# Medical conditions

**What this section holds.** 27 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 02-01 **CL-01. Type 1 diabetes on injections**: Everything a household needs to keep a person with type 1 diabetes alive when pharmacies, power and ambulances stop: what runs out, how to keep insulin good …
- → 02-02 **CL-02. Type 1 diabetes with an insulin pump and a sensor**: An insulin pump and a continuous glucose sensor do a great deal of the thinking in type 1 diabetes.
- → 02-03 **CL-03. Anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction, any cause)**: Anaphylaxis kills in minutes, and the only drug that stops it is epinephrine (adrenaline).
- → 02-04 **CL-04. Food allergy (child or adult)**: In a crisis, food becomes unlabelled, shared, donated, traded, scavenged, foraged and cooked in one pot over one fire.
- → 02-05 **CL-05. Type 2 diabetes (tablets and non-insulin medicines)**: Type 2 diabetes is the most common long-term condition in US households.
- → 02-06 **CL-06. Type 2 diabetes on insulin**: Many people with type 2 diabetes eventually need insulin, often a long-acting injection once or twice a day, sometimes with meal-time insulin as well.
- → 02-07 **CL-07. Asthma**: Asthma is common, usually well controlled, and turns dangerous fast when the inhaler is empty, the house is full of smoke, or the air is bitter cold.
- → 02-08 **CL-08. COPD and oxygen dependence**: COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is long-term lung damage that makes every breath work harder.
- → 02-09 **CL-09. High blood pressure and heart disease**: High blood pressure and heart disease are among the most common conditions in any household with adults over 40.
- → 02-10 **CL-10. Blood thinners (anticoagulants)**: Blood thinners stop clots that cause strokes, heart attacks and blocked lungs.
- → 02-11 **CL-11. Epilepsy and seizure disorders**: Most people with epilepsy control their seizures with daily medicine.
- → 02-12 **CL-12. Pregnancy, birth and the weeks after**: Giving birth without a skilled attendant is one of the most dangerous events this binder covers.
- → 02-13 **CL-13. Infant feeding: nursing and formula**: A baby's food cannot be stretched, swapped or skipped.
- → 02-14 **CL-14. Thyroid disease**: Thyroid disease is common, especially in women and older adults.
- → 02-15 **CL-15. Kidney disease and dialysis**: This is the hardest case in the library, and the module says so plainly.
- → 02-16 **CL-16. Mental-health medicines**: Many people take daily medicine for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, psychosis, ADHD or sleep.
- → 02-17 **CL-17. Opioid dependence and chronic pain**: Opioids are strong pain medicines (oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, fentanyl, methadone and others).
- → 02-18 **CL-18. Immunosuppression and transplant**: Some people live with a weakened immune system: transplant recipients on anti-rejection medicine, people on cancer treatment, and people on strong medicines …
- → 02-19 **CL-19. Celiac and severe gut disease**: This module covers two kinds of gut disease that make an emergency harder.
- → 02-20 **CL-20. Adrenal insufficiency**: In adrenal insufficiency the body cannot make enough **cortisol**, the hormone that keeps blood pressure and blood sugar up and that the body makes more of d…
- → 02-21 **CL-21. Dementia and elderly care**: Older people, and anyone with dementia (memory and judgement failing because of a brain disease such as Alzheimer's), are the most likely to be hurt by an em…
- → 02-22 **CL-22. Mobility impairment**: For someone who uses a wheelchair, walker or crutches, or who needs help to stand, move or turn in bed, an emergency changes three things at once: **getting …
- → 02-23 **CL-23. Hearing and vision aids**: Glasses, contact lenses, hearing aids and cochlear implants are easy to forget in a preparedness plan, until they are lost in an evacuation or the batteries …
- → 02-24 **CL-24. Sleep apnoea (CPAP)**: In obstructive sleep apnoea the airway closes again and again during sleep.
- → 02-25 **CL-25. Contraception and menstrual health**: Birth control and period care are among the most under-planned supplies in any household.
- → 02-26 **CL-26. Severe obesity and bariatric surgery**: This module covers two related situations.
- → 02-27 **A condition that is not in the library**: The condition library has 26 modules (→ 12-11).

pages.body:
# CL-01. Type 1 diabetes on injections

**What this page is for.** Everything a household needs to keep a person with type 1 diabetes
alive when pharmacies, power and ambulances stop: what runs out, how to keep insulin good without
a fridge, what goes wrong and how fast, what to do in the two emergencies (sugar too low, and
the acid build-up called DKA), and what to stock. It never tells you how much insulin to give.
That comes from the prescriber, written in the blanks on this page while you can still ask.
Pumps and sensors have their own module (→ 02-02); read this one first either way.

{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder so you can help someone else, or add the condition later in settings.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **Insulin cannot be skipped, stretched or replaced.** A person with type 1 diabetes makes no
>   insulin. Without it, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) follows and kills; the ADA's disaster sheet
>   says even a few hours of interrupted insulin can bring on life-threatening DKA (ADA,
>   Switching Between Insulin Products). Nothing grown, foraged or bought over a counter replaces it.
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Freezing breaks the insulin and it
>   can look normal afterwards; FDA and the American Diabetes Association both say do not use it
>   (floor, → 30-01).
> - **Heat is different from freezing.** Warm insulin loses strength slowly. Whether to use it
>   past the published window is your household's decision card: {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
> - **This page never calculates, adjusts or suggests a dose.** Your doses, and what to do when
>   sick or short, come from the prescriber and go in the blanks below. FDA's emergency
>   switching text is printed as published in part 8, for the prescriber to confirm.

## Do this now

**Low blood sugar: shaky, sweaty, pale, confused, odd behaviour, or "feels low":**
1. If they can swallow safely: **fast sugar now**. CDC's 15-15 rule: eat or drink 15 grams of
   fast carbohydrate (glucose tablets or gel by their label, or half a cup, 4 ounces, of juice or
   regular soda), wait 15 minutes, check sugar; if still below 70 mg/dL, repeat (CDC, Treatment of
   Low Blood Sugar).
2. **Not awake, cannot swallow, or having a seizure: nothing by mouth.** Give **glucagon** exactly
   as its label shows. Roll them onto their side (→ figure below). Stay with them. CDC says to get
   emergency medical care right after a glucagon injection: if any exists, send for it.
3. When they are awake and can swallow, give food. Check sugar again within the hour.

**Signs of DKA: thirst, peeing a lot, vomiting, belly pain, deep fast breathing, fruity breath, confusion:**
1. **Check ketones** (urine strip or blood meter). **Keep giving the person's insulin.** CDC's
   sick-day advice is to keep taking insulin as usual (CDC, Managing Sick Days); not eating is
   not a reason to stop it.
2. **Fluids, small sips often.** Follow the sick-day plan the prescriber wrote in part 6.
3. ADA says a blood ketone level of **1.6 mmol/L or higher** needs emergency care; CDC says
   ketones in the urine mean the emergency room (ADA, DKA; CDC, Managing Sick Days). If any care
   exists, go now (→ 01-07).

{{figure fig-recovery-position}}

## 1. What it is

Type 1 diabetes means the body has stopped making insulin, the hormone that lets sugar from food
into the cells. Without injected insulin, sugar piles up in the blood, the body burns fat
instead, and the acids from burning fat (ketones) poison the blood (ADA, DKA).

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | What happens when it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| **Insulin** | Your days on hand (part 7). One opened vial or pen lasts only as long as its label allows. | DKA, which can start within hours (ADA). **This is the household's master clock.** |
| Syringes or pen needles | Count them with the insulin. | A vial you cannot draw from is not usable insulin. |
| Glucose meter strips and lancets | Your check rate times your count. | Dosing blind; lows go unnoticed. |
| Ketone strips | Opened bottles have a printed use-within date; check yours. | DKA is caught late. |
| Glucagon | Printed expiry. | No way to treat a low in someone who cannot swallow. |
| Fast sugar | Anything sweet works; it is cheap now. | Lows cannot be treated. |
| Meter batteries | Printed on the meter. | No readings. |

**Write the master clock where everyone sees it:**
`total units of insulin on hand ÷ average units used per day = days of insulin`
Units on hand ________ ÷ units a day ________ = **________ days**, on ________ (date).
Copy it to → 23-02 and check it weekly. The units-per-day figure comes from the person's own
log or the prescriber, never from this page.

**The opened-vial clock matters.** Once a vial or pen is opened, or kept out of the fridge, its
label gives a number of days before it must be discarded; FDA's emergency guidance is up to 28
days at 59 to 86 °F (FDA, Insulin Storage and Switching). If the person uses less than one vial
in that time, the rest is lost. Open one at a time, oldest first, and ask the prescriber whether a
smaller package would waste less.

## 3. Storing insulin without power

**The published rules (FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products
in an Emergency; ADA, Insulin Storage and Syringe Safety):**

| Situation | Rule as published |
|---|---|
| Normal storage, unopened | Refrigerator, about **36 to 46 °F**. |
| No power, opened or unopened vial or cartridge | May be kept at **59 to 86 °F for up to 28 days** and still work (FDA). Each product's label gives its own in-use days; some are shorter. Write yours in part 12. |
| Above 86 °F | Strength drops; the longer and hotter, the more. FDA: under emergency conditions you might still need to use insulin stored above 86 °F, and replace it as soon as properly stored insulin is available. Your household's line: {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09). |
| Frozen | **Do not use** (FDA, ADA). Floor: discard. |
| Insulin taken out of its original vial or diluted | Discard within two weeks (FDA). |
| Looks wrong | Regular (clear) insulin with particles or discoloration, or NPH (cloudy) insulin with "frosting" or crystals on the inside of the bottle or small particles or clumps, is not used (ADA). |
| Expired | ADA says do not use past the expiry date. Your household's line on expired medicine: {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05). |

**Planning context, not permission:** a Cochrane review found that unopened vials and cartridges
of specific types of **human** insulin kept their strength for up to six months at up to 77 °F
(25 °C) and up to two months at up to 99 °F (37 °C) (Cochrane, Human insulin less
temperature-sensitive than previously thought). The review was about human insulin; it does not
cover the newer "analog" insulins that many people now use. Freezing is a cliff; heat is a slope.

**The cold ladder, best first** (→ 29-07 explains each step):
1. A **powered fridge or 12-volt compressor cooler** on a battery or solar, set so it **cannot
   freeze**, with a thermometer inside (→ 09-10).
2. **Winter cold, buffered:** an insulated cooler in a cold spot, never directly against ice or a
   frozen wall, checked with a **min/max thermometer** (one that remembers the highest and lowest
   reading). Outdoors, a garage or a car swings below freezing at night. Aim for the label's 36
   to 46 °F, and never let it freeze.
3. **Ice or cold packs with a barrier**: a towel or a box between the ice and the insulin so it
   cannot freeze (→ figure).
4. **Evaporative cooling pouches** in warm months: they keep insulin below air temperature with
   only water (→ 12-21).
5. **The coolest stable place in the house**: basement, interior closet, a cooler buried in the
   ground, checked by thermometer.

{{figure fig-insulin-cooler-barrier}}

{{photo insulin-outage-spot}}

**Supplies have bands too.** Meter strips and ketone strips read wrong if they freeze, cook or
get damp: keep them capped, dry, and in the room where the people are. Glucagon is a
room-temperature product; read its label and keep it out of the fridge, the car and the cold
garage.

## 4. Day by day without it

This is what public sources describe when insulin stops. It is here so nobody mistakes the
early hours for a reprieve.

- **First:** blood sugar rises. Thirst and peeing increase (CDC, Diabetic Ketoacidosis).
- **Then:** ketones appear and rise. Tiredness, headache, sick stomach.
- **DKA:** vomiting, belly pain, deep fast breathing, fruity breath, confusion, then collapse.
  Hospital treatment is fluids, salts and insulin through a drip (CDC).
- **How fast:** ADA says DKA can develop quickly, and its disaster sheet says even a few hours
  of interrupted insulin can bring it on (ADA, DKA; ADA, Switching Between Insulin Products).
  Do not plan on days. **Without insulin, nothing at home reverses it.**

**"Rationing" insulin does not work.** Taking less than the body needs leads to DKA, not to
savings. What you can ration is **waste**: cold-chain failures, spilled or frozen vials, a pen
discarded half full. That is why storage gets so much space on this page.

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

**Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia), the fast danger.** Below 70 mg/dL is low (CDC). Signs: fast
heartbeat, shaking, sweating, nervousness, irritability or confusion, dizziness, hunger; then
weakness, trouble walking or seeing clearly, acting strange, seizures, fainting (CDC, Low Blood
Sugar). Lows are more likely with physical activity, too little carbohydrate for the insulin
taken, alcohol, and at night (CDC). Activity can keep lowering sugar for up to 24 hours
afterwards (NIDDK, Low Blood Glucose). **Treat first, check second** if no meter is at hand. The first-aid steps are in "Do
this now" above. **Every adult must be able to give glucagon.** Not "has watched"; has done it
with a trainer or a practice kit.

**DKA, the slow danger.** CDC's emergency list: blood sugar staying at **300 mg/dL or above**,
fruity breath, vomiting so persistent no food or fluid stays down, trouble breathing, several
DKA signs together (CDC, Diabetic Ketoacidosis). ADA adds blood ketones **1.6 mmol/L or higher**
(ADA, DKA). There is no household cure for DKA beyond insulin and fluids. **The defence is
catching ketones early**, which is why ketone strips are on the stock list.

**Decide now what "emergency" means when there is no emergency room.** For most households it
is the trigger to move toward working medical care (→ 01-02, → 01-07). Write the household's
answer: ______________________________________________

## 6. Sick-day basics

Illness, even a cold or diarrhoea, pushes blood sugar up and can start DKA in a person who is
taking their insulin. CDC's published sick-day steps (CDC, Managing Sick Days):
- **Keep taking insulin** (and any diabetes pills) as usual.
- **Check blood sugar every 4 hours** and write it down.
- **Drink plenty of water** to prevent dehydration.
- **Try to eat as normal.** If meals are impossible, CDC says to take about **50 grams of
  carbohydrate every 4 hours**, for example 1½ cups of unsweetened applesauce or 1½ cups of
  fruit juice.
- **Weigh daily** (losing weight without trying is a sign of high sugar) and **check temperature
  morning and evening** (fever may mean infection).
- **Test urine for ketones** (an over-the-counter kit); if ketones are present, call the doctor
  right away.

CDC's emergency-room list for a sick person with diabetes, as published: trouble breathing;
ketones in the urine; cannot keep liquids down for more than 4 hours, or food for more than 24
hours; losing 5 pounds or more during the illness; blood sugar lower than 60 mg/dL; vomiting
and/or severe diarrhoea for more than 6 hours; temperature over 101 °F for 24 hours.

**Dehydration multiplies everything.** High sugar drains water; vomiting and diarrhoea drain more.
Oral rehydration solution is the treatment; the World Health Organization's home recipe is 1
litre of safe water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt (WHO, Cholera
Q&A), with the safety notes on → 12-05. The sugar in it counts: write it in the log.

**Ask your prescriber now, while you can, and write it here:**
- How to change insulin when sick and not eating: ______________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________________________________________
- The sugar level at which to check ketones: ____________ What to do at each ketone level:
  ______________________________________________________________________________________________
- How to treat a low when vomiting (some prescribers use small glucagon doses; only theirs counts):
  ______________________________________________________________________________________________

## 7. What to stock, and how much

The binder shows the arithmetic; you fill it in from your own bottles. The medicines tagged for this condition in settings are printed; if none are tagged, every household medicine row is, so use the ones for this condition. **Days on hand = on hand ÷ used per day.**

| Medicine or supply | On hand | Used per day | Days on hand | Days you want | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds_for.CL-01 as m}}
| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{else}}
{{#each meds as m}}
| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{/each}}
{{/each}}
| Syringes or pen needles (match the insulin strength, usually U-100) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Meter strips (count rises without a sensor) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Lancets | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Ketone strips (urine or blood) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Glucagon (earliest expiry: ____) | ____ | emergency | | ____ | ____ |
| Glucose tablets, gel, juice | ____ | as needed | | ____ | ____ |
| Spare meter and its batteries | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Sharps container (a rigid screw-cap bottle works) | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Min/max thermometers (one per storage spot) | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

**A second insulin type is the most common gap.** If the person uses only one kind (only
long-acting, or only rapid-acting), ask the prescriber now whether the household should hold the
other kind as a backup, and what the plan for it is. **Syringes must match the insulin strength.**
Insulin syringes are marked in units for one concentration; most US insulin is U-100. A
mismatched syringe is a dosing error. Check the vial and the syringe every time.

Used needles go in a heavy plastic bottle with a screw cap (FDA, Best Way to Get Rid of Used
Needles). Never share a syringe (ADA).

{{photo low-sugar-kits}}

> **Before the collapse:** ask the prescriber for the largest emergency supply they will write,
> move to 90-day fills, and refill at the earliest allowed date. Rotate: newest to the back of the
> fridge, use from the front. Ask whether manufacturer or nonprofit assistance programs can lower
> the cost if cost limits the buffer. In many states, older human insulins (Regular and NPH) can be
> bought at the pharmacy counter without a prescription; you must ask the pharmacist, and the
> rules differ by state. Ask your pharmacist what your state allows, and write it here: __________

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

| Source | Realistic? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Your pharmacy and others | First | A printed prescription, ID and the family medical summary (→ 25-09) help at any counter. |
| Hospitals, clinics, urgent care, disaster clinics, Red Cross, health department | Yes, while they run | Insulin is a recognised disaster need. A clinician there can direct a switch. |
| Other people with diabetes | Real | Neighbours and community groups (→ 18-01). Giving or taking someone else's prescription is a decision card: {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16). |
| Veterinary insulin | **No** | Different products and strengths; not an equivalent. |
| Unlabelled vials, or insulin of unknown storage | **No** | Unknown strength; may have been frozen. |

**Check anything you get:** product name, strength (U-100 or other), expiry, and appearance. Ask
how it was stored. Frozen at any point means discard (floor).

**If the only insulin you can find is a different kind** (for example, older Regular and NPH
instead of the person's usual insulin): switching changes timing and amounts. FDA and the ADA
both publish emergency switching guidance, and both say switching should be done with a
physician and close sugar monitoring (FDA; ADA, Switching Between Insulin Products in Disaster
Response Situations). **The two documents do not give the same amounts**: the ADA sheet, written
for health professionals, lowers the dose in most switches, while FDA's mostly keeps the same
number of units. That disagreement is one more reason to have the prescriber decide now. In the
Large download both documents are bound behind this page. **This binder does not convert
doses**; FDA's published text follows, for your prescriber to confirm.

### As published, for your prescriber to confirm

FDA's emergency guidance on switching insulin is printed here **exactly as published**, so that
you can show it to the prescriber **now** and have them confirm or change it for this person
(FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency,
content current as of 09/28/2026). It is not this binder's advice, and the binder does not work
out any amount from it. Brand names are FDA's examples.

> **FDA:** "Always switch insulin under a doctor's care, with close monitoring of your blood
> sugar. If you cannot reach a doctor during an emergency, follow the guidance below — but
> monitor your blood sugar closely and see a doctor as soon as you can."

> **FDA, Short-acting (regular insulin) and Rapid-acting Insulins:** "In an emergency, you can
> switch one brand of regular insulin (such as Humulin R or Novolin R) for another brand of
> regular insulin, or for a rapid-acting insulin (such as Apidra, Fiasp, Humalog, or NovoLog),
> and vice versa. Use the same number of units.
>
> Inject regular insulins approximately 30 minutes before the start of each meal. Rapid-acting
> insulins begin working more rapidly than regular insulin and are to be injected no more than
> 15 minutes before the start of each meal to avoid dangerously low blood sugar levels."

> **FDA, Intermediate and Long-acting Insulins:** "In an emergency, you can switch one brand of
> intermediate-acting insulin (such as, Humulin N, Novolin N) for another intermediate-acting
> insulin on a unit-per-unit basis. You can also switch intermediate-acting insulins for
> long-acting insulins (e.g., Lantus, Toujeo, Tresiba) on a total unit-per-day basis, or vice
> versa.
>
> Important: If you switch from a once-daily long-acting insulin (e.g., Lantus, Toujeo, Tresiba)
> to an intermediate-acting insulin, keep your total daily dose the same but split it into two
> equal injections. Give half in the morning with breakfast and half in the evening with dinner
> to avoid a dangerously low blood sugar.
>
> If you switch from an intermediate-acting to a once-daily long-acting insulin, add up the total
> amount of intermediate-acting insulin units for one day, and give it as a single long-acting
> insulin dose once a day.
>
> Close monitoring of blood sugar and adjustment of your insulin dose may be needed in the
> transition."

**Prescriber, please read the FDA text above and confirm it for this person, or write what to
do instead.** Person: ____________________
Agree as printed ☐  Change as written here: _________________________________________________
_____________________________________________________________________________________________
Prescriber: ____________________ Initials: ______ Date: __________

**Ask your prescriber now, while you can, and write it here:** "If all we can get is ________
insulin, what do we give, how much, and when?"
_____________________________________________________________________________________________
_____________________________________________________________________________________________
Prescriber: ____________________ Date: __________

## 9. Power and devices

On injections, the only powered item that matters is **cold storage in summer** (→ 09-10). A
glucose meter runs for months on its small battery; keep spares. If the person uses a phone app
or a sensor, see → 02-02 and → 09-06. Nothing in this module is lost to an EMP (an
electromagnetic pulse; → 27-03) except the meter: keep a spare meter, still boxed, with its
batteries, in a metal box.

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- **Insulin rides on a person, never in a trunk or a parked car.** In winter, inside the coat
  against the body; in summer, in an evaporative pouch or insulated bag out of the sun
  (→ 12-21, → 01-07).
- **The go-bag holds a complete kit** (→ 22-06): insulin for the trip and more, syringes or pen
  needles, meter, strips, ketone strips, glucagon, fast sugar, the sharps bottle, the written plan
  from this page, and a copy of the prescription.
- **Exertion, cold and missed meals make lows more likely.** Check more often on the road and
  carry fast sugar in a pocket, not in a pack.
- **Count the clock before you leave.** If the days of insulin are fewer than the days the trip
  might take plus a margin, the trip is toward resupply or care, not away from it (→ 01-02).

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Heat-exposed insulin:** {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
- **Expired medicine and supplies:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **Using or giving someone else's prescription:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **When to leave home:** {{choice DC-19}} (→ 30-20). For this condition, the insulin clock is
  usually the trigger. Write the number of days at which you start looking for resupply
  (________) and the number at which you move toward care (________).
- **Frozen insulin is not a card.** It is a floor: discard (→ 30-01).

pages.body:
# CL-02. Type 1 diabetes with an insulin pump and a sensor

**What this page is for.** An insulin pump and a continuous glucose sensor do a great deal of
the thinking in type 1 diabetes. They also add things that run out and break: pump supplies,
sensors, batteries, a phone, and sometimes software with an expiry date. This module is the
device layer. It sets out the **fallback ladder** from full automation down to a syringe and a
fingerstick meter, so that a dead battery or an empty box of sensors is an inconvenience and not
a crisis. **Read → 02-01 too**: the insulin, the cold chain, the emergencies and the sick-day
rules there apply in full.

{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder so you can help someone else, or add the condition later in settings.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **A pump holds only fast-acting insulin and has no reserve in the body.** When a pump stops,
>   for any reason, ketones can build within hours. **Never leave a pump failure "until
>   morning".** Go down the ladder within the hour.
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Freezing breaks the insulin and it
>   can look normal afterwards; FDA and the American Diabetes Association both say do not use it
>   (floor, → 30-01).
> - **The bottom rung must already be in the house:** injectable insulin, syringes or pens, a
>   meter and strips, and the prescriber's written fallback plan. A pump household without them
>   is one broken device away from DKA.
> - **This page never calculates or converts a dose.** The fallback plan is the prescriber's,
>   written in part 7 below. FDA's emergency switching text is printed there as published,
>   for the prescriber to confirm.

## Do this now: the device has failed

1. **Is it the device or the insulin?** Check for an alarm, a kinked or pulled-out tube or pod, a
   wet or bloody site, an empty reservoir. Check sugar with a fingerstick, and ketones.
2. **Try one fix, quickly:** new site and supplies, fresh battery or charge, restart the
   controller or phone. Give it no more than the time the system's own manual allows.
3. **Not fixed within the hour: go down the ladder** (part 4). Pump without automation if the
   pump still works; otherwise **injections, using the prescriber's plan in part 7.**
4. **Check sugar and ketones often for the first two days** after a change. The sick-day and
   emergency rules are on → 02-01.

## 1. What it is

Type 1 diabetes means the body makes no insulin (→ 02-01). An **insulin pump** is a small
device that drips fast-acting insulin under the skin all day through a tube or a stick-on
"pod". A **continuous glucose monitor (CGM)** is a sensor worn on the skin that reads sugar
every few minutes and sends it to a reader or a phone. When the pump and sensor talk to each
other and adjust insulin automatically, it is called a **closed loop** or **automated insulin
delivery**.

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| Insulin | Days on hand (→ 02-01, part 2). | DKA within days. |
| Pump supplies: reservoirs or pods, infusion sets, inserters | Changed every few days by label. Count changes left. | Step down to injections. |
| Sensors | Each lasts a set number of days by label; most cannot be restarted. | Step down to fingersticks; strip use rises sharply. |
| Pump and controller power | Hours to days per charge or battery. | No delivery, or no control. |
| Phone (if it is the controller or reader) | A day or two per charge; breaks, gets lost. | Use the backup controller, then step down. |
| Software (some systems) | Some phone apps and home-built systems stop working after a set date unless rebuilt or renewed. | The app will not open; step down. |
| Adhesive patches, tape, skin wipes | Count them. | Sites fall off early, wasting supplies. |

**Write the device clocks here** and on → 23-02:
Pump supplies: ________ changes × ________ days each = ________ days.
Sensors: ________ × ________ days each = ________ days.
Software expiry date (if any): ________ Renew or rebuild before: ________

**Sensors:** wear each one for its full labelled session; some makes allow a short grace period
after the session ends (for example, one maker's 10-day sensor reads for a further 12 hours;
Dexcom, G7 sensor wear time FAQ). Change at a convenient hour, inside that window. Protect the
site with an overpatch so knocks and sweat do not end it early. Decide now at what sensor count
you stop wearing them daily and save the last ones for illness and travel: ________.

## 3. Storing insulin and supplies without power

**Insulin:** the published rules, the cold ladder and the frozen-insulin floor are on → 02-01
part 3; nothing changes for a pump user. FDA's emergency guidance adds two pump lines, printed
as published (FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an
Emergency, content current as of 09/28/2026):

> **FDA, Special Storage: Insulin Pumps:** "Insulin in the pump's infusion set (such as the
> reservoir, tubing, catheters) should be thrown away after 48 hours. Unless your pump device's
> instructions are different. For example, NovoLog, Kirsty, and Humalog U-100 specify up to 6–7
> days in the reservoir; Fiasp PumpCart specifies 4 days. Always follow the specific product's
> prescribing information and your pump device's instructions for use.
>
> If the pump insulin is exposed to temperatures above 98.6°F, throw it away."

Write your own insulin's and pump's reservoir time here: ________ (→ 29-14). A pump worn under clothes in a heatwave, or left in the sun, is the
case to watch.

**Devices and sensors have storage bands too.** Read each box (→ 29-14) and write the band
below. Two examples from labels: one tubeless pod's FDA device record gives **32 to 86 °F**
(FDA AccessGUDID, pod device record); one sensor's user guide gives **36 to 86 °F** (Dexcom, G7
User Guide). A frozen or cooked pod or sensor may fail when you start it, wasting days of
supply at the worst moment. **Spare supplies live in the room where the people live**, not a
cold garage, a car, or an unheated storeroom.

| Item | Storage band from its label | Where we keep it |
|---|---|---|
| Pump supplies (reservoirs, sets, pods) | ________ | ________ |
| Sensors | ________ | ________ |
| Meter strips, ketone strips | ________ | ________ |
| Spare pump, controller, phone | ________ | ________ |

## 4. Day by day without it: the fallback ladder

Each step down trades convenience for reliability. **Never jump further down than the failure
forces; never stay above a step that has stopped working.**

{{figure fig-device-fallback-ladder}}

| Rung | What it is | Needs | What you lose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Full automation** | Pump and sensor adjust insulin together. | Pump, supplies, sensor, controller or phone, power, insulin. | Nothing. |
| **2. Backup controller or reader** | A spare phone, the pump maker's own handheld controller, or a second reader app. | The spare, charged, already set up. | Little, if it was prepared. |
| **3. Pump without automation** | The pump runs its programmed basal rates; you give meal and correction doses by button. | Pump, supplies, insulin, sugar readings, the settings copy below. | Automatic adjustment, especially overnight. Check more often. |
| **4. Injections with a sensor** | Long-acting insulin for the background, fast-acting for meals, by syringe or pen. | Both insulin types, syringes or pens, **the prescriber's plan (part 7)**. | The pump's fine control. |
| **5. Injections with a fingerstick meter** | As rung 4, sugar read by finger. | Meter, many strips, lancets. | Overnight warning. Set an alarm for a night check. |
| **6. Fast-acting insulin only** | No long-acting insulin in the house. | Frequent small injections around the clock, on a plan **only the prescriber can write**. | Sleep and margin. A bridge to getting long-acting insulin, not a way to live. |

**Rungs 4 and 5 are how most of the world manages type 1 diabetes, and they need no
electricity.** They are also the rungs pump households most often fail to prepare: no
long-acting insulin, no syringes, no written plan.

**Two things that surprise people:**
- **Some pumps and pods are tied to the controller that started them.** On some systems a pod
  started by a phone app cannot be taken over by the maker's handheld controller or another
  phone; you must start a new one (LoopDocs, Omnipod FAQs). Read your system's manual now and
  write the rule here: ______________________________________________
- **Some phone apps and home-built systems expire.** A build may stop opening after a fixed
  number of days and cannot be renewed without internet and a computer (LoopDocs, Updating or
  Rebuilding). Write the date and renew before it.

**Home-built ("do-it-yourself") closed loops exist.** Some people run open-source software that
links a pump and a sensor. FDA has warned against using devices not authorised for sale in the
United States (FDA Safety Communication, 2019). This binder does not cover building or
configuring them. **If your household uses one, save its full documentation offline now**, on
every phone and on paper for the key pages, because the community websites will not be there
when the internet is gone (LoopDocs; AndroidAPS documentation).

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

Everything on → 02-01 part 5 applies: low blood sugar and DKA, with the same first aid.
Device-specific signs:
- **Sugar rising for hours with no explanation:** assume the pump is not delivering. Check
  ketones, give insulin by syringe or pen per the prescriber's plan, change the site.
- **A sensor reading that does not match how the person looks or feels:** check with a
  fingerstick before acting. Treat the person, not the number.
- **Alarm fatigue at night:** if the sensor is gone, set a timed alarm for a night fingerstick.

## 6. Sick-day basics

The sick-day rules on → 02-01 part 6 apply. With a pump, add one: **when ketones are present,
many prescribers want correction insulin given by syringe or pen, not through the pump, and the
site changed**, in case the pump is the problem. Ask yours.

**Ask your prescriber now, while you can, and write it here:** sick-day changes for a pump user;
when to switch to injections; the ketone level that means "change everything now".
_____________________________________________________________________________________________
_____________________________________________________________________________________________

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**First, copy the pump's settings to paper.** You already run every setting; this puts them
where a dead battery cannot take them. Copy them from the pump or app screens, date them, and
re-copy after every change. Photograph each screen too.

```
DATE COPIED: ____________      (re-copy after every settings change)
Basal program (time: rate per hour) ______________________________________
Total daily basal (the pump shows it) ________ units
Carbohydrate ratio(s) ____________________________________________________
Correction factor(s) _____________________________________________________
Target sugar ____________   Average total daily insulin (from the pump) ________ units
```

{{photo pump-settings-screens}}

**Then the plan that turns those settings into injections.** FDA and the ADA publish emergency
guidance on switching from a pump to injections, and both say it should be done with a
physician (FDA; ADA, Switching Between Insulin Products in Disaster Response Situations). **The
two documents do not give the same amounts**: FDA's pump section replaces the pump's doses unit
for unit, while the ADA sheet, written for health professionals, works from body weight instead.
That disagreement is one more reason to have the prescriber write the plan now. Both documents
are bound behind this page in the Large download. **This binder does not convert
doses**; FDA's published text follows, for your prescriber to confirm.

### As published, for your prescriber to confirm

FDA's emergency guidance on switching insulin is printed here **exactly as published**, so that
you can show it to the prescriber **now** and have them confirm or change it for this person
(FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency,
content current as of 09/28/2026). It is not this binder's advice, and the binder does not work
out any amount from it. Brand names are FDA's examples.

> **FDA:** "Always switch insulin under a doctor's care, with close monitoring of your blood
> sugar. If you cannot reach a doctor during an emergency, follow the guidance below — but
> monitor your blood sugar closely and see a doctor as soon as you can."

> **FDA, Insulin Pumps:** "If your pump supplies are not available or your pump is not working
> properly, you may need to switch to injected insulin. This should be done with a doctor's
> guidance and close blood sugar monitoring whenever possible."

> **FDA, Insulin Pumps, Using a Different Insulin in Your Insulin Pump:** "In an emergency, you
> may be able to swap one rapid-acting insulin (such as Apidra, Fiasp, Humalog, Novolog) for
> another on a unit-per-unit basis. Check your pump's instructions to make sure the available
> insulins are compatible with your devices.
>
> Note: Not all rapid-acting insulins are approved for pump use. Merilog (insulin aspart-szjj) is
> not currently labeled for insulin pump use. Humalog U-200 and Lyumjev U-200 must NOT be used in
> insulin pumps. Always check the specific insulin product labeling before use in a pump."

> **FDA, Insulin Pumps, Switching from an Insulin Pump to Injected Insulin:** "If you must switch
> from your pump to injected insulin, use the following guidance:
>
> - Replace your pump's total 24-hour basal (background) dose with insulin on a unit-per-unit
>   basis.
> - For intermediate-acting insulin, split the 24-hour basal (background) dose into two equal
>   injections per day. For example, if your 24-hour basal (background) dose is 24 units, inject
>   12 units twice daily.
> - For long-acting insulin, give the full 24-hour basal (background) dose as one injection per
>   day.
> - If regular or rapid-acting insulin is also available, use it with each meal. Match your
>   pump's bolus (mealtime) dose on a unit-per-unit basis.
>   - For example, if your pump gives a bolus (mealtime) of 5 units to cover breakfast, inject 5
>     units of regular or rapid-acting insulin to cover that meal"

> **FDA, Intermediate and Long-acting Insulins:** "In an emergency, you can switch one brand of
> intermediate-acting insulin (such as, Humulin N, Novolin N) for another intermediate-acting
> insulin on a unit-per-unit basis. You can also switch intermediate-acting insulins for
> long-acting insulins (e.g., Lantus, Toujeo, Tresiba) on a total unit-per-day basis, or vice
> versa.
>
> Important: If you switch from a once-daily long-acting insulin (e.g., Lantus, Toujeo, Tresiba)
> to an intermediate-acting insulin, keep your total daily dose the same but split it into two
> equal injections. Give half in the morning with breakfast and half in the evening with dinner
> to avoid a dangerously low blood sugar.
>
> If you switch from an intermediate-acting to a once-daily long-acting insulin, add up the total
> amount of intermediate-acting insulin units for one day, and give it as a single long-acting
> insulin dose once a day.
>
> Close monitoring of blood sugar and adjustment of your insulin dose may be needed in the
> transition."

> **FDA, Short-acting (regular insulin) and Rapid-acting Insulins:** "In an emergency, you can
> switch one brand of regular insulin (such as Humulin R or Novolin R) for another brand of
> regular insulin, or for a rapid-acting insulin (such as Apidra, Fiasp, Humalog, or NovoLog),
> and vice versa. Use the same number of units.
>
> Inject regular insulins approximately 30 minutes before the start of each meal. Rapid-acting
> insulins begin working more rapidly than regular insulin and are to be injected no more than
> 15 minutes before the start of each meal to avoid dangerously low blood sugar levels."

**Prescriber, please read the FDA text above and confirm it for this person, or write what to
do instead.** Person: ____________________
Agree as printed ☐  Change as written here: _________________________________________________
_____________________________________________________________________________________________
Prescriber: ____________________ Initials: ______ Date: __________

**Ask your prescriber now, while you can, and write it here** (have them write it, and initial it):
- Long-acting insulin product: ______________ Amount: ________ When: ______________
- Meals and corrections by syringe or pen: ___________________________________________
- When to stop the pump after the first long-acting dose: ____________________________
- If only fast-acting insulin is available (rung 6): __________________________________
- If only Regular and NPH are available: ____________________________________________
Prescriber: ____________________ Initials: ______ Date: __________

**Stock arithmetic.** Days on hand = on hand ÷ used per day. The medicines tagged for this condition in settings are printed; if none are tagged, every household medicine row is, so use the ones for this condition.

| Medicine or supply | On hand | Used per day | Days on hand | Days you want | Still to get |

{{/each}}

| Pump supplies (reservoirs, sets or pods) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Sensors | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |

| **Syringes or pen needles** (match the insulin strength) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Meter, strips (count at fingerstick rate), lancets | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Ketone strips | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Pump batteries or charger, cables | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Overpatches, tape, skin wipes | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Glucagon, fast sugar, sharps bottle | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

{{photo device-spares-box}}

> **Before the collapse:** ask the prescriber for a long-acting insulin prescription to keep as
> a backup, and syringes or pens. Practise one injection day with their agreement, so the first
> time is not the real one. Ask the pump maker about a loaner or backup pump program, and keep
> the maker's support number and your pump's serial number on → 25-09.

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

Insulin sources are on → 02-01 part 8. For devices:
- **Pump supplies and sensors fit only their own system.** Another brand's pods or sensors will
  not work. Write your exact part numbers here: ________________________________
- **Other people with the same system** are the realistic source of spare supplies (→ 18-01).
- **Syringes** are sold without a prescription in many states, at the pharmacist's discretion;
  ask yours now.
- **Never use a pump with insulin it was not made for** without checking its manual; FDA notes
  pump users should check that a substitute insulin is compatible with the device (FDA).

## 9. Power and devices

- **Every powered item, with its charge clock,** goes on → 09-06: pump (battery type or
  charging), controller, phone, sensor reader. Phones are the weak link: keep them charged from a
  power station or solar (→ 29-02), and keep a spare charged.
- **Heat and cold:** do not leave pumps, phones or supplies in a car, in direct sun, or in a
  freezing room. Batteries lose capacity in the cold; keep the pump under clothing.
- **EMP and geomagnetic storms** (→ 27-03): a spare controller, a spare phone with the app
  installed, and a spare meter, stored in a closed metal box, give the best chance of surviving.
  The bottom of the ladder (syringes, insulin, a battery meter in a metal box) is the part that
  survives for certain.
- Write each device's charge clock: pump ________ controller ________ phone ________ reader ________

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- **Injections travel better than a pump**: no charging, no pairing. On a long move, carry the
  full injection kit even if the pump is running (→ 01-07, → 22-06).
- Insulin on a person, never in a trunk (→ 02-01 part 10). Spare pods and sensors in the cabin,
  inside their storage band.
- **Before leaving, renew any software that expires during the trip,** charge every device, and
  pack the paper settings copy and the prescriber's plan.
- A serious device failure on the road is a reason to head for the nearest working care.

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Heat-exposed insulin:** {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
- **Expired supplies and medicine:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **Someone else's prescription or supplies:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **When to leave:** {{choice DC-19}} (→ 30-20).
- **Frozen insulin is a floor, not a card:** discard (→ 30-01).

pages.body:
# CL-03. Anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction, any cause)

**What this page is for.** Anaphylaxis kills in minutes, and the only drug that stops it is
epinephrine (adrenaline). This module is the response every adult in the house must be able to
do without reading, then the parts that change when there is no ambulance: how to keep
epinephrine working through heat and cold, what to do with expired devices, how many to hold,
and what to ask the prescriber now. Food allergy prevention is on → 02-04.

{{#if has.condition.CL-03}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder because anaphylaxis can strike someone with no known allergy, from a sting, a food or a medicine.{{/if}}

Your household's allergy rows: {{#each allergies as a}}**{{a.member}}**: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}; carries epinephrine: {{a.carries_epinephrine}}). {{else}}none entered.{{/each}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **Epinephrine first.** At the first sign of a serious reaction, give it at once. Delay is
>   the main cause of death. When unsure, give it (AAAAI; CDC).
> - **Antihistamines and asthma inhalers do not treat anaphylaxis.** They are never a substitute
>   for epinephrine (CDC, Recognizing and Responding to Anaphylaxis).
> - **Use the device in reach.** Whether an expired or once-frozen device is used when nothing
>   else exists is your household's decision card: {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
> - **This page prints published dose bands as published.** Which device a person carries is the
>   prescriber's choice, written on the signed action plan.

## Do this now

1. **Give epinephrine.** Auto-injector into the **outer thigh**, through clothing if needed,
   following the device's own instructions. For one common pen the label says hold it in place
   for **3 seconds** (count slowly 1, 2, 3), then rub the spot for 10 seconds (FDA, EpiPen
   label). For a nasal spray, one spray into one nostril (FDA, neffy label).
2. **Note the time.** Say it aloud or write it.
3. **Call for help** if any exists: 911, and say "anaphylaxis".
4. **Position:** lying flat with legs raised. Vomiting: on their side. Struggling to breathe:
   sitting up. **Do not stand them up or walk them** (AAAAI).
5. **Second dose** if not improving or symptoms return: AAAAI's plan says a second dose may be
   given **5 to 15 minutes** after the first; the nasal spray's label says a second spray in the
   same nostril **starting 5 minutes** after the first.
6. **Wheeze or cough after eating, in someone with asthma: epinephrine first, inhaler after.**
7. **Stay with them for hours.** Symptoms can come back without a new exposure (a "biphasic"
   reaction). Keep a second device in reach. Nothing to eat or drink until they are clearly well.

{{figure fig-auto-injector-outer-thigh}}

{{figure fig-anaphylaxis-positions}}

## 1. What it is

Anaphylaxis is a sudden, severe allergic reaction that involves the whole body. The airway can
swell shut and blood pressure can fall until the person collapses. Common triggers are foods,
insect stings, medicines and latex; sometimes no trigger is found.

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| **Epinephrine devices** | Printed expiry on each device. Damaged by heat, freezing and light. | No treatment. Avoidance is the only defence. |
| Trainer devices | Do not expire, but get lost. | Carers lose practice. |
| Antihistamines (for itching and hives only, after epinephrine) | Printed expiry. | Comfort only; not life-saving. |
| Asthma inhalers, if the person has asthma | Dose counter. | Asthma makes reactions worse (→ 02-07). |

**Write the clock:** devices in date ________; earliest expiry ________; expired devices kept
________ (sorted newest first). Update at every inventory (→ 22-04) and on → 26-08.

## 3. Storing epinephrine without power

The labels, as published:

| Product | Store at | Excursions allowed | Never |
|---|---|---|---|
| Auto-injector (EpiPen and EpiPen Jr label) | **68 to 77 °F** | **59 to 86 °F** | Refrigerate or freeze; leave in a car or glove box. Keep in its carrier tube: epinephrine is damaged by light (FDA, EpiPen label). |
| Nasal spray (neffy label) | **68 to 77 °F**, in its blister pack | **Up to 122 °F** for a few days | Freeze. The label says it freezes below **5 °F** and **will not spray** if frozen; if a frozen one is needed in an emergency, do not wait for it to thaw: use another device and seek care (FDA, neffy label). |
| Other devices | Read the label (→ 29-14) and write it here: ________ | ________ | ________ |

**Check the window.** The liquid should be clear and colourless. Brown, pink, cloudy or with
particles means replace it (FDA, EpiPen label). Whether a discoloured or expired device is used
when nothing else exists is on the card (→ 30-05).

**What testing outside the label found** (planning context, printed as published):
- 40 EpiPen and EpiPen Jr devices up to 50 months past expiry all still held at least 80
  percent of the labelled dose (Cantrell and others, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- EpiPens frozen for 24 hours and thawed delivered the same dose volume as unfrozen ones
  (Cooper and others, American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, 2018).

**Cold weather is the bigger risk.** In a house heated to one room (→ 08-01), the epinephrine
lives in the warm room, not in the coat on a cold hook or a pack by the door. Outdoors in
winter, carry it **inside your layers, against the body**. In summer, never in a parked car; an
insulated pouch out of the sun. Evaporative pouches are made for cooling and are not a fix for
cold (→ 12-21, → 29-07).

{{photo epinephrine-locations}}

## 4. Day by day without it

There is no "day by day" in anaphylaxis: a reaction runs its course in minutes to hours.
Without epinephrine, a severe reaction can kill (CDC). **When devices run out, the person's
only protection is strict avoidance of the trigger** (→ 02-04 for food). That is a thin margin,
and it should shape decisions about food, travel, and how close to stay to working care
(→ 01-02).

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

Anaphylaxis usually involves **more than one body system**, but a severe reaction in one system
is still anaphylaxis (AAAAI; CDC).

| System | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Skin | Hives, flushing, itching; swelling of lips, tongue, eyelids, face |
| Breathing | Cough, wheeze, hoarse voice, throat tightness, trouble breathing or swallowing |
| Gut | Vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps |
| Circulation | Pale or blue colour, weak pulse, dizziness, fainting, collapse |
| Behaviour (young children) | Sudden irritability, frantic crying, clinging, going quiet, "my mouth feels funny" |

**In a small child, trust behaviour.** A child who has just eaten and suddenly changes may be
reacting before any rash. If the person stops breathing, start CPR (→ 12-18).

**Antihistamines** may be given for itching and hives **after** epinephrine, by the prescriber's
plan. FDA warns that diphenhydramine must not be used to make a child sleep, and is not for
children under 2 (FDA, Drug Safety Communication).

## 6. Sick-day basics

- **Asthma, colds and other illness make reactions more severe.** Keep asthma well controlled
  (→ 02-07).
- **Exercise, heat, alcohol and some medicines** can make a reaction worse or trigger one in a
  person with a known allergy; the prescriber can tell you which apply.
- **After any reaction, the person is "sick" for the rest of the day:** watch them, keep a
  device in reach, no new foods.
- Vomiting and diarrhoea during a reaction can dehydrate a child; small sips once breathing is
  clearly normal (→ 12-05).

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**Published dose bands, printed as published.** The prescriber picks the device and writes it
on the action plan; this table is so you understand the plan and know when to ask for a change.

| Source | Weight band as published | Device and dose |
|---|---|---|
| FDA, EpiPen label | 15 to 30 kg (33 to 66 lb) | EpiPen Jr, 0.15 mg |
| FDA, EpiPen label | 30 kg (66 lb) or more | EpiPen, 0.3 mg |
| FDA, neffy label (ages 4 and up) | 15 kg to less than 30 kg | neffy 1 mg, one spray |
| FDA, neffy label | 30 kg or more | neffy 2 mg, one spray |
| AAP clinical report, Epinephrine for First-aid Management of Anaphylaxis (2017) | 7.5 to 15 kg (about 16 to 33 lb) | 0.15 mg auto-injector is acceptable when a 0.1 mg device is not available |
| AAP clinical report and AAP action plan | About 25 kg (55 lb) and up | AAP suggests the 0.3 mg device from this weight; the label says 30 kg. The prescriber decides. |

Weights on file (re-weigh children every few months; the band can change):
{{#each members as m}}{{m.label}}: {{m.weight_text}}. {{else}}No members entered yet.{{/each}}

**How many devices.** Devices come in two-packs, and a reaction may need two doses. Each place
the person spends time needs a pair: on the person, the home's warm room, the go-bag. When
asking the prescriber, say plainly that you are planning for a time with **no ambulance**.
The EpiPen label says that if more than two injections are needed for one reaction, only a
healthcare provider should give more (FDA, EpiPen label).

**Ask your prescriber now, while you can, and write it here:**
- Device and dose for each person, and the weight at which to change: ___________________
- How many devices to hold for a time with no ambulance: ____________
- What to do if two doses are not enough and no help is coming: _________________________
  ______________________________________________________________________________________
- If the household holds epinephrine vials and syringes as a deep backup: the exact amount to
  draw up for each person, with which syringe, written by the prescriber: ____________________
  ______________________________________________________________________________________
- Antihistamine for each person, product and amount, for itching and hives after epinephrine:
  ______________________________________________________________________________________
Prescriber: ____________________ Date: __________

{{photo action-plan-signed}}

**Stock arithmetic.** The medicines tagged for this condition in settings are printed; if none are tagged, every household medicine row is, so use the ones for this condition.

| Medicine or supply | On hand | In date | Earliest expiry | Pairs wanted | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{else}}
{{#each meds as m}}
| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{/each}}
{{/each}}
| Epinephrine devices | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Trainer device for each device type | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Insulated pouch for each carry set | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Min/max thermometer where devices are stored | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Medical ID (bracelet or card) | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

**Everyone who cares for the person practises with a trainer**, for every device type in the
house: they inject differently. Rehearse the whole sequence, not just the click (→ 24-02).

> **Before the collapse:** get a signed action plan from the prescriber, refill before expiry,
> and set calendar reminders for every expiry date. Ask about a needle-free nasal device as a
> second form: its label allows short heat excursions that would ruin an auto-injector, but it
> fails if frozen (FDA, neffy label).

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

- **There is no household substitute for epinephrine.** Antihistamines are not one; inhalers are
  not one.
- **Pharmacies, clinics and disaster medical points** are the realistic resupply. Keep the
  prescription printed (→ 25-09).
- **Other households** with allergic members may hold devices. Using someone else's prescription
  is a decision card: {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16). Decide it before a reaction, not
  during one.
- **When scavenging**, check expiry and the window. A device left in a hot car or a frozen
  vehicle has had a hard life; your household's rule on using it is on → 30-05.

## 9. Power and devices

Epinephrine needs no power. Some auto-injectors have a small battery for spoken instructions;
the injection still works if the voice fails. Nothing here is lost to an EMP (→ 27-03). The
power question is **heat in summer**: if the house has no cooling, find the coolest stable spot
and use a thermometer.

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- **Devices travel on the person, inside layers in winter, out of the sun in summer.** Never in
  a trunk, a roof box or a parked car (→ 01-07).
- **Two devices at least in every carry set**, plus the action plan and the prescription
  (→ 22-06).
- **Communal, donated and roadside food is the highest-risk food on a move** (→ 02-04). Carry
  enough safe food that the allergic person never needs it.
- **Know where care is** along the route, and decide in advance that a reaction on the road means
  heading for it.

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Expired, frozen or heat-exposed epinephrine:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **Unlabelled, traded or scavenged food for the allergic person:** {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19).
- **Someone else's prescription:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **When to leave:** {{choice DC-19}} (→ 30-20). Running out of in-date devices, or of safe food,
  is a reason to move toward supply.

## 12. My meds

pages.body:
# CL-04. Food allergy (child or adult)

**What this page is for.** In a crisis, food becomes unlabelled, shared, donated, traded,
scavenged, foraged and cooked in one pot over one fire. Every one of those is a way for a
food-allergic person to eat their allergen. When epinephrine is limited and no ambulance comes
(→ 02-03), **avoidance stops being the cautious option and becomes the main defence.** This
module is how to build a food supply around the allergic person, read labels while they exist,
cook without cross-contact, and handle the food you did not buy.

{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder for guests, neighbours, and allergies that appear later.{{/if}}

Your household's allergy rows: {{#each allergies as a}}**{{a.member}}**: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}). {{else}}none entered.{{/each}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **A reaction is treated on → 02-03: epinephrine first.** This page is prevention.
> - **If you cannot name every ingredient and how it was prepared, the allergic person does not
>   eat it** unless your household has chosen otherwise on the card: {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19).
> - **Severity can change over time.** A food that once caused hives can cause anaphylaxis later.
>   Treat the symptoms in front of you, not the history (AAAAI).

## Do this now

**The person may have eaten their allergen:**
1. **Watch them closely** and keep epinephrine in hand. Any sign of anaphylaxis (→ 02-03):
   **give epinephrine at once.**
2. **Stop the meal.** Keep what they ate (the package, the dish) to work out what it was.
3. **Do not make them vomit.** Wipe the mouth and hands.
4. **Stay with them for hours**, with a device in reach.

**Preparation, this week:**
1. **Post the allergen card** where food is made: each person's allergens, the words to look for
   on labels, and "if in doubt, no".
2. **Mark the safe food** "SAFE FOR ______" in thick marker, and store it apart.
3. **Ask the allergist the questions in part 7** and write the answers.

{{photo allergen-card}}

## 1. What it is

A food allergy is the immune system treating a food as an attack. Reactions range from itching
and hives to anaphylaxis, which can kill in minutes. There is no household cure; the plan is to
avoid the food and to be ready to treat a reaction.

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| **Safe, labelled food** | Count it separately from the household's food (→ 04-01). It is usually the shorter clock. | The person depends on food nobody can verify. |
| **Epinephrine** | Printed expiry (→ 02-03). | No treatment for a reaction. |
| Labels and ingredient lists | Gone once food is repackaged, traded or donated. | Verification is impossible. |
| Dedicated cookware | Lost, borrowed, mixed up. | Cross-contact. |
| Wash water and soap | Scarce off-grid (→ 13-10). | Pans and hands carry traces. |

**Write the clock:** safe food for ________ (person) lasts ________ days; on → 23-02 as its own
line.

## 3. Storing safe food without power

- **Keep the labels.** Cut out and file the ingredient panel of anything you repackage into
  buckets or jars, and tape it inside the lid. A bucket of unlabelled flour is a hazard.
- **Label twice, in thick marker:** "SAFE FOR ______" or "NOT SAFE". Assume the person serving
  is tired, cold and working in poor light.
- **Store safe food apart**, on its own shelf or bin, **above** other food so nothing spills into
  it.
- **Depth matters more for the allergic person.** Others can eat whatever is available; they
  cannot. Their staples should have the longest clock in the pantry.

{{photo safe-food-shelf}}

## 4. Day by day without it

When safe food runs short, the pressure to "just try" a doubtful food rises every day. That is
the danger point. Plan now:
- **Who eats the safe food, and when.** Sharing the allergy-safe food with everyone shortens the
  allergic person's runway; holding it as their reserve means everyone else eats other food first.
  This is a decision card: {{choice DC-26}} (→ 30-27).
- **Hunger is survivable; anaphylaxis without epinephrine may not be.** If safe food runs out and
  only unverifiable food remains, that is a reason to move toward supply (→ 01-02), the same way a
  short medicine clock is.

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

Any sign of anaphylaxis after eating, in more than one body system or severe in one: hives with
vomiting, swelling of lips or tongue, cough, wheeze, hoarse voice, faintness, or in a small
child a sudden change in behaviour (CDC; AAAAI). **Epinephrine first** (→ 02-03).

## 6. Sick-day basics

- **During illness, keep to food the person has always tolerated.** A sick day is the wrong day
  to find out something new.
- **Oral rehydration** (→ 12-05): commercial packets list their ingredients; check them. The WHO
  home recipe is water, sugar and salt only (WHO, Cholera Q&A).
- **Medicines and supplements can hide allergens** (for example in coatings and flavourings).
  Ask the pharmacist now and note any on the card.

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**Labels, while they exist.** US law requires packaged foods to declare the **nine major food
allergens**: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and
sesame (FDA, Food Allergies: What You Need to Know). They appear in the ingredient list or a
"Contains" line. Three things catch people out:
- **Anything outside those nine is not called out.** Banana, mustard, legumes other than peanut
  and soy, and many others are found only by reading the **full ingredient list**.
- **"May contain" and "made in a facility with" lines are voluntary** and do not follow a
  standard. Treat them as a yes until the allergist says otherwise.
- **Highly refined oils made from a major allergen are exempt** from the allergen declaration
  under US labelling law (FDA, Food Allergies). Some allergic people tolerate them; that is an
  allergist's call, not a book's.

**What a food allergy does to a normal stockpile.** Many classic prepper staples hold common
allergens: peanut butter, canned fish, powdered egg, soy-based "vegetable oil", ration bars,
freeze-dried meals, trail mix, bread and crackers (often sesame, egg, soy, milk, wheat). **Build
the allergic person's supply from single-ingredient staples you can verify**: plain rice, plain
oats, plain dried beans (other than their allergen), plain flour if tolerated, sugar, salt, plain
canned vegetables and fruit, meat you preserved yourself. Check every freeze-dried pouch and bar
by its label (→ 04-19).

**Ask the allergist now, while you can, and write the answers here:**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Does a trace or "may contain" matter for this person? | ______________________ |
| Highly refined oils from the allergen: tolerated? | ______________________ |
| Baked forms (egg or milk baked into bread): tolerated? | ______________________ |
| Related foods that may cross-react (other nuts, legumes, shellfish, edible insects)? | ______________________ |
| Safe brands they reliably eat | ______________________ |
| Can new foods be introduced, and under what conditions? | ______________________ |
| Can cooking steam or smoke from the allergen cause a reaction? | ______________________ |

**Stock arithmetic.** The medicines tagged for this condition in settings are printed; if none are tagged, every household medicine row is, so use the ones for this condition.

| Item | On hand | Used per day | Days on hand | Days you want | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds_for.CL-04 as m}}
| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{else}}
{{#each meds as m}}
| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{/each}}
{{/each}}
| Safe staple: ____________ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Safe staple: ____________ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Safe staple: ____________ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Safe snacks for the go-bag | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Dedicated pot, pan, spoon, cutting board (one colour) | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Thick markers and labels | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Allergen card, wallet copy and go-bag copy | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

Here the "pharmacy" is the food supply.

**Cooking over one fire without cross-contact:**
- **Cook the allergic person's food first**, in clean, dedicated cookware, before the allergen
  enters the kitchen.
- **One colour of pot, pan, spoon and board** for safe food, stored apart. A single shared spoon
  defeats everything else.
- **Scarce wash water makes dedicated gear more important, not less**, because thorough washing
  between uses stops being possible (→ 13-10).
- **Surfaces and hands:** boards, the table, the grill grate, the server's hands.
- **Children share food.** Small children hand each other things; the whole household enforces
  the rule constantly (→ 20-02).

**The three highest-risk sources:**
1. **Donated and communal food.** Well meant and impossible to verify. Take it for the others if
   you wish (→ 18-01).
2. **Traded food.** The same problem, plus a reason for the trader to overstate it (→ 18-02).
3. **Foraged food.** Unlabelled by definition, with misidentification risk too (→ 05-06). The
   allergic person should not be the one who tries a new wild food.

Your household's rule for these is the card: {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19). Food past its date,
dented cans and food from a failed freezer are a separate card: {{choice DC-14}} (→ 30-15).

**When scavenging for the allergic person:** sealed, labelled, intact original packaging only;
single-ingredient wherever possible. Bulk bins, repackaged goods and damaged labels are out.
Your own garden is the best possible source: you know everything in it.

**Raising food at home** can bring an allergen on site (hens bring eggs; fishing brings fish).
That can be managed with separate handling and cookware, but ask the allergist first.

## 9. Power and devices

None for the allergy itself. Epinephrine storage is on → 02-03. A **freezer failure** forces
quick decisions about food; the allergic person's safe frozen food is eaten or preserved first,
by them.

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- **Carry the allergic person's food for the whole trip and more.** Shelter meals, roadside
  charity and communal pots are the highest-risk food they will meet (→ 01-07, → 22-03).
- **The allergen card** goes with them, in their pocket and in the go-bag: allergens, "no
  unlabelled food", epinephrine location, and how to give it.
- **Say it plainly** to anyone who feeds them, every time.

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Unlabelled, traded or scavenged food for the allergic person:** {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19).
- **Allergy-safe food held in reserve for the allergic person:** {{choice DC-26}} (→ 30-27).
- **Food past its date, dented cans, failed freezer:** {{choice DC-14}} (→ 30-15).
- **Expired epinephrine:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **When to leave:** {{choice DC-19}} (→ 30-20). Running out of safe food is a trigger.

## 12. My meds

Medicines your household tagged for this condition in settings are printed below. **If none
are tagged, every medicine row your household entered is printed instead: tick the rows for
this condition (epinephrine, antihistamines, inhalers)** and cross out the rest. Fill any blank columns by hand from the boxes
and bottles, and add untagged medicines in the empty rows.
