pages.title: CL-23. Hearing and vision aids

photo_slots.caption: Each person's written glasses or contact lens prescription

pages.body:
# CL-23. Hearing and vision aids

**What this page is for.** Glasses, contact lenses, hearing aids and cochlear implants are easy
to forget in a preparedness plan, until they are lost in an evacuation or the batteries run out.
Without them, a person may not hear a warning shout, read a label, see a hazard, drive, shoot, or
do half the jobs in this binder. Everything on this page is cheap to fix now and hard to fix
later: spares, batteries, a written prescription, and a plan for warnings that does not depend on
hearing or sight.

{{#if has.condition.CL-23}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder because most adults wear glasses at some point; check part 7 anyway.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **Never rinse or store contact lenses in tap water or untreated water.** FDA warns that water
>   can carry germs that cause serious eye infections (FDA, Focusing on Contact Lens Safety).
>   In an emergency, switch to glasses.
> - **Someone who cannot hear must still get warnings:** a smoke alarm with a strobe or bed
>   shaker, and a household signal (part 4; USFA, Smoke Alarms).
> - **Hearing-aid and coin batteries are dangerous if swallowed.** Keep them away from small
>   children and from anyone confused.

## Do this now

1. **Count spare glasses, contact lens supplies and hearing-aid batteries**, and write the days
   on hand in part 7.
2. **A red, painful eye with blurred vision** in a contact lens wearer: take the lens out, wear
   glasses, and get care (part 5).
3. **Agree the household's warning signals** for someone who cannot hear or see well (part 4).
4. **Put the written glasses prescription in this binder** (photo slot below).

## 1. What it is

**Vision aids** are glasses, contact lenses, magnifiers and, for low vision, larger print and
better light. **Hearing aids** are small amplifiers worn in or behind the ear; since 2022 some are
sold over the counter to adults with mild to moderate hearing loss (FDA, OTC Hearing Aids: What
You Should Know). A **cochlear implant** is a surgically placed device with an outer sound
processor that runs on batteries. Some household members use none of these and still have
reduced hearing or sight; noise from generators, tools and firearms damages hearing for good
(CDC/NIOSH, About Noise and Hearing Loss).

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| Disposable hearing-aid batteries | Days per battery (the person knows); count spares. | The aid is silent. |
| Rechargeable hearing aids and implant processors | A day or so per charge; need power. | Silent until charged. |
| Glasses | Until lost or broken. | Cannot see well. Spares solve it. |
| Daily or monthly contact lenses | Days of lenses and solution. | Switch to glasses. |
| Contact lens solution | Bottles on hand. | **Do not substitute water** (SAFETY). |
| Reading glasses, magnifiers | Until lost. | Cannot read labels or doses. |

## 3. Storing the devices without power

- **Hearing aids:** dry and cool; out of the bathroom, the car and direct sun. A drying jar or
  a sealed box with a desiccant pack overnight. Open the battery door at night to save the battery.
- **Hearing-aid batteries:** in their original card at room temperature; pull the tab only when
  using one. Write the size here: ________ (→ 29-14).
- **Glasses:** a hard case, always. Spares in the go-bag and the car.
- **Contact lenses and solution:** sealed, out of heat and freezing; check expiry.
- **Cochlear implant processors and chargers:** dry, protected from impact; a spare processor if
  the clinic provides one.

## 4. Day by day without it

**Without hearing aids:** missed warnings, missed instructions, isolation and frustration.
**Without glasses:** falls, injuries with tools and fire, misread labels and medicine doses,
inability to drive or keep watch.

**Warnings that do not depend on hearing** (Ready.gov, Individuals with Disabilities; USFA, Smoke
Alarms):
- **Smoke and CO alarms** with strobe lights or a bed shaker for a person who is deaf or hard of
  hearing.
- **A household signal:** a flashlight flicked on and off, a tap on the shoulder, a written card
  ("FIRE: OUT NOW", "STAY INSIDE", "WE ARE LEAVING"). Agree the signals with everyone (→ 15-07).
- **Weather and hazard alerts** by text, a light or vibration as well as sound (→ 15-01).
- **A notepad and pencil** in every room and every go-bag; a whiteboard by the door.
- **At night,** the person sleeps where someone can reach them quickly.

**For someone who is blind or has low vision:** keep things in fixed places, clear walkways,
good light, tactile marks (a rubber band, a dot of glue) on medicine bottles and supply bins,
and a sighted guide for evacuation (→ 10-01).

**Protect the hearing you have:** earplugs or ear muffs near generators, chainsaws and firearms
(CDC/NIOSH, About Noise and Hearing Loss).

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

- **Contact lens eye infection:** a red, painful eye, blurry vision, light hurting, discharge.
  Remove the lens, do not put another in, wear glasses, get care (FDA, Focusing on Contact Lens
  Safety; → 12-04).
- **Sudden loss of vision, flashes and floaters, or a curtain across vision:** urgent eye care.
- **Eye injuries and chemicals in the eye:** MedlinePlus first aid (MedlinePlus, Eye
  Emergencies); do not rub; flush chemicals with lots of clean water.
- **Sudden hearing loss in one ear,** or an ear that is painful, swollen or draining after an
  infection: get care.
- **A swallowed button or hearing-aid battery,** especially in a child: get care at once.

## 6. Sick-day basics

- **Colds and ear infections** can block hearing aids and make them painful; leave them out while
  the ear is sore and draining.
- **When ill, switch from contacts to glasses.**
- **Clean hands before touching eyes, lenses or aids** (→ 13-02).

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**Get from your eye doctor and audiologist now, while you can, and write it here:**
- Glasses prescription for each person (the full numbers, for both eyes): _______________
- Contact lens prescription and brand: ______________________________________________
- Hearing aid make, model, battery size, and programme settings: ________________________
- Cochlear implant: processor model, battery type, the clinic's number: __________________
Date: __________

{{photo glasses-prescription}}

**Stock arithmetic.** Days on hand = on hand ÷ used per day.

| Supply | On hand | Used per day or week | Days on hand | Days you want | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spare pair of glasses for each wearer | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Reading glasses (several strengths), magnifier | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Contact lenses | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Contact lens solution | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Hearing-aid batteries (by size) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Drying jar, desiccant, cleaning brush | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Cochlear implant batteries, spare cable or coil | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Strobe or bed-shaker alarm, notepads, whiteboard | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Earplugs and ear muffs | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Small screwdriver kit for glasses | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

{{/each}}{{/each}}

> **Before the collapse:** the eye doctor must give you a copy of your glasses prescription after
> an eye exam, under the federal Eyeglass Rule (FTC, Eyeglass Rule). Ask for it and file it here.
> Buy a spare pair of glasses (inexpensive online or at discount shops) and a pair of
> prescription sunglasses or safety glasses. Ask the audiologist for an older hearing aid as a
> backup, or consider an over-the-counter aid as a spare for adults with mild to moderate loss
> (FDA, OTC Hearing Aids).

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

- **Reading glasses** (magnifying, for close work) are sold everywhere and are easy to scavenge;
  they do not correct distance vision or astigmatism.
- **Prescription glasses** belonging to someone else rarely match; a near match can be better
  than nothing for a short time, but it may cause headaches and is unsafe for driving.
- **Hearing-aid batteries** are sold in pharmacies and big stores; the size is on the pack.
- **Contact lenses:** do not use someone else's. Switch to glasses.
- **Medicines** for eye or ear infections: someone else's prescription is a card:
  {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16). Expired eye drops: {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05); once opened, eye
  drops can grow germs.

## 9. Power and devices

- **Rechargeable hearing aids and implant processors** need charging every day. Charging cases
  usually charge from USB, so a power station or small solar panel can run them (→ 09-06,
  → 09-10, → 29-02).
- **Disposable zinc-air batteries need no charging** and are the most resilient choice in a long
  outage; keep a stock even if the person uses rechargeables.
- **EMP and storms:** a spare charger, cable and processor in a metal box (→ 27-03, → 27-02).

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- **Glasses on the face, spares in the go-bag** (→ 22-03, → 22-06), hearing aids in and a
  battery card in a pocket.
- **Tell rescuers and shelter staff** that the person is deaf, hard of hearing, blind or low
  vision; a card saying so helps (→ 25-09).
- **The communication plan** (→ 15-03, → 00-04) should include how this person will be reached
  if separated: text, written notes, a meeting place.

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Expired medicine or eye drops:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **Someone else's prescription:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).

The five questions to settle for every condition, and the whole library, are on → 12-11. The
household's full medicine stockpile is on → 12-07.

## 12. My meds

Rows marked ✓ are the medicines your household tagged for this condition in settings (eye
drops, ear drops). If none is tagged, every medicine row your household entered is printed with
a ☐ instead: **tick the rows for this condition** and cross out the rest. Fill any blank columns
by hand, and add missing medicines in the blank rows. Write glasses and hearing aid details in
part 7.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

pages.title: CL-24. Sleep apnoea (CPAP)

photo_slots.caption: The CPAP power supply label (volts, amps or watts) and the DC cable, if you have one

pages.body:
# CL-24. Sleep apnoea (CPAP)

**What this page is for.** In obstructive sleep apnoea the airway closes again and again during
sleep. A **CPAP** machine (continuous positive airway pressure) blows air through a mask to hold
it open. CPAP needs power every night. **For most people a few nights without it are not an
emergency**, but weeks without it bring dangerous daytime sleepiness at exactly the time when
people are driving, using tools, keeping watch and making hard decisions. This module covers the
power budget, running the machine off-grid, what happens without it, and what else helps.

{{#if has.condition.CL-24}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}{{#if has.cpap}}**Someone in your household uses CPAP.** This module applies to them.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder so you can help someone else, or add the condition later in settings.{{/if}}{{/if}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; a generator running at night for
>   a CPAP, while everyone sleeps, is the classic case (floor, → 30-01; CDC, Carbon Monoxide
>   Poisoning: Basics).
> - **Do not drive or run dangerous tools while very sleepy.** Drowsy driving kills (part 5).
> - **Alcohol and sleeping pills make apnoea worse** (NHLBI, Sleep Apnea).

## Do this now

**Power is out tonight:**
1. **Run the CPAP from a battery or power station, humidifier off** (part 9). The heated
   humidifier is usually the biggest power user; the manual says how much.
2. **No power at all:** sleep on the side, head and chest raised on pillows, no alcohol or
   sedatives (part 4).
3. **Generator:** outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows and doors, exhaust pointed away,
   CO alarms inside (CDC; → 09-04).
4. **Next day:** no driving if sleepy; nap when you can.

## 1. What it is

**Obstructive sleep apnoea** means the throat relaxes and closes during sleep, stopping breathing
for seconds at a time, many times an hour. The person wakes briefly each time, often without
knowing it, so sleep is broken and oxygen drops (NHLBI, Sleep Apnea). Loud snoring, gasping and
daytime sleepiness are common signs. Over years it strains the heart and raises blood pressure.
**CPAP** keeps the airway open with gentle air pressure (NHLBI, CPAP). Some people use a mouth
device or have had surgery instead; they need no power.

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| Power for the CPAP | Every night. Battery hours depend on the machine and the settings (part 9). | Sleep without CPAP (part 4). |
| Distilled water for the humidifier | Nights per jug. | Run with the humidifier off. |
| Masks, cushions, tubing, filters | Cushions and filters wear out over weeks to months. | Leaks, sore skin, dirty air. |
| The person's alertness | A few bad nights. | Dangerous daytime sleepiness. |

## 3. Storing the device without power

- **Machine:** dry, clean, out of heat and freezing. If it has been very cold, let it warm to room
  temperature before use so condensation does not form inside.
- **Spare mask, cushions, tubing and filters** sealed, out of sun.
- **Water tank:** empty it daily and let it dry; stale water grows germs.

## 4. Day by day without it

What public sources describe: without treatment, breathing pauses return, sleep is broken, and
daytime sleepiness builds. NHLBI lists daytime sleepiness, trouble concentrating, morning
headaches and irritability, and warns that untreated sleep apnoea raises the risk of accidents
(NHLBI, Sleep Apnea). **One night** is usually just a bad night. **Several nights to weeks:** the
sleepiness and poor judgement become a real hazard. Over months: blood pressure and heart strain
(→ 02-09).

**What helps without CPAP** (NHLBI, Sleep Apnea; CDC, About Sleep):
- **Sleep on the side,** not the back; a rolled towel or a backpack worn in bed stops rolling over.
- **Raise the head and chest** with pillows or blocks under the head of the bed.
- **No alcohol and no sedating medicines** at night unless the prescriber has said they are
  safe; they relax the throat further. If the person takes opioids or sedating mental-health
  medicines, see → 02-17 and → 02-16.
- **A regular sleep time,** a dark, quiet, cool room, and naps by day if possible (→ 21-07).
- **Weight loss** helps many people over months (→ 02-26).

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

- **Falling asleep while driving, working with tools, cooking on a fire or on watch.** Stop the
  task; someone else takes over.
- **Gasping, choking awake, or blue lips at night** that do not settle with position change.
- **Morning confusion or severe headache,** especially with heart or lung disease: possible low
  oxygen or high carbon dioxide; get care. Someone on oxygen too: → 02-08.
- **Headache, dizziness or nausea in several people** in a house with a generator or heater:
  carbon monoxide (→ 29-03). Get everyone into fresh air.

## 6. Sick-day basics

- **A cold or blocked nose** makes the mask hard to use; a full-face mask or saline rinse can help.
  Ask the prescriber now.
- **Sedating cold medicines** worsen apnoea; check the label.
- **Clean the mask and tubing** more often when sick, with mild soap and water, and let them dry
  completely (→ 13-02).

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**Ask the sleep doctor or equipment supplier now, while you can, and write it here:**
- The machine's make, model and pressure setting: ______________________________________
- Does it have a DC (12-volt) cable or a battery made for it? ______________________________
- The power it draws with and without the humidifier, from the label or manual: ___________
- Can it run safely from a power station or inverter? ____________________________________
- If CPAP is impossible for weeks, what else should we do? ________________________________
Doctor or supplier: ____________________ Date: __________

{{photo cpap-power-label}}

**Night budget.** Nights on battery = battery watt-hours available ÷ watt-hours the machine uses
per night. The power station's watt-hours are on its label and on → 28-01; your household total
is {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh. The machine's use per night comes from its manual or a plug-in
meter test, not from this page.

| Supply | On hand | Used per night or month | Nights on hand | Nights you want | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Battery or power station watt-hours for CPAP | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Distilled water | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Mask cushions | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Filters | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Tubing, spare mask, headgear | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| DC cable or approved battery | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Wedge pillow or blocks for raising the bed | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
{{#each meds_for.CL-24 as m}}| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{else}}{{#each meds as m}}| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{/each}}{{/each}}

> **Before the collapse:** run the CPAP for one night on your power station and write down how
> much charge it used, with and without the humidifier. That one test is worth more than any
> table. Ask the supplier about the maker's DC cable. Tell your electric company you use a
> medical device ({{ contacts.utility.electric.provider }}, {{ contacts.utility.electric.phone }}).
> Keep the prescription and settings on → 25-09.

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

- **Medical equipment suppliers and pharmacies** while they run; masks and tubing are standard
  sizes within each system.
- **Another person's CPAP** can be borrowed only if it is cleaned well and its pressure is right
  for this person; pressure settings are prescribed. That is the same trade-off as someone else's
  prescription: {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **Distilled water** can be replaced by running the humidifier dry (off). Do not use tap or
  untreated water in the tank; it leaves minerals and can grow germs.

## 9. Power and devices

- **CPAP is a medical load on the household power plan** (→ 09-01, → 09-06, → 09-10). Put it on
  the list with its nightly watt-hours.
- **Humidifier off** reduces power use the most; the heated tube too, if fitted.
- **A DC cable from the maker** runs the machine straight from a 12-volt source without the
  losses of an inverter (→ 29-02). Use only the maker's cable or one the supplier approves.
- **Power stations:** charge by day from solar, car or generator; run the CPAP at night
  (→ 28-01). Read your own machine's label (→ 28-07).
- **Car battery:** possible with the right DC cable, but a car battery run flat may not start
  the car. Keep the engine off while sleeping; never run it in a garage (floor).
- **EMP and storms:** a spare power supply in a metal box (→ 27-03).

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- The machine, mask, tubing, power supply and DC cable go with the person (→ 01-07, → 22-06).
  Shelters may have power outlets; ask for a spot near one (American Red Cross, Power Outage
  Safety).
- On the road: side-sleeping and a raised head if the CPAP cannot run.
- **Driver rota:** the person with untreated apnoea drives short legs only, and never while sleepy.

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Someone else's prescription or equipment:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).

The five questions to settle for every condition, and the whole library, are on → 12-11. The
household's full medicine stockpile is on → 12-07.

rows for this condition** and cross out the rest. Fill any blank columns by hand, and add

pages.title: CL-25. Contraception and menstrual health
pages.body:
# CL-25. Contraception and menstrual health

**What this page is for.** Birth control and period care are among the most under-planned
supplies in any household. Pill packs run out on a fixed date; a shot is due every few months;
pads and tampons are bulky and run out fast. **A pregnancy in a long emergency carries real risk**
(→ 02-12), so for many households contraception is a safety supply, not a private detail. This
module covers the supply clocks, what still works when the pharmacy is closed, emergency
contraception, period care without stores, and the warning signs that need care.

{{#if has.condition.CL-25}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder because most households include someone who has periods; part 4 and part 5 apply to them.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **Toxic shock syndrome is rare but can kill.** Use the lowest-absorbency tampon that works
>   and change it as the package says; know the signs (part 5; FDA, The Facts on Tampons).
> - **Very heavy bleeding, or severe one-sided belly pain with a missed period, is an emergency**
>   (part 5).
> - **This page never calculates, adjusts or suggests a dose or schedule.** Each method's own
>   leaflet is the instruction.

## Do this now

1. **Count the supply clock** for each method (part 2) and write the date it runs out in part 12.
2. **Unprotected sex, or a method failed (missed pills, broken condom):** emergency contraception
   (part 4) as soon as possible, as its label says.
3. **Soaking a pad or tampon every hour for several hours, or fainting:** part 5.
4. **Stock reusable period products now** and learn to use them (part 4, → 13-08).

## 1. What it is

**Contraception** prevents pregnancy. Methods differ in how well they work, how long they last
and what they need: some are a daily pill, some a weekly patch or monthly ring, some an injection
every 3 months, some a device that works for years (an IUD or implant), some a barrier used each
time (CDC, Contraception and Birth Control Methods). **Menstrual health** covers period care,
pain, heavy bleeding, and the supplies and hygiene they need.

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| Pills | Packs on hand; each pack lasts a set number of days (the pack says). | Protection ends; it can end within days of missed pills (the leaflet says). |
| Patch, ring | Patches or rings on hand; each lasts a set time (the box says). | Protection ends. |
| Injection | Next injection date on the clinic card. | Protection ends after the due date; check the leaflet. |
| IUD or implant | The removal or replacement date on the card. Lasts years. | The most resilient methods in a long emergency. |
| Condoms | Count them; one each time. | No barrier, no protection from infections. |
| Pads, tampons | Count them; several per day of a period. | Reusable products or improvised cloth. |
| Pain relievers | Count them (→ 12-13). | Heat, rest and movement only. |

## 3. Storing the medication without power

- **Pills, patches, rings:** in their packs, at room temperature, dry, out of sun and heat. Not in
  a car or a hot attic. Pills left in serious heat are the household's call: {{choice DC-08}}
  (→ 30-09).
- **Condoms:** cool, dry, away from sharp objects; check the expiry date. Heat and age weaken
  latex. Oil-based lubricants (petroleum jelly, cooking oil) damage latex condoms.
- **Pads, tampons, cups:** sealed, dry. A cup in its cloth bag, clean and dry.
- **Expired pills or condoms** when nothing else exists: {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).

## 4. Day by day without it

**When a method runs out.** Pregnancy becomes possible quickly after pills, patches and rings
stop; after the injection, fertility can take longer to return but cannot be counted on to stay
away. There is no danger to the body in stopping these methods suddenly; the risk is pregnancy.

**How well each method works, as published.** CDC lists the percentage of women who become
pregnant in the first year of **typical use** (CDC, Contraception and Birth Control Methods):

| Method | Pregnancies per 100 women in a year, typical use |
|---|---|
| Implant | 0.1 |
| Hormonal IUD | 0.1 to 0.4 |
| Copper IUD | 0.8 |
| Injection | 4 |
| Pill, patch or ring | 7 |
| Male condom | 13 |
| Withdrawal | 20 |
| Fertility awareness methods | 2 to 23 |
| Spermicide | 21 |

**Methods that need no supply:**
- **Fertility awareness** (tracking the cycle by dates, temperature and cervical mucus) needs
  training and discipline; its range in the table shows how much that matters (WHO and Johns
  Hopkins, Family Planning: A Global Handbook for Providers). Learn it from a book or a trained
  teacher now, not in a crisis.
- **Breastfeeding** prevents pregnancy reliably only under strict conditions described in the
  WHO handbook (the baby is under 6 months, fed only at the breast day and night, and periods have
  not returned). Outside those conditions it cannot be relied on (→ 02-13).
- **Withdrawal** and **abstinence**: honest numbers are in the table.

**Emergency contraception.** Levonorgestrel pills (sold as Plan B One-Step and generics) are sold
without a prescription and without an age limit (FDA, Plan B One-Step Information). FDA says it
works best the sooner it is taken after unprotected sex; the label gives the time window. **Keep a
pack in the medical kit; it is one of the most useful things a pharmacy run can buy.** It is not
for regular use.

**Over-the-counter daily pill.** Since 2023 FDA has approved a progestin-only daily pill for sale
without a prescription (FDA, First Nonprescription Daily Oral Contraceptive). Its leaflet says
how to take it and what to do after a missed or late pill.

**Period care without stores** (CDC, Menstrual Hygiene; → 13-08):
- **Menstrual cups** last years; rinse and reinsert as the maker says, and clean between cycles as
  the instructions say (boiling is common). They need clean hands and a little water.
- **Cloth pads and period underwear** last years; wash with soap, rinse well, dry fully, ideally
  in sunlight (→ 13-04).
- **Improvised pads** from clean, absorbent cotton cloth folded in layers.
- **Hands:** wash with soap before and after changing any product (CDC, Menstrual Hygiene;
  → 13-02).
- **Pain:** heat on the lower belly, gentle movement, and over-the-counter pain relievers as
  their labels say (→ 12-13).
- **Iron:** heavy periods drain iron. Iron-rich foods (beans, lentils, meat, leafy greens) in the
  food plan (→ 04-18).

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

- **Toxic shock syndrome:** FDA lists sudden high fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, a sunburn-like rash,
  dizziness or fainting, and muscle aches (FDA, The Facts on Tampons). **Remove the tampon or cup
  and get care.**
- **Heavy menstrual bleeding:** CDC describes soaking through one or more pads or tampons every
  hour for several hours in a row, needing two products at once, passing clots the size of a
  quarter or larger, or a period lasting more than 7 days (CDC, Heavy Menstrual Bleeding). With
  dizziness, a racing heart or fainting, it is an emergency.
- **A missed period with severe one-sided belly pain, shoulder-tip pain, or fainting** can be a
  pregnancy outside the womb (ectopic), which can bleed inside. Get care at once.
- **Bleeding in pregnancy:** → 02-12.
- **Fever with belly pain and unusual discharge** after sex or an IUD insertion: infection
  (→ 12-04). Antibiotics without a prescription are a card: {{choice DC-16}} (→ 30-17).

## 6. Sick-day basics

- **Vomiting or severe diarrhoea** soon after a pill can mean it was not absorbed. The pill
  leaflet says what to do; follow it.
- **Some antibiotics, seizure medicines and herbal products** can make hormonal methods work less
  well; the leaflet lists them. Use condoms as a backup when in doubt.
- **Fever with a tampon or cup in place:** remove it and think of toxic shock (part 5).

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**Ask the prescriber or clinic now, while you can, and write it here:**
- The longest supply of this method they can prescribe: _____________________________
- If the method runs out, what should we switch to? _____________________________________
- For the injection: can it be given at home, and how? __________________________________
- When the IUD or implant is due for replacement: _______________________________________
- Is emergency contraception suitable for this person, and is there anything to know about it?
  ______________________________________________________________________________________
Prescriber or clinic: ____________________ Date: __________

**Stock arithmetic.** Days on hand = on hand ÷ used per day (for pills, one pack covers the days
printed on it).

| Medicine or supply | On hand | Used per day or cycle | Days or cycles on hand | Wanted | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds_for.CL-25 as m}}| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{else}}{{#each meds as m}}| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{/each}}{{/each}}| Condoms | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Emergency contraception pill | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Pregnancy tests | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Menstrual cup (one per person, right size) | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Cloth pads or period underwear | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Disposable pads and tampons (the buffer) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Pain relievers, hot-water bottle | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

> **Before the collapse:** ask for a 12-month supply of pills, patches or rings if the insurer
> allows; rules differ by state, so ask the pharmacist. Consider whether a long-acting method (IUD or implant) suits the
> person before a crisis. Buy emergency contraception and pregnancy tests. Buy and practise with a
> menstrual cup or cloth pads now. Note the method and replacement dates on → 25-09.

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

- **Pharmacies, clinics and disaster medical points** while they run. Condoms, emergency
  contraception and the over-the-counter daily pill need no prescription.
- **Someone else's pill packs** are a card: {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16). Pill types differ; the
  leaflet in the pack is the instruction for that type, and switching types can leave a gap in
  protection.
- **Scavenging:** sealed packs only, in date. Pads, tampons and cups are good finds in any store
  or home.

## 9. Power and devices

None. A fertility-tracking app on a phone needs charging; a paper chart and a thermometer do not.

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- Pills and the current pack on the person, out of heat; condoms, emergency contraception and a
  cycle's worth of period products in the go-bag (→ 22-03, → 22-06).
- Travel and stress can delay periods and cause missed pills; keep the leaflet.
- Shelters may have little privacy or water; a cup or a few days of disposables, a zip bag for
  used products, and hand sanitiser make it manageable (→ 01-07).

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Expired pills or condoms:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **Heat-exposed medicine:** {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
- **Someone else's prescription:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **Antibiotics without a prescription:** {{choice DC-16}} (→ 30-17).

The five questions to settle for every condition, and the whole library, are on → 12-11. The
household's full medicine stockpile is on → 12-07.

## 12. My meds

Rows marked ✓ are the medicines your household tagged for this condition in settings. If none
is tagged, every medicine row your household entered is printed with a ☐ instead: **tick the
rows for this condition** and cross out the rest. Fill any blank columns by hand, and add
missing medicines in the blank rows. For an IUD, implant or injection, write the replacement or due date under
"Expires".

pages.title: CL-26. Severe obesity and bariatric surgery
pages.body:
# CL-26. Severe obesity and bariatric surgery

**What this page is for.** This module covers two related situations. **Severe obesity** brings
practical problems in a long emergency: moving and evacuating, heat, skin care, equipment that
does not fit, and the conditions that often come with it (diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep
apnoea). **Bariatric (weight-loss) surgery** changes how the body takes in food and medicine for
life: the person needs vitamins every day, cannot eat large or sugary meals, may absorb some
medicines poorly, and can become seriously ill from vomiting. Emergency food is often exactly
the wrong food. This module covers both, without judgement.

{{#if has.condition.CL-26}}**Someone in your household has this condition.** This module is at the front of the medical section for you.{{else}}**Nobody in your household is marked with this condition.** The module stays in the binder so you can help someone else, or add the condition later in settings.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY**
> - **After bariatric surgery, vomiting that will not stop is an emergency.** It can lead to a
>   vitamin B1 (thiamine) shortage that damages the brain (Mechanick et al., 2019 guideline;
>   part 5).
> - **After gastric bypass, avoid anti-inflammatory pain relievers** (NSAIDs such as ibuprofen,
>   naproxen and aspirin) unless the surgeon says otherwise; they cause ulcers at the join
>   (Mechanick et al., 2019 guideline; → 12-13).
> - **This page never calculates, adjusts or suggests a dose.**

## Do this now

1. **Bariatric surgery: keep taking the daily vitamins and minerals.** Count them; write days on
   hand in part 12.
2. **Vomiting for more than a day, or any vomiting with confusion, unsteady walking or eye
   problems:** get care (part 5).
3. **Severe belly pain after bariatric surgery,** especially with a fast heartbeat or fever: get
   care.
4. **Heat:** shade, water, rest, cool cloths; people with more body weight overheat sooner
   (→ 17-04).
5. **Evacuation:** plan the transport and helpers now (part 10).

## 1. What it is

**Severe obesity** is a level of body weight high enough to affect health and daily function. It
often comes with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea and joint pain (NIDDK,
Bariatric Surgery). **Bariatric surgery** makes the stomach smaller and, in some operations,
bypasses part of the small intestine. The common operations are the **sleeve gastrectomy**, the
**gastric bypass**, the **adjustable band**, and the **duodenal switch** (NIDDK, Bariatric
Surgery). After surgery a person eats small amounts, needs protein first, and takes vitamins and
minerals for the rest of their life. Some people instead take weekly or daily weight-loss
injections.

## 2. What runs out, and how fast

| What | Clock | When it is gone |
|---|---|---|
| Daily vitamins and minerals after surgery | Days on hand (part 7). | Shortages build over weeks to months (part 4). |
| Protein foods and supplements | Days of protein on hand. | Weakness, hair loss, slow healing. |
| Weight-loss injections | Pens on hand; most need a fridge before first use (label). | Appetite returns over weeks; no immediate danger. |
| Medicines for linked conditions | See → 02-05, → 02-09, → 02-24. | As those modules say. |
| Equipment that fits | Blood pressure cuff in the right size, clothing, a sturdy chair, a cot rated for the weight. | Wrong readings, falls, injury. |

## 3. Storing the medication without power

- **Vitamins and tablets:** original containers, cool and dry, out of sun. Chewable and liquid
  forms (often prescribed after surgery) can spoil in heat; check them.
- **Weight-loss injections:** read the box for the fridge rule before first use and the days a pen
  may be kept out of the fridge after; write them here: ________ (→ 29-07, → 29-14). After a heat
  excursion: {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
- **Expired vitamins or medicine** when nothing else exists: {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).

## 4. Day by day without it

**After bariatric surgery, without the vitamins.** The 2019 guideline lists the shortages that
are common after surgery: vitamin B12, iron, calcium and vitamin D, folate, thiamine (B1), and in
some operations the fat-soluble vitamins (Mechanick et al., 2019 guideline). They develop over
weeks to months: tiredness, pale skin and breathlessness (anaemia), numbness and tingling, weak
bones, poor night vision. Thiamine can run low within weeks if the person is vomiting or barely
eating.

**The food plan after surgery** (NIDDK, Bariatric Surgery; NIDDK, Dumping Syndrome):
- **Small meals, eaten slowly, protein first.** Canned meat and fish, beans, eggs, powdered milk,
  peanut butter and protein powder belong in the stockpile (→ 04-18).
- **Little sugar and refined starch.** Many emergency rations are sweet or starchy. After a
  gastric bypass, sugary food can cause **dumping syndrome**: within minutes, nausea, cramps,
  diarrhoea, dizziness and a racing heart; or one to three hours later, sweating, shakiness and
  weakness from low blood sugar (NIDDK, Dumping Syndrome).
- **Drink between meals, not with them,** and sip all day to avoid dehydration.
- **The household's calorie plan** assumes ordinary eating (→ 04-01). For this person, plan by
  protein and small portions instead, and ask the dietitian now how much.

**Medicine absorption after surgery.** Some medicines, especially extended-release and
long-acting tablets, may be absorbed differently after some operations (Mechanick et al., 2019
guideline). The prescriber may already have switched forms. Do not crush or break tablets unless
the pharmacist says that form allows it. Alcohol is absorbed faster and hits harder after
surgery.

**Severe obesity, day to day, off-grid:**
- **Heat:** people with more body weight are at higher risk of heat illness (CDC, About Heat and
  Your Health). Shade, water, rest in the heat of the day, cool cloths (→ 17-04).
- **Skin:** skin folds stay damp and break down; wash, dry fully, and keep them aired (→ 13-02).
  Long sitting or lying causes pressure sores (MedlinePlus, Preventing Pressure Ulcers; → 02-22).
- **Sleep apnoea** is common; see → 02-24.
- **Physical work:** build up gradually; joints and heart need pacing.

**Weight-loss injections stopped:** appetite and weight return over weeks to months. There is no
known immediate danger in stopping. **Do not restart at the old dose after a gap without asking**:
the label has restart rules, and the prescriber decides.

## 5. Warning signs that mean an emergency

- **Vomiting that does not stop,** or vomiting with **confusion, unsteady walking, double vision
  or jerky eye movements**: possible thiamine shortage, which can cause permanent brain damage;
  get care urgently (Mechanick et al., 2019 guideline).
- **Severe belly pain after bariatric surgery,** especially with fever, a racing heart or
  vomiting: a leak, an ulcer or a twisted bowel; get care.
- **Black or bloody stool, or vomiting blood:** a bleeding ulcer.
- **Food that will not go down,** with pain and drooling: something is stuck.
- **Heat stroke:** hot skin, confusion, collapse (→ 17-04).
- **A swollen, painful calf, or sudden breathlessness and chest pain:** a blood clot; more likely
  after long sitting on a trip.

## 6. Sick-day basics

- **Dehydration comes fast** after bariatric surgery because the stomach holds little. Sip fluids
  all day; oral rehydration solution for vomiting or diarrhoea (the WHO home recipe: 1 litre safe
  water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, half a level teaspoon salt; WHO, Cholera Q&A; safety notes on
  → 12-05). Sip it slowly; the sugar can trigger dumping in some people.
- **Pain relievers:** after bypass, acetaminophen as its label says, not NSAIDs, unless the
  surgeon has said otherwise (→ 12-13).
- **Weight-loss injections** commonly cause nausea and vomiting; with vomiting or diarrhoea from
  any cause, ask the prescriber now whether to hold the next dose.

## 7. What to stock, and how much

**Ask the surgeon, dietitian or prescriber now, while you can, and write it here:**
- The exact vitamins and minerals this person needs every day, by name and form:
  ______________________________________________________________________________________
- If vitamins run short, which matter most? ___________________________________________
- What to do for vomiting, and when it becomes an emergency: _____________________________
- Which pain relievers are safe: ______________________________________________________
- Medicines that should be in a different form because of the surgery: _________________
- Protein target per day, and good stored foods for it: _________________________________
Surgeon or dietitian: ____________________ Date: __________

**Stock arithmetic.** Days on hand = on hand ÷ used per day. The medicines tagged for this
condition in settings are printed; if none is tagged, every medicine row is, and you use the
ones for this condition.

| Medicine or supply | On hand | Used per day | Days on hand | Days you want | Still to get |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds_for.CL-26 as m}}| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{else}}{{#each meds as m}}| {{m.name}} {{m.strength}} ({{m.member}}) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
{{/each}}{{/each}}| Vitamins and minerals after surgery (each one) | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| Protein foods and powder | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ | ____ |
| ORS sachets, or salt, sugar and measuring spoons | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Large blood pressure cuff, batteries | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Skin-fold care: soap, cloths, barrier cream | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |
| Sturdy chair, commode or cot rated for the person's weight | ____ | | | ____ | ____ |

> **Before the collapse:** ask for the full list of lifelong supplements in writing and stock
> several months. Note the type and date of surgery on → 25-09; any doctor treating the person
> later needs to know it. Check that the go-bag clothes, rain gear and any evacuation equipment
> fit.

## 8. Sourcing when the pharmacy is closed

- **Vitamins and minerals** are sold over the counter everywhere and are easy to scavenge; match
  the names and forms the surgeon wrote. Chewable or liquid forms may be needed in the first
  months after surgery.
- **Someone else's prescription** is a card: {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **Protein:** canned meat and fish, beans, eggs, milk powder; traded food rich in protein is
  worth more to this person than bread.
- **Equipment:** medical supply stores and hospitals stock larger cuffs, chairs and commodes.

## 9. Power and devices

None for the vitamins. A refrigerated injection needs the cold ladder (→ 29-07). A CPAP, if used,
needs power (→ 02-24). An electric blood pressure cuff runs on batteries.

## 10. Travel and evacuation

- **Plan transport now:** the vehicle seat and belt, a seat-belt extender if needed, helpers, and
  for someone who cannot walk far, the carrying plan (→ 02-22, → 01-07).
- Carry vitamins, protein snacks, water and the medical summary (→ 22-06, → 25-09).
- On long rides: stand and walk at every stop, flex the calves, drink water (blood clots).
- Shelter cots may not be rated for the person's weight; bring a pad and ask for a sturdy bed.

## 11. Decision cards that apply

- **Expired medicine or vitamins:** {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05).
- **Heat-exposed refrigerated injections:** {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
- **Someone else's prescription:** {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).

The five questions to settle for every condition, and the whole library, are on → 12-11. The
household's full medicine stockpile is on → 12-07.

## 12. My meds

Rows marked ✓ are the medicines your household tagged for this condition in settings. If none
is tagged, every medicine row your household entered is printed with a ☐ instead: **tick the
rows for this condition** and cross out the rest. Fill any blank columns by hand, and add
missing medicines in the blank rows. **Add a row for each daily vitamin and mineral.**

# Water

**What this section holds.** 10 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 03-01 **How much water we need (household math)**: Water is the fastest survival clock in the house: you can go weeks without food but only days without water.
- → 03-02 **Storing water safely**: How to store drinking water so it is still safe when you need it: which containers, how to clean them, where to keep them, and how to get the water already i…
- → 03-03 **Pool and hot tub water: utility water, and distilling it to drink**: A swimming pool or hot tub is a large store of water already at your house.
- → 03-04 **Purifying water: boil, chemical, filter**: How to make fresh water (rain, snow, rivers, ponds, wells, doubtful tap water) safe to drink, with or without fuel.
- → 03-05 **Rain catchment and melting snow and ice**: Rain and snow are the cheapest water you can get in fuel terms: they need disinfecting, not distilling.
- → 03-06 **Water when everything is frozen**: Winter brings two separate water problems: **your plumbing freezing and bursting** (which can flood the house and destroy the water you have), and **every ou…
- → 03-07 **Judging and testing water quality**: How to rank water sources from bad to worse, what a real test can tell you, and which tests to buy now while labs and shops are open.
- → 03-08 **Keeping stored and pool water from going bad (algae, bacteria, mosquitoes)**: Standing water left alone goes bad: green, slimy, smelly, and full of mosquito larvae.
- → 03-09 **Filter care: straws, bottles, squeeze and gravity filters**: How to choose, use, clean, store and retire the portable water filters most households buy.
- → 03-10 **Well water without power**: Getting water out of a drilled well when the grid is down, at your own home or at any place you might go that has one.

pages.body:
# How much water we need (household math)

**What this page is for.** Water is the fastest survival clock in the house: you can go weeks
without food but only days without water. This page turns the CDC planning figure into your
household's numbers: how much to store, and how many days the water you already have will
last. Every other water page uses the numbers printed here.

> **CAUTION.** The numbers below are planning minimums built on the CDC figure, not comfort
> levels. Heat, hard work, illness, pregnancy and nursing all push real need higher. Plan above the
> minimum, never below it.

## Do this now

1. **Know your two numbers.**
   - **Floor:** {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons a day for the whole household. This
     is the bare minimum. It is the number you fall back to in a crisis, never the plan.
   - **Plan:** {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day. Store to this number.
2. **Three days is the minimum store. Two weeks is the goal.** For your household, two weeks
   at the plan rate is **{{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gallons**.
3. **Know your runway.** You have {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gallons stored. At the floor
   rate that is about **{{ derived.water.stored_days }} days**. At the plan rate it is
   shorter. Recount every week during an emergency.
4. **Store more if** anyone is sick, pregnant or nursing, if it is hot, or if people are
   doing hard physical work.
5. **Never ration drinking water to the point of thirst.** FEMA's advice: drink the amount you
   need today and try to find more for tomorrow (→ 03-05 rain and snow{{#if has.pool}}, → 03-03 your pool{{/if}}{{#if has.well}}, → 03-10 your well{{/if}}).

## Why these numbers

The CDC planning figure is **1 gallon per person per day**, with **at least a 3-day supply**
at home and a **2-week supply** if you can manage it (CDC, How to Create and Store an
Emergency Water Supply). That gallon is not all for drinking. FEMA says a normally active
person needs about three quarters of a gallon of fluid a day from water and other drinks; the
rest covers cooking, dishes, brushing teeth and basic washing (FEMA, Ready.gov Water).

**Needs go up.** The CDC says to store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot
climates. FEMA adds that children, nursing mothers and sick people may need more, that a
medical emergency may need extra water, and that **in very hot weather water needs can
double** (FEMA, Ready.gov Water). Hard physical work raises it too. A grid-down summer with laundry by
hand and wood to haul is not a quiet day on the couch.

### How your numbers are worked out

The binder builds your **floor** from your household profile. The 1 gallon per person is the
CDC figure. The CDC and FEMA say to store more for pregnancy, nursing, infants and pets but
publish no exact amount, so the extra amounts below are this binder's planning allowances, not
published figures:

| Who | Added to the daily floor |
|---|---|
| Each person | 1 gallon |
| Each pregnant or nursing member | 0.5 gallon more |
| Each infant (formula mixing and washing) | 0.5 gallon more |
| Each pet | 0.25 gallon (a cat drinks far less, a big dog may drink more; check yours) |

Your household: **{{ household.size }} people**, floor **{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}
gallons a day**.

The **plan** figure is the floor plus a 30 percent margin ({{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }}
gallons a day). The margin is also this binder's planning allowance, not a published figure.
It covers heat, sickness, spills and the water that cooking eats.
If your food store leans on freeze-dried or dehydrated meals, those meals are rehydrated with
water that counts against the day, so treat the plan number as the least you need
(→ 07-07).

| | Per day | Two weeks |
|---|---|---|
| Floor (crisis ration) | {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gal | floor x 14 |
| Plan (store to this) | {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal | {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal |

### People who need extra care

{{#if has.infant}}- **Your infant.** Any water used for bottles, formula, cups or feeding must
  be safe water: boiled or treated, never raw pool or surface water. Infants are the least
  able to survive a stomach illness from bad water (→ 20-05).
{{else}}- **Infants.** Any water used for bottles, formula, cups or feeding must be safe water:
  boiled or treated, never raw pool or surface water. Infants are the least able to survive a
  stomach illness from bad water (→ 20-05).
{{/if}}
{{#if has.nursing}}- **The nursing member.** FEMA says needs rise while nursing. The margin
  in your plan number exists for her. Hers is never the line to ration.
{{else}}- **Anyone nursing** may need more water, says FEMA. Never ration a nursing mother's
  share.
{{/if}}
- **Diabetes.** Dehydration and high blood sugar feed each other: high sugar makes the body
  pass more urine, which concentrates the sugar further. Keep drinking water within reach of
  a person with diabetes, day and night, and give them a larger share
  {{#if has.condition.CL-01}}(→ 02-01){{else}}(→ 02-05){{/if}}. Some households agree in
  advance that this person gets water first if supply runs short. That is a conversation to
  have now, not during the shortage.
- **Children** get a full share. Do not shortchange them.
{{#if has.pets}}- **Your pets drink treated water too.** Raw pool or pond water can make an
  animal sick, and there may be no vet. Keep pets away from the pool and pour their water from
  the treated supply (→ 20-09).
{{else}}- **Pets** drink treated water, the same as people (→ 20-09).
{{/if}}

### Water that is not drinking water

Flushing a toilet uses gallons each time. Laundry and bathing use more. **Do not spend stored
drinking water on these.**
{{#if has.pool}}Your pool is for that: raw pool water flushes toilets, washes floors and
fights fires perfectly well (→ 03-03).{{else}}Use rain barrels, a pool or pond, or other
untreated water for flushing and washing floors (→ 03-05, → 13-01).{{/if}}

### The runway

**Runway = stored gallons ÷ gallons used per day.** That is how many days you have before you
*must* be producing water. Divide by the plan figure while things are normal; divide by the
floor only after you have already cut back to the floor. Write the number on the consumables
table (→ 23-02). For most households the honest answer is under two weeks, which is why rain,
snow{{#if has.pool}}, the pool{{/if}}{{#if has.well}}, the well{{/if}} and a way to treat
water matter so much.

## Gear and supplies

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Food-grade water containers (5 to 7 gal jugs, or a 55-gal drum) | The bulk of the store | Jugs can be moved. A full 55-gal drum weighs about 460 lb and never moves again |
| Bottled water by the case | Safest water with no preparation | The CDC calls it the safest reliable emergency source |
| Bathtub water bladder | Fills a tub cleanly before the water stops | Read the capacity on the package; only useful if filled *before* pressure is lost (→ 03-02) |
| Labels and a marker | Track what is left | Date each container; mark drums in gallons |
| A runway card | Know the number without doing maths under stress | Write "stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }}" on the container |

**If you don't have it, use what is in the house:**

{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}- **Your water heater** holds about {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gallons. It can be
  scalding hot, and gas heaters keep heating while gas flows. Never drain it from memory: use
  the step-by-step procedure on → 03-02.
{{else}}- **A tank water heater**, if you have one or find one, holds tens of gallons (the size
  is on its label). FEMA lists it as a safe water source in the home. It can be scalding hot;
  use the step-by-step procedure on → 03-02.
{{/if}}
- The water in your **pipes** and **ice** in the freezer, which FEMA lists as safe sources.
- Toilet **tanks** (the box behind the seat, never the bowl), only if no cleaning tablet or dye
  is in them. They are the last of the in-house reserves: FEMA's guide says not to drink tank
  water, so disinfect it before drinking (→ 03-04), or keep it for washing and flushing.
- Any clean food-grade container: soda bottles, juice jugs. **Not** milk jugs (milk protein
  is hard to clean out and the water spoils), and never containers that held chemicals.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} a day (÷ {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}
  only once you have already cut back to the floor). Recount weekly.
- **Ration:** cut washing and cooking water first, never drinking water. Move washing and
  flushing to untreated water at once; that alone can halve how fast stored water goes.
- **Resupply:** rain and snowmelt first, because they cost the least fuel to make safe
  (→ 03-05). In winter, snow is often the easiest large source (→ 03-06).{{#if has.pool}}
  Distilling pool water works but burns a lot of fuel (→ 03-03).{{/if}}{{#if has.well}} Your
  well can still give water without power (→ 03-10).{{/if}}

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** build the two-week store now, while it is a shopping trip.
- **B (moving):** water weighs 8.34 lb per gallon, so you can carry very little. Carry one
  to two days per person and a way to treat more (→ 03-04), and plan the route around water.
  For {{ household.size }} people that is roughly {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} to twice
  that in gallons. Load it low in the vehicle, over the rear axle, strapped down; never in a
  roof box and never loose in the passenger area (→ 22-05). Fill containers from the tap on
  the way out if there is time.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** find out before you go where the water comes from.
  On **town or district water**, pressure dies when the grid's pumps stop, so the first job
  on arrival is to **fill every container and tub at once**, then set up rain catchment
  (→ 03-05). On a **private well**, the pump needs power; → 03-10 explains how to get water out
  without it. Either way the daily maths becomes a hauling and treating problem, not a storage
  problem.
{{#if has.destinations}}
  Your destinations:
{{#each destinations as d}}  - **{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}). Water source: {{ d.water_source_text }}
{{/each}}
{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 03-02 storing water · → 03-03 pool water · → 03-04 purifying water · → 03-05 rain and snow ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 03-10 well water without power · → 23-02 consumables table ·
→ 22-05 vehicle loading

# Storing water safely

**What this page is for.** How to store drinking water so it is still safe when you need it:
which containers, how to clean them, where to keep them, and how to get the water already in
your house (including the water heater) out safely.

> **CAUTION.** Stored water goes bad because of **what you put it in** and **what you touch it
> with**, far more often than because of age. A contaminated 55-gallon drum is not a water
> supply; it is 55 gallons of disease. Follow the container and handling rules exactly.
>
> **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
> mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Fill everything when the forecast turns bad, not when the power fails.** Ice storm
   warning, blizzard warning, hurricane watch, severe thunderstorm watch: fill the bathtub
   bladder and every container then. City water pressure can hold for a while after a grid
   failure, depending on the utility's storage tanks and backup power, but it **fades before
   it stops**: weak flow upstairs first, then sputtering and air. **By the time you notice,
   you are at the end of the buffer, not the start.** A bathtub bladder fills slowly even at
   full pressure and far more slowly at low pressure; time yours once. This is the only water
   job with a hard deadline.
2. **When pressure comes back after an outage, assume the water is contaminated.** Empty
   pipes suck in dirty water at leaks and joints. Filter and chlorinate (→ 03-04) until the
   water utility says it is safe.
   {{#if has.municipal_water}}Your water utility: {{ contacts.utility.water.provider }},
   phone {{ contacts.utility.water.phone }} (check it against a current bill).{{/if}}
3. **Use food-grade containers** with tight lids: water jugs and drums made for drinking
   water, or clean 2-liter soda bottles. **Never** reuse containers that held chemicals, and
   do not use milk jugs.
4. **Sanitize before filling:** wash with soap, rinse, then mix **1 teaspoon of unscented
   5 to 9 percent household bleach in 1 quart of water**, cover the container and shake so the
   solution touches every inside surface. Wait **at least 30 seconds**, pour it out, let it air
   dry (CDC). Bleach basics: → 29-05.
5. **Label** every container **"DRINKING WATER"** with the **date filled**.
6. **Store at 50 to 70 °F, out of direct sunlight**, away from gasoline, pesticides and
   other toxic substances (CDC).
7. **Replace home-filled water every 6 months.** Store-bought sealed bottles: use the printed
   date.
8. **Never put hands or a dirty cup into stored water.** Pour it, or use a clean scoop kept
   only for that.

## Why it works this way

Tap water from a city system leaves the plant with a little chlorine in it. That chlorine
fades in storage. Once it is gone, whatever got in (from the container, the air or a hand)
can multiply. That is why the CDC's rules are mostly about **clean containers, sealed lids
and clean handling**, not about water "expiring" (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency
Water Supply).

{{#if has.well}}Well water usually has no chlorine in it to begin with, so clean handling
matters even more. Until your well has a clean test result (→ 03-07), treat well water with
the CDC bleach dose (→ 03-04) before you store it.{{/if}}

### Container choices

| Option | Gallons | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bottled water, sealed | varies | Safest, no preparation, portable | Costs most per gallon; bulky |
| 5 to 7 gal jugs | 5 to 7 | Can be moved when full, stack, good for leaving home | Modest volume; about 40 to 60 lb each full |
| 55-gal food-grade drum | 55 | Cheapest per gallon; two weeks in one container | About 460 lb full: it never moves again; needs a pump |
| Bathtub bladder | about 100 | Huge and cheap | Only works if filled **before** the water stops |
| Clean 2-liter soda bottles | 0.5 | Free, tough, good for freezing and for children to carry | Work to fill and rotate |

### Where to put it

A basement or an inside room is best: dark, cool, steady temperature. {{#if has.basement}}Your
basement is the right place.{{/if}} {{#if has.garage}}**An attached garage is the wrong place
for winter.** In a grid-down cold spell the garage drops below freezing and bottles split.
Move any water stored there inside before winter, or on the first day of an outage at the
latest (→ 03-06).{{/if}} Water expands when it freezes: leave a little air space at the top of
any container that might get cold, and never use glass for cold storage.

**Write down where your water is** so anyone in the house can find it (→ 22-04).

{{photo stored-water-location}}

### Handling

One person's dirty hands can spoil a whole drum. Use a spigot, pump or pour spout kept only
for water; keep it capped; never pour unused water back into the container.

**If stored water tastes flat,** pour it back and forth between two clean containers to put
air back in it, or add a pinch of salt per quart. The CDC suggests this for boiled water and it
works the same here.

## The water heater: the biggest store already in your house

{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}Your tank water heater holds about {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }}
gallons.{{else}}A tank water heater holds 30 to 80 gallons. If you have one, or reach a house
that does, this applies.{{/if}} It is also the most dangerous water in the house to get at
carelessly.

- **It is hot.** CPSC urges setting water heaters to 120 °F, and many are set hotter. CPSC
  says most adults suffer third-degree burns after six seconds in 140 °F water, and most
  scald injuries and deaths are to young children and elders (US Consumer Product Safety
  Commission, Tap Water Scalds).
- **A gas heater keeps heating** while gas flows, grid or no grid. An electric one stops when
  the power stops, but stays hot for many hours.
- **Until you drain it, it is your only safe hot washing water.** Use it for the first days'
  hand washing and dishes before you drain it for drinking (→ 13-02, → 13-10).

{{photo water-heater-drain-valve}}

**Draining the water heater: six steps, in this order** (FEMA, Food and Water in an Emergency,
gives the same order: power or gas off, cold inlet closed, a hot tap open, drain at the
bottom, refill before the heat goes back on).

1. **Turn the heat off.** On a gas heater, turn the gas control to **OFF** (not "pilot"). On an
   electric heater, switch its breaker off. Draining with the burner or elements live will
   fire them on an emptying tank and ruin it.
2. **Close the cold-water inlet valve** on the pipe at the top of the tank.
3. **Open a hot tap** somewhere higher in the house (a bathroom sink) and leave it open. This
   lets air in so the tank will drain.
4. **Put a hose or bucket on the drain valve at the base, then open it slowly. THE WATER CAN BE
   SCALDING.** Wear gloves and long sleeves and keep children out of the room. If you can, let
   the tank cool for hours first, or run the first water into a lidded bucket and walk away
   from it.
5. **The first water out carries sediment** (sand and scale from the bottom of the tank).
   Let it settle, pour off the clear water and throw away the sludge. If the tank has sat for
   weeks, treat the water before drinking (→ 03-04).
6. **Do not turn the heat back on until the tank is full again:** inlet valve open, hot tap
   running steadily with no air. A heater fired empty burns out. On a gas heater, turning it
   back on means relighting the pilot by the lighting label on the heater. If the gas to the
   house was also shut off, FEMA says a professional is needed to turn it back on. Whether you
   relight gas appliances yourself when nobody can come is a household decision:
   {{choice DC-28}} (→ 30-29).

Every other page that says "drain the water heater" means this procedure.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Food-grade water jugs, 5 to 7 gal | Water you can move; for leaving home | Rigid, with a spigot or cap you trust |
| 55-gal food-grade drum, bung wrench and pump | Bulk storage | Put it where it will live for ever before you fill it |
| Bottled water by the case | Safest, no preparation | Use by the printed date |
| Unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 percent | Cleaning containers **and** treating water | Buy fresh; use within a year (EPA) (→ 29-05) |
| A scoop, pour spout or pump kept only for water | Keeps hands out of the supply | Store it capped and clean |
| Waterproof labels and a marker | Date and name every container | "DRINKING" or "UTILITY" |
| Bathtub bladder | Large cheap volume at the warning stage | Practice putting it in the tub once |

**If you don't have it:**

- Clean 2-liter soda bottles are good containers: free and strong.
- Food-grade buckets from bakeries or restaurants. Ask what was in them; avoid anything oily.
- The water heater (above), the water in the pipes and ice in the freezer (FEMA). Toilet
  tanks (never bowls) with no cleaning tablet in them are the last reserve: FEMA says not to
  drink tank water, so disinfect it first (→ 03-04) or keep it for washing and flushing.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day, your plan rate
  from → 03-01. The floor rate ({{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}) is a crisis ration, not the
  number to divide by.
- **Ration:** the moment the tap is in doubt, stop using stored water for anything but
  drinking, cooking, infant feeding and medical needs. Everything else uses rain or untreated
  water.
- **Resupply:** refill containers with treated rain, snowmelt or other treated water
  (→ 03-04, → 03-05, → 03-06). **Clean the container again** before each refill.
- **Rotation is the quiet failure.** Water you stored and forgot is water you will not trust
  when it matters. Put the six-month swap on the calendar with the smoke-alarm batteries.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** fill the bladder and every container the moment a warning is
  issued, before pressure is lost.
- **B (moving):** only jugs and bottles travel. Water weighs about 8.34 lb a gallon; carry one to two
  days and a way to treat more, not a week.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** set up storage at once (a cistern, drums or barrels) so
  you are not hauling water every day. The same cleaning rules apply to anything you press
  into service.

## Cross-references

→ 03-01 daily water needs · → 03-04 purifying water · → 03-05 rain barrels ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 03-08 keeping water from going bad · → 22-04 where everything is ·
→ 29-05 chlorine products

pages.body:
# Pool and hot tub water: utility water, and distilling it to drink

**What this page is for.** A swimming pool or hot tub is a large store of water already at
your house. This page explains what that water is good for, why you cannot simply drink it,
and how to distil it (boil it and collect the steam) when you must.
{{#if has.pool}}Your pool holds about {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons.{{else}}{{#if has.hot_tub}}Your hot tub holds about {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons.{{/if}}{{/if}}

> **SAFETY.**
> - **A saltwater pool cannot be made drinkable by boiling, bleach or an ordinary filter.**
>   None of them removes salt, and drinking salt water makes dehydration worse. Only
>   **distillation** removes salt.
> - **Pool and hot tub water also holds chemicals:** chlorine or bromine, stabilizer
>   (cyanuric acid), and sometimes algaecide or metals. Distillation removes salts and most of
>   these.
> - **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.
>   Pool supplies include acids ("pH down", muriatic acid); keep them apart. The mix gives off
>   chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine
>   products. Pool chemicals count as chlorine products. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Use stored, tap or bottled water first.** Distilling is slow and burns a lot of fuel. It
   is the fallback, not the main supply.
2. **Use untreated pool water freely for everything except drinking and cooking:** flushing
   toilets, washing floors, cleaning, fighting fires. This is the pool's real value: once the
   pool covers flushing and washing, every gallon of stored water can go to drinking.
3. **Never drink saltwater pool water straight, boiled or bleached.** The salt stays in.
4. **Drinking fresh (chlorine) pool water without distilling it is a decision.** Your
   household's choice: {{choice DC-13}} (→ 30-14). Whatever you chose, follow it the same way
   every time. **Hot-tub water is distilled before drinking under every option on the card.**
5. **To distil:** boil the water and catch the **steam**, which turns back into clean water.
   The salt and most chemicals stay behind in the pot. Method below.
6. **Cover the pool** to cut evaporation and keep out leaves, animals and children.

## What kind of water is in it

| Water | What is in it | Without distilling it is | To drink |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Saltwater pool** (salt chlorinator) | Dissolved salt, chlorine made from the salt, stabilizer, maybe algaecide or metals | Utility water only | **Distil.** No other home method removes salt |
| **Chlorine pool** (fresh water) | Chlorine, stabilizer, maybe algaecide or metals; bacteria and algae once the pump stops | Utility water | Distil; or the household's choice on → 30-14 |
| **Hot tub or spa** | Bromine or chlorine, body oils and sweat from bathers, often a warm breeding ground for germs | Utility water | **Distil.** No option on → 30-14 drinks it undistilled |

A home saltwater pool is much less salty than the sea, but **far too salty to drink**. Your
salt chlorinator's manual gives the salt level it runs at; write it here: ______ ppm ("ppm"
means parts per million, → 29-05). Less salty does not mean safe to sip.

**The trade-off for fresh pools, in one sentence:** filtering and chlorinating a fresh pool
uses far less fuel than distilling it, but leaves in the stabilizer, algaecide and any metals
that distilling would remove. The card lays out the risks and options (→ 30-14). FEMA's
own list of household water sources says not to drink from swimming pools or spas (FEMA,
Food and Water in an Emergency).

## Why distillation works

Distillation boils water into steam and turns only the steam back into liquid. Salt, metals
and most chemicals do not boil off with the water, so they are **left behind** in the pot.
FEMA and the Red Cross say distillation removes germs that resist boiling and chlorine, **as
well as heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals**, and that salt water is used only if it
is distilled first (FEMA, Food and Water in an Emergency; AWWA, distillation in an emergency).
Boiling and bleach kill germs but leave salt and chemicals in place (EPA).

### The cup-on-lid still (FEMA and Red Cross method)

{{figure fig-cup-on-lid-still}}

1. **Pre-filter:** pour the water through a cloth or coffee filter to remove leaves, insects
   and grit. This keeps the pot cleaner and the still faster.
2. Fill a pot **halfway** with the filtered water.
3. Tie a cup to the handle of the pot lid so that, when the lid is put on **upside down**, the
   cup hangs **right side up** inside the pot. The cup must **not** touch the water.
4. Put the lid on upside down. Steam hits the lid, runs to the low middle point and drips into
   the cup.
5. **Boil for 20 minutes.** The water that drips from the lid into the cup is distilled
   (FEMA). Let it cool before drinking.

**Yield:** measure it. Pour the cup into a measuring cup after a timed run and write the
result here: ______ cups an hour. FEMA says a normally active person needs about three quarters of
a gallon of fluid a day (FEMA, Ready.gov Water; → 03-01): about 12 cups each, for each of your
{{ household.size }} people, before cooking. Divide by your measured rate to see how many
hours of boiling that takes. For most households the cup-on-lid still is a
demonstration and a stopgap, not a supply. That is why the tube still below, fuel, and rain
and snow (→ 03-05) matter.

### The larger still: pot, lid and tube condenser

The cup-on-lid wastes most of the steam. Piping the steam out through a tube and cooling it
outside the pot captures nearly all of it: same fire, several times the water.

{{figure fig-tube-condenser-still}}

**Materials (stores in a shoebox):**

- **10 to 20 ft of soft copper tubing, 3/8 or 1/2 inch.** Copper carries heat away fast and
  handles steam. Food-grade silicone tubing is fine for a short flexible joint. **Never use
  vinyl or PVC tubing**: it releases chemicals at steam temperature.
- **A lid you can seal the tube into:** drill a spare pot lid and fit a compression or barbed
  fitting, or, with no tools, seal heavy aluminum foil over the pot with the tube pushed
  through and crimped tight.
- **A cooling bath:** a bucket or basin of cold water (snow in winter works well) that the
  copper coil runs through, sloping **downhill** the whole way to the collection jar.
- A collection jar, and cloth or coffee filters.

**Running it:** pot half full of pre-filtered water at a low rolling boil. Steam leaves
through the tube, turns to water in the cold coil and drips into the jar. Keep the bath cold
(change the water or add snow). Keep the tube sloping so water cannot pool in it. **Never let
the pot boil dry**: the salts scorch and the pot warps. Throw away the salty liquid left in
the pot.

{{photo pool-still-setup}}

**Rules that keep the water clean:**

- Before the first drinking batch, run a new copper coil once with vinegar and water, then
  once with plain water. New copper carries oil from manufacturing.
- **Lead-free fittings only.** No lead solder, no brass of unknown origin.
- Pour the leftover brine far from gardens and rain barrels. Salt kills soil.
- **Do not look for a reverse-osmosis unit** to use on pool water. Home units need water
  pressure, power and replacement membranes. A still is the practical route.

**Planning numbers: measure your own still once.** No published table gives the output of a
home-built still; it depends on the seal, the fire and how cold the coil is.

- **Yield:** time a run with a watch and measure the water in the jar. Write it here:
  ______ quarts an hour.
- **Fire time:** 4 quarts make a gallon, so hours of fire per gallon = 4 ÷ your quarts an
  hour = ______. Your household's drinking share alone is several gallons a day, so
  **distilling cannot carry a household by itself.** Run the still on fires already burning
  for heat and cooking (→ 06-04), and use it to cover dry spells. Rain and snow must be the
  main supply.
- **Wood:** weigh the wood you burn during that timed run, and divide by the gallons you
  made: ______ lb of wood per gallon. Turning water into steam takes several times the heat of
  bringing it to a boil, and an open fire wastes most of its heat, so expect it to be a large
  number. Put it on the consumables table (→ 23-02).
- **Check the output:** a cheap TDS meter ("total dissolved solids", a pen that reads how much
  is dissolved in water) should read near zero on distilled water. If it reads salty, the
  seal is leaking boiling splash into the tube. Reseat the seal and fix the slope.

**Do not distil on battery power.** Turning water to steam takes several times the energy of
bringing the same water to a boil, and a battery holds very little heat energy by that
standard. {{#if has.power_station}}Your power stations hold about
{{ gear.station_wh_total }} watt-hours in total.{{else}}A power station's label gives its
watt-hours.{{/if}} An electric distiller's label gives its watts and the liters it makes per
hour. Watts ÷ liters per hour = watt-hours per liter; divide the station's watt-hours by that
to see how few liters a full charge would make.
Distillation is a wood-fire job. An electric countertop distiller running on a strong solar
day nets only a few liters: useful for drinking water, never the household's supply
(→ 09-02).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Large stockpot with a domed lid that can sit upside down | The still | Stainless steel; a rounded lid sends drips to the center |
| Heat-safe cup and wire or cord | Catches the distilled water | A metal cup will not melt |
| 10 to 20 ft soft copper tubing, 3/8 to 1/2 inch, and a fitting | The tube still | Never vinyl tubing |
| A drilled spare lid, or heavy aluminum foil | Seals the tube into the pot | Foil needs no tools |
| Cloth or coffee filters | Pre-filter | Cheap; stock many |
| Unscented bleach or pool shock | Disinfecting distilled water before storage | **Dose only from → 03-04.** Pool shock only by the two-step method there, never as dry granules |
| TDS meter | Confirms the still is working | Reads near zero on good distillate |
| Food-safe storage containers | Finished water | Label "DRINKING" and "POOL / UTILITY" |
| Electric countertop distiller | Much faster if you have power | Power hungry; a supplement only |

**If you don't have it:**

- Any pot with a bowl set inside and an upside-down domed lid is a still. Weight the center of
  the lid so drips fall into the bowl.
- Clear tubing and two sealed containers over heat make a rough condenser.
- Plastic sheeting over a frame floating on the pool surface makes a solar still: slow, but it
  needs no fuel. Measure its daily output before you count on it.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** a pool is a lot of *volume*. Your real limits are **fuel to boil it** and
  **time**. Wood or propane (→ 06-04) is the binding constraint, not water.
- **Ration:** distil only what you need to drink and cook with. Use untreated pool water for
  all washing, flushing and cleaning.
- **Resupply:** rain and snowmelt need only disinfecting, **not** distilling, which takes far
  less fuel (→ 03-05). In wet or snowy months, use those first and save the pool for dry
  spells.
- **Gardens:** do not water a garden with saltwater-pool water. Salt harms soil and plants.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** the pool is a large reserve already in place. Once the grid is
  down, **stop adding chemicals by default**, cover the pool, and treat it as your utility
  tank. Keeping a measured chlorine level to slow algae is an option with its own rules
  (→ 03-08).
- **B (moving):** you cannot take the pool. Carry stored or distilled water, and know the
  water sources on the route.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** a still kit is light. Bring it for brackish or doubtful
  sources even if you do not expect to need it. Fresh well water is disinfected, not
  distilled (→ 03-10).

## Cross-references

→ 03-01 how much you need · → 03-04 purifying fresh water · → 03-05 rain and snow ·
→ 03-08 keeping pool water from going bad · → 06-04 wood supply · → 30-14 the pool-water card ·
→ 29-05 chlorine products
