pages.body:
# Purifying water: boil, chemical, filter

**What this page is for.** How to make fresh water (rain, snow, rivers, ponds, wells, doubtful
tap water) safe to drink, with or without fuel. Salt water is different: it needs → 03-03.
New to the words? "Disinfect", "micron", "virus" and "turbidity" are explained in → 29-06;
bleach and pool shock in → 29-05.

> **SAFETY.**
> - Bad water causes diarrhea. In an infant, a young child, an elder or a person with
>   diabetes that is not an inconvenience: it is dehydration and a medical emergency with no
>   clinic to go to (→ 12-05).
> - **You cannot boil or disinfect away fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material**
>   (CDC). If water may hold those, do not use it; distil it (→ 03-03) or find another source.
> - **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.
>   The mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine
>   products. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Cloudy water: clear it first.** Pour it through clean cloth, paper towel or a coffee
   filter, or let it settle and pour off the clear water. Then disinfect.
2. **Boiling is best.** Bring the water to a **rolling boil for 1 minute**. Above about 5,000
   feet, boil for **3 minutes** (EPA says above 5,000 ft; CDC says above 6,500 ft; use the
   lower, safer figure). {{#if is.high_altitude}}**Your home is at about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft: boil for 3 minutes.**{{else}}Your home is at about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft.{{/if}}
   Let it cool, then store it covered.
3. **No fuel? Use plain unscented household bleach (5 to 9 percent): 8 drops per gallon.**
   Stir, wait **30 minutes**, then drink. **Double the bleach** if the water is cloudy,
   colored or very cold.
4. **Filters do not remove viruses.** After filtering, still disinfect with chemicals or
   boiling.
5. **Salt water needs distilling, not this page** (→ 03-03).

## Three different jobs

People mix these up all the time.

- **Clarifying** removes dirt and particles (settling, cloth, filters).
- **Disinfecting** kills germs (boiling, chlorine, UV, sunlight).
- **Distilling** removes salts and chemicals (→ 03-03).

Boiling and bleach disinfect. They do **not** remove salt or chemicals.

## 1. Boiling: the most reliable

The CDC says boiling is the best way to kill germs. **One minute at a rolling boil**: a true
tumbling boil, not the first small bubbles. Let it cool on its own; do not add cold untreated
water to speed it up. A flat taste is normal: pour it between two clean containers to put air
back in, or add a pinch of salt per quart.

The catch is **fuel**. Boiling a household's water every day burns a lot of wood or gas
(→ 06-04). That is why chemical treatment is the everyday method when the water is already
clear.

## 2. Chlorine bleach: cheap, small, no fuel

Use **unscented liquid household bleach**. Check the label for "sodium hypochlorite" and its
percentage. Do not use scented, color-safe, splash-less or "with cleaners" bleach. **If the
label gives directions for disinfecting drinking water, follow the label.**

**CDC table** (CDC, How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency), printed as published:

**Bleach dosing: 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite concentration**

| Water | Drops | Milliliters | Measuring spoon |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 quart or liter | 2 drops | 0.1 mL | too small to measure |
| 1 gallon | 8 drops | ½ mL | a little less than ⅛ teaspoon |
| 5 gallons | 40 drops | 2½ mL | ½ teaspoon |

**Bleach dosing: 1% sodium hypochlorite concentration**

| Water | Drops | Milliliters | Measuring spoon |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 quart or liter | 10 drops | ½ mL | ⅛ teaspoon |
| 1 gallon | 40 drops | 2½ mL | ½ teaspoon |
| 5 gallons | 200 drops | 12½ mL | 2½ teaspoons |

*If water is cloudy, murky, colored, or very cold, double the bleach amount.* (CDC)

**EPA table** (US EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water), printed as published, for
bleach labelled 6 or 8.25 percent:

| Volume of water | Amount of 6% bleach to add | Amount of 8.25% bleach to add |
|---|---|---|
| 1 quart/liter | 2 drops | 2 drops |
| 1 gallon | 8 drops | 6 drops |
| 2 gallons | 16 drops (1/4 tsp) | 12 drops (1/8 teaspoon) |
| 4 gallons | 1/3 teaspoon | 1/4 teaspoon |
| 8 gallons | 2/3 teaspoon | 1/2 teaspoon |

The two tables agree on the common case (8 drops a gallon for ordinary 6 percent bleach). Use
whichever matches the percentage on your label; for 1 percent bleach only the CDC table
applies.

Stir well and let stand **at least 30 minutes**. **Double the dose** for water that is
cloudy, murky, colored or very cold. The water should then have a slight chlorine smell. **If
it does not, repeat the dose and let it stand another 15 minutes** (EPA).

**Very dirty water that will not clear** after settling and filtering is a decision. The
published method is to clear the water first and then use the label or table dose (doubled for
cloudy water). Some households go further, adding more chlorine and waiting longer, which
raises the chlorine they drink and still may not reach germs hidden in dirt. Your household's
choice: {{choice DC-23}} (→ 30-24).

**Limits that matter:**

- Chemicals **do not work as well as boiling against parasites** (tiny organisms with tough
  shells).
- Iodine will **not** kill *Cryptosporidium*, a common parasite. **Chlorine dioxide tablets
  will**, if you follow the label exactly.
- **Do not drink iodine-treated water** if pregnant, with thyroid problems, or with iodine
  sensitivity, and nobody should drink it for more than a few weeks.

## 2b. Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite): the long-storage chemical

Liquid bleach loses strength in storage: EPA says to use bleach stored at room temperature for
less than a year. Dry, sealed **granular calcium hypochlorite** ("pool shock") keeps far
better as long as it stays dry and cool, and a small amount treats a very large volume of
water. It is used
in **two steps**. This is the US EPA's published emergency method:

**Step 1. Make a stock solution** (somewhere with fresh air; wear eye protection):
**One heaping teaspoon (about 1/4 ounce) of high-test granular calcium hypochlorite into 2
gallons of water.** Stir until the particles have dissolved. EPA says this makes a chlorine
solution of about 500 milligrams per liter.

**The stock is itself a poison**, far stronger than drinking water. Keep it in a container
nobody could mistake for drinking water, **labeled "CHLORINE STOCK: DO NOT DRINK"** in
marker, lid on, up high and out of children's reach (→ 20-02). If anyone swallows it, call
Poison Control and see → 12-17.

**Step 2. Treat the water:** add **1 part stock solution to each 100 parts of water**: EPA
says this is about **1 pint (16 ounces) of stock per 12.5 gallons** of water. Worked out from
the same 1-in-100 ratio, that is about 1.3 fl oz (about 2½ tablespoons) of stock per gallon,
or about 6.4 fl oz per 5 gallons. Stir and wait **30 minutes** before drinking (the same wait
as bleach), and expect a slight chlorine smell. If the taste is strong, pour it between clean
containers and let it stand a few hours (EPA).

**Rules that keep this safe:**

- **Read the label:** calcium hypochlorite must be the only active ingredient, with **no
  algaecides, clarifiers or stabilizers**. "Multi-action" shock products cannot be made
  drinkable. Write the percentage from the label here: ______ percent.
- Add granules **to water**, never water to granules. Use plastic or glass, never metal.
- **Do not keep mixed stock solution**: diluted chlorine loses strength (CDC says diluted
  bleach solutions work less well after 24 hours). Mix it fresh each time.
- Never use pool shock as dry granules in drinking water, and never dose it like bleach
  drops.

**Storing pool shock.** Calcium hypochlorite is a strong oxidizer: it **feeds a fire**,
**gives off chlorine when it gets wet or hot**, and its dust burns skin, eyes and lungs. ATSDR says to store it dry, in a well-ventilated
place **below 120 °F**, separated from acids, ammonia and other chlorinating or oxidizing
chemicals (CDC and ATSDR, Medical Management Guidelines for Calcium Hypochlorite). Store it:

- in its sealed bag inside a lidded plastic bucket, labeled "POOL SHOCK: OXIDIZER";
- **off the floor** (a flood or wet floor reaching it releases chlorine), dry, away from
  furnaces, water heaters and other heat;
- **never near fuel, acids, ammonia or ammunition** (→ 06-06), and **never on the same shelf
  or in the same bucket as trichlor or dichlor pool tablets** (they are other chlorinating
  chemicals, which ATSDR says to keep separate): calcium hypochlorite and trichlor can make
  chlorine gas or fire on contact;
- away from electronics and power stations (the fumes corrode them);
- where children cannot reach it.

If your only good dry spot is also your shelter room, a sealed, lidded bucket on a shelf
removes the two triggers that matter most: water and heat.

{{photo water-treatment-kit}}

## 3. Filters: clear water and remove parasites, not viruses

Portable filters do **not** remove all germs. The CDC says a filter needs an **absolute pore
size of 0.3 micron or smaller** to remove bacteria, and **1 micron or smaller** for parasites
such as *Giardia* and *Cryptosporidium* (a micron is a thousandth of a millimeter, → 29-06).
**No common portable filter removes viruses.** So filter first, then disinfect. Filter care:
→ 03-09; filter specifications: → 28-06.

## 4. UV and sunlight: the backups

- A portable **UV pen or bottle** works on small amounts of **clear** water.
- **Solar disinfection (SODIS):** fill **clean, clear plastic bottles** with clear water (not
  colored or scratched plastic: the sunlight has to get through). Lay them on their side in
  the sun for **6 hours** if sunny or **2 days** if cloudy. A dark surface underneath helps
  (CDC).
- Neither works on cloudy water.

**Never** drink water from car radiators or home heating boilers.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 percent, fresh | Main fuel-free treatment | Use within a year (EPA); write the purchase date and the percentage on it |
| Calcium hypochlorite (pool shock), additive-free | Keeps far better than liquid bleach if dry and cool | Strong oxidizer; store as above |
| Chlorine dioxide tablets | The chemical that handles *Cryptosporidium* | Follow the label timing exactly |
| Gravity or pump filter, absolute pore size 0.3 micron or smaller | Clears water and removes parasites and bacteria with no fuel (CDC) | Still disinfect afterwards for viruses |
| Coffee filters, clean cloth | Pre-filter, always step one | Cheap; stock many |
| Large stockpot with lid | Boiling in volume | Also the still (→ 03-03) |
| Medicine dropper and measuring spoons | Measure bleach accurately | Guessing a dose is how people get sick |
| Clean lidded containers | Hold treated water | Label "TREATED" with the time |

Write where your treatment kit is kept: __________ (→ 22-04).

**If you don't have it:**

- **Pool shock** is concentrated chlorine; additive-free pool shock is usable for drinking
  water by the two-step method above.
- Any tightly woven cloth (a T-shirt, a bandana) pre-filters; fold it in layers.
- Clear PET bottles of 2 liters or less plus sunshine is disinfection with no equipment.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** count bottles of bleach and strips of tablets. Bleach older than a year is
  weaker than the tables assume (EPA). Pool shock kept dry and cool lasts much longer.
- **Ration:** use chemicals for clear water and save fuel. Boil when the water is doubtful,
  someone is sick, or you cannot measure a dose with confidence.
- **Resupply:** boiling always works if you have fuel. Sunlight works with nothing but
  bottles. A good filter reduces how much chemical you need.
- **The real failure:** running out of *clean container space*, not treatment. Keep clean,
  labeled containers ready so treated water does not get dirty again.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** clear tap or stored water usually needs nothing. Treat rain and
  snow (→ 03-05){{#if has.pool}}, and distil pool water (→ 03-03){{/if}}. Keep both bleach and
  tablets.
- **B (moving):** tablets and a small filter: light, no fuel, fast. Treat everything you pick
  up on the way, no exceptions.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** a well or spring is usually fresh and needs only
  disinfecting. Test it when you can (→ 03-07); until then, treat it as unsafe.

## Cross-references

→ 03-03 pool water · → 03-05 rain and snow · → 03-06 winter water · → 03-07 testing ·
→ 03-08 keeping water from going bad · → 03-09 filter care · → 06-04 fuel ·
→ 12-05 dehydration · → 29-05 chlorine products · → 30-24 extra-strength chlorination card

pages.body:
# Rain catchment and melting snow and ice

**What this page is for.** Rain and snow are the cheapest water you can get in fuel terms:
they need disinfecting, not distilling. This page covers catching rain, melting snow and
ice, and keeping both safe.

> **CAUTION.** Rain is clean when it leaves the sky and dirty by the time it leaves your roof:
> bird droppings, grit, roofing residue and whatever blew onto it. **Treat harvested rain
> before drinking it** (CDC, Collecting Rainwater and Your Health). Snow is the same, plus
> whatever it landed on.

## Do this now

1. **Put barrels or any clean containers under downspouts.** A modest rain fills them.
2. **Always treat before drinking:** filter out the grit, then boil or disinfect (→ 03-04).
   Rain needs **disinfecting only**, not distilling.
3. **Skip the first flush.** The first rain off the roof in a storm carries the most dirt,
   germs and chemicals (CDC). Send it away from the barrel and collect what comes after.
4. **Melt snow with a little water already in the pot.** Never eat snow to stay hydrated: it
   costs body heat you cannot spare (→ 03-06).
5. **Screen where the water comes into every barrel, or empty the barrel at least every 10
   days.** That is the CDC's rule for stopping mosquitoes breeding in it (CDC, Collecting
   Rainwater and Your Health; → 03-08).

## Setting up a barrel

- **Stand it on level, solid ground or a sturdy platform.** A full 55-gallon barrel holds
  about **460 lb of water** (55 gal x 8.34 lb). On a slope or soft ground it can tip over or
  split; a falling barrel can crush a child.
- **Lid and screen on**, against mosquitoes and debris (→ 03-08).
- **Draw from a spigot or a pump**, never by dipping.
- **A pump or hose used for drinking water is "WATER ONLY" for ever.** Anything that has
  touched fuel, diesel exhaust fluid or chemicals never touches drinking water again. Mark the
  pump "WATER ONLY" in marker and keep it in a separate bag from any fuel pump. Before first
  use, rinse barrel and pump with the container-cleaning solution on → 03-02 (1 teaspoon
  bleach per quart of water, 30 seconds), then with clean water.
- **No roof? Make a funnel.** A tarp strung as a funnel, or an upside-down ceiling-leak
  diverter hung from posts or a line with a hose to the barrel, collects rain without the
  roof's grit. (If your roof is leaking, that job comes first: → 16-12.)
- **Freeze rule: drain the barrel and bring it in before a hard freeze.** Water expands as it
  freezes and splits barrels and pumps. In winter, snowmelt replaces it.

Write where your barrel, pump and treatment supplies are kept: __________ (→ 22-04).

{{photo rain-barrel-setup}}

## How much water a roof gives

**One inch of rain on 1,000 square feet of roof is about 623 gallons** (arithmetic: one inch
of water over one square foot is 144 cubic inches, which is 0.623 gallon). Some of it is lost
to the first flush, splash and overflow; measure what your barrels actually catch in one
storm and compare.

The roof footprint (length x width of the house from outside, not the sloped surface):
{{ dwelling.roof_area_sqft }} sq ft. Then:

- **Gallons per inch of rain, before losses** = roof square feet x 0.623 =
  {{ derived.rain_gal_per_inch }}
- Your area gets about **{{ region.home.precip_in }} inches of rain a year** and
  **{{ region.home.snow_in }} inches of snow**.

Even one downspout on a modest roof section fills a 55-gallon barrel in an ordinary rain. For
most houses, **storage barrels and treatment are the limit, not the rain.**

> **Before the collapse:** a few states limit how much rainwater a household may collect or
> how it may be used. Your state's water-rights agency can tell you. This never decides
> whether you collect water to survive.

## What is actually in it

The CDC says rain picks up germs and chemicals from the air, the roof, gutters, pipes and
storage: bird droppings, dust, smoke, and metals such as lead or copper from roofing
materials. Dirt and germs wash off the roof most after several dry days. The CDC prefers tap or
bottled water to rainwater for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth. When rain is what you
have, treat everything anyone drinks.

**Never mix rainwater into treated water.** The CDC warns that adding rain to treated water
(bottled or tap) can contaminate it. Keep "TREATED" and "RAW" containers strictly apart, and
never connect a catchment line to house plumbing.

**Roofing matters.** Asphalt shingles shed grit and some chemicals; metal roofs are the
cleanest common surface. Do not collect from anything with lead flashing, treated wood or moss
killer. If the roof is doubtful, use the water for flushing, washing and the garden, and drink
from a cleaner source.

**Treatment chain:** screen out leaves at the gutter → let it settle in the barrel → draw from
a spigot above the sediment → **filter** → **boil or disinfect** (→ 03-04) → store clean
(→ 03-02).

{{figure fig-first-flush-diverter}}

## Snow and ice

- **Melt, don't eat.** Eating snow lowers your core temperature and costs more energy than it
  gives back. Melt it and drink it warm.
- **Prime the pot.** Put an inch of water in the pot first, then add snow a little at a time.
  Snow packed into a dry hot pot scorches and can ruin the pot.
- **Volume is disappointing.** Fresh fluffy snow is mostly air: a full pot melts down to a
  small puddle. Wet, dense snow and ice give far more.
- **Ice beats snow** for yield and fuel. Take icicles or hard-packed snow over powder.
- **Take clean snow.** Not near roads (salt, exhaust), not near the driveway, not discolored,
  not where pets or wildlife have been. The middle of an untouched yard, or a clean tarp, is
  best.
- **Still treat it.** Snow is not sterile. Clean fresh snowmelt is usually low-risk and has
  little sediment, but it gets the same treatment as rain.

{{#if is.snow_region}}**Where you live, snow is a real reserve.** A snowbank is a large store
of water sitting in the yard for months. In deep winter, snowmelt often beats every other
source on effort, but it costs **fuel**, so it competes with cooking and heat (→ 06-04).{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rain barrels, food-grade, with spigot (two or more) | The catchment | Link in a row; raise them for gravity flow |
| Drum pump or siphon, marked WATER ONLY | Empties the barrel into jugs without dipping | Never used for fuel |
| Downspout diverter and first-flush device | Skips the dirtiest runoff | Can be built from pipe |
| Fine screen, gutter guards, barrel screens | Blocks leaves and mosquitoes | Mosquito control is not optional (→ 03-08) |
| Clean tarp and cord | Catch rain or clean snow away from the roof | The cleanest catchment surface you can own |
| Large melting pot | Snow to water in volume | A dark pot melts faster in sun |
| Filter and treatment supplies | Rain and snow both need them | → 03-04 |
| Food-grade containers | Move it to storage | → 03-02 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Any clean container under a downspout:** trash cans, storage totes, buckets. Volume beats
  neatness.
- A **tarp strung as a funnel** into a barrel.
- Kiddie pools, coolers and totes all hold water; cover them against mosquitoes and debris.
- A **sled** is the best tool for hauling snow to the pot.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** rain and snow are seasonal and you cannot schedule them. Collect hard whenever
  they come, not when you need them.
- **Ration:** use rain and snowmelt for drinking and cooking *first*, because they are cheap
  in fuel.{{#if has.pool}} Save the pool for washing and flushing.{{/if}}
- **Resupply:**{{#if has.pool}} the pool (→ 03-03) is the constant backstop: huge volume,
  high fuel cost. Rain is the opposite: free but irregular. Run both.{{else}} keep stored water
  (→ 03-02) for dry spells and look for other sources (→ 17-07).{{/if}}
- **The fuel trade:** melting snow and boiling rain both burn fuel. In a hard winter, water and
  heat compete for the same woodpile. Put both in the consumables table (→ 23-02).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** barrels on downspouts and snow from the yard are quiet water
  sources that nobody sees you collect, unlike hauling from a public source.
- **B (moving):** a tarp and a pot make rain and snow your water anywhere. This is the most
  portable water skill in the binder.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** scale it up: a cistern, more roof, more barrels. Clean
  and disinfect a new or unused cistern before trusting it (CDC, Cistern Safety and
  Disasters). Where a destination is on town or district water with no well, pressure dies
  with the grid, and **roof catchment becomes the water plan**, not a supplement: fill every
  container on arrival (→ 03-01), then live on the roof. Do the roof sum for each place you
  might go, and send barrels ahead if you can.
{{#if has.destinations}}
{{#each destinations as d}}  - **{{ d.name }}** gets about {{ d.region.precip_in }} inches of rain a year. Roof size: ______ sq ft; gallons per inch: ______; barrels there: ______
{{/each}}
{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 03-02 storing water · → 03-04 purifying water · → 03-06 winter water ·
→ 03-08 mosquitoes in barrels · → 06-04 fuel for melting · → 17-07 drought ·
→ 03-10 well water · → 01-05 destination water

pages.body:
# Water when everything is frozen

**What this page is for.** Winter brings two separate water problems: **your plumbing freezing
and bursting** (which can flood the house and destroy the water you have), and **every
outdoor source turning solid**. This page covers both.
{{#if is.cold_winters}}Your January nights average about {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F, so
this page applies to you every winter.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.** Never thaw a pipe with an open flame: that is how houses burn down. Never eat
> snow to stay hydrated: that is how people become hypothermic (dangerously cold inside).

## Do this now

1. **Before the cold:** drain and store garden hoses. Close the inside valve to each outdoor
   tap and leave the outdoor tap **open** so trapped water can expand without bursting the
   pipe.
2. **During deep cold:** let taps on outside walls **drip**, and **open the cabinet doors**
   under sinks so house heat reaches the pipes.
3. **If the power fails in winter:** fill every container with water **at once**, before pipes
   freeze or pressure is lost: tub, pots, jugs, bottles.
4. **If a pipe freezes** (a tap gives only a trickle):
   - **keep the tap on the frozen line open**: as the ice melts, running water helps melt the
     rest (American Red Cross);
   - **warm the pipe starting from the tap end** and working back toward the frozen part, with
     a hair dryer, an electric heating pad or towels soaked in hot water. **Never a blowtorch,
     a kerosene or propane heater, a charcoal stove or any open flame** (American Red Cross);
   - **if the pipe has split or starts leaking, close the main water valve at once.** A frozen
     pipe often cracks and only leaks once it thaws, so check the whole run before you trust
     it, and check the other taps: if one pipe froze, others may have too.
5. **Melt snow; never eat it.** Put a little water in the pot first (→ 03-05).

{{photo water-main-shutoff}}

Your main water shutoff is at: __________ (→ 22-04). Practice finding it in the dark now.

## Why pipes burst

Water expands as it freezes, with enough force to split metal or plastic pipe. The break is
often not found until the ice thaws and the pipe floods. The pipes at risk are in unheated
space: along outside walls, in crawlspaces, in the garage, in any unheated corner of a
basement.

**In a grid-down winter this gets worse.** With no furnace, the house cools toward the outside
temperature, and pipes *inside* start to freeze too. If you are heating only one room
(→ 08-01), the rest of the plumbing is exposed. Often the right move is to **drain the system
on purpose** rather than fight it:

1. **Fill every container first.** Draining means no running water at all. Fill first, drain
   second.
2. Shut off the main water valve.
3. Open the lowest tap and any drain valves; open the taps upstairs to let air in.
4. Flush the toilets to empty the tanks.
5. **Drain the water heater** using the six-step procedure on → 03-02. Do not do it from
   memory: the heat must go off first and the water can be scalding. Until you drain it, that
   tank is your safe **hot washing water** (a gas heater keeps it hot while gas flows), so use
   it for the first days' washing before you empty it.
6. Pour plumbing (RV) antifreeze, the non-toxic kind, into sink and tub drain traps and toilet
   bowls if you have it.

A drained system cannot burst. Toilets without water: → 13-05.

## Where winter water comes from

| Source | Effort | Fuel cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stored water indoors | None | None | Keep it where it cannot freeze |
| Snow | Low (shovel) | **High** (melting) | Fluffy snow melts to a small fraction of its volume |
| Ice (icicles, hard-packed snow) | Low | Medium | More water per pot than powder |
| Pool or hot tub under its cover and ice | Medium (procedure below) | High if distilled | Still there; saltwater still needs distilling (→ 03-03) |
| Rain barrels | none | none | Usually frozen solid; drain them before the hard freeze |
| A well | Depends | Depends | → 03-10 |

### Drawing from a pool in winter: the cover comes first

{{#if has.pool}}This applies to your pool.{{else}}This applies if you have, or reach, a pool
with a safety cover.{{/if}} **A safety cover is a drowning barrier for small children, and it
matters as much in January as in July.** Never cut the cover, never fold it back in a way that
defeats it, never leave it open or half open. Cold adds another reason: a cover peeled back
in freezing weather can stiffen and ice into its tracks, and then it cannot be closed again.

1. **First choice: draw without touching the cover.** Use a skimmer opening at deck level, if
   it sits outside the cover and is open to the pool, or the cover's own pump or drain
   access. A bottle on a pole through the skimmer fills buckets slowly but touches nothing.
   **Check this before the first freeze:** many skimmers sit under the cover's lid box, are
   plugged for winter, or sit above a lowered water level. Skimmer reachable with the cover
   closed: ☐ yes ☐ no. Checked on: ________. If no, step 2 is your first choice and snow is the
   better answer.
2. **If you must open the cover: the smallest corner only, an adult there the whole time.**
   Open only enough at the shallow end for a bucket, draw fast, and **close and secure it at once**,
   before anything else. In freezing weather, check that ropes and tracks are free of ice and
   that you *can* close it **before** you open it. If you cannot be sure of closing it, do not
   open it: melt the snow lying on top of it instead.
3. **If there is ice under the cover:** break through **at the access point only**: one hole
   the size of the bucket, chipped with a bar (never an axe swung over water). Draw, then
   cover the hole again and **mark the spot** with a flag or stake at the edge so the next
   person knows where the ice is thin. Never walk on the cover or the ice.
4. **Watch the water level.** Read your cover's manual now for the water level it needs:
   some covers are designed to sit on, or be supported by, the normal water level (→ 03-08). Winter draws count. Draw sparingly; snow and ice around the yard are the bulk
   source.

### Protect what you have

{{#if has.garage}}Water stored in an unheated garage will freeze and can split its containers.{{else}}Water stored in any unheated space will freeze and can split its containers.{{/if}}
Keep the working supply inside the heated part of the house. Leave air space at the top of
any container that might freeze. Do not store water in glass where it can freeze.

**Winter is also a refrigerator.** The cold that threatens your pipes also keeps food
(→ 04-09). But some medicines must never freeze.

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}> **Floor:** A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded. It loses strength with no
> way to tell. Keep insulin and other refrigerated medicines in the heated room, never on a
> windowsill or in an unheated space (→ 29-07).
{{else}}> **Floor:** A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded. It loses strength with no
> way to tell. If anyone in your group uses refrigerated medicine, keep it from freezing
> (→ 29-07).
{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pipe insulation sleeves, heat tape | Prevention beats repair | UL-listed heat tape only (American Red Cross) |
| Hair dryer, heating pads, towels | Thawing pipes safely | Never an open flame |
| The main shutoff, its tool, and knowing where the drain valves are | Draining before a burst | Practice in the dark now |
| Plumbing or RV antifreeze (non-toxic) | Protects drain traps and toilets once drained | |
| Snow shovel, sled, large pot | Collecting and hauling snow | The sled saves the most work |
| Insulated containers or a cooler | Keeps stored water from freezing | Also keeps it cool in summer |
| Headlamps | All of this happens in the dark at 5 p.m. | → 10-01 |

**If you don't have it:**

- Towels soaked in hot water thaw a pipe with no equipment.
- Foam pool noodles, rags or blankets make rough pipe insulation.
- Any tarp collects clean snow; any dark container melts it faster in the sun.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** in winter the limit is **fuel to melt**, not water. Track wood or propane
  against the melting load (→ 23-02).
- **Ration:** melt in big batches while a fire is already going for cooking or heat. Never
  light a fire just to melt snow (→ 06-04).
- **Resupply:** ice before snow; on bright days, set dark containers of snow in the sun for
  free melting.
- **The real winter failure** is a burst pipe flooding the house while everyone keeps warm in
  one room. Drain the system early rather than gambling.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** fill everything, then drain the plumbing if the house is going
  cold. Snow from a fenced yard is clean and private.
- **B (moving):** winter travel with young children is among the riskiest moves in this
  binder. Carry water inside your coat against your body or it freezes; melt snow at stops
  (→ 11-02).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** protect barrels, cisterns and tanks against freezing.
  A well pump needs power; hand pumps, bailers, generators and keeping the wellhead from
  freezing are on → 03-10.

## Cross-references

→ 03-05 rain and snow · → 03-02 storing water and draining the water heater ·
→ 03-04 purifying water · → 03-08 pool cover rules · → 03-09 a frozen filter is a dead filter ·
→ 08-01 heating one room · → 08-03 winterizing the home · → 08-05 hypothermia and frostbite ·
→ 11-01 layering · → 13-05 winter sanitation

pages.body:
# Judging and testing water quality

**What this page is for.** How to rank water sources from bad to worse, what a real test can
tell you, and which tests to buy now while labs and shops are open.

> **CAUTION.** You cannot see, smell or taste the things that matter most: bacteria, nitrate
> and most chemicals. **Clear water is not safe water** (→ 29-06). Treat every unknown source
> as contaminated and disinfect it (→ 03-04). This page helps you choose between sources; it
> is not a way to declare water safe by looking at it.

## Do this now

1. **Test now, while labs exist.** If you have a well or might ever use one, get a baseline
   test through a **state-certified lab** for **total coliform bacteria, nitrate, total
   dissolved solids and pH**: the CDC's yearly list (CDC, Guidelines for Testing Well Water).
   Your county or state health department can name a certified lab.
2. **Nitrate matters most for infants.** EPA says infants under six months who drink water
   with nitrate above the limit can become seriously ill and, untreated, may die ("blue-baby
   syndrome": their blood cannot carry oxygen properly). Know the number before you ever mix
   formula with well or surface water. **Boiling does not remove nitrate** (EPA: boiling does
   not remove salts or most chemicals), and because some water boils away, what is left is
   slightly stronger.{{#if has.infant}} You have an infant: this is your
   most important water test.{{/if}}
3. **Buy test strips now** (free chlorine, pH, nitrate, hardness) and a pocket TDS meter. They
   are cheap, small, and impossible to buy later.
4. **At a new site with a well**, the first job is a coliform and nitrate test. Treat every
   gallon until you have the result (→ 03-04), and carry the kit so you can test on the first
   day. Record it below.
5. **When in doubt, distil** (→ 03-03). It is the only home method that deals with salt, most
   chemicals and germs in one step.

## What testing can and cannot tell you

**Private wells are not regulated.** The EPA's public-water rules do not apply to them;
nobody checks or treats that water but you (CDC, Private Drinking Water and Public Health).
The CDC recommends testing a well **at least once a year** for **total coliform, nitrate,
total dissolved solids and pH**, and testing again when someone in the house becomes pregnant
or a child joins the household, after flooding or nearby land disturbance, after well repairs,
or when the water's taste, color or smell changes.

| Test | What it means | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Total coliform** | Indicator bacteria. If they are present, harmful bacteria, viruses or parasites probably are too | The disease test. Positive means do not drink it untreated |
| **Nitrate** | Runoff from fertilizer, animal waste, septic systems, sewage (CDC; EPA) | **Dangerous to infants.** A real risk in farm country |
| **TDS** (total dissolved solids) | How much salt and mineral is dissolved in the water | Tells you whether distilling is needed (pool water, brackish sources) |
| **pH** | How acidic the water is | Affects pipe corrosion and how well chlorine works |

**Disinfecting does not remove nitrate, salts or most chemicals** (EPA, Emergency Disinfection
of Drinking Water). Boiling leaves them in, slightly concentrated as water boils off. That is the most dangerous misunderstanding in
emergency water, and it is why nitrate and TDS deserve a real test.

### Well test record

Fill this in at the wellhead, for your well or any well you use.

{{#each destinations as d}}**{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}): water source {{ d.water_source_text }}
{{/each}}

- Well: __________ Date sampled: ________ Lab or kit: ________
- Total coliform: ☐ absent ☐ PRESENT (treat all water until it is fixed, → 03-04, → 03-10)
- Nitrate: ________ mg/L. **Over 10 mg/L (EPA's drinking-water limit, measured as nitrogen)
  is not safe for an infant's formula or feeding** (US EPA, National Primary Drinking Water
  Regulations). Check which unit your lab or strip reports. Use other water for the baby;
  boiling does not help.
- TDS: ________ ppm · pH: ________
- Retest due (one year, or after flooding): ________

## Judging a source in the field

Use this to *choose between* sources and to decide how hard to treat. Never to skip
treatment.

**Prefer, in this order:** stored or bottled water → rain caught off a clean surface → clean
snow or ice → a working well or spring → a clear flowing stream → a still pond → pool water
(needs distilling).

**Warning signs that push a source down the list or off it:**

- **Any smell of fuel, solvent or chemicals:** reject it. Boiling, bleach and filters do not
  fix that, and boiling makes some of it worse.
- **A sheen, foam or oily rainbow on the surface:** reject.
- **A strong rotten-egg or sewage smell:** reject for drinking.
- **Dark color, very cloudy, floating material:** do not use it. If you must, clear it, then
  distil rather than only disinfect.
- **Dead animals, mats of algae or livestock upstream:** heavy germ load. Boil or distil,
  never chemicals alone.
- **Downstream of a crop field, feedlot, road or industrial site:** assume nitrate and
  chemicals. Distil only.
- **Near a flooded area:** assume sewage and chemicals are mixed in (→ 17-03).

{{#if is.rural}}**Farm country.** Where crops and livestock surround you, surface water often
carries nitrate and manure runoff, and spring floods mix sewage with field runoff. Rain, snow
and distilled water are often *safer* than the nearest creek: the opposite of what instinct
says.{{else}}**Towns and cities.** Urban streams and ponds collect road runoff, sewage
overflows and industrial waste. Rain off a clean surface and snow are usually safer than any
nearby creek or pond.{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lab test of any well you might use | The only real answer on nitrate and coliform | State-certified lab; keep the report behind this page |
| Nitrate and nitrite test strips | The contaminant most dangerous to infants | Cheap; check the expiry date |
| Pocket TDS meter | Shows how salty a source is and whether a still is working | → 03-03 |
| Free-chlorine and pH strips | Confirms disinfection worked | Also for pool water (→ 03-08) |
| Total-coliform home test kits (present or absent) | Home check for bacteria | Not lab grade, far better than guessing |
| Clear glass sample jars with lids | Judge clarity, settling and smell in good light | |
| Printed results sheet | The numbers survive a dead phone | File it behind this page |

**If you don't have it:**

- **A clear jar and daylight.** Fill it, let it stand an hour, look at what settles and what
  floats, and smell the air at the top. Crude, but it separates obviously bad from possible.
- **Distilling** (→ 03-03) removes what you cannot test for. Slow and fuel hungry, but it is
  the honest answer.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** test strips expire. Check dates and rotate them like batteries.
- **Ration:** test the *source*, not every batch. Once a source is known and unchanged, treat
  it the same way every time, and re-test only when something changes: heavy rain, flooding,
  a new smell, or anyone falling ill.
- **Resupply:** when tests run out, rank sources and use the strongest treatment you can
  afford in fuel. Distil anything doubtful.
- **The health signal:** if people start having diarrhea, treat the water supply as guilty
  until proven otherwise (→ 12-05).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** city water is tested until it is not. Once the grid is down,
  treat the last tap water as stored water and everything after as unknown.
- **B (moving):** no lab, no time. Rank the source, treat everything, and prefer rain, snow
  and springs over standing water.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the first job at a new place is learning its water.
  Bring strips; test a well or spring before it becomes the family supply, and re-test after
  floods. On town water plus roof catchment, test the catchment.

## Cross-references

→ 03-04 purifying water · → 03-03 distilling · → 03-05 rain and snow · → 17-03 floods ·
→ 03-10 well water without power · → 20-01 infant needs · → 12-05 illness and dehydration

pages.body:
# Keeping stored and pool water from going bad (algae, bacteria, mosquitoes)

**What this page is for.** Standing water left alone goes bad: green, slimy, smelly, and full
of mosquito larvae. This page explains how to slow that down, how to stop mosquitoes breeding
in it, and how to make bad water usable. It matters most for pools, hot tubs, rain barrels and
ponds, but stored drinking water is covered too.

> **SAFETY.**
> - Water that has "gone bad" carries **bacteria and parasites that cause diarrheal
>   disease**, which can kill infants and young children, and **breeds mosquitoes** that
>   spread **West Nile virus** and other illnesses. **Never drink scummy, green or smelly
>   water untreated.** For drinking, distil it (→ 03-03).
> - **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
>   mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine
>   products. (→ 30-01)
{{#if has.young_child}}> - **A pool is a drowning hazard for your young children.** Every rule below keeps the
>   cover closed except for the minutes you are drawing water with an adult present.
{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Cover the pool or tub.** The single most useful move. A solid cover blocks sunlight (which
   stops algae), keeps debris out, and **stops mosquitoes laying eggs**.
2. **Treat the pool as utility water**, not drinking water. You cannot keep a pool swimming-
   clear without power, so don't try. Keep it usable for flushing, washing and firefighting,
   keep the cover on against mosquitoes, and **distil the small amount you drink** (→ 03-03). Drinking
   fresh pool water any other way is a household decision: {{choice DC-13}} (→ 30-14).
3. **Kill mosquito larvae** in standing water you will **not** drink, with **Bti "mosquito
   dunks" or "bits"**. EPA has judged that Bti does not pose a risk to people. CDC says to use
   larvicides only in water that will not be used for drinking and that cannot be covered,
   emptied or removed, and to follow the label for how much and how often. Water you may
   drink, even after distilling, is covered and screened instead.
4. **Empty every other container of standing water** in the yard each week: buckets, tires,
   toys, gutters, plant saucers.
5. **Replace stored drinking water about every 6 months** (CDC). Keep it cool, dark and
   sealed (→ 03-02).

## If your pool has an automatic (electric) safety cover

**If the cover cannot be worked without power, the pool is not a water source.** Find the
manual override in the cover's manual now, while the power is on, and practice it.

- **Some covers open with a hand tool but close only by pulling, which can take two strong
  people.** Your manual says which kind you have. **Confirm you can close it before you ever
  open it.** With children in the house, an open pool you cannot close is a worse problem than
  a water shortage.
- **Never fully open it.** Open only a bucket-sized gap at the shallow end, draw water, close
  it. The barrier stays in place. **Never cut the cover.**
- **Check the manual for the water level the cover needs.** Some covers are designed around the
  normal water level; drawing the pool down can weaken the barrier. Draw sparingly and watch
  the level, winter included (→ 03-06).
- **Keep the override tool with the pool equipment**, and write here what it is and where it
  lives: __________

{{photo pool-cover-override}}

## Why pool water turns bad

A pool stays clear because a **pump** moves the water, a **filter** strains it, and
**chlorine** kills germs and algae. Cut the power and all three stop. Soon the chlorine is used
up, sunlight feeds **algae** (green, then black), leaves and debris rot,
**slime and bacteria** grow, and the still surface becomes a **mosquito nursery**. It goes
from a pool to a pond.

## Three ways to control it

### 1. Block sunlight and debris (cheapest; always do it)

A cover (solid is better than mesh for this) stops algae growing and mosquitoes laying eggs.
A shaded, covered pool goes bad far more slowly than an open, sunny one.

### 2. Keep some chlorine in it (optional; uses up your stock)

If you want clearer utility water and have the chemicals, keep a **free-chlorine level**
("free chlorine" is the chlorine still able to kill germs; → 29-05) using a pool test kit as
your guide.

**Chlorine products, best to worst for long storage:**

- **Calcium hypochlorite** ("cal-hypo", pool shock): a lot of chlorine per pound, and it keeps
  far better than liquid bleach **dry, sealed, below 120 °F, and away from anything flammable
  and from other pool chemicals** (CDC/ATSDR). Store it as described on → 03-04.
- **Sodium hypochlorite** (liquid pool chlorine, or plain unscented bleach at 5 to 9 percent):
  easy to measure, but **loses strength in storage** (EPA: use bleach less than a year old) and
  is mostly water, so heavy to store.
- **Dichlor granules:** contain stabilizer (cyanuric acid), dissolve cleanly, store well.
- **Trichlor tablets:** release slowly, store very well, acidic, need a floating feeder.
  **Never store trichlor with calcium hypochlorite, or use a scoop that touched one for the
  other.** ATSDR says to keep calcium hypochlorite separated from other chlorinating agents;
  the two can react to make chlorine gas or fire. Keep them on different walls.

**How much:** do not dose from memory. **Measure with strips or a kit, and add small amounts
to stay in the range CDC gives for pools: 1 to 4 ppm chlorine, pH 7.0 to 7.8** (CDC,
Guidelines for Keeping Your Pool Safe and Healthy), then test again. For a stronger "shock" dose, follow
the product label for your pool's gallons and confirm with the test kit, because strengths
vary.

**Reality check:** keeping a whole pool chlorinated for months uses a lot of chemical. It is
usually better to **cover it and distil what you drink**, and spend chlorine only where
it is worth it.

### 3. Kill the mosquitoes (always, in warm months)

- **Bti** (*Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis*) dunks or bits are a natural bacterium that
  kills mosquito larvae when they eat it. The EPA has registered it and **judged that it does
  not pose a risk to people**, and no resistance to it has been documented (US EPA, Bti for
  Mosquito Control). CDC lists buckets, rain barrels, gutters, tires, pool covers that collect
  water and non-chlorinated pools as places to treat, but **only water that will not be used
  for drinking** (CDC, Larvicides). Re-apply as the label says.
- **Methoprene** (a growth regulator that stops larvae becoming adults) and **surface oils or
  films** (which smother larvae at the surface) are the other two larvicide types if Bti is not
  available (CDC, Larvicides for Mosquito Control).
- **A tight cover** stops egg-laying, and it is the method for any water you may drink.
- **Around the yard:** get rid of all other standing water weekly, screen rain barrels
  (→ 03-05), keep gutters clear. Even small containers breed mosquitoes.

## Making bad water usable

- **For drinking:** strain out the chunks (cloth or coffee filter), then **distil** (→ 03-03).
  Distilling deals with algae, bacteria and chemicals in one step.
- **To clear cloudy water** before disinfecting (if you are not distilling): let it **settle**,
  or use **alum** (a powder sold for pickling that makes particles clump and sink). CDC's
  method: stir about 1/4 teaspoon of alum powder into 1 quart of cloudy water, stir often for a
  few minutes, add more until clumps form, let them settle, then pour through a coffee filter or
  clean cloth. Alum removes most but not all germs, so **then** disinfect (→ 03-04) (CDC Yellow
  Book, Water Disinfection for Travelers).
  Disinfecting alone does not clear algae or particles, and dirty water uses up chlorine, so
  clear it first.
- **For utility use** (flushing, firefighting, laundry): use it as it is.
- **"Utility" stops where mouths begin.** Dishes, hands before cooking, food surfaces, teeth
  brushing and washing a child's face all get **treated** water, or a sanitizing final rinse
  (→ 13-10). Stale raw water on an eating surface ends up swallowed.
- **"Utility" stops at broken skin.** Untreated pool or pond water (and salty water from a
  saltwater pool) on an open cut, a cracked winter hand or a scraped knee is an infection
  route. Wash wounds with treated water only (→ 12-02), and keep anyone with open cuts away
  from pool-water chores.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Solid pool cover, or a heavy tarp with tie-downs | Blocks sun, debris and mosquitoes | The most useful single item here |
| Bti mosquito dunks and bits, a season's worth or more | Kills larvae; EPA finds no risk to people | Non-drinking water only (CDC); re-apply per the label |
| Calcium hypochlorite (pool shock) | Compact, long-keeping chlorine | Store as on → 03-04 |
| Pool test kit or chlorine and pH strips | Dose by measuring, not guessing | CDC's pool range: 1 to 4 ppm chlorine, pH 7.0 to 7.8 |
| Unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 percent | Disinfecting stored or cleared water | **Dose only from the table on → 03-04** |
| Alum | Clears cloudy water before disinfecting | Small amount; settle, then pour off |
| Fine mesh, cloth or coffee filters | Strain debris and algae | Before distilling or clearing |
| Food-safe containers and labels | Rotating stored drinking water | "DRINKING" or "UTILITY" |
| Long-handled skimmer or brush | Remove debris and algae mats | Filtering by hand |

**If you don't have it:**

- Any tarp with weights makes a pool cover. Even partial shade cloth slows algae.
- Plain unscented bleach stands in for pool chlorine for a while (weaker; use more, by test).
- Screen or netting over barrels stops egg-laying if you have no larvicide.
- A thin film of cooking oil on the surface of a **non-drinking** container smothers larvae.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the label says how long each Bti dunk lasts; count months of mosquito season
  times the number of pools and containers. Calcium hypochlorite keeps well dry and cool; liquid
  bleach should be used within a year (EPA). **A cover does not run out**, which is why it is the backbone
  of the plan.
- **Ration:** stop chlorinating for clarity. Spend chemical only on hygiene and on batches you
  will disinfect. Rely on cover, Bti and distilling.
- **Resupply:** pool shops, hardware stores and pool sheds are where chlorine and dunks are
  found. Bleach is everywhere but weak and does not keep. Long term, **prevention beats
  treatment**: keep water covered and shaded.
- **Disease is the real cost of failure.** A mosquito-borne illness or a diarrhea outbreak
  with no clinic is a catastrophe, not an inconvenience.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** a covered pool is a large reserve for sanitation and utility
  water. If you will distil drinking water from it (→ 03-03), keep larvicides out of it (CDC)
  and rely on the cover.
- **B (moving):** you leave the pool behind. What travels is the skill: larvae control and
  clearing water at any source you camp near.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** ponds, stock tanks and rain barrels all breed mosquitoes
  and grow algae. Same three levers: cover or shade, larvicide, clear then disinfect or distil.

## Cross-references

→ 03-02 storing water · → 03-03 distilling pool water · → 03-04 purifying water ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 06-06 chemical storage · → 13-03 greywater · → 17-03 floods ·
→ 30-14 the pool-water card

pages.body:
# Filter care: straws, bottles, squeeze and gravity filters

**What this page is for.** How to choose, use, clean, store and retire the portable water
filters most households buy. Specifications by filter class are on → 28-06; what "micron" and
"virus" mean is on → 29-06.

> **SAFETY. A filter fails silently.** A damaged filter looks and works exactly like a good
> one: water still comes out. **You will not know.**
>
> **Freezing is the failure that matters.** Water left inside a used hollow-fiber filter (a
> bundle of tiny porous tubes) expands when it freezes and splits the fibers. The makers of
> these filters warn against it, and **the damage cannot be seen**: the filter still flows,
> but it no longer filters.{{#if is.cold_winters}} Where you live, a used filter left in a
> vehicle or an unheated garage overnight is the most likely way to lose your water
> treatment (→ 03-06, → 22-05).{{/if}}
>
> **Most filters do not remove viruses** (CDC). Filtering is not the end of the chain
> (→ 03-04).

## Do this now

1. **Find every filter you own and write on it, in marker, whether it has ever been used and
   whether it has ever been below freezing.** A filter with an unknown history cannot be
   trusted.
2. **Move used filters out of garages and vehicles** for the winter. They live in the heated
   part of the house (→ 08-01).
3. **Buy the backflush syringe or cleaning tool for your filter now,** and spare elements
   (→ 26-04). A filter without its cleaning tool has a much shorter life.
4. **Practice the full chain once:** pre-filter → filter → disinfect with chemical or boiling
   → store covered (→ 03-04). Doing it for the first time in an emergency is how steps get
   skipped.

{{photo our-filters}}

## What each type is for

| Type | How it works | Best for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Straw** | You suck water through it at the source | Emergency use by one person; go-bag weight | **You cannot store or carry treated water.** Useless for cooking, or for a child who cannot suck hard |
| **Bottle filter** | Filter built into a bottle | One person on the move | Small; the filter limits the flow |
| **Squeeze** | Squeeze a pouch through a filter in the line | Light, fast, fills containers | Pouches split; carry spares |
| **Gravity** | Hang a bag and let it drip through | **Households.** Volume with no effort | Bulky; slow when cold or clogged |
| **Pump** | Hand pump through a cartridge | Shallow or awkward sources | Moving parts and seals that break |
| **Ultrafilter (0.01 micron)** | Hollow fiber with pores small enough for viruses | Removes viruses too, says the CDC | Costs more, slower, needs more pressure |

**For a household of {{ household.size }}, a gravity filter is the right main filter**, with a
squeeze filter to carry and a straw only as a go-bag backup. **Do not build the household
plan on straws.**

## What filters do and do not remove

The CDC is direct: **pore size is the main thing that decides how well a filter works**, and
**many filters do not reliably remove viruses.** Its advice for anyone using a microfilter is to
treat the water with chlorine as well, to deal with viruses (CDC, Water Disinfection for
Travelers).

So the chain is:

1. **Pre-filter:** cloth, coffee filter, or let it settle (→ 03-04).
2. **Filter:** removes parasites and bacteria, and clears the water.
3. **Disinfect:** chlorine or boiling. **This is the virus step.**
4. **Store:** in a covered, clean container (→ 03-02).

The CDC also notes that filtering **does not prevent the water getting dirty again in
storage.** A perfectly filtered gallon poured into a dirty jug is dirty water.

**Ultrafilters at 0.01 micron are the exception:** the CDC says they should remove viruses,
bacteria and parasites. If you own one, know it. If you do not, **assume you need step 3.**

## Freezing: read this twice

Once a hollow-fiber filter has been used, water stays inside the fibers. **When that water
freezes it expands and splits them.** After that the filter passes water freely, and passes
everything in the water with it.

- **There is no reliable field test.** You cannot see, taste or measure it at home.
- **Makers say to protect these filters from freezing.** Your filter's own instructions
  govern.
- **A brand-new filter that has never been wet is not at risk.** The danger starts the first
  time it gets wet.
- **The rule: if a used filter has been below freezing, or you cannot be sure, retire it.**
  Use it only to pre-filter dirty water, or throw it away. **Do not gamble a child's health on
  it** (→ 12-05).

**What that means in practice:**

- Used filters do not live in a garage, a shed or a vehicle in winter.
- The vehicle kit gets **chemical treatment and a metal cup for boiling**, not the good filter
  (→ 22-05, → 03-04).
- After winter use, **shake it as dry as you can and bring it inside** (→ 03-06). In very cold
  weather, carry it inside your coat.

## Clogging and backflushing

The CDC notes that filters **eventually clog** with particles and then need replacing,
maintenance or repair. Slower flow is normal ageing, not necessarily failure.

**Pre-filtering is the biggest single thing that extends filter life.** Cloth, a coffee filter,
or letting sediment settle and pouring off the clear water costs nothing and makes the element
last many times longer.

**Backflushing** means pushing clean water backwards through the element to knock trapped dirt
loose. It restores flow on filters designed for it:

- [ ] Backflush with **clean, already-treated water**, never dirty source water.
- [ ] Use the syringe or tool made for **your** filter, by its instructions.
- [ ] Do it when flow slows noticeably, and before storage, not after.
- [ ] Some filters are shaken, tapped or scrubbed instead (ceramic elements are scrubbed and
  slowly wear thin). Know which you have.
- [ ] Never poke anything into the element to clear it.

## Storing a filter between uses

- **Dry it as far as its instructions allow** before long storage, then keep it **inside,
  above freezing**.
- **Some filters are stored with a preservative solution and some must not be.** Your
  instructions govern; there is no universal rule.
- **Keep new spare elements sealed and dry.** They keep well, and they are the part that runs
  out (→ 26-08).
- **Label each filter with the date of first use** and roughly how much water has gone
  through it.

## When to retire a filter

Retire it (not "keep an eye on it") if any of these is true:

- [ ] It has been below freezing after being used, or you cannot be sure it has not.
- [ ] It was dropped hard, or the housing is cracked or damaged.
- [ ] Flow does not come back after a proper backflush.
- [ ] It has passed its rated volume, or you have lost track of the volume.
- [ ] It was stored wet and smells, or shows mold or growth.
- [ ] Its history is unknown: scavenged, borrowed or found (→ 22-02).

**A retired filter still has a job:** pre-filtering muddy water before boiling. Mark it clearly
so it is never used as a main filter again.

## Why spare elements are the real purchase

The housing lasts. **The element is what wears out**, and a filter with no spare has a hard
deadline. Buy at least two spares with each filter and count them in → 23-02. That count is
your real filtering runway, not the filter itself (→ 23-04).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravity filter and 2 spare elements** | Household volume with no effort | The main filter; elements are the consumable |
| **Squeeze filter and spare pouches** | Portable; fills containers | Pouches split before elements fail |
| **The backflush tool for your model** | Restores flow, extends life | Buy it with the filter |
| Straw filters, two | Go-bag backup only | Not a household plan |
| **Chemical disinfectant** | **The virus step** filters miss | → 03-04 |
| Cloth or coffee filters | The cheapest life-extender there is | Stock many |
| A clean container for backflush water | Never backflush with source water | |
| Permanent marker | First-use date, volume, freeze history | The habit that makes this page work |

**If you don't have it:** cloth and settling clear water. **Boiling replaces filtering
entirely** and needs nothing but fuel (→ 03-04, → 06-04). Sand-and-charcoal home-made filters
clear water but **do not make it safe**: they are a pre-filter, and the disinfecting step still
applies.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the rated volume per element, and **far less on dirty water** without
  pre-filtering. Write the number in → 23-02.
- **Ration:** pre-filter everything. Use the filter for drinking and cooking water, not
  washing (→ 13-04).
- **Resupply:** spare elements while shops exist. **After that there is none**, which is why the
  boiling path matters.
- **Substitute:** **boiling**, at a fuel cost (→ 06-04). Chemicals deal with germs but not
  cloudiness or chemicals (→ 03-04). **Filters are a stock that runs down; boiling is the
  answer that lasts** (→ 23-04).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** gravity filter at the sink, chemicals as backup, spares stocked,
  everything above freezing.
- **B (moving):** the squeeze filter and chemical treatment travel. **The good filter does not
  sit in a cold vehicle** (→ 22-05).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** protect the elements you have and move the daily load onto
  boiling, because a filter you cannot replace is a filter on a countdown.

## Cross-references

→ 03-04 the treatment chain (filtering is step 2 of 4) · → 03-02 clean storage ·
→ 03-06 winter water · → 03-07 judging the source · → 28-06 filter specifications ·
→ 26-04 checklist · → 26-08 dates · → 23-02 your real runway

pages.body:
# Well water without power

**What this page is for.** Getting water out of a drilled well when the grid is down, at your
own home or at any place you might go that has one. A drilled well's water really comes from
an **electric pump** at the bottom of a narrow pipe: no power, no pump, no water, unless you
have planned one of the four ways round it below.
{{#if has.well}}Your home is on a well: this page is for you now.{{else}}Your home is on
{{ dwelling.water_supply }}. Keep this page for a destination, a relative's farm, or a
neighbor's well.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.** Two ways to get hurt here.
> - **Electricity.** Generator-to-pump wiring is dangerous (→ 09-04, → 09-08, → 29-04).
>   **Floor:** Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or
>   an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a
>   double-male ("suicide") cord. Backfeeding electrocutes line workers and neighbors and
>   starts fires. (A cord-and-plug conversion is not a connection to house wiring; whether to do
>   one yourself is a decision card, → 30-08.) (→ 30-01)
> - **Floor:** Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
>   open window. Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning. (→ 30-01)
> - **Contamination.** One dirty rope lowered down the well can foul the water everyone
>   drinks. Everything that goes down the pipe is clean.

## Do this now

1. **Buy a well bucket (cylinder bailer) and enough rope to reach the water, with margin.** It
   fits in a tote, and it is the one option that works on any drilled well with no power and
   no information. An ordinary bucket will not fit down a well.
2. **Fill in the well survey below** for your well and any well you might use. Ten minutes at
   the wellhead with a flashlight and a phone camera answers every open question on this page.
   Pull a water sample the same visit (→ 03-07).
3. **At someone else's place, ask what already exists.** A working farm has often solved this
   before: a standby or tractor-driven generator, a windmill stock well, a spring. Plugging
   into their system may be the right first move. Arrive assuming nothing is there for you.
4. **Do not open a well cap casually.** Sealed is safe. Open it only with clean hands, cleaned
   gear and a reason.

## What a drilled well is

{{figure fig-drilled-well-parts}}

- **The casing:** a steel or plastic pipe a few inches across (measure yours at the cap), set
  down to the water-bearing rock or gravel, often a hundred feet or more. A sanitary **well
  cap** seals the top. Below it is a narrow, dark, wet tube.
- **The submersible pump:** an electric pump hanging near the bottom on a **drop pipe**,
  pushing water up. Home pumps run on either **240 volts** or **120 volts**; the breaker and
  the pump's control box tell you which (below). That one fact decides the generator question.
- **The pitless adapter:** the underground fitting where the water line leaves the casing
  **below the frost line** and runs to the house. It is why a well works in winter.
- **The pressure tank and switch:** inside the house or a well house, a tank (its size is on
  the label) holds water under pressure so the pump starts and stops instead of running at
  every tap. The pressure switch turns the pump on and off; it is often set to start the pump
  at 30 or 40 psi and stop it about 20 psi higher, at 50 or 60 psi (University of
  Nebraska-Lincoln Extension).

{{photo wellhead}}

## Four ways to get water with no grid, fastest first

### 1. What is left in the pressure tank (minutes of water, not days)

The tank keeps delivering until its pressure is gone, and it holds far less usable water than
its size suggests. In the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension table, a 30-gallon
galvanized steel tank gives about **4 to 5 usable gallons**, and an 82-gallon one about 8.5 to
12, depending on the switch setting (University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension, Private
Drinking Water Wells, Table I). Draw it into containers
from the lowest tap, on purpose, before it disappears into toilet flushes and hand washing.

### 2. A generator to run the pump (the fast fix, if the electrics match)

Check, in this order:

- **Pump voltage.** Find the well pump's breaker in the panel. **A double-width (2-pole)
  breaker means a 240-volt pump; a single breaker means 120 volts.** Confirm on the pump's
  control box or nameplate.
- **Generator voltage.** Read the generator's label. **A 120-volt-only generator cannot run a
  240-volt pump at any wattage.** Many small and inverter generators are 120 volts only.
  {{#if has.generator}}Your generator: {{ gear.generator_watts }} running watts. Its output
  (check the label): {{ gear.generator_volts }}.{{/if}}
- **Starting surge.** Pump motors draw several times their running watts for a moment to
  start. The generator size your pump needs is in the pump maker's manual or on its control
  box (look for a generator sizing table by horsepower); write it in the survey below. **Size
  the generator to the start surge, not the running number.** A "soft-start" kit fitted to
  the pump circuit reduces the surge; its maker states by how much.
- **Connection.** Through a transfer switch or interlock, or by a proper connection at the
  pump's own disconnect: **never backfed through a wall outlet** (floor above; → 09-04,
  → 09-08). Rewiring a pump to a plug yourself is a decision with its own card: your choice
  {{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08).
- **Run it hard and briefly.** Run the generator, refill the pressure tank and every
  container, shut down. A well pump is the textbook short, heavy job for a generator (→ 09-04).

{{photo well-breaker-and-tank}}

### 3. The well bucket (no power, no information needed: buy now)

A home well casing takes no ordinary container. A **purpose-made well bucket** is a slim
cylinder of galvanized steel or plastic pipe, narrower than the casing (check the clearance
beside the drop pipe in your survey), with a one-way valve in the foot. Its label gives how
much it holds per pull. Lower it
on rope past the drop pipe and the pump wires (go slowly; do not snag the wire), let it fill,
haul it up. Slow, honest work, and it works at any depth your rope reaches. This plus good rope
is the guaranteed floor under this whole page.

### 4. A deep-well hand pump (the permanent fix)

Purpose-built deep-well hand pumps (for example the Simple Pump or Bison types) fit **beside
the existing electric pump in the same casing**, under a two-hole well cap. One maker states
its pump fits alongside the existing submersible in casings 4 inches and larger and lifts from
static water levels **up to 325 feet** (Simple Pump Co., Deep Well Hand Pumps). The cheap
"pitcher pumps" sold for shallow wells work by suction and cannot lift from a deep well. **You
cannot choose one without the survey:** casing inside width, how far down the water stands,
and how much room the drop pipe leaves. Before the collapse, it is the project that turns a
well from grid-dependent to hand-powered for good.

## Keeping the wellhead from freezing

The buried line and pitless adapter are safe below the frost line. What freezes is the
**equipment above ground**: the pressure tank, the switch and exposed pipe in a well house or
basement. In a grid-down winter with the building unheated: insulate the tank and pipes, heat
a small well house if you safely can, or **drain the above-ground side between generator
runs** and treat each run as "fill everything, then drain" (→ 03-06). Never leave a full
pressure tank in a space going below freezing. The capped casing itself survives winter fine.

## Keeping the well clean

A well is the one water source that one careless draw can *ruin*, for everyone who drinks
from it.

- **Everything that goes down the casing is clean.** Wipe the bailer and the first several
  feet of rope with the container-cleaning solution on → 03-02 (1 teaspoon of 5 to 9 percent
  bleach per quart of water, 30 seconds), then rinse with treated water. The drinking-water
  dose on → 03-04 is far too weak to clean a surface. Keep the rope in a sealed bag, never
  coiled on the ground, and wash your hands first.
- **Keep the cap on** except during a draw. Rodents, insects and surface water running down the
  casing are the classic ways wells get contaminated.
- **Keep fuel, the generator and animals well away from the wellhead**, and check that the
  ground slopes *away* from the casing so surface runoff drains away from the well (US EPA,
  Protect Your Home's Water). Keep latrines and septic systems well away too
  (→ 13-07, → 13-12).
- **After anything gets in** (bailer work, pump repair, flood water over the wellhead):
  disinfect the well as below and re-test before trusting it (→ 03-07). Treat all water until
  then (→ 03-04).

> **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The
> mix gives off chlorine gas. (→ 30-01)

### Disinfecting ("shock-chlorinating") a well: the CDC method

Do this after flood water covers the wellhead, after any work down the casing, or after a
positive coliform test. It takes a day; everyone uses stored or treated water meanwhile.
Steps from the CDC (How to Disinfect Wells After an Emergency), in plain words, for a drilled
or driven well:

> **Before the collapse:** CDC says to contact the local or state health department or the
> agriculture extension agent first, and that wells should be disinfected by a well or pump
> contractor. If the water smells of fuel or chemicals, disinfection will not make it safe:
> use another source.

**Safety first (CDC):** turn off all electricity to the well before clearing debris; do not
enter a well pit (gases build up in them); wear goggles or a face shield; work with fresh air.

1. **Run the water until it is clear**, from the outside tap closest to the well, so dirty
   water stays out of the house plumbing. With no pump, bail until it runs clear.
2. **Close the valves to any water softener** (strong chlorine can damage it).
3. **Work out the depth of water in the well**: total well depth minus the depth down to the
   water (from the survey, the well record, or a weighted line). Find the bleach amount in
   the table below. Use only unscented household bleach.
4. **Mix that bleach with 3 to 5 gallons of water** in a 5-gallon bucket.
5. **Remove the vent cap and pour the mixture into the well** through a funnel. Keep clear of
   all electrical connections.
6. **Circulate it:** attach a clean hose to the nearest outside tap and run water back down
   the well for thorough mixing (this needs the pump, so a generator; see above). Rinse the
   inside of the casing with the hose or a bucket for 5 to 10 minutes. If the pump cannot run,
   mix it by bailing and pouring water back into the well with a bucket (CDC gives this for
   wells without a pump).
7. **Open every tap in the house** and run each until you smell a **strong chlorine (bleach)
   smell** at it. Then close them all.
8. **Leave it at least 12 hours.** Nobody drinks, cooks with or bathes in the water.
9. **Drain it:** run a hose from an outside tap onto an area **with no plants**, such as a
   driveway, until the chlorine smell is gone. Do not drain it into streams or ponds (CDC),
   and keep it out of a septic system as far as you can (strong chlorine kills the bacteria a
   septic tank needs, → 13-12). Then run the indoor taps until the smell is gone.
10. **Until the water is tested, boil it** (rolling boil, 1 minute) or use another source.
    **Wait at least 7 to 10 days**, then have the water tested for total coliform and E. coli
    or fecal coliform (→ 03-07). Testing cannot be done until all the chlorine is flushed out.
    CDC then advises two more tests, one in the next 2 to 4 weeks and another in 3 to 4
    months.

If coliform bacteria show up, CDC says to disinfect again and retest. If they keep showing up,
contamination is still getting in (a cracked casing, surface water, a nearby septic system or
latrine): find the cause rather than re-shocking again and again. Bored or dug wells have
their own CDC table and are harder to disinfect; this page covers drilled and driven wells.

**Approximate Amount of Bleach for Disinfection of a Drilled or Driven Well** (CDC, printed as
published. CDC's notes: use only unscented household liquid chlorine bleach; bleach
concentrations are generally between 5 and 9 percent; quantities are approximate, rounded to
the nearest practical measurement, and calculated to reach a chlorine concentration above
100 mg/L):

| Depth of water | 2 inches | 4 inches | 6 inches | 8 inches | 10 inches | 24 inches | 36 inches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 feet | 3/4 tbsp | 3 1/4 tbsp | 1/2 cup | 3/4 cup | 1 1/4 cups | 7 cups | 1 gal |
| 20 feet | 1 1/2 tbsp | 6 1/2 tbsp | 1 cup | 1 1/2 cups | 2 1/2 cups | 14 cups | 2 gal |
| 30 feet | 2 1/4 tbsp | 9 3/4 tbsp | 1 1/2 cups | 2 1/4 cups | 3 1/4 cups | 1 1/4 gal | 3 gal |
| 40 feet | 3 tbsp | 13 tbsp | 2 cups | 3 cups | 5 cups | 1 3/4 gal | 4 gal |
| 50 feet | 3 3/4 tbsp | 1 cup | 2 1/2 cups | 3 3/4 cups | 6 1/4 cups | 2 1/4 gal | 5 gal |
| 100 feet | 7 1/2 tbsp | 2 cups | 5 cups | 7 1/2 cups | 12 1/2 cups | 4 1/2 gal | 10 gal |

Columns are the diameter of the well casing. tbsp: tablespoon; gal: gallon; 1 cup = 8 fluid
ounces = 16 tablespoons; 1 gallon = 16 cups. For water deeper than 100 feet the CDC table
stops; the target is the same strong chlorine smell at every tap.

If you have only pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), dissolve it in a bucket of water first;
never pour dry granules down a well. The strong chlorine smell at every tap is still the
target (→ 29-05).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Cylinder well bucket (bailer)** | Works with no power and no information | Narrower than your casing with room beside the drop pipe, with a foot valve |
| Rope long enough to reach the water with margin, and a carabiner | Reaching the water | Braided rope; kept bagged and clean |
| Well-cleaning kit | Protects the well during draws; disinfects it | Fresh unscented bleach, gloves, eye protection, a sealed rope bag, a clean 5-gallon bucket, a funnel, a garden hose |
| Soft-start kit | Reduces the generator surge the pump needs | Fit after the survey: pump horsepower and voltage first |
| A spare pressure switch, and knowing how it works | The most common well electrical failure | Photograph the existing switch during the survey |
| Water test supplies | Same visit as the survey | → 03-07 |

**If you don't have it:**

- A bailer can be made from **plastic pipe narrower than the casing, a foot check valve and an
  eye bolt**: farm store parts and one afternoon.
- A neighbor's larger generator that can supply 240 volts can run a pump yours cannot: a
  mutual-aid trade waiting to happen (→ 18-01).
- A windmill or solar stock well elsewhere on a farm is water already solved. Ask where the
  animals drink in winter.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the groundwater is effectively unlimited at household scale. The runway is
  **generator fuel**, or **arms and rope** with the bailer. Your
  {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day (→ 03-01) divided by what one pull brings up
  is the number of pulls a day: count it once.
- **Ration:** the well changes none of the treat-and-test rules. Until test results are in,
  treat every gallon you draw (→ 03-04).
- **Resupply:** roof catchment, stock tanks, and snowmelt in winter (→ 03-06). A hand pump is
  the permanent way off the fuel treadmill.
- **The failure to fear** is not a dry well. It is a **fouled** one: a contaminated casing
  after careless draws or a flood. Discipline at the wellhead is the whole game.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if has.well}}fill in the survey now, buy the bailer and rope,
  and know your pump's voltage and your generator's.{{else}}you are on {{ dwelling.water_supply }}.
  If any place you might go has a well, buy the bailer and rope now and pack them with the
  survey sheet and test strips.{{/if}}
- **B (moving):** wells along a route are sealed and private. Carry water (→ 03-01).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** on arrival, water is job one (→ 01-04). Check what is left
  in the pressure tank, find out what the place already uses to run the pump, and fall back to
  the bailer the same afternoon if needed. Do not wait for a perfect generator answer before
  you start drawing and treating water.

### Well survey (photograph everything)

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which well (home or destination): | ________ |
| Casing diameter (measure the cap): | ________ in |
| Total well depth / depth down to the water (well record, owner, or a weighted line): | ________ / ________ ft |
| Pump voltage (breaker poles and control box): 120 V ☐ 240 V ☐ | Horsepower: ________ |
| Pump breaker location and amps: | ________ |
| Pressure tank location and size: | ________ |
| Well house? Heated how in winter? | ________ |
| Generator on site (watts; can it supply 240 V?): | ________ |
| Generator size the pump maker gives for this pump: | ________ |
| Hand pump, windmill or stock wells nearby: | ________ |
| Well log or driller's record available? | ________ |
| Water sample taken (→ 03-07)? ☐ coliform ☐ nitrate | Date: ________ |

{{#if has.destinations}}Destinations to survey:
{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}): well? ☐ yes ☐ no ☐ unknown
{{/each}}{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 03-07 testing water · → 09-04 generators · → 09-08 wiring and safety · → 28-03 generator
specifications · → 30-08 the cord-and-plug card · → 01-04 arrival · → 03-06 freezing ·
→ 03-04 treat until tested · → 13-12 septic
