# Food storage and preservation

**What this section holds.** 19 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 04-01 **Calorie planning and stockpile math**: How much food your household needs each day, how to turn that into pounds of food on a shelf, and how to work out how many days the food you already have wil…
- → 04-02 **Building a shelf-stable pantry**: How to build a store of food that keeps without a fridge, in the right order, on a budget, and in a way that it actually gets eaten and replaced.
- → 04-03 **Long-term bulk staples: grains, beans, sugar and salt**: How to pack dry staples (rice, wheat, beans, oats, sugar, salt) so they keep for years or decades, which foods do not keep, and how to cook stored beans safely.
- → 04-04 **Water-bath canning (high-acid foods)**: How boiling-water canning works, which foods it is safe for, how to adjust for your altitude, and when to throw a jar out.
- → 04-05 **Pressure canning (low-acid foods) and botulism safety**: How to can vegetables, beans, meat, poultry, fish, soups and stocks safely, how to set the pressure for your altitude, and what to do with a jar you are not …
- → 04-06 **Drying food**: How to dry fruit, vegetables, herbs and meat so they keep for months with no jars, no lids and no electricity, and the one food (meat) where drying needs str…
- → 04-07 **Smoking and curing meat**: The difference between curing (the step that preserves meat) and smoking (which flavours or cooks it), how to use curing salt safely, and when pressure canni…
- → 04-08 **Fermentation and root cellaring**: Two ways to keep vegetables for months with no jars-per-batch, no fuel and no electricity: fermenting them in salt brine (sauerkraut is the model), and stori…
- → 04-09 **Using winter as a freezer, and where it does not work**: In a cold winter, the outdoors, an unheated garage or the unheated rooms of the house can keep food cold or frozen with no power at all.
- → 04-10 **Rotation, dating and inventory**: How to keep a food store fresh and counted, what the dates on food packages mean, and how to run the "pantry week" that finds problems before an emergency does.
- → 04-11 **Protecting stored food from pests and rodents**: How to keep mice, rats and insects out of stored food, what to do when they get in, and how to clean up after rodents without catching a disease from the dust.
- → 04-12 **Fats and oils: storage and rendering**: Why fat matters more than most food plans allow, how long each kind keeps, and how to render animal fat into cooking fat that stores for months.
- → 04-13 **Salt, sugar, vinegar and honey: the preserving staples**: The four foods that make almost all other food preservation work: why to stock them, how much, how to store them, and the one safety rule about honey.
- → 04-14 **Dairy: powdered, canned and shelf-stable**: Which kinds of milk and dairy keep without a fridge, how long each keeps, which ones young children need, and why none of them replaces infant formula.
- → 04-15 **Storing eggs without refrigeration**: Which eggs can be kept without a fridge and which cannot, the storage methods that are tested and the traditional ones that are not, how to check an egg, and…
- → 04-16 **Sprouting grains and beans for fresh food**: How to turn dry beans, lentils and grains you already store into fresh green food in a few days, on a counter, with no soil, light or fuel, and who should ea…
- → 04-17 **Food safety when the power fails**: What to do with the food in your fridge and freezer from the moment the power goes out: how long it stays safe, what to eat first, what to throw out, and how…
- → 04-18 **Meal planning and cooking from stores**: How to plan a small set of meals that your household can cook from stored food every day, using little fuel, that everyone in the house can safely eat, and t…

pages.title: Calorie planning and stockpile math
pages.body:
# Calorie planning and stockpile math

**What this page is for.** How much food your household needs each day, how to turn that into
pounds of food on a shelf, and how to work out how many days the food you already have will
last (your **runway**). Every other food page uses the numbers printed here.

> **CAUTION.** Calories are only half of a food plan. If anyone in the house has a food
> allergy, diabetes, celiac disease or another condition that limits what they can eat, their
> safe food is a second, separate number, and it is usually the one that runs out first. Plan
> both numbers together, or you will find the problem when it is too late to fix (→ 02-04).

## Do this now

1. **Know your daily number.** Your household needs about **{{ derived.calories.day }}
   calories a day** at an ordinary, moderately active level. Two weeks is about
   **{{ derived.calories.two_weeks }} calories**.
2. **Plan more in winter and for hard work.** Cold, hauling wood and water, and washing by
   hand all burn more. For most adults the "active" column of the same government table is
   200 to 400 calories a day higher than the moderate one (USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines
   2020-2025, Appendix 2).
3. **Count, do not estimate.** Your current estimate is **{{ gear.food.pantry_days }} days**
   of pantry food and **{{ gear.food.freeze_dried_servings }} freeze-dried servings**. Most
   households are wrong about this number. Count the shelf once, with the method below.
4. **Track any restricted diet separately.** If one person can eat only some of the food,
   work out their runway from their safe food only.
5. **Build in stages:** two weeks, then one month, then three months. Depth of food you
   already eat beats variety.
6. **Write the runway down** where everyone can see it (→ 23-02, → 22-04).

## How your number is worked out

The binder adds up one line per person from the published USDA/HHS table of estimated
calorie needs, using the **moderately active** column (USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines for
Americans 2020-2025, Appendix 2).

{{#each members as m}}
- **{{m.label}}**: {{m.age_text}}, {{m.sex}}. Daily need from the table below: ________ calories.
{{else}}
- No household members are entered yet. Add them in settings and this list fills in.
{{/each}}

**Household total: {{ derived.calories.day }} calories a day.** If the total shows a blank,
someone's age is missing in settings.

| Age | Male, moderately active | Female, moderately active |
|---|---|---|
| 12 to 23 months | about 1,000 (kit uses the top of the published 700 to 1,000) | about 1,000 |
| 2 | 1,000 | 1,000 |
| 3 | 1,400 | 1,200 |
| 4 to 5 | 1,400 | 1,400 |
| 6 | 1,600 | 1,400 |
| 7 to 8 | 1,600 | 1,600 |
| 9 | 1,800 | 1,600 |
| 10 | 1,800 | 1,800 |
| 11 | 2,000 | 1,800 |
| 12 to 13 | 2,200 | 2,000 |
| 14 | 2,400 | 2,000 |
| 15 | 2,600 | 2,000 |
| 16 to 18 | 2,800 | 2,000 |
| 19 to 25 | 2,800 | 2,200 |
| 26 to 45 | 2,600 | 2,000 |
| 46 to 50 | 2,400 | 2,000 |
| 51 to 65 | 2,400 | 1,800 |
| 66 and over | 2,200 | 1,800 |

Source: USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025, Appendix 2, printed as
published. Where sex is not entered the binder uses the higher figure, so the store is not
planned short.

- **Pregnant:** the binder adds **340 calories a day** (the published second-trimester
  figure; the Guidelines give nothing extra in the first trimester and 452 in the third).
  **Nursing:** it adds **330** (the published figure for the first 6 months of nursing; the
  Guidelines give 400 for months 7 to 12). All come from the same Guidelines and are printed as
  published. Plan the larger figure by hand for a pregnancy in its last three months or a baby
  over 6 months.
- **Babies under 12 months are not in the food total.** The Guidelines give no calorie figure
  for them: they live on breast milk or infant formula. Their plan is on → 02-13 and → 20-05.
  **Powdered or canned milk is not infant formula** (→ 04-14).
- **Toddlers 12 to 23 months need whole-fat food.** The dairy rule for them is on → 04-14 and
  the feeding plan on → 20-05.

## Turning calories into pounds

Rules of thumb that make this workable (worked from USDA FoodData Central values per 100 g;
your own labels govern):

- **1 lb of dry staples (rice, beans, flour, oats) is about 1,500 to 1,750 calories.** Dry
  white rice is about 1,650, dry white beans about 1,520, all-purpose flour about 1,650, oats
  about 1,760.
- **Pounds of dry staples per day, if you ate staples alone:** {{ derived.calories.day }} ÷
  1,600. Multiply by 30 for a month and by 90 for three months.
- **Fats and oils are about 4,000 calories per pound** (cooking oil is about 4,010), more than
  double any grain. They are the easiest way to close a calorie gap in a small space (→ 04-12).

### The runway is a sum

Count every layer: staples, canned goods, fats, and freeze-dried food. The number that goes on
the consumables table (→ 23-02) is:

> **(calories of staples on hand + calories of canned and other food on hand + calories of
> freeze-dried food on hand, from → 04-19) ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }} = days of runway**

No single layer is the number. If one person eats a restricted diet, work out their runway
the same way **from their safe food only**, using their own line from the table above.

How to count calories on hand: read the label (calories per serving × servings per package;
→ 29-14). For bulk buckets, weigh them and use the per-pound figures above. A kitchen scale
helps; → 29-13 has ways to estimate without one.

### The water cost: when water is short, eat the food that brings its own

Freeze-dried food is the best food when water is plentiful and the worst when it is not,
because you must add your stored water to eat it (→ 07-07, → 03-01). When the water runway is
the shorter one, turn the menu around:

| Food | Water it costs you to eat | Eat it when water is |
|---|---|---|
| **Canned goods** | **Lowest**: packed in their own liquid; drink it | **Short: eat these first** |
| Dry staples (rice, beans, oats) | Middle: real cooking water, some absorbed | Adequate |
| **Freeze-dried meals** | **Highest**: about 2 cups per pouch (the label governs) | **Plentiful: eat these last** |

## Medical diets change the plan

- **Food allergy.** One allergic person can remove a large share of the usual preparedness
  pantry. Build the family's staples from **single-ingredient foods** everyone can eat, keep any
  separate supply physically apart and labelled, and track the allergic person's safe-food
  runway as its own number: everyone else can eat almost anything; they cannot. Whether the
  rest of the household also eats that safe food, or keeps it as the allergic person's reserve,
  is a decision card: sharing shortens their runway, reserving means everyone else eats other
  food first. {{choice DC-26}} → 30-27. → 02-04. {{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Someone in your household has an allergy marked
  severe enough for anaphylaxis.** Their safe-food runway is the number that binds.{{/if}}
- **Diabetes.** Carbohydrate is dosing information, not just calories. Write the carbohydrate
  content on each container of staples; repeat known meals with known carbohydrate; keep fast
  sugar for treating lows separate and protected (→ 02-01, → 02-05, → 04-18).
- **Celiac disease and other gut conditions:** → 02-19.
- **Unlabelled, traded or scavenged food for someone with a food allergy** is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.

## What to store, by role

| Role | Foods | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Calorie base** | Rice, wheat, oats, corn, beans, potatoes | Cheap, dense, long-storing (→ 04-03) |
| **Fat** | Oil, lard, tallow, shortening | Calorie density; cooking (→ 04-12) |
| **Protein** | Dried beans, canned meat and fish, jerky | Beans and grain eaten together give complete protein |
| **Vitamins** | Canned and dried vegetables and fruit, sprouts (→ 04-16) | Scurvy (vitamin C lack) is a real risk over months |
| **Morale** | Sugar, coffee, tea, spices, cocoa | Not optional over months (→ 21-02) |
| **Medical** | Fast sugar for diabetics, oral rehydration salts | → 02-01, → 12-05 |

**Do not overlook vitamins.** A family living on rice and beans for six months develops real
deficiencies. Sprouting (→ 04-16), preserved vegetables and a garden (→ 05-01) are the
practical answers. A multivitamin is cheap insurance; check its label for allergens.

## Building it in stages

1. **Two weeks** of normal food you already eat.
2. **One month,** adding bulk staples and fats (→ 04-02, → 04-03).
3. **Three months,** adding the ability to preserve food (→ 04-04 to → 04-08).
4. **Beyond that** needs **production**: garden, animals, hunting, trade (Section 05, → 18-02).

**Storage alone does not carry a household through a long grid-down.** Every stored pound is
eaten once. Storage buys time to start producing.

## Leaving home: calories per pound decide what rides

When you leave home (Phase B) the limit is weight and space in the vehicle, not shelf space
(→ 01-03). Load by calories per pound, with one exception that comes first.

| Food | About calories per lb | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rendered fat, lard, shortening | **4,000** | Densest food in the house (→ 04-12) |
| Cooking oil | **4,000** | Jugs pack tight |
| Sugar | 1,750 | Dense and keeps for ever (→ 04-13) |
| Jerky | **1,800** | Ready-to-eat protein (USDA FoodData Central: about 410 calories per 100 g) |
| Freeze-dried pouches | Read the label: calories per serving × servings, ÷ the pouch weight in lb | Ready to eat; needs your water (→ 04-19) |
| Dry staples | 1,500 to 1,750 | Needs cooking fuel and water |
| Canned goods | **About 100 to 700** (vegetables low, meat and fish high) | You are hauling its water: cheap water, expensive weight |

(Figures worked from USDA FoodData Central per 100 g: oil 884, sugar 387; canned salmon 153,
canned capers 23. Labels govern.)

**One 50-lb bin, worked out** (use your own labels' figures; these are examples):

- of **dry staples** at about 1,600 per lb = about **80,000 calories**
- of **canned goods** at an assumed 500 per lb = about **25,000 calories**
- of **freeze-dried** pouches: work out calories per lb from the label, × 50

Divide each by {{ derived.calories.day }} to get household-days per bin. Same bin, same weight,
about three times the difference between staples and cans. Load dense.

**Grab order (write it on the bin lids):**

1. **Any allergy-safe or medical-diet bin, first, always.** It is the one kind of food that
   scavenging and charity cannot replace (→ 02-04). Density does not apply to it.
2. **Fats and oils:** the most calories per pound.
3. **Freeze-dried pouches:** dense and no cooking, but check the water plan (→ 03-01).
4. **Sugar, jerky, dry staples:** dense, but staples need fuel and water to become food.
5. **Canned goods last,** and only if weight remains; or on purpose, as food-plus-water for
   the first day on the road.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bulk staples: rice, beans, oats, flour, sugar, salt | The calorie base | Storage method → 04-03 |
| Cooking oil, shortening, lard | Calorie density | Check labels for allergens (→ 04-12) |
| Plain canned vegetables, fruit, meat | Vitamins and protein | Single-ingredient, readable labels |
| Separate stock for any restricted diet | Usually the binding number | Track its own runway; who eats it is DC-26 (→ 30-27) |
| Kitchen scale and measuring cups | Real numbers; carbohydrate counting | Also for canning and curing |
| Written inventory and calorie sheet | Planning needs numbers | → 22-04, → 23-02 |
| Multivitamins | Cheap insurance against deficiency | Check allergens on the label |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Single-ingredient staples in sealed original packaging** are the safest food to scavenge
  or trade for, and the easiest to check for allergens.
- Garden produce (→ 05-01) is fully traceable.
- Fats are the hardest food to find later and the most valuable per pound. Get them early.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** total calories on hand (every layer, summed) ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }}. Write
  it on → 23-02. Then work out each restricted diet's separate runway from that person's safe
  food only; it is usually shorter.
- **Ration:** many households cut adult portions before children's. Keep a diabetic's
  carbohydrate steady rather than cut. Never ration an allergic person into eating unchecked
  food.
- **Resupply:** production (Section 05), preserving gluts (→ 04-04 to → 04-08), trade (→ 18-02).
- **The honest limit:** storage buys months. Only production buys years.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** build the stockpile now; it is the cheapest phase to do it in.
- **B (moving):** you carry days, not months: dense, ready to eat, and safe for everyone who
  travels (→ 01-03). Use the grab order above.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** storage plus growing; the planting calendar becomes the
  plan (→ 25-01).

## Cross-references

→ 04-02 building a pantry · → 04-03 bulk staples · → 04-12 fats · → 04-19 freeze-dried food ·
→ 03-01 water · → 02-04 food allergy · → 02-01 diabetes · → 02-13 infant feeding ·
→ 23-02 consumables table

pages.title: Building a shelf-stable pantry

photo_slots.caption: Our deep pantry: where it is, which shelf is oldest, where the can openers live

pages.body:
# Building a shelf-stable pantry

**What this page is for.** How to build a store of food that keeps without a fridge, in the
right order, on a budget, and in a way that it actually gets eaten and replaced. "Shelf-stable"
means sealed food that keeps at room temperature: cans, jars, boxes and dry goods.

> **CAUTION.** The pantry that saves you is the one you **actually eat from**. A wall of
> unfamiliar buckets you never open is a museum, not a food supply: you will not know how to
> cook it, whether your family will eat it, or whether **everyone in the house can safely eat
> it** (→ 02-04). Build a deep version of your normal diet, and rotate through it.

## Do this now

1. **Buy what you already eat,** in the forms you already cook. Then buy more of it.
2. **Check every label against every allergy in the house** before you buy in bulk (below).
3. **Store the deep stock where you can see it** and use it. Out of sight is out of rotation.
4. **Date everything on purchase,** in marker, on the item.
5. **Add a little each shopping trip** rather than one big buy. It is cheaper and builds the
   habit.
6. **Buy two manual can openers.** It is the single most forgotten item.

## Build it in layers

| Layer | Target | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Working pantry** | 1 to 2 weeks | Normal food, just more of it. Deep and familiar |
| **2. Extended** | 1 month | Canned goods, pasta, rice, oil, shelf-stable milk |
| **3. Bulk staples** | 3 months or more | Grains, beans, flour, sugar, salt in proper storage (→ 04-03) |
| **4. Preserving equipment** | Ongoing | Jars, lids, salt, a canner, a dehydrator (→ 04-04 to → 04-08) |
| **5. Production** | Years | Seeds, garden, animals (Section 05) |

**Most people jump to layer 3 and skip layers 1 and 2.** That is backwards. The first two
weeks are the emergency you are most likely to face, and they cost the least to prepare for.
Your household's two-week calorie number is on → 04-01.

## The allergen check: do this before you buy in bulk

US food labels must name nine major allergens: **milk, egg, fish, shellfish, tree nuts,
peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame** (FDA, Food Allergies). Sesame was added most recently.
How to read the ingredient list and the "Contains" line: → 29-14.

{{#each allergies as a}}
- **{{a.member}}:** {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}})
{{else}}
- No allergies are entered for your household. If that changes, add them in settings.
{{/each}}

Traps that catch people:

- **"Vegetable oil"** in the US is usually **soybean oil.** Highly refined oils are treated
  differently under the labelling law, so ask the allergist whether a refined oil is safe for
  your allergic person before you stock it (→ 04-12).
- **Soy lecithin** is in a huge range of packaged food, especially anything with chocolate.
- **Sesame** turns up in breads, buns, crackers, seasoning blends and hummus.
- **Egg** is in pasta, baked goods, mayonnaise and many prepared mixes.
- **An allergen that is not one of the nine never appears in a "Contains" line.** Read the
  whole ingredient list for it.
- **Most freeze-dried "bucket" systems and ration bars contain soy, and many contain egg.** Do
  not buy a year of food an allergic person cannot eat. → 04-19 has a product-by-product check.
- **Recipes change without notice.** A product that was safe last year is not checked this
  year. Read the label on the package in your hand.

**Keep a photo or the cut-out label** of anything you repackage (→ 04-03). Feeding an allergic
person unlabelled, traded or scavenged food is a decision card: {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.

## The rotation habit

**First in, first out** (FIFO): the oldest food gets eaten first. The mechanics matter more
than the intention:

- **Date everything** on purchase, in large marker, where you can read it.
- **Shelve new behind old,** so the oldest is what your hand reaches.
- **Cook from the deep stock** on a regular rotation, and replace what you use.
- **Run a "pantry week"** every few months: cook only from stores. It finds what has expired,
  what nobody will eat, and what you do not know how to cook (→ 04-10).

{{photo pantry-shelves}}

## What actually keeps

| Food | Realistic shelf life | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Salt, sugar, honey | **Indefinite** | Buy heavily (→ 04-13) |
| White rice, dried beans, wheat berries | Decades, properly stored | → 04-03 |
| Rolled oats, pasta, flour | 1 to 5 years | Flour is the shortest; whole-grain flour goes rancid |
| Canned goods | Years, if the can is sound | USDA: safe indefinitely if not frozen or kept above 90 °F and in good condition; quality fades (USDA FSIS, Shelf-Stable Food Safety) |
| Cooking oil | 1 to 2 years | Rancidity is the limit (→ 04-12) |
| Powdered milk | Years | → 04-14 |
| Freeze-dried | Long, if stored cool | Manufacturer claims assume cool storage (→ 04-19) |
| Spices | Years (flavour fades) | Morale value (→ 21-02) |

Dented, rusted, bulging or leaking cans: → 04-10 and → 04-17.

## Money and pacing

- **A little every trip** beats one large purchase. It spreads the cost and builds the habit.
- **Buy sales in bulk** on things that keep: salt, rice, canned goods.
- **Prioritise by what fails first:** water (→ 03-02), then calories, then variety.
- **Do not buy anything you have not cooked.** Test it first.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Sturdy shelving in a cool, dark place | What you can see gets rotated | A basement or interior closet is usually best |
| Permanent markers | Date everything | Buy a pack |
| Airtight containers, food-grade buckets | Bulk storage (→ 04-03) | Screw-top ("gamma") lids for working buckets |
| **Two manual can openers** | The most forgotten item | One always fails |
| Written inventory sheet | You cannot plan what you have not counted | → 22-04 |
| Saved labels for repackaged food | Allergen checking | Tape inside the lid |
| A separate, labelled shelf for any allergy-safe food | Physical separation | → 02-04 |

**If you don't have it:**

- Any shelf, any cool dark corner, any sealed container.
- **Single-ingredient staples in original sealed packaging** are the best thing to acquire:
  cheap, easy to check, and the safest for anyone with an allergy.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** see → 04-01. Track the household total and any restricted diet's separate number.
- **Ration:** eat perishables first, then the working pantry, then bulk staples. Where one
  person eats an allergy-safe diet, whether their safe stock is shared by everyone or held as
  their reserve is a decision card: sharing shortens their runway, reserving means everyone
  else eats other food first. {{choice DC-26}} → 30-27. Write it on the allergy plan (→ 02-04).
- **Resupply:** preserving (→ 04-04 to → 04-08) and production (Section 05).
- **The rotation failure:** the most common way a stockpile fails is quietly expiring while
  unused. A pantry you cook from never has that problem.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** build it now: this is the cheapest, easiest phase.
- **B (moving):** you take days of food, not months: dense, no-cook, safe for everyone
  (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the pantry seeds the new site; bring staples and seeds,
  leave the shelving.

## Cross-references

→ 04-01 calorie math · → 04-03 bulk staples · → 04-10 rotation and inventory ·
→ 04-19 freeze-dried food · → 04-12 fats · → 04-13 salt and sugar · → 02-04 food allergy ·
→ 22-01 acquisition list

pages.title: Long-term bulk staples: grains, beans, sugar and salt

photo_slots.caption: Our bulk buckets: where they sit, how they are labelled, which one is the working bucket

pages.body:
# Long-term bulk staples: grains, beans, sugar and salt

**What this page is for.** How to pack dry staples (rice, wheat, beans, oats, sugar, salt) so
they keep for years or decades, which foods do not keep, and how to cook stored beans safely.

> **CAUTION.** Two real hazards. **Moisture:** sealing damp food in an oxygen-free bucket grows
> mould and, in the wrong conditions, botulism (a deadly toxin, → 29-08). **Only dry,
> low-moisture foods go into oxygen-free storage.** **Rodents and insects:** a chewed bucket is
> a lost bucket, and they will find it (→ 04-11).

## Do this now

1. **Store only truly dry staples** in sealed, oxygen-free containers: white rice, wheat,
   dried beans, oats, pasta, sugar, salt, powdered milk.
2. **Never** seal moist food, fresh produce, brown rice (its oil goes rancid) or anything oily
   in oxygen-free storage.
3. **Use food-grade buckets, Mylar liner bags and oxygen absorbers** for anything you want to
   keep for a decade (method below).
4. **Label the outside** with contents, weight and date, plus **the ingredient label** if
   anyone in the house has a food allergy (→ 02-04).
5. **Lift it off concrete** and keep it cool, dark and dry.
6. **Dried kidney-type beans must boil hard before any slow cooking** (rule below).

## What stores for decades, and what does not

| Food | Realistic life (sealed, cool) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **White rice** | 25 to 30 years | The benchmark storage staple |
| **Wheat berries** (whole wheat grains) | 25 to 30 years | Needs a grain grinder (→ 16-01) |
| **Dried beans, lentils** | 25 to 30 years (harder to cook with age) | Soak longer as they age |
| **Rolled oats** | 20 to 25 years | Good with children |
| **Pasta** | 20 to 25 years | Check for egg in the ingredients |
| **Sugar, salt** | **Indefinite** | No oxygen absorbers with sugar: it sets hard |
| **Powdered milk** | 10 to 20 years (nonfat) | → 04-14 |
| **Brown rice** | **6 to 12 months** | Its oil goes rancid: **not** a long-term staple |
| **Whole-grain flour** | Months | Same problem; store the **grain**, not the flour |
| **Cooking oil** | 1 to 2 years | Cannot be stored long; rotate (→ 04-12) |
| **Nuts and seeds** | Months to 1 year | Oil content; also common allergens |

**The pattern: oil is what spoils.** Whole grains keep far longer than flour, white rice far
longer than brown. **Store the raw material and process it as you need it**, which is why a
hand grain grinder is an important purchase.

## The container system

1. **Food-grade bucket** (HDPE plastic marked food-safe), 5 or 6 gallons.
2. **Mylar liner bag.** This is the real oxygen and moisture barrier; plastic alone lets air
   through slowly.
3. **Oxygen absorbers,** sized to the volume: **about 2,000 cc per 5 to 6 gallon Mylar-lined
   bucket; 300 to 500 cc per #10 can or 1-gallon bag** (Utah State University Extension).
   They remove oxygen, which kills insects and slows rancidity. **They start working the moment
   the pack is opened and are spent after about 30 minutes in air.** Open the pack, work fast,
   and **reseal the unused absorbers in a jar or vacuum bag within 15 to 30 minutes.** A Mylar
   bag that has pulled tight by the next day is working. **Absorbers are not desiccants** (they
   do not dry food): the food must already be dry (under about 10 percent moisture) or you have
   sealed in mould.
4. **Seal the Mylar** with a clothes iron or a hair straightener, then lid the bucket.
5. **Label the outside:** contents, weight, date packed, and the ingredient label.

{{figure fig-mylar-bucket-pack}}

**No oxygen absorbers with:** sugar or brown sugar (they set into a brick), salt (not needed),
or anything with real moisture or oil in it.

**A working bucket** with a screw-top ("gamma") lid for the staple you are eating now, plus
sealed buckets for the deep stock, is the practical arrangement.

## Where to store it

- **Cool, dark, dry, steady.** Heat shortens storage life fast (→ 04-19 has the Utah State
  figures).
- **Off the concrete:** pallets, boards or shelving. Concrete wicks moisture and swings in
  temperature.
- {{#if has.basement}}**Your basement is usually the best place.**{{else}}**An interior closet
  or the coolest room is usually the best place.**{{/if}} Attics and garages are not: too hot
  and too changeable.
- **Spread it out.** Do not keep everything in one place (fire, flood, theft).

{{photo bulk-bucket-store}}

## Allergen discipline for bulk food

Repackaging throws away the label. If anyone in the house has a food allergy (→ 02-04):

- **Cut out the ingredient panel and tape it inside the lid,** or file it in a sheet.
- **Label the bucket boldly** as safe or not safe for that person.
- **Never share scoops** between an allergen-containing bucket and a safe one.
- **Single-ingredient staples** (plain rice, plain beans, plain oats) are the safest to
  bulk-store because there is nothing hidden to check.

## Using bulk staples

- **A grain grinder** turns wheat into flour; a hand-cranked one works with no power (→ 16-01).
- **Beans need long cooking.** Pair them with an insulated "haybox" cooker (→ 07-02) to cut
  fuel.
- **The kidney-bean rule.** For any *Phaseolus* bean (kidney, red, white, pinto, black):
  **soak at least 5 hours, THROW AWAY the soak water, then hold a full rolling boil for at
  least 10 minutes (FDA says 30) BEFORE any haybox or slow finish.** Raw or half-cooked
  kidney beans carry a natural toxin (a lectin called phytohaemagglutinin): **4 or 5 raw
  beans can cause hours of violent vomiting and diarrhoea** (FDA, Bad Bug Book). A slow,
  low-temperature cook (about 80 °C, 176 °F) makes it **worse**, not better. Never cook dry
  beans from raw in a haybox alone. Canned beans are already safe.
- **Sprouting** turns stored grains and beans into fresh greens in winter (→ 04-16).
- **Old beans get harder.** Soak longer, cook longer, or use a pressure cooker.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Food-grade buckets (many) | The container | 5 to 6 gallon; often free from bakeries |
| **Mylar liner bags** | The real oxygen and moisture barrier | Sized to the bucket |
| **Oxygen absorbers** | Stops insects, slows rancidity | About 2,000 cc per 5 to 6 gal bucket; 300 to 500 cc per #10 can; reseal spares within 15 to 30 min |
| Screw-top ("gamma") lids | Working buckets you open often | A few |
| Impulse sealer or a clothes iron | Sealing Mylar | An iron works |
| **Hand grain grinder** | Wheat is useless without it | Test it now |
| Bulk white rice, wheat, beans, oats, sugar, salt | The calorie base | → 04-01 |
| Pallets or shelving | Off the concrete | Often free |
| Labels, marker, saved ingredient panels | Rotation and allergen safety | → 02-04 |
| Rodent-proof outer protection | They chew buckets | → 04-11 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Bakery and restaurant buckets** are often free and food-grade. Ask what was in them; avoid
  anything oily or strong-smelling.
- Glass jars with tight lids are excellent for smaller amounts.
- Metal cans and bins stop rodents better than plastic (→ 04-11).
- Original packaging inside a sealed tote is a reasonable first step.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** pounds on hand ÷ daily use (→ 04-01). Bulk staples are the backbone of the
  household runway.
- **Ration:** stretch grains with sprouting (→ 04-16) and beans; add fat for calories (→ 04-12).
- **Resupply:** growing grain at household scale is hard on a small lot, so **bulk staples are
  a finite, buy-it-now resource.** The move is to garden vegetables (→ 05-01), game (→ 05-07)
  and trade (→ 18-02).
- **The honest limit:** you cannot store your way to years. You can store your way to a year,
  and use that year to start producing.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** buy and pack now. Cool storage, spread out, labelled.
- **B (moving):** buckets are heavy; take what fits, and know what you are leaving (→ 01-05).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** better storage space; same rules. Rodent pressure is
  usually higher (→ 04-11).

## Cross-references

→ 04-01 calorie math · → 04-02 pantry · → 04-11 pests · → 04-12 fats · → 04-16 sprouting ·
→ 07-02 haybox for beans · → 16-01 grain grinder · → 02-04 food allergy

pages.title: Water-bath canning (high-acid foods)
pages.body:
# Water-bath canning (high-acid foods)

**What this page is for.** How boiling-water canning works, which foods it is safe for, how to
adjust for your altitude, and when to throw a jar out. It teaches the method. The tested
recipes, with their process times, are in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning. If canning
words are new to you, read → 29-08 first.

> **SAFETY.** Botulism is a toxin that paralyses, including the breathing muscles. It is
> invisible, has no smell or taste, and can kill.
>
> **Floor:** **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not
> canned.** Botulism has no field treatment and the food looks and smells normal (→ 30-01).
>
> High-acid foods only in a boiling-water canner; everything low-acid goes to a pressure
> canner (→ 04-05). **Never** invent a recipe, never cut the acid, and never use an old family
> recipe that contradicts current USDA guidance. **Use a current tested recipe every time.**

## Do this now

1. **Have the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015 revision) where you can read it with
   no internet.** {{#if size.large}}Your binder carries it: the Introduction and all seven
   Guides are bound at the end of this section, after the last food-storage page, and the
   "Sources for this page" list below links to each one. If a Guide could not be downloaded
   when the binder was made, it is named on the "Sources not captured" page in Section 25:
   get a paper copy of that one.{{else}}Your binder is the Small download, which cites the
   Guide but does not carry it. Make the Large or Everything download, or keep a paper copy.
   **Without it, this binder holds no tested recipe and no process time, and you must not can
   from memory.**{{/if}} A current tested recipe book is a sensible second copy.
2. **Water-bath ONLY these:** fruits, jams and jellies, pickles, and **properly acidified**
   tomatoes and salsas.
3. **Never water-bath:** vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, beans, soups or anything low-acid.
   Those are pressure-canning foods, no exceptions (→ 04-05).
4. **Acidify tomatoes. For whole, crushed or juiced tomatoes: per PINT, 1 tablespoon bottled
   lemon juice OR ¼ teaspoon citric acid; per QUART, 2 tablespoons bottled lemon juice OR
   ½ teaspoon citric acid** (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 3). Put it in the jar before filling.
   **Bottled** juice only: fresh lemons vary. Vinegar of 5 percent acidity also works, at
   4 tablespoons per quart, but may change the flavour (Guide 3). Salsas and mixed tomato
   recipes print their own acid amounts: use the recipe's. Tomatoes are not reliably acidic
   enough on their own, and pH strips are unreliable in coloured food: the acid goes in
   whatever a strip says.
5. **Adjust the process time for your altitude** (table below). If the recipe prints its own
   altitude table, **the recipe's table governs.**
6. **Before eating ANY home-canned tomatoes or low-acid food, yours or anyone else's, boil it
   hard in an open pan for 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft of elevation,** liquid
   included (CDC, Botulism Prevention). Your times are in the table below. Heat destroys the
   toxin; this is the cheap backstop when the process is doubtful or unknown (a traded jar, a
   jar you are unsure of). **It does not rescue a bulging, leaking or foul jar: those are thrown
   away unopened.** The same rule is on → 04-05.

## Your altitude

Water boils at a lower temperature the higher you live, so boiling-water processes need more
time up high.

Your home is about **{{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft** above sea level.
{{#if is.high_altitude}}**That is above 5,000 ft: every recipe needs its altitude row, and the
extra time is large.**{{/if}}
{{#each destinations as x}}
- {{x.name}}: about {{x.region.elevation_ft}} ft.
{{/each}}

**Boiling-water canner: time to add to the recipe's process time** (South Dakota State
University Extension, Altitude Adjustments for Home Canning). The USDA recipes print their own
altitude rows, usually in these same steps to 6,000 ft (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 1, the
peaches example); **when the recipe has its own table, it governs.** The 8,001 to 10,000 ft row
is from the Extension table only.

| Elevation | Add to the process time |
|---|---|
| 0 to 1,000 ft | Nothing: use the recipe time |
| 1,001 to 3,000 ft | **5 minutes** |
| 3,001 to 6,000 ft | **10 minutes** |
| 6,001 to 8,000 ft | **15 minutes** |
| 8,001 to 10,000 ft | **20 minutes** |

**CDC pre-eating boil** for home-canned tomatoes and low-acid food: boil 10 minutes, and add
1 minute for each additional 1,000 ft of elevation (CDC, Botulism Prevention). This table counts
any part of 1,000 ft as a whole 1,000, so it never gives less time than CDC; boiling longer does
no harm.

| Elevation | Boil hard, open pan, before eating |
|---|---|
| Sea level | 10 minutes |
| Up to 1,000 ft | 11 minutes |
| 1,001 to 2,000 ft | 12 minutes |
| 2,001 to 3,000 ft | 13 minutes |
| 3,001 to 4,000 ft | 14 minutes |
| 4,001 to 5,000 ft | 15 minutes |
| 5,001 to 6,000 ft | 16 minutes |
| 6,001 to 7,000 ft | 17 minutes |
| 7,001 to 8,000 ft | 18 minutes |
| 8,001 to 9,000 ft | 19 minutes |
| 9,001 to 10,000 ft | 20 minutes |

## Why acidity decides everything

*Clostridium botulinum* spores are common in soil and are **not killed by boiling water**.
What stops them is **acid**: at pH 4.6 or below (→ 29-08), the spores cannot grow and make
toxin. So:

- **High-acid (pH 4.6 or lower):** fruit, pickles, properly acidified tomatoes. Boiling water
  is enough, because it only has to kill the organisms that spoil food, not botulism spores.
- **Low-acid (pH above 4.6):** vegetables, meat, fish, beans. These **must** reach the
  temperatures only a pressure canner reaches (→ 04-05).

**This is not a preference. It is the whole reason home canning is safe or lethal.**

## The method

1. **Inspect jars.** Throw out any with chips or cracks. **Use new lids each time;** bands are
   reusable.
2. **Wash and heat** the jars; keep them hot so they do not crack.
3. **Prepare the food to a tested recipe,** including the acid it specifies.
4. **Fill the jars,** leaving the **headspace** (empty space at the top) the recipe gives. It
   decides whether a seal forms.
5. **Remove air bubbles,** wipe the rim completely clean (a smear of food stops a seal), fit the
   lid, and screw the band on fingertip-tight, not hard.
6. **Load the canner,** jars on a rack, with **at least 1 inch of water over the jar tops**
   (at least 2 inches if the process is longer than 30 minutes) (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 1).
7. **Bring to a full rolling boil, then start timing.** Add the altitude time from the table.
8. **Turn off the heat, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars out** and set them on a towel,
   undisturbed, for 12 to 24 hours.
9. **Check the seals:** the lid is pulled down (concave) and does not flex. **Any unsealed jar
   goes in the fridge and is eaten now,** or is reprocessed with a new lid.
10. **Remove the bands, wipe, label with contents and date,** and store cool and dark.

{{figure fig-jar-headspace-and-seal}}

## When to throw it out: no exceptions

Throw away, without tasting, any jar that:

- has a **bulging or unsealed lid,** or spurts when opened
- shows **mould, cloudiness or bubbling**
- smells **wrong**
- has leaked, or has food dried under the lid

**Never taste to check.** Put it where children and animals cannot reach it. Eating food from
a doubtful but sealed, normal-looking jar is a decision card: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15. Bulging,
leaking or spurting jars are not part of that choice: they are thrown away.

## Canning without the grid

Water-bath canning works over an outdoor fire (→ 07-01) or a camp burner (→ 07-05): it needs only
a big pot, a rack and a hard, steady boil.

- **It uses a lot of fuel** (→ 06-04). Do a full canner load per fire, not one jar.
- **Holding a rolling boil for the whole process time** is the real challenge on wood. Build
  the fire for it and have wood ready.
- **A windbreak cuts the fuel cost a great deal** (→ 07-01).
- **Open flame indoors** (a camp stove in the kitchen) is a decision card: {{choice DC-20}}
  → 30-21.

## Allergen note

Home canning suits a food-allergic household: you know every ingredient because you put it in
(→ 02-04). **Label the allergy-safe jars distinctly** and keep them apart. Watch for shared
equipment and surfaces, and for recipes that add a common allergen.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Boiling-water canner and rack (or a big stockpot and rack) | The vessel | Deep enough for 1 to 2 in of water over the jars |
| **Mason jars** (pints and quarts), many | Reusable for decades | Check for chips every use |
| **Lids: a large stock** | **Single-use: the real consumable** | Buy deep, or a reusable-lid system |
| Bands | Reusable | A few spares |
| Jar lifter, funnel, bubble tool, magnetic lid lifter | Safety and speed | Cheap kit |
| **USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015), all seven Guides** | The tested recipes and times | Bound in the Large and Everything downloads; a paper copy is good insurance |
| pH strips (optional) | Curiosity only | **Never a substitute for the printed acid amounts** |
| Bottled lemon juice, citric acid, 5 percent vinegar | Acidifying | → 04-13; bottled for known acidity |
| Labels and marker | Contents and date | Not optional |

**If you don't have it:**

- Any large pot with a rack (or a folded towel on the bottom) works as a canner.
- **Jars are easy to find second-hand; lids are not.** Lids are the thing to stockpile.
- Commercial food jars (from pasta sauce and the like) are generally **not** suitable: mason
  jars are made for the heat stress.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** **lids** are the limiting consumable. Count them: one lid per jar per batch.
- **Ration:** keep canning for foods that really need it; use drying (→ 04-06), fermenting
  (→ 04-08) and winter cold (→ 04-09) for the rest. None of those use lids.
- **Resupply:** reusable-lid systems are a real long-term answer; buy some now. Fermenting and
  drying need no consumables at all.
- **The strategic point:** canning is your highest-quality preserving method and the most
  dependent on consumables. Fermenting and drying are the methods that last.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** learn it now, on the kitchen stove, with a tested recipe.
- **B (moving):** jars are heavy and fragile; this does not travel.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the core way to keep a garden surplus; pair it with
  fermenting and drying to save lids.

## Cross-references

→ 04-05 pressure canning (everything low-acid) · → 29-08 canning words · → 04-06 drying ·
→ 04-08 fermenting · → 04-13 salt, sugar and vinegar · → 07-01 canning over a fire ·
→ 30-01 the floors · → 30-15 questionable food

pages.body:
# Pressure canning (low-acid foods) and botulism safety

**What this page is for.** How to can vegetables, beans, meat, poultry, fish, soups and stocks
safely, how to set the pressure for your altitude, and what to do with a jar you are not sure
about. The tested recipes, with their times and pressures, are in the USDA Complete Guide to
Home Canning. If canning words are new to you, read → 29-08 first.

> **SAFETY. THIS IS THE MOST DANGEROUS PAGE IN THE FOOD SECTION.**
>
> **Floor:** **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not
> canned.** Botulism has no field treatment and the food looks and smells normal (→ 30-01).
>
> Low-acid foods (vegetables, meat, poultry, fish, beans, soups, stocks) can only be home-canned
> safely in a **pressure canner**. A boiling-water canner **cannot** reach the temperature that
> destroys botulism spores. Getting this wrong makes jars that look, smell and taste normal and
> can kill your family. **Use a current tested recipe with its pressure and time, every batch.**

## Do this now

1. **Never** water-bath a low-acid food. Not "just this once", not a family recipe, not a recipe
   from a website or video.
2. **Have the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015) where you can read it with no
   internet.** Guides 1, 4 and 5 carry the low-acid and meat processes. {{#if size.large}}Your
   binder carries them: they are bound at the end of this section, after the last food-storage
   page, and the "Sources for this page" list below links to each one. If a Guide could not be
   downloaded when the binder was made, it is named on the "Sources not captured" page in
   Section 25: get a paper copy of that one.{{else}}Your binder is the Small download, which
   cites the Guide but does not carry it. Make the Large or Everything download, or keep a
   paper copy. **Without it, this binder holds no tested process for any low-acid food.**{{/if}}
3. **Set the pressure for your altitude** (table below). Time stays as the recipe says; only the
   pressure changes. If the recipe's own table differs, **the recipe's table governs.**
4. **Get a dial gauge tested every year** (Extension offices did this before the collapse). **A
   dial gauge that reads more than 2 psi off is replaced, not "corrected for"** (USDA Complete
   Guide, Guide 1). **Weighted gauges** need no testing, which is a real advantage off-grid.
5. **Vent the canner for 10 minutes of steady steam** before bringing it to pressure (USDA
   Complete Guide, Guide 1). Trapped air lowers the real temperature and is a classic cause of unsafe batches.
6. **Run the full process time.** Do not shorten it because the fire is dying.
7. **Backstop before eating ANY home-canned low-acid food, yours or anyone else's: boil it hard
   in an open pan 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft of elevation,** liquid included (CDC,
   Botulism Prevention). Your time is in the table below. Heat destroys the toxin; this is the
   one cheap safety net for a jar from a doubtful or unknown process. **It does not rescue a
   bulging, leaking or foul jar: those are thrown away unopened.**

## Your altitude

Your home is about **{{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft** above sea level.
{{#if is.high_altitude}}**That is above 5,000 ft. A dial gauge needs at least 13 psi there, and
more higher up; check the table every time.**{{/if}}
{{#each destinations as x}}
- {{x.name}}: about {{x.region.elevation_ft}} ft.
{{/each}}

**Pressure to use, by gauge type.** The rows to 8,000 ft are the steps printed in the USDA
vegetable and meat tables (USDA Complete Guide, Guides 4 and 5). USDA's tables stop at
8,000 ft; the 8,001 to 10,000 ft row is from South Dakota State University Extension (Altitude
Adjustments for Home Canning). The recipe's own table governs if it differs.

| Elevation | Weighted gauge | Dial gauge |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 1,000 ft | **10 psi** | **11 psi** |
| 1,001 to 2,000 ft | **15 psi** | **11 psi** |
| 2,001 to 4,000 ft | **15 psi** | **12 psi** |
| 4,001 to 6,000 ft | **15 psi** | **13 psi** |
| 6,001 to 8,000 ft | **15 psi** | **14 psi** |
| 8,001 to 10,000 ft | **15 psi** | **15 psi** |

A weighted gauge has only two settings that matter here: 10 psi is good only to 1,000 ft;
above that, use 15.

**CDC pre-eating boil:** 10 minutes, plus 1 minute for each additional 1,000 ft of elevation
(CDC, Botulism Prevention). Counting any part of 1,000 ft as a whole 1,000, which never gives
less than CDC: sea level 10 minutes; up to 1,000 ft 11; 1,001 to 2,000 ft 12; 2,001 to 3,000 ft
13; and one more minute for each further 1,000 ft (the full table is on → 04-04).

## Why pressure is not optional

Botulism spores survive boiling. Water boils at **212 °F** at sea level, and no amount of longer
boiling makes a low-acid food safe. The spores are destroyed reliably only at the higher
temperatures a **pressure canner** reaches, **about 240 to 250 °F (116 to 121 °C)** depending on
the pressure held (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 1). That is why USDA processes for home-canned vegetables other than tomatoes
have used pressure only since 1943, and why boiling-water, oven and "open-kettle" canning have
been called unsafe for low-acid food ever since (NCHFP, Principles of Home Canning). In a
sealed, airless, low-acid jar at room temperature, surviving spores grow and make **botulinum
toxin**, one of the most poisonous substances known.

**There is no look, smell or taste test.** That is the whole reason canning rules are rigid.

**A pressure cooker is not necessarily a pressure canner.** Many electric multi-cookers are
**not** tested for canning low-acid food. Use equipment the maker states is for canning.

## The method

1. **Use a tested recipe** for that exact food. Note its **pressure, time and altitude
   adjustment.**
2. **Prepare jars and food. Hot pack or raw pack exactly as the recipe says** (the time was
   tested for that pack, not the other); fill to the stated headspace; wipe rims; new lids;
   fingertip-tight bands. **Use the jar sizes the recipe lists.** Half-gallon jars are for very
   acid juices only, never for low-acid food (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 1).
3. **Add the stated amount of water** to the canner (usually 2 to 3 inches of hot water, USDA
   Guide 1; pressure canners use far less water than water-bath canners).
4. **Lock the lid; heat until a steady stream of steam comes from the vent; vent for the full
   stated time** (commonly 10 minutes).
5. **Close the vent** (put the weight on or close the petcock); let the pressure rise to the
   level for your altitude.
6. **Start timing only when the correct pressure is reached.** If the pressure drops below the
   target at any point, **bring it back up and start the timing again from zero.**
7. **Turn off the heat; let the pressure fall to zero on its own.** **Never** cool it with water
   or lift the weight early: that causes liquid loss, seal failure and burns.
8. **When the gauge reads zero: remove the weight (or open the petcock), WAIT 10 MINUTES, then
   unfasten the lid and lift it away from your face** (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 1). Opening
   early means liquid loss, failed seals and a steam burn. Lift the jars out and leave them
   undisturbed 12 to 24 hours.
9. **Check seals, remove bands, label with contents and date,** store cool and dark.

{{figure fig-pressure-canner-parts}}

{{photo our-pressure-canner}}

## Canning meat: the big win

This is how you keep a deer or a batch of chickens without a freezer (→ 05-09). Canned meat is
shelf-stable, ready to eat, and needs no fuel later to cook it.

- **USDA and NCHFP have specific procedures for meat, poultry and game** (Guide 5; NCHFP,
  Canning Meat, Poultry and Game). Use them.
- **Can it promptly** after butchering; meat does not wait. USDA's meat recipes start from
  chilled meat (Guide 5): keep it at 40 °F or colder, below the 40 to 140 °F danger zone,
  until it goes in the jars (→ 04-09, → 04-17).
- **Batch it.** A whole animal is many jars and a lot of fuel (→ 06-04).

## Pressure canning without the grid: the honest difficulty

- **You must hold a steady pressure for a long time.** On a wood fire that means constant
  attention and feeding; much harder than a water bath (→ 04-04).
- **A propane burner is far easier to control** than wood (→ 07-05). It is one of the best uses
  of stored propane. Run it outdoors.
- **Floor:** **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.**
  Vapour ignition (→ 30-01). Change cylinders with the burner off and cool.
- **Open-flame cooking indoors** is a decision card: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21.
- **Do not can on an unsteady fire** with a heavy canner and small children nearby. Burns and a
  tipped canner are the realistic injuries.

## If a jar fails

- **Unsealed within 24 hours:** refrigerate and eat now, or reprocess with a new lid.
- **Any bulging lid, spurting liquid, cloudiness, mould or bad smell:** **throw it away without
  tasting,** where children and animals cannot get it.
- **If you think a batch was processed wrongly** (pressure dropped, wrong time, unknown recipe),
  the published advice is to treat the whole batch as unsafe. Whether a household eats a sealed,
  normal-looking jar after the CDC boil when food is short is a decision card: {{choice DC-14}}
  → 30-15. Bulging, leaking, spurting or foul jars are not part of that choice: they are
  thrown away.
- **Home-canned food from someone else** has an unknown process. For anyone with a food allergy
  it also has unknown ingredients: {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pressure canner** (not just a pressure cooker) | The only safe low-acid method | "Pressure canner" usually means 16 quarts or more; USDA's tested times were set in 17- to 21-quart canners, and smaller cookers are not recommended (NCHFP) |
| **Weighted gauge** (or a tested dial gauge) | Weighted needs no yearly test | A big off-grid advantage |
| Spare gasket, safety plug, weights | The canner's wear parts | Model-specific; buy now |
| Mason jars and a **large stock of new lids** | The consumable | → 04-04 |
| **USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015)** | Guides 1, 4 and 5 carry the low-acid and meat processes | Bound in the Large and Everything downloads; a paper copy is good insurance |
| Jar lifter, funnel, headspace tool | Safe handling | Cheap |
| Propane burner and fuel | Controllable heat for long processes | → 07-05; outdoors |
| Timer and thermometer | Process discipline | A wind-up timer works |
| Labels and marker | Contents, date, batch | Not optional |

**If you don't have it:**

- **There is no substitute for a pressure canner** for low-acid food. Without one, keep
  low-acid food by **drying** (→ 04-06), **fermenting** by a tested recipe (→ 04-08),
  **curing and smoking** (→ 04-07) or **freezing and winter cold** (→ 04-09). Not by
  water-bath canning.
- Used canners are common. **Replace the gasket and have a dial gauge tested** before you trust
  one.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** lids again, plus the canner's gasket. **Buy spare gaskets now:** a perished gasket
  makes the canner useless, and it is a model-specific part.
- **Ration:** pressure-can the foods that most need it (meat especially); dry or ferment the rest.
- **Resupply:** reusable lids; and for meat, **curing, smoking and drying** (→ 04-07) are the old
  answers that need no jars at all.
- **Fuel is the other cost:** long processes on wood are expensive (→ 06-04). Batch hard.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** learn it now on a stove with a tested recipe and a working gauge.
- **B (moving):** it does not travel: heavy, fragile, fuel-hungry.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the key skill for keeping game and a garden surplus. Set up
  an outdoor burner station for it.

## Cross-references

→ 04-04 water-bath canning (high-acid only) · → 29-08 canning words · → 30-01 the floors ·
→ 04-06 drying · → 04-07 curing and smoking · → 04-09 winter cold · → 05-09 butchering ·
→ 07-05 propane burners · → 06-04 fuel

pages.title: Drying food
pages.body:
# Drying food

**What this page is for.** How to dry fruit, vegetables, herbs and meat so they keep for months
with no jars, no lids and no electricity, and the one food (meat) where drying needs strict
rules.

> **CAUTION.** Drying is the preserving method that uses up nothing: no jars, no lids, no
> pressure. But **drying meat is not like drying apples.** Jerky carries real risk from germs
> that survive gentle drying, and it must follow the USDA procedure, which heats the meat, not
> just dries it. Fruit and vegetables are forgiving; meat is not.

## Do this now

1. **Dry any surplus.** It is the cheapest way to keep a harvest, with no lids.
2. **Dry until truly dry.** Fruit should be leathery with no moist pockets; vegetables brittle.
   Under-dried food goes mouldy in storage.
3. **Condition dried fruit:** pack it loosely in a jar for **7 to 10 days,** shaking daily. If
   droplets form on the glass, it needs more drying (NCHFP, Drying Foods).
4. **Dry at the right temperature** (dehydrator, or oven with the door cracked): **fruit and
   vegetables about 135 to 140 °F; herbs about 95 to 115 °F; jerky 130 to 140 °F or higher**
   (NCHFP). Too hot hardens the outside and traps moisture inside; too cool grows mould before
   it dries.
5. **Store airtight, cool and dark.** Light and warmth ruin dried food fast.
6. **Jerky: follow the numbered steps below every time.** Heat the meat to **160 °F (poultry
   165 °F) BEFORE drying;** dry at **130 to 140 °F or higher;** **never sun-dry or air-dry
   meat.**

## Why it works

Removing water stops germs and moulds growing. It also removes weight and bulk: dried food is
**light, compact, and needs no fuel to keep.** In a long grid-down that is hard to beat.

| Method | Needs | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Electric dehydrator** | Power | Fastest and best controlled; use while the grid or solar allows |
| **Solar drying** | Sun, screens, airflow | Free; works best in dry, sunny weather (→ 07-03). **Fruit, vegetables, herbs only: NEVER meat** |
| **Air drying** | Dry air, airflow | Herbs, peppers, beans hung in bunches. **Never meat** |
| **Oven or beside a stove** | Low heat, door cracked | Wasteful unless the fire is lit anyway; the one fuel method that can hold jerky at 130 °F or more |
| **Above a wood stove** | Heat you already have | Good for plant food; **not for meat unless a thermometer at the rack reads 130 °F or more the whole time** |

**The habit that matters:** whenever a fire is going for cooking or heat, **something should be
drying near it.** That is free preserving (→ 06-04).

{{figure fig-drying-rack-over-stove}}

## What dries well

- **Very well:** apples, pears, plums, berries, tomatoes, peppers, onions, garlic, green beans,
  corn, peas, herbs, and fruit purée spread thin as **fruit leather.**
- **Well, with blanching:** most vegetables. Blanching (a short dip in boiling water or steam)
  keeps colour and vitamins and stops the enzymes that spoil flavour.
- **Poorly:** fatty foods. **Fat goes rancid** and cannot be dried out. That is why jerky must be
  lean meat with the fat cut off.
- **Allergies:** dried fruits get mixed together casually. If anyone in the house is allergic to
  a fruit you dry, keep it separate and clearly labelled (→ 02-04).

## Jerky: the one to do carefully

*E. coli* O157 and *Salmonella* **survive ordinary low-temperature jerky drying.** That outbreak
history is why USDA's procedure heats the meat, not just dries it. The steps, with the numbers
(USDA FSIS, Jerky and Food Safety; NCHFP, Drying Foods):

1. **Lean meat, all fat trimmed.** Slice about ¼ inch thick; partly frozen meat cuts evenly.
   Venison and other game (→ 05-09) suit it well.
2. **Marinate COLD:** in the fridge or measured outdoor cold below 40 °F (→ 04-09), never on the
   counter. **Throw the marinade away** afterwards. Salt and acid help but are not the safety
   step.
3. **Heat the strips to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F) BEFORE drying:** steam, roast or simmer them in
   the marinade, and **check with a thermometer.** (Less preferred: dry first, then 10 minutes
   in a 275 °F oven, only if your oven holds 275 °F.)
4. **Dry at 130 to 140 °F or higher** (dehydrator, or oven with the door cracked) until a cooled
   strip **cracks but does not snap.** Usually 4 to 12 hours.
5. **Store airtight, cool and dark; use within 1 to 2 months** at room temperature (longer cold).
   Check for mould. Home jerky does not keep for ever.
6. **NEVER sun-dry or air-dry meat.** Not on screens, not in a hot car, not over a wood stove
   without a thermometer. Plant food, yes; meat, no.

## Storing dried food

- **Airtight:** jars with lids, vacuum bags, or sealed buckets with screw lids.
- **Cool and dark.** Heat and light are what destroy dried food in storage.
- **Oxygen absorbers** extend storage life a lot for long-term packs (→ 04-03).
- **Check now and then** for moisture, mould or insects (→ 04-11).
- **Label with contents and date:** dried vegetables become hard to recognise.

## Rehydrating and using

- Soak in water, or add straight to soups and stews, where they soak up liquid as they cook.
- **Dried food plus a haybox** (an insulated box, → 07-02) is a very fuel-efficient meal: boil
  briefly, insulate, and let it soften for hours with no more fuel.
- Grind dried vegetables to a powder for instant soup base and hidden nutrition for children.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Electric dehydrator | Fast and controlled while you have power | Trays; a thermostat helps |
| **Drying screens or racks** (food-safe mesh) | Solar and stove-top drying | Stackable; easy to make |
| Cheesecloth or fine netting | Keeps insects off solar-dried food | Essential outdoors |
| Airtight jars, buckets, vacuum bags | Storage is half the method | Plus oxygen absorbers |
| Oxygen absorbers | Big shelf-life gain | Cheap; buy now |
| **Thermometers:** instant-read, and one that reads at the drying rack | 160 °F before drying; 130 to 140 °F while drying | → 07-01 |
| Sharp knife or mandoline | Even thickness dries evenly | → 16-02 |
| Labels and marker | Dried food is hard to identify later | Not optional |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Clean window screens** (food-safe, no paint or rust) on blocks make good drying racks.
- Racks near a wood stove use heat you are already paying for (plant food only, unless measured).
- A car in summer sun works as a dehydrator for fruit and vegetables (on screens, covered
  against insects). Never meat.
- String and a dry room dry herbs, peppers and beans with nothing else.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** drying itself uses **nothing.** Storage containers and oxygen absorbers are the
  only parts that run out.
- **Ration:** none needed. Dry whenever you have surplus and sun or a fire already lit.
- **Resupply:** jars can be reused for ever for dried food; a tight lid is enough to keep out
  moisture and insects, no new canning lid needed.
- **The strategic point:** canning is limited by lids (→ 04-04) and freezing by weather or power
  (→ 04-09), so **drying and fermenting (→ 04-08) are the two preserving methods that can run
  indefinitely.** Learn both properly.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** dry the garden and any bulk buy; use the dehydrator while power
  lasts.
- **B (moving):** dried food is the best food to carry: light, compact, no cooking needed.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** solar and stove-top drying at scale; pair it with a haybox
  for fuel-free meals.

## Cross-references

→ 04-04 canning (lid-limited) · → 04-07 curing and smoking · → 04-08 fermenting ·
→ 04-11 pests in storage · → 07-02 haybox cooking · → 07-03 solar · → 05-09 game meat

pages.title: Smoking and curing meat

photo_slots.caption: Where our curing salt is locked up, labelled POISON - NOT SALT

pages.body:
# Smoking and curing meat

**What this page is for.** The difference between curing (the step that preserves meat) and
smoking (which flavours or cooks it), how to use curing salt safely, and when pressure canning
or drying is the better choice.

> **SAFETY.** Curing meat is the place, outside canning, where home preserving is most likely
> to cause **botulism** (→ 29-08). Two rules: **use a tested recipe with the stated curing salt
> and amounts,** and understand that **cold smoking does not cook or preserve meat by itself.**
> It flavours it; the *cure* does the preserving. Improvised curing of large cuts is genuinely
> dangerous. **Nitrite curing salts are poisonous in small amounts: lock them away from
> children and never measure them by eye.**
>
> **Floor:** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning (→ 30-01, → 29-03). A smoker or
> charcoal fire stays outdoors, away from doors and windows.

## Do this now

1. **Use a tested recipe** (NCHFP, USDA or Extension) for anything cured. Salt and nitrite levels
   are the safety control, not seasoning. Nitrite and nitrate salts are toxic enough that they
   are used only in the amounts a researched recipe sets (Oregon State University Extension,
   Making Cured Bacon at Home, PNW 784, 2025).
2. **Know which you are doing:** **hot smoking** cooks the food (safe once it reaches a safe
   inside temperature); **cold smoking** is flavour only (the meat must be cured first and is
   often still raw).
3. **Buy curing salt now.** It is cheap, keeps well, and will be hard to get later. **Know which
   one you are buying; they look alike and are not interchangeable:**
   - **Cure #1** (also sold as Prague Powder #1, Insta Cure #1 or "pink salt"; 6.25 percent
     sodium nitrite, the rest table salt): for bacon, ham, sausage, corned meat, **anything
     that will be cooked or smoked.** **Rate: 1 LEVEL TEASPOON per 5 lb of meat, NEVER MORE,
     unless the tested recipe or the cure's own label says less** (Oregon State University
     Extension, PNW 784). By weight that is about 5.7 g of Cure #1 per 5 lb (2.27 kg) of meat:
     the same nitrite level US federal rules allow in commercial sausage, ¼ oz of sodium nitrite
     per 100 lb of chopped meat (USDA FSIS, 9 CFR 424.21). Weigh the meat; weigh the cure.
   - **Cure #2** (Prague Powder #2; nitrite plus nitrate): **ONLY for dry-cured whole-muscle or
     salami recipes that hang for weeks** (the nitrate converts slowly). **Not for bacon**
     (Oregon State University Extension, PNW 784), **jerky or anything eaten within days.**
   - Both are dyed pink and look like pink table salt. **Label "POISON: NOT SALT", never put it
     in a shaker, keep it locked** (→ 20-02). Nitrite stops the blood carrying oxygen
     (methemoglobinemia). People have died after using sodium nitrite in place of table salt,
     and after swallowing a single tablet that held about two-thirds of a gram of nitrite
     (ATSDR, Toxicological Profile for Nitrate and Nitrite, 2017). **A level teaspoon of Cure #1
     holds about a third of a gram of sodium nitrite: treat any swallowed amount as an
     emergency, above all in a small child.** If anyone swallows it: → 12-17, and call Poison
     Control (1-800-222-1222) while phones work.
4. **Keep meat cold while curing: 40 °F or colder, not frozen** (a fridge, or measured outdoor
   or garage cold with a thermometer, → 04-09; Oregon State University Extension, PNW 784).
   Curing does not rescue meat that has already sat warm.
5. **Stockpile plain salt heavily** (→ 04-13). It is the master preservative.

{{photo curing-salt-storage}}

## Curing and smoking: the difference that matters

| Process | What it does | Safe on its own? |
|---|---|---|
| **Curing** (salt, with or without nitrite; dry rub or brine) | Draws out water, slows bacteria, and with nitrite specifically blocks botulism | **This is the preserving step** |
| **Hot smoking** (the meat reaches its safe inside temperature, FoodSafety.gov chart, → 07-01) | Cooks and flavours | Safe once it reaches that temperature, but it is **cooked meat**, not shelf-stable, unless it was also cured |
| **Cold smoking** (smoke kept cool enough that the meat does not cook) | Flavour and surface drying only | **Not safe alone:** the meat must be properly cured first |

**The most common dangerous mistake** is cold smoking uncured meat and treating it as
preserved. It is raw meat held for hours at the temperatures bacteria like best.

## Why nitrite exists

Curing salts contain **sodium nitrite** because it blocks *Clostridium botulinum* in the
airless inside of cured meats. That is why traditional bacon, ham and sausage recipes include it,
and why "just use sea salt" is not the same thing for those products (NCHFP, Curing and Smoking
Meats for Home Food Preservation).

**Handle with respect.** The pink dye is there so it is not mistaken for table salt. **Measure
carefully, by weight if you can: 1 level teaspoon (about 5.7 g) of Cure #1 per 5 lb of meat is
the ceiling, and a tested recipe sets the method. Store it locked.** With small children in the house, treat it like any other
poison (→ 20-02).

## What works without nitrite

- **Heavy salt cures and dry-salting** (salt pork, salt fish): old, effective, and dependent on
  **a lot of salt** and cool temperatures.
- **Drying** (→ 04-06): jerky, by the USDA procedure.
- **Pressure canning** (→ 04-05): often the **better** answer for game meat: shelf-stable, ready
  to eat, no nitrite, no cold storage (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 5).

**For most households, pressure canning is the safer and simpler way to keep a deer** (→ 05-09).
Curing and smoking are worth learning as the no-jars, no-lids alternative and for the food
quality, but they are less forgiving.

## Smoking on what you have

An outdoor fire pit, grill or improvised smokehouse (→ 07-01) can hot smoke well:

- **Keep a low, steady fire with plenty of smoke:** hardwood coals plus damp chips (→ 06-02).
- **Use thermometers** for both the chamber and the inside of the meat. Guessing is how people
  get sick.
- **Hot smoke to a safe inside temperature** (→ 07-01 has the numbers; Oregon State Extension's
  smoked bacon is taken to 160 °F inside) and treat the result as cooked food, not
  shelf-stable.
- **Do not smoke with softwoods** (pine, spruce) or any treated or painted wood: resinous smoke
  tastes terrible and treated wood is poisonous (→ 06-05).
- **Cold smoking** is only practical in cold weather, when the air keeps the chamber cool and
  the meat cold. {{#if is.cold_winters}}Your winters make that possible; the cure still
  has to be right.{{else}}In a mild climate it is hard to do safely; hot smoke instead.{{/if}}

## Storage after curing

- **Cool, dark and airy** for hanging cured meat; humidity matters.
- **Watch for mould.** Some white surface mould is normal on traditional cures; fuzzy black or
  coloured mould is not.
- **Plan curing by season.** Winter gives the cold; summer does not (→ 04-09).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Curing salt: Cure #1** (and Cure #2 only if you will dry-cure) | The botulism control in cured meat | 1 level tsp per 5 lb meat, never more; labelled **POISON: NOT SALT**; **locked** |
| **Plain salt, in bulk** | The master preservative | → 04-13; buy a lot |
| **A tested recipe for each product** | The method and amounts | NCHFP, USDA or Extension; in the Large and Everything downloads, the "Sources for this page" list below links to each bound document |
| Digital thermometers (chamber and probe) | Safety, not preference | Two is one, one is none |
| Smoker, or a smoking setup on an outdoor fire | Hot smoking | Can be improvised; always outdoors |
| Hardwood chips or chunks (not softwood) | Smoke flavour | Fruit wood, hickory, oak |
| Food-safe crocks or tubs for brining | Curing vessels | Non-reactive: no bare aluminium or copper |
| Meat hooks, twine, cheesecloth | Hanging and protecting | Also drying (→ 04-06) |
| Scale that reads grams | Cure amounts are by weight: 5.7 g Cure #1 per 2.27 kg meat | Precision matters here |

**If you don't have it:**

- A **barrel, an old fridge shell or a wooden box** makes a smokehouse with a separate firebox.
- Salt-only cures are the old fallback, with more salt, colder temperatures and more care.
- **The best substitute for curing is pressure canning** (→ 04-05) or drying (→ 04-06).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** **curing salt** and **salt.** Most households cannot make either; both are
  stockpile items.
- **Ration:** use nitrite cures only for the products that need them; use plain salt cures,
  drying and canning for the rest.
- **Resupply:** salt is a top barter good (→ 18-02) because everyone needs it and few can make it.
- **The seasonal point:** curing and smoking pair naturally with **autumn hunting** (→ 05-07) and
  **winter cold.** Plan the year around that rhythm.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** smoke smell travels and announces meat (→ 14-03). Think about
  timing and how often.
- **B (moving):** cured and dried meat travels very well; the process does not.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the classic partner to hunting and livestock. Build a
  smokehouse if you settle.

## Cross-references

→ 04-05 pressure canning (often the better choice for game) · → 04-06 drying · → 04-13 salt ·
→ 05-07 hunting · → 05-09 butchering · → 06-02 fire control · → 20-02 poisons and children ·
→ 30-01 the floors

photo_slots.caption: Our cold storage spots: the humid corner for roots, the dry corner for onions and squash

pages.body:
# Fermentation and root cellaring

**What this page is for.** Two ways to keep vegetables for months with no jars-per-batch, no
fuel and no electricity: fermenting them in salt brine (sauerkraut is the model), and storing
raw crops cool in a "root cellar", which can be any cold, dark corner with the right humidity.

> **CAUTION.** Fermentation is safe **because of the salt strength and the absence of air.**
> Get the salt amount from a tested recipe and keep the vegetables **under the brine.** Too
> little salt, or vegetables exposed to air, and the wrong organisms grow. A good ferment smells
> sour and clean; **slimy, foul, pink or fuzzy means throw it out.**

## Do this now

1. **Learn sauerkraut first.** Cabbage and salt, nothing else. It is the most forgiving ferment
   and a real source of vitamin C through winter.
2. **Measure the salt exactly** to the recipe. It is the safety control, not seasoning.
3. **Keep everything under the brine** with a weight, a bag of brine, or a cabbage leaf on top.
4. **Ferment cool:** 60 to 75 °F. Above 75 °F kraut may go soft; below 60 °F it may not ferment
   (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 6).
5. **Store raw what keeps raw:** potatoes, carrots, beets, cabbage, onions, squash, apples.

## Why fermentation matters

- **Almost nothing runs out.** Salt, water, vegetables, a crock. No lids, no new jars each batch.
- **No fuel at all,** unlike canning (→ 04-04), which uses a lot (→ 06-04).
- **Nutrition.** Fermented vegetables keep their vitamins well and give **vitamin C through
  winter,** the old answer to scurvy.
- **It scales with a garden** (→ 05-01): cabbage is easy to grow and turns directly into months
  of stored food.

## How it works

Salt makes conditions where **lactic acid bacteria** (which tolerate salt) outgrow the organisms
that spoil food. They make lactic acid, the pH drops (the food becomes more acidic, → 29-08), and
the food preserves itself. Air is the enemy: the food must stay **under** its brine.

**The method (sauerkraut):**

1. **Shred the cabbage.** Weigh it.
2. **Add salt at the tested rate.** The USDA rate for sauerkraut is **3 tablespoons of canning
   or pickling salt per 5 lb of shredded cabbage** (USDA Complete Guide, Guide 6). Weigh the
   cabbage so the salt matches it. Other vegetables have their own tested rates: **use the
   Guide, not memory.** {{#if size.large}}Guide 6 is bound in your binder at the end of this
   section, after the last food-storage page; the "Sources for this page" list below links to
   it.{{else}}Your binder is the Small download, which only cites Guide 6; the Large and
   Everything downloads carry it. Keep a paper copy.{{/if}}
3. **Massage or pound** until the cabbage releases its own liquid.
4. **Pack it into a crock or jar,** pressing down so the brine covers everything.
5. **Weight it down** so nothing floats. If the juice does not cover the cabbage, add brine
   that was boiled and cooled: 1½ tablespoons of salt per quart of water (Guide 6).
6. **Cover loosely:** gas must escape. An airlock lid or a cloth works.
7. **Ferment cool.** USDA: **70 to 75 °F for about 3 to 4 weeks; 60 to 65 °F for 5 to 6 weeks;
   below 60 °F it may not ferment; above 75 °F it may go soft.** Taste as it goes.
8. **Skim any surface film.** When it tastes right, move it somewhere cold to slow it down.

**Judging it:** a good ferment smells **sour, clean and cabbagey;** cloudy brine is normal.
**Throw it out** if it is slimy, foul, pink or red, or has fuzzy mould. A thin white film on the
surface (kahm yeast) is common and can be skimmed off.

**Do not water-bath-can a ferment casually.** Heat kills the live cultures, and canning
fermented food needs its own tested recipe (→ 04-04).

## Root cellaring: storage that costs nothing

Many crops keep raw for months, with **no processing at all,** in the right conditions. The
temperatures below are Iowa State University Extension's (Storing Winter Storage Vegetables,
reviewed 2025); rows without a number keep the general rule.

| Crop | Wants | Keeps |
|---|---|---|
| **Potatoes** | 40 °F, dark, humid; **never next to apples** | Months |
| **Carrots, beets, turnips** | Just above freezing (32 to 35 °F), very humid: pack in damp sand | Beets 1 to 3 months; carrots and turnips longer |
| **Cabbage** | Cold, humid | Months (and it smells) |
| **Onions, garlic** | Cold (32 to 40 °F), **dry,** airy | Months |
| **Winter squash, pumpkins** | Cool (50 to 55 °F), **dry**; away from ripening fruit | Weeks (acorn) to months (butternut, Hubbard) |
| **Apples** | Cold, humid, **away from potatoes** | Months |

**Two rules:** **apples and other ripening fruit give off ethylene gas,** which makes potatoes
sprout and shortens squash storage; keep them apart (Iowa State University Extension).
And **onions and squash want dry air** while roots want humid air: two different corners.

**Where to do it.** {{#if has.basement}}Your basement is the asset here.{{else}}Any unheated room,
closet against an outside wall, crawlspace or shed that stays cold but above freezing will
work.{{/if}} In a grid-down winter, if you heat only one room (→ 08-01), the unheated rest of
the house becomes a working cold store (→ 04-09). {{#if !is.cold_winters}}Where winters
are mild, a cool spot is harder to find; the crops above still keep for weeks to a few months in
the coolest place you have.{{/if}}

{{photo root-cellar-corner}}

## Allergen note

Fermenting suits a food-allergic household: cabbage, salt and water, all easy to check
(→ 02-04). Watch for recipes that add soy sauce, fish sauce or sesame, as some kimchi-style
recipes do. Keep allergy-safe batches separate and labelled.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Fermentation crock, or wide-mouth jars | The vessel | Crocks are traditional; jars work |
| **Fermentation weights** | Keeping food under brine is the safety control | Glass weights, or a boiled stone |
| Airlock lids (or cloth and a band) | Lets gas out, keeps air off | Cheap |
| **Salt: a large quantity** | The preservative | → 04-13; **non-iodised** canning salt for ferments |
| **Kitchen scale** | Weigh the vegetables so the salt matches the recipe | The safety-critical tool |
