| **USDA Complete Guide, Guide 6** (fermented foods and pickled vegetables) | Tested rates | Bound in the Large and Everything downloads |
| Damp sand and bins or crates | Roots keep for months | Free |
| Thermometer and humidity gauge for the cold store | Know your conditions | Cheap |
| Shredder, mandoline or cabbage knife | Prep in volume | → 16-02 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Any food-safe bucket** with a plate and a weight ferments cabbage well.
- A **boiled rock** or a water-filled bag makes a weight.
- Sand, leaves or straw in crates for root storage; an unheated corner as the cellar.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** **salt** is the only real consumable, and it does not spoil. Buy a lot now
  (→ 04-13). Everything else is reusable.
- **Ration:** none needed. This is the method to lean on because it uses almost nothing.
- **Resupply:** salt is the one thing to stockpile heavily; most places cannot make it.
- **The strategic point:** **fermenting, drying and root cellaring together need no lids, no fuel
  and no electricity.** In a long emergency they are the preserving system; canning is the
  luxury while lids last.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** ferment now for practice; use the coldest part of the house as a
  cellar in winter.
- **B (moving):** does not travel: crocks are heavy and ferments need stillness.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the core preserving method alongside drying. Build a real
  root cellar if the site allows.

## Cross-references

→ 04-04 canning · → 04-06 drying · → 04-09 winter cold storage · → 04-13 salt ·
→ 05-01 growing cabbage and roots · → 06-04 fuel (fermenting uses none)

pages.title: Using winter as a freezer, and where it does not work

photo_slots.caption: Our outdoor cold store: north side, shaded, off the ground, animal-proof, thermometer inside

pages.body:
# Using winter as a freezer, and where it does not work

**What this page is for.** In a cold winter, the outdoors, an unheated garage or the unheated
rooms of the house can keep food cold or frozen with no power at all. This page says how to do
that safely, and says plainly where and when it does **not** work.

> **CAUTION.** Outdoor temperature is not a thermostat. A sunny afternoon on a south wall can
> push food into the danger zone (40 to 140 °F) while the air is still below freezing.
> **Measure, do not assume.**
>
> **Floor:** **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Loss of potency with no
> way to tell (→ 30-01). The cold that keeps food also destroys insulin and some other
> refrigerated medicines (→ 29-07).

## Do this now

1. **Put a thermometer wherever you store food in the cold.** A min/max thermometer (one that
   remembers the highest and lowest reading) tells you what actually happened at midday and
   overnight.
2. **Keep food at 40 °F or below at all times,** and at 0 °F or below if you are treating it as
   frozen (FoodSafety.gov; NCHFP, Freezing Foods).
3. **Store it in the shade, on the north side,** off the ground and out of the sun.
4. **Protect it from animals:** dogs, cats, raccoons, bears and rodents will find it.
5. **Throw out perishable food that has been above 40 °F for 2 hours or more** (→ 04-17).
6. **Keep insulin and other refrigerated medicines in a separate, warmer place,** with their own
   thermometer (→ 02-01, → 29-07).

## Does this work where you live?

**Winter cold storage only works while the food stays at 40 °F or below, every hour of every
day.** That means sustained cold, not the odd frost.

Your home: January average low **{{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F**, record low
**{{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F**, USDA hardiness zone **{{ region.home.zone }}**.

{{#if is.cold_winters}}**Your home has cold winters** (January average low below 20 °F). In
the coldest months, outdoor and unheated-garage storage can work as a freezer. The months either
side are unreliable: measure every day.{{else}}**Your home does not have reliably cold winters.**
Do not plan on winter as a freezer. Use outdoor cold only as a short-term refrigerator on
measured cold nights, and rely on shelf-stable methods (→ 04-05 to → 04-08) and any powered
cold you have (→ 04-17).{{/if}}

**Where it does not work:**

- **Anywhere daytime highs regularly climb above 40 °F in winter.** That covers most of the
  South, the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plains, the Pacific coast, the low deserts of the
  Southwest, and Hawaii. Food stored outside there spends hours in the danger zone most days.
- **Places with repeated freeze-thaw swings.** A winter that crosses freezing week after week is
  the dangerous case: food thaws above 40 °F, refreezes overnight, and **looks fine.** You will
  not know it happened unless a min/max thermometer tells you.
- **Any spot in direct sun,** even in a cold place.
- **Warm spells.** Sudden thaws and warm dry winds (chinooks east of the Rockies) can raise the
  temperature 40 °F or more in hours. Have a plan to cook or preserve fast.
- **Spring, everywhere.** It ends, often abruptly.

{{#each destinations as x}}
- **{{x.name}}:** January average low {{x.region.jan_low_f}} °F. Check this page's rules before
  counting on cold storage there.
{{/each}}

**In humid places the other problem is moisture.** Opened dried food picks up water fast in a
humid summer, and mould follows. Favour **sealed original packs and Mylar with oxygen
absorbers** (→ 04-03), reseal opened containers at once, and use opened packs sooner (→ 04-19).

## Where it works: what it gives you

In a place with reliable hard freezes, cold storage with no power lets you:

- **Freeze a whole deer** (→ 05-09) instead of racing to can it.
- **Stretch the contents of a fridge and freezer** when the grid fails (→ 04-17).
- **Keep cooked food, dairy and produce** cold with no fuel cost.

## The traps

| Trap | Why it bites | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Sun** | Direct sun on a container can lift it above freezing even at 20 °F air temperature | North side, shade, insulated container |
| **Thaw and refreeze** | Repeated cycles ruin quality and are a safety risk | An insulated container damps the swings; a min/max thermometer catches them |
| **Warm spells** | Swings of 40 to 50 °F in a day happen in some regions | Min/max thermometer; a plan to process food fast |
| **Animals** | Everything wants your meat | Secure, raised, hard-sided container |
| **"Cold enough"** | Air temperature is not food temperature | Measure the **food,** not the air |
| **Spring** | It ends, often suddenly | Have the food preserved (→ 04-05, → 04-06) first |

## Doing it properly

- **Use insulated containers (coolers) outside.** It sounds backwards, but insulation buffers
  the swings in both directions.
- **North side of the house, shaded, raised** off the ground, secured against animals.
- **An unheated garage or porch** is often better than fully outdoors: darker, steadier, and
  harder for animals.
- **The unheated part of the house** works as a refrigerator once you heat only one room
  (→ 08-01).
- **Freeze in meal-sized portions** so you never thaw more than you will eat.
- **Wrap well.** Dry winter air causes freezer burn (a quality problem, not a safety one).

{{photo outdoor-cold-store}}

## Food cold, medicine not frozen

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Someone in your household takes a refrigerated medicine.** {{/if}}This
page and the medicine pages pull in opposite directions. **Food wants to be frozen. Insulin must
never freeze;** freezing destroys it and it can look normal afterwards (FDA, Information
Regarding Insulin Storage). Keep food and medicine in **completely different places,** each with
its own thermometer. Do not let "the cold room" become one shared storage idea. → 02-01, → 29-07.

## When it thaws

- **At 40 °F or below the whole time:** still safe; use it or re-preserve it.
- **Above 40 °F for 2 hours or more:** throw out perishables (meat, poultry, fish, eggs,
  leftovers). Do not taste to check (→ 04-17).
- **Partly thawed but still with ice crystals and at 40 °F or below:** generally safe to
  refreeze, with some loss of quality (FoodSafety.gov).
- **When in doubt, throw it out.** Food poisoning without a clinic is a medical emergency
  (→ 12-05). How strictly your household applies the published rules when food is short is a
  decision card: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15.

## The end of the season

**Winter storage has a hard deadline.** Before the thaw, convert anything you want to keep into a
shelf-stable form: **pressure canned** (→ 04-05), **dried** (→ 04-06), **cured** (→ 04-07) or
**fermented** (→ 04-08). Plan that conversion **before** the thaw, not during it: a warm week
with a deer in the garage is a crisis.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Min/max thermometers** (several) | The whole safety case rests on measuring | One per storage spot |
| Coolers or insulated containers | Buffer swings outdoors | Hard-sided, animal-resistant |
| Hard-sided secure bins or a chest | Animal protection | Latching |
| Heavy freezer wrap, bags, butcher paper | Prevent freezer burn | In bulk |
| Labels and marker | Contents, date, portion | Not optional |
| A shaded north-side spot, cleared | Site preparation | Free |
| A plan and gear to make food shelf-stable | Spring is a deadline | → 04-05 to → 04-08 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Snow** packed around a container is good insulation and cooling.
- A buried or snow-banked cooler stays very steady.
- An unheated garage, porch, shed or the north side of the house.
- Any hard container with a weight on the lid keeps most animals out.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** this is **seasonal, not used up.** {{#if is.cold_winters}}At your home, roughly the
  coldest months; the shoulder months are unreliable, so measure.{{else}}At your home, little or
  none: plan on other methods.{{/if}}
- **Ration:** none, but do not let free cold make you lazy about preserving. It ends.
- **Resupply:** the shelf-stable methods (→ 04-05 to → 04-08) carry food through the rest of the
  year.
- **The yearly rhythm (cold climates):** hunt and slaughter in autumn and early winter, hold in
  winter cold, convert to shelf-stable before the thaw, live on stores through summer, grow and
  preserve through the season (→ 25-01).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** garage, north side, and the unheated part of the house. Watch for
  animals and for neighbours noticing (→ 14-03).
- **B (moving):** frozen food does not travel; dried and canned food does.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** often more space, outbuildings and a real cellar (→ 04-08).
  Check the destination's climate against the list above before counting on it.

## Cross-references

→ 04-17 food safety in a power outage · → 04-05 to → 04-08 making food shelf-stable ·
→ 04-03 sealed storage for humid places · → 02-01 insulin must not freeze · → 29-07 refrigerated
medicines · → 08-01 the cold house as a refrigerator · → 03-06 winter water

pages.title: Rotation, dating and inventory
pages.body:
# Rotation, dating and inventory

**What this page is for.** How to keep a food store fresh and counted, what the dates on food
packages mean, and how to run the "pantry week" that finds problems before an emergency does.

> **CAUTION.** The most common way a food stockpile fails is not disaster. It is **quiet
> expiry.** Food bought once and never looked at again becomes a pile of unknowns exactly when
> you need certainty. Rotation is boring, and it is the difference between a supply and a guess.

## Do this now

1. **Date every item on purchase,** in marker, large enough to read on a dim shelf.
2. **Shelve new behind old** so your hand always reaches the oldest first.
3. **Count everything once,** on paper, and keep the sheet with the food (→ 22-04).
4. **Run a "pantry week"** every few months: cook only from stores.
5. **Recount and work out the runways every three months,** and write them on → 23-02.

## Dates: what they mean and what they do not

- **"Best if used by", "sell by" and most "use by" dates are about quality, not safety,** for
  shelf-stable food. **Infant formula is the exception:** its use-by date matters (USDA FSIS,
  Food Product Dating). How to read the different date formats: → 29-14.
- **USDA:** canned food is safe indefinitely if it was not frozen or kept above 90 °F and the
  can is in good condition; **throw out cans that are dented, leaking, bulging or rusted**
  (USDA FSIS, Shelf-Stable Food Safety). High-acid canned food (tomatoes, fruit) keeps its
  best quality for a shorter time than low-acid food (meat, vegetables).
- **The real limits** are: rancid fat in oils and whole grains (→ 04-12), rust or seam damage in
  cans, moisture in dry goods, and any broken seal.
- **Your own purchase-date mark is often more useful** than the printed date: it tells you how
  long *you* have had it.
- **How strictly to follow the dates** when food is short is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15. Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are not part of that choice:
  they are thrown away.

## The rotation system that works

1. **One direction.** New goes in at the back or top; you take from the front or bottom.
2. **Group by type,** not by purchase date; rotate within each group.
3. **Working stock at eye level,** deep stock below or behind.
4. **Open one at a time.** An open bucket or box is on the clock; finish it before opening the
   next.
5. **Write down what you take.** A pencil on a clipboard by the shelf is enough.

## The inventory sheet

Keep it simple enough that you will keep it up:

| Item | Unit | Qty | Date packed | Where | Safe for each allergy? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| White rice | 5-gal bucket | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Pinto beans | 5-gal bucket | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Cooking oil | quart | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Canned tomatoes | can | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |

**The two columns that matter most:** **date** (rotation) and, if anyone in the house has a food
allergy, **safe or not** (→ 02-04). For freeze-dried food, use the fuller table on → 04-19. The
binder's expiry tracker is → 26-08.

## Pantry week: the check that finds real problems

Every few months, cook **only** from stores for a week. It shows:

- Food nobody will eat (stop buying it).
- Food you do not know how to cook (learn now).
- Missing basics: the spice, the fat, the can opener.
- Items past their useful life.
- **Whether everyone in the house, including anyone on a restricted diet, can actually eat a
  week of your stored food.** This is the most important finding.

**Do one in winter, cooking outdoors** if you can (→ 07-01), and you will learn more in a
weekend than in a year of reading (→ 24-02).

## Working out the runways

Every three months, update → 23-02:

- **Household food-days** = total calories on hand ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }} (→ 04-01).
- **Each restricted diet's food-days,** from that person's safe food only; usually the shorter
  number.
- **Water-days** (→ 03-01), **fuel-days** (→ 06-04), and **medicine-days** for anyone on daily
  medicine (→ 12-07).

Those numbers are the dashboard for the stay-or-go decision (→ 01-02).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Permanent markers (a pack) | Date everything | Cheap, always missing |
| Clipboard and printed inventory sheets | Kept up beats elegant | Keep it with the food |
| Shelving that lets you rotate front to back | The system works or it does not | |
| Labels for repackaged goods, saved ingredient panels | Allergen safety (→ 02-04) | Tape inside the lid |
| A reminder every three months | Habits decay | Same day you test the smoke alarms |

**If you don't have it:**

- Paper and pencil beat any app that needs a charged phone.
- Any shelf can be arranged front to back; masking tape and marker label everything.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** this page makes the runway numbers rather than using anything up.
- **The failure to avoid:** finding in month three that half the pantry expired in year one, or
  that the deep stock is full of something an allergic person cannot eat. Both are prevented by
  a marker and an hour every three months.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** build the habit now; it is the cheapest discipline in the binder.
- **B (moving):** the inventory sheet tells you what to take in minutes (→ 01-06).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** count everything again on arrival; the numbers all change.

## Cross-references

→ 04-01 calorie math · → 04-02 pantry · → 22-04 household inventory · → 23-02 consumables
table · → 26-08 expiry tracker · → 29-14 reading a label · → 24-02 drills

pages.title: Protecting stored food from pests and rodents
pages.body:
# Protecting stored food from pests and rodents

**What this page is for.** How to keep mice, rats and insects out of stored food, what to do
when they get in, and how to clean up after rodents without catching a disease from the dust.

> **CAUTION.** Rodents do not just eat food. **They spoil far more than they eat,** with urine
> and droppings that carry disease. **Food that rodents have touched is thrown away.** In a
> grid-down with no clinic, a preventable stomach illness in a small child or an elder is an
> emergency (→ 12-05). **Deer mice carry hantavirus** in much of the US; people catch it from
> rodent urine, droppings and saliva, often by breathing dust stirred up while sweeping. CDC
> says 38 percent of people who develop the breathing symptoms of the illness (hantavirus
> pulmonary syndrome) may die, and there is no specific treatment (CDC, About Hantavirus,
> 2024). **Never sweep or vacuum droppings: wet them first** (steps below).
>
> **Floors:** **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.**
> Chlorine gas (→ 30-01). **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or
> chlorine products.** Fixed in every source (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Store food in hard containers, not bags.** Mice chew through plastic bags, cardboard and
   thin plastic buckets easily.
2. **Seal entry points.** A mouse fits through a hole the width of a pencil, about ¼ inch
   (CDC, How to Seal Up to Prevent Rodents).
3. **Keep food off the floor and away from walls,** so you can see and clean behind it.
4. **Clean up crumbs and spills at once.** A clean store room does not attract pests.
5. **Use snap traps, not poison,** where there are children or pets (below).

## The three threats

| Pest | What they do | Control |
|---|---|---|
| **Mice and rats** | Chew containers, foul food with urine and droppings, spread disease | Hard containers, sealing gaps, traps, cats |
| **Pantry insects** (weevils, meal moths) | Infest grain, flour and beans, usually from the store | Freezing, oxygen absorbers, sealed containers |
| **Ants and cockroaches** | Foul food, spread germs | Cleanliness, sealed food |

## Rodents: keep them out first

- **Hard containers:** metal cans and bins, glass jars, or **plastic buckets inside a metal
  container.** A plastic bucket alone is not rodent-proof for long.
- **Seal the building:** steel wool held in with caulk or spray foam for small holes; hardware
  cloth (stiff wire mesh), metal sheeting or cement for larger ones (CDC). Check around pipes, vents, the dryer vent, foundation gaps, and where cables and pipes
  come in.
- **Remove hiding places:** woodpiles against the house (→ 06-03), clutter, cardboard.
- **Traps beat poison** in a house with children or pets: snap traps inside covered boxes.
  Poison can kill a pet that eats a poisoned mouse and can poison a curious child (→ 20-02).
- **Check regularly.** Droppings, gnaw marks and greasy rub marks along walls are the signs.

**In a grid-down, rodent pressure rises:** food is scarcer for them too, buildings are less
disturbed, and nearby houses may stand empty. Expect more, not fewer.

## Insects: kill them before storage

Pantry insects usually arrive **inside** the food from the store, as eggs.

- **Freeze new grain and flour at 0 °F or colder for 3 days; large packages and buckets for
  7 days** (Kansas State University Extension, Controlling Stored-Food Insects, MF-2270). A
  home freezer, or measured winter cold that stays that low (→ 04-09). Heat works too: flour,
  beans and whole grain spread in shallow pans in a 150 °F oven for 15 to 20 minutes (same
  source).
- **Oxygen absorbers** in sealed Mylar (→ 04-03) suffocate any survivors.
- **Bay leaves** in containers are a traditional, mild deterrent; harmless.
- **Look when you open a package:** webbing in the corners, clumps, or small moths in the pantry
  mean an infestation. Seal it off and deal with it before it spreads.

## If contamination happens

- **Food rodents have touched: throw it away.** Do not cut out the "good part." Urine and
  droppings spread beyond the visible damage.
- **Sealed metal or glass containers** that were only gnawed on the outside are fine: the
  contents are protected. That is exactly why hard containers matter.
- **Clean up the CDC way. This is hantavirus prevention, not tidiness.** Deer mice shed the virus
  in urine, droppings and nests; people catch it by breathing the dust. CDC's steps (CDC, Clean
  Up After Rodents, 2024):
  1. **Open all doors and windows for 30 minutes before you start, and stay out** while it airs.
  2. **Never sweep or vacuum** droppings, urine or nest material: that puts the virus in the air.
  3. **Rubber or plastic gloves on.** Spray the droppings, urine and nest **thoroughly** with a
     disinfectant or **bleach solution: 1½ cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water (1 part
     bleach to 9 parts water), mixed fresh. Let it soak 5 minutes** (or as the disinfectant
     label says). Bleach basics: → 29-05. Use bleach and water only, nothing else mixed in.
  4. **Wipe up with paper towels** and put them in a covered rubbish bin that is emptied often.
  5. **Then mop or sponge the whole area** (floors, counters, cabinets, drawers) with
     disinfectant.
  6. **Wash gloved hands** with soap and water or disinfectant **before taking the gloves off,
     then wash bare hands** with soap and warm water.

  A dead mouse or a nest: gloves on, spray it and the area around it with disinfectant, put it
  (and any used trap) in a plastic bag, knot it, put that in a second bag, knot it, and put it in
  a covered bin (CDC). Food the rodents touched is thrown away; wash dishes and utensils they
  reached before use. **Anyone who develops fever, tiredness and muscle aches (thighs, hips,
  back), then cough and shortness of breath, 1 to 8 weeks after contact with rodents: → 12-05,
  and say the word "hantavirus"** (CDC).
- **Insect-infested dry goods** are more a quality problem than a safety one, but with little
  water for sorting and washing, throwing them out is usually the practical answer.

## Pets, food and hygiene

{{#if has.cats}}Your cats{{else}}Cats{{/if}} are genuinely useful for rodent control around
stored food. The other side:

- **Keep litter boxes far from food storage and preparation** (→ 13-01).
- **Wash hands** after handling pets or litter, especially before food work (→ 13-02).
- **Pet food is rodent food too:** store it in the same hard containers (→ 20-09).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Metal bins or galvanised cans with lids** | Truly rodent-proof | Buckets go inside them |
| Glass jars with tight lids | Small amounts, rodent-proof | Free from many foods |
| **Hardware cloth and steel wool** | Sealing entry points | ¼-inch mesh |
| Snap traps (many) | Safer than poison with children and pets | Inside covered boxes |
| Oxygen absorbers | Kill insect eggs in sealed storage | → 04-03 |
| Gloves, bleach or disinfectant, spray bottle, paper towels, plastic bags | The CDC clean-up | 1½ cups bleach per gallon of water (1 to 9); 5-minute soak; **wet, never sweep or vacuum**; store bleach where children cannot reach it |
| Headlamp | Checking dark corners | → 10-01 |
| Bay leaves | Mild insect deterrent | Cheap |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Metal filing cabinets, ammunition cans, coffee tins and old chest freezers** (unplugged) all
  make good rodent-proof food storage.
- Hardware cloth in gaps; expanding foam **with** steel wool packed in first (foam alone gets
  chewed through).
- Winter cold (→ 04-09) can stand in for a freezer to kill insect eggs, if a thermometer shows
  0 °F or colder for the whole 3 to 7 days.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** traps and sealing materials are small consumables; the containers last.
- **Ration:** protect the **bulk staples** first. A lost bucket of rice is weeks of food.
- **Resupply:** metal containers are easy to scavenge.
- **The losses compound:** pests do not take a fixed amount; an unchecked infestation destroys a
  stockpile bit by bit. A monthly look is the whole defence.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** seal the house now; use metal containers for the deep stock.
- **B (moving):** food in a vehicle draws animals at stops; keep it sealed and inside.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** rodent pressure is usually much higher, especially in
  outbuildings. Metal containers become essential.

## Cross-references

→ 04-03 bulk storage containers · → 04-02 pantry · → 04-09 winter cold · → 20-09 pets ·
→ 13-02 hygiene · → 12-05 illness · → 20-02 poisons and children · → 29-05 bleach

pages.title: Fats and oils: storage and rendering
pages.body:
# Fats and oils: storage and rendering

**What this page is for.** Why fat matters more than most food plans allow, how long each kind
keeps, and how to render animal fat into cooking fat that stores for months.

> **CAUTION.** Fat is the **most calorie-dense food you can store** (about 4,000 calories per
> pound, more than double any grain) and the **first to go rancid.** It is also a common hiding
> place for allergens: in the US, "vegetable oil" usually means **soybean oil,** and soy is one
> of the nine major allergens (FDA, Food Allergies). Read every label.

## Do this now

1. **Stock fat on purpose.** It is where calories hide in a small space, and stored-food diets
   most often fall short on fat.
2. **Read every oil label** if anyone in the house has a food allergy (→ 02-04). "Vegetable oil"
   is the trap. Single-source oils name what they are: olive, canola, corn, sunflower, coconut.
3. **Ask the allergist about highly refined soybean oil.** Refined oils are treated differently
   under US labelling law, and the answer opens or closes a large amount of shelf-stable food.
   {{#if has.anaphylaxis}}Someone in your household has an allergy marked for anaphylaxis: get
   this answer in writing for the allergy plan.{{/if}}
4. **Store cool, dark and sealed.** Heat, light and air make fat rancid.
5. **Learn to render** (below). It turns animal fat you would otherwise waste into months of
   cooking fat and soap (→ 13-09).

## Why fat matters more than people plan for

- **Calorie density:** about 4,000 calories per pound against about 1,600 for grain. A gallon of
  oil is roughly **30,000 calories** in a container you can carry.
- **Eating and cooking:** rice and beans with no fat is a bleak, hard-to-eat diet. Fat makes
  stored food into meals people finish, which matters a great deal with children.
- **Nutrition:** fat carries the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and is a real need.
- **Other uses:** soap (→ 13-09), lamps (→ 10-02), lubrication, waterproofing.

## Shelf life: the limit

| Fat | Shelf life (cool, dark, sealed) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Coconut oil** | 2 to 3 years or more | Very stable; solid at room temperature |
| **Olive oil** | 1½ to 2 years | Check for blends |
| **Canola, corn, sunflower** | 1 to 2 years | Single-source; **not** "vegetable oil" |
| **Shortening (canned)** | 2 to 5 years or more | Very stable sealed; check for soy |
| **Lard, tallow (rendered, sealed)** | 1 to 2 years at room temperature; longer cold | Well rendered is very stable |
| **Butter: COMMERCIALLY canned, or ghee** | 1 to 2 years or more | Ghee (butter with the milk solids removed) keeps far better than butter |
| **Nuts and seeds** | Months | High oil; also common allergens |

**Never home-can butter, milk, cheese or any dairy.** There is no tested process for it (NCHFP);
the fat shields botulism spores from the heat. **Floor:** **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to
the published time and pressure, or not canned.** Botulism has no field treatment and the food
looks and smells normal (→ 30-01). Make ghee and keep it cool, or freeze butter.

**Rancid fat smells like crayons or old paint.** It is not immediately dangerous, but it tastes
bad and has lost nutrition, and children will simply refuse it.

**The rotation rule:** fat is the **one bulk food you cannot store for decades.** Buy amounts you
will actually use up in a year or two, and keep buying (→ 04-10).

## Rendering: the renewable source

Rendering is melting raw animal fat slowly and straining it, which turns it into cooking fat that
keeps. It makes fat **renewable** rather than purely stored, if you hunt (→ 05-07) or keep
animals (Section 05).

**Method:**

1. **Cut the fat small** (or grind it). Trim off meat and blood; they cause spoilage.
2. **Heat low and slow:** a heavy pot over low coals (→ 06-02) or a Dutch oven (→ 07-04). A
   little water at the start stops scorching; it boils off.
3. **Let it melt out** over hours. Do not brown it: high heat gives dark, strong-tasting fat.
4. **Strain** through cloth into clean jars.
5. **Cool and seal.** Well rendered fat is white or pale and smells clean.
6. **The crisp bits left over** (cracklings) are food.

**Sources:** pork fat makes **lard** (good for cooking and baking); beef and deer fat make
**tallow** (harder; better for candles, soap and waterproofing than for baking; deer tallow is
waxy and strong-tasting). Poultry fat renders easily and tastes good.

**For hunting households:** deer are lean, and deer fat is not prized for cooking. If you want
rendered cooking fat, pork and beef fat are far better. A butcher may sell it cheaply now.

## Storage in practice

- **Cool, dark, sealed:** a cool shelf, not above the stove.
- **Small containers** so you open one at a time; each opening starts the clock.
- **Metal or glass** over plastic for long storage.
- **Keep a "used grease" jar** for cooking fat: strain and reuse it several times, then use the
  last of it for soap (→ 13-09) rather than throwing it away.

## The allergen check, again

If anyone in the house has a food allergy (→ 02-04):

- **"Vegetable oil" usually means soybean oil.** Avoid it unless the allergist clears refined soy.
- **Shortening** and **margarine** often contain soy.
- **Buy single-source oils** and keep the label (→ 04-03).
- **Fat you rendered yourself is fully traceable,** which makes it one of the safest fats in the
  house for an allergic person.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cooking oil: **single-source, label checked** | Calories and cooking | Olive, canola, corn, coconut |
| Coconut oil, canned shortening | Longest-keeping fats | Check ingredients |
| Ghee or **commercially** canned butter | Keeps far better than butter | **Never home-canned dairy** |
| Heavy pot or Dutch oven for rendering | Turns waste fat into food | → 07-04 |
| Straining cloth and wide-mouth jars | Rendering and storage | Reusable |
| Grease jar kept by the stove or fire | Reuse, then soap | → 13-09 |
| Labels and dates | Fat is the fastest-rotating bulk food | → 04-10 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Fat from anything you butcher or hunt** (→ 05-09): render it rather than throw it away.
- Bacon grease and cooking drippings, strained and kept.
- **Fat from a butcher** is often cheap or free now; buy it and render it while that is easy.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** count in **pounds or quarts,** and remember it is the **shortest-lived** bulk food
  (1 to 2 years, not decades).
- **Ration:** spend fat on flavour and calories, not on deep frying. Reuse cooking grease.
- **Resupply:** **rendering** is the renewable answer, from hunting (→ 05-07), livestock
  (Section 05) or trade. It is one of the few foods with a real renewable path at household scale.
- **The long-term point:** grains keep for decades; **fat does not.** In a long emergency,
  rendered animal fat is how you get calorie density.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** buy and rotate; render fat from any meat you process.
- **B (moving):** fat is the best calories-per-pound food to carry; a jar of rendered fat is
  remarkable energy in a small space.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** rendering becomes routine; pair it with hunting and
  butchering (→ 05-09).

## Cross-references

→ 04-01 calorie math · → 04-03 bulk storage · → 04-10 rotation · → 02-04 food allergy ·
→ 05-09 butchering and fat · → 13-09 soap · → 10-02 fat lamps

pages.title: Salt, sugar, vinegar and honey: the preserving staples
pages.body:
# Salt, sugar, vinegar and honey: the preserving staples

**What this page is for.** The four foods that make almost all other food preservation work:
why to stock them, how much, how to store them, and the one safety rule about honey.

> **CAUTION.** These four are the chemical basis of nearly all food preserving. They keep
> essentially **for ever,** they are **cheap now,** and most households **cannot make any of
> them** at useful scale. That makes them the best value-per-dollar stockpile in the food
> section. **One safety rule: never give honey to a baby under 12 months.** It can carry
> botulism spores that a baby's gut cannot handle (→ 20-01).

## Do this now

1. **Buy salt in quantity. Then buy more.** It is the master preservative and it never expires.
2. **Stock sugar and honey** for preserving, calories and morale (→ 21-02).
3. **Stock vinegar of known strength (5 percent acidity)** for pickling. Canning recipes assume
   it.
4. **Keep them dry and sealed.** They do not spoil, but they cake, absorb moisture and attract
   pests (→ 04-11).
5. **No honey for any baby under 12 months.** {{#if has.infant}}**You have a child under 2 in the
   house: check the age before anyone offers honey,** including honey in baked goods or
   medicine.{{/if}}

## Salt: the one you cannot replace

Salt is the base of curing (→ 04-07), fermenting (→ 04-08), brining, and preserving meat and
vegetables. It also seasons food that is otherwise dull, which matters more over months than
people expect.

- **Storage: indefinite.** Keep it dry; it cakes but stays usable.
- **Kinds:** plain, non-iodised **canning or pickling salt** for ferments and cures: **iodised
  salt and anti-caking agents can discolour ferments and cloud brine.** Keep both: iodised for the
  table (iodine is a real nutritional need) and plain for preserving.
- **Quantity:** far more than you think. Curing meat uses pounds at a time.
- **Most households cannot practically make food salt.** It is a stockpile item, and so an
  excellent **barter good** (→ 18-02).
{{#if has.saltwater_pool}}- **Your saltwater pool** holds a large amount of dissolved salt, and
  distilling pool water (→ 03-03) leaves concentrated brine behind. That residue is
  **emergency-grade, not food-grade:** pool water carries cyanuric acid (a chlorine stabiliser)
  and whatever else was ever added to it. Treat boiled-down pool salt as a true last resort for
  preserving brines, never the plan, and never as table salt for children.{{/if}}

## Sugar and honey

- **Sugar** keeps indefinitely if dry. Used for jams, preserving fruit, baking and morale. **Do not
  pack sugar with oxygen absorbers:** it sets into a solid brick (→ 04-03).
- **Honey** keeps practically for ever. Crystallising is normal and reverses with gentle warmth. It
  is a real morale food.
- **Never for babies under 12 months.** Honey can contain *Clostridium botulinum* spores. An older
  child's or adult's gut handles them; a baby's cannot. This is a hard rule (→ 20-01, → 02-13).

## Vinegar

- **Use vinegar of known acidity (5 percent)** for canning. Recipes are calculated on it, and
  homemade vinegar of unknown strength is **not safe** for canning (→ 04-04).
- **Keeps indefinitely.**
- **Uses beyond food:** cleaning and descaling when other cleaners run out (→ 13-03). **Floor:**
  **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** Vinegar is an
  acid; the mix gives off chlorine gas (→ 30-01).
- **You can make vinegar** from fruit or cider with a "mother" culture. It is fine for eating and
  cleaning, but **not for canning,** because you cannot check its acidity.

## The barter angle

Salt and sugar are close to ideal trade goods (→ 18-02): everyone wants them, they keep for ever,
they divide into small amounts, and few people can make them. Unlike ammunition (→ 14-08),
trading them puts no risk in someone else's hands.

## Storage

- **Airtight and dry.** Moisture is the only enemy.
- **Food-grade buckets** for bulk salt and sugar; a working container in the kitchen.
- **Off concrete,** cool and dark (→ 04-03).
- **Pest-proof:** sugar draws insects and rodents (→ 04-11).

## Quantities to think about

| Item | A serious household stock | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Salt** | **50 lb or more** | Curing alone uses pounds; cheap; keeps for ever |
| Sugar | 25 to 50 lb | Preserving, baking, morale |
| Honey | Several pounds | Keeps for ever; morale |
| Vinegar (5 percent) | Several gallons | Pickling, cleaning |
| Canning or pickling salt | A separate stock | Ferments and cures (→ 04-08) |
| Curing salt (nitrite) | Small, labelled, **locked** | → 04-07; poisonous in small amounts |

These are starting points for an ordinary household; scale them to your {{ household.size }}
people and to how much you plan to cure and ferment.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bulk salt** (plain and iodised) | The master preservative | The cheapest high-value stockpile there is |
| Bulk sugar | Preserving and morale | Dry, sealed, no oxygen absorbers |
| Honey | Keeps for ever; morale | **Not for babies under 12 months** |
| Vinegar, 5 percent acidity | Canning and cleaning | Known strength matters |
| Airtight buckets or containers | Moisture is the only threat | → 04-03 |
| Kitchen scale | Cure and ferment amounts are by weight | → 04-08 |
| Labels | Tell canning salt from curing salt | Critical: curing salt is poisonous |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Vinegar can be made** from fruit or cider: fine for eating and cleaning, **never for canning.**
- Maple sap can be boiled down to syrup where the trees grow; it takes an enormous amount of fuel
  (→ 06-04).
- **Salt has no substitute.** That is exactly why you stockpile it now.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** simply the amount you bought ÷ how fast you use it. These do not spoil.
- **Ration:** salt used for **preserving** creates stored food; salt used for seasoning is spent.
  Put preserving first.
- **Resupply:** trade (→ 18-02) is the realistic route.
- **The strategic point:** of everything in this section, **salt is the highest-value,
  lowest-cost, longest-lasting purchase you can make today.** If the budget is tight this month,
  buy salt.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** buy in bulk now.
- **B (moving):** salt is heavy but valuable; carry some. It is compact currency (→ 18-02).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** essential for preserving game and garden produce; a top
  trade good with neighbours.

## Cross-references

→ 04-04 canning (needs known-strength vinegar) · → 04-07 curing · → 04-08 fermenting ·
→ 18-02 barter · → 20-01 no honey for babies · → 13-09 soap (uses fat and lye, not salt)

pages.title: Dairy: powdered, canned and shelf-stable
pages.body:
# Dairy: powdered, canned and shelf-stable

**What this page is for.** Which kinds of milk and dairy keep without a fridge, how long each
keeps, which ones young children need, and why none of them replaces infant formula.

> **CAUTION.** **Powdered or canned milk is not infant formula.** Giving a baby under 12 months
> improvised milk instead of breast milk or formula is dangerous. The infant feeding plan is on
> → 02-13 and → 20-05. **Children 12 to 23 months drink plain whole milk, not reduced-fat** (CDC,
> Foods and Drinks for 12 to 24 Month Olds), so their stored milk is **whole-milk powder or UHT
> (long-life boxed) whole milk, not the nonfat powder** that keeps longest. **Never home-can any
> dairy** (below).

## Do this now

1. **Stock powdered milk.** It is the most storable dairy, and it makes stored grain far more
   appealing to children.
2. **If you have a child 12 to 23 months old,** stock **whole-milk powder and/or UHT whole milk**
   for them, label it, and rotate it. The nonfat powder is for everyone else.
   {{#if has.toddler}}**You have a child in this age range.**{{/if}}
3. **If you have a baby under 12 months,** stock **infant formula,** not milk, even if the baby
   is breastfed (as a backup), and follow → 02-13 and → 20-05. Formula's use-by date matters
   (→ 04-10). {{#if has.infant}}**You have a child under 2 in the house.**{{/if}}
4. **Check labels for allergens.** Milk is one of the nine major allergens; dairy blends and
   "non-dairy" creamers often contain soy or tree nuts (→ 02-04).
5. **Store cool, dark and sealed.** Fat content limits shelf life.
6. **Rotate.** Dairy is not a decades item, apart from nonfat powder (→ 04-10).

## The options

| Product | Shelf life (cool, sealed) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Nonfat dry milk** | **10 to 20 years** | The storage champion: no fat to go rancid. Not for children 12 to 23 months as their main milk |
| **Whole dry milk** | 2 to 5 years | Better taste, shorter life (fat). The toddler's powder; rotate it |
| **Evaporated milk (canned)** | 1 to 2 years or more | Ready to use; heavy |
| **Sweetened condensed milk** | 1 to 2 years or more | Sugar preserves it; morale food |
| **UHT boxed milk** (long-life) | 6 to 12 months | Tastes closest to fresh; short life. Whole UHT is the toddler's other option |
| **Commercially canned or powdered butter, ghee** | 1 to 2 years or more | → 04-12 |
| **Hard cheese, wax-sealed** | Months | Keeps without a fridge surprisingly well |
| **Powdered cheese, powdered buttermilk** | Years | Flavour for plain food |

**Never home-can butter, milk or cheese.** There is no tested process for it (NCHFP); the fat
shields botulism spores from the heat. **Floor:** **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the
published time and pressure, or not canned.** Botulism has no field treatment and the food looks
and smells normal (→ 30-01).

**Nonfat dry milk is the backbone:** sealed, it keeps for decades, and it reconstitutes for
drinking, baking and cooking.

## Why it matters with children

- **Calcium and protein** for growth.
- **Fat for toddlers.** From 12 to 23 months, whole milk, not reduced-fat, is the rule (CDC).
  Log the toddler's whole-milk stock as theirs on → 22-04.
- **Familiarity.** Small children under stress eat familiar things. Milk on oatmeal turns stored
  grain into breakfast rather than a fight (→ 20-03).
- **Calories** in a form children accept.
- **Morale.** Hot chocolate in a cold house is worth far more than its calories (→ 21-02).

## The allergen check

If anyone in the house has a food allergy (→ 02-04):

- **Milk itself** is a major allergen. A milk-allergic person needs a different calcium and
  protein plan; ask their doctor while you can.
- **Blends and mixes** (hot chocolate, creamers, "milk alternatives") often contain **soy** or
  **tree nuts.**
- **Plain nonfat dry milk** is usually a single ingredient: the easiest to check.
- **Keep the label** when you repackage (→ 04-03).

## Using it

- **Mix it ahead and chill it.** Powdered milk tastes much better cold and after a few hours'
  rest.
- **Cook with it** if people will not drink it: oatmeal, gravy, baking, soup.
- **Use it to enrich plain food:** a scoop of dry milk in bread, porridge or soup adds protein and
  calories.
- **Reconstituted milk is perishable.** Treat it exactly like fresh milk: the 40 °F and 2-hour
  rule applies (→ 04-17). Whether to use dairy that has been warm, or past its date, when food is
  short is a decision card: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15.

## Is dairy renewable?

- **Not realistically in town.** A dairy animal does not work on a small lot.
- **Goats** are the small-scale option at a rural site (Section 05): a real long-term dairy source,
  and a serious daily commitment.
- **So at home, dairy is a stored, finite resource.** Plan it that way and favour the long-life
  forms.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Nonfat dry milk (bulk)** | Decades of storage | Repackage as on → 04-03 |
| **Whole-milk powder and/or UHT whole milk** | For children 12 to 23 months | Rotate (2 to 5 years; 6 to 12 months); label it |
| **Infant formula** (if there is a baby under 12 months) | The only safe substitute for breast milk | → 02-13, → 20-05; mind the use-by date |
| Evaporated and condensed milk (cans) | Ready to use; morale | Rotate |
| Shelf-stable boxed milk | Closest to fresh | Short life: rotate hard |
| Powdered cheese, buttermilk | Flavour for plain food | Small, big effect |
| Ghee or **commercially** canned butter | Fat and flavour | → 04-12; never home-canned dairy |
| Airtight containers and oxygen absorbers | Dry milk keeps far longer sealed | → 04-03 |
| Whisk or shaker jar | Mixing without lumps | Small but useful |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Hard, waxed cheeses** keep for months without a fridge.
- Canned milk is common in pantries and stores.
- **For cooking,** dry milk replaces fresh milk in nearly every recipe.
- **Do not improvise infant nutrition.** → 02-13 and → 20-05. For a toddler, the shelf substitute
  is whole-milk powder or UHT whole milk, not nonfat.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** pounds of dry milk ÷ use. It multiplies comfort and nutrition more than calories,
  but it is what makes the calorie base edible for children.
- **Ration:** many households keep it for the children and for cooking, not for adults' drinks.
- **Resupply:** trade (→ 18-02); goats at a rural site; otherwise accept that it is
  finite.
- **The gap it leaves:** calcium and vitamin D. Sprouts (→ 04-16), greens (→ 05-01), canned
  fish with soft bones (if no one is allergic to fish), and bone broth from game (→ 05-09) help.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** stock deep now; it is cheap and keeps well.
- **B (moving):** dry milk is light and dense; worth carrying for children.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** goats become possible; until then, the same stored supply.

## Cross-references

→ 04-03 bulk storage · → 04-12 fats · → 04-01 calorie math · → 04-17 reconstituted milk is
perishable · → 02-13 infant feeding · → 20-05 infant feeding plan · → 02-04 food allergy

pages.title: Storing eggs without refrigeration
pages.body:
# Storing eggs without refrigeration

**What this page is for.** Which eggs can be kept without a fridge and which cannot, the storage
methods that are tested and the traditional ones that are not, how to check an egg, and how to
cook eggs safely.

> **SAFETY.** **US store-bought eggs are washed,** which removes the egg's natural protective
> coating (the "bloom"). Washed eggs **must be kept cold** and cannot be stored by the
> traditional room-temperature methods below. Eggs can carry *Salmonella* (a germ that causes
> severe diarrhoea and fever) **inside** the shell; cooking eggs firm is what controls it.
> **Egg is one of the nine major food allergens** (FDA, Food Allergies): if anyone in the house
> is allergic to egg, read → 02-04 before deciding to store eggs at all.

## Do this now

1. **Know which eggs you have.** **Washed (store) eggs** are kept at **40 °F or below** (FDA,
   What You Need to Know About Egg Safety). In
   an outage, that means measured cold (→ 04-09) or eat them first (→ 04-17). **Unwashed,
   freshly laid eggs** (your own hens or a farm) are the only eggs the methods below apply to.
2. **Cook eggs and egg dishes to safe temperatures:** eggs until yolk and white are firm; egg
   dishes to **160 °F** (FDA; FoodSafety.gov). With no medical care, cook them through.
3. **Crack every stored egg into a separate bowl first** and smell it.
4. **Use the tested long-term methods first:** freezing (out of the shell) and drying fully
   cooked egg.
5. **If anyone in the house is allergic to egg,** decide as a household, with the allergist's
   advice, whether eggs belong in the house at all (below). {{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Someone in
   your household has an allergy marked for anaphylaxis.** Check whether egg is on their
   list.{{/if}}

## The allergy question comes first

{{#each allergies as a}}
- {{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}})
{{else}}
- No allergies are entered for your household.
{{/each}}

Eggs are one of the best food returns from a small yard (→ 05-04): protein, fat and calories.
For a household where someone has an egg allergy, they are also a dangerous food. The honest
options:

| Option | What it means |
|---|---|
| **No eggs in the house** | Simplest and safest for the allergic person. Loses a very efficient protein source |
| **Eggs, strictly controlled** | Sealed storage out of reach, dedicated cookware and surfaces, cooked when the allergic person is not in the kitchen, thorough cleaning |
| **Eggs kept or traded elsewhere** | Produced and traded away, or kept at a neighbour's |

**Ask the allergist** while you can, including whether the person tolerates **baked** egg, which
changes the picture a great deal. Write the answer in the allergy plan (→ 02-04, → 02-03).
Traded or scavenged food containing egg for an allergic person: {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.

## Washed and unwashed: the fact that decides everything

A freshly laid egg has a natural coating (the **bloom**) that seals the shell and keeps bacteria
out. **US commercial eggs are washed,** which removes it, so they need refrigeration.

**Unwashed, freshly laid eggs** keep their bloom, which is why the traditional methods start
from them. No source used here gives a safe time for keeping them out of the fridge:

- **The safe storage temperature is 40 °F or below** (FDA). Penn State Extension notes that a
  pantry or basement is very unlikely to reach and hold that.
- **Use unrefrigerated eggs first,** and check each one (below).
- **Do not wash them until you use them.** Brushing, washing or rough handling damages the bloom
  (Penn State Extension).

## Long-term methods (unwashed eggs only)

Two methods are **tested and recommended** (freezing, and drying cooked egg). Two are
**traditional and not recommended by Extension** (water glassing and oiling).

| Method | How | Planning life | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Freezing** (out of the shell) | Break each egg into a saucer and check it, mix yolk and white, freeze in portions (NCHFP, Freezing Eggs) | Months (needs a freezer or measured hard-freeze cold, → 04-09) | **Recommended** (NCHFP; Penn State Extension). First choice when cold is available |
| **Drying** | **Fully cooked** (scrambled hard), dried, powdered | Quality varies; keep it dry and sealed | Cooked first, so the *Salmonella* question is settled before storage (→ 04-06) |
| **Cool storage** | Unwashed eggs kept as cold as you can, dark | No tested time: use them first | Refrigeration at 40 °F or below is the published standard (FDA); a cellar is usually warmer |
| **Water glassing** | Clean, unwashed, uncracked eggs under a pickling-lime (calcium hydroxide) and water solution in a sealed food-safe container, kept cool | No tested storage time | **Not recommended** by Utah State University Extension ("not considered safe"), Kansas State University Research and Extension, or Penn State Extension. Decision card DC-27 |
| **Oiling** | Fresh unwashed eggs coated in food-grade mineral oil, stored cool, small end down | No tested storage time | Not tested; no source used here recommends it |

**Why Extension says no to water glassing:** *Salmonella* can get inside the egg while it forms
in the hen, and there is no way to know it is there (Utah State University Extension, Storing
Eggs Safely, 2023; Kansas State University Research and Extension, Storing Eggs Safely, 2020).
Penn State Extension adds that the membrane under the shell lets water, and any germs in it,
into the egg, and that a pantry or basement will not stay cold enough to stop germs already
inside from growing (How to Safely Handle and Store Eggs from Your Home Flock, 2024). Oiling has
no published testing either way; the same germs-inside problem applies.

**The trade-off.** Some households water-glass anyway, because the alternative is no eggs
through a winter with no fresh food. The card's "with rules" option means all of these, every
time: only clean, unwashed, uncracked fresh eggs; food-grade pickling lime; a sealed container
kept as cool as possible, for the shortest time you can manage; every egg checked before use
(below), and any cracked, floating or off egg thrown out; every egg cooked until yolk and white
are firm (160 °F in dishes); and none for anyone allergic to egg. Thorough cooking is what
reduces the *Salmonella* risk; it does not make the method tested, and there is no tested
storage time. Whether your household water-glasses at all is a decision card: following
Extension means no stored eggs once cold storage fails; water-glassing accepts a *Salmonella*
risk that cooking reduces but does not remove. {{choice DC-27}} → 30-28.

**Pickling lime is caustic.** Store it sealed and out of children's reach (→ 20-02). A bucket of
eggs in solution on the floor is exactly the wrong container in a house with small children:
sealed, labelled, raised, out of reach.

## Checking an egg

- **Candling:** in a dark room, hold the egg against a bright flashlight. A sound egg shows a
  small air pocket at the wide end and a faint yolk shadow. **A large air pocket, a dark or moving
  mass, blotches, cracks, or a bad smell on opening: throw it out.**
- **Float test:** in water, a fresh egg sinks and lies flat; an older one stands on end; **one
  that floats is old: throw it out.** This measures the air pocket, not safety, but it is a useful
  first screen.
- **Crack it into a separate bowl first,** always, so one bad egg does not ruin a dish, and so you
  can smell it. **Bad eggs are unmistakable.**
- **Throw out cracked, leaking or bad-smelling eggs.**

{{figure fig-candling-an-egg}}

## Safe cooking

- **Eggs:** until yolk and white are firm (FDA).
- **Egg dishes** (quiche, frittata, custard): **160 °F** (FDA; FoodSafety.gov).
- **Casseroles:** **165 °F** (FoodSafety.gov).
- Runny eggs are a higher-risk food; with no medical care, cook them through. Children, older
  adults, pregnant women and anyone with a weak immune system (including people with diabetes)
  are most at risk from *Salmonella* (FDA).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Sealed, labelled container out of reach** | Allergen control and child safety | → 02-04 |
| Freezer containers or small bags | Freezing beaten egg in portions | The recommended method |
| Dehydrator or drying racks | Drying cooked egg | → 04-06 |
| Bright flashlight | Candling | → 10-01 |
| Instant-read thermometer | 160 °F egg dishes | → 07-01 |
| Pickling lime (only if you choose to water-glass) | Traditional, not recommended method | Food-grade calcium hydroxide; caustic; store locked |
| Food-grade mineral oil (only if you choose to oil eggs) | Traditional, not recommended method | Food grade only |
| **Dedicated cookware and utensils** for any allergic person | Avoids cross-contact | A distinct colour (→ 02-04) |
| Egg cartons | Storage and trade | Free |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Unwashed farm eggs** are the practical source if you do not keep hens.
- **Egg replacers for baking** (ground flax and water, commercial replacers): check every replacer
  for other allergens, such as soy (→ 02-04).
- Without eggs, **beans, meat and dairy** cover the protein role.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** with hens, eggs are a **flow, not a store** (→ 05-04). Laying drops sharply in winter
  with short days, which is when you most need the calories.
- **Ration:** preserve a summer surplus to cover the winter slump: freeze or dry cooked egg where
  you can.
- **Resupply:** hens, trade with neighbours, or do without.
- **If someone in the house is allergic to egg:** eggs may be worth more as a trade good
  (→ 18-02) than as stored food. Decide on purpose, and write the decision in the allergy plan.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** controlling an allergen is hardest in a small shared kitchen.
- **B (moving):** eggs travel badly; do not carry them.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** hens are more practical; the same rules apply, plus coop
  hygiene (→ 05-04).

## Cross-references

→ 05-04 backyard chickens · → 04-06 drying · → 04-09 winter cold · → 04-17 food safety in an
outage · → 07-01 safe cooking temperatures · → 02-04 food allergy · → 02-03 anaphylaxis ·
→ 30-15 questionable food · → 30-28 water-glassed eggs

pages.title: Sprouting grains and beans for fresh food
pages.body:
# Sprouting grains and beans for fresh food

**What this page is for.** How to turn dry beans, lentils and grains you already store into fresh
green food in a few days, on a counter, with no soil, light or fuel, and who should eat sprouts
cooked rather than raw.

> **CAUTION.** Sprouting is the cheapest fresh food you can have in a long winter, and **sprouts
> are a known higher-risk raw food:** the warm, wet conditions that grow them also grow bacteria.
> **FDA advises that children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune
> systems should not eat raw sprouts of any kind; cooking sprouts thoroughly kills the bacteria**
> (FoodSafety.gov/FDA, Sprouts: What You Should Know). Rinsing does not remove bacteria that are
> inside the sprout. Keep jars scrupulously clean.

## Do this now

1. **Buy sprouting seed now,** and note that **the dry beans and grains you already store will
   sprout,** which makes this nearly free.
2. **Set up two jars** with mesh lids and start a rotation, so something is always ready.
3. **Rinse twice a day, morning and night.** That is the whole technique and the whole safety
   control.
4. **Do not sprout anything someone in the house is allergic to** (→ 02-04).
5. **Cook sprouts** (steamed, or stirred into soup until steaming hot, 165 °F) **for children,
   older adults, anyone pregnant and anyone with a weakened immune system.**
   {{#if has.child}}You have children in the house: their sprouts are cooked.{{/if}}
   {{#if has.elder}}You have an older adult in the house: their sprouts are cooked.{{/if}}
   {{#if has.pregnant}}Someone in the house is pregnant: her sprouts are cooked.{{/if}}

## Why this matters

In winter, with no garden and no shops, a diet of stored grain, beans and canned goods has
enough calories but **too few vitamins.** That is the classic long-winter deficiency problem;
historically, scurvy (lack of vitamin C).

**Sprouting fixes it with what you already store.** A handful of dry beans becomes fresh green
food in 3 to 5 days, on a kitchen counter, with **no soil, no light, no garden and no fuel.**
Sprouting raises vitamin content, including vitamin C, which dry seeds have almost none of.

**It also multiplies volume** several times over, which stretches stored staples.

## What to sprout

| Seed | Days | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Lentils** | 2 to 4 | Easiest; the best first choice |
| **Mung beans** | 3 to 5 | The classic bean sprout; forgiving |
| **Alfalfa, clover** | 4 to 6 | Small, mild, high yield |
| **Radish, broccoli** | 3 to 5 | Peppery; strong nutrition |
| **Wheat, barley, hull-on oat groats** | 2 to 3 | From bulk storage (→ 04-03). **Rolled, steel-cut or hulled oats will not sprout:** only whole groats with the hull |
| **Chickpeas, peas** | 2 to 4 | Hearty; good cooked. Chickpeas and peas are legumes, like peanuts: ask the allergist before giving them to someone with a peanut allergy |
| **Sunflower** | 2 to 3 | Hulled seed |
| **Soy, sesame** | — | Common allergens: skip them if anyone in the house is allergic |
| **Kidney beans** (and other *Phaseolus* beans) | — | **Do not eat raw sprouted kidney beans.** They contain a natural toxin; boil them hard as on → 04-03 (FDA, Bad Bug Book) |

**Use seed sold for sprouting or for food,** not garden seed. Garden seed is often coated with
fungicide and is **not food** (→ 05-03).

## The method

1. **Rinse and look over** a few tablespoons of seed; throw out damaged ones.
2. **Soak** overnight (4 to 12 hours, depending on the seed) in a clean jar.
3. **Drain completely.** Standing water is what spoils a batch.
4. **Rinse and drain twice a day,** morning and evening.
5. **Keep at room temperature, out of direct sun,** tilted mouth-down so it drains.
6. **Ready in 2 to 6 days:** eat when the sprout is about as long as the seed.
7. **Keep finished sprouts cold** and use them within a few days.

{{figure fig-sprouting-jar}}

**Signs it has failed:** a musty or sour smell, sliminess, or visible mould. **Throw the batch
out** and sterilise the jar; do not try to rinse it back to health.

## Safety, honestly

Sprouts are on every food-safety agency's higher-risk list. The bacteria come **in the seed;** a
contaminated batch of seed is multiplied by the warm, wet jar, and rinsing does not reach bacteria
inside the sprout. Commercial sprouting seed is sometimes sanitised; **beans from a storage bucket
are not.** Apply the strict version:

- **Scrupulously clean jars and lids** (boiling water between batches).
- **Clean water for rinsing** (→ 03-04).
- **Rinse well and drain completely,** twice a day, without fail.
- **Cook sprouts** for children, older adults, anyone pregnant and anyone with a weakened immune
  system (→ 02-18): lightly steamed, or added to soup, to 165 °F. Cooking removes almost all of
  the risk and keeps most of the nutrition. Healthy adults can reduce their own risk the same way.
- **Do not eat a batch that smells wrong.**
- If someone gets sick after eating sprouts: → 12-05.

Indoor microgreens (grown in soil and light, cut above the soil) are another winter green, and
some households prefer them for children (→ 05-14).

## Fitting it into the routine

- **Two jars on a rotation** give a continuous supply from a few tablespoons of seed a week.
- **It needs no fuel and no light,** a rare thing in this binder (→ 06-04).
- **Children can help with supervision.** Rinsing jars is a job a small child can share with an
  adult, but the adult owns the hygiene (→ 20-07), and children's sprouts are cooked.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Wide-mouth jars (several) | The sprouting vessel | You may already have canning jars (→ 04-04) |
| **Mesh sprouting lids,** or cheesecloth and bands | Rinse and drain without losing seed | Cheap; buy several |
| Sprouting seed (lentil, mung, alfalfa, radish) | Dedicated and food-grade | Stored food beans and grains also sprout |
| A rack or bowl to hold jars tilted | Draining is the safety control | Improvised is fine |
| Clean water | Rinsing twice daily | → 03-04 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Cheesecloth, window screen or a clean sock** with a rubber band replaces a sprouting lid.
- **Your stored lentils, mung beans, wheat and peas** are sprouting seed; no special purchase
  needed.
- Any jar, any bowl, any counter.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** effectively unlimited while you have dry seed, and sprouting **multiplies** the
  volume, so it stretches the pantry.
- **Ration:** none needed; it is a net gain.
- **Resupply:** save seed from the garden (→ 05-03), or trade for it.
- **The strategic point:** of every method in this section, sprouting has the best ratio of
  nutrition to cost, fuel, space and effort. **In a long winter it is the single best answer to
  the vitamin problem.**

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** run it all winter on the kitchen counter.
- **B (moving):** a jar and a handful of lentils travel; you can sprout on the road.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the same, plus a real garden in season (→ 05-01).

## Cross-references

→ 04-03 bulk staples (the seed source) · → 04-01 nutrition planning · → 04-18 meal rotation ·
→ 02-04 food allergy · → 05-03 seed saving · → 05-14 indoor growing · → 12-05 illness

pages.title: Food safety when the power fails

photo_slots.caption: Our freezer inventory card, taped to the lid

pages.body:
# Food safety when the power fails

**What this page is for.** What to do with the food in your fridge and freezer from the moment
the power goes out: how long it stays safe, what to eat first, what to throw out, and how to
stretch the cold.

> **SAFETY.** **Never taste food to find out whether it is safe** (FoodSafety.gov). Food
> poisoning without a working hospital is not an inconvenience: vomiting and diarrhoea mean
> dehydration, which is dangerous for babies, small children, elders and anyone with diabetes
> (→ 12-05). **When in doubt, throw it out.**
>
> **Floor:** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning (→ 30-01).
>
> **Floor:** **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Loss of potency with no
> way to tell (→ 30-01). Medicines follow different rules from food (→ 29-07).

## Do this now: the first hour

1. **Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut.** Every opening costs hours of safe storage.
2. **A closed fridge keeps food safe for up to 4 hours.**
3. **A full freezer keeps food safe for about 48 hours; a half-full one about 24 hours,** with
   the door kept shut.
4. **Throw out perishable food** (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, leftovers) that has been
   **above 40 °F for 2 hours or more.**
5. **Move insulin and other refrigerated medicines to their own managed cold,** with its own
   thermometer (→ 02-01, → 29-07). {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Someone in your household
   takes a refrigerated medicine: do this first.**{{/if}}
6. **In cold weather, use the outdoors, but measure it** (→ 04-09).
7. **Put a thermometer in the fridge and the freezer** if they are not already there.

(All times and temperatures: FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During a Power Outage; CDC gives the
same 4, 48 and 24 hours in Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency.)

## The clock

| Appliance | Safe holding time, door kept shut |
|---|---|
| **Refrigerator** | **Up to 4 hours;** after that, perishables (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, leftovers) are thrown out |
| **Freezer, full** | **About 48 hours** |
| **Freezer, half full** | **About 24 hours** |

**Every door opening sets you back.** Decide what you need *before* you open it, take it all at
once, and close it.

## The danger zone

Bacteria multiply fast between **40 °F and 140 °F**. The rule that follows: **perishable food
above 40 °F for 2 hours or more is thrown out.**

**Put an appliance thermometer in the fridge and the freezer now,** so that when the power comes
back (or when you check) you know what actually happened instead of guessing. It costs a few
dollars and it is the difference between a decision and a coin toss.

## The eating order

1. **Fridge perishables first:** meat, dairy, leftovers, opened items. Cook them now, to safe
   inside temperatures (→ 07-01).
2. **Freezer contents next,** as they thaw. **Cook thawed meat while it is still cold,** or
   preserve it (→ 04-05).
3. **Then the pantry** (→ 04-02).
4. **Then bulk staples** (→ 04-03).

**Cook a large batch early.** Cooking **resets** the clock; it does not stop it. Cooked food and
leftovers follow the **same 40 °F and 2-hour rule** as raw food (FoodSafety.gov). The gain is
that it feeds people now and turns a spoilage problem into meals. **Eat it or chill it;** in cold
weather that can mean outside in measured cold (→ 04-09), never "it's cooked, it'll keep on the
counter."

## Stretching the freezer with the power you have

The 48-hour and 24-hour times above are for a freezer with **no power.** If you have stored
power, it can buy more time, but it competes with medical needs and other loads for the same
energy (→ 09-01).

{{#if has.power_station}}- **Your power stations** total **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh.** The
  binder's rough estimate is that this runs a typical full-size fridge (about 1.2 kWh a day) for
  **about {{ derived.station_fridge_days }} days** per full charge. It is an estimate; your own
  appliance may use more or less (→ 09-03, → 29-02).{{else}}- **A power station** (a large
  rechargeable battery with outlets, → 29-02) can run a fridge or freezer for a day or more,
  depending on its size and the appliance (→ 09-03).{{/if}}
- **Find your own appliance's daily use** on its yellow EnergyGuide label: kilowatt-hours per
  year ÷ 365 = kilowatt-hours per day (→ 29-14). Compare it with your stored watt-hours
  (1 kWh = 1,000 Wh).
{{#if has.generator}}- **Your generator** can recharge batteries or run the freezer directly in
  short runs, as long as fuel lasts (→ 09-04). Outdoors only, as the floor above says.{{else}}- A
  **generator** can run the freezer in short runs while fuel lasts (→ 09-04). Outdoors only, as
  the floor above says.{{/if}}
{{#if has.solar}}- **Solar** gives partial refills. In winter, short days and snow cut output
  hard; a December day may not carry a freezer (→ 09-05).{{/if}}

**The moment the outage looks longer than your fuel, stop bridging and start triage:**

1. **Any frozen food that someone on a restricted diet depends on, first.** Allergy-safe or
   medical-diet food is the one category that scavenging, charity and barter **cannot replace**
   (→ 02-04). Cook it, or move it to your coldest backup.
2. **Raw meat second:** the biggest loss and the best to convert. Cook it or pressure-can it
   (→ 04-05) while it is still at 40 °F or below.
3. **Cooked food and leftovers:** eat these in the first day's big meals.
4. **Bread and frozen fruit last:** FoodSafety.gov lets these be kept or refrozen even after
   2 hours above 40 °F, unless mouldy, slimy or yeasty-smelling. **Frozen vegetables are
   thrown out after 6 hours above 40 °F.**

**Keep a freezer inventory card.** Tape a card to the freezer lid and update it whenever the
contents change: what is inside, where (top or bottom), and which items are allergy-safe or
medical-diet food. Then triage decisions get made **without opening the door,** and the card
answers "is it worth running the generator?" with a list instead of a guess.

{{photo freezer-inventory-card}}

## Making the cold last

- **Dry ice or block ice:** CDC advises buying it to keep food cold if the power could be out for
  a long time (CDC, Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency). Handle dry ice with gloves,
  never bare hands, and **never in a closed space with people** (it turns to carbon dioxide gas,
  which pushes out the air).
- **Block ice** lasts longer than cubes.
- **Fill empty freezer space** with jugs of water. A full freezer stays cold much longer, and the
  frozen jugs become drinking water later (→ 03-02).
- **Blankets over the freezer** (not covering any vents) help hold the cold.
- **In cold weather, the outdoors is a freezer,** with the cautions on → 04-09.

## What to keep and what to throw out

| Food | If above 40 °F for 2 hours or more |
|---|---|
| Meat, poultry, fish, eggs | **Throw out** |
| Leftovers, casseroles, cooked dishes | **Throw out** |
| Soft cheeses, milk, cream, yogurt, reconstituted powdered milk | **Throw out** |
| Hard cheeses (cheddar, Swiss, parmesan), processed cheese | Keep |
| Shredded and low-fat cheeses | **Throw out** |
| Butter, margarine | Keep |
| Opened creamy dressings | **Throw out** |
| Opened mayonnaise, tartar sauce, horseradish | **Throw out** if above 50 °F for 8 hours or more |
| Opened vinegar-based dressings, peanut butter, jelly, mustard, ketchup, pickles | Keep |
| Fresh fruit and vegetables, **uncut** | Keep |
| Fresh fruit and vegetables, **cut**; cooked vegetables, cooked pasta, rice and potatoes | **Throw out** |
| Bread, rolls, cakes without custard fillings | Keep |
| Unopened shelf-stable items | Keep |

(FoodSafety.gov's full chart lists more foods. In the Large and Everything downloads it is bound
in this binder: the "Sources for this page" list below links to it.)

**Thawed food that still has ice crystals and is at 40 °F or below** can generally be refrozen,
with some loss of quality (FoodSafety.gov). Fully thawed and warm is thrown out.

**Infant formula** that has been mixed follows its own, shorter rules (→ 02-13, → 20-05).

## The judgment rule

**No smell test. No taste test.** The germs that cause food poisoning do not reliably announce
themselves. How strictly your household follows these published lines when food is truly short
is a decision card: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15. Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are not part of
that choice: they are thrown away.

## Medicine is not food

This page is about food. **Insulin and other refrigerated medicines follow different numbers and
fail the opposite way:** they must stay cool but **must never freeze** (FDA, Information Regarding
Insulin Storage). Do not let "keeping things cold" become one shared job. Give medicine its own
container and its own thermometer (→ 02-01, → 29-07).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Appliance thermometers** (fridge and freezer) | Know what actually happened | A few dollars each |
| **Instant-read food thermometer** | Cooking safely (→ 07-01) | And a spare |
| Water jugs to fill freezer space | Holds cold longer; becomes drinking water | Free |
| Coolers | Gather together what you are keeping | Also → 04-09 |
| Blankets for the freezer | Buys hours | Do not cover vents |
| A known dry-ice source | Extends a freezer by days | Find it before you need it |
| **Freezer inventory card,** taped to the lid | Triage without opening the door | Mark allergy-safe and medical-diet items |
| Charged power station, or generator fuel | The powered bridge | → 09-03, → 09-04 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Snow and ice** in winter (→ 04-09).
- Coolers packed with snow; an unheated garage or the north side of the house.
- **Cooking and eating** is always a valid way to "preserve" food.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** refrigerated food is measured in **hours,** not days. Plan to turn it into meals or
  preserved food at once.
- **Ration:** eat the most perishable first; do not "save" meat that is on the clock.
- **Resupply:** pressure canning (→ 04-05) turns thawing meat into shelf-stable food, the best
  answer to a freezer full of meat in a long outage, if you have jars, lids and fuel.
- **The season matters:** a summer outage is a food emergency within hours; a winter outage in a
  cold place is an opportunity (→ 04-09). Know which one you are in.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** this page is the first-day food plan (→ 01-01, → 09-16).
- **B (moving):** take shelf-stable food only; leave the fridge behind.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the same rules; less resupply, so making food shelf-stable
  matters more.

## Cross-references

→ 04-09 winter cold storage · → 04-05 pressure canning thawing meat · → 04-01 calorie math ·
→ 09-01 power priorities · → 09-03 batteries · → 09-04 generators · → 02-01 insulin ·
→ 02-04 food allergy · → 07-01 safe cooking temperatures · → 12-05 illness

pages.title: Meal planning and cooking from stores
pages.body:
# Meal planning and cooking from stores

**What this page is for.** How to plan a small set of meals that your household can cook from
stored food every day, using little fuel, that everyone in the house can safely eat, and that
people will keep eating for months.

> **CAUTION.** In most households several limits meet at every meal: **fuel** (→ 06-04),
> **anyone's food allergy or restricted diet** (→ 02-04), and, if anyone has diabetes,
> **steady carbohydrate** (→ 02-01, → 02-05). A meal plan built around only one of them fails
> on the others. Plan them all at once, now, while it is a planning exercise and not a nightly
> crisis.

## Do this now

1. **Build a rotation of 7 to 10 meals** you can cook from stores, that everyone eats and
   everyone can safely eat.
2. **If anyone has diabetes, write the carbohydrate per serving on each recipe.** For them it
   is dosing information (→ 02-01, → 02-05).
3. **Cook once a day, in a batch.** Every fire lit is fuel spent (→ 06-04).
4. **Test the rotation now** with a pantry week (→ 04-10), cooking outdoors on your backup
   stove or fire if you can.
5. **Keep one "everyone's favourite" meal** in reserve for a bad day. Morale is a system
   (→ 21-02).

## The limits, and why they point the same way

| Limit | What it asks for |
|---|---|
| **Fuel** | Batch cooking, long-simmer foods finished in a haybox, few separate cooking sessions (→ 07-02) |
| **Allergies and restricted diets** | Every ingredient checked; the restricted food cooked first, in its own cookware (→ 02-04, → 02-19) |
| **Diabetes** | A known, repeatable amount of carbohydrate per serving so insulin or medicine works predictably (→ 02-01, → 02-05) |

**The good news:** these point the same way, toward **a small rotation of simple, repeated,
one-pot meals made from single-ingredient staples.** Repetition is efficient, easy to check and
predictable. It is also monotonous, which is what the morale ideas below are for.

## A workable rotation

Built from staples (→ 04-03). Check each one against every allergy in your house and swap
ingredients where needed.

| Meal | Base | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Beans and rice** | Beans, rice, fat, salt, spice | The backbone. Haybox-friendly (kidney-bean rule below) |
| **Lentil soup** | Lentils, dried vegetables, fat | Fast, forgiving, good for children |
| **Porridge** | Oats, dry milk, sugar | Warm breakfast; morale (→ 04-14) |
| **Flatbread** | Flour, water, salt, fat | No yeast needed (→ 07-04) |
| **Stew with canned or preserved meat** | Meat, roots, grain | Uses home-canned meat (→ 04-05) |
| **Rice pudding** | Rice, dry milk, sugar | Dessert from staples; worth its weight in morale |
| **Potato or root hash** | Stored roots, fat | Seasonal (→ 04-08) |
| **Sprouts, steamed or stirred into the soup pot** | Sprouts (→ 04-16) | The winter fresh food. Cooked for children, older adults, anyone pregnant and anyone with a weakened immune system (FDA) |
| **Soup from dried vegetables** | Dried garden produce (→ 04-06) | Softens while it cooks |

**If anyone has diabetes, write the carbohydrate per serving next to each one.** Do it now, with
a scale and a printed reference, not later by candlelight.

## Cooking with less fuel

- **One fire, many jobs** (→ 06-02): the meal, tomorrow's beans, boiled water, hot-water bottles.
- **Soak beans and grains first.** It cuts cooking time a great deal.
- **Haybox finish** (an insulated box that keeps a hot pot cooking, → 07-02): boil hard **at
  least 10 minutes,** then insulate for hours. Nearly free.
  - **Dry kidney-type beans** (any *Phaseolus* bean: kidney, red, white, pinto, black): **soak at
    least 5 hours, throw the soak water away, and hold a full rolling boil at least 10 minutes
    (FDA says 30) BEFORE the box.** Never from raw in a haybox alone; a low, slow cook makes the
    bean toxin worse (FDA, Bad Bug Book; → 04-03).
  - **Hold rule:** food that has sat in the box more than about 4 hours, or is no longer too hot
    to touch (about 140 °F, the top of the danger zone), is **boiled again before anyone eats
    it.** The box is a cooker, not a warmer for ever.
- **Cook once a day, eat twice;** reheat small portions on little fuel.
