- **Lid on, windbreak up:** the two cheapest savings you have (→ 07-01).

## If anyone has diabetes

- **Steady beats varied** for dosing, especially without a glucose monitor (→ 02-01, → 02-02).
- **Write the carbohydrate on the pot,** or keep a card with the rotation's counts.
- **Keep fast sugar for treating lows separate and protected,** never dependent on what is
  cooking.
- **Sick days change everything.** When the person cannot eat normally, CDC's sick-day guidance
  is **about 50 grams of carbohydrate every 4 hours** in a form they can keep down, such as
  juice, regular soda or applesauce (CDC, Managing Sick Days). The rest of the sick-day plan is
  on → 02-01 or → 02-05. **Stock those foods specifically** and do not let them be eaten as treats.

## If anyone has a food allergy or restricted diet

- **Cook the allergic person's portion first,** in their own cookware, before other foods come
  into the kitchen (→ 02-04).
- **Simplify:** if the whole household eats the same safe meal, most of the problem goes away.
  That is a strong reason to build the rotation around what the most restricted person can eat.
- **Label leftovers** clearly; a mislabelled container is an exposure.
- Celiac disease (gluten): → 02-19.

## Morale: not optional over months

- **Keep spices, sugar and something sweet.** They cost little to store and transform dull food
  (→ 04-13, → 21-02).
- **Mark occasions.** Birthdays, holidays, a set day of the week: a different meal on a known day
  gives the week a shape (→ 21-04).
- **Let children help.** A child stirring, kneading flatbread or rinsing sprouts is busy rather
  than anxious (→ 20-07).
- **Hot drinks** in a cold house are worth far more than their calories.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Written meal rotation, with carbohydrate counts if needed | Fuel, allergies and dosing solved in advance | Laminate it |
| Spices, salt, sugar, cocoa | Morale and flavour | Cheap; big effect (→ 04-13) |
| Haybox (or a cooler and blankets) | Fuel-free finishing | → 07-02 |
| Large pot and Dutch oven | Batch cooking | → 07-04 |
| **Separate cookware for any allergic person** | Avoids cross-contact | → 02-04 |
| Sick-day carbohydrate (juice, applesauce, regular soda), if anyone has diabetes | Sick days | A protected stock |
| Kitchen scale and a printed carbohydrate reference | Counting without a phone | Keep with the rotation |
| Insulated containers | Keep food hot for staggered meals | Also → 07-02 |

**If you don't have it:**

- Almost any one-pot mix of grain, legume, fat and salt is nutritionally sound.
- Dried vegetables and sprouts add nutrition to anything.
- Wild game and foraged food extend the rotation (Section 05), with your allergy rules applied.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** this page does not use anything up; it decides **how fast everything else goes.**
  Good meal planning stretches both food (→ 04-01) and fuel (→ 06-04).
- **Ration:** many households shrink adult portions before children's. Keep a diabetic's
  carbohydrate steady rather than cutting it. Where one person eats an allergy-safe diet,
  whether their safe stock is shared or held as their reserve is a decision card: sharing
  shortens their runway, reserving means everyone else eats other food first.
  {{choice DC-26}} → 30-27 (→ 02-04).
- **Resupply:** garden, game and trade (Section 05, → 18-02).
- **The combined effect:** batch cooking plus a haybox plus lids on pots can cut cooking fuel by
  more than half. Over a winter, that is a lot of wood (→ 06-04).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** set the rotation and the daily cooking rhythm early; it gives the
  day a structure, which helps morale (→ 21-02).
- **B (moving):** no-cook and one-pot only; restricted-diet food carried separately (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** the same rotation, plus whatever the site produces.

## Cross-references

→ 04-01 calorie math · → 04-10 pantry week · → 04-16 sprouts · → 04-13 spices and salt ·
→ 02-01 diabetes · → 02-04 food allergy · → 07-02 haybox · → 21-02 morale

photo_slots.caption: Our freeze-dried shelf: where it is, how the allergy-safe stock is kept apart

pages.body:
# Freeze-dried meals: buying, checking and storing a stockpile

**What this page is for.** How freeze-dried meals fit into a food store, how much to buy for your
household, how to check every product for allergens, how much water they need, and how to store
them so the long shelf life on the label is true.

> **SAFETY.** **Commercial freeze-dried and "emergency food" products very often contain soy, egg,
> milk or wheat, and recipes change without notice** (→ 04-02). If anyone in the house has a food
> allergy, every pouch must be **checked against their allergy list before purchase, checked again
> at purchase, and kept apart** (protocol below). A stockpile that skips that check can be a
> stockpile of allergy triggers with a 25-year shelf life (→ 02-04, → 02-03).

## Do this now

1. **Read the directions on every product and write down its TYPE:**
   - **"Add boiling water, wait"** = **true freeze-dried.** It is already cooked; cold-water
     soaking works too (slowly).
   - **"Boil" or "simmer X minutes"** = **dehydrated or blended "emergency food"** (most bucket
     systems, many "just add water" pasta and rice blends). Its pasta, beans and textured soy are
     **not precooked;** it needs **a real boil on a stove** (→ 07-05, → 07-01) and is **NOT a
     cold-water meal.**
   - **Water per pouch is the label's figure.** About 2 cups is only a planning average.
2. **Run the allergen protocol below on every product before buying** if anyone in the house has
   a food allergy. No exceptions, no "same brand, probably fine".
3. **Fill in the inventory table** as you buy. An uncounted stockpile cannot be planned with.
4. **Mark every container** safe or not safe for each allergic person, in bold marker, and shelve
   the safe stock separately.
5. **Store cool, dry and sealed:** not the garage, not the attic. Heat is what breaks the
   "25-year" claim.
6. **Count the water these meals need** into your water plan (→ 03-01).

## Where freeze-dried food fits

| Property | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Long dating** ("25 years" is a manufacturer claim, for cool storage) | Buy once; less rotation work (see the rotation note below) |
| **No cooking: only hot water** (true freeze-dried) | About 2 cups of boiling water per pouch (the label governs); about 55 Wh at an electric kettle, more from a battery after inverter losses (→ 07-06). No fire, no pot to wash. **Dehydrated "simmer" products do not qualify:** they need a stove |
| **Cold-water fallback** (true freeze-dried only) | Softens in cold water in **1 to 2 hours:** a zero-energy meal when power is rationed (→ 07-07). **Never for a "boil/simmer" product** |
| **Weight** | The most calories per pound of any ready-to-eat food (→ 04-01); good for leaving home |

**Staples are cheaper per calorie** (→ 04-03), and freeze-dried food does not replace them. It is
the **ready-to-eat, no-fuel, travels-well layer** on top. Both count toward the runway (→ 04-01,
→ 23-02).

## How much to buy

Your household needs about **{{ derived.calories.day }} calories a day** (→ 04-01 shows how
that is worked out from the published USDA/HHS table for your {{ household.size }} people).

> **target days × {{ derived.calories.day }} ÷ calories per serving (from the label) = servings
> to stock**

| Target | Calories needed | Servings to stock |
|---|---|---|
| 2 weeks | {{ derived.calories.two_weeks }} | {{ derived.calories.two_weeks }} ÷ ______ calories per serving = ______ |
| 1 month | {{ derived.calories.day }} × 30 = ______ | ÷ ______ = ______ |
| 3 months | {{ derived.calories.day }} × 90 = ______ | ÷ ______ = ______ |

**Check it a second way.** Count meals, not just calories: {{ household.size }} people × 3 meals
a day × the number of days, and compare that with the label's servings. Plan from the calories,
not the serving count: a label's serving size may not match what your household eats. You have **{{ gear.food.freeze_dried_servings }}
servings** logged now.

**Run the same line for any restricted diet alone,** using that person's own figure from
→ 04-01 and only the products marked safe for them. That runway is computed separately and is
usually the one that matters most.

**Babies under 12 months** are not in these numbers: they need breast milk or infant formula
(→ 02-13, → 20-05). Freeze-dried meals are not baby food.

## The allergen protocol

Most commercial freeze-dried meals contain **soy** (soy protein, soy lecithin, "vegetable oil"),
many contain **egg, milk or wheat,** and **sesame** turns up in seasoning blends. US labels must
name the nine major allergens: milk, egg, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and
sesame (FDA, Food Allergies). How to read a label: → 29-14.

{{#each allergies as a}}
- **{{a.member}}:** {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}})
{{else}}
- No allergies are entered for your household. If none applies, skip to the inventory table.
{{/each}}

1. **BEFORE purchase:** get the full ingredient list and "Contains" line for the exact product and
   size, and check it against every allergy above. **An allergen outside the nine never appears in
   a "Contains" line:** read the full list. Check the maker's "made in a facility with" statements
   and follow the allergist's advice on traces.
2. **AT purchase:** read the physical label on the units in your hand again. **Recipes change;** a
   product checked last year is not checked today. Write the date you checked it.
3. **AFTER purchase:** mark every container safe or not safe, log it in the table below, and shelve
   the safe products **physically apart:** their own bin, their own shelf, above the others.
4. **A product that fails any step is not for that person,** and is marked and stored that way.

**Where this fits with → 04-02:** that page warns against buying a year of unchecked bucket food,
and the warning stands. This protocol is the discipline that makes the category usable: checked
single products, not blind buckets. Feeding an allergic person food you could not check:
{{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.

{{photo freeze-dried-shelf}}

## Inventory table

The products on your shelf are a fact you record here. Keep it current: it feeds every runway
number on → 04-01 and → 23-02.

| Product (maker and exact name) | **Type: FD (add water, wait) or DEHYD (boil X min)** | Water per pouch (label) | Servings | Calories per serving | **Safe for each allergy? (date checked)** | Bought | Lot number, best-by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |

**Totals:** calories on hand ______ · **allergy-safe calories on hand ______** (track separately).

## The water these meals need

Freeze-dried food **uses your water;** that is the price of the convenience.

- **Your plan figure is {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day** for the household
  (→ 03-01). Treat it as the least you need if you will eat mostly freeze-dried food.
- **About 2 cups of boiling water per pouch** (the label governs): small boils, about 55 Wh each
  at an electric kettle (→ 07-06).
- **Cold water works for TRUE freeze-dried pouches:** 1 to 2 hours instead of about 10 minutes,
  worse texture, no energy (→ 07-07). A "boil/simmer" product needs the stove.
- **When water is short, eat this food LAST.** Canned food brings its own water; freeze-dried
  food takes yours (→ 04-01 has the table).

## Storage: heat is the enemy of the 25-year claim

The long shelf-life figures assume **cool storage.** Utah State University Extension's research
summary is blunt: the ideal is **40 to 70 °F**, and the same stored wheat that kept about 25 years
in a cool basement kept **about 5 years in a hot garage or attic** (Utah State University
Extension). Treat every "25-year" label as conditional on:

- **Cool:** a basement or interior closet. **Never** the garage, the attic, or a vehicle or
  trailer parked in the sun.
- **Dry:** dried food that picks up moisture grows mould and bacteria. Off the concrete floor,
  low humidity. {{#if is.hot_summers}}Your summers are hot: find the coolest place in the house
  for this.{{/if}} In humid places this matters twice as much (→ 04-09).
- **Sealed:** unopened original packaging (cans, pouches with oxygen absorbers). **An opened
  container is ordinary food:** reseal it and use it within weeks, faster in humid weather
  (USDA FSIS, Shelf-Stable Food Safety).
- **Dark, and off concrete.**

## Rotation: 25-year food does not rotate like a pantry

"First in, first out" (→ 04-02, → 04-10) does not fit food you may not outlive. Instead:

- **Check seals once a year:** walk the shelf and look at every can and pouch for swelling,
  punctures, crushed seams and rodent damage (→ 04-11). Throw out swollen or punctured ones.
  Log the check on → 23-02.
- **Eat one pouch of each product each year.** It confirms people will eat it, teaches the
  preparation, and catches a bad batch. Replace what you eat.
- **Re-check the allergy marks** at the same yearly walk: anything opened, water-damaged or
  unlabelled loses its "safe" mark until checked again.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Checked freeze-dried products, logged above | The stockpile | Check BEFORE buying; mark at purchase |
| A separate bin or shelf for allergy-safe stock | Physical separation | Above other food (→ 02-04) |
| Bold markers and labels | Safe or not safe | Re-mark at every yearly check |
| Printed ingredient labels or photos, filed | Re-checking without internet | Tape inside the bin lid |
| Water storage sized to your plan figure | The paired consumable | → 03-01 |
| Kettle or small pot, measuring cup | About 2 cups boiling per pouch | An insulated bottle saves energy |
| This page's inventory table, kept current | Runway input | Feeds → 04-01 and → 23-02 |

**If you don't have it:**

- Scavenged freeze-dried food is **not for an allergic person unless the label is intact and
  passes the full protocol.** For them, sealed single-ingredient staples are the safest find.
- Home-dried food (→ 04-06) is the home-made cousin: heavier and shorter-lived, but fully
  traceable.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** total logged calories ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }}, **plus** the staples runway
  (→ 04-01). The figure on → 23-02 is the SUM. Work out each restricted diet's runway separately.
- **Ration:** it is the best travel and no-fuel food. Many households save it for moving days and
  days when power or fuel is rationed, and eat staples on ordinary days when the stove works.
  Where one person eats an allergy-safe diet, whether their safe pouches are shared or held as
  their reserve is a decision card: sharing shortens their runway, reserving means everyone else
  eats other food first. {{choice DC-26}} → 30-27 (→ 02-04).
- **Resupply:** most households cannot make freeze-dried food; the substitutes are drying
  (→ 04-06), canning (→ 04-04, → 04-05) and production (Section 05).
- **The honest limit:** this layer is bought, not renewable. It buys months of certainty;
  Section 05 buys years.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** buy and check now; store cool; do the yearly seal walk.
- **B (moving):** the densest ready-to-eat calories you own; first into the vehicle after any
  allergy-safe or medical-diet bin (→ 04-01 grab order, → 01-03).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** bridge food while production starts. In humid places the
  sealed-container and reseal rules get stricter (→ 04-09).

## Cross-references

→ 04-01 runway and grab-load math · → 04-02 the unchecked-bucket warning (stands) · → 04-03
staples · → 03-01 water · → 07-07 rehydrating · → 02-04 food allergy · → 04-10 inventory ·
→ 04-11 pests

pages.body:
# Food production and foraging

**What this section holds.** 19 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 05-01 **A small high-yield garden for your climate**: How to get the most food from a small garden where you live: when to plant, what to grow first, and how to squeeze a yard.
- → 05-02 **Season extension: row cover, low tunnels and cold frames**: Cheap covers that let you plant earlier in spring and keep harvesting later in fall, beyond the frost-free window on → 05-01.
- → 05-03 **Seed saving and a survival seed stock**: How to build a seed stock that keeps a garden going for years, and how to save your own seed so it never runs out.
- → 05-04 **Backyard chickens**: Whether a small flock of hens suits your household, and how to keep them through a hard winter, a feed shortage and the diseases that matter.
- → 05-05 **Meat rabbits in a small yard**: Why rabbits are often the best-fitting livestock for a small lot, and how to keep them healthy, fed and productive, including the diseases that wipe out a herd.
- → 05-06 **Foraging wild plants, and the deadly look-alikes**: The rules for eating wild plants anywhere in the US, the pairs of plants that kill people who confuse them, and the few starter plants that are hard to get w…
- → 05-07 **Hunting for food**: What hunting can realistically add to a household's food, how to take game cleanly and keep the meat, and the lead problem that matters for children and preg…
- → 05-08 **Fishing and ice fishing**: Why fishing is one of the best food-gathering methods there is, how to fish passively, how to keep the catch safe to eat, and how not to die on the ice.
- → 05-09 **Field dressing and butchering**: Turning a large animal, usually a deer, into safe meat: the order of work, the disease checks, the cuts, and how to keep it.
- → 05-10 **Container and vertical growing in a small space**: How to grow real food in pots, bags and buckets and up fences and trellises, on a patio, a balcony, a driveway or a small yard.
- → 05-11 **Soil, compost and fertility without bought inputs**: How to keep garden soil fertile year after year without buying fertilizer: compost, manure, mulch and cover crops, and how to handle manure and human waste w…
- → 05-12 **Pollination and garden pests without chemicals**: Which crops need insects to make food, how to pollinate them by hand, and how to control pests when there is nothing to buy.
- → 05-13 **Perennials, fruit trees and berries for your zone**: Food plants that come back every year: what grows in your zone, how long each takes to bear, and how to keep them alive and multiplying.
- → 05-14 **Growing indoors: microgreens and seed starting in winter**: Fresh greens in the dead of winter from a windowsill, and starting garden transplants indoors so the outdoor season produces more.
- → 05-15 **Trapping small game and pest animals**: Why traps beat guns for small game in a long emergency, how to set them where animals travel, and how to keep children, pets and yourself safe from the traps…
- → 05-16 **Processing poultry and small game**: Turning a chicken, a rabbit or a trapped animal into clean, safe meat: the order of work, the hygiene that protects you, and how to handle it with children a…
- → 05-17 **Wild edibles by season**: **When** and **where** to look for wild food through the year, so you can plan and preserve.
- → 05-18 **Garden calendar for each destination**: A destination can sit in a different climate from home, and then the home calendar (→ 05-01) is wrong there.
- → 05-19 **Foraging and field hazards at each destination**: What is different about wild food and outdoor hazards at each place this household might go: the plants, the snakes, the ticks, and the allergy risks that li…

pages.body:
# A small high-yield garden for your climate

**What this page is for.** How to get the most food from a small garden where you live: when
to plant, what to grow first, and how to squeeze a yard. Your frost dates and zone are printed
below from your home region's data. The methods work anywhere in the US.

> **CAUTION.** Be honest about what a small backyard garden does: **it will not feed a family.**
> It supplies vitamins, variety, morale and **food whose every ingredient you know**, which
> matters if anyone has a food allergy (→ 02-04). Calories still come from stored staples
> (→ 04-03) and protein from animals, fish and game. Plan the garden for **nutrition and
> traceability**, not survival calories, and you will be right about it.

## Do this now

1. **Learn your frost window.** At home the median **last spring frost is
   {{ region.home.last_frost }}** and the median **first fall frost is
   {{ region.home.first_frost }}**: about **{{ region.home.growing_days }} frost-free days**.
   "Median" means half of all years are worse. Plan tender crops to be ripe well before the
   first frost date, not on it. Write your own observed dates here each year:
   last spring frost ________ · first fall frost ________.
2. **Start seeds indoors on the packet's schedule**, counted back from the date they go
   outside: about 5 to 6 weeks for tomatoes, 9 for peppers, 10 to 11 for cabbage-family crops and
   14 to 15 for onions (University of Minnesota Extension, Starting Seeds Indoors; → 05-14).
3. **Sow cool-season crops before the last frost.** Peas, spinach, lettuce and radish can be
   sown straight into the garden once the soil is 40 to 50 °F (University of Minnesota
   Extension, Planting the Vegetable Garden).
4. **Build the soil now** (→ 05-11). Soil takes years; seeds take days.
5. **Buy and store seed now** (→ 05-03), choosing varieties that ripen inside your season.

## Why / how it works

### Your season, in one table

Words first. A **frost** is a night cold enough (32 °F or below) to kill tender plants; the
frost dates in this binder are for that 32 °F mark, from NOAA's climate normals (→ 32-00).
**Cool-season crops** (peas, lettuce, spinach, kale, cabbage, radish, carrots, onions,
potatoes) tolerate light frost and grow best in cool weather. **Warm-season crops** (tomatoes,
peppers, beans, squash, cucumbers, corn, melons) are killed by frost and want soil at 50 to
60 °F or warmer before they go in (University of Minnesota Extension).

| Milestone | When, at home |
|---|---|
| Start seeds indoors | 5 to 15 weeks before transplanting (onions earliest, then cabbage family, peppers, tomatoes); transplants go out after {{ region.home.last_frost }} |
| Sow cool-season crops outside | Before {{ region.home.last_frost }}, once the soil is 40 to 50 °F |
| **Last spring frost (median)** | **{{ region.home.last_frost }}** (a cold year runs later) |
| Transplant warm-season crops | After the last frost, once nights stay warm |
| **First fall frost (median)** | **{{ region.home.first_frost }}** (a cold year comes earlier) |
| Frost-free days | **{{ region.home.growing_days }}** |
| Hardiness zone (for perennials, → 05-13) | **{{ region.home.zone }}** |
| Season extension | Weeks before and after the frost dates, under cover (→ 05-02) |

**Will a crop fit?** Every seed packet prints "days to maturity". Count that many days forward
from the date you plant (or transplant) it. If the answer lands comfortably before
{{ region.home.first_frost }}, it fits. If it lands close, pick a faster variety, start it
indoors, or cover it at the end (→ 05-02). A fenced town yard is often slightly warmer than
open country, and a low spot is often colder; your own written dates beat the median.

**Hardiness zone** (from the USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map) is the average coldest winter
night, in bands of 10 °F. It decides which **perennials** (plants that live for years) survive
your winter. It does not decide when to plant vegetables; frost dates do.

### Crop guidance by zone band

Find the row that holds your zone ({{ region.home.zone }}) and your frost-free days
({{ region.home.growing_days }}). If the two point to different rows, trust the frost-free
days for vegetables. These are rough bands; your state's Extension planting chart is the
local authority.

| Band | What the season is like | What that means in the garden |
|---|---|---|
| **Zones 3 to 4, short season** | Late spring, early fall, one warm stretch | One main planting. Start tomatoes, peppers and squash indoors. Choose short-season varieties (the shortest "days to maturity" on the rack). Potatoes, cabbage, carrots, peas and greens are the reliable crops. Season extension (→ 05-02) adds real weeks at both ends. |
| **Zones 5 to 6, middle season** | One full warm season, cool spring and fall shoulders | A spring cool-season planting, a summer warm-season planting, and a fall cool-season planting sown in late summer. Most of the crop list works. |
| **Zones 7 to 8, long season** | Early spring, late fall, hot summers | **Two full plantings**: a spring garden and a fall garden. Potatoes twice. Heat-tolerant crops such as sweet potatoes, okra and southern peas (cowpeas) thrive. Fungal disease and summer heat, not cold, are the main limits. Your state Extension planting chart gives the spring and fall dates. |
| **Zones 9 and warmer, mild winter** | Frost rare or absent; summer is the hard season | Cool-season crops grow **through the winter**. Midsummer heat stops many crops from setting fruit, so plant warm-season crops in late winter and again in late summer. Shade cloth and water become the limits. |

Your binder carries a month-by-month planting calendar for home in → 25-01, and one for each
destination in → 05-18.

### What to grow in a small space, ranked by usefulness

| Priority | Crops | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Calorie-dense** | Potatoes, winter squash, dry beans, corn (if space); sweet potatoes in long-season bands | The only garden crops that meaningfully add calories |
| **2. Storage crops** | Carrots, beets, onions, garlic, cabbage | Keep for months in a cool place with no processing (→ 04-09) |
| **3. High-yield producers** | Zucchini, tomatoes, cucumbers, kale, chard | Large output per square foot |
| **4. Fast / succession** | Radish, lettuce, spinach, turnip greens | Several harvests per season |
| **5. Preserving crops** | Tomatoes, cucumbers (pickles), cabbage (kraut) | Feed the preserving chain (→ 04-04, → 04-08) |
| **6. Perennial** | Rhubarb, asparagus, berries, herbs | Plant once, harvest for years (→ 05-13) |

**Potatoes deserve a special mention.** In most of the country they are the highest-calorie
crop a small garden can grow, they store well somewhere cool and dark (→ 04-09), and they
contain none of the common food allergens. In the warmest bands, plant them early so they are
dug before summer heat.

### Making a small yard produce

- **Intensive spacing** (blocks or "square-foot" grids) instead of long rows. Rows waste
  space in a small yard.
- **Grow up** (→ 05-10): pole beans, cucumbers, tomatoes and small squash on trellises.
- **Succession planting:** as soon as one crop finishes, another goes in the same spot.
- **Interplanting:** fast crops (radish, lettuce) between slow ones (tomatoes, squash).
- **Containers** on the patio and along the fence add real growing area (→ 05-10).
- **Full sun:** at least 6 hours of direct sun a day (Iowa State University Extension). Map your yard's sun before
  you dig: check it in the morning, at noon and in late afternoon.

{{photo garden-sun-map}}

### One weed to learn before you weed

**Poison hemlock comes up in garden beds** across most of the country. Its first-year rosette
(a low circle of leaves) is the plant gardeners most often mistake for parsley or carrot tops,
and it is deadly to eat (→ 05-06). Before the first weeding each spring, look at the hemlock
plate on → 05-06: finely divided, fern-like, glossy leaves on hairless stems that are often
blotched with purple. Any carrot-family plant you did not sow comes out with gloves on and goes
in the trash: not the compost, not the rabbits (→ 05-05), and never into a child's hand.

### Water, and one important warning

- A vegetable garden needs **about 1 inch of water a week** from rain or watering: **62 gallons
  for every 100 square feet** (University of Minnesota Extension, Watering the Vegetable Garden).
  In a dry spell that is a lot of hauling.
- **Do not water the garden with saltwater-pool water** (→ 03-03). Salt damages soil and kills
  plants, and the damage lasts for seasons.
- **Rain barrels are the right source** (→ 03-05). Used wash water ("greywater") works with
  care (→ 13-03).
- **Mulch heavily** with straw, leaves or cardboard. It is the cheapest water saving there is,
  and it smothers weeds.
- Your home gets about **{{ region.home.precip_in }} inches of precipitation a year**. In the
  wetter bands, raised beds for drainage matter more than watering.

### Food allergies and the garden

{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}Someone in this household has a food allergy (→ 02-04). {{/if}}Garden
produce is the most traceable food you can have: you planted it, you know what it is, and there
is no label to misread. Two cautions: **do not grow a crop that is one of your household's
allergens** (soybeans as edamame, for example, or sesame), and keep allergen-free produce
handling separate from any allergen-containing food preparation (→ 02-04).

### Keeping it quiet

A visibly productive garden in a hungry neighbourhood is an advertisement (→ 14-03). A fence
helps. Consider growing calorie crops out of sight and ornamental-looking edibles (kale, chard,
herbs) where they show.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Open-pollinated or heirloom seed** | You can save it year to year (→ 05-03) | Not hybrids, if you plan to save seed |
| Hand tools: spade, fork, hoe, rake, trowel | No power needed | → 16-01 |
| Watering cans, hose, rain barrels | Hauling water is the daily reality | → 03-05 |
| Compost bin or pile | Fertility without bought inputs | → 05-11 |
| Trellises, stakes, twine | Growing up multiplies yield | → 05-10 |
| Mulch (straw, leaves, cardboard) | Saves water, stops weeds | Usually free |
| Row cover, plastic, a cold frame | Season extension at both ends | → 05-02 |
| Soil test | Know what you are working with | Extension offices test soil while they operate |
| **Your state Extension's printed vegetable guide** | Local varieties and timing | Keep it with your documents (→ 19-01) |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Containers:** buckets, totes, feed sacks: anything that holds soil and drains.
- **Trellis:** a fence, a livestock panel, branches, string.
- **Mulch:** leaves, grass clippings, cardboard, newspaper.
- **Compost:** kitchen scraps and leaves. **Cat litter and dog waste never go in food-garden
  compost** (→ 05-11).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** a garden is a **flow**, not a store, and it is seasonal. Outside your frost-free
  window it produces little or nothing unless covered, which is exactly when stored food
  matters most. In the mildest bands the gap is summer heat rather than winter.
- **Ration:** preserve the surplus rather than eating it all fresh (→ 04-06, → 04-08).
- **Resupply:** seed saving (→ 05-03) makes the garden renewable; sprouts and microgreens
  (→ 04-16, → 05-14) cover the fresh-food gap.
- **The honest limit:** a backyard garden supplies a share of your vegetables for part of the
  year. Treat it as nutrition insurance and morale, and keep the calorie plan resting on stored
  staples and protein.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** small, intensive, vertical, fenced. Start improving the soil this season.
- **B (moving):** carry seed (→ 05-03). It is light, and it is next year's food.
- **C (establishing):** a destination may be in a different band from home. Use its own
  calendar (→ 05-18), not this one.

pages.body:
# Season extension: row cover, low tunnels and cold frames

**What this page is for.** Cheap covers that let you plant earlier in spring and keep
harvesting later in fall, beyond the frost-free window on → 05-01. At home that window runs
from about **{{ region.home.last_frost }}** to **{{ region.home.first_frost }}**
({{ region.home.growing_days }} days).

> **CAUTION.** Season extension is one of the highest-value garden techniques there is, but
> covered structures **overheat very fast** on a sunny day, even in early spring when the air
> outside is near freezing, and can cook everything inside. Plastic covers must be opened every
> day to let the heat out (UGA Extension, Low Hoop Houses). **Vent it, and put a thermometer in
> it.**

## Do this now

1. **Build or buy one cold frame this season.** It is the cheapest way to add real weeks.
2. **Put a thermometer inside** every covered structure, and open it on sunny days.
3. **Plant cool-season crops early**: before {{ region.home.last_frost }}, once the soil is 40 to
   50 °F (University of Minnesota Extension, Planting the Vegetable Garden).
4. **Plan a fall planting**, not just a spring one. Fall is usually the easier win.
5. **Use row cover**: cheap, light, reusable, and it buys several degrees.

## Why / how it works

### The words

- **Row cover** (floating row cover): a thin, white, see-through fabric laid loosely over
  plants. Light and rain pass through; frost and insects mostly do not.
- **Low tunnel**: wire or plastic hoops over a bed, covered with plastic or row cover.
- **Cold frame**: a bottomless box with a clear lid (an old window works), set on the soil.
- **Hoop house**: a walk-in tunnel greenhouse. A real building project.

### What each method buys

| Method | Frost protection | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Row cover** | A few degrees; heavier fabric gives more (read the label) | Very low | Lay directly on crops; also keeps out pests (→ 05-12) |
| **Low tunnel** | Typically 2 to 8 °F warmer inside than out (UGA Extension) | Low | The best value per dollar |
| **Cold frame** | More than a tunnel, with a solid frame and a clear lid | Low to moderate | Durable; reusable for decades |
| **Cold frame inside a low tunnel** | Substantial | Low | Layering multiplies protection |
| **Hoop house / greenhouse** | Large | High | A project, not a weekend |
| **Deep mulch** | Protects roots | Free | Lets carrots and parsnips sit in the ground into winter |

**Fabric must reach the ground on all sides** to hold in the heat that rises from the soil
overnight (UGA Extension). **Layering is the trick.** Row cover inside a low tunnel is much
warmer than either alone.
That is how gardeners in cold places pick greens in midwinter.

{{figure fig-cold-frame}}

### The seasons you gain

**Spring:** sow cool-season crops (spinach, lettuce, radish, kale, peas) weeks before the
ground would otherwise be ready. Warm the soil first with clear plastic for a week or two.

**Fall: the easier and more reliable win.** Sow in late summer so crops mature as the days
shorten, then cover them. Hardy greens (spinach, kale, corn salad) and roots (carrots,
parsnips) hold under cover well past the first frosts, and **carrots get sweeter after
frost**.

**Parsnip foliage burns skin.** Garden parsnip is the same species as wild parsnip, with the
same sap: wear gloves and long sleeves when weeding or harvesting parsnip tops in sun, or you
get the blistering burns described on → 05-06.

**Winter:** in the northern half of the country, growth nearly stops in midwinter whatever
the temperature, because the days are too short. Covered beds become **storage in place**: you
are picking what already grew. That is still fresh food from the yard in January. In the
mildest climates ({{ region.home.zone }} is your zone; see the bands on → 05-01), covered
greens keep growing slowly all winter.

### Building a cold frame

- **Frame:** scrap lumber, straw bales, concrete blocks, or an old window frame.
- **Lid:** an old storm window, a salvaged glass door, rigid clear plastic, or plastic sheeting.
  Never use treated wood that touches food-crop soil (→ 05-10).
- **Slope the lid toward the south** so it catches low winter sun and sheds snow and rain.
- **Insulate the north wall** and bank the sides with leaves, straw or snow.
- **Add thermal mass**: jugs of water inside soak up daytime heat and give it back at night
  (the same idea as → 08-04).
- **Hinge or prop the lid** so venting is easy, because you will vent often.

**Venting is where people fail.** More cold-frame crops are killed by heat than by cold. On
any sunny day near freezing, prop the lid. Make it a habit, or use an automatic vent opener (a
wax-filled piston that opens the lid as it warms, with no power).

{{photo cold-frame}}

### Snow is insulation

Snow on and around a covered bed protects it: the soil beneath stays warmer than bare frozen
ground. Leave light snow on a low tunnel; **clear heavy, wet snow** before it collapses the
hoops.

### No fuel needed

Nothing here burns fuel (→ 06-04), uses power, or needs supplies beyond the covers themselves.
That makes season extension one of the few food methods in this binder that costs nothing to
run. Build it now, while materials are easy to get.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Floating row cover** (rolls) | Cheapest degrees per dollar | Reusable for years |
| Hoops (wire, plastic pipe, metal conduit) | Low tunnels | Cheap to make |
| Greenhouse plastic or clear sheeting | Tunnels and frames | UV-stabilised lasts longer |
| **Old windows or glass doors** | Cold-frame lids | Often free from remodels |
| **Min/max thermometer** for each structure | Tells you when to vent | Essential |
| Automatic vent opener (wax piston) | Vents with no power and no attention | Worth buying |
| Straw bales | Walls, insulation, mulch | Cheap where farms are near |
| Clips, clamps, sandbags | Holding covers down in wind | Wind is the usual enemy |
| Deep mulch (leaves, straw) | Overwintering roots in the ground | Free |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Old windows, storm doors, shower doors**: free cold-frame lids.
- **Milk jugs or clear tubs** with the bottom cut out as covers over single plants.
- **Straw bales in a rectangle with a window on top** make a complete cold frame.
- Bedsheets and blankets as emergency frost covers for one night. Take them off in the morning.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** frames last for years. **Plastic sheeting breaks down in sunlight** within one to
  three seasons and is the main consumable. Keep spare sheeting and clips.
- **Ration:** cover the highest-value crops (winter greens for vitamins) rather than trying to
  cover everything.
- **Resupply:** glass and rigid panels outlast plastic; salvage them now. Straw and leaves are
  free insulation.
- **Why it matters:** every extra week of fresh greens at either end of the year is a week less
  on stored food and sprouts alone (→ 04-16).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** build a cold frame from salvaged windows this season.
- **B (moving):** row cover is light and packs small. Take some.
- **C (establishing):** scale up to low tunnels or a hoop house. Wind protection matters more
  in open country.

pages.body:
# Seed saving and a survival seed stock

**What this page is for.** How to build a seed stock that keeps a garden going for years, and
how to save your own seed so it never runs out.

> **CAUTION.** **Hybrid (F1) seed does not breed true.** "Hybrid" or "F1" on the packet means
> the plant is a cross of two parent lines; seed saved from it grows into a scattered, often
> useless mix. For a renewable garden you must buy **open-pollinated** or **heirloom** seed
> (varieties that come back true from their own seed). Separately, **treated seed** (coated
> with a fungicide, usually dyed pink, blue or green) **is not food**: never eat it and never
> sprout it (→ 04-16).

## Do this now

1. **Buy open-pollinated or heirloom seed**, not hybrids, for anything you mean to save.
2. **Buy a real seed stock now** and store it cool, dark, dry and sealed.
3. **Learn the easy three first: beans, peas and tomatoes.** They pollinate themselves and save
   reliably with almost no technique.
4. **Label everything** with variety and year. Unlabeled seed is a guess.
5. **Split the stock.** Keep a working stock at home and a sealed duplicate somewhere else
   cool and dry: with family, at a destination{{#if has.destinations}} (→ 05-18 lists the
   varieties suited to each of yours){{/if}}, or in a second building. One cache can be lost;
   two rarely are.
6. **Test germination** on older seed each spring before you rely on it.

## Why / how it works

### One season or many

A stored seed packet feeds you once. **A saved-seed cycle feeds you indefinitely.** In a long
emergency, seed becomes one of the most valuable things a household can have, for food and for
trade (→ 18-02).

Most modern commercial seed is hybrid, bred for uniformity in the first generation only.
Renewable gardening means choosing open-pollinated varieties **before** you need them.

### Easy to hard, for saving

**Pollination** is how a flower is fertilised so it makes seed. **Self-pollinating** crops
fertilise themselves inside one flower. **Cross-pollinating** crops are fertilised by pollen
carried by insects or wind from another plant, so two varieties growing near each other mix.

| Difficulty | Crops | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Easy**: self-pollinating | **Beans, peas, tomatoes, lettuce** | Little or no crossing; just dry and store |
| **Moderate**: needs isolation | **Peppers**, squash, cucumbers, melons, corn | Cross readily. Sweet and hot peppers in one yard **will** cross, and the next generation is a hot/sweet lottery. Isolate, bag the blossoms, or grow one variety |
| **Hard**: biennial (two-year cycle) | **Carrots, beets, cabbage, onions** | Flower only in their second year. Where the ground freezes hard, dig them in fall, store them cool (→ 04-09) and replant in spring; left in frozen ground they die. In mild-winter climates they can stay in the ground |
| **Specialist** | Potatoes | Grown from saved tubers ("seed potatoes"), not true seed |

**Start with the easy tier.** Beans and peas self-pollinate, dry on the plant, store for years,
and are rich in calories and protein.

**Keeping varieties true, in one table:**

| Crop | To keep it true |
|---|---|
| Beans, peas, lettuce, tomato | A few feet between varieties is enough |
| **Peppers** | **Bag the blossoms** (tie a scrap of row cover over a flower cluster until fruit sets) **or grow one variety** |
| Squash, cucumber, melon | One variety per species, or hand-pollinate at dawn and tape the flower shut (→ 05-12) |
| Corn | One variety, or keep it far from any other corn: wind carries corn pollen, and popcorn crosses with sweet corn (University of Minnesota Extension) |
| Cabbage family, beets, chard, onions, carrots | One variety flowering per year (beets and chard cross; so do all the cabbage-family crops) |

### Saving the easy three, and peppers

- **Beans and peas:** let the pods dry brown and rattly on the plant (up to a month after you
  would pick them to eat). Dry them indoors at least two weeks before shelling, dry further
  indoors, store.
- **Tomatoes:** scoop the seeds and gel into a jar with a little water, swirl it twice a day and
  let it ferment until the seeds sink, within about five days (University of Minnesota
  Extension, Saving Vegetable Seeds). Pour off the liquid, rinse, then dry thoroughly on a
  plate.
- **Peppers:** from a bagged blossom or your only variety, let the fruit ripen fully, scrape the
  seed, dry it.

**Dry is everything.** Seed stored with any moisture moulds or dies. Dry it longer than feels
necessary, then store it with a desiccant (a drying agent such as silica gel packets).

### Storing seed

- **Cool, dark, dry and steady.** Between 32 and 41 °F is ideal, so a refrigerator works,
  sealed in a glass jar (University of Minnesota Extension). Otherwise a basement or the coldest
  corner of the house, sealed.
- **Sealed jars with silica gel.** Silica gel can be dried out again in a warm oven and reused.
- **Freezing extends life a lot** for thoroughly dried seed, if it stays sealed against
  moisture. A winter outbuilding or a freezer works.
- **Label:** variety, year saved, where it came from.

### How long seed lasts

Approximate seed life, stored cool and dry (University of Illinois Extension, Will My Seeds
Still Grow?):

| Seed | Approximate life |
|---|---|
| Onion, parsnip, parsley | 1 year |
| Leek, sweet corn, pepper, okra | 2 years |
| Bean, pea, carrot, broccoli, kohlrabi, spinach, celery | 3 years |
| Tomato, beet, cabbage, cauliflower, kale, squash, pumpkin, watermelon, chard, eggplant | 4 years |
| Cucumber, muskmelon, radish, collards, endive | 5 years |
| Lettuce | 6 years |

The University of Minnesota advises using your own saved seed within a year where you can; older
seed sprouts less and grows weaker plants.

**Germination test** (University of Illinois Extension): put 10 seeds on a damp paper towel,
fold it into a bag or box so it stays damp, label it, and leave it somewhere warm (no light
needed) for the days to sprouting on the packet. **All 10 sprout:** sow as normal. **7 to 9:**
sow more thickly. **6 or fewer:** replace the seed if you can; the plants it makes will be
weak.

### Building the stock

Buy for **calories, storage and reliability in your season** (bands on → 05-01):
- **Beans (dry and green), peas**: protein, easy saving.
- **Seed potatoes**: highest calorie return in most gardens. Buy certified seed potatoes;
  grocery potatoes may be treated to stop sprouting.
- **Winter squash**: calories and long storage.
- **Carrots, beets, cabbage, onions**: storage crops.
- **Tomatoes, cucumbers**: preserving crops (→ 04-04).
- **Kale, chard, spinach, lettuce**: fast greens and season extension (→ 05-02).
- **Long-season bands only:** sweet potato slips, okra, southern peas (cowpeas).
- **Herbs**: flavour matters more than you think over months (→ 21-02).

**Leave out any crop that is one of your household's food allergens** (→ 02-04).
{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}This household has a food allergy on record: check the stock list against it.{{/if}}

### Seed as currency

Seed is close to an ideal trade good (→ 18-02): light, storable, valuable, divisible, and **it
multiplies**. Giving seed away costs you almost nothing and builds goodwill and a wider local
food supply.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Open-pollinated or heirloom seed**, several years' stock | The renewable foundation | **Not** hybrid |
| Certified seed potatoes (each spring) | Highest calorie crop | Not grocery potatoes |
| Airtight jars and **silica gel** | Dryness is everything | Re-dry the gel with heat |
| Envelopes, labels, marker | Variety and year | Unlabeled seed is useless |
| Fine screens or plates for drying | Processing saved seed | Improvise |
| Paper towels and bags | Germination tests | Free |
| **A printed seed-saving reference** | Isolation distances, techniques | Keep with your documents (→ 19-01) |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Dry beans from the grocery store usually grow.** So do whole dried peas and popcorn.
- **Neighbours and local gardeners** are the best source of varieties that already suit your
  climate (→ 18-01).
- Any dry jar in any cool corner beats no storage.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** seed life is measured in years (table above), but **a saved-seed cycle never runs
  out**.
- **Ration:** always save more seed than you think you need, and **never eat the seed stock**.
  That is the classic famine mistake.
- **Resupply:** trade with neighbours (→ 18-02), grocery dry beans, and perennials that need no
  replanting (→ 05-13).
- **Why it matters:** seed is the only food input in this binder that **multiplies**. A handful
  of beans becomes pounds.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** buy the stock, learn the easy three, save seed this season, and place the
  duplicate while trips are ordinary.
- **B (moving):** seed is light and it is next year's food: **take it** (→ 01-03). With a
  duplicate already placed, a lost load is not a lost garden.
- **C (establishing):** more space means easier isolation of the harder crops. A longer season
  at a destination ripens seed from biennials and late crops more reliably (→ 05-18).

{{photo seed-store}}

# Backyard chickens

**What this page is for.** Whether a small flock of hens suits your household, and how to keep
them through a hard winter, a feed shortage and the diseases that matter.

> **CAUTION.** Three things go wrong with backyard hens. **Bird flu (avian influenza)** kills
> flocks and has infected people who handled sick birds (CDC). **Salmonella** lives on healthy
> birds, their eggs and their coop, and it makes small children seriously ill (CDC, Backyard
> Poultry). And **heat lamps burn coops down**. Each has a rule on this page.
{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}> **This household has a food allergy on record.** If egg is one of the allergens, keeping hens
> means producing that allergen daily at home. Read the allergy section before buying birds.
{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **If anyone in the household is allergic to egg, decide the allergy plan first**, with the
   allergist while one is available (→ 02-04). Below.
2. **Choose cold-hardy breeds** if your winters are cold
   ({{#if is.cold_winters}}yours are: January lows average {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F{{else}}January lows at home average {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F{{/if}}).
3. **Build the coop with hardware cloth**, not chicken wire, and a solid latching door.
4. **Plan the feed.** Chickens eat grain. Store it like human food (→ 04-03).
5. **Learn the bird-flu signs now** (below). A bird that died on its own is never food.
6. **Consider rabbits as well or instead** (→ 05-05): comparable protein, better manure, quiet,
   no egg allergen.

> **Before the collapse:** many towns and cities limit backyard poultry: how many birds, no
> roosters, a permit for the coop, a distance from neighbours' houses, permits for ducks,
> turkeys or geese. Check your city or county ordinance before buying birds. This never decides
> how you keep animals to survive.

## Why / how it works

### If someone in the house is allergic to egg

Egg is one of the major food allergens in the US (FDA, Food Allergies). A flock means handling
that allergen every day, on hands, clothes, surfaces and in the kitchen. Many families manage
it, but it is a decision to make deliberately (→ 02-04, → 02-03).

| Consideration | Detail |
|---|---|
| **What you gain** | Renewable protein and fat from scraps and yard forage; manure for the garden (→ 05-11) |
| **What you risk** | Daily handling of the allergen; egg residue on hands, clothes, surfaces and in the kitchen |
| **What helps** | Egg handling entirely outside; dedicated coop clothing and boots; washing before contact with the allergic person; dedicated cookware; eggs stored sealed and out of reach (→ 04-15); no egg cooking while the allergic person is in the kitchen |
| **A middle path** | Keep hens and **trade the eggs** (→ 18-02) instead of eating them. The allergen stays on the property, but the kitchen exposure shrinks a lot |
| **The alternative** | **Rabbits** (→ 05-05): similar protein, no allergen |

Write the household's decision and the allergist's input here: ______________________

### Breeds and space

Where winters are cold, choose medium to large, cold-hardy, dual-purpose breeds (eggs and meat;
University of Minnesota Extension, Raising Chickens for Eggs): **Rhode Island
Red, Plymouth Rock, Wyandotte, Orpington, Australorp, Brahma, Chantecler.** **Small combs are
better:** large single combs get frostbite. Rose-comb and pea-comb breeds handle cold better.
Where summers are hot, lighter breeds and shade matter more than combs.

**Space:** at least **3 to 5 square feet of indoor floor per bird**, and **one nest box for every
4 to 5 hens** (University of Minnesota Extension). Six hens need 18 to 30 square feet inside; give
more where birds are shut in all winter, and as large an outdoor run as you can. Crowding turns a
winter coop into pecking and disease.

### Winter management

- **Dry and draft-free, but ventilated.** Moisture, not cold, causes frostbitten combs and
  breathing problems. This is the most common beginner mistake.
- **Avoid heat lamps.** Cold-hardy hens do not need heat; a dry coop and deep litter is the
  method. Heat-lamp fires destroy coops, and they spread to garages and
  houses, especially where fuel is stored nearby (→ 06-06). A lamp over dusty bedding is how
  you lose the birds and the house.
- **Deep litter:** keep adding bedding (straw, wood shavings) on top. The lower layers compost
  in place, give off a little warmth, and become garden material in spring (→ 05-11).
- **Water freezes.** Without power you haul and thaw water at least twice a day, every day, all
  winter (→ 03-06). That is the real daily labour.
- **Laying drops sharply** as days shorten. Without added light, expect few or no eggs in the
  darkest months.
- **Predators:** raccoons, foxes, hawks, dogs and, in a crisis, people. Hardware cloth (welded
  wire mesh with small openings), buried at the edges, and a solid door.

{{photo coop}}

### Feed: the honest constraint

**Chickens eat grain.** In a long emergency:
- Kitchen scraps and garden waste help but will not sustain a flock.
- **Free-ranging** gives real forage in summer and almost nothing in a cold winter.
- **Sprouted grain** (→ 04-16) stretches feed a lot.
- **You turn stored grain into eggs at a loss in calories.** The gain is protein quality and
  fat, not energy.

Plan feed storage the way you plan human food, in rodent-proof bins (→ 04-11), and count it in
the runway (→ 23-02).

### Health and hygiene

- **Salmonella:** wash hands after touching birds, eggs, feeders or the coop. CDC advises that
  children under 5 not handle or touch backyard poultry (CDC, Backyard Poultry). Do not kiss or
  snuggle birds, and keep coop shoes outside the house.{{#if has.young_child}} This household
  has a child under 6: keep them out of the coop and away from bird handling.{{/if}}
- **Bird flu (avian influenza, HPAI H5N1)** has been found in backyard flocks across the
  country, and people have been infected through unprotected contact with sick birds (USDA
  APHIS, Defend the Flock; CDC, Preventing Bird Flu Infections). **Signs: sudden death, more
  birds dying, swelling of the head, comb or wattles, purple combs, wattles or legs, gasping,
  a sharp drop in laying, soft or misshapen eggs** (USDA APHIS, How To Spot Sickness). If you see
  them, assume bird flu: **do not eat them, do not compost them**, wear gloves, a mask and eye
  protection to handle them (CDC), bury them deep. While phones work, report sick or dying birds
  to your state veterinarian or to USDA at 1-866-536-7593 (USDA APHIS).
  **Prevention:** keep feed and water where wild birds, especially ducks and geese, cannot reach
  them, and keep wild birds out of the coop.
- **A bird that died on its own is never food** (→ 05-16).
- **Collect eggs often and throw away cracked ones** (CDC, Backyard Poultry). How to keep
  them, washed or unwashed, is on → 04-15; whether to store them in lime water ("water-glassing")
  is a decision card (→ 30-28): {{choice DC-27}}.
- **Cook poultry to 165 °F and egg dishes to 160 °F** (FoodSafety.gov).
- **Put the coop away from the house**, downwind, and well away from stored water (→ 03-08).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Allergy decision written (if egg allergy) | It governs everything else | Before any birds |
| Ordinance checked, permit if needed | Pre-collapse | Your city or county |
| Secure coop: **hardware cloth**, solid door | Predators | Not chicken wire |
| Deep bedding (straw, shavings) | Dry warmth and compost | → 05-11 |
| Rodent-proof feed bins | Feed is the real constraint | → 04-11 |
| Waterers and a freeze plan | Daily winter labour | → 03-06 |
| **Coop-only clothing and boots** | Salmonella, bird flu, allergen | Never worn in the house |
| Gloves and masks | Handling sick or dead birds | Keep a box by the coop |
| Instant-read thermometer | 165 °F poultry, 160 °F egg dishes | → 07-01 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Rabbits** (→ 05-05) instead, if the fit is poor.
- Coops build easily from salvaged lumber and pallets.
- Neighbours with hens may trade eggs for produce or labour (→ 18-02).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** **feed** is the limit, not the birds. Count it like human food (→ 23-02).
- **Ration:** sprouted grain (→ 04-16) stretches feed; free-ranging helps in summer only.
- **Resupply:** without bought feed, the flock must shrink to what scraps, garden waste and
  forage can support. Realistically that is a very small number of birds.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** ordinance, neighbours, noise and any egg allergy all argue for a deliberate
  decision.
- **B (moving):** **poultry travels badly**: heat stress, water and crates on the road. Caged
  rabbits travel better (→ 05-05). Treat a flock as a home or destination commitment.
- **C (establishing):** easier: space, forage, fewer neighbours. The allergy question and the
  winter water hauling come with you.

pages.body:
# Meat rabbits in a small yard

**What this page is for.** Why rabbits are often the best-fitting livestock for a small lot,
and how to keep them healthy, fed and productive, including the diseases that wipe out a herd.

> **CAUTION.** Rabbit is **extremely lean**. A diet that leans on rabbit without a fat source
> causes "rabbit starvation" (protein poisoning): nausea, weakness and diarrhoea even while
> eating plenty. **Rabbit must be paired with fat** (→ 04-12). And **two diseases can kill a
> whole herd in days** (below).

## Do this now

1. **Start with a trio:** one buck (male), two does (females). That is a working breeding unit.
2. **Plan a fat source** alongside them (→ 04-12).
3. **Vaccinate the breeding stock against RHDV2 while veterinarians are available**, and
   quarantine every new rabbit for 30 days (below).
4. **Plan for summer heat**, not winter cold. Heat kills rabbits.
5. **Be honest with children** about what the animals are for, before they name them
   (→ 20-03).

> **Before the collapse:** many towns count rabbits with chickens under a backyard-livestock
> limit, with setbacks from neighbours' houses and permits above a certain number. A doe's
> litters can push you past a cap fast; ask your city how young rabbits being raised for meat
> are counted. This never decides how you keep animals to survive.

## Why / how it works

### Why rabbits fit a small lot

| Factor | Rabbits | Chickens (→ 05-04) |
|---|---|---|
| Food allergen | None of the major allergens | Eggs are a major allergen |
| Noise | Silent | Hens cluck; roosters are a neighbour problem |
| Space | Very small; hutches stack | Coop plus run |
| Travel | **Caged rabbits travel**, with care about heat | Poorly |
| Cold | **Excellent**; they tolerate cold far better than heat | Good with the right breeds |
| Feed | Hay, forage, garden waste, pellets | Grain-dependent |
| **Manure** | **Will not burn plants**; still must be composted or autumn-applied (below) | "Hot": must be composted first |
| Output | Meat | Eggs and meat |
| Fat | **Very lean: a real limit** | Eggs supply fat |

**The manure is a serious argument.** Rabbit droppings are low in ammonia, so they do not burn
plants the way chicken manure does. But "will not burn plants" is not "safe to eat from": they
carry what any raw manure carries (*E. coli*, *Salmonella*, coccidia). **Compost them, or spread
them raw only on beds that will not be harvested for 120 days; never side-dress crops eaten
raw.** The 120-day interval is the US organic rule for raw manure on crops whose edible part
touches the soil (7 CFR 205.203). Details on → 05-11.

### Productivity

A trio produces a substantial amount of meat a year. Rabbits breed readily and grow fast. On a
small lot this is the highest protein output per square foot you are likely to get.

**But count the feed.** Rabbits turn feed into meat; they do not make calories from nothing.
Their advantage is that they eat **hay, weeds, garden waste and forage** instead of grain.

### Weather

- **Cold:** rabbits handle it well. Dry, draft-free hutches with deep bedding and wind
  protection.
- **Water freezes** at least twice a day in hard cold (→ 03-06). That is the real winter work.
- **Heat is the real danger.** Rabbits die of heat far more readily than of cold. Shade,
  airflow and water in the hottest weeks.{{#if is.hot_summers}} Your July highs average
  {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F: plan shade and airflow before the first heat wave.{{/if}}

### The two diseases that kill meat rabbits

- **Coccidiosis** (a gut parasite) is the main killer of young rabbits in small hutches.
  Prevention is the whole answer: **wire floors, feeders and water off the floor, clean water,
  no droppings in the feed.** At slaughter, **a white-spotted liver in a domestic rabbit is
  liver coccidiosis**: the meat is edible cooked to 160 °F; throw out the liver. **The same
  spotted liver in a wild rabbit means tularemia, and the whole animal is thrown out**
  (→ 05-15, → 05-09). Keep the two facts side by side.
- **RHDV2 (rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus 2)** has spread through wild and domestic rabbits
  in many US states in recent years. It kills **70 to 90 % of infected rabbits: sudden deaths in
  rabbits that looked healthy, sometimes with bleeding from the nose or mouth**. It spreads by
  contact with sick rabbits, carcasses, blood, urine and droppings, and on insects, scavengers and
  birds (Minnesota Board of Animal Health, Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease). If it happens: do not
  eat them, double-bag the carcasses, disinfect hutches and tools with **1 part household bleach
  to 9 parts water, left on 10 minutes, then rinsed and dried** (Minnesota Board of Animal
  Health; → 29-05), and, while phones work, report it to your state veterinarian. **Vaccinate the
  breeding stock while veterinarians exist**; the vaccine is sold through vets. **Quarantine any
  new rabbit for 30 days** before it meets the herd (Minnesota Board of Animal Health).
- **Introduce fresh greens to young rabbits gradually.** A sudden switch to wet greens causes
  the gut illness that kills them. Hay first, greens a little at a time.

### Feeding

- **Hay is the staple.** Grass hay stores well.
- **Garden waste, weeds and forage:** dandelion, plantain, clover, carrot tops.
- **Pellets** while you can buy them; plan for the day you cannot.
- **Grow fodder:** sprouted grain (→ 04-16) and cut greens.
- **Never feed anything from the toxic-plant list** (→ 05-06). The hemlocks kill rabbits as
  surely as people.

### The lean-meat problem

Rabbit meat carries very little fat. A diet of little but rabbit causes protein poisoning. It
killed explorers and trappers, and it is why rabbit alone is not a survival plan.

**Pair rabbit with:** stored fats and oils (→ 04-12); rendered fat from fattier animals; and
carbohydrates from stored grain (→ 04-03). **Cook rabbit to 160 °F** (FoodSafety.gov).

### Children and the animals

Children bond with animals. What works for many families: keep breeding stock as named animals
and the young raised for meat unnamed; involve the children in care but not slaughter; be
honest and matter-of-fact (→ 20-03). Do the processing out of sight (→ 05-16).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hutches: wire floors, sheltered, off the ground | Housing; wire floors control coccidiosis | Big enough for a doe to stretch out full length and sit up; more for a doe with a litter |
| Breeding trio (1 buck, 2 does) | The working unit | Meat breeds such as New Zealand and Californian |
| **Dry, rodent-proof hay storage** | The staple feed | → 04-11 |
| Water bottles or crocks, and a freeze plan | Twice-daily winter work | → 03-06 |
| Nest boxes | For does giving birth ("kindling") | Simple wooden boxes |
| Shade cloth, airflow for summer | **Heat kills rabbits** | The real seasonal risk |
| RHDV2 vaccination record | Proof of protection | From your vet |
| Instant-read thermometer | 160 °F | → 07-01 |
| **A fat source** | Rabbit alone is not enough | → 04-12 |

{{photo hutches}}

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- Hutches build easily from salvaged lumber and welded wire.
- **Weeds and garden waste** are free feed all summer. Dandelion and plantain are excellent.
- Wild rabbits can be trapped (→ 05-15), with the same lean-meat caution and the tularemia
  check.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** **hay and feed**. The herd renews itself; the feed does not.
- **Ration:** forage and garden waste first; sprout grain to stretch feed (→ 04-16).
- **Resupply:** rabbits are the most feed-flexible small livestock. Weeds, hay and garden
  trimmings go a long way.
- **Why it matters:** a breeding trio is **renewable protein**, and its manure feeds the garden
  (→ 05-11): two loops closed at once.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** often the best-fitting livestock for a small fenced yard.
- **B (moving):** caged rabbits can travel in a trailer or vehicle (→ 22-05). **Heat is the
  whole risk:** travel in the cool hours, never seal live animals in an unvented box in warm
  weather, shade at every stop, water at every stop. In a heat wave, honestly reassess whether
  they come.
- **C (establishing):** more forage and space; the stock you bring is the seed of the next herd.
