# Foraging wild plants, and the deadly look-alikes

**What this page is for.** The rules for eating wild plants anywhere in the US, the pairs of
plants that kill people who confuse them, and the few starter plants that are hard to get
wrong. **It is about risk, not a field guide.** The plates on this page exist so you can
recognise the plants that kill, not so you can identify food.

> **SAFETY.** **No wild plant or mushroom is eaten on a "test"; identification or nothing.**
> The deadly ones are not detectable by taste tests and the dose is small (→ 30-01).
> **Water hemlock is the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America** (USDA
> Agricultural Research Service); a piece of root 2 to 3 cm long (about an inch) can kill an
> adult (CDC MMWR, Water Hemlock Poisoning, 1994). It grows in wet ground in every region and
> resembles plants people forage. There is no antidote.

> **If someone has eaten a suspect plant:** call **Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222**, while
> phones work, and keep a piece of the plant. **Do not make them vomit.** Water hemlock sickness
> starts within 15 to 90 minutes of eating (CDC MMWR, 1994), and seizures can follow within the
> hour (USDA Forest Service). In a seizure: lay the person on their side, keep the airway clear, give
> nothing by mouth, and protect them from injury until the seizure passes. Wash skin that
> touched the sap; the poison (cicutoxin) is absorbed through skin (CDC MMWR, 1994). → 12-17.

## Do this now

1. **Study the plates for your home region below**: the hemlocks first, then their
   look-alikes. Twenty minutes now.
2. **Buy two regional field guides with photographs**, for your own part of the country, and
   learn plants **now**, in your own yard, while a mistake costs nothing.
3. **Learn the poisonous plants first**, before any edible one.
4. **Never use a "universal edibility test."** It does not protect against the plants that
   kill. Where the military handbook in Section 31 (→ 31-17) describes one, the floor above governs.
5. **Positive identification or nothing:** several matching features, the right habitat, the
   right season, checked against two sources.
6. **Write the household's rule for anyone with a food allergy** (below, → 30-19).

## Why / how it works

### What foraging is worth

Wild plants are mostly water and fibre. A day of foraging yields greens and a few calories:
worth it for **vitamins and variety**, not for keeping a family alive. Its real value:
- **Micronutrients** in spring, when stored food is nutritionally thin (→ 04-18).
- **Variety and morale** (→ 21-02).
- **Seasonal fruit and nuts** you can dry and keep (→ 05-17).

Trapping (→ 05-15), fishing (→ 05-08) and hunting (→ 05-07) return far more calories per hour,
at far lower risk. The garden (→ 05-01) is foraging with the risk removed.

### The killers that grow almost everywhere: learn these first

| Plant | Where | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Water hemlock** (*Cicuta* species) | **Wet** ground: ditches, stream banks, wet meadows, springs, pond edges | The most violently poisonous plant in North America. Resembles wild carrot and parsnip family plants |
| **Poison hemlock** (*Conium maculatum*) | **Drier** disturbed ground: fields, **garden beds**, ditches, fence lines, roadsides | Deadly to eat, even a small amount. **Its first-year rosette comes up in garden beds and is mistaken for parsley or carrot tops** (→ 05-01) |
| **Death camas** (several species) | Grassland, open woods, mostly in the West and Plains | Looks like wild onion **but has no onion smell**. All species are deadly |
| **Nightshades** | Disturbed ground, gardens, fence lines | Berries attractive to children |
| **Wild mushrooms** | Everywhere | Treat as off limits (below) |

**Two that hurt without being eaten:**

| Plant | Where | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Wild parsnip** | Roadsides, ditches, old fields | **Sap burns and blisters skin in sunlight.** Yellow flowers: the easy tell from the white-flowered hemlocks |
| **Poison ivy** (and poison oak, poison sumac) | Edges, fence lines, woods, riverbanks | Blistering rash on contact. Poison ivy has **three leaflets**. The oil stays active on clothes, tools and pets' fur, and **burning it puts the oil in your lungs** (→ 17-05) |

### The hemlocks, side by side

Both hemlocks are **tall** (water hemlock up to about 6 feet, USDA Forest Service; poison
hemlock up to 2 to 3 metres, about 6 to 10 feet, USDA ARS), with **hollow stems that branch at
the top**, often **mottled or streaked with purple**. **Smell proves nothing, either way.** Crushed poison
hemlock usually smells musty or mousy; water hemlock's root smells of carrot or parsnip. A
carrot-family plant that smells "right" can still be hemlock. **Do not crush and sniff unknown
plants as a test.** Use stem, leaf and habitat.

| | Poison hemlock | Water hemlock |
|---|---|---|
| **Ground** | **Dry** disturbed ground | **Wet** ground |
| **Stem** | Smooth, hairless, **purple blotches** | **Purple streaks**, stout |
| **Leaf** | Very finely divided, **fern-like lace** | **Coarsely toothed** leaflets whose **side veins run to the notches between the teeth, not to the tooth tips**: the one leaf feature that separates water hemlock from the edible carrot-family plants (USDA ARS; USDA Forest Service) |
| **Root** | Long white taproot | **Chambered** rootstalk with poisonous liquid. Confirmation only; **never cut one open to check** |

{{figure fig-hemlock-leaf-veins}}

**The carrot family (Apiaceae) is the family to avoid entirely.** It contains wild carrot
(Queen Anne's lace), wild parsnip, and both hemlocks. Unless you are genuinely expert, **eat
nothing from this family.** The downside is death; the upside is a poor root vegetable you
could have grown.

### The look-alike pairs

These are the pairs where people die. Learn the dangerous half first.

| You are looking for | It is confused with | The difference |
|---|---|---|
| Wild carrot, wild parsnip, wild celery | **Water hemlock, poison hemlock**, fool's parsley | Do not eat this family at all (above) |
| Wild onion, wild garlic | **Death camas**, fly poison, star-of-Bethlehem, daffodil bulbs | **Onion smell from every bulb, checked with clean hands** (onion on your fingers carries to the next bulb). If any bulb in a clump does not smell of onion, throw out the whole clump |
| Ramps (wild leeks, eastern woods) | **Lily-of-the-valley, false hellebore**, autumn crocus | Crush a leaf from **each** plant: no onion-garlic smell means poison. False hellebore has pleated leaves on a stem |
| Cattail shoots | **Blue flag iris** (and other irises), toxic to gut and skin | Only harvest shoots or roots from a stand you identified **by its brown spikes the previous summer**. Cattail leaves are flat and spongy with a rounded base; iris leaves fan out from a flat base |
| Wild grape | **Moonseed**, poisonous; also Virginia creeper and pokeweed | Grapes have **tendrils** and several small seeds; moonseed has **no tendrils** and **one crescent-shaped seed**: cut a fruit and look. Virginia creeper has five separate leaflets; pokeweed is an upright plant with berries in long strings on magenta stems |
| Milkweed shoots | **Dogbane**, a heart poison, in the same ground with the same milky sap | Left off the edible list in this binder: the features are too fine for printed text |
| Elderberry (cooked) | **Water hemlock** in the same wet ground; **pokeweed**; red elderberry | Elderberry is a woody shrub with paired leaves; hemlock is a soft, hollow-stemmed plant that dies back each winter. Pokeweed berries hang in long strings on soft magenta stems. Red elderberry has dome-shaped flower clusters and red berries. Raw elderberries and all green parts of elder cause vomiting: cook the berries |
| Dandelion | Common groundsel | Dandelion has one flower per **hollow, leafless** stalk and leaves only at the ground; groundsel has leafy branching stems with many small flower heads |
| Purslane | **Spotted spurge** (milky sap, irritant) | Break a stem: purslane has clear juice and fleshy leaves; spurge has **milky** sap and thin leaves |
| Chokecherry | Common buckthorn | Chokecherries hang in long strings; buckthorn berries cluster tight against the twig, often with a thorn at the twig tip |
| Blueberries | **Nightshades** (deadly nightshade, black nightshade) | Learn blueberries in person first; never let children pick dark berries unsupervised |
| Staghorn sumac (red upright cones) | **Poison sumac** | Poison sumac has **drooping white berries** and grows in swamps |
| Morel mushrooms | **False morels**, which can kill | See mushrooms, below. Not on the edible list |

### Mushrooms: the honest rule

**Do not forage mushrooms in a survival situation.** Deadly species in every region look like
edibles. Symptoms of the worst (amatoxin, in death caps and destroying angels) are **delayed by
hours**, seem to improve, and then the liver fails. There is no treatment available to you, and
the food value is negligible. **It is the worst risk-reward trade in foraging.**

### Your home region's plates

{{plates}}

The plates in this section are the deadly plants and look-alikes recorded for your home region
({{ region.home.ecoregion }}, {{ region.home.state_name }}). **Every state's page in Section 32
lists its ecoregions (→ 32-00), and the national plate pages carry every plate in the binder:
deadly plants and look-alikes (→ 32-60) and safe starters (→ 32-61).** Look at a destination's
plates before you go there (→ 05-19).

**What the plates can and cannot do.** They can make you say *"that might be hemlock: stay
away."* They cannot make you say *"that is safe to eat."* Recognising danger is a low bar, and
photographs clear it. Positive identification of food is a high bar: it needs a real guide, the
plant in your hand, and ideally a person who knows it.

### Rules that keep you alive

1. **Identification or nothing.** Several features, the right habitat, the right season, two
   sources. No taste test, no edibility test (→ 30-01).
2. **Learn the poisonous plants first.**
3. **Never eat from the carrot family** unless you are expert.
4. **No mushrooms.**
5. **One new plant at a time**, a small amount, then wait and watch before eating more, and only
   for **plants you have already identified for certain**: this checks personal tolerance and
   allergy. It is not a way to identify anything.
6. **Never children first.** Teach "we only eat what a grown-up hands us."
7. **Cover up and wash.** Long sleeves and gloves in brush; wash skin and clothes after, and
   wash pets that have been in it (→ 20-09).
8. **Avoid contaminated ground:** roadsides (exhaust, salt), sprayed lawns and rights-of-way,
   industrial sites, and floodwater ground (→ 03-07).
9. **Cook what can be cooked.** Cooking reduces some toxins and kills parasites. It never makes a
   poisonous plant safe.

### The safe, hard-to-mistake starters

These grow across most of the country, mostly as **weeds in your own yard**. Learn them in
person, from a guide and ideally a person who knows them. Check that each one appears on your
region's safe-starter plates (→ 05-17, → 32-61); not every plant grows everywhere. Each one's
look-alike is in the table above.

- **Dandelion:** leaves, roots, flower buds. Hard to mistake once you check the stalk (hollow,
  leafless, one flower).
- **Broadleaf plantain:** common lawn weed; leaves edible.
- **Lamb's quarters and amaranth (pigweed):** good cooked greens, **with a caution**: both build
  up nitrate and oxalate. Boil them and throw out the water; eat them as part of a varied diet,
  not a staple; skip plants from heavily manured or drought-stressed ground. Nitrate is most
  dangerous to babies and toddlers (it stops blood carrying oxygen). Write the household's rule
  for young children here: ______________________{{#if has.young_child}} (this household has a
  child under 6){{/if}}.
- **Purslane:** succulent garden weed. Clear juice, never milky (spurge, above).
- **Stinging nettle:** cooked only (cooking removes the sting). Wear gloves to pick it.
- **Wild onion and garlic:** **only if every bulb smells of onion** (look-alike table above).
- **Cattail:** only from a stand identified by its brown spikes (above), and beware the water it
  grows in (→ 03-07).
- **Berries you already know:** mulberry, raspberry and blackberry, wild plum. **Chokecherry
  and wild plum pits contain cyanide-forming compounds: never crush or eat the pits.**

### Food allergies and wild food

Wild food is **unlabeled by definition**, and nobody can tell you what it was processed with.
**Any wild nut is a tree nut.** For anyone with a food allergy the risk of a reaction adds to
the risk of misidentification, and in a crisis neither can be treated properly.

Allergies on record in this household:
{{#each allergies as a}}- **{{a.member}}**: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}})
{{else}}- None entered.
{{/each}}

Whether a food-allergic person eats unlabeled, wild or traded food at all is a decision card
(→ 30-19). The household's choice: {{choice DC-18}}. → 02-04, → 02-03.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Two regional field guides with photographs** | Cross-checking is the safety method | For your own region, not a national guide |
| A poisonous-plants guide | Learn these first | Regional |
| Hand lens | Identification detail (leaf veins) | Cheap |
| Gloves | Wild parsnip sap, nettles, poison ivy, hemlock | Always when handling unknowns |
| Basket or cloth bags | Collecting | Keeps plants whole and identifiable |
| Notebook | What you find, where and when | Builds local knowledge over years |
| Digging tool | Roots | → 16-01 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Your own lawn and garden weeds** are the highest-value, lowest-risk foraging there is.
- **A knowledgeable local person** is worth more than any book (→ 18-03).
- **The garden** (→ 05-01) is foraging without the risk. Prefer it.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** foraging is **seasonal and local**. In cold regions there is almost nothing from
  the first hard frost to spring, which is when you most need food (→ 05-17).
- **Ration:** taking a whole patch destroys it. Take a fraction; leave the rest.
- **Resupply:** the garden, sprouting (→ 04-16), trapping, fishing and hunting: all higher
  return, all lower risk.
- **The conclusion:** learn foraging as a **supplement and a skill**, practise it now while
  errors are survivable, and never let the food plan depend on it.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** yard weeds and parks. Watch for sprayed ground and for being seen.
- **B (moving):** little value while travelling. Tired, hurried and on unfamiliar ground is
  exactly when people make fatal identification errors.
- **C (establishing):** more ground and better plants, but the same rules, and further from help.
  Check the destination's plates in Section 32 (→ 32-00) and → 05-19 before you forage there.

pages.body:
# Hunting for food

**What this page is for.** What hunting can realistically add to a household's food, how to
take game cleanly and keep the meat, and the lead problem that matters for children and
pregnancy. Laws appear only as notes for while government works.

> **CAUTION.** Hunting gives the **largest single return** of any food-gathering method: one
> deer is a lot of protein. But it is **seasonal, and useless without a way to keep the meat.**
> A deer taken with no plan for keeping the meat is mostly waste. And **a lead-core bullet puts
> lead in the meat** (below), which matters most for children under 6 and anyone pregnant. If
> you are new to firearms, read → 29-11 first.

> **Before the collapse:** seasons, licences, tags, legal methods and calibres, hunter-education
> cards, blaze-orange rules and non-toxic-shot rules are set by your state's fish and wildlife
> agency and change every year. Hunt legally now; it is how you learn the ground and the people.
> Keep the agency's printed hunting guide with your documents (→ 19-01). This never decides a
> survival procedure.

## Do this now

1. **Get licensed and hunt now**, in normal times. Skill, access and local knowledge cannot be
   learned during a crisis.
2. **Solve preservation before you shoot** (→ 05-09, → 04-05): jars, lids, salt and fuel ready.
3. **Decide the bullet now:** copper (solid, "monolithic") bullets for deer keep lead out of the
   meat. Steel or bismuth shot for birds the children will eat.
4. **Arrange access now:** public land, and permission from landowners. That takes time.
5. **Practise with the gun you will actually use** (→ 14-09).

## Why / how it works

### What you can hunt

Game differs by region; your state's hunting guide lists what lives near you. Across most of the
US the useful groups are:

| Game | Typical firearm | Yield |
|---|---|---|
| **Deer** (whitetail almost everywhere; mule deer in the West) | Centrefire rifle, or shotgun with slugs. **Copper bullets** (below) | **The most meat of any common game**: the big prize |
| **Elk, moose, pronghorn** (where present) | Centrefire rifle | Very large, regional |
| **Wild turkey** | Shotgun | Substantial |
| **Upland birds** (pheasant, grouse, quail, dove) | Shotgun | Small |
| **Waterfowl** (ducks, geese) | Shotgun with **steel or bismuth shot** | Good, and fatty, which matters (→ 04-12) |
| **Rabbit, hare, squirrel** | **.22 LR** rifle or shotgun | Small, steady, near towns |
| **Feral hogs** (mainly the South) | Centrefire rifle | Large and fatty. Wear gloves: they carry diseases (→ 05-09) |

"Centrefire" and "rimfire" (.22 LR) are explained on → 29-11 and → 14-04.

### The calorie reality

- **One deer is weeks of protein for a family**, if you can keep it (→ 05-09).
- **A day of small-game hunting** might give a rabbit or two: real food, not comparable.
- **Ammunition matters** (→ 14-08). A deer costs very little ammunition. Shooting squirrels with
  centrefire is waste. **Use .22 LR for small game**; that is its job.
- **Traps and snares** (→ 05-15) take small game while you do other work, with **no ammunition
  at all**. In a long emergency they beat hunting for small game.

### The yearly rhythm

- **Fall: hunt.** Animals are fat and the cold helps you keep meat.
- **Late fall and winter: preserve.** Can (→ 04-05), cure and smoke (→ 04-07), dry (→ 04-06),
  or hold in winter cold where it is cold enough (→ 04-09).
- **Winter: live on it**, plus stored staples.
- **Spring and summer: garden** (→ 05-01), fish (→ 05-08), prepare for fall.

**Missing the fall window can cost you the year.** That is why hunting in normal times matters:
you learn the timing while it is not urgent.

### Field to table, in brief

1. **Shoot cleanly.** A wounded animal that runs is meat lost and needless suffering.
2. **Field dress immediately** (→ 05-09). Body heat spoils meat fast.
3. **Cool it fast.** Easy in cold weather; in a warm early season it is the whole problem.
4. **Butcher and preserve promptly**; cold weather buys time, warm weather does not. Pressure canning (→ 04-05) is the most
   reliable answer without a freezer. **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published
   time and pressure, or not canned.** Meat is a low-acid food (→ 30-01).
5. **Cook it through.** FoodSafety.gov gives **160 °F for venison and rabbit, wild or
   farm-raised**, whole cuts and ground alike. Cooking does not remove the chronic wasting disease
   agent in deer (Minnesota DNR; → 05-09): test where CWD is known, and never eat an animal that
   tested positive or looked sick (CDC).

### Lead in the meat

Lead-core bullets break up inside the animal. In a Minnesota DNR study, lead particles turned
up **as far as 18 inches from the wound channel**, too small to see, feel or notice when chewing,
and Minnesota testing found lead fragments in **26 % of packages of ground venison** and 2 % of
whole-muscle cuts. **Pregnant women and children under 6 should never be in a position to eat
lead particles** (Minnesota DNR, Tips for Deer Hunters).
{{#if has.young_child}}This household has a child under 6.{{/if}}{{#if has.pregnant}} This household has a pregnant member.{{/if}}

- **Copper (monolithic) bullets** for deer fragment very little. Buy them now.
- **If a deer was shot with lead:** trim liberally around the wound channel (there is no
  distance known to be safe) and throw out all bloodshot meat. Ground meat, trim, stew meat and sausage from that deer carry the most
  risk, because fragments get mixed through them. Whole-muscle cuts far from the wound carry the
  least.
- **Lead shot in birds and rabbits:** pick out the pellets; steel or bismuth shot keeps lead out
  of the pot.

### Taking game when there are no rules

When there is no warden, the limits that remain are real ones:
- **Take what feeds you, take it cleanly, and do not strip the local herd.** Deer near a town
  can be shot out in one hungry season and take years to recover.
- **Land access:** a landowner who knows and trusts you is worth more than gear (→ 18-01).
- **Shooting at home:** whether anyone fires a gun on your own property (for small game, pests
  or practice) is a decision card, because of what lies beyond the target (→ 30-12). The
  household's choice: {{choice DC-11}}. A suppressor (→ 14-10) changes the noise, not the
  backstop.

### The long view

In a long emergency, **game near towns will be hunted hard** and populations will drop fast.
Expect diminishing returns after the first season. Small game and trapping (→ 05-15) last
longer than deer near population centres. Treat a good fall as a windfall to preserve, not an
income.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Your state's current hunting guide, printed** | Pre-collapse rules; the maps and species notes inside outlast the law | → 19-01 |
| Rifle zeroed for hunting, **copper bullets** | One clean shot; no lead in the meat | → 14-04, → 14-09 |
| Shotgun with **steel or bismuth shot** | Birds and waterfowl | Lead-free for what children eat |
| **.22 LR and a deep stock of ammunition** | Small game, the sustainable kind | → 14-04 |
| Sharp knives and a sharpener | Field dressing | → 16-02 |
| Game bags, rope, gloves | Handling and cooling meat | Cheap |
| Sled or cart | Dragging a deer out | |
| **Preservation ready before the season** | Jars, lids, salt, fuel | → 04-05, → 04-07 |
| Blaze orange | Not being mistaken for game | Pre-collapse: often required |
| Instant-read thermometer | Cooking temperatures | → 07-01 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Traps and snares** (→ 05-15): no ammunition, work while you sleep.
- **Fishing** (→ 05-08): often a better return per hour than small-game hunting.
- **Local knowledge** from experienced hunters is the most valuable thing to gather now
  (→ 18-03).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** ammunition (→ 14-08) and seasons. The binding limit is usually **ammunition and
  preservation capacity**, not game.
- **Ration:** one clean shot, close range, no hopeful shooting. .22 LR for small game; save
  centrefire.
- **Resupply:** trapping and fishing scale better and cost nothing to run.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** in town, hunting means leaving town: fuel, time and access all matter. Small
  game and birds within reach are the realistic option.
- **B (moving):** a hunting rifle is a weight decision (→ 01-03); a .22 LR is the light,
  high-use choice.
- **C (establishing):** hunting becomes central; land access and neighbours matter more than
  gear. Learn the destination's game and habitat on ordinary visits.

pages.body:
# Fishing and ice fishing

**What this page is for.** Why fishing is one of the best food-gathering methods there is, how
to fish passively, how to keep the catch safe to eat, and how not to die on the ice.

> **SAFETY.** **Ice kills people every winter.** No ice is ever guaranteed safe, and a fall into
> cold water brings on hypothermia fast, even on a day above 40 °F (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia;
> → 08-05). **Under
> 4 inches of new, clear ice, nobody goes out** (Minnesota DNR). **Never eat local freshwater
> fish raw, lightly pickled or cold-smoked** unless it was first frozen solid at −4 °F for
> 7 days: it can carry the broad fish tapeworm, and salting, smoking or pickling does not kill it
> (CDC). **Cook fish to 145 °F**, or until the
> flesh is opaque and flakes apart (FoodSafety.gov).

## Do this now

1. **Get licensed and fish now.** Fishing is one of the best calorie-per-effort methods there
   is, and it uses no ammunition (→ 14-08).
2. **If anyone in the household reacts to fish, set the separation rule before the first fish
   comes home** (below, → 02-04).
3. **Never go on ice alone, never onto moving water in winter, and never without a spud bar and
   the table below.**
4. **Learn passive methods**: set lines and limb lines fish while you do other work.
5. **Find your state's fish-consumption advisories** for the waters you fish, and write the ones
   that matter on this page.

> **Before the collapse:** licences, limits, seasons and which waters allow set lines, trotlines,
> nets or traps are set by your state's fish and wildlife agency; fish-consumption advisories
> come from the state health or environment agency. Keep the printed fishing guide with your
> documents (→ 19-01). This never decides a survival procedure.

## Why / how it works

### Why fishing beats most food gathering

- **No ammunition:** it costs line, hooks and time.
- **Passive methods work while you sleep:** set lines, limb lines, traps and weirs.
- **Renewable** in a way that local deer are not (→ 05-07).
- **Year-round** in many places: open water spring to fall, **ice fishing in winter** where
  lakes freeze, which is exactly when nothing else produces.
- **Fish is a useful fat source** in a lean season (→ 04-12).

**Panfish** (perch, crappie, bluegill, sunfish) and **catfish** are the practical targets:
abundant, catchable in numbers and reliable. Trophy fish are not a food plan.

### Passive methods

- **Set line:** a baited hook on a line tied to a stake or the bank, left in place.
- **Limb line:** the same, tied to an overhanging branch so the branch flexes.
- **Trotline:** a long main line across the water with short baited lines hanging from it,
  spaced so the hooks cannot tangle.
- **Fish trap or weir:** a funnel or fence that lets fish in and makes them hard to leave.

In an emergency, set what feeds you, **check every line daily** (fish spoil and suffer on an
unchecked line), and **pull any line you are not fishing**. These are the rules that matter
when there is no warden.

### Water quality and advisories

- **After a flood, assume contamination** (→ 17-03). Prefer moving, cleaner water, cook
  thoroughly, and avoid fishing just downstream of towns, sewage outfalls or feedlots (→ 03-07).
- **Mercury:** FDA and EPA advise **anyone who is or might become pregnant, anyone
  breastfeeding, and children aged 1 to 11** to choose fish lower in mercury (FDA/EPA, Advice
  about Eating Fish). **For fish caught by family or friends: check the local advisory, and if
  there is none, eat only one serving that week and no other fish.** Larger carp, catfish, trout
  and perch are more likely to carry advisories. A child's serving is about 1 ounce at age 1 to
  3, 2 ounces at 4 to 7, 3 ounces at 8 to 10 and 4 ounces at 11 (FDA/EPA). Cooking does not
  remove mercury.
- **Your state's advisories** name specific lakes, species and sizes. Write the ones for your
  waters here: ______________________
{{#if has.young_child}}- This household has a young child: follow the FDA/EPA advice and child servings above.{{/if}}
{{#if has.pregnant}}- This household has a pregnant member: follow the FDA/EPA advice above.{{/if}}
{{#if has.nursing}}- This household has a nursing mother: follow the FDA/EPA advice above.{{/if}}

### Ice fishing: the winter advantage and the winter danger

Where lakes freeze, ice fishing is one of the few things that produces food in midwinter
({{#if is.cold_winters}}your January lows average {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F{{else}}your
lakes may not freeze reliably; January lows at home average {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F{{/if}}).

**But ice is genuinely dangerous:**
- **No ice is ever "safe" ice.** Thickness varies a great deal across one lake: currents,
  springs, inlets and pressure ridges all make weak spots.
- **Check the thickness yourself, again and again**, as you go out. Do not trust someone else's
  tracks.
- **Clear, solid ice is stronger** than white, slushy or refrozen ice.
- **Never go alone, and never onto moving water in winter.** River ice over current can be thick
  at the bank and gone in the middle. Tell someone where you are and when you will be back.
- **Early and late season, and any warm spell, are the most dangerous times.**
- **Wear ice picks around your neck:** two spiked handles that let a person drag themselves out.
  Carry rope and a throwable float too.
- **If someone goes in: do not go in after them.** Reach, throw or extend something. Get them
  out, then treat for hypothermia at once (→ 08-05), including CPR for a person with severe
  hypothermia (→ 12-18): **cold and apparently dead is not the same as dead** (CDC).

**The decision table (Minnesota DNR, for new, clear ice):**

| Clear ice | Load |
|---|---|
| **Under 4 in** | **Stay off** |
| **4 in** | Walking, ice fishing on foot |
| 5 to 7 in | Snowmobile or small ATV |
| 7 to 8 in | Side-by-side ATV |
| 9 to 10 in | Small car or SUV |
| 11 to 12 in | Medium SUV or small truck |
| 13 in | Medium truck |

**White ice (snow that melted and refroze on top) is only about half as strong as new, clear
ice: double every figure** (Minnesota DNR). Ice can be two feet thick in one place and one inch
thick a few yards away, so check with a spud bar (a heavy steel chisel on a pole) or an auger
**again and again** as you go out, and again on the way back if the day warmed. Many families never drive onto ice at all. Write
yours: vehicles on the ice? ________

{{figure fig-ice-thickness}}

**Children and ice:** whether children go onto ice, and with what rules, is part of the
household's worksheet on children and dangerous jobs (→ 30-25). The household's choice:
{{choice DC-24}}.

{{photo ice-kit}}

### If anyone reacts to fish

Fish is a major food allergen. If anyone in the household reacts to fish (→ 02-04):
- **A dedicated cooler, board, knife and pan** for fish, stored apart.
- **Clean fish outdoors**, away from the kitchen.
- **Cook the allergic person's food first**, before fish enters the kitchen.
- **Wash hands and surfaces** thoroughly afterwards.
- **Label any preserved fish clearly.** Smoked or canned fish in an unlabeled jar is exactly the
  failure to avoid.

### Keeping the catch

- **Eat fresh** where possible. Fish spoils fast.
- **No raw, pickled or cold-smoked local fish** unless first **frozen solid at −4 °F (−20 °C)
  for 7 days**: pike, walleye, perch, salmon and other freshwater fish can carry the broad fish
  tapeworm (CDC). An unheated building in winter does not reliably hold −4 °F. Pickled fish
  starts from hard-frozen fish or it is not made.
- **Winter cold** (→ 04-09) where it is reliably below freezing.
- **Smoking** (→ 04-07): traditional and excellent for fish.
- **Pressure canning** (→ 04-05): fish has its own published procedures; follow them exactly.
  **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not canned.**
- **Salting and drying** need a lot of salt (→ 04-13).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Your state's fishing guide, printed** | Pre-collapse limits, plus lake maps and species lists | → 19-01 |
| Rod, reel, and **a large stock of line, hooks, weights, lures** | The real consumables | Hooks and line run out first |
| **Hand ice auger** (no fuel) | Winter access | Works for ever |
| **Ice picks (worn), rope, throwable float** | What saves a life | Cheap; wear them |
| Spud bar | Checking ice as you go | Non-negotiable |
| Ice shelter and warm gear | Hours in the cold | → 11-01, → 08-05 |
| Set-line and trotline gear | Passive fishing | |
| Dedicated fish cooler, board, knife, pan | Allergy separation, hygiene | Mark them |
| Instant-read thermometer | 145 °F | → 07-01 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Hooks, line and a stick** catch fish. The reel is a convenience.
- Hooks from wire, safety pins or bone.
- Fish traps and weirs are ancient, passive and effective.
- Any hand auger or a chisel opens a hole in ice, slowly.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** **hooks and line** are the real consumables. Stock them deeply: they weigh nothing
  and cost little.
- **Ration:** passive set lines catch more per unit of effort and tackle.
- **Resupply:** improvised hooks and cordage; traps and weirs; trade (→ 18-02).
- **Why it matters:** fishing may be the most **sustainable** protein you have: no ammunition,
  works in winter where lakes freeze, and runs passively.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** nearby rivers and lakes. Watch water quality (→ 03-07).
- **B (moving):** a hand line and hooks weigh nothing. Carry them.
- **C (establishing):** often better water and less competition; set lines become genuinely
  productive. In warmer regions, watch for venomous snakes at the water's edge (→ 05-19).

pages.body:
# Field dressing and butchering

**What this page is for.** Turning a large animal, usually a deer, into safe meat: the order of
work, the disease checks, the cuts, and how to keep it. It is a sequence reminder, not a
substitute for hands-on teaching or an illustrated guide.

> **SAFETY.** Three hazards. **Spoilage:** body heat ruins meat within hours. **Contamination:**
> a cut gut spreads bacteria over the carcass. **Disease:** chronic wasting disease (CWD) in
> deer, elk and moose is caused by a prion, an infectious protein, and **cooking or freezing
> does not remove it** (Minnesota DNR, CWD Questions and Answers): never eat meat from an animal
> that tested positive, looked sick or was found dead, however it is cooked (CDC). **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not
> canned** (→ 30-01): meat is low-acid. And **sharp knives and tired hands cut people**; with no
> emergency room a deep hand cut is a serious injury (→ 12-02).

## Do this now

1. **Have the preservation plan ready before you hunt** (→ 05-07): jars, lids, salt and fuel.
2. **Field dress immediately.** The clock starts the moment the animal is down.
3. **Keep it clean and keep it cool.** Those two rules cover most of meat safety.
4. **Where CWD is known, test every deer before anyone eats it, while testing exists**, and hold
   the meat until the result is back. **Bone it out; do not saw through the spine.**
5. **Practise on small game first** (→ 05-16). Rabbits and birds teach the anatomy cheaply.

> **Before the collapse:** many state wildlife agencies run CWD testing in the hunting season,
> often free, with head drop-off sites. Use it while it exists.

## Why / how it works

### The three rules

1. **Speed.** Body heat spoils meat from the inside. Gut it fast.
2. **Cleanliness.** Do not cut the stomach, intestines or bladder. If you do, wash the mess
   away at once and trim generously.
3. **Cooling.** Get the carcass cool quickly. In cold weather this is easy; in a warm early
   season it is the whole problem.

### Field dressing, in outline

"Field dressing" means removing the guts where the animal fell.

1. **Position** the animal, ideally head uphill.
2. **Open the belly carefully:** a shallow cut through the hide only, with your fingers guiding
   the blade so it does not cut the gut.
3. **Free and remove the guts** without cutting the bladder or intestines.
4. **Remove the diaphragm, heart and lungs.** Save the **heart and liver** if you want them.
   **Not the spleen and not the lymph nodes** (CWD, below).
5. **Drain and wipe out** the body cavity: clean water if you have it, otherwise cloth or grass.
6. **Prop the cavity open** and get air moving through it.
7. **Hang it, skin it, let it cool.** In cold weather, hanging for a few days improves the meat.

**Save the fat** (→ 04-12): deer fat renders for tallow, candles and soap even if it is not
prized for cooking. **Save the bones** for broth, cooked on a fire that is already lit. **Save
the hide** if you have the skill and time.

### Disease and safety

- **Chronic wasting disease** is in deer in many states, and **cooking does not remove the
  prion** (Minnesota DNR). CDC's advice: **strongly consider testing before eating** where CWD
  is known; wear gloves; avoid handling the brain and spine; do not use your kitchen knives; never
  eat an animal that tested positive, looked sick or was found dead (CDC, About Chronic Wasting
  Disease). Penn State Extension adds: **bone out the meat** and do not saw through bone or cut
  through the brain or spinal cord; **do not eat brain, spinal cord, eyes, spleen, tonsils or
  lymph nodes**; wash hands and tools after (Penn State Extension, Precautions for Deer Hunters).
- **Lead fragments** (→ 05-07): lead particles from a lead-core bullet were found **as far as
  18 inches from the wound channel**, too small to see, feel or notice when chewing, and there is
  no distance that is known to be safe. **Trim liberally** and throw out bloodshot meat.
  **Pregnant women and children under 6 should never be in a position to eat lead particles**
  (Minnesota DNR, Tips for Deer Hunters). Copper bullets fragment very little.
- **Wear gloves.** Nitrile gloves are cheap and sensible.
- **Do not eat an animal that looked or behaved sick:** thin, confused, or with abnormal tissue.
- **Tularemia** ("rabbit fever") is a real risk in rabbits and hares. **The field check:** a wild
  rabbit whose **liver shows many white spots about the size of a pinhead is thrown out whole**:
  bury it, eat none of it, wash up (Missouri Department of Conservation, Rabbit: Safety and
  Health). **Gloves when dressing rabbits, no rubbing eyes or face, clean the knife after** (CDC):
  the germ gets in through skin and eyes. Cold weather reduces but does not remove the risk. (The
  same spotted liver in a **domestic** rabbit is coccidiosis, → 05-05.)
- **Wash hands and tools thoroughly**, and keep the work away from your water supply (→ 03-08).

### Butchering into usable cuts

- **Break it down** into backstraps (loins), tenderloins, shoulders, hindquarters, ribs, neck
  and trim, **boning out, not sawing through the spine** (CWD, above).
- **Prime cuts** (backstraps, tenderloins, whole hindquarter muscles) for roasting or steaks.
- **Everything else** (shoulders, neck, ribs, trim) becomes **ground meat, stew meat, jerky or
  canned meat**. In a survival setting this is most of the animal. From a lead-shot deer this is
  also the meat most likely to hold fragments.
- **Cooking:** FoodSafety.gov gives **160 °F for venison and rabbit, wild or farm-raised**, whole
  cuts and ground alike. Check the thickest part with a thermometer (→ 07-01).
- **Trim silver skin** (the tough shiny membrane) and connective tissue.
- **Keep it cold throughout.** Work in batches so the rest stays cool.

### Preserving: decide before you start

| Method | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pressure canning** (→ 04-05) | **The most reliable without a freezer** | NCHFP has game procedures; shelf-stable and ready to eat |
| **Winter cold / freezing** (→ 04-09) | Everything, when reliably below freezing | Free but temporary; measure it with a thermometer |
| **Drying / jerky** (→ 04-06) | Lean cuts | Follow the tested procedure; meat drying is not fruit drying |
| **Curing and smoking** (→ 04-07) | Traditional | Needs the correct cure and salt |
| **Fresh** | Straight away | Eat the organs and trim first |

**Pressure canning is usually the right answer for a deer** in a long outage: shelf-stable, no
ongoing cold, and the meat comes out ready to eat with no more fuel (National Center for Home
Food Preservation, Canning Meat, Poultry and Game; → 29-08).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharp knives** (skinning and boning) and a steel or stone | The core tools | Sharp is safer than dull (→ 16-02) |
| Bone saw or hacksaw | Quartering | **Not through a deer's spine or skull** (CWD): bone out instead |
| **Nitrile gloves**, by the box | Disease protection | Use them |
| Game bags | Keeping meat clean while it cools | Reusable |
| Gambrel, rope, or block and tackle | Hanging a deer | A tree limb and rope work |
| Large cleanable cutting surface | Butchering | |
| Coolers and ice, or reliable winter cold | Cooling is a safety step | Measure it |
| **Preservation gear ready** | Jars, lids, salt, canner, fuel | → 04-05, → 04-07 |
| Instant-read thermometer | Cooking temperatures | → 07-01 |
| **Illustrated butchering guide, printed** | Anatomy under pressure | → 19-01 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- One good sharp knife does everything; the rest is convenience.
- Rope over a branch replaces a gambrel.
- Clean bedsheets as game bags; a door on sawhorses as a table.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the consumables are **gloves, jars and lids** (→ 04-05) and **salt** (→ 04-13).
  Knives last if you keep them sharp (→ 16-02).
- **Ration:** use every part: organs, bones for broth, fat for rendering, hide if you can.
- **Resupply:** salt and canning lids are the items to stock now.
- **Why it matters:** a deer is only food if you can **keep** it. Butchering skill without
  preserving capacity turns a whole deer into a few days of eating and a lot of waste.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** butchering in a town backyard raises visibility and sanitation problems
  (→ 14-03, → 13-03). Plan where, and how to get rid of the remains.
- **B (moving):** you are not butchering on the move; carry preserved meat.
- **C (establishing):** far easier: space, distance from neighbours, cold outbuildings for
  hanging.

pages.body:
# Container and vertical growing in a small space

**What this page is for.** How to grow real food in pots, bags and buckets and up fences and
trellises, on a patio, a balcony, a driveway or a small yard.

## Do this now

1. **Count your real sun.** Check the space at about 9 a.m., noon and 4 p.m. and mark where you
   get **6 or more hours of direct sun** (Iowa State University Extension). That map, not the size of the space, sets how much food
   you can grow. A fenced town lot usually has less full sun than it looks.
2. **Buy containers big.** The most common failure is a pot too small: it dries out by noon and
   the plant stalls. Use the size table below and err large.
3. **Stock the growing mix now.** Potting mix, compost and fertilizer are the inputs you cannot
   scavenge quickly. → 05-11 for making your own.
4. **Put containers where you can water them from stored water** without carrying buckets across
   the yard. In an outage, water is measured by the gallon (→ 03-02).

## Why / how it works

**Containers trade soil volume for control.** You can grow food on a driveway, a deck, a
balcony, a south-facing wall, or the hot strip along a fence. You control the soil completely,
which matters in town where ground soil may hold lead, old fill or weedkiller. But you accept
three permanent costs:

1. **Water.** A container has no deep soil to draw from. In summer a 5-gallon pot in full sun
   can need water **every day**, sometimes more than once (University of Minnesota Extension). Push a finger an inch down; if it is dry,
   water until it runs out of the bottom. **Every container needs drainage holes**; without them
   the roots drown.
2. **Nutrients.** Every watering washes nutrients out of the bottom. Container plants must be
   **fed through the season**: a slow-release fertilizer mixed in at planting plus a weak
   liquid feed while watering is the Extension baseline (University of Minnesota Extension).
   Without shops, that becomes compost and compost tea (→ 05-11).
3. **Cold.** A container freezes from all sides; garden soil does not. Where winters freeze hard
   ({{#if is.cold_winters}}yours do{{else}}check your zone, {{ region.home.zone }}{{/if}}),
   containers are a **one-season** setup unless you sink them in the ground, mulch them deeply,
   or move them under cover. Perennials in pots often die over a hard winter.

**Growing up buys area, not sunlight.** Training cucumbers, pole beans, peas and small squash up
a fence or a livestock-panel arch gives far more yield per square foot of ground: more leaf in
the light, fruit off the dirt, and less disease because leaves dry faster. It does **not** make
sun. Put trellises on the **north** side of a bed so they shade nothing you are growing.

### What pays in a container

Choose crops with high value per square foot and a long harvest, not bulk calories.

| Tier | Crops | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best** | Bush or cherry tomatoes, peppers, bush beans, chard, kale, leaf lettuce, spinach, herbs | Long harvest, compact, tolerate small roots |
| **Good with a trellis** | Pole beans, peas, cucumbers, small winter squash | Vertical space is free space |
| **Works but greedy** | Potatoes in grow bags, bush zucchini, paste tomatoes | Need the biggest containers you have |
| **Don't bother** | Sweet corn, field pumpkins, melons, sprawling vines | Terrible calories per square foot in a pot |

### Container size: the rule that matters most

| Crop | Minimum volume | Practical |
|---|---|---|
| Lettuce, spinach, radish, herbs | 1 to 2 gal | Wide and shallow beats deep |
| Bush beans, chard, kale | 3 to 5 gal | |
| Peppers, bush tomatoes | 5 gal absolute floor | **7 to 10 gal** is the difference between a plant and a crop |
| Potatoes | 10 to 15 gal grow bag | Yield grows with volume |

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Fabric grow bags (5 to 15 gal) | Cheap, fold flat, store for years | Best storage-space-to-growing-space ratio |
| Bagged potting mix and compost, several seasons' worth | The input you cannot improvise fast | Stores dry; rotate |
| Slow-release and water-soluble fertilizer | Containers leach; unfed pots stall | Fertilizer is an early shortage item |
| Livestock panel(s) and metal fence posts | An arch trellis that lasts decades | A 16-ft panel bent into an arch is the classic |
| Jute or sisal twine | Trellising and tying; it composts | |
| Watering can with a fine head | Precise watering from stored water | |
| Drip line or soaker hose | Cuts water use a lot | Keep a manual backup |
| Shade cloth (30 to 40 %) | Saves greens in a heat wave | Doubles as a frost layer (→ 05-02) |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **5-gallon buckets:** food-grade if you can get them. Drill 6 to 8 half-inch drainage holes
  near the bottom edge.
- **Totes, coolers, tubs, feed sacks, woven bags, laundry baskets lined with landscape fabric.**
  Anything that holds soil and drains.
- **Trellis:** the existing fence, branches lashed into an A-frame, old bed springs, chain-link
  panels, concrete mesh, string grids.
- **Growing mix:** finished compost cut with garden soil and something for structure: shredded
  leaf mould, sand, or crumbled charcoal. **Wood ash is not a substitute** (it raises soil pH
  hard).
- **Do not reuse:** containers that held fuel, solvent, pesticide or unknown chemicals; treated
  lumber as bed sides for food; tyres.

## When it runs out

- **Potting mix and compost** are the real limit in year two. Start a compost system **now**
  (→ 05-11). Reuse container soil: empty it, mix in fresh compost, replant. Growing the same crop
  in the same tired mix year after year builds up disease.
- **Fertilizer:** substitute compost, compost tea, well-rotted manure (→ 05-11), **urine heavily
  diluted with water, applied to soil, never to leaves, and not in the last month before you
  harvest anything eaten raw**, wood ash **sparingly** for potassium, and crushed eggshell or bone
  for calcium. All are slower and weaker than bagged fertilizer: plan for lower yields.
- **Water:** a container garden is a standing daily demand. Budget it against Section 03 before
  you plant, and mulch every container. Rinse water without soap stretches the supply; never put
  greywater on leaves you will eat raw (→ 13-03).
- **Seed:** → 05-03. Save from open-pollinated varieties only.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** in an apartment or small lot this **is** the garden: containers plus fence
  trellises on the sunny side, placed so a frost warning means carrying pots under cover rather
  than losing the crop.
- **B (moving):** rigid containers full of soil do not travel. **Fabric grow bags fold flat**
  and go with the seed (→ 05-03); dump the soil and keep the bags. Harvest everything edible
  before you leave.
- **C (establishing):** containers become the starter garden while you break ground, and a
  permanent home for anything that must come indoors.

pages.body:
# Soil, compost and fertility without bought inputs

**What this page is for.** How to keep garden soil fertile year after year without buying
fertilizer: compost, manure, mulch and cover crops, and how to handle manure and human waste
without making anyone sick.

> **CAUTION.** Two real hazards. **Raw manure and human waste carry germs** that cause serious
> diarrhoeal illness; they must be composted properly and kept away from food crops and water
> (→ 13-01). And **cat and dog waste never go into food-garden compost**: cat faeces can carry
> *Toxoplasma*, a parasite that is a particular danger in pregnancy and to small children
> (→ 20-09).

## Do this now

1. **Start composting now.** Fertility takes years to build and cannot be improvised in a crisis.
2. **Compost everything organic you have:** kitchen scraps, leaves, grass, cardboard, paper.
3. **Sheet-mulch new beds:** cardboard, then leaves and compost on top. It builds soil while you
   wait.
4. **Get a soil test** through your state Extension service while it operates.
5. **Never compost cat litter or pet faeces** for a food garden.

## Why / how it works

### Fertility is the limit nobody plans for

You can store seed, tools and water. **You cannot store soil fertility.** Every harvest takes
nutrients out, and in a long emergency there is no bag of fertilizer to put them back. The
households still producing in year three are the ones that built a **closed loop**: everything
organic goes back into the soil.

### Compost basics

| Ingredient | Examples | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Greens** (nitrogen-rich) | Kitchen scraps, grass clippings, fresh manure, green weeds | Feed the microbes |
| **Browns** (carbon-rich) | Dry leaves, straw, cardboard, paper, sawdust, wood chips | Structure and air |
| **Water** | | Damp as a wrung-out sponge |
| **Air** | Turning the pile | Stops it going sour and smelly |

**Mix browns and greens**, with more browns than greens by volume. Too much green goes slimy
and smells; too much brown just sits there. A pile about **3 to 5 feet each way** works best:
smaller does not heat, larger does not let air and water in, and an active pile heats to
**130 to 160 °F** (University of Minnesota Extension, Composting in Home Gardens).

**Hot or cold:** a hot pile (turned, balanced, big enough) heats up and finishes in months, and
the heat helps kill germs and weed seeds. A cold pile works too; it takes a year or more and
does not kill germs or seeds.

**Where winters freeze, the pile freezes and stops.** That is fine: it starts again in spring.
Keep adding to it.

### Free inputs, especially in town

- **Leaves:** the best free soil input. Neighbours bag them up every fall. Collect them.
- **Grass clippings:** high nitrogen; use in thin layers.
- **Cardboard and paper:** carbon, and the base of sheet mulching. Remove tape and glossy print.
- **Wood ash** (→ 06-02): potassium and lime. **Use sparingly**; it raises soil pH and too much
  harms soil. Test before adding it, especially where soils are already alkaline.
- **Kitchen scraps:** the daily input.
- **Coffee grounds** from cafés while they exist.

### Manure: useful and hazardous

- **Plant-eater manure** (rabbit, chicken, horse, cow, goat) is excellent fertility.
- **Rabbit manure is the standout** because it is "cold": low in ammonia, so it will not burn
  plants (→ 05-05).
- **Chicken manure is "hot"**: it must be composted before use or it burns plants.
- **"Will not burn plants" is not "free of germs."** Rabbit droppings carry *E. coli*,
  *Salmonella* and other germs like any raw manure. **Compost all manure before it touches food
  crops, or spread it raw only on beds that will not be harvested for 120 days; never on crops
  eaten raw, never as a side-dressing on growing food plants.** The US organic rule sets
  **120 days** between raw manure and harvest for crops whose edible part touches the soil, and
  **90 days** for others (7 CFR 205.203). With children eating from the garden, the longer gap
  is the one to use.
- **Never use dog or cat waste** on food gardens.

### Human waste: the honest version

In a long outage, human waste is a sanitation problem (→ 13-01) and a possible fertility
resource.
- **It carries serious germs.** Composting it safely needs sustained heat, long curing and
  discipline. It is not a casual project (→ 13-06).
- **The safe compromise** for most households: compost it separately, cure it for a long time,
  and use the result on **non-food** plantings (fruit-tree drip lines at most, ornamentals,
  windbreaks), not vegetables.
- **Keep it far from any water source:** well, rain barrel or pool (→ 03-08). CDC's well
  guidance treats nearby human and animal waste as a contamination risk to wells (CDC,
  Guidelines for Testing Well Water).
- **With small children in the house**, err strongly toward caution: getting this wrong means
  diarrhoeal illness in the most vulnerable people (→ 12-05).

### Building beds fast: sheet mulching

The way to turn lawn into garden with no digging:
1. **Lay cardboard directly on the grass**, overlapping, and wet it.
2. **Pile leaves, compost, grass clippings and straw** on top, in a thick layer.
3. **Wait a season**, or plant straight into pockets of compost.

It smothers grass, feeds the soil, holds water, and needs no tools and no fuel. Fall is the
ideal time to start it, ready for spring planting.

### Keeping fertility in the loop

- **Compost everything:** kitchen, garden, paper, leaves.
- **Cover crops** where you have space: clover and vetch take nitrogen from the air into the
  soil; cereal rye holds soil over winter.
- **Rotate crops** so the same family does not drain the same bed year after year.
- **Return what you harvest:** stalks, husks and trimmings go back.
- **Mulch permanently.** Bare soil loses water, structure and nutrients.

### Know your soil

A soil test tells you the **pH** (how acid or alkaline the soil is) and which nutrients are
short. Soils differ a lot across the country: many wet, wooded regions have acid soils that
need lime; many dry western soils are alkaline and should never get wood ash. Test before you
add lime or ash; overdoing either locks up nutrients.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Compost bin(s) or a pallet enclosure | Holds and speeds the process | Pallets are often free |
| Garden fork or pitchfork | Turning compost | → 16-01 |
| **Cardboard** (stockpile it) | Sheet mulching and carbon | Free |
| Leaves (collect every fall) | The best free input | |
| Soil test | Know your starting point | Do it now |
| Cover crop seed (clover, vetch, rye) | Nitrogen and structure | Store with seed (→ 05-03) |
| Wheelbarrow or garden cart | Moving material is the real labour | |
| Straw bales | Mulch, compost carbon, cold frames (→ 05-02) | |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Leaves, cardboard, grass and kitchen scraps** are free and plentiful in town: one of the few
  things town does better than country.
- Wood ash from the fireplace, sparingly, after a soil test.
- Manure from neighbours' animals, composted before use.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** fertility declines over seasons if you take out more than you put back. It is
  invisible until yields drop.
- **Ration:** put the compost on the beds growing calorie crops rather than spreading it thin.
- **Resupply:** leaves and cardboard are close to unlimited in a residential area; manure if you
  or neighbours keep animals; cover crops fix nitrogen for free.
- **Why it matters:** of everything in Section 05, **soil is the slowest to build and the
  fastest to neglect.** A compost pile started this month is the best thing you can do for the
  garden three years from now.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** free leaves and cardboard everywhere. Start now; build beds by sheet mulching.
- **B (moving):** you cannot take soil. Take seed (→ 05-03) and knowledge.
- **C (establishing):** test the soil at the destination before choosing a garden site; farm
  manure or woodland leaves may be the local unlimited input (→ 05-18).

pages.body:
# Pollination and garden pests without chemicals

**What this page is for.** Which crops need insects to make food, how to pollinate them by hand,
and how to control pests when there is nothing to buy.

> **CAUTION.** **Stinging insects:** encouraging bees into the yard raises sting exposure. Anyone
> can have a first severe reaction to a sting, and epinephrine is the answer (→ 02-03).
> {{#if has.epinephrine}}Make sure every adult knows where the household's epinephrine is before
> you plant a flower strip.{{else}}Know the signs of a severe reaction before you plant a flower
> strip.{{/if}} **Every "natural" pesticide is still a pesticide.** Homemade nicotine tea, sprays
> of unknown strength and borrowed farm chemicals can poison people, pets and soil. Do not
> improvise chemistry near where children play.

## Do this now

1. **Learn which of your crops actually need an insect.** Many do not. If
   pollinators crash, you want to know at once which beds are at risk (table below).
2. **Learn to hand-pollinate squash, cucumbers and melons.** Five minutes a morning, and the vine
   crops no longer depend on insects.
3. **Stop spraying anything broad-spectrum** (anything that kills all insects). In a long outage,
   beneficial insects are the only pest control left, and they come back more slowly than pests.
4. **Walk the garden every morning with a jar of soapy water.** Hand-picking is the most
   effective no-input pest control there is.

## Why / how it works

### Which crops need pollinators

| Needs insects | Pollinates itself (shake or wind is enough) | Wind-pollinated | Eaten before it flowers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Squash, zucchini, pumpkin, cucumber, melon (separate male and female flowers) | Tomato, pepper, eggplant, bean, pea | Sweet corn | Lettuce, spinach, chard, kale, radish, carrot, beet, onion, potato, herbs |
| Apple, plum, cherry, pear and most tree fruit (usually needs a **second compatible variety**) | Strawberry (better with insects) | | |
| Raspberry, blueberry (better and bigger with insects) | | | |

Read that twice. **Most of a survival garden's calories (potatoes, roots, greens, beans, corn,
tomatoes) do not depend on bees.** The vine crops and fruit trees do. That tells you where to
spend effort (University of Minnesota Extension, Fruits and Vegetables That Require
Pollination).

**Squash-family crops ("cucurbits") are the special case.** They carry **separate male and
female flowers**, and an insect has to carry pollen from one to the other. Female flowers have a
tiny fruit already formed behind the bloom; males sit on a plain stem. Poor pollination gives
shrivelled, curled or half-formed fruit that rots at the flower end. Bumblebees and native squash
bees are the best pollinators of squash; they work early in the morning, when the flowers are
open.

{{figure fig-squash-male-female-flowers}}

**Hand-pollinating squash, cucumbers and melons (at dawn; the flowers close by midday):**
1. Find an open **male** flower. Pick it and peel the petals back to show the pollen-covered
   centre.
2. Find an open **female** flower (tiny fruit behind the bloom).
3. Dab the male centre onto the centre of the female flower. One male does several females.
4. A soft brush or a cotton swab does the same job without picking the male.

**Tomatoes and peppers** under cover or indoors (no wind): flick or gently shake the flower
clusters daily. They pollinate themselves; they just need the vibration.

### Keeping the pollinators you need

Bees need **flowers from spring through fall**, not one burst. The near-free version: let some
herbs, cabbage-family crops and greens **bolt** (go to flower) instead of pulling them. Dill,
cilantro, basil, mustard, radish and arugula flowers draw pollinators. Add a strip of native
wildflowers for your region along the fence. **Leave a patch of bare, untilled ground:** many
native bees, including squash bees, nest in soil and will not use a bee house (Iowa State
University Extension).

### Pest control with nothing in the shed

Work down this ladder in order. Each step is cheaper and less harmful than the next.

1. **Prevention.** Rotate crops so last year's pest does not wake up under this year's host.
   Clear crop debris in fall (pests spend the winter in it). Space plants for airflow. Water the
   soil, not the leaves: wet leaves breed fungus.
2. **Barriers.** **Floating row cover is the most valuable pest tool in a no-chemical garden**:
   it keeps out flea beetles, cabbage worms, squash vine borer and cucumber beetles. **Row cover
   keeps pollinators out too**, so take it off squash-family crops when they flower, or
   hand-pollinate under it. Collars of cardboard or tin cans around transplants stop cutworms.
   Fine mesh over cabbage-family crops all season nearly ends cabbage worms.
3. **Hand-picking.** Every morning: Colorado potato beetles and their orange egg clusters (check
   under leaves), tomato hornworms, squash bugs and their bronze egg patches, cabbage worms,
   Japanese beetles. Drop them in soapy water. **A board laid flat on the soil overnight**
   collects squash bugs underneath; flip it in the morning.
4. **Encourage predators.** Lady beetles and their alligator-shaped larvae, lacewings, ground
   beetles, tiny parasitic wasps, hoverflies. They come for the same small flowers the
   pollinators want: dill, fennel, cilantro, yarrow. **Learn to recognise the larvae** so you do
   not crush your allies. A hornworm covered in white rice-like cocoons is being eaten by
   parasitic wasps: leave it.
5. **Physical.** A strong water spray for aphids. Beer traps or hand-picking at night for slugs.
   Diatomaceous earth on dry soil only (it stops working when wet and kills beneficial insects
   too): spot use, never on flowers.
6. **Last resort: soap.** Insecticidal soap, or a **very weak** plain-soap spray, kills
   soft-bodied insects on contact only. It also kills beneficial insects it lands on. Spray in
   the evening, on the pest, never the whole garden. Do not make stronger chemistry.

**Companion planting:** the folk claims ("marigolds repel everything", "basil protects
tomatoes") are mostly unsupported by trials. What **is** supported is the underlying idea:
**variety and continuous flowers support predators and pollinators** (University of Minnesota
Extension, Companion Planting). Interplant flowers freely; do not plan food security around a
marigold.

### Common garden pests across most of the US

| Pest | Attacks | What works |
|---|---|---|
| Colorado potato beetle | Potato, eggplant, tomato | Hand-pick adults and crush egg clusters daily; rotate far |
| Squash vine borer | Squash, zucchini, pumpkin | Row cover until flowering; bury vine joints so they root; slit the stem and remove the grub |
| Squash bug | Squash family | Board trap; crush bronze eggs under leaves |
| Cucumber beetle | Cucumber, melon, squash | Row cover early; they spread bacterial wilt, so this one matters |
| Cabbage worm / looper | Cabbage, kale, broccoli | Fine mesh all season |
| Flea beetle | Cabbage family, eggplant | Row cover on transplants until established |
| Aphid | Everything | Water spray; let the lady beetles work |
| Japanese beetle | Beans, raspberry, fruit | Hand-pick into soapy water at dawn; **do not use pheromone traps**: they draw in more than they catch |
| Grasshopper (dry years) | Everything | Physical barriers; poultry (→ 05-04); often you accept the loss |
| Deer, rabbit, raccoon | Everything | Fencing |

Your region will have its own extras; your state Extension service's pest guide lists them
(University of Minnesota Extension, Yard and Garden Insects).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Floating row cover (100-ft roll or more) and hoops | Best no-chemical pest tool; also frost cover | Light weight for summer, heavier for → 05-02 |
| Fine insect mesh | Season-long cabbage worm control | Lasts years if stored dry |
| Insecticidal soap concentrate | Last-resort soft-bodied pests | Concentrate stores longer |
| Soft brush or cotton swabs | Hand-pollination | |
| 10× hand lens | Telling a pest from a beneficial larva | |
| A printed pest guide for your region | You will not remember 20 insects | |
| Native wildflower seed for your region | Continuous bloom, resident pollinators | Perennial; plant once |
| Diatomaceous earth (food grade) | Spot use for slugs and crawling pests | Useless wet |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Row cover:** old sheer curtains, tulle, window screen, cheesecloth, worn sheets on hoops
  (heavier: watch the heat).
- **Hoops:** plastic pipe, heavy wire, willow branches bent green, metal conduit.
- **Cutworm collars:** toilet-paper tubes, cut cans, cardboard strips, cups with the bottoms cut
  out.
- **Traps:** a flat board for squash bugs; a shallow dish of beer or yeast and sugar water for
  slugs.
- **Pollination brush:** a feather, a paintbrush, or the male flower itself.

## When it runs out

- **Insecticidal soap:** use a **very weak** plain-soap solution (pure soap, not detergent and
  not dish soap with degreasers), sprayed on the pest in the evening, rinsed off food before
  eating. Test on a few leaves first: soap burns leaves in heat. **Do not** move on to homemade
  nicotine, bleach or borrowed farm chemicals: the poisoning risk to children and pets is real
  and the benefit small.
- **Row cover** is the consumable that matters. It tears and breaks down in sun. **Keep spares
  and patch with tape.** When it is gone: hand-picking discipline, and plan as if you will lose
  a share of cabbage-family and squash-family crops.
- **Pollinators** can crash after a hard chemical year, a brutal winter or habitat loss. Your
  hedge is **hand-pollination** plus favouring crops that do not need insects.
- **Bought predators** (lady beetles, nematodes) end when shops do. Habitat is the permanent
  replacement: plant it now; it takes two or three seasons to establish.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** fence out the animals; row cover and morning hand-picking for the insects. Let
  herbs flower along the fence.
- **B (moving):** carry seed, not plants. Wildflower seed weighs nothing.
- **C (establishing):** bigger plantings can absorb losses, and native habitat nearby usually
  means plenty of pollinators. Pest pressure shifts toward grasshoppers, deer and voles: fencing
  and poultry matter more than sprays.

# Perennials, fruit trees and berries for your zone

**What this page is for.** Food plants that come back every year: what grows in your zone, how
long each takes to bear, and how to keep them alive and multiplying.

> **The most time-sensitive page in Section 05.** Everything here takes **years** to produce. A
> tree planted the week the grid goes down feeds no one for several years. Act on this page
> **now**, while nurseries, water and spare time exist.

## Do this now

1. **Plant something perennial this season.** Rhubarb and raspberries are the fastest
   meaningful returns in most climates, often a partial crop the year after planting.
2. **Check your state Extension service's recommended fruit variety list before you buy.** Your
   zone is **{{ region.home.zone }}**. Many varieties sold nationally are not reliable in very
   cold zones, and many need more winter cold than the warmest zones give. Buying the wrong tree
   costs you years.
3. **Buy fruit trees in pairs.** Most apples, pears and plums need a **second, different,
   compatible variety** nearby to set fruit. A lone apple tree can be a lifetime of leaves.
4. **Site them permanently and correctly:** full sun, out of the frost pocket at the bottom of
   the slope, and where they will not shade your vegetable beds as they grow.
5. **If you have an agreed destination, plant fruit there too, now**, with the owner's
   permission{{#if has.agreed_destination}} (→ 05-18 has each destination's zone){{/if}}. A tree
   planted this year is bearing before you might need it.

## Why / how it works

**Perennials are the opposite trade from the vegetable garden.** They cost years of patience and
permanent space up front. In return they produce **without seed, tilling, transplanting or yearly
inputs**: exactly what matters when supply chains are gone. A vegetable garden fails completely
if you lose a season to illness or a move. A raspberry patch keeps going.

**Hardiness is pass or fail.** Your **USDA hardiness zone** is the average coldest winter
night in your area, in 10 °F bands (USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map). A plant rated two zones
warmer than yours is not stunted by a hard winter; it is dead. In the warmest zones the problem
reverses: many apples, pears, cherries and peaches need a certain amount of winter cold
("chill hours") to flower, and a mild winter leaves them barren. Choose "low-chill" varieties
there.

### What grows by zone band

Rough bands. Your state Extension list is the local authority.

| Band | Reliable choices | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Zones 3 to 4** | Rhubarb, asparagus, raspberries, currants, gooseberries, haskap (honeyberry), aronia, elderberry, very hardy apples, hardy plums, sour cherries, cold-hardy grapes, hybrid hazelnuts | Prefer varieties from northern university breeding programmes; that is what those programmes are for |
| **Zones 5 to 6** | All of the above plus most apples, pears, plums, many grapes, blueberries (in acid soil), strawberries; peaches in sheltered spots | The widest choice for temperate fruit |
| **Zones 7 to 8** | Peaches, pears, apples (fewer in hot humid areas), figs (with winter protection at the cold end), persimmons, blackberries, blueberries, muscadine grapes in the Southeast | Disease pressure from humidity; choose resistant varieties |
| **Zones 9 and warmer** | Citrus, figs, pomegranates, low-chill peaches and apples; avocado and mango in the warmest areas | Winter cold is short or absent; water and heat are the limits |

Your zone, **{{ region.home.zone }}**, puts you in one row. Any perennial you plant should be
rated for your zone or colder.

### Time to first real harvest

| Crop | First real harvest | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Rhubarb** | Year 2 (light), year 3 full | Very tough. **Leaves are poisonous**: stalks only |
| **Raspberry, blackberry** | Year 2 | Fastest fruit calories. Spreads by itself, which is a feature |
| **Strawberry (June-bearing)** | Year 2 | Renews itself by runners |
| **Asparagus** | Year 3 | Then productive for 15 to 20 years |
| **Currant, gooseberry** | Years 2 to 3 | Very hardy; tolerate some shade |
| **Aronia, elderberry** | Year 3 | Hardy native shrubs; best cooked or preserved |
| **Haskap (honeyberry)** | Year 3 | Earliest fruit of the year; needs **two different varieties** |
| **Plum** | Years 3 to 5 | Often needs a compatible pollinator |
| **Apple** | Years 4 to 7 (dwarf sooner) | The long game; storage apples are worth the wait |
| **Pear** | Years 4 to 7 | |
| **Grape** | Years 3 to 4 | Needs a trellis or fence |
| **Peach** (zones 5 and warmer) | Years 3 to 4 | Short-lived tree; replant from time to time |
| **Hazelnut (hybrid)** | Years 4 to 7 | One of the faster nut crops |

### Pollination is a design rule

Most apples, pears and plums are **self-unfruitful**: they need pollen from a **different
variety** that flowers at the same time (University of Minnesota Extension, Growing Apples).
Haskaps need a matched partner. Sour cherries, most peaches, and most raspberries, currants and
strawberries are self-fertile. Before you plant, write down which tree pollinates which. In a
small yard, a **multi-graft tree** (several varieties on one trunk) solves pollination in one
planting hole.

{{photo fruit-pairs}}

**Rootstock decides size and lifespan.** Fruit trees are grafted (joined) onto a root system
chosen for size. Dwarf trees fruit sooner and stay pickable without a ladder, but need
**permanent staking** and more watering. Standard trees take longer, grow big, live longer and
stand on their own. In town, dwarf or semi-dwarf; on open land, standard trees are the legacy
planting.

### Food trees you did not plant

Towns and farm country are full of **abandoned apple trees, wild plum thickets, mulberries,
chokecherries, serviceberries and nut trees**, planted or naturalised decades ago. Map them now
(→ 05-17), the way you would map water.

### The two ways young trees die

- **Rabbits and voles girdle young trunks** (chew the bark all the way round), often under
  snow, and kill the tree. Every young tree gets a **hardware-cloth or spiral trunk guard**,
  from the ground to above the expected snow line, from day one.
- **Deer** rub antlers on young trunks in fall and browse low branches. Cage young trees where
  deer roam.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bare-root fruit trees, **in compatible pairs** | Cheapest way to buy trees | Check the Extension list first |
| Raspberry canes, rhubarb and asparagus crowns | Fastest perennial food per dollar | Rhubarb and asparagus can outlive you |
| Hardware cloth and trunk guards | Rabbits and voles kill more young trees than cold does | Check every fall |
| Bypass pruners, loppers, pruning saw | Perennials need yearly pruning | Keep sharp (→ 16-02) |
| Tree stakes and soft ties | Dwarf trees need permanent support | Not bare wire against bark |
| Deep mulch (wood chips, straw) | Moisture, weeds, root insulation | Keep mulch off the trunk |
| Grafting knife and grafting tape | Propagate more trees | The skill that makes fruit renewable (→ 24-01) |
| Wire or panel trellis | Grapes and cane berries | |
| Netting | Birds take the whole berry crop otherwise | |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Free plants:** raspberries, blackberries and elderberry send up suckers; a neighbour's patch
  is a free start. Rhubarb divides. Strawberries send runners. Currants and grapes root from
  **hardwood cuttings** taken while dormant.
- **Wild rootstock:** wild plum, chokecherry and wild apple can be grafted onto.
- **Trunk guards:** split plastic pipe, wrapped window screen, metal flashing.
- **Mulch:** shredded leaves, wood chips from storm debris.

## When it runs out

Perennials do not run out; they **decline**, slowly enough to miss.
- **Water:** a young tree needs deep watering through its first two or three summers. Plant in
  **fall or early spring** so roots establish before heat, and site trees where stored or used
  water can reach them.
- **Renewal:** raspberries need old canes cut out every year; strawberry beds need renovating
  every few years; fruit trees need yearly pruning. **The skill is the consumable**: learn
  pruning now.
- **Propagation is the resupply.** With no nurseries, new plants come from **cuttings, suckers,
  divisions, runners and grafting**: all free, from what you already have.
- **Preserving is the other half.** Fruit arrives all at once and will not wait: dry it
  (→ 04-06), can it (→ 04-04) or make fruit leather. Plan preserving capacity **before** the
  harvest.
- **Nut trees and allergies:** tree nuts are a major food allergen. If anyone in the household
  is allergic to tree nuts (→ 02-04), nut trees may not be worth planting at all; if they are
  planted, harvest, processing and storage happen away from that person's food, with dedicated
  tools.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** plant now along fences and in corners where they do not shade vegetable beds.
  Berries, rhubarb and asparagus give the best return on a small lot.
- **B (moving):** you cannot take a tree. You **can** take dormant cuttings, seed, and rhubarb or
  asparagus crowns wrapped damp.
- **C (establishing):** perennials pay off most here. Old farmsteads often hide apple, plum,
  mulberry and asparagus gone wild along fence lines. Inventory before you plant.
