# Growing indoors: microgreens and seed starting in winter

**What this page is for.** Fresh greens in the dead of winter from a windowsill, and starting
garden transplants indoors so the outdoor season produces more.

> **CAUTION: food safety.** **Sprouts and microgreens are not the same, and the risk is not the
> same.** **Sprouts** are germinated seeds eaten whole, grown warm and wet: the same conditions
> that grow *Salmonella* and *E. coli*, and sprouts have caused many documented outbreaks.
> **Microgreens** are seedlings grown in a growing mix and cut above the seed, which is much
> safer. For young children, the elderly, pregnant women and anyone sick or with weak immunity,
> **default to microgreens, or cook sprouts.**{{#if has.young_child}} This household has a child
> under 6.{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}} This household has an elder.{{/if}}{{#if has.pregnant}} This
> household has a pregnant member.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Buy microgreen seed by the pound, not the packet.** Sunflower, pea, radish and broccoli
   seed keep for years cool and dry, and a pound goes a long way.
2. **Grow one tray this week and eat it.** It takes 7 to 21 days from sowing to harvest (Penn
   State Extension, Growing Microgreens): cheap practice.
3. **Find your best south-facing window.** Winter sun through it is weak but free.
4. **Check seed against your household's food allergies** before you buy (→ 02-04). Soybean and
   sesame are common sprouting seeds and major allergens.

## Why / how it works

**What indoor growing is for.** It is **not** calories. A windowsill will never feed a family.
It delivers what stored food is worst at: **fresh vitamins and minerals, plus flavour and
morale, in midwinter** (→ 04-18).

### 1. Microgreens: the best return; master this one

Seedlings cut young, about 1½ to 3 inches tall, 7 to 21 days after sowing. Grown in a shallow
tray of potting mix, watered from below, cut above the soil with clean scissors (Penn State
Extension, Growing Microgreens).
- **Light:** a bright south window is enough for most; more light means less stretching. They
  need far less light than a full-grown plant, which is why this works with the grid down.
- **Yield:** a standard 10 × 20-inch tray gave about a third of a pound per crop in Penn State's
  trials, from about one tablespoon (10 to 15 grams) of seed.
- **Best crops:** sunflower (most bulk), pea shoots (sweet; children eat them), radish (fast,
  spicy), broccoli, kale, mustard, arugula, beet, cabbage.
- **Food safety:** wash hands before sowing and harvesting; clean trays and scissors; **cut above
  the seed and roots**.
- **Mould or roots?** Fine white root hairs are normal and disappear when sprayed with water.
  Real mould is grey or green, smells musty and spreads: that tray goes out. Prevent it with
  thinner sowing, air movement and less standing water.

### 2. Seed starting: the highest leverage

Every transplant you start indoors in late winter is a plant producing outdoors in summer. In
short-season climates (→ 05-01, your frost-free days: {{ region.home.growing_days }}), tomatoes,
peppers, cabbage-family crops and onions often **only** make a crop if started indoors.
- **Light is where people fail.** A window alone usually gives pale, stretched, weak seedlings.
  If you have any power (→ 09-02), a cheap LED shop light 2 to 4 inches above the plants for
  12 to 16 hours a day, with a dark period each night, is one of the best uses of stored power in
  late winter (University of Minnesota Extension, Starting Seeds Indoors).
- **Warm to sprout, cool to grow.** Most seeds want warm soil to sprout, then cooler, brighter
  conditions to grow stocky.
- **Damping off** (seedlings collapsing at the soil line) is a fungus of overwatered, still,
  dirty conditions. Prevent it with clean containers, fresh sterile mix, watering from below and
  **moving air**.
- **Harden off** over about two weeks before transplanting: a little more outdoor time each day
  (University of Minnesota Extension).
  Skip it and the first wind or sun kills them.

### 3. Full-grown food plants indoors: the weakest option

Herbs (basil, chives, parsley, mint), leaf lettuce and dwarf peppers can be kept alive indoors
all winter, with **slow growth, small yields and heavy light needs**. Herbs are worth it; they
transform stored food. A tomato crop in the living room in midwinter is not.

### Sprouts: read this before you do it

Sprouts need no soil and no light, which makes them tempting. If you sprout (→ 04-16): use seed
**sold for sprouting**, rinse at least twice a day, keep them well drained, chill them when done
if you can, and **cook them** for young children, elders, pregnant women and anyone sick or with
weak immunity. Cooking removes most of the risk.

**Never sprout or eat treated garden seed** (dyed pink, blue or green). It is coated with
pesticide and is not food (→ 05-03).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bulk microgreen seed (sunflower, pea, radish, broccoli) | Fresh greens all winter | Store cool, dry, dark (→ 05-03) |
| 10 × 20-inch trays, some with holes, some without | Grow tray plus a bottom-watering tray | Get more than you think; they crack |
| Clear domes | Sprouting | Or a second tray turned upside down |
| Potting mix or coir, several seasons | You cannot scavenge sterile mix | Same stock as → 05-10 |
| LED shop light and timer | What makes seed starting work | Runs from a modest solar setup (→ 09-02) |
| Seedling heat mat | Sprouting in a cold house | Low watts, high payoff |
| Small fan | Prevents damping off; stronger stems | Any USB fan |
| Spray bottle, fine-headed watering can | Seedlings drown easily | |
| Clean scissors | Harvest | Keep them for this job |
| Wire shelf unit | Three or four growing levels in a corner | |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Trays:** foil roasting pans, clear produce boxes, cut-down milk jugs, baking sheets lined with
  plastic.
- **Domes:** plastic wrap, a clear lid, a cut soda bottle.
- **Light:** the south window; a mirror or white board behind the tray nearly doubles the light;
  any 12-volt LED strip off a battery (→ 10-01).
- **Medium:** sifted compost, coir, or for microgreens a damp paper towel, burlap or felt mat
  (they live mostly on the seed's own reserves).
- **Heat:** the warmest room (→ 08-01), a jug of hot water under the tray.

## When it runs out

- **Seed** is the true consumable. Buy bulk now and rotate. Later, grow some plants out to seed
  to feed the tray (→ 05-03). Sunflowers are the easy one: they set huge amounts of seed.
- **Potting mix:** spent microgreen mix goes to compost (→ 05-11) and comes back as growing mix.
  Do not reuse a tray of mix without refreshing it; mould problems build up.
- **Light and power:** if power shrinks (→ 09-01), drop the full-grown plants first, keep **seed
  starting** (highest leverage) and **microgreens** (least light). Windowsill microgreens are
  the last fresh food you will have.
- **Warmth:** if the house is heated to one room (→ 08-01), the growing shelf lives in that room.
  Warm-season seeds stall in a cold room; plan the calendar around the room you can actually keep
  warm.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the winter fresh-food system: a wire shelf, a few trays on rotation, the south
  window. It also gives children something growing in winter (→ 21-02).
- **B (moving):** seed travels; trays do not. Carry microgreen seed.
- **C (establishing):** the same system, plus a real seed-starting setup for spring transplants.

pages.body:
# Trapping small game and pest animals

**What this page is for.** Why traps beat guns for small game in a long emergency, how to set
them where animals travel, and how to keep children, pets and yourself safe from the traps and
from the diseases wild animals carry.

> **SAFETY.** **Traps injure children and pets:** the trap does not know whose foot it has.
> **Wild rabbits and hares carry tularemia:** gloves, the spotted-liver check, cook to 160 °F
> (CDC; FoodSafety.gov). **Wild meat-eaters (bear, wild boar, fox; treat raccoon and opossum the
> same) can carry trichinosis:** cook every part right through, to at least 160 °F; freezing does
> not reliably make their meat safe (CDC). **Raccoon droppings carry a roundworm whose eggs can
> damage the brain and eyes, mostly in young children** (CDC): handle droppings, carcasses and gut
> piles as hazardous waste.

## Do this now

1. **Learn and practise now**, while a mistake costs nothing. Trap-setting has a real learning
   curve.
2. **Never set traps where children or pets go.** Map every set and show the household.
3. **Wear gloves when handling rabbits and hares, and check the liver** (below).
4. **Understand why it matters:** traps work **while you sleep and use no ammunition**
   (→ 14-08).

> **Before the collapse:** trapping is regulated by your state's wildlife agency: which species
> may be trapped (often only "furbearers" such as raccoon, opossum, muskrat and beaver; often
> **not** cottontail or squirrel), licences, trap types, tags and how often traps must be
> checked. Practise legally now, on the species your state allows. Keep the printed rules with
> your documents (→ 19-01). This never decides a survival procedure.

## Why / how it works

### Why trapping beats hunting for small game

| | Hunting | Trapping |
|---|---|---|
| **Ammunition** | Used per animal | **None** |
| **Your time** | Hours per attempt | Set once, check daily |
| **Works while** | You are there | You do other work, or sleep |
| **Scale** | One shooter, one place | Many sets, many places |
| **Noise** | Announces you (→ 14-03) | **Silent** |

In a long emergency where ammunition is finite, a trapline is the sustainable way to take small
game. A dozen sets checked each morning is a real food system.

### The rules that remain when nobody enforces any

- **Check every set every morning.** A late check means spoiled meat and a suffering animal.
- **Do not strip the ground you live on.** Heavy trapping near a town empties the local rabbit
  and squirrel population in one winter and leaves you with nothing in year two. Move the line
  and leave breeding stock.
- **Children and pets first** (below).
- **Only where you have a right to be.** A trapline on an armed neighbour's land is a security
  problem, not a food system (→ 14-03).

### Target species

Which animals are near you depends on your region; these are widespread.
- **Rabbits and hares:** the main small-game target. Cage traps and snares on their runs.
  **Gloves, the spotted-liver check, 160 °F.**
- **Squirrels:** common, even in town.
- **Raccoon, opossum:** edible **cooked right through, to at least 160 °F** (trichinosis, below). Also pests that
  raid stored food (→ 04-11). **Raccoon droppings and latrine sites are hazardous** (below).
- **Muskrat, beaver** where present: good meat, and **fat**, which matters (→ 04-12).
- **Rats and mice** around food storage: a different job, and always worth doing (→ 04-11).
- **Armadillo** (in the South): can carry the bacterium that causes leprosy (Hansen's disease).
  Gloves and thorough cooking, or leave them.

### Where to set: the actual skill

Trapping is reading animal behaviour, not buying traps.
- **Set on trails, runs and funnels:** fence lines, hedgerows, the edge of cover, under low
  branches, along water. Places animals already travel.
- **Look for sign:** droppings, tracks, chewed plants, worn paths in grass or snow.
- **Snow shows you exactly where animals move.**
- **Baited sets** draw animals in; **blind sets** sit on a trail with no bait.
- **Check every day.**

### Children and pets

- **Never set a trap where children play or pets roam.**
- **Map every set** and show every adult. An unmapped trap is a hazard you made and forgot.
- **Cage (live) traps are the safest** around a household: they hold without injury, and a pet
  can be released unharmed.
- **Body-grip traps** (which close on the body and kill quickly) **and foothold traps are
  indiscriminate**: never near a home with pets or small children.
- **Snares:** use ones with locks and stops that can be released; a snare that cannot be
  released cannot release a cat or dog.
- **Teach children the rule:** do not touch; come and tell an adult (→ 20-02). Whether older
  children help with trapping is part of the household's worksheet on children and dangerous
  jobs (→ 30-25): {{choice DC-24}}.
{{#if has.pets}}- **This household has pets** (→ 20-09). Cage traps only anywhere they can reach.{{/if}}

{{photo trap-map}}

### Handling and disease

- **Tularemia:** wild rabbits and hares carry it. **The field check:** a rabbit whose **liver
  shows many white spots about the size of a pinhead is thrown out whole**: bury it, wash up, eat
  none of it (Missouri Department of Conservation, Rabbit: Safety and Health). **Nitrile or latex
  gloves when dressing, no rubbing eyes or face, clean the knife**: the germ gets in through skin
  and eyes. Avoid animals that seemed sick or sluggish. **Cook to 160 °F** (FoodSafety.gov). Waiting
  for cold weather to trap rabbits reduces the risk but does not remove it (Missouri Department
  of Conservation; CDC, Tularemia Prevention). Flu-like illness after handling rabbits needs a
  doctor, while there is one: say "possible tularemia". (The same spotted liver in a
  **domestic** rabbit is coccidiosis, → 05-05.)
- **Bear, wild boar, fox and other wild meat-eaters: trichinosis** (CDC, Trichinellosis); treat
  raccoon and opossum the same way. FoodSafety.gov gives no separate figure for these animals:
  cook all of it right through, to at least the **160 °F** it gives for venison and rabbit. Do not
  rely on freezing, smoking, curing or drying: they do not reliably kill the worms in wild meat
  (CDC).
- **Raccoon roundworm (*Baylisascaris*):** eggs in raccoon droppings can damage the brain and
  eyes (blindness, coma); most infections are in young children who put dirt in their mouths
  (CDC).
  **Gloves; no children anywhere near carcasses, gut piles or raccoon latrines** (raccoons use
  the same toilet spots: flat roofs, woodpiles, the base of big trees, decks); **burn or
  deep-bury gut piles; never process near the kitchen; wash hands and tools** (→ 13-02).
- **Rabies:** raccoons, skunks, foxes and bats. **Never handle an animal that acts strangely.**
- **Fleas and ticks** leave a dead animal looking for a new host. Handle accordingly.

### The lean-meat caution again

Wild rabbit is **extremely lean** (→ 05-05). A diet that leans on it without fat causes protein
poisoning. **Pair trapped small game with stored fat** (→ 04-12).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Cage (live) traps**, several | Safest around children and pets | Also for pest control |
| Body-grip or foothold traps (if you trap furbearers) | Species-specific | Never near the house |
| **Snare cable or wire** with locks, stops and swivels | Light, cheap, effective | Releasable |
| Your state's trapping rules, printed | Pre-collapse practice; species biology outlasts the law | → 19-01 |
| **Nitrile gloves** by the box | Tularemia and general hygiene | Always |
| Stakes, wire, pliers, hatchet | Setting and anchoring | → 16-01 |
| Notebook and **map of sets** | Safety and daily checks | Non-negotiable with children |
| Instant-read thermometer | 160 °F | → 07-01 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Wire, cord and scrap** make snares and deadfalls: ancient technology that needs almost
  nothing.
- Cage traps can be built from wire mesh.
- **Mouse and rat traps** you already own protect stored food (→ 04-11).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** traps last; wire and cable are minor consumables. **One of the few food systems in
  this binder with almost no running cost.**
- **Ration:** move the trapline instead of over-trapping one area.
- **Resupply:** wire, cord and knowledge.
- **Why it matters:** as ammunition runs down (→ 14-08), trapping becomes **more** valuable, not
  less.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** in town, neighbours, pets and children limit this heavily. Pest control around
  stored food is always appropriate.
- **B (moving):** a few snares weigh nothing; set them at camp and check at dawn.
- **C (establishing):** a real trapline becomes practical, and may be the most sustainable meat
  source on rural land.

pages.body:
# Processing poultry and small game

**What this page is for.** Turning a chicken, a rabbit or a trapped animal into clean, safe meat:
the order of work, the hygiene that protects you, and how to handle it with children around.

> **SAFETY.** **Raw poultry carries *Salmonella* and *Campylobacter*.** Cross-contamination
> during processing is a real illness risk, and with no medical care a bad stomach illness in a
> baby, an elder or someone with a chronic condition is an emergency (→ 12-05). **Cook poultry to
> 165 °F and rabbit to 160 °F** (FoodSafety.gov). **A bird that died on its own is never food.**
> Work **outside**, keep it clean, and keep children away from raw carcasses and the water used.
> **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not canned**
> (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Process outdoors**, away from the kitchen, the garden and any stored water (→ 03-08).
2. **Set up before you start:** kill area, scald or skin area, gutting area, chilling container,
   in that order, so nothing moves backwards.
3. **Plenty of clean water.** This is a water-hungry job (→ 03-01).
4. **Gloves and dedicated tools.** Raw poultry never touches anything used for other food,
   especially any allergy-safe cookware (→ 02-04).
5. **Chill the carcass fast**, then preserve or cook.

## Why / how it works

### First rule: what is never food

**A bird that died on its own is never food**, and neither is any bird from a flock with sudden
multiple deaths, swollen heads or purple combs or wattles. Assume bird flu (→ 05-04; USDA APHIS,
Defend the Flock): gloves, a mask and eye protection, do not compost it, bury it deep, and process
nothing from that flock. While phones work, report sick or dying birds to your state veterinarian
or to USDA at 1-866-536-7593 (USDA APHIS).

At gutting, **a liver with lumps or spots of any size, or fluid in the body cavity, means that bird
is not used** (University of Minnesota Extension, Home Processing of Poultry).

### Poultry: the sequence

1. **Hold back feed** for several hours beforehand (water available). A full crop and gut make
   gutting messier and riskier.
2. **Kill quickly and humanely.** A killing cone (a funnel that holds the bird head-down) and a
   very sharp knife is the standard method. Speed and calm handling matter for welfare and for
   the meat.
3. **Bleed out** fully.
4. **Scald or skin.**
   - **Scalding** (a short dip in hot water, well below boiling) loosens feathers for plucking.
     Hold the bird by the feet, dip it head first and move it up and down and side to side.
     University of Minnesota Extension gives: **young birds 125 to 130 °F for 30 to 75 seconds;
     older birds near 140 °F for 30 to 75 seconds; ducks and geese 160 to 170 °F for 1 to
     2 minutes.** Check the water with a thermometer and keep a pot of boiling water nearby to
     top it up. The bird is ready when the tail and wing feathers pull out easily. Too hot tears
     the skin; too cool and the feathers hold. Pluck straight away.
   - **Skinning** is faster and needs no hot water. You lose the skin and some fat, but when fuel
     is short (→ 06-04) you avoid heating a big pot.
5. **Pluck** (if scalded): main feathers, then the small pin feathers.
6. **Gut it** ("eviscerate"): cut carefully around the vent (the rear opening), then remove the
   insides **without cutting the intestines or the gall bladder** (bile ruins meat). Save heart,
   liver and gizzard if you want them.
7. **Rinse and chill at once** in ice and water until the carcass is down to **40 °F**, then cold
   storage. Small birds take a couple of hours (University of Minnesota Extension).
8. **Rest** the carcass cold before cooking or preserving; a just-killed bird is tough.

### Rabbit: simpler

1. **Kill quickly and humanely.**
2. **Skin:** rabbit hide peels off readily.
3. **Gut it**, avoiding the bladder and intestines.
4. **Rinse, chill, rest.**
5. **Gloves, and check the liver before keeping the meat.** In a **wild** rabbit, **many
   pinhead-size white spots on the liver mean possible tularemia: throw out the whole animal,
   bury it, wash up, eat none of it** (Missouri Department of Conservation, Rabbit: Safety and
   Health; CDC; → 05-15). In a
   **domestic** rabbit the same spots are coccidiosis: the meat is fine cooked to 160 °F; throw
   out the liver (→ 05-05). No rubbing eyes or face while skinning; clean the knife after.

### Raccoon and opossum, if the trapline brings them

The same sequence as rabbit, with two hard rules (→ 05-15): **cook every part right through,
checked with a thermometer.** FoodSafety.gov gives no separate figure for raccoon or opossum; use
at least the 160 °F it gives for venison and rabbit. Freezing, curing, smoking and drying do not
reliably kill the trichinosis worms of wild meat-eaters (CDC, Trichinellosis). And treat raccoon
**droppings and fur as hazardous**: they carry a roundworm whose eggs can damage the brain and
eyes, mostly in young children who put dirt in their mouths (CDC, Baylisascaris). Gloves, no
children anywhere near the carcass or gut pile, burn or deep-bury the remains, never process near
the kitchen.

### Hygiene: the part that protects you

- **One-way workflow.** Dirty (kill, feathers, guts) → clean (rinse, chill). Never carry a clean
  carcass back through the dirty area.
- **Dedicated tools and surfaces** for raw poultry, never the ones used for allergy-safe food.
- **Wash hands** at every change of task (→ 13-02).
- **Get rid of guts and feathers properly:** bury deep away from water and the garden, or compost
  with care (→ 05-11). Left out, they draw predators, rats (→ 04-11) and attention (→ 14-03).
- **Clean and sanitise tools** after: hot soapy water, then a bleach solution if you have it (→ 29-05 for the mix).

### Preserving

- **Pressure canning** (→ 04-05): published procedures exist for poultry and rabbit (National
  Center for Home Food Preservation, Canning Meat, Poultry and Game). The best answer without
  refrigeration.
- **Winter cold** (→ 04-09), where it is reliably below freezing.
- **Broth from the carcass:** bones, feet and backs make nourishing stock on a fire that is
  already lit.
- **Fat:** poultry fat renders easily (→ 04-12), a real advantage of birds over lean rabbit.

### Children

If children helped care for the animals, they may have named them. Handle it deliberately:
- **Be honest and matter-of-fact.** Evasion often frightens children more than the truth.
- **Process out of sight** of small children; involve them in care and cooking, not slaughter.
- **Let them opt in later** as they grow. Whether and when older children take part is on the
  household's worksheet for children and dangerous jobs (→ 30-25): {{choice DC-24}}.
- **Do not force it**, and do not make a spectacle of it (→ 20-03, → 21-03).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Very sharp knives** and a steel or stone | Humane and safe | Sharp is safer (→ 16-02) |
| Killing cone | Control and humane killing | Can be made from sheet metal |
| Large pot for scalding, and a thermometer | Scalding | Skinning avoids this |
| **Nitrile gloves** by the box | Germ protection | Especially for rabbits |
| Dedicated cutting surface and tubs | One-way clean workflow | Cleanable |
| Cold water or ice bath | Fast chilling is a safety step | → 04-09 in winter |
| **Instant-read thermometer** | 165 °F poultry, 160 °F rabbit | → 07-01 |
| Soap, bleach, brushes | Sanitising | → 13-02 |
| Shovel | Burying remains, away from water | → 13-03 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- A traffic cone, a bucket with a hole cut in it, or a cord from a branch all work as restraints.
- **Skinning instead of scalding** saves fuel and equipment.
- Any large tub for chilling; clean snow works in winter.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the consumables are **gloves, soap and fuel** (for scalding and canning). Knives
  last.
- **Ration:** skin rather than scald to save fuel; process in batches so one setup serves several
  animals.
- **Resupply:** everything here can be improvised except sharp knives and cleanliness.
- **Why it matters:** processing skill turns livestock (→ 05-04, → 05-05) and traps (→ 05-15)
  into food. **Practise now**, on a bird or two, while hot water comes from a tap.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** neighbours, sight lines, smell and disposal all matter (→ 14-03). Work
  discreetly and clean up thoroughly.
- **B (moving):** you are not processing livestock on the road.
- **C (establishing):** set up a dedicated processing area away from the house and water.

# Wild edibles by season

**What this page is for.** **When** and **where** to look for wild food through the year, so you
can plan and preserve. It is a calendar, not a field guide: it cannot tell you **what** you found.
Read → 05-06 before you pick anything.

> **SAFETY.** **No wild plant or mushroom is eaten on a "test"; identification or nothing.**
> The deadly ones are not detectable by taste tests and the dose is small (→ 30-01). **Water
> hemlock, the most violently toxic plant in North America (USDA ARS), where a 2 to 3 cm piece of
> root can kill an adult (CDC MMWR, 1994), grows in wet ditches and low meadows in every region,
> and comes up in spring looking like a carrot-family green.** **Mushrooms are
> deliberately left off this page**: deadly look-alikes exist and printed text is not an adequate
> teacher.

## Do this now

1. **Map before you forage.** Walk your neighbourhood, trails, parks and field edges now, with
   fuel and time and no urgency, and mark on a paper map (→ 25-04) where the **mulberries, wild
   plums, serviceberries, crabapples, abandoned fruit trees and nut trees** are. Those are the
   calories.
2. **Buy one good field guide with photographs for your own region.** A national guide is a poor
   substitute.
3. **Learn three plants completely, not thirty badly.** Good first three in most of the US:
   **dandelion, mulberry, and one wild fruit common near you** (wild plum, blackberry or
   serviceberry).
4. **Learn water hemlock and poison hemlock cold** (→ 05-06). The plants that hurt you matter
   more than the ones that feed you.
5. **Look at your region's plates** (below) and at Section 32 for anywhere you might go.

## Why / how it works

**Set your expectations.** Wild plants are a **supplement**, not a food supply. Wild greens are
mostly water and vitamins; berries are seasonal and brief; the real wild calories are **animal**
(→ 05-07, → 05-08, → 05-15) and **starchy roots and nuts**, which take real work. Foraging's honest
role:
1. **Vitamins and variety** against a stored-food diet (→ 04-18).
2. **Seasonal bulk you can preserve:** fruit dried or made into leather (→ 04-06).
3. **Knowledge that scales** when you have more ground.

**Your green window at home** runs roughly from the last spring frost
(**{{ region.home.last_frost }}**) to the first fall frost (**{{ region.home.first_frost }}**):
about **{{ region.home.growing_days }} days**. The productive foraging season is shorter still: a
spring greens flush, an early-summer berry run, a late-summer fruit and nut glut. In cold regions,
**much of the year offers almost nothing wild and green**; that gap is closed by storing, not by
foraging. In mild-winter regions the greens season runs through the cool months and summer heat
is the lean time. **Plan the wild harvest around preserving it.**

### The calendar, by season

Dates shift with latitude, elevation and the year. Use your frost dates as the anchor and your
own notes as the truth. Not every plant grows in every region: check each against your region's
plates and your field guide.

**Early spring (the weeks around the last frost): the greens flush**
Wild greens are tender and worth eating for a short window; most turn bitter and tough once the
plant flowers.
- **Dandelion:** young leaves before flowering, roots, flower buds. Lawns everywhere. The easiest
  plant on this page: one yellow flower on each hollow, leafless stalk. Groundsel, the look-alike,
  has leafy, branching stems with many small flower heads (→ 05-06).
- **Stinging nettle:** cooked only (cooking removes the sting). Moist edges, ditches, old
  farmsteads. Gloves.
- **Lamb's quarters, purslane, plantain, violet, chickweed:** common yard and garden weeds into
  summer. **Lamb's quarters and amaranth build up nitrate and oxalate:** boil and throw out the
  water, eat them as part of a varied diet, skip plants from heavily manured or drought-stressed
  ground, and use the household's rule for young children (→ 05-06). **Purslane** has clear
  juice; spotted spurge, which grows in the same cracks, has milky sap and is not food.
- **Wild onion and wild garlic:** **every bulb must smell of onion, checked with clean hands**;
  death camas, fly poison, star-of-Bethlehem and daffodil have onion-like bulbs, no onion smell,
  and are poisonous (→ 05-06). Ramps grow only in parts of the East; a ramp look-alike in a shady yard is more
  likely lily-of-the-valley.
- **This is peak hemlock season.** Young carrot-family plants (a lacy leaf, a hollow stem, a wet
  spot) are where people die. If you cannot identify it beyond doubt, walk away.

**Late spring to early summer: early fruit, the last greens**
- **Mulberry:** planted and wild trees in towns across most of the country; heavy drops; nothing
  dangerous looks like a mulberry tree with mulberries on it. Dries well.
- **Serviceberry (Juneberry):** wild stands and ornamental plantings.
- **Wild strawberry; black and red raspberry; blackberry and dewberry** (thorny canes on edges
  and old fields).
- **Elderflower:** the bloom tells you where to come back for berries.
- Most greens are now bitter or gone to seed.

**Late summer to early fall: the glut, and the reason to have jars ready**
Almost everything worth preserving comes at once.
- **Wild plum:** thickets on fence lines and field edges. Excellent dried, as sauce or leather.
- **Chokecherry:** astringent raw; good cooked into syrup or jelly. **The pits contain
  cyanide-forming compounds: never crush or grind them.** Chokecherries hang in long strings;
  buckthorn berries, the look-alike, cluster tight against the twig.
- **Elderberry:** **cook them**; raw berries and all green parts cause vomiting. Pokeweed, whose
  berries hang in long strings on soft magenta stems, is poisonous (→ 05-06).
- **Crabapple, wild and abandoned apple and pear:** cook or dry.
- **Wild grape and muscadine:** **moonseed is the poisonous look-alike.** Grapes have tendrils
  and several small seeds; moonseed has no tendrils and one crescent-shaped seed: cut a fruit and
  look before eating any. Virginia creeper berries (five leaflets per leaf) are not grapes.
- **Pawpaw** (eastern woods): eat only ripe flesh; skin and seeds cause stomach upset; try a
  small amount first.
- **Sunflower, amaranth and lamb's-quarters seed:** real calories, tedious to process. **Rinse
  amaranth and lamb's-quarters seed well before using it as grain** (it carries soapy, bitter
  compounds called saponins).
- **Nuts: black walnut, hickory, hazelnut, acorns, pecan in the South.** **The wild calorie crop
  in much of the country.** Acorns need **leaching** (soaking out the bitter tannins): **cold-water
  leaching (repeated changes of water over several days) keeps the starch usable for flour;
  hot-water leaching is faster but cooks the starch, so the meal will not bind.** White-oak-group
  acorns (rounded leaf lobes) need far less leaching than red oaks (pointed lobes): start there.
  Black walnut hulls stain and irritate skin (wear gloves), and **water the hulls soaked in kills
  fish and garden plants**: dump it nowhere near a pond, rain barrel or bed. **Tree nuts are a
  major food allergen** (below).

**Fall into early winter (after the first frost): roots and the last fruit**
- **Burdock, Jerusalem artichoke, cattail roots:** starchy calories, dug.
  **Not wild parsnip, wild carrot or any carrot-family root. Ever.** A first-year parsnip or carrot
  rosette beside a young hemlock is exactly the fatal mistake, and wild parsnip sap burns skin.
  **Cattail grows in the same wet ground as water hemlock**, and its shoots resemble blue flag
  iris: harvest only from a stand identified by its brown spikes the previous summer (→ 05-06).
- **Rose hips:** best after the first frost; high in vitamin C; dry them for tea.
- **Persimmon** (South and East): wait until fully soft and wrinkled, usually after frost; unripe
  fruit is fiercely astringent.
- **Highbush cranberry, hackberry:** frost sweetens some fruit.
- **Nuts continue.** Squirrels are competition: be early.

**Winter: little or nothing in cold regions**
- **Rose hips still on the cane; hackberries on the tree; dried staghorn sumac heads** (red,
  upright, fuzzy cones; soaked for a sour vitamin-C drink). **Poison sumac has drooping white
  berries and grows in swamps.**
- **Inner bark** of pine and some other trees is last-resort survival food, not food.
- **In cold regions, winter is hunting, trapping, ice fishing and stored food** (→ 05-07,
  → 05-08, → 05-15). **Winter is the reason you preserve in late summer.**
- In mild-winter regions, cool-season greens (chickweed, dandelion, wild mustards) return through
  the winter.

### Your home region's plates

{{plates}}

The plates in this section are the edible plants recorded for your home region ({{ region.home.ecoregion }},
{{ region.home.state_name }}). Their deadly look-alikes are on → 05-06. **Every state's page in
Section 32 lists its ecoregions (→ 32-00), and the national plate pages carry every plate in the
binder: safe starters (→ 32-61) and deadly plants (→ 32-60).**

### The rules that keep you alive

1. **Identification or nothing.** Not "probably", not "it looks like the picture." Several
   matching features, the right habitat, the right season. No taste or edibility test
   (→ 30-01).
2. **Never eat from a carrot-family plant.**
3. **Never forage where you do not know the spray history.** Roadsides, rail lines, park edges,
   power-line corridors and lawns are often sprayed with weedkiller. Ditches collect road salt
   and runoff.
4. **One new food at a time, a small amount, one person, then wait and watch before eating
   more**, even when the plant is correctly identified: some people react to correctly identified
   wild plants.
5. **Cook what must be cooked:** nettle, elderberry, acorns. (Milkweed is deliberately left off:
   its look-alike, dogbane, is a heart poison, and printed features are not enough to tell them
   apart.)
6. **Food allergies:** wild food is unlabeled and any wild nut is a tree nut. Whether a
   food-allergic person eats it at all is the household's decision card (→ 30-19):
   {{choice DC-18}}. → 02-04.
7. **Children eat only what an adult hands them.** A toddler will eat berries off a bush because
   they saw you do it.
8. **Pets too:** several wild plants are toxic to cats and dogs, and pets chew greens (→ 20-09).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Field guide with **photographs**, for your region | The only thing that makes foraging safe | Paper, not an app |
| Paper map of your area | Mark fruit trees, thickets, nut trees now | → 25-04 |
| Baskets, buckets, mesh bags | Berries crush in a plastic sack | Rigid containers for fruit |
| Pruners and a small folding saw | Harvesting high fruit | Same tools as → 05-13 |
| Digging fork or a sturdy digging knife | Roots | |
| Heavy gloves | Nettle, thorns, poison ivy, walnut hulls | |
| Drying racks or a dehydrator | The glut arrives in a few weeks | → 04-06 |
| Jars and lids | Preserving capacity **before** the harvest | → 04-04 |
| Nut cracker or a board-and-hammer setup | Black walnuts and hickories | |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Containers:** any bucket, pillowcase, cut jug, or a jacket tied off at the sleeves.
- **Drying:** window screens on blocks, a car dashboard in late summer, a line in a hot attic.
- **Acorn processing:** a bucket and many changes of water; grind with two stones, a hand mill or
  a meat grinder.
- **What you cannot substitute:** the field guide and the identification skill.

## When it runs out

Wild food does not run out so much as **arrive and vanish**. The failure is being unready during
the short window when a plant is ripe.
- **Runway:** almost none without preserving. A plum thicket is ripe for days, not weeks. **Preserving
  capacity is the limit, not the plants.**
- **Competition:** in a long emergency every wild food near town is stripped fast, by people and
  by deer, birds and raccoons. **Town fruit trees will be picked clean in the first season.**
- **Substitute:** **planted perennials** (→ 05-13): the same fruit, on ground you control.
  Foraging carries the first season; planting carries the years after.
- **The skill does not deplete.** Everything you learn to identify this year, you know for good.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** towns are full of planted mulberry, crabapple, serviceberry and abandoned
  fruit trees. Expect competition in a real event.
- **B (moving):** foraging on the move is a snack, not a meal plan. Do not detour for wild food,
  and do not eat anything unverified while tired and hungry: that is when people make fatal
  mistakes.
- **C (establishing):** more ground and less competition. **Walk the property in each season of
  the first year** and write down what grows where; the destination's plates are in Section 32
  and its hazards on → 05-19.

pages.body:
# Garden calendar for each destination

**What this page is for.** A destination can sit in a different climate from home, and then the
home calendar (→ 05-01) is wrong there. This page sets out each destination's season next to
home's, what changes, and what to do before you ever need it. The crop rankings and methods on
→ 05-01 still apply everywhere.

## Do this now

1. **Compare each destination's season with home's** (table below). A difference of more than a
   few weeks changes what you plant and when.
2. **Get the destination state's Extension planting chart, print it, and keep it with the
   destination's papers** (→ 19-01). It is the local authority.
3. **Place a duplicate seed stock at each agreed destination** (→ 05-03), sealed with
   desiccant, with the owner's permission. Seed already there is a garden that starts the day
   you arrive.
4. **Buy varieties suited to each destination's band** and store them with that cache.
5. **Get a soil test at the destination** on an ordinary visit (→ 05-11).

## Why / how it works

### Home and each destination, side by side

| Place | Zone | Last spring frost | First fall frost | Frost-free days | Precipitation | January low | July high |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Home** ({{ region.home.county }}, {{ region.home.state_name }}) | {{ region.home.zone }} | {{ region.home.last_frost }} | {{ region.home.first_frost }} | {{ region.home.growing_days }} | {{ region.home.precip_in }} in | {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F | {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F |
{{#each destinations as x}}| **{{x.name}}** ({{x.county}}, {{x.state_name}}) | {{x.region.zone}} | {{x.region.last_frost}} | {{x.region.first_frost}} | {{x.region.growing_days}} | {{x.region.precip_in}} in | {{x.region.jan_low_f}} °F | {{x.region.jul_high_f}} °F |
{{else}}| **No destinations entered** | | | | | | | |
{{/each}}

Find each destination's zone in the bands on → 05-01. A longer season usually means a **second
full planting** (a fall garden), earlier potatoes, and crops that do not ripen at home. A wetter
place swaps drought for **fungal disease and waterlogged ground**. A colder or higher place
shortens everything and makes season extension (→ 05-02) essential.

### Each destination's calendar

Fill this in from the destination state's Extension chart on an ordinary visit, then trust a soil
thermometer over the calendar. The anchor dates are printed for you.

{{#each destinations as x}}
#### {{x.name}} ({{x.status_text}})

Zone **{{x.region.zone}}**. Median last spring frost **{{x.region.last_frost}}**; median first
fall frost **{{x.region.first_frost}}**; about **{{x.region.growing_days}} frost-free days**;
about **{{x.region.precip_in}} inches** of precipitation a year.

| When | What to plant there |
|---|---|
| 5 to 15 weeks before transplanting (→ 05-01) | Start onions, cabbage family, peppers, tomatoes indoors: ______________________ |
| Before {{x.region.last_frost}}, soil 40 to 50 °F | Cool-season crops outside (potatoes, peas, onions, greens, roots): ______________________ |
| After {{x.region.last_frost}}, nights warm | Warm-season crops (beans, corn, squash, tomatoes, peppers; sweet potatoes in long seasons): ______________________ |
| Midsummer | Second warm-season planting, if the season allows: ______________________ |
| Late summer, counting back from {{x.region.first_frost}} | **The fall garden:** cabbage family, greens, roots, fall potatoes in long seasons: ______________________ |
| Around {{x.region.first_frost}} | Garlic; hardy greens under row cover to overwinter (→ 05-02): ______________________ |
| Winter | Harvest stored roots and covered greens: ______________________ |

Verified against the Extension chart on (date): __________ by: __________

Seed cache placed there? ____ (date: ______) Where exactly: ______________________
Soil test done? ____ pH: ______ Lime or other amendment needed: ______________________

{{else}}
No destinations are entered. Add them in settings, or plan from the home calendar (→ 05-01,
→ 25-01).
{{/each}}

### What usually changes in a longer, warmer season

- **Plantings per year:** two full gardens, spring and fall, instead of one. Potatoes twice: an
  early spring planting dug before summer heat, a midsummer planting dug in fall. The
  destination state's Extension chart gives the dates.
- **The fall planting is often the better one:** fewer insects, milder finish, greens sweetened
  by light frost.
- **Overwintering:** spinach, kale, collards and garlic planted in fall feed you through a mild
  winter under cover.
- **Variety choice:** the short-season problem becomes a **heat and disease** problem. Choose
  heat-setting, disease-resistant tomatoes; early northern types stop setting fruit in a hot
  summer.
- **Crops worth adding:** sweet potatoes (a top survival calorie crop where the season allows),
  okra, southern peas (cowpeas).
- **Plan seed for two plantings**, not one: more of the succession crops in that cache.

### What usually changes in a wetter climate

- **Watering mostly disappears** as a chore; watering new transplants and trees still matters.
- **Fungal disease replaces drought as the main plant killer:** blights, mildews and rots thrive
  in humidity. The answers: **wide spacing, morning sun, water the soil not the leaves, mulch to
  stop soil splashing onto leaves, resistant varieties, and prompt removal of diseased leaves**
  (→ 05-12's no-chemical ladder).
- **Raised beds** on wet clay ground: waterlogged roots rot.
- **Soil is often acidic** in wet, wooded regions: test before adding lime or wood ash; over-liming
  locks up nutrients as surely as acid does (→ 05-11).

### What usually changes in a shorter, colder season

- One planting, short-season varieties, transplants started indoors (→ 05-14).
- Season extension at both ends (→ 05-02) and storage crops that keep through winter.
- Perennials rated for that destination's zone or colder (→ 05-13).

### Fruit at a destination

If a destination is agreed and the owner welcomes it, **plant fruit trees there now**: a tree
planted this year bears before you might need it. Choose for that destination's zone (→ 05-13).
If anyone in the household is allergic to tree nuts, plant fruit, not nut trees.

## Gear / items

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Duplicate seed cache at each agreed destination** | The garden starts on arrival | Sealed, with desiccant (→ 05-03) |
| Varieties suited to that destination's band | The home list may be wrong there | Open-pollinated where possible |
| **The destination state's printed Extension chart** | The local calendar | → 19-01 |
| Raised-bed materials or a plan | Drainage on wet ground | Untreated wood for food beds |
| Row cover | Frost edges and overwintering | Same stock as → 05-02 |
| Soil test | Know the starting point | First visit |

**Scavenge or substitute:** the host's existing tools, hoses and outbuildings: inventory before
buying duplicates. Leaves and wood chips on wooded land are endless mulch and compost carbon.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** a garden is a seasonal flow wherever it is. A longer season shortens the gap stored
  food must bridge; a shorter one lengthens it.
- **Resupply:** seed saving (→ 05-03) often works better in a longer season, where biennials and
  late crops ripen seed reliably.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** buy the destination-band seed, place the caches, and verify frost dates and
  soil while travel is easy.
- **B (moving):** with caches in place, you carry nothing extra for the garden.
- **C (at a destination):** run that destination's calendar, not home's. First season: beds near
  the house, potatoes and beans first, and a fall garden the same year if the season allows.

pages.body:
# Foraging and field hazards at each destination

**What this page is for.** What is different about wild food and outdoor hazards at each place
this household might go: the plants, the snakes, the ticks, and the allergy risks that lie on the
ground. Everything on → 05-06 (killers first, identification or nothing, no mushrooms) applies in
full. This page adds what changes when the ground is new to you.

> **SAFETY.** **No wild plant or mushroom is eaten on a "test"; identification or nothing.**
> The deadly ones are not detectable by taste tests and the dose is small (→ 30-01). **Snakebite:
> do not cut the wound, suck the venom, apply a tourniquet or ice, or give alcohol; keep the
> person still and get them to medical care, because antivenom is the treatment and only
> hospitals have it** (CDC/NIOSH, Venomous Snakes). **A fever or rash in the weeks after a tick
> bite is a tick-borne disease until proven otherwise** (CDC, What to Do After a Tick Bite;
> CDC, Ehrlichiosis).

## Do this now

1. **Look at each destination's plates** (below, and that state's page in Section 32, → 32-00)
   before your next visit: the deadly plants first, then the edibles.
2. **Find out which venomous snakes live at each destination** (the state Extension service
   publishes a guide) and write them in the table below.
3. **Treat outdoor clothing with permethrin** before tick season, and pack fine-tipped tweezers in
   every kit (below).
4. **Write down the nearest hospital** to each destination that can treat snakebite and severe
   allergic reactions (→ 25-03, → 01-07).
5. **Set the household's ground rules for children and food allergies** before the first walk,
   and brief every adult who will watch the children there, including the hosts.

## Why / how it works

### Each destination at a glance

| Destination | Ecoregion | Zone | July high | Annual precipitation | Plates |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each destinations as x}}| **{{x.name}}** ({{x.county}}, {{x.state_name}}) | {{x.region.ecoregion}} | {{x.region.zone}} | {{x.region.jul_high_f}} °F | {{x.region.precip_in}} in | Below; {{x.state_name}} page in Section 32 |
{{else}}| **No destinations entered** | | | | | |
{{/each}}

{{#each destinations as x}}
#### {{x.name}}

- Venomous snakes there: ______________________ (from the state Extension snake guide)
- Ticks there, and the diseases they carry: ______________________
- Poison ivy, oak or sumac there: ______________________
- Wild foods worth learning there (from the plates below): ______________________
- Nut trees on or near the property (hickory, walnut, oak, pecan): ______________________
- Nearest hospital for snakebite and anaphylaxis, and drive time: ______________________
- Checked on (date): __________

Plates recorded for {{x.name}}:

{{plates}}

{{/each}}

### Nuts underfoot and food allergies

Much of the country, especially wooded land in the East and South, drops **hickory nuts, walnuts,
pecans and acorns** every fall. Hickory nuts, walnuts and pecans are **tree nuts**, a major food
allergen. At a wooded destination the allergen is not in a labelled package; it is **on the
ground, at a small child's height**, disguised as the easiest food on the property.

If anyone in the household has a tree-nut allergy (→ 02-04, → 02-03):
1. **No ground-snacking.** Nothing picked up from the ground or off a plant goes in any child's
   mouth.
2. **Adults check everything.** Any wild or gathered food is identified, checked against the
   allergy list and handed over by an adult.
3. **Nut processing happens away from the allergic person entirely**, with dedicated tools,
   washed hands and the debris cleaned up. Consider not gathering nuts at all.
4. **Epinephrine goes on every walk** if it has been prescribed (→ 02-03).
5. **Fall is the danger season:** the ground is thickest with nuts when everyone is outside.

Whether a food-allergic person eats any wild, gathered or traded food is the household's decision
card (→ 30-19): {{choice DC-18}}.

### Mushrooms: the honest rule, again

**Do not forage mushrooms in a survival situation** (→ 05-06). Some regions make the temptation
worse because **morels** are famous and locally plentiful in spring. If anyone hunts them in normal
times, with an expert, know the killers:
- **False morels** look wrinkled or brain-like rather than honeycomb-pitted, and are chambered or
  stuffed inside rather than hollow. They **can be deadly.** A true morel is **hollow from cap tip
  to stem base**, with the cap joined to the stem.
- **Destroying angels:** clean, all-white gilled mushrooms of the woods. **Symptoms are delayed,
  seem to improve, then the liver fails.** This is why "a white mushroom in the woods" is never
  food.
- **Chanterelle versus jack-o'-lantern:** jack-o'-lanterns (violently sickening) grow in clusters
  on wood and have true gills.

**In a crisis: no mushrooms.** Nothing about a crisis makes the odds better.

### Venomous snakes

The venomous snakes of the US are the **pit vipers** (rattlesnakes, copperheads and cottonmouths)
and the **coral snakes** of the South (CDC/NIOSH, Venomous Snakes). Which ones live where varies by
state; write yours in the destination notes above.

| Snake | What to look for | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Copperhead** | Coppery-tan with **hourglass-shaped crossbands** seen from the side; superbly camouflaged in leaf litter | Woods in the East and South |
| **Rattlesnakes** | Heavy body, blotches or chevrons, a **rattle** on the tail; usually rattles, not always | Many species across the country |
| **Cottonmouth (water moccasin)** | Heavy, dark, blocky head; threatened, it holds its ground and gapes a **white mouth**. Harmless water snakes look similar: treat every snake at the water's edge as venomous | Streams, ponds and swamps in the South and Southeast |
| **Coral snake** | Red, yellow and black rings | Southern states |

**Avoidance is nearly everything:** boots and long trousers off mowed ground; **never put hands
or feet where you cannot see** (woodpiles, rock ledges, stepping over logs); a light at night in
warm months; children on cleared paths; leave every snake alone. **Never handle a venomous
snake, not even a dead one or its cut-off head, and never try to pick one up or trap it**
(CDC/NIOSH, Venomous Snakes). Clear brush, rock piles and lumber near the house and play areas.
Look before you step down a bank or reach into brush at the water's edge (→ 05-08).

**Snakebite response (CDC/NIOSH):**
1. **Move away from the snake.** No second bite, no revenge hunt; do not pick it up or trap it,
   even dead.
2. **Do NOT cut the wound, suck the venom (no suction kits), apply a tourniquet, ice or electric
   shock, or soak the wound in water.** No alcohol, and no aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen for the
   pain.
3. **Remove rings, watches and tight clothing** near the bite before swelling starts.
4. **Keep the person calm and still**, lying or sitting with the bite in a comfortable, neutral
   position. Wash the bite with soap and water and cover it with a clean, dry dressing.
5. **Get to medical care at once; do not wait for symptoms. Antivenom is the treatment and only
   hospitals have it.** The bitten person does not drive. Mark the edge of the tenderness or
   swelling on the skin with a pen and write the time beside it; repeat as it spreads.
6. **If care truly cannot be reached:** rest, fluids, wound care and watching for infection
   (→ 12-04) are what you have. That is why **avoidance is the real medical plan.**

### Ticks

Ticks carry several serious diseases, and some regions have very heavy tick loads (the lone star
tick across the South and East above all). Two to know by name:
- **Alpha-gal syndrome:** a lone star tick bite can cause an **allergy to red meat** (beef, pork,
  venison, rabbit and other mammals), with reactions **usually 2 to 6 hours** after eating red
  meat or dairy: hives, stomach symptoms, up to anaphylaxis (CDC, Alpha-gal Syndrome; CDC,
  Symptoms of Alpha-gal Syndrome). For a household whose protein
  plan is game and livestock, this is a serious threat.
- **Ehrlichiosis:** **fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, sometimes an upset stomach, 1 to
  2 weeks after a bite.** It can become severe; **doxycycline is the treatment** (CDC,
  Ehrlichiosis; → 12-04).

**The routine (CDC, Preventing Tick Bites):**
- **Permethrin on clothing and boots** (0.5 % clothing treatment, sprayed on fabric and dried
  before wearing; **never on skin**). **Wet permethrin is highly toxic to cats**: keep cats away
  until it is dry (→ 20-09). Retreat as the label says. An EPA-registered repellent (DEET or
  picaridin) on skin.
- **Trousers tucked into socks; light-coloured clothes; stay in the middle of paths.**
- **Daily full-body tick checks on everyone** after any time outdoors. Children at bath time:
  hairline, ears, waistband, groin, behind the knees. Check pets too.
- **Removal: clean, fine-tipped tweezers, grip as close to the skin as possible, pull straight
  out with steady, even pressure.** No twisting or jerking; no petroleum jelly, heat or nail
  polish. Wash the site and your hands; write the date down and watch for fever or rash for
  several weeks (CDC, What to Do After a Tick Bite).
- **Dry clothes into a dryer on high heat for 10 minutes** after field days kills ticks that
  rode home (CDC, Preventing Tick Bites).

{{figure fig-tick-removal}}

### Chiggers and poison ivy

- **Chiggers:** tiny mites in brush and tall grass that leave intensely itchy welts at the
  waistband and sock line. Permethrin-treated clothing helps; a soapy shower soon after exposure
  helps. The risk is scratched-open skin getting infected (→ 12-04).
- **Poison ivy** is far heavier in some regions, including **thick, hairy climbing vines** on the
  trees you would cut for firewood. Three leaflets; leafless winter vines still carry the oil;
  **never burn it** (the smoke injures lungs, → 17-05). Wash skin, tools and clothes after
  clearing; pets carry the oil on fur.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Permethrin clothing treatment (0.5 %)** | Ticks and chiggers | Dry fully before wearing; toxic to cats when wet |
| Fine-tipped tweezers, several | Correct tick removal | One in every kit (→ 12-01) |
| DEET or picaridin repellent | Skin-side protection | Stock several seasons |
| Snake boots or tall leather boots, long trousers | Snake country | For brush work especially |
| **Field guides with photographs for each destination's region** | The two-source rule (→ 05-06) | |
| **Epinephrine on every walk**, if prescribed | Allergies | → 02-03 |
| This page, filled in, with each destination's papers | The response is knowledge, not gear | |
| Strong soap | Removing poison ivy oil | Soap and cold water work if prompt |

**Scavenge or substitute:** the hosts and neighbours at a destination know its snake spots, tick
seasons and berry patches. **Local knowledge is the best field guide** (→ 18-03).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** permethrin and repellent are consumables. Stock several seasons; clothing treatment
  goes furthest.
- **Ration:** when repellent is gone, clothing discipline, path discipline and daily checks do
  most of the work, and cost nothing.
- **There is no substitute for antivenom.** Avoidance is the plan.

## Phase notes

- **B (moving):** the tick routine applies from the moment you leave the vehicle on any leg
  through tick country; treat travel clothes before you leave.
- **C (at a destination):** set the children's and allergy ground rules the first day; clear brush
  and rock near the house the first week; start the tick-check routine the first night.

pages.body:
# Fire and fuel

**What this section holds.** 9 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 06-01 **Starting fire reliably (multiple methods)**: Without power, fire cooks food, makes water safe and keeps people warm.
- → 06-02 **Sustaining and banking a fire**: A fire you keep going is worth far more than one you relight.
- → 06-03 **Firewood: species, cords, seasoning, splitting**: Firewood is only fuel if it is dry, and only enough if you measure it honestly.
- → 06-04 **When the wood runs out (burn rate and sourcing)**: A woodpile that lasts a whole winter of evening fires can be gone in weeks once it is the only way to cook and boil water every day.
- → 06-05 **Alternative fuels (propane, charcoal, kerosene, biomass)**: Wood is the long-term fuel, but it is slow and needs seasoning.
- → 06-06 **Storing fuel safely (gasoline, propane, kerosene)**: Stored fuel is the most dangerous thing in a prepared house.
- → 06-07 **Moving and transferring fuel (siphoning)**: Pouring, pumping and siphoning fuel is when it hurts people.
- → 06-08 **Carrying fuel on the road (cans, propane, trailers)**: If the household has to drive somewhere far away with no working fuel stations, it may carry extra fuel.
- → 06-09 **Chimneys and creosote (inspection, sweeping, chimney fire)**: A fireplace or wood stove used every day all winter builds tar in its chimney faster than anything else.

pages.body:
# Starting fire reliably (multiple methods)

**What this page is for.** Without power, fire cooks food, makes water safe and keeps people
warm. It is also the fastest way to lose a house. This page covers when not to light a fire,
how to build one that catches the first time, and which ways of lighting it still work when it
is cold and wet.

> **CAUTION.** **Never burn treated, painted or pressure-treated wood, plywood, particleboard,
> plastics or trash**: the smoke is toxic (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices). Inside the house, fire for heat or
> cooking belongs only in an installed, vented fireplace or wood stove, because every flame
> makes carbon monoxide (CO), a gas you cannot see or smell (CDC; → 29-03). **Never use
> gasoline to start or restart a fire** (CPSC; → 29-01). **Fuel is never stored or transferred
> near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour ignition. **Children do not have access
> to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in every source. Lighters and
> matches count as fuel here.

## Do this now

1. **Keep three different ways to light a fire, in three places**: lighters, storm-proof
   matches, and a ferrocerium rod (below).
2. **Keep manufactured tinder** (fire-starter cubes or similar). It works wet, cold and
   one-handed, which is exactly when you need it.
3. **Practise once in bad weather now.** Lighting a fire with numb hands in freezing wind is a
   different skill from lighting one in the yard in summer.
4. **Keep dry kindling inside**, under cover, before every storm.
5. **Clear the spot**: nothing that burns within a few feet, and water or an extinguisher
   beside you (→ 29-12).

{{photo ignition-kits}}

## The gate: when not to light an outdoor fire

Knowing how to light a fire includes knowing when the answer is no. Run these checks before
any open fire outdoors.

| Check | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Burn ban?** | Counties and states ban open burning in dry spells because the grass and brush really will carry fire. Under a ban: contained appliances only (a camp stove outdoors), no open flame. The reason holds whether or not anyone enforces it |
| **Red Flag Warning?** | The National Weather Service's warning for **critical fire weather: strong wind plus very low humidity over dry fuels** (the glossary's example criteria: sustained wind of 15 mph or more and humidity of 25 percent or less, after a dry spell). Criteria vary by state and office (NWS Glossary, Red Flag Warning). **On a Red Flag day, no open fire**, no ash dumping outside and no spark-making work outdoors (→ 17-05) |
| **Wind right now?** | Wind carries embers past any fire ring you control. Pick a wind limit before you need it, lower than the conditions that bring a Red Flag Warning, and write it here: no open fire above ______ mph |
| **Dry-fuel season?** | Any time the grass is brown and cured, and any drought. Treat every other check one step more cautiously |

{{#if is.wildfire_region}}Your home county is rated for wildfire risk. Treat dry, windy days as
no-fire days by default (→ 17-14).{{/if}}{{#if is.drought_region}} Your home county is rated for
drought; dry spells can last for months.{{/if}}

> **Before the collapse:** burn bans for {{ home.county }} are issued by the county or state.
> Check the current status while there is someone to issue it.

**How you hear it with no internet.** Red Flag Warnings and fire-weather watches come over a
NOAA Weather Radio (→ 15-01, → 29-09). When no warning service exists, the wind check and the
season check still work: **you can always feel the wind and look at the grass** (→ 17-10).

## Why fires fail

A fire needs fuel, heat and air. Fires almost always fail for one of three ordinary reasons:
**wet fuel**, **too big too fast**, or **not enough air**. Build small, build dry, leave gaps.

## The fuel ladder: the part beginners skip

You need **four sizes**, all ready **before** you strike anything:

1. **Tinder** catches a spark: a cotton ball smeared with petroleum jelly, birch bark, dryer
   lint, fatwood shavings, char cloth, a commercial fire starter.
2. **Kindling**: from pencil-lead to pencil thickness. Dry twigs, thin split shavings.
3. **Small fuel**: finger to wrist thickness.
4. **Fuel wood**: the real logs (→ 06-03).

**Have three times more kindling than you think you need.** Running back for more while a weak
flame dies is the most common failure.

{{figure fig-fuel-ladder}}

## Ways to light it, ranked for reliability

| Method | Reliability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Butane lighter** | High, when warm | **Fails in the cold**: butane boils at 31 °F, so below freezing it barely turns to gas (NIOSH Pocket Guide, n-Butane). Keep one in an inside pocket against your body |
| **Storm-proof or waterproof matches** | High | Work cold and wet; there are only so many. Keep them in a waterproof case with the striker |
| **Ferrocerium ("ferro") rod** | Very high | A metal rod that throws hot sparks when scraped. Works wet and cold, for a great many strikes. **Needs good tinder** and practice |
| **Magnifying lens** | Depends on weather | Free and unlimited, but needs bright sun, which winter often does not give |
| **Battery and steel wool** | Good improvised method | A 9-volt battery touched to fine steel wool lights it at once. **Store them apart**: together in a drawer they are a fire hazard |
| **Bow drill or other friction** | Low | Hard, especially in damp cold. Learn it; do not rely on it |

**The cold-weather lesson:** a lighter kept in your pocket works; a lighter left in a cold shed
often will not. Keep ignition warm and dry, on your body.

## Building it: a method that works in the wet

1. **Platform.** Lay split wood or bark so the tinder is not on cold, wet ground or snow.
2. **Windbreak.** Your body, a wall of split wood, or the fireplace itself.
3. **Tinder bundle** on the platform.
4. **Kindling** over it in a teepee or lean-to, with air gaps.
5. **Light the tinder low, on the side the wind is coming from**, and shield it.
6. **Feed small first.** Add bigger pieces only once the flame is steady.
7. **Do not smother it.** Most dying fires need air and patience, not more wood.

**In snow or rain**, the platform matters more than anything else. A fire on snow melts itself
out. Build up, not down.

## Tinder you can make or find

- **Cotton balls and petroleum jelly** in a pill bottle: cheap, nearly waterproof, burn for
  minutes.
- **Fatwood**: resin-rich pine. Lights when damp and shaves easily.
- **Birch bark**: burns even when wet.
- **Dryer lint** from natural fibres, **char cloth**, waxed cardboard, egg-carton-and-wax pucks.
- **Cattail fluff, dry grass, milkweed down** where they grow.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lighters, a bag of them | Easiest method; cheap; good barter | Keep some on your body in winter |
| Storm-proof matches and a waterproof case | Work when lighters fail | Include the striker |
| Large ferrocerium rod and striker | A great many lights | Practise **before** you need it |
| Commercial tinder or fire-starter cubes | Work wet, cold, one-handed | Cheap; keep plenty |
| Fatwood | Natural, keeps indefinitely, lights damp | |
| Dry kindling stored inside | The real bottleneck | Restock before every storm |
| Hatchet and knife | Dry wood is **inside** wet wood: split it to reach it | → 16-01, → 16-02 |
| Fire extinguisher and a bucket of water | Things go wrong | Beside the fire, not behind it (→ 29-12) |
| Metal ash bucket with a lid | **Hot ashes start house fires.** USFA: metal container with a lid, outside, at least 10 feet from the house | Never a cardboard box or plastic bin (→ 06-02) |

**If you do not have it:**

- A 9-volt battery and steel wool is the best improvised way to light a fire in a house.
- Petroleum jelly, lip balm, candle wax and cooking oil all help weak tinder burn longer.
- Paper, cardboard and untreated wood scraps are everywhere in town (→ 06-04).
- **Never gasoline.** It flashes, explodes and kills people every year (CPSC; → 29-01).

## When it runs out

- **Count** lighters and matches. A ferro rod lasts for a great many strikes, which is why it
  belongs in every kit: it turns something you use up into something that lasts.
- **Use one lighter until it is empty** rather than starting several.
- **Keep a fire going rather than relighting it** (→ 06-02). Banked coals save lighters,
  matches and kindling all at once.
- Lighters and matches are common things to scavenge and good to barter (→ 18-02).

## Fire indoors

A fireplace or wood stove is the only indoor place for a wood fire. Before the first fire of
the season, check the chimney (→ 06-09). Using one that has not been inspected this year is a
trade-off: {{choice DC-21}} → 30-22. Candles and open-flame cooking indoors are a separate
trade-off: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21. Keep battery CO alarms on every level and where people
sleep, as the floors page says (→ 30-01, → 08-02).

## Children and fire

{{#if has.young_child}}There is a child under 6 in this household. Lighters, matches and
ferro rods stay locked or out of reach, and a marked line around any fire is a household rule
for everyone (→ 20-02).{{else}}Lighters and matches stay out of reach of any visiting children,
and a marked line around any fire keeps everyone back (→ 20-02).{{/if}} Whether older children
light or tend fires is the household's call: {{choice DC-24}} → 30-25.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if has.outdoor_fire}}your outdoor fireplace or fire pit is
  your cooking and boiling fire (→ 07-01).{{else}}a fire-pit ring, a rocket stove (→ 07-02) or
  a camp stove outdoors (→ 07-05) does the cooking.{{/if}}{{#if has.fireplace}} The indoor
  fireplace is for heat once the chimney is checked (→ 06-09).{{/if}}{{#if has.wood_stove}} The
  wood stove is for heat once the chimney is checked (→ 06-09, → 08-08).{{/if}} Keep kindling
  and ignition indoors and dry, and one set in each go-bag (→ 22-03).
- **B (on the move):** ignition on your body, tinder in a pocket, a ferro rod as backup.
  Practise with gloves on.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** more natural tinder and wood, often harsher weather. A
  reliable ignition kit is a survival item.

pages.body:
# Sustaining and banking a fire

**What this page is for.** A fire you keep going is worth far more than one you relight. It
saves matches, lighters, kindling and time. This page covers how to keep a fire steady, how to
"bank" it so it survives the night, where the wood's heat actually goes, and what to do with
the ashes.

> **CAUTION.** **Ashes stay hot long after the fire looks dead.** Ash carried out in a paper
> bag or a plastic bin is a classic cause of house fires. **Metal container with a lid, outside,
> at least 10 feet from the house, every time** (USFA, Fireplace and Wood Stove Safety). **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine
> products.** Fixed in every source. Keep an extinguisher or water within reach of every fire
> (→ 29-12).

## Do this now

1. **Bank the fire overnight** instead of letting it die: rake the coals together, cover the
   edges with ash, add a large log. In the morning the coals relight with kindling and no
   match.
2. **Burn dry, seasoned wood only.** Wet wood wastes its energy boiling off its own water and
   builds creosote in the chimney (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices; CSIA; → 06-09).
3. **One fire, many jobs.** Cook, boil water, heat stones, dry clothes and melt snow in the
   same burn (→ 06-04).
4. **Ashes into a metal bucket with a lid.** Never paper, never plastic, never in a shed.
5. **Save the ash**: it has uses (below).

## Keeping it going

- **Coals do the work.** Flames look impressive; a deep bed of coals cooks, gives steady heat
  and relights easily.
- **Feed steadily, not in bursts.** One piece at a time keeps the coal bed stable. Three at
  once smother it and make smoke instead of heat.
- **Air control:** more air burns hotter and faster; less air burns slower and longer. In an
  open fireplace or fire pit you control air by how you place and space the wood.
- **Two logs burn better than one**, because they heat each other. Three is better still: the
  gaps between them are where the fire lives.

## Banking: the skill worth practising

Banking keeps live coals overnight so you wake to a fire, not a chore.

1. Let the fire burn down to a good bed of coals.
2. **Rake the coals into a compact pile.** A mound holds heat far better than a spread.
3. Put **one or two large, dense logs** on top (oak, hickory, ash and other dense woods,
   → 06-03).
4. **Cover the edges with ash.** Ash insulates and slows the fire to a smoulder.
5. In the morning, rake the ash off, expose the coals, add fine kindling and blow gently.

Done well, this holds live coals overnight. In a long outage, a fire you bank instead of
relighting is a large saving in matches, lighters, tinder and effort.

{{figure fig-banked-fire}}

**In a wood stove or fireplace indoors:** a fire turned down to smoulder all night makes more
creosote than a small hot fire; EPA says a smouldering fire is neither safe nor efficient in most
appliances (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices; CSIA). Bank with dry wood, and check the chimney often
in a season of heavy use (→ 06-09, → 08-08).

## Where the wood's heat actually goes

- **An open fireplace is a poor heater.** MU Extension puts a conventional fireplace at about 10
  percent efficiency, and some pull more warm room air out of the house than they put back (MU
  Extension, G5450). Treat an open fireplace as a place to cook and
  boil water, with its heat as a bonus. A wood stove, with a door and an air control, heats far
  better (→ 08-08).
- **A contained fire beats an open one for cooking.** A rocket stove (→ 07-02) does the same
  cooking on much less wood, and less again with a lid, a windscreen and a haybox (an insulated
  box that finishes the cooking without fire).
- **Dry wood is the cheapest efficiency there is.** MU Extension gives hardwood about 7,100 BTU
  per pound air-dried to 20 percent moisture against about 4,900 fresh-cut: dry wood puts far more
  of its energy into your pot instead of boiling off water (MU Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating,
  G5450; → 06-03).
- **Cook while the fire is already lit.** Every fire lit for one job is waste.

## Ashes: do not just throw them away

- **Hot ashes go in a metal bucket with a lid**, outside, at least 10 feet from the house and
  away from anything that burns (USFA), and stay there until they are cold all the way through.
- **Uses:** grip on icy paths, a light dressing on acid garden soil, soap-making (→ 13-09),
  scouring greasy pots, and covering each layer in a latrine (→ 13-01).
- **Do not** put large amounts in compost, put them on acid-loving plants, or keep them near
  stored drinking water.

## Fire safety with children

- **Never leave a fire unattended**, indoors or out, while children are awake.
- **A physical barrier** (a screen or fence) around any fire a child can reach.
- **Teach the boundary early**: a marked line nobody small crosses (→ 20-02).
- **Long-handled tools** so nobody reaches over the flame.
- Whether older children tend the fire is the household's call: {{choice DC-24}} → 30-25.

{{#if has.young_child}}This household has a child under 6. A screen in front of every fire is
not optional.{{/if}}

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Metal ash bucket with a tight lid** | Prevents the classic ash fire | And a metal shovel |
| Poker, shovel, tongs | Move coals without reaching in | Long handles |
| Heavy leather gloves | Wood and hot tools | Welding gloves are ideal |
| Bellows or a blow tube | Revives banked coals with no fuel | A length of metal pipe works |
| Grate or andirons | Air underneath burns better | Helps any fire |
| Moisture meter | Shows whether wood is really dry | Cheap; big efficiency gain (→ 06-03) |
| Fire extinguisher and water | Things go wrong | → 29-12 |
| Spark screen | Embers travel, especially in wind | Essential with children near |

**If you do not have it:**

- A metal trash can with a lid becomes an ash bucket.
- Any metal pipe becomes a blow tube; a rolled magazine works as a fan.
- Bricks, blocks or stones build a windbreak and reflect heat back at you.

## When it runs out

This page is itself a way to save: what it saves is ignition (→ 06-01) and wood (→ 06-04).

- **Bank** rather than relight; **batch** every heat job into one burn; use a **contained
  stove** for cooking.
- Nothing here needs restocking. It is a skill, and a skill does not run out. **Practise
  banking now**, while a failure just means lighting the fire again.
- Efficient burning, dry wood and banking together make a woodpile last much longer.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if has.outdoor_fire}}the outdoor fireplace or fire pit is for
  cooking and boiling.{{else}}an outdoor fire is for cooking and boiling.{{/if}} Bank it if you
  will use it again the same day; otherwise put it **fully** out. An unattended outdoor fire
  near fences and neighbours is a real risk.
- **B (on the move):** small, contained fires only, and fully out before you move on: drown,
  stir, drown again, until it is cold to the back of your hand.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** a banked stove overnight is the old rhythm, and how people
  lived through winters before matches were cheap.
