pages.body:
# Firewood: species, cords, seasoning, splitting

**What this page is for.** Firewood is only fuel if it is dry, and only enough if you measure
it honestly. This page explains how to measure a woodpile, why moisture matters more than
anything else, which kinds of trees burn best, how to dry ("season") wood, and how to split it
without hurting yourself.

> **CAUTION.** Two things here hurt people. **Splitting injuries**: an axe glancing off a log
> is a leg wound, possibly with no emergency room. **Burning the wrong material**: never burn
> treated, painted or pressure-treated wood, plywood, OSB, particleboard, driftwood or trash.
> The smoke is poisonous and the residue damages the chimney (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices;
> MU Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating).

## Do this now

1. **Measure your stack honestly, in cords.** A **cord is 128 cubic feet**: a stack 4 ft high,
   4 ft deep and 8 ft long. A "face cord" or "rick" is one row 4 ft high and 8 ft long but only
   16 to 24 inches deep, so a **third to a half** of a cord, and it is often sold as a "cord" (MU
   Extension, G5450). This is where people badly overestimate what they have.
2. **Get a moisture meter** (a cheap hand tool with two pins) and check what you own. The
   target is **below 20 percent** (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices).
3. **Start seasoning now.** Fresh-cut hardwood is very wet (about 75 percent moisture by MU
   Extension's measure, so close to half its weight is water) and needs **at least six months**
   of drying (EPA), a year for dense hardwoods (MU Extension).
4. **Stack it off the ground, covered on top, open on the sides.** Wood dries by moving air,
   not by being wrapped in a tarp.
5. **Split it.** Split wood dries much faster than whole rounds.

{{figure fig-cord-measure}}

This household's firewood on hand: **{{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords**.

{{photo woodpile}}

## Moisture is everything

University of Missouri Extension gives these figures for hardwood (MU Extension, Wood Fuel for
Heating, G5450):

- one pound of **oven-dry** hardwood holds about **8,600 BTU** (a BTU is a unit of heat);
- **air-dried to about 20 percent** moisture: about **7,100 BTU per pound**;
- **fresh-cut at about 75 percent** moisture: about **4,900 BTU per pound**.

That is roughly **a third of the energy lost** to boiling off the wood's own water. Wet wood
also gives a smoky, hard-to-manage fire and builds **creosote** in the chimney, a tar that can
catch fire and can block the flue (→ 06-09, → 08-02). **Green (fresh-cut) wood in a crisis is
close to useless.** That is the strongest reason to season wood ahead, every year.

## Species: a cord is not a fixed amount of heat

At the same moisture, **heavier (denser) wood holds more heat**: a given volume of oak or hickory
gives more heat than the same volume of cottonwood or willow (MU Extension, G5450). MU Extension
puts a seasoned cord of oak or other dried hardwood at about **3,600 lb**. A cord of a light wood
weighs much less and carries much less usable heat.

The groups below are common US firewood trees sorted by heat per cord, the same classes used on
the region plates in Section 32 (MU Extension, G5450; → 32-00). They are general:
which of them grow near you depends on your region.

| Burn quality | Common US examples | Best use |
|---|---|---|
| **High (dense hardwoods)** | Oaks, hickories and pecan, sugar maple, white ash, beech, yellow birch, black locust, honey locust, Osage orange (hedge), mulberry, ironwood (hophornbeam), mesquite | **Overnight burns, cold nights, banking** (→ 06-02) |
| **Medium** | Elm, red and silver maple, green ash, paper birch, cherry, walnut, hackberry, sycamore, most pines (ponderosa, lodgepole, loblolly, shortleaf and other southern pines), Douglas-fir, larch (tamarack), junipers and eastern redcedar | General burning |
| **Low (light woods)** | Cottonwood, aspen, willow, basswood, boxelder, tuliptree (yellow-poplar), eastern white pine, spruces, true firs, hemlocks, northern white-cedar, western redcedar | Quick cooking heat and kindling. Burn fast and leave little coal |

**Pines and other conifers** are resinous: fine outdoors and as kindling, and in a flue burn them
only dry and hot, and check the chimney more often (→ 06-09). Osage orange throws many sparks: not
for an open fireplace without a screen (MU Extension).

**Strategy:** burn the light, fast woods for **cooking**; save the dense woods for **overnight
heat and banking** (→ 06-02).

**Elm is common and famously hard to split.** Use a maul and wedges, or leave it in rounds for
long overnight burns.

**Your region's trees.** Your home ecoregion is **{{ region.home.ecoregion }}**. The firewood
trees recorded there are listed below; the high-heat ones come first, with photographs. Each
state's page in Section 32 lists the trees of every ecoregion in that state (→ 32-00). **Learn
the bark**: in winter, and on a log already on the ground, bark and grain are all you have to go
on.

{{plates}}

## Seasoning properly

- **Split first, then stack.** Bark is waterproof; the split faces are where water leaves.
- **Off the ground**: pallets, rails or scrap lumber. Wood touching the ground rots and soaks
  water back up.
- **Cover the top only.** A tarp over the whole pile traps moisture.
- **Sun and wind**, not shade. A spot with sun and moving air dries fastest.
- **Single rows dry faster** than deep blocks.
- **Time:** at least **six months** for most woods (EPA); dense hardwoods such as oak need a year
  or more (MU Extension), and the slowest oaks up to two years.
- **Check with the meter** instead of guessing. Split a piece and test the fresh face: a
  surface that reads 20 percent may read 35 percent inside.

## Splitting safely

- **Chopping block** at about knee height. Never split on the ground.
- **Feet apart and out of the swing line.** If the blade glances off, it should hit the block
  or the dirt, not your shin.
- **Maul for splitting, axe for felling and limbing.** A splitting maul has a wedge-shaped head
  that does the work; a sharp felling axe gets stuck in rounds (→ 16-06).
- **Wedges and a sledgehammer** for knotty, twisted and stringy wood such as elm.
- **Nobody near you while you split**, especially children: keep everyone well clear of the
  swing and of flying chips and pieces.
- **Frozen wood splits easier.** Winter is a good time to split.
- **Stop when you are tired.** Most splitting injuries happen on a tired swing.

Whether teenagers split wood is the household's call: {{choice DC-24}} → 30-25.

{{figure fig-splitting-stance}}

## Stacking and storage

- Keep a **working supply** near the door (a few days' worth, under cover) and the **main
  stack** further out.
- **Bring tomorrow's wood inside** to warm and dry; it lights far better.
- **Mice, rats and insects** live in woodpiles. Keep the main stack away from the house.
- **Do not stack against the house**: moisture, pests and fire spread.
- **A big woodpile shows the street you have supplies** (→ 14-03). Think about what can be
  seen.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Splitting maul | The main tool | And a spare handle |
| Two or more splitting wedges and a sledgehammer | Knots, big rounds, elm | Steel wedges |
| Bow saw and spare blades | Cuts wood with no fuel, quietly | Keep plenty of blades |
| Chainsaw with fuel, bar oil, files, spare chain | Fast while fuel lasts | Runs out: back it up with hand tools |
| Felling axe with a file or stone | Limbing and felling | Keep sharp (→ 16-02) |
| **Moisture meter** | Know what will burn | The cheapest efficiency purchase there is |
| Chopping block | Safety and speed | A big round of tough wood such as elm |
| Pallets or rails | Keep the stack off the ground | Free from many businesses |
| Tarps (top cover only) | Keep rain off, let air through | Weight with rocks or tie down |
| Heavy gloves, eye protection, sturdy boots | Splitting injuries | Steel toes if you have them |
| Log carrier or sled | Hauling in snow | Saves your back |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Standing dead and storm-downed wood** is already partly seasoned: the best crisis fuel.
- Untreated pallets and clean scrap lumber burn fine. Pull the nails; **never** treated wood.
- Fruit-tree and hedge prunings, windbreak thinnings.
- A car jack, or wedges and a sledgehammer, can stand in for a log splitter.

## When it runs out

- **Count** your days of wood: cords on hand divided by cords burned per day (→ 06-04).
  Recount honestly.
- **Stretch it:** light woods for cooking, dense woods overnight; bank the fire (→ 06-02); heat
  one room instead of the house (→ 08-01).
- **Always be seasoning next season's wood.** In a long emergency the rhythm becomes: burn this
  year's, cut and stack next year's.
- **The trap:** a pile of green wood is not a fuel supply. Staying a season ahead is the whole
  discipline of heating with wood.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if is.urban}}town lots have little room and few trees. Storm
  debris and scrap are the main resupply (→ 06-04).{{else}}storm debris, deadfall and windbreak
  thinnings are the nearest resupply (→ 06-04).{{/if}} Season everything you gather.
- **B (on the move):** carry no wood; gather dry, standing dead wood at stops.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** more wood, but you must cut and season **ahead**. A winter's
  heat is several cords. Build a woodshed early.

pages.body:
# When the wood runs out (burn rate and sourcing)

**What this page is for.** A woodpile that lasts a whole winter of evening fires can be gone in
weeks once it is the only way to cook and boil water every day. This page shows how to work out
how long your wood will last, how to make it last longer, where more comes from, and what not to
burn when you get desperate.

> **SAFETY.** Two ways this kills.
> 1. **Desperation fuel.** Burning treated lumber, plywood, painted, stained or
>    pressure-treated wood, or trash releases poisons (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices; MU
>    Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating). Never burn them,
>    especially where anyone breathes the smoke.
> 2. **Carbon monoxide (CO).** Every fire makes CO, a gas you cannot see or smell (CDC; → 29-03).
>    **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>    window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
>    mitigation that works every time. An outdoor fire, fire pit, rocket stove or grill is
>    outdoor equipment: it never comes inside, not even "for a while" (→ 08-02, → 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Assume your woodpile is smaller than you think.** Count it in cords (→ 06-03). This
   household's count: **{{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords**.
2. **Know your cooking fires.** Have at least two ways to cook outdoors in case one fails: an
   outdoor fireplace or fire-pit ring (buildable from blocks or scrap steel), a rocket stove
   (→ 07-02, the most wood-efficient), or a camp stove on propane (→ 07-05).{{#if has.outdoor_fire}}
   Your outdoor fireplace or fire pit is one of them.{{/if}}
3. **Separate the two jobs.** Cooking needs **small, hot, short** fires. Heating needs **large,
   long** fires. Doing both on one outdoor fire burns wood fast. **Cooking and boiling water
   come first** (survival); get heat by the methods in Section 08 (→ 08-04).
4. **Cut use now.** Cook on a rocket stove or small contained fire. Cook in batches and boil
   water in bulk while a fire is going.
5. **Start finding more wood before you are low**, not after.

## How long will it last? Do the arithmetic

1. **Count cords on hand.** A cord is 128 cubic feet (4 × 4 × 8 ft). A face cord or "rick" is
   the same height and length but only one row deep, usually 16 to 24 inches, so it is a third to
   a half of a cord (MU Extension, G5450). Be honest.
2. **Estimate daily use** for how you actually burn: cooking only, or cooking and heating. Weigh
   or count what you burn in a normal day for a few days, and use the average.
3. **Divide** cords on hand by cords per day. That is your **runway**, in days.

Write it here and on the master consumables table (→ 23-02):

| Cords on hand | Cords burned per day | Days of wood |
|---|---|---|
| ______ | ______ | ______ |

A household heating with wood through a cold winter burns **several cords a season**, far more
than a small backyard stack holds.{{#if is.cold_winters}} Your home has cold winters: expect
the high end.{{/if}} If your arithmetic says "weeks", believe it and start finding wood now.

## Three things that change the arithmetic

**Moisture.** Wet ("green") wood wastes much of its energy boiling off its own water, makes
little heat, and coats the chimney with **creosote**, a tar that can catch fire (→ 06-09).
Firewood should be **seasoned to below 20 percent moisture** (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices).
That takes **at least six months** split, stacked and covered on top (EPA), and **most dense
hardwoods need at least a year** (MU Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating, G5450). Green wood in a
crisis barely works. A cheap moisture meter tells you what will actually burn.

**Species.** Dense hardwoods such as oak and hickory hold far more heat per cord than light
woods such as cottonwood, willow, boxelder or white pine: MU Extension rates the first "high"
and the second "low" (MU Extension, G5450; → 06-03). A "cord" is not a fixed amount of survival:
if your wood is light, plan on considerably more volume for the same heat.

**Drying time.** Dense woods dry slowly: oak and hickory often need a year or more (MU
Extension). Light woods often dry in one summer. Wood cut this year from the best trees may not burn well until next
winter. Cut standing dead wood first for wood you can burn now.

## Somewhere else may be a different wood world

The trees, and so the firewood, change across the country. Plan each place on its own trees,
not on a generic "cord".

- **Home ({{ region.home.ecoregion }}):** see your region page and its firewood trees (→ 32-00).
{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{d.name}}, {{d.county}}, {{d.state_name}} ({{d.region.ecoregion}}):** see the region page for that state (→ 32-00). If it is open prairie or desert, expect little wood and plan cooking on other fuels (→ 06-05) and heat by other means (→ 08-04).
{{/each}}

Two traps: **in places with little wood**, a cord of light wood gives much less heat than a cord
of oak, so cord arithmetic silently shrinks. **In places with the best wood**, none of it burns well
for about a year after you cut it, so start cutting and stacking on the first visit.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rocket stove or efficient wood cookstove | Cooks on much less wood than an open fire, and less again with a lid, windscreen and haybox | The biggest single wood saver (→ 07-02) |
| Axe, maul, splitting wedges | Turn rounds into splits that burn | Keep sharp (→ 16-02) |
| Bow saw, spare blades, hand saw | Cut with no power or fuel | Quiet and reliable |
| Chainsaw with fuel, bar oil, files (optional) | Fast while fuel lasts | Runs out; back up with hand tools |
| Moisture meter | Know what will burn | Prevents creosote trouble |
| Tarps, a woodshed, pallets | Season and keep wood dry off the ground | Wet wood is nearly no wood |
| Work gloves, eye protection, first-aid kit | Cutting injuries are common | → 12-01 |
| Fire extinguisher and water | Chimney fires and stray embers | → 29-12; CO alarms → 08-02 |

**If you do not have it, scavenge:**

- **Standing dead trees and fallen limbs**: already partly seasoned, the best crisis wood.
- **Storm debris, downed branches, untreated pallets, untreated scrap lumber, fruit-tree and
  hedge prunings.** In town, wind-downed limbs are plentiful after storms.
- **Bundle small stuff.** Twigs and yard waste burn better tied in bundles or fed to a rocket
  stove.
- **Never burn:** pressure-treated, painted or stained wood; plywood, OSB or particleboard (the
  glues); driftwood (salt); trash; plastics. All release toxic smoke (EPA).

## When it runs out

- **Recount weekly** as the pile shrinks, and update the runway (→ 23-01).
- **Warm the people, not the space:** clothing (→ 11-01), one small heated room (→ 08-01),
  sleeping close together, insulation. Cook in batches so one fire does many meals. Bank coals
  so you relight without wasting kindling (→ 06-02).
- **Other fuels:** propane for cooking is compact and clean (stored as → 06-06); charcoal
  (outdoors only), compressed fire logs and dense biomass (→ 06-05).
- **Always be drying next season's wood.**
- **The trap to avoid:** running the pile to zero, then burning wet, green or toxic wood in
  desperation. Stay a month ahead, and keep a **reserve** you do not touch until you are truly
  cornered.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** the backyard stack plus storm debris; propane as the compact
  backup for cooking. Outdoor fires are for cooking and boiling, not whole-house heat.
  {{#if has.wood_stove}}The wood stove is your heat; guard its wood for that job.{{/if}}
- **B (on the move):** do not haul wood. Carry a compact stove and a little fuel; gather on the
  way.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** more wood, but you must **cut and season ahead**; a winter's
  heat is several cords. Thin windbreaks gently: they protect the house from wind first and are
  fuel second. Keep the chimney clean (→ 06-09). Build a woodshed and stay a season ahead.

pages.body:
# Alternative fuels (propane, charcoal, kerosene, biomass)

**What this page is for.** Wood is the long-term fuel, but it is slow and needs seasoning.
Stored fuels such as propane, kerosene and charcoal bridge the gap. This page compares them,
shows how far a tank goes, and explains how to divide a limited supply between cooking, heat and
power so the same tank is not promised three times.

**New to fuels?** Read → 29-01 first. It explains what gasoline, diesel, kerosene, propane,
butane, white gas, lamp oil and charcoal are, how to tell them apart, the usual can colours, and
which can ever be used indoors. This page assumes it.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
>   mitigation that works every time. Charcoal makes lethal carbon monoxide (CO). CDC: never
>   burn charcoal indoors, and a fireplace is indoors (CDC; → 29-03).
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
>   ignition.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed
>   in every source.
> - **Never burn treated or painted wood, plywood, particleboard or trash**: toxic smoke and
>   residue (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices; MU Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating).
>
> Every fuel here can kill by CO, fire or explosion. Read → 08-02 and → 06-06 alongside this page.

## Do this now

1. **Propane is the best compact backup for cooking.** It keeps for years in a sealed cylinder,
   lights instantly and makes no smoke. It is limited and you cannot make more.
2. **Charcoal is outdoor-only. Always.**
3. **Stock some now.** Fuel limits water treatment, cooking and warmth all at once. A few 20-lb
   propane cylinders are among the most useful things a household can buy.
4. **Divide your propane on paper** between its jobs (worksheet below).
5. **Plan the move to wood** (→ 06-04). Stored fuels are a bridge; wood is the long game.
6. **Store fuel safely, outside the living space** (→ 06-06).

## The fuels compared

| Fuel | How long it keeps | Cooking | Heat | Indoors? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Propane** | Does not go stale in a sealed cylinder; the cylinder has its own date (→ 29-14) | Excellent | Good, in heaters rated for it | **Only appliances rated for indoor use**, with ventilation | Best compact backup. Cannot be made |
| **Wood** | Years if seasoned and dry | Good | Good | Installed, vented appliance only | Renewable, can be scavenged: the long game (→ 06-03) |
| **Charcoal** | Years if dry | Very good | — | **Never** | Steady heat outdoors; deadly indoors |
| **Wood pellets** | Years if dry | With a pellet stove | Good | Pellet stove only | Dense and clean, but needs its own stove, which usually needs electricity |
| **Kerosene** | Keeps longer than gasoline when full, sealed and dark, but water creeps in. Jar-test before use; how old is too old is a household choice (→ 30-18) | Kerosene stove | High | **Only K-1 kerosene, only in heaters or lamps made for indoor use**, with ventilation and a CO alarm (→ 08-10) | Usual can colour: blue |
| **Gasoline** | **Months, not years.** Stabiliser added when fresh slows ageing but cannot fix stale fuel (Honda Power Equipment, Fuel Recommendations) | Some camp stoves | — | **Never for heat or light** | Vehicles and most generators. Dangerous to store (→ 06-06). Usual can colour: red |
| **Butane canisters** | Years | Good | — | Not indoors (CDC: never a camp stove indoors) | **Fails in the cold**: butane boils at 31 °F (NIOSH) |
| **Compressed sawdust logs ("bio-bricks")** | Years, if dry | Yes | Good | Vented appliance | Excellent to stockpile: dense, dry, no seasoning |
| **Paper logs (homemade)** | Months to years | Poor | Poor | Vented appliance | Free from junk mail and cardboard |
| **Dung, dried plant matter** | Seasonal | Yes | Low | Vented appliance, ventilated room | Old last resort; smoky |

**Old fuel.** Whether to burn kerosene, diesel or gasoline that has been stored a long time is a
trade-off: fresh fuel only, or a jar test first. {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18.

## The shape of it

- **Propane, charcoal, kerosene and gasoline run out.** You will not make more. Spend them on
  the jobs that are hard any other way: a fast meal, boiling water in bad weather, running a
  generator to charge medical devices.
- **Wood and other plant fuel are renewable.** Slower, dirtier, more work, and the only thing
  that lasts.
- **So:** use stored fuels early while you get organised, then move to wood and efficiency
  (→ 07-02 rocket stove) as the emergency goes on. Do not burn through propane being
  comfortable in month one and reach month six with a woodpile you never started seasoning.

## How far a 20-lb propane cylinder goes

A BTU is a unit of heat. A full 20-lb cylinder holds about **430,000 BTU**. One heater maker's
figures show it: its manual gives **48 to 110 hours** per 20-lb cylinder, from high (9,000 BTU/h)
to low (4,000 BTU/h) (Enerco Group, portable radiant heater owner's manual), and 48 × 9,000 is
about 430,000. The US Department of Energy gives propane about 91,000 BTU per gallon (DOE
Alternative Fuels Data Center, Fuel Properties Comparison).

**Check the label first.** Most "20-lb" cylinders at exchange cages are filled to **15 lb**, not 20
(NIST, Liquefied Petroleum Gas 20 Pound Cylinders). A 15-lb fill holds three quarters as much:
about 320,000 BTU (→ 28-04).

**The method:** hours per cylinder = 430,000 (or 320,000 for a 15-lb fill) ÷ the appliance's BTU
per hour, from its label (→ 29-14). Real use is lower in hard cold.

- **Cooking:** read the burner's BTU rating on the stove's label. For example, a burner rated
  10,000 BTU/h would run about **43 hours** on a full 20-lb cylinder at full flame. Real cooking
  rarely runs a burner wide open the whole time. Stove technique: → 07-05.
- **Portable propane heater:** the manual figures above; use your own heater's rating (→ 08-09,
  → 28-04).
- **Generator:** run time per cylinder depends entirely on the model and the load. Use your
  generator's manual (→ 09-04, → 28-03).{{#if has.generator}} Your generator: {{ gear.generator_watts }} running watts, fuel: {{ gear.generator_fuel }}.{{/if}}

## The same tank, promised three times

The common trap: the same propane is "the generator supply", "the cooking backup" and "the
heater fuel" in three different plans. **Divide it on paper** before the outage, and recheck
whenever a cylinder moves from one job to another.

This household has **{{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }}** 20-lb cylinders and **{{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }}**
1-lb cylinders.

| Job | Cylinders set aside | Not to be spent on |
|---|---|---|
| Cooking (→ 07-05) | ______ | ______ |
| Heat (→ 08-09){{#if has.propane_heater}} — you have a portable propane heater{{/if}} | ______ | ______ |
| Generator (→ 09-04){{#if has.generator}} — fuel: {{ gear.generator_fuel }}{{/if}} | ______ | ______ |
| Float (the cylinder in use; first spent, first refilled) | ______ | — |

**Things that help:**
- Decide which job each cylinder serves, and write what it may **not** be spent on.
- Know what can stand in for propane in each job. Gasoline may stand in for it in a dual-fuel
  generator; kerosene may stand in for it as heat. Often **nothing stands in for propane as
  quick, smoke-free cooking**, so keep enough back for cooking.
- Write a **refill trigger**: for example, the first empty cylinder is refilled that same week
  while refills still exist.
- Keep a **reserve** you never spend on comfort: for storms, illness and a quick meal for a sick
  child.

**Two propane decisions on other pages.** Refilling small 1-lb cylinders from a 20-lb tank:
{{choice DC-03}} → 30-04. A cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03.
Fire codes based on NFPA 58, the propane code, limit cylinders kept inside a home to the 1-lb
class (NFPA 58; Minnesota State Fire Marshal, LP Gas Inside Buildings).

## Charcoal: useful, and lethal indoors

Charcoal is tempting: cheap, keeps for years if dry, and gives steady, controllable cooking heat.
**It also makes a lot of CO**, and CDC says never burn it indoors (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning:
Basics). A fireplace is indoors. **Outdoors only, every time, whatever the weather.** If it is too
cold to cook outside, use a different method, not a different room.

**You can make charcoal** from wood by burning it with little air. In a long emergency it is a
useful skill: charcoal is lighter than the wood it came from, keeps better, and burns hotter and
cleaner.

## Homemade and scavenged fuels

- **Paper logs:** soak shredded paper and cardboard, press into logs, dry them **completely**.
  Free, but they burn quickly.
- **Compressed sawdust logs:** worth stockpiling now: dense, dry, no seasoning, compact.
- **Untreated pallets and scrap lumber:** plentiful in town (→ 06-04). Pull the nails and make
  sure it is untreated. Treated lumber is often green-tinged or stamped, and burning it is
  poisonous.
- **Never burn:** pressure-treated, painted or stained wood; plywood, OSB or particleboard;
  driftwood; railroad ties; plastics; foam; trash.

## The cold-weather footnote

**Butane canister stoves largely stop working below freezing**: butane boils at 31 °F, so below
that it will not turn to gas. **Propane keeps working** in far colder weather: it boils at −44 °F
(NIOSH Pocket Guide, n-Butane and Propane).{{#if is.cold_winters}} With your cold winters,
that alone makes propane the better backup stove fuel.{{/if}}

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 20-lb propane cylinders (several) and adapter hoses | Best compact cooking backup | Stored outdoors or detached (→ 06-06) |
| 1-lb propane cylinders | Portable; the size some indoor-rated heaters take | Refilling them is a decision (→ 30-04) |
| Charcoal, in dry bags | Steady outdoor cooking heat | **Outdoor use only** |
| Compressed sawdust logs | Dense, dry, no seasoning | Store dry |
| Kerosene (K-1) and a heater rated for indoor use | High heat output | Ventilation and a CO alarm (→ 08-10) |
| Fuel stabiliser | Slows gasoline ageing | Add when the fuel is fresh; date the can (→ 06-06) |
| Approved, labelled fuel cans | Safety; not mixing fuels up | → 06-06 |
| **CO alarm** | Any fuel, any time | → 08-02 |

**If you do not have it, scavenge:**
- **Untreated pallets, scrap lumber, storm debris**: the biggest fuel source in town (→ 06-04).
- **Paper and cardboard**, pressed into logs.
- **Part-used propane cylinders** from grills are common and often overlooked.
- Wood you turn into **charcoal** yourself keeps better than the wood did.

## When it runs out

- **Count cylinders in cooking days**, not pounds: how many days of meals one cylinder cooks for
  your household. Write it on → 23-02.
- **Save propane for what is hard with wood**: boiling water fast in a blizzard, cooking when it
  is dangerous to be outside, a quick meal for a sick child. Do ordinary cooking on wood
  (→ 07-01, → 07-02).
- **Wood can be found and grown; propane and kerosene cannot.** Every efficiency gain (rocket
  stove, banked fire, batch cooking) stretches both.
- **Decide in advance what part of the propane you will never spend on convenience.**

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** propane plus an outdoor wood fire (→ 06-04) covers nearly
  everything. Scrap wood in town is plentiful.
- **B (on the move):** a small propane or multi-fuel stove and a little fuel; gather wood at
  stops. Butane fails in winter.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** wood becomes the main fuel and propane becomes precious. Start
  making and storing charcoal, and cut and season wood a year ahead.

pages.body:
# Storing fuel safely (gasoline, propane, kerosene)

**What this page is for.** Stored fuel is the most dangerous thing in a prepared house. This
page covers where each fuel is kept, how to label it so nobody pours the wrong one, how to keep
it from going bad, what must never be stored next to it, and how to keep children away from it.

**New to fuels?** Read → 29-01 first: it explains what gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane
are and how to tell them apart.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
>   ignition.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed
>   in every source.
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
>   mitigation that works every time.
> - **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** Chlorine gas.
>
> **Gasoline vapour is heavier than air. It flows along the floor and can be lit by a water
> heater's pilot light across the room** (Maryland Department of the Environment, Gasoline Safety;
> CPSC, Fuel Container Safety). If you
> smell strong fuel vapour indoors or in a garage: no light switches, no engines, no flames;
> get everyone out; open doors from outside if you can.

## Do this now

1. **Label every can today**, in large letters you can read by headlamp: "GASOLINE — NOT FOR
   HEATERS", "KEROSENE — HEATER ONLY", "DIESEL". **Before any pour: read the label aloud, smell,
   then pour.** Kerosene smells oily, like lamp fuel; gasoline is sharp and stings the eyes.
2. **Keep gasoline and kerosene apart**: not on the same shelf, not touching, a gap you can see.
3. **Propane cylinders outdoors**, upright, valves closed and capped, away from doors, windows
   and vents, and **at least 5 feet from anything that can light them** (NFPA 58, as quoted in
   Hawaii Gas, Gas Engineering Guide).
4. **Never pour or transfer fuel indoors or in a garage.** Carry the can outside, pour, cap it,
   carry it back (→ 06-07).
5. **Never store gasoline in the house or basement** (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety). **Propane
   cylinders larger than 1 lb live outdoors**, never in a basement; bringing one inside is a
   decision card, not a winter habit (→ 30-03).
6. **Approved fuel containers only**, labelled. Never milk jugs, drink bottles or unlabelled cans.
7. **Away from anything that sparks or burns**: water heater, furnace, pilot lights, electrical
   panel, woodpile.
8. **Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) far away from all fuels.** It is a strong oxidiser and
   can react dangerously with petroleum (→ 29-05, → 03-08).
9. **A fire extinguisher outside the storage area**, so you never reach through a fire to get it
   (→ 29-12).

## What this household keeps, and where

| Fuel | On hand | Container and label | Where it is kept |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gasoline | {{ gear.fuel.gasoline_gal }} gal | ______ | ______ |
| Diesel | {{ gear.fuel.diesel_gal }} gal | ______ | ______ |
| Kerosene | {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal | ______ | ______ |
| Propane, 20-lb | {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} cylinders | Cylinders | ______ |
| Propane, 1-lb | {{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }} cylinders | Cylinders | ______ |

Distance from the fuel to the nearest pilot light, igniter, heater or engine: ______ ft.

{{photo fuel-store}}

## Can colours, and why the label wins

In the US, fuel cans are usually coloured by an industry convention, not a law: **red for
gasoline, yellow for diesel, blue for kerosene** (→ 29-01). Heater makers lean on it: one common
kerosene heater manual says store kerosene only in a blue container clearly marked "kerosene",
never a red one, because red containers are associated with gasoline (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo,
kerosene heater manual).

**Use the convention, but trust the label.** Cans get reused, faded and borrowed, and some
households have cans in other colours. So:

- **Every can is labelled with its fuel**, whatever its colour.
- **A can with a missing or unreadable label is not poured into anything** until you know what is
  in it.
- **Read aloud, smell, then pour.** Gasoline in a kerosene heater causes a flare-up, fire or
  explosion (heater maker's manual).

{{figure fig-fuel-can-colours}}

## The attached garage

The garage is where most families keep fuel, and it is a hard place for it: pilot lights,
igniters, a car engine, tools that spark, and a shared wall and door with the house. Vapour
flowing along the floor finds them. Keeping fuel there is a trade-off the household decides,
with rules for how: {{choice DC-05}} → 30-06.

{{#if has.garage}}Your home has an attached garage. Whatever the choice, the transfer rule holds:
**never pour or transfer fuel inside the garage, power on or off.** A fuel-fired appliance that
cannot light during an outage lights again the moment power returns, and a vapour cloud lasts
longer than the pour.{{/if}}

> **Before the collapse:** model fire codes and your local fire code limit how much gasoline may
> be kept in an attached garage. Ask your fire department while it can answer. The physics is
> the same either way.

{{figure fig-vapour-flow}}

## Gasoline: the dangerous one

It is not the liquid that explodes, it is the **vapour**. Gasoline gives off enough vapour to
burn at temperatures far below zero (its flash point is about −45 °F), and a mixture of only
about 1.4 percent gasoline vapour in air can light (NIOSH Pocket Guide, Gasoline). The vapour is
**heavier than air**, so it sinks, flows along the floor and pools in low spots (Maryland
Department of the Environment, Gasoline Safety). A can leaking in a basement corner can be set
off by a furnace igniter on the other side of the room.

- **Detached storage is the standard**: a shed or an outdoor locker, ventilated, shaded, locked.
- **Approved, sealed containers**; newer ones have a flame arrester (a mesh at the spout that
  stops a flame entering the can) (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety). Keep cans out of direct sun.
- **Never fill a can sitting inside a vehicle or on a plastic truck-bed liner**: a static spark
  can light the vapour. Set it on the ground, nozzle touching the can (NIOSH, Fire Hazard from
  Filling Portable Gas Cans; → 06-07).
- **Never siphon by mouth.** Use a pump (→ 06-07).

### Gasoline goes stale: months, not years

Gasoline ages. Air and heat break it down, ethanol in pump gas draws water from the air, and
stale gas causes starting and running problems in small engines (Honda Power Equipment, Fuel
Recommendations). **Untreated gasoline keeps for months, not years.** Stabiliser slows this if it
is added when the fuel is fresh; it cannot fix fuel that is already stale, and it has its own
shelf life (Honda).

**A simple rotation that works:**
- Add stabiliser **when you fill the can**. Write the date and "STABILISED" on the can.
- **Keep cans nearly full** (no more than about 95 percent, so the fuel has room to expand;
  Maryland Department of the Environment). Less air in the can means less ageing and less water
  (Honda).
- On a set schedule, **pour each can into a vehicle's tank and refill it fresh**. Put the date on
  the rotation tracker (→ 26-08).
- Ethanol pulls water from the air (Honda), so where ethanol-free gasoline is sold, it avoids
  that problem in stored cans and small engines.

**Old gasoline** (or kerosene, or diesel): whether to use it is a decision card with a jar test on
it. {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18.

> **Before the collapse:** gasoline too old to use goes to your county or city household
> hazardous waste collection. Never pour it on the ground, down a drain, or burn it (Maryland
> Department of the Environment, Gasoline Safety).

**Generator fuel.** Use only the fuel your generator's manual names, and follow its steps for
switching fuels and for storage. Stale gasoline in a carburettor is the usual reason a stored
generator will not start (→ 09-04).{{#if has.generator}} Your generator's fuel: {{ gear.generator_fuel }}.{{/if}}

**Never gasoline in a heater or lamp.** No gasoline ever goes in a kerosene heater or any kerosene
appliance.

## Propane

- Cylinders are tough, but must be **upright, secured, and outdoors**. Heat raises the pressure;
  the relief valve then vents **flammable gas**.
- **At least 5 feet from anything that can light it**: an air-conditioner unit, a running
  generator, a grill in use. NFPA 58 sets 5 feet from a cylinder's relief valve to any outside
  ignition source (NFPA 58, as quoted in Hawaii Gas, Gas Engineering Guide). More is better.
- Heater makers say the same in their own words: cylinders are stored outdoors, never in a
  building or garage (Enerco Group, portable radiant heater manual). Fire codes based on NFPA 58
  limit cylinders kept inside a home, attached garages included, to the 1-lb class (NFPA 58;
  Minnesota State Fire Marshal, LP Gas Inside Buildings).
- **Never in a basement.** Propane is **heavier than air** (NIOSH Pocket Guide, Propane) and
  pools in low spaces.
- **Check for leaks with soapy water** brushed on the connection: growing bubbles mean a leak.
  **Never with a flame.**
- **Valves closed and capped** when not in use. Do not overfill.
- **Cold performance is good**: one of propane's real advantages (→ 06-05).
- Running a heater from a 20-lb cylinder: the cylinder stays outdoors (→ 08-09). A cylinder
  larger than 1 lb indoors is a decision card: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03.

{{photo propane-spot}}

## Kerosene

Kerosene gives off much less vapour than gasoline, so it is easier to store. It still burns.

**Grades: the difference that matters.**
- **K-1 (also written 1-K): clear, low-sulfur.** **The only grade for any heater used in, or
  vented into, living space** (MU Extension, Unvented Portable Kerosene Heaters, G1999). Heater
  makers say the same: "never use any fuel other than water-clear 1-K kerosene" (GHP
  Group/Dyna-Glo manual). Buy it clear and undyed where you can.
- **K-2 and red-dyed kerosene:** higher sulfur, sootier, more fumes. Outdoor use only; it fouls
  wicks and burners faster. Pump kerosene of unknown grade is treated as K-2.
- Never lamp oil in a heater, never gasoline in anything that burns kerosene.

**Storage.**
- **Labelled cans** (blue is the usual colour), away from anything that sparks, out of the living
  space, **cool and out of the sun** (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo manual).
- **Keep cans nearly full.** A part-full can "breathes" damp air as temperatures swing, and
  water condenses inside (the heater manual warns the same of part-empty storage tanks); water and
  dirt clog wicks and burners.
- **Date every can** and burn the oldest first.
- **Refuel heaters outdoors, with the heater cold**, never hot or running (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo
  manual; → 08-10).

**The jar test before burning stored kerosene.** Pour a sample into a clean, clear glass jar and
let it stand. Good fuel is **clear and bright**. Water sits as a layer or droplets at the bottom;
contamination shows as cloudiness, yellowing, sludge or anything floating. A common heater maker
says never use kerosene stored from one season to the next (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo manual). Whether
to follow that, or to jar-test and use older fuel, is a decision card: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18.

**How long your kerosene lasts.** Hours of heat = gallons on hand ÷ the heater's burn rate in
gallons per hour (from its manual). This household: **{{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal** ÷ ______
gal per hour = ______ hours. Wick heater manuals warn that turning the wick down to save fuel
makes odour, soot and carbon monoxide. To make the fuel last longer, **heat a smaller room
(→ 08-01), not a smaller flame.**

## Diesel

Diesel behaves like kerosene: little vapour, but water and sludge collect at the bottom of the
can or tank and plug filters, and it thickens in hard cold (→ 29-01). Label it, keep cans full and
sealed, date them, and follow your additive's label. Diesel goes **only** in diesel engines and
in heaters whose exhaust is ducted outdoors.{{#if has.diesel_vehicle}} You have a diesel
vehicle: keep its fuel clearly apart from gasoline.{{/if}}

## What must never be stored together

| Keep apart | Why |
|---|---|
| Fuels and **pool shock (calcium hypochlorite)** | An oxidiser: with combustible material it can start a fire or react explosively (CDC/ATSDR, Calcium Hypochlorite; → 29-05) |
| Fuels and anything that lights: water heater, furnace, garage heater, electrical panel, engines | Vapour travels to the flame or spark |
| **Kerosene and gasoline** | One wrong pour puts gasoline in a heater: an explosion (→ 08-10) |
| Fuels and living or sleeping space | Vapour, fire, carbon monoxide |
| Fuels and stored food and water | Contamination |
| Pool chemicals, acids and ammonia products, from each other | Toxic gases |

**The food-and-water row matters more than people think.** CDC says water contaminated with fuel
or toxic chemicals **cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting** (CDC, How to Make Water Safe
in an Emergency). A fuel spill into stored water ruins the water for good (→ 03-04).

**Pool and cleaning chemicals** cause their own accidents. Store them dry, off the floor, in their
original containers, never where something above them gets watered, liquids never with dry
chemicals, and each type in its own place, with fuel somewhere else again. Check them every few
months for caking, staining, warmth or damaged packaging. If chemicals are ever found reacting
(fuming, hot, bubbling): **do not add water, do not try to neutralise them, do not seal the
container**; keep everyone upwind and away. Poison Control: **1-800-222-1222**; with no phone,
→ 12-17. More on chlorine products: → 29-05.

## Children

- **Locked storage, and child-resistant caps.** CPSC requires child-resistant closures on
  portable gasoline, diesel and kerosene containers; keep the cap on every time (CPSC, Fuel
  Container Safety). A curious small child and an unlocked fuel can is a catastrophe.
- **Never pour fuel into a drink bottle or food container.** This is how children are poisoned
  (CPSC). No exceptions, not even "just for a minute". If a child swallows any fuel or lamp oil:
  **do not make them vomit** (MedlinePlus, Poisoning first aid); **call Poison Control,
  1-800-222-1222** (→ 12-17).
- **Teach the rule** as an absolute line (→ 20-02).

{{#if has.child}}There are children under 13 in this household. Every fuel store is locked, every
time.{{/if}}

## How much is sensible

More fuel is more capability and more risk.

- **Gasoline:** only what you will rotate through the **vehicles** and the generator, if it burns
  gasoline. Detached storage is the standard.
- **Propane:** several 20-lb cylinders is a large capability for a modest risk. Kept outdoors, it
  is the safest stored fuel for a home. Dividing it between jobs: → 06-05.
- **Kerosene:** only if you own an appliance that burns it.
- **Diesel:** only if you own a diesel engine or a ducted heater that burns it.
- **Wood is the safest bulk energy store** (→ 06-03): it does not explode, leak or go stale.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Approved fuel cans, labelled by fuel | Safe and unmistakable | Never unlabelled or old food containers |
| Fuel stabiliser | Slows gasoline ageing | Add when you buy, not later |
| Detached or outdoor lockable storage | Keeps vapour and children out | Ventilated, shaded |
| ABC fire extinguisher mounted **outside** the storage | Reachable without entering a fire | Check it yearly (→ 29-12) |
| Siphon or transfer pump | Never siphon by mouth | Cheap (→ 06-07) |
| Spray bottle of soapy water | Propane leak checks | Never a flame |
| Cylinder caps and a strap | Upright and secured | Protects valves |
| Spill absorbent (cat litter or sand) | Contain leaks | And a shovel |
| Fuel log: what, how much, date bought | Rotation | → 26-08 |

**If you do not have it:**
- Metal cabinets and outbuildings can serve as detached storage: ventilated, locked, shaded.
- Sand or cat litter for spills; a shovel to move soaked soil.
- **Do not improvise fuel containers.** This is the one place where "make do" is truly dangerous.

## When it runs out

- **Track quantity and age.** A full can of old fuel may not run the generator when you need it.
- **Save liquid fuels for the jobs only they can do**: generator runs for medical devices
  (→ 09-06), fast cooking in extreme weather.
- **In a long emergency, liquid fuels do not come back. Wood does.** Plan the change (→ 06-05).
- **Fuel in vehicle tanks:** many modern cars have screens that block siphoning, and fuel-tank work
  is dangerous. Treat getting fuel out of a tank as a real technical job (→ 06-07).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** a detached shed or outdoor locker is best; nothing in the house or
  basement; propane outdoors. Never pour or transfer in the house or garage.
- **B (on the move):** carrying fuel in a vehicle with people in it is a decision card; the full
  road rules are on → 06-08.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** more room and more distance from neighbours, same rules. Keep
  fuel in a separate structure well away from where people sleep.

pages.body:
# Moving and transferring fuel (siphoning)

**What this page is for.** Pouring, pumping and siphoning fuel is when it hurts people. This page
covers the tools that make it safe, the static-electricity rules for filling cans, why the
hose-down-the-filler-neck trick rarely works on modern cars, how to judge old fuel you find, and
what to do about a spill.

**New to fuels?** → 29-01 explains gasoline, diesel and kerosene and how to tell them apart.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
>   ignition. Transfer outdoors, engines off, nobody smoking.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed
>   in every source.
> - **Never siphon by mouth.** Gasoline irritates the lungs when breathed in and the stomach
>   lining when swallowed, and high exposures can harm the nervous system (CDC/ATSDR, ToxFAQs
>   for Automotive Gasoline). If anyone swallows fuel: **do not make them vomit** (vomiting can
>   carry it into the lungs; MedlinePlus, Poisoning first aid); **call Poison Control,
>   1-800-222-1222**; with no phone, → 12-17.
> - **Static can light it.** **Put the can on the ground to fill it**: never inside a vehicle,
>   a trunk, a pickup bed or on a trailer floor. **Fill slowly** (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety;
>   Maryland Department of the Environment, Gasoline Safety; NIOSH).
> - **Taking fuel that is not yours is theft** (→ 22-02).

## Do this now

1. **Buy a shaker (jiggle) siphon and a hand transfer pump.** They cost little and **remove any
   reason to put a hose in your mouth.** Put one in each vehicle kit (→ 22-05).
2. **Find out what your own vehicles allow.** Open the filler and look in. If you cannot see down
   into the tank, a hose will not go down it (below). Find out before an emergency.
3. **Buy two or three approved fuel containers** and label each with its fuel and the fill date
   (→ 06-06).
4. **Never keep fuel in the living space, and never in glass or a food or drink container.**

## Why "a hose down the filler neck" usually fails now

On most modern vehicles, **it does not work**:

- **Anti-siphon screens and rollover valves** sit in the filler neck to stop fuel escaping in a
  crash. A hose hits them and stops.
- **The filler neck bends**, so even without a screen a hose will not reach the fuel.
- **Forcing a stiff hose past them can damage the neck** and leave a leaking tank.

Hybrid fuel systems are often sealed even more tightly; some run pressurised tanks. **Assume a
modern car's tank cannot be siphoned until you have checked.** For a household with modern cars,
**the fuel you can reach is the fuel in your cans**, which is why the cans stay full and rotated
(→ 06-06). The car's tank gives its fuel back by driving.

**Check each vehicle once, in daylight, and write it down:**

{{#each vehicles as v}}- **{{v.type_text}}** ({{v.fuel_text}}): filler neck checked on ______. A hose passes / is blocked. Reachable fuel-rail valve (method 3): yes / no. Service manual kept at: ______.
{{else}}- Vehicle: ______. Filler neck checked on ______. A hose passes / is blocked. Reachable fuel-rail valve: yes / no. Service manual kept at: ______.
{{/each}}

Siphoning still matters for equipment with open, reachable tanks: older vehicles, mowers, boats,
ATVs, generators.

## The four ways to move fuel, best first

**1. Shaker (jiggle) siphon: the one to own.** A hose with a one-way valve on the end. Drop the
valve end in the fuel, **jiggle it up and down a few times**, and gravity does the rest. **No
mouth suction at any point.**
- **The receiving can must sit lower than the fuel you are drawing from.** Gravity does the work.
- Cheap, nothing to break, works on any tank it can reach.

**2. Hand or battery transfer pump.** A pump with an inlet hose and an outlet hose. Works uphill,
faster, and does not care which container is higher. **The right tool for moving fuel between
containers**, which is most of what you will do: topping up a generator from a can, emptying a
can into a car.

**3. The fuel-rail valve on fuel-injected engines.** Many fuel-injected vehicles have a valve on
the engine's fuel rail that looks like a tyre valve (a **Schrader valve**). The car's own fuel
pump can push fuel out through it.
- **Real hazards:** a pressurised fuel system, a hot engine bay, electrical connections near fuel
  vapour.
- **It differs by vehicle.** Not every vehicle has a reachable valve, and how the pump is
  switched on differs by model.
- **Learn it on your own vehicle, from its own service manual, in daylight, before you need it.**
  Do not improvise it from a general description, including this one.

**4. A drain plug, or dropping the tank.** Some tanks have a drain plug; most modern ones do not.
Dropping a tank is a real job with the vehicle properly supported. Last resort.

## The static rules: the part people skip

CPSC, the petroleum industry and NIOSH agree (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety; Maryland Department of
the Environment, Gasoline Safety, quoting the American Petroleum Institute; NIOSH, Fire Hazard from
Filling Portable Gas Cans in Pickup Trucks and Cars):

1. **Put the container on the ground to fill it.**
2. **Never fill a container inside a vehicle, a trunk, a pickup bed or on a trailer floor.**
   NIOSH traced fires to cans filled on plastic bed liners.
3. **Touch the can with the nozzle before you open it, and keep the nozzle touching the can's
   opening** while filling.
4. **Fill slowly.** Fast flow builds static and splashes.
5. **Fill to no more than about 95 percent**, so the fuel has room to expand.
6. No smoking, no flames, engine off, nothing in your other hand.
7. **Do not get back into the vehicle in the middle of filling** and then return to the nozzle:
   that is how people build a charge on themselves (Petroleum Equipment Institute, Stop Static).

{{figure fig-fill-on-ground}}

**Why it matters.** CPSC: if fuel vapour escapes from a container and meets a spark or flame, it
can ignite and **flash back into the container**, causing an explosion that can severely burn
people nearby. Each year thousands of people go to emergency departments with burns from
flammable liquids (CPSC).

**Flame jetting** is the failure worth knowing by name. CPSC describes it as an outside flame
suddenly igniting fuel vapour inside a container and forcefully throwing burning vapour and
liquid out of its mouth, like a blowtorch.

**That is why the container matters as much as the method.** Since **July 2023**, CPSC has
required portable fuel containers to carry **flame mitigation devices** (flame arresters) that
prevent flame jetting and container rupture. **Cans made before then may not have one.**
Replacing old gas cans is a cheap, concrete safety upgrade: put it on the shopping list (→ 26-09).

**Child-resistant closures:** CPSC requires them on portable gasoline cans, and its updated
requirements for gasoline, diesel and kerosene containers took effect in December 2022 (CPSC). {{#if has.child}}With children in this household, buy
containers that have them (→ 20-02).{{else}}Buy containers that have them.{{/if}}

**Never use gasoline to start or restart a fire**, including one you think has gone out (CPSC;
→ 06-01).

## Containers

- **Approved fuel containers only**: designed, vented and sealed for the job (OSHA, Flammable
  Liquids, 29 CFR 1910.106; CPSC).
- **Never glass. Never a food or drink container.** Ever.
- **Label every container** with its fuel and fill date. The usual US colours are **red for
  gasoline, yellow for diesel, blue for kerosene** (→ 29-01), but **the label, not the colour, is
  what you trust**. Read it aloud, smell, then pour (→ 06-06).
- **Leave room at the top**: fill to no more than about 95 percent. Fuel expands as it warms
  (Maryland Department of the Environment).
- **Store outside the living space**, away from anything that sparks and out of children's reach
  (→ 06-06).
- **Fuel inside a passenger vehicle** (in the cabin or an SUV's cargo area) is a trade-off the
  household decides: {{choice DC-06}} → 30-07. Road rules: → 06-08.

## Where fuel is found

Your own first:

| Source | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Vehicles** | The biggest reservoir and the hardest to reach on modern cars |
| **Mowers, snowblowers, trimmers, chainsaws** | Easy to reach, often **old** fuel |
| **Boats, ATVs, motorcycles, tractors** | Often reachable tanks; boats can hold a lot |
| **Generators** | Including your own (→ 09-04) |
| **Propane cylinders** | Grills, camp stoves, RVs. **Propane does not go stale** (→ 06-05) |
| **Kerosene heaters, lamp oil** | → 06-06 |

## Judging old fuel you find

Old gasoline is the most likely thing you will find, and it can wreck an engine you depend on.

- **Smell it.** Fresh gasoline smells sharp. Stale gasoline smells sour or varnishy, like old
  paint.
- **Look at it** in a clean, clear glass jar against something white. Fresh gasoline is nearly
  clear to pale straw. Dark, orange or cloudy is bad.
- **Look for a water layer** at the bottom. Gasoline with ethanol takes up water and separates. A
  visible layer means it cannot be used as it is.
- **Filter it** through a fine-screen funnel before use.
- **Diesel** keeps longer than gasoline, but microbes grow in it where water collects, and it
  thickens ("gels") in hard cold without treatment.{{#if is.cold_winters}} Your winters are cold
  enough for this.{{/if}}

**Whether to burn old fuel at all is a household decision**, and the jar test above is part of
it: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18. If you do use questionable fuel, try it first in an engine you do not
depend on, never first in the generator that runs medical equipment or the vehicle you would leave
in.

## Spills

1. **Stop the source, then air the place out.** Vapour is heavier than air and pools low
   (Maryland Department of the Environment).
2. **Soak it up** with sand, cat litter or absorbent pads. **Do not hose it into a drain**
   (Maryland Department of the Environment).
3. **Nothing that sparks** until the vapour has cleared: no light switches, no starting a vehicle.
4. **Fuel-soaked clothing comes off at once** (Maryland Department of the Environment), outside,
   and never goes in a dryer.
5. **Skin:** wash with soap and water. **Eyes:** flush with a gentle stream of clean, cool water
   for 15 minutes (MedlinePlus, Eye emergencies).
6. **Swallowed or breathed in:** **Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222**. No phone: → 12-17. Do not make
   the person vomit; get them to fresh air; watch their breathing closely, for as long as → 12-17
   says.

## The legal and ethical line

**Taking fuel from a vehicle that is not yours is theft**, and any working authority will treat it
so. **Your own vehicles and equipment, and fuel you are given or trade for, are not in question**
(→ 22-02, → 18-02).

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Shaker (jiggle) siphon** | Starts itself; no mouth; nothing to break | Buy two: one per vehicle kit |
| **Hand or battery transfer pump** | Container to container, works uphill | The one you will use most |
| **Approved fuel containers** (several) | The only safe storage | Label fuel and fill date |
| Funnel with a fine filter screen | Keeps dirt and water out of an engine | |
| Clean clear glass jar | Judging old fuel by eye | |
| Fuel stabiliser | Slows ageing | → 06-06 |
| Absorbent (sand, cat litter, pads) | Spills | Keep it where the fuel is |
| Nitrile gloves and eye protection | Fuel on skin and in eyes | |
| **Fire extinguisher rated for flammable liquids** | Where fuel is handled and stored | → 29-12 |
| Each vehicle's service manual | Method 3 differs by vehicle | |

**If you do not have it:** clear tubing and a hand pump beat any improvised arrangement. **Never
substitute your mouth for a pump**, and there is no acceptable improvised fuel container.

## When it runs out

- **Gasoline goes stale on the shelf** (→ 06-06). Count it in **hours of generator run time**, not
  gallons (→ 09-04, → 23-02).
- **Batch** every generator run (→ 09-04); keep vehicle fuel for the vehicle.
- **Resupply:** your own equipment first, then propane exchange while it exists, then trade
  (→ 18-02). **There is no renewable source of gasoline**, which is why long-term power plans rest
  on solar (→ 09-02).
- **Propane keeps for years and does not go stale.** A dual-fuel generator run on propane avoids
  every stale-gasoline problem on this page (→ 06-05, → 09-04).{{#if has.generator}} Your
  generator's fuel: {{ gear.generator_fuel }}. Use only what its manual names, and switch fuels by
  its procedure.{{/if}}

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** own the tools, know your vehicles, keep containers labelled and
  rotated.
- **B (on the move):** fuel is range, and range is the plan (→ 01-03). A siphon and a funnel belong
  in the vehicle kit (→ 22-05). Carrying fuel on the road: → 06-08.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** fuel becomes a finite resource. Keep it for setting up (tools,
  pumps, hauling) and run daily life on wood and solar.

pages.body:
# Carrying fuel on the road (cans, propane, trailers)

**What this page is for.** If the household has to drive somewhere far away with no working fuel
stations, it may carry extra fuel. This page covers where fuel rides, how to load cans and propane
so they cannot leak, tip or light, how much to carry, and what to check at every stop.

**New to fuels?** → 29-01 explains gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
>   ignition. Engine off, nobody smoking, when you pour.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed
>   in every source. Children stay belted in the vehicle at fuel stops.
> - **Never fill a can inside a vehicle, a trunk, a pickup bed or on a trailer floor.** Put it on
>   the ground (CPSC; Maryland Department of the Environment, Gasoline Safety; NIOSH; → 06-07).
> - **Nobody ever rides in a trailer.**
>
> **A closed box in summer sun concentrates vapour.** Cans breathe as they warm, and in a closed
> cabin, trunk or trailer the vapour has nowhere to go. Propane is worse: heavier than air, it
> pools on the floor. Everything below reduces a hazard that cannot be removed.

## Where fuel rides: a decision

Carrying fuel inside the passenger space (the cabin, or an SUV's or van's cargo area that shares
the cabin's air) is a trade-off the household decides: {{choice DC-06}} → 30-07.

The order that keeps it away from people, best first:

1. **Outside the vehicle**: roof rack, hitch-mounted cargo carrier, pickup bed, or an open
   trailer.
2. **An enclosed trailer, vented**, with the steps below.
3. **Inside the passenger space** only if the household's card allows it, with the card's rules.

{{#if has.vehicle}}Your vehicles: {{#each vehicles as v}}{{v.type_text}} ({{v.fuel_text}}){{#if has.trailer}}, can tow: {{v.can_tow}}{{/if}}; {{/each}}{{/if}}
{{#if has.trailer}}**You have a trailer**, so outside carry is possible. The trailer steps below
apply to you.{{else}}**You have no trailer in your settings.** Outside carry means a roof rack,
a hitch-mounted carrier or a pickup bed. If none of those exist, the passenger-space card
applies (→ 30-07).{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Write the load plan on the trip card** (→ 01-03): which cans, where each rides, who checks
   them at stops.
2. **Mount propane outside** on a rack or carrier: open-air carriage is far better than inside
   any box.
3. **Check every can**: approved, made after July 2023 (has a flame mitigation device, → 06-07),
   sealed, and labelled with its fuel. Replace any that are not before the first loaded trip.
4. **If you carry fuel in a closed trailer:** check that its roof vent works, or decide which
   door can be safely cracked open while driving. A closed trailer with no vent should not carry
   gasoline in summer.
5. **Practise the load once in the driveway** (cans, straps, barrier, vent) so the first real
   load is not also the first attempt.

{{photo fuel-load}}

## Labels and colours on the road

The usual US colours are **red for gasoline, yellow for diesel, blue for kerosene** (→ 29-01).
A helper or a tired adult at a dark rest stop will trust the colour, so **the label is what
matters**:

- **Every can is labelled** with its fuel in large letters: "GASOLINE — NOT FOR HEATERS",
  "KEROSENE — HEATER ONLY", "DIESEL".
- **If two fuels ride in the same load, they ride apart** (separate tubs, or opposite sides of
  the barrier), every can labelled first.
- **At loading and again at the pour: read the label aloud, smell, then pour.** A can with a
  missing or unreadable label is not poured into anything.
- **Trip fuel is the vehicle's fuel.** Other fuels ride only if the destination plan needs them.
  Write it on the trip card: kerosene riding? yes / no.

## Can to tank: the transfer pump

A hand transfer pump moves fuel from a can into the tank at a stop without lifting a full can to
the filler, and spills less (→ 06-07, method 2).

- **One pump, one fluid. Label each pump with its fluid.** A gasoline pump never moves kerosene;
  a pump used for water never touches fuel, and a fuel pump never touches water.
- The → 06-07 rules apply: outdoors, engine off, no flames or smoking, children belted in the
  vehicle.
- **The pump rides with the fuel**, in a lidded fuel tub. A wet pump gives off vapour and never
  rides in the cabin.
- **Never transfer fuel in a garage** before you leave, even "a quick top-up": roll the vehicle
  out and pour outside (→ 06-06).

## Gasoline in an enclosed trailer: the honest version

{{#if !has.trailer}}(This applies to any closed space fuel rides in: a trunk, a closed
cargo carrier, a cargo van.){{/if}} No arrangement of a closed box makes gasoline in summer sun
safe. What you can do is stack every step:

1. **Approved fuel cans only**, sealed, caps tight, spouts stowed. Never improvised containers
   (→ 06-07).
2. **Upright and strapped.** Cans cannot tip, slide or rub. A can rubbing a strap for hundreds of
   miles wears through.
3. **Full cans**, filled to about 95 percent so the fuel has room to expand (Maryland Department
   of the Environment). A nearly full can has little vapour space; a half-empty can is mostly
   vapour. Fill before you leave.
4. **At the back, by the door**: last in, first out, shortest reach, first to air out when the
   doors open.
5. **Vent the box**: roof vent open, or a door cracked. Moving air is the single best step.
6. **Nothing shares the box with fuel** except behind a barrier: fuel in its own lidded tubs, a
   tarp or plastic-sheet wall between fuel and food, water and clothing. Vapour soaks into
   cardboard and fabric, and water that fuel gets into cannot be made safe (CDC, How to Make
   Water Safe in an Emergency; → 03-04).
7. **Nothing that sparks in the box**: no powered devices, no loose battery packs against metal,
   no lantern "just stored" with the fuel.
8. **Air it out before unloading**: doors open, walk away, let it breathe several minutes before
   anyone works inside. Longer on a hot day.

{{figure fig-trailer-fuel-load}}

**A yardstick from the US Department of Transportation.** DOT's "materials of trade" rules were
written for work vehicles, not family cars, so they are a guide here, not a law: no more than **8
gallons per container**, packaging that is leak-tight, closed, secured against shifting and
protected from damage, and no more than **440 lb** in all (49 CFR 173.6; US DOT/PHMSA, Materials
of Trade Exceptions). Ordinary 5-gallon cans sit inside it. Many small containers are better than
one large one.

## Propane: worse than gasoline in a closed box

Gasoline vapour needs a leak or a breathing cap. **Propane in a closed box needs only a weeping
valve, or the relief valve opening on a hot day**, and then it pools on the floor, heavier than
air, until it finds a spark. The propane industry's rules for cylinders on the road (PERC, Safety
Guide for Portable Propane Cylinders):

- **Upright, always.** A cylinder on its side can put liquid propane at the relief valve. Never
  carry one lying down.
- **Valve closed, plugged or capped**, held against tipping (a rack, a crate-style holder, or a
  ratchet strap to an anchor).
- **A ventilated space only.** The propane code also limits how much propane may ride in a closed
  vehicle; whatever your local figure, treat it as a ceiling, not a plan (NFPA 58).
- **Where it rides, best first:** (1) an open rack or exterior mount; (2) inside a closed trailer
  only with the vent open and the cylinders by the door; (3) never in the passenger space for
  longer than the card allows (→ 30-07).
- **Unload cylinders as soon as you arrive.** Do not leave them in a parked, sun-heated trailer or
  car.

## How much: carry what the arithmetic needs, not what fits

The trip fuel table on → 01-03 is the authority. Work it out there for each destination:

1. Distance to the destination, including a detour.
2. The vehicle's range on a full tank, **towing if you will tow** (towing uses more fuel; measure
   it on a loaded practice drive).
3. The gap between them, with a margin. That gap, in gallons, is what the cans must hold.

{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{d.name}}** (about {{d.approximate_miles}} miles): cans needed ______ ; cans owned ______ .
{{else}}- Destination: ______ (about ______ miles): cans needed ______ ; cans owned ______ .
{{/each}}

**Propane** travels for the stay at the destination: take what the stay needs, mounted outside
first.

Every extra can adds weight{{#if has.trailer}} against the trailer's cargo limit (on its data
plate; → 16-11){{/if}}, more vapour, and more value visible at stops (→ 17-11).

## Stop discipline

- **Park in shade** if there is any. Sun on a dark box drives vapour.
- **At every stop, walk round the load.** Check straps; smell at the door seam or around the cans.
  **A gasoline or propane smell at a closed door stops everything**: doors open, everyone away,
  find the source before driving on.
- **Children stay in the vehicle, belted, engine off, at every fuel stop.** Nobody is near a
  trailer while its doors are open and it airs out.
- **No smoking, no flames, no refuelling while trailer doors are open** downwind.
- Fuel stops are also when you are most exposed on the road. Keep them short (→ 17-11).

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Approved 5-gallon fuel cans, enough for the trip arithmetic | The range margin | Made after July 2023, child-resistant (→ 06-07) |
| Labels for every can | Colour alone fails | Large, readable by headlamp |
| Hand fuel transfer pump | Can to tank without lifting | One fluid only, labelled |
| Exterior propane rack or mount | Gets propane out of any box | Roof, hitch, trailer tongue or rear |
| Cylinder holders or ratchet straps and anchors | Upright and immovable | One per cylinder |
| Lidded fuel tubs and a tarp or plastic sheeting | The barrier from food and water | Fuel tubs carry nothing else |
| Ratchet straps and anchor points | Cans that cannot move | Check at every stop |
| ABC fire extinguisher, reachable from outside the load | Fire at a stop | A second one in the vehicle (→ 22-05, → 29-12) |
| Spill absorbent and nitrile gloves with the fuel | A leaking can at a stop | → 06-07 |

**If you do not have it:** straps and tubs can be improvised. **Fuel containers and propane
mounts cannot**: an unsecured cylinder or an unapproved can is the one corner never to cut.

## When it runs out

- **The cans are the range margin** (→ 01-03). A can spent on the way is range spent: recompute
  the gap at every fuel stop against the trip card's turn-back points.
- **Trip fuel feeds the vehicle only.** Do not let a cold night talk anyone into burning trip fuel
  in other equipment.
- **Resupply:** in a partial disruption, cash and small-town pumps on the way (→ 01-03, → 19-02).
  Every gallon bought is a can kept full.
- **Nothing replaces range.** If the fuel aboard plus the tank cannot close the distance, the
  answer is the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02), not hope.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** this page waits. Storage is → 06-06. Keep cans full and rotated so
  leaving is a loading job, not a shopping trip.
- **B (on the move):** this page is for now. Load plan on the trip card; checks at every stop.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** {{#if has.trailer}}the trailer becomes local hauling: same rules,
  shorter runs, same habit of airing it out before unloading.{{else}}local hauling follows the
  same rules, with shorter runs.{{/if}}
