pages.body:
# Chimneys and creosote (inspection, sweeping, chimney fire)

**What this page is for.** A fireplace or wood stove used every day all winter builds tar in its
chimney faster than anything else. That tar is what starts chimney fires, and in a long emergency
no fire department may come. This page covers how creosote forms, how to inspect and sweep the
flue yourself, how to burn so it stays clean, and what to do in a chimney fire. Running the stove
itself is → 08-08; carbon monoxide alarms are → 08-02.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Chimney fire** (a roar like a freight train in the chimney, flames or heavy sparks from the
>   top, a hot chimney wall): **everyone out first**, then the steps in "Chimney fire" below.
>   **While anything still works, call 911.**
> - **A CO alarm sounds, or people get headache, dizziness or nausea near the fire:** everyone
>   out to fresh air, then → 08-02. A blocked flue sends smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) back into
>   the room, and CO has no smell (CDC; → 29-03).
> - Creosote is what burns in a chimney fire. "Clean chimneys don't catch fire" (CSIA,
>   Preventing Chimney Fires).

## Do this now

1. **Book a professional sweep and inspection while you can.** NFPA 211, the national chimney
   standard, says chimneys, fireplaces and vents are inspected **at least once a year**, and CSIA
   and the US Fire Administration say the same (CSIA, Homeowner FAQs; USFA, Fireplace and Wood
   Stove Safety). A professional now gives you a known clean starting point.
2. **Buy a rod-and-brush kit sized to your flue**, and keep it where the fireplace or stove is.
   If a destination has the wood heat, the kit belongs there.
3. **Keep chimney-fire suppressant flares** (sticks you light and drop in the firebox) beside
   each fireplace or stove.
4. **Learn the flashlight-and-mirror check below**, while a professional's verdict is still
   available to compare yours against.

**Using a fireplace or stove that has not been inspected this year** is a trade-off the household
decides: {{choice DC-21}} → 30-22.

{{#if has.fireplace}}Your home has an indoor fireplace.{{/if}} {{#if has.wood_stove}}Your
household has a wood stove.{{/if}}

## Words used here

- **Firebox:** where the fire burns.
- **Flue:** the passage inside the chimney that carries smoke out.
- **Damper:** the metal plate that opens and closes the flue.
- **Cleanout door:** a small metal door at the bottom of some chimneys, for removing soot.
- **Creosote:** black tar from wood smoke that sticks to the flue. It burns very hot.

## How creosote forms

Wood smoke is unburned fuel: water vapour, a fog of tar, other gases and particles. When the smoke
meets a **cool flue wall, it condenses** and sticks (CSIA). CSIA names three things that speed it
up: restricted air, unseasoned wood, and a cooler-than-normal chimney:

- **Smouldering, air-starved fires**, such as the overnight "turn it way down" habit, or a stove
  packed full for a long burn (CSIA).
- **Unseasoned wood**: energy goes into boiling water, the fire burns cool, and the smoke is wet
  and heavy (CSIA; → 06-03).
- **A cold flue**: an oversized flue, or one on a cold outside wall, and burning resinous softwood
  or trash low and slow.

## The three forms

CSIA describes creosote as crusty and flaky, tar-like and sticky, or shiny and hardened, often all
three in one chimney, and **all of it highly combustible** (CSIA, Preventing Chimney Fires). Sweeps
call these stages 1 to 3:

| Stage | Looks like | Removal |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Light, flaky, sooty dust | An ordinary brush takes it off. This is what routine sweeping keeps to |
| **2** | Crusty, tar-like flakes | A brush struggles; crusty deposits that fracture when hit may need rotary cleaning (CSIA) |
| **3: glaze** | Hard, shiny or tacky black glaze, like poured tar that set | Normal brushing will **not** remove it; a professional uses chemical treatment first (CSIA, Homeowner FAQs). With no professional, a flue you may have to stop using for good |

**Never reach stage 3.** Prevention (hot fires, dry wood) is cheap; removing glaze without a
professional is close to impossible (CSIA).

{{figure fig-creosote-stages}}

## Inspecting: flashlight and mirror

Do this **before the first fire of the season**, and again on a fixed day every few weeks while
you burn every day. The scrape test below tells you whether that is often enough.

1. **Cold flue, damper open.** From the firebox, or the cleanout door at the bottom, hold a
   **mirror** angled to see up the flue and shine a **strong flashlight** on it.
2. **What you want to see:** the flue lining with no more than a dusty grey-black film.
3. **Scrape test:** drag a screwdriver along the flue wall. **About 1/8 inch of sooty buildup
   means sweep before the next fire**, sooner if there is any glaze (CSIA, Homeowner FAQs).
   **Shiny, tarry glaze**
   (stage 3): stop using the flue until a professional deals with it; with none available, treat
   it as a flue you may have to give up.
4. **Also look for:** cracked or shifted flue tiles, daylight where there should be none, nests
   or other blockages, stains on the outside brick.

{{figure fig-flue-inspection-mirror}}

{{photo flue-check}}

## Sweeping with a proper brush

- **The kit:** a brush **matched to the flue's shape and size** (wire for a masonry flue, plastic
  for a metal liner) and fibreglass rods that screw together. **Measure the flue first**: a
  wrong-size brush polishes without cleaning.
- **From the top:** on the roof, push the brush on its rods the full length of the flue in
  overlapping strokes. Roof work is its own danger: a harness or rope, **never alone, never on
  ice**.
- **From the bottom:** push the same brush up from the firebox or cleanout. Messier, but no roof.
  Seal the fireplace opening with a sheet taped in place and work the rods through a slit.
- **Afterward:** shovel the fallen creosote out of the cleanout and firebox. It burns: metal
  bucket with a lid, outside, like ashes (→ 06-02).
- **How often:** whenever the scrape test says so. With daily winter burning, expect to sweep
  **in mid-season, not just once a year**.
- Wear a dust mask and goggles: creosote dust is nasty to breathe.

## Burning so the flue stays clean (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices)

- **Hot, lively fires**: flames, not smoulder. EPA: for most appliances a smouldering fire is
  neither safe nor efficient. If the chimney is rolling thick smoke, the flue is being painted
  with fuel.
- **Seasoned wood below 20 percent moisture only** (EPA). The moisture meter goes wherever the
  wood heat is (→ 06-03).
- **No trash, no cardboard, no painted, coated or pressure-treated wood** (EPA). Resinous softwood
  such as pine is fine burned hot and fast, and dangerous burned low and slow.
- **Small hot fires beat one big damped-down fire.** The overnight smoulder makes more creosote
  than anything else. Banking done right: → 06-02. Stove operation: → 08-08.
- **Watch the chimney top from outside**: thin, nearly clear smoke means a clean burn; thick dark
  smoke means a cool, dirty one.

## Chimney fire, when no fire department is coming

You will know it: a **roar like a freight train or a jet** in the flue, flames or dense sparks from
the chimney top, cracking sounds, a hot chimney wall.

1. **Everyone out of the house.** Gather outside, away from the wall the chimney is on. People
   first, house second.
2. **Cut the air.**
   - **Wood stove:** close the air inlets and the door.
   - **Open fireplace:** close the glass doors, or cover the opening with a fire blanket or sheet
     metal if there are none. **Do not close the damper while anything is still burning in the
     firebox**: it pushes the firebox's smoke and CO into the room. A chimney fire dies when it
     cannot breathe.
3. **Chimney-fire suppressant flare**, if you have one: light it and place it in the firebox as
   its instructions say. Its smoke starves the fire all the way up the flue.
4. **Garden hose on the roof and around it**: wet the roof, the eaves, and anywhere embers land.
   **Do not pour water down the flue**: the burst of steam and sudden cooling can crack the flue
   and let fire into the walls. Thermal shock is how chimney fires crack tiles and open a path to
   the house framing (CSIA).
5. **Watch the attic and walls for hours afterward**: a hand on the chimney wall, your nose in the
   attic. Chimney fires relight, and they slowly char the wood framing around the chimney. Keep
   checking, again and again, through the next day.
6. **The flue is now out of use** until it has been inspected bottom to top. A chimney fire burns
   at around 2,000 °F and can melt mortar, crack tiles and collapse liners; a damaged factory-built
   metal chimney must be replaced (CSIA, Preventing Chimney Fires). No fires until damage and
   stage-3 glaze are ruled out.

**While anything still works, the answer is 911.** This procedure is for when it does not. An
extinguisher (→ 29-12) is for a fire that has escaped the firebox into the room, not for the flue.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rod-and-brush kit sized to your flue | The sweep itself | Kept where the fireplace or stove is; measure the flue first |
| A spare brush head | Brushes wear | Wire for masonry, plastic for liners |
| Chimney-fire suppressant flares (two or more per fireplace or stove) | The no-fire-department response | Firebox use, per the instructions |
| Inspection mirror and a strong flashlight | The regular check | Any mechanic's mirror works |
| Moisture meter | Prevention | Also on → 06-03's list |
| Drop cloths, tape, dust mask, goggles | Sweeping from below is filthy | |
| Metal bucket with a lid | Swept creosote and ashes | Never plastic or cardboard |
| Roof safety: harness or rope, ladder standoff | Sweeping from the top | Never alone, never on ice |
| Smoke and CO alarms near every fireplace and stove | Warning of fire and of a blocked flue | → 08-02, → 29-12 |

**If you do not have it:** a heavy chain lowered and rattled, or a weighted sack of straw pulled
through, are the old improvised sweeps. Far worse than a brush and hard on flue tiles, but better
than burning over stage-2 buildup. There is no improvised answer to stage-3 glaze.

## When it runs out

- **Brushes and rods last years; suppressant flares are used once.** Count them per fireplace or
  stove, and restock while stores exist.
- **The real thing you spend is a clean flue.** Every hot, dry, well-seasoned fire spends less of
  it; every smoulder spends more.
- **If the sweep kit is gone,** burn hotter, smaller, drier fires and inspect **more** often, not
  less.
- **The trap:** by late winter nobody wants to sweep. The scrape test does not care.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** professional sweep and inspection every year while you can buy it.
  Buy the kits now.
- **B (on the move):** at an arrival point where nobody has burned recently, the first fire gets
  the flashlight-and-mirror check **first**.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** you are the chimney sweep now. Regular inspection in season,
  sweep when the scrape test says so, and the burning rules above become house rules. Where the
  only wood is light and fast-burning (→ 06-04), the same rules apply even to small fires.

pages.body:
# Cooking on an open fire: fire pit, outdoor fireplace or hearth

**What this page is for.** How to cook real meals over wood: on a fire pit, an outdoor fireplace,
or an indoor fireplace or wood stove built for fire. Coals, heat zones, safe temperatures, and
how to keep allergens and children away from the fire.

> **CAUTION.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window** (→ 30-01). A fire pit, a grill and charcoal are **outdoor equipment** and never come
> inside (→ 08-02, → 29-03). An indoor fireplace or wood stove is the only place fire cooking
> happens inside, and that is a decision card (below). Cooking over live fire with small children
> nearby needs a hard boundary. And **undercooked meat is a serious risk when there is no
> emergency room**: use a thermometer; FoodSafety.gov is clear that colour is not a reliable sign
> of doneness.

## Do this now

1. **Cook over coals, not flames.** Flames scorch the outside and leave the middle raw. Burn down
   to a deep bed of glowing coals first; that is the cooking surface.
2. **Use a thermometer:** **165 °F for all poultry, 160 °F for ground meat and for venison and
   rabbit, 145 °F for whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal with a 3-minute rest**
   (FoodSafety.gov).
3. **Make every fire do several jobs:** cook the meal, boil water (→ 03-04), heat wash water, dry
   boots. Never light a fire for one job (→ 06-04).
4. **Mark a child line** around the fire and enforce it every time (→ 20-02).
5. **If anyone has a food allergy, cook their food first**, in their own marked cookware (procedure
   below, → 02-04).

## Why / how it works

### Coals, not flames

A wood fire has three useful stages:
1. **Flames:** for boiling water fast and for light. Bad for food.
2. **Coals:** steady, controllable heat. **This is where you cook.**
3. **Embers and ash:** dying heat for simmering, keeping food warm and banking the fire (→ 06-02).

Build the fire, let it burn down until the flames die back to a glowing bed, then rake the coals into
zones. Burn only dry, seasoned, untreated wood; wet wood smokes and gives little heat (EPA, Burn
Wise; → 06-03).

### Heat zones: the trick that makes fire cooking work

Rake the coals into:
- **A hot zone** (deep coals) for searing and boiling.
- **A medium zone** (thinner coals) for most cooking.
- **A cool zone** (few or no coals) to move food to when it is getting ahead of you.

Move the **food**, not the fire. That is your stove dial.

{{figure fig-coal-heat-zones}}

### Methods

| Method | What it needs | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Grate over coals** | A grill grate | Everyday cooking, boiling, searing |
| **Dutch oven in or over coals** | Cast iron with a lid | Stews, beans, bread, anything long (→ 07-04) |
| **Tripod and hanging pot** | Chain or tripod | Soup, stock, boiling water in bulk |
| **Directly on coals** | Nothing | Potatoes, onions, foil-wrapped food |
| **Flat stone** | A dry, flat stone | Flatbread; a hot stone is a griddle |
| **Skewers** | Green sticks or metal | Quick protein |
| **Ash baking** | Coals and ash | Root vegetables buried in embers |

### Cold-weather realities

{{#if is.cold_winters}}Your January lows average {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F, so outdoor
cooking in deep cold is the normal case, not the exception.{{else}}Outdoor cooking in cold, wet or
windy weather needs planning.{{/if}}
- **Everything takes longer.** Cold pots, cold food, wind stripping heat. Plan for double.
- **Wind is the enemy.** A windbreak of split wood, blocks or sheet metal cuts cooking time and
  saves real fuel.
- **Prepare inside, cook outside.** Chopping with numb hands is miserable and dangerous.
- **Cook once, eat twice.** Cook big in the cold, reheat on a smaller fire or the kettle (→ 07-06).
- **Keep water off your gloves.** Wet gloves in deep cold are a cold injury (→ 08-05).
- **Light the path.** It is dark early in winter (→ 10-01).

{{photo outdoor-cook-spot}}

### Cooking on an indoor fireplace or wood stove

A built, chimneyed fireplace or wood stove is the one place fire cooking can happen indoors.
It runs under the wood-heat rules on → 08-08, not this page's:
- **CO alarm in the room, working, before the first cooking fire** (→ 29-03). The damper stays
  open for the burn and is **never closed on live coals**: coals make carbon monoxide for hours
  after the flames die (→ 08-08).
- **Cook on coals, not flames:** burn down to a bed, set a Dutch oven on and among the coals
  (→ 07-04) with coals on the lid. Flames up the flue are heat and creosote (tar that builds up in
  chimneys and catches fire, → 06-09), not cooking.
- **Keep the child line.** An indoor hearth tempts small children more, not less.

Two decision cards cover this. **Open-flame cooking indoors** (→ 30-21): {{choice DC-20}}.
**Using a fireplace or stove that has not been inspected this year** (→ 30-22): {{choice DC-21}}.
{{#if has.fireplace}}This household has an indoor fireplace.{{/if}}{{#if has.wood_stove}} This
household has a wood stove.{{/if}}

### Food safety without a fridge

- **Use a thermometer.** Appearance and colour do not reliably show doneness (FoodSafety.gov).
- **Poultry 165 °F. Ground meat, venison and rabbit 160 °F. Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and
  veal 145 °F plus a 3-minute rest. Fish 145 °F** (FoodSafety.gov).
- **Never partly cook food to finish later.** That is how you grow bacteria.
- **Cool leftovers fast.** In winter, use the cold as a refrigerator (→ 04-09), with a
  thermometer, and do not let food freeze and thaw over and over.
- **Wash hands and surfaces** with what water you have (→ 13-02). A stomach illness in a baby, an
  elder or someone with a chronic condition is an emergency with no medical care (→ 12-05).

### Food allergies at the fire: the procedure

One fire, one grate, one pot is the classic cross-contact setup ("cross-contact" means a trace
of an allergen getting onto safe food). With no ambulance, it is the biggest cooking risk for an
allergic person. Run it the same way every time, numbered so anyone at the fire can follow it:
{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}This household has a food allergy on record (→ 02-04).{{/if}}

1. **The allergic person's food cooks FIRST**, in clean cookware from their own **colour-marked
   pot-and-utensil set**, before anything else touches the heat.
2. **Serve it and cover it** before any of the household's allergens enter the cooking area.
3. **Their utensils are washed and racked separately.** The stirring spoon is never shared, not
   once.
4. **When shared heat cannot be avoided** (one grate, one lid), lay **foil** as a barrier between
   the shared metal and their food.
5. **Wash order: their gear first, in clean water**, never after allergen cookware has been
   through it.
6. **When one pot must feed everyone**, the whole meal is built **only from ingredients safe for
   the allergic person**. There is no "take their portion out before the sauce goes in."
7. **Hands are washed** between handling any allergen and handling their food.

The zero-contact alternative, a verified pouch prepared in its own pouch, is on → 07-07.

### Children and fire

Whether children help at the fire (tending, cooking, carrying hot water) is part of the
household's worksheet on children and dangerous jobs (→ 30-25): {{choice DC-24}}.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy grill grate that fits your fire pit or fireplace | The core cooking surface | Cast iron or heavy steel |
| Cast-iron Dutch oven with legs and a flat, rimmed lid | The most versatile fire cookware | Also bakes (→ 07-04) |
| Cast-iron skillet and griddle | Everyday cooking | Nearly indestructible |
| Large stockpot with lid | Boiling water in bulk | |
| **Instant-read thermometer**, and a spare | Food safety | Cheap, essential |
| Long tongs, spatula, poker | Reach without leaning over fire | Long is safer |
| Heavy leather or welding gloves | Handling hot iron | Two pairs |
| Tripod and chain, or grate supports | Hanging pots | Height is heat control |
| Windbreak (sheet metal or blocks) | Faster cooking, less fuel | |
| **Colour-marked cookware set**, if anyone has a food allergy | Cross-contact control | Stored apart (→ 02-04) |
| Fire extinguisher and a water bucket | Cooking fires happen | Within reach (→ 29-12) |
| Battery CO alarm, for any indoor hearth | CO | → 08-02 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **An oven rack makes a good grill grate. Not a refrigerator shelf:** many are plated with
  metals that give off toxic fumes over fire.
- **Flat stones as griddles, dry ones only:** wet or porous rock can crack or burst when heated.
- Green hardwood sticks as skewers and pot supports.
- Foil for wrapping food in coals; a metal sheet as a windbreak.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** this is a firewood question (→ 06-04). An open fire is the **least** fuel-efficient
  way you have to cook.
- **Ration:** move everyday cooking to a **rocket stove** (→ 07-02), which uses **much less
  wood** than an open fire for the same cooking; keep the open fire for
  big-batch cooking, boiling volume, and when you want the heat anyway.
- **Resupply or substitute:** solar cooking in summer (→ 07-03) costs no fuel; propane (→ 07-05)
  for speed and bad weather; the kettle (→ 07-06) wherever there is stored power.
- **The efficiency stack:** windbreak, a lid on every pot, coals not flames, and batch cooking
  together can cut wood use by more than half, which is the same as doubling your woodpile.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** set up the outdoor spot properly: grate, windbreak, work surface, child line.
  Smoke and cooking smells advertise that you have food (→ 14-03).
- **B (moving):** small, contained fires only; a grate and a pot travel well. Check fire danger
  before lighting anything in dry country (→ 17-05).
- **C (establishing):** build a roofed outdoor kitchen with a windbreak, then work toward a vented
  indoor stove for winter.

pages.body:
# Rocket stoves, hayboxes and fuel-efficient cooking

**What this page is for.** How to cook more food on less wood: the rocket stove, the "haybox"
that finishes cooking with no fuel at all, the vacuum flask, and the small habits that add up.

> **CAUTION.** A rocket stove is a **fuel-burning appliance**: it makes carbon monoxide (CO), an
> invisible gas that kills (→ 29-03). It stays **outdoors**, never in a closed room, tent or
> garage, unless it is a stove designed, installed and vented for indoor use (CDC, Carbon Monoxide
> Poisoning; → 08-02). It gets extremely hot and tips easily: with children around, where you put
> it matters as much as how well it burns. And **dry kidney-type beans must be boiled hard before
> any slow or haybox cooking** (below).

## Do this now

1. **Get or build a rocket stove.** For everyday cooking it uses **much less wood** than an
   open fire: the biggest fuel saving you can make (→ 06-04).
2. **Feed it small:** twigs, sticks and split scraps, fuel you would not bother putting on a
   fireplace.
3. **Always put a lid on the pot.** It is the biggest free saving there is.
4. **Set it on a level, non-combustible surface**, out of the wind, away from where children run.
5. **Make a haybox** (an insulated box for a hot pot) this week. It costs nothing.

## Why / how it works

### Why a rocket stove is so much better

A rocket stove is an **insulated L- or J-shaped burn chamber**. Three things happen:
1. **The fire is contained**, so heat goes into the pot instead of the sky.
2. **The insulated chamber runs very hot**, so it burns the smoky gases from the wood too: more
   complete burning, less smoke, more heat from the same wood (the principle EPA describes for
   efficient wood burning; EPA, Burn Wise).
3. **The short vertical chimney makes a strong draft**, pulling air through the fuel; that is the
   "rocket" roar.

A handful of sticks boils a pot of water. An open fire loses most of its heat to the air. Expect
**a real saving** over an open fire in practice, but not the "ten times" that gets
repeated. Plan your woodpile on that basis (→ 06-04). With a lid, a windscreen and a
haybox on top, the saving grows further.

{{figure fig-rocket-stove-cutaway}}

### Where the fuel goes: the efficiency stack

Every one of these is free and they add up:

| Habit | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Lid on the pot** | Large: the biggest single free saving |
| **Rocket stove instead of open fire** | Very large |
| **Windbreak** | Large, especially in winter |
| **Dry, seasoned, split-small fuel** | Large (wet wood wastes its heat boiling off water; University of Missouri Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating; → 06-03) |
| **Pot sized to the stove** | Moderate |
| **One fire, many jobs** | Large |
| **Soak beans and grains first** | Large: cuts boiling time a lot |
| **Haybox finishing** (below) | Very large for slow-cooked food |
| **Turn it off early**: let held heat finish the job | Moderate |

### The haybox: the cheapest trick there is

Bring food to a **full rolling boil, right through the pot, not just at the edges**, then move the
covered pot into a heavily insulated box: blankets, straw, crumpled paper, or a cooler stuffed
with towels. It keeps cooking for hours **with no fuel**. Stews, grains, soups and soaked beans
finish well this way. **Boil hard, then insulate.** It also keeps food hot for people eating at
different times.

{{figure fig-haybox}}

**Two rules the box does not forgive:**
- **Dry kidney beans (and other dry beans of the same family: red, white, pinto, black): soak at
  least 5 hours, THROW AWAY the soak water, then boil in fresh water for at least 30 minutes
  BEFORE the box (FDA). Never cook dry beans from raw in a haybox or any slow, low-heat method.**
  Raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a natural toxin (phytohaemagglutinin): **as few as 4 or
  5 raw beans can cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea** within 1 to 3 hours, and slow cookers,
  which are what a haybox becomes after the first minutes, do not get hot enough to destroy it
  (FDA, Bad Bug Book). Canned beans are already
  safe; dry beans from storage (→ 04-03) are not until boiled.
- **The box must keep food hot, above 140 °F.** Bacteria multiply fast in the "danger zone"
  between 40 and 140 °F (CDC, Preventing Food Poisoning). **Check with a thermometer before
  serving.** Food still above 140 °F is fine; food that has just dropped below it is **reheated
  to 165 °F** before serving (CDC); food that has sat below 140 °F for **more than 2 hours** is
  thrown out (CDC's 2-hour rule). An overnight haybox has spent hours in the danger zone. It is
  not breakfast.

### The vacuum flask: the haybox's twin

A good stainless vacuum flask, preheated with hot water and filled full, keeps water **hot** for
many hours, less if it is part-empty or was not preheated. The label states how hot after how
long. Boil once in the morning, fill the flasks, and pour from them all day:
- Freeze-dried pouches with a longer rest (→ 07-07), hot drinks, instant foods, hot-water bottles.
- **Flask water is hot, not boiling.** Not for directions that require boiling water, and not
  for sanitising.

One boil instead of three is a large saving with any heat source: kettle (→ 07-06), rocket stove,
propane or fire.

### Buying or building

- **Buying:** a manufactured rocket stove is inexpensive and sturdy.
- **Building:** the classic homemade version is a large can with a smaller can or pipe as the burn
  chamber and wood ash or vermiculite packed between them as insulation; masonry versions use
  brick or block. What matters: **insulation around the burn chamber**, a **short chimney**, and a
  **shelf** so fuel feeds in sideways while air passes underneath.
- **Have both** if you can: one bought, one improvised, and the knowledge to build another.

### Safety with children

- **Stability first.** A rocket stove with a full pot is top-heavy and very hot. Put it on level,
  non-combustible ground where nobody runs past.
- **The chimney is very hot and does not look it.** Teach the boundary (→ 20-02).
- **Never indoors, never in a tent, never in a garage** (→ 08-02).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Manufactured rocket stove | The biggest fuel saving you can buy | Steel, with a pot support |
| Pots with **tight lids** | Free efficiency | Sized to the stove |
| Windscreen | Big saving outdoors | Sheet metal or foil-covered board |
| Haybox: a cooler or box and blankets | Fuel-free finishing | Any cooler works |
| Stainless vacuum flasks | One boil covers the day | Preheat before filling |
| Hatchet or small saw for kindling | Rocket stoves eat small fuel | → 16-01 |
| Heat-proof gloves and a stable base | Burns and tipping | Non-combustible surface |
| Materials for a second stove (cans, insulation) | Spare and skill | Practise building one now |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Cans, buckets and ash or vermiculite** build a working rocket stove for almost nothing.
- **Bricks or concrete blocks** stack into a rocket-style stove in minutes with no tools.
- A **hobo stove** (a large can with air holes) is far better than an open fire, if cruder.
- Any cooler, box or pile of blankets becomes a haybox; any insulated jug or wrapped pot stands in
  for a flask, for shorter times.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the stove does not run out; steel slowly burns through with heavy use, which is why
  a spare or the skill to build one matters.
- **Ration:** this page **is** the rationing plan for wood (→ 06-04). Stove, lid, windbreak and
  haybox together make everyday cooking cheap in fuel.
- **Resupply:** solar cooking (→ 07-03) in summer costs nothing; the open fire (→ 07-01) when you
  want the heat as well.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** everyday outdoor cooking; the open fire for batch cooking and boiling volume. A
  rocket stove also makes far less smoke, so it draws less attention (→ 14-03).
- **B (moving):** a small rocket or twig stove is ideal: it burns sticks you gather, so you carry
  no fuel.
- **C (establishing):** build a masonry version and a haybox. Fuel efficiency matters more when you
  cut all your own wood.

pages.body:
# Solar cookers

**What this page is for.** Cooking with sunlight: no fuel, no smoke, no carbon monoxide. What a
solar cooker does well, what it cannot do, and how to build one from boxes and foil.

> **CAUTION.** Solar cooking is **free but slow and depends on the weather**, and it does not
> excuse you from food safety: meat must still reach safe internal temperatures, checked with a
> thermometer (165 °F poultry, 160 °F ground meat, venison and rabbit, 145 °F whole cuts of beef,
> pork, lamb and veal with a 3-minute rest; FoodSafety.gov). Do not make a solar cooker your only plan for anything that must be cooked
> through.

## Do this now

1. **Use it all summer** for anything slow (beans, grains, stews, bread, rehydrating dried food)
   and save every stick of wood for winter (→ 06-04).
2. **Start early.** Solar cooking needs the middle of the day; food goes in by mid-morning.
3. **Use dark, thin-walled pots with lids**, under a clear cover.
4. **Turn it to face the sun every hour or two**, unless the design is very wide-angle.
5. **Check meat with a thermometer**, always.

## Why / how it works

Sunlight passes through a clear cover, is soaked up by dark surfaces, and the heat is trapped:
a greenhouse in a box. **Reflectors** bounce extra light in; **insulation** keeps the heat from
escaping. A decent box cooker reaches **slow-oven temperatures** on a clear day (check it
with an oven thermometer). Plenty for stews, beans, rice, bread and casseroles; not searing heat.

### What it is good for

| Great | Poor |
|---|---|
| Beans, lentils, grains, rice | Searing or frying |
| Stews, soups, casseroles | Fast cooking on demand |
| Bread and baked goods | Cloudy days, winter, evenings |
| Rehydrating dried food (→ 07-07) | Large amounts quickly |
| **Heating water** (below) | Anything you need in 20 minutes |
| Keeping food hot | |

### Your sun

- **Summer** in most of the US has long days and strong sun: from late spring to early fall a
  solar cooker can carry a real share of the cooking. Your home gets about
  **{{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }} peak sun hours a day in June** and
  **{{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} in December** ("peak sun hours" are explained on → 09-02).
- **Winter** is weak almost everywhere north of the southern tier: short days, low sun, cold air
  fighting you. Treat solar as a **seasonal fuel-saver**, not a year-round method. The further
  south you are, the longer its season.
- **The point is shifting fuel across the year:** every meal cooked by sun in summer is wood or
  propane you still have in winter.

### Water: an important second use

Heat makes water safe, and a solar cooker can heat water without fuel. Keep the methods apart
(→ 29-06 explains the water words):
- **CDC's solar disinfection method (SODIS)** uses **clear plastic bottles laid on their side in
  full sun for 6 hours (sunny) or 2 days (cloudy)**, and works on **clear water only** (CDC, How to
  Make Water Safe in an Emergency; → 03-04).
- **A solar cooker** heats water faster and hotter. If you rely on heat rather than a rolling boil,
  use a **water pasteurisation indicator (WAPI)**: a small tube of wax that melts when the water
  has been hot enough. Do not guess.
- **When in doubt, boil** (→ 03-04). The fuel saving is not worth a sick child.

### Types

- **Box cooker:** an insulated box with a clear lid and reflectors. The best all-rounder; holds
  heat.
- **Panel cooker:** reflective panels aimed at a dark pot inside a clear bag. Cheap, folds flat.
- **Parabolic cooker:** a dish focusing sunlight to a point. Hottest and fastest, but needs
  constant aiming and is **an eye and burn hazard**. Not for use around small children.

### Build one

A working box cooker: **a cardboard box inside a larger box**, the gap packed with crumpled
newspaper or wool; the inside lined with **aluminium foil**; a **dark pot** inside; and a **clear
plastic or glass lid**. Add foil-covered flaps as reflectors. It costs almost nothing and works,
and it is a good project to build with children (→ 20-03).

{{figure fig-solar-box-cooker}}

**Practical notes:** black pots with lids; do not open it to look (each peek loses heat); put an
oven thermometer inside so you know what you are getting; expect two to four times the usual
cooking time.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A solar oven, bought or built | Fuel-free summer cooking | Box type for capacity |
| Dark, thin-walled pots with tight lids | Soak up and hold heat | Black enamel or dark cast aluminium |
| Oven thermometer | Know the real temperature | Cheap |
| Instant-read food thermometer | Same safety rules as any cooking | → 07-01 |
| Water pasteurisation indicator (WAPI) | Shows water got hot enough | Cheap, reusable |
| Foil, cardboard, clear plastic sheet | Build and repair reflectors and covers | |
| Oven bags or a clear dome | Traps heat around the pot | Big gain |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Two cardboard boxes, newspaper, foil and a clear lid** make a working oven.
- A **car windshield sunshade** becomes a panel cooker with a little shaping.
- Any dark pot; a glass bowl or clear plastic bag as the cover.
- Reflective emergency blankets make good reflectors.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** nothing runs out but the sun and the season. Foil and plastic covers wear out in
  sunlight; keep spares.
- **Ration:** nothing to ration. Use it whenever the sun is out, so you can save wood and propane
  for when it is not.
- **Resupply:** the rocket stove (→ 07-02) and the open fire (→ 07-01) on cloudy days and in
  winter.
- **The yearly rotation:** solar in summer, wood in winter, propane held in reserve. That is how
  a limited fuel supply lasts a year rather than a season.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** a yard or balcony with sun is enough, and it makes **no smoke and no smell**,
  which draws less attention than a fire (→ 14-03).
- **B (moving):** a folding panel cooker weighs almost nothing, but you rarely have the hours
  while moving.
- **C (establishing):** excellent: space, sun, and a strong reason to save wood.

# Dutch-oven cooking and baking without an oven

**What this page is for.** The cast-iron Dutch oven: how to control its heat with coals, how to
bake bread with no kitchen oven and no yeast, and how to keep cast iron for a lifetime.

> **CAUTION.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window** (→ 30-01). Charcoal for Dutch-oven baking is **outdoor only**: it gives off carbon
> monoxide, an invisible gas that kills (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning; → 29-03). Cast iron full of
> hot food is **heavy and stays hot a long time**: a serious burn and crush risk around children.
> And baking does not exempt meat from safe temperatures (→ 07-01).

## Do this now

1. **Own at least one cast-iron Dutch oven**, the "camp" style with three legs and a flat, rimmed
   lid: the most versatile single cooking pot for off-grid life.
2. **Learn one bread you can make from stored staples** and practise it now, while a failure is
   only a bad loaf.
3. **Coals on the lid, not just underneath.** That is what turns a pot into an oven.
4. **Dry and oil your cast iron** after every use; rust is the only thing that kills it.
5. **If anyone has a food allergy**, bake their food first, in their own marked pan (→ 07-01,
   → 02-04).

## Why / how it works

### Why cast iron

It works on coals, in a fireplace, on a rocket stove, on a grate or on a stove; it holds and
evens out heat; it lasts generations; and it needs no electricity, no non-stick coating and no
spare parts. **Cast iron is the cookware that outlives the crisis.**

A **camp Dutch oven** (three legs, flat lid with a raised rim) is the key piece: the legs hold it
above coals, and the rimmed lid holds coals **on top**, so heat comes from both directions, like a
real oven.

### Controlling the temperature with coals

A starting rule, from the Missouri Department of Conservation (Dutch Oven Cooking 101); check
with a thermometer, because wind, cold and the brand of charcoal all change it:
- **Total charcoal briquettes = 2 × the oven's diameter in inches, for about 325 °F.** A 12-inch
  oven → **24 briquettes**; a 10-inch → 20.
- **For baking, two-thirds of them on the lid and one-third underneath.** 12-inch oven →
  **16 on the lid, 8 underneath.** The other way round burns the bottom before the top browns.
- **Add or remove 2 briquettes to change the heat by about 25 °F.** For about 350 °F in a
  12-inch oven, 26.
- **In cold or wind, expect to need more**, and check with the thermometer.

| Job | Heat pattern |
|---|---|
| **Baking** (bread, biscuits, cake) | Most coals **on the lid**, few underneath |
| **Roasting** | Even, top and bottom |
| **Simmering, stewing** | Mostly underneath, few or none on top |
| **Frying** | All underneath |

{{figure fig-dutch-oven-coals}}

**Turn it to avoid hot spots:** every 15 minutes, lift the oven and turn it a quarter turn, and
turn the lid a quarter turn the other way (Missouri Department of Conservation). That habit is
the difference between burnt and even.

**Keep coals coming:** briquettes last about 30 minutes (Missouri Department of Conservation);
wood coals less.
For long bakes, keep a second fire making fresh coals (→ 06-02).

**Use a thermometer** rather than trusting coal counts: an oven thermometer inside the pot, an
instant-read for meat.

### Bread without an oven, or without yeast

Bread matters more than people expect: calories, morale, and a use for the stored grain and flour
(→ 04-03).
- **Yeast breads** need yeast: stock it, or keep a **sourdough starter** alive (a living mix of
  flour and water that leavens bread indefinitely and can be shared with neighbours).
- **Soda breads and quick breads** need only baking soda or baking powder: cheap and long-lasting.
- **Flatbreads:** flour, water, salt, a hot skillet or flat stone. No leavening, fast, reliable.
  **This is the bread to know.**
- **Bannock and ash cakes:** dough cooked on a stick, in a skillet, or straight in clean embers.

### Other ways to bake

- **A skillet and lid** with coals on top stands in for a Dutch oven.
- **Two skillets** clamped rim to rim make an improvised oven.
- **A metal box or tin in the coals** bakes well.
- **The haybox** (→ 07-02) will not bake, but it finishes anything simmered.

### Care

- **Season:** a thin coat of oil, heated until it bonds to the iron; repeat. Well-seasoned iron is
  nearly non-stick.
- **Clean** with hot water and a brush or chain-mail scrubber rather than heavy soap scrubbing;
  dry at once over heat, then wipe with oil.
- **Never store it damp.**
- **Wood ash** is a good scouring powder for greasy iron (→ 06-02).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Camp Dutch oven (legs, rimmed lid), 10 to 12 inch | The core off-grid oven | Bigger for a larger household |
| Cast-iron skillet(s) with a lid | Everyday cooking, flatbread | 10 to 12 inch |
| Lid lifter and heavy gloves | Lifting a lid covered in coals | A hook is safer than pliers |
| Long tongs or a small shovel for coals | Placing coals | |
| Oven thermometer and instant-read thermometer | Real temperatures | Cheap |
| Charcoal briquettes, stored dry | Predictable, countable heat | **Outdoor only** |
| Lid stand or trivet | A place to set a hot lid | Keeps ash out of food |
| Flour, salt, baking soda and powder, yeast | Bread from stored staples | Rotate (→ 04-03) |
| Sourdough starter | Renewable leavening | |
| Marked cookware, if anyone has a food allergy | Cross-contact control | → 02-04 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- Any **heavy pot with a tight lid** works as a Dutch oven: bury it in coals with coals on the lid.
- **Flat, dry stones** as griddles for flatbread.
- A **metal biscuit tin or ammunition can** as a small oven in coals.
- Green sticks for bannock; children can cook their own with an adult at the fire (→ 20-02).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** cast iron does not run out. The consumables are **fuel** (→ 06-04), **charcoal** and
  **leavening**.
- **Ration:** bake in batches while the coals are hot: bread, then a stew, then wash water, all
  from one fire.
- **Resupply:** a sourdough starter replaces bought yeast for good; flatbread needs no leavening
  at all.
- **Morale:** fresh bread in a hard winter is worth more than its calories (→ 21-02).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** a Dutch oven in fire-pit or fireplace coals is your oven. Practise one loaf now.
- **B (moving):** cast iron is **heavy**: one skillet at most; flatbread on a hot stone travels.
- **C (establishing):** a Dutch oven and an outdoor fire pit cover all baking; a masonry oven later
  if you settle long-term.

pages.body:
# Propane and camp stoves, and why they stay outdoors

**What this page is for.** Choosing and using camp stoves and grills safely, making a limited
fuel supply last, and lighting a gas range when the power is out. It starts with the rule that
keeps people alive in winter outages.

> **SAFETY.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
> mitigation that works every time (→ 30-01). **The same applies to camp stoves and grills built
> for outdoor use:** CDC says never use a portable gas camp stove indoors, never burn charcoal
> indoors, and **never use a gas oven or range to heat your home** (CDC, Carbon Monoxide
> Poisoning; CDC, Winter Weather). Carbon monoxide (CO) has no smell and no colour (→ 29-03).
> "Cracking a window" does not make it safe. **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open
> flame or a running appliance** (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Cook outdoors** with any camp stove, grill or charcoal, including in winter. Build a
   sheltered outdoor spot (windbreak, roof or tarp, light) so weather is never the reason to bring
   it inside.
2. **Choose propane or white gas over butane** where winters are cold: butane canisters lose
   pressure badly in the cold and may barely work; propane keeps working, more weakly.
3. **Store cylinders outdoors**, upright and secured, away from doors, windows and anything that
   sparks (→ 06-06).
4. **Keep battery CO alarms** on every level and where people sleep (→ 08-02).
5. **Count what you have:** {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} 20-lb cylinders and
   {{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }} 1-lb cylinders on hand. If the same tanks also feed a heater or a
   generator, decide now how much is for cooking (→ 06-05).
6. **Save propane for what it does best:** fast boiling, bad weather, illness, and cooking when
   the kettle (→ 07-06) is down and a fire is not practical.

## Why / how it works

### The single rule

Every appliance that burns fuel makes carbon monoxide. Appliances built for **outdoor use** have
no venting and no oxygen-depletion sensor, because they assume unlimited fresh air. Indoors, in a
closed room, in winter, with a family asleep, that assumption kills.

**The tempting scenario:** it is bitterly cold, the power is out, and cooking outside is
miserable. "Just ten minutes, with the window open." That is how people die, and it is worth
deciding **now**, in advance, that the answer is always no. Set things up so the temptation never
comes: a sheltered outdoor cooking spot with a windbreak, a roof or tarp, and a light. An
afternoon's work in fall removes the risk in winter.

{{photo sheltered-cook-spot}}

### Choosing a stove

The fuels are explained on → 29-01.

| Type | Fuel | Cold performance | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Two-burner propane camp stove** | 1-lb cylinders, or a 20-lb tank with an adapter hose | **Fair to good** | The best all-round backup for a family |
| **Single-burner propane** | 1-lb cylinders | Fair to good | Compact, cheap, good as a spare |
| **Butane canister stove** | Butane cartridges | **Poor in the cold** | Fine in summer; unreliable exactly when you need it |
| **Liquid-fuel (white gas) stove** | White gas or multi-fuel | **Excellent** | Best in deep cold; needs priming and care |
| **Alcohol stove** | Denatured alcohol | Moderate | Simple, quiet, low output |
| **Wood or twig stove** | Sticks | Good | No fuel to carry (→ 07-02) |

A two-burner propane stove with a **20-lb tank and adapter hose** gives a great many cooking
hours cheaply, **outdoors**. If the same tank also runs a heater or a generator, one tank cannot
serve both on the same night.

### Getting the most from the fuel

- **Lids on pots**, always (→ 07-02).
- **A windscreen:** outdoors, wind can double fuel use.
- **Size the flame to the pot:** flames licking up the sides are wasted fuel.
- **Simmer once it is up to temperature;** do not keep it at a hard boil.
- **A 20-lb tank and adapter** is cheaper per meal than 1-lb cylinders.

### Propane in deep cold

Propane feeds a stove by its vapour pressure, and vapour pressure falls as it gets colder. A
**1-lb cylinder** chilled well below freezing, and chilling itself further as it is used, loses
pressure: the flame weakens, and a part-full cylinder can sputter out while still holding fuel. A
20-lb tank does better (more mass, more liquid) but weakens too in hard cold. Keeping a cylinder
warmer (inside a coat, never near a flame) helps a little.

**Do not plan a bitter-cold night around a camp stove.** In deep cold, the better answers are an
electric kettle indoors (→ 07-06: no flame, no CO) or a wood fire outdoors. Propane is the
mild-weather and shoulder-season fast burner; in deep cold it is a backup, with a warmed cylinder,
a windbreak and short boil-only sessions. White-gas stoves are the cold-weather exception.

### Grills

A propane or charcoal grill is a real outdoor cooking appliance, and most households have one.
**Same rule: outdoors only, always.** A grill in a garage with the door open has killed whole
families.

### Cylinders: the three decisions

- **A cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house** is a decision card (→ 30-03). Propane is
  heavier than air: a leak pools at floor level and finds a flame. The household's choice:
  {{choice DC-02}}.
- **Refilling 1-lb cylinders from a bigger tank** is a decision card (→ 30-04). Makers say
  disposable cylinders are never refilled. The household's choice: {{choice DC-03}}.
- **Storing propane or other fuel in an attached garage** is a decision card (→ 30-06). The
  household's choice: {{choice DC-05}}.

> **Before the collapse:** fire codes limit how much propane may be stored in or near a home
> (NFPA 58, Liquefied Petroleum Gas Code), and many rental agreements forbid it indoors entirely.

### Lighting a gas range when the power is out

{{#if has.gas_any}}This household has natural gas or propane service, so this matters to you.{{else}}This
matters at any destination or shelter with gas service.{{/if}} In most electrical outages **natural
gas keeps flowing**, and a propane tank on site keeps feeding the house, so a gas range is often
a working stove when the lights are not.
- **The electric igniters will be dead. Light the burner with a match: flame FIRST.** Strike the
  match or click the lighter, hold it at the burner, and **only then** turn the gas on. Gas on
  first while you fumble for a light pools gas around your hand. If a burner does not light within
  a couple of seconds, gas off, wait for it to clear, try again.
- **Most modern gas ovens will not work without power.** Their gas valve depends on an electric
  igniter and control board, and they cannot be safely lit by hand. Plan on **stovetop only**;
  bake in a Dutch oven outdoors (→ 07-04). Check your range's manual.
- **A range is for cooking, never for heat** (CDC). Keep sessions to cooking length, open the
  kitchen to the rest of the house, and keep the CO alarm on that level working.
- **Open-flame cooking indoors** (a match-lit range, an indoor hearth) is a decision card
  (→ 30-21). The household's choice: {{choice DC-20}}.

### Safe temperatures

A camp stove does not change the numbers: **165 °F poultry, 160 °F ground meat, venison and
rabbit, 145 °F whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal with a 3-minute rest** (FoodSafety.gov). Use a thermometer (→ 07-01).

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Two-burner propane camp stove | Cooks real family meals | Simple, repairable models |
| 20-lb tank(s) and an adapter hose | Cheapest fuel per meal | Stored outdoors (→ 06-06) |
| 1-lb propane cylinders | Portable; go-bags | See the refill card (→ 30-04) |
| A spare stove on a different fuel | Redundancy | White gas for deep cold |
| **Battery CO alarms** | Non-negotiable near any burning fuel | → 08-02 |
| Windscreen | Big outdoor fuel saving | Foil or sheet metal |
| Sheltered outdoor cooking spot (roof or tarp, windbreak, light) | Removes the reason to cook indoors | Build it before winter |
| Fire extinguisher | Cooking fires | → 29-12 |
| Instant-read thermometer | Food safety | → 07-01 |
| Spare regulator, hose, O-rings | Stoves fail at the fittings | Cheap insurance |
| Long matches or a lighter | Lighting a range or stove with no igniter | |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Grill tanks** from abandoned grills are a common find, often part-full. Check the valve and
  the date stamp; treat any that hiss as leaking.
- A **rocket stove** (→ 07-02) does everything a camp stove does, on free fuel, more slowly.
- **Alcohol stoves** can be made from cans. **Yellow-bottle fuel-line antifreeze is methanol. It
  burns, with three cautions: the flame is nearly invisible in daylight (never refuel a stove that
  might still be lit; pour water on it first); its vapour and fumes are toxic (outdoors only); and
  swallowed, as little as 2 tablespoons can kill a child, and blindness is common and often
  permanent** (MedlinePlus, Methanol Poisoning). If anyone swallows it: Poison Control,
  1-800-222-1222, and do not make them vomit. **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel,
  medications or chlorine products** (→ 30-01): locked, labelled, never in a drink bottle
  (→ 12-17). Red-bottle (isopropyl) antifreeze is a poor, sooty fuel.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** count cooking days against the share of propane that is really for cooking, and
  write it on → 23-02. If heat or a generator also needs the tanks, cooking's share may be days,
  not a season.
- **Ration:** propane for **speed and weather**: a hot meal in a blizzard, boiling water when it
  is dangerous to be outside long, cooking for someone sick. Everyday boiling goes to the kettle
  (→ 07-06) or wood (→ 07-02).
- **Hold a reserve.** Decide now how much propane you will **never** spend on convenience.
- **Resupply:** wood (→ 06-04) is renewable; propane is not. Plan the change before you are forced
  into it.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** kettle for everyday boils, propane for speed and weather, wood for volume, solar
  in summer. Build the sheltered outdoor spot so winter never forces a bad decision.
- **B (moving):** a small propane or white-gas stove; **never** run it inside a vehicle or tent,
  including to warm up. White gas wins in deep cold.
- **C (establishing):** propane becomes precious and hard to replace; wood becomes the main fuel.
  Bring the adapter hose and any remaining tanks.

pages.body:
# Electric kettle cooking from stored power

**What this page is for.** Using an electric kettle (and, optionally, an induction plate) run from
a power station or solar as an everyday stove in an outage: what it can cook, how much power it
takes, and when to stop and move to another method.

> **CAUTION.** This is the one cooking method that is safe **indoors**: no flame, no fuel, no
> carbon monoxide (CO). Every fuel-burning cooker stays outdoors (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning;
> → 08-02). The cautions here are electrical and thermal: a kettle draws a lot of power and must
> be budgeted against the station like any big load (→ 09-16), and a just-boiled kettle is a scald
> hazard. Pour at the counter; never carry boiling water over children.

## Do this now

1. **Read your kettle's rating plate** for its watts (→ 29-14), and your power station's label for
   its maximum continuous output. The kettle's watts must be **below** the station's output.
   Most kettles draw 1,200 to 1,800 W.
2. **Medical loads come first.** If anyone depends on a refrigerated medicine, oxygen or CPAP,
   that device's power is never the one spent on the kettle (→ 09-10).
3. **Boil in full litres, not cupfuls.** One litre (about 4 cups) covers two pouches whose labels
   each ask for 2 cups (→ 07-07).
   Batching is free efficiency.
4. **Boil in the afternoon, from the day's solar surplus**, not at night from stored charge
   (→ 09-16).
5. **Fill vacuum flasks with every surplus boil** (→ 07-02): hot water banked is a boil you do not
   pay for twice.
6. **When the stations are low and there is no sun, stop** and move to the next method (→ 07-05,
   → 07-01, → 07-02), outdoors.

## Why / how it works

### Why a kettle, of all things

The general rule for stored power is **never make heat with electricity**: heat is what drains a
battery fastest (→ 09-01). Boiling small amounts of water is the exception, because a kettle puts
nearly all its energy straight into the water, and because much emergency food needs **only hot
water**: freeze-dried pouches (→ 04-19), instant staples, hot drinks, washing-up water.

**And it works in the cold, indoors.** Every other method in this section means standing over a
flame outdoors or at a vented hearth. The kettle runs **indoors, silently, with no CO and no fuel**,
in a closed-up room with the family around it.

### The power arithmetic

Words first (→ 29-02): **watts (W)** are how fast something uses power; **watt-hours (Wh)** are how
much energy it uses in total, and how much a battery holds.

- **Heating water takes a fixed amount of energy.** Heating 1 litre from cold tap water to boiling
  takes roughly 100 Wh of heat (physics: about 1.16 Wh per litre per °C). Add kettle and inverter
  losses and **plan on about 135 Wh out of the battery per one-litre boil**, the figure used across
  Section 09 (→ 09-03).
- **A freeze-dried pouch** takes the water on its label; a pouch that asks for 2 cups (about half
  a litre) is roughly half a litre-boil.
- **Boils per full charge ≈ station Wh × 0.85 ÷ 135** (the 0.85 allows for the part of the battery
  you cannot use and inverter losses; → 09-03).

**Your stations:**
{{#each stations as s}}- {{s.model}}: {{s.wh}} Wh → ______ litre-boils per full charge
{{else}}- No power station entered.
{{/each}}
Total: **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh** × 0.85 ÷ 135 = ______ litre-boils per full charge, before
any other load.

**Solar refill** ({{#if has.solar}}your panels total {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W{{else}}no panels
entered{{/if}}; method on → 09-02): daily Wh ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.75. At home that is
{{ gear.solar_w_total }} × {{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }} × 0.75 = ______ Wh on a clear June day,
and {{ gear.solar_w_total }} × {{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} × 0.75 = ______ Wh on a clear
December day. Overcast days give far less, and snow on the panels gives nothing (→ 09-05).

**Measure it once:** boil 1 litre from cold on your station and write the station's own Wh
drop here: ______ Wh (date ______). That number replaces every estimate above.

{{photo kettle-station}}

### What boiling water alone cooks

- **Freeze-dried pouches** (→ 07-07) and anything labelled "add boiling water".
- **Instant staples:** oatmeal, instant rice and potatoes, couscous, quick noodles.
- **Hot drinks:** a big morale item in a cold house.
- **Washing-up and wash water**, including any allergy-safe cookware (→ 02-04).
- **Hot-water bottles** for beds: the same boil, one more job.

It does **not** fry, sear, simmer a pot or bake. For that, see induction below, or the fuel
methods.

### An induction plate: real cooking on stored power

A portable **induction plate** heats the pan directly with a magnetic field. Like the kettle it is
efficient, flameless and safe indoors, and it turns "boiling water only" into eggs, pancakes,
soup from staples and skillet meals. It needs **iron or steel cookware** (a magnet sticks to the
bottom); cast iron works (→ 07-04). Check that its watts fit under your station's output, and count
it like the kettle. It is an optional buy, not a requirement.

### Limits: read these before relying on it

- **One big load at a time.** A kettle at full draw leaves little room on most stations. Kettle
  **or** a furnace blower **or** heavy charging: one after the other, not together.
- **Never on the station that carries a medical device or a medicine fridge** unless you decide
  so deliberately, against that device's needs (→ 09-10).{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}} This
  household has refrigerated medicine.{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}} This household uses CPAP.{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}
  This household uses oxygen.{{/if}}
- **The kettle dies with the stations.** No sun, empty batteries and no generator to recharge
  (→ 09-04) means this method is over until recharge. Keep a **stovetop kettle** that works on
  every fuel.
- **A 12-volt kettle** on a vehicle or station 12 V socket avoids inverter losses but takes far
  longer per litre: background flask-filling only, never dinner.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Electric kettle, stainless inside | The everyday indoor stove | Watts below your station's output |
| Power station(s) | Stored power | → 28-01 |
| Solar panels | Daily refill | → 09-02 |
| Stainless vacuum flasks | One boil serves the day | Routine on → 07-02 |
| Whistling stovetop kettle | Works on every fuel when power is gone | |
| Induction plate (optional) | Real cooking, indoors, no CO | Needs iron or steel pans |
| Measuring cup | Exact water per pouch, no waste | Lives with the pouches (→ 07-07) |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- Any household kettle whose rating plate fits your station.
- A coffee maker or electric skillet works but wastes power; prefer the kettle for anything that
  is really a water job. Check the watts first.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the station charge. Track it in litre-boils (about 135 Wh each) against the day's
  solar; → 09-16 decides which station carries what.
- **Ration:** flask every surplus boil (→ 07-02); cold-water rehydration of true freeze-dried
  pouches uses no energy (→ 07-07); hot drinks are the first thing cut; medical loads are never
  the cut.
- **Resupply:** sun (→ 09-05), a generator run outdoors (→ 09-04), then the fuel methods: propane
  (→ 07-05), wood (→ 07-01, → 07-02), outdoors.
- **In a long event,** electricity from the sun renews daily; propane does not. Use this method as
  long as the sun allows before spending tanks.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the everyday indoor method, all winter, with combustion cooking outdoors as the
  backup.
- **B (moving):** the kettle travels with a station; boil at stops from vehicle charging or sun,
  and cold-rehydrate on the road.
- **C (establishing):** at a destination with a working gas range or hearth, the kettle becomes the
  quiet, fuel-free option rather than the only indoor one.

pages.body:
# Freeze-dried and dehydrated meals: rehydrating them safely

**What this page is for.** How to turn emergency food pouches into safe meals: telling the two
kinds of "just add water" food apart, how much water, how long to wait, cold-water rehydration
when there is no heat, feeding small children, and preparing an allergic person's meal with no
chance of cross-contact.

> **SAFETY.** **Two lines that must never blur.** **Allergy:** if anyone in the household has a
> food allergy, their meal is a **checked pouch prepared in its own pouch with their own marked
> tools**; it never touches the family pot, spoon or counter (→ 02-04; FDA, Food Allergies).
> **Scald:** a just-filled pouch is boiling water in a floppy bag. Stand it in a bowl or pot on a
> hard surface, never on a lap or a sleeping bag, and test the temperature before any child eats
> (→ 12-03). And **only true freeze-dried food may be rehydrated with cold water** (below).

## Do this now

1. **Read the pouch first: two kinds of food wear the same label.**
   - **"Add boiling water, wait" = true freeze-dried:** already cooked before drying; the method
     on this page applies, and cold water works.
   - **"Boil" or "simmer X minutes" = a dehydrated blend** (many bucket kits and "just add water"
     pasta or rice meals): its pasta, beans and textured soy protein are **not pre-cooked**. It
     needs a **real boil on a stove** (→ 07-05, → 07-01). **It is not a cold-water meal**, and a
     kettle pour alone will not make it safe or edible. Note the type in your inventory (→ 04-19).
2. **Water per pouch = the figure on the label.** Products differ; measure it. Extra water is
   wasted energy and soup where you wanted stew.
3. **Boil in batches:** one litre of water is about two pouches (→ 07-06).
4. **Seal the pouch and wait** the time on the label (15 minutes or less for one common maker's
   meals; Mountain House FAQ). Stir once half-way,
   reseal, keep waiting. Opening early gives crunchy centres and loses heat.
5. **The allergic person's pouch first**, with their own marked tools, before any other pouch or
   pot is opened (procedure below).
6. **No way to boil? Cold water works, for true freeze-dried pouches only:** same pouch, cold or
   room-temperature water, **at least twice the label's hot-water time** (one common maker's
   advice; Mountain House FAQ), longer in a cold room; check that the centre is soft. It is safe
   because the food was fully cooked before it was dried; it is just cold and less cheering. **A "boil or simmer" pouch in cold water is
   raw pasta and raw beans: wait for a stove.**

## Why / how it works

### Why true freeze-dried food is safe cold

True freeze-dried meals are cooked, then frozen and dried under vacuum, and sealed; makers of
true freeze-dried meals state that they are pre-cooked (for example, Mountain House FAQ). Kept
intact they keep on the shelf for years. Adding water **reconstitutes** them;
it does not cook them. That is why cold water is safe for them and not for dehydrated blends that
were never cooked.

### In the pouch or in a pot

| | **In the pouch** | **In a pot** |
|---|---|---|
| Dishes and wash water | **None**: the pouch is the bowl | Pot, bowls, spoons (→ 13-02) |
| Cross-contact risk | **No shared surfaces** | The one-pot problem (→ 07-01) |
| Texture | Fair; corners rehydrate unevenly | **Better**: stir, simmer, adjust |
| Portioning | One pouch, fixed | **Easy**: split, thin, stretch |
| Heat in a cold room | Poor; wrap it in a towel | Better under a lid; best in a haybox (→ 07-02) |

**For an allergic person the pouch is a real safety gain.** Prepared in its own bag with its own
tools, a checked meal has no route to the family's food: no shared pot, no shared spoon, no shared
serving surface. That is more control than a shared pot can give.

### The allergic person's pouch: the fixed sequence

{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}This household has a food allergy on record (→ 02-04).{{else}}Use this
sequence for anyone with a food allergy, including a guest.{{/if}}

1. **Checked pouch only.** The label has been read against the person's allergen list and the pouch
   is marked as checked, with the date (→ 04-19). No mark, no meal. Labels can change between
   batches of the same product.
2. **Clean hands**, washed after touching any other food.
3. **Open it with their own marked scissors**, fill with measured boiling water **before** any other
   pouch is opened at that station, stir with **their own spoon only**, seal.
4. **Rest, cool, serve** in the pouch or their own marked bowl. Their tools are washed first, in
   clean water, and kept apart.

{{photo allergy-pouch-kit}}

Allergies on record:
{{#each allergies as a}}- **{{a.member}}**: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}})
{{else}}- None entered.
{{/each}}

Whether the allergic person ever eats unlabeled, traded or scavenged food is a decision card
(→ 30-19). The household's choice: {{choice DC-18}}. Whether the allergy-safe pouches are held as
that person's reserve while everyone else eats other stock first is a second card (→ 30-27). The
household's choice: {{choice DC-26}}.

### Feeding small children

{{#if has.young_child}}This household has a child under 6.{{/if}}
- **Cooling takes time.** Food made with boiling water is still scalding **after** the rest
  time, and longer if wrapped for warmth. Stir to let steam out, taste a test
  spoonful, and check it on your wrist like a bottle.
- **Thin and mash for toddlers:** a splash of warm (not boiling) water and a mash with the spoon
  makes most pouch meals soft. Cut or mash anything chunky; choking rules do not relax in an
  emergency (→ 20-01).
- **Serve from their own bowl**, not from spoons going in and out of the family pouch.
  Half-eaten rehydrated food spoils like any cooked food (→ 04-17).
- Rice and potato meals rehydrate softest and are usually the reliable children's meals; note
  the favourites in the inventory (→ 04-19).

### Respect the rest time

The wait is not a suggestion: water is still soaking in and heat is doing the work. Opening early
loses heat and leaves hard centres. In a cold room, wrap the resting pouch in a towel or put it in
the haybox (→ 07-02).

### Adding calories

Freeze-dried meals are often lean for people working hard in a cold house. The household's daily
need is about **{{ derived.calories.day }} calories** (→ 04-01). The densest food in the pantry is
**fat** (→ 04-12): a spoonful of oil, ghee or lard stirred in after rehydrating adds calories and
fullness for no extra water or fuel. For an allergic person, the fat passes the same label check
as everything else (some oils contain soy or other allergens).

### Every pouch drinks water

This food uses water; that is the price of its shelf life. Plan stored water **above** the
drinking floor when freeze-dried food is a large part of the diet (→ 03-01: your planning figure
is {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day for the household). When water is scarcer than
energy, eat freeze-dried food **last**: canned food carries its own water.

## Gear / items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pouch stock, logged with type (true freeze-dried or dehydrated blend) | The food | → 04-19 |
| **Allergy kit: marked scissors, spoon and bowl** | In-pouch preparation, no cross-contact | Kept with the allergy-safe pouches |
| Measuring cup | Exact water per pouch | Lives with the pouches |
| Stainless vacuum flasks | Meals later in the day without another boil | → 07-02 |
| Oil, ghee or lard | Extra calories | → 04-12; check labels for allergens |
| Towels or a haybox | Hot rest in a cold room | → 07-02 |
| A bowl or pot to stand hot pouches in | Scald prevention | |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- Any zip-top bag or lidded jar rehydrates loose freeze-dried food; allow a longer rest.
- No marked scissors? A knife **washed and dried first, used on the allergic person's food only**,
  then straight back to their wash rack.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the pouch count and calorie arithmetic are on → 04-19. If anyone has a food allergy,
  count their safe pouches separately: that number is usually the one that runs out first.
- **Ration:** cold-water rehydration (true freeze-dried only) uses no energy; half-pouch meals
  stretch the count; add fat before opening a second pouch.
- **Resupply:** none; this food is bought. Stored staples (→ 04-03), home-dried food (→ 04-06) and
  food production (Section 05) come next.
- **Spend it on the right days:** travel days and days with little power, not days when the kettle
  is running comfortably on sun.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the everyday supper of a long outage: kettle (→ 07-06), pouches, flask.
- **B (moving):** the travelling food. Cold-rehydrate at stops if you cannot boil. The allergy kit
  and safe pouches are packed first and kept within reach.
- **C (establishing):** the bridge stock while gardens and animals come in. The in-pouch procedure
  for an allergic person matters **more** in a shared or borrowed kitchen, not less.

# Heating and cold-weather shelter

**What this section holds.** 10 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 08-01 **Heating one room instead of the house**: When the power or the fuel supply fails in winter, the most useful single decision is to **stop heating the whole house and heat one room**.
- → 08-02 **Carbon monoxide: the silent killer**: Carbon monoxide (CO) is the gas that kills families in cold outages.
- → 08-03 **Winterizing the home and preventing frozen pipes**: The cheap, boring work done in autumn that does more for a winter outage than any gadget: protecting the pipes, sealing draughts, insulating, and knowing how…
- → 08-04 **Emergency heat options and their risks**: A plain comparison of every way to stay warm when the power or fuel fails, from the furnace you already own to a candle, with what each one can do to you.
- → 08-05 **Hypothermia and frostbite: prevent, spot, treat**: How to recognise and treat the two cold injuries: **hypothermia**, when the whole body gets too cold, and **frostbite**, when skin and the tissue under it fr…
- → 08-06 **Trapping heat: tents indoors and insulation tricks**: What works when the fuel is gone or low: stop heating air and start trapping body heat.
- → 08-07 **Ducted diesel and kerosene heaters: install and operation**: How the class of small forced-air heaters often called "diesel heaters" or "parking heaters" works, how to install one through a window so its fumes stay out…

- → 08-09 **Portable propane heaters (Buddy family): setup, safe use and troubleshooting**: How to set up, light, run, shut down and troubleshoot the small portable propane heaters sold for indoor emergency use: the "Buddy" family (small, mid and la…
- → 08-10 **Wick kerosene heaters: setup, safe use and troubleshooting**: How to set up, fuel, light, run, shut off, clean and troubleshoot a portable **wick kerosene heater** of the round "convection" type sold for indoor use.
