pages.body:
# Heating one room instead of the house

**What this page is for.** When the power or the fuel supply fails in winter, the most useful
single decision is to **stop heating the whole house and heat one room**. Everyone lives and
sleeps in that room. This page shows how to choose that room in your own home, how to close it
off, what the heater in it needs, and when it is time to stop holding the house. Carbon monoxide
(CO), the poison gas every flame makes, is explained on → 29-03; read → 08-02 before you bring
any heat source into the room.

> **SAFETY.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
> mitigation that works every time (→ 30-01). A heater sold for indoor use is different: it may
> be used inside, but only by its manual, with a working battery CO alarm in the room first,
> the manual's air openings open, and an adult in the room while it burns. Whether one may
> burn while people sleep is a decision card, not a default: {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02).
> **CDC says people who are asleep can die from CO before they have any symptoms** (CDC,
> Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

## Do this now

1. **Pick the warm room today, in writing** (box below). Small, few outside walls, enough floor
   for everyone to sleep, and able to meet your heater's air rules.
2. **Put a battery CO alarm and a smoke alarm in it** before any heater is lit: CO alarm on the
   wall opposite the heater, at the height of sleeping heads (→ 08-02).
3. **Close off the rest of the house.** Shut doors. Hang blankets over doorways and stairwells.
4. **Everyone sleeps in the warm room**, children and pets included. Body heat counts.
5. **Move cold-sensitive medicines there** (→ 29-07). Insulin must never freeze (→ 30-01).
6. **Fill every water container, then drain the plumbing** in the parts of the house that will
   freeze (→ 03-06).
7. **Tape the action ladder (below) inside the door,** next to a thermometer.

## Why it works

Heating a whole house with a wood fire or a portable heater is close to impossible. A house is
built to be heated by its furnace, and anything smaller loses the race against the walls and
windows. One room is a small fraction of the house's volume, so the same fuel lasts many times
longer. That is the difference between a woodpile or a fuel can lasting days and lasting weeks.

**Even better than heating a room is heating the people in it.** Layers (→ 11-01), sleeping
bags, shared body heat and a small shelter inside the room (→ 08-06) keep a family safe at room
temperatures that would otherwise be miserable. The room just has to be warm enough for that to
work.

## Choosing the room in your home

| What to look for | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Size | The smallest room that fits everyone sleeping |
| Outside walls | Fewest; an inside room loses heat slowest |
| Windows | Few, but a south-facing one gives free heat on sunny days |
| A real chimney | A room with a working, inspected fireplace or wood stove wins by default (→ 08-08) |
| Water and kitchen | Close is a plus for cooking and washing |
| Your heater's air | It can give the openings your heater's manual requires (table below) |
| Clearances | Floor space for the heater's clearances plus a barrier children cannot get past |

**Your home on file:** a {{ dwelling.type }}, basement: {{ dwelling.basement }}, main heat:
{{ dwelling.primary_heat }}.

{{#if has.apartment}}**In an apartment.** Your neighbours' walls, floor and ceiling are often
warmer than the outside air, so a room in the middle of the unit, away from the outside wall,
holds heat well. You cannot close off a stairwell, but you can close your own doors and hang
blankets. Building smoke and CO travel between units: keep your CO alarm working even if you
burn nothing yourself.

> **Before the collapse:** the national propane code (NFPA 58) does not allow propane cylinders
> larger than the 1-lb camping size to be stored or used inside a home (Minnesota State Fire
> Marshal, LP Gas Inside Buildings), and many leases forbid fuel heaters. Read yours.

{{/if}}{{#if has.mobile_home}}**In a mobile or manufactured home.** The rooms are small and the
walls are thin, so the whole home cools fast once heat stops. Choose the room with the fewest
outside walls and windows. Before using any fuel-burning heater, read its manual for a
mobile-home or RV warning: some unvented heaters may not be used in one at all. A small room
also reaches a heater's ventilation limit sooner (see the volume method below).

{{/if}}{{#if has.basement}}**Your basement.** Walls set in the ground lose heat slowly, because
the soil around them stays far warmer than winter air. That makes a basement room a strong warm
room for **non-burning** heat: bodies, blankets, a heated blanket on a battery, or a vented
furnace. For a **fuel-burning heater** it is a weak choice unless it has an outside door or
window at ground level: the heater needs that window for its air, and **propane is heavier than
air**, so a leak flows down into a basement and pools there until it reaches a flame
(Enerco/Mr. Heater, Buddy owner's manual). {{#if has.walkout}}Your basement is a **walkout**: a
room on the walkout side, with its door or window at ground level, can serve both purposes. With
a propane heater, a door cracked at the floor on that side is also a low air opening, and any
room holding a gas water heater or furnace pilot stays shut off from it.{{else}}Your basement is
not a walkout, so use it for a fuel-burning heater only if a room there has a window that opens
to the outside, and never with propane.{{/if}}

{{/if}}{{#if has.shelter_room}}**Your windowless room ({{ dwelling.shelter_room }}).** A room
with no windows is excellent at holding body heat and is a fine warm room if your heat comes
from bodies, bedding or electricity. It is the **wrong** room for any fuel-burning heater:
every portable heater needs fresh-air openings to the outside, and a propane heater on a hose
needs a window or door the hose can pass through.

{{/if}}**The trade-off to settle on paper.** "Inside room, few outside walls" pulls toward a room
without windows. Every fuel-burning portable heater needs a window. **If your heat will come from
a flame, a room with one window or outside door you can open beats an inside room**, and you
insulate the rest of that room's glass (→ 08-03). If your heat will come only from bodies,
bedding and battery power, the inside room wins.

### The heater's air: what the manuals require

| Heater class | What the manual requires | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Portable propane heater (Buddy family) | Fresh-air openings of 9 square inches (a 3 × 3 in opening) at ceiling level **and** at floor level; no other fuel-burning appliance in the space; the 20-lb tank outdoors, fed by the maker's hose | → 08-09 |
| Wick kerosene heater | If the room has less than 200 cubic feet of air per 1,000 BTU/h of heater, open a window at least 1 inch or keep doors to other rooms open; never a bathroom or small closed room | → 08-10 |
| Ducted diesel or kerosene heater | Combustion intake and exhaust both outside, sealed | → 08-07 |
| Fireplace or wood stove | A sound, inspected chimney | → 08-08 |

Sources: Enerco/Mr. Heater, Portable Buddy owner's manual; GHP Group/Dyna-Glo, Portable
Kerosene Heater owner's manual. **Your own heater's manual governs;** these are the figures from
one common model of each class.

**The volume method (wick kerosene heaters).** Measure the room: length × width × ceiling height
in feet = cubic feet. Divide the heater's BTU/h rating by 1,000 and multiply by 200: that is the
room volume the manual wants. Example: a 10,500 BTU/h heater wants 2,100 cubic feet, about a
13 × 20 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling. A smaller room means the window stays cracked at least an
inch whenever it burns. A warm room is usually smaller than this, so plan on the window being
open.

**A towel stuffed around a hose gap is a draught seal, not ventilation.** The openings the manual
asks for are still required.

{{figure fig-warm-room-layout}}

### Commit the warm room (fill in now, in ink)

> **OUR WARM ROOM IS:** ______________________
> **Room size L × W × H = ________ cu ft** (needed for the kerosene volume rule)
> **Window or outside door that opens for air:** ______________________
> **High and low openings for a propane heater will be:** ______________________
> **Where the heater stands, and the barrier around it:** ______________________
> **CO alarm goes:** ______________________ (opposite wall from the heater, pillow height)
> **Backup room if this one is damaged:** ______________________
> **Decided on:** ____________ **by:** ______________________

Once written, stage the blankets, hooks, sleeping bags, thermometer, alarm and window film in
that room now, not during the outage.

{{photo warm-room}}

{{photo warm-room-co-alarm}}

## The indoor-temperature action ladder

Tape a copy inside the warm-room door, beside the thermometer. Each rung is a decision made in
advance so nobody argues about it at 2 a.m. The temperatures are your household's to set; write
them in. The actions are what each rung should trigger.

| Warm-room reading | Action, starting now |
|---|---|
| **___ °F and falling** | **Consolidate.** Everyone moves into the warm room. Close off the rest of the house; door blankets up. Install and test the CO alarm now so a heater is ready |
| **___ °F** | **Protect the plumbing:** drip vulnerable taps, open cabinet doors under sinks, fill every container, and drain the rest of the house if the cold will keep falling (Red Cross; → 03-06). **Everyone sleeps in the warm room.** Light **one** heater if you have one, by its manual |
| **___ °F** | **Watch the people:** touch checks on children and elders (back of the neck, chest; → 08-05, → 11-02). Move medicines to the warmest spot in the room. Count fuel-hours left (→ 23-02). Start thinking about whether to leave (→ 01-02) |
| **___ °F and falling, no heat source recovering** | **The house can no longer be kept safe.** Make the go/no-go decision now, in daylight if at all possible (→ 01-02). When to leave is your household's own worksheet: {{choice DC-19}} (→ 30-20) |

**Run one fuel heater at a time.** The propane class's manual forbids other fuel-burning
appliances in the space, and two unvented burners add their CO and their oxygen use together.

## Heat while people sleep

Both common portable heater manuals say never run them while sleeping, and CPSC says never to
operate unvented fuel-burning appliances in any room where people are sleeping (CPSC, Carbon
Monoxide Questions and Answers). Running one overnight
keeps the room warm but leaves CO and fire with no one awake to notice them; turning it off
means a cold night, which is hardest on babies and frail elders. That trade-off is the
household's to decide, on the card, with its mitigations listed there (lowest correct setting,
alarm at pillow height, the manual's openings, a barrier, an adult who wakes to check):
{{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02). Whatever the choice, the heater pages (→ 08-09, → 08-10) explain
what "lowest setting" means for each class, because on a wick heater a turned-down wick makes
smell and CO, not savings (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo, Portable Kerosene Heater owner's manual).

## Small children in the warm room

The American Academy of Pediatrics publishes **no numeric minimum room temperature** for babies.
Its guidance is to dress the baby for the room, keep loose bedding out of a baby's sleep space,
and avoid overheating (AAP, How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe). CDC lists **babies sleeping in
cold bedrooms** among the people most at risk of hypothermia (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia). So in
a cold house the baby sleeps in the warm room, dressed in layers and a sleep sack, and is checked
by touch.

{{#if has.infant}}Your household has a child under 2: {{#each infants as c}}{{c.label}}
({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}Whether a small child shares an adult bed for warmth is a decision
card, with the AAP rule for babies under 1 printed on it: {{choice DC-09}} (→ 30-10).{{else}}If a
baby or toddler joins the household, whether a small child shares an adult bed for warmth is a
decision card: {{choice DC-09}} (→ 30-10).{{/if}}

**Hot-water bottles and fire-warmed stones pre-warm a bed and come out before a child gets in.**
Skin that is asleep or numb burns without waking. **No electric blanket on or around a baby or
toddler** (→ 08-04, → 11-02).

## Sealing the room, and its limits

- **Blankets over doorways** and at the top or bottom of stairs. A stairwell is a chimney.
- **Towels and draught stoppers** at door gaps; window film, plastic sheeting or bubble wrap on
  the glass (→ 08-03).
- **Curtains closed at night**, south-facing ones open on sunny days.
- **Cover the floor** with rugs, blankets or cardboard. Cold comes up through it.
- **Do not make it airtight.** Draught-proofing is not the same as sealing. With a heater
  burning, the openings its manual requires stay open the whole time.

## The rest of the house

- **Let it go cold, on purpose.** Drain the plumbing (→ 03-06) or you trade a heating problem for
  a flood.
- **Cold rooms become food storage** (→ 04-09), but insulin and other medicines that must not
  freeze stay in the warm room (→ 29-07).
- **Walk the house twice a day:** burst pipes, snow load, and any smoke or CO drifting into
  unused rooms.

## Living in one room

Several people{{#if has.pets}} and their pets{{/if}} in one room for weeks is hard. Plan it as a
people problem, not only a heat problem: a sleeping spot for each person, a play corner if there
are children, a daily routine, and some way for each adult to get an hour of quiet (→ 21-02).
Morale in a one-room winter is part of survival.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Battery CO alarm** for the warm room (you have {{ gear.co_alarms }}) | The only thing that detects CO | Plug-in alarms without a battery fail in an outage (→ 08-02) |
| Smoke alarm and an extinguisher in the room | Fire is the other way heaters kill | → 29-12 |
| Heavy or moving blankets, hooks or nails | Close off doorways and stairs | Cheap; large effect |
| Window film, bubble wrap or plastic sheeting | Cuts the biggest heat loss | → 08-03 |
| Cold-rated sleeping bags, child sizes too | Heat the people, not the room | |
| Foam pads, rugs, cardboard | Insulate from the floor | Sleeping on a cold floor is dangerous |
| Two thermometers: the room and where the baby sleeps | Know the real temperature | |
| A heater sold for indoor use, its manual and fuel | Supplemental heat | → 08-04 for the options |
| Headlamps and battery lanterns | The room is dark early | → 10-06 |

**No gear?** Curtains, comforters, tarps and cardboard make door covers and window insulation.
Furniture pushed against outside walls adds a still-air layer. A tent pitched inside the room is
the cheapest large gain of all (→ 08-06).

## When it runs out

- This page **is** the fuel strategy: shrinking the heated space is the biggest lever on how long
  fuel lasts (→ 06-04).
- **Ration in steps:** heat one room, then only the sleeping shelter inside it (→ 08-06), then
  only the people: layers, body heat, pre-warmed beds.
- **Spend effort on insulation first.** It is the only "fuel" that never runs out.
- **The last resort** is leaving: if the fuel is gone and the house cannot be kept safe, that is
  the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02), not something to endure with small children or frail elders.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** set the room up before you need it.
- **B (moving):** the same idea, smaller: the smallest insulated space you can warm with bodies.
  Never an unvented burner in a closed vehicle or tent (→ 08-02).
- **C (established somewhere else):** the same choice, often with a real stove. Pick the room
  with the chimney, after inspecting it (→ 08-08).

pages.body:
# Carbon monoxide: the silent killer

**What this page is for.** Carbon monoxide (CO) is the gas that kills families in cold
outages. This page explains it in a few lines (the full explainer is → 29-03), sets out the rules
for every kind of fuel-burning device, tells you where to put CO alarms and what their numbers
mean, and gives the step-by-step for a suspected poisoning, including what to do when no one
answers 911. It outranks every other heating page.

> **SAFETY.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
> mitigation that works every time (→ 30-01). **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an
> open flame or a running appliance** (→ 30-01). CO cannot be seen, smelled or tasted. More
> than 400 Americans die from unintentional CO poisoning each year, and people who are asleep
> or drunk can die before they ever feel ill (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

## Do this now

1. **Put battery CO alarms on every level of the home and outside each sleeping area** (CPSC),
   and one in the warm room at pillow height (→ 30-02). Test each one. You have listed {{ gear.co_alarms }}.
2. **Never use a gas oven or range to heat the house.** It is not a heater (CDC).
3. **Never use a camp stove, grill or charcoal indoors** (CDC; → 07-05).
4. **Generators outdoors only, more than 20 feet from any window, door or vent** (CDC; → 09-04).
5. **Know the signs:** headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain,
   confusion. They feel like flu (CDC). **If several people, or the pets, feel ill at once and
   better outdoors, get everyone out into fresh air now.**

## What CO is, in brief

Anything that burns fuel makes CO: furnaces, water heaters, stoves, portable heaters,
fireplaces, generators, vehicles, charcoal (CDC). It takes the place of oxygen in your blood. The
first symptoms are the same as flu, so people lie down to rest and do not get up.

**Who is hurt first.** CDC names infants, older adults, and people with chronic heart disease,
anaemia or breathing problems as higher risk (CDC). One CO alarm maker's manual adds that young
children and pets may be the first affected (First Alert, CO alarm user's manual). {{#if has.young_child}}Your household has a child under 6: if a child
is unusually sleepy or sick while anything is burning indoors, treat it as CO until you know
otherwise.{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}} Your household has an older member, who may show it early
too.{{/if}}

**Why the alarm matters more than your senses.** A sleeping person cannot notice symptoms.
That is the reason for the alarm.

## The grid-down trap

Every winter outage produces the same deaths, in the same order:

1. The power fails and the house gets cold.
2. Someone puts the generator in the garage "out of the snow", or lights charcoal in the
   fireplace, or runs the camp stove indoors "just to take the chill off".
3. Everyone gets sleepy.
4. Nobody wakes up.

**Outdoor equipment stays outdoors.** An outdoor fire pit, a grill or a generator is exactly right
outside and deadly inside.

## Rules by device

| Device | Indoors? | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Portable generator | **Never** | Outdoors, more than 20 ft from windows, doors and vents (CDC); floor rule (→ 30-01; → 09-04) |
| Charcoal or a charcoal grill | **Never** | Outdoors only; floor rule (→ 30-01) |
| Any engine, including a vehicle | **Never** in a garage, even with the door open | Floor rule (→ 30-01) |
| Gas camp stove | **Never** | Outdoors (→ 07-05) |
| Gas oven or range used as a heater | **Never** | It is not a heater (CDC) |
| Portable propane or kerosene heater **sold for indoor use** | Yes, by its manual | Its manual's air openings; CO alarm first; one at a time; an adult awake in the room. Overnight use is a decision card: {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02). → 08-09, → 08-10 |
| Ducted diesel or kerosene heater | Yes, if intake and exhaust are both sealed and outside | CO alarm in the room anyway (→ 08-07) |
| Installed fireplace or wood stove | Yes, if the chimney is sound and clear | Inspect before use: {{choice DC-21}} (→ 30-22; → 08-08) |
| Candles and oil lamps | A decision card | {{choice DC-20}} (→ 30-21) |

## The numbers: what a CO reading means

An alarm with a digital readout turns CO into a number, in **parts per million (ppm)**: how many
CO molecules there are in every million molecules of air (→ 29-03). Three published sets of
figures help you read it.

**What the home alarm standard requires.** UL 2034, as printed in a First Alert CO alarm manual
(CPSC says alarms are designed to sound before levels become life-threatening):

| CO level | What the alarm standard requires |
|---|---|
| 30 ppm, steady | No alarm, even after 30 days |
| 70 ppm | Alarm within 1 to 4 hours |
| 150 ppm | Alarm within 10 to 50 minutes |
| 400 ppm | Alarm within 4 to 15 minutes |

**What the levels do to people** (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Questions and Answers): long exposure at
about 1 to 70 ppm usually causes no symptoms, though people with heart disease may get more chest
pain. Sustained above 70 ppm, symptoms become noticeable: headache, tiredness, nausea. Sustained
at 150 to 200 ppm, disorientation, unconsciousness and death are possible.

**What ordinary homes read** (EPA, Carbon Monoxide's Impact on Indoor Air Quality): 0.5 to 5 ppm
in homes without gas stoves; 5 to 15 ppm near a properly adjusted gas stove; 30 ppm or more near a
badly adjusted one.

What to do with a reading. This column is deliberately cautious:

| Reading | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Steady, above the ordinary-home levels, alarm silent** | Something is making CO. **A silent alarm is not proof of safety.** Ventilate, check every burning appliance and flue, and do not sleep with an unexplained steady reading |
| **30 to 70 ppm** | A source is running and winning, often with no symptoms yet, which is the trap. Ventilate now; find and shut off the source. Nobody sleeps until it reads low and the cause is known |
| **Alarm sounding, or above 70 ppm sustained** | **Everyone out to fresh air;** burning appliances off (one-adult re-entry rule below); air the house fully before anyone returns |
| **150 ppm and higher** | **Leave immediately. Carry the children, count heads, nobody goes back in** |

Two readings deserve special fear: **any reading while people were asleep**, and a **peak on the
alarm's memory you cannot explain**. Both mean you find the source before the next night.

## Where the alarms go

- **Minimum:** one on every level and one outside each sleeping area (CPSC). With only one
  alarm, it goes where people sleep, which in an outage is the warm room (→ 08-01).
- **Height and placement: follow your alarm's own manual.** Makers differ: one common manual
  allows a wall or a tabletop (First Alert); CPSC says a plug-in outlet or high on the wall, never
  in a kitchen or above a fuel-burning appliance (CPSC). **In the warm room, put it at pillow
  height**, the height of sleeping heads (→ 30-02).
- **Distance from the heater.** Many alarm manuals give a minimum distance from fuel-burning
  appliances; one common manual says 20 feet from a furnace or other fuel-burning heat source
  (First Alert). A small warm room often cannot meet it. Then put the alarm on the **wall opposite the heater, at pillow height, never directly
  above it**, and treat a short alarm at lighting as "ventilate and check", never as "pull the
  battery". An alarm pulled for being annoying is not there at 3 a.m.
- **Never in still-air or blowing-air spots:** not within 4 inches of the corner where wall meets
  ceiling, not where curtains or furniture can cover it, not near a fan, heat vent or open window,
  because blowing air can keep CO from reaching the sensor (First Alert; CPSC). A heater's cracked
  window or air openings count: keep the alarm away from them.
- **Not in bathrooms or above heat sources:** one common manual says at least 10 feet from a bath
  or shower, because constant high humidity or heat can shorten the sensor's life (First Alert).
- **Battery alarms only count in an outage.** A plug-in alarm with no battery backup is useless
  when the power is out.

{{figure fig-co-alarm-placement}}

{{photo co-alarm-warm-room}}

{{photo co-alarm-other}}

**Blocked vents are the quiet version of this.** Snow drifting over a furnace, water heater or
dryer vent, or a bird's nest in a chimney, sends exhaust back into the house. **After every heavy
snow, clear the outside exhaust vents.**{{#if has.gas_any}} Your home has gas service, so this
applies to your furnace and water heater vents.{{/if}}

{{photo exhaust-vents}}

## If you suspect CO

1. **Get everyone outside into fresh air immediately,** pets included.
2. **Do not go back in** to open windows or look for the source first. Out, then think.
3. **Call 911** if it works. CO poisoning needs medical care; some effects are delayed.
4. **Do not go back in** until the source is found and shut off and the house is aired out.
5. **Count heads.** Confusion is a symptom: someone affected may not follow instructions.

**If there is no 911:**

- **Fresh air is the field treatment** (MedlinePlus, Carbon monoxide poisoning). There is no home
  antidote. Hospitals give oxygen; the household version is time in clean air. Keep everyone outside, **resting** (exertion makes it
  worse), warm (→ 08-05), for hours, not minutes. A safely parked vehicle running outdoors with
  a clear tailpipe, or a neighbour's house, can be the warm spot.
- **Anyone who was confused, staggering, vomiting or unconscious** gets the longest rest and a
  watcher. Permanent brain damage can follow, and impaired thinking can come back after one to two
  weeks without symptoms (MedlinePlus). Write down
  who was exposed and how badly, in case care becomes reachable.
- **One clear-headed adult goes back in**, briefly, holding their breath, with doors open, to shut
  off the source and open windows. The house then airs out until the alarm is silent on fresh
  batteries before anyone sleeps in it.
- **Find the cause before the next night.** The stove, flue or heater that did it will do it
  again. The alarm going quiet is not a diagnosis.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Battery CO alarms**: every level, outside sleeping areas, the warm room | The only thing that detects CO | Test as its manual says (one common manual: weekly); the test button checks the circuit, not the sensor (CPSC); replace at the end-of-life date printed on the unit, and at once on an end-of-life chirp |
| CO alarm with a **digital peak readout** | Shows what happened while you slept | CDC suggests considering one |
| A deep supply of the alarms' batteries | Alarms fail silent without them | Check twice a year (CDC) |
| Heavy outdoor extension cord, 25 ft or more | Lets the generator sit 20+ ft from the house | Rated for the load (→ 09-04) |
| Chimney inspection or brush | A blocked flue makes CO and fire | → 06-09 |
| A snow shovel by the vent side of the house | Clear vents after storms | |
| The manual for every fuel-burning heater | "Sold for indoor use" is on the label, not a guess | → 29-14 |

**There is no substitute for a CO alarm.** No sense, no plant, no rule of thumb detects CO. If you
have exactly one, it goes where people sleep. Ventilation helps, but a cracked window does not
make an unsuitable burner safe indoors.

## When it runs out

- **Alarms run out twice:** batteries, and the sensor itself, which expires at the date printed
  on the unit even if never used. Write that date here: ____________. Keep spares.
- **Never ration alarms away from sleepers.** One working alarm goes where people sleep.
- **The rule that never runs out:** nothing that burns fuel comes inside except heaters sold for
  indoor use, run by their manuals, and never those without a working alarm. Teach it to the whole
  family (→ 20-04).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the highest-risk phase. There is a garage, a generator, a grill and a cold
  house. Most CO deaths happen here.
- **B (moving):** never run a vehicle in an enclosed space to keep warm, and never bring a stove
  into a tent or car to sleep. Warmth comes from insulation and layers (→ 11-01). A stranded car
  in snow: clear the tailpipe first (→ 22-05).
- **C (established somewhere else):** an unfamiliar stove or heater is an unknown. Inspect the
  flue before first use, and put an alarm in the sleeping room on day one.

pages.body:
# Winterizing the home and preventing frozen pipes

**What this page is for.** The cheap, boring work done in autumn that does more for a winter
outage than any gadget: protecting the pipes, sealing draughts, insulating, and knowing how to
drain the house if it has to go cold. A burst pipe in an unheated house wrecks the building and
your water supply at the same time.

> **CAUTION.** **Never thaw a pipe with an open flame** (Red Cross; → 03-06). A snow-buried
> exhaust vent pushes carbon monoxide back into the house: clear vents after every storm
> (→ 08-02). **Never use automotive antifreeze in drains or toilets** (below).

## Do this now (before the cold)

- **Outdoor taps:** drain and store hoses. Close the inside shutoff valve to each outdoor tap,
  then **open the outdoor tap and leave it open** so trapped water can expand without splitting
  the pipe (Red Cross).
- **Insulate pipes** in the basement, crawlspace, garage and along outside walls, hot and cold
  lines both (Red Cross).
- **Seal leaks:** weatherstrip doors, caulk window gaps, draught stoppers, foam gaskets behind
  outlet covers on outside walls.
- **Insulate the attic, basement and crawlspace.** Insulation keeps those spaces, and the pipes in
  them, warmer (Red Cross).
- **Find the main water shutoff**, keep the tool with it, and practise turning it in the dark.
- **Stage the warm-room kit now** (→ 08-01): blankets, hooks, window film.

{{photo main-water-shutoff}}

## Pipes

Water expands as it freezes and splits metal or plastic pipe. The breaks happen first in
**unheated space:** outside walls, crawlspaces, garages and cold basement corners. In deep cold,
**let vulnerable taps drip** (moving water resists freezing) and **open the cabinet doors under
sinks** so house heat reaches the pipes (Red Cross).

**In a winter outage the whole house becomes unheated space.** Either keep enough heat
everywhere to protect the plumbing, which costs a great deal of fuel, or **drain the system on
purpose** (→ 03-06) and live without running water. For a long outage, draining is usually
right, but **fill every container first** (→ 03-02).

{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}### The water heater when the house is drained

A tank water heater ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gallons on file) is the biggest volume of
water left to freeze and split, and it is **drinkable reserve water first** (→ 03-02). In order:

1. **Turn its heat off.** {{#if has.gas_any}}Gas: control knob to **OFF**, not "vacation" or
   "pilot". The gas shutoff procedure is on → 16-12.{{else}}Electric: its breaker off.{{/if}}
2. **Close the cold-water inlet valve** on top of the tank.
3. **Wait.** The water stays scalding for hours. Once it is safe to touch, draw it off through the
   drain valve into clean containers, or run a hose from the drain valve to a floor drain and
   open a hot tap upstairs so air can enter.
4. **Restart only after it is full again,** with the inlet open, and only by the instructions on
   its label. Heating an empty tank destroys it.
   Relighting a gas water heater's pilot yourself when the gas company cannot come is a
   decision card: {{choice DC-28}} → 30-29.

{{photo water-heater-valves}}

{{/if}}### Antifreeze for drains and toilets

When a house is drained, pour antifreeze into sink traps and toilet bowls so the water left in
them cannot freeze and crack them. **Use only pink RV or marine antifreeze, which is propylene
glycol.** **Never automotive antifreeze (ethylene glycol):** it is sweet-tasting and brightly
coloured, so it gets swallowed, and swallowing more than a taste can cause serious illness or
death (CDC/ATSDR, Ethylene Glycol ToxFAQs). A toilet bowl or floor drain is exactly where a child
or a pet will find it.

## The building envelope, biggest gains first

| Fix | Effort | Payoff |
|---|---|---|
| Attic insulation | High | Large and permanent |
| Window film, plastic sheeting, bubble wrap | Low | Very high per dollar |
| Weatherstripping and door sweeps | Low | High: draughts are constant loss |
| Caulking gaps, outlet gaskets | Low | Moderate but adds up |
| Heavy curtains, closed at night | Low | Real and immediate |
| Blankets over unused doorways and stairs | Low | Essential for the warm room (→ 08-01) |
| Rugs and foam on bare floors | Low | Comfort and real loss reduction |

Storm windows and thermal curtains help in a normal winter and matter a great deal in an abnormal
one. **Bubble wrap pressed onto glass misted with water** is a cheap substitute.

## Snow and the house

- **Clear exhaust vents after every storm:** furnace, water heater, dryer. A buried vent pushes
  CO inside (→ 08-02).
- **Watch the roof load** after heavy wet snow, especially low-slope sections and porch roofs.
- **Ice dams:** heat leaking into the attic melts snow that refreezes at the eaves and backs water
  under the shingles. Good attic insulation and ventilation prevent them.
- **Keep paths clear** to the woodpile, the generator spot and the vehicle. In a blizzard, the
  path you did not clear yesterday is the one you cannot use today (→ 17-01).

## Before a forecast storm

1. Fill every water container and the bathtub (→ 03-02).
2. Charge everything, medical devices first (→ 09-06).
3. Bring several days of firewood under cover.
4. Stage the warm room (→ 08-01).
5. Check CO and smoke alarm batteries (→ 08-02).
6. Move medicines that must not freeze or overheat to the safe spot (→ 29-07).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pipe insulation sleeves; UL-listed heat tape (Red Cross) | Prevents the costly failure | Hot and cold lines |
| Window film kits or bubble wrap | Cheapest large gain | Enough for the warm room at least |
| Weatherstrip, door sweeps, caulk, outlet gaskets | Stops constant loss | Autumn job |
| Thermal curtains, blankets and hooks | Night insulation and closing off rooms | Also the warm-room kit |
| Main water shutoff tool, kept at the valve | Drain fast when needed | |
| **RV or marine antifreeze, pink, propylene glycol only** | Protects traps and toilets in a drained house | Never automotive (ethylene glycol) |
| Roof rake | Snow load and ice dams | Long handle, used from the ground |
| Two or more snow shovels | Vents, wood, ways out | One stays inside by the door |

**No gear?** Plastic sheeting, cardboard and tape over windows; foam pool noodles and rags as
pipe wrap; rolled towels as draught stoppers; furniture against outside walls; any blanket on a
few nails becomes a door curtain.

## When it runs out

- **Insulation does not run out.** That is why it is the best investment. The consumables here
  (tape, film, antifreeze) are minor.
- **Short of materials?** Insulate the **warm room first**, then the pipes that matter, then the
  rest.
- **Resupply:** cardboard, cloth and plastic sheeting are everywhere and all work.
- **Every bit of insulation permanently cuts the fuel you burn** (→ 06-04).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** do all of it in autumn. It is the highest return per dollar and hour in the
  binder.
- **B (moving):** the skill that travels is insulating a small space fast: the same tricks work in
  a vehicle or a borrowed room.
- **C (established somewhere else):** on day one, check the building: where the wind gets in,
  where the pipes run, and where the snow drifts.

pages.body:
# Emergency heat options and their risks

**What this page is for.** A plain comparison of every way to stay warm when the power or fuel
fails, from the furnace you already own to a candle, with what each one can do to you. Each
option is ranked by risk, and the heater pages hold the procedures. Fuels are explained on
→ 29-01, carbon monoxide (CO) on → 29-03, power stations on → 29-02.

> **SAFETY.** Every option here can hurt you in a different way: **carbon monoxide**, **house
> fire**, or **burns to a child**. Only a device's own label and manual decide whether it may be
> used indoors; follow the manual over anything written here. **Never run a generator, charcoal,
> or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes
> with no warning; alarms fail; there is no mitigation that works every time (→ 30-01). **Never
> use a gas oven or range to heat the house** (CDC). Battery CO **and** smoke alarms in the heated
> room before anything is lit (→ 08-02).

## Do this now

1. **Rank your own options** with the table below and write your order here:
   1 ________ 2 ________ 3 ________ 4 ________.
2. **Insulation, layers and body heat are always on** and cost no fuel (→ 08-01, → 08-06).
3. **Before you light any heater:** CO alarm and smoke alarm up and tested; extinguisher within
   reach (→ 29-12); the manual's air openings open; a barrier if there are children or pets.
4. **One fuel-burning heater at a time.** Never two unvented heaters together.
5. **Overnight heat is a decision card,** not a default: {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02).

## Your home on file

Main heat: **{{ dwelling.primary_heat }}**.
{{#if has.unvented_heater}}Heaters you listed: {{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}} {{h.model}};
{{/each}}{{else}}You have not listed a portable heater.{{/if}}
{{#if has.power_station}}Power stations on file: {{ gear.station_wh_total }} watt-hours in
total.{{/if}}{{#if has.generator}} Generator: {{ gear.generator_watts }} running watts,
{{ gear.generator_fuel }}.{{/if}}

## The options, honestly assessed

| Option | Heat | Indoors? | Main risks | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Insulation, layers, body heat** | Passive | Yes | None | Always on (→ 08-06, → 11-01) |
| **Your gas furnace on battery or generator power** | Whole house | Yes, it is the furnace | None new, **if** it can be safely connected (below) | Often the best heater you already own |
| **Heated blanket on a power station** | Person-level | Yes | Burns and overheating for babies | Warm the bed, not the room (below) |
| **Portable propane heater sold for indoor use** (Buddy family) | Good | Yes, by its manual | CO, low oxygen, fire, propane leak | Oxygen-depletion and tip-over shutoffs; tank outdoors (→ 08-09) |
| **Wick kerosene heater sold for indoor use** | High | Yes, by its manual | CO, fumes, fire, **wrong fuel** | The common model's manual lists a tip-over shutoff, no oxygen-depletion sensor (→ 08-10) |
| **Ducted diesel or kerosene heater** | High | Yes, if installed with intake and exhaust outside | CO if the install leaks | → 08-07 |
| **Wood stove or fireplace** (installed, vented) | High (stove); low (open fireplace) | Yes | Chimney fire; CO if the flue is blocked | Inspect first: {{choice DC-21}} (→ 30-22; → 08-08) |
| **Outdoor fire pit or outdoor fireplace** | High, outdoors | **No** | CO, fire | Cook and boil there; it is not house heat (→ 07-01) |
| **Generator running an electric heater** | Moderate | **Generator outdoors only** | CO; burns fuel fast | Usually a poor use of fuel (→ 09-01) |
| **Candles and tea-light "heaters"** | Negligible | A decision card | **Fire** | Not a heat source (below) |
| **Gas oven or range** | — | **Never** | CO | Not a heater. People die doing this (CDC) |
| **Charcoal, grill, camp stove** | — | **Never** | CO | Floor rule (→ 30-01) |

Spec tables for common heater models are on → 28-04.

## The gas furnace: the heater you may already have

{{#if has.gas_any}}Your home has gas service.{{/if}} **In many electrical outages the gas keeps
flowing.** The gas supply runs largely separately from the electric grid, so a gas furnace is
often fully fuelled and stopped only because its **blower and controls** have no power. **Read
your furnace's data plate** for the watts or amps it draws (→ 29-14); that number decides what can
run it.

- **Run it in bursts:** long enough to lift the whole house a few degrees, then off, and let the
  house coast on its stored heat. Repeat. Warm the house before bed and at waking; hold the warm
  room with blankets and bodies between bursts (→ 08-01). Time your own bursts with a thermometer.
- **Power it from a power station or a generator outdoors.** Divide the station's usable
  watt-hours by the blower's watts for a rough runtime (→ 29-02); solar recharge stretches it
  (→ 09-05).

**The connection must be safe, and must be arranged in advance.** Most furnaces are wired
directly into the house, so nothing can plug into them. **Never connect a generator to house
wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never
backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide") cord.** Backfeed electrocutes line
workers and neighbours and starts fires (→ 30-01; → 29-04). A third route is converting the
furnace to a cord and plug, so that the furnace unplugs from its own wall outlet and plugs into
the generator or power-station cord; that is not a connection to house wiring. Whether your
household does that conversion itself or has an electrician do it is a decision card:
{{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08). The write-up is on → 09-04.

{{photo furnace-data-plate}}

## Heated blankets: warm the bed, not the room

A heated blanket draws a small fraction of what a plug-in space heater does; read both labels
(typical appliance figures are on → 29-02). On a power station it can warm a bed for far longer
than a space heater would run on the same charge. Work out your own runtime from the labels
(→ 29-02).

**No electric blanket on or around a baby or toddler.** The AAP keeps loose bedding out of a
young child's sleep space and warns against overheating (AAP, How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby
Safe). A small child can neither escape nor report a blanket that is too hot. Use it to pre-warm
a bed and switch it off before the child gets in, or to warm the adults, whose bodies then warm
the shared sleeping space (→ 11-02). {{#if has.young_child}}Your household has a young child:
this applies.{{/if}} Bed-sharing for warmth is its own card: {{choice DC-09}} (→ 30-10).

## Portable fuel heaters sold for indoor use

{{photo heater-barrier}}

These are **unvented**: no chimney, so their exhaust stays in the room and they use the room's
air (oxygen). Without enough air they can give off excessive CO (Enerco/Mr. Heater, Buddy owner's
manual), and the kerosene class's manual warns of indoor air pollution (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo,
Portable Kerosene Heater owner's manual). Burning fuel also adds water vapour to the room.

- **Propane heaters of the Buddy family** carry an **oxygen depletion sensor (ODS)**, a safety
  system that shuts the heater off when there is not enough fresh air, and a **tip-over switch**.
  Neither measures CO. The manual requires air openings high and low. It allows emergency indoor
  heating on a 1-lb cylinder, a remote tank of up to 20 lb only **outdoors** on the maker's hose,
  and says never bring a refillable cylinder indoors (Enerco/Mr. Heater, Buddy owner's manual). Bringing a larger tank inside is a
  decision card: {{choice DC-02}} (→ 30-03). Procedures: → 08-09.
- **Wick kerosene heaters:** the common model's manual lists a tip-over (jar) shutoff and no
  ODS. It burns about 13 hours on a tank, needs water-clear 1-K kerosene only, and is refuelled
  outdoors and cold (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo, Portable Kerosene Heater owner's manual). Procedures:
  → 08-10.

**The rules for either, from their manuals:**

- **Follow the manual** for room size, air openings, clearances and fuel.
- **CO alarm running** in the same room, at pillow height (→ 08-02).
- **An adult in the room** while it burns. Never left unattended.
- **No fuel stored in the living space** (→ 06-06). **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an
  open flame or a running appliance** (→ 30-01).
- **One at a time.** The propane class's manual forbids other fuel-burning appliances in the
  space.
- **Overnight:** both manuals say never while sleeping, and CPSC says never run an unvented
  fuel-burning appliance in a room where people sleep (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Questions and
  Answers). Keeping one burning trades CO and fire
  risk against a dangerously cold night; the household decides on the card: {{choice DC-01}}
  (→ 30-02).
- **Moisture:** burning fuel adds water vapour. In a closed room that means condensation, damp
  bedding and mould, and damp bedding is a cold-injury risk (→ 08-05). Vent briefly.

## Candles

Candles give almost no heat against a house's losses, and an open flame in a blanket-draped room
full of people is a fire risk bought for nothing. The US Fire Administration says use flashlights,
not candles, in a power outage (USFA, Candle Fire Safety). Whether your household uses any open
flame indoors is a decision card: {{choice DC-20}} (→ 30-21). A stranded car is the one place a
single candle's heat matters, with a window cracked and an adult awake beside it (→ 22-05).

## Fire risk with children

{{#if has.child}}Your household has children.{{/if}} A small child and any hot surface is a burn
waiting to happen.

- **A physical barrier** around any heater or stove: a hearth gate or a furniture perimeter.
- **Never leave a burning heater unattended,** and never with children in the room unsupervised.
- **Clearances:** keep bedding, door blankets, curtains and toys out of the manual's clearance.
  Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from any heat source (USFA, Heating Fire Safety). A
  blanket hung to trap heat is a fire hazard if it can swing into the heater.
- **Teach the rule** early and often (→ 20-02).

## Passive heat that costs nothing

- **South-facing windows:** curtains open in sun, closed at dusk.
- **Thermal mass:** jugs of water near (not on) a heat source soak up heat and give it back
  overnight.
- **Hot-water bottles or heated stones** wrapped thickly in cloth, in the bedding before you get
  in. **They pre-warm a child's bed and come out before the child gets in** (burns on skin that
  cannot report it). Never a hot stone straight against skin or bedding.
- **Cooking heat:** if you cook indoors on an appliance allowed indoors, that heat is already paid
  for.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Battery CO alarm **and** smoke alarm for the heated room | The two ways heaters kill | → 08-02 |
| Fire extinguisher (ABC), plus a second | Fire is the other killer | Within reach, not behind the heater (→ 29-12) |
| Hearth gate or barrier | Keeps children off hot surfaces | |
| Heater sold for indoor use, its manual, its fuel | Supplemental heat | → 08-09, → 08-10, → 28-04 |
| Safe furnace connection, arranged in advance | Unlocks the furnace option | → 09-04, → 30-08 |
| Heavy extension cord rated for the furnace load | Power station or generator to furnace | |
| Hot-water bottles | Heat the bed, not the room | |
| Wool blankets, cold-rated sleeping bags | Passive warmth | → 08-06 |
| Thermometer | Know if the room is improving | |

**No gear?** Heated stones from an outdoor fire, wrapped thickly in cloth. Water jugs as thermal
mass. Insulation from cardboard, foam, rugs, bubble wrap and newspaper.

## When it runs out

- **Count your fuel:** propane cylinders, kerosene gallons, cords of wood (you have listed
  {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} 20-lb propane tanks, {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gallons of
  kerosene, {{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords of wood). Write the hours each gives on → 23-02,
  using the runtimes on → 08-09 and → 08-10.
- **Ration:** heat the room while awake; shrink the space (→ 08-01, → 08-06) before burning more.
- **Resupply:** wood is the most findable fuel in a long outage (→ 06-04); propane and kerosene
  are not. Plan the move to wood and insulation.
- **The endpoint:** with no fuel, survival is insulation, layers, body heat and a very small
  shelter. That is why → 08-06 is not a curiosity.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** furnace bursts if it can be safely connected, heated-blanket nights,
  insulation always, a portable heater as backup, one at a time, alarm first.
- **B (moving):** **no unvented burner in a vehicle or tent while sleeping.** Warmth is layers and
  insulation (→ 11-01).
- **C (established somewhere else):** a properly installed, inspected wood stove is the goal
  (→ 08-08).

pages.body:
# Hypothermia and frostbite: prevent, spot, treat

**What this page is for.** How to recognise and treat the two cold injuries: **hypothermia**, when
the whole body gets too cold, and **frostbite**, when skin and the tissue under it freeze. In an
outage both happen indoors as well as out. Keep the "Do this now" list where everyone can see it.

> **SAFETY.** Hypothermia is a **medical emergency**. A body temperature below **95 °F** is
> hypothermia (CDC). **Confusion is a symptom,** so the person affected is the least able to
> notice it: someone else has to watch. **Severe hypothermia can look like death: handle the
> person gently, keep warming, and do CPR anyway** (CDC). Never rewarm frostbite with a fire,
> stove, heater, heating pad or electric blanket: numb skin burns without feeling it (CDC).

## Do this now

1. **Watch others, not yourself.** Adults: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, **fumbling hands**,
   memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness. Babies: **bright red, cold skin and very low energy**
   (CDC). A quiet, floppy baby in a cold house is an emergency, not a good sleeper.
2. **Hypothermia:** into warmth, **wet clothes off**, warm the **centre first** (chest, neck, head,
   groin) with dry layers and **skin-to-skin contact**. Warm drinks only if fully awake. **No
   alcohol.** Nothing by mouth if not alert (CDC).
3. **Frostbite: do not rub it,** do not rub snow on it, do not warm it at a fire. Use **warm, not
   hot, water: 98.6 to 102 °F (37 to 39 °C) by thermometer,** or, with no thermometer, water an
   unhurt hand can stay in for 30 seconds without discomfort; or body heat such as an armpit.
   Rewarming is done at **about 30 minutes,** when the part is red or purple and soft again
   (Wilderness Medical Society guideline, as summarised by AAFP).
4. **Both at once? Treat the hypothermia first.**
5. **No pulse or breathing you can find? CPR, and keep warming** (CDC; → 12-18).
6. **The stop line:** when your NWS office ({{ region.home.nws_office }}) issues an **Extreme Cold
   Warning**, nobody goes outside except for essential minutes, and children stay in (→ 29-10).
   Your office's criterion: wind chill at or below ______ °F.

## Hypothermia

The body loses heat faster than it makes it. Below 95 °F core temperature, thinking and
coordination go first, then consciousness. **Wet speeds it up:** CDC notes hypothermia can happen
even above 40 °F if someone is chilled by rain, sweat or cold water. That is why sweating while
hauling wood in winter is dangerous (→ 11-03), and why a soaked child on a cool spring day is at
risk too.

**CDC lists older people with poor food or heating, babies sleeping in cold bedrooms, people who
stay outdoors a long time, and people who drink alcohol among those most at risk** (CDC,
Preventing Hypothermia). A grid-down winter house fits that list.

**Who to watch in your household:**

{{#each members as m}}- {{m.label}} ({{m.age_text}})
{{/each}}
{{#if has.infant}}- **Babies and toddlers** have a lot of skin for their size, shiver poorly and
  cannot tell you. They chill fastest and quietest. **A baby never sleeps in a cold room**
  (→ 08-01, → 11-02).
{{/if}}{{#if has.child}}- **Children** play until they are soaked and cold.
{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}- **Older members:** NWS notes that the body gets less good at signalling
  cold with age and that older people tend not to shiver effectively (NWS, During Extremely Cold
  Weather). Check them as often as the children.
{{/if}}- **Anyone with diabetes who uses insulin or other medicine that can cause low blood sugar.**
  Cold, work and missed meals all upset blood sugar, and **low blood sugar looks like
  hypothermia:** confusion, fumbling, slurred speech, drowsiness. If you find such a person
  confused in the cold, **check blood sugar and treat a low while you warm them.**
  {{#if has.condition.CL-01}}Your household has type 1 diabetes: → 02-01, → 02-02.{{/if}}

**Treatment, in order (CDC):**

1. Get the person into a warm room or shelter.
2. **Take off wet clothing.**
3. **Warm the centre of the body first** (chest, neck, head, groin) with dry blankets, clothing,
   towels, or **skin-to-skin contact** under loose dry layers.
4. Warm, non-alcoholic drinks **only if the person is fully awake** (CDC says never give drinks to
   someone unconscious).
5. Afterwards, keep them dry and wrapped, head and neck included.
6. **Get medical help** if any exists.

**Do not:** rewarm fast in a hot bath, give alcohol, give anything by mouth to someone not alert,
or let them "walk it off".

**Severe hypothermia: do not assume death.** CDC says a person with severe hypothermia may be
unconscious and **may not seem to have a pulse or to be breathing.** Handle them gently, get help,
and **do CPR even if the person seems dead**, continuing until they respond or help arrives, and
**keep warming them during CPR** (CDC). Cold and apparently dead is not the same as dead.

## Frostbite

Freezing of skin and the tissue under it, usually the **nose, ears, cheeks, chin, fingers and
toes**. First signs: **redness or pain**. Then numbness, skin that feels waxy or firm, and loss of
colour (CDC). **Numbness is the danger:** people keep working and make it far worse. How fast
exposed skin freezes depends on temperature and wind together; read it from the NWS wind chill
chart (→ 11-01).

**Treatment cautions (CDC):**

- **Do not rub** the area or rub snow on it.
- **Do not warm it with a fireplace, heat lamp, radiator, stove, heating pad or electric
  blanket.** It is numb and burns easily.
- **Do not walk on frostbitten feet or toes** unless you must.

**Rewarming (Wilderness Medical Society guideline, as summarised by AAFP):**

- Water at **98.6 to 102 °F (37 to 39 °C).** The injured person cannot judge "warm", so **check the
  water with a thermometer, or test it for 30 seconds with an unhurt hand** (it should feel warm,
  never hot). Top it up as it cools.
- **About 30 minutes** is the usual end point: the part turns red or purple and becomes soft.
  Expect real pain as feeling returns.
- Afterwards: dry, loose, clean dressing, gauze between fingers or toes, raise the limb, no walking
  on it.
- **Do not thaw if it might freeze again.** Refreezing does far worse damage than staying frozen
  until you can rewarm for good. This is a real choice when travelling (→ 01-03).
- **If hypothermia and frostbite are both present, treat the hypothermia first.** Core before
  extremities.

## Prevention is the whole game

- **Layer and stay dry** (→ 11-01, → 11-03). Sweat is the enemy; vent before you overheat.
- **Cover the extremities:** hat, a scarf or knit mask over face and mouth, mittens (warmer than
  gloves), water-resistant coat and boots, several loose layers (CDC; → 11-04).
- **Eat and drink.** Food makes heat; people get dehydrated in winter because they do not feel
  thirsty (→ 03-01).
- **Work in shifts and check each other's faces** every few minutes in hard cold. You cannot see
  your own white cheek.
- **A hard rule for children:** a time limit outside set before going out, and inside at once if
  any clothing gets wet.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Thermometer that reads **low** temperatures | Ordinary fever thermometers may not read the hypothermia range | Needed to confirm below 95 °F |
| A thermometer for water | Frostbite rewarming water must be 98.6 to 102 °F | A kitchen or bath thermometer |
| Wool blankets, cold-rated sleeping bags | Rewarming and sleeping warm | Wool insulates when damp |
| Chemical hand and body warmers | Heat with no fire | **Over clothing only, never against skin, never on numb skin, never inside a small child's mittens or boots:** they get hot enough to burn skin that cannot feel or pull away |
| A dry change of clothes per person | "Take off wet clothing" needs something dry to put on | |
| Emergency reflective blankets or bivvies | Hold body heat | Cheap and tiny |
| Room thermometer | Know how cold the house really is | Especially where a baby sleeps |
| Spare hats, mittens, face masks | Extremity cover is the first defence | |
| Makings for warm sweet drinks | Rewarming a conscious person | Also morale |

**No gear?** Another person's body heat is the most reliable rewarming tool there is: skin to skin
under dry layers. Newspaper, cardboard and dry leaves are real insulation inside clothing and
bedding.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** hand warmers and dry clothing are the consumables here; fuel is the deeper one,
  because a warm room prevents all of this (→ 08-01).
- **Ration:** when fuel is short, heat the **people**, not the space: layers, shared body heat, a
  small sleeping area (→ 08-06). Never let a baby's sleeping space go cold.
- **The quiet failure:** everyone gets a little colder each day, judgment slips, and nobody notices.
  In a cold house, take temperatures and look at each other's faces daily.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** most outage hypothermia happens indoors. Keep one warm room (→ 08-01) and check
  children and elders often.
- **B (moving):** the highest-risk activity in winter. Sweat, wind and wet feet are the killers;
  do not thaw frostbite if it may refreeze.
- **C (established somewhere else):** more exposure, more distance from help, harder work. Face
  checks and dry spares become routine.

pages.body:
# Trapping heat: tents indoors and insulation tricks

**What this page is for.** What works when the fuel is gone or low: stop heating air and start
trapping body heat. A tent or blanket fort inside the warm room, insulation under you, shared
warmth, pre-warmed bedding, and using a vehicle as a short warming refuge without poisoning
anyone.

> **CAUTION.** **Nothing that burns goes inside a small enclosed sleeping space:** no heater, no
> stove, no candle. In a tent or fort that means carbon monoxide or a fire around sleeping people
> (CDC; → 08-02). Warmth inside the shelter comes from **insulation and bodies only.** **Never run
> a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window** (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Pitch a tent inside the warm room** (→ 08-01). It is the cheapest, most effective cold-weather
   move in this section: a small space warmed by the people in it.
2. **Insulate from the floor first.** A cold floor draws heat out of anyone lying on it. Foam
   pads, cushions, cardboard, rugs: a thick layer of anything.
3. **Sleep together** in one shelter. Body heat is shared heat.
4. **Hot-water bottles into the bedding before you get in, and out before a child gets in.**
5. **Nothing burning inside the shelter. Ever.**

## Why small is warm

A resting person gives off heat all the time. That heat is lost in a whole house and noticeable
in a small tent. Shrinking the space is how body heat starts to matter. As fuel gets short, step
down:

**House → one room (→ 08-01) → tent inside the room → sleeping bags inside the tent → layers
inside the bags.** Each step is a smaller space with the same heat source: you.

{{figure fig-heat-ladder-house-to-bag}}

## Building the indoor shelter

- **A camping tent indoors** is ideal: it is made to trap warmth and it stands on its own. Drape
  blankets over it for more.
- **No tent?** Build a blanket fort with real structure: a table with blankets over it, or cord
  strung across the room. Children can help, which is good for morale (→ 21-02).
- **Floor first, then walls, then roof.** Most people insulate over before under and stay cold.
- **Keep it small.** Snug is warm; a big fort is a cold fort.
- **Leave a small opening.** Breath is water vapour, and a sealed shelter gets damp; damp bedding
  is a cold-injury risk (→ 08-05).

{{photo indoor-shelter}}

### Insulation, by what you probably have

| Material | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Foam sleeping pads, cushions | Under bodies | Best floor insulation |
| Cardboard | Under everything | Free, effective, plentiful |
| Rugs, blankets, comforters | Floor and walls | Layer generously |
| Newspaper | Inside clothing, under bedding | Really does insulate |
| Bubble wrap | Windows, walls | Traps air |
| Dry leaves, straw | Under a pad or inside a liner | Rural option |
| Curtains, towels, clothing | Everywhere | Nothing is too small |

## Bedding that works

- **Loft is warmth.** Squashed insulation does not insulate; do not cram a bag so tight that it
  flattens.
- **Wool over cotton.** Wool insulates when damp; cotton is dangerous when wet (→ 11-05).
- **Hat in bed.** Cover the head and neck as well as the body (CDC wraps a chilled person's head
  and neck too).
- **Dry sleep clothes.** The day's sweat will chill you all night (→ 11-03).
- **A wrapped hot-water bottle at the feet**, put in before you get in.
- **Babies and toddlers:** warmth is worn, not piled on. Layers and a sleep sack, no loose
  bedding in a baby's sleep space (AAP); keep the room and shelter warm instead (→ 11-02).
  Whether a small child shares an adult bed for warmth is a decision card: {{choice DC-09}}
  (→ 30-10).

## A vehicle as a warming refuge at home

{{#if has.vehicle}}You have a vehicle. {{/if}}A car's cabin is a small insulated space with a real
heater. Used at home it has its own rules:

- **In the open, never in the garage,** not with the door open, not "for a few minutes". Park it
  clear of the house's windows and vents (→ 08-02).
- **Clear the tailpipe of snow before every warming session.** A drifted-over exhaust fills the
  cabin with CO (NWS, What To Do If You're Caught in a Winter Storm).
- **Run it about 10 minutes each hour with a window open a little,** the same rule NWS gives for a
  stranded car (NWS; → 22-05). The cabin holds the heat between runs.
{{#if has.hybrid}}- **A hybrid** in its ready mode starts the engine only as needed to hold the
  battery and cabin temperature, which uses far less fuel than idling a conventional engine and
  can charge devices too (→ 09-11). The tailpipe and garage rules still apply.
{{/if}}- **Children are never alone in it,** awake or asleep.
- **If it becomes a daily refuge, put a battery CO alarm in the cabin.** Repetition is when the
  tailpipe check gets skipped.
- **A refuge, not a bedroom.** Nobody sleeps overnight in a running vehicle. A parked, unheated car
  is just a small cold room: insulate it like one.

## Children

Small children in a tent for weeks is either miserable or an adventure, and that depends mostly on
how the adults frame it. Make it a fort. Let them help build it. Give it a name. It costs nothing
and pays back in behaviour and morale (→ 21-02, → 20-03).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Camping tent big enough for the household ({{ household.size }} people) | The indoor shelter | A cheap dome tent works |
| Closed-cell foam pads, one per person | The floor layer | Also for travel |
| Cold-rated sleeping bags, all sizes | Where the warmth lives | Child sizes too |
| Wool blankets | Insulate when damp | |
| Hot-water bottles | Pre-warm bedding | |
| Emergency reflective blankets | Reflect body heat | Cheap; stock several |
| Cord, hooks, nails | Hang blankets, build structure | |
| Wool hats and socks for sleeping | Head and feet | A dry sleep set |

**No gear?** Cardboard is the most underrated insulation there is. Sofa cushions make a floor and a
wall. Newspaper between two blankets makes a warm quilt. A parked car, insulated with blankets and
**without** the engine running, is a usable small shelter.

## When it runs out

- **Insulation is found, not used up.** This is the heat plan with no depletion clock, which is why
  it is the end of the fuel ladder.
- **Nothing to ration.** Shrink the space further, add layers, share heat.
- **Fuel buys comfort; insulation and body heat buy survival.** Practise one cold weekend now; it
  teaches more than reading (→ 24-02).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** tent inside the warm room. Practise one weekend while you still have heat, so
  children find it fun.
- **B (moving):** the same skills in a vehicle or rough shelter: insulate from the ground, keep it
  small, nothing burning inside.
- **C (established somewhere else):** the same, plus natural insulation (straw, leaves, snow) and a
  proper vented stove if the building has one.

pages.body:
# Ducted diesel and kerosene heaters: install and operation

**What this page is for.** How the class of small forced-air heaters often called "diesel heaters"
or "parking heaters" works, how to install one through a window so its fumes stay outside, how to
power and fuel it, and how it fails. These heaters were made for trucks and boats and are widely
sold for home and cabin use. This page gives the method; **your own unit's manual gives the
numbers (start current, running power, fuel use, exhaust temperature, altitude setting) and
governs.** Spec tables for common models are on → 28-04.
Diesel and kerosene are explained on → 29-01.

> **SAFETY.** This class is the safest serious fuel heat in this section **only if it is installed
> right:** combustion air comes from **outside**, exhaust goes **outside**, and only clean heated
> air enters the room. Installed wrong (exhaust inside, intake inside, a leaking joint) it is just
> another carbon monoxide (CO) source. **Sealed combustion is a design goal, not a guarantee: a
> battery CO alarm runs in the heated room every time** (CDC; → 08-02). **Fuel is never stored or
> transferred near an open flame or a running appliance** (→ 30-01): fill it with the heater off
> and cool, outdoors.

{{#if has.diesel_heater}}**Your household listed a ducted heater:** {{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}} {{h.model}}; {{/each}}{{/if}}

## Do this now (the week you get one)

1. **Do the window-board install as a dry run** in daylight and above freezing, not for the first
   time in an outage by headlamp.
2. **Make the window board:** plywood or rigid foam cut to one warm-room window opening, with two
   sealed pass-throughs for the **combustion intake** and the **exhaust**, both ending outdoors.
   Label it and store it with the heater.
3. **Stage the fuel** your manual names (diesel or kerosene), in approved, labelled cans
   (→ 06-06). **Winter diesel gels**: use winter-blend fuel or an anti-gel additive.
4. **Battery CO alarm in the room it heats,** every run (→ 08-02).
5. **Test-run it monthly in season** through the window board, so the pump, glow plug and
   controller are known to work before you need them.

## How this class works

Portable propane and kerosene heaters burn the room's air and leave their exhaust in the room
(→ 08-09, → 08-10). A ducted heater is different in kind. Its burner is a **sealed loop**: outside
air in, burn, exhaust out. A separate fan blows room air across a hot metal box (the heat
exchanger) and back out of a duct as clean hot air. Nothing the flame touches should mix with the
air you breathe. That is why this class can run for hours in a lived-in room, **provided the
install is tight and the alarm is watching for the day it is not.**

It needs electricity: a **glow plug** (a small electric heater element) lights the fuel, then a fan
and a small dosing pump run all the time. Some units carry their fuel tank inside the unit itself,
which puts fuel inside the warm room; fill such a tank outdoors with the heater cold, and keep all
other fuel out of the living space (→ 06-06). Where fuel is stored is a decision card if the place
is an attached garage: {{choice DC-05}} (→ 30-06).

## The window-board install

{{figure fig-ducted-heater-window-board}}

1. Cut plywood or rigid foam to fill the chosen window opening snugly; foam-tape or weatherstrip
   the edges.
2. Make two holes through the board: **combustion intake** and **exhaust**, spaced apart as the
   manual says, both opening outdoors. The warm-air duct stays entirely indoors.
3. **Seal every joint on the exhaust run** with the supplied clamps and exhaust sealant. A leaking
   exhaust joint indoors defeats the whole design.
4. Close the window down onto the board and stuff and tape the gaps. **Know which sealing is
   which:** the board's edges are for comfort; the exhaust joints are for life.

{{photo ducted-window-board}}

### Exhaust rules

- **Slope the exhaust slightly down and away** so condensation drains out, not back into the
  burner.
- **End it away from any window, door or vent,** and clear snow from around it after every storm
  (→ 08-02).
- **It gets very hot,** hot enough to burn skin and scorch what it touches; your manual gives the
  figure. Keep the pipe off siding, buried combustibles and cord, use the supplied heat wrap and
  standoffs, and keep it where a child cannot touch it.
- **Never shorten the exhaust or run it indoors "temporarily".** There is no temporary CO.

{{photo ducted-exhaust-outside}}

## Fuel

- **Diesel or kerosene,** as your manual allows. Both are distillate fuels, close relatives of
  heating oil (EIA, Diesel Fuel Explained; EIA, Heating Oil Explained; → 29-01). Never gasoline.
- **Winter diesel gels** in cold weather, and the heater's thin fuel line clogs first. Use winter
  blend or anti-gel (→ 06-06).
- **Refuel outdoors, with the heater off and cool.**
- **Old or water-contaminated fuel** clogs the pump and fouls the burner. Whether old fuel is used
  after a test is a decision card: {{choice DC-17}} (→ 30-18).

## Power

- **At start:** the glow-plug cycle draws heavily for a few minutes. Your manual states the
  current the 12 V supply must deliver; write it here: ______ A.
- **Running:** a much smaller draw that depends on the power level; your manual gives it: ______ A
  (or W) at low, ______ at high.
{{#if has.power_station}}- Your power stations ({{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh in total) can run one
  from a 12 V outlet or through the unit's AC adapter; divide watt-hours by the running watts for a
  rough runtime (→ 29-02).
{{/if}}- **Let it finish its shut-down cycle.** The unit runs its fan after the flame is out to cool the
  burner. Cutting power to a hot heater damages the burner.

## CO plan anyway

Sealed combustion fails in dull ways: a cracked exhaust joint, a worn burner gasket, a kinked
intake that pulls room air, snow over the exhaust. **The CO alarm in the heated room is the
backstop for all of them.** Some units have a built-in CO sensor; treat it as a bonus, not a
replacement for the room alarm you test monthly. If the alarm sounds: everyone out, heater off,
→ 08-02.

## Altitude and won't-start

- **Altitude:** thin air makes the mixture too rich, which smokes and soots. Many controllers have
  an altitude ("plateau") mode that cuts the fuel rate; your manual says from what height to use
  it: ______ ft.
  {{#if is.high_altitude}}Your home is above 5,000 ft: check your controller's setting.{{/if}}
- **Won't start in the cold:** usually fuel (gelled diesel, or air in the line after refuelling:
  repeat the priming cycle) or a weak power supply that sags under the glow-plug load. Check the
  voltage under load before blaming the unit.
- **Smoke at start:** a little white smoke from a cold start is normal. **Continuous black smoke means
  too much fuel**: wrong altitude setting or a fouled burner. Glow plugs and burners can be cleaned
  by the manual's maintenance section.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| The heater and its manual | Your unit's numbers | Keep the manual with it |
| Pre-cut window board with sealed pass-throughs | The install is the safety | Made in advance, labelled |
| Exhaust extension, clamps, high-temperature sealant | Reach outdoors, sealed | Every joint clamped |
| Diesel or kerosene, anti-gel for diesel | Fuel that flows in the cold | → 06-06 |
| 12 V cable or AC adapter | Its power | Supply good for the start current |
| **Battery CO alarm for the heated room** | The backstop | Test before each season |
| Spare glow plug and burner gasket | The parts that fail | Cheap now, unobtainable later |

**No heater?** Any rigid sheet (plywood, foam board, doubled cardboard faced with foil tape) can
become a window board, but the exhaust sealing cannot be improvised loosely. Without the heater,
fall back on → 08-04 and → 08-06.

## When it runs out

- **Fuel is countable:** your manual lists fuel use per hour at each power level. Write it here:
  ______ per hour at low, ______ at high. Log cans on → 23-02.
- **Ration:** run it in bursts to warm the room, then coast under insulation (→ 08-01). Overnight,
  bedding and shared warmth save fuel.
- **Resupply:** diesel is often the most findable liquid fuel in rural areas; kerosene usually is
  not (→ 06-05). The glow plug and gaskets are the non-fuel clock: keep spares.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** a strong warm-room heater for a long winter outage: window-board install,
  battery power, CO alarm.
- **B (moving):** these began as vehicle heaters. A vehicle install is an option **only** with the
  same rules: exhaust fully outside and sealed, CO alarm in the cabin, never improvised at a rest
  stop (→ 22-05).
- **C (established somewhere else):** a good backup to wood heat (→ 08-08): it heats a room without
  tending a fire.
