pages.body:
# Running wood heat that actually heats

**What this page is for.** How to run a wood stove or fireplace so it gives real heat without
burning the house down or filling it with carbon monoxide (CO): checking the chimney, testing the
wood, building a fire that burns clean, the damper, the night, the ashes, and children near the
hearth. It is written for tired people new to wood heat, at home or wherever you end up.

> **SAFETY.** The two killers are **chimney fire** (from creosote, the tar that smoky fires and
> wet wood leave in the chimney) and **CO** (from a blocked flue, or a damper closed on live
> coals). Battery CO alarm in the room with the fire, smoke alarm on that level (→ 08-02).
> Whether to light a fireplace or stove that has not been inspected this year is a decision card:
> {{choice DC-21}} (→ 30-22). **Chimney fire response is on → 06-09: know it before the first
> fire.**

{{#if has.wood_stove}}Your household has a wood stove.{{/if}}{{#if has.fireplace}} Your home has an
indoor fireplace.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Before the first fire anywhere:** look up the flue with a strong light, with the fire out and
   the flue cold. Look for nests, shiny or crusty soot glaze, cracks, fallen brick or a blockage.
   NFPA 211, the chimney standard, calls for an inspection at least once a year (as quoted by
   CSIA, Homeowner Resources and FAQs; CSIA, Preventing Chimney Fires). The full check is on
   → 06-09.
2. **Test the wood.** Burn wood **under 20% moisture** (EPA, Burn Wise). Use a moisture meter on a
   freshly split face. Wet wood makes smoke, creosote and half the heat (→ 06-03).
3. **CO alarm and smoke alarm** in the room, fresh batteries.
4. **A metal ash can with a tight metal lid,** outside on dirt or concrete, before the first burn.
5. **Set the child line:** a physical barrier, children kept back, and anything that can burn at
   least 3 feet from the fireplace or stove (USFA, Fireplace and Wood Stove Safety), taught before
   the first fire, not after the first burn (→ 20-02).

## The open-fireplace truth

**An open fireplace can cool a house overall.** MU Extension puts a traditional fireplace at about
10 percent efficiency, sometimes worse than nothing: it can draw up to 300 cubic feet a minute of
already-warm room air up the chimney, and cold outside air comes in through every crack to replace
it (University of Missouri Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating, G5450).

What an open fireplace is still good for:

- **Light, morale and cooking coals:** real value, honestly priced.
- **Real heat only with hardware:** a **fireplace insert** (a stove built into the opening) can
  raise a fireplace's efficiency to as much as 40 percent (MU Extension, G5450).
- **When it is not burning, close the damper.** An open damper is a hole in the roof. (Never with
  live coals: below.)

## Building a fire that heats

- **Top-down lighting:** big splits on the bottom, smaller pieces crosswise above, kindling and
  tinder on top. It warms the chimney fast, burns clean from the start and needs little tending at
  first.
- **Small hot fires beat a big smouldering one.** EPA says build hot fires: for most appliances a
  smouldering fire is neither safe nor efficient (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices). Smoke cools in
  the chimney and sticks as creosote; restricted air and wet wood speed it up (CSIA, Preventing
  Chimney Fires). If you cannot see flames, you are making creosote, not heat.
- **Plenty of dry kindling** at every start and every reload onto coals: start small and hot, then
  add larger pieces with space for air between them (EPA).
- **Never burn** garbage, plastic, painted or pressure-treated wood, or glossy paper (EPA): toxic
  indoors and hard on the chimney.

## The damper

- **Fully open to light** and for the first minutes of every reload. Flame needs air and the
  chimney needs heat to draw.
- **Turn it down in steps** once the fire is burning strongly, watching that flames stay present
  and no smoke rolls into the room.
- **Never closed with live coals.** Burning coals still make CO after the flames die (→ 29-03), and
  a closed damper sends it into the sleeping house. EPA also says keep a stove's doors closed except
  when loading, because CO can be released into the home (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices). Close it only when the ashes are truly out, with
  the CO alarm working.

## Overnight: burn down, don't smoulder

**USFA's advice is to put the fire out before you go to sleep or leave the house** (USFA, Fireplace
and Wood Stove Safety). Loading the stove full and choking the air for an "all-nighter" is the
opposite: CSIA names overloading the firebox for a longer burn and closing the air down too far as
causes of creosote buildup (CSIA, Preventing Chimney Fires), and it adds CO risk while everyone
sleeps. So **let the last load burn down before sleep, never choke it, leave the damper open while
any coals are live, and take the night on bedding:** bags, wool, hot-water bottles, shared warmth
(→ 08-06). A well-warmed room and real bedding ride out the night. Relight in the morning
(→ 06-02).

## Ashes

**Metal can, metal lid, outside, at least 10 feet from the house** (USFA, Fireplace and Wood
Stove Safety), on a surface that cannot burn (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices); never a paper bag,
plastic bin or the porch. "Cold-looking" ash can hide live coals, so the can stays out there until
the ash is cold right through. Cold ash is useful afterwards: grit on icy paths, the garden.

{{photo ash-can}}

## The wood itself

- **Under 20% moisture,** seasoned at least six months, split, stacked off the ground and covered on
  top only (EPA, Best Wood-Burning Practices; → 06-03).
- **Dense hardwoods** such as oak and hickory give more heat per load and long-lasting coals; they
  want a hot start. **Light woods** such as cottonwood burn fine but give much less heat for the
  same volume, so plan more wood, more reloads and more cutting (→ 06-04).
- Your home region's firewood trees are on the regional plates (→ 06-04).

## Children and the hearth

{{#if has.young_child}}Your household has a young child.{{/if}} Barrier first (a hearth gate or a
furniture perimeter), a screen in front of an open fireplace (USFA), children kept well back, tools
and lighters out of reach, no child
alone in the room with a live fire, and the rule practised (→ 20-02). **Stove glass and metal stay
hot long after the flames are gone**; that is the burn that actually happens.

{{photo hearth-barrier}}

## If the chimney roars

A low rumble like a freight train, loud cracking and popping, dense smoke or flame from the top of
the chimney (CSIA), a glowing stovepipe: that is a chimney fire. **The response is on → 06-09:** shut the air, get everyone out, follow it. This
page does not repeat it so that there is only one version.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Moisture meter** | The difference between heat and creosote | Cheap pin type; test fresh split faces |
| Metal ash can with tight lid, metal shovel | The ash rule made physical | Stays outside |
| **CO and smoke alarms**, spare batteries | The two ways wood heat kills | Carry one CO alarm when you travel (→ 22-03) |
| Hearth gate or barrier | The child line | |
| Fireplace gloves, poker, tongs | Tending without burns | |
| Fire extinguisher (ABC) near, not behind, the hearth | The first seconds of a fire | → 29-12 |
| Chimney brush sized to the flue | A mid-winter sweep | → 06-09 |
| Splitting maul, wedges, saw | Wood is labour | → 16-06 |

**No gear?** No moisture meter: knock two splits together; a sharp crack is dry, a dull thud is wet;
checked, cracked end grain and loose bark are dry signs (→ 06-03). No ash can: any all-metal
container with a metal lid; a galvanised trash can works; nothing plastic, ever. No hearth gate:
a furniture perimeter, a taped line, and constant adult eyes.

## When it runs out

- **The woodpile is countable** (→ 06-04).
- **Ration:** shrink the heated space (→ 08-01), burn small hot fires in the day, take nights on
  bedding. A smouldered fire wastes wood and builds the creosote that ends the chimney.
- **Resupply:** standing dead wood and fallen wood first (→ 06-04). Green wood cut now is next
  winter's fuel.
- **The real clock is often the chimney, not the pile.** A chimney fire or a choked flue ends wood
  heat instantly; clean burning and sweeping (→ 06-09) keep it going.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** if your home has no indoor wood appliance, an outdoor fire pit is for cooking
  only (→ 07-01, → 08-02).
- **B (moving):** on arrival anywhere with a stove or fireplace: flue check, alarms up, wood test,
  before the first fire, however cold the trip was.
- **C (established somewhere else):** this is the daily routine wherever wood is the heat.

pages.body:
# Portable propane heaters (Buddy family): setup, safe use and troubleshooting

**What this page is for.** How to set up, light, run, shut down and troubleshoot the small
portable propane heaters sold for indoor emergency use: the "Buddy" family (small, mid and large
sizes from one maker) and similar radiant heaters from other makers. The figures on this page come
from the owner's manual of one widely sold model, the Portable Buddy MH9BX (Enerco/Mr. Heater,
Portable Buddy Radiant Heater operating instructions and owner's manual). **Other sizes and makers
differ:** their spec tables are on → 28-04, and **your own heater's manual and data plate govern.**
Propane is explained on → 29-01, carbon monoxide (CO) on → 29-03.

> **SAFETY.** This is an **unvented** heater: it burns the room's oxygen and its exhaust stays in
> the room. "Approved for indoor use" means it has safety shutoffs; **it does not mean it cannot
> poison you.** Four rules from its manual and this binder: **(1)** a tested battery CO alarm is up
> **before** it is lit (→ 08-02); **(2)** the manual's fresh-air openings are open the whole time it
> burns; **(3)** never unattended; **(4)** a cylinder larger than 1 lb stays **outdoors**. **Fuel is
> never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance** (→ 30-01). If the CO
> alarm sounds or anyone gets a headache, dizziness or nausea: heater off, everyone out, → 08-02.

{{#if has.propane_heater}}**Your household listed:** {{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}} {{h.model}}; {{/each}}Propane on hand: {{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }} 1-lb cylinders, {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} 20-lb tanks.{{/if}}

{{photo propane-heater-plate}}

## Do this now: the sequence, every time

1. **CO alarm first.** Battery in, hold TEST until it sounds. In the warm room at pillow height, on
   the wall opposite the heater, not above it, not in a still-air corner, not by an air opening
   (→ 08-02).
2. **Fresh air:** open the manual's openings (below) before lighting.
3. **Clearances:** 30 in above, 24 in in front, 6 in each side; on a level, hard surface out of foot
   traffic; children and pets kept back by a barrier (→ 20-02).
4. **Fuel:** a 1-lb cylinder attached outdoors, or a 20-lb tank **outdoors** on the maker's hose
   through a cracked window or door, with the fuel filter fitted. Soapy-water leak test on every
   connection.
5. **Light** by the steps below. **An adult stays in the room while it burns.**
6. **Shut down** before leaving the room: tank valve closed, let the line burn empty, knob to OFF.
7. **One fuel-burning heater at a time.** The manual says do not use other fuel-burning appliances
   inside.

## What "indoor-approved" means, and what it does not

The manual certifies the heater to **ANSI Z21.103, unvented portable gas camp heaters for indoor
and outdoor use,** and calls it a heater for **recreational and emergency indoor use**. Check the
data plate on yours for the certification mark (→ 29-14). Two built-in protections earn that:

- **Oxygen depletion sensor (ODS).** A safety system built into the pilot that turns the heater
  off when not enough fresh air is available. The manual says: if it shuts off, do not relight
  until you provide fresh air; if it keeps shutting off, have it serviced. **An ODS shutoff means
  the room ran short of air. It is a warning, not a nuisance.**
- **Tip-over switch.** Shuts the heater off if it tips or is knocked hard.

**Neither one measures CO.** A dirty burner, a blocked pilot, or a knob left between settings makes
CO while the oxygen is still fine. The manual itself warns that without enough air for burning and
ventilation the heater may give off excessive carbon monoxide. The alarm is your only CO detector
(CDC; → 08-02).

## The manufacturer's numbers (one model; check yours)

| Item | Portable Buddy MH9BX manual |
|---|---|
| Heat input | **4,000 BTU/h on LO, 9,000 BTU/h on HI** |
| Fuel use, shown as runtime | **3 to 6 hours per 1-lb cylinder; 48 to 110 hours per 20-lb tank,** shorter below 20 °F |
| Required fresh air | **9 square inches (a 3 × 3 in opening) at ceiling level and at floor level** |
| Other fuel appliances in the space | Not allowed |
| Permitted settings by room | Bathroom: LO only. Bedroom: HI or LO |
| Sleeping | "Never operate the heater while sleeping" |
| Clearances to anything that burns | Top 30 in, front 24 in, sides 6 in, rear 0 in |
| Safety devices | ODS and tip-over switch |
| Altitude | Weak burning and **possible shutoff above 7,000 ft** |
| Lowest room temperature on the spec plate | **0 °F** |
| Emergency indoor heating | On a disposable 1-lb cylinder |
| Larger cylinder | A remote refillable cylinder of up to 20 lb, **only when the cylinder is outdoors**, on the maker's hose (the manual words this for recreational enclosures such as cabins, tents and trailers) |
| Cylinders indoors | "Never bring a refillable propane cylinder indoors"; cylinders not connected for use are stored outdoors, not in a building or garage |

Source: Enerco/Mr. Heater, Portable Buddy owner's manual. Larger "Big Buddy" class heaters burn more
fuel per hour and smaller ones less; read yours (→ 28-04).

## Fresh air

- **Two openings of at least 9 square inches each: one high, one low.** In practice: a window or
  door cracked to give at least a 3 × 3 in opening near the ceiling, and another near the floor,
  for example an upper window sash dropped an inch across its width plus a door to the rest of the
  house open at the floor.
- A towel stuffed around a hose gap is a draught seal, **not** one of these openings.
- The heater also makes **water vapour**: condensation and damp bedding follow in a closed room, and
  damp bedding is a cold-injury risk (→ 08-05).
{{#if is.high_altitude}}- **Your home is above 5,000 ft.** The manual warns of possible shutoff
  above 7,000 ft. If it shuts off at altitude: fresh air, wait 5 minutes, relight.
{{/if}}
## Heat while people sleep

The manual says **never operate the heater while sleeping**, and CPSC says never run an unvented
fuel-burning appliance in any room where people are sleeping (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Questions and
Answers). Running it overnight keeps the room
warm but leaves CO and fire with no one awake to catch them; turning it off means a cold night,
which matters most for babies and frail elders. The household decides on the card:
{{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02). If the household's answer allows overnight use, on this class "lowest
setting" means **LO**, both openings open, the heater behind its barrier on the far side of the room
from the sleepers, and whoever checks looks at the burner tile, the alarm and the openings. **If you
wake to a cold heater, the ODS may have shut it off because the room was short of air: ventilate
before relighting.**

## Placement

| Direction | Minimum clearance to anything that burns |
|---|---|
| Top | 30 in |
| Front | 24 in |
| Sides | 6 in |
| Rear | 0 in |

Level, hard ground, out of traffic. Never on a bed, couch or rug edge (some carpet or vinyl may
discolour under it). **Never warm or cook food on it**: the manual says that can defeat the safety
systems. **Never move it while lit**: a bump trips the tip-over switch, and the grille is hot. Keep
door blankets, curtains and toys out of the clearances.

{{photo propane-heater-setup}}

## Cold-weather limits

The spec plate lists a **0 °F** minimum room temperature, and the manual says runtimes drop **below
20 °F**. With the tank outdoors on a very cold night, the propane itself is the limit: **a heater
that sputters or dies with the tank outside in deep cold has a cold-fuel (low-pressure) problem,
not an air problem.** Shelter the tank from wind, switch to a fuller tank, or use another heat
source. **Never warm a tank with a flame, a heater or anything but air.**

## Lighting, step by step (manual)

**With a hose to a 20-lb tank:**

1. Control knob at **OFF**. Swing the regulator outward.
2. Screw the **fuel filter** onto the heater's regulator, then the hose onto the filter; screw the
   hose's other end into the tank valve. Hand-tight; **no thread sealant**; do not overtighten.
3. **Open the tank valve.** Soapy-water test **both ends.** Bubbles mean a leak: stop.
4. Turn the knob to **PILOT** and press it in to spark. **With a hose, the first light takes
   longer**, because air in the hose has to clear. If it does not light, hold the knob down about
   **30 seconds**, release, and press again; repeat until the pilot lights.
5. Once the pilot lights, **keep holding the knob down 30 to 60 seconds** (this heats the pilot's
   sensor), then release. The pilot must stay lit.
6. Press slightly and turn to lock on **HI**; leave it on HI until the burner tile glows **bright
   orange** (a few minutes from cold). Then choose LO or HI. **Never leave the knob between the
   locked positions**: poor burning and more CO.

**With a 1-lb cylinder:** attach and remove it **outdoors only, with the heater cool and no flame
nearby**. Screw it in clockwise, hand-tight; soapy-water test; then steps 4 to 6. Only 1-lb
(16.4 oz) cylinders made for this purpose.

**Normal at first use:** smoke and smell from the grille paint (once), the reflector discolouring, a
narrow unlit border around the tile, condensation on the cylinder. **Not normal:** visible flames on
the tile; turn it off.

## Shutting down

- **Hose:** close the **tank valve first**, let the heater burn the gas left in the hose until it
  goes out, then press and turn the knob to OFF. If it was set up but never lit, the manual says
  purge the line **outdoors** by holding the control down.
- **1-lb cylinder:** knob to OFF; remove the cylinder **outdoors, once cool**. The manual says
  cylinders must be disconnected from the heater when not in use.
- The wire guard stays hot for a long time; let it cool before storing.

## The heat-powered fan (accessory)

The maker's add-on fan is **thermoelectric**: it runs on the heater's own heat, with no batteries or
electricity. Install it only with the heater **off and cool**, seated tight against the heater with
no gap. Light on **HI**; it takes **3 to 5 minutes** to start spinning, then LO is fine. **Never put
anything in front of or on the fan.** If it has not started after 15 minutes, shut down, cool, reseat
it and retry (Enerco/Mr. Heater, Buddy power fan installation instructions).

## The propane source

**Why a 20-lb tank lives outdoors:**

1. **Size.** A full 20-lb grill tank holds about twenty times the propane of a 1-lb cylinder; most
   are sold filled to 15 lb (NIST, LPG 20 Pound Cylinders). One pound of propane makes about
   8.6 cubic feet of gas, so a full 20-lb tank holds about **170 cubic feet** of gas (a 15-lb fill
   about 130). Propane burns once it makes up **2.1 %** of the air (Matheson, propane data sheet).
   At 2.1 %, 170 cubic feet is enough to make about 8,000 cubic feet of air able to burn: more than
   a whole room (→ 28-04). A leak indoors is not a whiff.
2. **It sinks and pools.** Propane is heavier than air (manual). It flows along floors, down stairs
   and into **basements**, below your nose, toward the furnace and water-heater flames.
3. **Warmth makes it vent.** A cold tank brought into a warm house builds pressure, and its relief
   valve is built to open and release gas when the pressure is too high (YSN/Flame King, Training
   Program 1A), indoors as well as out.
4. **The rule says so.** The manual allows a cylinder of up to 20 lb **only when the cylinder is
   outdoors**, and says **never bring a refillable propane cylinder indoors**. The national
   propane code (NFPA 58) limits cylinders kept or used inside a home, attached garages included,
   to the 1-lb size (Minnesota State Fire Marshal, LP Gas Inside Buildings), and a propane training
   course written to that code allows at most two 1-lb cylinders stored in a home (YSN/Flame King,
   Training Program 1A).

**The hose method.** The manual's own line for emergency heating in a home names the 1-lb
cylinder; it allows the outdoor tank and hose for recreational enclosures. Many households run the
hose into the warm room anyway; the decision card treats the cylinder-outside, hose-through-a-window
route as one of its options and lists what makes it safer: {{choice DC-02}} (→ 30-03). If you use
it:

- **Tank outdoors,** upright, on a board off snow and ice, out of the wind if possible, valve closed
  until you are ready to light.
- **The maker's hose** through a cracked window or door at ground level; a towel around the gap so
  the hose is not pinched. The heater sits within the hose's reach of that window, which is why the
  warm room has to be chosen with this in mind (→ 08-01). **Never a fully below-ground room with
  propane.**
- **Fuel filter on.** The manual strongly recommends the maker's fuel filter with any remote tank,
  and requires it with some of its hoses: hoses shed an oily residue that clogs the regulator and
  pilot, and the manual's remedy for that is a new control valve and regulator. Check your hose's
  tag against the manual's accessory list. Replace the filter yearly; write the date on it.
- **Only the maker's hoses.** The manual forbids hand-made or third-party accessories.
- **Inspect the hose every use:** cracks, cuts, wear mean replace it first.
- **No second regulator.** The heater's own regulator must always be in place.

{{figure fig-propane-heater-hose-route}}

{{photo propane-tank-outside}}

**Bringing a tank larger than 1 lb inside** (for example when the window route is frozen shut) is a
trade-off between a cold room and a propane leak that pools at floor level until it finds a flame;
the manual and the propane code both say no. The household decides on the card, which lists the
conditions for each option: {{choice DC-02}} (→ 30-03).

## Refilling 1-lb cylinders

The green 1-lb cylinders are made to be filled once at the factory. Adapters sold for refilling them
from a 20-lb tank exist. The heater's maker allows only disposable 1-lb cylinders on the heater and
says never bring a refillable cylinder indoors; the refillable-cylinder maker says a disposable
single-trip cylinder must never be refilled. The risks are overfilling (a 1-lb cylinder has no
overfill stop, so an overfilled one vents gas when it warms indoors) and a worn valve leaking in the
room. Whether your household refills at all is a decision card: {{choice DC-03}} (→ 30-04).

**If the card's answer is to refill by weight, this is the cylinder maker's method** (YSN/Flame King,
Training Program 1A; Flame King, 1-lb refillable cylinder product information):

- **Only cylinders built and stamped as refillable.** The foot ring carries the specification, the
  **tare weight (TW, the empty weight)**, the date made, and a 12-year requalification requirement.
  **Never refill a disposable (single-trip) cylinder.**
- **Outdoors, away from any flame or spark,** gloves and long sleeves: liquid propane causes
  frostbite burns.
- Supply valve **closed** before connecting. **Turn the 20-lb tank upside down** in a stable stand
  so liquid flows, and **never leave it inverted longer than 10 minutes.**
- **Never put a refillable 1-lb cylinder in a fridge or freezer,** and never use one that has been
  in one.
- **Fill limit: 80 percent liquid**, which leaves a 20 percent vapour space for the liquid to
  expand. The training's method is the bleed vent: open the fixed liquid level gauge, and **when
  white fog (liquid propane) comes out of the bleed vent, stop at once** and close it (YSN/Flame
  King, Training Program 1A).
- **Weight check:** the cylinder's rated content is 16.4 oz, about 1 lb (Flame King). So a full
  cylinder should weigh no more than its stamped TW plus about 1 lb: for the training's example
  cylinder, TW 1.5 lb, about 2.5 lb. Weigh every filled cylinder on a kitchen scale; heavier means
  overfilled.
- **Overfilled:** bleed it down outdoors until the weight is right. **Leaking:** set it outdoors away
  from everything; do not use it.
- **Soapy-water test** the filled cylinder's valve. **Retire any cylinder that hisses or whose valve
  is bent or stiff.**
- Put the 20-lb tank back **upright**, valve closed.

## Troubleshooting (manual)

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **No spark** when the knob is pressed | Broken electrode, loose igniter wire, bad igniter | Parts replacement, not a field fix. Use other heat (→ 08-04) |
| **Spark but no pilot** | No gas: tank valve closed, tank empty, 1-lb not fully seated | Open the valve; change cylinder outdoors; check the filter is fitted where required |
| | Air in the hose (first light) | Hold the knob in at PILOT about 30 s, release, repeat |
| | Knob not exactly at PILOT; pilot blocked | Reseat at PILOT; clean the pilot with air (never a needle or wire) |
| **Pilot goes out when the knob is released** | Not held long enough | Hold 30 to 60 s after it lights |
| | Pilot flame not reaching its sensor; tip-switch wires loose | Clean the pilot; reconnect tip-switch wires |
| **Burner tile will not light** | Burner orifice blocked; knob not locked on HI | Lock on HI; clean per manual |
| **Shuts off after running** | **ODS tripped: the room is short of air** | **Stop. Do not just relight.** Open both openings, wait 5 minutes, relight. If it keeps happening, stop using it |
| | Bumped or tipped | Set it level, out of traffic; relight |
| | Oily contamination from a hose without a filter | New control valve and regulator; this is why the filter is on |
| **Weak flame, short runtime in deep cold** | Cold tank, low pressure | Use a 20-lb tank; shelter it from wind; never heat it |
| **Flames on the tile, yellow pilot, flame rolling over the top** | Dust, lint or spider webs inside | Off; cool; clean per manual. Persistent: service |
| **Smell of gas** | Leak at a connection, hose or cylinder | **Light nothing. Put out flames. Close the tank valve. Leave, and let the gas clear at least 5 minutes before relighting** (manual). Soapy-water test every joint. Propane sinks: smell low. **Persistent smell: everyone out; call the gas supplier or fire department from outside** |
| **Fan not spinning** | Takes 3 to 5 min on HI; not seated; blocked | Wait on HI; after 15 min shut down, cool, reseat |
| **CO alarm sounds, or headache, dizziness, nausea** | CO | **Heater off, everyone out to fresh air**, → 08-02 |

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| The heater, its manual, its data plate photographed | Your model's numbers | Keep the manual in its bag |
| **Battery CO alarm** | No alarm, no heater | → 08-02 |
| The maker's hose and fuel filter | 20-lb tank stays outdoors | Spare filter; replace yearly |
| 1-lb cylinders and/or 20-lb tanks | Fuel | Stored outdoors (→ 06-06) |
| Soapy-water spray bottle | Leak test every connection, every time | Dish soap and water |
| Barrier | Children and pets | → 20-02 |
| Extinguisher | The fire that gets past the heater | → 29-12 |
| Refillable cylinders, adapter, kitchen scale | Only if the card says refill | → 30-04 |

**There is no substitute for the CO alarm.** Neighbours' grill tanks fit the maker's hose.

## When it runs out

- **Runtime:** use the manual's figures above: 3 to 6 hours per 1-lb, 48 to 110 hours per 20-lb, less
  in deep cold. Log cylinders on → 23-02. Propane is often shared with cooking and the generator
  (→ 06-05): decide how it is split before the outage.
- **Ration:** burst-heat the warm room, then off; bedding and bodies carry most nights (→ 08-06).
- **Substitute:** a wick kerosene heater (→ 08-10), then insulation and layers (→ 08-06).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the warm-room heater with the tank outdoors and the hose through a window, alarm
  first, never unattended.
- **B (moving):** the manual forbids use in a moving vehicle. Never as a sleeping heater in a tent or
  car (→ 08-02).
- **C (established somewhere else):** the same rules. The manual allows a cabin with a window or roof
  vent that gives the required openings.

pages.body:
# Wick kerosene heaters: setup, safe use and troubleshooting

**What this page is for.** How to set up, fuel, light, run, shut off, clean and troubleshoot a
portable **wick kerosene heater** of the round "convection" type sold for indoor use. The figures
here come from the owner's manual of one common 10,500 BTU/h model, the Dyna-Glo WK11C8 (GHP
Group/Dyna-Glo, Portable Kerosene Heater owner's manual). **Other models differ:** spec tables are
on → 28-04, and **your own heater's manual and data plate govern.** Kerosene and the other fuels it
must never meet are explained on → 29-01; carbon monoxide (CO) on → 29-03.

> **SAFETY.** This is an **unvented** heater: it burns room air and its exhaust stays in the room.
> Its manual warns of indoor air pollution and calls for more air in a small room (GHP
> Group/Dyna-Glo manual). **1-K kerosene only. Gasoline in this heater can cause an explosion or
> uncontrolled flames** (manual). A tested battery CO alarm is up **before**
> it is lit (→ 08-02). **Never leave it unattended** (manual). **The common model's manual lists no
> oxygen depletion sensor,** so the alarm is the only thing watching. **Fuel is never stored or
> transferred near an open flame or a running appliance:** refuel outdoors, heater off and cold
> (→ 30-01). **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products**
> (→ 30-01): drinking or breathing in kerosene can cause hydrocarbon pneumonia, a lung injury
> (MedlinePlus, Hydrocarbon pneumonia; → 12-17). Never dry clothes on or over it; never put anything on its top.

{{#if has.kerosene_heater}}**Your household listed:** {{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}} {{h.model}}; {{/each}}Kerosene on hand: {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gallons.{{/if}}

{{photo kerosene-heater-plate}}

## The can rule

**Kerosene goes in a can that is not red, clearly marked KEROSENE.** The manual says store it only
in a blue container marked "KEROSENE", never a red one, because red containers are associated with
gasoline (manual; → 29-01). **Read the label aloud, sniff, then pour. An unlabelled can,
or any doubt, and you do not pour.** Never dyed (red) kerosene, 2-K kerosene, "lamp oil", camp fuel,
diesel, alcohol or anything else in this heater.

{{photo kerosene-cans}}

## Do this now: the sequence, every time

1. **CO alarm first.** Battery in, hold TEST until it sounds. In the warm room at pillow height, on
   the wall opposite the heater, not above it, not in a still-air corner, not by the cracked window
   (→ 08-02).
2. **Fuel outdoors, heater cold,** from the KEROSENE can, by siphon pump, watching the gauge. **If
   the tank had run dry, wait 60 minutes before lighting** so the wick soaks (manual). Set a timer.
3. **Placement:** **36 in clear above and in front** (manual; give it 36 in all round if you can),
   level floor, out of traffic and draughts, behind a barrier (→ 20-02). **Nothing on the top plate;
   nothing drying on, over or near it** (manual).
4. **Air:** the window cracked **at least 1 inch** in a small room (below).
5. **Light, then check the flame at 5 to 7 minutes,** and every 30 minutes after. An adult stays in
   the room while it burns.
6. **Off and confirmed out** before leaving the room.
7. **One fuel-burning heater at a time.** Never moved or carried while lit.
8. **Never where fuel vapour may be present** (manual), which means never run it in a garage or room
   where fuel is stored.

## The manufacturer's numbers (one model; check yours)

| Item | Dyna-Glo WK11C8 manual |
|---|---|
| Heat output | **10,500 BTU/h** maximum |
| Fuel tank | **1.1 US gallons**, built in, with a fuel gauge |
| Fuel use | **0.079 gallons per hour** at maximum |
| Burn time | **About 13 hours** per tank |
| Fuel | Water-clear **1-K kerosene** only |
| Ignition | Push-lever glow igniter on **2 C batteries**, or a match |
| Clearances | **36 in** above and in front |
| Ventilation | If the room has **less than 200 cubic feet per 1,000 BTU/h**, open a window **at least 1 inch** or keep doors to other rooms open; never a bathroom or small closed room |
| Correct flame | **½ inch above the flame spreader**, even all round |
| Safety device | **Tip and jar shut-off** (drops the wick); no oxygen depletion sensor listed |
| Wick height (when fitting a new wick) | 5/16 in above the collar |
| Sleeping | Turn it off and make sure it is out **before going to bed** |
| Altitude | The manual cited here gives no altitude limit that this kit has checked; if yours does, write it here: ______ |

**Runtime from your stock:** gallons on hand ÷ the manual's gallons per hour = hours of burn. With
the figures above, 1 gallon is about 12½ hours at full output. The manual says the heater is meant
to run at its correct flame, not turned down: a low wick makes smell, tar and CO instead of savings.

## Ventilation (manual)

In an ordinary, not unusually tight house, air leaks supply what the heater needs. **But if the room
has less than 200 cubic feet of air per 1,000 BTU/h** of heater, keep the doors to the next rooms
open or **open a window at least 1 inch**. For a 10,500 BTU/h heater that is 2,100 cubic feet, about
a 13 × 20 ft room with an 8 ft ceiling. **Never in a bathroom or any small room with the door
closed.** A warm room is usually small and sealed on purpose (→ 08-01), so **plan on the window
being cracked at least 1 inch whenever it burns.** That does not replace the CO alarm.

{{photo kerosene-heater-setup}}

## Heat while people sleep

The manual says turn it off and make sure it is out before going to bed, and CPSC says never run
an unvented fuel-burning appliance in any room where people are sleeping (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide
Questions and Answers). Keeping it burning keeps the room warm, but this heater has no oxygen
sensor listed, so CO and fire would have only the
alarm and whoever wakes to check. The household decides on the card: {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02).
If the household's answer allows overnight use, on a wick heater **"lowest" does not mean a
turned-down wick**, which smokes and makes CO: it means the wick exactly at the manual's ½-inch
flame, checked before bed and at every check; the tank filled before bed (a tank running dry
overnight gives a dying, smoky flame); the window cracked at least 1 inch; the heater behind its
barrier on the far side of the room; the alarm on the opposite wall at pillow height.

## First-time setup (in daylight, before you need it)

1. Unbox (keep the box for summer storage). Assemble by the manual. **Never run it without its
   guard or grille.**
2. Batteries into the igniter holder.
3. **Fill outdoors** (below), then **wait at least 60 minutes before lighting** so the wick soaks.
   Lighting early traps air in the wick and can ruin it.
4. **First burn outdoors** on a calm day: the factory oils burn off with a smell.

## Refuelling: outdoors, cold

- Heater **off and cool.** Carry heater, KEROSENE can and siphon pump outside.
- Siphon: tighten the cap on top of the pump, straight tube in the can, flexible tube in the heater's
  fill opening, squeeze the bulb.
- **Watch the gauge.** Near full, loosen the pump cap: the flow stops. **Do not overfill.** Let the
  pump drain before pulling it out.
- Wipe spills before the heater comes back inside. Fill cap on tight.
- **Tank was dry? Wait 60 minutes** before lighting. A top-up of a tank that was not empty needs no
  wait.
- Where the cans are stored matters: away from the living space and any flame (→ 06-06). Storage in
  an attached garage is a decision card: {{choice DC-05}} (→ 30-06).

## Lighting

1. Turn the **wick knob** to raise the wick all the way.
2. **Push the ignition lever:** the glowing igniter touches the wick. When it catches, release; the
   burner drops back over the wick.
3. **Turn the burner knob side to side** a few times so the burner sits evenly.
4. **Match backup** (dead batteries): wick fully up, lift the burner by its knob, touch a match to the
   top edge of the wick, lower the burner, turn it to seat. **Leave no match debris** in the burner.

## Flame height

{{figure fig-kerosene-flame-height}}

- **Check at 5 to 7 minutes** (the flame builds as the burner warms), then **every 30 minutes**: as
  the room and tank warm, the flame climbs.
- **Correct: a ½-inch flame above the flame spreader, even all round,** seen through the glass.
- **Too high: smoke and soot.** Lower the wick.
- **Too low: smell and carbon monoxide.** Never run below the wick stop.
- **Smell:** slight at start-up and shut-down is normal; after 5 to 10 minutes it should be very
  slight. Strong or continuing smell is not normal (table below).
- Do not touch the burner knob once the flame has settled; it is very hot.

{{photo kerosene-flame}}

## Shutting off

Push **down on the shut-off knob** with one hand while holding the **wick knob** with the other; ease
your grip and let the spring lower the wick. Turn the wick knob down as far as it goes. After 10 to 15
seconds, lift the burner by its knob and **look: no flame.** Wait **at least 10 minutes before
relighting**; a hot relight gives a strong smell and can flare up.

## The tip and jar shut-off

A pendulum drops the wick if the heater is knocked or tipped. **Test it weekly in season:** heater
off, wick fully up, grab the grille and give a firm shake. You should hear a snap and the wick drops.
If the wick knob then turns further down, the wick is gummed: dry-burn it. **Wick will not rise?**
Push the safety reset lever, then turn the wick up.

## Wick care: the job that keeps it safe

Tar and carbon build up on the wick. A tarred wick smokes, smells, will not lower fully, and **can
fail to go out.** The manual makes this the owner's job.

- **Dry burn (clean burn):** within 7 days of first use, then **every 2 tankfuls or weekly** in
  season, and whenever the wick feels hard. **Outdoors only,** calm day. Burn the tank nearly empty;
  when the flame starts dying, raise the wick fully and let it burn out. Wait 60 minutes, relight, let
  it burn out again. Cool, then brush the wick top with a stiff old toothbrush.
- **Monthly:** heater off and cool, batteries out, grille and burner off, wick raised level with the
  guide; scrape tar off the wick guide with a flat screwdriver.
- **Replace the wick** when cleaning does not fix slow lighting, a stiff knob, smell while burning,
  low heat or damage. **Water-contaminated fuel cannot be dry-burned out:** drain, clean the tank,
  new wick, soak it 60 minutes in fresh 1-K. **Use the maker's wick for your model** (part number on
  the plate or in the manual). After any wick change: set the height by the manual, even all round,
  and **test the shut-off.**

## Fuel quality

- **Water-clear 1-K only.** Water or dirt in the fuel ruins the wick and makes the heater smoke,
  smell and flicker out (manual).
- **Old kerosene:** the manual says never use kerosene stored from one season to the next, because
  old kerosene does not burn properly. Whether old fuel is used after a jar test is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-17}} (→ 30-18). Either way, an unlabelled or cloudy can is never poured (→ 06-06).

## Summer storage

Rinse the tank with a little kerosene and pour it **all** out (never water). Burn the heater dry with
the wick fully up, **outdoors**. Batteries out. Clean tar off the wick knob, guide and burner. Store
with the **wick fully lowered**, in the original box with the manual and siphon pump, somewhere
ventilated.

## Troubleshooting (manual)

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Will not light** | Tank empty | Fill outdoors with clear 1-K; 60-minute soak if it ran dry |
| | Igniter does not glow | New batteries; then a new igniter plug; or a match |
| | Igniter touching the side of the wick | Lower the wick slightly |
| | Water in the kerosene | Drain; new wick; refill with clear 1-K |
| **Smokes** | Flame too high | Lower to ½ in |
| | Draught; burner not level | Move it; turn the burner side to side to seat it |
| | Tar on the wick; bad fuel | Dry burn or new wick; drain and refill |
| **Strong smell** after the first 5 to 10 minutes | Flame too **low**; tar; bad fuel; hot relight | Set ½ in; dry burn; fresh 1-K; wait 10 min before relighting. **Persistent smell or any CO alarm: off, ventilate, → 08-02** |
| **Flame low, uneven, flickers out** | Water in fuel; tar; burner not seated | Drain, new wick, refill; dry burn; reseat |
| **Wick burns down fast** | **A volatile fuel mixed in: gasoline, camp fuel, alcohol, thinner** | **Off, cool, outdoors:** drain and clean the tank, new wick, clear 1-K. Find out how it happened (labels) |
| **Wick will not rise** | Safety shut-off tripped | Push the reset lever, then turn up |
| **Wick sticks, will not lower fully** | Tar; water in fuel | Dry burn; new wick. **If it will not go out:** keep pushing the shut-off; if flame continues, treat as below |
| **Tall flames, flare-up, flames outside the burner** | Runaway flame, hot relight, wrong fuel | **Push the shut-off knob if you can reach it safely. Get the children out. Do not carry it** |
| **Heater surrounded by flames** | — | **Everyone out.** Extinguisher if safe (→ 29-12); otherwise smother with blankets and wet the blankets. **Never water straight onto the heater** |
| **CO alarm sounds, or headache, dizziness, nausea** | CO | **Off, everyone out to fresh air**, → 08-02 |

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| The heater, siphon pump, manual | Your model's numbers | Keep the box for storage |
| 1-K kerosene in labelled, non-red cans | Fuel | → 06-06 |
| **Battery CO alarm** | The only thing watching | → 08-02 |
| Spare wicks for your model | The wear part | Maker's part only |
| Spare C batteries | The igniter | A match also works |
| Fire extinguisher in the warm room | While it burns | → 29-12 |
| Stiff brush, small pliers, flat screwdriver | Wick care | |
| Barrier | Children and pets | → 20-02 |

## When it runs out

- **Runtime:** gallons ÷ the manual's gallons per hour. Log cans on → 23-02.
- **Ration:** burst-heat the warm room while awake; bedding and bodies carry the night (→ 08-06).
  **Never turn the wick down to stretch fuel:** it makes CO, not savings.
- **Substitute:** a propane heater (→ 08-09), then insulation and layers (→ 08-06). Kerosene is hard
  to find in a long outage.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** a steady warm-room heater for long burns. Fuel stays outside the living space;
  filling happens outdoors.
- **B (moving):** never in a vehicle or tent.
- **C (established somewhere else):** the same rules; buy fresh 1-K when you can.

pages.title: What actually needs power (load triage)
pages.body:
# What actually needs power (load triage)

**What this page is for.** Before you buy a single panel, battery or generator, decide what *must*
run when the grid is down, add up how much energy that takes in a day, and size everything else to
that number. Most households do it backwards: they buy a generator or a "solar generator" first and
then find out what it can run. This page is the list and the arithmetic. If watts and watt-hours
are new to you, read → 29-02 first; this page uses them without re-explaining.

## Do this now
- **Buy a plug-in watt meter (the kind a lamp plugs into) and measure your real devices.** The
  label on an appliance gives its *maximum* draw, not what it uses over a day. A refrigerator
  labelled 700 W may average 60 to 90 W across a day because the compressor cycles on and off.
  Guessing here is the single biggest cause of systems that turn out too small.
- **Fill in the table at the bottom of this page** with measured numbers. It is the input to
  → 09-02, → 09-09 and → 09-10. Nothing downstream works without it.
- **Sort every load into the four tiers below and put the tier on a label on the device.** You
  make these decisions once, calmly, now, not at 2 a.m. in a cold house.
- **Know your Tier 0 loads by name.**
  {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}This household has a refrigerated medicine: keeping it cold is a
  Tier 0 load and usually the biggest one (→ 09-10).{{/if}}
  {{#if has.cpap}}A CPAP machine is on the Tier 0 list (→ 02-24, → 09-06).{{/if}}
  {{#if has.oxygen}}An oxygen concentrator is on the Tier 0 list, and it is a large load
  (→ 02-08, → 09-06).{{/if}}
  Everything else on this page is comfort by comparison.

## Why it works this way

**The number that matters is the watt-hour (Wh).** Watts are how fast a device uses energy;
watt-hours are how much it used. Watts × hours = watt-hours: a 10 W LED bulb for 5 hours is
50 Wh. A battery is rated in watt-hours, or in amp-hours at a voltage (amp-hours × volts =
watt-hours; a 100 Ah 12 V battery is roughly 1,200 to 1,280 Wh depending on whether you count it
at 12.0 or 12.8 V). Every sizing decision in this section is that one piece of arithmetic
(→ 29-02).

**Two numbers describe every load, and you need both:**
- **Power (W)** decides whether a battery and its inverter can run the device *at all*. A
  1,500 W microwave trips a 300 W power station instantly, however large its battery is.
- **Energy (Wh per day)** decides how long you can keep doing it.

**Heat and motors are the two budget-killers.** Anything that makes heat (kettle, toaster, hair
dryer, space heater, coffee maker) or drives a compressor or motor (refrigerator, freezer, well
pump, furnace blower) draws ten to a thousand times what electronics draw. **A survival power
system does not make heat.** Heat comes from fire and fuel (Sections 06, 07 and 08). Electricity
is for information, medicine and light.

**Two deliberate exceptions** (→ 07-06):
- **Boiling small amounts of water.** An electric kettle is efficient, silent and makes no carbon
  monoxide. Budget about **110 Wh per litre boiled, about 55 Wh per freeze-dried meal**. A vacuum
  flask filled from one morning boil roughly halves that.
- **Heated blankets (50 to 100 W)** warm the person, not the room: the best heat per watt you
  can get from a battery.

### The four tiers

**Tier 0: life-critical. This is the reason the system exists.**

| Load | Why | Typical draw |
|---|---|---|
| Phone(s) used for medical devices, alerts and contact | Information; for some households the phone runs a medical device (→ 09-06) | About 10 to 20 Wh a day with the screen mostly off |
| Cooling for refrigerated medicine | Some medicines lose strength when warm (→ 29-07, → 09-10) | **200 to 1,500 Wh a day, depending on what does the cooling** |
| Medical devices that plug in or charge (CPAP, oxygen concentrator, pump accessories, nebuliser) | Breathing and medicine delivery (→ 09-06) | From a few Wh to hundreds; read the label and measure |
| One reliable light source at night | Falls, stairs, children, injuries | 10 to 50 Wh a day |

**Tier 1: high value, low cost.** Radio and scanner (→ 15-02, → 15-04), headlamps and
rechargeable AA and AAA cells (→ 10-01), a small fan to move warm air in one room (→ 08-01), a
tablet or laptop holding this binder, rechargeable tool batteries, a water filter pump.

**Tier 2: quality of life, when there is a surplus.** A refrigerator or freezer for food (as
opposed to medicine), laundry, children's devices for morale (→ 21-02), power tools, a sewing
machine.

**Tier 3: do not run these on batteries.** Electric space heat, electric cooking, electric water
heating, air conditioning, a well pump on a small system, a clothes dryer. **These are fuel jobs,
not electricity jobs.** Each one empties a battery bank in well under a day and buys almost
nothing.

### Typical draws (planning placeholders; measure your own)

| Device | Typical W | Typical Wh per day | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phone charge | 5 to 20 W | 10 to 20 Wh | 0 |
| LED bulb or lantern | 3 to 10 W | 15 to 50 Wh | 0 or 1 |
| Headlamp recharge | 2 to 5 W | 5 to 10 Wh | 1 |
| Handheld radio charge | 5 W | 10 to 20 Wh | 1 |
| Laptop | 30 to 65 W | 100 to 300 Wh | 1 or 2 |
| CPAP-class medical device | 30 to 60 W | 200 to 400 Wh | 0 if you use one |
| 12 V compressor cooler (medicine) | 40 to 60 W while running | 200 to 500 Wh | 0 |
| **The power station's own draw** (its idle use while it runs a load) | commonly 3 to 10 W, more with the AC inverter on | 70 to 240 Wh | 0: unavoidable; keep it small by using the 12 V port and switching the AC inverter off (→ 09-10) |
| Full-size refrigerator (efficient, modern) | 60 to 150 W average | 800 to 1,500 Wh | 0 or 2 |
| Chest freezer | 40 to 100 W average | 600 to 1,200 Wh | 2 |
| Box fan | 50 to 100 W | 400 to 800 Wh | 1 or 2 |
| Microwave | 1,000 to 1,500 W | | 3 |
| Electric kettle | 1,200 to 1,800 W | | 3, except the small-boil exception above (→ 07-06): tea and meals yes, bulk heating never |
| Space heater | 1,500 W | 36,000 Wh per day if run continuously | 3, never |
| Well pump | 1,000 to 2,500 W, much more at start | | 3 on small systems (→ 03-10) |

Look hard at the space heater row. One space heater running all day uses about 36,000 Wh. Compare
that with what your panels make on a clear December day (→ 09-05): for most households it is a
few hundred to a couple of thousand watt-hours. That is why heat comes from combustion, clothing
and one warm room (→ 08-04), not from batteries.

{{#if has.house_connection}}A furnace blower is a motor load (often several hundred watts running,
two to three times that for a moment at start). It can run from a generator or a large station
only through a safe connection: this household's is "{{ gear.house_connection }}" (→ 09-04).
{{else}}A gas furnace needs electricity for its blower and controls. It can run from a generator
or a large station only through a safe connection: a transfer switch or interlock fitted by an
electrician, or a cord-and-plug conversion, which is a decision card (→ 09-04, {{choice DC-07}},
→ 30-08). Never by plugging a generator into an outlet (→ 30-01).{{/if}}

### Doing the triage
1. List every device you would want. Measure or estimate its watts and hours per day.
2. Multiply for watt-hours per day. Add up each tier.
3. **The Tier 0 total is your must-have design number.** Add about 30% for inverter and charging
   losses (inverters are typically 85 to 90% efficient, and batteries lose a little too).
4. **Tier 0 plus Tier 1 is the realistic target.** If that is affordable, build to it.
5. **Everything above Tier 1 is a fair-weather bonus** you run only on a sunny surplus day.
6. **Check the plan against December, not June** (→ 09-05). A system sized in summer
   disappoints in the month you need it most.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Plug-in watt meter | Turns guesses into a real design | The highest-value purchase in this section |
| DC watt meter (inline 12 V or USB) | Measures the DC side: 12 V loads, USB loads, panel output | For → 09-09 |
| This page's table, filled in | The design document for everything downstream | Copy the totals to → 23-02 |
| Label maker or masking tape and marker | Tier label on every device | Removes decisions from a crisis |
| Power strips with switches | Kills standby draw at once | Standby draw adds up over weeks |
| USB power banks, 20,000 mAh or larger | About 70 Wh each; covers phone loads for days (→ 09-06) | The cheapest useful battery there is |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Measuring without a meter:** appliance labels give maximum watts (a ceiling, not a daily
  figure, → 29-14); a car's 12 V socket fuse rating bounds what you can pull from it; the
  percentage drop on a power station over a known time is a crude but usable meter.
- **Storage:** laptop batteries, tool batteries with USB adapters, car batteries (with the
  cautions in → 09-14), any power bank in a drawer.
- **Cutting the load beats making power.** A headlamp instead of a room light, a hand-crank radio,
  cooking on fire, hanging laundry: every watt you do not need is a watt you do not have to make,
  store and maintain.

## When it runs out
- **Batteries are the consumable, not panels.** Panels degrade slowly over decades; batteries wear
  out in years and faster if abused (→ 09-03, → 09-07). Your power runway is a battery question.
- **Ration by tier, in order.** Tier 3 is already off; drop Tier 2, then Tier 1. **Tier 0 is
  defended to the end**, and if Tier 0 cannot be met, that is not a power problem, it is a medical
  emergency and an input to the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02).
- **Substitutes for each tier:** light → lamps and flashlights first, candles only with care
  (→ 10-02; candles indoors are a decision, {{choice DC-20}}, → 30-21); refrigeration → cold
  storage and evaporative cooling (→ 04-09, → 12-21); information → this binder and a hand-crank
  radio; tools → hand tools (→ 16-01).
- **Write the Tier 0 number on the consumables table (→ 23-02)** and track how many days of it
  your storage holds, the same way you track food and water.

## Our loads

{{#if has.power_station}}Our power stations total **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh**.{{/if}}
{{#if has.solar}}Our panels total **{{ gear.solar_w_total }} W**. On a clear December day at
home ({{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} peak sun hours) that is roughly
{{ gear.solar_w_total }} × {{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} × 0.75 = ________ Wh; in June
({{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }} sun hours), ________ Wh (method on → 09-02).{{/if}}
{{#if has.generator}}Our generator is rated **{{ gear.generator_watts }} W** running on
{{ gear.generator_fuel }} (→ 09-04).{{/if}}

Measure each device, then write it in. Correct in pencil as you learn.

| Device | Measured W | Hours per day | Wh per day | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}| Medicine cooler (→ 09-10) | | 24 (cycling) | | 0 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}| CPAP (→ 09-06) | | | | 0 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}| Oxygen concentrator (→ 09-06) | | | | 0 |
{{/if}}| Phones and medical charging | | | | 0 |
| Night light or headlamp recharge | | | | 0 |
| Power station idle draw | | 24 | | 0 |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| **Tier 0 subtotal** | | | | |
| **Tier 0 × 1.3 = design target** | | | | |
| **Tier 0 + Tier 1 subtotal** | | | | |

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** the whole system lives here: panels in the yard, batteries indoors where they
  stay warm (→ 09-07), Tier 0 and Tier 1 running.
- **B (moving):** you carry a fraction: a folding panel, one power station or battery, power
  banks and the medical loads. **Tier 0 only.**
- **C (settled somewhere new):** rebuild bigger. This is also where fuel generation (→ 09-04) is
  least sustainable and solar matters most, because there is no fuel resupply.

## Cross-references
→ 09-02 solar basics and sizing · → 09-03 batteries and power stations · → 09-05 solar in winter ·
→ 09-09 a small solar build · → 09-10 power for refrigerated medicine · → 09-16 outage day one ·
→ 29-02 batteries and power stations explained · → 28-07 reading your own gear

pages.body:
# Solar power basics and sizing

**What this page is for.** How a solar setup is put together, how to work out how many panels and
how much battery you need, and the one wiring mistake that destroys equipment on the first cold
morning. Do the load list on → 09-01 first; you cannot size anything without its watt-hour number.
Volts, amps and watts are explained on → 29-02.

> **CAUTION.** A grid-tied rooftop solar array **shuts down when the grid goes down**, by design,
> to protect line workers. If your house has rooftop solar with no battery and no inverter that
> can run on its own (often called "islanding" or "backup-capable"), **you will have no power in
> an outage despite the panels on the roof.** Find out which kind you have before you need it.
> Also: **a panel in daylight is live.** There is no off switch on a solar panel; you cover it or
> you disconnect it.

## Do this now
- **Finish → 09-01 first.**
- **If the house has rooftop solar, find out whether it is grid-tied, hybrid or off-grid.** Grid-tied
  without a battery is no help in an outage. This is a phone call to the installer today.
- **Size on the December number, not the June number** (→ 09-05). This is where most plans fail.
- **Start small and modular.** A few hundred watts of panels, a lithium iron phosphate battery or a
  power station, and a good charge controller cover Tier 0 and much of Tier 1. Buy parts you can
  add to, not a sealed box you cannot expand.
- **Read the label on every panel and station you own** and write the numbers in the tables on
  → 09-03 (how to read them: → 28-07).

## Why it works this way

**Four parts, four jobs.** Every solar setup, from a folding kit to a whole-house array, is the
same four blocks (US Department of Energy, Solar Photovoltaic System Design Basics):

| Part | Job | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **Panels** (PV modules) | Turn light into DC electricity | No generation. Very reliable; decades of life |
| **Charge controller** | Regulates panel output into the battery safely | Overcharges and destroys the battery, or will not charge |
| **Battery** | Stores energy for night and cloud | Power only while the sun shines |
| **Inverter** | Turns battery DC into 120 V AC for household plugs | Only DC devices work |

A **power station** is all of these except the panels, in one box (→ 09-03).

**Skip the inverter where you can.** Running 12 V DC loads directly (USB charging, LED lights, a
12 V compressor cooler) avoids the 10 to 15% lost in each conversion. Direct DC is the easiest
efficiency gain there is. Run the medicine cooler and the lights on DC; keep the inverter for the
few things that truly need AC.

**"Sun hours" is the sizing unit.** A panel rated 100 W makes 100 W only in full, square-on,
clear-sky noon sun at a mild temperature: a laboratory condition. A "peak sun hour" is one hour of
that full-strength sun; a December day may give two or three of them even though it is light for
eight or nine. Real daily output is roughly:

**Daily Wh ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.75**

The 0.75 covers wiring and controller losses, dust, heat and imperfect aim. Be pessimistic.

**Your home's sun hours** (from the region data for {{ region.home.county }} County,
{{ region.home.state_name }}): June **{{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }}**, December
**{{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }}**. Use December for sizing. Overcast and snow cut December far
below even that (→ 09-05).

**Size the system with this arithmetic:**
1. **Daily need** (Wh per day) from → 09-01, including the 1.3 loss factor.
2. **Panel watts needed ≈ daily need ÷ (December sun hours × 0.75).**
   Example: 600 Wh per day ÷ (2.5 × 0.75) ≈ **320 W of panel** to break even on a clear December
   day. Yours: ________ Wh ÷ ({{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} × 0.75) = ________ W.
3. **Battery ≈ daily need × days of autonomy** (days you can run with no sun at all). Two to three
   days is the practical minimum where overcast or snow can last several days. Then divide by the
   usable depth of discharge (→ 09-07): lithium iron phosphate about 80 to 100%; lead-acid only
   about 50%, so a lead-acid bank must be **twice** the size.
   Example: 600 Wh × 3 days = 1,800 Wh usable → about 2,000 Wh of lithium iron phosphate, or about
   4,000 Wh of lead-acid.
4. **Inverter size ≈ the largest set of AC loads that run at the same time**, plus headroom for
   motor start (a compressor can pull 3 to 5 times its running watts for a second).
5. **Charge controller** must handle the panels' voltage and current with margin. **MPPT beats
   PWM**, typically by 15 to 30%, and by more in cold weather and low light. (MPPT and PWM are the
   two kinds of controller; MPPT converts surplus panel voltage into extra charging current, PWM
   throws it away.) Buy MPPT. Every power station has an MPPT controller inside.

### Series and parallel: the wiring choice that matters most

{{figure fig-series-vs-parallel}}

When you connect two or more panels you choose:
- **Series** (plus of one panel to minus of the next, in a chain): the **voltages add**; the
  current stays at the level of the weakest panel. Three panels of about 20 V each make a string of
  about 60 V.
- **Parallel** (all pluses together, all minuses together, usually with a Y-branch connector): the
  **currents add**; the voltage stays near the lower panel's voltage.

**The failure modes are not the same.** **Too much voltage kills a charge controller instantly
and permanently.** Too much current, at most station and controller inputs, is simply clipped:
the input takes what it can use and ignores the rest. (Check your manual: if it lists a maximum
short-circuit current, stay under that too.) So when in doubt, **choose the configuration with the
lower voltage.**

**Cold raises panel voltage.** A panel is rated at 77 °F (25 °C). For every degree colder, its
open-circuit voltage (Voc, the voltage with nothing connected, printed on the label) rises a
little: typically about 0.3% per °C. A string that is safely under a controller's limit on a mild
afternoon can be over it at sunrise on a clear, frozen morning. Cold never raises current, so
**series is the configuration winter can push over the edge, and parallel is the one it cannot.**

**The cold-voltage check, every time you plan a series string:**
1. Add up the label **Voc** of every panel in the string (warm Voc).
2. **Multiply by 1.20.** At a typical 0.3% per °C, a factor of 1.20 covers panel temperatures down
   to about −40 °F. Your home's record low is **{{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F**; if your
   panel's label gives a larger temperature coefficient, or you are planning for colder, work it
   out: factor = 1 + (coefficient as a decimal, without its minus sign) × (25 − lowest
   temperature in °C). Example: 0.003 × (25 − (−40)) = 0.195, so a factor of about 1.20.
3. **The result must be below the station's or controller's maximum PV input voltage**, with a
   margin. A few volts of margin is no margin.
4. Never drop the factor because "it is only 20 degrees this morning". Every winter morning is far
   below the 77 °F rating.

The worked tables for your own panels and stations, and which configuration goes into which
station, are on → 09-03. The short version that prevents almost every disaster: **a station with
a high input-voltage ceiling and a low current limit takes series strings; a station with a low
voltage ceiling and a high current limit takes parallel pairs or single panels, never a series
string that its ceiling cannot hold cold.**

### Mounting decisions that matter
- **Face true south.** A compass points to magnetic north, which can be well off true north in
  much of the country. Set panels by the shadow at solar noon (when shadows are shortest, they
  point true north).
- **Tilt steep in winter.** Roughly your latitude plus 15° catches the low winter sun and sheds
  snow (→ 09-05). Adjustable tilt is worth the trouble twice a year.
- **Shade is disproportionately bad.** Shading part of one panel can cut the output of the whole
  series string, not just that panel. Trees, chimneys, a neighbour's roof and the low winter sun
  angle all matter.
- **Ground-mount or portable is better than roof for an emergency setup.** You can sweep snow off
  it, re-aim it, move it, and bring it inside at night. A roof array in a blizzard is
  unreachable, and a lit house in a dark neighbourhood is a signal (→ 14-03).
{{#if has.solar}}
**Our panels:**

| Panel | Watts each | How many | Voc (label) | Isc (label) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each panels as p}}| {{p.model}} | {{p.watts}} | {{p.count}} | ______ V | ______ A |
{{/each}}

Total: **{{ gear.solar_w_total }} W**. Model-by-model figures for common panels and controllers:
→ 28-02.
{{/if}}

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rigid panels, 100 to 200 W each, several | Modular, cheap per watt, decades of life | More smaller panels give more redundancy than one big one |
| One folding or portable 100 to 200 W panel | Phase B, and aiming at the low winter sun | The panel that leaves with you |
| **MPPT** charge controller with voltage headroom | 15 to 30% more harvest; survives the cold-voltage rise | Check its maximum PV input voltage against the cold check above |
| Lithium iron phosphate battery, 100 Ah (about 1.2 kWh) or more, or a power station | Deep cycles, long life | Note the **cold-charging limit** (→ 09-07) |
| Pure sine inverter, 300 to 1,500 W | Medical gear and electronics want pure sine | Modified sine can damage or buzz some devices |
| 12 V DC distribution: sockets, USB, fuse block | Skips inverter losses | The efficient path for Tier 0 |
| Fuses, breakers, correctly sized wire | Not optional (→ 09-08) | Fire risk otherwise |
| Adjustable tilt mounts or a simple A-frame | Winter angle and snow shedding | Buildable from 2×4s |
| Soft broom or snow rake with a non-abrasive head | A snowed-over panel makes nothing | Never a metal scraper |
| Multimeter | Checks Voc and polarity before every first connection | → 09-12 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Panels** from RVs, campers, boats, construction signs, solar yard lights and derelict arrays.
  **Large grid-tie panels are high-voltage** (30 to 40 V or more each) and need an MPPT controller
  that accepts that input; they are not a direct 12 V battery charger.
- **Controllers and inverters** from RVs, boats and campers; car inverters for small AC loads.
- **Batteries** from vehicles, boats, RVs, UPS units, floor scrubbers, mobility scooters and golf
  carts (→ 09-13, → 09-14).
- **Mounts:** 2×4 A-frames, pallets, fence posts, a ladder, a leaned sheet of plywood: anything
  that holds a panel steep and facing south.
- **Wire:** automotive and battery cable, welding cable. **Do not undersize it** (→ 09-08).

## When it runs out
- **Panels are the durable part.** They lose a fraction of a percent a year and can last 25 years
  or more. Hail is the real risk: store a spare panel flat and indoors.
- **The controller and inverter are the fragile electronics.** They fail from heat, water, surges
  and reversed polarity. **Buy a spare charge controller now**; without it the panels cannot
  safely charge anything. It is the highest-value spare in this section.
- **The battery is the true consumable** (→ 09-03, → 09-07).
- **When generation drops below Tier 0** (a snowed-in December week), fall back in order: stored
  battery, then a short generator run to bulk-charge the bank (→ 09-04), then vehicle and
  hand-crank charging (→ 09-11), then shedding to Tier 0 alone (→ 09-01).

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** ground-mounted or yard-deployed panels you can sweep and re-aim, batteries
  **indoors** where they stay warm (→ 09-07).
- **B (moving):** one folding panel, one battery or station, power banks. Solar on foot or in a
  vehicle is a **trickle**: it keeps a phone and a small medical device alive, not a household.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the permanent build. More panel than you think you need, real
  ground-mount racking, a battery room that stays above freezing. **Over-panel deliberately**:
  extra panels are cheap and they are what carry you through December.

## Cross-references
→ 09-01 load triage, do this first · → 09-03 batteries, stations and your wiring tables ·
→ 09-05 solar in winter, read before finalising any size · → 09-07 battery chemistry ·
→ 09-08 wiring and fusing · → 09-09 step-by-step build · → 28-02 panels and controllers ·
→ 29-02 batteries and power stations explained
