pages.body:
# 12 V wiring, fusing and electrical safety

**What this page is for.** The rules that keep a battery system, a solar setup or a car-battery
inverter from starting a fire: wire sizes, fuses, working habits, and the AC side (inverters and
extension cords). Read it before you cut a single wire. Volts and amps are explained on → 29-02;
the house panel and breakers on → 29-04.

> **SAFETY. Low voltage is not low danger.** A 12 V battery bank will not shock you through dry
> skin, which is exactly why people get careless with it. What it *will* do is push **hundreds of
> amps** into a short circuit: enough to melt a wrench instantly, ignite wire insulation inside a
> wall or a joist, and start a fire behind something you cannot see. **Undersized wire and missing
> fuses are the most common causes of home-built off-grid fires.** The rules on this page are not
> optional: **fuse every conductor at the battery, size wire for current AND length, no bare
> terminals, and take off rings and watches before you touch a battery bank.**
> **Never connect a battery system, an inverter or a power station to house wiring.** Generators
> and house wiring are on → 09-04: **never connect a generator to house wiring without a transfer
> switch, interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion with the main breaker locked off; never backfeed
> through an outlet** (it electrocutes line workers and neighbours and causes fires, → 30-01). Doing
> a cord-and-plug conversion yourself is a decision card: {{choice DC-07}} (→ 30-08). Anything else
> in a wall belongs to a qualified electrician (OSHA, Electrical).

## Do this now
- **Buy a fuse block, an assortment of fuses, and more wire than you think you need, heavier than
  you think you need.** Cheap now, unobtainable later.
- **Put a main fuse or breaker on the battery positive terminal, within inches of it.** If you do
  exactly one thing from this page, do that.
- **Get a proper crimping tool and heat-shrink terminals.** Twisted-and-taped joints are a common
  source of DC fires: a bad connection makes heat.
- **Fire extinguisher and smoke alarm in the room where the batteries live** (→ 09-03).
- **Cover the battery terminals** with boots or caps. {{#if has.young_child}}A young child with a
  spoon and an uncovered battery bank is a serious hazard.{{/if}}
- **Draw the wiring diagram on paper, with every fuse rating, and keep it in this binder.**
  {{photo wiring-diagram}}

## Why it works this way

### Why 12 V systems bite
Power is volts × amps. To deliver **600 W**:
- at **120 V AC** you need **5 amps**: thin lamp cord handles it.
- at **12 V DC** you need **50 amps**: cable about the size of jumper leads.

**Same power, ten times the current.** Every problem in DC wiring comes from that:
- **Voltage drop.** Resistance in a long, thin wire eats voltage. Lose 1 V out of 12 and you have
  lost over 8% of your power as heat in the wire. Aim to keep drop under **3%** on important runs.
  **Length matters as much as thickness**, and you must count **both** conductors (out and back).
- **Heat.** An undersized wire carrying 50 A gets hot along its whole length. Inside a wall, under
  insulation, or bundled, it can reach ignition temperature without tripping anything, because
  **there is nothing to trip if you did not fuse it.**
- **Connections.** A loose or corroded joint has resistance; resistance makes heat; heat raises
  resistance. That runaway is why crimped and sealed connections matter more in DC than people
  expect.

### Wire sizing (conservative planning guidance; check against a real ampacity table)
Lower gauge number = thicker wire. For a **12 V** system, keeping voltage drop reasonable, counting
the **round-trip** length:

| Current | ≤10 ft round trip | ≤20 ft | ≤30 ft |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 A | 16 AWG | 14 AWG | 12 AWG |
| 10 A | 14 AWG | 12 AWG | 10 AWG |
| 20 A | 12 AWG | 10 AWG | 8 AWG |
| 30 A | 10 AWG | 8 AWG | 6 AWG |
| 50 A | 8 AWG | 6 AWG | 4 AWG |
| 100 A | 4 AWG | 2 AWG | 1/0 AWG |
| 200 A (inverter cables) | 1/0 to 2/0 AWG | 2/0 to 4/0 AWG | keep it short |

**Rules of thumb:** keep battery-to-inverter cables **as short as possible**; between two sizes,
**take the thicker**; prefer **fine-stranded copper** (marine or welding cable) over solid or
aluminium. **Never use aluminium wire on battery terminals.**

### Fusing: the rule set
**The fuse protects the WIRE, not the device.** Size it to the wire's capacity, not to what you wish
the device could draw.

1. **Main fuse or breaker at the battery positive, within about 7 inches of the terminal**, rated at
   or below the capacity of the cable it protects. This is the fuse that prevents the catastrophic
   fault.
2. **A fuse on every branch circuit**, at the source end, sized to that branch's wire.
3. **A fuse between the solar panels and the charge controller, and between the controller and the
   battery**, as the controller's manual says. **Three or more panel strings in parallel need a fuse
   on each string**; two do not.
4. **The inverter gets its own heavy fuse** (class T or similar): inverters pull very large currents.
5. **Use DC-rated fuses and breakers.** An AC-rated switch or breaker on DC can fail to break the arc:
   **DC does not pass through zero volts the way AC does, so a DC arc keeps burning.** That is why
   "it's just a light switch" is wrong on a 12 V system.
6. **Never replace a fuse with a bigger one to stop it blowing.** The fuse is telling the truth.
   Find the fault.

### Working habits
- **Take off rings, watches and metal bracelets.** A ring bridging a battery terminal heats red-hot
  and cannot be pulled off in time.
- **Insulate the wrench.** Tape all but the working end, or use insulated tools.
- **Disconnect negative first, reconnect negative last.** Then a slipped wrench touching the frame is
  harmless.
- **Cover every terminal:** boots, caps or heat-shrink.
- **Do not work on a live system tired, cold or rushed.** Most of these accidents happen at the end
  of a long day.
- **Reversed polarity kills electronics.** Reversing the leads on a charge controller or inverter
  usually destroys it instantly. **Check twice with the meter.** Red and black consistently; label
  both ends of every cable.
- **Strain relief and abrasion protection.** Wire rubbing on a metal edge eventually wears through and
  shorts. Use grommets, loom and clamps.
- **Keep DC wiring physically separate from house AC wiring**, and never run it into house circuits.

### The AC side
- **Pure sine inverters** for anything sensitive: medical gear, laptops, chargers. Modified sine can
  damage some devices and makes others buzz and run hot.
- **Ground the system as the inverter's manufacturer says.** Grounding on a portable system is
  subtle; follow the manual, do not improvise.
- **GFCI protection** (the outlets with test and reset buttons) on any outlet near water: kitchen,
  bathroom, outdoors.
- **Extension cords: heavier than you think, fully unrolled.** A coiled cord under load heats up; a
  16 AWG cord running a heater is a fire. Generator cords: → 09-04.
- **Never chain extension cords or power strips.**
- **Anything permanent, anything in a wall, anything touching house circuits: a qualified
  electrician**, except the cord-and-plug conversion if your household has chosen to do it
  ({{choice DC-07}}, → 30-08).

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| DC fuse block and assorted blade fuses | Branch protection | A wide spread of ratings |
| Main fuse and holder (ANL, MRBF or class T) | The battery-terminal fuse | The most important single part here |
| DC-rated breakers, a few sizes | Resettable; also a disconnect switch | **Must be DC-rated** |
| Battery cable: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 AWG | You will always want more | Fine-stranded, marine or welding grade |
| Ratcheting crimper, lugs, heat-shrink | Good connections do not make heat | Cheap tool, prevents the common fire |
| Heat gun or lighter for heat-shrink | Sealed, waterproof joints | |
| Digital multimeter | Polarity, voltage, continuity, current | Learn it before you need it |
| DC clamp meter | Measures current without breaking the circuit | Diagnosis without disassembly |
| Terminal boots, wire loom, grommets, clamps | Prevent shorts and abrasion | |
| Insulated wrenches or tape | Prevents the dropped-wrench short | |
| Labels or tape and marker | Label both ends of every cable | |
| Fire extinguisher and smoke alarm | This page is about fire | In the battery room |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Wire:** vehicle wiring harnesses, jumper cables (excellent heavy cable), welding leads, battery
  cables from scrapped vehicles, speaker wire (light duty only), house cable from construction (solid
  core: acceptable for fixed runs, poor where it flexes).
- **Fuses:** every vehicle has blade fuses in a labelled box, in exactly the ratings you want. **One
  of the best things to salvage from a vehicle.** Also fusible links and midi and maxi fuses.
- **Fuse blocks, switches, sockets and USB outlets** from vehicles, boats and RVs.
- **Connectors:** vehicle harness connectors, Anderson-style plugs from equipment (→ 09-12).
- **What you must not substitute: a fuse.** **Never use a nail, a bolt, foil or a coin in a fuse
  holder.** That is how a fault becomes a house fire. With no fuse of the right rating, use a smaller
  one and accept the nuisance trips.

## When it runs out
- **Wire, fuses and connectors are consumables** in an active system: corrosion, vibration, rodents
  and repairs eat them. Stock generously now; they do not expire.
- **Corrosion is the slow failure.** In an unheated or humid space, terminals corrode, resistance
  rises and things quietly get hot. Inspect each season: green or white powder, discolouration,
  melted insulation, anything warm to the touch under load. **A warm connector is a warning.**
- **Rodents chew wire** (→ 04-11). Run cable in conduit or loom and check after any rodent sign.
- **Substitute:** heavier salvaged cable can always replace lighter; a DC-rated breaker can replace a
  fuse; a switch plus a fuse can replace a breaker. **Nothing replaces the fuse itself.**
- **The skill is the real asset:** sizing wire, crimping a lug, reading a meter, finding a short.
  Practise it now on a bench in daylight (→ 24-01). Burns first aid: → 12-03.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** build it properly the first time, with real fuses and real crimps, where children
  cannot reach it. Label everything. Keep the diagram on paper.
- **B (moving):** a portable system is short runs and plug connections. Secure against vibration,
  protect against abrasion, fuse it anyway, keep cables out from underfoot.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** longer runs mean thicker wire and more voltage drop. This is where
  **24 V or 48 V** systems make sense: they cut current, and so wire size, proportionally.

## Cross-references
→ 09-03 batteries · → 09-04 generators, backfeed and house connections · → 09-07 battery chemistry
· → 09-09 small solar build (this page in practice) · → 09-12 connectors and testing · → 29-04

pages.body:
# Building a small solar system step by step

**What this page is for.** A step-by-step build of a **portable, self-contained 12 V DC system**:
panels, a charge controller, a battery, fuses and a small inverter in one box. It plugs into nothing
and touches no house wiring. It is the repairable, expandable alternative (or companion) to a power
station (→ 09-03). Read → 09-08 before you cut a wire.

> **CAUTION.** This build is safe only if it is fused and wired correctly (→ 09-08). The moment you
> want it to power house circuits, it is a different project and it belongs to a licensed
> electrician.
>
> **Before the collapse:** a portable system that plugs into nothing usually needs no permit; anything
> wired to a building, or on a roof, generally does.

## Do this now
- **Build it now, while there is no pressure.** A system assembled on a calm weekend and actually
  used is worth ten still in boxes.
- **Then use it every month.** Run the lights from it for an evening; charge the phones from it.
  **Find the failures now**, when the fix is a trip to the store.
- **Draw the wiring diagram on paper, with fuse ratings, and keep it in this binder.** You will not
  remember it in a year, and a stranger may need to work on it.

## Why it works this way

### The design
Roughly **400 to 800 W of panels, 1.2 to 2.5 kWh of lithium iron phosphate, an MPPT controller and a
small pure sine inverter**, built as separate parts in a portable box, sized from your → 09-01 load
numbers and your **December** sun hours ({{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }} at home, → 09-05). It covers
Tier 0 and much of Tier 1 and grows by adding panels or a second battery.

{{figure fig-small-solar-system-layout}}

**Worked example: do this arithmetic with your own numbers.**
```
Tier 0 + Tier 1 daily need (from 09-01) ......   550 Wh/day
x 1.3 for inverter/charge losses ............   715 Wh/day  <- design target
December sun hours (09-05) ..................   2.5
Panel watts = 715 / (2.5 x 0.75) ............   ~380 W  -> buy 400-600 W (over-panel)
Battery for 3 days' autonomy = 715 x 3 ......   ~2,150 Wh usable
   LiFePO4 (use ~90%) .......................   ~2,400 Wh  -> 2 x 100 Ah 12 V
   Lead-acid (use ~50%) .....................   ~4,300 Wh  -> 4 x 100 Ah 12 V, and heavy
Inverter = largest set of AC loads at once ..   ~600 W running -> 1,000 W pure sine
```
Yours:
```
Daily need ________ Wh  x 1.3 = ________ Wh   December sun hours ________
Panel watts = ________ / (____ x 0.75) = ________ W
Battery = ________ x ____ days = ________ Wh usable
Inverter = ________ W
```

### The parts, in the order you will wire them
1. **Panels:** two to four rigid 100 to 200 W panels, plus one folding portable panel.
2. **Panel wiring:** MC4 connectors and extension cable; a **PV disconnect or breaker**.
3. **MPPT charge controller:** sized for the panels' current, with a **maximum PV input voltage
   that survives the coldest morning** (→ 09-02).
4. **Main battery fuse:** on the battery positive terminal, within inches.
5. **Battery:** lithium iron phosphate with a battery management system that blocks cold charging
   (→ 09-07).
6. **Shunt battery monitor:** between the battery negative and everything else.
7. **DC fuse block:** feeds the 12 V loads (USB, lights, cooler).
8. **Inverter:** on its own short, heavy, fused cables straight to the battery.

### Build it: the sequence
**Step 0: lay it out dry, on the floor, unconnected.** Check every cable reaches, every fuse rating
matches its wire, and you know what each wire does. Label both ends of everything now.

**Step 1: mount the electronics on a board.** Charge controller, fuse block, monitor display and
switches on a piece of plywood; battery below or beside it in its box. A **power box** on a hand
truck or in a crate is portable, protects the parts and keeps small children out. Leave ventilation
for the inverter and controller: they make heat.

**Step 2: battery negative to the shunt, shunt to the negative bus.** All negatives return through
the shunt, or the monitor reads nothing.

**Step 3: main fuse on the battery positive**, then to the positive bus. **This fuse goes in last,
after everything else is wired:** it is your master disconnect during the build.

**Step 4: charge controller to the battery**, fused as its manual says, **correct polarity**. Most
MPPT controllers must see the **battery first, panels second**; read the manual, because the wrong
order damages some controllers.

**Step 5: loads.** Fuse block off the positive bus; each branch (USB outlets, 12 V socket, LED
lights, the cooler) fused for its own wire size (→ 09-08).

**Step 6: inverter** on its own short heavy fused cables straight to the battery, not through the
fuse block.

**Step 7: panels last.** Wire the panels with the **PV breaker off** or the panels covered.
Series raises voltage (good for long runs and MPPT, but run the cold-voltage check on → 09-02);
parallel raises current (more tolerant of shade). {{figure fig-series-vs-parallel}} Then connect the
panels to the controller and switch on.

**Step 8: commission it.** Measure everything: battery voltage, panel open-circuit voltage, charging
current, load current. Confirm the controller shows charging. **Then run a real load and watch what
happens.**

**Step 9: test the failure modes on purpose.**
- Cover the panels: does it run cleanly on battery?
- Pull a fuse: does only that branch die?
- Run the bank down to 50%: how long did it take? **Write the number down.**
- Charge from low on a cloudy day: how much did you really get?
- {{#if is.cold_winters}}Leave the panels out on a January day: what does the cold do to the
  harvest and the voltage?{{else}}Run it through the hottest week: what does heat do to the
  controller and the battery?{{/if}}

**Step 10: document it.** Wiring diagram, fuse ratings, charging voltages and measured runtimes, on
paper, in this binder. {{photo power-box}}

### Common mistakes, all avoidable
- **Undersized wire between battery and inverter.** The classic fire.
- **No main battery fuse.** The classic catastrophic fire.
- **Controller maximum PV voltage too low for a cold clear morning.** A dead controller.
- **Lead-acid discharged below 50% again and again.** A dead bank in one season.
- **Lithium iron phosphate charged below freezing.** A permanently damaged battery.
- **Sizing on yearly-average sun hours.** Works in July, fails in January.
- **An inverter far larger than needed.** Big inverters have real idle draw that quietly eats the
  bank. Size it to the load and **switch it off when unused.**
- **Building it and never using it.** The most common failure of all.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 400 to 600 W of panels and one folding portable | Generation, plus the panel that travels | Over-panel for December |
| MPPT controller with generous voltage headroom | Efficiency and cold-weather survival | **Buy a spare**: the highest-value spare in this section |
| One or two 100 Ah lithium iron phosphate, low-temperature protection | Two to three days' autonomy | → 09-07 |
| 1,000 W pure sine inverter | AC when you need it, off when you do not | Watch the idle draw |
| Main fuse, fuse block, assorted fuses | Not negotiable | → 09-08 |
| Shunt battery monitor | The only honest fuel gauge on lithium | |
| Cable in several gauges, lugs, crimper, heat-shrink | Build and repair | Buy extra |
| MC4 connectors, PV extension cable, PV breaker | Panel side | → 09-12 |
| Plywood board, crate or toolbox, hand truck | Portable, child-safe | |
| Multimeter and DC clamp meter | Commissioning and diagnosis | |
| Adjustable A-frame mount (2×4s) and a snow broom | Steep winter tilt, sweepable | → 09-05 |

Panels and controllers by class: → 28-02.

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Panels** from RVs, campers, boats, signs and solar yard lights; **grid-tie panels are
  high-voltage: MPPT only** (→ 09-02).
- **Controllers, inverters, fuse blocks and DC sockets** from RVs, boats and campers: these are
  complete 12 V systems on wheels.
- **Batteries** from vehicles, UPS units, scooters, golf carts (→ 09-13, → 09-14).
- **Cable** from jumper cables, welding leads and vehicle harnesses; **fuses from any vehicle's fuse
  box**.
- **Mounting** from 2×4s, pallets, fence posts, angle iron.
- **Enclosure:** a plastic tote, an ammunition can, a toolbox, a crate.

## When it runs out
- **Keep a spare charge controller.** It is the small, cheap, fragile part whose failure stops the
  whole system. Panels and wire rarely fail; controllers and inverters do.
- **The batteries' life is the system's life** (→ 09-07). Log capacity over time.
- **Repairability is the design goal.** This is why a component build beats a sealed power station
  over the long term: **every part can be replaced with something salvaged.** Keep the diagram,
  spare parts and tools.
- **Shed by tier** as capacity fades (→ 09-01), and move loads to midday.
- **Practise the drill:** once a year, run the household from this system for a full weekend, in
  **winter** (→ 24-04). It is the only honest test.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** the power box lives indoors (warm battery); panels deploy in the yard on an
  adjustable frame you can sweep. Keep it on a cart so it can move fast.
- **B (moving):** the folding panel, one battery and the power banks go. **Design the box so the
  battery and controller come out in five minutes without tools**: decide that when you build it.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** rebuild larger and permanent. Longer runs make **24 V or 48 V** worth
  it (→ 09-08). Bring the small system: it becomes the backup and the portable unit.

## Cross-references
→ 09-01 load triage · → 09-02 sizing and the cold-voltage check · → 09-05 winter numbers · → 09-07
chemistry · → 09-08 wiring and fusing, read first · → 09-10 sizing for medicine cooling · → 24-04

pages.body:
# Power for refrigerated medicine

**What this page is for.** Some medicines must stay cool: insulin, some injectable and biologic
drugs, some liquid antibiotics, some eye drops. Keeping them cool without the grid is often the
hardest electrical problem in the household. This page covers how to make and budget the
electricity, how to cut the load, and the non-electric paths to cold. **It does not tell you what
temperature or how long your medicine can tolerate.** That is on its label, in its condition module,
and on → 29-07.

> **SAFETY.** Take storage temperatures, in-use times and discard decisions **from the medicine's
> label and the condition module**, never from this page. Two rules apply everywhere:
> **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Freezing destroys potency with no way to
> tell, and the published guidance is unanimous (→ 30-01). **Too cold is as dangerous as too warm.**
> Using a medicine after it has been too warm for longer than its published window is a decision
> card: {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).
> For reference, unopened insulin is stored refrigerated at 36 to 46 °F (2 to 8 °C), not frozen (US
> FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage; American Diabetes Association, Insulin Storage).

## Do this now
- **Measure the real daily watt-hours of whatever you would use to cool medicine.** A full-size
  kitchen refrigerator and a small 12 V compressor cooler differ by nearly ten times, and that
  decides whether your system is adequate or hopeless. Plug it into a watt meter for 24 hours and
  write the number here: ________ Wh per day.
- **If you do not yet own a medicine cooler, a small 12 V compressor cooler is the purchase that
  matters.** Compressor, never thermoelectric (see below).
- **Build the non-electric cold plan at the same time** (→ 04-09, → 12-21). Electricity is one path to
  cold; it should never be the only one.
- **Turn off any power-saving ("ECO") setting on the station port the cooler will use.** Many
  stations switch an output off after an hour or more of tiny load, and a compressor cooler resting
  between cycles looks like nothing is plugged in. If the cooler's display is ever dark, re-enable
  the port and check the thermometer (→ 09-03).
- **Run the cooler for 24 hours on the station you will use, with a min/max thermometer inside,**
  before you ever need it. Confirm it holds the medicine's range; leave that thermometer in the
  cooler's box as the designated one. {{photo med-cooler}}
- **Decide the go/no-go trigger now, in writing:** if you cannot keep the medicine usable *and*
  cannot replace it, that is a decision about leaving (→ 01-02), not something to ride out.

## Why it works this way

### Why refrigeration is the expensive load
Cooling is a heat pump. It runs a motor and fights the room temperature all day, every day. That is a
different shape of load from a phone:

| Device | Typical running W | Typical Wh per day | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phone | 5 to 20 W briefly | **10 to 20 Wh** | Trivial |
| **12 V compressor cooler (small, well insulated)** | 40 to 60 W while running | **200 to 500 Wh** | Duty cycle depends heavily on room temperature |
| Dorm or mini fridge (AC, cheap, poorly insulated) | 60 to 90 W | **600 to 1,000 Wh** | Often *worse* than a modern full-size fridge |
| Full-size efficient refrigerator | 60 to 150 W average | **800 to 1,500 Wh** | Big, but modern ones are surprisingly efficient |
| **Thermoelectric ("Peltier") cooler** | **45 to 60 W continuous** | **1,000 to 1,400 Wh** | **Runs constantly and cools only about 30 to 40 °F below the room. Avoid.** |

**Read the thermoelectric row carefully.** Those coolers are cheap, common and sold as "12 V
refrigerators", and they are the **worst choice** here. They never cycle off, use more energy than a
real refrigerator, and on a hot day may not reach a useful temperature at all. A 12 V compressor
cooler costs several times more and uses a fraction of the power.

### Sizing against reality
**Worked example:** a cooler at about **350 Wh a day**, with 400 W of panels at a northern location
(→ 09-05):

| Condition | Panel yield | Cooler need | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| June, clear | about 1,800 Wh | 350 Wh | Easy: big surplus |
| December, clear, panels swept | about 750 Wh | about 250 Wh (colder room = less work) | Workable, with margin |
| December, overcast | about 150 to 300 Wh | about 250 Wh | **Break-even at best: living off the battery** |
| Blizzard, panels buried | **0** | about 250 Wh | **Battery only: three days ≈ 750 Wh for the cooler alone** |

That table is the argument for over-paneling (→ 09-05), for three or more days of battery, and for
the non-electric paths below.

**How long our stations run the cooler** (estimates; the percentage on the screen is the truth):

Days per charge ≈ station Wh × 0.85 ÷ (cooler Wh per day + 24 × the station's idle watts).

The station's **idle draw** matters: with the AC inverter on, a station can use nearly as much
running itself as a small cooler uses. **Run the cooler from the 12 V port with the AC inverter off.**
Measure the idle: fully charged, inverter on, nothing plugged in, note the percentage after 12 hours.

| Station | Wh | Idle W (measured) | Cooler Wh per day | Days per charge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each stations as s}}| {{s.model}} | {{s.wh}} | ______ | ______ | ______ |
{{else}}| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
{{/each}}

For a **full-size refrigerator** (about 1,200 Wh a day), our whole bank of
{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh gives roughly **{{ derived.station_fridge_days }} days**: an estimate
that leaves out idle draw and anything else plugged in. Measure your own as above. Pick the
percentage at which you move the cooler to the next station, and write it here: ______ %.

**Having two stations makes the electric path redundant:** one dead inverter or one failed battery
no longer ends it. Either station's 12 V port can run the cooler, with ECO off on whichever it moves
to.

### Two ways to set up day to day
- **Station as a UPS:** the medicine lives in the cooler, the cooler on a station that stays plugged
  into the wall in pass-through or UPS mode (if your station supports it, → 09-03). A grid failure
  is then a switchover of milliseconds. Costs: the station is tied up, and it sits at full charge.
- **Kitchen fridge, cooler ready:** the medicine lives in the kitchen fridge; the cooler, the station
  and the designated thermometer are staged. When the power fails, you set up the cooler and move
  the medicine once the cooler reads within the label range (step by step on → 09-16). Costs: it
  depends on someone doing it within the first hours.

Our set-up: ________________________________________.

{{#if is.cold_winters}}
### The winter insight: cold can be free
For several months a year here the outdoors is a refrigerator, and often a freezer. A well-managed
insulated container in an unheated space, a shaded north side, a snow cache or a buried container can
hold refrigerator temperatures with **zero watts** (→ 04-09). Two cautions:
- **A garage with a thermostat-controlled heater is not "unheated" while the grid is up.** It
  becomes passive cold only when that heater is off.
- **Freezing is the winter danger.** The problem flips from "make cold" to "hold a narrow band and
  never freeze". That is a job for insulation, thermal mass and a **thermometer with min/max memory**,
  checked daily, not for a compressor.

**The seasonal pattern:**
- **Winter:** passive cold with freeze protection and a min/max thermometer. Electrical cooling load
  near zero, just when solar is weakest.
- **Summer:** solar is strongest, and so is the cooling load. Run the compressor cooler on the
  surplus.
- **Spring and autumn:** mixed. Cooler when it is warm; passive cold on cold nights; watch the
  thermometer.
{{else}}
### Where winters are mild
Here, cooling is a year-round load. The battery and panel margin matter more, and the evaporative
and ground-cooling paths below are your non-electric options. Winter nights can still dip below
freezing: keep a min/max thermometer in any passive store.
{{/if}}

### Making the cooling load smaller: cheaper than making more power
1. **Insulate the container heavily.** Extra rigid foam around a small cooler cuts the duty cycle a
   lot. Insulation costs nothing to run.
2. **Cool a small volume.** You are cooling **vials and pens**, not groceries.
3. **Add thermal mass.** Water bottles or gel packs inside hold the temperature through the night and
   a cloudy stretch, so the compressor can run at midday when the sun is up.
4. **Site it cool:** the coolest room, out of the sun, away from any heater.
5. **Open it rarely.** Every opening dumps the cold air.
6. **Run it on 12 V DC directly:** no inverter, no 10 to 15% conversion loss, no inverter idle draw.
7. **Pre-cool at midday** and let it coast overnight.

### Other medicines with temperature rules
{{#if has.epinephrine}}**Epinephrine auto-injectors** are a different problem from insulin: they are
generally stored at room temperature, protected from light, and **not refrigerated or frozen** (US
FDA, EpiPen prescribing information). **Their winter risk is freezing.** In a house heated to one
room, the auto-injectors stay in the warm room with you, not in a cold car or a go-bag in the
garage. Check the label and → 02-03.
{{else}}**Epinephrine auto-injectors**, if anyone ever carries them, are stored at room temperature
and **not refrigerated or frozen** (US FDA, EpiPen prescribing information); their winter risk is
freezing (→ 02-03).
{{/if}}
Test strips, glucagon and other supplies have their own ranges; see their modules. The electrical
answer is the same: small insulated volume, thermometer, seasonal plan.

### Redundancy: because this load is life-critical
Have **three independent paths to cold**, and know which one you are on:
1. **Electric:** a 12 V compressor cooler on a station or battery.
2. **Passive:** an insulated container using outdoor cold, ground temperature or a snow or ice cache
   (→ 04-09), with freeze protection.
3. **Evaporative or cold water:** evaporative cooling pouches made for medicine (→ 12-21), a wet
   cloth over a container in moving air, a sealed container in a cold stream or well.

Plus a **min/max thermometer** on the store, checked and logged daily. **Without a thermometer you
have a guess, not a cold chain.**

### Our refrigerated medicines
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}This household has at least one medicine marked refrigerated.{{/if}}
The household's medicine list (the "refrigerated" column shows which ones this page is about):

| Who | Medicine | Strength | Refrigerated? | Label storage range (copy from the label) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as m}}| {{m.member}} | {{m.name}} | {{m.strength}} | {{m.refrigerated}} | ______ |
{{else}}| | | | | |
{{/each}}

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **12 V compressor cooler**, small (15 to 25 qt) | The right electric cooling device: a fraction of the energy of anything else | **Never** thermoelectric |
| Rigid foam board and tape to over-insulate it | Cuts the duty cycle; costs no watts | Cheapest efficiency gain there is |
| **Min/max digital thermometers** with an external probe, several | You cannot manage a cold chain you cannot measure | Spare batteries |
| Insulated medicine travel case or evaporative pouches | Phase B and daily carry | → 12-21 |
| Gel packs or water bottles for thermal mass | Coast overnight and through cloud | Free if you use water |
| Battery capacity beyond the → 09-09 build, or a second station | This load is the reason to over-size | |
| A second cooling method, tested | Redundancy | Test it before you need it |
| Insulated cooler and a way to cache snow or ice | The winter and shoulder-season answer where it is cold | → 04-09 |
| Notebook for a daily temperature log | Turns a guess into evidence | Keep it with this binder |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Insulation:** foam board, packing foam, bubble wrap, blankets, straw, sawdust, leaves: anything
  that traps air. Doubling insulation roughly halves the energy.
- **Passive cold:** a shaded pit on the north side, a basement floor, a buried container, a snow
  cache, a spring, a creek, a well. Ground a few feet down is remarkably stable.
- **Evaporative cooling:** a wet towel over a container in moving air; the pot-in-pot with damp sand
  between. Works best in dry heat.
- **Vehicle:** a running car's 12 V socket can power a cooler (→ 09-11). **Never leave medicine in a
  car in summer heat or a hard freeze.**
- **What you cannot substitute:** the thermometer, and the label's temperature rules.

## When it runs out
- **When the power runs out, cold does not have to.** Fall back in this order: **electric cooler →
  passive cold → evaporative, ground or water cooling →** the room-temperature times printed on the
  medicine's label and in its module.
- **Runway: work two numbers and write them on → 23-02:** (a) days of battery that will run the
  cooler alone with no generation, and (b) **days of medicine supply left**. **Whichever is shorter
  is your real clock**, and it is very often (b).
- **Ration:** shed every other load to defend this one. Shrink to the smallest cooled volume. Run
  the cooler at midday from direct generation and coast on thermal mass at night.
- **Resupply:** cooling can be improvised; **the medicine often cannot.** Medicine supply is a main
  input to the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02).
- **Escalation, written as decisions, not worries:**
  - Cold chain cannot be held **and** the weather is warm → act today.
  - Medicine supply below your written threshold with no resupply path → go/no-go (→ 01-02).
  - Cannot power the medical devices **and** cannot keep the medicine usable → the highest-priority
    emergency in this binder: the condition module and → 01-02, now.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** cooler on a station or battery when it is warm; passive cold with freeze
  protection when it is cold; thermometer logged daily. Build and **prove** all three paths.
- **B (moving):** an insulated case and thermal mass, or evaporative pouches (→ 12-21). **Cold is a
  packing problem while moving**, unless the vehicle can run the cooler. In winter the risk flips to
  freezing: keep medicine inside your clothing layers, not in an outside pocket or a pack strapped
  to a vehicle.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** a root cellar or buried store gives stable cool temperatures year
  round with zero energy (→ 04-09). Keep the 12 V cooler as the summer fine-control on top of it.

## Cross-references
→ 29-07 refrigerated medicines explained · → 09-01 load triage · → 09-03 stations, ports and ECO
settings · → 09-05 winter solar · → 09-06 device charging · → 09-16 outage day one (when and where
the cooler is set up) · → 04-09 winter cold storage · → 12-21 evaporative cooling pouches · → 01-02
go/no-go · → 30-09 heat-exposed medication card

pages.title: Hand-crank, vehicle, wind and other backup generation
pages.body:
# Hand-crank, vehicle, wind and other backup generation

**What this page is for.** Everything here is a backup to solar and batteries, not a plan: what you
use when the panels are buried, the controller has failed, or you are on the move. It ranks the
options by what they actually deliver, and covers the one that is dangerous, a running vehicle.

> **CAUTION: the vehicle is the dangerous one.** A car used as a generator is a fuel-burning engine
> and makes **carbon monoxide**, which you cannot see or smell and which can kill within minutes
> (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics). **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors,
> in a garage, or near an open window** (→ 30-01): not in an attached garage, not even with the door
> open. Outdoors, exhaust away from the house, carbon monoxide alarms on every level (→ 08-02). In
> snow, **check the tailpipe is not buried**: a drifted exhaust pushes carbon monoxide straight into
> the cabin, and it kills people in vehicles in snowstorms.

## Do this now
- **Buy a hand-crank weather radio with a USB output.** It needs nothing and covers information
  (→ 15-02) and a trickle of emergency phone charge.
- **Learn how to charge from your vehicles**, and keep the cables that do it in the vehicle kit
  (→ 22-05): a high-wattage USB-C car charger for phones and power banks, and the station
  maker's car-charging cable if your station has one.
- **Keep vehicle fuel tanks above half, always.** Half a tank is a real power reserve and a head
  start if you have to leave.

## Why it works this way

**Sort the options by what they deliver:**

| Method | Realistic output | Honest verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Hybrid vehicle in "ready" mode** | Hundreds of watts of charging, engine starting and stopping only as needed | The best vehicle option, far more fuel-efficient than idling a conventional engine |
| Conventional vehicle alternator, engine idling | **500 to 2,000 W** | Good, but fuel-hungry at idle. Limited by fuel |
| Vehicle 12 V socket, engine off | About 100 W from the 12 V battery | Small loads only; do not flatten a battery you need to start the vehicle (→ 09-14) |
| Small wind turbine (400 to 1,000 W rated) | Very variable; often 10 to 30% of rated over time | Worth it only with open exposure and a tall tower |
| Hand crank (radio, charger) | **2 to 6 W while cranking hard** | Real but tiny: a phone charge is an hour or more of work |
| Bicycle generator | 50 to 150 W by a fit person, briefly | Exercise, not a power supply |
| Thermoelectric (TEG) stove generator | 5 to 15 W while a fire burns | Free power from a fire you were burning anyway |
| Micro-hydro | 100 W or more, continuously, with real drop and flow | The best of all, **if** you have year-round moving water |

### The vehicle as a generator
**The vehicle is a generator, not a battery.** The engine and alternator make the power; the 12 V
battery only buffers it.

**Our vehicles:**
{{#each vehicles as v}}- {{v.type_text}} ({{v.fuel_text}})
{{else}}- None recorded.
{{/each}}

**Conventional vehicles.** An idling conventional engine burns a lot of fuel to make a trickle of
electricity: very inefficient. Run it in **batches** at a meaningful load, as with a generator
(→ 09-04): charge hard, then shut down. Its fuel is also your evacuation range.

**Hybrids.** A hybrid in "ready" mode, with everything else off, starts and stops its engine by
itself to keep the large traction battery charged. It does not idle continuously: it runs the engine
a few minutes at a time at an efficient load and is silent in between. **That makes charging devices
in ready mode extremely fuel-efficient.** The carbon monoxide rules do not change: **the engine will
start on its own; never ready mode in a garage, and never with a snow-drifted tailpipe.**

**Hybrid cautions:**
- A hybrid's **12 V battery is a small auxiliary battery**, often an AGM type, whose job is to boot
  the computers. It is smaller than a normal starting battery. **Do not deep-cycle it with the
  vehicle off**: take it low and the vehicle may not enter ready mode, the hybrid version of "will
  not start". In ready mode the vehicle maintains it.
- **Jump rules differ** (→ 09-14). Check the owner's manual for the jump point and rules.
- **The high-voltage traction battery is not user-accessible. Never tap, probe or wire to it.**
  Orange cables mean hundreds of volts.

{{#if has.ev}}**Electric vehicles.** An EV is a very large battery. Read its owner's manual for an
accessory or "camp" mode that keeps the 12 V system powered, and for any built-in AC outlet or
vehicle-to-load adapter. The traction-battery rule above applies.{{/if}}

**What each vehicle path charges:**

| Load | Path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Phones, power banks, small DC stations | High-wattage USB-C car charger in the 12 V socket | The main use: refills the pocket tier |
| A 12 V medicine cooler | 12 V socket, directly | Native 12 V; no adapter needed (→ 09-10) |
| A larger power station | The station maker's 12 V car-charging cable | **Slow: often about 100 to 200 W**, so an all-day trickle, not a bulk refill |
| AC loads | An inverter on the 12 V system, fused (→ 09-08) | Small inverters only through the socket (typically fused 10 to 15 A) |

### Wind: worth it only in the right place
Wind can produce at night, in overcast, and in the middle of a dark winter that has flattened your
solar, and in many open places the windiest months are the least sunny. The caveats are real:
- **Small turbines routinely make far less than their rating**, because the rating assumes a wind
  speed you rarely get.
- **Height is everything.** A turbine on a short pole between houses and trees is close to useless.
  Real production needs a **tall, clear tower**: impractical and conspicuous on a town lot, and often
  against local rules.
- **Moving parts fail:** ice, hail, bearings, gusts.
- **It is noisy and visible** (→ 14-03).

**Verdict: not in town; worth evaluating at a rural site** with open exposure and room for a tower.
A supplement to solar, never a replacement.

### Thermoelectric: small, free, and it fits a wood plan
A TEG (thermoelectric generator) makes a few watts from the temperature difference across a burning
stove. Little, but **you are already burning that fire** to cook or heat, so it is free, it works at
night and in a blizzard, and a few watts charges a phone over a few hours. A good winter backup.

### Hand crank and pedal: the honest floor
Hand-crank output is **a few watts of hard, continuous cranking**: charging a phone from empty is an
hour or more of steady work. Do not build a plan on it. **Do** own a hand-crank radio: the radio
itself uses almost nothing, and information with **no** power dependency is worth a lot (→ 15-02).
A bicycle generator does better but needs a stand, a generator head, a controller and a willing
rider: a settled-site project, not a preparation.

### Micro-hydro: the one that would change everything
Year-round moving water with real drop produces **continuously, day and night, in winter**: the best
off-grid power there is. Put it on the criteria list when choosing a rural site (→ 01-05). Many
streams freeze or dry up.

> **Before the collapse:** water rights and permits apply to diverting a stream.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Hand-crank weather radio with USB out | Information with no power dependency | Also a light and a tiny charger |
| High-wattage USB-C car charger | The right way to charge the pocket tier from a vehicle | One per vehicle |
| Station's 12 V car-charging cable | Trickle-charges a station while driving | Check it is in the kit |
| DC-DC charger | Charges a separate battery bank from an alternator properly | Settled-site or scavenged-vehicle tool |
| 1,000 W inverter with battery clamps and an inline fuse | Turns any vehicle into AC power | Fuse it (→ 09-08) |
| Heavy jumper cables | Charging, jump-starting, salvage cable | |
| TEG stove generator | A few watts from a fire you are burning anyway | Best when solar fails |
| Spare vehicle battery, maintained | Portable storage and a starting reserve | Rotate it |
| **Carbon monoxide alarms** | Any engine anywhere near the house | The recurring answer in this section |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Alternators** from any scrapped vehicle can be belt- or hand-driven into a crude generator.
  Needs a regulator and real speed: a genuine project.
- **Permanent-magnet motors** from treadmills, scooters, power tools and washing machines run
  backwards as generators; treadmill motors are the classic home-built turbine head.
- **Bicycle dynamos and hub generators:** small, but made for this.
- **Every abandoned vehicle** is a lead-acid battery, a 12 V socket and potentially an alternator
  (→ 09-13).
- **What you cannot improvise well:** a charge controller and a good charger. Buy spares.

## When it runs out
- **Vehicle generation ends when the fuel ends**, and that fuel is also your evacuation range.
  Budget it on → 23-02 as **both** miles and watt-hours, and decide in advance which use wins.
- **Hand crank and TEG never run out:** the only truly renewable generation you can carry. That is
  why they are the floor, small as they are.
- **Wind and hydro run as long as you can maintain them;** bearings, blades and controllers are the
  consumables.
- **The order of fallback as things degrade:** solar → generator → vehicle → wind or hydro if built →
  TEG on the cooking fire → hand crank → **nothing, and each medical device falls back to the
  non-electric method in its condition module** (→ 09-06). Every rung buys time; none is permanent.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** the vehicles are the big backup (hybrids in ready mode where you have them) and
  the hand-crank radio is the floor. Tanks above half. **No engine running in the garage, ever.**
- **B (moving):** the vehicle *is* the power system while you drive: the USB-C charger keeps phones
  and small medical devices alive, and a 12 V cooler runs from the socket. On foot: a folding panel
  and power banks, with the hand crank as reserve.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** where wind and micro-hydro become worth building. Evaluate the wind
  and water **before** choosing the site (→ 01-05).

## Cross-references
→ 09-04 generators and carbon monoxide · → 09-14 car batteries and hybrid 12 V rules · → 09-06
charging medical devices · → 09-08 wiring and fusing · → 08-02 carbon monoxide safety · → 22-05 the
vehicle kit · → 15-02 radios

photo_slots.caption: Our adapter kit laid out and labelled

pages.body:
# AC versus DC, cables, connectors and adapters

**What this page is for.** Making mismatched equipment work together: which connectors you will
meet, how to charge things efficiently, and how to test a scavenged power source before it destroys
something. Volts, amps and watts: → 29-02. House wiring: → 29-04.

> **CAUTION.** Mismatched equipment is exactly when people connect something backwards and destroy
> it, or start a fire. **Three rules prevent almost every disaster here: check polarity before
> connecting, check voltage before connecting, and fuse the battery side** (→ 09-08). **Anything
> touching house wiring is an electrician's job** (OSHA, Electrical).

## Do this now
- **Buy a cheap multimeter and learn three measurements:** DC volts, AC volts, continuity. It costs
  less than a tank of fuel and is the difference between "I found a power supply" and "I destroyed my
  battery bank".
- **Build the adapter kit** listed below. It is small and cheap and it turns salvaged parts into
  working power (→ 09-13). {{photo adapter-kit}}
- **Label every cable you own:** voltage, polarity, what it belongs to.
- **Put a known-good charging set in the go-bag** (→ 22-03): the cable and charger that definitely
  work, not the drawer of maybes.

## Why it works this way

### AC and DC: the practical difference

| | **DC (direct current)** | **AC (alternating current)** |
|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | Current flows one way, steadily | Current reverses direction many times a second |
| **Where you meet it** | Batteries, solar panels, USB, vehicles, 12 V gear | Wall outlets, generators, inverter outputs |
| **Typical voltages** | 3.7, 5, 12, 20, 24, 48 V | 120 V (240 V for big appliances) |
| **Polarity** | **Matters. Backwards can destroy things instantly** | No polarity in the same sense |
| **Danger** | Low shock risk at 12 V; **high fire risk**: huge current into a short | **High shock risk.** 120 V can kill |

Almost everything you store energy in is **DC** (batteries, panels), and almost everything made for a
wall outlet is **AC**. Converting between them costs energy.

### The rule that saves the most power: run DC loads on DC
An **inverter** turns battery DC into household AC. That costs energy as heat, and the inverter draws
power just by being switched on, even with nothing plugged in.

```
BATTERY (12 V DC) --> 12 V DC device                  best: no conversion
BATTERY (12 V DC) --> USB adapter --> phone           very good: one small conversion
BATTERY (12 V DC) --> INVERTER --> wall charger --> phone
                                                      worst: two conversions,
                                                      and the inverter idles all day
```
**Charging a phone through an inverter and a wall charger is the most wasteful way.** Use a **12 V
to USB adapter.** {{#if has.condition.CL-02}}Where a phone runs a medical device, as in this household
(→ 09-06), that habit meaningfully extends the battery bank.{{/if}}

**When you do need the inverter:** for anything that only exists as AC (most kitchen appliances, power
tools, some medical equipment). **Switch it off when not in use**, and use a **pure sine** inverter
for anything sensitive (→ 09-08).

### The voltage ladder

| Voltage | What lives there |
|---|---|
| **3.6 to 3.7 V** | A single lithium cell |
| **5 V** | USB-A, basic USB-C charging, most small electronics |
| **12 V nominal** | Vehicles, most portable solar setups, RV and marine gear. **Real range about 11.8 to 14.6 V** depending on charge and charging |
| **9, 15, 20 V** | USB-C Power Delivery levels; laptops typically 20 V |
| **18 to 24 V** | Cordless tool packs |
| **24 and 48 V** | Larger off-grid systems: fewer amps, thinner wire |
| **120 V AC** | Wall outlets, inverter output |

**Watts = volts × amps** (→ 25-02). A 60 W load is 5 A at 12 V or 0.5 A at 120 V, which is why 12 V
needs much thicker wire for the same job (→ 09-08).

### The connectors you will actually meet
Salvaged power fails at the connector far more often than at the battery.

| Connector | Where it lives | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **MC4** | Solar panels, almost universally | Weatherproof, locking. **Panels are live in daylight; treat them as live.** The + side has the male pin. {{figure fig-mc4-polarity-check}} |
| **12 V socket** ("cigarette lighter") | Vehicles, power stations, RVs | Convenient, **loose-fitting, limited current**: typically fused around 10 to 15 A |
| **Anderson Powerpole** | Ham radio, RV, home-built systems | **Excellent**: genderless, high current, hard to connect wrong. Worth standardising on |
| **XT60 / XT90** | Hobby gear, e-bikes, many power station solar inputs | High current, polarised |
| **Barrel jack** (commonly 5.5 × 2.1 mm) | Small electronics, routers, LED strips, some panels and stations | **Polarity varies by device**: centre-positive is common, not universal. **Check first** |
| **Ring and spade terminals** | Battery posts, fuse blocks | The workhorse of permanent 12 V wiring |
| **Alligator clips** | Testing and temporary connections | **Never for anything permanent or unattended** |
| **USB-A** | Older everything | About 5 V, low power |
| **USB-C** | Phones, laptops, modern power banks and panels | See below |

### USB-C Power Delivery
- **USB-C can carry far more than 5 V.** With **Power Delivery (PD)** the device and charger agree on a
  higher voltage (commonly 9, 15 or 20 V), so one connector charges a phone or a laptop.
- **Not every USB-C cable carries full power.** Some are data-only or low-power; cables rated for the
  highest power are electronically marked. **A phone that charges slowly may just have the wrong
  cable.**
- **Buy a couple of known-good, high-rated USB-C cables and label them.** Test them. One in the
  go-bag and one in each vehicle (→ 22-05).
- **A 12 V to USB-C PD adapter** charges phones and laptops straight from a battery, a station's 12 V
  port or a vehicle with one conversion. One of the highest-value small purchases in this section.

### Polarity: the mistake that destroys things
**Reversed polarity on DC can kill a device instantly, and on a battery it can start a fire.**
- **Red, a marked stripe or a ridged conductor = positive** by convention. **Convention is not a
  guarantee** on salvaged gear.
- **Check with the multimeter before connecting.** Every time, on anything salvaged. A **minus sign**
  on the meter's reading means your probes are on the opposite conductors: the red probe is on
  negative.
- **Barrel jacks:** look for the polarity symbol printed near the socket.
- **Fuse the positive lead close to the battery** (→ 09-08). A fuse turns a polarity mistake into a
  blown fuse instead of a fire.

### Wire: what to keep and what to salvage
- **Thicker is safer.** Undersized wire heats up (→ 09-08).
- **Stranded flexes, solid does not.** Use stranded anywhere that moves or vibrates.
- **Extension cords are AC wire.** In a pinch they work as heavy DC wire, but keep them fully unrolled
  under load: a coiled cord heats (OSHA).
- **Worth salvaging:** jumper cables (very heavy), speaker wire, thermostat wire (light duty only),
  vehicle harnesses, welding cable.
- **Never assume a salvaged cable's rating.** If you cannot read a gauge marking, size
  conservatively.

### Testing before you connect anything salvaged
```
1. LOOK      Damage, corrosion, melted insulation, swelling, burnt smell?  -> reject
2. MEASURE   DC volts across the output. Note the POLARITY the meter shows.
3. COMPARE   Does that voltage match what the load expects? Within its range?
4. FUSE      Put a suitably rated fuse in the positive lead first.
5. CONNECT   Smallest, least valuable load first. Never a medical device first.
6. WATCH     Heat, smell, buzzing. Check it again after 10 minutes.
```
> **Never test a new supply on a phone or device that someone's health depends on.** Prove it on a
> headlamp or a cheap USB light first (→ 09-06).

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Multimeter** and a spare battery for it | The most useful electrical tool you can own | DC volts, AC volts, continuity |
| **12 V to USB-C PD adapter** | Charges phones with one conversion | High value |
| **Known-good, high-rated USB-C cables** | Cables fail more than batteries | Label and test |
| **12 V socket splitter with inline fuses** | One outlet into several, safely | → 09-08 |
| **Anderson Powerpole set and crimper** | Standardise DC connections | Hard to get wrong |
| **MC4 connectors, Y-branch pair and spanner** | Solar side, including salvaged panels | → 09-03 |
| **Assorted barrel-jack adapters** | Salvaged small electronics | Check polarity every time |
| **Ring and spade terminals, heat-shrink, crimper** | Proper battery connections | Not twisted wire and tape |
| **Inline fuse holders and assorted fuses** | Stops a mistake becoming a fire | → 09-08 |
| **Alligator test leads** | Testing only | Never permanent |
| **10 to 12 AWG stranded wire, red and black** | Fixing and extending | Buy more than you think |
| Electrical tape, heat-shrink, cable ties, marker | Labelling and insulation | |

**Scavenge or substitute:** jumper cables are excellent heavy DC conductors; vehicle 12 V sockets,
fuse blocks and harnesses are reusable (→ 09-13); computer power supplies, wall chargers and car
chargers are everywhere and each is a labelled DC source: **read the label, check with the meter,
then use it**.

## When it runs out
- **Runway:** connectors and wire do not wear out fast, but **every repair uses some**, and crimp
  terminals and fuses go fastest.
- **Ration:** reuse terminals where safe; **never reuse a fuse by bridging it. A bridged fuse is the
  most dangerous "repair" in this section.**
- **Resupply:** vehicles, appliances and abandoned electronics are full of wire, terminals and fuses
  (→ 09-13, → 22-02).
- **Substitute:** proper crimps > soldered joints > twisted and taped. All three beat nothing, but only
  the first two belong in anything left unattended.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** standardise now: one DC connector family, labelled cables, a stocked adapter kit.
- **B (moving):** the 12 V socket adapters, the USB-C PD adapter and known-good cables travel
  (→ 22-05).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the adapter kit and multimeter let you use whatever you find. **Bring
  the connectors; you will not find the right ones when you need them.**

## Cross-references
→ 09-08 fusing and wire sizing, read before wiring anything · → 09-03 batteries and the MC4 polarity
check · → 09-06 charging medical devices · → 09-13 what to scavenge · → 09-09 the small build ·
→ 25-02 conversions and math · → 22-02 scavenging field guide

pages.title: Scavenging electrical power: what to harvest
pages.body:
# Scavenging electrical power: what to harvest

**What this page is for.** What is worth taking from vehicles, buildings and abandoned equipment to
keep your power going in a long event, what is not worth the risk, and how to tell a useful battery
from scrap. Read → 09-12 first: without a multimeter and an adapter kit, most of what you could
harvest is unusable.

> **SAFETY. Four things on this page can kill or burn you, and they are not the obvious ones.**
> **(1) Stored charge.** Capacitors inside inverters, power supplies, microwave ovens and old CRT
> televisions hold a **lethal charge long after unplugging.** **Do not open them.**
> **(2) Lithium packs.** Damaged or mishandled cells go into thermal runaway, an intense,
> self-sustaining fire (NFPA, Lithium-Ion Batteries). **Do not take packs apart for cells.**
> **(3) Solar panels are live in daylight.** They make voltage whenever light falls on them; there is
> no off switch (US Department of Energy, Solar Photovoltaic System Design Basics).
> **(4) Anything connected to house wiring or a running generator.** That is electrician territory
> (OSHA, Electrical) and the backfeed floor: **never connect a generator to house wiring without a
> transfer switch, interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion with the main breaker locked off; never
> backfeed through an outlet** (→ 09-04, → 30-01).

## Do this now
- **Read → 09-12 first.**
- **Learn the resting voltages for lead-acid** (→ 09-07): they tell a useful battery from scrap with
  no special equipment.
- **Decide the lithium rule now, calmly: take whole packs with their matching chargers, never loose
  cells.** That rule is the whole safety margin.
- **Scavenging is no substitute for owning a system** (→ 09-09). It extends what you have; it does not
  produce anything (→ 23-04).

## Why it works this way

### What is actually worth taking
Ranked by usefulness for the risk and effort:

| Rank | Item | Why | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Lead-acid batteries:** car, truck, marine, RV, golf cart, floor scrubber, mobility scooter | Everywhere, testable with a meter, no fire risk in normal use | Acid, weight, hydrogen when charging: **ventilate** |
| **2** | **Wire, terminals, fuses, fuse blocks, 12 V sockets** | The consumable every repair uses (→ 09-12) | Low |
| **3** | **Vehicle 12 V accessories:** chargers, inverters, socket splitters | Built for exactly this voltage | Low |
| **4** | **UPS units** (office and computer battery backups) | **Underrated.** A sealed lead-acid battery, a charger and an inverter in one box | Stored charge in the inverter: **do not open it** |
| **5** | **Solar:** garden and path lights, sign and construction panels, RV panels | Free DC, no fuel, silent | Live in daylight; theft risk on the last two |
| **6** | **Alternators, small motors** | Generation potential (→ 09-11) | Needs a mechanical drive you probably do not have |
| **7** | **Whole cordless tool, e-bike or laptop packs, with their charger** | Usable **as a pack**, on its own charger | **High: see the lithium section** |
| **(none)** | **Loose lithium cells, opened packs** | | **Do not** |

### Lead-acid: the one you can judge
In depth on → 09-03 and → 09-07; the field version:
- **Resting voltage tells you most of what you need.** A 12 V lead-acid battery at rest reads about
  **12.6 to 12.7 V full**, about **12.0 to 12.1 V at 50%** (as low as you should take it), and below
  about **11.8 V you are damaging it.**
- **A battery at 0 V, or with a cracked case, bulging sides or leaking acid, is scrap.** Leave it.
  Batteries that have sat flat for months are usually beyond recovery.
- **Deep-cycle beats starting.** Marine, RV, golf-cart and floor-scrubber batteries are built to be
  drained; car starting batteries die fast if cycled (→ 09-14).
- **Carry them upright, wear eye protection and gloves,** and never let a metal tool bridge the
  terminals: that is an instant, violent short (→ 09-08).
- **Charge in a ventilated space.** Charging lead-acid makes hydrogen.

### UPS units: the best-value scavenge nobody thinks of
Every office, server closet and home desk has one. A UPS is effectively a **pre-built 12 V system in
a box**: a sealed lead-acid battery, a charger and an inverter.
- **The battery is the useful part:** usually a standard 12 V sealed lead-acid, easy to remove from
  its own compartment.
- **The inverter section holds stored charge. Do not open the electronics.** Take the battery from its
  compartment; leave the rest sealed.
- **The whole unit is useful as-is** if you have any AC to charge it from, as a small buffer for a
  critical load.

### Solar you can actually find
- **Garden and path lights:** a tiny panel, a small cell and an LED each. Trivial one by one; **in
  quantity a useful trickle**, and free indoor light as they are (→ 10-03).
- **Sign, construction, RV and boat panels:** real panels, usually with **MC4 connectors** and often
  a controller and battery attached.
- **Treat every panel as live.** **Cover it with something opaque before handling the connectors,**
  and never bridge the leads.
- **Read the label** for the open-circuit voltage before connecting anything. A panel meant for a 24 or
  48 V system will not behave the way you want on a 12 V controller, and may exceed your station's
  input limit (→ 09-02, → 09-03).
- **A panel is useless without a charge controller.** Connecting a panel straight to a battery can
  destroy the battery. Take the controller if there is one (→ 09-09).

### Vehicles: a rolling parts bin
Beyond the battery (→ 09-11 covers running a vehicle as a generator, and the carbon monoxide rule):
- **Alternator:** real generation potential, but it needs to be spun fast by something.
- **Inverters, 12 V sockets, fuse blocks, relays and the wiring harness:** all reusable in a 12 V
  system (→ 09-12).
- **Heavy cable:** battery and starter cables are excellent conductors.
- **Fuses:** every vehicle carries an assortment, and fuses are consumed by every mistake.

### Lithium: the honest and unpopular position
Tool packs, laptop batteries, e-bike and scooter packs and power station cells are everywhere and hold
real energy. **They are also the most dangerous thing in this section.**

**The rule: use whole packs with their own chargers, or leave them.** Why:
- **Damaged or mishandled lithium cells can go into thermal runaway**, an intense, self-sustaining
  fire that is very hard to extinguish and gives off toxic smoke (NFPA, → 09-07).
- **Cells in a pack are spot-welded, not screwed.** Getting them apart is exactly the handling that
  punctures or shorts them.
- **The pack's battery management system is the safety device.** Remove it and you have removed the
  protection against overcharge, over-discharge and imbalance.
- **You cannot tell a good salvaged cell from a bad one by looking.**

**The warning signs, worth memorising:** **heat, an odd smell, swelling or a change of shape.** Any of
those: get it away from people and buildings, outdoors, on a non-combustible surface, and do not try
to charge it.

**What is reasonable:**
- Take a tool pack **and its charger together**, and use it with the tool it belongs to.
- Take a power station or e-bike battery **whole and undamaged**, and use it as designed.
- **Store salvaged lithium outside the living space**, away from anything that would burn (→ 06-06),
  not in the basement beside the medical supplies.
- **Never charge salvaged lithium unattended, overnight or indoors.**

### What is NOT worth taking
- **Microwave ovens and CRT televisions** for parts: the stored charge is lethal.
- **Anything with a cut or damaged mains cord.**
- **Sealed inverter or electronics housings:** you cannot repair them and they hold charge.
- **Batteries that are swollen, leaking, cracked or read 0 V.**
- **Solar panels with shattered glass or peeling backing:** degraded, and a shock hazard when wet.
- **Anything still connected to a building's wiring.** That is not scavenging; it is working on live
  wiring (OSHA, → 09-08).

### The legal and ethical line
**Taking property that is not yours is theft**, and while the law works, the law applies. Sign and
construction solar arrays belong to someone. **Ask, trade or leave it** (→ 18-02, → 22-02): the
relationships outlast the panel.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Multimeter** | Nothing on this page works without one | → 09-12 |
| **Insulated gloves and eye protection** | Acid, sparks, shorts | → 16-01 |
| Battery terminal cleaner and puller | Corroded terminals are the usual failure | |
| **Insulated wrenches**, or tape over the metal | Bridging terminals is the classic injury | → 09-08 |
| Battery carry strap | They are heavier than they look | |
| **Spare charge controller** | A salvaged panel is useless without one | → 09-09 |
| MC4 and Anderson connector kit | Connect what you find | → 09-12 |
| Assorted fuses and holders | Consumed by every mistake | → 09-08 |
| Hydrometer or battery tester | Judging lead-acid properly | → 09-07 |
| **Fire extinguisher of the right class** | Especially with any lithium around | → 29-12 |

**Scavenge or substitute:** a cheap 12 V bulb makes a crude load tester; jumper cables move charge
between batteries; a vehicle's own charging system will charge a salvaged lead-acid battery (→ 09-11).

## When it runs out
Scavenged electricity is **substitution, never production** (→ 23-04).
- **Runway:** salvageable batteries degrade whether used or not. Most abandoned lead-acid is scrap
  within a couple of years; lithium packs age out too.
- **Ration:** treat every working battery as a consumable; do not deep-cycle a starting battery for
  convenience.
- **Resupply:** vehicles are the deepest reservoir, and they are finite.
- **Substitute:** **solar is the only electricity that keeps coming** (→ 09-02): panels last decades,
  and the batteries are the consumable.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** buy the multimeter and the adapter kit, and note what exists nearby. Take nothing
  that is not yours.
- **B (moving):** almost nothing here is worth the weight while moving: cables, adapters and a
  multimeter, not batteries.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** farms and outbuildings hold batteries, wire, panels and controllers,
  with less competition than town. Bring the connectors.

## Cross-references
→ 09-12 connectors and testing, read first · → 09-03 and → 09-07 judging lead-acid · → 09-08 fusing
and shorts · → 09-09 building with what you have · → 09-11 vehicle generation · → 09-14 car batteries
· → 22-02 scavenging guide and its ethics · → 23-04 resource lifecycles
