pages.body:
# Car batteries in practice: getting energy out and back in

**What this page is for.** How much energy is really in a car battery, the three ways to get it out,
the four ways to put it back, how to take one out of a vehicle safely, and the rules for hybrids,
whose 12 V battery is a different animal. Chemistry and resting voltages: → 09-07.

> **SAFETY. A car battery is the most dangerous-feeling-harmless object in the garage.** It will not
> shock you through dry skin, which is why people get careless with it.
> **(1) Explosive gas.** Charging batteries give off hydrogen; ventilation must prevent "the
> accumulation of an explosive mixture" (OSHA, 29 CFR 1926.441). **No sparks, flames or smoking near
> a charging battery. Never charge one in a sealed space.**
> **(2) Short-circuit current.** A wrench dropped across the terminals delivers hundreds of amps at
> once: it welds itself in place, glows, and can burst the battery.
> **(3) Acid.** OSHA requires face shields, aprons and rubber gloves for handling batteries, with
> drenching facilities nearby. **Eye protection, always.**
> **(4) Never charge or jump a frozen or damaged battery.** It can rupture.
> **(5) Engines.** Charging from a running vehicle: **never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine
> indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning
> (→ 30-01; CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

## Do this now
- **Read the label on each battery you own** and write down the **RC** (reserve capacity) or **Ah**,
  not just the CCA. CCA tells you nothing about how much energy is stored. {{photo vehicle-battery-labels}}
- **Buy a cheap voltmeter or multimeter** (→ 09-12). Resting voltage is your fuel gauge.
- **Buy one small inverter (150 to 300 W) with a 12 V plug, and one larger one (1,000 W or more) with
  battery clamps and an inline fuse.** Together they cover almost everything (→ 09-08).
- **Set the household rule now: the batteries in the vehicles you drive are not a power bank.** They
  are your ability to start and leave (→ 01-03). Hybrids are stricter still: read the box below.

## Why it works this way

### Hybrids are different
Everything below about worked examples, big inverters clamped to posts and harvesting energy assumes
a **conventional vehicle with a conventional starting battery.** A hybrid is a different machine:
- **Its 12 V battery is a small auxiliary battery**, not a starting battery. It boots the computers
  and closes the high-voltage contactors; the traction battery starts the engine. It is smaller than
  a normal starting battery, so **the arithmetic below does not apply to it. Do not deep-cycle it
  with the vehicle off:** take it low and the vehicle will not enter ready mode, the hybrid version of
  "will not start".
- **Draw power in ready mode** (→ 09-11): the vehicle maintains its own 12 V system and runs the
  engine only as needed. With ready mode on, the auxiliary-battery problem disappears. Same carbon
  monoxide rules: the engine starts by itself.
- **Jump rules differ.** Many hybrids accept a jump only at a marked 12 V jump point (the battery may
  not be under the hood), and only to boot the computers. **Never use a hybrid's 12 V system to
  crank-start a conventional car:** the burst can exceed what the small battery and its wiring are
  built for. A dead **traction** battery is not a jumper-cable
  problem.
- **The high-voltage traction battery is not user-accessible. Never tap, probe or wire to it.**
  Orange cables mean hundreds of volts.
- **What still applies to hybrids:** the voltmeter habit, terminal care, the freeze and
  deep-discharge cautions, and the rule that the vehicle battery's job is mobility.

**Our vehicles:**
{{#each vehicles as v}}- {{v.type_text}} ({{v.fuel_text}}): battery Ah or RC ______ · conventional
  or hybrid ______ · jump point ______
{{else}}- None recorded.
{{/each}}

The rest of this page is for **conventional vehicles and the spare and scavenged batteries**
(→ 09-13).

### How much energy is in there
**The label usually shows CCA: ignore it for this.** Cold cranking amps measures a short, violent
burst to turn a starter. It says nothing about stored energy.

**What you want is Ah (amp-hours) or RC (reserve capacity, in minutes).** If you only have RC:
```
Ah  ~=  RC (minutes) x 25 / 60        RC is measured at a 25 A draw
Wh   =  Ah x 12.6 V                   (nominal, full)
```
**Worked example, a typical car battery:**
```
RC 100 minutes  ->  100 x 25 / 60  ~=  42 Ah
42 Ah x 12.6 V                     ~=  530 Wh  NOMINAL (all of it)
Lead-acid: take only 50%           ~=  265 Wh
STARTING battery, to keep it alive: less again  ~=  130-200 Wh REALISTIC
Minus inverter losses (10-15%)     ~=  120-175 Wh AT THE OUTLET
```

**What one car battery actually runs:**

| Load | Roughly |
|---|---|
| **Phone (10 to 20 Wh a day)** (→ 09-06) | **A week or more.** The best use of it |
| LED lantern or headlamps | Many nights |
| Laptop (50 to 60 Wh a charge) | Two or three charges |
| CPAP or similar (30 to 60 W) | Part of a night |
| **Refrigerator (1,000 to 2,000 Wh a day)** (→ 09-10) | **A few hours at most. Do not plan on it** |
| Anything with a heating element | **Minutes. Never** |

> **The lesson:** a car battery is a useful reservoir for **small DC loads and charging**, and
> nowhere near enough for refrigeration or heat. That is why medicine cooling has its own page
> (→ 09-10).

### Starting versus deep-cycle

| | **Starting battery** (cars, trucks) | **Deep-cycle** (marine, RV, golf cart, floor scrubber) |
|---|---|---|
| Built for | Short high-current bursts | Being drained and refilled again and again |
| Deep discharge | **Kills it quickly**, sometimes in a dozen cycles | Designed for it (still only to about 50%) |
| Use as storage? | Gently, in an emergency | **Yes: this is the one you want** |

Every abandoned RV, boat, golf cart and floor scrubber holds the better battery (→ 09-13).

### Getting energy out: three paths, best first
**1. Straight 12 V DC: the efficient path.** A socket adapter or clamps to a **12 V to USB-C PD
adapter** (→ 09-12). One conversion, no inverter idling. **For phones and medical devices this is the
right way** (→ 09-06).

**2. Small inverter (150 to 300 W) in the 12 V socket.** For small AC things. Limited by the socket's
fuse (typically 10 to 15 A, so roughly 120 to 180 W continuous). **Do not exceed it.**

**3. Large inverter (1,000 W or more) clamped to the terminals.** For real AC loads. Rules (→ 09-08):
- **Fuse the positive lead close to the battery**, sized to the cable.
- **Heavy, short cable:** a 1,000 W inverter at 12 V pulls roughly 85 to 100 A.
- **Connect the inverter's negative last; disconnect it first.**
- **Engine running for anything substantial** (outdoors, never in a garage), or you flatten the
  battery fast.

**Watch the voltage, not the clock:** about **12.6 to 12.7 V full**, **12.0 to 12.1 V at 50%** (stop
there), and **below about 11.8 V you are damaging it.** On a battery in a vehicle you want to drive,
**stop well above that.**

### Putting energy back: four ways, best first
**1. Alternator, through a proper charger or DC-DC charger** (→ 09-11). Controlled and fast. Run the
engine at a meaningful load **in batches**, not idling for hours: idling burns a lot of fuel for very
little power, and that fuel is also your range (→ 01-03). **Never in an attached garage** (CDC; CPSC,
Portable Generator Safety; → 08-02).

**2. Solar through a charge controller** (→ 09-02, → 09-09). The only renewable path: slow, silent,
every sunny day. **A panel connected straight to a battery with no controller will damage it.**

**3. Mains or generator AC through a proper battery charger** (→ 09-04). A smart charger with a
lead-acid profile; batch-charge while the generator is running for other loads anyway.

**4. Another vehicle, by jumper cables.** Emergency only. It moves charge crudely and does not fill a
bank.

**While charging (OSHA 1926.441):** ventilate; keep vent caps in place on flooded batteries to avoid
electrolyte spray; eye protection; no sparks or flames.

### Taking a battery out of a vehicle
```
[ ] Engine off, key out. Eye protection and gloves on.
[ ] DISCONNECT NEGATIVE (-) FIRST, then positive (+).
    Negative first means a slipped wrench touching the body cannot short anything.
[ ] Tape over the wrench, or use insulated tools. NEVER let a tool bridge the posts.
[ ] Release the hold-down clamp. Lift with your legs: they are heavy.
[ ] Carry and store UPRIGHT. Flooded batteries spill acid.
[ ] REINSTALLING: positive (+) FIRST, negative (-) LAST.
[ ] Store CHARGED, cool, and never fully flat.
```

### Building a small bank from several batteries
Worth doing at a settled site; not in a hurry.
- **Parallel for more capacity at 12 V** (all positives together, all negatives together).
- **Only parallel batteries of the same type, capacity and age, at the same state of charge.**
  Otherwise the good one endlessly drains into the bad one.
- **Never mix lead-acid with lithium** in one bank (→ 09-07).
- **Fuse each battery's positive lead individually** (→ 09-08).
- **Ventilate**, and keep flooded batteries out of the living space (OSHA).
- **Use equal-length cables** to each battery, or the nearest one does all the work.

### Keeping them alive
Lead-acid dies from neglect far more often than from use (→ 09-07):
- **Never leave one flat.** A flat battery sulfates and may not recover. A flat battery is also the
  one that **freezes** in winter, and **a frozen battery must never be charged or jumped.**
- **Top up flooded cells with distilled water only**, plates covered.
- **Clean corroded terminals:** corrosion looks minor and destroys capacity.
- **Cold cuts capacity a lot.** A battery that runs your lights for a week in July does far less in
  January (→ 09-05).
- **Recharge promptly after every use.** That one habit is most of a battery's life.

### The rule that outranks all of this
**Do not flatten the battery in a vehicle you may need to drive.** The vehicle is your way out
(→ 01-03), it can be shelter, and it is your fastest charging source (→ 09-11). **Harvest from spare
and scavenged batteries first;** take an in-service vehicle battery down only for a phone, and only
when it will be recharged soon.

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Multimeter or voltmeter** | Your only fuel gauge | → 09-12 |
| **12 V to USB-C PD adapter** | The efficient path for phones and medical devices | → 09-06 |
| Small inverter (150 to 300 W, 12 V plug) | Small AC loads, no wiring | |
| **Large inverter (1,000 W or more) with clamps** | Real AC loads | **Fuse it** (→ 09-08) |
| **Inline fuse holders and fuses (100 A class and up)** | The difference between a mistake and a fire | → 09-08 |
| Heavy short cables, ring terminals, crimper | 12 V means big amps | → 09-12 |
| **Smart lead-acid battery charger** | Charging properly from AC | → 09-04 |
| **DC-DC charger** | The right way to charge from an alternator | → 09-11 |
| Charge controller | The only safe way to charge from a panel | → 09-09 |
| Heavy jumper cables | Emergency transfer; excellent salvage wire | → 09-13 |
| **Eye protection, rubber gloves** | OSHA requires them for a reason | |
| Terminal cleaner, distilled water, battery strap | Maintenance and carrying | |
| Vented battery box | Contains a flooded battery indoors | |

**Scavenge or substitute:** every vehicle, RV, boat, tractor, golf cart and mobility scooter holds a
battery, and **the deep-cycle ones are the prize** (→ 09-13). A 12 V bulb makes a crude load tester.
**A vehicle's own charging system will recharge a salvaged battery**: often the fastest route back to
usable power (→ 09-11).

## When it runs out
- **Runway:** a car battery is **hundreds of watt-hours per cycle**, not thousands: days of phone and
  light, **not refrigeration.**
- **Ration:** stop at 50% resting voltage, and much sooner on a battery you need for starting.
- **Resupply:** recharging is the resupply: alternator, solar or generator. **The battery is storage,
  never a source.**
- **Substitute:** solar with a controller is the only renewable input (→ 09-02). Salvaged lead-acid
  extends storage but generates nothing (→ 09-13).
- **The long view:** salvageable lead-acid degrades whether used or not: years, not decades.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** keep the vehicle batteries healthy and charged; harvest from spares, not from the
  vehicles you drive.
- **B (moving):** the vehicle battery's job is **starting the vehicle**. Charge phones and run a
  cooler only with the engine running or a hybrid in ready mode, and stop there (→ 22-05).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the vehicle becomes a real power asset: alternator charging plus a
  salvaged deep-cycle bank, with solar as the daily input (→ 09-11, → 09-02).

## Cross-references
→ 09-07 chemistry, voltages and the 50% rule · → 09-13 finding more batteries · → 09-08 fusing, read
before clamping any inverter · → 09-12 connectors and testing · → 09-11 alternator charging and the
carbon monoxide rule · → 09-06 medical devices · → 22-05 the vehicle kit

pages.body:
# Generator maintenance, storage and fuel rotation

**What this page is for.** A generator almost never dies from running. **It dies from sitting**, and
it fails on the one night you need it. This page is the routine that prevents that: a fuel-storage
strategy, exercise runs, oil, the service list, the no-start sequence and the log. Safety, siting and
the first start are on → 09-04.

> **CAUTION. The safety rules do not change because you are only doing maintenance.** **Never run a
> generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window**: carbon monoxide
> kills in minutes with no warning (→ 30-01). Run it outdoors, 20 feet or more from the house,
> exhaust pointed away (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety). {{figure fig-generator-siting}}
> **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance** (vapour ignition,
> → 30-01). Never refuel it hot or running. Store fuel in approved, closed containers, cool,
> ventilated, away from ignition and out of children's reach (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety; → 06-06).
> **Your engine's manual governs every interval and specification on this page.**

## Do this now
- **Choose an exercise cadence and put it on the calendar:** at least a few times a year, under load,
  logged. Ours: every ______ , on ______ (fuel). Tie two of the runs to the spring and autumn kit-check
  weekends (→ 24-03).
- **Keep the starting battery charged** the way the manual says (some manuals want a regular charge in
  months it has not run; if the charger is not a maintainer, unplug it after the manual's maximum
  time). A flat starting battery is the likeliest no-start after missing oil.
- **Print your model's manual and keep it with the machine.** Oil type, capacity and intervals are
  model-specific, and you will not have the internet. Copy the key numbers onto → 09-04.
- **Buy the maintenance kit now** (oil, oil filter if fitted, air filter, spark plug) and store it
  **with** the generator.
- **Write the run hours, last oil change, oil grade and fuel state on a label on the machine.** Nobody
  remembers. {{photo generator-label}}

## Why it works this way

### The three things that kill generators
1. **Stale fuel in the carburettor.** Ethanol gasoline absorbs water, separates, and leaves varnish in
   passages narrower than a pin. **The most common cause of a no-start.**
2. **No oil, or oil never changed.** Small engines hold very little oil and forgive nothing.
3. **Rodents.** Nests in the shroud and air box; chewed wiring. Stored equipment is where mice live.

**All three are prevented by one habit: run it under load a few times a year, and look at it while you
do.**

### Fuel: pick a storage state and stick to it
There are three defensible strategies. **The failure is having none.**

| Strategy | How | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Run it dry** | Shut the fuel valve and let the engine stall, so the carburettor empties | Gasoline machines used now and then |
| **Store it wet, stabilised** | Fill with stabilised, ideally ethanol-free fuel; run it long enough to draw stabilised fuel through the carburettor | Machines that must start instantly |
| **Never wet it: run on propane** | Dual- and tri-fuel machines | **The strongest option for long storage** |

> **On a multi-fuel generator, running on propane and never putting gasoline in it removes the most
> common failure entirely.** Propane does not go stale, does not absorb water, and leaves nothing in
> the carburettor to varnish (→ 06-05). Once gasoline has been used, **follow the manual's storage
> table** for draining the fuel tank and carburettor bowl by how long it will sit. Copy it here:
>
> | Will sit for | What the manual says to do |
> |---|---|
> | ______ | ______ |
> | ______ | ______ |
> | ______ | ______ |

{{#if has.generator}}Our generator runs on: **{{ gear.generator_fuel }}**.{{/if}} **Whichever
strategy you choose, write it on the label**, so the next person to touch it (including you in three
years) knows what state the machine is in. A generator stored with gasoline in it in an attached
garage is fuel storage in the garage: a decision card, {{choice DC-05}} (→ 30-06).

### The exercise run: what "running it" actually means
A thirty-second idle proves almost nothing.
```
[ ] OUTDOORS, 20+ ft from the house, exhaust pointed away. CO alarms working.  (09-04)
[ ] Check the oil BEFORE starting. Every time. Ten seconds.
[ ] Start it. Note how easily it started, and on which attempt.
[ ] LOAD IT: a space heater, kettle, battery charger, power station on charge.
    A generator run with no load does not clear its carburettor or warm properly.
    (A new machine: stay within the manual's break-in limit.)
[ ] Run 20-30 minutes under that load.
[ ] Listen and look: surging, misfiring, smoke colour, fuel or oil leaks, hot smells.
[ ] Shut down per the manual. If storing dry, shut the fuel valve and let it stall.
[ ] Log the date, run hours, and anything you noticed.
```
**If it runs on more than one fuel:** run it on propane most times, and on gasoline only as often as
your storage strategy needs.

### Oil: the ten-second check that saves the machine
- **Check the level before every run.** Small engines use and lose oil.
- **Change it on the manual's schedule**, and early on a new machine (break-in). If oil has sat unused
  for years, **change it anyway**: it absorbs moisture.
- **Use the grade the manual gives for the temperatures you will run in.** Cold starting is a real
  load on thick oil; manuals usually list a lower-viscosity grade for cold weather. Ours: ________ ,
  capacity ________. Keep two changes' worth with the machine and write the grade on the label.
- **A low-oil shutdown is a protection, not a gauge:** a machine that stops on low oil was already
  running low.
- **Store used oil in a sealed container** and dispose of it properly; never pour it out (→ 13-03).

### The rest of the service list

| Item | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Air filter** | Check every run; clean or replace per the manual | Also where rodents nest |
| **Spark plug** | Inspect yearly; replace per the manual | Its colour tells you how the engine is running |
| **Fuel filter** | Per the manual | Cheap; replace rather than clean |
| **Fuel lines and primer bulb** | Inspect yearly | Rubber ages even unused. Cracked = replace |
| **Propane hose and regulator** | Inspect yearly | Same ageing. Leak-check with soapy water, never a flame |
| **Starting battery** | Keep charged per the manual; expect to replace | Left unmaintained it sulfates (→ 09-14) |
| **Valve clearance, carburettor rebuild** | Long interval, per the manual | A real job: learn it now or plan to live without it |
| **Cooling fins and air intake** | Every run | Debris and nests cause overheating |

### Fuel rotation: the part that quietly expires
Stored fuel that is never rotated becomes the thing that ruins the engine you were saving it for
(→ 06-06, → 29-01).
```
[ ] LABEL every can with contents and FILL DATE.                       (06-07)
[ ] Rotate stored gasoline through the VEHICLES on a schedule, and refill
    the cans with fresh. Vehicles tolerate older fuel far better than small engines.
[ ] Buy ethanol-free fuel for small engines if you can get it. It stores better.
[ ] Use stabiliser per ITS instructions, added when the fuel is FRESH:
    stabiliser does not repair fuel that has already gone off.
[ ] Putting old or questionable fuel in the generator is a decision: DC-17.
[ ] Propane needs no rotation at all. That is the reason to prefer it. (06-05)
[ ] Record fill dates on 26-08 with everything else that expires.
```
Old fuel: {{choice DC-17}} (→ 30-18).

### When it will not start: work in this order
Do not skip to the carburettor; most no-starts are the first four lines.
```
1. FUEL     Is there fuel? Is the valve OPEN? Is the fuel FRESH?
2. SWITCH   Ignition or battery switch on? Choke set right for a cold engine?
3. OIL      Low-oil shutdown stops many machines from starting. Check the level.
4. LOAD     Anything plugged in? Some machines will not start under load.
            Unplug everything, start, then add load.
5. SPARK    Plug fouled, wet, or wrong gap? A spare plug is the cheapest test there is.
6. AIR      Filter blocked, or a nest in the intake?
7. FUEL DELIVERY  Old fuel or a gummed carburettor. On a dual- or tri-fuel
            machine, TRY IT ON PROPANE: if it runs on propane, the problem
            is the gasoline side. A diagnosis and a workaround in one.
8. BEYOND THAT  Carburettor cleaning or rebuild. Learn it now, or accept the limit.
```
> **The propane test on line 7 is the most useful diagnostic a multi-fuel owner has**, and it keeps
> you running while you deal with the fuel side.

### The maintenance log
```
DATE       RUN HRS   WHAT WAS DONE                      FUEL STATE   NEXT DUE
________   _______   ________________________________   __________   ________
________   _______   ________________________________   __________   ________
________   _______   ________________________________   __________   ________
________   _______   ________________________________   __________   ________
FUEL STATE: DRY (carburettor empty) · WET-STAB (stabilised fuel) · LP (propane only)
```

## Gear and items

**Have it now (buy toward this):** engine oil of the manual's grade (several changes' worth), oil
filter if fitted, **two air filters**, **two spark plugs** and the right plug wrench, fuel filter, spare
fuel line, **fuel stabiliser**, a funnel with a screen, an oil drain pan and a sealable container, a
bottle of soapy water for gas leak checks, **the printed manual**, and a label and marker for the
machine. Store it all **with the generator**. Specs by generator class: → 28-03.

**Scavenge or substitute:** oil in the right grade from vehicle stocks; plugs and filters from other
small engines are sometimes interchangeable, **so check the part numbers; do not guess**; fuel line
from other equipment. **What you cannot substitute is the manual's specifications:** print it while you
can.

## When it runs out
- **Runway:** maintenance parts are consumables. **Count oil changes, not hours:** a generator with fuel
  and no oil is finished.
- **Ration:** stretch intervals only if you must, and never the oil.
- **Resupply:** other small engines (mowers, snowblowers, chainsaws) are the parts bin (→ 22-02).
- **Substitute:** none for oil. **Plan for the generator to be a memory by month two and be fine
  anyway**: solar and batteries are the long-term answer (→ 09-02).

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** exercise runs on your cadence, the starting battery kept charged, fuel rotated,
  parts stocked, log kept.
- **B (moving):** it travels only outside the passenger cabin, or stays behind (→ 09-04).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** use it hard for setting up (pumping, building), then keep the
  remaining fuel and parts for real emergencies.

## Cross-references
→ 09-04 generators: safety, siting, first start and house connections · → 06-06 storing fuel · → 06-07
moving fuel and judging old fuel · → 06-05 propane · → 09-14 the starting battery · → 26-08 expiry
tracking · → 24-03 the seasonal practice weekends · → 28-03 generators by class

pages.body:
# Outage day one: the live grid-down procedure

**What this page is for.** The page you run, in order, when the grid drops. It defends the loads that
matter most (→ 09-01): medical devices, refrigerated medicine, phones, light and, in cold weather,
heat. It then sets up the next morning's charging. The last part is a hard-limits card for your
stations and panels: print it and keep it with the panels.

> **SAFETY.** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
> window**: carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail (→ 30-01). Generator outdoors
> only, 20 feet or more from the house, exhaust away (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety).
> **Never connect a generator to house wiring without a transfer switch, interlock, or a cord-and-plug
> conversion with the main breaker locked off. Never backfeed through an outlet**: it electrocutes
> line workers and neighbours and causes fires (→ 30-01). The same goes for a power station's AC
> output.
> **The one wiring mistake that destroys a station instantly** is a panel string whose voltage is over
> the station's solar input limit. Use only the configurations on the card at the bottom. When in
> doubt, stop and read the card.

## Do this now (the power just went out)
1. **Is it just us?** Look outside. If neighbours have power, check the main breaker and the panel
   ({{photo breaker-panel}}). Report the outage: {{ contacts.utility.electric.provider }},
   {{ contacts.utility.electric.phone }}.
2. **Medical devices first.** {{#if has.cpap}}CPAP onto its battery or a station tonight. {{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}Oxygen: switch to cylinders or the portable concentrator's battery now and start
   counting hours. {{/if}}Phones and medical devices onto power banks (→ 09-06).
3. **Keep the fridge and freezer shut.** A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about 4 hours; a
   full freezer about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24 (USDA and HHS, Food Safety During a Power
   Outage; → 04-17).
4. {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Refrigerated medicine: set up the cooler within the first hour**
   (step 3 below), and move the medicine once the cooler's thermometer reads within the label range.
   {{else}}Any refrigerated medicine: set up a cooler within the first hour (step 3 below).{{/if}}
5. **Switch off and unplug non-essential loads and sensitive electronics** so a surge when the grid
   returns cannot damage them (American Red Cross, Power Outage Safety). Leave one light switched on so
   you know when power is back. Leave smoke and carbon monoxide alarms alone.
6. **Light: flashlights and lanterns, not candles** (US Fire Administration, Candle Fire Safety).
   Candles indoors are a decision: {{choice DC-20}} (→ 30-21).
7. **If you smell gas, leave first and call from outside** ({{ contacts.utility.gas.phone }}; FEMA,
   Utility Shut-off and Safety).
8. **Decide what kind of outage this is** (→ 17-08): hours, overnight, or unknown. Overnight or
   unknown: carry on down this page.

## Before any outage
- **Print this page and the card at the bottom; keep the card in the panel bag.** {{photo panel-bag}}
- **Photograph the breaker panel and mark the fridge, freezer and furnace breakers.**
  {{photo fridge-breaker}}
- **Know your posture for refrigerated medicine** (→ 09-10): either the cooler lives on a station in
  UPS mode, or the medicine lives in the kitchen fridge and the cooler, station and designated
  thermometer are staged. Ours: ________________________________.
- **Test the cooler for 24 hours on the station's 12 V port** with the designated thermometer inside;
  turn the station's power-saving ("ECO") setting off for that port (→ 09-03).
- **Stations:** stored at 40 to 60%, charged to 100% when a storm is forecast. Power banks charged.
  Panel bag staged with cables, Y-branch and multimeter. {{photo station-ports}}
- **Carbon monoxide alarms installed** (we have {{ gear.co_alarms }}), tested, spare batteries.
- **Walk this sequence once on a calm day and time it.** The first real run should be the second run.

## The sequence

### T+0: the first hour
1. **Fridge and freezer shut** (above). Start the clock.
2. **Kill non-essential house loads.** Walk the house once: power strips off, unplug anything with a
   standby light. Five minutes; it stretches every stored watt-hour and protects against the surge when
   power returns.
3. **Set up the medicine cooler** (if anyone uses refrigerated medicine):
   - Cooler, station and the designated thermometer to the **warm room** (→ 08-01), away from any
     heater; never an unheated room in winter.
   - **Plug the cooler into the station's 12 V port, not the AC outlets.** The inverter's idle draw
     alone can be most of what the cooler uses. Switch the 12 V port on; **power-saving mode off.** If
     the cooler's display is ever dark, re-enable the port.
   - **Thermometer inside, lid shut.** Move the medicine in **only when the thermometer reads within
     the label range** (for insulin, 36 to 46 °F, 2 to 8 °C, never frozen: US FDA, Information
     Regarding Insulin Storage). Wrap the medicine so it never touches the cooler walls; if it reads
     too cold, raise the setting.
4. **Runtimes to plan on** (→ 09-10): each station's days for the cooler, worked out there. **The
   percentage on the screen is the truth.** Move the cooler to the next station at ______ %.
5. **Before dark:** every phone and power bank charging from the remaining station capacity; set out
   tomorrow's panel plan in your head.

{{#if has.well}}**Water:** the well pump stops with the power (→ 03-10).{{/if}}

### T+0 to T+6 hours: heat (any outage in cold weather, or when the house is cooling)
{{#if is.cold_winters}}**In a winter as cold as yours, heat is the clock right behind medicine.**{{else}}When it is cold, heat is
the clock right behind medicine.{{/if}} Start while the house still holds its warmth, not late at
night. In this order (→ 08-04):
1. **Furnace, only if gas still flows and a safe connection exists.** Our connection:
   **{{ gear.house_connection }}**. A station or generator can run the blower only through a transfer
   switch or interlock, or a cord-and-plug conversion ({{choice DC-07}}, → 30-08; how to use it:
   → 09-04). Run the blower in bursts, coast, repeat. **Never backfeed.** {{figure fig-generator-connection-options}}
2. **Close down to one warm room** (→ 08-01): blankets over doorways, everyone (and the medicine) in
   one room. The warm room must meet the heater's air rules.
3. **Carbon monoxide alarms on and tested BEFORE any heater is lit:** one in the warm room, one where
   people sleep (→ 08-02).
4. **One combustion heater at a time.** Portable heater manuals generally forbid another fuel-burning
   appliance in the same space. Kerosene: → 08-10. Propane: → 08-09; a cylinder larger than 1 lb
   indoors is a decision: {{choice DC-02}} (→ 30-03). Shared propane also feeds the generator and
   any cooking stove: count it (→ 06-05).
5. **Overnight:** an unvented heater running while people sleep is a decision card:
   {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02). Whatever you chose, heated blankets from a station for the sleepers
   help either way (→ 09-01). Anyone waking with a headache or nausea: everyone out to fresh air.

### The first morning: panel deployment
{{#if has.solar}}Our panels: {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W.{{/if}} Deploy in this order, unless the
station's manual says otherwise: **position the panels → chain them as the card says → lay the cable →
plug into a station that is switched off → switch on.**

**Decision rule: charge whichever station is lowest.** Use **only the standing configurations on the
card** (worked out on → 09-03). {{figure fig-series-vs-parallel}}
- **Before the first connection of any string, measure its voltage (Voc)** with the multimeter: red
  probe to the + end (the MC4 connector with the male pin). **A minus sign means a connector is
  reversed: swap it.**
- **Re-check the card every time you move panels between stations.**
- **Suitcase kits:** the panel's bare MC4 leads only. A separate controller box never joins a string
  or a station.
- **Wind:** stake or weight kickstand panels. **Concealment:** out at dawn, in at dusk, never left
  unattended (→ 14-03).

### Who runs on what

| Load | Runs on | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Medicine cooler | **A station's 12 V port, power-saving off, AC inverter off** | Tier 0; no inverter loss; give it a dedicated station if you have two (→ 09-10) |
| CPAP, oxygen concentrator | Its own battery pack or DC cord, then a station | Tier 0 (→ 09-06) |
| Phones, medical charging, power banks | Power banks and the smallest station | Keeps the pocket tier off the big stations |
| Kettle boils, heated-blanket sessions | **Whichever station is fullest** | Big optional draws come from surplus, never from the cooler's station |
| Furnace blower | A station or generator, **only through the safe connection** | Never backfed (→ 09-04); check the start surge first |
| Lights, radio, laptop | Power banks and the smallest station first | Tier 1 stays off the AC tier when it can |

### The daily rhythm
- **Charge at midday; run loads while the sun is up.** Every watt-hour used while the panels are
  producing is storage you did not need (→ 09-05).
- **Kettle and blanket sessions in the afternoon**, from the day's surplus, not at 10 p.m. from the
  night's reserve.
- **The cooler's station is topped up before dark, every day.** The one hard daily requirement.
- **Panels in at dusk**, folded, indoors: inspection, concealment and hail insurance in one habit.

{{#if is.cold_winters}}### Winter variant
- **Panels go out only in usable sun.** A grey whiteout day is not worth the cold exposure or the wind
  risk (→ 09-05).
- **Stations charge INDOORS, above 32 °F, always.** Lithium iron phosphate charged below freezing is
  permanently damaged (→ 09-03). Run the panel cable in through a window or door gap with a towel seal.
- **Check winter's gift first:** below-freezing outdoor air may let the cooler's job move to passive
  cold, with freeze protection and a min/max thermometer (→ 09-10, → 04-09).
{{/if}}

### When solar fails for two days or more: the generator bridge
{{#if has.generator}}Our generator: {{ gear.generator_watts }} W, {{ gear.generator_fuel }}.{{/if}}
Outdoors, 20 feet or more, exhaust away, carbon monoxide alarms on (→ 09-04). Run it long enough to
refill a station at the station's **standard** charge rate on a 12 AWG cord, then off. That cycle is
the storm plan, not continuous running. In deep cold, start it warm and bring it back in between
runs (→ 09-04). **If it has never been run, follow the first-start steps on → 09-04 (oil
first).**

### When the power comes back
1. Leave the generator running only until the house is back on the grid; then switch it off, outdoors.
2. If the furnace or a pump was on the generator cord, **unplug it from the cord, plug it back into its
   wall receptacle**, then switch the breakers back on (→ 09-04).
3. Plug things back in one at a time.
4. Check the fridge and freezer and decide on food (→ 04-17). Medicine goes back to its normal
   storage.
5. Recharge everything, return stations to storage charge later, and write what happened in the log.

## Hard-limits card: print, cut out, keep with the panels
*(Fill in from the labels and the worksheet on → 09-03. Cold rule: a string's Voc × 1.20 must stay
below the station's maximum input voltage, with margin: → 09-02.)*

| Station | Solar input: max V · max A · max W · socket | OK to connect | **NEVER** |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each stations as s}}| {{s.model}} ({{s.wh}} Wh) | ______ V · ______ A · ______ W · ______ | ______________ | ______________ |
{{else}}| ______ | ______ V · ______ A · ______ W · ______ | ______________ | ______________ |
{{/each}}

**Standing configurations:** (1) ______________ → ______ · (2) ______________ → ______ ·
(3) ______________ → ______.

**Never-rules for every station:**
- Measure Voc with the multimeter before any first-time connection; a **minus sign** means a reversed
  connector.
- The × 1.20 cold factor is never dropped on a "mild" morning.
- No series string whose cold voltage reaches a station's maximum input, in any season.
- No suitcase controller box, its clips or its adapter tips in a string or a station.
- No station's AC output into house wiring or a wall outlet, ever.
- No charging any lithium station below 32 °F.
- Power-saving mode off on any port running a medicine cooler.
- Generator outdoors only, 20 feet or more, exhaust away.

## When it runs out
- **Day three or later with no sun and no generator fuel:** shed to Tier 0 (→ 09-01), move the
  cooler's job to passive cold if the season allows (→ 09-10), and charge phones from a vehicle
  (→ 09-11, → 09-14).
- **If a station dies:** with two or more, the system is redundant: the cooler runs on any station's
  12 V port (power-saving off on whichever it moves to). One dead unit is a log entry, not a crisis.
- **If Tier 0 cannot be met**, that is a go/no-go input (→ 01-02), not something to endure.

## Phase notes
- **A (at home):** this page as written.
- **B (moving):** this page does not apply. Phase B power is power banks, the smallest station and the
  vehicle (→ 09-06, → 09-11).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the same sequence; the generator bridge matters more until solar is
  set up (→ 09-04).

## Cross-references
→ 09-03 stations, panels and the wiring worksheet behind this card · → 09-10 the medicine cooler ·
→ 09-04 generator bridge and house connections · → 09-05 winter solar · → 09-06 medical devices ·
→ 09-01 load triage · → 08-04 the heat ladder · → 08-01 the warm room · → 08-02 carbon monoxide ·
→ 04-17 food safety in an outage · → 17-08 power grid failure · → 00-06 the first 60 minutes

# Lighting

**What this section holds.** 6 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 10-01 **Lighting options ranked (safety and runtime)**: When the power goes out, the house goes dark for many hours every day.
- → 10-02 **Fuel lamps and candles (fire risk)**: This is a page of last resort.
- → 10-03 **DIY lamps and conserving light**: The cheapest light is the light you never have to make.
- → 10-04 **Making candles and oil lamps**: Batteries and bought fuel run out; fat and wax can be renewed.
- → 10-05 **Light discipline and blackout at night**: In a long outage, a lit window in a dark street is visible a long way, and it tells people something.
- → 10-06 **The winter light budget (watt-hours, cells and fuel)**: → 10-01 says which lights to use.

pages.body:
# Lighting options ranked (safety and runtime)

**What this page is for.** When the power goes out, the house goes dark for many hours every
day. This page ranks the ways to light it, by safety first and then by how long each runs on what
you have stored. It explains why battery LED lights win, how to choose a light for each job, and
why the batteries, not the lights, are what you run out of.

> **CAUTION. In a power outage, use flashlights, not candles** (US Fire Administration, Candle
> Fire Safety). Every light that burns something is a distant second choice to an LED, and has
> its own rules on → 10-02. Nothing that burns fuel goes in a bedroom, near bedding, or left
> alone, and anything burning indoors needs a working carbon monoxide (CO) alarm (→ 08-02,
> → 29-03). Whether to use candles and oil lamps indoors at all is a household decision:
> {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21. **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or
> chlorine products.** Fixed in every source. Lamp oil counts.

## Do this now

1. **A headlamp beside every bed, one in each coat pocket, one by the back door.** Headlamps
   beat flashlights for almost everything: both hands stay free, which matters when you carry a
   child, cook on a fire or work on batteries.
2. **Use as few battery sizes as possible.** AA is the most common and the easiest to find.
   Rechargeable AA cells and a USB charger turn every light into one your stored power can
   refill. Any new light you buy should take the same cells as the rest.
3. **Test everything today.** Dead cells, corroded contacts and lights "in a drawer somewhere"
   are the usual outage discovery.
4. **Count the dark hours.** Look up tonight's sunset and tomorrow's sunrise, and do it again in
   December. {{#if is.cold_winters}}In a northern winter the dark lasts most of the day, for
   months.{{else}}Even in the south, winter nights are long.{{/if}} Light is a daily consumable,
   and it drives both your power budget (→ 09-01) and morale (→ 21-02). The arithmetic is on
   → 10-06.

{{photo bedside-lights}}

## The night light that is never optional

Some households have a job that must happen in the dark: checking blood sugar and drawing up
insulin, a night feed, putting on a CPAP mask or checking an oxygen line, giving a medicine on a
schedule.{{#if has.condition.CL-01}} This household has a member with type 1 diabetes (→ 02-01).{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-02}} This household has a member on an insulin pump or sensor (→ 02-02).{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-06}} This household has a member with type 2 diabetes on insulin (→ 02-06).{{/if}}{{#if has.infant}} There is an infant in this household: night feeds and changes need light.{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}} A member uses CPAP.{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}} A member uses oxygen.{{/if}}
That job gets its own light, not "whatever is around":

- **A headlamp reserved for it, kept on charge at the bedside.** It never leaves the bedside and
  is never borrowed for the yard, the car or a game. The predictable failure is that it gets
  borrowed "just once" and is somewhere else at 3 a.m.
- **Red light to move, white light to read.** Red keeps your night vision and does not wake the
  house. But check before trusting it: some meter screens fade under red light, and syringe and
  dose markings are fine lines that need enough light to read **correctly**. **A misread dose is
  worse than lost night vision.** Use red to get up; use a short burst of white, aimed down and
  shielded, for reading and measuring. Test both tonight with the real meter or device.
- **A second identical headlamp in the medical kit** (→ 22-06): same model, same buttons, so the
  habit carries over and the bedside light and the grab-and-go light are never the same missing
  light.
- **The rule:** the night-time care job never depends on finding a light.

## The ranking

Rank every option on four things: safety, how long it runs on stored energy, how you get more,
and the quality of the light. LEDs win the first three so clearly that everything else is a
fallback.

| Option | Safety | Efficiency | How you get more | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **LED headlamp** | Excellent | Excellent: tens of hours on low | Rechargeable or AA cells | **First choice for tasks and moving around** |
| **LED lantern** (AA or USB-rechargeable) | Excellent | Excellent | Rechargeable or AA cells | **First choice for a room** |
| **LED flashlight** | Excellent | Excellent | Rechargeable or AA cells | Good, but uses a hand |
| **USB light run from a power bank or power station** | Excellent | Excellent | Solar, if you have it (→ 09-03) | The house solution if you own stored power |
| 12-volt LED strip wired to a battery | Excellent | Best on paper: no conversion loss | Solar | A later project (→ 09-08) |
| Solar garden or path light | Excellent | Dim, but free | Sun | Bring them in at dusk |
| Chemical light stick | Excellent | Single use | None | Children, marking, one-time use |
| **Oil or kerosene lamp** | **Fire, CO, fumes** | Good run time, warm light | Needs fuel | Backup only (→ 10-02) |
| **Candle** | **Worst: about 20 home candle fires are reported every day in the US** (USFA, citing NFPA) | Poor | Can be made (→ 10-04) | Last resort, with rules |
| Propane or white-gas lantern | **Fire and serious CO** | Bright | Needs fuel | **Outdoors only** |
| Fireplace or stove glow | Already burning | Free | Wood | Background light only, not for tasks |

## Your stored power is your lighting grid

If you own power stations or power banks (→ 29-02), they already are the lighting system. Plan it
as an allocation, not a wish:

- **Small loads on small sources.** USB lanterns, headlamp charging and AA charging run off power
  banks and the smallest station first, so the big stations are kept for big jobs.
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **Never the station that keeps refrigerated medicine cold.** A
  lantern charging there is spending the medicine's watt-hours (→ 09-16).
{{/if}}- **Area lighting is cheap.** An LED string or a couple of plug-in LED lights drawing 5 to
  10 watts in all costs a large station very little per evening hour. Put it on whichever station
  is fullest.
- **A wired 12-volt LED circuit** (→ 09-08) is a reasonable later project. Nothing here waits for
  it.

{{#if has.power_station}}Your stations: {{#each stations as s}}{{s.model}} ({{s.wh}} Wh); {{/each}}total {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh. → 10-06 turns that into hours of light.{{/if}}

## The numbers that matter

These are **typical planning figures**, not measurements of your lights. Your own lights'
packaging lists their run time on each mode; use those numbers in → 10-06.

- **A modern LED headlamp on low (10 to 50 lumens)** typically draws about 0.1 to 0.5 watts and
  runs for tens of hours on one set of three AA or AAA cells. **On high (200 to 300 lumens)** it
  draws a few watts and lasts only a few hours. Three cells hold only a few watt-hours, so both
  numbers cannot be large. **Low is almost always enough**: your eyes adapt in a dark house. High
  is for going outside.
- **A 20,000 mAh power bank** (about 70 watt-hours at its 3.7-volt cell rating) runs a 2-watt
  lamp for about 30 hours, after conversion losses.
- **Lighting is a small load** next to refrigeration (→ 09-10), which is why it is affordable even
  on a small solar setup, and why it should be electric rather than flame.
- **A candle gives a small fraction of the useful light of an LED lantern**, and brings fire risk.

## Choosing light by job, not by device

- **Moving around and tasks:** headlamp on low; red at night to keep your night vision.
- **A room or gathering:** one lantern on a table, bounced off a white ceiling. Spread-out light
  feels far brighter than a point of light and is easier on the eyes over a long evening.
- **Children's rooms:** a dim, **flameless** night light. A small child in a dark house is a
  safety and morale problem (→ 20-02). Battery LED, always. **Never a candle or fuel lamp in a
  room where children sleep** (USFA).{{#if has.young_child}} This household has a child under 6:
  put a night light in every room they sleep in.{{/if}}
- **Outside:** a bright flashlight, used **sparingly** (→ 10-05).
- **Reading and long evenings:** a warm, dim, spread-out lamp. Here light becomes a morale
  question: long nights are hard on people, and good light matters more than you would guess.

## Red light, and why it is worth the habit

After a few minutes in the dark your eyes adapt, and a burst of white light undoes that for many
minutes. Red light does not. Red is also much harder to see from outside (→ 10-05) and disturbs
sleep less for everyone in the room. Buy headlamps with a red mode and make it the default indoors
at night.

## Batteries: the real bottleneck

**The lights are not what runs out; the cells are.**

- **Pick one main cell size**, usually AA, and buy new lights to match. If you already own lights
  that take another size (often AAA), stock that size too and stop there.
- **Rechargeable NiMH cells and a USB charger** let solar or stored power feed every light
  (→ 09-07).
- **Keep a reserve of alkaline cells** as well: they keep for years and need no charging. **Store
  them out of the devices**: alkaline cells leak and ruin the contacts. Check stored lights twice a
  year.
- **Lights with a built-in rechargeable cell** are efficient and handy, but when the cell dies the
  light is finished. **Prefer lights that take cells you can replace**; ideally own some of each.
  Charge lithium devices where you can see them, not on a bed or sofa (NFPA, Lithium-Ion
  Batteries).
- **Cold cuts run time.** In an unheated space expect much less from any battery. Keep spare cells
  warm (→ 09-07).

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| LED headlamps: one per person ({{ household.size }} people) plus spares | Hands-free is the whole game | **Red mode**; same cells as your other lights |
| LED lanterns, AA or USB-rechargeable, three or four | Room light for long nights | Spread-out, warm, dimmable |
| Rechargeable NiMH cells (plenty) and a USB charger | Makes lighting solar- or station-powered | The core of the plan |
| Alkaline cell reserve | Keeps for years; no charging | Stored **outside** devices |
| Children's flameless night lights | Safety and sleep | Dim, warm, never a flame |
| Clip-on book light | Long-evening morale | Low draw |
| White paper, foil or a white sheet | Spreads light and makes a room feel much brighter | Costs nothing |
| Chemical light sticks (a box) | Children, marking hazards, one-time use | No heat, no flame, no batteries |
| Spare lights and cells in each go-bag | Redundancy | → 22-03 |
| 12-volt LED strip, wire, fuses | Later efficiency project | → 09-08; low priority |

**If you do not have it, scavenge:**
- **Lights** from vehicles (dome, map and work lights), bike lights, emergency exit signs, solar
  path lights, phone flashlights, cordless-tool work lights.
- **Batteries** from remotes, toys, clocks, keyboards, cameras and every drawer in the house. If
  you take them from smoke alarms, **replace them**. **Count your batteries now.**
- **12-volt lighting** from RVs, campers and boats: built for exactly this.
- **Diffusers:** a plastic milk jug over a headlamp makes a lantern; a jar of water in front of a
  light spreads it.
- **Reflectors:** foil, white paint, a mirror, a pale wall. **Bouncing light off a white ceiling is
  the cheapest lighting upgrade there is.**

## When it runs out

- **Count cells, not lights.** Estimate hours per set (usually far more than you think on low) and
  write the total on → 23-02. Most households find they have **weeks to months** of LED light: rare
  good news.
- **Stretch it, in this order:** (1) low or moonlight mode, always; (2) **one light for the
  household, not one each**: gather in the heated room in the evening (→ 08-01), which saves fuel,
  light and morale at once; (3) **shift the day earlier**: get up with the sun, do everything in
  daylight, sleep through the long winter nights; (4) red or dim only; (5) flame as a last resort
  with the rules on → 10-02.
- **Resupply:** solar into rechargeable cells is the renewable loop, which is why one cell size
  matters. Scavenged alkalines stretch it. Beyond that, → 10-04: making candles and lamps from fat
  and wax.
- **Never swap an unattended candle in for a lamp.** That trade has killed more people than the
  dark ever will.
- **The real risk is morale.** Long dark days for months are hard on adults and harder on
  children. Budget light for **evening gathering, reading and children's routines** on purpose
  (→ 20-02, → 21-04).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** LEDs off power banks and the smallest station; area light in the one
  heated room when there is spare power; headlamps everywhere; children's night lights on; the
  bedside care light on charge. A lit house in a dark street is visible a long way (→ 10-05).
- **B (on the move):** headlamps, red mode, spare cells. **Light discipline is a safety rule on the
  move**: one dim red headlamp per adult, children kept close.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** the same LED plan, plus more freedom to use flame lamps in a
  building you control, and a real reason to make candles and lamp oil (→ 10-04). On arrival, walk
  the building and find out what actually lights, and whether any circuits run from a generator,
  before assuming any house lighting exists. **A bin of lanterns, headlamps, chargers and cells**
  travels with you, or is placed at the destination ahead of time.{{#if has.agreed_destination}}
  For your agreed destination, ask the people there about lights and generator circuits now, not
  on arrival.{{/if}}

# Fuel lamps and candles (fire risk)

**What this page is for.** This is a page of last resort. Batteries eventually run out, so this
page covers candles, oil and kerosene lamps, lanterns and homemade fat lamps: which are least bad,
the rules that keep them from burning the house down, and how to keep children from drinking the
fuel.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **In a power outage, use flashlights, not candles** (US Fire Administration, Candle Fire
>   Safety). About 20 home candle fires are reported in the US every day (USFA, citing NFPA).
>   USFA says **do not use lit candles in bedrooms, bathrooms or sleeping areas.**
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed
>   in every source. Lamp oil, kerosene and lighters count.
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
>   ignition. Fill lamps away from any flame, never while lit or hot.
> - **Swallowed lamp oil or kerosene:** these thin fuels slip into the lungs and cause a chemical
>   pneumonia, and **vomiting can carry more of it into the lungs.** **Do not make them vomit;
>   wipe out the mouth; call Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222** (CDC MMWR; MedlinePlus, Poisoning
>   first aid). Coughing, choking or fast breathing means it reached the lungs. How long to keep
>   watching, and the full protocol: → 12-17.
>
> **Four hazards:** (1) **fire**; (2) **carbon monoxide (CO) and fumes**: any flame in a closed
> room uses oxygen and makes CO, which you cannot smell (→ 29-03); (3) **burns and spilled fuel**:
> a knocked-over oil lamp spreads burning liquid; (4) **swallowing the fuel**.

**Whether to use candles and oil lamps indoors at all** is a household decision:
{{choice DC-20}} → 30-21. This page gives the rules for doing it as safely as it can be done.

## Do this now

1. **Make LED the default; this page is the backup** (→ 10-01).
2. **Smoke alarms and CO alarms on every level, battery-powered, tested**, before any lamp is ever
   lit indoors. Test them monthly (USFA, Smoke Alarms). This is the prerequisite, not an extra
   (→ 29-12).
3. **Set the house rules now, out loud, with every adult, and teach the children:** no flame in
   bedrooms; no flame left alone, ever, even for a minute; no flame under anything that can burn;
   no child carries a flame; nothing burning when everyone goes to sleep.
4. **Buy proper lamps and the fuel they were made for, together.** The homemade versions on
   → 10-04 are for when you have no choice; a real lamp with a glass chimney and its own fuel is
   far safer.
5. **An extinguisher in each room where flame is used**, plus a pot lid or fire blanket in the
   kitchen (→ 29-12, → 12-03).
6. **Store lamp fuel as a poison:** original child-resistant container, capped, up high or locked;
   **never poured into a drink bottle, jar or cup**; filled lamps out of children's reach even when
   cold; fill lamps where the children are not.

## The rules, in order of how often they are broken

1. **Never leave a flame alone.** Blow it out when you leave the room and when you go to bed. This
   one rule prevents most candle fires (USFA).
2. **Never in a bedroom, a bathroom or where anyone sleeps** (USFA). A candle left burning "just
   while we fall asleep" is the classic fatal fire.
3. **At least 12 inches clear of anything that can burn** (USFA): curtains, bedding, paper, books,
   decorations, clothes drying near the stove, firewood.
4. **On a sturdy, uncluttered surface that cannot burn and cannot tip.** Never on a shelf, never on
   a table a child can pull, never where it can be bumped in the dark.
5. **Out of reach of children and pets. Physically** out of reach, not "probably high enough".
6. **Ventilate.** A sealed, winterised room (→ 08-03) with a burning lamp builds CO and uses up
   oxygen. **Crack a window.** This is the tension that makes flame light dangerous in winter: the
   house is sealed for warmth and the lamp needs air.
7. **Keep hair, sleeves and loose clothing away.** A long sleeve over a candle is a common burn.
8. **Extinguisher, lid and water within arm's reach before you light.**
9. **Trim wicks and use proper holders.** A long wick makes a big, smoky flame; a proper holder
   catches drips and does not tip.
10. **Never move a burning oil lamp, and never refill one that is lit or hot.**

{{photo lamp-station}}

## The devices, worst to best

### Candles: the worst option, and the most tempting

Cheap, everywhere, need nothing. Also a leading cause of fires, very little usable light, and
easily knocked over. If you use them:

- **Enclosed jar or hurricane candles only**: the flame inside glass that does not tip easily and
  cannot easily touch anything.
- **No tapers or pillar candles on an open surface.**
- **Never carried by anyone.** Carry a headlamp; leave the candle where it stands.
- **Never in a child's room, never overnight.**
- **Battery "flameless candles" are a good substitute** where you want the feel without the risk;
  USFA recommends them. Put them in the children's rooms.

### Kerosene and lamp-oil lamps: the traditional answer, with real caveats

A proper wick lamp with a glass chimney gives good, steady, warm light for hours on a little fuel,
and a little heat.

- **Use only the fuel the lamp is made for**: lamp oil, or **K-1 clear kerosene** in a kerosene
  lamp (→ 29-01). **Never gasoline, camp fuel (white gas), alcohol or diesel in a wick lamp**: it
  causes fires and explosions and is a documented way people die. The lamp maker's instructions
  decide what fuel it takes.
- **"Lamp oil" is a category, not one thing.** Clear, highly refined paraffin lamp oil is fine in a
  flat-wick kerosene lamp. **Citronella or "tiki torch" oil and coloured or scented decorative oils
  are outdoor-only**: soot and irritating fumes. They are the most common thing in a garage
  labelled "lamp oil". Read the label before it goes in a lamp.
- **Kerosene grades:** only clear K-1 belongs indoors; red-dyed or unknown pump kerosene is treated
  as the sootier K-2 and kept outdoors (MU Extension, G1999; GHP Group/Dyna-Glo kerosene heater
  manual: "never use any fuel other than water-clear 1-K"; → 06-06).
- **Labels:** kerosene is usually kept in a **blue** can, gasoline in **red**. Trust the label,
  not the colour: **read it aloud, smell, then pour** (→ 06-06).
- **Old kerosene:** water gets into part-full cans, and wet or dirty fuel smokes, smells and makes
  more CO. Date every can, burn the oldest first, and jar-test before filling (→ 06-06). Whether to
  burn kerosene that has been stored a long time is a household decision: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18.
- **Fill outdoors or over a tray**, the lamp cold and out.
- **Ventilate.** Kerosene lamps make CO, soot and fumes, and they smell.
- **Trim the wick** so it burns clean. A smoking lamp puts soot in your lungs and on the ceiling.
- **Storage:** fuel cans stay outside the living space (→ 06-06). Only the day's fill comes inside,
  in its labelled container.{{#if has.kerosene_heater}} Your kerosene heater shares the same
  fuel stock: count both jobs against it (→ 08-10, → 10-06).{{/if}}

This household's kerosene on hand: **{{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal.** Lamps owned: ______ ;
chimneys intact: ______ ; spare wicks: ______ ; stored where: ______ . Count the fuel in hours of
light on → 10-06.

### Pressurised liquid-fuel and propane lanterns: bright, hot, and for outdoors

A pressurised camping lantern is very bright and makes **serious** amounts of CO and heat.
**Outdoors only.** A garage with the door open is not ventilated (→ 08-02). The mantles (the small
fabric bags that glow) are fragile and get used up: stock spares, or the lantern is useless.

### Alcohol lamps: clean-burning, in a purpose-built lamp only

Denatured alcohol burns clean, with little soot or smell. But an **alcohol flame can be nearly
invisible in daylight**, and spilled burning alcohol spreads and is hard to see.

- **Only a purpose-built, sealed alcohol lamp or stove** (a closed reservoir with its own wick or
  burner).
- **Alcohol never goes in an open or improvised wick lamp** (→ 10-03, → 10-04): it turns to vapour
  and the jar becomes a fireball. An open dish of alcohol is not a lamp.
- **Denatured alcohol contains methanol.** Swallowed methanol can cause blindness and death, and
  breathing a lot of its vapour is as harmful as swallowing it (CDC/NIOSH, Methanol). Same storage
  rules as lamp oil, same Poison Control number (→ 12-17).

### Fat, tallow and oil lamps: the ones you can make

Any fat or vegetable oil with a wick will burn (→ 10-04). Dim, smoky and smelly, but **renewable**,
which is why it is in this binder. In a jar, low, stable, and watched.

## Children and pets, specifically

- **Nothing burning at floor level or anywhere a pet can reach.** Cats jump onto every surface;
  assume any flat surface is reachable. A cat's tail crosses a flame without the cat noticing.
- **Nothing burning where a crawling or toddling child is awake.**
- **Nothing a child can drink.** Lamp oil and kerosene look like water or juice in a clear
  container. Original containers, capped, up high or locked.
- **Teach young children the rule in words they will repeat:** "Fire stays where a grown-up puts
  it. We don't touch, we don't carry, we tell a grown-up." Then give each child **a headlamp of
  their own**: a light they are allowed to use makes the rule about flame much easier to keep
  (→ 20-04).
- **Flameless lights in the children's rooms, always.**
- **When everyone sleeps, everything is out.** No exceptions.

{{#if has.child}}This household has children under 13: every rule in this section applies.{{/if}}{{#if has.pets}} This household has pets: nothing burning on any surface they can reach.{{/if}}

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Smoke and CO alarms on every level, battery** | The prerequisite for any flame indoors | Test monthly; spare batteries (→ 29-12) |
| Fire extinguishers, one per room where flame is used | Within reach **before** you light | Know how to use one (→ 29-12) |
| Fire blanket or pot lids | Smothering a small fire or burning oil | Kitchen and lamp areas |
| Kerosene lamps with glass chimneys | Real light, hours per fill, stable base | Spare chimneys and wicks |
| K-1 clear kerosene or lamp oil | The fuel the lamp is made for | Labelled, dated, jar-tested; child-resistant container (→ 06-06) |
| Spare wicks, mantles and chimneys | The parts that end a lamp's life | Stock plenty: they disappear later |
| Enclosed jar or hurricane candles | Contained flame, if you use candles at all | No open tapers |
| **Battery flameless candles** | USFA-recommended substitute; safe for children's rooms | A set |
| Long-reach lighter and strike-anywhere matches in a waterproof case | Light at a distance | → 06-01 |
| Trays or tiles that cannot burn, under each lamp | Catch drips, stop spread | Cheap |
| A headlamp for every person, children included | Removes the **reason** to carry a flame | The real fix |

**If you do not have it:**
- **Lamps:** a jar, a lid punched for a wick, and oil (→ 10-04). Contained, low, stable.
- **Wicks:** cotton string, cotton fabric strips, mop cotton, cotton shoelaces, jute twine. **Never
  synthetic fabric**: it melts and drips flame instead of wicking.
- **Fuel:** cooking oil, rendered fat, tallow, old candle wax, paraffin. **Never gasoline, camp fuel
  or solvents in a lamp.**
- **Holders:** canning jars, cans, ceramic dishes, hurricane glass.
- **Reflectors:** foil behind a lamp sends its backward light forward, for free (→ 10-03).
- **What you cannot improvise:** a working smoke alarm and a working CO alarm. Buy several now, with
  batteries.

## When it runs out

- **Lamp oil and candles go fast** in daily use: a lamp may run a handful of hours per fill, and
  winter nights are long. Count fuel in **hours of light** and write it on → 23-02. Most households
  have days, not months.
- **One lamp for the household**, in the gathered room (→ 08-01), not one each, and only during the
  evening. **Shift the day earlier**: daylight is free.
- **Resupply:** → 10-04: tallow and fat candles, oil lamps from cooking fat, old candle wax
  remelted. Sustainable at a low level, and worth practising **before** the store-bought candles
  are gone.
- **Move back toward LED as flame fuel runs low**, not deeper into flame. Rechargeable cells and a
  solar panel are a renewable light supply (→ 09-02); candles are not.
- **The habit that outlasts every fuel:** sleeping when it is dark. It costs nothing.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** flame is backup only, in the one heated gathered room, watched, with
  alarms and an extinguisher. Children's rooms get flameless lights. A flickering window is visible
  a long way (→ 10-05).
- **B (on the move):** **no open flame while moving with children.** Headlamps only. A lamp in a
  vehicle or tent is a fire and CO hazard in a small space, and it ruins everyone's night vision.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** more room to use flame safely in a building you control, and the
  phase where making candles and lamp oil (→ 10-04) becomes a real, renewable part of the
  household: tallow from butchered animals (→ 05-16), fat from cooking, wax from bees if you keep
  them.

pages.body:
# DIY lamps and conserving light

**What this page is for.** The cheapest light is the light you never have to make. This page is
mostly about conserving it: using daylight, bouncing the light you have, and rearranging the day.
Homemade lamps come at the end. Anything here that involves a flame follows every rule on → 10-02.

> **CAUTION.** Flame indoors is a household decision ({{choice DC-20}} → 30-21); if you use it,
> every rule on → 10-02 applies. **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or
> chlorine products.** Fixed in every source. **Dark stairs are one of the most likely serious
> injuries in a long outage**, and there may be no emergency room: light them (below).

## Do this now

1. **Put something white where you will spend winter evenings.** A white ceiling or a white sheet
   on the wall behind a lamp can roughly double the useful light in a room, free, for good, with no
   batteries. This is the best lighting improvement in the binder.
2. **Move the household's evenings into one room** (→ 08-01). One lamp lighting one room where
   everyone is, instead of four lamps in four rooms, cuts lighting use by most of it, and the room
   is warmer and better for morale (→ 21-04).
3. **Rearrange for daylight now.** Put the table, the work surface and the children's play area by
   the best windows. In winter, useful daylight is short; **being in the right place to use it is
   free light.**
4. **Mark the stairs** with glow tape and put a night light at the top and bottom (below).
5. **Practise the homemade lamp once, outdoors, in daylight.** Building an oil lamp for the first
   time at night in a crisis is how accidents happen.

## Conservation first: the gains are huge

**1. Set the day by the sun.** Write down sunrise and sunset in late December where you live.
Moving the household's waking hours earlier (up at first light, main work in daylight, dinner at
dusk, bed early) can cut the hours you need artificial light by half or more. **This is the
biggest saving available, and it costs nothing.** It is how everyone lived until recently. Long
nights also mean long sleep, which is not a bad thing (→ 21-07).

**2. Gather the household.** One heated, lit room in the evening (→ 08-01). Light, heat, keeping
an eye on children, conversation and fuel all improve at once.

**3. Bounce, don't beam.** A bare light sends most of its output where nobody is looking, and a
point of light makes harsh shadows that tire the eyes.
- **Aim a lantern at a white ceiling** instead of at the room. The whole ceiling becomes the light.
- **Foil or a mirror behind a lamp** sends the backward half forward.
- **White sheets, white paper or pale walls** make the same light go further.
- **A see-through diffuser** (a milk jug, a bottle of water, a jar, tracing paper) spreads a
  headlamp into soft room light. **A headlamp strapped around a jug of water is an excellent
  improvised lantern.**

**4. Light the task, not the room.** You rarely need a lit room. You need light **on the book, the
cutting board, the wound, the pump**. Headlamps and clip lights use a tiny fraction of the energy
of lighting a whole room.

**5. Use the lowest setting that works.** Your eyes adapt. In a dark house a "moonlight" mode is
often plenty, and low runs many times as long as high (your light's packaging gives both run
times). Make low the default; keep high for outside.

**6. Red at night.** Keeps your night vision, disturbs sleeping children less, and is far harder to
see from outside (→ 10-05).

**7. Let daylight in.** Light-coloured curtains open on the sunny side by day (and closed at night
for warmth, → 08-03); snow outside a sunny window is a huge natural reflector; a mirror placed to
bounce daylight into a dark corner is an old trick that works.

**8. Do the light-needing work together.** Reading, mending, cleaning and paperwork in one lit
block, not five.

## The stairs: where light is a safety system

**A fall on dark stairs is a serious injury**, and in a long outage there may be no emergency
room. Engineer the stairs; do not improvise them.

- **Glow-in-the-dark (photoluminescent) safety tape on every stair edge.** It charges from daylight
  or lamplight and glows for hours, right where feet go: **no power, no batteries, no upkeep.** A
  strip along the edge of each step marks every tread in a fully dark house. Buy real
  photoluminescent safety tape, not novelty stickers.
- **A small night light at the top and bottom of the stairs**: plug-in while the grid is up,
  battery or USB LED after. A typical LED night light draws about half a watt, so two of them
  through a 12-hour winter night use about 12 watt-hours (a planning figure; check your own), and
  they are a **fixed line in the light budget** (→ 10-06).
- **Wrap the ends of the handrail** with the same glow tape. Make one hand on the rail the habit for
  every adult, every trip, especially when carrying anything.
- **Never carry a small child on dark stairs.** Light first: the night lights on, or your headlamp
  lit **before** you pick the child up. An adult with a child in both arms cannot catch the rail.
  If the light is not there, make it there first.{{#if has.infant}} There is an infant in this
  household: this rule applies every day.{{/if}}{{#if has.toddler}} There is a toddler in this
  household: gate the stairs and light them.{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}} An older member lives here:
  light and mark the stairs before anything else.{{/if}}{{#if has.mobility_aid}} A member uses a
  walker or wheelchair: light every route they use at night.{{/if}}

{{figure fig-stair-glow-tape}}

{{photo stair-marking}}

## Homemade light, safest first

**Headlamp and jug = lantern.** Strap a headlamp around a see-through jug of water, beam pointing
in. A soft lantern at once: no flame, no extra battery. **The best improvised light on this page;
make it your default.**

{{figure fig-jug-lantern}}

**Solar path lights, brought indoors.** Put them outside in the morning, bring them in at dusk. Dim,
but free and completely safe. **Good children's night lights.**

**12-volt LED strip from a battery.** Cut to length, stuck to a shelf edge, aimed at the ceiling.
The most efficient permanent light you can build (→ 09-08).

**Salvaged vehicle lights.** Dome lights, map lights and LED work lights run straight off 12 volts
and are everywhere.

**A water bottle in front of a light.** A clear bottle of water in front of a small light spreads
and softens it. Free and safe.

**Improvised oil lamp (a flame: all of → 10-02 applies).** A jar, a lid or float that cannot burn,
a cotton wick, and any liquid cooking oil or rendered fat:
- Wick: cotton string, a cotton fabric strip, jute twine. **Never synthetic: it melts and drips
  flame.**
- Keep the wick short: just enough showing for a small, steady flame. A long wick smokes.
- The oil does not catch fire easily; **the wick burns and draws the oil up.** That makes an oil
  lamp safer than a puddle of fuel, but a tipped lamp still spreads burning oil.
- **Contained, low, stable, on a surface that cannot burn, watched; never in a bedroom, never
  overnight, never where a child or pet can reach.**

**Candle from scraps.** Melt old candle stubs in a double boiler (**never** directly on the heat:
wax fires are serious) and pour into a jar around a cotton wick (→ 10-04).

**Fire glow.** A wood stove or fireplace that is already burning gives real background light for
free. Not enough for tasks, but enough to move around by.

## What not to improvise

- **No gasoline, camp fuel, white gas, alcohol or solvent in a homemade wick lamp.** This is how
  people are killed and burned. Heavy oils and fats only. (A purpose-built, sealed alcohol lamp is a
  different device, → 10-02, and denatured alcohol is a poison as well as a fuel.)
- **No open dish of burning liquid**, ever, especially alcohol: its flame can be nearly invisible.
- **No flame in a bedroom, left alone, or where children sleep.** Repeated because it is the rule
  people break.
- **No opening lithium batteries** to take out cells for light projects (→ 09-07; NFPA, Lithium-Ion
  Batteries).
- **No flame in a tent, a vehicle or any small closed space**: carbon monoxide, fabric and no room
  to escape (→ 08-02).

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| White paint, white sheets or white poster board | Roughly doubles the light in a room, free, for good | The best-value lighting purchase |
| See-through jugs and bottles (keep a few) | Headlamp diffusers: instant lanterns | Free |
| Aluminium foil, small mirrors | Reflectors behind lamps; bounce daylight | Cheap |
| Clip-on lights and small clamps | Task light exactly where needed | Low draw |
| 12-volt LED strip, connectors, fuses | Efficient permanent room light | → 09-08 |
| Cotton string or cotton fabric for wicks | The consumable in every homemade lamp | **Cotton only** |
| Wide-mouth canning jars and lids | Lamp bodies, candle moulds | Endlessly useful |
| Trays and tiles that cannot burn | Under every lamp | Cheap insurance |
| Solar path lights (several) | Free, safe background light and children's night lights | Out each morning |
| Photoluminescent safety tape (a roll) | Stair edges and handrail ends: no-power fall prevention | Real safety-grade tape |
| Two small night lights for the stairs | The stairs are never dark | A fixed line on → 10-06 |

**If you do not have it:**
- **Reflectors:** foil, chip bags, mirrors, white-painted plywood, aluminium flashing, a polished pot
  lid.
- **Diffusers:** milk jugs, soda bottles, plastic food tubs, frosted glass, a white T-shirt over an
  LED lamp (**never over a hot lamp or a flame**).
- **Lamp bodies:** cans, jars, ceramic bowls, a hollowed potato or turnip (a real old-fashioned
  lamp), a shell.
- **Wicks:** cotton shoelaces, mop strands, twisted cotton balls, torn cotton sheet, jute twine.
- **Fuel:** cooking oil, bacon grease, rendered tallow (→ 05-16), old candle stubs.
- **Light sources:** vehicle bulbs, bike lights, solar garden lights, a phone screen on its lowest
  brightness for close work, emergency exit-sign LEDs.

## When it runs out

- **Conservation never runs out.** Shifting the day, gathering in one room and reflectors keep
  working when every battery is dead.
- **Wick material** is the quiet consumable of every homemade lamp. Cotton string, rag and jute are
  cheap now; an old cotton sheet is a large supply.
- **Oil and fat compete with food.** **Burning fat for light is burning calories.** In a real
  shortage that is a real decision, and it usually favours eating the fat and going to bed early.
  Track it on → 23-02.
- **The fallback ladder:** LED on solar, then LED on stored cells, then the glow of a fire you were
  burning anyway, then a contained oil lamp, then **sleep**. Sleeping through the dark is not a
  failure; it is how people have always lived, and it costs nothing.
- **Spend light on morale, on purpose** (→ 21-02, → 21-04). Children need light for bedtime
  routines, stories and school work (→ 20-03); adults need enough to read and to feel the evening
  exists. Budget a fixed lit block each evening and protect it.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** white ceiling, one gathered room, headlamp-and-jug lanterns, solar
  path lights in at dusk, stairs marked and lit. Day shifted early in winter.
- **B (on the move):** headlamps on low, red mode, a jug diffuser at rest stops. **No flame.** Light
  discipline is a safety matter (→ 10-05).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** build permanent 12-volt lighting and pale, reflective interior
  surfaces; use flame more freely in a building you control; start making your own fuel and wicks
  (→ 10-04) so lighting becomes renewable instead of stocked.
