pages.body:
# Making candles and oil lamps

**What this page is for.** Batteries and bought fuel run out; fat and wax can be renewed. This page
shows how to render fat into tallow, make jar candles, and make simple oil lamps from cooking oil,
safely. Making them is more dangerous than burning them.

> **SAFETY.**
> 1. **Melting wax and rendering fat is a hot-fat fire hazard.** Wax or fat heated too far
>    **catches fire**, and **water on a wax or grease fire flashes the hot fat into a fireball.**
>    Melt **low and slow, in a double boiler (a pot inside a pot of water), never on direct heat,
>    never left alone.** A metal lid and a fire blanket or extinguisher within reach (→ 29-12). If
>    it smokes, it is too hot: turn off the heat. If it catches fire: lid on, heat off, do not move
>    the pot, **never water**.
> 2. **Everything you make is still an open flame.** Every rule on → 10-02 applies: contained,
>    stable, watched, out of reach of children and pets, never in a bedroom, never overnight.
>    **USFA still says use flashlights, not candles** (USFA, Candle Fire Safety). Flame indoors is a
>    household decision: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21.
> 3. **Bought lamp oil or kerosene in any of these lamps is a poison in the room.** Cooking oil and
>    tallow are food; lamp oil and kerosene are thin fuels a child can breathe into the lungs with
>    one swallow. **Do not make the child vomit**: vomiting can carry more into the lungs. **Call
>    Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222**; with no phone, → 12-17 (CDC MMWR; MedlinePlus, Poisoning
>    first aid).
> 4. **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in
>    every source. Children stay out of the kitchen while fat is hot.

{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}**Food allergy in this household.** Rendering fat and melting wax use
pots, jars and utensils. Keep this work entirely off the allergic person's dedicated cookware, and
do not render fat from anything they react to (→ 02-04).{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Practise once, now, outdoors or with a window open, with an extinguisher beside you.** Hot fat
   is unforgiving; do not meet it for the first time by lamplight.
2. **Start saving wax and fat.** Candle stubs, old jar candles, broken crayons, bacon grease, beef
   fat trimmings, cooking fat past food use. It costs nothing and it is a real light reserve.
3. **Stock cotton wick material**: cotton butcher's twine, cotton string, an old cotton sheet.
   **Cotton only.** Synthetic melts and drips flame.
4. **Buy wide-mouth canning jars in quantity.** They hold candles, lamps, food and half the
   improvisations in this binder.

## The raw materials

- **Tallow** (rendered beef, lamb or deer fat): the traditional candle fat. Hard at room
  temperature, so a tallow candle stands up. Modest smell. **The best candle material you can
  produce yourself.**
- **Lard** (rendered pork fat): softer. Better in a jar lamp than as a standing candle.
- **Any cooking oil** (vegetable, olive, canola, bacon grease): liquid, so it can only be a **lamp**,
  never a candle. The easiest lamp fuel there is.
- **Beeswax and paraffin:** the good stuff. Beeswax is renewable if you keep bees; paraffin comes
  from old candles. **Remelted candle stubs are free candles** and the easiest win here.

## Rendering fat (making tallow)

1. **Trim the fat** and cut it small, or grind it. More surface means faster, cleaner rendering.
2. **Melt it low and slow**: a heavy pot on the lowest heat, or a double boiler, with a little water
   in the bottom at the start to stop scorching. **Low. Slow. Watched.** If it smokes, the heat is
   too high.
3. **When the solid bits (cracklings) turn golden and sink, strain** through cloth into a clean
   jar. Strain twice: impurities make a candle smoke.
4. **Cool.** It sets white and firm, and keeps a long time cool and covered. Rancid fat still burns;
   it just smells worse.
5. **Cracklings are food** if the fat came from food-safe handling: treat them like any cooked meat
   (→ 04-12; FoodSafety.gov, Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures).

**Throughout:** hot fat, a flame or hot stove, and a distracted adult is the recipe for a kitchen
fire. **Lid within reach. Extinguisher within reach. Never water on a fat fire. Children out of the
kitchen.**

## Making candles

1. **Melt wax or tallow in a double boiler**: a can or jar standing in a pot of simmering water.
   **Never direct heat.** The water bath cannot get hotter than boiling, 212 °F (100 °C) at sea
   level, and that is what makes it safe. Paraffin melts at about 115 to 154 °F, and its **flash
   point**, where its vapour can catch fire, is about 390 °F (NIOSH Pocket Guide, Paraffin wax
   fume): a pot on direct heat can get there, a water bath cannot. Tallow and other fats also
   smoke and then catch fire when overheated. Melt only until it is liquid and pour soon after;
   your wax may differ, so stay low. **Smoke means you are already too hot: turn off the heat.**
2. **Prepare the wick.** Cotton string, ideally dipped in melted wax and pulled straight first (a
   "primed" wick burns better). **Wick size matters most:** too thin and the candle drowns in its
   own melted wax; too thick and it smokes and burns fast. **Expect to experiment**: start with
   three strands of cotton butcher's twine braided, for a jar candle.
3. **Anchor the wick** at the bottom (a washer, a nut, a blob of hardened wax) and hold it straight
   and centred, tied to a pencil laid across the jar's mouth.
4. **Pour slowly** into the jar or mould. Too hot and it shrinks and cracks; too cool and it does
   not fill.
5. **Cool slowly, undisturbed.** A dip usually forms around the wick; top it up with a second pour.
6. **Trim the wick short** before lighting. A long wick is the main cause of smoking, sooty
   candles.

{{figure fig-double-boiler}}

**Jar (container) candles are safer than standing candles**: the flame is enclosed, the melted wax
stays put, and the jar does not tip easily. **Make jar candles.**

**Dipped candles** are made by dipping a wick into melted tallow again and again, cooling between
dips, over dozens of dips. Traditional and slow, and the candles stand free and can tip. A useful
skill, a less safe product.

## Making an oil lamp (easier and better than candles)

Faster, cheaper and safer, and it uses liquid oil or fat directly.

**Float-wick jar lamp:**
1. A wide-mouth jar, half to two-thirds full of oil or melted fat.
2. A **float** to hold the wick upright: a bottle cap, or a disc of cork or metal with a hole
   punched through, floating on the oil, the wick threaded through it.
3. **Only a short stub of wick above the float**, just enough for a small flame. More smokes
   badly.
4. Light it. The float keeps the flame at the surface as the oil drops; it burns until the oil is
   gone and then goes out.

{{figure fig-float-wick-lamp}}

**Lid-wick jar lamp:** punch a hole in a metal jar lid, run the wick through with its tail in the
oil, screw the lid on. Even simpler. Keep the exposed wick short.

**Why oil lamps are fairly forgiving:** the oil in the jar is far below the temperature at which it
catches fire. **The wick burns, drawing oil up.** A knocked-over lamp still spreads burning oil, so
**containment and stability matter absolutely**, but it is not a pool of fuel waiting for a spark.

**Never in a wick lamp: gasoline, camp fuel, white gas, naphtha, alcohol or any solvent.** They turn
to vapour and the lamp becomes a bomb. **Heavy oils and fats only.** (Alcohol belongs only in a
purpose-built, sealed alcohol lamp or stove, → 10-02, never an improvised jar.) If you put **bought
lamp oil or K-1 kerosene** in a jar lamp instead of cooking oil, it is a poison too: see the safety
box above and → 12-17.

## Getting usable light out of it

Homemade light is dim: a candle or fat lamp gives a small fraction of an LED lantern's light. Use
→ 10-03: bounce it off a white ceiling, put foil behind it, put two or three small lamps where you
are working rather than one in the middle of the room, and keep it close to the task.

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Wide-mouth canning jars (many) | Candle jars, lamp bodies, everything else | Buy in quantity |
| **Cotton** wick material: butcher's twine, string, rag | The consumable in every candle and lamp | **Never synthetic** |
| A melting pot or large can, and a pot for the water bath | The double boiler is the safety mechanism | Kept apart from food cookware |
| Candy or fat thermometer | Keeps you well below the smoke and flash points | Paraffin melts by about 154 °F; its flash point is about 390 °F (NIOSH) |
| Fire extinguisher, metal lid, fire blanket | Hot-fat fire: **never water** | Within reach before you start (→ 29-12) |
| Fine strainer and cloth | Clean tallow burns cleaner | Strain twice |
| Washers, nuts or bottle caps | Wick anchors and floats | Easy to improvise |
| Beeswax or paraffin | Better light than fat | Also waterproofs cloth and thread (→ 16-04) |
| Hot pads, long tongs, apron | Burns are the common injury | → 12-03 |

**If you do not have it:**
- **Wax:** old candles and stubs, tea lights, broken crayons, wax toilet-bowl rings (really used for
  this), cheese wax, canning wax, beeswax from a hive.
- **Fat:** trimmings from any butchered animal (→ 05-09), bacon grease, drippings saved in a jar,
  fat from poultry and rabbits (→ 05-16), suet.
- **Wicks:** cotton shoelaces, mop strands, twisted cotton balls, torn cotton sheet, jute twine.
- **Containers:** cans, jars, ceramic dishes, shells, a hollowed potato or turnip.
- **Moulds:** cans, cardboard tubes lined with paper, ice trays, small jars.
- **What you cannot improvise:** the double-boiler discipline. Improvising **that** is how kitchens
  burn.

## When it runs out

- **The limit is fat, and fat is food** (→ 04-12). Burning tallow for light is burning calories. In
  a real shortage that trade usually loses: **eat the fat, go to bed early, and light the evening
  with the fire you are already burning.** List fat on the master consumables table (→ 23-02) as
  one resource shared between food, cooking, soap and light.
- **How long it lasts:** a small jar lamp burns for many hours on a modest amount of oil; a jar
  candle runs for many hours too. Still a countdown unless you are producing fat.
- **Resupply:** animals you butcher (→ 05-09, → 05-16), cooking fat saved instead of thrown out, and
  beeswax if you keep bees. **Beekeeping is one of the few truly renewable light sources**, and it
  gives food and pollination too (→ 05-12).
- **Move back up the ladder to LED on solar** (→ 09-02) whenever you can. Homemade flame is the floor
  of the lighting plan, not the goal.
- **The skill is the asset.** Rendering, wicking and pouring are learnable in an afternoon and
  impossible to learn from a book at midnight. Practise now (→ 24-01).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** practise and stockpile. Save every candle stub and every jar of
  grease. Make a few jar candles so you know your wick size works.
- **B (on the move):** do not make candles on the move. Carry a couple of finished jar candles at
  most and rely on headlamps (→ 10-01).
- **C (settled somewhere new):** this becomes part of the household economy: tallow from every
  animal butchered, beeswax if you keep hives, a shelf of jar candles, lamp oil from cooking fat.
  Light stops being a countdown and becomes a crop.

pages.body:
# Light discipline and blackout at night

**What this page is for.** In a long outage, a lit window in a dark street is visible a long way,
and it tells people something. This page covers how to keep light inside when you choose to, and
the things blackout must never do.

> **CAUTION. One rule beats everything on this page: nothing done for light discipline may block a
> fire exit, muffle a smoke or carbon monoxide (CO) alarm, or slow getting everyone, children
> first, out of the house.** A window cover that cannot be opened, or an escape window taped shut,
> trades a small risk for a large one. **Fire and CO kill far more people than discretion protects.**
> Design the blackout so every exit still works in the dark, by feel, in seconds. Alarms stay
> uncovered and audible from where people sleep (USFA, Smoke Alarms; → 08-02).

## Do this now

1. **Walk outside your house tonight, after dark, with the lights on inside.** Look at it from the
   street, the alley and the neighbours' side. **That is what other people see.** Most households
   have never done this and are surprised.
2. **Measure your windows and buy or make covers now**: blackout curtains, cardboard cut to fit, or
   heavy blankets on a tension rod. They double as **winter insulation** (→ 08-03): a purchase that
   pays twice.
3. **Set the household rule and teach the children:** "When it's dark, we keep the light inside."
   Give each child a red headlamp of their own, so the rule comes with a tool (→ 20-04).
4. **Switch every headlamp's default to red**, and put lanterns on their lowest setting.

## What light discipline means here

It is not paranoia and not tactics. **In a truly dark neighbourhood, a lit window is visible a very
long way, and it is information.** It says: this house has power, so it has fuel or solar; it is
occupied; these people are prepared. In a short outage, with everyone in the same position, that
is harmless.

In a **long** event, when the street has been dark for weeks and yours is the one window glowing,
it is a different signal. The point of this page is to make that a **choice** you make on purpose,
not an accident of habit (→ 14-03).

**Be proportionate.** In a two-day ice storm you do not black out; you help your neighbours and
leave the porch light on so the plough driver sees the driveway. The judgement is about how long it
has lasted and what is happening around you (→ 14-01).

## Outside light: two modes

Solar motion lights on the approaches (→ 14-12) and "no light outside" are both right, in different
situations:

| Mode | What it looks like | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Deterrence** | Solar motion lights on and covering the approaches; a house that looks occupied and cared for | Normal times, short outages, and whenever the aim is a lived-in look that makes the house a harder target than the next |
| **Blackout (low profile)** | No outside light at all; motion lights switched off or bagged; the measures on the rest of this page | A long event where a lit house is information, not deterrence |

- **Which mode you are in is a security decision** made on → 14-01 and → 14-12. This page only makes
  both modes ready.
- **Deterrence mode costs nothing from the light budget** (→ 10-06): solar motion lights draw nothing
  from stations, banks or cells. The only argument against them is visibility, and it only wins in
  blackout mode.
- **Switching must be fast and reversible.** Know how each motion light turns off (switch, bag or
  unplug), and practise the change once.

## How you are seen at night

- **Eyes adapted to the dark are very sensitive.** A single candle can be seen a long way across open
  ground on a clear night. A lit window is unmistakable.
- **Snow makes it worse.** Fresh snow reflects light everywhere, so light from a window lights up the
  yard.{{#if is.snow_region}} Your area gets real snow: winter is your most visible season, not the
  least.{{/if}}
- **Sound and smell carry too.** Wood smoke on a cold, still night carries a long way, and a
  generator (→ 09-04) is heard much further than any light is seen. **Light discipline without noise
  and smoke discipline is for show.**
- **Movement catches the eye more than steady light.** A swinging flashlight beam draws far more
  attention than a dim steady glow.
- **Cold air is clear air.** Crisp, still winter nights are the best conditions for seeing far.

## What to do, easiest first

1. **Choose the room.** Use an interior room, a basement, or a room whose windows face away from the
   street. **The most effective step, and free**, and it fits with gathering heat and light into one
   room (→ 08-01, → 10-03).
2. **Cover the windows.** Blackout curtains, heavy blankets, cardboard, foam board or a tarp. **Cover
   the whole opening, edges included**: the glow around the edges is what is actually seen. Rigid
   foam board cut to a snug fit is excellent: it blacks out, insulates, and pops out at once if you
   need the window to escape.
3. **Low, warm, indirect light.** Bounce a dim light off a wall or ceiling instead of lighting the
   room (→ 10-03). Less escapes, and it is more pleasant.
4. **Red light indoors at night.** Keeps night vision, spills less, and is much harder to see from a
   distance than white.
5. **Lights off before a door opens.** An open door with light behind it is a beacon and ruins
   everyone's night vision.
6. **No light outside, in blackout mode.** A flashlight in the yard is seen far beyond where you can
   see with it. Move by dark-adapted eyes, or a red light held low and shielded with your hand. (In
   deterrence mode the motion lights stay on; the rule about **carried** light applies in both.)
7. **Vehicles.** Dome lights, headlights and reversing lights are very visible. Know how to disable
   the dome light (pull its fuse or bulb) if you will load a vehicle at night (→ 01-03).
8. **Screens.** A phone at full brightness is a bright light in a dark room and shows through a
   covered window. Lowest brightness, facing away from windows.

{{photo window-covers}}

## Children

- **Children need light.** Dark halls and stairs cause falls; dark bedrooms cause fear (→ 20-08).
  **Nothing about discipline overrides a child's safety.**
- The answer is **dim, warm, low and inside**: a flameless night light on the floor of an interior
  room feels safe to a child and cannot be seen from outside.
- **Teach it as a game, not a threat.** "We keep our light inside so it stays cosy." Young children
  can learn this; framing it around danger frightens them and works worse (→ 20-04, → 21-01).
- **Give each child a red headlamp of their own.** Children follow rules they have equipment for.
- **Babies and toddlers cannot be reasoned with**, so the room does the work: window covers, lights
  out of reach, a night light where they sleep.{{#if has.infant}} There is an infant in this
  household.{{/if}}{{#if has.toddler}} There is a toddler in this household.{{/if}}

## What blackout must never do

- **Never block an escape window or door.** Every cover comes off from inside, in the dark, by feel,
  in seconds. **Test it with the lights out.**
- **Never cover or muffle a smoke or CO alarm.**
- **Never seal a room so completely that air stops moving**, especially with any flame or
  fuel-burning appliance in it (→ 08-02). Winterising and blackout both push toward sealing; **CO
  risk pushes back, and it wins.**
- **Never make the stairs dark.** Falls in a dark house are among the most likely injuries in a long
  outage, and there may be no emergency room (→ 10-03).
- **Never let discipline stop you signalling for help.** If someone is hurt or you need to be found,
  **light is a tool**: signal on purpose (→ 15-07).

## Gear

**Have now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Blackout curtains or panels for every window | Light and heat kept in, one purchase | Full coverage, edges included |
| Rigid foam board cut to the window openings | Blacks out **and** insulates; pops out for escape | Best two-in-one option (→ 08-03) |
| Heavy blankets and tension rods or clips | Cheap fallback, up in minutes | |
| Red-mode headlamps for everyone | Night vision, little spill, low draw | Children included |
| Red film or red tape for existing lights | Turns white lights red | Cheap |
| Dim, warm flameless night lights | Child safety without a visible signal | Interior rooms |
| Duct tape and cardboard | Seal edge leaks fast | Keep a roll with the covers |
| Dark tarps | Door curtains, porch screening, wind block | Many uses |

**If you do not have it:**
- **Window covers:** cardboard, moving blankets, comforters, garbage bags taped up, plywood, foam
  packing sheets, rugs on a rod, a mattress leaned against a window (never over an escape window).
- **Red light:** red marker on a clear lens, red cellophane, a red balloon stretched over a
  flashlight, brake-light bulbs.
- **Less spill:** a jug over a headlamp aimed at the floor (→ 10-03).
- **A door "airlock":** a blanket hung inside the door, so opening it does not flood light out. It
  also cuts heat loss (→ 08-03).

## When it runs out

- **Light discipline is a habit, not a supply.** It costs nothing. What runs out is the **discipline**
  in month three, when everyone is tired. **Make it a habit now.**
- **The habit that replaces everything:** be asleep when it is dark. Long winter nights and an early
  bedtime (→ 10-03, → 21-07) leave little light to discipline.
- **Review it on a schedule.** What made sense in week six may be unnecessary in month six, or the
  reverse. Tie the review to your situational-awareness routine (→ 14-01). **Neither permanent
  paranoia nor permanent carelessness is a plan.**
- **The failure to avoid:** blacking out so thoroughly that you cannot hear an alarm, cannot get out
  of a window, or trip on a dark stair with a child in your arms. **Discretion is worth something. It
  is not worth a broken hip or a house fire.**

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if is.urban}}the phase where this matters most: you are surrounded by
  neighbours, some in worse shape than you.{{else}}neighbours are fewer, but a lit window still
  carries.{{/if}} Interior room, covered windows, low warm light, outside light by the declared mode.
  Pair it with noise and smoke discipline (→ 09-04, → 14-03).
- **B (on the move):** discipline is safety. Red light only, shielded and low, never standing against
  a light behind you. Children stay physically close: a small child in the dark on the move can be
  lost in seconds.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** fewer eyes, but longer sight lines. In open country a light can be
  seen for **miles**. Same measures; a lit window matters more when it is the only one for a long
  way.

pages.body:
# The winter light budget (watt-hours, cells and fuel)

**What this page is for.** → 10-01 says which lights to use. This page works out what they cost
each night in stored power, how many rechargeable cells that takes per winter, how much lamp fuel
a winter would use, and whether it fits the power plan on → 09-01. A **watt-hour** (Wh) is a
measure of stored energy: one watt for one hour (→ 29-02). Every figure here is a planning number
for the type of device. Measure your own gear and write over the numbers in pen.

## Do this now

1. **Fill in the lights inventory** at the bottom of this page. Cells, fuel and chargers all start
   from knowing what the house holds. Ten minutes with a box.
2. **Measure your real lanterns and night lights** with a plug-in watt meter if you have one
   (→ 09-01), and correct the budget table.
3. **Know your tier:** AUSTERE is the life-critical floor; COMFORT is what a working household
   wants. Know which one tonight calls for.

## How long is your dark season?

Write down sunset and sunrise at home in mid-December, and how many nights of the year you need
light for a long evening:

- Hours of darkness in mid-December: ______ h
- Nights in the long-dark season: ______

{{#if is.cold_winters}}Your home has cold winters, which in the US mostly means the northern states,
where mid-December darkness runs to roughly 15 hours or more. Budget for the long end.{{else}}Your
winters are milder, and your December nights are likely shorter than in the far north, but they are
still long. Use your own numbers.{{/if}}

## The nightly budget: two tiers

**COMFORT: the full plan, about 45 to 50 Wh a night (planning figures)**

| Load | Draw | Hours a night | Wh a night |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 LED lanterns (gathered room and kitchen), low to medium | about 3 W each | about 5 | about 30 |
| 2 night lights (stair top and bottom, or stairs and a child's room) | about 0.5 W each | about 12 | about 12 |
| Headlamps in use (low mode, everyone) | about 1 W (real low modes draw 0.1 to 0.5 W; 1 W is the cautious figure) | 2 to 3 in all | 2 to 3 |
| Topping up the bedside care headlamp (→ 10-01), plus charging losses | — | — | about 2 |
| **COMFORT total** | | | **about 45 to 50** |

**AUSTERE: the floor, about 15 to 20 Wh a night**

| Load | Draw | Hours a night | Wh a night |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 LED lantern, low, one gathered room only | about 2 W | about 5 | about 10 |
| 1 night light: the stairs are never dark (→ 10-03) | about 0.5 W | about 12 | about 6 |
| Headlamps, including any night-time care job (→ 10-01) | about 1 W | 1 to 2 in all | 1 to 2 |
| **AUSTERE total** | | | **about 15 to 20** |

**How this fits → 09-01.** The power-priorities page puts "one reliable light source at night" in the
life-critical tier at **10 to 50 Wh a day**.

- **AUSTERE (15 to 20 Wh)** buys one lit gathered room for the evening, stairs that are never dark,
  and the night-time care light. It sits inside the life-critical line, and power banks alone can
  carry it for days. **This is the number the system is designed to defend.**
- **COMFORT (about 50 Wh)** adds a second lit workspace, a night light in each child's room, and a
  longer evening for reading, school work and morale (→ 21-04). The extra comes **from surplus**,
  on whichever station is fullest (→ 09-16), and it is the first lighting load dropped when the sun
  does not come out.

### Your stored power, in nights of light

{{#if has.power_station}}Your power stations:

| Station | Capacity |
|---|---|
{{#each stations as s}}| {{s.model}} | {{s.wh}} Wh |
{{/each}}| **Total** | **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh** |

{{/if}}**The method:** nights of light = usable watt-hours ÷ Wh per night. Count about 85 percent of a
station's rated capacity as usable (inverter and other losses; → 29-02).

| | Usable Wh | ÷ Wh per night | = Nights |
|---|---|---|---|
| COMFORT | ______ | 50 | ______ |
| AUSTERE | ______ | 20 | ______ |

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Not from the medicine's station.** Count only the stations and banks
that are not keeping refrigerated medicine cold (→ 09-16).{{/if}} Light is cheap next to
refrigeration; the point of two tiers is knowing which one you are running.

## Cells per winter: the worksheet

Planning values: a **NiMH AA** rechargeable cell holds about **2.4 Wh** usable; a **NiMH AAA** about
**1.0 Wh** (1.2 volts times typical capacity). Assume about **500 recharges** per cell, so a cell
recharged daily lasts **three winters or more**. Rechargeable cells are a durable asset, not a
consumable, as long as the USB charger and a charging source last (→ 09-06).

**Fill in from your measured gear:**

1. Cells used up per day in AA and AAA devices (headlamps, night lights, a meter): **___ AA and
   ___ AAA.** (USB-rechargeable lanterns draw from power banks instead and do not count here.)
2. Times 2 for rotation: one set in the device, one on the charger: **___**
3. Times 2 again for a run of sunless days. Winter solar is feast or famine (→ 09-05): **___**
4. **Rechargeable stock to own = line 1 × 4.**

**Example:** a household using about 6 AA and 4 AAA a day on COMFORT needs about **24 NiMH AA and
16 NiMH AAA**.

**Alkaline reserve.** Alkaline cells keep for years and are the buffer when charging fails. Divide
the reserve by cells used per day. For example, 24 alkaline AA at 6 a day is about 4 days, around 5
with alkaline's better performance at low draw; at AUSTERE (2 to 3 cells a day) the same reserve
lasts about a week and a half. With the recharge loop running, the NiMH stock covers the whole
season, winter after winter.

**Without rechargeables:** 6 to 10 throwaway cells a day across a long winter is **on the order of a
thousand cells.** That one line is the whole argument for rechargeables and a charger (→ 09-06).

**Recharging in winter.** Your home gets about **{{ region.home.sun_hours_dec }}** peak sun hours a
day in December, against **{{ region.home.sun_hours_jun }}** in June. Winter is when you need the
most light and harvest the least, so size the cell stock for December (→ 09-05).

## Kerosene: gallons per winter

Planning figure: **a flat-wick kerosene lamp burns very roughly 1 ounce of fuel per lamp-hour**. It
varies with wick width and height: measure yours once and write it here: ______ oz per hour.

- **Backup use**, one lamp about 2 hours a night: over 140 nights that is about 280 lamp-hours, or
  roughly **2 to 2.5 gallons**. Adjust for your season length above.
- **Everyday use**, two lamps 5 hours a night over 140 nights: about 1,400 lamp-hours, roughly **11
  gallons**, plus wicks, chimneys, soot and carbon monoxide (→ 10-02). This is why kerosene is the
  backup and LED on stored power is the plan.

This household's kerosene: **{{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal.**{{#if has.kerosene_heater}} **Your
kerosene heater burns the same fuel.** Every gallon in a lamp is hours of heat gone; look up the
heater's burn rate in its manual (→ 08-10). In winter, light with LEDs and save the kerosene for
heat.{{/if}}

- **Labels:** kerosene usually lives in **blue** cans, gasoline in **red**. Trust the label, not the
  colour: read it aloud, smell, then pour (→ 06-06).
- **Rotation:** date every can, burn the oldest first, keep cans full, sealed and dark, and jar-test
  before every fill: clear, no water layer, no cloudiness, no sludge (→ 06-06). Cloudy or wet
  kerosene fouls wicks, smokes and makes more carbon monoxide. How old is too old is a household
  decision: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18.

## The seasonal correction

The budget is sized for the December worst case. In midsummer the nights are short, the lit evening
nearly disappears, and the budget falls to little more than the night lights, just when solar
harvest peaks. **Size everything to December. Do not size anything to July.**

## Lights inventory: fill this in

The binder does not know how many lights the house holds or where they are. Count once and write it
here; update it when things move. This table feeds → 22-04 and the cell targets above.

| Item | Count | Cell type or fuel | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| LED headlamps (red mode) | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| — of which: the bedside care light (→ 10-01) | ___ | ___ | bedside |
| — of which: its twin in the medical kit (→ 22-06) | ___ | ___ | medical kit |
| LED flashlights | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| LED lanterns | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Night lights (stairs, children's rooms) | ___ | ___ | ___ |
| Solar path lights | ___ | solar | ___ |
| Kerosene lamps (→ 10-02) | ___ | fuel: ___ | ___ |
| Candles (count as hours, not sticks) | ___ h | wax | ___ |
| NiMH AA / AAA cells | ___ / ___ | — | ___ |
| Alkaline AA / AAA reserve | ___ / ___ | — | ___ |
| USB chargers for AA and AAA (→ 09-06) | ___ | — | ___ |
| Power banks | ___ | ___ Wh each | ___ |

{{photo light-bin}}

**Buy toward the gaps only.** The inventory decides the shopping list, not the other way round
(→ 26-09).

## When it runs out

- **The budget does not run out; the inputs do.** Track cells, the alkaline reserve and kerosene
  hours on → 23-02. The recharge loop (panel or station, then bank, then charger, then cells) is the
  renewable core; everything else is buffer.
- **What to drop when power is short:** the COMFORT extras first (second lantern, children's-room
  night lights, the long evening), then shorten the lit block. **The stair night light and the
  bedside care light go last, after everything else in the house.**
- **If the arithmetic stops working** (dead stations, dead cells), the answer is the conservation
  ladder on → 10-03, not more flame: shift the day to daylight, one room, sleep the long nights.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** run AUSTERE by default in a real outage, COMFORT when the stations are
  full and the sun is out. Power banks and the smallest station carry it either way.
- **C (settled somewhere new):** rebuild this table for the new place: different house, different
  stairs, a different length of dark. The lighting bin travels with its own copy of the inventory
  (→ 10-01).

pages.body:
# Layering for extreme cold

**What this page is for.** How to dress so that cold, wind and wet do not injure anyone: the layer
system, why sweat is the main danger, the wind chill table with frostbite times, dressing for a
cold house indoors, and a count sheet of what each person needs.

> **SAFETY.** In hard cold, clothing is life-support equipment. **Exposed skin can freeze in
> minutes**: read the time from the NWS wind chill chart for today's temperature and wind, not
> from a guess (NWS, Wind Chill Chart). **The two things that injure are wet and wind.** Being
> wet, from rain, sweat or cold water, can bring on hypothermia even above 40 °F (CDC, Preventing
> Hypothermia). **Cotton, when wet, is dangerous** (→ 11-05). Shivering hard, confused,
> clumsy, or no longer shivering while still cold: that is hypothermia, → 08-05 now.

{{#if is.cold_winters}}**Your home climate:** January average low about {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F,
record low {{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F, about {{ region.home.snow_in }} inches of snow a year.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Lay out what each person actually owns,** by person, against the count sheet below. Most
   families find plenty of adult coats and no real deep-cold gear for the children (→ 11-02). Do it
   in early autumn.
2. **Buy base layers first:** wool or synthetic long underwear, top and bottom, **two sets per
   person** so one dries while the other is worn.
3. **Take every cotton item out of the winter kit:** cotton socks, cotton long johns, hoodies as
   outer layers, jeans.
4. **Read the wind chill table before anyone goes out.** "It's −5 and windy" and "20 minutes to
   frostbite" are different facts, and only the second changes what people do.
5. **Set your stop line:** when your NWS office ({{ region.home.nws_office }}) issues an **Extreme
   Cold Warning** (the product called a Wind Chill Warning before October 2024; NWS; → 29-10),
   nobody goes out except for essential minutes with no skin showing,
   children stay in, and vehicles stay home. Criteria are set by each office (NWS, Wind Chill
   Chart). Your office's criterion: wind chill at or below ______ °F.

## The system, not the coat

Think in layers, not in one warm coat. A layer system adapts to how hard you are working, lets you
shed heat before you sweat, and dries in stages.

| Layer | Job | Material | How it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Base** (against skin) | Move sweat away from the skin | Merino wool, polyester, polypropylene | **Cotton holds sweat and chills you** |
| **Mid** (insulation) | Trap air: this is the warmth | Fleece, wool, down, synthetic fill | Squashed or wet: no loft, no warmth |
| **Outer** (shell) | Block wind and water | Windproof or waterproof-breathable nylon | Not windproof; or so airtight you soak it from inside |
| **Extremities** | Head, hands, feet, face | Wool, insulated, windproof | Where frostbite happens (→ 11-04) |

{{figure fig-layer-system}}

**Insulation is trapped air, not fabric.** That explains everything else:

- **Several thin layers beat one thick one:** more trapped air, and you can adjust.
- **Squashed insulation does not insulate.** Tight boots, a pack strap crushing a puffy jacket,
  sitting on your down layer: all make cold spots.
- **Wet insulation does not insulate.** Water pushes out the air and carries heat away far faster
  than air does.
- **Wind strips away the warm air layer.** That is what wind chill is, and why a windproof shell
  over modest insulation beats thick insulation that the wind blows through.

## The rule that matters most: don't sweat

**Sweat is one of the main ways people get into trouble in hard cold,** and it happens while they
feel great. You shovel, carry wood or walk, you overheat, you sweat into your base layer, then you
stop and **that wet layer chills you**. OSHA lists wetness, dressing improperly and exhaustion
among the risk factors for cold stress (OSHA, Cold Stress).

- **Start slightly cold.** Comfortable standing still means overdressed for working.
- **Vent before you sweat, not after:** open zips, open the front, take the hat off. Your head is
  your fastest thermostat.
- **Shed a layer before hard work;** put it back the moment you stop.
- **The C-O-L-D memory aid:** keep it **C**lean (dirty insulation mats down), avoid **O**verheating,
  wear it **L**oose and in **L**ayers, stay **D**ry.

## What to wear, roughly

A starting point, not a rule: adjust by how you feel standing still, and let the wind chill chart
below decide the face and the time limit.

| Conditions | What is needed |
|---|---|
| Around freezing, dry, calm | Base + light mid + shell |
| Well below freezing, light wind | Base + fleece + insulated shell; hat, gloves |
| Below zero °F | Base + heavy mid + insulated parka; wool hat and hood, mittens, insulated boots, face covered |
| Wind chill in a frostbite band on the chart | Everything: **no exposed skin at all**, goggles or a face mask, mittens over liner gloves, and **a time limit outdoors set before going out** |
| Working hard in any of these | **Fewer layers than standing still.** Vent hard; layer up the moment you stop |

**Extremities are where people get hurt** (→ 11-04). Mittens are much warmer than gloves because
the fingers share heat; a thin liner glove inside lets you do fiddly work briefly without bare skin.

## The wind chill table

Values from the **NWS wind chill chart** (public domain). Read across from the air temperature and
down from the steady wind speed; the cell is the wind chill in °F (NWS, Wind Chill Chart).

| Air temp ↓ / Wind → | 10 mph | 15 mph | 20 mph | 25 mph | 30 mph | 35 mph | 40 mph |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **10 °F** | −4 | −7 | −9 | −11 | −12 | −14 | −15 |
| **5 °F** | −10 | −13 | −15 | −17 | −19 | −21 | −22 |
| **0 °F** | −16 | −19 | −22 | −24 | −26 | −27 | −29 |
| **−5 °F** | −22 | −26 | −29 | −31 | −33 | −34 | −36 |
| **−10 °F** | −28 | −32 | −35 | −37 | −39 | −41 | −43 |
| **−15 °F** | −35 | −39 | −42 | −44 | −46 | −48 | −50 |
| **−20 °F** | −41 | −45 | −48 | −51 | −53 | −55 | −57 |
| **−25 °F** | −47 | −51 | −55 | −58 | −60 | −62 | −64 |

**Frostbite time on exposed skin: read it from the NWS chart's shading, not from the wind chill
number alone.** The chart shades frostbite time by temperature and wind together, so the same wind
chill can fall in a different band at a different wind speed. At ordinary winds of 10 to 25 mph,
read from the chart itself (NWS, Wind Chill Chart, 2001 graphic):

- **About 30 minutes** begins at a wind chill of about −19 to −24 °F. NWS's own example: 0 °F
  air with a 15 mph wind is −19 °F, and exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes.
- **About 10 minutes** begins at about −37 °F with a 25 mph wind, about −42 °F at 20 mph, and
  about −45 °F at 10 to 15 mph. The stronger the wind, the sooner this band starts.
- **About 5 minutes** begins at about −58 to −64 °F with a 20 to 25 mph wind, and about −71 °F
  at 15 mph. At 10 mph the table above never reaches it.

**When the number sits near a boundary, use the shorter time.** Example: −20 °F air with a 20 mph
wind reads **−48 °F: about ten minutes to frostbite** on any exposed skin (NWS chart). The chart was
built for adults, so **be more cautious with children, older people and anyone in poor health**
(NWS; → 11-02).

## Wet cold near freezing

Places that get ice storms and days of wet weather around 30 °F injure people through **wet**, not
deep cold.{{#if is.cold_winters}} Your home has deep cold; if you travel or move south, you may meet
this instead.{{/if}}

- **A waterproof shell over wool or synthetic fill beats down.** In freezing rain the shell does the
  work, and the insulation under it must keep working when damp. **Down fails wet** (→ 11-05).
- **Trench foot** (non-freezing cold injury) is the wet-feet injury: no freeze needed, and OSHA
  says it can happen at temperatures as high as 60 °F if feet stay wet (OSHA, Cold Stress;
  → 11-04). **Dry socks whenever they are damp; feet dried, warmed and checked at every change;
  boots dried every night** (→ 11-03).
- **Pack for it:** rain shell, waterproof boots and extra wool socks outrank an expedition parka.

## The gear under the layers

Some people carry things in the cold that must stay working: an insulin pump or glucose sensor, a
phone that runs a medical app, fast sugar, epinephrine, an inhaler.

- **Dress so one device site can be reached without undressing:** a half-zip or button-front base
  layer over a belly site, or a sleeve that pushes up over an arm site.
- **Phones and spare batteries ride in an inner pocket, against the body.** Cold kills lithium
  batteries fast (→ 09-06).
- **Fast sugar in a chest pocket reachable with the shell on,** never buried in a pack.
- **Cold fingers do not bleed for a finger-stick test:** warm the hands in the armpits first. Keep the
  meter and strips warm too.
- **Low blood sugar and hypothermia look alike.** When in doubt, test (→ 08-05).
- **Medicines that must not freeze** ride inside the layers too.
{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}Your household has type 1 diabetes: → 02-01, → 02-02.{{/if}}{{#if has.epinephrine}} Your household carries epinephrine: → 02-03.{{/if}}

## Living in a cold house

If the house is heated to one room (→ 08-01), **you dress for indoor cold too.** In a cold house,
people live in base layers, wool socks, a fleece and a hat **indoors, all day.** That is normal, it is
how people lived before central heat, and it cuts the fuel you burn (→ 06-04).

**Sleeping cold is a skill:** change into dry base layers before bed (never sleep in what you sweated
in), a wool hat and socks, and insulation **under** you as well as over. A cold mattress or floor
takes enormous heat. Sleeping together shares heat.

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Cotton anywhere in the system,** especially socks and base layers.
- **Boots laced too tight:** cuts circulation and freezes toes.
- **Skipping the hat** because the coat is warm.
- **Bare hands "just for a minute"** at −20 °F. Keep liner gloves on.
- **Sweating into your only dry base layer.**
- **A shell that is not windproof.**
- **Alcohol:** it makes you feel warm while you lose heat faster, and it impairs judgment. CDC
  lists drinking alcohol as a hypothermia risk, and OSHA says no alcohol in the cold (CDC; OSHA).
- **Not eating or drinking.** Staying warm burns calories, and you get dehydrated in the cold without
  feeling thirsty (→ 03-01).

## Count sheet (fill in, in pencil)

A suggested starting count per person, built on the rule of two (one worn, one drying); change it
to suit your climate. Write the number each person owns; circle any shortfall. The household
inventory (→ 22-04) audits this sheet.

| Item | Suggested per person |
|---|---|
| Wool or synthetic base layer sets (top and bottom) | 2 |
| Mid layers (fleece or wool) | 2 |
| Windproof or waterproof shell | 1 |
| Insulated parka | 1 |
| Insulated bibs or snow pants | 1 |
| Wool sock pairs | 6 |
| Mitten pairs | 2 |
| Liner glove pairs (not for babies) | 2 |
| Wool hats | 2 |
| Balaclava or neck gaiter | 1 |
| Insulated waterproof boots | 1 pair |
| Boot liners or felt insoles | 2 pairs |

| Person | Base | Mid | Shell | Parka | Bibs | Socks | Mittens | Liners | Hats | Gaiter | Boots | Boot liners |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each members as m}}| {{m.label}} ({{m.age_text}}) | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ | ___ |
{{/each}}

Children's counts are in their **current** size; the next sizes are on → 11-09.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Wool or synthetic base layers, 2 sets per person** | The foundation | Highest-value clothing purchase |
| Wool or fleece mid layers, 2 per person | The insulation | Fleece dries fast; wool works damp |
| Insulated parka and windproof shell | Blocks the wind | A hood matters in hard cold |
| Insulated bibs or snow pants | Legs get forgotten | Bibs beat pants for children |
| **Wool socks, 6 pairs per person** | The most-used, most-failed item | |
| Wool hats, 2 per person; balaclava or gaiter | Thermostat and face cover | One always gets lost |
| **Mittens** and liner gloves | Mittens are warmer; liners let you work | Spares: they get wet and lost |
| Insulated waterproof boots, sized for thick socks | → 11-06 | Tight boots freeze toes |
| Goggles or wraparound glasses | Wind, blowing snow, snow glare | |
| Wool blankets, sleeping bags | Sleeping cold and travel | |

**No gear?** **Wool** from thrift stores, closets, blankets and army surplus is the best cold-weather
scavenge: it keeps insulating when damp. Down comforters cut and sewn into vests (→ 16-04); fleece
blankets as mid layers. A trash bag or tarp as an emergency shell (vent it, or you soak yourself from
inside). Newspaper stuffed between layers really works. Wool sweaters cut into socks; two thin pairs
for one thick. A cut sleeve as a gaiter; a T-shirt as a balaclava. **Do not** build a cold-weather
system from cotton hoodies and jeans.

## When it runs out

- **Clothing runs out by wearing out and getting wet,** not by being used. The consumables are **socks
  and gloves**.
- **Drying is the real bottleneck** (→ 11-03). In a cold house wet gear can take days; gear that is
  not dry is not insulation. That is why two sets of everything is the real requirement.
- **Rotate:** wear one set, dry one set. **Change base layers before bed, every night.**
- **Repair rather than replace** (→ 11-07).
- **Substitute:** wool blankets become ponchos, vests and liners; layering more thin things replaces
  one lost thick thing. **Trapped air is the goal.**
- **Children outgrow everything:** see → 11-02 and → 11-09. It is a standing line on → 23-02.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** dress for a cold house indoors and the full system outdoors. Start the rotation
  and drying routine early (→ 11-03).
- **B (moving):** the highest-risk clothing situation. Adults carrying children sweat while the
  children, not moving, freeze (→ 11-02). Vent constantly, stop before you sweat, check the children
  every few minutes, and **strongly prefer not to move in winter** (→ 01-02, → 01-03). One clothing
  bag per person, and the children's next-size bag, travel with you (→ 22-05).
- **C (established somewhere else):** more outdoor work means more sweat and more wet gear. Build a
  drying setup near the stove before the first hard freeze (→ 11-03).

pages.body:
# Keeping babies and children warm

**What this page is for.** Why small children get cold faster than adults and show it later, how to
dress them, the car-seat rule, warning signs by age, how to warm a cold child, and how a small child
sleeps safely in a cold house.

> **SAFETY.** **Small children get cold much faster than adults and are much worse at telling you.**
> They have a lot of skin for their size, shiver less (a baby may not shiver at all), and a carried
> or seated child makes almost no heat while the adult carrying them sweats. **A quiet, sleepy,
> unusually still child in the cold may be hypothermic** (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia; → 08-05).
> Check the child **by touch**, not by asking. **Never leave a baby or toddler unattended near any
> heat source:** a stove, a fireplace, a fuel heater or a hot-water bottle burns a small child badly
> and fast (→ 20-02).

**Children in your household:**
{{#each children as c}}- {{c.label}}, {{c.age_text}}
{{else}}- None listed. Keep this page for visiting or future children.
{{/each}}

## Do this now

1. **Get the next sizes now.** Children outgrow winter gear every year, and babies and toddlers
   faster: their clothing sizes step every few months (→ 11-09). In a long outage there is no store.
   A reasonable target is two sizes ahead for older children{{#if has.toddler}}, and for your
   toddler **three sizes ahead**{{else}} and three for a toddler{{/if}}. The ledger that tracks
   this is → 11-09.
2. **Wool or synthetic base layers, not cotton,** for every child.
3. **Start the touch-check habit:** feel the **back of the neck and the belly**, not the hands (small
   hands run cold normally). Often outdoors, every few minutes when a child is carried or pulled on
   a sled, and regularly through the day in a cold house. Set the interval before you go out, and
   shorten it as the wind chill drops (→ 11-01).
4. **Teach children old enough to talk to report:** "Tell a grown-up if any part of you hurts,
   tingles, or stops feeling" (→ 20-04). Babies cannot, so they are checked, always.

## Why children are different

- **Skin area for their size.** A small body loses heat much faster for the heat it can make; the
  younger the child, the worse.
- **Poor shivering.** Babies barely shiver.
- **Passive.** A carried, sledded, stroller-bound or car-seated child makes almost no heat while the
  adults around them work hard and feel warm. **The adult is a bad thermometer for the child.**
- **They don't report.** They get quiet, clingy, sleepy or fussy, which looks like ordinary child
  behaviour.
- **They get wet:** snow down the neck, wet mittens, a soaked nappy, drool, puddles. **Wet is a fast
  route to cold injury**: CDC notes hypothermia can happen above 40 °F in someone who is wet (CDC,
  Preventing Hypothermia; → 11-03).
- **Frostbite on cheeks, ears and fingers.** The NWS wind chill chart was tested on adults only;
  NWS says use it as a starting point and be even more cautious with children (NWS, Wind Chill
  Chart; → 11-01).

## Dressing children

The same three layers as → 11-01, with these differences:

- **One-piece garments win.** A bunting or one-piece snowsuit for a baby or toddler and **bib
  overalls** for an older child close the waist gap where snow gets in and warmth gets out.
- **One more layer than an adult** in the same conditions, because the child is not working (AAP:
  as a rule of thumb, infants wear one more layer than adults).
- **Mittens, always, on a string through the sleeves.** Keep spare pairs; they will be wet.
- **Hats that cover the ears and stay on:** a balaclava or a chin-strap hat for a toddler.
- **Boots sized for thick wool socks,** not tight (→ 11-06).
- **Neck gaiter, not a scarf.** A loose scarf on a small child is a strangling hazard on play
  equipment, sleds and machinery.

## Car seats and puffy coats

**No puffy coat under the harness.** A bulky coat squashes in a crash and leaves the harness loose
enough for the child to be thrown out of it (AAP, Winter Car Seat Safety Tips; NHTSA, Car Seats and
Booster Seats).

1. **Dress the child in thin, warm layers:** base layer plus a fleece.
2. **Buckle the harness snug over the thin layers.** Pinch test at the shoulder: if you can pinch a
   fold of webbing, tighten it.
3. **Put the warmth over the buckled harness:** a blanket tucked around, a coat put on backwards over
   the arms, or a car-seat poncho.

**In a cold car at night, the layer over the harness must be one an adult can take off from the front
seat** (a blanket or poncho, not a zipped suit): once the car warms, a bundled child overheats and
cannot tell you (AAP). Also follow the car seat maker's instructions.

{{figure fig-car-seat-warmth-over-harness}}

## Warning signs by age

**Older children:** unusual quiet, stumbling, clumsy hands, slurred or slow speech, complaining and
then **stopping** complaining, pale or waxy skin on cheeks, ears or fingers, "my fingers don't feel
like anything".

**Babies and toddlers:** CDC's signs in infants are **bright red, cold skin and very low energy**
(CDC, Preventing Hypothermia). Watch also for unusually sleepy or hard to wake, quiet or floppy,
a weak cry, a cold belly and back of neck, not wanting to feed.

**Any of these: get warm now, and → 08-05.** In a baby, **sleepy and hard to wake in the cold is an
emergency,** not a nap.

## Warming a cold child, gently

- **Inside and out of every wet layer at once.**
- **Dry, warm layers;** cover the head.
- **Skin-to-skin under a blanket** with an adult: one of the best ways to rewarm a small child.
- **Warm drinks** for a child who is fully alert and swallowing normally; never a drink for a child who is
  unconscious (CDC), and nothing for one who is too drowsy to swallow safely.
- **No direct heat on cold skin:** not a stove, heater, hot water or heating pad. Cold, numb skin burns
  without feeling it (CDC, Preventing Frostbite).
- **No rubbing frostbitten skin.**
- **Chemical hand warmers get hot enough to burn,** and a small child cannot take one out or say it
  hurts. Keep them **outside** clothing, in an adult's or an older child's pocket, never inside a
  small child's mittens or boots, never on numb skin. The packets are also a choking and chewing
  hazard: keep them out of reach.
- **Warm the room, not the child directly** (→ 08-01), and add body heat.

## Living in a cold house with children

- **Children live in the warm room** (→ 08-01), not in their own cold bedrooms.
- **Base layers, wool socks and hats indoors.** Normal in a cold house.
- **Off the cold floor.** Children sit and play on the floor, the coldest surface in the room. A foam
  pad, rug or blanket layer under them matters more than most people expect.
- **Older children's sleep:** dry base layers changed before bed, wool socks, a hat, insulation under
  as well as over.

## Cold-room sleep for babies and toddlers

The American Academy of Pediatrics publishes **no numeric minimum room temperature** for babies. Its
guidance: dress the baby for the room, keep loose bedding out of a baby's sleep space, and avoid
overheating (AAP, How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe). CDC lists **babies sleeping in cold bedrooms**
among those most at risk of hypothermia (CDC). In a cold house:

- **Warmth is worn, not piled on.** A snug base layer, a fleece footed sleeper over it, and **one
  wearable sleep sack** rated for the room; a thicker (higher-TOG, a warmth rating) sack is sold for
  cold rooms. Follow the room-temperature chart on its label. AAP: if you are worried about a baby
  getting cold, dress them in layers or use a wearable blanket, generally one layer more than you
  are wearing; no loose blankets, no weighted sleepers (AAP, How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe).
  **Do not stack two sacks:** overheating raises the risk of SIDS (sudden infant death) too (AAP).
  A sack cannot be kicked off at 3 a.m.; a blanket can.
- **The overheating check:** feel the **neck and chest.** Sweating, a hot chest or flushed skin
  means take a layer off (AAP). Cool hands and feet are normal.
- **The baby sleeps in the warm room**, next to the adults (→ 08-01).
- **Bed-sharing for warmth is a decision card.** The AAP says share a room with your baby for at
  least the first 6 months, but **never a bed**: the baby sleeps on their own firm, flat surface
  (AAP). The card offers
  bed-sharing on cold nights only for children over 12 months, with its own rules:
  {{choice DC-09}} (→ 30-10).
  {{#if has.infant}}Your children under 2: {{#each infants as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}check each one's age against the card.{{/if}}
- **Hot-water bottles and fire-warmed stones pre-warm the bed and come out before a child gets in.**
  Sleeping or numb skin burns without waking, and a small child cannot move away (→ 21-07). **Never an
  electric or heated blanket on or around a baby or toddler** (→ 08-04).
- **If a heater runs at night,** it runs only under the household's answer on the overnight-heater
  card: {{choice DC-01}} (→ 30-02).
- **Feed them often.** Staying warm burns calories, and small children have small reserves.
  {{#if has.nursing}}A nursing parent needs extra food and water in the cold house too (→ 20-05,
  → 03-01).{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-04}} For a child with a food allergy, every one of those
  calories comes from safe food (→ 02-04).{{/if}}
- **Watch hydration.** Children do not feel thirsty in the cold, and dehydration makes them colder
  (→ 03-01).

{{photo child-sleep-setup}}

## Nappies and cold

A wet nappy against skin in a cold house drains heat continuously and damages skin. **Change often and
fast, in the warm room** (→ 20-06). This competes directly with your water and washing budget.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Winter gear in the next sizes** (three for toddlers, two for older children) | They outgrow it and there is no store | Tracked on → 11-09 |
| Wool or synthetic base layers, 2 to 3 sets per child (suggested) | Cotton fails; children get wet | Thrift stores |
| One-piece snowsuit (baby, toddler) or bibs (older) | Closes the waist gap | |
| Wool socks, 6 pairs per child | Always wet, always lost | Count sheet on → 11-01 |
| Mittens, 3 pairs per child, and mitten clips | Warmer than gloves | Clipped through the sleeves |
| **Car-seat poncho** per child in a car seat | Warmth over the buckled harness | Keep with the vehicle kit (→ 22-05) |
| Wearable sleep sacks: one mid-weight, one cold-room weight | The warm sleep layer; never stacked | Next size too |
| Balaclava or chin-strap hats, 2 per child | Covers ears; stays on | Not a loose scarf |
| Neck gaiters | Scarves can strangle | |
| Insulated waterproof boots, sized with room | Tight boots freeze toes | Next size too |
| Foam pads or rugs for floor play | Children live on the coldest surface | |
| Kid-sized wool blankets | Layering and wrapping | |
| Waterproof outer layer | Snow play soaks them in minutes | → 11-03 |
| Room thermometer | Know what you are keeping | |

**No gear?** Thrift stores and hand-me-downs are the whole strategy: start now. **An adult wool sweater
cut down and resewn** makes several toddler garments (→ 11-07). Wool blankets become ponchos, buntings
and wraps. Adult socks become toddler leg warmers. A down comforter section sewn into a bunting is
light and very warm. A trash bag with arm holes over a snowsuit for short supervised periods only:
**never for sleep, never over the head.** **Body heat** is the best resource you have: a child
carried inside your coat is warmer than in any garment.

## When it runs out

- **Children's clothing runs out by growth, not wear,** and no care prevents it. Next sizes stockpiled
  now is the only real answer (→ 11-09, → 23-02).
- **Socks and mittens are the fast consumables.** Stock heavily; learn to darn (→ 11-07).
- **Resupply:** cut down adult clothing; trade with other households, one of the easiest trades there
  is, since every family has outgrown gear (→ 18-02).
- **Ration outdoor time** by the NWS chart's frostbite time for today's temperature and wind (→ 11-01),
  and **not at all** under an Extreme Cold Warning, never by how much the children want to go out.
- **The substitute that always works:** an adult's body heat.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** children live in the warm room, in layers, off the cold floor, checked by touch.
  Outdoor play is good for morale; keep it time-limited and follow it with a full dry-out.
- **B (moving):** **the most dangerous situation for small children.** Carried children freeze while
  carrying adults sweat. Check them every few minutes, keep them inside your layers where possible,
  stop and rewarm at the first sign, and **strongly prefer not to move in winter** (→ 01-02).
- **C (established somewhere else):** more outdoor work and more chance of a child out of sight in the
  cold. Set firm boundaries and check-ins (→ 20-02).

pages.body:
# Staying dry, and drying gear without a dryer

**What this page is for.** How clothes get wet in winter and how to stop it, how to dry clothes and
boots in a cold house with no dryer, and how to deal with the damp air that drying creates.

> **CAUTION.** **Wet is what turns cold into injury.** Wet clothing loses much of its insulation and
> pulls heat from the body faster than dry. CDC says hypothermia can happen even above 40 °F in
> someone who is wet from rain, sweat or cold water, and OSHA lists wetness among the causes of
> cold stress (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia; OSHA, Cold Stress). Two hazards on this page: **(1) fire:** clothing hung on or too
> near a stove or heater is a classic house fire; **(2) damp air:** drying laundry in a sealed winter
> house puts a lot of water into the air, which condenses on cold surfaces and grows mould. **Never
> use an unvented fuel heater to speed drying in a closed room** (→ 08-02), and never hang anything
> on or over a portable heater (→ 08-10).

## Do this now

1. **Build a drying setup before the first hard freeze:** a rack or line **near, never on,** the heat
   source, placed so nothing can fall onto it.
2. **The two-set rule:** everyone has two of everything, one worn, one drying (→ 11-01).
3. **Change base layers before bed, every night, for everyone.** Sleeping in a damp layer is how a
   warm household ends up cold at 3 a.m.
4. **A boot tray and a drying spot by the door,** and the rule that wet gear goes there at once.

{{photo drying-setup}}

## How clothes get wet, and how to stop each one

1. **Sweat, the biggest.** Vent **before** you overheat (→ 11-01). Most winter wet comes from inside
   the clothes.
2. **Snow and rain.** Windproof or waterproof shell, gaiters, bibs, hood, and brushing snow off
   **before** coming inside: snow melted indoors is water in your gear.
3. **Wet work.** Hauling water (→ 03-02, → 03-06), washing, melting snow, animal chores. Waterproof
   gloves and a dedicated "wet work" outer set.
4. **Children** in snow are soaked within the hour (→ 11-02). Plan for it.

## Why drying is hard in a winter outage

Drying needs **heat, moving air, and somewhere for the moisture to go.** In a cold outage you are short
of all three:

- The house is **cold** (→ 08-01), so water evaporates slowly.
- The house is **sealed** for warmth (→ 08-03), so moisture has nowhere to go.
- **Cold air holds very little water.** Outside air is very dry, so bringing some in and warming it
  dries things fast, but every bit of air you heat costs fuel.

**Expect wet gear to take a day or more to dry in a cold house.** Heavy boots and thick mittens can
take **several days.** Plan around that.

## Methods that work

1. **Near the heat, never on it.** A rack or line at a safe distance from the stove or heater, where
   rising warm air reaches it. **Never draped on a stove, stovepipe, fireplace screen, or anywhere it
   can fall in.** Never left drying by a fire overnight.
2. **High up.** Warm air rises: a line near the ceiling of the heated room dries far faster than a
   rack on the floor. It is the best free drying spot you have.
3. **Freeze-drying outdoors.** Hang wet laundry outside in below-freezing air. It freezes stiff, then
   the ice turns straight to vapour and the clothes end up dry. It takes a day or more, works best in
   dry, sunny cold, and **uses no fuel at all.** Bring items in stiff and let the last moisture leave
   indoors.{{#if is.cold_winters}} Your winters are cold enough for this on most dry days.{{/if}}
4. **Wring, roll and press first.** Wring hard, then **roll the garment in a dry towel and stand on
   it.** This removes a surprising amount of water and cuts drying time a lot.
5. **Moving air.** A small fan across a rack dries far better than more heat in still air: a very
   good use of a little electricity (→ 09-01).
6. **Body heat, carefully.** Damp (not soaked) socks and mittens can be dried inside your clothing
   against your body while you sleep. It works and costs nothing.
7. **Boots** dry from the inside out and take longest:
   - **Pull out the liners and insoles** and dry them separately: that is most of the job.
   - **Stuff newspaper inside** and replace it as it gets damp.
   - **Never dry boots on a stove:** heat ruins the glue, cracks leather and shrinks the fit (→ 11-06).
   - A boot dryer on battery or solar power is a small load and worth it if you have the watts.

## Managing the damp you create

Drying inside a sealed winter house puts water into the air. It condenses on the coldest surfaces
(windows, outside walls, corners), where it grows mould and soaks insulation.

- **Vent on purpose.** A window opened wide for a short time swaps humid air for very dry cold air,
  and costs less heat than people fear because you are swapping air, not chilling the walls.
- **Dry in the heated room, and vent that room,** rather than spreading wet gear through the house.
- **Keep indoor relative humidity between 30 and 50%, never above 60%** (EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold,
  Moisture and Your Home). A cheap hygrometer reads it. In deep cold the practical ceiling is lower,
  because cold glass condenses moisture long before the room feels damp.
- **Watch the windows.** Water or frost on the inside of the glass means the humidity is already too
  high for that surface: vent now.
- **Watch for mould** in corners, behind furniture and on outside walls. It is bad for everyone,
  especially small children.
- **The tension is real:** → 08-03 says seal the house; this page says vent it. The answer is **brief,
  targeted venting of the room where the moisture is made.**

## The rotation

- **Two sets of everything per person, one worn, one drying.**
- **Wet gear off at the door and straight to the drying spot.**
- **Base layers changed before bed,** every night.
- **Socks changed more often than you think.** Damp socks in boots lead straight to trench foot and
  frostbite (→ 11-04).
- **Nothing goes into a drawer damp.**

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Folding drying racks, 2 or 3 | The core of the system | Near, never on, the heat |
| Clothesline and pegs, indoor and outdoor | High line indoors; freeze-drying outside | |
| **Two full sets of everything per person** | One worn, one drying | → 11-01 |
| Towels kept for roll-pressing | Mechanical water removal | |
| Boot tray; boot dryer or rack | Boots take days otherwise | |
| Newspaper | Boot stuffing; also insulation | |
| Small 12 V fan | Moving air multiplies drying | → 09-01 |
| Gaiters and waterproof overmitts | Stop wet at the source | |
| A "wet work" waterproof outer set | Water hauling, chores, washing | |
| Hygrometer | Tells you when to vent: 30 to 50% | Cheap; prevents mould |
| Wringer or mop-bucket wringer | Serious water removal | → 13-04 |

**No gear?** Racks and lines from cord, wire, broom handles across chair backs, a ladder laid flat.
Boot stuffing: newspaper, dry cloth, dry grass, uncooked rice in a sock. Desiccants: silica packets
saved from packaging, uncooked rice. Waterproofing: trash bags as overmitts and gaiters; a tarp
poncho; beeswax rubbed into leather and canvas (→ 10-04); plastic bags between sock layers as a
vapour barrier (it keeps the boot's insulation dry at the cost of a damp inner sock). Pressing: a dry
towel, a flat surface and your weight.

## When it runs out

- **Drying capacity, not clothing, is the real limit.** If you can dry one set a day, you can get one
  set wet a day. **That limits work, not just laundry.** Do wet work in one block, then dry.
- **Fuel is the hidden cost:** drying near the stove costs wood (→ 06-04). Outdoor freeze-drying is
  free.
- **Ration:** fewer garments, worn longer. **A base layer worn three days but kept dry beats a clean
  one that is damp.** Dryness beats cleanliness here, within hygiene limits (→ 13-02).
- **Never get everything wet at once.** If the whole household soaks its gear in one afternoon, you
  have days with no dry outer layers. **Stagger the wet work.**
- **Substitute: wool.** Wool keeps insulating when damp, so it survives a failed drying system in a
  way cotton and down cannot (→ 11-05).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** rack and high line in the heated room, freeze-drying outside on dry cold days, boot
  tray by the door, everyone on the two-set rotation.
- **B (moving):** **assume you cannot dry gear while moving in winter.** Staying dry (venting,
  waterproof shells) matters most on the move, and it is a strong argument against winter travel
  (→ 01-02, → 01-03). Carry a spare dry base layer per person sealed in a bag as an emergency
  reserve.
- **C (established somewhere else):** more outdoor work, more wet gear, and space to build a drying
  room near the stove. Build it early.

pages.body:
# Feet, hands and face: protecting the extremities

**What this page is for.** How to keep fingers, toes, ears, nose and cheeks from cold injury: why they
go first, the two foot injuries (frostbite and trench foot), mittens versus gloves, the face, and a
check-and-respond routine.

> **CAUTION.** **Extremities are where cold actually injures people.** Hypothermia takes the core;
> **frostbite takes fingers, toes, ears, nose and cheeks**, often while the rest of you feels fine
> (CDC, Preventing Frostbite). Exposed skin can freeze in minutes in hard cold; read the time on the
> NWS wind chill chart for today's conditions (→ 11-01). **Frostbitten skin goes numb: the warning is
> the absence of a warning.** If a body part stops hurting and starts feeling like nothing, that is
> the emergency: → 08-05.

## Do this now

1. **Mittens, not gloves, for everyone,** with a thin liner glove inside for brief fiddly work.
2. **Far more wool socks than seems reasonable.** Socks are the highest-turnover item in this
   section.
3. **Check that boots fit with thick socks on.** Snug with thin socks means a frostbite trap with thick
   ones (→ 11-06).
4. **The face-check habit:** in hard cold, look at each other's faces every few minutes. White or waxy
   patches on cheeks, nose and ears are visible to a companion and invisible to the person who has
   them.

## Why the extremities go first

When the core gets cold, the body **deliberately** cuts blood flow to the hands, feet and skin to
protect the heart and brain. Two useful consequences:

1. **Cold hands are often a core problem.** If your hands will not warm up, **put on a hat and another
   mid layer.** Warming the core brings blood back to the hands; another glove does much less.
2. **Anything tight makes it worse:** tight boots, tight socks, tight cuffs, watch bands, sitting
   cross-legged for a long time. **Snug is the enemy.**

Nicotine narrows blood vessels; alcohol sends core heat to the skin and loses it; dehydration
thickens the blood. All three make cold injury more likely. The Wilderness Medical Society's advice
for preventing frostbite includes avoiding alcohol and anything that reduces blood flow, and not
wearing tight clothing or footwear (AFP, Frostbite: Prevention and Initial Management).

## Feet

Feet are hardest to protect: **inside a closed container that fills with sweat, standing on frozen
ground, doing all the work.**

**Two different injuries, both serious:**

- **Frostbite:** tissue actually freezes. Needs temperatures below freezing.
- **Trench foot (non-freezing cold injury):** feet kept wet and cold **above** freezing. No freeze
  needed, just wet socks and time; OSHA says it can happen at temperatures as high as 60 °F if feet
  stay wet. Painful and disabling (OSHA, Cold Stress). When drying is hard (→ 11-03), it is a likely
  injury.

**The rules that prevent both:**

- **Wool socks. Never cotton.**
- **Change socks whenever they are damp,** often more than once a day when working. Carry a spare pair
  in an inside pocket, where body heat keeps it dry and warm.
- **Boots roomy enough for thick socks with wiggle room** (→ 11-06).
- **Dry the boots, not just the socks:** pull the liners, stuff with newspaper (→ 11-03).
- **Vapour-barrier socks:** a plastic bag between a thin inner sock and a thick outer sock keeps sweat
  out of the boot's insulation. The inner sock gets damp; change it. Useful on long cold days.
- **Air the feet daily:** dry, warm, bare feet by the heat for a while, then dry socks. This one habit
  prevents most foot problems.
- **Loosen laces when sitting still.**

## Hands

- **Mittens over gloves.** Mitten with a liner glove inside is the best system: pull the mitten off for
  a task, work quickly in the liner, mitten back on.
- **Never bare hands on cold metal.** Skin sticks and tears, and metal pulls heat out very fast. This
  matters around tools, vehicles and firearms (→ 14-05).
- **Keep a spare pair of mittens dry,** always.
- **Chemical hand warmers** are cheap, keep for years, and help anyone standing still outside. **They
  get hot enough to burn.** Use them outside clothing or in a pocket, never against bare or numb skin,
  never inside a small child's mittens or boots (→ 11-02). Keep the packets away from small children,
  who chew them.
- **Idle hands get cold.** Move your fingers, swing your arms, put your hands in your armpits. **The
  armpits and groin are the warmest places on the body** and the fastest way to rewarm hands.

## Face, ears and nose

- **The first place frostbite shows, and the last place anyone checks.**
- **Balaclava or face mask plus goggles** in wind. In hard cold, **nothing exposed.**
- **Watch each other:** white, waxy or grey patches on cheeks, nose and ear tips (CDC).
- **Breath freezes in the mask:** a scarf or mask over the mouth collects moisture and freezes against
  the face. A gaiter you can turn to a dry section, or a mask built to vent, works better.
- **Eyes:** wind and blowing snow hurt and blur vision; in bright snow, **snow blindness** is real.
  Sunglasses or goggles in sun, even in winter, especially with fresh snow (→ 17-01).

## Check and respond

**Check** often in hard cold, at an interval you set before going out and shorten as the wind
chill falls toward the chart's frostbite bands (→ 11-01); **check children more often than adults,
and every few minutes when a child is carried** (→ 11-02):

- Can everyone feel and wiggle all fingers and toes?
- Is anyone's face showing white or waxy patches?
- Is anyone unusually quiet?
- Are anyone's socks wet?

**Respond at once:**

- Numb, white, waxy or hard skin: **stop, get inside, → 08-05.**
- **Do not rub** frostbitten skin (CDC).
- **No direct high heat:** stove, heater, hot water. Numb skin burns without feeling it (CDC).
- **Do not thaw a frostbitten foot if the person then has to walk on it and it may freeze again.**
  A frostbitten part is rewarmed only if there is no risk of it refreezing (AFP, Frostbite;
  → 01-03).
- **Skin-to-skin** (armpits, groin, a companion's belly) is the safe way to rewarm cold-but-not-frozen
  fingers and toes.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Wool socks, many pairs per person** | Highest-turnover item | Merino or wool blend; never cotton |
| Thin liner socks | Wicking layer under thick socks | Fewer blisters, less wet |
| **Mittens, 2 to 3 pairs per person** | Warmer than gloves | Plus overmitts for wet work |
| Liner gloves, 2 to 3 pairs per person | Fine work without bare skin | |
| Balaclavas or neck gaiters, 2 per person | Face and ears; turn to a dry section | Not a loose scarf for children |
| Goggles or wraparound sunglasses | Wind, blowing snow, snow blindness | |
| Chemical hand and toe warmers | Cheap, long shelf life | Outside clothing only |
| Waterproof overmitts | Wet work without soaking insulation | |
| Insulated boots and spare liners | → 11-06 | Liners dry separately |
| Vapour-barrier bags (bread bags) | Keep boot insulation dry | Free |
| Lip balm and skin ointment | Cracked lips and split fingertips hurt and can get infected | → 12-02 |
| Nail clippers | Long toenails in tight boots cause injury | |

**No gear?** Socks from wool sweaters cut and sewn (→ 11-07), or two thin pairs for one thick. Mittens
from sweater sleeves sewn shut, or a wool sock over a glove. Overmitts from plastic bags or a tarp
scrap. A cut sleeve as a gaiter; a T-shirt as a balaclava; a scarf for adults only. Any sunglasses; a
slit visor cut from cardboard or bark is the traditional snow-blindness fix. A warm (not hot) water
bottle or hands in armpits instead of warmers; nothing hot goes inside a child's mitten. Bread or
grocery bags as vapour barriers.

## When it runs out

- **Socks and gloves are the true consumables of this section.** Stock heavily, learn to darn
  (→ 11-07), keep every wool sweater as raw material.
- **Runway:** count pairs per person and divide by real daily changes. Outdoor winter work can use **two
  pairs of socks a day.** Write that on → 23-02.
- **Ration:** dry and rewear rather than wearing fresh every time. **A dried, reworn wool sock beats a
  damp clean one.** Give the best socks to whoever works outside most.
- **The permanent substitute is behaviour:** shorter exposures, more warming breaks, checking each
  other, and not doing outdoor work under an Extreme Cold Warning (→ 29-10) when it could wait.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** exposures are short (the yard, the woodpile, the water haul). The risk is a routine
  chore done carelessly in hard cold. Dry mittens by the door; check faces when anyone comes in.
- **B (moving):** **the highest-risk page in this section for travel.** Long exposure, wet feet, no
  drying, and the refreezing problem. Spare dry socks changed at every stop; face checks at every stop,
  children included.
- **C (established somewhere else):** daily outdoor work means daily wet feet and hands. Build the
  drying setup and the "air the feet by the heat" habit early.
