pages.body:
# Materials: wool, synthetics and what fails

**What this page is for.** Which fabrics keep you warm when wet, which melt near fire, how to tell an
unlabelled fabric by a burn test, what to wear for saw and wood work, and how to make materials last.

> **CAUTION. Two material facts matter more than any brand.**
> **(1) Cotton is dangerous in the cold.** Wet cotton loses most of its insulation and holds water
> against your skin, and being wet can bring on hypothermia even above 40 °F (CDC, Preventing
> Hypothermia). OSHA and CDC guidance is to dress properly for cold and wet and to get out of wet
> clothing (OSHA, Cold Stress; CDC). Not in base layers, not in socks, not in the
> winter kit.
> **(2) Synthetics melt.** Fleece, nylon and polyester near an open flame or a hot stove **melt onto
> skin** and cause burns far worse than a fabric that just chars. **Wear wool, not fleece, around
> fire** (→ 06-01, → 07-01, → 12-03).

## Do this now

1. **Sort the winter kit by fibre.** Read the labels. Much of what you thought was cold-weather
   clothing will be cotton.
2. **Start buying wool secondhand:** sweaters, blankets, army surplus. It is cheap, lasts decades, and
   is the most valuable material in this section.
3. **Set aside a "fire clothing" set:** wool or heavy cotton canvas outer layers for stove and fire
   work.
4. **Learn the burn test** (below) to identify unlabelled scavenged fabric.

## The fibres in one table

| Fibre | Warm when wet? | Dries | Near flame | Durability | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Wool (especially merino)** | **Yes: the key property** | Slow | **Chars, puts itself out** | Very good | **The survival fibre** |
| **Polyester fleece** | Somewhat | **Fast** | **Melts: dangerous** | Good | Excellent mid layer; never near fire |
| Polypropylene | Somewhat | Very fast | **Melts** | Good | Good base layer; holds odour |
| Nylon | No insulation | Fast | **Melts** | **Excellent** | Shells, packs, outerwear |
| **Down** | **No: collapses** | **Very slow** | Burns | Good if dry | Warmest per ounce **if dry** |
| Synthetic fill | Somewhat | Moderate | Melts | Good | **More reliable than down in a wet winter** |
| **Cotton** | **No: dangerous** | **Very slow** | Chars, burns | Good | **Not in the winter kit; fine in summer** (→ 11-08) |
| Canvas or duck (cotton) | No | Slow | Chars | **Excellent** | Good work shell in dry cold |
| Linen | No | Fast | Chars | Good | Summer only |
| Silk | Poorly | Fast | Chars | Fair | Light base layer |
| Leather | No | Very slow | Chars | Excellent | Boots, gloves, wind blocking |

## Why wool

- **It insulates when wet.** Wool fibres are crimped and hold air even damp: the most important
  property when drying is hard (→ 11-03). **Wool survives the failure of your drying system.**
- **It resists fire:** it chars and puts itself out instead of melting. The right fibre for tending a
  stove or outdoor fire.
- **It resists odour** and can be worn much longer between washes than synthetics, which matters when
  washing costs water, fuel and drying (→ 13-04).
- **It is warm across a wide range** and breathes, so you sweat into it less.
- **It is everywhere:** sweaters, blankets, army surplus, coats. **A wool blanket is raw material** for
  socks, mittens, liners and a poncho (→ 11-07).
- **Downsides:** slow to dry, heavier than synthetics, itchy in coarse grades (merino is not), eaten by
  **moths** (store clean and sealed), and it shrinks if washed hot or agitated. **Wash wool cool and
  gently; never wring it hard.**

## Where synthetics win

- **Fleece dries fast:** a real advantage when drying is limited.
- **Polypropylene base layers** wick hard and dry fastest of all.
- **Nylon shells** are the only practical windproof and waterproof layer, and in hard wind the shell
  does more work than any insulation.
- **Synthetic fill keeps some loft when damp,** which makes it safer than down for a wet winter.

**Remember: they melt.** Fleece near the stove, a nylon shell brushing a stovepipe, synthetic long
johns while tending a fire: these cause burns that melt into the skin and are much harder to treat
(→ 12-03). **Wool or canvas for fire work.**

## Down: wins and losses

Down is the warmest insulation for its weight and packed size, **in dry cold.** Wet down clumps and
gives almost **no** insulation, and it takes a very long time to dry in a cold house. **In a wet or
long winter outage, make synthetic fill the main insulation and down the layer you keep dry.** If you
own down, protect it carefully.

## The burn test for unlabelled fabric

Useful when scavenging (→ 22-02). Snip a small piece, hold it with tweezers over something that cannot
burn, and light it **outdoors or over a sink**:

| Fibre | How it burns | Smell | What is left |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Wool** | Slowly, **puts itself out** | Burning hair | Black bead that crushes |
| **Cotton or linen** | Fast and steady, keeps burning | Burning paper | Soft grey ash |
| **Polyester** | **Melts and shrinks away,** drips | Sweet chemical | **Hard black bead** |
| **Nylon** | Melts, drips, puts itself out | Celery-like, chemical | Hard grey-tan bead |
| **Acrylic** | Melts and burns readily | Sharp chemical | Hard, irregular black bead |
| **Rayon** | Fast, like cotton | Burning paper | Little ash |

**Hard bead: it melts; keep it away from fire and do not trust it wet. Crushable bead and a hair smell:
wool; keep it.**

## Other materials

- **Canvas or duck cotton:** excellent abrasion resistance for work layers, chaps, tool rolls, aprons.
  Not a base layer, but a good wind-blocking, spark-resistant work shell in dry cold.
- **Leather:** gloves, boots, repairs. Durable and wind-blocking, slow to dry, needs conditioning with
  beeswax and oil (→ 10-04).
- **Fur and hides:** if you process animals (→ 05-09, → 05-15), hides are insulation. Tanning is a real
  skill and a long project.
- **Sheepskin and shearling:** the best boot-liner material there is.

## Saw and wood work: the saw does not negotiate

Wood heat usually means a chainsaw (→ 06-04, → 16-06). With an emergency room, saw protection is
sensible; without one, a chainsaw cut to the leg can be a barely survivable wound (→ 12-02). OSHA's
logging standard requires chain-saw operators to wear cut-resistant leg protection from the thigh to
the top of the boot and cut-resistant foot protection, with head, eye and face protection where
objects can fall or fly (OSHA, Logging Operations, 29 CFR 1910.266). The household list, with hearing added:

- **Chainsaw chaps or cut-resistant trousers.** The thigh is where saws land. Cut-resistant fibres pull
  out and jam the chain. Check the label for the cut-resistance standard. Wear them for **every** cut,
  including "just one quick cut". **No chaps, no saw** is a sensible household rule.
- **Eyes and face:** safety glasses under a mesh face screen for saw work. Safety glasses at least for
  splitting and for hammering wedges: steel chips from a struck wedge blind people.
- **Hearing:** muffs or plugs every session. Hearing lost to a saw does not come back, and hearing is a
  security sense (→ 14-01).
- **Hands:** snug grip gloves for control; padded anti-vibration gloves on long sessions.
- **Feet:** steel or composite toe boots for felling, cutting rounds and splitting. The winter boot and
  the safety-toe work boot may have to be two different boots.
- **Nothing loose near a running saw:** no scarves, drawstrings, flapping cuffs or untucked shirts;
  long hair tied back. Snug wool or canvas outer layers are right for both fire and saw.

## Care that makes materials last

- **Wool:** cool water, gentle, no wringing, dry flat. Store clean and sealed: **moths prefer dirty
  wool.** Cedar or lavender in storage.
- **Synthetics:** wash cool; fabric softener ruins wicking. They hold odour, so they need washing more
  often.
- **Down:** keep it dry; store it **loose**, not compressed (long compression kills loft).
- **Waterproof shells:** the coating wears off; re-treat with wax or a water-repellent spray. **Once
  the shell soaks through, the whole layer system fails.**
- **Everything:** mend small holes at once (→ 11-07).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Merino wool base layers, 2 sets per person** | Warm when damp, low odour, comfortable | The keystone purchase |
| Wool sweaters and blankets | Layers now, raw material later | Thrift stores, surplus |
| Fleece mid layers | Fast-drying insulation | **Never near fire** |
| Nylon windproof and waterproof shells | Wind is the danger | Re-treat yearly |
| Synthetic-fill parka or vest | More reliable than down when wet | |
| Canvas work jacket or bibs | Abrasion and spark resistance | The right kind of cotton |
| Leather work gloves and conditioner | Wood, tools, wire, fire | |
| Water-repellent spray or wax bar | Restores a dead shell | |
| Mothproof storage | Wool's real enemy | Store clean |
| Darning wool, needles, patches | → 11-07 | |
| Chainsaw chaps, safety glasses and face screen, hearing protection, saw gloves, safety-toe boots | Saw and wood work | → 22-01 |

**No gear?** Wool is the top clothing scavenge: sweaters, blankets, coats, army surplus, felt. Fleece
blankets as mid layers (→ 11-07). Nylon from tents, tarps, packs and jackets for shells and repairs.
Down from comforters and old sleeping bags. Canvas from tarps, awnings and work clothes. Leather from old
coats, boots, belts and furniture. Insulation in a pinch: newspaper between layers, dry grass or cattail
fluff inside a shell, bubble wrap. **Skip** cotton for the winter system and synthetics for fire work.

## When it runs out

- **Fabric lasts a long time,** and every house nearby is full of it. In a long outage you are unlikely
  to run out of fabric if you can rework it (→ 11-07, → 16-04).
- **What does run out:** waterproof coatings (re-treat with wax), elastic (perishes), zippers (fail and
  are hard to replace: **stock spares**), thread. **Thread and needles are tiny, cheap and almost
  impossible to improvise. Stock them heavily.**
- **Protect the good things:** wear cheap layers for dirty work and save merino and the good shell for
  cold work.
- **Substitute up the chain:** wool blanket into socks, mittens, liners, poncho; sweater into children's
  clothes (→ 11-02); tarp into a shell; comforter into a parka.
- **The very long term:** hides from animals you process, and one day wool from sheep where land allows.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** sort by fibre, purge cotton from the winter kit, stock wool, set aside fire clothing.
- **B (moving):** wool and synthetics only; nothing cotton. A windproof shell is worth more than an extra
  insulation layer in wind. Keep the spare dry base layer sealed in a bag.
- **C (established somewhere else):** more abrasion, more fire work, more wet: canvas, leather and wool
  earn their keep, and reworking fabric becomes routine.

pages.body:
# Boots, traction and winter footwear

**What this page is for.** What makes a winter boot work, how to fit it, how to stop falls on ice, and
how to keep boots alive through a long winter.

> **CAUTION.** **A fall on ice is a serious injury in a winter outage,** and with no emergency
> room behind it a broken wrist, hip or a head injury is a crisis (→ 12-09, → 12-19,
> → 12-16). **An adult carrying a small child across ice is the situation to design against.**
> Traction devices cost little and prevent it. **The second hazard is the boot itself: a boot that is
> too tight freezes your feet,** because squeezed circulation makes frostbite more likely; frostbite
> prevention guidance says avoid tight footwear (AFP, Frostbite; → 11-04).

## Do this now

1. **Traction devices for every adult, and a pair by every door.** Buy spares: the rubber perishes and
   they get lost.
2. **Try boots on with the thick wool socks you will wear.** Toes touching, or toes that cannot wiggle:
   **go up a size.**
3. **Choose boots with removable liners.** With no dryer, a boot you cannot dry is a boot you lose for
   days (→ 11-03).
4. **Children's boots: size up, and buy the next size ahead** (→ 11-02, → 11-09).

{{photo door-traction-station}}

## What makes a winter boot work

1. **Room for thick socks and air.** Insulation is trapped air, and toes must move. **Snug boots are
   cold boots.**
2. **A removable liner.** The liner soaks up sweat and takes a day or more to dry inside the boot. Pull
   it, dry it separately, and the boot is wearable tomorrow. This feature is worth more than extra
   insulation in an outage.
3. **A waterproof lower or rubber bottom:** snow, slush, meltwater on the entry floor.
4. **A thick, insulating sole.** Cold comes up through the sole from frozen ground; a thin sole means a
   cold foot whatever is above it.
5. **Height and a good cuff,** with **gaiters** for deep snow.
6. **Traction that works on ice,** not just snow.

**Boot temperature ratings are marketing figures** measured under assumptions that usually involve
walking. Use them only to compare boots, not as a promise for standing still.

### The cold-country answer

**Pac boots** (a rubber lower, a leather or nylon upper, and a removable felt or wool liner) are the
traditional and still-correct answer for deep cold: waterproof below, very warm, and the liner comes
out to dry. They are clumsy for long walks. **Insulated leather work boots** are better for walking and
working and worse for standing still in hard cold. **Rubber overboots** pull over ordinary shoes for
chores. Ideally own both kinds: one for standing and chores, one for distance.

## Traction: the injury-prevention item

Ice under snow is invisible, and freeze-thaw cycles glaze everything.

| Device | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Coil or spring traction devices** | Packed snow, general walking | Cheap, light, easy on and off |
| **Spike or stud devices** | Bare ice | Best grip; take them off inside |
| **Short hex-head screws in the sole lugs** | Improvised, permanent, cheap | Works well |
| Studded rubber overshoes | Chores | Slip over boots |
| Grit on the path | The path itself | Below |

**Treat the ground, not just the feet:** wood ash from the stove (→ 06-02), sand, cat litter or gravel on
the path from the door to the woodpile and the water. You walk that path many times a day all winter;
make it safe once.

## Falls, seriously

- **Most falls happen on routine trips:** carrying something, in the dark, in a hurry.
- **Carrying a child raises the stakes:** you cannot put your hands out. **Do not carry a small child
  across ice:** clear and grit the path, make two trips, or use a sled.
- **A sled** moves children, water and wood across snow and ice without carrying.
- **Light the path** (→ 10-01). Winter evenings are long.
- **Walk flat-footed with short steps, hands out of pockets.** Teach children the same.

## Fit, socks and frostbite

- **Fit with the socks you will wear,** in the afternoon (feet swell).
- **Toes must wiggle.** If not, circulation is squeezed and you will get cold or frostbitten feet
  whatever the rating (→ 11-04).
- **Do not over-lace.** Loosen when sitting still.
- **Two thin socks can beat one thick one** (a wicking liner and a wool outer), **only if the boot is
  not then tight.**
- **A vapour barrier** (a bread bag between liner sock and outer sock) keeps the boot's insulation dry
  over a long day (→ 11-04).

## Care and repair

- **Dry the liners every night:** pull them out, stand them near (not on) the heat, stuff the shells with
  newspaper (→ 11-03).
- **Never dry boots on the stove:** it ruins the glue, cracks leather and shrinks the fit.
- **Condition leather** with beeswax or oil a few times a season (→ 10-04).
- **Repair early:** a small sole separation becomes a lost boot. Shoe adhesive, contact cement,
  stitching (→ 16-05).
- **Rotate pairs** so each dries fully.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pac boots with removable liners**, per person | Standing in deep cold; liners dry separately | Sized for thick socks |
| Insulated leather work boots, per adult | Walking and working | Waterproofed |
| **Spare liners** for each pair | The wear item and the drying bottleneck | Rarely stocked |
| **Traction devices, 2 or more per adult** | Fall prevention | They perish; keep spares |
| Rubber overboots | Slush, chores, mud | |
| Gaiters | Snow out of the boot top | |
| Sled | Moves children, water and wood | |
| Grit, sand or ash bucket by the door | Treat the path | |
| Boot repair kit: adhesive, contact cement, awl and thread | Sole separation is the common failure | → 16-05 |
| Beeswax or leather conditioner | Waterproofing wears off | |
| Boot dryer or rack | Days versus overnight | |
| **Children's boots in the next size** | They outgrow them yearly | → 11-09 |

**No gear?** Traction: short hex-head screws driven into the lugs; chain or wire wrapped over the boot;
rope wound round the sole. Overboots: heavy plastic bags taped at the top (no grip: add the screws).
Liners: wool felt, layered wool socks, sheepskin, cut-up wool blanket. Insoles: felt, foam pad,
cardboard for a while, dry grass. Gaiters: cut trouser legs, tarp scraps. Repairs: wire, cord and duct
tape hold a failing boot long enough to get home.

## When it runs out

- **Boots are among the hardest things to improvise and the worst to lose.** A household without
  working boots in winter cannot fetch water or wood. Treat boots as **critical equipment.**
- **Runway:** a good pair lasts years; **liners and soles wear out.** Stock spare liners and repair
  supplies now.
- **Ration:** rotate pairs, dry nightly, condition, repair at once. **Keep one good pair per adult as
  untouchable** and use lesser footwear for dirty work.
- **Children again:** boots are outgrown fast. Next sizes ahead, on → 11-09 and → 23-02.
- **Traction devices perish:** check them every autumn.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** short trips, many times a day, on ice: exactly the frequent-fall pattern. Grit the
  paths, cleats by the door, a sled for children and loads.
- **B (moving):** boots are the most important equipment on a winter move. Spare dry socks at every
  stop, gaiters, a repair kit. A failed boot on the move in winter is an emergency (→ 01-03).
- **C (established somewhere else):** daily outdoor work. Two pairs per adult, spare liners, a drying
  spot by the door.

pages.body:
# Repairing and extending clothing

**What this page is for.** The four repairs that keep most clothing working, how to make clothes last,
how to remake adult clothing into what you need (especially children's clothes), and what to stock.
Damaged or wet clothing stops protecting you from cold (OSHA, Cold Stress; CDC, Preventing
Hypothermia), so repair is part of staying warm.

In a long emergency the clothing in your closets may be the last you can buy. The question becomes how
long you can keep it working and what you can make from what is around you. **Fabric is one of the few
things that is truly plentiful;** the limits are **skill, needles and thread.**

## Do this now

1. **Buy a real sewing kit and a large stock of thread, needles and pins.** They are tiny, cheap, never
   expire, and are nearly impossible to improvise. **Thread is the consumable that limits everything
   here.**
2. **Learn four things this month:** sew on a button, darn a sock, patch a knee, fix a zipper pull.
3. **Start a rag bag and a parts bin.** Every worn-out garment gives up its buttons, zippers, elastic,
   snaps, cord and usable fabric before anything is thrown away.
4. **Fix things now, while it is easy.** Five minutes on a small tear saves a garment.

## The four repairs that matter most

**1. Darning socks.** Socks wear out fastest (→ 11-04), and darning is easy:

- Put a smooth round object inside the sock (a darning egg, a light bulb, a smooth stone) to hold the
  shape.
- Sew a row of parallel stitches **across** the hole in one direction, then **weave** over and under
  through them at right angles, filling the hole with new fabric.
- **Wool yarn on wool socks:** matching the fibre keeps warmth and stretch.
- **Reinforce before it is a hole,** when the heel goes thin.

{{figure fig-darning-steps}}

**2. Patching** knees, elbows and seats:

- **Patch from the inside** where the garment is under strain and should lie flat.
- **Patch from the outside** where it gets rubbed (canvas knees, work gear).
- **Round the corners;** square corners peel.
- Iron-on patches do not last on hard-use clothes; **stitch round the edge** and they become a real
  repair.

**3. Seams and buttons.** Sew a split seam with **backstitch** along the original line, then a second
pass. **Backstitch, not running stitch, for anything under load.** A button takes five minutes.

**4. Zippers,** the most common serious failure in outerwear:

- **Teeth separating behind the slider** with teeth intact: often fixed by squeezing the slider gently
  with pliers; it has spread and stopped meshing.
- **Missing pull:** a paperclip, a split ring or cord.
- **Missing stop at the end:** stitch a hard bar of thread across the track.
- **Replacing a whole zipper is a real project,** which is why **spare zippers are worth stocking.**
- **Backup fastenings:** buttons, snaps, hook-and-loop, toggles, a cord and loop. **A coat that closes
  with buttons is a working coat.**

## Making things last

- **Reinforce before failure:** a second layer at knees, elbows, seat and cuffs of work clothes while
  they are new.
- **Patch shells at once.** A pinhole in a waterproof shell lets water in and the whole layer system
  fails (→ 11-05). Adhesive nylon repair tape works; keep a roll.
- **Re-waterproof** once a year with wax or spray.
- **Replace elastic;** it perishes with age. Stock some.
- **Wash less, gently.** Every wash costs water, fuel and drying (→ 13-04) and wears the garment. Wool can
  often be aired instead of washed.
- **Store correctly:** clean, dry, sealed against moths (wool), loose (down).

## Remaking

| Source | Becomes |
|---|---|
| **Adult wool sweater** | Two or three pairs of children's mittens, a child's vest, sock liners, boot liners |
| **Wool blanket** | Poncho, vest, mittens, boot liners, leg wraps, a child's coat |
| **Fleece blanket** | Mid-layer jacket, children's layers, hats, neck gaiters |
| **Down comforter** | Vest, a baby's bunting, a jacket liner |
| **Tarp or tent fly** | Windproof shell, gaiters, overmitts, rain poncho |
| **Old jeans or canvas** | Patches, knee reinforcement, tool rolls, aprons |
| **Leather coat or sofa** | Glove palms, boot patches, straps |
| **Adult clothes generally** | The next size up for children (→ 11-02) |
| **Worn-out anything** | Buttons, zippers, elastic, snaps, cord, thread, rags |

**Cutting down adult clothes for children is the most valuable remaking skill,** because children's
clothing runs out by growth and nothing prevents it (→ 11-09).

**Felting wool:** washing wool hot and agitating it on purpose makes a dense fabric that can be cut
without hemming. It is excellent for mittens, boot liners and insoles, and it rescues shrunken sweaters.

## Tools and skill

Very little: needles in several sizes (including a heavy one for canvas and leather), strong thread,
scissors, pins, a thimble and patience. A **sewing machine** multiplies your work while there is power;
a **hand-crank or treadle machine** is one of the great pieces of grid-free equipment. **The skill is the
real asset,** and one of the most tradeable there is (→ 18-03).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Thread: large spools, several weights and colours** | The limiting consumable | Include heavy-duty and upholstery thread |
| **Needles: many, several sizes** | They bend, break and vanish | Include leather and curved needles |
| Wool darning yarn and a darning egg | Socks wear fastest | |
| Fabric scissors and a seam ripper | Sharp scissors make everything possible | Do not cut paper with them |
| Pins, many safety pins, thimble | A safety pin is a repair in itself | |
| **Spare zippers, buttons, snaps, hook-and-loop, elastic** | Parts that fail and cannot be made | Small and cheap |
| Patches: canvas, denim, nylon repair tape | The common repairs | |
| Awl and waxed thread | Boots, packs, heavy gear (→ 16-05) | |
| Water-repellent spray or wax bar | Restores waterproofing | Yearly |
| Sewing machine; hand-crank or treadle if found | Speed now; no power needed later | |
| Rag bag and parts bin | Nothing is thrown away whole | |

**No gear?** Fabric is in every closet, curtain, sheet, blanket, tarp, tent and sofa. Thread: unravel it
from a tightly woven edge; dental floss for heavy repairs; **the inner strands of paracord make
excellent thread.** Needles are the hard one: **stock real needles now.** Buttons from other garments,
carved wood or bone, cut plastic. Elastic: a drawstring channel, ties, hook-and-loop. Darning egg: a
light bulb, a smooth stone, a doorknob. Patches: any sturdy fabric; old jeans are ideal.

## When it runs out

- **Fabric lasts a very long time; thread and needles do not.** Stock thread and needles in quantities
  that feel absurd.
- **Runway:** a household that sews can keep clothing working for years; one that cannot is limited to
  what is intact now, often a season or two in hard use.
- **Ration:** repair early (cheap) rather than late (costly in thread and fabric). Keep the best thread
  for load-bearing repairs.
- **Resupply:** unpicking seams from unwanted garments gives usable thread; the parts bin is a real
  supply.
- **The ladder:** repair, patch, remake, felt, improvise. Each step uses more skill and less material.
- **Very long term:** spinning and weaving, and fibre animals where land allows. It starts with being
  able to sew (→ 24-01).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** learn the four repairs, build the kit, start the rag bag and parts bin, reinforce work
  clothes.
- **B (moving):** a small repair kit: a few needles, strong thread, safety pins, nylon repair tape, a
  spare zipper pull, duct tape. A failed coat zipper or boot seam on a winter move is an emergency
  (→ 11-06).
- **C (established somewhere else):** repair becomes routine work, and remaking is how growing children
  get clothed. Sewing is one of the most natural things to trade (→ 18-03).

pages.body:
# Summer heat and sun protection

**What this page is for.** How to dress, work, drink and cool a house when summer heat arrives and
there is no air conditioning: the heat-illness warning signs, clothing that keeps you cooler, running a
house cool without power, and protecting children.

> **CAUTION.** **Heat kills too.** A summer outage means no air conditioning in a house built to be
> air-conditioned. **Heat stroke is a medical emergency:** high body temperature, hot skin (dry or
> damp), confusion, collapse (CDC/NIOSH, Heat-Related Illnesses). Small children overheat faster than
> adults and a baby cannot tell you. **Never leave a child in a parked vehicle,** for any length of
> time (NWS, Heat Safety). Treatment for heat illness is on → 17-04 and → 12-05.

{{#if is.hot_summers}}**Your home climate:** July average high about {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F,
record high {{ region.home.record_high_f }} °F.{{else}}Even where summers are mild, a heat wave without
power is dangerous; this page applies when it comes.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Know the heat alerts.** NWS issues a **Heat Advisory** for dangerous heat and an **Extreme
   Heat Warning** (called an Excessive Heat Warning before March 2025) for extremely dangerous heat
   (NWS, Understanding Heat Alerts). Under a warning: heavy work stops in the heat of the day, and
   children and older people stay in the coolest place you have.
2. **Wide-brim hats and light long-sleeved sun shirts for everyone,** children included. Covering up
   beats sunscreen over a long event: **sunscreen runs out, cloth does not.**
3. **Stock sunscreen anyway,** check its dates, and plan as if it will run out.
4. **Find the coolest part of the house** (a basement, the north side, the ground floor) and make it the
   hot-day room, the summer version of the winter warm room (→ 08-01).
5. **Work out the summer water figure** (→ 03-01). Heat and hard work raise water needs a great deal
   (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply).

## Dressing for heat

The instinct is to wear less. **In strong sun, the better answer is to wear more of the right thing:**
lightweight, loose-fitting, light-coloured clothing over the skin (NWS, During a Heat Wave).

- **Loose and light-coloured.** Air moving between fabric and skin cools you; tight clothes block
  evaporation.
- **Cover up in direct sun.** A light long-sleeved shirt blocks the sun's heat and prevents sunburn,
  and **sunburn reduces the body's ability to get rid of heat** (NWS, During a Heat Wave).
- **A wide brim, not a ball cap.** Ears and the back of the neck are where people burn.
- **Cotton and linen are good in heat.** This is the one place cotton is right, the opposite of winter
  (→ 11-05): the water it holds cools you as it evaporates.
- **Light merino works in heat too,** and resists odour when washing is expensive.
- **Wet a shirt or bandana** and wear it. Evaporation cools for free, best in dry heat.

## The heat-illness ladder

Know the stages; the signs and first aid are from CDC/NIOSH (Heat-Related Illnesses) and repeated on
→ 17-04:

- **Heat cramps:** muscle cramps, heavy sweating. Rest, cool down, drink.
- **Heat exhaustion:** heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, cool clammy skin. **Stop,
  move somewhere cool, loosen clothing, cool the body, sip fluids.** This is the warning stage.
- **Heat stroke: a medical emergency.** High body temperature, hot skin (dry **or** damp), confusion,
  slurred speech, loss of consciousness. **Cool the person fast and get help.** Confusion in a hot
  person is the sign that matters most.

**Who is at greater risk:** infants and young children, people 65 and older, pregnant women, people
working in the sun, and people with chronic illness (CDC, About Heat and Your Health; NWS, Heat
Safety).{{#if has.young_child}} Your household has a young
child.{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}} Your household has an older member.{{/if}} **Heat and diabetes affect
each other:** high blood sugar increases urination and dehydration, and dehydration affects blood sugar;
plan fluids and checks and follow your clinician's sick-day guidance.{{#if has.condition.CL-01}} Your
household has type 1 diabetes: → 02-01.{{/if}}

## Cooling a house with no air conditioning

The winter warm room run backwards:

- **Closed by day, open by night.** Windows and heavy curtains closed against the sun in the day; **open
  everything once it is cooler outside than inside,** usually late evening. Cross-ventilate overnight,
  close up again at dawn. **This one habit is most of what you have.**
- **Block the sun before it reaches the glass.** Outside shade (awnings, tarps, trees, plywood over
  south and west windows) works far better than inside curtains.
- **Live low.** Heat rises; the basement or ground floor is cooler.{{#if has.basement}} Your basement is
  the summer room.{{/if}}
- **A fan is worth far more than its watts** (→ 09-01), used the right way. At night a fan in a
  window pulling cool air in transforms a room (NWS). **Above 90 °F indoors, do not point a fan at
  a person**: CDC says a fan can then raise body temperature, and NWS says the hot blowing air
  dries you out faster (CDC, About Heat and Your Health; NWS, During a Heat Wave). Use it to move
  hot air out instead, and cool people with water.
- **Do not cook indoors.** Cook outdoors (→ 07-01, → 07-02, → 07-03).
- **Wet towels and damp sheets** in a breezy window cool the incoming air, especially in dry heat.
{{#if has.pool}}- **Your pool** ({{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons) is a real cooling asset for people
  and as a cool mass of water. Drinking it is a different and much harder problem (→ 03-03).
{{/if}}
## Work, rest and water

- **Move the workday:** heavy work early morning and evening; rest through the hottest hours.
- **Work-rest cycles and fluids:** rest in shade often and drink before you are thirsty. For heat
  cramps, NIOSH's first aid is water plus a snack or a drink that replaces salts and carbohydrates
  every 15 to 20 minutes, and no salt tablets (CDC/NIOSH, Heat-Related Illnesses). In real heat the
  rest is longer than people want.
- **Water is the limit** (→ 03-01). Heat plus hard work can multiply water needs; reconcile that with
  storage, purification (→ 03-04) and the garden.
- **Salt matters** when sweating heavily for days: replace it with food or an electrolyte drink, not
  salt tablets (CDC/NIOSH). Keep salt available (→ 04-13).
- **Urine colour** is a free rough check of hydration: light yellow or clear usually means you are
  drinking enough; dark means drink more (CDC, About Heat and Your Health).

## Sun protection that does not run out

- **Cloth is the sunscreen that never expires:** long sleeves, brimmed hats, a neck cover.
- **Sunglasses:** real eye protection, with no eye doctor available.
- **Shade structures:** tarps, awnings, shade cloth over work and play areas. Build once; use every
  summer.
- **Sunburn is an injury:** it impairs cooling, hurts, blisters and can get infected (→ 12-03).

## Children in summer

- **Babies and toddlers cannot cool themselves well or tell you.** Watch for hot skin, flushing, unusual
  fussiness or sleepiness, and **fewer wet nappies** (a hydration sign).
- **Hats and sun shirts on every child** outdoors.
- **Never leave a child in a parked vehicle,** in any weather. NWS says it is never safe, even in
  winter; inside temperatures rise fast and kill (NWS, Heat Safety).
- **Water play cools and lifts morale, under the water-watcher and barrier rules on → 20-02,** which do
  not relax in a heat wave: an exhausted household and an inviting pool or tub is how drownings happen.
- **Shade the play area.**

## Medicines in the heat

Heat damages some medicines, especially insulin and others kept in the fridge (→ 29-07). Evaporative
cooling pouches help (→ 12-21). Using a medicine after a heat excursion is a decision card:
{{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09).{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}} Your household has refrigerated medicines:
plan their cooling with your summer power budget (→ 09-10).{{/if}}

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Wide-brim hats for everyone | Sunscreen that never runs out | Chin straps for small children |
| Light long-sleeved sun shirts | Cooler than bare skin in sun | Light colours, loose |
| Loose cotton or linen clothing | The one place cotton is right | |
| Sunglasses for everyone | Eye protection | Spares |
| Sunscreen | While it lasts | Watch the dates |
| Bandanas or neck covers | Wet them for evaporative cooling | |
| **12 V fans** | Best comfort per watt | → 09-01 |
| Shade cloth or tarps and poles | Shade work, play and garden areas | |
| A water bottle per person | Encourages drinking | → 03-01 |
| Electrolyte powder or salt | Days of heavy sweating | → 04-13 |
| Window screens or netting | Open windows at night without insects | → 03-08 |
| Indoor and outdoor thermometer | Tells you when to open the house | |

**No gear?** Any light long-sleeved shirt; a bandana under a cap to cover the neck; a brim from cardboard
and tape. Shade from tarps, sheets, plywood, cardboard on sunny windows. Cooling from wet cloth on the
neck and wrists, a damp sheet in a breezy window, a basin of water for the feet. Netting, tulle or
cheesecloth stapled over window openings is worth doing, because open windows at night are the core of
summer cooling and insects come in through open windows (→ 03-08).

## When it runs out

- **Sunscreen runs out; cloth and shade do not.** Plan around covering up and shade from the start.
- **Water is the real summer shortage** (→ 03-01, → 23-02). Work out the summer number, not the average.
- **Ration by shifting the work, not the water.** Rest in the heat, work in the cool hours, accept a
  slower pace.
- **Substitute:** shade for sunscreen; night ventilation for air conditioning; the lowest floor for the
  whole house; outdoor cooking for indoor.
- **Refrigerated medicines need the most cooling in summer,** when solar output is also highest. Plan the
  two together (→ 09-10).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the coolest room by day, night ventilation, outdoor cooking, a shaded play area.
- **B (moving):** summer travel is more survivable than winter travel, but it is a **water** problem,
  and water is heavy. Move early and late, rest in shade at midday, cover up, carry more water than
  feels necessary (→ 03-01).
- **C (established somewhere else):** less shade, more sun, more outdoor work. Build shade early and plan
  the day around the heat.

pages.body:
# Children's sizing ledger and next-size pipeline

**What this page is for.** Children's clothing is the one supply that runs out whatever you do: they
grow. This page is the household's tool for staying ahead: measure each child, record what fits, list
the next sizes you own and where they are stored, and check it every season. The reasons and the
clothing rules are on → 11-02. **Everything below is filled in by the household, in pencil: it
changes.**

> **CAUTION.** US children's clothing is sized by age, so the labels themselves show the pace: baby
> sizes step every 3 to 6 months (0-3, 3-6, 6-9, 9-12, 12-18, 18-24 months), and from toddler sizes
> on (2T, 3T, 4T, then 4, 5, 6) about one size a year. A child's own pace varies; the measurements
> below are what count. In a long emergency there is no store for the next size. **A reasonable
> target: the next two sizes for older children and the next three for toddlers,** or buy for a
> toddler twice a year.

## Do this now

1. **Measure each child and fill in the current-size table.** Height, weight and what actually fits
   today, not the label on the coat they are wearing.
2. **Walk the closets and bins and fill in the next-size grid.** You may own more of the next size than
   you think (hand-me-downs, gifts, end-of-season buys).
3. **Circle every empty box in the next-size column** and put those items on the next thrift-store
   trip. Next-size gaps are urgent; the size after is this year's project.
4. **Add "re-measure the children" to the seasonal calendar** (→ 24-03), and "buy the toddler's next
   size" to spring and autumn. Growth does not announce itself.

## Current sizes (re-measure every season)

| Child | Age | Date measured | Height | Weight | Clothing size | Boot size | Mitten size | Coat size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each children as c}}| {{c.label}} | {{c.age_text}} | ___ / ___ / ___ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| {{c.label}} | | ___ / ___ / ___ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| {{c.label}} | | ___ / ___ / ___ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
{{else}}| (no children listed) | | | | | | | | |
{{/each}}

When the table fills up, print the page again: the history shows how fast each child is growing.

## The next-size grid

"N" is the child's current size. Tick the box when the item is **in hand**, and write **where it is
stored** (a bin in the house, the vehicle, a destination). One grid per child. For a toddler, fill the
N+3 column too: a toddler moves through sizes faster than an older child, so N+2 may be only about
a year of runway.

{{#each children as c}}
**{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}): current size N = ______**

| Garment | N+1 | Stored | N+2 | Stored | N+3 (toddlers) | Stored |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base layer sets (×2) | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Mid layers or fleece (×2) | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Snowsuit, bunting or bibs | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Winter coat or parka | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Waterproof shell | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Insulated boots | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Wool socks (×6) | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Mittens (×3) | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Hats or balaclava (×2) | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Sleepers and sleep sacks (babies and toddlers) | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
| Everyday clothes bundle | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ | ☐ | ______ |
{{/each}}

## How to buy

- **Thrift stores and end-of-season sales are the whole strategy.** Buy next winter's size in late
  winter or spring, not in November. Children's winter gear is nearly free in spring and unobtainable
  in a crisis.
- **Buy by the grid, not on impulse:** fill the empty boxes first. A third fleece in the current size is
  worth less than one shell two sizes up.
- **Counts follow the count sheet on → 11-01** (sock and mitten counts apply to stored sizes too). The
  household inventory (→ 22-04) audits this page, and growth is a standing line on → 23-02.
- **Outgrown gear is trade goods** (→ 18-02): every family with children needs the next size.

## Where the bins are

A next-size bin stored where you would go is one you do not have to carry (→ 01-05). Only store gear at
a destination where the people there have agreed to it.

| Bin | Contents (sizes) | Lives at | Placed on | Last checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Next sizes: home | ______ | ______ | ___ / ___ / ___ | ___ / ___ / ___ |
| Next sizes: vehicle or travel bag | ______ | ______ | ___ / ___ / ___ | ___ / ___ / ___ |
{{#each agreed_destinations as d}}| Next sizes: {{d.name}} | ______ | ______ | ___ / ___ / ___ | ___ / ___ / ___ |
{{/each}}

Current-size hats, mittens and boots for each child also ride in each vehicle (→ 22-05); that cache is
separate from these bins and is checked on the same seasonal rhythm.

{{photo next-size-bins}}

## Hand-me-downs: inspect before counting

Clothing an older child outgrows can wait in a labelled bin for a younger one, which halves the buying.
**But children wear gear out:** toes worn through, knees gone, zippers dead, elastic perished by the time
it is needed. **Inspect before ticking a hand-me-down as "in hand".** Repair what can be repaired now
(→ 11-07), and treat worn-out items as raw material, not stock. A worn-out boot discovered in a crisis is
worse than a known gap.

## When it runs out

- **This ledger is the plan** for the fastest-depleting supply in the house. At the pace the size labels
  imply, a full grid buys roughly two years for an older child at N+2, less for a toddler; your own
  measurements tell you the real runway.
- **Beyond the grid:** cut down adult clothing (→ 11-07, → 16-04), trade outgrown gear (→ 18-02), and
  keep measuring.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** measure every season, fill gaps at thrift prices, label bins by size so anyone can
  find them.
- **B (moving):** the current-size bags and the next-size bin travel with you (→ 22-05). Bins already at
  a destination mean less to carry.
- **C (established somewhere else):** the ledger becomes the trade sheet: what your children need next
  and what they have outgrown is what other households want to swap (→ 18-02).

- → 12-02 **Bleeding control and wound care**: Stopping serious bleeding in the first minutes, then cleaning and caring for a wound over the following weeks so it does not become infected.

pages.body:
# Building a real first-aid and trauma kit

**What this page is for.** It lists what to buy and store so your household can handle the
injuries and illnesses that actually happen when no clinic is open. It is a supply list only.
How to use each item is on the treatment pages it points to.

> **Supplies are the smaller half of this.** A kit you do not know how to use is a bag of
> expensive props. **Take a Stop the Bleed course and a hands-on first-aid and CPR course
> now**, while classes still exist. They are short and inexpensive, and they are worth more
> than anything on this list. Nobody in your household needs to be a doctor; this binder is
> written for people who are not.

> **Life-critical medicines do not go in this kit.** Epinephrine auto-injectors (a pen that
> injects adrenaline into the thigh for a severe allergic reaction, → 02-03), insulin
> (→ 02-01, → 02-02) and any other medicine someone cannot go without belong in their own
> known place, reachable in seconds, never buried in a general first-aid bag.
> {{#if has.epinephrine}}Your household carries epinephrine: everyone, including older
> children, should know exactly where it is.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Take the courses.** Stop the Bleed (about an hour) and a Red Cross or equivalent first
   aid and CPR class. Every adult who could be the one responding.
2. **Count what you already own** against the "buy first" table below and write the counts on
   → 22-04. Assume you do not have a trauma kit until those counts are written down.
3. **Check everyone's tetanus vaccination** while clinics are open. A puncture wound with no
   clinic and an out-of-date tetanus shot is a dangerous combination, and it is easy to fix
   now (CDC, About Tetanus; → 12-04).
4. **Build the everyday kit first, then the trauma kit.** You will use adhesive bandages,
   tweezers and pain relief a hundred times for every time you need a tourniquet.
5. **Put a trauma kit where wood is cut and fires are lit.** Axes, saws, chainsaws and stoves
   are where serious injuries happen (→ 16-06, → 06-01).
6. **Stock quantities, not a boxed kit.** Commercial kits hold about six of everything. For
   {{ household.size }} people in a long event you want **boxes** of gauze, not packets.
7. **Photograph where each kit lives** and add the photo below and on → 12-08.

{{photo kit-locations}}

## Design the kit around what will actually happen

Forget television. In a long emergency at home, the realistic list of injuries and illness
looks like this:

| How often | What | Where it is covered |
|---|---|---|
| **Constant** | Cuts, scrapes, splinters, blisters, minor burns | → 12-02, → 12-03 |
| **Very likely** | Axe, saw and knife wounds from processing wood and food | → 12-02 |
| **Very likely** | Burns from stoves, open fires and hot liquids{{#if has.child}}, especially children{{/if}} | → 12-03 |
| **Very likely** | Diarrhoea and vomiting; dehydration (losing more water than you take in) | → 12-05 |
| **Likely** | Sprains, falls{{#if is.cold_winters}} on ice{{/if}}, broken bones | → 12-09, → 11-06 |
| **Likely** | Infected wounds, the thing that kills when there are no antibiotics | → 12-04 |
| **Likely** | Cold injuries | → 12-10, → 08-05 |
| **Likely** | Dental problems | → 12-06 |
| **Ongoing** | Long-term conditions and the medicines they depend on | → 12-11 |
| Less likely | Massive bleeding; this is what the trauma kit is for | → 12-02 |

**Design for the top of that list.** Most of your supplies should be gauze, tape, wound
cleaning and burn care, not exotic gear.

## The three tiers (detail on → 12-08)

1. **Everyday kit**: in the kitchen, used weekly. Bandages, antiseptic, tweezers, pain
   relief{{#if has.child}}, children's supplies{{/if}}.
2. **Trauma kit**: for serious bleeding. Small, fast to reach, in the places injuries happen:
   the woodpile or work area, the vehicle, the go-bag.
3. **Long-haul supplies**: the bulk stock. Boxes of gauze, tape, saline, splint material and
   over-the-counter (OTC, no prescription needed) medicines in quantity. Stored, rotated,
   counted.

## The core list

**Bleeding and wounds** (→ 12-02)
- **Tourniquet ×2 to 3** (a strap with a stick-like handle, the windlass, that you twist to
  stop blood flow to a limb), and **training in how to use one.** Buy a genuine
  windlass-type tourniquet of a model the Stop the Bleed course teaches. Cheap copies can snap
  or slip under load.
- **Hemostatic gauze ×2 to 4** (gauze treated with a substance that speeds clotting) and plain
  **compressed gauze** in quantity.
- **Pressure bandages ×2 to 4** (a roll bandage with a built-in pad and a clip you can put on
  with one hand; often sold as "emergency" or "Israeli-type" bandages).
- **Sterile gauze pads** in many sizes, **by the box**. This is your highest-volume item.
- Roller gauze, self-adherent wrap, medical tape (cloth and paper).
- Non-adherent dressings (pads that do not stick to a wound) and large abdominal pads.
- **Nitrile gloves by the box.** Not latex: latex allergy is common. Gloves protect the
  person giving care, which matters when there is no clinic for them either.
- Trauma shears, fine-point tweezers for splinters, an irrigation syringe (20 to 60 mL) for
  washing wounds.
- Sterile saline or clean drinkable water for washing wounds (→ 03-04).
- Wound-closure strips and skin adhesive. **Read → 12-14 before closing any wound.** Most
  wounds in a long emergency should not be closed.
- Antiseptics: povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine, alcohol wipes.
- Antibiotic ointment (→ 12-07).

**Burns** (→ 12-03)
- Sterile non-adherent burn dressings, clean cling film (a recommended burn covering), and
  plenty of clean water for cooling.

**Splints and support** (→ 12-09)
- **Moldable padded splint ×2** (a flexible aluminium-and-foam strip you bend to shape),
  elastic bandages, triangular bandages, athletic tape, a sling.

**Checking a patient**
- Thermometers (**several**, plus batteries), a blood pressure cuff, a pulse oximeter (a
  fingertip clip that reads oxygen level and pulse; needs batteries), a good headlamp
  (→ 10-01), a notepad and pen for a treatment log, and a watch with a second hand.

**Medicines**: see → 12-07 and → 12-13. Follow the label. For children, use only the
published dosing tables on → 12-13 and the label; never guess.

**Reference books on paper**
- A real first-aid manual. *Where There Is No Doctor* and *Where There Is No Dentist*
  (Hesperian) are widely used for exactly this situation. Buy physical copies.
- Your **family medical summary** (→ 25-09): conditions, medicines, allergies, blood types,
  vaccination dates. Written down, in this binder.

**For your household's own conditions**
{{#each members as m}}
- **{{m.label}}**: conditions {{m.conditions}}; allergies {{m.allergies}}. The supplies for
  these come from that condition's page (→ 12-11), not from this kit.
{{else}}
- No members are entered yet. Add them in settings so this list fills in.
{{/each}}
- Life-critical medicines (epinephrine, insulin, glucagon, rescue inhalers, seizure
  medicines) stay in their own known place. → 12-11 lists every condition page.

## The mistakes to avoid

- **Buying a boxed kit and calling it done.** A "300-piece" kit is mostly adhesive bandages. It
  is a restock source, not a plan.
- **Skipping the training.** Supplies without skills is the most common failure.
- **Burying the trauma kit in a closet.** Serious bleeding is a minutes problem. The kit has
  to be where the injury happens.
- **Nothing in the vehicle or the go-bag.**
- **Ignoring expiry dates.** Sterile packaging degrades; medicines lose strength. Count
  everything twice a year (→ 22-04).
{{#if has.child}}- **No children's sizes.** Small bandages, a child-suitable thermometer,
  children's medicine strengths and an oral dosing syringe. A one-year-old and a four-year-old
  need different everything.
{{else}}- **No children's sizes.** Even without children at home, you may be caring for
  someone else's child. Keep a few small bandages and children's medicine strengths.
{{/if}}- **Latex.** Use nitrile.

## Two things that prevent more harm than any kit treats

1. **Handwashing and clean water** (CDC, About Hygiene; → 13-02). Preventing infection is far
   cheaper than treating it when there are no antibiotics (→ 12-04).
2. **Not getting hurt.** Sharp tools used carefully (→ 16-02), traction on ice (→ 11-06), fire
   discipline (→ 10-02){{#if has.child}} and children kept away from the stove (→ 20-02){{/if}}
   prevent more harm than any amount of gauze fixes.

## Buy first: the life-saving core

Write what you own in the second column. Anything blank is the first thing to buy (also on
→ 22-07).

| Item | Owned (count) | Why it is first |
|---|---|---|
| **Genuine tourniquets ×2**, plus one for practice | ____ | The only fix for a limb bleed that pressure cannot hold (→ 12-02) |
| **Hemostatic gauze ×2** plus compressed gauze | ____ | Wounds in the groin, armpit and neck; packing |
| **Pressure bandages ×2** | ____ | One-handed and fast |
| **Oral rehydration salts (ORS) packets**, enough for at least 20 litres | ____ | Dehydration from diarrhoea is one of the biggest killers when water is unsafe (→ 12-05) |
| **Children's acetaminophen and ibuprofen in the strengths the published tables use, plus two oral dosing syringes** | ____ | The tables on → 12-13 are useless without the bottles and syringes |
| **CPR pocket mask**, adult and child sizes | ____ | → 12-18 |

## Build toward this

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop the Bleed course plus first-aid and CPR course** | Worth more than the whole kit | Every adult; refresh every few years |
| Genuine tourniquets ×2 to 3 | Copies fail under load | Train with a practice one |
| Hemostatic gauze ×2 to 4 | Bleeding pressure alone will not stop | Check expiry |
| Pressure bandages ×2 to 4 | One-handed use | |
| **Gauze pads and rolls by the box** | Highest-volume item by far | Assorted sizes |
| Nitrile gloves by the box | Protects the caregiver; no latex | Several sizes |
| Moldable splints ×2 plus elastic bandages | Falls and broken bones (→ 12-09) | Reusable |
| Trauma shears, fine tweezers, irrigation syringe | The three most-used tools | |
| Antiseptics (iodine, chlorhexidine) | Wound cleaning | Bulk |
| Non-adherent burn dressings plus cling film | Burns are a top-three likely injury | → 12-03 |
| Thermometers ×2 to 3 plus batteries | Fever is a critical signal (→ 12-04) | {{#if has.child}}Include one suited to small children{{else}}One spare{{/if}} |
| Blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter | Checking a patient with no clinic | Batteries |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* and *Where There Is No Dentist* on paper | The reference that matters | Physical copies |
| Family medical summary, printed | Conditions, medicines, allergies, blood types | → 25-09 |
| Labeled, sealed, waterproof containers | Findable in the dark, by anyone | Contents list on the outside |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Dressings:** clean cotton cloth, boiled and dried; clean sheets torn into strips.
  Sanitary pads and disposable diapers make good absorbent dressings: they come sealed and soak
  up a lot.
- **Washing wounds:** a clean squeeze bottle, a plastic bag with a pinhole, any syringe, and
  clean drinkable water (→ 03-04). Pressure and volume matter more than sterility.
- **Splints:** cardboard, magazines, sticks, foam pads, rolled newspaper (→ 12-09).
- **Tape:** duct tape or electrical tape over gauze, not directly on skin.
- **Slings and triangular bandages:** a T-shirt, a pillowcase, a scarf.
- **Cold packs:** snow, ice, a bag of anything frozen.
- **Tourniquet:** improvised tourniquets often fail. Buy real ones. If you must improvise, it
  needs a wide strap and a rigid stick to twist. Read → 12-02 first.
- **From other houses (→ 22-02):** medicine cabinets, veterinary supplies, first-aid stations
  in workplaces and vehicles, school and church kits.

## When it runs out

- **Gauze, tape and gloves run out fastest.** One significant wound with dressing changes for
  two weeks uses an astonishing amount. Stock in bulk and list it on → 23-02.
- **Count dressing changes, not packets.** One wound, changed twice a day for ten days, is
  twenty dressings, for one injury.
- **Ration:** wash and reuse cloth dressings, boiled, dried and stored clean. This is how it
  was done for most of history and it works. Keep sterile commercial dressings for fresh, deep
  or dirty wounds.
- **Resupply:** scavenging (above) and trade. Medical supplies are among the most valuable
  trade goods there are (→ 18-02). That cuts both ways: you can get them, and people will want
  yours. Think about what you tell others (→ 14-03).
- **Substitute:** clean cloth for gauze, boiled water for saline, honey as a wound dressing
  (→ 12-02), soap and water for antiseptic. **Cleanliness substitutes for almost everything;
  nothing substitutes for cleanliness.**
- **What cannot be substituted:** epinephrine, insulin and the other life-critical medicines
  on the condition pages (→ 12-11). Everything else on this page has a workaround.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** all three tiers set up. Everyday kit in the kitchen, trauma kits at the
  work area and in the vehicle, bulk stock stored and counted. Take the courses now.
- **B (moving):** a compact kit per adult: tourniquet, pressure bandage, gauze, tape, gloves,
  blister care, pain relief, **and each person's life-critical medicines first** (→ 22-03,
  → 01-07). Blisters and cold injury are the realistic problems on the move.
- **C (resettled):** further from help, more dangerous work (axes, animals, building), so you
  need more capability, not less. A trauma kit at every work site, a real supply store, and
  ideally someone in the group with real medical training (→ 18-03).

pages.title: Bleeding control and wound care
pages.body:
# Bleeding control and wound care

**What this page is for.** Stopping serious bleeding in the first minutes, then cleaning and
caring for a wound over the following weeks so it does not become infected. It is a reminder
card for people who have taken a hands-on course, not the course itself.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Reading this page does not make you able to do this.** Bleeding control is a physical
>   skill. **Take a Stop the Bleed course now**, while classes exist. It takes about an hour.
> - **Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no help
>   will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).** Re-bleeding and clot release
>   kill. While help can come, this is one of the binder's floors (→ 30-01): it is not offered
>   as a choice.
> - **Severe bleeding kills in minutes.** That is why the trauma kit lives where the work
>   happens (→ 12-01, → 12-08).
> - **Infection is the bigger long-term killer** when there is no clinic (→ 12-04). A wound
>   you survive in the first hour can still kill in the second week. Cleaning matters as much
>   as stopping the bleeding.

## Do this now: serious bleeding

1. **Make the scene safe.** Stop the chainsaw, step off the ice. A second casualty helps
   nobody.
2. **Find the bleeding.** Cut or pull clothing away. Blood soaks into dark cloth unseen.
3. **Press hard** on the wound with gauze or cloth and a gloved hand. **Do not lift to check.**
4. **Arm or leg still bleeding through pressure? Tourniquet:** 2 to 3 inches above the
   wound, never over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops **and** there is no pulse
   below it. Still bleeding? A second tourniquet above the first. **Write the time on it.
   Never loosen it while help can still come.**
5. **Groin, armpit or neck?** Pack the wound with gauze and press hard.
   **Chest or belly?** Do **not** pack. Cover and press.
6. **Keep them warm and lying flat.** Watch breathing. Then read → 12-16.

{{figure fig-tourniquet-placement}}

## Do this now: preparation

- **Take the Stop the Bleed course.** Every adult who might respond. Then buy genuine
  tourniquets and a practice one, and drill putting one on yourself, one-handed, in the dark,
  with gloves on.
- **Put a trauma kit where wood is cut.** Axe and saw injuries to the leg and foot are among
  the most likely serious bleeding events in a long emergency (→ 16-06). Until you have
  counted tourniquets, hemostatic gauze and pressure bandages on → 22-04, assume you do not
  have them (→ 12-01, "buy first").
- **Check tetanus vaccination dates for everyone** while clinics are open (→ 12-04, → 25-09).
- **Stock gauze in bulk.** One serious wound managed for two weeks uses far more dressing
  than any commercial kit contains.

## The order of operations for serious bleeding

This is the framework taught by Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons). Learn it in a
class; use this page as the reminder.

1. **Your own safety first.** Falling wood, a running saw, a fire, thin ice.
2. **Find the bleeding.** Look and feel. Use trauma shears to cut clothing away.
3. **Firm, direct pressure** with a gloved hand and gauze or cloth, **hard**, and **do not
   lift to check.** Most bleeding stops with steady direct pressure. It is the single most
   effective action and it needs no equipment.
4. **On an arm or leg, if pressure is not controlling it, use a tourniquet** (Stop the Bleed):
   - **2 to 3 inches above the wound, on the limb, never over a joint.** The bone of the
     knee or elbow stops the strap from squeezing the artery. If the wound is at or just below
     a joint, go above the joint.
   - **Tighten until the bleeding stops and there is no pulse below it**, then lock the
     windlass (the twisting handle) in its clip.
   - **If it still bleeds, put a second tourniquet above the first.**
   - **Write the time on it**: on the strap, the skin, the forehead, anywhere it will be seen.
   - It will hurt a great deal. That is expected.
   - **Small children:** a windlass tourniquet closes down on most children from about 2 years
     old. On an infant's or toddler's thinner limb it may not. Use direct pressure and packing
     instead.{{#if has.young_child}} You have a young child: practise direct pressure and
     packing on a pillow, not only the tourniquet.{{/if}}
5. **Junctional wounds** (groin, armpit, neck, where a tourniquet cannot go): **pack the wound**
   with hemostatic or plain gauze, pushing it in firmly until the wound is filled, and hold
   hard pressure. Packing is exactly what the course teaches. **Never pack a wound in the
   chest or abdomen** (Stop the Bleed): packing there pushes into the organs. Cover it and hold
   firm pressure. That is an injury to move toward whatever care exists (→ 12-16).
6. **Keep them warm** (→ 08-05), **lying flat**, and watch them. Blood loss plus cold is a
   dangerous combination{{#if is.cold_winters}}, and in your winters "keep them warm" is not
   an afterthought{{/if}}.

{{figure fig-wound-packing}}

### Once a tourniquet is on

**Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no help
will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).** Loosening lets the wound bleed
again and can release clots into the blood, and both kill. While help can come, this is a floor
(→ 30-01).

Be honest about what this means with no hospital. A tourniquet left on for many hours costs
the limb below it. Keep the person warm, keep them lying down, give fluids by mouth if they are
awake and can swallow, and move toward any care that exists (→ 12-16).

**When no help will ever come.** Military guidance for long, remote care converts a tourniquet
to wound packing and a pressure bandage under strict conditions (not in shock, the wound watched
closely, not an amputation, early, never after 6 hours), and tells people without medic training
to leave it on (TCCC Guidelines, 2026). Keeping it on risks the limb; converting risks the
bleeding starting again. Your household's choice: {{choice DC-25}} → 30-26.

**Myths that persist anyway:** a tourniquet does **not** automatically cost the limb when care
arrives within a few hours; pressing "pressure points" and raising the limb are **not**
substitutes for direct pressure; and **improvised tourniquets often fail** because they are too
narrow or lack a rigid windlass. Buy real ones.

## Cleaning a wound: the part that decides the outcome

With no clinic and possibly no antibiotics (→ 12-04), **cleaning the wound is your infection
control.**

- **Wash your hands first** (CDC, About Hygiene) and put on gloves. Every time.
- **Irrigate (flush) with lots of clean drinkable water.** This is the core of it. **Volume and
  pressure matter more than sterility.** A large syringe, a squeeze bottle, or a plastic bag
  with a pinhole gives the pressure. Use far more water than feels necessary.
- **Remove dirt and debris**: grit, splinters, gravel, bark, cloth. Anything left in the wound
  becomes an abscess (a pocket of pus) later. Use fine tweezers and good light (→ 10-01).
- **Antiseptics** (iodine, chlorhexidine) are for the **skin around** the wound. Strong
  antiseptics poured into a wound damage healthy tissue as well as germs. Clean water is the
  workhorse.
- **Dress it:** a non-stick layer against the wound, absorbent gauze over it, secured.
- **Change the dressing regularly and look at the wound every time.** This is how you catch
  infection early (→ 12-04).

## When not to close a wound

**Read → 12-14 before closing anything.** In brief: **closing a dirty wound traps the infection
inside.** Wounds that are dirty, deep, punctures, bites, more than several hours old, or from an
axe or chainsaw in a dirty place should generally **be left open**, packed lightly, and allowed
to heal from the bottom up. It is slower and uglier, and far safer without a surgeon and
antibiotics.

## The wounds a long emergency produces

| Wound | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Axe or hatchet to the foot or shin** | The classic wood-splitting injury. Deep, dirty, often bleeds hard. Sharp tools and a correctly placed chopping block prevent it (→ 16-06) |
| **Chainsaw** | Ragged, very dirty, severe. Chaps and protective gear are the answer; treatment without a surgeon is poor |
| **Knife, from butchering and cooking** | Frequent, usually clean, often deep in the hand (→ 05-09) |
| **Splinters and punctures** | Small and easy to dismiss, and the classic route to tetanus and abscesses |
| **Animal bites and scratches** | Always treated as dirty. Never close. High infection risk (→ 20-09, → 05-15) |
| **Burns** | Handled differently; see → 12-03 |
| **Crush injuries** | Falling wood, vehicles, machinery. Damage inside may be worse than what shows |
{{#if has.child}}| **Children's cuts and scrapes** | Constant. Clean well, cover, watch. Most are trivial; a few are not |
{{/if}}

## Eye injuries: shield, flush, or dark rest

Wood chips, wire ends, sunlight off snow. The three responses are very different, and mixing
them up is what costs sight.

- **Something stuck in or through the eye: shield it. Never remove it, never press**
  (MedlinePlus, Eye emergencies). Use rigid protection that rests on the bone around the eye,
  not on the eye: **a clean paper cup, or half a foam cup, taped over the eye socket.** Cover
  the other eye too if the person can bear it, because the eyes move together and movement
  grinds the object. No rubbing, no rinsing around it. **Nothing to eat or drink** (it may need
  surgery). Move toward whatever care exists (→ 12-16). The shield's job is to change nothing
  on the way.
- **Loose grit, eyelash or sawdust:** blinking and tears clear most of it. Help with a **gentle
  flush of clean water** (MedlinePlus). Never fingers or tweezers on the eyeball, and **never
  rub.**
- **Scratched eye (corneal abrasion):** the grit is out but it still feels like glass:
  scratchy pain, tears, light hurts. Flush once, then **stop touching it.** MedlinePlus says
  the discomfort of a minor scratch settles within a day or two. If pain gets worse, redness
  spreads, there is discharge, or sight gets worse instead of better, treat it as an infection
  (→ 12-04). Tight patching is no longer routine; do not press or rub an injured eye. Dark
  glasses for comfort are fine.
- **Snow blindness:** hours on snow or water glare, then that evening both eyes burn, water,
  and cannot stand light (American Academy of Ophthalmology, What Is Photokeratitis). It is a
  sunburn of the clear front of the eye. **It heals by itself, gradually, in about a day or
  two.** Treatment is dark rest: contact lenses out, a dim room or covered eyes, a cool cloth
  over closed lids, comfort measures from → 12-13. **Prevention is the real medicine:
  UV-blocking sunglasses or goggles on every snow and ice day (→ 11-08).** The field
  improvisation works: cardboard, bark or cloth with two narrow horizontal slits, tied on.
  Both eyes at once plus a day of glare means snow blindness; one eye, or no glare, means look
  for the other causes above.
- **Chemical splash in the eye** is covered on → 12-03 and → 12-17: flush with lukewarm water
  for 15 to 20 minutes, from the nose side outward, lids held open, starting now. It is more
  urgent than anything else in this list.

## Watching for infection: the second-week killer

Check at every dressing change and know the signs (→ 12-04; CDC, About Sepsis):
- Redness, swelling, warmth and pain that **increase after day two or three.** Normal healing
  gets less uncomfortable, not more.
- **Red streaks** spreading from the wound.
- **Pus or a foul smell.**
- **Fever, chills, feeling unwell all over.**
- **Confusion, fast breathing, fast heartbeat, extreme discomfort**: signs of **sepsis**, the
  body's overwhelming reaction to infection, a life-threatening emergency.

**Tetanus** (lockjaw, a germ from soil that causes muscle spasms) is a real risk with punctures
and dirty wounds. Early signs are jaw stiffness and muscle spasms. **There is no home treatment
once it starts.** The defence is the vaccine. After any wound, ask whether a booster is due now.
The CDC wound rule (CDC, About Tetanus; full table on → 12-04): **a clean minor wound needs a
booster if the last dose was 10 or more years ago; any other wound (dirty, puncture, bite,
burn, crush, frostbite) needs one if it was 5 or more years ago, ideally within 48 to 72
hours; fewer than 3 lifetime doses plus a dirty wound also calls for tetanus immune globulin**,
which only a clinic has. Everyone's dates belong on → 25-09.

## Honest limits

With no clinic, some injuries are beyond what a household can manage: bleeding inside the body
you cannot reach, deep chest or belly wounds, broken bones that cut off blood to a limb, severe
head injuries, and infections that outrun what you have. **→ 12-16 covers those decisions.**
Knowing your limits in advance is part of the plan. Prevention (→ 16-02 sharp tools, → 16-06
safe technique, → 11-06 traction) does more than any treatment page.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop the Bleed training** | The skill, not the gear, saves the life | Every adult; refresh |
| Genuine tourniquets ×2 to 3, plus a practice one | Copies fail | Count on → 22-04 |
| Hemostatic gauze ×2 to 4 | Wounds you cannot put a tourniquet on | Check expiry |
| Compressed and roller gauze, **in bulk** | The volume item | Boxes |
| Pressure bandages ×2 to 4 | One-handed, fast | |
| **Large irrigation syringe (20 to 60 mL)** | Flushing pressure is the infection control | Cheap; get several |
| Nitrile gloves by the box | Protects you and the wound | Not latex |
| Fine tweezers, magnifier, headlamp | Splinters and debris | Good light matters |
| Trauma shears | Cut clothing away fast | |
| Antiseptic (iodine, chlorhexidine) | Skin around the wound | Bulk |
| Non-stick dressings, abdominal pads, tape | Weeks of dressing changes | Quantity |
| Medical-grade honey (or plain honey) | Traditional wound dressing with real evidence | See below |
| A trauma kit at the work area and in the vehicle | Minutes matter | → 12-08 |
| Chainsaw chaps, safety glasses, cut-resistant gloves | **Prevention beats all of it** | → 16-06 |
| UV-blocking sunglasses or goggles for each person; a rigid eye shield (or clean paper cups) | Snow blindness; shielding a stuck object | → 11-08 |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* on paper | The reference | → 12-01 |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Dressings:** clean cotton cloth, boiled and dried; **sanitary pads and diapers** (sealed,
  very absorbent, excellent for this); clean torn sheets.
- **Flushing:** any squeeze bottle, a plastic bag with a pinhole, a turkey baster, and clean
  drinkable water (→ 03-04).
- **Honey** on clean wounds and burns has traditional and evidence-supported use: it fights
  germs and keeps the wound moist. **Not for deep punctures, and never for a baby under 12
  months** (risk of infant botulism, a rare paralysing illness).
- **Sugar packing** of infected wounds is another traditional method with real history.
- **Tape:** duct tape over gauze, not directly on skin; cloth strips tied.
- **Sterilising instruments:** boiling for a sustained time; flame for metal.
- **What you cannot improvise well:** a tourniquet, hemostatic gauze, and the training. Get all
  three now.

## When it runs out

- **Dressings go fastest.** One significant wound dressed twice a day for two weeks is dozens
  of dressings. Count in dressing changes, not packets (→ 23-02).
- **Ration:** wash and reuse cloth dressings, boiled, dried, stored clean. Keep sterile
  commercial dressings for fresh, deep or dirty wounds and for the first days.
- **Resupply:** medicine cabinets and workplace kits (→ 22-02); trade (→ 18-02); cloth, which is
  plentiful (→ 11-05).
- **Substitute:** clean cloth for gauze; boiled water for saline; soap, water and flushing for
  antiseptic; honey or sugar for antibiotic ointment on suitable wounds.
- **What cannot be substituted is cleanliness** (→ 13-02). Clean hands, clean water and clean
  cloth at every dressing change prevent far more harm than any supply here treats. When
  supplies run low, be more careful, not less.
- **The real answer is prevention.** Sharp tools that cut instead of glancing off (→ 16-02), a
  proper stance, chaps, gloves, not swinging an axe when exhausted or cold, traction on ice
  (→ 11-06). The wound you do not get costs nothing to treat.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** trauma kit at the work area and in the kitchen. Wood splitting and cooking
  are where the injuries are. Use clean water for flushing generously while you have it.
- **B (moving):** a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for each adult, reachable with one hand.
  Water for flushing is scarce on the move, so wound cleaning gets worse exactly when dirt goes
  up. Clean thoroughly at the next stop with real water.
- **C (resettled):** more axe work, more animals, more building, further from help. More
  capability, not less. A trauma kit at every work site, and protective gear treated as
  required.

pages.title: Burns (high risk around fire)
