- **Containers:** metal ammunition cans (waterproof, tough, obvious), tool boxes, dry bags,
  tackle boxes, clear plastic bins, gallon zip bags inside a backpack.
- **Labels:** tape and a marker. **Do it now**; unlabelled kits are half-useless.
- **Vehicle kit container:** a small duffel you can carry away if you end up walking.
- **Prompt cards:** index cards in a zip bag.

## When it runs out

- **The everyday kit runs out constantly.** That is normal and it is the signal to draw from the
  long-haul stock. Track it: "the bandages are gone" is easy to notice and easy to keep not
  fixing.
- **The long-haul stock decides how long you can manage injury and illness.** Estimate in
  **dressing changes and sick-days**, not in items (→ 12-02, → 12-05, → 23-02).
- **Ration:** as the long-haul stock falls, move the everyday kit toward washable cloth
  dressings (→ 12-02) and keep sterile commercial materials for fresh, deep or dirty wounds.
  **Never rob the trauma kit to restock the everyday kit.** That is the discipline that matters.
- **Resupply:** scavenging (→ 22-02), trade (→ 18-02), cloth from the household's fabric
  (→ 11-05).
- **Organisation itself is free.** Even with almost no supplies, the right things in the right
  places, and people who know where they are, is most of the value.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** all five kits placed, mapped, labelled and counted. Restock the everyday kit
  weekly from the long-haul stock.
- **B (moving):** the go-bag module and vehicle kit are what you have. **Life-critical medicines
  are the core**, and everything else competes with water and warmth for weight. Keep a
  tourniquet reachable one-handed, not at the bottom of a pack.
- **C (resettled):** rebuild the same structure: a trauma kit at every work area, an everyday
  kit in the living space, long-haul stock dry and above freezing. **Map and label again**; a
  kit nobody can find in an unfamiliar building is a kit you do not have.

pages.title: Splints, sprains and broken bones
pages.body:
# Splints, sprains and broken bones

**What this page is for.** Recognising a broken bone (fracture), splinting it, caring for
sprains, and planning for the weeks when an injured adult cannot work.

> **SAFETY**
> - **An open fracture, with bone through the skin, is a surgical emergency** with a very high
>   infection risk (→ 12-04). It is beyond household care.
> - **Do not try to straighten (realign) a broken bone from this page.** Realigning is a
>   procedure with real risk to nerves and blood vessels. It is taught hands-on in wilderness
>   first-aid courses; take one now (→ 24-01). The one exception, a limb with no pulse below the
>   break when no care is coming, is a decision card (→ 30-30).
> - **After any high-energy fall, check the head, neck, back, pelvis and belly before the
>   obvious limb.**
> - **A person lying still on cold ground is becoming hypothermic** (dangerously cold; CDC,
>   Preventing Hypothermia). Insulate them from the ground at once.

## Do this now: suspected broken bone

1. **Check the whole person first** after a big fall: head (→ 12-19), neck and back, pelvis,
   belly. Suspected neck, back, pelvis or hip injury: **do not move them** unless they are in
   immediate danger where they lie.
2. **Stop any bleeding** (→ 12-02). Bone showing? Cover it with a clean dressing; do not push it
   back.
3. **Check beyond the injury: colour, warmth, pulse, feeling, wiggle.** Write it down.
4. **Splint it as you found it.** Joint above and joint below. Pad every gap.
5. **Check colour, warmth, pulse and feeling again.** Worse? Loosen the splint at once.
6. **Get them off the cold ground, warm, and give pain relief** (→ 12-13).
7. **Re-check the splint every hour or so.** Swelling keeps building for hours.

{{figure fig-splint-joint-above-below}}

## Do this now: preparation

- **Buy traction cleats for boots and keep sand or ash for paths** (→ 11-06). Prevention is
  cheap compared to the injury.
- **Buy two moldable padded splints and elastic bandages**: light, reusable, and they make any
  fracture manageable.
- **Take a hands-on first-aid course that covers splinting.** Having done it once beats reading
  about it.
- **Plan for "one adult is down" now**: who does what, what gets dropped{{#if has.child}}, what
  the children can safely help with (→ 20-07){{/if}}, and how the household runs short-handed.
  Write it on → 00-07.

## Recognising what you are dealing with

You often cannot tell a bad sprain from a broken bone without an X-ray. **When in doubt, treat
it as broken.** Splinting a sprain costs a few days of inconvenience; walking on a fracture
costs far more.

**Signs of a broken bone:**
- **Deformity**: an angle, shortening, a limb that looks wrong
- **A crack or snap** heard or felt at the time
- **Cannot bear weight or use the limb at all**
- **One spot that is extremely painful to press**
- **Grating** when it moves
- **Fast, heavy swelling and bruising**
- **A wound over the suspected break**: assume it is an open fracture

**Signs it is an emergency beyond splinting:**
- **Bone showing, or a wound over the break** (open fracture)
- **The hand or foot beyond the injury is pale, cold, blue, numb or has no pulse.** Blood flow
  may be cut off, and the limb can be lost within hours. If any care exists, go now (→ 12-16).
  When no care is coming, published first-aid guidance says to try to bring the limb back toward
  its normal position, and wilderness first aid teaches gentle traction for it (MedlinePlus,
  Broken Bone; Wilderness First Aid Scope of Practice); splinting as found risks the limb, one
  gentle pull risks pain and added injury. Your household's choice: {{choice DC-29}} → 30-30.
  It must be learned hands-on, not from a page.
- **Suspected spine, neck, pelvis or hip fracture**: do not move the person except to save them
  from an immediate hazard
- **Suspected skull fracture or significant head injury** (→ 12-19)
- **Thigh bone (femur) fracture**: major internal bleeding risk
- **Several fractures, or a fracture with shock** (pale, cold, clammy, fast weak pulse,
  confused)

## Splinting: the principles

**The goal is to stop the injured part moving.** A splint reduces pain, prevents more damage and
lets the person be moved.

1. **Check circulation, feeling and movement beyond the injury before and after splinting**:
   colour, warmth, pulse, feeling, wiggle. **If splinting makes any of these worse, loosen it at
   once.** This is the most important step and the most often skipped.
2. **Splint it in the position found** where possible. Do not force a limb straight.
3. **Hold still the joint above and the joint below** the break.
4. **Pad everything**: bony points, gaps, anywhere the splint touches. Unpadded splints cause
   pressure sores over hours and days.
5. **Secure firmly but not tightly, and check again as swelling builds.** A splint that was fine
   at noon can cut off blood by evening. **Re-check repeatedly.**
6. **Raise the limb** where you can, and use cold early to limit swelling. Wrap ice or snow in
   cloth; never put it straight on skin.
7. **Treat the person, not just the limb**: pain relief (→ 12-13), fluids, warmth.
   {{#if is.cold_winters}}In your winters, a person lying still outdoors is a hypothermia case in
   progress (→ 08-05).{{/if}} Get insulation under them first.

## Sprains and strains

Most soft-tissue injuries are managed with **rest, cold early on, compression and raising the
limb**, then a gradual return to use.
- **If they cannot bear weight at all, treat it as a fracture** until shown otherwise.
- **Compression wraps must not be so tight they block circulation.** Same check as above.
- **Return to use gradually.** Keeping it still too long causes stiffness and weakness, which
  means a slower return to being useful.

## What a household can manage, and what it cannot

| Injury | Household capability |
|---|---|
| Finger or toe | Usually manageable: tape it to its neighbour (buddy-taping) or splint |
| Wrist or forearm | Splint and hold still; **may heal crooked without realignment** |
| Ankle | Splint, no weight on it; long recovery; **a major loss of working hands** |
| Collarbone | Sling and support; usually heals |
| Ribs | Pain relief and **deep-breathing exercises**: the danger is pneumonia from shallow breathing, not the bone. **Never tape, strap or bind the chest**: it stops the deep breaths that prevent pneumonia |
| **Open fracture** | **Beyond household care.** Clean dressing, splint, do not push bone back in, treat as a life-threatening infection risk (→ 12-04) |
| **Thigh bone** | Beyond household care; major bleeding risk |
| **Spine, pelvis, hip** | **Do not move.** Beyond household care |
| **Skull or significant head injury** | Beyond household care; watch for worsening (→ 12-19) |

**→ 12-16 covers what to do when something is beyond you and there is no hospital.** Think it
through before it happens.

## The part people do not plan for: losing a pair of hands

A broken bone takes an adult out of the work for weeks or months.
- **An adult on crutches cannot haul water, split wood{{#if has.young_child}} or carry a small
  child{{/if}}.**
- The other adults now do **everything**, including caring for the injured one.
- **If the injured person is the one who manages someone's medicines or medical devices**,
  someone else must already know how (→ 12-11). Every adult in the household should be able to
  do every life-critical medical routine.
- **Plan it in advance** (→ 00-07): what gets dropped, who can help, what neighbours could do
  (→ 18-01), and how long the household can run short-handed.
- **An injured adult may make leaving impossible** (→ 01-02).

## Prevention: where the leverage is

- **Traction on ice; sand and light the paths** (→ 11-06, → 10-01).{{#if is.cold_winters}}
  Falls on ice are the most likely source of a broken bone in your climate.{{/if}}
{{#if has.young_child}}- **Do not carry a small child across ice.** Clear the path or use a sled.
{{/if}}- **Ladder discipline.** Most household falls from height involve ladders, and there is
  no emergency room.
- **No sharp or heavy tool work when exhausted, cold or in poor light** (→ 16-06).
- **Sleds and carts instead of carrying** heavy loads on uneven or icy ground.
- **Handrails and lit stairs** in a dark house (→ 10-01).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Moldable padded splints ×2 to 3** | Light, reusable, fit anything | The core item; count on → 22-04 |
| Elastic bandages, several sizes | Compression and securing splints | High turnover |
| Triangular bandages and slings | Arm and shoulder injuries | Cheap; many uses |
| Athletic tape, self-adherent wrap | Buddy-taping, securing | Bulk |
| Padding: rolled gauze, foam, cloth | **Unpadded splints cause pressure sores** | Never skip |
| Crutches, cane or walker | Weeks of limited movement | Thrift stores; nobody has these until they need them |
| Cold packs (or snow, wrapped) | Early swelling control | |
| **Traction cleats; sand or ash for paths** | The prevention that matters most | → 11-06 |
| Sled or garden cart | Move loads and people without carrying on ice | → 11-06 |
| *Where There Is No Doctor* on paper | Real fracture guidance | → 12-01 |
| Written "one adult down" plan | The capability problem, solved in advance | → 00-07 |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Splint material:** cardboard (excellent: stiff, light, bendable when scored), rolled
  magazines or newspaper, sticks, a rolled foam sleeping pad, wooden slats, a broom handle,
  metal flashing, a book.
- **Padding:** clothing, towels, blankets, foam, moss, dry grass. **Use plenty.**
- **Securing:** torn cloth strips, cord, duct tape (**not directly on skin**), belts, elastic
  from clothing.
- **Sling:** a T-shirt, pillowcase, scarf, or the person's own shirt front pinned up.
- **Crutch:** a forked branch padded at the top, a hoe or rake handle, ski poles, a chair pushed
  as a walker.
- **Cold:** snow in a bag, ice, cold water, anything frozen. **Wrap it; never ice straight on
  skin**, especially when frostbite is a risk.

## When it runs out

- **Splint supplies barely run down.** Splints are reusable, elastic bandages wash, and
  cardboard is free. Supply is not the limit here.
- **What runs down is working hands, for weeks.** Put "one adult unavailable for 6 to 12 weeks"
  on the planning list and work out what it means for water, wood, food and medical care.
- **Ration work, not supplies.** Drop everything non-essential. Water, warmth, food and medical
  care come first; the garden and projects stop.
- **Substitute:**{{#if has.child}} children can genuinely help with small tasks, and it is good
  for them (→ 20-07);{{/if}} neighbours are a real resource, and this is the kind of concrete,
  bounded request that builds mutual aid (→ 18-01).
- **The permanent answer is prevention.** Cleats, sand, light, sleds, handrails, and no
  dangerous work when tired. All cheap, and the injury they prevent could halve the household's
  working strength for two months.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):**{{#if is.cold_winters}} ice is the hazard.{{/if}} Sand and light the path from
  the door to the woodpile and the water, keep cleats by the door, and use a sled for anything
  heavy.
- **B (moving):** **an injury on the move is one of the worst situations in the binder.** It
  can strand the household in the open. Move deliberately, do not carry more than you can
  manage, and treat an injured adult as a reason to stop and shelter (→ 01-02, → 01-03).
- **C (resettled):** more heavy work, more ladders, more animals, further from help. **Build the
  safety in early**: good steps, handrails, lit paths, carts. Keep splint material and crutches
  where they can be found.

pages.title: Cold injuries quick reference
pages.body:
# Cold injuries quick reference

**What this page is for.** A one-screen card to find the essentials on hypothermia, frostbite
and trench foot fast. The full guidance is on → 08-05; read it before you need this card.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Confusion in someone who is cold means hypothermia is serious.** They will not recognise
>   it themselves.
> - **Shivering that stops while the person is still cold is a severe warning sign, not
>   improvement.**
> - **Never rub frostbite, never use direct heat on it, and never thaw a part that may refreeze.**
> - Export this card to the vehicle kit and go-bag copies (→ 25-08).

## The three cold injuries

| | **Hypothermia** | **Frostbite** | **Trench foot (non-freezing)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| What | **Core** body temperature falling | Tissue actually **freezing** | Long hours **wet and cold**, above freezing |
| Where | Whole person | Fingers, toes, ears, nose, cheeks | Feet |
| Needs freezing temperatures? | **No**: happens above freezing, especially when wet | **Yes** | **No** |
| Key sign | **Shivering, then confusion, then shivering stops** | **Numb, white or waxy, hard** | Painful, pale, wet, wrinkled, numb |
| Emergency? | **Yes** | **Yes** | Serious, less sudden |

## Hypothermia: the one that kills

**Recognise** (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia):
- **Early:** shivering, cold, clumsy hands, tiredness
- **Worse:** **confusion, slurred speech, poor judgement, stumbling**, fumbling
- **Severe:** **shivering stops** while still cold, drowsiness, unconsciousness
- **In a baby:** bright red **or** pale cold skin, very low energy, weak cry, hard to wake.
  **Feel the belly and the back of the neck, not the hands** (→ 11-02).

> **The most important sign is confusion.** Remember "the umbles": stumbles, mumbles, fumbles,
> grumbles. Judge people by how they act, not by what they say.

**Respond:**
1. **Get out of the cold, wind and wet.**
2. **Remove all wet clothing.** Wet clothing is how heat is lost (→ 11-03).
3. **Dry layers; cover the head; insulate from the ground**, which steals heat fast.
4. **Warm the core gently**: blankets, dry clothes, skin-to-skin with a warm person, warm (not
   hot) drinks **only if fully awake and swallowing normally.**
5. **Handle gently.** Rough handling of a severely hypothermic person is dangerous.
6. **No alcohol. No rubbing. No hot-water bath. No direct high heat.**
7. **Keep watching.** People can get worse after being brought inside.

## Frostbite: where cold freezes tissue

**Recognise** (CDC, Preventing Frostbite):
- **Numbness**: the tissue stops hurting, which is the trap
- White, greyish-yellow or **waxy** skin
- Skin that feels **unusually firm or hard**
- Clumsiness in the affected part
- On rewarming: pain, tingling, redness, blisters

**Respond:**
1. **Get inside.** Off with wet gloves, socks and boots.
2. **Do not rub or massage** the area. It damages frozen tissue.
3. **No direct heat**: stove, fire, heater, hot water. **Numb skin burns without feeling it.**
4. **Rewarm in water at 98.6 to 102 °F (37 to 39 °C).** Numb skin cannot judge "warm", so
   **use a thermometer, or test with your own uninjured elbow** (comfortably warm, never hot).
   **15 to 30 minutes, until the part is soft and pink or red-purple**, topping up with warm
   water to hold the temperature. **Hotter burns the numb tissue; cooler does not thaw it**
   (Wilderness Medical Society frostbite guidelines, 2019 update; CDC). Body heat (armpits, a
   companion's belly) is the fallback when no warm water can be made. **Only if it will not
   refreeze** (next step).
5. **Do not thaw a part that might refreeze before you reach safety.** Refreezing thawed tissue
   is much worse. **This is a real decision on the move** (→ 01-03).
6. **Do not walk on thawed frostbitten feet.**
7. **Do not break blisters.** Cover, protect, watch for infection (→ 12-04).

**How fast skin freezes:** read the National Weather Service wind chill chart at today's actual
temperature and wind (NWS, Wind Chill Chart; → 29-10). In severe cold with wind, exposed skin
can freeze in **minutes**.{{#if is.extreme_cold}} Your home's record low is
{{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F.{{/if}}

## Trench foot (non-freezing cold injury)

**Happens above freezing**: wet socks and cold, for hours. **Likely in a grid-down winter when
drying things is hard** (→ 11-03).
- **Recognise:** feet painful, numb, pale or blotchy, wrinkled, swollen; may turn red and very
  painful on warming.
- **Respond:** **dry the feet**, warm them gradually, raise them, put on dry socks, keep them dry,
  and walk on them as little as possible. **Prevention is dry socks, changed often** (→ 11-04).

## Prevention card

- **Wet plus wind are the killers**, not just temperature.
- **Do not sweat.** Open layers before you overheat (→ 11-01).
- **No cotton** (→ 11-05).
- **Change into dry base layers before bed, every night.**
- **Hat on**: the fastest thermostat you have.
- **Mittens over gloves.**
- **Boots loose enough to wiggle your toes** (→ 11-06).
- **Eat and drink.** Staying warm burns calories, and dehydration in cold is easy.
- **No alcohol.**
{{#if has.child}}- **Check children by touch, not by asking** (→ 11-02): belly and back of the neck.
{{/if}}- **Check each other's faces** for white patches.
- **Check the wind chill chart** before going out. Set a time limit and keep it.

## When it is beyond you

- Severe hypothermia (unconscious, not shivering, very cold)
- Deep frostbite with blackened or hard tissue
- Any cold injury in a baby or toddler that does not improve quickly
- Cold injury together with another serious injury, or in someone with a condition from → 12-11
  (diabetes especially)

**Get professional care wherever it exists.** If it does not, → 12-16.

pages.title: Long-term conditions without a clinic: the condition library index
pages.body:
# Long-term conditions without a clinic: the condition library index

**What this page is for.** Every long-term condition this binder covers, in one table: what
it is, what runs out and how fast, the sign that means an emergency, and the page with the
full module. Your household's conditions are listed first. Then the questions to settle for
each condition while help still exists.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Never stop a medicine suddenly without knowing whether that is dangerous.** Several
>   medicines cause serious harm when stopped at once. Ask the prescriber which, now.
> - **The binder never calculates, stretches or adjusts a dose.** Published tables are printed
>   as published. Everything about your own medicines comes from your bottles and your
>   prescriber, written in the "my meds" table (→ 12-07).
> - **Some medicines have no household substitute**: insulin, epinephrine, and others marked on
>   the condition pages. For those, the plan when supply runs out is a decision, not a
>   substitution (→ 01-02).

## Conditions in this household

{{#each members as m}}
- **{{m.label}}** ({{m.age_text}}): conditions {{m.conditions}}; allergies {{m.allergies}}.
{{else}}
- No members entered yet. Add them in settings and tick their conditions.
{{/each}}

**Your modules, read these first:**

{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}- **CL-01 Type 1 diabetes (injections)** → 02-01
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}- **CL-02 Type 1 diabetes with pump and sensor** → 02-02
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-03}}- **CL-03 Anaphylaxis (any cause)** → 02-03
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}- **CL-04 Food allergy (child or adult)** → 02-04
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-05}}- **CL-05 Type 2 diabetes (tablets and non-insulin)** → 02-05
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-06}}- **CL-06 Type 2 diabetes on insulin** → 02-06
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-07}}- **CL-07 Asthma** → 02-07
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-08}}- **CL-08 COPD and oxygen dependence** → 02-08
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-09}}- **CL-09 High blood pressure and heart disease** → 02-09
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-10}}- **CL-10 Blood thinners (anticoagulants)** → 02-10
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-11}}- **CL-11 Epilepsy and seizure disorders** → 02-11
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-12}}- **CL-12 Pregnancy, birth and after birth** → 02-12
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-13}}- **CL-13 Infant feeding (nursing and formula)** → 02-13
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-14}}- **CL-14 Thyroid disease** → 02-14
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-15}}- **CL-15 Kidney disease and dialysis** → 02-15
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-16}}- **CL-16 Mental-health medicines** → 02-16
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-17}}- **CL-17 Opioid dependence and chronic pain** → 02-17
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-18}}- **CL-18 Immunosuppression and transplant** → 02-18
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-19}}- **CL-19 Celiac and severe gut disease** → 02-19
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-20}}- **CL-20 Adrenal insufficiency** → 02-20
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-21}}- **CL-21 Dementia and elderly care** → 02-21
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-22}}- **CL-22 Mobility impairment** → 02-22
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-23}}- **CL-23 Hearing and vision aids** → 02-23
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-24}}- **CL-24 Sleep apnoea (CPAP)** → 02-24
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-25}}- **CL-25 Contraception and menstrual health** → 02-25
{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-26}}- **CL-26 Severe obesity and bariatric surgery** → 02-26
{{/if}}

A condition you typed that is not in the library is on → 02-27, with the module's twelve
headings left blank for you to fill from the prescriber and the pharmacy leaflet.

## Do this now

1. **Read the module for each condition above**, start to finish, while nothing is wrong.
2. **Fill in the "my meds" table** (→ 12-07) from the bottles: name, strength, schedule, fridge
   or not, and **what the prescriber says to do if doses are missed**, in their words.
3. **Write each person's supply clock** (days of medicine and supplies on hand) on → 23-02, and
   update it as you use them.
4. **Make sure at least two adults can do every life-critical routine**: give the injection, use
   the auto-injector, change the device, recognise the emergency. Not "has watched"; **has
   done it.** → 12-09 explains why.
5. **Write the family medical summary** (→ 25-09): every condition, medicine, allergy,
   prescriber and blood type, on paper.

> **Before the collapse:** book a conversation with each prescriber. Say it plainly: "I'm doing
> emergency preparedness. If we could not reach care for a long time, what should I have, what
> should I know, and what warning signs must I not miss?" Clinicians have this conversation
> regularly. For each medicine, ask what happens if supply runs low or stops, which medicines
> must never stop suddenly, and what to do if a dose is missed. Write the answers in the "my
> meds" table and on the condition page.

## The full library

"Yes" marks a condition someone in your household has. The supply clock and emergency sign are
one-phrase reminders; the module has the detail.

| Yours | Id | Condition: what it is | What runs out | Emergency sign | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| {{#if has.condition.CL-01}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-01 | **Type 1 diabetes (injections)**: The body makes no insulin; insulin by injection keeps the person alive. | Insulin every day; it needs cold storage and has a limited life once opened. | Vomiting, deep fast breathing, fruity breath, confusion (high-sugar crisis); or shaking, sweating, confusion, passing out (low sugar). | → 02-01 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-02}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-02 | **Type 1 diabetes with pump and sensor**: As type 1, with insulin given by a pump and sugar read by a sensor. | Pump supplies, sensors and charging on top of insulin; when a device fails, back to injections. | As type 1, plus a pump or sensor failing with no injection supplies to fall back on. | → 02-02 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-03}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-03 | **Anaphylaxis (any cause)**: A sudden, severe allergic reaction that can close the airway or drop blood pressure. | Epinephrine auto-injectors expire; heat and freezing damage them. | After a trigger: trouble breathing, swelling of tongue or throat, faintness, widespread hives. Epinephrine now. | → 02-03 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-04}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-04 | **Food allergy (child or adult)**: A food that the immune system reacts to, sometimes with anaphylaxis. | Safe, labelled food; traded or scavenged food may hide the allergen. | Any sign of anaphylaxis after eating (as CL-03). | → 02-04 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-05}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-05 | **Type 2 diabetes (tablets and non-insulin)**: The body uses insulin poorly; managed with diet, tablets or non-insulin injections. | Pills on hand; most tablets keep well. | Extreme thirst and urination with confusion (very high sugar); shaking and confusion on some drugs (low sugar). | → 02-05 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-06}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-06 | **Type 2 diabetes on insulin**: Type 2 diabetes that now needs insulin injections. | Insulin cold storage and supply, as type 1. | Low sugar: shaking, sweating, confusion, passing out; or very high sugar with confusion. | → 02-06 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-07}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-07 | **Asthma**: The airways tighten and swell; inhalers open and calm them. | Inhaler canisters empty; smoke, cold air and dust make attacks more likely. | Cannot speak in full sentences, lips going blue, rescue inhaler not helping. | → 02-07 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-08}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-08 | **COPD and oxygen dependence**: Long-term lung damage; some people need extra oxygen. | Oxygen concentrators need power; cylinders run empty. | Severe breathlessness, blue lips, new confusion or drowsiness. | → 02-08 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-09}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-09 | **High blood pressure and heart disease**: Strain on the heart and blood vessels, managed with daily medicines. | Daily pills; some are dangerous to stop suddenly. | Chest pain or pressure; sudden face droop, arm weakness or slurred speech (stroke). | → 02-09 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-10}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-10 | **Blood thinners (anticoagulants)**: Medicines that slow clotting to prevent strokes and clots. | Daily pills; missed doses raise clot risk. | Bleeding that will not stop, any head injury, black or bloody stool; sudden leg swelling or breathlessness. | → 02-10 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-11}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-11 | **Epilepsy and seizure disorders**: The brain has repeated seizures; daily medicine prevents them. | Daily medicine; missed doses cause seizures. | A seizure that does not stop, or one after another without waking up. | → 02-11 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-12}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-12 | **Pregnancy, birth and after birth**: Carrying a baby, giving birth, and the weeks after. | The due date; prenatal vitamins; birth supplies. | Heavy bleeding, severe headache or vision changes, seizure, severe belly pain, trouble breathing. | → 02-12 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-13}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-13 | **Infant feeding (nursing and formula)**: Feeding a baby by breast or bottle. | Formula and safe water; the nursing parent's food and water. | A baby with few wet diapers, no tears, sunken soft spot, or too sleepy to feed. | → 02-13 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-14}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-14 | **Thyroid disease**: The thyroid gland makes too little or too much hormone. | Daily tablet; a long clock, and the tablets keep well. | Extreme drowsiness and confusion; or a racing heart with fever and agitation. | → 02-14 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-15}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-15 | **Kidney disease and dialysis**: The kidneys cannot clean the blood; some people need dialysis. | Dialysis sessions; every missed session counts. Fluid and potassium limits. | Breathlessness, swelling, an irregular heartbeat, confusion. | → 02-15 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-16}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-16 | **Mental-health medicines**: Medicines for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, psychosis and more. | Daily medicine; several are dangerous to stop suddenly. | Thoughts of suicide, losing touch with reality, severe withdrawal (→ 12-15). | → 02-16 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-17}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-17 | **Opioid dependence and chronic pain**: The body depends on opioid medicines, or pain is long-term. | Daily medicine; withdrawal begins when it stops. | Overdose: slow or no breathing, tiny pupils, cannot be woken. Naloxone. | → 02-17 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-18}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-18 | **Immunosuppression and transplant**: Medicines or illness that weaken the body's defence against infection. | Anti-rejection or immune medicines daily; missed doses risk rejection. | Any fever or sign of infection. | → 02-18 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-19}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-19 | **Celiac and severe gut disease**: Food or gut disease that causes damage, pain or diarrhoea. | Safe food supply; dehydration risk. | Dehydration, blood in the stool, severe belly pain. | → 02-19 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-20}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-20 | **Adrenal insufficiency**: The body cannot make enough of the stress hormone cortisol; daily steroid replaces it. | Daily steroid; illness and injury need extra, as the prescriber wrote. | Vomiting, severe weakness, collapse (adrenal crisis). | → 02-20 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-21}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-21 | **Dementia and elderly care**: Memory and judgement failing; frailty in old age. | Medicines someone must manage; warmth; supervision. | Sudden worse confusion, a fall, getting cold, wandering off. | → 02-21 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-22}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-22 | **Mobility impairment**: Needing a wheelchair, walker or help to move. | Batteries for powered chairs; spare parts; helpers. | Pressure sores turning red-hot or smelly; being unable to leave in an evacuation. | → 02-22 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-23}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-23 | **Hearing and vision aids**: Hearing aids, glasses, contact lenses. | Hearing-aid batteries; spare glasses; a written prescription. | Lost or broken aids in an emergency or evacuation. | → 02-23 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-24}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-24 | **Sleep apnoea (CPAP)**: Breathing stops repeatedly in sleep; a CPAP machine keeps the airway open. | Power every night. | Dangerous daytime sleepiness when driving or working. | → 02-24 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-25}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-25 | **Contraception and menstrual health**: Birth control and period care. | Pill packs and supplies run out. | Very heavy bleeding; signs of pregnancy (→ 02-12). | → 02-25 |
| {{#if has.condition.CL-26}}**Yes**{{/if}} | CL-26 | **Severe obesity and bariatric surgery**: Very high body weight, or after weight-loss surgery. | Lifelong vitamins after surgery; medicines absorbed differently. | Vomiting that will not stop, severe belly pain. | → 02-26 |

## For every condition, answer five questions

Do this for every condition in the household, with the prescriber while you can.

1. **What is the supply clock?** Days of medicine and supplies on hand, from the "my meds"
   table. It changes daily and belongs on → 23-02.
2. **What happens when it runs low?** Ask the prescriber what to do if doses are missed, and
   write their answer down. **This is a prescriber question, never one to work out alone under
   stress, and never one this binder answers.**
3. **What are the warning signs?** Written down, specific, known to every adult. What does
   "getting worse" look like, and when does it become an emergency?
4. **What is the fallback?** Is there a simpler version of the treatment that needs no power or
   device? For diabetes on a pump, it is insulin by syringe and a fingerstick meter (→ 02-02).
   Knowing the fallback turns a device failure into an inconvenience instead of a crisis.
5. **What is the decision point?** At what supply clock does this become the reason to move,
   seek care or change the plan? **Decide in advance and write it down** (→ 01-02, → 01-07).

## Principles for any long-term condition

- **Daily habits matter more when supply is short**: food, activity, sleep, stress and warmth all
  affect long-term conditions, and all are things you control.
- **Illness knocks long-term conditions off balance** (→ 12-05; CDC, Managing Sick Days). Plan
  for the combined event, not the single one. Ask each prescriber for written sick-day
  instructions.
- **Stress is physical, not just emotional** (→ 21-01). Months of crisis affect blood sugar,
  blood pressure, sleep and immunity.
- **Storage without power** is its own skill. Refrigerated medicines (→ 29-07, → 12-21), heat
  exposure and freezing (→ 12-07) each have published rules. Your household's choices on the
  related trade-offs: heat-exposed medicine {{choice DC-08}} (→ 30-09); expired medicine
  {{choice DC-04}} (→ 30-05); someone else's prescription {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16).
- **Write everything down.** Symptom, sugar and medicine logs (→ 25-05) replace the clinic's
  chart, and they matter enormously if you reach care.

## The honest part

**A household cannot make insulin, epinephrine or most other medicines.** No preparation changes
that. What preparation does:
- **Lengthens the supply clock**: a legitimate buffer, good storage, careful use (→ 12-07).
- **Makes the fallbacks work**, so a dead battery or a broken device is not a crisis.
- **Buys decision time**, so the decision to stay or go (→ 01-02) is made early, deliberately,
  with the resources to act on it.
- **Prevents the avoidable crises**: allergen discipline, sick-day management, infection
  prevention.

That is a great deal of value. It is not the same as solving the problem, and this binder does
not pretend otherwise. **For many conditions, the realistic best outcome in a long event is
reaching working medical care in time.** That is why the supply clock is a trigger on → 01-02,
and why closeness to surviving medical care belongs on the list when choosing a destination
(→ 01-05).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **A conversation with each prescriber** | The most valuable item in this section | Before the collapse |
| **Family medical summary, printed** | Conditions, medicines, allergies, blood types, prescribers | → 25-09 |
| The largest legitimate medicine buffer | The supply clock is everything | 90-day fills, early refills (→ 12-07) |
| Each module's supply list, in full | What that condition depends on | → 02-NN pages above |
| Power-free fallback supplies | Work when devices fail | Each module's "power and devices" part |
| Cooling for refrigerated medicines | Cold chain without the grid | → 12-21, → 09-10 |
| **Written care instructions any adult can follow** | The usual carer may be the one hurt | → 12-09 |
| Symptom, sugar and medicine logs | Replace the clinic's chart | → 25-05 |
| Written decision points | So → 01-02 is not improvised | → 01-02 |
| Medical ID for each person with a condition | Matters if people are separated | Cheap |

## When it runs out

- **Write the plan now, calmly:**
  - **Supply clock thresholds** for every life-critical medicine, with dates, checked weekly
    (→ 23-02).
  - **A trigger** at which the household stops sheltering and seeks resupply or care (→ 01-02).
    **Set it early enough that you still have the resources to act**, not at the last dose.
  - **A resupply plan**: where, who, what is realistic.
  - **A conversation, in advance, among the adults** about what happens if resupply fails
    (→ 12-16, → 21-03). Hard, and far better had now.
- **Rationing a prescription medicine is a prescriber's decision**, made in advance and written
  in the "If doses are missed" column. Never improvise a lower dose from a book.
- **Scavenging and trade:** pharmacies and clinics early in an event may still have supply; that
  window closes fast. Other households, nurses, pharmacists and doctors in the community are
  enormously valuable (→ 18-01, → 18-03). Never take unlabelled medicine (→ 12-07).
- **The strategic move is community and location.** A group with medical skill, or a place near
  surviving care, changes this problem more than any stockpile.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the best phase for this. Pharmacies, clinicians and supply may work for a
  while. **Use that window hard** for building the buffer and for the conversations. Track the
  supply clock from day one.
- **B (moving):** life-critical medicines are the most important cargo, protected from heat and
  cold, carried on a person (→ 22-03, → 01-07). **The reason to move is often the medicine
  itself** (→ 01-02). A serious medical event on the road means heading for the nearest working
  care; the destination can wait.
- **C (resettled):** no resupply and further from care. Find out where the nearest working
  medical care is and write it on → 25-03.

pages.title: Pregnancy, childbirth and women's health
pages.body:
# Pregnancy, childbirth and women's health

**What this page is for.** Planning for pregnancy in a long emergency, the warning signs that
must never be dismissed, contraception and menstrual supplies as preparedness items, and
everyday women's health. The full pregnancy, birth and after-birth module is → 02-12; infant
feeding is → 02-13; contraception and menstrual health is → 02-25.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Childbirth without a skilled attendant is one of the highest-risk situations in this
>   binder.** Deaths of mothers and babies in childbirth fell because of skilled attendants,
>   clean technique, the ability to stop heavy bleeding, and surgery when needed. **None of
>   those can be improvised from a book.**
> - **This page is planning, prevention and warning signs. It is deliberately not a delivery
>   manual.** If pregnancy is possible or present, the right preparation is **a trained
>   attendant identified in advance**, a real midwifery reference, and **being near working
>   care when the time comes** (→ 01-02, → 01-05).
> - **Learn the urgent maternal warning signs** (CDC, Hear Her; below) and post them. Many
>   mothers' deaths follow warning signs that were missed or dismissed.

{{#if has.pregnant}}> **Someone in your household is pregnant.** Read → 02-12 today. Write the due date
> on → 25-09 and make the decision on → 01-02 early, well before that date.{{/if}}

## Urgent maternal warning signs (CDC, Hear Her)

During pregnancy and in the year after birth, any of these needs care at once:
- Severe headache that will not go away or gets worse
- Dizziness or fainting
- Changes in vision
- Fever
- Trouble breathing
- Chest pain or a fast-beating heart
- Severe belly pain that will not go away
- Severe nausea and vomiting
- Baby's movements stopping or slowing during pregnancy
- Vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking during pregnancy
- Heavy bleeding or fluid leaking after pregnancy
- Swelling, redness or pain in a leg
- Very bad swelling of the hands or face
- Overwhelming tiredness
- Thoughts of harming yourself or the baby
- **"Something just doesn't feel right."** That is on the CDC's list because it matters. **Take
  it seriously when she says it.**

If any care exists, go. If not, → 12-16.

## Do this now

- **Decide, as a household, your position on pregnancy during a long crisis: explicitly, all
  the adults concerned, in advance.** It is a hard conversation and far better had calmly than
  after the fact. Whatever you decide, decide deliberately.
- **If the answer is "not now", stock contraception in depth**, watching expiry dates. It is
  cheap, light, and **removes the highest-risk medical scenario from the plan.**
- **Stock menstrual supplies deeply, and get reusable ones** (→ 13-08). The need goes on for
  years; menstrual cups and cloth pads end the dependency.
- **Find out now whether anyone in your circle has midwifery, nursing or obstetric training**
  (→ 18-01, → 18-03). That person is worth more than any supply on this page.

> **Before the collapse:** if long-acting contraception (an implant or IUD) fits your plans, ask
> a clinician now; it lasts for years with nothing further needed. Ask about extended fills for
> any prescription method (→ 12-07). If anyone is or may become pregnant, ask about prenatal
> care, prenatal vitamins and what their own risks are.

## Why this page matters even if nobody is pregnant

This binder plans for **months to years.** Over that time, in a household with adults of
reproductive age, pregnancy is a realistic possibility, planned or not, and it is **the single
highest-risk medical event that could plausibly happen.** Planning ahead is far better than
facing it unprepared.

**Contraception and menstrual supplies are consumables with a supply clock**, like food, and
they belong on → 23-02.

## Contraception as a preparedness item

Bluntly: **when childbirth is dangerous and there is no obstetric care, reliable contraception
is a life-safety item** (CDC, Contraception and Birth Control Methods).
- **Long-acting methods** (implants, IUDs) are placed by a clinician and then need nothing for
  years. If they fit your plans, doing it before a crisis removes the problem for the duration.
- **Prescription methods** need ongoing supply: ask about extended fills (→ 12-07).
- **Barrier methods** (condoms) keep for years in cool, dry storage, need no prescription, and
  **also reduce the spread of infections.** Stock them.
- **Fertility-awareness methods** need training and consistency and are less reliable than the
  above. They need no supplies, which is their advantage.
- **Whatever you use, stock extra and check expiry dates.**

## If pregnancy happens

**The goal becomes reaching skilled care by the time of delivery.** That is the plan; everything
else is backup.
- **Use any prenatal care that exists.**
- **Nutrition matters enormously**, and a stored-food diet has gaps (→ 04-18). **Prenatal
  vitamins, folic acid and iron** are cheap, keep well, and are worth stocking even with no
  current pregnancy.
- **Higher-risk pregnancies need care even more:** a first pregnancy, past complications,
  twins, and existing long-term conditions, **diabetes** especially, which greatly complicates
  pregnancy (→ 12-11).
- **The weeks after birth are dangerous too.** Heavy bleeding, infection, high blood pressure
  and blood clots can happen days or weeks later. Keep watching for the warning signs above.

## The realistic risks of an unattended birth

Stated plainly so the planning is honest (WHO, Maternal Health):
- **Heavy bleeding after birth (postpartum haemorrhage)**: the leading cause of mothers' deaths
  worldwide. Managing it takes medicines and skills a household does not have.
- **Labour that cannot progress (obstructed labour)**: needs surgery. There is no home answer.
- **Infection** of the mother or the newborn (→ 12-04).
- **Newborn problems**: trouble breathing at birth, being born early, getting cold. A newborn
  in a cold house is at serious risk.
- **Dangerously high blood pressure in pregnancy (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia)**: can kill, and
  is why blood pressure is checked in pregnancy.

**This list is the argument for → 01-02 and → 01-05.** A known pregnancy with a due date is one
of the strongest reasons to be near working medical care, and it should outweigh most other
considerations when deciding where to be.

## Newborns and infant feeding

- **Breastfeeding is the most robust way to feed a baby in a crisis**: no supply chain, no water
  treatment, no sterilising bottles, the right temperature, and it passes on protection against
  infection (CDC, Breastfeeding). Its advantages in a grid-down situation are enormous.
- **It needs the mother to be well fed and well watered.** A nursing mother needs much more food
  and fluid, and that goes on the food and water plan (→ 04-18, → 03-01).{{#if has.nursing}}
  Your household's daily water figure already includes extra for nursing
  ({{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons a day minimum).{{/if}}
- **If formula is needed**, it requires **safe water and clean preparation** (→ 03-04, → 20-05).
  Stock formula and safe water if there is any chance of needing it, and learn the preparation
  in advance.
- **Newborns lose heat very fast.** Skin-to-skin with a parent, a hat and a warm room (→ 08-01)
  matter more for a newborn than for anyone else (→ 11-02).
- Full detail: → 20-05 and → 02-13.

## Everyday women's health

- **Menstrual supplies**: a need for years. **Reusable cups and cloth pads end the dependency**,
  need only water and soap, and are the best purchase in this category (→ 13-08).
- **Urinary tract infections** are common, become serious if untreated (→ 12-04), and are more
  likely with less washing and less water. **Drinking enough and hygiene are the prevention**
  (→ 13-02).
- **Yeast and other infections** are more common with less washing; over-the-counter treatments
  are worth stocking (→ 12-07).
- **Long-term conditions and prescriptions**: same framework as → 12-11.
- **Menopause and other changes**: discuss supply and management with a clinician now.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Contraception, in depth** | Removes the highest-risk scenario | Ask about long-acting options now |
| **Reusable menstrual supplies (cups, cloth pads)** | Ends the supply dependency | → 13-08 |
| Disposable menstrual supplies as a buffer | Bridge and backup | Bulk |
| Prenatal vitamins, folic acid, iron | Cheap contingency that keeps well | Rotate |
| **The CDC warning signs above, posted** | Missed signs are how mothers die | Show every adult |
| Blood pressure cuff | High blood pressure is a leading risk | General use too (→ 12-01) |
| OTC treatments for urinary and yeast infection symptoms | Common with less washing | Check allergies |
| Clean birth supplies (if pregnancy is possible) | Sterile gloves, clean cloths, cord ties, bulb syringe, blankets | **Supplies do not replace an attendant** |
| Infant formula and safe water (contingency) | If breastfeeding is not possible | → 20-05, → 03-04 |
| A real midwifery reference and *Where There Is No Doctor* | Have it before you need it | Paper |
| **A trained attendant identified in your community** | Worth more than everything above | → 18-01, → 18-03 |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Menstrual:** clean cotton cloth, folded and washed. Historically standard and it works
  (→ 13-08). It needs water and soap, which is why → 13-09 matters.
- **Clean birth supplies:** boiled cloth, boiled string for tying the cord, a clean surface,
  clean hands. **Cleanliness is the one thing improvised supplies can truly deliver**, and it
  matters more than any equipment.
- **Newborn warmth:** skin-to-skin with a parent is the best method there is and needs nothing.
- **What you cannot improvise:** a skilled attendant, a way to stop heavy bleeding, surgery and
  blood. **That is why the plan is to be near care.**

## When it runs out

- **Contraception and menstrual supplies are the consumables here.** Put both on → 23-02.
  **Reusable menstrual supplies end one of those lines for good.**
- **If contraception is finite and the decision is "not now", its supply clock is a planning
  limit.** Settle it with a clinician before it becomes urgent.
- **Substitute for menstrual supplies:** clean cloth, washed and reused. Adequate, and it makes
  water and soap a women's health need (→ 13-02, → 13-09).
- **There is no substitute for obstetric care.** The strategy is: **avoid needing it, or be
  near it.**
- **Community is the real answer.** A midwife, nurse or doctor in your circle changes this more
  than any stockpile (→ 18-01, → 18-03). Find out now who is out there.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** clinics and pharmacies may work for a while. **Use that window** for
  contraception decisions, extended prescriptions and any delayed care. Being near a hospital is
  an asset worth weighing.
- **B (moving):** **do not move a woman late in pregnancy or soon after birth unless there is no
  alternative.** If there is a pregnancy, make the decision to move (→ 01-02) **early**, well
  before the due date, and move *toward* care.
- **C (resettled):** furthest from care. **If pregnancy is possible or present, closeness to
  working obstetric care should be a main reason for choosing a destination** (→ 01-05), above
  land, water and defensibility.

pages.title: Pain, fever and over-the-counter medicine reference
pages.body:
# Pain, fever and over-the-counter medicine reference

**What this page is for.** Using over-the-counter (OTC) pain and fever medicines safely, the
American Academy of Pediatrics' published children's dosing charts, the fever warning signs in
children, and pain relief that needs no medicine.

> **SAFETY**
> - **Read the package. Every time.** For adults, the label's directions govern. For children,
>   the only doses in this binder are the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) charts below,
>   printed as published. **This binder never calculates, adjusts or suggests a dose.**
> - **The three ways households hurt themselves with OTC pain relievers:**
>   1. **Overdose.** Above the daily maximum, acetaminophen can cause **liver failure**;
>      ibuprofen and similar drugs cause stomach bleeding and kidney damage. **The daily
>      maximum is a ceiling, not a suggestion.**
>   2. **Doubling up without knowing.** Cold, flu and sinus products **already contain pain
>      relievers.** Taking one with a separate pain reliever is a very common accidental
>      overdose. **Read every ingredient list.**
>   3. **Children.** Children's doses go **by weight**, measured with a **dosing syringe**, never
>      a kitchen spoon. Some medicines are **not for children at all.**
> - **Check every liquid, chewable and suspension against everyone's allergies** (→ 25-09):
>   flavourings and suspension bases can contain food allergens (FDA, Food Allergies).
> - **Never aspirin or other salicylates for children or teenagers** (Reye's syndrome, → 12-07).

## Do this now: a child has a fever

1. **Check the red flags below first.** A baby under 3 months with a fever of 100.4 °F (38 °C)
   or higher is an emergency, full stop.
2. **Weigh the child** (or use the weight on → 25-09 if it is recent).
3. **Read the bottle's strength** (mg per mL). It must match the chart column exactly.
4. **Find the weight row**, measure with a dosing syringe, and **write the time down** (→ 25-05)
   so two tired adults never double-dose.
5. **Keep them drinking** (→ 12-05). Comfort is the goal, not the thermometer number.

## Do this now: preparation

- **Buy accurate dosing syringes and cups** and keep them with the medicines.
- **Read the label of every OTC product you own** and mark the ones with a hidden pain reliever.
- **Write everyone's weight down** and update children's weights every few months (→ 25-09).
- **Check every product against the household allergy list.**

> **Before the collapse:** ask your pharmacist which OTC products suit each person in your
> household, and how to combine or alternate them for significant pain. Ask your child's doctor
> to confirm the chart row for each child's weight and the bottle you own, and write the answer
> on → 25-09 with the date. For anyone nursing, ask which products are fine (→ 12-07). These are
> free, five-minute conversations that make this page safe to act on.

## Children's dosing charts (AAP, as published)

Below are the American Academy of Pediatrics' two printable charts, transcribed in full: every
weight band, every product column, the dose line and the note printed on each chart (AAP,
HealthyChildren: Acetaminophen pictographic dosing chart, 2026 edition; Ibuprofen dosing chart,
2024). The rules beside them come from the AAP's own dosing-table pages (AAP, HealthyChildren:
Acetaminophen Dosing Tables for Fever and Pain in Children; Ibuprofen Dosing Table for Fever and
Pain). A dash (—) means the chart prints no dose for that product at that weight. **Find the
column that matches the bottle in your hand, then the weight row. Use weight; use age only if
you do not know the weight** (AAP).

### Acetaminophen (AAP chart, as published)

**Printed on the chart:** "Dose: For products labeled for children and infants, DO NOT GIVE MORE
THAN 5 DOSES IN 24 HOURS. For children over 12 years, extra strength tablets/gelcaps can be given
every 6 hours. DO NOT GIVE MORE THAN 6 EXTRA STRENGTH TABLETS/GELCAPS IN 24 HOURS. Acetaminophen
should not be given to children under two years of age without the guidance of a doctor."

| Weight | Age | Infants' Acetaminophen (160 mg / 5 mL) | Children's Acetaminophen (160 mg / 5 mL) | Children's Acetaminophen Chewables (160 mg) | Children's Acetaminophen Dissolvable Packets (160 mg / powder pack) | Adults' Acetaminophen Tablets (325 mg; regular strength) | Adults' Acetaminophen Tablets (500 mg; extra strength) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 to 11 pounds (3 to 5 kilograms) | 0 to 3 months | 1.25 mL | — | — | — | — | — |
| 12 to 17 pounds (5 to 7 kilograms) | 4 to 11 months | 2.5 mL | — | — | — | — | — |
| 18 to 23 pounds (8 to 10 kilograms) | 12 to 23 months | 3.75 mL | — | — | — | — | — |
| 24 to 35 pounds (11 to 15 kilograms) | 2 to 3 years | 5 mL | 5 mL | 1 tablet | — | — | — |
| 36 to 47 pounds (16 to 21 kilograms) | 4 to 5 years | — | 7.5 mL | 1 ½ tablets | — | — | — |
| 48 to 59 pounds (22 to 26 kilograms) | 6 to 8 years | — | 10 mL | 2 tablets | 2 packets | 1 tablet | — |
| 60 to 71 pounds (27 to 32 kilograms) | 9 to 10 years | — | 12.5 mL | 2 ½ tablets | 2 packets | 1 tablet | — |
| 72 to 95 pounds (33 to 43 kilograms) | 11 years | — | 15 mL | 3 tablets | 3 packets | 1 tablet | — |
| 96 pounds or more (44 kilograms or more) | 12 years or older | — | — | — | — | 2 tablets | 2 tablets |

**AAP's table notes for acetaminophen** (AAP, Acetaminophen Dosing Tables):
- "For children under 12 years, give every 4 hours while symptoms last. Do not give more than 5
  doses in 24 hours."
- "Acetaminophen should not be given to children under 2 years of age without the guidance of a
  doctor. Fever in the first 12 weeks may signal a serious infection and needs immediate medical
  attention." The 0 to 3 month row is on the chart; **a baby under 3 months with a fever is an
  emergency first** (red flags below).
- "Do not give 500 mg oral extra strength products to children under 12 years of age." "Do not
  give 650 mg oral extended-release products to children under 18 years of age."
- Use the dosing syringe that comes with the medicine; "Never use a kitchen teaspoon or
  tablespoon."

### Ibuprofen (AAP chart, as published)

**Printed on the chart:** "Dose: Give every 6 hours if needed, for fever or pain. DO NOT GIVE
MORE THAN 4 DOSES IN 24 HOURS. Do NOT use with any other medicine containing ibuprofen."

| Weight | Age | Infant's Ibuprofen Drops (50 mg / 1.25 mL) | Children's Liquid Ibuprofen (100 mg / 5 mL) | Children's Ibuprofen Chewable Tablets (100 mg) | Adult's Ibuprofen Tablets (200 mg) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 to 11 pounds (up to 5 kilograms) | 0 to 5 months | — | — | — | — |
| 12 to 17 pounds (about 6 to 7 kilograms) | 6 to 11 months | 1.25 mL | 2.5 mL* | — | — |
| 18 to 23 pounds (about 8 to 10 kilograms) | 12 to 23 months | 1.875 mL | 4 mL* | — | — |
| 24 to 35 pounds (about 11 to 15 kilograms) | 2 to 3 years | 2.5 mL | 5 mL* | 1 tablet | — |
| 36 to 47 pounds (about 16 to 21 kilograms) | 4 to 5 years | 3.75 mL | 7.5 mL* | 1 ½ tablets | — |
| 48 to 59 pounds (about 22 to 26 kilograms) | 6 to 8 years | 5 mL | 10 mL* | 2 tablets | 1 tablet |
| 60 to 71 pounds (about 27 to 32 kilograms) | 9 to 10 years | — | 12.5 mL* | 2 ½ tablets | 1 tablet |
| 72 to 95 pounds (about 33 to 43 kilograms) | 11 years | — | 15 mL* | 3 tablets | 1 ½ tablets |
| 96 pounds or more (44 kilograms or more) | 12 years or older | — | 10 mL + 10 mL = 20 mL* | 4 tablets | 2 tablets |

"\*Note: This dosage is for children's liquid ibuprofen products given by dropper. See the
previous column for correct dose-by-weight for infant ibuprofen drops, which are more
concentrated." (AAP chart.) **Infant drops (50 mg in 1.25 mL) and children's liquid (100 mg in
5 mL) are different strengths: read the bottle before every dose.**

**AAP's table notes for ibuprofen** (AAP, Ibuprofen Dosing Table):
- "Do not use ibuprofen in children who are less than 6 months old unless your child's doctor
  tells you to." The chart prints no dose below 6 months.
- "You can give ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours if needed." (The printed chart says every 6 hours,
  no more than 4 doses in 24 hours. Never closer together than 6 hours.)
- "It is also best not to give medicines with more than one ingredient in it to children less
  than 6 years of age."

### Rules that go with both charts

- **The label on the bottle you own governs if it differs.** Check the strength (mg per mL) every
  time; it must match the column you read.
- **Never aspirin for children** (Reye's syndrome, → 12-07).
- **Do not alternate the two drugs on an improvised schedule.** If a clinician gave you a written
  alternating plan, follow it exactly.
- **Write every dose down with the time** (→ 25-05).

{{#if has.child}}**Your children** (weights as typed in settings; re-weigh every few months):
{{#each members as m}}
- {{m.label}}: age {{m.age_text}}, weight {{m.weight_text}}
{{/each}}
Find each child's row yourself, from a current weight and the bottle in your hand.{{/if}}

## Fever in children: the red flags and two scary nights

From the AAP (When to Call the Pediatrician: Fever). **Any of these is an emergency, not a sick
day:**
- **A baby under 3 months with a fever of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, taken rectally.**
- Unusually drowsy, floppy or hard to wake
- Not drinking; no wet diapers
- Stiff neck, or a rash of tiny purple-red spots that do not fade when pressed
- Laboured or grunting breathing
- A seizure
- Crying that cannot be consoled at all

If care exists, go. If not, → 12-16. **Medicine treats comfort; it never replaces this check.**

**Febrile seizure** (a seizure brought on by fever; most common from about 6 months to 5 years):
terrifying, usually brief, and usually stops by itself. **On their side, protect from injury,
nothing in the mouth, time it.** Longer than about 5 minutes, one seizure after another, jerking
on one side only, or a child who does not wake up properly afterwards is an emergency: move
toward whatever care exists (→ 01-02).

**Croup** (most common at 1 to 3 years): a barking, seal-like cough with noisy breathing in,
worse at night. The first home measure is **calm plus cool night air**: bundle the child up and
step outside for 10 to 15 minutes. **Struggling to breathe at rest, drooling or unable to
swallow, or blue lips is an emergency.**

## What pain and fever medicine is actually for

With no clinic, these medicines do three valuable things:
1. **Let an injured or sick person sleep**, which is part of recovery.
2. **Let a feverish person drink and eat**, which is what actually prevents dehydration (→ 12-05).
3. **Keep people functional.** Someone in severe pain makes bad decisions.

**They do not treat the cause.** Masking pain can hide a worsening infection or injury, **so keep
watching for the warning signs** (→ 12-04) even when someone feels better. **Feeling better on
medicine is not the same as getting better.**

## The categories (no doses, no brands)

| Category | What it does | Key cautions: **read the label** |
|---|---|---|
| **Acetaminophen** | Pain, fever | **Liver damage above the daily maximum.** Hidden in many combination products. Alcohol raises the risk |
| **NSAIDs** (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: ibuprofen, naproxen) | Pain, fever, **swelling** | Stomach bleeding, kidney effects; take with food; caution with dehydration, kidney disease and some conditions (→ 12-11) |
| **Aspirin** | Pain, fever, specific uses | **Not for children or teenagers** (Reye's syndrome). Bleeding risk |
| **Rub-on pain relievers** | Local muscle and joint pain | Not with heat; away from eyes and broken skin |
| **Antihistamines** | Allergy symptoms, itching; some cause drowsiness | **Not a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis** (→ 02-03). Children's diphenhydramine label: **do not use under 2; ages 2 to 5 only if a doctor directs.** **Never use it to make a child sleep** (FDA, Drug Safety Communication on diphenhydramine). Non-drowsy antihistamines made for children exist; the label gives the age and dose. Drowsy types dull adult judgement too |
| **Combination cold and flu products** | Several symptoms | **Contain pain relievers: the doubling-up trap** |

**Practical points:**
- **The two main pain relievers work differently**, which is why a clinician may advise using
  them in a pattern for significant pain. Ask your pharmacist before the collapse and write it
  down.
- **NSAIDs reduce swelling and acetaminophen does not**, which matters for sprains and tooth
  pain.
- **After a head injury (→ 12-19), use acetaminophen, not ibuprofen or another NSAID, while a
  bleed inside the skull is still possible** (the first 48 hours of the watch). NSAIDs thin the
  blood slightly; the headache pill should not add to a bleed you cannot see.

## Fever: the judgement, not the number

Fever is the body fighting infection. **You are treating the person's comfort and ability to
function, not the thermometer.**
- **Write temperatures down with the time** (→ 25-05). The trend matters more than any reading.
- **A comfortable, drinking, resting person with a fever is usually fine.** One who cannot
  drink, cannot rest, or is getting worse is not.
- **Fever plus confusion, fast breathing or a fast heartbeat may be sepsis** (→ 12-04; CDC,
  About Sepsis): an emergency whatever the number.
- **Fever in someone with a long-term condition can be a sick-day event** (CDC, Managing Sick
  Days). Diabetes, adrenal insufficiency and a weakened immune system each have their own rules
  (→ 12-11).
- **Most fevers come from viruses, where antibiotics do nothing** (CDC, Antibiotic Use; → 12-04).

## Pain relief without medicine: more important as supplies fall

Free, unlimited and effective:
- **Rest and keeping the injured part still**: for injuries, most of the treatment (→ 12-09).
- **Cold** early (swelling, fresh injury); **heat** later (muscle pain, stiffness). **No heat on
  a spreading infection.**
- **Raising** a swollen limb.
- **Positioning**: find the position that hurts least and support it with pillows and rolled
  blankets.
- **Distraction, slow breathing and calm.** Effective, especially for children (→ 20-08). Fear
  makes pain worse (→ 21-01).
- **Warmth and comfort.** A cold, frightened person in pain is worse off in every way.
- **Salt-water rinses** for tooth and throat pain (→ 12-06).
- **Sleep.** Protecting an injured person's sleep is real treatment (→ 21-07).

## Mistakes to avoid

- **Doubling up** through combination products: the most common real-world overdose.
- **Going over the daily maximum** because the pain is not controlled. **If the maximum is not
  working, the answer is not more; it is reassessment** (→ 12-16).
- **Dosing a child by guessing.** By weight, with a syringe, from the label or the AAP chart.
- **Aspirin for a child.**
- **Masking a worsening problem.** Keep checking the wound, the temperature and the trend.
- **Ignoring interactions** with prescriptions. Ask the pharmacist while you can.
- **An allergen hidden in a medicine.** Check every label.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Acetaminophen and ibuprofen, adult **and** children's | The most-used medicines in the binder | Bulk; rotate; children's bottles in the strengths the chart uses |
| **Dosing syringes and cups** | Accurate children's doses | Never a kitchen spoon |
| Thermometers ×2 to 3 plus batteries | Fever tracking | One suited to children |
| Antihistamines | Allergy symptoms, itching | **Not for anaphylaxis.** Check the age on the label |
| Rub-on pain reliever | Muscle and joint pain | |
| **Written pharmacist and doctor answers for your household** | Makes this page safe to act on | Before the collapse |
| **Weights and allergy list for everyone** | Children's doses and safety | → 25-09 |
| Symptom and temperature log sheets | Trends beat single readings | → 25-05 |
| Cold packs or snow, a heat source, pillows | The no-medicine half | Free |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Medicine cabinets (→ 22-02):** OTC pain relievers are among the most common and useful finds.
  **Original labelled containers only**; never unidentified pills.
- **Pain relief without medicine** (above) is the real substitute, and it does not run out.
- **Willow bark** contains a salicylate related to aspirin and has a long history. **It carries
  the same risks as aspirin, including not for children, and its strength is unreliable.** If
  you use it, learn it properly in advance.
- **Honey** for cough and sore throat has real support. **Never under 12 months** (infant
  botulism).
- **What you cannot improvise:** a reliable dose. That is why the no-medicine methods deserve
  more attention than they get.

## When it runs out

- **Pain relievers are among the fastest-used medicines**: headaches, sore backs, injuries,
  fevers, tooth pain, {{ household.size }} people, months. **Stock far more than a normal
  household** and list it on → 23-02.
- **Use them for function, not comfort alone, as supply falls**: letting a feverish child drink,
  letting an injured adult sleep, controlling tooth pain enough to eat. Use the no-medicine
  methods for ordinary aches.
- **Put the smallest, the sickest and the people the household depends on first.**
- **Expiry:** liquids and children's suspensions expire faster than tablets (→ 12-07). **Rotate
  the children's products most actively.** Splitting an adult tablet for a child is never done
  without a clinician's written instruction, and for some medicines not at all. Ask your
  pharmacist before the collapse.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** stock deep while pharmacies work, have the pharmacist and doctor
  conversations, start the logging habit. Nobody gives a child medicine without the label, the
  chart and the syringe.
- **B (moving):** a compact supply of both medicines, adult and children's, plus the dosing
  syringe, in the medical module (→ 22-03). Pain control on the move is about keeping people
  able to keep going.
- **C (resettled):** no resupply and more injuries. **Pain relief without medicine becomes the
  main tool**, and the stocked medicine a reserve for real need. Build the habit early.

pages.title: Wound closure, drainage, and when not to close
pages.body:
# Wound closure, drainage, and when not to close

**What this page is for.** Deciding whether a wound should be closed at all (usually not), the
safest ways to close the few that should be, packing an open wound, and why draining an abscess
is a procedure, not a home trick.

> **SAFETY**
> - **The most important thing on this page is a negative: most wounds in a long emergency
>   should not be closed.**
> - Suture kits are popular with preppers and are **one of the items most likely to cause harm
>   in untrained hands.** **Closing a dirty wound traps germs inside**, turning a wound that would
>   have healed slowly into an abscess, a deep infection or sepsis (→ 12-04), with no surgeon and
>   perhaps no antibiotics.
> - **The axe wound, the chainsaw wound, the animal bite, the puncture: the wounds a long
>   emergency produces are almost all wounds to leave open.**
> - **This page teaches no stitching or cutting technique.** Get *Where There Is No Doctor*, and
>   if you want real skill, get real training before you need it (→ 24-01).

## Do this now: should I close this wound?

1. **Clean it first, thoroughly** (→ 12-02). Always.
2. **Run the "do not close" list below.** Any one item: **leave it open**, pack it loosely, dress
   it.
3. **Clean, fresh, shallow, straight edges that meet without pulling, nothing on the list?**
   Closure strips or skin glue may be reasonable.
4. **Unsure? Leave it open.** A bigger scar is acceptable; a trapped infection is not.
5. **Check tetanus** (→ 12-04).

## Do this now: preparation

- **Learn the "do not close" list.** It is the part that saves people, and it is free.
- **Buy wound-closure strips and skin glue, not a suture kit**, as your first purchase. They
  handle the wounds a household should actually close, and they trap infection far less.
- **Buy far more gauze and flushing supplies than closure supplies** (→ 12-02). Cleaning and
  packing is what you will actually do.
- **Bring everyone's tetanus vaccination up to date** (→ 12-04; CDC, About Tetanus).

## Why an open wound is often the safer wound

A wound heals in one of two ways:
- **Closed (primary closure):** edges brought together; heals fast with a small scar. **Only
  right for clean, fresh, well-cleaned wounds.**
- **Left open (healing by secondary intention):** packed and allowed to fill in from the bottom.
  **Slower and uglier, and far safer for anything dirty.**

**With no surgeon and few antibiotics, leaving it open is your default.**

## The do-not-close list: learn it by heart

**Do not close a wound that is:**
- **Dirty**: soil, manure, rust, wood, bark, gravel, cloth fibres
- **A puncture**: deep, narrow, impossible to clean; the classic tetanus and abscess risk
- **An animal or human bite**: **always** dirty, always high infection risk (→ 20-09, → 05-15)
- **More than several hours old**: germs have multiplied
- **Already showing signs of infection** (→ 12-04)
- **Deep, with damage you cannot see the bottom of**
- **From crushing**, with damaged tissue at the edges
- **Over a joint, or where the edges will not line up**
- **Somewhere you are not sure what lies underneath** (tendons, nerves, arteries)
- **On the face, hands or genitals**: these need proper care for function and appearance; seek
  real care if it exists

**In other words: nearly everything an axe, a chainsaw, an animal or a fall on rough ground
produces.**

## The narrow case where closing is reasonable

- **Clean and fresh** (within a few hours) and thoroughly flushed (→ 12-02)
- **Straight edges** that meet easily without pulling
- **Not deep**, nothing left in it, no sign of dirt
- Somewhere a gaping wound would cause real trouble
- **You are sure what is underneath**

**Even then, closure strips or skin glue usually do the job**, and they have a big safety
advantage: **they come off instantly** if the wound starts to look infected. Removing stitches
from a swollen infected wound is far worse.

## Closure options, safest first

1. **Nothing**: clean, dress and let it heal open. Right for most wounds in a long emergency.
2. **Closure strips** (thin adhesive strips laid across the cut): no needle, easy to remove, good
   for shallow clean cuts. **Your main closure tool.**
3. **Skin glue (medical adhesive):** good for clean wounds that close without pulling. **Never
   inside a wound**: it goes on the surface across the closed edges.
4. **Stitches or staples:** real capability, real risk, **real training required.** Not from a
   book. If nobody in your household or community is trained, this option does not exist for
   you; the first three still do.

{{figure fig-closure-strips}}

## Packing an open wound

What you will do far more often than closing.
- **Flush thoroughly first** (→ 12-02): volume and pressure.
- **Pack loosely** with clean gauze so the wound stays open at the surface and heals from the
  bottom up. **A wound that seals over at the skin while still infected underneath is how
  abscesses form.**
- **Change the packing regularly and look at the wound every time.**
- **Watch for infection signs** at every change (→ 12-04).
- A significant wound needs this for **weeks**. That is a lot of dressing material (→ 12-02).

## Abscesses and drainage

A closed pocket of pus does not clear with antibiotics alone; **it needs to drain.** Draining it
is a historically standard treatment, and it is also a **procedure**:
- **Location matters enormously.** An abscess on the face, neck, hand or groin, or near large
  blood vessels, is dangerous to open and can go badly wrong.
- **Some swellings are not abscesses**, and cutting into them causes serious harm.
- **After draining, the cavity is packed and heals from the bottom**, as above.
- **Warm compresses** may bring a shallow abscess to a head so it drains by itself. Try that
  first.
- **This binder gives no cutting procedure.** Read a real reference in advance and get hands-on
  training if you want the skill. Tooth abscesses: → 12-20.

## Aftercare: where the outcome is decided

- **Clean hands and gloves at every dressing change** (CDC, About Hygiene). This is the whole
  game.
- **Look at the wound every time.** Less redness and pain is normal; more is a warning (→ 12-04).
- **Keep it clean and slightly moist.** Modern practice favours moist healing over letting a wound
  dry into a hard scab.
- **Honey** on suitable clean wounds has traditional and evidence-supported use. **Never for a
  baby under 12 months** (infant botulism).
- **Support the person:** food, protein, fluids, warmth, sleep. A well-fed, warm, rested person
  heals much better.
- **Keep wounds over joints still** so they are not reopened again and again.
- **Tetanus** (CDC, About Tetanus): no home treatment once it starts. **The booster decision is
  the part you can act on: → 12-04 prints the CDC rule** (clean minor wound: booster if 10 or
  more years since the last dose; any other wound: if 5 or more years, within 48 to 72 hours;
  fewer than 3 lifetime doses plus a dirty wound: tetanus immune globulin too).

## The realistic picture

With clean water, careful flushing, clean dressings and patience, **a household can manage a
great many wounds well.** People did it for centuries. What they could not do, and you cannot
either, is rescue a wound closed over dirt, or an infection that has spread through the body.
**The discipline of not closing is the most valuable thing on this page, and it costs nothing.**

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Closure strips, many, several widths** | The main closure tool; removable | Buy generously |
| Skin glue (medical adhesive) | Clean wounds that close without pulling | Check expiry |
| Tincture of benzoin or adhesive prep | Makes closure strips actually hold | Underrated |
| **Gauze for packing, bulk, several widths** | What you will use for weeks | The real consumable |
| Large flushing syringe (20 to 60 mL) | Cleaning is the treatment | Get several (→ 12-02) |
| Sterile saline or clean water in quantity | Volume matters | → 03-04 |
| Fine tweezers, artery forceps, good light | Removing debris | Headlamp (→ 10-01) |
| Nitrile gloves by the box | Every dressing change | Not latex |
| Non-stick dressings, tape | Over the packing | Bulk |
| Raw or medical-grade honey | Traditional dressing with support | **Never under 12 months** |
| ***Where There Is No Doctor* on paper** | Real guidance on closure and abscesses | Read it in advance |
| Suture or staple kit | **Only with real training** | Otherwise leave it out |

## Scavenge or substitute

- **Closure strips:** thin strips of strong medical tape (cloth or paper) laid across the wound.
  **Works surprisingly well** on shallow clean cuts. Never duct tape directly on skin.
- **Packing:** clean cotton cloth, boiled, dried and torn into strips (→ 12-02).
- **Flushing:** any squeeze bottle, a bag with a pinhole, a turkey baster, plus clean drinkable
  water.
- **Honey and sugar** for suitable wounds: both have real traditional use.
- **Instruments:** sterilised by boiling for a sustained time.
- **What you cannot improvise:** the judgement about **whether** to close, and the training to do
  it. That is why the negative rule at the top is the real content of this page.

## When it runs out

- **Packing gauze is the consumable that matters.** One significant wound over weeks uses an
  enormous amount. Count in dressing changes (→ 12-02, → 23-02).
- **Ration:** boil and reuse cloth for packing and outer layers; save sterile commercial material
  for the first days and the deepest, dirtiest wounds.
- **Resupply:** cloth is plentiful (→ 11-05); scavenged medical supplies (→ 22-02); trade
  (→ 18-02).
- **Substitute:** **clean water, clean cloth and clean hands stand in for nearly everything
  here.** They do not stand in for surgery, or for the judgement about when a wound is beyond you
  (→ 12-16).
- **The permanent answer is prevention.** Sharp tools (→ 16-02), correct technique (→ 16-06),
  chaps and gloves, and no dangerous work when cold, tired or rushed. The wound you do not get
  needs no dressings.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** clean water is plentiful; **flush generously.** This is the time to read the
  reference and, if you want the skill, get real training while it exists.
- **B (moving):** water for flushing is scarce exactly when dirt is worst. **Clean as well as you
  can, close nothing, dress it, and clean it properly at the next real water source.**
- **C (resettled):** more wounds from axes, animals and building, further from help. **Stock
  packing deeply**, keep the flushing kit near the work areas, and hold the do-not-close line even
  when a wound looks tempting.

pages.title: First response to a mental-health crisis
pages.body:
# First response to a mental-health crisis

**What this page is for.** The sharp end of mental health: someone in danger, someone who
cannot function, and keeping psychiatric medicines going. Ordinary stress, fear, grief and the
long grind of a crisis are in Section 21 (→ 21-01, → 21-02, → 21-03), which is where most of the
real work happens.

> **If anyone is in crisis and any phone or internet works: call or text 988** (988 Suicide and
> Crisis Lifeline). In a disaster, SAMHSA's **Disaster Distress Helpline is 1-800-985-5990 (call
> or text, 24/7)**. The **National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233 (text START to
> 88788).** All three are printed here so they can be read with no internet; copy them onto the
> wall. **These may keep working when much else does not.** Communications fail unevenly, and a
