pages.body:
# Human waste without plumbing

**What this page is for.** What to do when the toilet stops working: how to tell what is
broken, how to build and run a bucket toilet, and where the waste goes. Getting this right is
one of the highest-value things in this binder, and it costs almost nothing.

> **SAFETY.** **Sanitation failure is one of the classic ways a survivable situation becomes a
> deadly one.** Poor sanitation spreads diarrheal diseases such as cholera and dysentery, and
> typhoid and intestinal worms; WHO counts hundreds of thousands of deaths a year from unsafe
> sanitation, mostly from diarrhea (WHO, Sanitation fact sheet). **Human waste that gets into
> land or water spreads disease to everyone downstream** (CDC, About Global Sanitation).
>
> Diarrhea dehydrates infants and young children dangerously fast (→ 12-05), and it is a
> serious sick-day event for anyone with diabetes{{#if has.condition.CL-01}} (→ 02-01){{/if}}.
>
> **Always: gloves for handling waste, hands washed with soap and water straight after, and
> waste kept far from anything anyone drinks, eats or touches** (CDC, Protecting Workers
> Handling Human Waste or Sewage).

## Do this now

1. **Buy the bucket-toilet kit today:** two 5-gallon buckets, a snap-on toilet seat lid,
   heavy-duty bags, and a large bag of cover material (sawdust, wood shavings, peat moss or
   dry leaves). Small cost; enormous problem solved.
2. **Stock heavy-duty contractor bags**, several boxes.
3. **Buy far more toilet paper than seems reasonable, and a bidet bottle or peri bottle** (a
   squeeze bottle for rinsing with water). It uses a fraction of the paper and works better.
4. **Decide now where waste goes:** the container, the storage spot and the final disposal
   (→ 13-07). Deciding during the crisis is how mistakes happen.
5. **Know your sewer situation.** If the sewer works but there is no water pressure, you can
   usually still use the toilet by **pouring a bucket of water into the bowl** to flush it.
   That is the easiest answer; check it first.
   {{#if has.septic}}Your house is on a septic system: it needs no power to work (→ 13-12).{{/if}}

## First: work out what is actually broken

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| **No water pressure, sewer working** | **Pour-flush with a bucket of water.** Water you would not drink is fine: rain, snowmelt, pool water. **Best option; check it first** |
| **Sewer backed up or broken** | Stop using the toilet at once. Use the bucket system below |
| **Pipes or the drain line frozen** | → 13-05. Do not pour water into a frozen line |
| **Flooding, sewer backing up into the street** | Do not use the toilet; sewage will come back up into the house |
| **Septic system** | **Keep using it carefully: → 13-12.** A gravity septic system needs no power, only water and a working drain field (EPA) |

**A pour-flush uses about as much water as the toilet's own flush:** EPA says newer
high-efficiency toilets use 1.6 gallons or less, and many older ones 3.5 to 5 gallons (US EPA,
How to Care for Your Septic System). That is a lot when water is rationed (→ 03-01). **Pour it
fast, straight into the BOWL, not the tank.** Try it once now with a marked bucket to learn
the least that clears your toilet. **Flush for solids only and let urine collect between flushes.** "If it's yellow, let
it mellow" is correct water-saving practice in a crisis.{{#if has.pool}} Your pool can supply
flush water (→ 03-03).{{/if}}

### Protecting the house from sewer backup

When town sewers fail, sewage can rise back up through the lowest drains in the house: basement
floor drains, showers and toilets. Heavy rain, more than power loss, is the usual cause, and
storms often bring both.

- **Know your lowest drains.** {{#if has.basement}}In your basement, find the floor drain, any
  shower, and any toilet.{{else}}Find the lowest floor drain, shower and toilet in the house.{{/if}}
- **Drain plugs** (rubber expanding or mechanical gripper plugs sized to the drain) can sit in
  floor drains and showers that you are not using. Pour water in a floor drain first: if it
  runs to a sump pit rather than the sewer, it cannot back up from the sewer.
- **A backwater valve** (a one-way flap in the main drain, fitted by a plumber) is the
  permanent fix. Before the collapse it is worth asking a plumber about.
- **An inflatable drain plug through the main cleanout** (the capped access pipe on the main
  drain) seals the whole house drain at one point. While it is in, **nothing drains in either
  direction.** Tie its safety cord so it cannot be lost in the pipe.
- **Stage towels and a wet-dry vacuum** by the lowest fixture. Write where your main cleanout
  is: __________ (→ 16-12).

## The bucket toilet: the standard answer

Simple, cheap and effective, and it works indoors in winter, which very few alternatives do.

{{figure fig-bucket-toilet}}

**Build it:**

1. **Two 5-gallon buckets:** one in use, one being emptied and cleaned.
2. **A snap-on toilet seat lid.** Comfort matters more than you would think over months, and
   the lid seals in smell.
3. **A heavy-duty bag** lining the bucket, or **no bag** if the waste is going to a compost
   system (→ 13-06).
4. **Cover material** in a second container beside it: sawdust, wood shavings, peat moss,
   shredded dry leaves, dry grass, sand or wood ash.
5. **A scoop.**

**Use it:**

- **Put a layer of cover material in the bottom before first use.**
- **Cover every deposit completely** with a scoop of material. **This is the whole trick.**
  Covering controls smell almost entirely and keeps flies off, and flies carry disease.
- **Keep the lid closed.**
- **Collect urine separately if you can.** Urine is most of the volume, and it is what makes
  the bucket heavy, smelly and quick to fill. A separate jug or bucket for urine makes the
  solids bucket last much longer and cuts smell sharply. **This is the biggest single improvement you can
  make.**
- **Wash hands with soap and water straight afterwards** (→ 13-02). Put a handwashing station
  right next to the toilet. This is not optional.

{{photo toilet-setup}}

**Empty it:**

- **Gloves and, ideally, rubber boots** (CDC).
- **Where it goes** depends on your situation: bagged and stored, a compost system (→ 13-06),
  or a properly placed latrine (→ 13-07). **Never into a storm drain, a creek, a ditch, or
  anywhere water flows.**
- **Wash hands. Every time. Properly.**

### Bucket maths for your household

No federal source publishes a table of how fast a household uses these. **Count your own:**
run the bucket toilet for a weekend now (or count the first week of a real outage) and fill in
the rates. Then the runway is simple division.

| Supply | Your rate for {{ household.size }} people (count it) | On hand | Days it lasts (on hand ÷ rate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bucket bags** | ______ a day | ______ | ______ |
| **Cover material** | ______ buckets a week | ______ | ______ |
| **Toilet paper** | ______ rolls a week | ______ | ______ |
| **Bucket changes** (solids bucket full) | every ______ days | | |

Separating urine and using a bidet bottle both slow every row. Write the results into the
consumables table, in the sanitation rows (→ 23-02).
{{#if has.infant}}Diapers are counted separately (→ 13-08).{{/if}}

### When the bucket is full

1. **Tie the bag off** with the air pressed out, gloves on.
2. **Double-bag it.** Use a contractor-weight outer bag.
3. **Into a lidded, animal-proof storage container**, outdoors, away from living space, water
   storage and food. In winter, the cold side of the house: **frozen waste is inert and does
   not smell.**
4. **When trash collection and sewers are gone for good:** bury it by the distances on
   → 13-07 (at least 100 feet from any well, spring or surface water, downhill, with at least
   5 feet of dry soil between the bottom of the pit and the water table), or add it to a
   running compost or latrine system (→ 13-06). The 200-foot figure on → 13-07 is for shallow
   catholes while traveling, not for pits; the two do not conflict.
5. **Wash hands with soap. Every time.**

{{photo waste-storage}}

## The hard part: where does it actually go?

This is the part people skip, and the part that matters.

{{#if is.urban}}**In a town or city this is genuinely difficult.** A town lot has no room for a
latrine at safe distances from neighbors and water (→ 13-07), neighbors close on all sides,
local rules about waste, and sometimes a high water table or a river nearby.{{else}}**Even on
a rural property,** check the distances to wells, streams and the house before choosing a spot
(→ 13-07).{{/if}}

**Realistic options at home, best first:**

1. **Pour-flush while the sewer works.** By far the best. Check it first, and keep checking.
2. **Bag and store**, sealed in heavy bags in a sealed container in a cold place, until
   disposal or until service comes back. **Winter helps a lot: waste freezes and stops
   smelling.** This is the realistic short-to-medium-term answer in town.
3. **A composting system** (→ 13-06), if you have yard space, discipline and time. Composting
   human waste properly takes a long time and real management; done badly it is a disease
   hazard.
4. **A properly placed pit** (→ 13-07): usually not possible on a town lot.

> **Before the collapse:** local codes govern waste disposal, pits and composting toilets. They
> never decide whether you keep waste away from water to stay alive.

**Be honest that option 2 piles up.** A household produces a steady, large volume. **Work out
where a month's worth goes before you are a month in.**

## Rules that prevent a disease outbreak

1. **Waste never goes near water, food or food preparation** (CDC, WHO): not the water store,
   not the edible parts of the garden, not the kitchen.
2. **Handwashing with soap and water after every use.** The single most effective control
   (→ 13-02).
3. **Cover everything:** smell, flies and exposure, all at once.
4. **Gloves for handling and emptying**, and wash hands afterwards anyway.
5. **Tools and containers kept only for this**, never used for anything else. Label them.
6. **Keep children away from the waste system entirely** (→ 20-02), and manage diapers
   separately (→ 13-08, → 20-06).
7. **Anyone sick uses their own container if possible** (→ 13-11); treat their waste as more
   dangerous.
8. **Flies carry disease; they are not just a nuisance.** Cover, seal and screen.

## Toilet paper and the water-versus-paper trade

- **Stock deeply.** Bulky but cheap, and good for morale.
- **A bidet bottle or peri bottle** uses a little water, cuts paper use sharply and is more
  hygienic. A very good preparedness purchase almost nobody makes.
- **Cloth wipes**, washed (→ 13-04), are the long-term answer, at a cost in water and soap.
  Wash them completely apart from all other laundry.
- **Nothing but human waste and toilet paper goes into a system you will compost**: no wipes,
  no plastic, no hygiene products.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 5-gallon buckets, four or more | The system, plus spares | Food-grade if possible |
| Snap-on toilet seat lids, two | Comfort and smell over months | A few dollars each |
| **Heavy-duty contractor bags, by the box** | Containment; running out is the failure point | Thick; double-bag |
| **Cover material in bulk** (sawdust, shavings, peat) | Smell and fly control: the whole trick | Wood shavings are cheap |
| **A separate urine container** | Makes the solids bucket last far longer; cuts smell | A jug or second lidded bucket |
| Rubber gloves and rubber boots | CDC-recommended protection | Kept for this job only |
| **Handwashing station beside the toilet** | The most effective disease control | A jug with a tap, soap, towel |
| Soap in quantity | → 13-02, → 13-09 | The most important medical supply you own |
| Toilet paper, deep stock | Bulky, cheap, morale | Rotate |
| **Bidet or peri bottle** | Little water, big paper saving, more hygienic | Underrated |
| Sealed outdoor storage container | Holding bagged waste | Lidded, animal-proof |
| Bleach or disinfectant | Cleaning buckets and the area | → 13-11 |
| Lime or wood ash | Extra smell control in a pit | → 13-07 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Buckets:** restaurants, bakeries, building sites, hardware stores.
- **Cover material:** sawdust from firewood cutting (→ 06-04), shredded dry leaves, dry grass,
  peat, sand, dry soil, wood ash, shredded paper.
- **Bags:** any heavy plastic; double up thin ones.
- **Seat:** a wooden frame over the bucket, a foam pool noodle split along its length and
  pressed over the rim (comfortable), or the seat from your own toilet.
- **Handwashing:** a jug with a spigot, a bottle with a pinhole, or a **tippy-tap** (a hanging
  jug tipped by a foot lever: a standard, very effective low-water design).
- **Toilet paper:** washable cloth wipes, newspaper (crumple it to soften it), or water and the
  left hand as much of the world uses. **All of these raise the need for handwashing**, which is
  fine as long as you actually do it.

## When it runs out

- **Bags and cover material are the consumables.** Bags are the harder one: stock boxes now.
  **A bucket system without bags becomes a compost system** (→ 13-06), which works but needs
  land and management.
- **Runway:** use the bucket maths above and keep the consumables table (→ 23-02) up to date
  with real use.
- **Ration:** **separate urine**, the biggest extender. Get cover material from your own yard
  and firewood. Pour-flush whenever the sewer works.
- **Substitute:** cover material is almost unlimited (sawdust, leaves, ash, soil). **What you
  cannot substitute is somewhere for it to go**, which is why → 13-07 matters, and why this is
  harder in town than at a rural site.
- **Long term, a proper system:** composting (→ 13-06) or a correctly placed latrine (→ 13-07)
  on land. **In town, over a long event, waste disposal is a real reason to consider leaving**
  (→ 01-02), alongside water and food.
- **What never runs out is discipline:** cover it, wash your hands, keep it away from water.
  Those three habits prevent most of what this page warns about.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** check the sewer first and pour-flush if it works. Otherwise a
  bucket toilet indoors, urine separated, waste bagged and stored in a sealed container in a
  cold spot. Plan the disposal path before storage fills.
- **B (moving):** bury waste properly and away from water (→ 13-07), pack out what you must,
  and **carry soap and hand sanitizer**. Hygiene slips exactly when illness would be most
  dangerous (→ 12-05).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** finally solvable properly. **Place the latrine or compost
  system correctly on the first day** (→ 13-07): well away from and downhill of any water
  source, away from the garden and the kitchen. On a septic system, → 13-12 is the first move.
  Getting this right at the start prevents the illness that would otherwise arrive in month
  two.

## Cross-references

→ 13-02 hygiene and handwashing · → 13-05 winter sanitation · → 13-06 composting toilet ·
→ 13-07 latrine siting · → 13-08 menstrual and diapers · → 13-11 disease outbreak ·
→ 13-12 septic · → 12-05 illness and dehydration · → 20-02 child safety ·
→ 23-02 consumables table

pages.body:
# Hygiene and handwashing (disease prevention)

**What this page is for.** Handwashing with soap and water is the most valuable medical step a
household with no clinic can take. This page covers when and how to wash, a low-water
handwashing station you can build, washing the body when water is short, and children.

> **SAFETY.** Handwashing with soap breaks the chain that carries germs from human waste to
> mouths (the "fecal-oral" route), which causes diarrheal illness: the most likely serious
> health problem a household will face without services (→ 12-05). It costs a little water and
> a bar of soap.
>
> **Wash with soap and water for at least 20 seconds** (CDC, About Handwashing), at the key
> moments below. Everything else in the medical and sanitation sections depends on this.

## Do this now

1. **Buy soap in quantity: more than you think, then more.** Bar soap keeps almost for ever in
   a cool, dry place. It is the cheapest medical supply you can own.
2. **Build a handwashing station** at the toilet (→ 13-01) and at the kitchen: **a jug with a
   spigot, soap and a towel.** It has to be effortless or it will not happen.
3. **Learn the tippy-tap** (below). It uses very little water per wash.
4. **Stock alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol** (CDC) for when
   water is short or you are on the move. Know its limits: it works less well on visibly
   dirty or greasy hands (CDC), and it does not work well against norovirus, the "stomach
   bug" (CDC, Preventing Norovirus; → 13-11).
5. **Learn to make soap** (→ 13-09) from wood ash and fat.

## The key moments

Washing at the *right times* beats washing constantly. The CDC says wash hands:

- **After using the toilet** or handling any waste (→ 13-01)
- **After changing a diaper**, or cleaning up a child who used the toilet (→ 20-06)
- **Before, during and after preparing food**
- **Before eating**
- **Before and after caring for anyone who is sick** (→ 13-11)
- **Before and after treating a wound or changing a dressing** (→ 12-02)
- **After touching animals, animal feed or animal waste** (→ 20-09, → 05-04)
- **After handling trash** (→ 13-03)
- **After blowing your nose, coughing or sneezing**
- **After touching anything from outside the household** during an outbreak

{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}**Food allergy in your household:** wash hands, and use a clean
towel, before preparing the allergic person's food, every time. Allergen proteins travel on
hands; handwashing is part of keeping them out (→ 02-04).{{else}}**Food allergies:** if anyone
you feed has one, wash hands with a clean towel before preparing their food. Allergen proteins
travel on hands (→ 02-04).{{/if}}

## How to wash properly (CDC)

1. **Wet hands** with clean running water, warm or cold, then apply soap.
2. **Lather with soap:** backs of hands, between fingers, under nails.
3. **Scrub for at least 20 seconds** (CDC's tip: hum a familiar tune twice, such as "Happy
   Birthday").
4. **Rinse** under clean running water.
5. **Dry** with a clean towel, or air dry.

**"Running" does not mean a tap.** Water poured from a jug by another person, a bottle with a
hole, or a tippy-tap all count. **What matters is that the rinse water runs off and away**,
rather than you rinsing in a basin of dirty water.

## The tippy-tap: a low-water station worth building

{{figure fig-tippy-tap}}

A jug hung from a frame with a small hole near the cap, tipped by a string tied to a foot
pedal:

- **Uses very little water per wash**, far less than a tap.
- **Hands-free:** you never touch the jug, so you do not dirty it.
- **Built from a jug, cord, two sticks and a nail.**
- **Soap hangs on a string beside it.**

**Build one at the toilet and one at the kitchen.** A fifteen-minute job.

{{photo handwashing-station}}

## Water for handwashing

Handwashing competes with drinking water (→ 03-01). Be deliberate:

- **A tippy-tap wash uses a small fraction of a tap wash.**
- **The CDC's emergency guidance:** wash with soap and water, use boiled or disinfected water
  when authorities advise extra precautions, and make a temporary station from a large water
  jug when there is no tap (CDC, Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency).
- **Some households use untreated rain, snowmelt or pool water for ordinary washes** to save
  treated water, relying on soap and water that runs off. If you do, three limits hold
  whatever you decide:
  - **never greywater** (used wash or laundry water, → 13-03): it carries the very germs
    handwashing exists to remove;
  - **never on open cuts or cracked skin**: those hands get treated water, and a wound is never
    washed in untreated water (→ 12-02). Saltwater-pool water on a cut is an infection route;
  - **the final rinse before preparing food, and before handling an infant, is treated water.**

  Your household's handwashing-water rule: ______________________________
- **Hand sanitizer (at least 60 percent alcohol)** where water is truly scarce. The CDC says it
  works less well on visibly dirty hands and does not handle everything (not norovirus), so it
  is a supplement, not a replacement.
- **Do not cut handwashing below the key moments.** If water is that short, the answer is the
  water plan (→ 03-01). The illness will cost far more water than the washing would have.

## Washing the body when washing is hard

Over months in a cold house with rationed water, full baths become rare. That is survivable.
The priorities:

- **The areas that matter: hands, face, feet, armpits, groin.** A "basin wash" of these with a
  cloth and a little warm water does most of the work and uses very little water.
- **Feet matter more than you would think.** Wash and dry them daily to prevent fungal
  infection and trench foot (feet damaged by days of cold and wet) (→ 11-04).
- **Teeth twice a day** (→ 12-06). This routine quietly lapses, and it costs teeth.
- **Hair** can go a long time; brushing spreads the natural oils. Lice and scabies (tiny mites
  that burrow in skin) are real in crowded conditions: **stock the treatments** (→ 12-07).
- **In cold, dry clothes matter more than clean ones** (→ 11-03), but change and wash
  underwear and socks regularly (→ 13-04).
- **Keep nails short.** Long nails hold dirt and bacteria, and tear.
- **Menstrual hygiene** has its own water and cleanliness needs (→ 13-08).
- **A weekly warm wash in the heated room is a real morale event**, not just hygiene
  (→ 21-02). Do not underrate it.

## Children

- **Young children can learn to wash properly** with practice. Make it a routine with a song
  to time it, and put the station at their height. **They will not do it unless it is easy and
  expected** (→ 20-04).
- **Babies and toddlers put everything in their mouths.** That is the highest-risk habit in any
  household for spreading stomach illness. **Wash their hands often, especially before
  eating**, and keep the waste system completely out of their reach (→ 13-01, → 20-02).
- **Every diaper change is a hygiene event:** hands washed after each change, one changing area
  kept for the job, waste contained (→ 20-06, → 13-08).
- **Model it.** Children do what adults do, not what adults say.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bar soap, a large stock** | The cheapest, most valuable medical supply | Keeps for years cool and dry |
| Liquid soap and refills | Convenient at stations | Bar soap stores better |
| **Hand sanitizer, at least 60 percent alcohol** | Backup when water is scarce or on the move | Not for norovirus; not on dirty hands |
| Jugs with spigots, two or three | Stations at toilet and kitchen | Or build tippy-taps |
| Basins or wash tubs, two or three | Basin washing; kept apart from dish tubs | Label them |
| Washcloths and towels, many | Basin washing; rotate and wash | → 13-04 |
| Nail brush, nail clippers | Dirt under nails carries germs | Cheap |
| Toothbrushes, toothpaste, floss, years' worth | → 12-06 | Children's sizes |
| Lice and scabies treatment | Crowded conditions | Check expiry dates |
| Lotion or petroleum jelly | Hands cracked by cold and washing get infected | Matters in winter; cracked hands get treated water |
| Wood ash and fat for soap making | The supply you can renew | → 13-09 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Soap:** any soap works for handwashing: dish soap, shampoo, laundry soap. **Then make your
  own** (→ 13-09).
- **A station:** a jug with a nail hole, a bottle with a pinhole in the cap, a tippy-tap from
  sticks and cord, a bucket with a hardware-store spigot.
- **Sanitizer:** it must be **at least 60 percent alcohol** (CDC). 70 percent isopropyl rubbing
  alcohol works. 40 to 50 percent spirits (vodka, whiskey) and 50 percent rubbing alcohol do
  **not**. **Do not improvise strengths**: weak alcohol does not work.
- **Towels:** any clean cloth, dried between uses. **Damp towels grow bacteria.**
- **Ash and sand** scrub hands when there is no soap. Better than nothing, and a real
  traditional method: the scrubbing plus the ash's alkali does real work.

## When it runs out

- **Soap is the one to plan for, and you can make it** (→ 13-09). Ash from the stove plus
  rendered fat is a renewable supply. **Practice before you need it.**
- **Runway:** a bar of soap lasts a household a surprisingly long time for handwashing. Count
  bars and put them in the consumables table (→ 23-02). Soap competes with nothing; there is no
  reason to under-stock it.
- **Ration:** wash at the key moments rather than constantly; use tippy-taps; never go below
  the key moments.
- **Substitute:** ash and sand scrubbing; hand sanitizer; and **more careful behavior**: not
  touching your face, keeping the waste system separate, keeping small children's hands out of
  their mouths as far as possible.
- **It compounds both ways.** Good hygiene prevents illness, which saves water, energy,
  supplies and the household's ability to function. A hygiene failure becomes a water crisis,
  a medical crisis and a labour crisis at the same time.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** water is still around, so make hygiene **easy and strict**. Build
  the stations, set the habits, and get children's routines in place now, so they survive later
  fatigue.
- **B (moving):** hygiene slips exactly when illness risk rises. **Hand sanitizer and a small
  bar of soap per person**; wash properly at every real water source; be strict before eating
  and after any waste handling.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** more animals, more dirt, more hard work, further from care.
  **Handwashing stations at the door and the toilet become permanent**, and soap making becomes
  a routine job (→ 13-09).

## Cross-references

→ 13-01 human waste · → 13-09 soap making · → 13-10 dishwashing · → 13-11 disease outbreak ·
→ 13-04 laundry · → 13-08 menstrual and diapers · → 12-05 illness and dehydration ·
→ 12-06 dental · → 03-01 water needs · → 20-06 diapers · → 11-04 foot care

pages.body:
# Greywater and trash management

**What this page is for.** What to do with used wash water and with trash when the drains
and the trash collection stop: how to reuse water safely, shrink the trash stream, deal with
medical sharps and cat litter, and keep rats and mice out.

> **CAUTION. Two hazards.**
> 1. **Greywater is not clean water.** Wash and rinse water holds soap, grease, food bits, skin
>    bacteria and, depending on what was washed, real germs. **It is never for drinking, never
>    for the edible parts of plants, and it turns foul within a day or two if stored.**
> 2. **Trash draws rodents, and rodents spread disease and wreck food stores** (→ 04-11).
>    When collection stops, **rodent control becomes a real health issue within weeks.**

## Do this now

1. **Buy several lidded, rodent-proof bins.** Metal cans with tight lids beat plastic, which
   rodents chew through.
2. **Start composting now** (→ 05-11). It takes the wet, smelly, rodent-drawing part out of
   your trash for good and makes soil for the garden.
3. **Catch greywater at the sink and wash basin:** a basin instead of a drain, so wash water
   becomes a resource.
4. **Work out where a month of trash goes** if collection stops. It piles up faster than
   people expect.

## Greywater: a resource with rules

**Greywater** is wash water: dishes, laundry, bathing, handwashing. **Blackwater** is toilet
waste (→ 13-01) and anything from diapers or cleaning up after a sick person. **They are
handled completely differently and never mixed.**

**Good uses of greywater** when water is rationed (→ 03-01):

- **Flushing:** pour it into the toilet bowl, when the sewer works. **The best single use.**
- **Plants you do not eat, trees and lawn.**
- **A fire-fighting reserve**, cleaning, washing dirty tools.
- **NOT for:** drinking, cooking, washing food, washing hands, or **the edible parts of food
  plants.**

**Rules that keep it safe:**

- **Use it the same day.** Greywater goes foul fast, within about a day in warm weather.
  **Don't store it.**
- **On the soil, not the leaves.** Pour it at the base of plants, never over anything eaten raw.
- **Watch what is in the soap.** For anything going on soil, use plain, biodegradable soap;
  avoid bleach, boron (borax) and heavy salts, which build up and damage soil.
- **Strain out the solids first:** a screen over the basin. Food bits make greywater rot and
  draw pests.
- **Never let it pool.** Standing water breeds mosquitoes (→ 03-08) and smells.
- **Keep it away from wells, water storage, and anywhere it can run into a neighbor's yard or a
  storm drain.**
- **In winter it freezes.** Choose a pouring spot that will not ice your path (→ 11-06).

**Cascade your water.** This is the whole idea, and it stretches supply a long way:
**clean water → rinsing → washing → dishwater → flushing or non-food plants.** Each drop is used
two or three times. Set the basins up so this happens without thinking.

{{figure fig-water-cascade}}

## Trash when there is no collection

**Shrink the stream first.** Every kind of waste you remove is one you do not have to store.

| Waste | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Food scraps** | **Compost** (→ 05-11), or feed to chickens (→ 05-04). Removes the smelly, rodent-drawing part |
| **Paper and cardboard** | **Burn** in the stove (untreated only, → 06-04), use as fire starter, compost, or use as mulch |
| **Wood scraps** | Firewood or kindling (untreated only) |
| **Metal cans** | Rinse (the rinse water is greywater), flatten and **keep**: metal is useful (→ 16-08) |
| **Glass jars** | **Wash and keep.** Jars are storage, lamps and containers (→ 04-08, → 10-04) |
| **Plastic containers** | Keep the useful ones: containers, scoops, funnels |
| **Fabric and clothing** | Rag bag, repair material, wicks, patches (→ 11-07, → 10-04) |
| **Batteries** | Do not burn; store safely (→ 09-03) |
| **Medical sharps, used pump pods** | **See below.** Rigid sealed containers marked SHARPS, never loose in the trash; **pump pods contain a battery: never burn** |
| **Hazardous** (chemicals, fuel, paint) | Sealed, labeled, away from living space and water (→ 06-06) |
| **Diapers** | **Blackwater: treat as human waste** (→ 13-01, → 20-06) |
| **Used cat litter** | **Never compost.** Scoop daily, bag, bury or store like human waste (below) |
| **What is actually left** | Contained, lidded, rodent-proof, away from the house |

**Do not burn:** plastics, treated or painted wood, rubber, foam, batteries, or anything with a
coating. The smoke is toxic (→ 06-04).

## Medical sharps

Anyone who injects medicine (insulin, other injections), uses lancets, wears an insulin pump or
a glucose sensor, or treats an animal with injections produces a **sharps waste stream that
never stops.** Glucose sensor applicators can hide a **spring-loaded needle** inside the plastic.
{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}Your household uses a pump or sensor: count a year's pods and
applicators from your own supply list (→ 02-02) and size the containers to that number.{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}Count a year's pen needles, syringes and lancets from your own supply
list and size the containers to that number.{{/if}}

**The rules:**

- **Rigid, sealed container (FDA).** Every sharp goes into a rigid, puncture-resistant, lidded
  container **straight after use**: a proper sharps container, or the standard substitute, a
  **heavy-duty plastic laundry-detergent bottle**. **Mark it SHARPS in marker, and tape the cap
  shut when it is about three-quarters full.** Overfilled containers are how people get stuck
  (US FDA, Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps). Keep it out of reach of
  children and pets (→ 20-02).
- **Insulin pump pods contain a battery. Never burn a pod, never crush one, never put one in a
  burn barrel or stove.** A damaged battery can vent or catch fire (→ 09-03). Store used pods
  sealed in their own rigid, labeled container and treat them as battery waste.
- **Long term, when collection never comes back:** sealed containers are small; **store them
  indefinitely, or bury them deep, away from water** by the distances on → 13-07 (100 feet or
  more from any well or surface water, above the water table). **Never the burn barrel, never
  loose in the ground, never the compost.**
- A needle stick from a used sharp is a wound plus an infection risk with no urgent care
  (→ 12-04). The container habit is cheap insurance.

{{photo sharps-container}}

## Used cat litter

{{#if has.cats}}This applies to your household.{{/if}}

- **Used litter is never compost and never goes on a garden.** Cat feces can carry
  *Toxoplasma gondii*, a parasite. **The CDC says it becomes infectious 1 to 5 days after it is
  passed, which is why the box is scooped daily**: daily scooping removes it before it is
  infectious (CDC, Preventing Toxoplasmosis).
- **Scoop daily into a bag; bury or store it exactly like human waste** (→ 13-01): sealed, away
  from living space, water and the garden.
- **Wear gloves** when handling litter or soil that may hold cat feces, and wash hands with
  soap afterwards (CDC).
- **Pregnancy:** toxoplasmosis during pregnancy can harm the unborn baby. **A pregnant person
  should not change the litter box if anyone else can. If she must: gloves, daily scooping,
  thorough handwashing** (CDC; → 12-12).{{#if has.pregnant}} This applies in your household
  now.{{/if}}
- Litter runs out. Dirt, sand, wood ash or shredded paper replace it (put it in → 23-02). The
  disposal rule never changes.

## Rodents: the part that becomes serious

When collection stops and food is stored, **rats and mice follow.** They spread disease, destroy
food (→ 04-11), chew wiring (→ 09-08), and get into insulation and vehicles.

- **Seal food in hard containers**, not bags (→ 04-03).
- **Lidded metal trash bins**, away from the house.
- **Compost properly.** A badly kept pile feeds rodents. Keep it hot, turned and contained, with
  **no meat or fat in an open pile** (→ 05-11).
- **Traps, and a lot of them.** Snap traps work and can be reused. Poison bait is a danger to
  children and pets: **use it with real care or not at all** (→ 20-02, → 20-09).
- **Pets help**, but a cat is not a pest-control program.
- **Seal entry points.** Rodents fit through very small gaps. Stuff gaps with steel wool and
  cover them with hardware cloth (stiff wire mesh). Sealing for heat also seals out rodents
  (→ 08-03).

## Winter changes things, mostly for the better

- **Frozen trash does not smell or draw flies.**
- **Rodents come indoors in winter**: sealing and trapping matter more, not less.
- **Greywater freezes:** plan where it goes, and expect ice.
- **Compost slows almost to a stop in a cold winter.** The pile still takes material; it just
  breaks it down in spring. Plan for the volume.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Metal lidded trash bins, two or three** | Rodents chew plastic | Away from the house |
| Wash basins or tubs, three or four | Cascading water; catching greywater | Label by use (dishes, laundry, body) |
| Sink strainers or screens | Solids out of greywater: no rot, no pests | Cheap |
| **Compost bin or tumbler** | Removes the worst part of the trash | → 05-11 |
| Heavy contractor bags | Containment | Shared with → 13-01 |
| **Snap traps, many** | Rodent control without poison | Reusable |
| Steel wool and hardware cloth | Sealing rodent entry points | → 08-03 |
| **Rigid sharps containers, several** (if anyone uses sharps) | Needles, lancets, applicators | A detergent bottle is acceptable: mark SHARPS, tape shut at three-quarters full |
| **A separate sealed container for used pump pods** (if used) | Battery inside: never burn | Rigid, labeled, away from heat |
| Litter scoop and bags (if you have cats) | Daily scooping prevents toxoplasmosis | Store or bury like human waste |
| Buckets for cascading water | Move greywater to its next use | Label them |
| A watering can kept for greywater | Pouring greywater onto soil | Never used with drinking-water gear |
| Work gloves | Handling trash | Wash hands after (→ 13-02) |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Containers:** buckets, drums, totes, metal cans from anywhere.
- **Strainers:** window screen over a basin, a colander, cloth over a bucket.
- **Rodent-proofing:** steel wool, sheet metal, hardware cloth, glass and metal containers.
- **Traps:** home-made bucket traps work; snap traps are better and cheap.
- **Compost bin:** a circle of wire fencing, pallets wired together, a pit, a pile.
- **What not to improvise:** a sharps container worse than the FDA fallback. A rigid, lidded,
  labeled heavy plastic bottle at minimum: **never a bag, never a thin milk jug, never anything
  unlabeled.**

## When it runs out

- **Trash bags are the consumable**, shared with → 13-01. **Stock boxes.** When they are gone,
  containers replace bags: buckets and cans that are emptied and cleaned, not thrown away.
- **The real shortage is space and disposal.** **Shrink the stream hard:** compost, burn what is
  safe to burn, and treat glass, metal, fabric and plastic as materials. **In a long event, most
  of what a household throws away is a resource** (→ 22-02).
- **Ration greywater by cascading it:** the same water doing three jobs.
- **The failure to avoid:** trash piling up uncontained near the house. That is how a rodent
  population starts, and once settled it is very hard to remove, and it threatens your whole
  food store (→ 04-11).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** collection may keep running for a while: use that window. Compost
  at once, set up the cascade, get rodent-proof bins before you need them. Neighbors'
  uncollected trash becomes your rodent problem too (→ 18-01).
- **B (moving):** pack out what you must, bury nothing that draws animals near where you sleep,
  and **never leave food waste at a camp.**
- **C (rural or at a destination):** more room and no collection at all, so **the system has to
  be complete from the first day**: compost, a burn pile (safe materials only, and mind the fire
  risk in dry grass, → 17-05), scrap and materials storage, and a greywater spot away from the
  well and the vegetable beds (→ 13-07).

## Cross-references

→ 13-01 human waste · → 13-04 laundry · → 13-10 dishwashing · → 13-11 disease outbreak ·
→ 05-11 compost · → 04-11 pests and rodents · → 06-04 what not to burn · → 13-07 burial
distances · → 22-02 scavenging

pages.body:
# Laundry without power

**What this page is for.** Washing clothes by hand when there is no washer, dryer or hot water
on tap: what to wash, how, and how to get it dry.

> **Laundry is a water problem, a fuel problem and a drying problem.**{{#if is.cold_winters}}
> In your winters, drying is the hardest of the three (→ 11-03).{{/if}} Expect a load to take
> a day or more to dry in a cold house. **Drying, not washing, limits how much laundry a
> household can actually do.**
>
> **Safety:** anything soiled with human waste or vomit, or from someone who is sick, is handled
> separately, with gloves, washed hot where possible and dried completely (→ 13-11; CDC). Don't
> mix it with the general wash.

## Do this now

1. **Buy a mop-bucket wringer or a hand wringer.** Squeezing water out mechanically is the
   biggest time-saver in the whole job: it turns a two-day dry into an overnight one.
2. **Get two or three wash tubs kept only for laundry** and label them (wash, rinse, soak).
   Keep them apart from dish tubs and body-washing basins (→ 13-10).
3. **Set up drying:** a high line in the heated room and a line outdoors (→ 11-03).
4. **Buy a washboard or a plunger-style agitator.** A clean new toilet plunger with holes
   drilled in it, pumped up and down in a bucket, is an effective washing machine for a few
   dollars.

## The reality: you will wash far less

In a grid-down winter, a household of {{ household.size }} cannot wash the way it does now. The
honest plan:

- **Wash what must be washed:** underwear, socks, diapers (→ 13-08), anything soiled, anything
  from a sick person, kitchen cloths, and dressings you plan to reuse (→ 12-02).
- **Air and spot-clean the rest.** Outer layers, sweaters and wool can go a long time. **Wool
  resists smell and can be aired instead of washed** (→ 11-05).
- **In cold, dry beats clean** (→ 11-03). A dry base layer worn three days is better than a
  freshly washed damp one. Dryness wins.

## The process

{{figure fig-plunger-agitator}}

1. **Sort:** heavily soiled, lightly soiled, and contaminated (waste, vomit, a sick person).
   Contaminated items are washed separately, with gloves.
2. **Shake out and brush off** dry dirt first. Free, and it saves water and soap.
3. **Pre-soak** heavily soiled items in warm soapy water. **Soaking does most of the work:**
   time stands in for scrubbing and hot water. An overnight soak beats hard scrubbing.
4. **Agitate:** a plunger in a bucket, a washboard for stubborn spots, or feet in a tub (good for
   bedding and big items). **Movement, not temperature, removes most dirt.**
5. **Wring hard, then rinse** in clean water, once or twice. Soap left in fabric irritates
   skin, especially children's.
6. **Wring again, then towel-press:** roll the item in a dry towel and stand on it. This removes
   a surprising amount of water and cuts drying time a lot.
7. **Dry:** a high line in the warm room, or **freeze-drying** outdoors (below).
8. **The wash and rinse water becomes greywater** (→ 13-03): flushing, non-food plants,
   cleaning.

{{photo laundry-setup}}

## Water and fuel

- **A hand-washed load uses far less water than a machine**, and you can reuse the water.
- **Clean first, dirty last.** Wash the cleanest items first and the dirtiest last in the same
  water. Rinse water from a clean load becomes wash water for a dirty one.
- **Hot water costs fuel** (→ 06-04, → 07-01). **Warm is usually enough** with soap and soaking.
  **Save truly hot water for contaminated items and diapers**, where it matters for killing
  germs.
- **Rain and snowmelt are ideal for laundry:** soft water lathers better and needs less soap
  (→ 03-05). Melting snow costs fuel, so weigh it.
- **Put laundry in the water budget** (→ 03-01, → 23-02). It is a real line.

## Drying in winter

- **Plan the week around drying.** Wash on a day you can dry.
- **Freeze-drying works.** Hang clothes outside in below-freezing air; the ice slowly turns
  straight to vapour. Bring them in stiff and finish indoors. **No fuel at all.**
- **Indoor drying adds damp to a closed-up house.** Vent on purpose and watch for condensation
  and mold (→ 11-03, → 08-03).
- **Never dry laundry on a stove or heater.** That is how house fires start (→ 12-03). **Near,
  never on.**
- **Stagger the wet work.** If everything is wet at once, nobody has dry clothes for days, in
  winter.

## Special cases

- **Diapers** (→ 13-08, → 20-06): the biggest and most important laundry in a house with a
  baby. Scrape solids into the toilet system (→ 13-01), soak, wash **hot**, rinse thoroughly
  (leftover soap causes rashes), and **dry completely**; sun and freeze-drying both help. This
  is steady, unavoidable work.{{#if has.infant}} It applies to you now.{{/if}}
- **Menstrual cloths** (→ 13-08): soak in **cold** water first (hot water sets blood), then
  wash.
- **A sick person's laundry** (→ 13-11): gloves, kept separate, hot water where possible, and
  dried completely (CDC).
- **Dressings you plan to reuse** (→ 12-02): **boiled**, not just washed, then dried clean and
  stored sealed.
- **Wool:** cool water, gentle, **no hard wringing** (it shrinks and mats into felt); dry flat
  (→ 11-05).
- **Cold hands.** Long sessions with wet hands in cold air chill you fast and crack skin
  (OSHA, Cold Stress). Wear rubber gloves, warm the water if you can, and take breaks.

## Soap

- **Laundry uses more soap than anything else in the house.** Stock it, and **learn to make
  it** (→ 13-09).
- **Less soap than you think** works with soaking and movement, and **less soap means fewer
  rinses**, which saves water. Too much soap is the common mistake.
- **Grated bar soap or home-made soap works** for laundry. Plain soap is better than detergent
  for greywater you will put on soil (→ 13-03).

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mop-bucket wringer or hand wringer** | The biggest saver of work and drying time | Transforms the job |
| Wash tubs or basins, three, labeled | Wash, rinse, soak; kept apart from dish tubs | Galvanised or plastic |
| **Plunger-style agitator** (or a plunger and a drill) | A hand washing machine for a few dollars | Drill holes in it |
| Washboard | Collars, cuffs, stubborn spots | Old-fashioned and effective |
| Clothesline and pins (indoor high line and outdoor) | Drying is the limit | → 11-03 |
| Drying racks, two or three | Near the heat, never on it | |
| Absorbent towels for pressing | Squeezing water out beats waiting for it to evaporate | |
| **Soap in bulk, or soap-making supplies** | Laundry uses the most soap | → 13-09 |
| Rubber gloves | Contaminated laundry, hot water, cracked winter hands | Kept for this job |
| Scrub brush | Spot cleaning | |
| Diaper pail with lid (with a baby) | Steady volume | → 13-08 |
| A large pot kept for boiling laundry | Diapers, contaminated items, dressings | Not the cooking pot |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Tubs:** any bucket, tote, bin, cooler or bathtub.
- **Agitator:** a plunger, a stick, a paddle, a clean boot, your feet.
- **Washboard:** a sheet of corrugated metal, a ridged panel, a smooth rock.
- **Wringer:** two people twisting the item in opposite directions; pressing between boards;
  rolling in a towel and standing on it.
- **Line:** cord, wire, rope, branches. **Pins:** clothespins, clips, split twigs, or just
  drape it.
- **Soap:** any soap; home-made (→ 13-09); water soaked through wood ash (lye water) is a
  traditional laundry cleaner. **It is caustic (burns skin): handle carefully and rinse
  thoroughly.**
- **Softener:** a splash of vinegar in the rinse (it also cuts soap residue).
- **Stains:** sunlight bleaches stains for free; cold water at once for blood; sun on cloth
  diapers removes stains and helps kill germs.

## When it runs out

- **Soap is the consumable, and you can make it** (→ 13-09). **Water and fuel are the ongoing
  costs.** Put all three in → 23-02.
- **Runway:** think in loads per week your **drying space** can handle, not in soap. That is the
  real limit.
- **Ration:** wash less, air more, spot-clean, and choose: **underwear, socks, diapers, kitchen
  cloths and anything contaminated get washed; outer layers get aired.** Wool takes this much
  better than cotton (→ 11-05).
- **Substitute:** sunlight and air for washing (real, if partial); freeze-drying for the dryer;
  ash lye for soap; soaking and movement for hot water and scrubbing.
- **Why it matters:** washing the things that matter properly (**diapers, a sick person's
  things, kitchen cloths, reused dressings**) is infection control (→ 13-11, → 12-04).
  Skipping *those* is how a shortcut becomes an illness. Skipping a sweater wash costs nothing.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** water is available; drying is the limit. Set up tubs, wringer and
  lines early, and start the "wash what matters" habit before everyone is tired.
- **B (moving):** no laundry on the move. **Rinse socks and underwear at water stops if you can
  dry them**; otherwise carry spares. **Wet clothing in winter is the danger** (→ 11-03), so
  carry dry spares rather than washing.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** room for a real setup: a summer washing area outdoors, a
  winter setup near the stove, long lines, space to freeze-dry. **A hand-crank wringer washer is
  a great find** (→ 16-05); watch for one.

## Cross-references

→ 13-02 hygiene · → 13-03 greywater · → 13-08 menstrual and diapers · → 13-09 soap making ·
→ 13-11 disease outbreak · → 11-03 staying dry · → 11-05 wool · → 03-01 water needs ·
→ 12-02 reusing dressings

pages.body:
# Sanitation when water lines are frozen

**What this page is for.** Keeping toilets, drains and washing going when the pipes freeze or
the house goes unheated, and planning for the spring thaw.
{{#if is.cold_winters}}Your January nights average about {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F: plan
for months of this, not a two-week outage.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION. Never thaw a frozen pipe with an open flame:** no blowtorch, no kerosene or
> propane heater, no charcoal stove (American Red Cross, Preventing and Thawing Frozen Pipes).
> An open flame on a pipe inside a wall or crawlspace is how houses catch fire. Use a hair
> dryer, an electric heating pad, towels soaked in hot water, or an electric space heater kept
> away from anything that can burn, working **from the tap end back toward the
> frozen part, with the tap open.**
>
> **A frozen supply pipe and a frozen drain pipe are different problems.** Pouring water into a
> frozen **drain** just backs sewage into the house. **Find out which is frozen before you pour
> anything.**

## Do this now

1. **Winterize before the first hard freeze** (→ 08-03): insulate exposed pipes, seal the
   crawlspace and the gaps where the walls meet the foundation, keep cabinet doors open on
   outside-wall plumbing, and know where the main shutoff is.
2. **Decide now whether you will drain the plumbing** if the house goes unheated. It is the
   final answer to frozen pipes, and a decision better made calmly.
3. **Set up an indoor bucket toilet now** (→ 13-01). In hard cold, outdoor options are often not
   usable.
4. **Stock RV antifreeze**, the non-toxic pink kind (propylene glycol), for drain traps and
   toilets. Cheap, and it prevents a specific, annoying failure.

## Why winter is the hardest case

Everything gets harder at once:

- **Water freezes:** the tap, the well pump, stored water, the rain barrel (→ 03-06).
- **Drain pipes freeze**, especially in cold or unheated parts of the house.
- **Outdoor options become impractical.** You cannot dig a latrine in frozen ground, and going
  outside in deep cold with a small child is a serious undertaking.
- **A septic drain field can freeze**, especially with little snow cover (University of
  Minnesota Extension) (→ 13-12).
- **Handwashing water is harder to get** (→ 13-02) exactly when the household is packed into
  one heated room and illness spreads most easily (→ 13-11).

**One large mercy: cold kills smell and flies.** Frozen waste does not smell and does not draw
insects. **Winter is easier for *storing* waste even as it is harder for *handling* it.**

## Which pipe is frozen, and what to do

| Situation | Response |
|---|---|
| **No water at the tap, house heated** | Probably a frozen supply pipe. Find it and thaw it, **never with flame**. Open the tap first so melt water can escape |
| **Water runs in but the drain will not take it** | **Frozen drain. Stop adding water.** It will back up. Warm the drain pipe if you can reach it; otherwise use the bucket toilet (→ 13-01) |
| **House going unheated** | **Drain the system, after every container is filled:** main water valve off, all taps open, toilets flushed, RV antifreeze in traps and toilet bowls, and **drain the water heater by the six-step procedure on → 03-02** (heat off first; the water can be scalding). Never from memory, never with the burner or elements on |
| **Pipe already burst** | Shut off the main at once. Deal with the water; repair is on → 16-05 |
| **Septic system** | Keep normal use if you can: regular use helps stop freezing (University of Minnesota Extension). Leave snow undisturbed, or add loose straw or mulch, over the tank and drain field (→ 13-12) |

Your main water shutoff is at: __________ (→ 22-04).

**Prevention beats all of it:** insulate, seal drafts near outside-wall plumbing, keep a
**slow drip running** through pipes at risk during extreme cold, and keep cabinet doors open so
warm air reaches the pipes.

## The winter toilet

**Indoor bucket toilet, in or near the heated room, urine separated.** This is the answer, and
it works.

- **Indoors.** Nobody, adult or child, should be going outside to a toilet at 3 a.m. in deep
  cold.
- **In or near the one heated room** (→ 08-01), screened for privacy. Months in one room make
  privacy a real morale issue (→ 21-02).
- **Separate urine.** Even more important in winter: you cannot easily pour liquid outdoors
  without making ice on the paths and a smell in spring.
- **Keep the cover material indoors too.** Sawdust left outside freezes into a useless block.
- **Bagged waste goes to a sealed outdoor container.** It freezes, stops smelling, and waits.
- **Handwashing station indoors with warm water** (→ 13-02). Cold hands do not get washed
  properly, and cracked winter skin gets infected (→ 12-04).

## Where frozen waste goes in spring

**Plan for the thaw.** A winter of frozen bagged waste becomes an urgent problem the week it
warms up.

- **Have the disposal plan before spring:** sewer service back, a properly placed pit (→ 13-07),
  or a compost system that can take it (→ 13-06). **Make the plan by late winter.**
- **Do not let it thaw in the yard.** It will smell, draw flies, and contaminate the ground and
  runoff.
- **Snowmelt moves everything downhill.** Anything buried or piled over winter ends up in the
  runoff. **Place it accordingly** (→ 13-07).

## Water for sanitation in winter

- **Snow is free water** (→ 03-05, → 03-06). **Melting it costs fuel** (→ 06-04). Melted snow
  is ideal for handwashing and laundry (soft water), and is treated before drinking (→ 03-04).
- **Reuse water hard** (→ 13-03). Every drop melted with hard-won fuel should do two or three
  jobs.
- **Keep water containers inside**, above freezing, or they burst.
- **Warm washing water matters.** Nobody washes properly in ice water, and hygiene that does not
  happen does not prevent disease. **Budget a little fuel for warm washing water.**

## Safety around all of this

- **No open flame for thawing pipes.** Repeated because it is the fire that burns houses down
  (→ 12-03).
- **No fuel-burning heater in a closed space without carbon monoxide precautions** (→ 08-02;
  carbon monoxide explained on → 29-03).
- **Ice on paths** from water poured outside: choose a spot away from walkways (→ 11-06).
- **Cold injury during outdoor chores:** hats, mittens, don't linger (→ 11-04, → 12-10; NWS,
  During Extremely Cold Weather).
- **Keep children away from the waste system** (→ 20-02), which is harder when everyone lives in
  one room.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Indoor bucket toilet (two buckets, seat, cover material) | The winter answer | → 13-01 |
| **Urine container** | Matters more in winter than any other season | A jug or a second bucket |
| Privacy screen or curtain | Months in one room | Cheap, and it matters |
| **RV antifreeze (propylene glycol, pink)** | Traps and toilets once the system is drained | Non-toxic type only |
| Pipe insulation, heat tape, foam sleeves | Prevention beats thawing | → 08-03 |
| Hair dryer, heating pad, electric space heater | **Thawing without flame** | Red Cross guidance |
| Sealed outdoor waste container | Freezes and waits for spring | Lidded, animal-proof |
| Indoor handwashing station and a way to warm water | Cold hands don't get washed | → 13-02 |
| A large pot for melting snow | Water from snow | → 03-06 |
| The main water shutoff and its tool | Burst-pipe response | Water heater draining: → 03-02 |
| Headlamps at the toilet area | It is dark by 5 p.m. | → 10-01 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Cover material:** sawdust from firewood cutting (→ 06-04); keep a supply **indoors** so it
  does not freeze solid.
- **Pipe insulation:** foam, towels, blankets, straw around exposed pipes.
- **Thawing:** warm towels applied again and again, a heating pad, a hair dryer, a lamp near
  (not touching) the pipe. **Never flame.**
- **Privacy:** a blanket on a rope, a folding screen, a corner behind furniture.
- **Snow melting:** any big pot on a stove that is already running for cooking (→ 07-01), not
  a separate fire.

## When it runs out

- **Cover material and bags** run out as on → 13-01, and you cannot easily gather frozen
  material outdoors. **Keep an indoor supply.**
- **Fuel is the winter multiplier.** Melting snow for washing competes with heating and cooking
  (→ 06-04). **Reuse water, melt on a fire that is already burning, and use snow directly where
  you can** (scrubbing, rinsing) instead of melting it first.
- **Runway:** in winter, storage gets easier (frozen waste waits) and water and fuel get
  tighter. **Plan the winter sanitation budget in fuel, not bags.**
- **The thing that does not wait is spring.** Have the thaw plan made by late winter (→ 13-06,
  → 13-07).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** the whole system indoors, waste frozen outdoors in sealed
  containers, water from snow and storage.
- **B (moving):** **avoid moving in deep winter unless you must** (→ 01-02). Sanitation on the
  move in hard cold means ground too frozen to dig, worse hygiene, and cold injury while doing
  it. Carry hand sanitizer and deal with waste well away from water and camp.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** you cannot dig a latrine in frozen ground, so **dig it in
  autumn** (→ 13-07). A septic system benefits from regular use and an insulating cover of snow
  or straw over the drain field (EPA). Plan the whole winter system before the first freeze.

## Cross-references

→ 13-01 human waste · → 13-02 hygiene · → 13-06 composting toilet · → 13-07 latrine siting ·
→ 13-03 greywater · → 03-06 winter water · → 03-02 draining the water heater ·
→ 08-03 winterizing · → 08-01 heating one room · → 17-01 blizzards and ice

pages.body:
# Building a composting or bucket toilet

**What this page is for.** The difference between a bucket toilet (collecting waste) and
composting human waste (treating it), and how to do the second one safely if you have the land
for it.

> **SAFETY. This page is deliberately cautious.**
>
> **Human waste carries germs that survive a long time:** bacteria, viruses, protozoa (single-
> celled parasites) and worm eggs. **Composting them to a truly safe standard needs sustained
> high temperatures throughout the pile and a long curing time.** A small backyard pile often
> does not get there, especially in a cold climate, where it stops working all winter.
>
> **This binder's advice:** build the bucket toilet (→ 13-01): it is safe, simple, and it
> works. **Treat composting as a way to dispose of waste and shrink its volume, not as a way to
> make compost for the vegetable garden. Do not put human-waste compost on food crops.** If you
> use it at all, use it on flowers, trees or areas where nothing is eaten, well away from
> anywhere water flows. The reason: you cannot tell by looking whether compost is free of
> germs, and an infection from food crops could reach the whole household.

## Do this now

1. **Build the bucket toilet** (→ 13-01). That is the part that matters, and it takes an hour.
2. **Stockpile cover material:** sawdust from firewood cutting (→ 06-04), wood shavings,
   shredded leaves, peat moss. **You need a lot, and indoors in winter** (→ 13-05).
3. **Choose the composting spot now, if you will have one:** well away from water, the edible
   garden, the neighbors, and anywhere children go (→ 13-07).
4. **Decide honestly whether you have the land, the time and the discipline.** On a small town
   lot the answer may be no, and bagging and storing (→ 13-01) is a legitimate answer.

> **Before the collapse:** most states and counties regulate composting toilets. Check your
> local rules. They never decide whether you keep waste away from water to stay alive.

## Two things people mix up

**A bucket toilet** is a *collection* system. Simple, safe, cheap, works indoors in winter.
**Covering each deposit with sawdust controls smell almost completely.**

**Composting human waste** is a *treatment* system that comes after collection. It is what
happens to the contents, and it is where the germ risk lives. **These are separate decisions.**
You can run a bucket toilet and bag the contents, or run a bucket toilet and compost the
contents; the collection is the same either way.

## What "safe" composting actually needs

To kill germs, a compost pile needs:

- **Sustained high ("thermophilic") temperatures throughout the pile**, not just in the middle;
- **turning**, so every part passes through the hot zone;
- **the right mix of carbon (dry brown material) and nitrogen (the waste), and moisture**, to
  keep the heat going;
- **a long curing time afterwards**: some germs, especially worm eggs, survive a long time;
- **enough volume**: small piles do not hold heat.

**In practice:**{{#if is.cold_winters}} where you live, a pile freezes solid for months each
year and does nothing.{{/if}} Summer piles can get genuinely hot, but getting every part of a
small backyard bin hot enough is hard to check and easy to get wrong. **You cannot tell by
looking whether compost is free of germs.** Use **time and distance** as your safety margin,
not confidence in the process.

## If you build a composting system anyway

{{figure fig-two-bin-humanure}}

**The two-bin method:**

1. **Bin one receives.** Bucket contents are tipped in and **covered at once** with a thick layer
   of carbon material (straw, leaves, sawdust). Covering stops smell, flies and exposure.
2. **When it is full, it rests:** closed and undisturbed for as long as you can possibly manage
   (this binder gives no safe minimum, because no published one fits a backyard bin; longer is
   always safer). Meanwhile bin two receives.
3. **Swap.**

{{photo compost-bins}}

**Building it:**

- **Closed on all sides**, with a lid or heavy cover. **Rodent-proof and child-proof** (→ 13-03,
  → 20-02): pallets lined with hardware cloth (stiff wire mesh), a wire bin, or a built box.
- **Placed by → 13-07:** downhill from and far from any water, far from the edible garden and
  the kitchen, away from the property line.
- **On soil, not concrete**, so liquid soaks into the ground rather than running off, but
  **only** if you are far from any water source and the water table is not shallow.
- **Never where snowmelt or heavy rain will run through it and away.**

**Rules for running it: all of them, every time.**

- **Cover every addition thoroughly.** This is the whole of the smell and fly control.
- **Nothing but human waste, toilet paper and carbon cover material.** No plastic, no wipes, no
  hygiene products, no diapers with plastic, no chemicals.
- **Gloves and boots for handling; hands washed with soap straight after** (CDC, Protecting
  Workers Handling Human Waste or Sewage).
- **Children never near it** (→ 20-02).
- **Tools kept only for this**, touching nothing else. Label them.
- **Do not turn a pile that has just had fresh material added:** it brings fresh waste to the
  surface.

## Urine, again

**Separating urine changes everything for a compost system:**

- Urine is most of the volume; separating it cuts what you handle sharply.
- It keeps the pile from going soggy and airless, which stops the heat and causes smell.
- **Urine from a healthy person is fairly low-risk** and can be diluted heavily and used on
  plants you do not eat and on trees. It is salty and rich in nitrogen, so **dilute it well,
  pour it on soil not leaves, and move where you pour it.** This binder gives no dilution
  figure because none is published for this use; dilute generously. The direction of the rule
  is solid: undiluted urine poured again and again in one place burns
  plants and builds salt in soil. **Never on the edible parts of food crops.**

## Winter

- **In a cold winter, a compost pile does nothing.** It freezes and waits.
- **You can keep adding to it**; it just stacks up until spring.
- **The pile may be where the winter's bagged waste goes** (→ 13-05), so **it needs room for a
  whole winter plus the year of curing.** That is usually bigger than people expect.
- **Plan the spring thaw** (→ 13-05): that is the week this becomes urgent.

## The honest comparison

| Option | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|
| **Bucket, bag, store or dispose** | Simple, safe, works indoors and in winter, no land needed | Bags run out; the pile of bags needs somewhere to go |
| **Bucket and compost** | No bags, smaller volume, nothing to buy | Needs land, discipline and time; **germ risk if done badly**; regulated; freezes in cold winters |
| **Properly placed pit latrine** (→ 13-07) | Simple and proven; nothing to buy | Needs land and safe distances; cannot dig frozen ground; groundwater risk |
| **Pour-flush while the sewer works** (→ 13-01) | **Best of all** | Uses water; needs a working sewer |

{{#if is.urban}}**For your town or suburban home: pour-flush if possible, otherwise bucket and
bag.** Composting belongs where land, distance and time exist.{{else}}**On a rural property**
with real distances to water, a two-bin system is workable; still pour-flush while you can.{{/if}}

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bucket toilet (→ 13-01) | The part that matters | Two buckets, seat, cover material |
| **Cover material in bulk** | Smell, flies, and the pile's carbon | Sawdust from firewood is free (→ 06-04) |
| **Urine container** | Cuts the problem by half or more | The best single improvement |
| Compost bin materials (pallets, hardware cloth, lid) | Closed, rodent-proof, child-proof | If you build one |
| **A fork or shovel kept only for this, labeled** | Never touches anything else | Not negotiable |
| Rubber gloves and rubber boots | CDC-recommended protection | Kept for this job |
| Long-stem compost thermometer | Shows what the pile is doing | Cheap; still not proof of safety |
| Straw, leaves, other carbon in bulk | The pile needs a lot | Free from the yard |
| Handwashing station next to it | Every single time | → 13-02 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Bin:** pallets wired together and lined, a wire ring, a barrel with the bottom cut out, a
  dug pit (→ 13-07).
- **Cover and carbon:** sawdust, wood shavings, shredded leaves, dry grass, straw, shredded
  paper and cardboard, peat, dry soil, wood ash.
- **Tools:** any fork or shovel, **permanently marked** so it never goes into the garden.
- **What you cannot substitute:** land, distance from water, and time. **If you do not have
  those, do not compost: bag it** (→ 13-01).

## When it runs out

- **The consumable is cover material**, and it is almost free if you cut firewood (→ 06-04) or
  rake leaves. **Keep an indoor winter supply** (→ 13-05).
- **What runs out is capacity.** The bins must hold everything your {{ household.size }} people
  produce in a year, **plus** a full curing period in which that material is not touched. Be
  honest about whether your lot can hold that.
- **Ration:** separate urine (the biggest cut), and use the sewer whenever it works.
- **Substitute:** bag and store; a pit latrine where the site allows (→ 13-07); the sewer.
- **The long-term answer is land**, where a properly placed latrine or compost system with real
  distances and a real curing area is straightforward, **built in the first weeks, before it
  is urgent** (→ 13-07).
- **What never runs out is the safety margin of time and distance.** When in doubt, wait longer
  and keep it further from everything.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** bucket toilet, urine separated, bagged and stored. **A compost
  system on a small lot is hard to place safely** and may not be allowed. Don't force it.
- **B (moving):** neither. Bury properly and away from water (→ 13-07), or pack it out.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** **this is where it belongs.** Real distances from water,
  real land, a two-bin system with a full year of curing, downhill and far from the well, the
  garden and the house. **Build it in the first month**, and still keep human-waste compost off
  food crops.

## Cross-references

→ 13-01 human waste (build this first) · → 13-07 latrine siting · → 13-02 hygiene ·
→ 13-03 rodents · → 13-05 winter sanitation · → 13-11 disease outbreak ·
→ 05-11 soil and compost (the food-safe kind) · → 20-02 child safety
