pages.body:
# Siting a latrine away from water

**What this page is for.** Where to put a pit toilet (latrine) so it does not poison the water,
how to build one, and how to deal with waste while traveling.

> **SAFETY. This is a decision you make once and cannot undo.** A latrine placed too close to,
> or uphill of, a water source contaminates that water, possibly for years, and possibly your
> neighbors' water too. **Groundwater contamination cannot be seen, and by the time people are
> sick the damage is done.**
>
> **Get it right on the first day at any new site.** It is one of the most important decisions
> in setting up at a new place (→ 01-04), and far easier to get right at the start than to fix
> later.
>
> **Safe distances depend on soil, slope and how deep the groundwater is.** The numbers here are
> the published emergency minimums (MSF; WHO and WEDC). When in doubt, go further.

## Do this now

1. **If a place has a working septic system, use it first** (→ 13-12): a gravity septic system
   needs no power, only water and a working drain field (EPA). A latrine is the fallback for
   when that system fails or is overloaded, which is exactly when you will need these numbers.
   {{#if has.septic}}Your home is on septic.{{/if}}
2. **When choosing any destination, look at where waste could safely go** (→ 01-05), alongside
   water, wood and access. **A site with nowhere safe to put waste is a worse site than it
   looks.**
3. **In town, a pit latrine is usually not possible** on a house lot: the distances cannot be
   met and neighbors are close. **Bucket and bag** (→ 13-01) is the answer at home in town.
4. **Learn the rules of thumb below** so you can apply them fast while traveling or at a new
   site.
5. **If you will need a pit in winter, dig it in autumn.** Frozen ground cannot be dug
   (→ 13-05).

> **Before the collapse:** state and county rules govern pits, privies and setback distances.
> Check them. They never decide whether you keep waste away from drinking water.

## The core rule

**Waste goes downhill from, and far away from, anything anyone drinks.** Water moves through
soil, and it moves downhill. Everything else is detail on that one rule.

## Cautious planning distances

{{figure fig-latrine-setbacks}}

**These are minimums to plan around. Further is better.** The published figures are metric:
30 metres is about 100 feet, 1.5 metres about 5 feet, 6 metres about 20 feet.

| From | Minimum distance | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **A well, borehole or spring** | **At least 100 ft (30 m)** (MSF, Medical Guidelines), and further in sandy or cracked rock ground | **Downhill of the well, never uphill** |
| **Any surface water** (creek, pond, river, ditch) | **At least 100 ft (30 m)** (WEDC, Emergency Sanitation), more on a slope | Includes drainage channels that only run in spring |
| The house or living space | **At least 20 ft (6 m)** (WHO, Technical Note 13), further if you can | Far enough for smell and flies, close enough to actually use in winter |
| The edible garden | Well apart | And downhill |
| Food storage, kitchen | Well apart | |
| Property line, neighbors | As far as possible | Their water matters too |
| **The groundwater (water table)** | **The bottom of the pit at least 5 ft (1.5 m) above the water table at its wettest season** (MSF; WEDC). Dig a test hole and wait a day to see if water seeps in | **The one people miss** |

**The water table matters most.** A pit dug into or near groundwater empties straight into the
water people pump from wells. **Near rivers and in low ground the water table can be very
shallow.** Dig a test hole first and look. If you hit water or wet, soggy soil, **that site is
wrong**: go higher, or use a system that does not soak into the soil (→ 13-06, or bag and
store, → 13-01).

## Reading the site

- **Slope and drainage.** Stand there in a rainstorm, or imagine snowmelt. **Where does the
  water go?** Everything you put in the ground goes with it. **Never uphill of a well, never in
  a drainage path, never where snowmelt sheets across.**
- **Soil.** Sandy and gravelly soils drain fast, so contamination travels far and quickly:
  **increase the distances a lot.** Heavy clay holds contamination closer but drains badly and
  can pool. Cracked bedrock is the worst: contamination travels a long way through the cracks
  with almost no filtering.
- **Flooding.** Never in a floodplain, a low spot, or anywhere a river can reach (→ 17-03).
  {{#if is.flood_region}}Your home area has a real flood risk.{{/if}}
- **Wind:** downwind of the living space if you can manage it.
- **The winter path.** A latrine you cannot safely reach in a blizzard is one people stop using
  (→ 13-05, → 11-06). **Close enough to reach, far enough to be safe**, with a shovelled,
  sanded path.
- **Existing systems.** If the site has a septic system, **use it** (→ 13-12). Find the tank and
  drain field before digging anything, to protect them, and because **a latrine dug through a
  drain field is dug into sewage.**
- **Your own well:** → 03-10.

{{photo latrine-site}}

## Building a pit latrine

1. **Dig a test hole first** to check for groundwater and rock.
2. **Dig deep and narrow rather than wide and shallow:** more room, less surface, less smell,
   easier to cover.
3. **Put a slab or platform over the pit.** A pit latrine with a slab counts as an "improved"
   facility in CDC's terms and one without a slab does not (CDC, About Global Sanitation): it
   keeps people from touching the waste and keeps rain out. **A wooden
   platform with a seat and a lid.**
4. **A lid that closes.** Flies breeding in a latrine and then landing on food is a textbook
   way disease spreads.
5. **Cover material beside it:** soil, ash, lime, sawdust. **A scoop after each use** controls
   smell and flies.
6. **A handwashing station at the latrine** (→ 13-02). A tippy-tap costs nothing, and it is the
   whole point.
7. **Close it well before it is full**, leaving room for a thick cap of soil: fill with soil,
   mound it so water runs off, mark it, and **do not plant food crops there.** Dig the next
   one somewhere else.
8. **Keep a record of where old pits are** (→ 25-04).

## Waste while traveling

- **A "cathole" 6 to 8 inches deep, at least 200 feet from water, camp and trails**; cover
  and disguise it when finished (National Park Service, Leave No Trace Seven Principles).
- **Pack out toilet paper and hygiene products** (NPS); **never leave them on the surface.**
- **Never near a water source anyone might drink from** (→ 03-04).
- **In frozen ground you often cannot dig:** pack it out. Carry bags for exactly this.
- **Wash hands:** carry sanitizer for when there is no water (→ 13-02).

The 100-foot pit distance and the 200-foot cathole distance do not conflict: a shallow,
unlined scrape on the move gets more distance.

## What goes wrong

- **Uphill of the well.** The most serious mistake.
- **Too shallow, or into groundwater.**
- **In a drainage path:** fine in August, a disaster in the spring melt.
- **Too far to use in winter**, so people start going closer to the house.
- **No lid, no cover material:** flies, smell and disease.
- **No handwashing station**, which cancels most of the benefit.
- **Digging where you will later want a well or a garden.**
- **Ignoring the neighbors' water.** In a community, sanitation is a shared problem (→ 18-01):
  one bad latrine uphill affects everyone.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Post-hole digger, spade, mattock, pry bar** | Digging a real pit | → 16-01 |
| Lumber for a platform and seat | Makes it an improved latrine | Solid, with a lid that closes |
| **Lime or wood ash** | Smell and germ control | Ash is free (→ 06-02) |
| Cover material and a scoop | Every use | Soil, sawdust, ash |
| **Handwashing station (tippy-tap)** | The point of the whole thing | → 13-02 |
| Screen or netting for the shelter | Flies spread disease | |
| A shovel kept only for the latrine | Touches nothing else | Label it |
| Marker stakes, a record of old pits | So nobody digs or plants there later | → 25-04 |
| Trowel and bags for traveling | Catholes, or packing out when frozen | → 22-03 |
| A site map with distances marked | Get the decision right once | → 25-04 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Platform:** pallets, planks, plywood, a seat taken from a house toilet.
- **Shelter:** tarps on a frame, salvaged siding, pallets. Privacy matters over months
  (→ 21-02), and a windbreak matters in cold.
- **Cover material:** soil from the digging (keep the dug-out pile beside the pit: it is your
  cover supply), ash, sawdust, leaves.
- **Digging hard ground:** soak it the day before to soften it; a mattock and pry bar. A fire
  built on the spot slowly thaws frozen ground (it works, slowly).
- **Handwashing:** a jug with a nail hole; a tippy-tap from sticks and cord.

## When it runs out

- **A pit fills.** Plan for **more than one pit** over a long event. Pick the second and third
  sites when you dig the first, so you are not choosing under pressure.
- **Capacity:** a household fills a pit faster than expected, **especially if urine goes in.**
  Separating urine (→ 13-01, → 13-06) makes a pit last much longer.
- **Runway:** estimate pit volume against your household's use and put it in → 23-02. A slow
  clock, but a clock.
- **Substitute:** compost system (→ 13-06), bag and store (→ 13-01), or the sewer or septic if it
  works.
- **What never runs out is the siting rule:** downhill, far from water, above the water table,
  out of the drainage path, with a lid and a handwashing station.
- **The community side matters over time** (→ 18-01). If neighbors are also improvising, **where
  they put waste affects your water.** Agreeing where waste goes is one of the most useful early
  conversations in a group, and one of the least contentious, because everyone benefits.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if is.urban}}generally not possible on a town lot: the
  distances cannot be met. **Bucket and bag** (→ 13-01), and treat sanitation as one of the real
  limits of staying put in a long event.{{else}}on a rural lot, do the site work now: test hole,
  drainage, distances from your well, and mark the spot.{{/if}}
- **B (moving):** catholes, 200 feet from water, buried and covered; pack out in frozen ground.
  **Never contaminate a water source you or others will use.**
- **C (rural or at a destination):** if there is a septic system, **operating it is the first
  move** (→ 13-12), not digging. The site work is still first-week work (→ 01-04): test-dig for
  groundwater, walk the drainage, **choose and mark the latrine site downhill and far from the
  well, and clear of the septic tank and drain field, before it is ever needed**, pick the next
  two pit sites, and dig a winter pit in autumn.
{{#if has.destinations}}
{{#each destinations as d}}  - **{{ d.name }}:** septic? ☐ yes ☐ no ☐ unknown. Latrine site marked: ☐
{{/each}}
{{/if}}

## Cross-references

→ 13-12 operating a septic system (first move where there is one) · → 13-01 human waste ·
→ 13-06 composting toilet · → 13-05 winter sanitation · → 13-02 hygiene · → 03-07 testing water ·
→ 17-03 floods · → 01-04 setting up at a new place · → 01-05 choosing a destination ·
→ 18-01 mutual aid · → 25-04 maps

pages.body:
# Menstrual supplies and diapering without stores

**What this page is for.** Two of the biggest, most relentless consumables in a household, and
the reusable alternatives that end the dependence on shops: menstrual cups and cloth pads, and
cloth diapers.

> **CAUTION.** A baby or toddler in diapers needs them every day: you cannot ration, put off or
> wait out that need. **Menstrual supplies are needed for years.** Together they are probably
> the two most under-planned consumables in most stockpiles.
>
> **Both are hygiene issues.** Wash hands before and after changing a menstrual product or a
> diaper (CDC). **A speck of stool too small to see holds millions of germs** (CDC): diapering
> is a direct route for stomach illness into a household with small children who touch
> everything (→ 13-02, → 12-05).

## Do this now

1. **Buy menstrual cups and cloth pads, and start using them now.** One of the most valuable
   purchases in this binder: **one purchase that permanently removes a recurring
   consumable.** There is a learning curve; get through it before a crisis.
2. **Buy cloth diapers and covers** in the sizes your child will need next.{{#if has.infant}}
   Even if you use disposables day to day, a stock of cloth diapers turns an impossible
   shortage into a laundry job.{{/if}}
3. **Stock disposables deeply as the buffer.** Bulky, but they get you through the first weeks
   without adding laundry to everything else.
4. **Set up the wash system now** (→ 13-04): a lidded pail, a tub kept for diapers, and a way to
   heat water.

## Menstrual supplies

**The reusable options:**

| Option | Lasts | Needs | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Menstrual cup** (a soft silicone cup worn inside, emptied and rinsed) | **Years** | Clean hands, water, boiling between periods | **The best preparedness item in this category.** Compact, no consumables, no laundry |
| **Cloth pads** | Years | Washing and drying | Easy to learn; can be made from cotton flannel |
| **Period underwear** | Years | Washing and drying | Comfortable; bulkier laundry |
| Disposable pads and tampons | One use | Storage space | The buffer, not the plan |

**A cup needs almost nothing in a crisis:** clean hands, a little water for rinsing, and
boiling between periods. It works on the move when nothing else does. Get one and learn it now.

**Hygiene rules (CDC, Menstrual Hygiene):**

- **Wash hands with soap and water before and after** changing any product.
- **Change regularly, and follow the product's own instructions.** CDC: change pads every few
  hours whatever the flow, more often for heavy periods; change tampons every 4 to 8 hours and
  never wear one longer than 8 hours; use the lowest absorbency you need. For tampons and cups
  the label matters: toxic shock syndrome (a rare, dangerous infection) is real.
- **Wash reusable products thoroughly and dry them completely.** Sunlight helps and is free
  (→ 13-04). Soak cloth in **cold** water first; hot water sets blood.
- **Throw away used disposables in a closed, lidded bin:** not into a compost system (→ 13-06)
  and not into a pit you will use later (→ 13-07).
- **Clean a cup daily, and boil it for 1 to 2 minutes after each period** (CDC), in a small
  pot on a fire already going for cooking (→ 07-01).

**Making cloth pads:** flannel or old cotton (a worn flannel sheet, a soft towel), several
absorbent layers, and a tightly woven or waterproof backing, sewn (→ 16-04). **Snap or tie it
around the underwear.** A straightforward sewing project that makes the supply renewable.

More on menstrual health and contraception: → 02-25.

## Diapering a baby or toddler

**This is the relentless one.** A baby or toddler goes through several diapers a day, every day,
for a year or more. Disposables at that rate are a very large volume of stock and of waste
(→ 13-03), and once they are gone, they are gone.

{{#if has.infant}}**Your household has a child in diapers.**{{/if}}

### Diaper worksheet: fill it in, then copy to → 23-02

No published figure fits every child: newborns use far more diapers a day than toddlers.
**Count your child's real week**, then work out the stock.

- Child's current diaper size: ______ · Next size up: ______
- Diapers on hand now (count the packs): ______
- Wipes packs on hand: ______ · Barrier cream tubes on hand: ______
- Real diapers per day this week (count once, honestly): ______
- **Days of stock = diapers on hand ÷ diapers per day = ______ days.**
- **A 90-day buffer = diapers per day x 90 = ______ diapers.** Round up: illness (diarrhea,
  → 12-05) raises the rate exactly when resupply is least likely.
- **Buy for the next sizes, not just today's.** A diaper one size too big still works (snugger
  waist, more leaks); one size too small does not close. A child outgrows a size during a long
  event, so split the stock across the current size and the next one or two, heavier on the
  next size (→ 11-09).
- **Wipes:** count how long one pack lasts: ______ days; packs for 90 days = 90 ÷ that =
  ______. Washcloths and warm soapy water are the fully renewable substitute.

### Cloth diapers: the system

{{figure fig-flat-diaper-fold}}

- **Enough diapers for at least two days of changes**, so you can wash every other day instead
  of daily: your diapers per day x 2, plus spares for the day they do not dry. **Flats** (a single large square of cotton you fold) or **prefolds** (a pre-sewn thicker
  rectangle), plus covers, are the toughest, cheapest and most repairable setup. **Flats dry
  fastest**, which matters a lot in a cold house (→ 11-03).
- **Covers** (waterproof outer pants): several per size; reused between changes unless soiled.
- **A lidded pail.** A dry pail (just a lidded container) is simpler and safer around a toddler
  than a pail full of water, which is a drowning risk.
- **Fasteners:** snap-style fasteners or safety pins, with spares.

{{photo diaper-station}}

**The routine:**

1. **Scrape or shake solids into the toilet system** (→ 13-01). Solids do not go in the wash.
2. **Store in the lidded pail** until wash day.
3. **Wash:** soak, then **hot water and soap**, agitate, **rinse thoroughly**: leftover soap
   causes rashes, so rinse more than you think (→ 13-04).
4. **After a stomach illness,** add a sanitizing rinse of diluted bleach to the diapers
   themselves, following the bleach label's laundry-sanitizing directions, then extra
   clean-water rinses. Never bleach the covers: bleach ruins the waterproof layer.
5. **Dry completely.** Sun-dry when you can (sunlight bleaches stains and helps kill germs, for
   free), freeze-dry outdoors in winter, or use the indoor line (→ 11-03).
6. **Wash your hands** properly after every change and after handling the pail (CDC).

> **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. Urine-soaked diapers
> contain ammonia: rinse them before any bleach rinse, and never add bleach to a pail of soiled
> diapers. The mix gives off toxic gas. (→ 30-01)

**Preventing rash matters more without a doctor:**

- **Change often.** A wet diaper against skin in a cold house is a rash risk and drains heat
  (→ 11-02).
- **Dry the skin fully** before the new diaper.
- **Air time:** a little time with no diaper, in the warm room, every day.
- **Barrier ointment:** stock it; petroleum jelly works (→ 12-07).
- **Rinse thoroughly** in the wash: soap residue is a leading cause of rash that will not go
  away.
- **Watch for rash that is not getting better.** It can turn into a yeast or bacterial infection
  that needs treatment (→ 12-07, → 12-04).

**Older children who are out of diapers** often go backwards under stress. That is normal and
common (→ 20-08). Have some larger cloth options and treat it as unremarkable.

## Water and work

**Both reusable systems swap a supply problem for a water-and-labour problem.**

- **Diaper laundry is an almost daily job:** real water, soap, fuel for hot water and drying
  space (→ 13-04, → 11-03).
- **In winter, drying is the limit:** that is why **flats** are the right choice, and why you
  keep more than two days' worth when drying is slow.
- **Put water, soap and fuel for diaper laundry in the household budget** (→ 03-01, → 23-02).
  It is easy to leave out.
- **This is the case for the disposable buffer:** use disposables during illness, on a move,
  in a cold snap when drying is impossible, and in the first chaotic weeks.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Menstrual cups, two per person who menstruates** | Years of use, no consumables, works on the move | **Learn to use them now** |
| **Cloth pads or period underwear** | Reusable backup | Can be made (→ 16-04) |
| Disposable menstrual supplies | Buffer for the first weeks and travel | Deep stock |
| **Cloth diapers, at least two days' changes plus spares (flats or prefolds)** | Flats dry fastest | Plus the next size |
| Diaper covers, six to eight | Reused between changes | Waterproof |
| Snap fasteners or pins | Fastening | Spares |
| **Lidded diaper pail** | Containment, smell, keeps a toddler out | Dry pail |
| A wash tub and large pot kept for diapers | Diaper laundry is its own job | → 13-04 |
| Barrier ointment or petroleum jelly | Rash prevention without a doctor | Many uses |
| **Disposable diapers, deep buffer** | Illness, travel, cold snaps, chaos | Your daily count x 90, split across sizes |
| Wipes, by your own count | 90 days' worth | Washcloths substitute |
| Soap in bulk | Diaper laundry uses a lot | → 13-09 |
| Drying lines and racks | The real limit | → 11-03 |
| Hand sanitizer at the changing area | For when washing is not immediate | Not a replacement (CDC) |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Cloth diapers:** flannel sheets, cotton towels, T-shirts, receiving blankets cut and hemmed.
  **A flat is just a square of absorbent cotton, folded.** The simplest design, and it works.
- **Covers:** wool "soakers" (wool resists water and breathes: a traditional, excellent choice,
  → 11-05), or a cover from any water-resistant fabric.
- **Menstrual cloth:** folded cotton flannel or towel, washed. This is what people used for most
  of history.
- **Fasteners:** safety pins (stock plenty), ties, a snug cover holding the folded cloth.
- **Pail:** any bucket with a lid.
- **What you cannot easily improvise:** a menstrual cup. **Buy them now:** small, cheap, and
  they last years.

## When it runs out

- **Disposables run out; reusables do not.** The reusable versions turn a hard shortage into an
  ongoing water, soap and labour cost, which is a much better problem to have.
- **What does run out:** soap (makeable, → 13-09), fasteners and elastic (**stock spares**,
  → 11-07), covers (they wear out: stock extras), and **the child's size** (buy ahead, → 11-09).
- **Runway:** count disposables in **days of child**, not packages: the worksheet above does
  it. Put the days in the diapers row of → 23-02 and re-count monthly as the rate and size
  change.
- **Ration:** **use disposables on purpose:** illness, cold snaps, travel, the first weeks.
  Cloth the rest of the time.
- **Substitute:** cotton cloth from any source. **Fabric is one of the most plentiful things in
  empty houses** (→ 22-02).
- **Trade:** children's supplies are one of the easiest, least tense things to barter (→ 18-02):
  everyone with children has outgrown gear and needs the next size.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** water and washing are available, so **run cloth as the default and
  keep disposables as the buffer.** Set up the pail, tub and line early and settle the routine
  while it is still easy.
- **B (moving):** **disposables, without hesitation.** You cannot wash and dry diapers on the
  move in winter, and a wet child in the cold is a serious problem (→ 11-02). The menstrual cup
  is the one item here that is actually *better* while traveling. Pack out diaper waste or bury
  it properly, away from water (→ 13-07).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** cloth throughout, with more drying space and water. **Build
  a real laundry setup near the stove** and make diaper washing a fixed daily job.

## Cross-references

→ 13-02 hygiene · → 13-04 laundry · → 13-01 human waste · → 13-09 soap making ·
→ 13-03 trash · → 12-12 women's health · → 12-04 infection · → 20-06 diapers and hygiene ·
→ 20-08 regression · → 11-03 drying · → 23-02 consumables

pages.body:
# Making soap from ash and fat

**What this page is for.** Why soap matters so much, and how soap is made from wood ash (or
bought lye) and animal fat, so that a household can keep making it once the shops are gone.

> **CAUTION. Lye causes severe chemical burns and can cause permanent blindness.** Sodium
> hydroxide and potassium hydroxide ("lye"), whether bought or made from wood ash, are strong
> caustics: they burn skin and eyes. **A splash in the eye is a medical emergency.** Mixing lye
> with water makes a lot of heat and can boil and spatter.
>
> **Always: eye protection (goggles, not glasses), gloves, long sleeves, outdoors or with real
> ventilation, and always add LYE TO WATER, never water to lye.** Keep plenty of clean water
> within reach. **Children and pets nowhere near it** (→ 20-02). **Floor:** Children do not have
> access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products (→ 30-01). Store lye the same way:
> locked and labeled.
>
> **This page gives no recipe and no ratios**, because lye made from ash has an **unknown and
> changing strength**, which is exactly what makes traditional soap-making unpredictable and
> sometimes caustic. **Learn from a real soap-making reference, practice with measured
> bought lye and a tested recipe first**, and only then try the ash version.

## Do this now

1. **Stock soap instead.** Bar soap keeps almost for ever, costs very little, and is the most
   valuable medical supply in the house (→ 13-02). **Buy far more than seems reasonable:** that
   is the real answer for the first year or two.
2. **Buy bought lye (sodium hydroxide) and a good paper soap-making book, and make one batch
   now, safely, with a tested recipe.** Learning with lye of known strength builds the skill
   without the risk.
3. **Save fat:** every trimming, every jar of drippings, every rendered batch (→ 04-12,
   → 10-04). Fat is the other half of soap.
4. **Save hardwood ash** from the stove, dry and clean, in a covered metal container.

## Why this matters more than it looks

**Soap is the most valuable medical supply a household with no clinic can have** (→ 13-02;
CDC). Handwashing with soap breaks the chain that causes the most likely serious illness
(→ 12-05). Soap also does laundry (→ 13-04), dishes (→ 13-10) and wound cleaning (→ 12-02).

**Soap is also one of the few manufactured goods a household can keep making**, from two things
it will have anyway: **wood ash from the stove** (→ 06-04) and **fat** from animals and cooking
(→ 05-09, → 05-16, → 04-12).

## The chemistry in one paragraph

Soap is what you get when a **strong alkali (lye)** reacts with **fat** ("saponification").
Historically the alkali came from **water trickled through hardwood ash**, which gives
**potassium hydroxide** ("potash lye") and makes a **soft, jelly-like soap**: good for laundry
and washing, not a hard bar. **Modern hard bar soap uses sodium hydroxide.** The difference that
matters: **bought lye has a known strength on its label, and ash lye does not.**

## Why the unknown strength is the whole problem

Soap-making is a ratio. Too little lye and you get greasy fat that spoils. Too much and you get
**caustic soap that burns skin**: exactly what you do not want on a child's hands or in a wound.

Ash lye strength changes with the kind of wood, how completely it burned, how the ash was
stored and how it was soaked. The traditional tests (whether an egg or potato floats in it,
whether it dissolves a feather) are **rough signs, not measurements**, which is why old-time
soap was often harsh.

**The safe path:**

1. **Learn with bought lye and a tested recipe.** Get the process, the safety habits and the
   feel for it.
2. **Then, if you need to, use ash lye**, testing cautiously, adding **extra fat** (so the soap
   stays mild even if the lye was stronger than you thought), and **testing the finished soap
   carefully before it touches anyone's skin, especially a child's.**
3. **When in doubt, add more fat.** Greasy soap is unpleasant. Caustic soap injures.

## Making lye from wood ash (an outline, not a procedure)

{{figure fig-ash-hopper}}

- **Hardwood ash only.** Softwood and pine ash is much weaker. Oak, ash, maple and similar
  hardwoods are what you want.
- **Clean white ash from a hot fire**, sieved of charcoal lumps, kept **dry** in a covered metal
  container. Ash that has got wet has already lost its strength.
- **Leaching:** water trickled slowly through a container of ash and collected underneath. The
  traditional "ash hopper" is a barrel with a false bottom and a spout. **Rainwater or other
  soft water works better than hard water.**
- **The result is a caustic liquid.** Treat it exactly like bought lye: goggles, gloves,
  ventilation, out of reach of children.
- **Boiling it down to make it stronger raises the danger a lot**: boiling caustic spatters.
  **This is where people get hurt.**

## Rendering the fat

Same method as → 10-04: **low and slow, in a heavy pot or a double boiler, watched, strained
through cloth.** Clean, well-strained fat makes better soap. **Melting fat is a real fire
hazard, and water on a fat fire makes it explode into flame** (→ 10-04).

**Fat sources:** beef or deer tallow (best for hard soap), lard, chicken and rabbit fat
(→ 05-16), strained used cooking oil, and rancid fat (**still fine for soap**: a good use for
fat that is no longer good food, → 04-12).

## Safety rules, all of them

1. **Goggles.** Not glasses. Eye splashes cause permanent damage.
2. **Chemical-resistant gloves and long sleeves.**
3. **Outdoors or with real ventilation.** Lye and water give off fumes.
4. **Always add lye to water, never water to lye.** The reverse can boil violently.
5. **The mixture gets very hot:** lye dissolving in water gives off a great deal of heat (CDC/
   ATSDR, Medical Management Guidelines for Sodium Hydroxide). Use heat-proof containers.
6. **Never aluminum.** Lye reacts with aluminum, tin and zinc and corrodes most metals (ATSDR);
   with aluminum it gives off hydrogen, a flammable gas. Use
   stainless steel, heavy plastic, or glass (lye slowly etches and weakens glass).
7. **Equipment kept only for soap**, never anything that touches food. {{#if has.condition.CL-04}}Never
   the allergy-safe cookware (→ 02-04).{{/if}} Label everything.
8. **Plenty of clean water within reach.** For a splash on skin, **flush with lots of water at
   once, and for a long time** (ATSDR). An eye splash is a medical emergency: lye can burn the
   eye badly, and ATSDR warns the damage may not be clear for days. Flush and keep flushing
   (→ 12-03). If anyone swallows lye, call Poison Control (→ 12-17).
9. **Children and pets nowhere near it:** the process and the curing soap.
10. **Fresh soap is caustic and must cure for weeks before use.** Do not rush it, and test it
    before it touches skin.
11. **Store lye and ash lye sealed, labeled and locked** (→ 06-06).

## What you get, realistically

- **Ash-lye soap:** soft, jelly-like, brown, and excellent for **laundry** (→ 13-04) and
  **general cleaning**, which use the most soap anyway.
- **Bought-lye tallow soap:** a real hard bar, good for hands and body.
- **Neither will look like shop soap**, and that is fine.
- **Soap is a very good barter good** (→ 18-02): everyone needs it, few can make it, and it
  keeps.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bar soap, a very large stock** | The real answer for the first year or two | Cheap now; keeps |
| **Bought lye (sodium hydroxide) and a tested recipe** | Learn safely with a known strength | Sealed, labeled, locked |
| **Goggles, chemical gloves, apron** | Protection that is not optional | Goggles, not glasses |
| Stainless steel or heavy plastic pots and utensils kept for soap | **Never aluminum, never food equipment** | Label them permanently |
| Digital kitchen scale | Soap is a ratio; cups and spoons are not accurate enough | Essential for a real recipe |
| Thermometer | Fat and lye temperatures matter | Kept for soap |
| Covered metal ash container | Dry ash keeps its strength | Also safe ash storage (→ 06-02) |
| Jars for saving fat | Every trimming and drippings | → 04-12 |
| A paper soap-making book | Ratios, safety, troubleshooting | **Learn before you need it** |
| Plenty of clean water | Splash response | Within arm's reach |
| Molds kept for soap | Paper-lined boxes, silicone, old pans | Never food containers |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Ash:** free from a wood stove (→ 06-04). **Hardwood only, kept dry.**
- **Fat:** butchering trimmings (→ 05-09, → 05-16), saved drippings, rancid fat, tallow rendered
  by → 10-04.
- **Ash hopper:** a barrel or bucket with a false bottom of gravel and cloth, a spout at the
  bottom, ash on top.
- **Containers:** stainless steel, heavy plastic buckets, glazed crockery. **Never aluminum.**
- **Molds:** paper-lined cardboard boxes, wooden frames, a loaf pan you will never cook in
  again.
- **Cleaning with no soap at all:** ash and sand scrub hands, and ash is mildly alkaline. A real
  traditional method, and better than nothing (→ 13-02).

## When it runs out

- **Making soap is the answer to soap running out.** But **the skill is the resource, not the
  supplies**, and it has to be learned before it is needed.
- **The inputs renew:** ash from a stove you are running anyway, fat from animals and cooking.
- **What limits you:** bought lye (finite: use it to learn), fat (which competes with food and
  light, → 04-12, → 10-04), and time.
- **Fat is food, light and soap at once.** In a real shortage, **rancid and inedible fat goes to
  soap.** That is why you save every scrap.
- **Ration:** home-made soap for laundry and cleaning (the big users); keep shop-bought bar soap
  for hands, bodies and wound care, where mildness and reliability matter most.
- **Trade:** soap is one of the best barter goods there is (→ 18-02). **A household that can make
  soap holds real value in a community** (→ 18-03).

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** stock soap deeply and **learn the process now**, with bought lye,
  outdoors, once. Start saving ash and fat. Do not make ash lye under pressure as your first
  attempt.
- **B (moving):** carry soap; do not make it. A small bar per person, and hand sanitizer
  (→ 13-02).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** **soap-making becomes a real household job:** the stove makes
  ash every day, animals give tallow (→ 05-16), and soap is made in batches a few times a year.
  Set up a permanent, safe, outdoor work area, well away from where children play.

## Cross-references

→ 13-02 hygiene (why this matters) · → 13-04 laundry · → 13-10 dishwashing ·
→ 10-04 rendering fat and the fire warnings · → 04-12 fats and oils · → 12-03 burns ·
→ 06-06 storing hazardous materials · → 20-02 child safety · → 18-02 barter ·
→ 24-01 skills checklist

pages.body:
# Dishwashing and kitchen hygiene with little water

**What this page is for.** Washing dishes properly with very little water, keeping food safe
without a fridge, and keeping allergy-safe food safe.

> **SAFETY. Two separate reasons this matters.**
>
> 1. **Food poisoning.** A kitchen with no fridge, no hot running water and food cooked over a
>    fire is a kitchen where germs spread easily. Diarrheal illness is the most likely serious
>    health problem without services (→ 12-05). It dehydrates babies fast and is dangerous for
>    anyone with diabetes.
> 2. **Allergen cross-contact.** **Sanitizer does not remove allergen proteins. Only washing
>    with soap and water does** (US FDA, Food Allergies). A plate that was rinsed but not
>    washed, or an allergic person's plate washed in a tub that just held egg, is a real risk.
>    {{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Someone in your household has a severe allergy.** The food-allergy
>    module governs (→ 02-04, → 02-03), and it does not relax because water is short.{{else}}If
>    anyone you feed has a food allergy, the food-allergy module governs (→ 02-04).{{/if}}
>
> **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The mix
> gives off toxic gas. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Set up the three-tub system** (below).{{#if has.condition.CL-04}} Add **a separate,
   clearly marked set of tubs and cloths for the allergic person's dishes**, labeled
   permanently with a different color, tape or paint.{{/if}}
2. {{#if has.condition.CL-04}}**Keep cookware, utensils and a cutting board only for the
   allergic person**, stored separately.{{else}}**If anyone you feed has a food allergy, keep
   cookware, utensils and a cutting board only for them**, stored separately.{{/if}}
3. **Get a good food thermometer, or two.** With no fridge and fire cooking, cooking to the
   safe temperature is the main food-safety control (FoodSafety.gov, Cook to a Safe Minimum
   Internal Temperature; → 04-17).
4. **Stock dish soap and bleach.** Both are cheap now and central to this page.

## The three-tub system: the standard low-water method

{{figure fig-three-tub-dishwashing}}

How commercial kitchens and campsites do it, with very little water.

1. **Scrape first, thoroughly.** Wipe plates with a paper towel, a cloth or a piece of bread;
   scrape food into the compost or waste (→ 13-03). **Scraping is what makes this use little
   water:** food bits foul the wash water fastest.
2. **Tub 1: WASH.** Hot water and soap. Wash from cleanest to dirtiest (glasses, then plates,
   then pots) so the water lasts.
3. **Tub 2: RINSE.** Clean warm water, to remove the soap.
4. **Tub 3: SANITIZE. 1 tablespoon of unscented 5 to 9 percent household bleach in 1 gallon
   of clean water; dishes fully under the water; then air dry** (CDC, Cleaning and Sanitizing
   with Bleach After an Emergency: wash with soap and hot clean water, rinse, sanitize in this solution,
   air dry). CDC gives no soak time for dishes; leaving them in while you wash the next load is
   a reasonable habit. Without bleach, dishes can go into boiling water instead (use tongs).
   **Clean first, then sanitize: sanitizing a dirty surface does not work** (CDC). **This tub is NOT drinkable.** Label it, mix it fresh daily, and keep children
   away from it. It is a weak sanitizing solution, not the much stronger disinfecting mixes in
   the table on → 13-11.
5. **Air dry on a rack.** **Do not towel dry:** a damp towel used all day spreads germs to
   everything it touches. Air drying is cleaner and needs no towels.

{{photo dish-tubs}}

**Water:** the three tubs use a small fraction of what running water does, and **the wash and
rinse water become greywater** for flushing or plants you do not eat (→ 13-03, → 03-01).

## Allergy-safe dishes: a completely separate track

This is not a variation on the above; it is a parallel system.
{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}It applies in your household.{{else}}It applies whenever anyone you
feed has a food allergy.{{/if}}

- **Their own tub, brush or cloth, and towel:** visibly different, never swapped.
- **Wash the allergic person's dishes FIRST**, in clean water, before anything else touches the
  tubs.
- **Soap and water, scrubbed by hand.** This is what removes allergen protein. **Rinsing is not
  enough. Sanitizer is not enough** (FDA).
- **Their own cookware, cutting board and utensils**, stored separately.
- **Wash hands with a clean towel before preparing their food** (→ 13-02).
- **Shared cooking surfaces are washed with soap and water before their food touches them:** a
  grill grate, a griddle, a Dutch oven that just cooked something with the allergen in it.
- **This holds when water is short.** If there is not enough water to do it properly, there is
  not enough water to feed them from shared equipment: **use their own gear and simple safe
  foods** instead of bending the rule.
- Feeding an allergic person traded, scavenged or unlabeled food is a separate decision:
  your household's choice {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19).

## Food safety without a fridge

- **Cook to temperature**, checked with a thermometer, by the FoodSafety.gov table (→ 04-17,
  → 05-16). This becomes the main control.
- **Keep raw and cooked completely apart:** different boards, plates and utensils. **Raw meat
  juices are the classic route.**
- **Do not keep cooked food warm for hours.** Eat it, or cool it and store it cold (→ 04-09),
  or preserve it (→ 04-04, → 04-06).
- **Cook only what will be eaten**, or plan the leftovers. **In winter, outdoor cold is free
  refrigeration** (→ 04-09); in summer it is not, and that is when food safety gets hard.
- **Reheat thoroughly.**
- **When in doubt, throw it out.** Food poisoning costs far more than a wasted meal (→ 12-05).

## Kitchen surfaces and cloths

- **Clean first with soap and water; sanitize after** (CDC). Cleaning removes dirt and germs;
  sanitizing reduces what is left. Doing only the second does not work.
- **Sanitize food-contact surfaces after raw meat** with the Tub 3 solution (1 tablespoon per
  gallon, air dry) (CDC). **To disinfect after illness, use the surface-bleach table on
  → 13-11, then rinse food-contact surfaces with clean water** before food touches them.
- **Dishcloths and sponges are the dirtiest things in most kitchens.** Wash and dry them daily,
  boil them now and then, and rotate them. A cloth that is always damp spreads more than it
  cleans.
- **Air dry everything:** surfaces, dishes, cloths. **Dry is hostile to bacteria; damp is
  welcoming.**
- **Separate cutting boards** for raw meat, for produce{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}, and for the
  allergic person{{/if}}.

## Short-water and no-water modes

| Water available | Approach |
|---|---|
| Normal | Three-tub system; reuse the greywater |
| Short | **Scrape harder**, wash fewer dishes (one plate per person, reused), heat less water, sanitize only what needs it |
| Very short | **Personal dishes:** each person has one plate, cup and set of utensils, wiped and reused; wash properly less often. **Allergy-safe dishes still get washed properly, always** |
| None | Eat from foil, leaves or clean hands; **cook one-pot meals** to cut dishes; **put handwashing before dishwashing** (→ 13-02) |

**When water is truly scarce, handwashing beats dishwashing.** Clean hands and a doubtful plate
is safer than dirty hands and a clean plate.

## One-pot cooking is a sanitation strategy

**Fewer dishes means less water, fuel and soap.** When all three are rationed, **one-pot meals
(stews, soups, skillet meals) are a sanitation decision as much as a cooking one** (→ 07-04,
→ 04-18). Cast iron cleans with hot water and a scraper and does not need soap for routine use,
but **it does need soap and scrubbing before it touches allergy-safe food.**

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Three wash tubs (wash, rinse, sanitize)** | The standard low-water system | Labeled, kept for dishes |
| **A separate, clearly marked tub set for allergy-safe dishes** (if needed) | Allergen control is not optional | Different color; never swapped |
| **Separate cookware, board and utensils for the allergic person** (if needed) | → 02-04 | Stored apart |
| **Food thermometers, two** | The main control with no fridge | FoodSafety.gov |
| Dish soap in bulk | Used heavily | Plus → 13-09 |
| Unscented bleach, 5 to 9 percent | Sanitizing: **1 tablespoon per gallon** (CDC); disinfecting by the → 13-11 table | Weakens over time; rotate (→ 29-05) |
| Dish rack or drying rack | **Air dry, don't towel dry** | Cleaner, saves towels |
| Several dishcloths and brushes | Rotate and dry daily | Boil now and then |
| Separate cutting boards (raw meat, produce, allergy-safe) | Stops germs and allergens crossing | Color-coded |
| Scrapers, spatulas | Scraping saves the water | |
| A large pot for heating wash water | On a fire already running | → 07-01 |
| Measuring spoons for bleach | Strength matters | 1 tablespoon per gallon for dishes; → 13-11 for surfaces |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Tubs:** buckets, totes, pots, a sink basin. **Keep the sets separate and marked.**
- **Sanitizing:** boiling water sanitizes washed dishes when you have no bleach.
- **Soap:** home-made (→ 13-09), or any soap. Plain soap is better than detergent for greywater
  you reuse (→ 13-03).
- **Scrubbers:** a cloth, a wad of grass, sand and a rag, a pine cone, steel wool, wood ash as a
  mild scrub.
- **Drying rack:** a wire shelf, sticks, a towel spread out (**then dry the towel**).
- **What you cannot substitute:** the separate allergen system. **Improvise the containers,
  never the separation.**

## When it runs out

- **Dish soap and bleach are the consumables.** Soap can be made (→ 13-09); **bleach cannot,
  and it weakens in storage.** Rotate it; **hot water and boiling replace sanitizer** when it is
  gone.
- **Water is the real limit** (→ 03-01). Put dishwashing in the water budget: it is a daily
  line and easy to forget.
- **Cut back in this order:** scrape harder → fewer dishes per person → personal dishes → wash
  properly less often → **one-pot cooking to remove the dishes entirely.** **Never cut the
  allergy-safe washing, and never cut handwashing** (→ 13-02).
- **The logic:** food poisoning costs huge amounts of water (→ 12-05), medicine and labour: far
  more than the water saved by cutting corners. In the kitchen, careful is cheaper than
  efficient.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** water is available; run the full three-tub system and any
  allergy-safe track. **Set the habits now:** routines from the first week are the ones that
  last.
- **B (moving):** one-pot cooking, few dishes, wipe and reuse, handwashing first. An allergic
  person eats from **their own sealed supplies** on the move rather than shared cooking: the
  safe simplification.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** more water and space; a summer washing station outdoors and
  a winter one near the stove. **More raw meat handling** (→ 05-09, → 05-16) means keeping raw
  and cooked apart and cooking to temperature matter more, not less.

## Cross-references

→ 13-02 hygiene · → 13-03 greywater · → 13-09 soap making · → 13-11 the surface-bleach table ·
→ 02-04 food allergy · → 04-17 food safety in an outage · → 04-09 cold storage ·
→ 07-04 one-pot cooking · → 12-05 illness and dehydration

pages.body:
# Preventing a disease outbreak in the household

**What this page is for.** Stopping an illness (especially a stomach bug) from spreading through
the whole household when you are living close together with no clinic: routes, the sick corner,
the cleanup, and the bleach strengths to use.

> **SAFETY. The whole household falling ill at once is one of the worst situations in this
> binder**, worse than most single injuries, because it takes away every adult's ability to haul
> water, tend the fire and care for the sick at the moment care is most needed.
>
> **For some people a routine stomach bug is not routine:** babies and young children dehydrate
> dangerously fast (→ 12-05), and vomiting and diarrhea are a dangerous sick day for anyone with
> type 1 diabetes{{#if has.condition.CL-01}} (→ 02-01){{/if}}.
>
> **The structural problem: you may be living in one heated room** (→ 08-01). That is right for
> heat, fuel and morale, and **the worst possible arrangement for containing an illness.** This
> page manages that tension on purpose.
>
> **Norovirus:** alcohol hand sanitizer is **not** good enough against it (CDC, Preventing
> Norovirus). **Soap and water.**
>
> **Floor:** Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners. The mix
> gives off a gas that can kill. (→ 30-01)

## Do this now

1. **Decide now where a sick person would go:** a second room you would heat, a corner you
   would screen off, or a marked "sick zone" in the warm room. **Deciding while everyone is well
   is far easier than at 2 a.m. with a vomiting child.**
2. **Stock unscented bleach (5 to 9 percent sodium hypochlorite) and learn the cleanup**: the
   surface table is below. Rotate bleach; it weakens in storage (→ 29-05).
3. **Stock oral rehydration salts (ORS) heavily** (→ 12-05). They matter most when this happens.
4. **Give everyone their own items now:** cup, plate, utensils, towel, marked with their name.
   Costs nothing, stops a lot of spread.
5. **Build the handwashing stations** (→ 13-02). The single control that does the most.

## How illness spreads, and what stops it

| Route | What spreads | The control |
|---|---|---|
| **Fecal-oral** (from stool to mouth) | Norovirus, diarrheal illness, hepatitis A | **Handwashing with soap** (→ 13-02), waste handling (→ 13-01), dishwashing (→ 13-10) |
| **Coughs, sneezes, breath** | Colds, flu, most chest illness | Distance, fresh air, covering coughs, separation |
| **Surfaces** | Norovirus survives a long time on surfaces | Clean, **then** disinfect (CDC) |
| **Food and water** | Food poisoning, waterborne illness | → 04-17, → 03-04, → 13-10 |
| **Shared items** | Everything | **Personal cups, plates, towels, bedding** |
| **Cleaning up vomit and stool** | Norovirus especially | **Gloves, bleach, careful cleanup, thorough handwashing** (CDC) |

## The one-room problem, handled honestly

You cannot fully isolate someone in a household living in one heated room. What you can do:

- **A sick corner:** the far end of the room, screened with a blanket, with the sick person's own
  bedding, cup, plate and bucket.
- **Air the room on purpose:** brief, wide-open airing several times a day. It costs less heat
  than people fear (→ 11-03), and it really does cut spread through the air.
- **One caregiver** where possible: ideally **not** someone with diabetes or another serious
  condition, and **not** the person who cooks. One person in and out, washing hands thoroughly
  every time.
- **Heat a second room if you possibly can** during an illness. **This is a good use of
  firewood** (→ 06-04): extra wood for a week to stop an outbreak taking the whole household is a
  good trade.
- **Children are the hardest part.** A sick child wants comfort, and a baby cannot be separated
  from its parents at all. **Accept that, and put your effort into the controls that work:**
  handwashing, surfaces, personal items, and containing vomit and stool.

## The sick kit

Put this together in advance, in one labeled container:

- **A bucket with a lid kept only for vomiting and waste** (→ 13-01), kept with the sick person
  and emptied carefully with gloves.
- **Gloves, and masks if you have them.**
- **Unscented bleach and a spray bottle**, for the table below.
- **Rags and paper towels kept for cleanup**, thrown away or washed separately (→ 13-04).
- **The sick person's own cup, plate, utensils, towel and bedding**, marked.
- **ORS packets, a thermometer, a symptom log** (→ 12-05, → 25-05).
- **A basin, a washcloth and a way to warm water.** Comfort matters, and it helps.

{{photo sick-kit}}

## The surface bleach table

**These are SURFACE strengths (CDC, Cleaning and Disinfecting with Bleach; CDC, Preventing
Norovirus). They are hundreds of times stronger than the DRINKING-water amounts on → 03-04 (a few
drops per gallon).** Never confuse the two tables. Bleach at surface strength in drinking water is
poisoning; bleach at drinking strength on a norovirus spill does nothing. **If a mixed jug has no
label, it is surface solution: pour it away. It is never drinkable.**

Published amounts, printed as published:

| Job | Recipe (per gallon of room-temperature water) | Contact time |
|---|---|---|
| **General surface disinfection** (counters, door handles, the sick corner) | **5 tablespoons (1/3 cup)** of household bleach, or 4 teaspoons per quart | **At least 1 minute, visibly wet** |
| **Norovirus: vomit and stool cleanup** | **5 to 25 tablespoons** of household bleach (5% to 8%) per gallon: a 1,000 to 5,000 ppm solution (CDC, Preventing Norovirus). **Use the strong end (up to 25 tablespoons, which is 1½ cups plus 1 tablespoon) on the spill itself and on porous or heavily soiled surfaces**; the low end on the hard surfaces around it | **At least 5 minutes** |

**Bleach strength:** the general recipe is for **plain unscented household bleach at 5 to 9
percent sodium hypochlorite** (CDC); CDC's norovirus recipe is written for 5 to 8 percent
bleach. The common US strengths (6 percent and 8.25 percent "concentrated") both fall in those
ranges, so the same spoon counts apply to either. If the label says anything outside 5 to 9
percent, or the product is splash-less, scented or a gel, do not use it for disinfecting.

**Rules that make the table work (CDC):**

- **Clean first, then disinfect.** Bleach on a visibly dirty surface does not work.
- **Mix it fresh every day.** Diluted bleach loses strength after about 24 hours. Date the jug.
- **NEVER mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner.** The fumes can kill. Open windows while
  using it indoors.
- **Food-contact surfaces and dishes:** after the contact time, **rinse with clean, safe water**
  before food touches them. The dish-sanitizing tub on → 13-10 uses a much weaker solution, not
  this table.
- **Wear gloves; keep it off skin and out of children's reach** (→ 20-02).

## Cleaning up vomit and diarrhea: the riskiest moment

Norovirus spreads very easily during cleanup (CDC).

- **Gloves, always.** A mask if you have one.
- **Contain it:** cover it with paper towels or disposable cloth first, then lift it away.
- **Clean, then disinfect** with the **norovirus-strength** solution from the table: 5 to 25
  tablespoons per gallon, at least 5 minutes wet. **Cleaning first is required.**
- **Handle soiled laundry carefully:** gloves, as little shaking as possible (shaking throws
  germs into the air), wash hot and separately, dry completely (→ 13-04; CDC).
- **Wash your hands with soap and water afterwards**, **not sanitizer alone** (CDC).
- **Air the room** afterwards.

## Watching the whole household

- **Log symptoms and times for everyone** (→ 25-05). Knowing who fell ill when tells you whether
  it is spreading and whether the controls work.
- **Watch babies and young children closest:** fewer wet diapers, floppiness or unusual
  sleepiness, no tears when crying (→ 12-05).
{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}- **Watch anyone with type 1 diabetes for ketones.** Illness plus
  vomiting is the road to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Ketone strips out and in use at the first
  sign of illness (→ 02-01).
{{else}}- **Anyone with diabetes:** illness plus vomiting is dangerous; follow their condition
  page's sick-day guidance (→ 02-01, → 02-05).
{{/if}}
- **Watch for signs it is beyond home care:** blood in stool, high fever, dehydration that does
  not improve with ORS, confusion, or signs of sepsis (a body-wide reaction to infection; → 12-04;
  CDC, About Sepsis).

## Prevention: where the real leverage is

This page's controls come after the ones that stop an outbreak starting:

1. **Handwashing at the key moments** (→ 13-02): **the single most effective thing.**
2. **Safe water** (→ 03-04).
3. **Keeping waste separate** (→ 13-01, → 13-07).
4. **Food safety:** cooking to temperature, raw and cooked kept apart (→ 13-10, → 04-17).
5. **Proper dishwashing** (→ 13-10).
6. **Personal items, not shared.**
7. **Managing outside contact.** Anyone who comes in (a neighbor, a trader, → 18-02) can bring
   illness. **Handwashing on arrival is a reasonable, friendly household rule.** Start it early.
8. **Keeping everyone fed, warm and rested.** A cold, hungry, exhausted household gets sicker and
   stays sicker (→ 08-01, → 21-07).

## If the whole household goes down anyway

It happens. Plan for it:

- **Put water and ORS where a sick person can reach them without going outside.** **The most
  important preparation:** everything else can wait; drinking cannot.
- **Simple food that needs no cooking** for the days nobody can cook (→ 04-18).
- **Keep the fire and the house going.** Even a barely functioning adult can keep one stove
  going. **Have enough wood indoors that nobody has to go out** for several days (→ 06-04).
- **Medical routines do not pause.** Insulin and other daily medicines continue through illness,
  and matter **more**, not less.
- **Neighbors** (→ 18-01). A household on good terms with its neighbors has somewhere to turn
  when everyone is ill at once.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Oral rehydration salts, heavy stock** | Matters most | → 12-05 |
| **Unscented bleach, spray bottle, measuring spoons** | Cleanup by the CDC table | Rotate: it weakens |
| Nitrile gloves, by the box | Cleanup and care | Non-latex |
| Masks | Chest illness; cleanup | Whatever you have |
| **A lidded bucket kept for sickness** | Vomit and waste, contained | And a spare |
| Personal cups, plates, utensils, towels, marked | Stops a lot of spread for free | Name them |
| Extra bedding | Sick person's bedding separate and washable | → 13-04 |
| A blanket or screen for a sick corner | Partial separation in one room | Cheap, real benefit |
| Thermometers, two or three | Track everyone | A child-friendly one |
| **Ketone strips** (type 1 diabetes) | Early warning for DKA | → 02-01 |
| Symptom log sheets | Who, when, what | → 25-05 |
| Soap in quantity and handwashing stations | The main control | → 13-02, → 13-09 |
| Several days of firewood indoors | Nobody has to go out while sick | → 06-04 |
| No-cook food for several days | For when nobody can cook | → 04-18 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Disinfectant:** bleach by the CDC table; boiling for anything that can be boiled; **soap and
  water with scrubbing does most of the work** even without a disinfectant.
- **ORS:** the WHO home recipe from salt, sugar and safe water, **read from → 12-05, never from
  memory.**
- **Separation:** a blanket on a rope, furniture, a screened corner, a second room heated for a
  while.
- **Personal items:** mark existing cups and plates with tape and marker.
- **Masks:** cloth is partial protection; better than nothing.
- **What not to substitute:** **alcohol sanitizer for handwashing during a norovirus outbreak**
  (CDC). Soap and water.

## When it runs out

- **Bleach is the consumable you cannot make**, and it weakens in storage. Rotate it; **boiling
  and thorough soap-and-water cleaning** replace most of what it does.
- **Soap can be made** (→ 13-09), and matters more anyway.
- **ORS is the stock that matters most** in a real outbreak (→ 12-05): count it in liters and in
  days of a sick child.
- **Water use jumps in an outbreak:** sick people drink more, and laundry, cleaning and washing all
  increase, while the people who haul water are ill. **That is a specific reason to store more
  water than the daily maths suggests** (→ 03-02, → 23-02).
- **When supplies run out, behavior substitutes:** thorough handwashing, personal items,
  separation, fresh air and careful cleanup need almost no supplies. **When the disinfectant runs
  out, be more careful, not less.**
- **The big point:** an outbreak is one of the few household emergencies that is **almost entirely
  preventable with cheap, boring, repeatable habits:** handwashing, safe water, keeping waste
  separate, and careful food handling. **The water, sanitation and food sections are the outbreak
  plan.** This page is what you do when they have been breached.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** crowding into one room is the risk. Build the stations, start the
  personal-item rule, decide the sick-corner plan, and **be willing to burn extra wood to heat a
  second room during an illness.**
- **B (moving):** hygiene slips and everyone is exhausted, which is exactly when illness spreads.
  **Hand sanitizer and soap for each person**, strict discipline before eating and after any waste
  handling, and treat all water (→ 03-04). **An outbreak while moving is a reason to stop and
  shelter** (→ 01-02).
- **C (rural or at a destination):** more room to isolate properly. But further from any care
  (→ 12-16), animals adding illnesses that pass from animals to people (→ 05-04), and a new water
  and sanitation setup that has to be right from the first day (→ 13-07). **Placing the latrine
  correctly at a new site is the best outbreak prevention there.**

## Cross-references

→ 03-04 the drinking-water bleach table (far weaker; never swap them) · → 13-02 handwashing ·
→ 13-01 human waste · → 13-10 dishwashing · → 13-04 laundry · → 13-07 latrine siting ·
→ 12-05 illness and dehydration · → 12-04 infection and sepsis · → 12-16 triage ·
→ 17-09 pandemic · → 08-01 heating one room · → 18-01 mutual aid

pages.body:
# Operating a septic system off-grid

**What this page is for.** A septic system is a buried sewage plant for one house. Most of them
need no electricity. This page explains how to keep one working when there is no pumping truck,
what must never go down the drain, and what to do when it struggles.
{{#if has.septic}}Your home is on septic: this page is for you now.{{else}}Your home is on
{{ dwelling.sewer }}. Keep this page for a destination or relative's house on septic.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Where a place has a working septic system, the first sanitation move is to operate it,
>   not to dig a latrine.** A working septic system is a complete, buried, already-placed
>   sanitation plant. Wrecking it through ignorance, then digging holes next to a well, is the
>   failure this page prevents.
> - **When the grid is down, there are no pumping trucks. The tank cannot be emptied. So
>   saving water is the maintenance:** every gallon you keep out, and every wrong thing you keep
>   out of the tank, is the only service it will get.
> - **A drain field with sewage coming to the surface is raw sewage, full of germs.** Do not dig
>   into it, keep children and pets away (→ 20-02), and do not try to fix it with a shovel.

## Do this now

1. **Gather the records** for your system, and for any destination on septic: where the tank is,
   when it was last pumped, and the installer or pumper's paperwork. Fill in the survey below.
2. **Find out whether it is a gravity system or a pumped one** (below). It changes everything.
3. **Read the never-flush list below once now.** Most septic damage comes from habits brought
   over from city sewers.
4. **Keep a bucket-toilet kit** (→ 13-01), including in any load you take to a destination on
   septic. It is the relief valve that lets a stressed septic system rest.

## How a tank and drain field work (EPA)

{{figure fig-septic-system}}

Household waste water runs down one main drain pipe into a buried, watertight **septic tank**.
There, **solids sink to the bottom as sludge; fats and grease float to the top as scum**; the
cleared liquid in the middle (**effluent**) flows out to the **drain field**, a shallow covered
trench system in dry soil. **The soil does the treatment:** as the liquid soaks down, the soil
filters it and its organisms eat the bacteria, viruses and nutrients before the water reaches
groundwater (US EPA, How Your Septic System Works).

Two facts drive everything on this page:

1. **The tank is alive.** Microbes digest the waste. Poison them (chemicals, heavy loads of
   bleach) and the tank becomes a dead box that passes solids out to the field.
2. **The field can only soak up so much.** Flood it with water and sewage comes up on the lawn or
   backs up into the house (EPA).

## What changes when the grid is down

- **No pumping trucks.** Tanks are normally pumped every 3 to 5 years (US EPA, How to Care for
  Your Septic System). Without pumping, sludge and scum build up until they escape to the field,
  which is the one failure you cannot repair. **So slow the clock: less water, fewer solids,
  nothing that kills the microbes.** A tank pumped recently starts with years of room.
- **Pumped and mound systems** (with electric float switches and an effluent pump) stop working
  without power and back up quickly. A gravity system is the good answer. Find out which yours is
  (survey below).
- **Well pressure may be gone too** (→ 03-10). Pour-flushing from a bucket (→ 13-01) still feeds a
  septic system fine, and naturally rations water.

## The never-flush list: tape it next to every toilet (EPA)

**Only human waste and toilet paper go in. Never flush:**

- **Wipes, even "flushable" ones** (baby wipes, wet wipes)
- **Cooking grease or oil**
- **Household chemicals:** gasoline, oil, pesticides, antifreeze, paint, paint thinner, photo
  chemicals, drain cleaner
- **Large volumes of toxic cleaners, including bleach** (EPA: never pour large volumes of toxic
  cleaners down the drain). Disinfecting batches (→ 13-11), sanitizing tubs and
  well-disinfection water (→ 03-10) poured down the drain can kill the tank's microbes. Pour
  those outside, away from water and the field
- **Pads, tampons, condoms, dental floss, diapers, paper towels, cigarette butts, coffee grounds,
  cat litter** (litter: → 13-03)
- **Medicines**

## Managing the water load: the real maintenance

- **Spread the load.** Do not do all the laundry in one day (EPA). Space laundry (→ 13-04) and
  bathing across the week so the field soaks up each dose before the next.
- **Send greywater elsewhere where it is lawful.** Wash-basin and laundry water poured onto soil
  (→ 13-03) is water the field never sees: the biggest single saving. **Never divert toilet
  waste.**

  > **Before the collapse:** greywater rules differ by state. Check before re-plumbing anything.

- **Fix every leak and drip.** A running toilet floods a field.
- **Flush on purpose:** "if it's yellow, let it mellow" (→ 13-01); solids get one honest flush.

## Finding the tank and the field

- **Paperwork first:** the county health or environmental office's permit drawings, the
  inspection from when the house was sold, the pumper's receipts (which also date the last
  pump-out).
- **Look:** follow the drain pipe where it leaves the house; EPA says the tank is usually about
  10 feet from the building (US EPA, Frequent Questions on Septic Systems). Look for tank lids
  or risers (often a black or green disc), a rectangle of grass that grows differently, snow that melts
  first.
- **Probe gently** with a thin rod along that line to find the tank's edges. **Do not drive
  machinery around guessing:** crushing a lid or a pipe causes the failure you fear.

{{photo septic-tank-lids}}

### Septic survey (one block per place)

**Home** ({{ dwelling.sewer }}):

- System type (gravity, pumped, mound, lagoon): __________ · Tank location: __________
- Last pumped: __________ · Drain field location: __________
- Pumper or installer, and who holds the records: __________

{{#if has.destinations}}{{#each destinations as d}}**{{ d.name }}** ({{ d.county }}, {{ d.state_name }}):

- Septic? Lagoon? Sewer? Other: __________ · Tank location: __________
- Last pumped: __________ · Drain field location: __________
- Who there knows the system: __________

{{/each}}{{/if}}

## Signs of failure, and what to do

**Signs (EPA):** sewage backing up into drains or toilets, slow drains, gurgling pipes · **standing
water, damp spots or soft, spongy ground over the tank or field** · sewage smell around the tank
or field · bright green, spongy, lush grass over the field even in dry weather.

**What to do, in order:**

1. **Stop putting water in. All of it.** Move the household to the bucket toilet (→ 13-01) at
   once: this is exactly what it is for.
2. **Let the system rest** for days, not hours. An overloaded field may recover once it drains
   down; there is no way to know how long without trying.
3. **Do NOT dig into a field with sewage on the surface:** the soil is soaked with germs. Fence it
   off from children and animals; sprinkle lime on pooling if you have it (→ 13-07).
4. **Start again slowly** with less water, and keep the bucket toilet in use for part of the
   household.
5. **If it will not recover,** the field is finished while the grid is down. A properly placed
   latrine (→ 13-07) becomes the main system.

## Winter (University of Minnesota Extension)

- **Snow and mulch are the insulation.** An undisturbed blanket of snow insulates the tank and
  field. In a cold snap with bare ground, a layer of mulch **8 to 12 inches** deep (straw,
  leaves, hay or any loose material that will not pack down) over the pipes, tank and field does
  the same job. Let the grass grow a little longer over it in late summer and fall.
- **Never drive over, park on, or pack down snow over the tank or field.** Packed snow loses its
  insulation and drives frost deep, and vehicles crush parts (EPA).
- **Regular warm water helps prevent freezing.** A house in daily use keeps its own lines warm; a
  little use beats none. Do not leave water running all the time to prevent freezing: it can
  overload the field. Fix dripping fixtures: a slow trickle freezes in the pipe.
- **If it freezes anyway:** stop using water, move to the bucket toilet, and wait for the thaw.
  **Do not add antifreeze, salt or septic additives, do not light a fire over the system to thaw
  it, and never pump sewage onto the ground** (University of Minnesota Extension) (→ 13-05).

## The bucket toilet is the relief valve

Every failure above (overload, freezing, overdue pumping, backup) has the same first move: **take
the load off by moving some or all of the household to the bucket system** (→ 13-01). That is why
the bucket kit goes with you even to a place with plumbing. A septic system that is rested
whenever it is stressed can run for years. One forced to take a full household's waste through
every stress will fail, for good, with no truck coming.

## Gear and supplies

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bucket toilet kit** | The relief valve for every failure | → 13-01, → 22-01 |
| Thin steel probe rod | Finding tank edges without machinery | A soil probe or a 4-ft rod |
| A printed never-flush list | Taped by every toilet | This page |
| Straw or leaf mulch | Winter insulation in bare-ground cold snaps | Gather on site |
| Basins for greywater | Water the field never sees | → 13-03 |
| Lime | Sprinkled on pooled sewage | → 13-07 |
| Gloves and rubber boots | Any contact with backup or surfaced sewage | → 13-01 |

**If you don't have it:**

- **Probe:** rebar, a straightened fence post, a sharpened dowel.
- **Mulch:** straw, hay, leaves, corn stalks: anything loose that will not pack down.
- **Records:** the county office, the pumper's office, neighbors who watched it go in.
- **What you cannot substitute: the field itself.** There is no improvised drain field. Protect
  the one you have.

## When it runs out

- **The tank runs out of room** on a clock of years, set by the last pump-out and slowed by saving
  water. Get the pump-out date onto the survey: it turns an unknown into a runway (→ 23-02).
- **Ration by diverting:** separating urine (→ 13-01) and diverting greywater (→ 13-03) can keep
  most of the household's liquid out of the tank.
- **Substitute:** the bucket toilet can take any share of the load for as long as needed; a
  properly placed latrine (→ 13-07) is the fallback if the system dies.
- **What never runs out:** the never-flush list and spreading the load. They cost nothing, and they
  are the whole difference between a system that outlasts the event and one that fails in the
  first spring.

## Phase notes

- **A (sheltering at home):** {{#if has.septic}}fill in the survey now, tape up the never-flush
  list, and start spreading the laundry across the week.{{else}}not your home system. Keep this
  page for any place you might go that is on septic.{{/if}}
- **B (moving):** nothing to operate (catholes and packing out: → 13-07). But arrival matters:
  **do not let a tired group run a week of laundry and baths into an unknown system on the first
  day.** Do the survey first.
- **C (rural or at a destination):** **operate the existing system as the main one; the latrine
  (→ 13-07) is the fallback, not the first move.** Check the system type on arrival; if it is a
  lagoon or a pumped system, the rules change: note it in the survey.

## Cross-references

→ 13-01 the bucket system this page leans on · → 13-07 latrine siting (the fallback) ·
→ 13-05 winter sanitation · → 13-03 greywater · → 13-11 disease outbreak ·
→ 01-05 choosing a destination · → 01-04 arrival · → 03-07 testing the well the field must not
touch

pages.body:
# Situational awareness and honest threat assessment

**What this page is for.** Security in a long emergency is mostly about noticing things early
and not walking into trouble. This page ranks the dangers a household really faces, shows how to
build a habit of noticing what is normal and what is not, and sets up a few family rules. It
does not teach fighting.

> **CAUTION.** The realistic threats when the power and services fail are **not** roving gangs.
> They are, in order: **fire, carbon monoxide, cold, medical failure, illness, accidents, and
> desperate ordinary people.** Planning for the dramatic scenario while ignoring the ordinary ones
> is the classic mistake, and it uses up attention you need elsewhere.

## Do this now

1. **Rank your real threats** with the table below and spend effort in that order.
2. **Know your block**: who lives where, who is elderly or alone, who has skills, who has medical
   needs. That knowledge is both security and community (→ 18-01).
3. **Walk and look twice a day**: around the property and down the street, morning and evening.
4. **Set a family duress word and rally points** (→ 15-03).
5. **Keep information flowing**: a weather radio and talking to neighbours tell you more than any
   weapon (→ 15-01, → 15-04).

## The honest threat ranking

| Rank | Threat | Why it is higher than you think |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Fire** | No 911, wood heat, candles, children. A house fire ends everything at once (→ 29-12) |
| 2 | **Carbon monoxide** | Silent, and the temptation to bring heaters and engines inside grows as it gets colder (→ 08-02, → 29-03) |
| 3 | **Cold and hypothermia** | Worst for {{#if has.infant}}your infant, {{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}your elders, {{/if}}small children, older people and anyone sick (→ 08-05) |
| 4 | **Medical failure** | A medicine or device someone depends on runs out; an allergic reaction or injury with no emergency room (→ 12-11) |
| 5 | **Illness and dirty water** | Diarrhoeal disease spreads fast, especially with small children (→ 03-04) |
| 6 | **Accidents** | Axes, saws, ladders, boiling water, with no ambulance |
| 7 | **Theft** | Real, but usually of property, not violence against people |
| 8 | **Desperate people asking for help** | Common; a social problem before it is a security one (→ 14-03) |
| 9 | **Organised violence** | Real, but rare, and it comes late if at all |

**Spend your preparation in that order.** A carbon monoxide alarm, a fire extinguisher and a good
first-aid kit protect against more likely deaths than any firearm. Outage guidance lists smoke
and carbon monoxide alarms, light that needs no grid power and a plan for heat among the basics
for the same reason (American Red Cross, Power Outage Safety).

## Awareness is a habit, not a state of alarm

- **Learn normal first.** You cannot notice something odd without knowing what normal is. What
  does your street sound like at 9 p.m.? Who walks a dog at 7 a.m.? Once the grid is down,
  normal changes: learn it again.
- **Things worth noticing:** vehicles that circle or park oddly; people looking at houses rather
  than walking past; sudden silence; dogs reacting; smoke where there should be none; a
  neighbour's routine breaking.
- **Trust the feeling, then check it.** Unease is often your brain spotting a pattern before you
  can name it. Do not dismiss it, and do not act on it blindly either.
- **Do not stare.** Noticing is not confronting. Note it, step back, talk it over.

## Three questions before you act

When something worries you, answer these first:

1. **What is actually happening?** What you saw, not what you guessed.
2. **What is the realistic worst case?** Not the imagined one.
3. **What is the least escalating response that works?** Almost always: step back, turn on a
   light, be seen, call a neighbour, lock a door. Not a weapon.

**Escalation is a one-way door.** The most important security skill is not winning a
confrontation; it is **not being in one** (→ 14-13). The household's written rule on force is
on → 14-11: {{choice DC-12}} → 30-13.

## Keeping watch: the realistic version

Films show a 24-hour armed watch. A household of {{ household.adults }} adults{{#if has.child}}
with children{{/if}} cannot keep that up and should not try: **lack of sleep will hurt you long
before an intruder does.**

- **Rely on locks, hardening and alarms** (→ 14-02, → 14-12) so that you can sleep.
- **Use layered early warning**: a dog, gravel under windows, a bell on a gate, motion lights.
- **Cooperate with neighbours.** A block that watches informally beats one exhausted household
  (→ 18-01).
- **If a real threat period arrives**, take turns on watch, but treat it as a short surge, not a
  permanent way of living.

## Information is the real awareness tool

- **NOAA Weather Radio** (→ 15-01): weather is the threat most likely to reach every household.
- **Scanner and radio traffic** (→ 15-04): what is actually happening in town.
- **Neighbours**: the best local information you will get.
- **Write down what you learn**, with the date, on paper. Rumour and fact separate quickly when
  they are written down.

## Family rules

- **Duress word:** an ordinary-sounding word that means "something is wrong, act now":
  __________ (keep it off any list a stranger could read; → 15-03).
- **Rally point if separated at home:** {{ contacts.meet.near_home }}. **Away from home:**
  {{ contacts.meet.in_town }} (→ 15-03).
- **Answering the door:** who does it, who does not, what is said: __________________________
- **Children's rules:** where to go, who to open the door for (nobody), what to say (nothing).
- **Practise them.** A rule nobody has rehearsed is a rule you do not have (→ 24-02).

## Gear

**Worth having now:**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NOAA weather radio | Weather is the most likely threat | → 15-01 |
| Scanner or handheld radio | Local information | → 15-04 |
| Motion-activated solar lights | Early warning with no wiring | Cheap, effective |
| Driveway or gate alarm, or a bell | Lets you sleep | A simple mechanical one works |
| Binoculars | Look without approaching | Also useful for weather and game |
| A written block map and neighbour list | Who is who, who needs help | → 18-01 |
| Notebook and pencil | Log what you see, dated | Separates rumour from fact |
| Fire extinguishers, smoke and CO alarms | The actual top threats | → 08-02, → 29-12 |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Gravel** under windows and along paths is a cheap, silent, reliable alarm.
- Tin cans on a string across a gate; a bell on a door.
- A dog is the best early-warning system there is (→ 14-12).

## When it runs out

- **Attention is the thing that runs out.** Constant high alert wears people out in days and
  damages judgement (→ 21-01).
- **Automate what you can** (alarms, lights, layout) so people only watch where they must. Sleep
  is a security measure.
- **Share the load with neighbours.** A shared watch is the only way to cover 24 hours for long.
- **The real failure:** exhaustion and fear leading to a bad decision, such as a confrontation
  that did not need to happen, or a missed CO alarm because everyone was watching the street.

## By phase

- **A (at home{{#if is.urban}}, in town{{/if}}):** neighbours close by mean more risk and more
  early warning. Invest in knowing your block.
- **B (on the move):** avoid crowds, narrow choke points and darkness; do not look worth stopping
  (→ 14-03).
- **C (rural or a new place):** fewer people, longer views, longer waits for help. Roads and
  approaches matter more; neighbours are farther away and count for more.
