# Hardening the home without trapping the family

**What this page is for.** Cheap changes to doors, windows, lights and gates that make an
opportunist pick another house and give you warning, without ever stopping your family getting
out in a fire.

> **CAUTION.** Two rules come before everything here. **First: never trap your family.** Bars,
> barricades and screwed-shut windows that stop an intruder also stop you escaping a fire, and
> **fire is a more likely killer than intrusion** (→ 14-01). **Second: work you do now, cheaply,
> in daylight, is worth ten times what you improvise in the dark.**

## Do this now

1. **Fix the door frame, not the lock.** Nearly every forced entry into a home is a kicked door
   splitting a soft wooden frame, not a picked lock.
2. **Put 3-inch screws** in every exterior door's hinges and strike plate (the metal plate the
   bolt goes into), long enough to reach the framing stud behind. A small box of screws and
   twenty minutes; it is the best-value security change in this binder.
3. **Add a reinforced strike plate** or a door-jamb reinforcement kit on exterior doors.
4. **Block sliding doors** with a bar or pin in the track.
5. **Keep a way out:** every bedroom needs an exit that opens from the inside without a key.
6. **Light the outside** with motion-activated solar lights on the approaches.

## The real weak point: the frame

A deadbolt is only as strong as the wood it goes into. Ordinary construction uses a soft pine
door frame with short screws into the trim. A single kick splits it.

{{figure fig-door-strike-3in-screws}}

**The fixes, best value first:**

1. **3-inch screws** in hinges and strike plates, reaching the stud behind the frame.
2. **Reinforced strike plate** (a long steel plate spanning several inches).
3. **Door-jamb reinforcement kit** (a full-length steel channel) for the main doors.
4. **Solid-core or steel exterior doors** if you are replacing a door anyway.
5. **A second deadbolt** or a floor-mounted brace for the most exposed door.

**Start with the doors people actually force:** the back door, the garage side door, and any
door hidden from the street.

## Windows and sliding doors

- **Sliding doors:** a bar or dowel in the track, plus an anti-lift screw in the upper track.
- **Ground-floor windows:** extra sash locks or pins. Security film on the glass does not stop it
  breaking, but it makes getting through quickly much harder.
- **Basement windows** are often the weakest point and rarely considered.
- **Never screw bedroom windows shut.** They are a way out in a fire. This is not negotiable
  {{#if has.child}}with children in the house{{else}}for anyone{{/if}}.

## Lighting and what can be seen

- **Motion-activated solar lights** on approaches need no wiring and keep working when the power
  is out, which is exactly when you need them.
- **Trim shrubs** away from doors and windows so nobody can hide there.
- **Keep climbing aids out of the yard**: bins, ladders and patio furniture near fences.
- **Balance this against not standing out (→ 14-03).** Floodlights on a dark street make your
  house the obvious one. Motion-activated lights are the compromise: dark until something moves.

## The garage

{{#if has.garage}}Your house has an attached garage.{{else}}If you have or move to a house with
an attached garage:{{/if}} it is a common weak point, with a house door that is often hollow
with a cheap lock, and an overhead door that can sometimes be released from outside.

- **Upgrade the house-to-garage door** like an exterior door, because it is one.
- **Protect the overhead door's emergency release** against someone hooking it from outside
  with a coat hanger: use a zip-tie that breaks when pulled hard from inside, or a release
  shield. **Never disable the release.** Without power it is the only way to open that door,
  and the garage is a second way out; disabling it breaks this page's first rule.
- **The carbon monoxide floor applies:** never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors,
  in a garage, or near an open window. Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning
  (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics; → 08-02).

## Gates and padlocks

If you have a fenced yard, padlocks on the gates turn the fence into a real boundary that slows
an opportunist and makes noise.

- **Open the packages now and put the keys where every adult can find them.** A padlock whose
  key is lost in a drawer locks *you* out. Write where the keys hang on the photo below or by
  hand; it does not go in your settings.
- **Check whether the locks are keyed alike.** Two padlocks of the same model are keyed
  differently unless they were sold as a keyed-alike set (the same key number on both
  packages). If they differ, put all the keys on one ring, tagged by gate, and make the spare
  ring match.
- **The lock is only as strong as the hasp and latch it hangs on.** A hasp screwed into soft wood
  where bolt cutters can reach it makes the padlock decoration. Bolt a shrouded hasp through the
  gate frame with carriage bolts (heads outside, nuts inside).
- **A locked gate must never trap anyone.** In a fire or a forced evacuation the gates are ways
  out. Everyone old enough knows where the key is, and the key ring hangs by the door you would
  leave through, not inside a safe. Firefighters and medics also need a way in: unlock when you
  call for help.
- **Lock the gates at the start of an event; unlock them only while someone is outside** (water
  hauling, generator runs). Add gravel, bells or cans on the gates for warning (→ 14-12).
- **Outdoor locks freeze and seize.** Every three to six months, and again before winter, blow
  the dust out of the keyway and put a light shot of **PTFE (Teflon) lock lubricant** in the
  keyway and shackle holes, then work the key several times. Regular lubrication helps stop locks
  freezing. **Not graphite, not silicone:** the manufacturer's own care guidance says never use
  either, and that graphite is often put on too heavily and jams the moving parts (Master Lock,
  Padlock care and lubrication). A jammed lock in deep cold is exactly the lock that traps your
  family. Frozen anyway? Warm the body of the lock with
  a hand warmer or warm water. **Never force the key.** Check the locks on your twice-yearly kit
  day (→ 22-03).

{{photo gate-lock-keys}}

## Layered, not fortified

Do not try to turn a house into a bunker. It does not work, it is expensive, it alarms the
neighbours (→ 14-03) and it creates fire traps. The goal is **delay, noise and visibility**:
enough that an opportunist chooses another house, and enough that you get warning.

| Layer | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Street and yard | Lighting, clear views, gravel, a dog (→ 14-12) |
| Perimeter (fence, if any) | Delay and a clear boundary |
| Structure | Doors, frames, windows, locks |
| Inside | A gathering room where the family goes |
| Response | Awareness, communication, neighbours (→ 14-01, → 18-01) |

## The inside gathering room

Pick the room where the family goes if something happens at night. In winter this is often the
room you are already heating and sleeping in (→ 08-01). It should have a solid door, a phone or
radio, a light, and nobody should have to cross the house to reach the children.

**Do not confuse it with the storm shelter.** Your tornado shelter{{#if has.shelter_room}}
({{ dwelling.shelter_room }}){{/if}} is chosen for different reasons: lowest floor, inside,
away from windows (→ 17-02, → 17-06). Know both, and which one is for which emergency.

## Fire: the rule that overrides the rest

- **Two ways out of every sleeping area**, always.
- **Smoke and CO alarms**, battery-powered and tested (→ 08-02).
- **Fire extinguishers** where fires start: kitchen, heater, fuel storage (→ 29-12).
- **Practise the exit with the children** (→ 24-02). A four-year-old needs to have done it, not
  just heard about it.
- **Never barricade a bedroom window** that is someone's way out.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **3-inch screws** (a box) | The best-value upgrade here | Hinges and strike plates, into studs |
| Reinforced strike plates or jamb kits | Stops the kicked-door failure | Main exterior doors |
| Sliding-door bars or track pins | Cheap, effective | Plus anti-lift screws |
| Window sash locks or pins | Ground floor and basement | Not on escape windows |
| Security window film | Slows fast entry through glass | Ground floor |
| Motion-activated solar lights | Warning without the grid | Approaches and dark sides |
| Reinforcement for the garage-to-house door | Common weak point | Treat it as an exterior door |
| Extra deadbolt or floor brace | Most exposed door | Opens without a key from inside |
| Smoke and CO alarms, extinguishers | The more likely threat | → 08-02 |
| Gravel on approaches | Free, silent alarm | → 14-01 |
| Outdoor padlocks for gates | Turns a fence into a locked boundary | Keyed-alike check above |
| PTFE lock lubricant | Keeps outdoor locks working in cold | Every 3 to 6 months and before winter; never graphite or silicone (manufacturer) |

**If you do not have it:**

- **A 2×4 across a door** in brackets is a strong barricade, but **only where it does not block
  a way out**, and it must lift off from inside.
- Furniture against a door for delay and noise.
- Bells, cans or gravel for warning; boards over broken glass.
- Doorstop wedges are cheap and surprisingly effective.

## When it runs out

Hardening does not get used up: it is a one-time job that keeps paying. Lumber and screws can be
found almost anywhere; the method matters more than the material. Most of it also helps in
normal life, and a reinforced, weather-sealed door doubles as winterizing (→ 08-03).

## By phase

- **A (at home):** do all of it now, in daylight, with a drill. Cheap and permanent.
- **B (on the move):** you are leaving the house; lock it and take what matters.
- **C (a new place):** look at unfamiliar buildings the same way (doors, windows, approaches),
  with more attention to long views and access roads.

pages.body:
# Not becoming a target

**What this page is for.** "Operational security", or OPSEC, means not giving away what you have.
This page covers the four ways a house gives itself away (light, smoke and smell, sound,
traffic), what to say and not say before anything happens, how to decide in advance what you
will give to people who ask, and how to keep a loaded vehicle from being a target.

> **CAUTION.** In a neighbourhood where everyone is cold and hungry, **the house that obviously
> has food, heat and light is the house people come to**: first to ask, later to demand. The
> opposite extreme is also a mistake: in a long crisis, **isolation is more dangerous than being
> seen**. The goal is not to be invisible. It is to **not stand out**, while being a known and
> valued part of the neighbourhood (→ 18-01).

## Do this now

1. **Say nothing now about what you store.** The most common failure happens years before the
   emergency, in casual conversation.
2. **Manage the four signatures:** light, smoke and smell, sound, and traffic.
3. **Look like everyone else** from the street: same darkness, same quiet, no visible stockpile.
4. **Do not post about preparedness** on social media, ever. It is a searchable inventory.
5. **Decide what you will give, and to whom, in advance** (below), so you are not making it up
   at the door{{#if has.child}} with your children watching{{/if}}.

## The four signatures

| Signature | What gives you away | How to control it |
|---|---|---|
| **Light** | Windows glowing on a dark street; flashlights outside | Blackout curtains, lights away from windows, low or red light (→ 10-05) |
| **Smoke and smell** | Woodsmoke, and especially **cooking smells** | Cook at midday when others do; a rocket stove makes far less smoke than an open fire (→ 07-02) |
| **Sound** | Generator, power tools, gunshots, loud voices, a barking dog | Site the generator away from the street and run it only for specific jobs; no shooting at home unless the household has chosen to (below) |
| **Traffic and movement** | Repeated trips, hauling, visitors, a loaded vehicle | Move supplies at quiet times; unload {{#if has.garage}}inside the garage{{else}}out of sight{{/if}} |

**Cooking smell is the underrated one.** On a cold, still evening the smell of food carries much
farther than you think, and nobody mistakes it. That is a real argument for **cooking once a
day, in daylight**, in a contained stove, rather than over a fragrant open fire at dusk
(→ 07-01).

**Generator noise is the loudest advertisement you can make.** It says *this house has fuel and
power*. Run it briefly, for specific jobs such as charging medical devices (→ 09-06), and place
it as far from the street as you can while keeping it **at least 20 feet from any door, window
or vent** (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics). **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any
engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no
warning; alarms fail; there is no mitigation that works every time (→ 08-02).

**Gunshots.** A shot fired at home, for pests, practice or sighting in a rifle, is heard all
around and tells everyone the house is armed and occupied; a missed shot also keeps going toward
whatever lies beyond the yard. Traps (→ 05-15) are quieter, work while you sleep and have no
backstop problem. Whether this household fires at home at all, and under what rules, is a
decision card: {{choice DC-11}} → 30-12.

## The long game: what you say before anything happens

- **Do not tell people what you have.** Not how much food, not ammunition, not fuel, not "we
  could last a year".
- **Do not post it.** Photos of a full pantry, a range trip or a new purchase are permanent,
  searchable and shareable.
- **Watch your delivery patterns.** Pallets of buckets and cases arriving again and again are
  noticed.
- **Teach the children at their level** (→ 20-04). A four-year-old repeats everything. The rule is
  not "keep secrets"; it is simply **"we don't talk about what's in our cupboards."**

## The balance: privacy and community

Hard-line secrecy is a poor long-term strategy where people live close together:

- **You cannot hide** a household of {{ household.size }}, its smoke and its daily activity from
  the houses next door. Trying looks strange, and strange draws attention.
- **Neighbours are your best early warning and your best defence** (→ 18-01). A block that
  cooperates is far safer than separate fortified houses that distrust each other.
- **You have needs too.** {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}Your household depends on refrigerated
  medicine; {{/if}}in a long crisis you may need the community more than it needs you.

**The workable posture: be a normal, helpful, unremarkable neighbour who does not discuss
supplies.** Contribute skills and labour openly; keep quantities private.

## Charity: decide it now

Someone will knock. Decide together, **before** it happens:

- **What will you give?** Food? Water? Nothing?
- **To whom?** Known neighbours? Anyone?
- **From where?** Keep a small, visible "give" supply apart from your main stores, so helping
  someone never shows how much you have.
- **Where is the line?** And what do you do if someone will not leave? (→ 14-13)
- **What do the children see and hear?** They will remember how it was handled.

Writing this down turns a frightening moment at the door into a policy you already agreed.

**Our policy:** ________________________________________________________________

______________________________________________________________________________

## On the move (phase B)

- **A visibly loaded vehicle is a target.** Cover loads; do not strap gear to the outside.
- **Do not display firearms** while travelling. It draws exactly the attention you want to avoid
  (→ 14-11).
- **Avoid choke points and crowds; travel in daylight** (→ 01-03).
- **Do not tell strangers where you are going.**

> **Before the collapse:** openly carrying or displaying a firearm in a vehicle or in public is
> unlawful in some states and some places. Your state's law, and the laws of every state on your
> route, apply while they are enforced.

### A trailer at stops

{{#if has.trailer}}Your household has a trailer.{{else}}If you tow a trailer:{{/if}} it solves
the space problem and creates a security one. It is a box of your supplies sitting in a parking
lot.

- **Coupler lock and hitch-pin lock at every stop.** A hitched trailer can be stolen by backing
  another vehicle under it and driving off in under a minute.
- **Tongue lock whenever it is unhitched**, including while it is staged at home.
- **Park where you can see it** from wherever you eat or refuel. At fuel stops, if there are two
  adults, one pumps and one stays with the children and the load (→ 01-03).
- **The cargo split:** **firearms, medicines, documents and cash ride in the cabin, never in the
  trailer** (→ 22-05, → 06-08). The trailer carries bulk: water, tools, totes. If it is stolen,
  you have lost weight, not the plan.
- **Overnight:** keep it where you can see it, backed against a wall or another vehicle so the
  doors cannot open, **or** move anything you cannot replace into the cabin before you sleep.
  Deciding "it's probably fine" without looking is the only wrong answer.
- **Keep it plain.** No stickers for guns, gear brands or "prepping", no visible racks of fuel
  cans. Plain and boring reads as "moving house", not "supplies".

## What OPSEC is not

- It is **not** suspicion of your friends and neighbours.
- It is **not** refusing all help. Giving and accepting help builds the network that keeps you
  safe.
- It is **not** a replacement for hardening (→ 14-02) or awareness (→ 14-01).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Blackout curtains or heavy drapes | Hides light; also insulates (→ 08-03) | Doubles as winterizing |
| Red-filter headlamps and lanterns | Low-visibility light inside and out | → 10-05 |
| Rocket stove or contained cooker | Far less smoke and smell than an open fire | → 07-02 |
| Long outdoor extension cord | Lets the generator sit farther away and quieter | Still at least 20 ft from doors and windows |
| Traps for pests and small game | Quiet, no backstop problem | → 05-15 |
| A small, separate "give" supply | Help without showing your depth | Cheap staples |
| A written charity policy | Decide once, calmly | This page |
| Opaque storage tubs or covers | Nothing recognisable through a window or open door | Cheap totes |

**If you do not have it:**

- Blankets and cardboard over windows do what curtains do, and insulate.
- A light kept behind a wall rather than in a window; light bounced off a ceiling.
- Cooking inside on the house's own range when it works removes the outdoor smell. **Never** use
  an unvented fuel-burner indoors because of carbon monoxide (→ 08-02); open flame indoors is a
  household decision: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21.

## When it runs out

- OPSEC uses almost nothing. It is discipline, and discipline does not run out, but it **fades**.
  After a few weeks people get careless with lights and noise. Make it a nightly routine, not an
  intention.
- Community goodwill is the renewable resource here (→ 18-01).
- **Every signature adds up to a reputation.** By the second month the neighbourhood has an
  opinion about which houses have supplies. Manage it from the first day, because you cannot undo
  it later.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** the phase where this page matters most{{#if is.urban}}, with houses close
  together and every signature carrying{{/if}}.
- **B (on the move):** look unremarkable; do not show gear or weapons; do not broadcast plans.
- **C (rural or a new place):** you cannot be invisible in a small community and should not try.
  Be known, be useful, keep quantities private.

pages.body:
# Caliber roles and the household firearms inventory

**What this page is for.** This page is logistics, not shooting. It answers two questions before
a crisis: **which gun does which job**, and **which ammunition is worth stocking deeply**. It ends
with an inventory log the household fills in by hand.

{{#if has.firearms}}Your profile says there are firearms in the home. Fill in the log at the
bottom and keep it current.{{else}}Your profile lists no firearms. This page stays in your binder
because firearms can be inherited, found or acquired in a long emergency, and someone has to know
what ammunition fits what. If that happens, start with → 29-11 and → 14-14, then use the log
below.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.** Never fire or load ammunition you have not matched to the marking on the gun. The
> caliber is stamped on the barrel; the headstamp on the base of the cartridge must match it
> (SAAMI, Generally Accepted Firearms and Ammunition Interchangeability). A cartridge that fits
> is not proof it is safe. New to firearms? Read → 29-11 first.

## Do this now

1. **Fill in the inventory log** below and keep it current. A count you have not written down is
   a guess.
2. **Stock by job, not evenly.** The calibers that do the most work deserve the most depth.
3. **If you own a .22 LR, stock it deeper than feels reasonable.** It is cheap and light, it feeds
   small game for years, and **it cannot be reloaded** (→ 14-08): what you have is what you get.
4. **Standardise where you can.** Fewer calibers means simpler supply, simpler spare parts and
   fewer ways to be short of the wrong thing.
5. **Count magazines like ammunition.** They wear out and get lost (→ 14-06).

## Words on this page

- **Caliber** is the size and type of cartridge a rifle or handgun is made for (".22 LR", "9mm").
  **Gauge** is the shotgun equivalent ("12 gauge"; a smaller number is a bigger bore). **Gauges
  are never interchangeable:** a 20-gauge shell dropped into a 12-gauge gun can slide forward and
  stick in the barrel, and the next 12-gauge shell fired behind it bursts the barrel (SAAMI,
  Generally Accepted Firearms and Ammunition Interchangeability). Keep each gauge in its own
  marked box.
- **Rimfire** cartridges (like .22 LR) have the priming compound in the rim; they cannot be
  reloaded. **Centerfire** cartridges have a replaceable primer in the centre of the base.
- **Platform** means a family of firearms that share parts, such as "AR-pattern rifle".

More words: → 29-11.

## Common calibers and their jobs

This table covers the calibers most common in US homes. It is general; your own firearms may
differ. Hunting methods, legal calibers and seasons are set by your state's wildlife agency and
change every year (→ 05-07).

| Caliber or gauge | Usual main job | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **.22 LR** (rimfire) | Small game, pests, training | Cheap, light, many rounds per pound. Cannot be reloaded |
| **9mm** | Handgun, defence | The most common centerfire handgun round in the US; best odds of finding more |
| **.45 ACP** | Handgun, defence | Heavier and less common than 9mm |
| **5.56 / .223** | Rifle: defence, varmints, general use | Very common. Read the barrel marking: SAAMI treats them as different cartridges, and the gun's maker decides what is safe |
| **.308** | Rifle: deer and larger game, longer range | Common hunting round; heavier |
| **Other hunting rifle calibers** (.30-06, .270, 6.5 Creedmoor and many more) | Rifle: deer and larger game | How easy each is to find varies a lot by caliber and region. Treat a less common one as finite |
| **12 gauge** | Shotgun: birds, small game, deer (slug), defence | The most versatile single firearm: birdshot, buckshot or slug. Very common |
| **20 gauge** | Shotgun: birds, small game | Less recoil; easier for smaller or newer shooters. Less common than 12 |

**When ammunition becomes scarce, what you can find follows what is common.** 9mm, 5.56/.223,
.22 LR and 12 gauge are the ones most likely to turn up. Two consequences:

- **Stock uncommon calibers now.** What you buy today may be your lifetime supply.
- **Common calibers have trade value, and that is the problem** (below).

## A hard note on ammunition as barter

Ammunition is very valuable in a crisis, which is exactly why trading it is dangerous. It arms
whoever you trade with, possibly against you, and it tells them you have more. If you trade it at
all, trade only with people you would trust armed, and never in a caliber that feeds your own
main firearms (→ 18-02, → 14-08).

## The case for standardising

Many calibers is a supply burden. You cannot carry them all, stock them all deeply, or keep the
cleaning gear, spare parts and know-how for each. Consider naming:

- **One main rifle caliber**
- **One main handgun caliber**
- **One small-game firearm** (often .22 LR)
- **One hunting rifle caliber**
- **One shotgun gauge**

Everything else becomes secondary: kept and maintained, but not what the plan depends on. Write
the decision in the log so the go-bag and vehicle load (→ 01-03) are not improvised.

## Matching firearms to game

→ 05-07 covers hunting. This only maps firearms to game in general terms.

- **Small game and pests:** .22 LR is the usual choice.
- **Upland birds:** 12 or 20 gauge with birdshot.
- **Waterfowl:** shotgun with **non-toxic shot** (steel, bismuth and others).
- **Deer:** a deer-legal rifle caliber, or a shotgun slug.

> **Before the collapse:** your state's wildlife agency sets legal methods, calibers, seasons and
> licences for hunting, and some calibers are not legal for deer in many states. Federal rules
> require non-toxic shot for waterfowl. Get the current regulations each year while they are
> published, and keep a copy in the binder kit.

## Inventory log (fill in by hand)

Update it after every purchase and every range trip. Keep a copy with your documents (→ 19-01).

**Never write serial numbers, safe combinations or where firearms are kept in this binder or in
the settings page.** Serial numbers belong on a separate paper record kept with your important
documents; the binder may be read by anyone who picks up the phone or tablet.

| Caliber or gauge | Firearms it feeds (type, not serial) | Rounds on hand | Magazines | Main job | Main or secondary? | Stock deeper? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| __________ | ______________ | ______ | ______ | __________ | ______ | ______ |
| __________ | ______________ | ______ | ______ | __________ | ______ | ______ |
| __________ | ______________ | ______ | ______ | __________ | ______ | ______ |
| __________ | ______________ | ______ | ______ | __________ | ______ | ______ |
| __________ | ______________ | ______ | ______ | __________ | ______ | ______ |
| __________ | ______________ | ______ | ______ | __________ | ______ | ______ |

**Also log:** suppressors and which firearms they fit (→ 14-10), optics and their battery types
(→ 14-09), spare-parts status for each platform (→ 14-06), and who in the household is trained
on each firearm (→ 14-14).

{{#if has.firearms}}{{#if !has.safe}}Your profile lists no safe. A lock for every firearm comes
before any more ammunition (→ 14-14).{{/if}}{{/if}}

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Deep stock of your small-game caliber | Most use per pound and dollar | Sealed containers (→ 14-07) |
| Extra depth in your least-common calibers | Hardest to find later | What you buy is what you will have |
| Non-toxic shot, if you hunt waterfowl | Required for waterfowl | Steel or bismuth |
| Slugs and buckshot, if you have a shotgun | Deer and defence from one gun | Check where they hit (→ 14-09) |
| Magazines, several per firearm | The most common failure point | Treat as consumable (→ 14-06) |
| The written inventory log | Planning needs numbers | Copy with documents (→ 19-01) |
| Current state hunting regulations, printed | Rules change every year | Print each year |

**If you do not have it:** common calibers are the substitute. Firearms in 9mm, 5.56/.223,
.22 LR and 12 gauge are more useful in a long emergency than unusual ones, because their
ammunition is what you will actually find.

## When it runs out

- **How long it lasts:** rounds on hand divided by realistic use per year, for each job. Hunting
  use is countable. **Practice is what actually drains a stockpile**, so budget it on purpose.
- **Stretch it:** practise with .22 LR instead of centerfire where you can: the same basics for a
  fraction of the cost, and it saves the ammunition that matters.
- **Resupply:** → 14-08, on reloading, commonality, and what can and cannot be made.
- **Dry practice** (an unloaded firearm, no ammunition in the room) keeps most skills alive at no
  cost in ammunition (→ 14-15).

## By phase

- **A (at home):** inventory and standardising, done now.
- **B (on the move):** you cannot carry it all. Decide in advance which firearms and calibers
  travel; ammunition is heavy (→ 01-03). Firearms ride in the cabin, locked (→ 14-03, → 14-14).
- **C (rural or a new place):** on most days small game and deer matter more than defence.

pages.body:
# Firearm maintenance and cleaning without resupply

**What this page is for.** Keeping firearms working for years with no gun shop: how to unload
safely before any work, what really stops guns working, how to fight rust in an unheated house,
what to use when gun oil runs out, and how to keep lead away from children. If you have never
handled a firearm, read → 29-11 first and ask someone who knows the specific gun to show you.

> **CAUTION.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.
> Fixed in every source (floor, → 30-01). In a long emergency the failures change: **rust and
> broken springs, not dirt**, take guns out of service. An unheated house swinging between cold
> and warm puts condensation on cold steel, and it works on every firearm at once while you are
> busy with other things.

## Do this now

1. **Before any maintenance, unload and check three times.** Magazine out and the magazine well
   checked; chamber checked **by eye and by finger**; **every round of ammunition carried out of
   the room**, including loaded magazines and loose rounds (the same routine as → 14-15); muzzle
   pointed at something that would stop a bullet the whole time. Cleaning and "cycling the
   action" (working the moving parts) are when unintended shots happen.
2. **Read the lead and solvent rules below** before the first cleaning: never in the kitchen,
   never on a food surface, gloves on, wash before touching children or food.
3. **Lubrication beats cleanliness** for reliability. A dirty, well-oiled rifle keeps working; a
   spotless dry one often does not.
4. **Wipe every firearm down monthly** in storage, and **at once** after damp, snow, or coming
   from cold into warm.
5. **Stock oil and grease like ammunition.** Cheap now, hard to get later.
6. **Clean rimfire (.22) and suppressed firearms more often.** Both get dirty fast (→ 14-10).

{{figure fig-unload-and-verify}}

## What really stops firearms working

| Cause | How often | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Magazines** | **Most common** | Replace; they wear out (→ 14-06) |
| **Too little oil** | Very common | Lubricate properly, more than you think |
| **Broken springs** | Common over time | Spare springs (→ 14-06) |
| **Rust and corrosion** | The long-term killer | Oil film, dry storage |
| **Worn extractor or ejector** (the parts that pull out and throw out the empty case) | Common after many rounds | Spares |
| **Carbon fouling** (burnt powder) | Least common real cause | Clean the parts where it builds up |

## Notes by type

**AR-pattern rifles** (the common semi-automatic rifle family):

- **Run it wet.** The bolt carrier group (the main moving part) needs a real film of oil on the
  bolt, cam pin and carrier rails. Too little oil causes far more stoppages than dirt.
- **Parts that need attention:** bolt lugs, the tail of the bolt (carbon builds behind the gas
  rings), the extractor and its spring, the cam pin, the inside of the carrier, and the chamber.
- **Gas rings wear.** A common check: a bolt pulled out to its extended position should hold its
  own weight when the carrier is stood on end. Keep spares (→ 14-06).
- **Do not over-scrub the bore.** A steel rod used hard without a bore guide does more harm over a
  lifetime than carbon ever would. A bore snake (a pull-through cord) and moderate solvent use is
  fine.
- **Suppressed rifles get dirtier and hotter**: more gas and carbon blows back into the action.
  They need more oil and more frequent attention (→ 14-10).

**Rimfire (.22 LR):** dirty ammunition with waxy bullets that fouls chambers and suppressors fast.
A neglected .22 becomes sluggish and unreliable. Clean the chamber and bolt face regularly. **A
rimfire suppressor must be taken apart and cleaned**, or lead and carbon will weld it solid
(→ 14-10).

**Shotguns:**

- Gas-operated semi-automatics are the sensitive ones. Keep the piston, gas ports and magazine tube
  clean; some use an O-ring that wears out.
- Pump-action shotguns are very tolerant; keep the action and magazine tube clean and lightly
  oiled.
- **Store with the action closed and springs relaxed** where the design allows, and keep the bore
  oiled. Long, thin barrels rust easily.

**Every firearm:** the printed manual is the authority on how it comes apart and goes back
together. Keep one for each (→ 19-01).

## Fighting rust: the priority when the heat is off

This is the part most people underestimate, especially in a house you are no longer heating
(→ 08-01).

- **Temperature swings make condensation.** A cold firearm brought into a warm room gets water
  on it and in it. Let it warm up **before** opening the case, then wipe it down.
- **A thin film of oil on every outside surface** is the basic protection. Check monthly.
- **Silicone-treated gun socks** and **VCI paper or emitters** (vapour corrosion inhibitor, a
  material that slowly releases a rust-preventing vapour) in storage containers add real
  protection.
- **Desiccant** (moisture-absorbing packets such as silica gel) in any sealed container, dried and
  reused. **Dry it outdoors or in the garage on a pan kept only for this, never in the kitchen
  oven:** desiccant that has lived in a gun case carries lead dust.
- **Do not store firearms in foam-lined cases long-term.** Foam holds moisture against the steel.
- **Watch the bore.** A rusted bore is the one damage you cannot easily undo.

## When the gun oil runs out

Purpose-made gun oil is best. After that, roughly in order of usefulness:

- **Motor oil** (any weight): works well, and you probably have some.
- **Automatic transmission fluid**: thin, spreads well, decent rust protection; a long-standing
  improvised gun oil.
- **Chainsaw bar oil or hydraulic oil**: sticky, good for long storage, poor in cold.
- **Axle or lithium grease**: sparingly, on rails and high-pressure points.
- **Rendered animal fat**: last resort. It can go rancid and attract pests, but it beats running
  dry.
- **Avoid:** water-displacing spray as a *lubricant* (fine for driving off water, poor as oil, and
  it can creep into cartridge primers), vegetable oils (they gum up), and anything that dries hard.

**In deep cold**, heavy oils and greases stiffen. Use **thinner** oil, not more of it.

## When solvent runs out

- **Hot soapy water** works for general fouling. Dry thoroughly and oil at once.
- **Mineral spirits or kerosene** cut carbon well. Store them as fuel (→ 06-06, → 29-01).
- **Do not** use household bleach or ammonia cleaners casually. Ammonia attacks copper and, left in
  place, can damage a bore.
- **Wood ash in hot water** makes a crude degreaser for very heavy fouling. **It is lye: caustic.**
  Gloves and eye protection; rinse well (→ 16-02 has the same warning for tools).

## Lead and solvent: keeping it away from children

Fouling from the bore and action is **lead-rich** (from primers and bullets), and solvents are
petroleum. The CDC states that **no safe blood lead level in children has been identified**,
that children under 6 are at highest risk because they put their hands in their mouths, and that
hobbies can bring lead home on hands, clothes and surfaces (CDC, Childhood Lead Poisoning
Prevention). → 14-08 says the same about reloading and casting. Every time:

- **Clean outdoors, in the garage, or in a room with a window open. Never in the kitchen, never on
  a table anyone eats at.** Lay down newspaper or a mat kept for this; it goes in the bin after.
- **Nitrile gloves on.** Patches, rags and used solvent go into a **lidded metal can** (a coffee
  can works) kept with the cleaning kit, out of children's reach.
- **Wash hands and forearms with soap and water** (hand sanitiser does not remove lead) and
  **change your shirt** before you pick up a child or make food.
- **Suppressor cleaning is the worst of it** (→ 14-10). Rimfire suppressor sludge is mostly lead:
  outdoors, gloves, and the sludge goes in the sealed can.

{{#if has.child}}There are children in your household: these rules are not optional.{{/if}}

## A realistic schedule

| When | What |
|---|---|
| **After every use** | Wipe down, check the bore is clear, light oil; clean if fired a lot |
| **After wet, snow, or cold-to-warm** | **At once**: full wipe-down and re-oil |
| **Monthly in storage** | **Unload and check first (above)**, look for rust, wipe, re-oil, work the action |
| **Every few hundred rounds** | Deeper clean of bolt and chamber; check springs and extractor |
| **Once a year** | Full take-down of the main firearms; replace worn springs (→ 14-06) |

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Gun oil and grease, **lots** | The real consumable | Buy in bulk now |
| A bore snake for each caliber | Fast, portable, no rod damage | One per caliber |
| Cleaning rods, bore guides, jags and brushes | Proper bore work | Coated rod, correct sizes |
| Carbon scraper (AR-pattern) | The one deposit that matters | Cheap |
| Solvent and mineral spirits | Removes fouling | Store as fuel (→ 06-06) |
| Patches, rags, nitrile gloves | Consumables; stock deep | Old T-shirts work; gloves block lead |
| Lidded metal can for used patches and rags | Keeps lead and solvent sealed | With the kit, out of children's reach |
| **Desiccant and VCI paper or emitters** | Rust is the long-term killer | Re-dry desiccant with heat, outdoors |
| Gun socks or oiled cases (not foam) | Storage protection | Avoid trapped moisture |
| Small brushes, picks, cotton swabs | Detail work | Dental picks are ideal |
| Headspace gauges, per centerfire caliber | Check after any barrel or bolt swap (→ 14-06) | Go/no-go at least |
| **Printed manual for every firearm** | How it comes apart; parts lists | Keep with documents (→ 19-01) |

**If you do not have it:** motor oil and transmission fluid are in every garage and vehicle. Any
cloth makes rags. A shoelace with a small weight makes a crude bore snake.

## When it runs out

- **Oil is the one to hoard.** It protects everything, and a rusted firearm is a permanent loss.
- **Protection first, cleanliness second.** If you have one ounce of oil left, it goes on outside
  surfaces and in the bore, not into a deep clean.
- **Firearms fail from neglect and tired springs, not from use.** A collection wiped down monthly
  and stored dry will outlast the crisis; one left in a damp basement for a year may not.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** monthly check; watch an unheated house for condensation.
- **B (on the move):** a small kit (oil, a bore snake, a rag, a multi-tool); keep firearms out of
  repeated cold-to-warm swings where you can.
- **C (rural or a new place):** damp outbuildings are hard on steel. Keep working firearms in the
  heated space with you, locked (→ 14-14).

pages.body:
# Spare parts and the armorer's kit

**What this page is for.** A firearm is a machine with parts that wear out, and in a long
emergency there is no gunsmith. This page lists the small parts worth buying now for the common
types of firearm, the tools to fit them, and the few jobs to learn before you need them. An
"armorer" is the person who maintains and repairs firearms.

{{#if has.firearms}}Your profile says there are firearms in the home. Work through the sections
below that match the types you own, and list your platforms in the log on → 14-04.{{else}}Your
profile lists no firearms. Keep this page for reference: if firearms come into the household,
start with → 29-11 and → 14-14, then come back here.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.** Unload and check every firearm before any work, and carry all ammunition out of the
> room (→ 14-05). **Springs and magazines fail long before barrels wear out**, and a rifle with a
> broken extractor spring and no spare does not work. Some jobs here change how safely a firearm
> fires: if you have not been shown how by someone qualified, leave barrels and bolts alone.

## Do this now

1. **List your platforms** (types of firearm that share parts, such as "AR-pattern rifle" or a
   particular pistol model) on → 14-04.
2. **Buy spring kits** for each platform. Springs are the main long-term wear item across every
   kind of firearm.
3. **Treat magazines as consumables** and stock deeply. They cause more stoppages than everything
   else combined.
4. **Learn to replace these parts now**, with the manual on a bench in daylight, not later by
   lamplight.
5. **Print the manual and the parts diagram** for every firearm and keep them with this binder's
   paper documents (→ 19-01).

## Springs and magazines first

**Springs deserve their own category.** Recoil and buffer springs, magazine springs, extractor
springs and trigger springs all tire. A full spring kit for each platform is cheap and is the most
cost-effective purchase in this section.

**Magazines: count them like ammunition.** In any semi-automatic they are the most frequent cause
of stoppages, and they cannot be repaired forever: followers (the platform the cartridges sit on)
crack, feed lips spread, springs weaken.

- **Stock heavily.** Cheap now, impossible later.
- **Mark and retire** a magazine that causes a stoppage. Do not keep mixing a bad one back in.
- **Loaded or empty in storage?** Good modern magazine springs tolerate long storage loaded, but
  rotating a few is sensible. Store them clean and dry (→ 14-05), and loaded magazines are
  ammunition: locked away from children (→ 14-14).
- **Keep spare followers and magazine springs.** They rebuild an otherwise good magazine.

## AR-pattern rifles

If you own more than one AR-pattern rifle, parts are cheap, standardised and mostly
interchangeable between them.

| Part | Why | Stock |
|---|---|---|
| **Complete bolt** (or bolt carrier group) | Highest-stress part; lugs and extractor live here | **2 or more** if you run several rifles |
| **Extractor, spring and insert or O-ring** | Classic failure; cheap | Several sets |
| **Ejector, spring and roll pin** | Small, easily lost, stops the rifle | Several |
| **Gas rings** | Wear item, cheap, easy | Several sets |
| **Firing pin and retaining pin** | Breakage happens | 2 or more |
| **Cam pin** | Rare failure but stops the rifle completely | 2 or more |
| **Gas tube and roll pin** | Can crack or clog | 1 to 2 |
| **Buffer spring** | Tires over time | 2 or more |
| **Lower parts kit** (springs and detents) | Tiny springs fly across rooms during repairs | 1 to 2 kits |
| **Castle nut and end plate** | Loosens with use | A spare |
| **Magazines** | **The most common failure point** | **As many as you can** |

## Handguns

| Part | Why |
|---|---|
| **Recoil spring assembly** | The scheduled wear item: replace on the maker's round count |
| Extractor and spring | Stoppages |
| Firing pin and spring | Breakage |
| Magazine springs and followers | Same as rifles |
| Sights and screws | They loosen |

## Shotguns

| Part | Why |
|---|---|
| Extractor, ejector and springs | Common failure |
| Magazine tube spring and follower | Tires |
| **Gas system O-rings and seals** (semi-automatics) | Classic wear item: cheap, stops the gun |
| Firing pin and spring | Breakage |

## Bolt-action rifles

Simpler and more durable, but stock a **firing pin spring**, an **extractor**, an **ejector
plunger and spring**, and **action screws**. Write down the **torque value** (how tight, from the
maker) for the action screws: it affects where the rifle shoots (→ 14-09).

## The armorer's tool kit

| Tool | For |
|---|---|
| **Armorer's wrench** for your platform | Castle nut, barrel nut, muzzle device on AR-pattern rifles |
| **Vise with receiver blocks** | Holding parts without crushing them |
| **Roll pin punches, starter punches, brass hammer** | Almost every take-down |
| **Torque wrench reading in inch-pounds** | Optic mounts, action screws, barrel nuts (→ 14-09) |
| **Headspace gauges** (go and no-go, for each centerfire caliber) | **Required after any barrel or bolt change** |
| Bench block, hex and Torx sets | General work |
| Digital calipers | Measuring, and reloading (→ 14-08) |
| Magnifier and a good light | Looking for cracks, worn lugs, tired springs |
| **Printed manuals and parts diagrams** | Doing it right under pressure |

**Headspace, in plain words:** the gap between the face of the bolt and the part of the chamber
that stops the cartridge. Too much and the case can rupture when fired. If a barrel or bolt is
ever swapped, checking headspace with gauges is not optional; it is the difference between a safe
firearm and a dangerous one. If nobody in the household knows how, do not swap barrels or bolts.

## Learn it now

Buying parts you cannot fit is a hobby, not preparedness. Before you need to, do each of these at
least once, with the manual and someone who knows how:

- Take apart and reassemble a bolt carrier group; replace the extractor and its spring.
- Replace a handgun recoil spring.
- Rebuild a magazine (spring and follower).
- Tighten an optic mount to the maker's torque and confirm the zero afterwards (→ 14-09).

Dates we did each: ______________________________________________

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Spare bolts or bolt carrier groups (AR-pattern) | Highest-stress part | Good quality, properly staked |
| Full spring kits for every platform | The main long-term wear item | Cheap; buy now |
| Bolt small-parts kits (extractor, ejector, pins, gas rings) | Parts that stop the firearm | Several sets |
| **Magazines, deep stock** | Most common failure point | Plus spare springs and followers |
| Handgun recoil springs and extractors | Scheduled wear | For each handgun |
| Shotgun O-rings, extractors, magazine springs | Cheap, stops the gun | For each shotgun |
| Armorer's wrench, vise blocks, punches, brass hammer | Doing the work | → 16-01 |
| **Inch-pound torque wrench** | Optics and actions | Zero depends on it |
| **Headspace gauges** | Safety after any barrel or bolt change | Go and no-go |
| Printed manuals and parts diagrams | The knowledge, offline | With documents |
| Thread locker, anti-seize, grease | Assembly | Small tubes |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Other firearms of the same pattern are parts sources.** A second rifle of the same type is,
  in effect, a spare-parts bin. This is the practical argument for owning common platforms
  (→ 14-04).
- Springs can sometimes be made from music wire, but the right strength and heat treatment matter.
  Treat a home-made spring as temporary.
- Ordinary hand tools (→ 16-01) cover much of the kit; the platform wrenches and headspace gauges
  have to be bought in advance.

## When it runs out

- **Count spares per platform, not overall.** Two bolts for four rifles is thinner than it sounds.
- **Keep the main firearms fully supported** and let secondary ones of the same pattern become
  parts donors.
- **Small parts are cheap insurance.** Springs, bolts and magazines bought today are worth more in
  the second year than another case of ammunition.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** buy the parts, learn the jobs, print the diagrams.
- **B (on the move):** a small repair kit: spare bolt or extractor kit, a punch, oil.
- **C (rural or a new place):** the full kit travels if the vehicle does; otherwise springs and
  small parts, which are light.

pages.body:
# Ammunition storage and how long it lasts

**What this page is for.** How to store ammunition so it stays safe and still works years from
now, where never to put it, what happens to it in a house fire, and how to check an old supply.

> **SAFETY.** Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.
> Fixed in every source (floor, → 30-01). Ammunition is locked, separately from firearms
> (→ 14-14). Two real hazards on this page: **fire** (badly stored ammunition, and especially
> loose smokeless powder, makes a house fire worse) and **quiet spoilage** (moisture ruining a
> supply you were counting on). The industry standard (SAAMI, Small Arms Ammunition: Properties
> and Storage): **avoid temperatures over 150 °F**, and keep ammunition **in its factory
> packaging**.

## Do this now

1. **Cool, dry, steady.** Not a hot attic, not a damp basement floor, not a vehicle in summer.
2. **Keep it in the factory carton**, then put the cartons inside sealed containers.
3. **Steel ammunition cans with good rubber gaskets, plus desiccant** (moisture-absorbing
   packets), are the practical answer.
4. **Lift it off concrete.** Concrete wicks moisture and sweats when temperatures swing.
5. **Store it away from fuels, solvents and pool chemicals** (→ 06-06). Oxidisers such as pool
   shock and propellant do not belong on the same shelf.{{#if has.pool}} Your household has a pool:
   wherever the pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) is kept, no ammunition or primers go on that
   shelf or the floor below it, and if the chemical bucket ever gets wet or the room smells of
   chlorine, the ammunition leaves the room first (→ 29-05).{{/if}}
6. **Write down lots and dates.** Use the oldest first.

## How long does ammunition last?

SAAMI publishes **no expiry date** for ammunition. Its position is that ammunition kept in its
factory packaging over extended periods, through the ordinary temperature and humidity changes of
homes and warehouses "from tropic to Arctic conditions", can be expected to perform
satisfactorily and safely (SAAMI, Small Arms Ammunition). Well-stored ammunition is commonly
kept for many years; what ruins it is not time so much as **moisture, heat and contact with oils
or solvents**.

| Enemy | What it does | Control |
|---|---|---|
| **Humidity** | Corrodes cases and primers; can reach the powder | Sealed containers and desiccant |
| **Heat over 150 °F** | Degrades powder and primers; SAAMI says avoid | Never an attic, never a car in summer |
| **Temperature swings** | Condensation inside containers | A steady place; sealed cans; desiccant |
| **Touching concrete** | Wicks moisture | Pallet, shelf or wood underneath |
| **Solvents, oils, water** | SAAMI: can reach the powder or primer and cause misfires, or a bullet stuck in the barrel | Never store ammunition with lubricants or solvents; never let it soak |
| **Physical damage** | Dented cases, bullets pushed in | Factory packaging |

## The cold-climate problem: temperature cycling

{{#if is.cold_winters}}Your home has cold winters, so this is your main risk.{{/if}} An unheated
garage or shed that swings from well below freezing to above it, again and again, pumps damp air
in and out of any unsealed container and condenses water on cold brass. That is how a supply
quietly corrodes over a couple of winters.

**The fix is sealing, not heating.** A gasketed steel can with fresh desiccant is stable almost
anywhere. Check the desiccant and dry it out again with heat, outdoors or in the garage on a pan
kept for this, **not in the kitchen oven**: desiccant from a gun room carries lead dust (→ 14-05).

## Where to store it

| Place | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Inside closet or heated, cooled living space** | **Best**: steady temperature and humidity |
| Basement, **off the floor**, sealed cans | Good; watch for damp |
| Detached shed or garage, sealed cans and desiccant | Acceptable if sealed |
| **Attic** | **No**: summer attics are among the hottest places in a house, and heat is what SAAMI says to avoid |
| **Vehicle**, long-term | **No**: SAAMI warns a closed car in the sun gets extremely hot |
| Next to fuels, solvents or pool chemicals | **No** (→ 06-06) |

**Spread it out.** Do not keep the whole supply in one place: a fire, a flood or a theft should
not be able to take all of it. Two or three locked places, and a current log (→ 14-04). Write the
places by hand on your own paper copy, not in the settings page.

## Fire: what actually happens

This drives the storage choices. Small arms ammunition burning in a fire does **not** behave like
a bomb: cartridges that are not inside a gun burst and pop; the bullets barely move, because
nothing confines them. SAAMI says small pieces of case and primer can fly short distances
(usually not over 50 feet) fast enough to injure, and that its member companies found they do
not get through firefighters' protective gear (SAAMI, Small Arms Ammunition). So keep people
without that gear well back, and tell firefighters it is there. **Loose smokeless powder** (the
propellant reloaders buy in bulk) is a different and more serious matter: once lit it burns until
it is gone, and if it is confined the pressure can burst its container like an explosion (SAAMI,
Smokeless Powder).

- **If you reload (→ 14-08), keep powder in its original containers, cool and dry, in a cabinet
  of insulating material such as wood, built so it can vent (a weak wall or seams), never in a
  sealed steel can or a safe.** Confinement is what turns a fast burn into a blast; SAAMI's
  smokeless powder guidance says keep it in the original approved containers and do not store it
  in close confinement (SAAMI, Smokeless Powder: Properties and Storage). **Keep the amount
  small**: many small containers are safer than one large one. Keep primers in their own trays,
  away from the powder.
- **Do not store powder next to ammunition, fuel or oxidisers such as pool shock.**
- **Tell everyone in the house where it is**, so anyone fighting a fire knows.
- **Never store ammunition or powder near a heat source or a wood stove.**

## Checking an old supply

- **Look for green or white corrosion** on cases and around primers. Surface tarnish is usually
  only cosmetic; corrosion at the primer or the case mouth is not.
- **Powder that smells acidic, like vinegar, or gives off reddish-brown fumes** (if you reload) is
  breaking down; SAAMI says dispose of it at once. Do not confuse it with ordinary solvent smells.
- **Ammunition that has been in a house fire, a flood, or got wet or scorched is scrapped**, not
  used or traded (SAAMI, Small Arms Ammunition).
- **Rimfire (.22) is often more vulnerable** than centerfire to moisture at the rim and case mouth;
  check it first.
- **Test-fire a sample** from an old lot before trusting it for hunting or defence.
- **Set aside, do not mix.** Doubtful ammunition goes in a marked can for practice only.

## How much?

There is no single right number. Plan by **job and rate of use** (→ 14-04):

- **Practice** is what actually uses ammunition. The fix is dry practice (→ 14-15) and .22 LR.
- **Hunting** is countable: a few rounds per animal, plus sighting in.
- **Defence** is unpredictable, and beyond a modest amount per firearm it is rarely what limits
  survival. Food, fuel and medicine are.

**A useful test:** what would still matter in year two? Usually small-game ammunition, a working
hunting rifle with ammunition for it, and enough for defence, not a mountain of one caliber.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Steel ammunition cans with intact rubber gaskets | The practical sealed container | Check the gasket; test the seal |
| **Silica gel desiccant, rechargeable** | Humidity is the real enemy | Re-dry with heat, outdoors |
| Humidity indicator cards | Show whether the seal is working | Cheap; one per can |
| Shelving or pallets | Off concrete | Any wood works |
| Waterproof labels and a log | Lot, date, caliber, count | Copy with documents (→ 19-01) |
| Original factory packaging | SAAMI's own recommendation | Keep the boxes |
| Wooden powder cabinet (if reloading) | Fire safety with loose powder | Vents if lit; original containers, small amount, primers apart; never sealed steel |
| Lockable containers in more than one place | Fire, theft and water resilience; children | → 14-14 |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Sealed plastic buckets with gasket lids**, plus desiccant, work instead of steel cans.
- **Rice** is a poor but real emergency desiccant; silica gel is far better.
- Any raised shelf beats the floor.

## When it runs out

- Storage does not use ammunition, but **bad storage destroys it**, and you find out when you need
  it.
- **Shoot the oldest and doubtful lots first**, in practice; keep the newest and best stored for
  hunting and defence.
- **Resupply:** → 14-08.
- **Inspect once a year**, on the same day as smoke-alarm batteries and water rotation.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** inside living space, spread out, sealed, logged, locked.
- **B (on the move):** ammunition is **heavy**: decide by job what travels (→ 01-03). Keep it out
  of direct sun in the vehicle, locked, in the cabin.
- **C (rural or a new place):** outbuildings swing in temperature; sealed cans with desiccant
  matter even more.

pages.body:
# Finding, stretching and reloading ammunition

**What this page is for.** In a long emergency the ammunition you have is, for most households,
all you will get. This page covers how to make it last, where more can honestly come from, what
reloading (re-assembling used cartridges) needs, and the hazards of lead.

> **SAFETY.** **Never guess a load.** Reloading is safe and routine when you follow current
> published data from the powder or bullet maker, and it destroys firearms and hands when you
> improvise. **No load data appears on this page, by design.** **Never try to make primers or
> powder at home**: both are dangerous chemistry and are where people are badly hurt. Children do
> not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products; that includes ammunition,
> lead and reloading components (floor, → 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Stretch first, find second.** Dry practice, .22 LR practice and careful hunting cut use far
   more than scrounging adds supply.
2. **If you intend to reload, set it up now**: press, dies, and above all **components**. It is a
   capability you build in advance, not improvise later.
3. **Primers are the bottleneck.** They cannot practically be made at home. If you stock one
   reloading component deeply, stock primers.
4. **Save your brass** (the empty cases). It is the one reusable component.
5. **Think hard before trading ammunition** (→ 18-02): you arm the person you trade with.

## Stretching what you have: the biggest lever

| Habit | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Dry practice** (unloaded, no ammunition in the room, → 14-15) | Keeps most shooting skills alive with **no** ammunition |
| **Practise with .22 LR** | The same basics for a fraction of the cost; saves centerfire |
| **Confirm the zero, do not redo it** | A few rounds to check, not a box (→ 14-09) |
| **Hunt carefully** | Closer shots, steady rests, fewer misses |
| **Traps and snares** | Take small game with **no** ammunition (→ 05-15) |
| **Stop casual shooting** | The largest avoidable drain |

**Traps deserve special mention.** In a long emergency they feed you while you do other work,
and they use nothing up. A rifle cartridge is a poor way to catch a rabbit if a snare will do it.

## Where ammunition really comes from

| Source | Realistic? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bought in advance** | **The only reliable one** | Everything else is speculation |
| Sporting goods, hardware and farm stores | Early on | Common calibers sell out first |
| Other shooters, trade | Real | See the warning below |
| Reloading your own | **Yes, if set up in advance** | Needs components you already own |
| Private and estate sales, now | Yes | Legal and often cheaper |
| "Scavenging" | Mostly fantasy | Ammunition does not lie around; assume nothing |

**The honest summary: your supply is what you buy before it matters.** Plan on that.

## Reloading: what it really needs

Reloading turns **brass + primer + powder + bullet** back into a cartridge. You need all four, plus
the tools. Brass can be reused many times; the other three are used up.

**Components, most critical first:**

1. **Primers**: **the hard bottleneck.** Cannot be safely made at home. Store cool and dry; they
   are sensitive to moisture and oil, so keep solvents away (→ 14-07).
2. **Powder**: buy in the container sizes you will use; store as SAAMI's smokeless powder
   guidance says (original containers, cool, dry, never closely confined; → 14-07). **Watch for
   breakdown** (a vinegar-like acid smell or reddish-brown fumes) and dispose of bad powder at
   once. Never salvage powder from old cartridges or mix powders (SAAMI, Smokeless Powder:
   Properties and Storage).
3. **Bullets**: buy now, and **cast later** from lead if you set up for it.
4. **Brass**: reusable; save every case. Inspect for splits, stretching and loose primer pockets.

**What you cannot do safely at home:**

- **Make primers.** The priming compound is sensitive explosive chemistry. Do not.
- **Make smokeless powder.** Do not.
- **Reload .22 LR** or any rimfire. **This is why .22 LR is stocked deep** (→ 14-04): you can
  never make more.
- **Reload shotgun shells without a press made for them**, though with one it is a real option.

## Casting bullets: the renewable part

Lead can be melted and cast into bullets, which makes **bullets** the one component you can
renew.

- **Lead sources:** older wheel weights, scrap lead, plumbing lead.
- **Needs:** a melting pot, a mould for your caliber, a sizing and lubricating setup, and an
  outdoor heat source (→ 07-01).
- **Cast bullets suit** handgun calibers and lower-speed rifle loads better than high-speed
  rifle loads. (Never .22 LR: rimfire is never reloadable.)

**Lead is a serious hazard, above all to children.** The CDC states that **no safe blood lead
level in children has been identified**, that children under 6 are at highest risk because they
put their hands in their mouths, and that **hobbies are a recognised way lead comes home**, on
clothes and hands (CDC, Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention).

- **Cast outdoors only**, well away from where children play. Never in the kitchen.
- **Never bring casting clothes, tools or residue into the living space.** Change and wash before
  touching children or food.
- **Store lead, moulds and cast bullets locked and out of reach.** A cast bullet is exactly what
  a toddler puts in their mouth.
- **Molten lead plus any moisture causes a violent steam explosion.** Everything that touches the
  pot must be bone dry.
- {{#if has.young_child}}**There is a child under 6 in your household.** Weigh honestly whether
  casting is worth it while they are this young.{{else}}With small children in the house, weigh
  honestly whether casting is worth it while they are young.{{/if}}

## Trading ammunition: the problem

Ammunition will be among the most valuable trade goods in a crisis. That cuts three ways:

1. **You arm whoever you trade with**, possibly against you.
2. **It tells them you have more** (→ 14-03).
3. **It draws coercion.** Being known as the house with ammunition is a danger, not an asset.

**If you trade at all:** only calibers you do **not** depend on, only with people you would be
comfortable seeing armed, in small amounts, and never in a way that shows how much you have.
There are better trade goods (→ 18-02).

## Setting up now: a realistic order

1. **Components first** (primers, powder, bullets): they are what vanish from shelves.
2. **A single-stage press, dies for your two most-used calibers, a scale and calipers.**
3. **Reloading manuals with current published load data, printed** (→ 19-01). Data on a phone is
   data you may not have.
4. **Practise now.** Load and shoot your own ammunition while you can check results safely.
5. **Casting** later, as the long-term extension.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Primers, deep stock** | The bottleneck; cannot be made at home | Cool, dry, away from solvents |
| Powder, in the containers you will use | Consumable | Store as → 14-07 |
| Bullets, or a casting setup | Renewable if you cast | Moulds in your calibers |
| Brass: **save all of it** | The reusable component | Sort by caliber, inspect |
| Single-stage press and dies | The core tool | Simple and durable |
| Scale, calipers, case trimmer, tumbler | Accuracy and safety | Digital, plus a beam scale as backup |
| **Printed load manuals** | Never guess | More than one source; keep them current |
| Shotshell press (optional) | Shotgun reloading | Wads, hulls, shot |
| Lead pot, moulds, sizer | Renewable bullets | **Outdoors only; lead is toxic** |
| Snares and trapping supplies | Game with **no** ammunition | → 05-15 |

**If you do not have it:** traps and snares are the real substitute for ammunition when the goal
is food. Lead can be scavenged if you can cast. Brass piles up wherever people shoot. **There is no
substitute for primers.**

## When it runs out

- **How long it lasts:** rounds on hand (→ 14-04), plus the cartridges you could reload. **Primers
  are the limit**: you can load only as many cartridges as you have primers.
- **Stretch it:** dry practice; .22 LR for practice; traps for small game; careful hunting.
- **After that:** accept that the supply is finite and move food-getting toward trapping, fishing
  and growing (→ 05-15, → 05-08). Plan your food so that it does **not** depend on ammunition.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** buy components, set up and learn the press, save brass.
- **B (on the move):** reloading gear is heavy and stays behind; carry loaded ammunition by job.
- **C (rural or a new place):** casting and reloading become valuable, and trapping matters more
  than shooting for daily food.

pages.body:
# Zeroing, optics and battery management

**What this page is for.** "Zeroing" means adjusting a sight so the bullet hits where you aim at
a chosen distance. This page covers choosing and recording a zero, keeping optics (scopes and red
dots) working when batteries are scarce, backup iron sights, and confirming a zero without using
much ammunition. New to firearms? Read → 29-11 first.

> **CAUTION.** Zeroing means live fire, and the four safety rules apply to every shot (→ 29-11):
> above all, know your target and what is beyond it. **Where** the household fires is a decision
> card: {{choice DC-11}} → 30-12. An optic is a **battery-powered part** on a mechanical tool. In
> a long emergency, two things end your ability to hit anything: **dead batteries** and **a zero
> you cannot check because ammunition is too precious**. Both are solved in advance, and almost
> nobody does it.

## Do this now

1. **Confirm and write down the zero of every rifle now**, while ammunition can still be bought.
   Put it on a card kept with the rifle.
2. **Know every optic's battery type** and stock **many** spares; count them like ammunition.
3. **Fit backup iron sights** to any rifle you depend on, and zero those too.
4. **If you shoot with a suppressor, zero with it on** (→ 14-10): the bullet's impact shifts.
5. **Tighten optic mounts to the maker's torque** and mark the screws so you can see if they move
   (→ 14-06).

## Choosing a zero

The zero you choose decides how much thinking you do under pressure. Common conventions:

| Firearm | Common approach | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **5.56 / .223 carbine** | **50/200-yard zero** | Little aiming adjustment needed across ordinary distances |
| **.308 and other deer rifles** | **100-yard zero** | A precise baseline to hold or adjust from |
| **.22 LR** | **50-yard zero** | Matches realistic small-game distances; drops fast beyond |
| **Shotgun with slugs** | **50-yard zero** | Practical slug distance |
| **Shotgun with shot** | **Pattern, do not zero** | Shoot each load at paper at your expected distance and look at the spread |

**Whatever you choose, write it down**, with the aiming adjustment ("hold") at the distances you
would really shoot. A zero you cannot describe is a zero you do not really have.

## The data card: the most valuable five minutes

Make one per rifle, protect it with a laminating pouch or clear tape, and keep it on the stock or
in the case. (Hunters call it a "dope card".)

{{figure fig-dope-card}}

```
RIFLE: ______________  CALIBER: ______  ZERO: ______ yd
LOAD:  ______________________  (bullet weight / brand / lot)
OPTIC: ______________  MOUNT TORQUE: ______ in-lb  BATTERY: ______
  50 yd  hold: ______      200 yd hold: ______
 100 yd  hold: ______      300 yd hold: ______
 SUPPRESSED shift: ______  IRONS zeroed: Y / N
 Zero confirmed (date): ______
```

**The ammunition matters.** Different loads, and even different lots of the same load, hit in
different places. If you stocked one hunting load, **zero for that load** and note it on the
card. Change loads and you have a new zero.

## Batteries: the dependency nobody plans for

- **List every optic's battery type** (CR2032, CR123A, AA, AAA) and standardise where you can.
- **Stock deeply.** Lithium primary (non-rechargeable) cells keep for years in storage and work
  in cold far better than alkaline (→ 29-02).
- **Cold cuts battery life.** A red dot that runs a year at room temperature runs noticeably less
  in sustained cold. Keep spares warm, in an inside pocket.
- **Alkaline batteries leak** and can destroy an optic left in storage. For anything stored with
  a battery in it, **use lithium** or take the battery out.
- **Know the run time.** Many red dots run a very long time; some magnified and lit scopes run far
  less. Turn them off, or use a motion-activated setting.
- **A magnified scope with an etched reticle still works with a dead battery**; only the
  illumination goes. **A red dot usually does not work at all.** That should shape what goes on
  the rifle you depend on most.

## Backup iron sights

- **Line them up with the red dot** ("co-witness") so switching is natural.
- **Zero the irons separately** and write it down. Iron sights never zeroed are decoration.
- **Practise using them**, including flipping up folding sights quickly.
- A rifle with iron sights never has a dead battery.

## Mounting and torque

- **Use a torque wrench that reads in inch-pounds** (→ 14-06). Too tight crushes scope tubes; too
  loose lets the optic shift, which shows up as a zero that wanders for no clear reason.
- **Mark the screws** with a paint line after tightening. One glance shows if anything moved.
- **Thread locker** only as the maker says.
- **Check the zero again after** any mount work, a hard drop, a long trip, or a barrel or bolt
  change.

## Zeroing without using much ammunition

- **Bore sight first** (look through the barrel of a bolt-action rifle, or use a laser or optical
  bore sighter) to get on paper in one or two shots instead of ten.
- **Shoot small groups from a steady rest:** three rounds, adjust, confirm. A careful process uses
  only a handful of rounds per rifle.
- **Confirm, do not redo.** Once zeroed, a periodic single-shot check at a known distance tells
  you what you need.
- **Dry practice** (→ 14-15) covers everything except recoil, and uses no ammunition.

## Optics care in the field

- **Lens covers on** when moving; grit is what scratches glass.
- **Do not wipe a dry lens.** Blow grit off first, then use a lens cloth.
- **Fogging:** a cold optic brought into a warm room fogs, like the condensation problem on
  → 14-05. Let it warm up before wiping.
- **Heat shimmer** ("mirage") rises off a hot suppressor and blurs the view (→ 14-10). Let it cool.
- **Store optics dry**, with alkaline batteries removed for long storage.

## Optic and battery log (fill in by hand)

| Rifle (type, not serial) | Optic | Battery type | Spares on hand | Irons? | Zero |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ____________ | ____________ | ______ | ______ | Y/N | ______ |
| ____________ | ____________ | ______ | ______ | Y/N | ______ |
| ____________ | ____________ | ______ | ______ | Y/N | ______ |

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Lithium batteries, deep stock, for each type** | The real optic dependency | Long shelf life; good in cold |
| Backup iron sights on rifles you depend on | Works with no battery | Zero them separately |
| **Inch-pound torque wrench** | Mounts that hold zero | Also → 14-06 |
| Bore sighter (laser or optical) | Zero with very little ammunition | Cheap; saves rounds |
| Data cards and laminating pouches | The numbers, on the rifle | Or clear tape |
| Lens pen, cloth, covers | Glass care | Blow off grit first |
| Rest, bipod or sandbag | A zero is only as good as what the rifle rests on | A bag of rice works |
| A spare optic, even a modest one | Optics fail | Already mounted if possible |
| Paper targets and a marker | Confirming zero | Print a stack now |

**If you do not have it:** iron sights replace everything electronic, which is the argument for
keeping at least one rifle with good irons. Cardboard and paint make targets; a rolled sleeping
bag makes a rest. CR123A and CR2032 cells turn up in cameras, sensors and other devices.

## When it runs out

- **Batteries, in hours of run time per optic.** Write the number in the log.
- **Stretch them:** turn optics **off** when not in use; use motion-activated settings; use iron
  sights for routine carry and save battery life for when it matters.
- **The lasting answer:** an etched-reticle scope or good iron sights never depend on a battery.
  Over several years, that is worth more than any electronic advantage.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** zero everything, make the data cards, stock batteries. Cheap and easy now.
- **B (on the move):** travel can shift a zero; confirm on arrival if you can spare a round and a
  safe place to fire it.
- **C (rural or a new place):** longer shots at game matter more; a confirmed hunting zero and a
  data card earn their keep (→ 05-07). In sustained cold, lithium batteries are clearly right.
