pages.body:
# Radio options: FRS, GMRS, MURS, CB, ham, scanners and satellite

**What this page is for.** Choosing radios that will actually work for your household when the
phones do not: which "service" does what, the FRS and GMRS channel table, how repeaters work,
buying advice, power, and the security cost of transmitting. Start with the plain-words
explainer on → 29-09 if any of these names are new.

> **CAUTION.** **The biggest mistake is buying handhelds and expecting the range on the
> package.** "35-mile" radios do not do 35 miles; typical numbers are on → 15-06, so read it
> before spending money. **Transmitting is announcing**: anyone listening learns that you
> exist, roughly where you are and what you are doing (→ 14-03). That is a trade-off to make on
> purpose.

> **Before the collapse:** power limits, frequencies and licences are federal rules (47 CFR
> Part 95 for FRS, GMRS, MURS and CB; Part 97 for amateur radio), and they change. Check the
> current rule, not this page. Transmitting outside a service's rules or your licence class is a
> federal violation while the FCC operates. A GMRS licence needs no exam, is issued to an adult
> (18 or older) for a ten-year term, carries an FCC fee, and lets the holder's immediate family
> (spouse, children, grandchildren, parents, grandparents, brothers and sisters, aunts, uncles,
> nieces, nephews, in-laws and step-relations) use the station (47 CFR 95.1705). An amateur
> licence needs an exam (→ 15-05). **Listening needs no licence.** A
> radio you are licensed and practised on now is worth far more than one you are guessing at
> later.

## Do this now

1. **Decide what you need radios for**, because it changes the answer:
   (a) **family coordination around the house and neighbourhood**; (b) **staying in touch while
   moving**; (c) **hearing what is happening in the region**; (d) **reaching real distance**. Most
   households need (a) and (c); (d) is amateur radio.
2. **For (a) and (b), buy GMRS radios** and get the GMRS licence: no exam, covers the family, more
   capable than FRS.
3. **For (d), start on the amateur (ham) Technician licence now** (→ 15-05). You cannot sit the
   exam after the grid goes down.
4. **For (c), buy a scanner or wideband receiver.** Listening is legal, useful, and does not
   broadcast your existence (→ 15-04).
5. **Write down what you own** (below) so the family plan on → 15-03 matches reality.

## The services compared

Orientation only; the explainer (→ 29-09) and the current federal rule give the details.

| Service | Licence | Typical range (terrain decides; → 15-06) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FRS** (Family Radio Service) | **None** | A few hundred yards to about a mile in town | Fixed antennas; **2 W (0.5 W on channels 8 to 14)**. Fine for the yard and the block |
| **GMRS** (General Mobile Radio Service) | **Licence, no exam, covers the family** | 1 to 5 miles typical; more with repeaters and better antennas | **The sweet spot for family use.** More power, removable antennas, repeaters allowed |
| **MURS** | **None** | About 1 to 3 miles | **5 channels** (151.820, 151.880, 151.940, 154.570, 154.600 MHz), **2 W**; fewer users; **outside antennas allowed** (top no higher than 60 ft above ground or 20 ft above the structure) |
| **CB** (Citizens Band) | **None** | 1 to 5 miles typical; sometimes very far | 40 channels near 27 MHz; **4 W AM, 12 W single-sideband**; still used by truckers; long antennas; **road information on the move** |
| **Amateur (ham)** | **Licence, exam** | Across town to across the world, by band, power and antenna | **The only option with real reach.** Repeaters, emergency nets |
| **Scanner or receiver** | **None** | Listening only | **Legal, useful, invisible.** Start here |

## What each is good for

**FRS and GMRS: family coordination.** One adult at the water source, one at the house; keeping
track of {{#if has.child}}children{{else}}people{{/if}} in a crowd; coordinating a move. **GMRS is
the better buy**: more power, better antennas, repeaters, and one licence covers the household.

**MURS:** a quieter alternative to FRS with the big advantage that you may fit a better antenna.

**CB: road information.** On the move by vehicle, CB is where road conditions circulate. Cheap,
no licence, and the antenna is the whole game.

**Amateur radio: real reach.** The only service that reliably gets beyond line of sight. In a
regional emergency, amateur operators run organised emergency nets and are often the last working
communications network (ARRL). It is also where the knowledge is: antennas, propagation, power,
repair (→ 15-05, → 15-06).

**Scanner or receiver: awareness without exposure.** Listening tells you what is happening
without telling anyone you are there (→ 14-03, → 15-04). For a household that values discretion,
this is the most valuable radio capability.

## What we own (fill in)

{{#if has.gmrs}}Your profile lists FRS or GMRS radios.{{else}}Your profile lists no FRS or GMRS
radios. If you buy some, they are the first hardware purchase in this section: matched pairs or
fours, same model.{{/if}}{{#if has.ham}} Your profile lists a ham radio or a licensed member
(→ 15-05).{{/if}}{{#if has.satellite}} Your profile lists a satellite messenger or satellite
internet (below).{{/if}}

- FRS or GMRS handhelds: model ____________ count ____ AA trays? ☐ programming cable? ☐
- GMRS licence: filed ☐ (date ______) granted ☐ call sign ______________
- Amateur licence holders and class: ___________________________________________
- Scanner or receiver: ____________ CB: ____________ Satellite: ____________

{{photo radios-and-chargers}}

## The FRS and GMRS channel table

All 22 shared channels, from 47 CFR Part 95 (§§ 95.563, 95.567, 95.1763, 95.1767). Print it;
it is public and rarely changes. Power figures are the legal maximums: the FRS limits and the
GMRS 5 W and 0.5 W limits are radiated power; the GMRS 50 W limit is for mobile, base and
repeater radios (fixed stations 15 W). Your family channel is chosen on → 15-03.

| Ch | MHz | Power | Ch | MHz | Power |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 462.5625 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 12 | 467.6625 | 0.5 W only |
| 2 | 462.5875 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 13 | 467.6875 | 0.5 W only |
| 3 | 462.6125 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 14 | 467.7125 | 0.5 W only |
| 4 | 462.6375 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 15 | 462.5500 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 5 | 462.6625 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 16 | 462.5750 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 6 | 462.6875 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 17 | 462.6000 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 7 | 462.7125 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 5 W | 18 | 462.6250 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 8 | 467.5625 | 0.5 W only | 19 | 462.6500 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 9 | 467.5875 | 0.5 W only | 20 | 462.6750 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 10 | 467.6125 | 0.5 W only | 21 | 462.7000 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |
| 11 | 467.6375 | 0.5 W only | 22 | 462.7250 | FRS 2 W / GMRS 50 W |

**"Privacy codes"** on these radios are tones (CTCSS or DCS) that only filter what **you** hear.
They hide nothing from anyone else (→ 15-03). **GMRS repeaters transmit on 462.550 to 462.725 MHz
(channels 15 to 22) and listen 5 MHz higher (467.550 to 467.725 MHz).** FRS radios can hear a
repeater's output but cannot talk through it; a repeater-capable GMRS radio can.

## Programming a repeater

A **repeater** is a radio on a tall tower that receives you and re-transmits at once, so radios
that cannot reach each other can both reach it (→ 29-09).

{{figure fig-line-of-sight-and-repeater}}

Any repeater needs three settings in your radio:

1. **The offset:** transmit 5 MHz above the frequency you listen on (GMRS repeaters are always
   +5 MHz; a radio's "repeater channel" mode usually does this for you).
2. **The transmit tone** (CTCSS or DCS): a tone the repeater needs before it will repeat you.
   **It is a key, not privacy**: everyone can still hear you.
3. **The test:** press to talk, give your call sign, and listen for the repeater's short "tail"
   after you let go. If nothing comes back, the tone or offset is wrong.

Our local repeater (if any): output ______ MHz, input ______ MHz, tone ______, open to the
public? ☐ Programmed ☐ (date ______) memory slot ______ tested on the air ☐ (date ______).
**Check it is still on the air twice a year**: repeaters are volunteer machines and come and go
(→ 15-05).

## Buying advice that matters

- **The antenna matters more than the radio.** A modest radio with a good antenna beats an
  expensive one with a stubby antenna, every time (→ 15-06).
- **Range claims are marketing.** Expect a small fraction of the number on the box in real
  terrain, and much less indoors or in town.
- **Buy radios that take common batteries (AA trays) or charge from 12 V** (→ 09-08). A radio with
  a battery pack you cannot replace is a temporary radio.
- **Buy in pairs or fours, all the same model**, so batteries, chargers and accessories swap and
  everyone knows how to use them.
- **Get spare batteries, spare antennas and a programming cable** while you can.
- **Practise now.** A radio nobody has used is not a capability.
- Spec tables for common radios: → 28-05.

## The security side

Every transmission is an announcement (→ 14-03):

- **Anyone with a scanner can hear you**, including on FRS, GMRS and CB, which are unencrypted by
  rule.
- **Finding a transmitter by direction is not exotic.** A transmitter used often can be located.
- **What you say matters.** What you have, where you are going and when the house is empty do not
  belong on an open channel.
- **What helps:** listen far more than you transmit; keep transmissions short and bland; use
  simple pre-agreed family codes (→ 15-07); and ask whether the coordination is worth the
  exposure.
- **In an ordinary emergency** (a blizzard, an outage, a tornado) the balance favours talking. In a
  long breakdown it shifts (→ 14-03).

## Power

Radios are a small load but a steady one if you listen all day (→ 09-01).

- **Handhelds:** rechargeable packs plus **AA battery trays** as backup, so they can be charged or
  fed from almost anything (→ 09-07).
- **Base and vehicle radios** run on **12 V DC directly** from a battery bank: efficient, no
  inverter (→ 09-08).
- **A scanner listening all day** is a real draw over 24 hours. Budget it.
- **Hand-crank radios** for when there is no power at all (→ 09-11).
- {{#if has.power_station}}**Your power station** (→ 09-03) can charge handhelds from its USB ports
  and run a scanner or base radio from its 12 V port. Keep any station reserved for medical or food
  loads for that job; radios charge from the others.{{else}}A power station or 12 V battery bank
  (→ 09-03) charges handhelds by USB and runs a base radio from 12 V.{{/if}}
- **In the vehicle:** a USB charger in the 12 V socket keeps handhelds topped up while driving.

## Satellite: messengers and satellite internet

Satellite devices reach past dead cell towers, but they depend on companies, networks and
accounts outside your control. **They are a layer in the plan, never the plan.**

- **Satellite messengers and phones with satellite texting** send short messages and SOS calls
  where there is no cell signal (→ 15-03).
- **Satellite internet dishes** (for example Starlink) give real internet, and with phone Wi-Fi
  calling turned on, a phone beside a working dish can make ordinary calls and texts.

**If you have satellite internet (or are thinking about it):**

- **It must be activated, with a paid account, before the emergency.** Activation runs through an
  app and the internet. Starlink's low-cost Standby Mode (low-speed messaging, weather and email,
  not video) is only available to customers who already have the kit on another plan, and since
  March 2026 it is for stationary use only: it switches off when the dish senses motion
  (Starlink, How does pausing service work; Starlink, Critical Information Summary; Mobile
  Internet Resource Center, 2026). Full-speed in-motion use needs a mobile plan. Check current
  plans and prices in the app while you still can.
- **It depends on things you do not control**: satellites, ground stations, billing and policy.
  It shines in a local or regional outage; a wider collapse, an account problem or a policy change
  can switch it off.
- **Power:** read the label for its voltage and watts (→ 28-07); smaller dishes run from a 12 V
  vehicle socket with an adapter, or from a power station. Run it in scheduled windows to stretch
  the battery.
- **Security:** a dish in the yard is visible and it transmits (→ 14-03).
- **The day it is activated:** turn on **Wi-Fi Calling** on every phone, join the dish's Wi-Fi,
  and test a voice call and a text **with cellular switched off**. That test is what proves it
  is a channel.

Ours: ☐ none ☐ messenger ☐ satellite internet. Plan ______ activated ______ Wi-Fi calling on
every phone ☐ tested ☐

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GMRS handhelds and a GMRS licence** | Family coordination; no exam; covers the household | Removable antennas; spare batteries |
| **Amateur Technician licence and a dual-band handheld** | The path to real capability | → 15-05 |
| **Scanner or wideband receiver** | Listen without transmitting | Legal, invisible, high value |
| Better antennas for everything | The antenna matters more than the radio | → 15-06 |
| AA battery trays for handhelds | Charge or feed them from anything | Often sold separately |
| Spare batteries, chargers, programming cable | The parts that fail or get lost | Buy while available |
| 12 V leads and fuses for base radios | Run straight off a battery bank | → 09-08 |
| CB (mobile or handheld) and a real antenna | Road information on the move | The antenna is the whole game |
| Hand-crank radio | Works with no power | → 09-11, → 15-01 |
| **A written family channel plan** | Everyone knows where to meet on the air | → 15-03, → 25-08 |
| Printed operating notes and licence details | Paper survives dead batteries | This binder |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Radios** turn up in vehicles, boats, businesses, marine sets and old scanners. **Vehicle radios
  receive AM and FM, and many receive the weather band.**
- **Antennas** are the best improvisation: wire, coaxial cable and a little knowledge make good
  ones (→ 15-06).
- **Power:** a battery bank, AA trays, a vehicle battery.
- **What you cannot scavenge is a licence and the skill.** Both take time and can only be got now
  (→ 15-05).

## When it runs out

- **Batteries are the consumable** (→ 09-07). Radios are a small load, so with solar and
  rechargeables this lasts a long time.
- **Hardware is what fails:** antennas break, connectors corrode, handhelds get dropped, battery
  packs die. **Stock spare antennas, cable, connectors and battery trays.**
- **Think about which capability you lose first.** Handhelds with proprietary packs go first;
  radios that take AA cells and run on 12 V last much longer. Buy accordingly.
- **Step down in order:** amateur, GMRS, FRS, then **signals without radio** (→ 15-07): whistles,
  mirrors, lights, flags, pre-agreed signals, and walking over to a neighbour (→ 18-01).
- **Knowledge does not run out.** Someone who understands antennas, propagation and 12 V power can
  keep communications going from salvage for a very long time (→ 15-05, → 15-06).

## By phase

- **A (at home):** GMRS for the household and the block, a scanner for awareness, the weather
  radio (→ 15-01), and amateur radio for regional news if someone is licensed. **Listen more than
  you transmit** (→ 14-03).
- **B (on the move):** GMRS handhelds keep the group together (this is where they earn their
  keep), CB for road information if driving, and great care about what you say on the air
  (→ 01-03, → 15-09).
- **C (rural or a new place):** distance becomes the problem and **amateur radio becomes the
  answer** (→ 15-05). At a rural site you can put up real antennas, so this is one capability that
  gets better (→ 15-06).

pages.body:
# Family communications plan: contacts, rally points, relay and cards

**What this page is for.** The situation this page exists for: **the household is separated when
something happens.** One adult at work and one at home; separated during a move; someone goes
for water and does not come back on time. This page is the plan: who to contact, where to meet,
how long to wait, how to leave notes, which channels to try in which order, and the cards that
let a stranger care for someone who cannot speak for themselves. It follows FEMA's family
communication plan approach (FEMA, Create Your Family Emergency Communication Plan).

> **CAUTION.** **Write the plan down, give copies to everyone, practise it once.** A plan that
> lives in one adult's head is not a plan. {{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**In your household,
> separation is also a medical problem:** someone has a severe allergy, and anyone who might end
> up caring for them needs the allergen list and the epinephrine plan on paper, in advance
> (→ 02-03).{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}} Someone depends on refrigerated medicine, which
> has to travel with them (→ 01-07).{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Fill in the one-page plan below**, print it, and put a copy in every wallet, every go-bag,
   the vehicle and this binder. Give one to the out-of-area contact.
2. **Make a medical card for everyone who needs one**: conditions, allergies, medicines, what to
   do, contacts. Laminate them. A stranger or neighbour may be the one reading it (→ 25-09).
3. **Agree an out-of-area contact.** In a regional emergency, local phone lines jam while
   long-distance calls and texts sometimes still get through. One relative or friend in another
   area whom everyone checks in with turns a scattered family into a connected one. FEMA's
   advice is the same: pick someone out of town, who may be easier to reach in a disaster.
4. **Teach every child old enough** their full name, their parents' names, the rally point,
   and any allergy, as a game (→ 20-04).
5. **Agree the rally points and wait times out loud**, every adult.

## The plan on one page

**Contacts**

| | Name | Phone | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Out-of-area contact (the relay) | {{ contacts.out_of_area.name }} | {{ contacts.out_of_area.phone }} | Everyone checks in here |
{{#each local_contacts as c}}| {{c.relationship}} | {{c.name}} | {{c.phone}} | {{c.notes}} |
{{/each}}| Clinician or pharmacy | ______________ | ______________ | Copy from → 25-03 |
| School or daycare | ______________ | ______________ | Write their release and reunification procedure (→ 00-04) |

**Rally points**

| | Place | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | Home | The default. Everyone comes home |
| **Secondary, near home** | {{ contacts.meet.near_home }} | If the house is unsafe or cannot be reached. Ask the people there first |
| **Out of the neighbourhood** | {{ contacts.meet.in_town }} | If the area is unsafe. Somewhere everyone can name |
| **Out of town** | {{ contacts.meet.out_of_town }} | Leaving the area (→ 01-03) |

**Wait times** (the household decides; write them in pen and initial):

- Separated in town: each of us goes to the primary rally point and waits ______ hours.
- If nobody comes, go to the secondary point and leave a note (below). Wait ______ hours.
- **Check in with the out-of-area contact** whenever you can, from wherever you are, using the
  relay script below.
- If we cannot reconnect within ______ hours, we: ____________________________________________
  ______________________________________________________________________________
- **Medical override.** If the missing person depends on a medicine, device or supply that they
  carry on their body, waiting uses up **their** supply, not yours. For them, shorten every wait
  above (our shortened times: ______), treat the search as a medical search from the start, and
  tell every contact and responder what the condition is (→ 12-11). The same applies if someone
  with a severe allergy is with the missing party and the epinephrine is with them.

## The note protocol: the low-tech thing that works

- **A pre-agreed hidden spot at each rally point** where notes are left. **Not on the door**: that
  tells everyone the house is empty (→ 14-03). Under a particular rock, inside a particular
  container, taped inside a particular place.
- **The note says:** who was here, the date and time, where they went, and when they expect to be
  back or where to follow. **Nothing about supplies, weapons or the household's situation.**
- **Everyone knows the spot, and everyone checks it.** Keep the spots off any list a stranger
  could read.

## Medical and identity cards

One card per person who could not explain their own needs to a stranger: every child, and every
adult with a condition, allergy or medicine that matters in an emergency. The household's
members, as entered in settings:

{{#each members as m}}- **{{m.label}}** ({{m.age_text}}). Conditions: {{m.conditions}}. Allergies:
  {{m.allergies}}. Medicines: {{m.meds}}.
{{/each}}

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Severe allergies in your household:**
{{#each allergies as a}}- {{a.member}}: **{{a.allergen}}** ({{a.severity}}). Carries epinephrine:
  {{a.carries_epinephrine}}.
{{/each}}{{/if}}

Each card carries:

- Full name, age, parents' or carers' names and phone numbers, the out-of-area contact.
- **Conditions and what an emergency looks like**, in plain words. For conditions that can look
  like drunkenness or confusion, such as low blood sugar, say so: it is what a bystander most
  needs to know (→ 12-11, and the person's own condition page in Section 02).
- **Allergies, and the severe ones in capitals**, with where the epinephrine is and how to use it
  (→ 02-03). For a child with a food allergy: **"Must not eat any food that an adult who knows this
  list has not approved"** (→ 02-04).
- Medicines (name and strength as on the bottle), and the clinician.
- For an infant or toddler: feeding needs (→ 20-05).

**Put the cards on the children**: a jacket pocket, a bracelet, a backpack, not only in an
adult's wallet.

## Channels, in the order they survive

1. **Text messages.** They use far less network capacity than calls and often get through when
   calls do not, and they leave the lines open for emergency workers. **Text first** (FEMA,
   Ready.gov Make a Plan). Three things few people know:
   - **911 connects from any phone on any carrier's tower**, even with no service plan: carriers
     must pass on every wireless 911 call (47 CFR 9.10). Call it rather than texting:
     text-to-911 works only where the local 911 centre accepts it. Ours: ☐ yes ☐ no ☐ unknown.
   - **A phone searching for a signal all day is flat by evening.** Use airplane mode between
     attempts (→ 15-09).
   - **Wi-Fi calling and app messaging work over any internet connection**, including a
     neighbour's or a satellite dish. Turn Wi-Fi calling on in each phone's settings now.
2. **The out-of-area contact.** Local lines jam; long distance sometimes does not.
3. **Satellite texting from the phone itself.** Some phones (for example iPhone 14 and later) can
   send an emergency SOS text with your location, and newer software can send ordinary texts, by
   satellite when there are no bars at all: clear sky, phone held up, follow the on-screen pointer
   (Apple Support, Emergency SOS via satellite). **Try the demo now** if your phone has it. A
   dedicated satellite messenger does the same job, **but only with a paid subscription.**
   Our phones with satellite texting: ______________________
4. **Satellite internet**, if the household has it and it is activated (→ 15-02). An inactive dish
   is not a channel.
5. **Radio** (→ 15-02): GMRS for local coordination, on a pre-agreed channel and schedule (below).
6. **Notes at the rally points.** The one that always works.
7. **Walking there** (→ 18-01). In a neighbourhood this is often the fastest and most reliable,
   and people forget it.
8. **Visual and sound signals** (→ 15-07): whistles, lights, a cloth in a window.

## The relay card: print it, and give the contact a copy

The out-of-area contact ({{ contacts.out_of_area.name }}) is the **switchboard**: in a crisis,
everyone reports to them, and they pass messages between family members{{#if has.destinations}}
and destinations (→ 15-08){{/if}} who cannot reach each other directly.

**The script: every call, text or relayed message uses these four lines, in this order:**

1. **WHO** is calling (name, and who is with them)
2. **STATUS**, one word: **OK / NEED HELP / MOVING**
3. **WHERE** (as specific as is safe to say, → 14-03)
4. **NEXT CHECK-IN**: when this person will report again

**The schedule** (the same words everywhere it is printed: → 00-04, → 15-08, → 25-08):
daily check-in with the relay at ______ (time and time zone); if missed, at ______ the next
morning; we treat someone as **overdue** after ______ missed check-ins in a row (what happens
then: → 15-08).

**On the relay's copy:** *"When anyone asks, pass on the latest WHO, STATUS, WHERE and NEXT
CHECK-IN you have for the others."*

Briefed (date) ____________ Agreed (date) ____________. A relay who has not heard the plan out
loud is a phone number, not a relay.

## The household channel ladder

P = try first, A = alternate, C = contingency, E = emergency or last resort. Fill it in; keep the
words short enough to copy onto a wallet card (→ 25-08).

| Situation | P | A | C | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Separated in town** | Text, then call | Out-of-area relay | GMRS channel ____, at the agreed times | Rally points and notes; walk there |
| **Regional outage** | Text; Wi-Fi calling over any working internet | Relay at the agreed time | Satellite text; GMRS or amateur radio (→ 15-05) | Notes at rally points; neighbours; signals (→ 15-07) |
| **On the road** | Text from named check-in towns (→ 15-09) | Another adult's phone on a different carrier | GMRS; CB channel 19 (road) and 9 (emergency); satellite SOS | Weather radio for news only; stop and wait (→ 15-09) |
| **At a destination** | Call or text home and the relay | The destination household's phones | Satellite text; GMRS at the agreed time (→ 15-08) | Relay; letters; travellers |

## The radio plan: pre-agreed

Radios only help if people listen at the same time.

- **Primary channel:** ______ **Backup channel or repeater:** ______ (→ 15-02). Use no "privacy
  code" for the family channel unless every radio is set the same: codes filter what you hear,
  they hide nothing.
- {{#if has.ham}}**Amateur frequencies** for the licensed members: ______ (→ 15-05).{{else}}If
  someone becomes licensed, add amateur frequencies here (→ 15-05).{{/if}}
- **Listening times:** for example five minutes on the hour: ______. **Listening all the time
  drains batteries and exposes you** (→ 14-03); set times do neither. (The weather radio is the
  exception: it stays on, → 15-01.)
- **Short and bland on the air.** Names and places only as needed; nothing about what you have
  (→ 15-07).

## Teaching the children

{{#if has.child}}You have children in the household.{{/if}}

- **A preschooler can learn** their full name, their parents' full names, the rally point, "I have
  allergies" if they do, and **"find a grown-up with a badge, or a grown-up with children"**.
  Practise it as a game, often, without making it frightening (→ 20-04, → 20-08).
- **They carry their card and know they have it.**
- **Babies and toddlers cannot do any of this**, so their identification and feeding information
  have to be **on them**.
- **Every child knows where the go-bags are**, and that one belongs to them.

## Practise it once

**Run one drill** (→ 24-02): "We're separated. What does everyone do?" Walk to the rally point.
Check the note spot. Try the radios. **You will find three things wrong with the plan, which is
the point.**

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **The printed plan, many copies** | Wallets, go-bags, vehicle, binder, relay | Update yearly (→ 25-10) |
| **Laminated medical and ID cards** | A stranger may be reading it | → 25-09 |
| Medical ID bracelets or tags for children and anyone with a condition | Works when the card is lost | Cheap; truly valuable |
| GMRS radios on the agreed channel | Local coordination | → 15-02 |
| A whistle for every person, children included | Carries farther than a voice; no power | → 15-07 |
| Paper, pencil, waterproof bags | The note protocol | Pencil works wet and cold |
| A printed local map with rally points marked | Phones die | → 25-04 |
| The relay's number, **memorised and written** | The one number everyone should know | |
| A small flashlight per person | Signalling and safety | → 10-01 |
| A phone with satellite texting, or a messenger with a subscription | Reaches the relay with no bars | Try the demo; note which phones have it |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Notes and markers:** chalk, pencil, tape, scratched into a surface, or a pre-agreed object
  moved to a pre-agreed place. A signal that is not writing is harder for others to read (→ 15-07).
- **Identification for children:** name and details on a card in a pocket, written inside a
  jacket, or written on the child's skin with a marker (a real practice in disaster response).
- **Signalling:** whistle, mirror, flashlight, a bright cloth in a particular window (→ 15-07).
- **Messages:** neighbours (→ 18-01). Where people know each other, word travels faster than any
  technology.

## When it runs out

- **The materials barely wear out**; what goes wrong is the plan's accuracy. Numbers change,
  children grow, rally points stop making sense, medical details change. **Review it every year**
  (→ 25-10) and after any change in anyone's health.
- **The phone network is what runs out**, usually early. **Everything after "text messages" on the
  channel list is designed to survive that**, which is why the notes and rally points matter more
  than the technology.
- **Being reunited quickly is worth more than almost any supply in this binder**, above all when
  someone's medicine, device or allergy plan is carried by a different person.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** phones while they work; radios, rally points and notes when they do not.
  **Neighbours are part of the plan** (→ 18-01): a neighbour who knows your children and their
  needs is a real safety asset.
- **B (on the move):** **the plan is most likely to be needed and hardest to follow here.**
  Everyone carries their card and whistle, everyone knows the next rally point before you set off,
  and **nobody goes ahead out of sight with a child** (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or a new place):** distances are longer and neighbours farther away, so **radio
  matters more** (→ 15-05, → 15-06). Set new rally points and note spots **on arrival**, and teach
  the children the new plan: their old one is now wrong.

pages.body:
# Monitoring the news, scanning, and judging what you hear

**What this page is for.** Listening is the most valuable and least risky thing a radio does. It
costs a little power, it is legal, and unlike transmitting, **it tells nobody you exist**
(→ 14-03). But in a crisis most of what circulates is wrong, exaggerated or out of date, and
constant bad news wears down a household's morale and judgement (→ 21-01, → 21-02). This page is
as much about **filtering and rationing** information as gathering it.

## Do this now

1. **Buy a scanner or a wideband receiver** and learn it before you need it (check first what is
   still listenable in your area; below).
2. **Buy a portable radio with shortwave.** When local sources go dark, shortwave still carries
   regional and world broadcasts, and it needs only batteries and a wire antenna.
3. **Fill in the frequency table below** while the internet still exists. **You will not be able
   to look these up later** (→ 25-03, → 25-08).
4. **Set an information routine now**: twice a day, at set times, for a fixed period. A habit set
   early is what keeps listening from becoming compulsive later.

## The layers, and how they fail

| Layer | What it gives you | How it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **NOAA Weather Radio** | Weather warnings, straight from the NWS (→ 15-01) | Usually among the last to go, but a transmitter can go off the air |
| **Local AM and FM** | Local conditions, official information | Stations run on generators for a while, then fade |
| **AM at night** | Distant stations: AM carries far after dark | Very durable; often the last broadcast standing |
| **Shortwave** | Regional and world broadcasts | **Least dependent on local infrastructure**; no licence to listen |
| **Scanner (public services)** | What is happening locally, right now | Many systems are digital, some encrypted; may go quiet |
| **Amateur bands** | **People on the ground, talking**: often the best real information (→ 15-05) | You need to know where to listen |
| **Internet and cell** | Everything, while it lasts | **Fails first, and early** |

**What to expect:** internet and cell go first; local broadcast lasts a while; **the weather
radio, AM at night, shortwave and amateur radio are what remain**, roughly in that order.

## What a scanner is really for

A scanner tells you what is happening **near you, now**: emergency responses, road closures,
where the problems are. That matters for the decision to stay or go (→ 01-02) and for awareness
(→ 14-01).

**Know before you buy:**

- **Many public-safety systems are digital and "trunked"** (shared among many users by computer).
  Hearing them needs a scanner made for that; an old analogue scanner may hear nothing useful.
- **Many police agencies now encrypt their radio traffic.** Encrypted traffic cannot be heard, and
  trying to decrypt it is unlawful. **No scanner hears it, and no plan should depend on it.** Fire,
  ambulance and state agencies vary: some talk groups stay open.
- **Amateur, marine and aviation bands are open** and are often more informative in a wide-area
  event.
- **The decision:** buy a digital scanner **only if** you have confirmed that local fire, EMS or
  state talk groups are still unencrypted. Otherwise a cheap analogue or wideband receiver covers
  everything else on this page. Our decision and date: ______________________

## The monitoring table (fill it in while the internet exists)

| What | Frequency or channel | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NOAA Weather Radio, home transmitter | {{#each region.home.nwr as t}}{{t.call}} {{t.freq}} MHz; {{/each}} | → 15-01 |
| Local police and sheriff | ____________ | Encrypted? ☐ yes ☐ no |
| Fire and EMS dispatch | ____________ | Digital? Encrypted? Check |
| State police and state agencies | ____________ | Some talk groups may be open |
| Amateur 2-metre: main local repeater | ____________ | → 15-05 |
| Amateur simplex calling frequencies | **146.520 MHz** (2 m), **446.000 MHz** (70 cm) | National calling channels |
| AM stations that carry far at night | ____________ | Many keep newsrooms on generator power |
| FM local news | ____________ | |
| Aviation emergency frequency | **121.5 MHz** (AM mode) | Emergencies and distress beacons; listen only, never transmit |
| Family GMRS channel and repeater | ____________ | → 15-02, → 15-03 |

Scanner: ☐ owned, model ____________ ☐ not owned.

## Amateur radio as a news source, even unlicensed

**You do not need a licence to listen.** In regional emergencies, amateur operators run
**organised emergency nets**: scheduled, disciplined traffic about real conditions on the ground
(ARRL, What is Ham Radio?). That is often the best information available in a disaster, and
listening is free. Learn where the local repeaters and nets are **now** and write them in the
table (→ 15-05).

## Judging what you hear: the part that matters most

In a crisis, information quality collapses. Ask:

- **Who is saying it, and how do they know?** "I can see the bridge is out" beats "someone said
  the bridge is out" by a huge margin.
- **When did it happen?** Crisis information goes stale in hours.
- **Is it specific?** "The road is flooded at the river crossing this morning" is usable; "the
  roads are bad" is not.
- **Do independent sources repeat it**, or is it one rumour going in circles?
- **Rumours travel faster and farther than facts**, and grow as they travel.
- **Be wary of news that is exactly what you feared, or exactly what you hoped.** Those are the
  stories people pass on without checking.
- **Write down what you hear, with the time and the source** (→ 25-05). Over days, patterns
  appear and rumours fall apart on their own.

## Rationing information

This is not a soft point. In a long crisis:

- **Constant bad news raises anxiety, spoils sleep and worsens decisions** (→ 21-01, → 21-07). It
  also drains batteries.
- **Set fixed listening times**, twice a day, for a set period. **Then turn it off and do the
  day's work.**
- **One adult listens and briefs the others**, rather than everyone soaking in it.
- **Children should not listen to disaster coverage.** {{#if has.young_child}}Young children
  absorb far more than adults think and have no way to make sense of it (→ 20-08).{{else}}Young
  children absorb far more than adults think (→ 20-08).{{/if}}
- **The information you need is usually small:** is the weather dangerous, are the roads passable,
  is help coming, has anything changed near us? A five-minute question, not an all-day one.

## Security

- **Listening is invisible.** Nobody can tell you are listening. That is the whole advantage
  (→ 14-03).
- **Do not repeat on the air what you hear**, and do not confirm details about your own situation.
- **A scanner heard from outside** at night breaks noise discipline (→ 10-05). Use an earpiece.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Scanner** (digital only if it helps where you live) | Local awareness, invisibly | Check what your area's systems need |
| **Portable radio with shortwave** | Survives when local infrastructure does not | Battery or crank; a wire antenna helps a lot |
| AM/FM portable radio | Local official news; AM carries far at night | Cheap, durable |
| NOAA Weather Radio | The alert layer | → 15-01 |
| Earpiece or headphones | Quiet; saves battery | → 10-05 |
| **A written frequency list for your area** | You cannot look it up later | → 25-03, → 25-08 |
| Wire, cable and connectors for receiving antennas | A long wire greatly improves shortwave | → 15-06 |
| Notebook and pencil for an information log | Patterns appear; rumours collapse | → 25-05 |
| Rechargeable AA and AAA cells and a charger | Listening is a small, steady load | → 09-07 |
| Hand-crank radio | Works with no power | → 09-11 |

**If you do not have it:**

- **A vehicle radio** gets AM and FM, and many get the weather band. A car is a listening post
  that runs a long time on its own battery.
- **Old scanners, marine radios, aviation receivers, amateur handhelds**: many receive far more
  than they transmit.
- **A long wire strung outside** is the biggest single improvement to any shortwave receiver
  (→ 15-06). Free.
- **Neighbours** (→ 18-01): someone on the block has a scanner, a licence or a working radio.
  Sharing information is one of the easiest kinds of mutual aid.
- **Your own eyes:** smoke, traffic, aircraft, whether streetlights are on, whether anyone is
  ploughing. What you see yourself is the best information there is (→ 14-01).

## When it runs out

- **Batteries are the only real consumable**, and listening is a small load (→ 09-01). Set
  listening times cut it to almost nothing.
- **What fades is the information itself**, in roughly this order: internet, cell, local
  broadcast, scanner traffic, weather radio, then shortwave and amateur radio. **Plan for the last
  two to be what you have**, and set up to receive them (→ 15-06).
- **In a long event the most reliable information becomes local and first-hand**: what you see,
  and what someone who was there tells you face to face (→ 18-01).
- **The failure to avoid is acting on a rumour**: leaving, trading away supplies, confronting a
  neighbour. **Write it down, wait for confirmation where you can, and prefer what you have seen
  yourself** (→ 01-02, → 14-01).

## By phase

- **A (at home):** the full set works. **Set the routine and the discipline now.** This is also
  when information most affects the stay-or-go decision (→ 01-02).
- **B (on the move):** the vehicle radio, a handheld scanner, and CB for road information
  (→ 15-02). **Route information is what you need**: closures, conditions, where people are
  gathering.
- **C (rural or a new place):** farther from local broadcast, but **far better for receiving**:
  space and height for real antennas (→ 15-06), less electrical noise. A rural site with a good
  wire antenna is a better listening post than a house in town.

pages.body:
# Amateur (ham) radio: licensing and getting started now

**What this page is for.** Amateur radio ("ham" radio) is the only communications option in
this binder with real reach, beyond line of sight and across a region or the country, **without
any infrastructure at all**. It is also where the knowledge lives: antennas, propagation, 12 V
power and repair (→ 15-06, → 09-08). This is a "do it this month" page: the licence, the skills
and the local network of people are all available now, cheaply, and not later.

> **Before the collapse:** transmitting on amateur bands requires an FCC licence while the FCC
> operates (47 CFR Part 97). The entry-level **Technician** exam is one written test of 35
> questions and needs **no Morse code** (47 CFR 97.501, 97.503; ARRL, Getting Licensed). Licences
> run for ten years (47 CFR 97.25) and expire quietly:
> write the expiry date down and renew in good time; an FCC fee may apply, so check the current
> fee when you apply. Part 97 also says nothing in its rules stops an amateur station using any
> means at its disposal for essential communication about the immediate safety of life when
> normal communications are down, or a station in distress from using any means to get help
> (47 CFR 97.403, 97.405). **Listening needs no licence at all.**

## Do this now

1. **Study for and take the Technician exam.** A few evenings of study, one test session, one fee.
   **The single most valuable action in this section.** Having more than one licensed adult means
   one person is not a single point of failure.
2. **Find the local amateur radio club and its nets** (scheduled on-air meetings). In an
   emergency these are the people on the air with real information, and being known to them
   beforehand matters (→ 18-01).
3. **Buy a dual-band handheld** (inexpensive) and **use it**: talk through the local repeaters,
   check into a net, get comfortable.
4. **Write the local repeaters into the table below** and check them by listening. Repeaters come
   and go.
5. **Then consider General.** Technician covers local and regional work; **General opens most of
   the HF bands, where long-distance capability lives.**

## Your licences

{{#if has.ham}}Your profile lists a ham radio or a licensed member.{{else}}Your profile lists no
licensed member yet.{{/if}}

| Person | Class | Call sign | Expires | Renewal on calendar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ______________ | ________ | ________ | ________ | ☐ |
| ______________ | ________ | ________ | ________ | ☐ |

Next exam: who ______________ target date ____________

## Local repeaters and frequencies (fill in and check by listening)

| Output (MHz) | Offset | Tone | Call sign | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ________ | ________ | ________ | ________ | Main 2-metre repeater: program this first |
| ________ | ________ | ________ | ________ | |
| ________ | ________ | ________ | ________ | |
| ________ | ________ | ________ | ________ | |

**National simplex calling frequencies** (radio to radio, no repeater): **146.520 MHz** (2 m) and
**446.000 MHz** (70 cm).

Local nets (name, day, time, frequency): __________________________________________________

Copy these into → 25-03 and → 25-08. You cannot look them up later.

## Why this matters more than any radio purchase

When cell networks, the internet and commercial broadcast all fail, **amateur radio keeps
working**, because it needs only a transmitter, an antenna and power, all of which a household can
supply (→ 09-02). In real disasters, amateur operators often provide the last working links,
running organised emergency nets and passing "health and welfare" messages (ARRL, What is Ham
Radio?).

**Three things you get:**

1. **Reach.** VHF and UHF (very and ultra high frequency) through repeaters cover a region; **HF
   (high frequency) covers hundreds to thousands of miles with no infrastructure at all.**
2. **Information.** Organised nets carry structured, first-hand reports (→ 15-04).
3. **Knowledge and people.** Antennas, propagation, power and repair, plus a local community of
   technically capable people who help each other (→ 18-01, → 18-03).

## The licence classes

| Class | What it opens | Exam |
|---|---|---|
| **Technician** | All amateur privileges above 30 MHz (VHF and UHF, local and regional repeaters), plus limited HF | Entry level, no code |
| **General** | **Most HF privileges**: long distance | A moderate step up |
| **Amateur Extra** | Full privileges | Hardest; not needed for anything in this binder |

Details: ARRL, Amateur Radio Licenses; the current Part 97 is the authority. **Technician now,
then General.**

## What you would use it for

- **Regional awareness**: nets during a blizzard, an ice storm, a flood or a wider emergency. The
  main one (→ 15-04).
- **Reaching family or contacts outside the region** when nothing else works (→ 15-03).
- **Keeping in touch with a rural site** at a distance no other service covers (→ 01-04).
- **Being useful to a wider community**: an amateur station in a neighbourhood is a real
  contribution (→ 18-01).
- **Listening**, which is legal unlicensed and often the point (→ 15-04).

## Equipment, in a sensible order

1. **A dual-band VHF/UHF handheld.** Inexpensive, works on local repeaters. **Buy a better antenna
   for it at once**: the supplied antennas are poor (→ 15-06).
2. **A better antenna**: a roll-up J-pole or a magnetic-mount antenna on the vehicle transforms a
   handheld.
3. **A mobile or base VHF/UHF radio** on **12 V** from a battery bank (→ 09-08): more power, a
   better receiver.
4. **An HF radio (with General)** and a **wire antenna** (→ 15-06). A wire dipole in a tree and a
   100-watt radio reach remarkably far.
5. **Power:** 12 V direct from a solar battery bank, no inverter (→ 09-08). Radios are an ideal
   solar load: modest, DC-native and used in short spells.
6. **Spares:** coaxial cable, connectors, wire, fuses, a spare handheld (→ 15-06).

## The skills that outlast the equipment

- **Antennas**: how they work, how to build one from wire, why height matters (→ 15-06).
- **Propagation**: why the same radio reaches 5 miles at noon and 500 at night.
- **12 V power and wiring**, directly useful for the power section (→ 09-08).
- **Repair and improvisation**: amateurs fix and build things, which a long emergency rewards.
- **Operating discipline**: passing accurate information, briefly, under pressure. Useful even off
  the air.

## How to operate

- **Identify with your call sign.** It is how nets know who is talking, and it gets you answered.
- **Plain language, no codes or encryption.** That is what a net can relay, and Part 97 requires
  it while it is enforced.
- **Skill and courtesy matter.** Amateur radio is a community with norms; a competent, known
  operator is the one who gets help in a crisis.
- **Every transmission is an announcement** (→ 14-03). Whether to transmit is a security
  decision, not only a rules question.

## Security

**Amateur transmissions are unencrypted by law, and a call sign is publicly linked to the licence
address.** For a household that values discretion that is a real consideration (→ 14-03). What
helps: **listen far more than you transmit**, keep transmissions practical and bland, and be
deliberate about what you say about your household. **A post office box as the licence mailing
address is a legitimate and common choice.**

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Technician licence, for more than one adult** | The point of this page | Free study material; one exam |
| **General licence** | HF: real distance | The next step |
| Dual-band VHF/UHF handhelds | Immediate capability; local repeaters | Inexpensive |
| **A real antenna for each handheld** | The supplied one is poor | Roll-up J-pole, magnetic mount |
| Mobile or base VHF/UHF radio, 12 V leads and fuse | More power, better receiver, solar-friendly | → 09-08 |
| HF radio and a wire dipole (after General) | Long distance | → 15-06 |
| Coax, connectors, wire, antenna tuner | Building and repairing | Stock spares |
| **The local repeater and net list, written** | You cannot look it up later | → 25-03, → 25-08 |
| A licence manual and study guide on paper | Study now, reference later | Physical copies |
| SWR meter or antenna analyser | Diagnoses antennas; protects the radio | Truly useful |
| Club membership | The people are the resource | → 18-01 |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Radios** from estate sales, swap meets ("hamfests"), clubs and other operators. The used
  amateur market is large and cheap, and older gear is often easier to repair.
- **Antennas**: wire, coax and knowledge build excellent antennas for almost nothing (→ 15-06).
- **Power:** a battery bank, a vehicle battery or a small solar panel (→ 09-02).
- **Knowledge:** free study material and a local club full of people who will teach you.
- **What you cannot scavenge is the licence and the practice.** Both take time, and only now
  works.

## When it runs out

- **Little here runs out.** Radios last decades, antennas are wire, and 12 V power comes from
  solar (→ 09-02).
- **What fails:** connectors corrode, cable degrades in sun, antennas come down in ice storms,
  handhelds get dropped. **Stock cable, connectors, wire and a spare radio.**
- **Power is the consumable, and it is small** (→ 09-01).
- **Knowledge gains value over time.** Someone who understands antennas and DC power can keep a
  station running from salvage and **build one for someone else** (→ 18-03).
- **The network of people fades if you are not part of it.** In an emergency you do not want to
  be a stranger with a radio; you want to be someone the local operators know.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** get licensed, get on the local repeaters, join a net, learn the frequencies,
  and **be known before anything happens.** In town a handheld and a modest antenna cover a lot.
- **B (on the move):** the handheld travels; a magnetic-mount antenna on the vehicle makes it far
  more useful (→ 15-09).
- **C (rural or a new place):** **this is where amateur radio becomes essential and works best**:
  real distances, and space and height for proper antennas (→ 15-06). A wire dipole between two
  trees and a 12 V solar bank make a capable long-distance station, which may be the household's
  only link to the wider world.

pages.body:
# Antennas, range and realistic expectations

**What this page is for.** How far radios really reach, why the antenna matters more than the
radio, how to build a working antenna from wire, and how to put one up without being killed by a
power line, a fall or lightning. Radio words are explained on → 29-09.

> **CAUTION. Three ways antenna work hurts people.**
> **(1) Power lines.** **Never put up an antenna, mast or wire where it could touch or fall onto a
> power line.** This kills people every year. Treat every line as live, keep the full length of
> the mast plus a wide margin away, and have a second person present.
> **(2) Falls.** Roof and ladder work, especially in ice or wind, is one of the likeliest serious
> injuries in this binder (→ 12-09). **Do antenna work in good weather, with help.**
> **(3) Lightning.** An outdoor antenna is a path for lightning into the house. **Ground the
> system and disconnect the cable when storms threaten.** A strike can destroy every radio you own
> and start a fire.

## Do this now

1. **Reset your expectations before spending money.** Range numbers on packaging are
   mountaintop figures. Typical numbers are in the table below.
2. **Buy a better antenna for every handheld.** The cheapest, biggest single improvement.
3. **Buy coaxial cable ("coax"), connectors and wire now.** Cheap, they do not expire, and they
   are the raw material for every antenna you will ever improvise.
4. **Put up one antenna and use it**, so you learn while it is a hobby and not an emergency.
5. **Test your own range** (below) and write it down.

## The one thing to understand: height beats power

For VHF and UHF radios (handhelds, FRS, GMRS, repeaters), **communication is essentially line of
sight**:

- **Doubling the power buys very little range.**
- **Raising the antenna buys a great deal.**
- **Hills, buildings and trees block signals**; height gets over them.

**A 5-watt handheld with a good antenna up high beats a 50-watt radio with a stubby antenna at
ground level.** That is why money and effort belong in the antenna.

{{figure fig-line-of-sight-and-repeater}}

## Typical ranges

These are typical figures for planning, not measurements or promises: terrain, buildings, trees,
weather and the antenna decide the real number, which is why you test your own (below).

| Setup | Typical range |
|---|---|
| **FRS handheld, in town, at ground level** | **A few hundred yards to about a mile** |
| FRS or GMRS handheld, open flat country | 1 to 3 miles |
| **GMRS handheld with a good antenna** | 2 to 5 miles |
| GMRS mobile with a roof antenna | 5 to 15 miles |
| **GMRS or amateur through a repeater** | **20 to 50 miles or more**: the repeater's height does the work |
| Amateur VHF/UHF radio to radio, good antennas, both raised | 10 to 30 miles |
| **CB with a proper (long) antenna** | 1 to 5 miles typical; sometimes very far when conditions allow |
| **Amateur HF with a wire dipole** | **Hundreds to thousands of miles**, varying with band, time of day and conditions |

**What the table shows:** handhelds are a **household and neighbourhood** tool. **Real distance
comes from repeaters (someone else's height) or from HF, which does not depend on line of
sight.**

**Flat country helps; buildings, trees and being indoors cut range hard.** Test your real range:
one person walks or drives away calling every block until contact is lost, from inside the house
and from outside. Write it down:

| Radio and antenna | From | Range reached |
|---|---|---|
| ______________ | inside the house | ______ |
| ______________ | outside | ______ |
| ______________ | through the repeater | ______ |

## Antennas, worst to best

1. **The stubby "rubber duck"** supplied on a handheld: a poor compromise.
2. **A longer whip**: a real improvement for a few dollars.
3. **A roll-up J-pole or slim-jim** (a flexible wire antenna) hung in a tree or from a curtain
   rod: cheap, packable, dramatically better. **For a handheld, the best value in this section.**
4. **A magnetic-mount antenna on a vehicle roof**: the metal roof and the height help a lot.
5. **A permanent outdoor vertical**, as high as can be safely put up.
6. **For HF: a wire dipole**: two lengths of wire and a centre feed point. Cheap, effective, and
   buildable from salvage (→ 15-05).

## Coax and connectors: the quiet failure

- **Coax loses signal**, more with length and frequency. A long run of cheap coax to a UHF antenna
  can throw away most of your signal.
- **Keep runs short**, use decent coax, and **do not coil the spare tightly.**
- **Water is the enemy.** Water in coax ruins it. **Seal every outdoor connector** with
  self-amalgamating tape, then electrical tape over it.
- **Sunlight destroys cheap coax jackets** within a few years. Check them.
- **Corroded connectors are a common, invisible cause of "my radio stopped working".** Inspect
  them every season, and **stock spare connectors and a crimper.**

## Building an antenna from wire

This works, and it is satisfying.

- **A dipole is two pieces of wire**, each a quarter of a wavelength long, fed in the middle by the
  coax. **The formula is one line:**
  **each leg (feet) = 234 ÷ frequency (MHz); whole dipole (feet) = 468 ÷ frequency (MHz)**
  (ARRL, Single Band Dipoles). Cut each leg a little long, hang it, and trim both ends equally
  until an SWR meter (which measures how well the antenna matches the radio) reads lowest. If the
  SWR falls as you tune lower in frequency, the antenna is still too long; if it rises, it is too
  short and needs wire added to both ends (ARRL). Worked out for common
  frequencies:

  | Use | Frequency | Each leg | Whole dipole |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Amateur 2-metre calling | 146.520 MHz | **19.2 in** | 38.3 in |
  | NOAA Weather Radio (receive) | 162.400 MHz | **17.3 in** | 34.6 in |
  | GMRS channel 15 | 462.550 MHz | **6.1 in** | 12.1 in |
  | CB channel 19 | 27.185 MHz | **8.6 ft** | 17.2 ft |
  | Amateur 40 metres (General licence) | 7.200 MHz | **32.5 ft** | 65.0 ft |

  For your own family channel or repeater: 234 ÷ ______ MHz = ______ ft each leg.

{{figure fig-wire-dipole}}

- **A ground-plane vertical** is one quarter-wave wire pointing up, over **several
  quarter-wave "radial" wires** (four is common) laid flat or drooping. **A replacement for a broken GMRS handheld
  antenna is the 6-inch quarter wave above, not "longer is better".** A random long wire is fine
  for *receiving* shortwave and broadcast; for *transmitting*, cut it to length and check the SWR.
- **Wire:** speaker wire, house wiring, fence wire, salvaged electrical cable (→ 09-08).
- **Insulators:** pieces of plastic bottle, wooden dowels, ceramic, plastic sheet.
- **Supports:** trees, a fence post, a pole, the house, a line thrown over a branch.
- **An SWR meter or antenna analyser** tells you whether it is right. **Without one you are
  guessing, and a badly mismatched antenna can damage the transmitter.** Buy one now.

## Keep people away from transmitting antennas

A transmitting antenna heats what is right next to it. **Any base or vehicle antenna, a 50-watt
GMRS mobile especially, goes where nobody, least of all a child, can touch it or stand within
arm's reach while it transmits**: roof peak or mast, not a deck rail or window ledge. With a 5-watt
handheld, keep the antenna a hand's width from your face and eyes, and never transmit with the tip
against anyone. Before the collapse, the FCC's radio-frequency exposure rules govern this;
afterwards it is still physics.

## Ice, wind and lightning

- **Ice storms bring antennas down.** Build for ice, use good supports, expect repairs after a
  storm (→ 17-01).
- **Wind:** guy (brace with ropes or wires) anything tall, properly (→ 17-18).
- **Lightning:** **ground the antenna system, and disconnect the cable when storms threaten.** A
  disconnected coax lying on the floor is a safe coax.
- **Snow on horizontal wires** makes them sag; leave slack and check after storms.

## Security

**A visible antenna is a visible capability** (→ 14-03). A big mast on a town lot says this house
has communications. **Wire antennas in trees are nearly invisible**, attic and indoor antennas
work (less well), and **a magnetic-mount antenna that comes off the vehicle leaves no trace.**
Weigh discretion against performance on purpose.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **A better antenna for every handheld** | Cheapest, biggest improvement | Longer whip; roll-up J-pole |
| Roll-up J-pole or slim-jim | Hang it in a tree; packable | Best value in this section |
| Magnetic-mount vehicle antenna | Roof height; removable | On the move; discretion |
| **Good coax, connectors, crimper** | The failure point nobody stocks | Buy extra; it does not expire |
| Self-amalgamating tape and electrical tape | **Sealing outdoor connectors** | Cheap; essential |
| Antenna wire, several hundred feet | Dipoles, radials, repairs | Stranded copper |
| Insulators, rope, pulleys | Getting wire up and keeping it there | → 16-03 for knots |
| **SWR meter or antenna analyser** | Stops guessing; protects the radio | Worth it |
| Grounding rod, ground wire, clamps | Lightning protection | Plus the disconnect habit |
| Lightning arrestor or coax switch | Fast disconnection | → 17-01 |
| Mast sections, guy line, stakes | Height is the whole game | Guy it properly |
| An amateur antenna book on paper | Designs beyond the dipole table | → 15-05 |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Wire:** speaker wire, electrical cable, fence wire, the centre conductor of salvaged coax.
- **Insulators:** plastic bottles, plastic pipe scraps, wooden dowels, ceramic pieces.
- **Supports:** trees (**the best mast you will ever have, and free**), fence posts, a fibreglass
  pole, a ladder, the house.
- **Mast:** conduit, a fence post, pipe, a cut sapling.
- **Ground plane:** wires laid on the ground, a vehicle roof, metal roofing.
- **Coax:** salvaged TV coax works for receiving and for some transmitting at lower frequencies.
  Not ideal; better than nothing.
- **Rope over a branch:** a weight on a line thrown over a high limb is the classic way to get wire
  into a tree (→ 16-03).

## When it runs out

- **Coax and connectors are the consumables**, and they fail invisibly from water, sunlight and
  corrosion. **Stock spares now**; they are the most under-stocked item in this section.
- **Antenna wire is nearly unlimited** from salvage (→ 22-02).
- **Sealing is the maintenance that matters.** A sealed system with good supports lasts years; a
  poorly sealed one fails in one wet season.
- **A ten-minute seasonal check** (connectors, cable jacket, supports, and everything after every
  ice storm and windstorm) prevents most failures.
- **Knowledge substitutes directly for money here** (→ 23-05): understanding wavelength, height
  and matching lets you build a working antenna from a fence and a spool of wire, indefinitely.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** modest and discreet: a wire in a tree, an attic antenna, or a magnetic mount on
  the vehicle. **Ground it and disconnect it in storms.** Test and write down your real range.
- **B (on the move):** a magnetic mount on the vehicle and a roll-up J-pole in a pack. A roll-up
  hung from a branch at a stop turns a handheld into something truly useful (→ 15-09).
- **C (rural or a new place):** **where antennas finally get to be good**: space, height, trees,
  no neighbours, little electrical noise. **A full-size HF dipole between two trees and a 12 V
  solar bank is a real long-distance station** (→ 15-05, → 09-02). Build it early, guy it for
  wind, and ground it for lightning.

pages.body:
# Signals without radio, and family codes

**What this page is for.** Signals that need no batteries, no licence and no network: whistles,
mirrors, lights, bright cloth, marks on the ground, and a handful of family codes agreed in
advance. They are the layer still working when everything else has failed.

> **CAUTION.** **If someone needs rescue, signal.** The discretion trade-offs on this page are for
> ordinary coordination. **They are never a reason to stay quiet when a person is injured, lost or
> freezing** (→ 12-16). **Give every person in the household a whistle**{{#if has.child}},
> children included{{/if}}: it carries far farther than a voice, especially a child's.

## Do this now

1. **Buy pealess whistles** (no ball inside to freeze) for everyone, and fix them to jackets and
   go-bags. Teach every child: **"If you're lost, stay where you are and blow it three times, over
   and over"** (→ 20-04).
2. **Agree the family signals** in the table below and write them here. Keep it to a handful: a
   code nobody remembers is worse than no code.
3. **Put a signal mirror and a flashlight in every go-bag and the vehicle** (→ 22-03, → 22-05).
4. **Teach children the "stay put" rule.** A lost child who stays in one place and makes noise is
   found; one who wanders is much harder to find.

## Distress signals everyone uses

Widely recognised, but **never assume they will be understood**:

- **Three of anything** (three whistle blasts, three shouts, three flashes) **means distress.** Two
  of anything is a common answer. **Gunshots as a signal: only in open wilderness, never in
  town**: where people live close together, three shots read as an attack, not a call for help,
  and every shot still needs a safe backstop (→ 14-11).
- **SOS**: three short, three long, three short, in any medium (light, sound, tapping).
- **Anything bright, moving and out of place**: a mirror flash, a signal fire, a coloured panel on
  snow, an X marked on the ground.
- **Patterns read as deliberate**; random noise reads as noise. **Signal in patterns.**

## Methods that work

| Method | Typical range (wind, weather and terrain decide) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Whistle** | **Far beyond a voice, with far less effort** | **The best single item here.** Works when you are exhausted or hoarse; carries through wind and snow |
| **Signal mirror** | **Miles in sunlight**, one of the longest-range signals there is | Needs sun; needs practice to aim |
| **Flashlight or headlamp** | Miles at night | Flash it; a steady light is easily missed |
| **Bright fabric or panel** | Visible far away on snow or from the air | **Orange or red on snow stands out** |
| **Fire and smoke** | Miles | Smoke by day (green leaves make white smoke), flame by night. **Fire risk** (→ 17-05) |
| **Marks on the ground** | From the air and the ground | An X, an arrow, tracks stamped in snow |
| **Banging on metal** | Several hundred yards | Carries better than shouting |
| **An object in a particular window** | The neighbourhood | Pre-agreed meaning; discreet (→ 10-05) |
| **Voice** | **The shortest range, and it tires you fastest** | Use the whistle instead |

{{figure fig-signal-mirror-aiming}}

**Weather changes everything.** Wind carries sound away, and blowing snow kills visibility
completely (→ 17-01). **In a whiteout, assume nobody can see or hear you beyond a very short
distance**, which is exactly why you do not travel in one. Cold also kills people who are lost and
waiting, so a lost person stays put **and** gets out of the wind (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia).

## The family signal set

Agree these, write them down, **practise them once.** Fewer is better.

| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **3 whistle blasts, repeated** | **"I need help / I'm lost."** Everyone stops and responds |
| **2 whistle blasts** | "I hear you" |
| **1 whistle blast** | "Where are you?" or check-in |
| **Flashlight, 3 flashes** | Distress, at night |
| **Flashlight, slow sweep** | "Here I am / come to me" |
| **An object in a window** (ours: ______________) | ______________ ("all clear", "come in" or "do not approach") |
| **A word in ordinary conversation** | **The duress word** (below) |
| **The hidden note spot** | The rally-point notes (→ 15-03) |

{{photo window-signal}}

## Family codes: a small number, agreed in advance

Two are really worth having:

1. **A duress word.** A word or phrase meaning *"I am saying this because someone is making me,
   or because something is wrong that I cannot say out loud."* Agreed between the adults (→ 14-01),
   never used casually, easy to slip naturally into a sentence. **It exists so that "come on in,
   everything's fine" can be a warning.** Do not write it anywhere a stranger could read it.
2. **A "come" and a "do not come" signal**: an object in a window, a mark on a gatepost, or a
   phrase on the radio (→ 15-02). Simple, unmistakable, and known to everyone.

**Keep the set small.** Elaborate codes fail under stress and give false confidence. Three or four
meanings everyone really remembers beat twenty clever ones.

**Be realistic about codes on open radio** (→ 15-02, → 14-03). FRS, GMRS, CB and amateur radio are
unencrypted, and anyone can listen. Simple codes hide meaning from casual listeners, not from
anyone paying attention; their real value is brevity and not broadcasting details.

> **Before the collapse:** amateur radio rules forbid messages coded to obscure their meaning
> (47 CFR Part 97; → 15-05). Keep codes off the amateur bands while the rule is enforced.

## Teaching the children

This is the part of the page with the most real-world value.

- **A young child:** whistle on their jacket, always. **"If you can't find a grown-up: stay where
  you are, blow your whistle three times, keep blowing it."** Practise it as a game, outdoors,
  until it is automatic (→ 20-04).
- **"Stay put" is the most important thing a lost child can do**, and it goes against their
  instinct to go looking. Practise it on purpose.
- **Teach them to answer** when they hear their name or a whistle. Some children hide when called,
  especially if they think they are in trouble. **Make it clear they are never in trouble for being
  lost.**
- **Babies and toddlers cannot signal**, so their identification is on them (→ 15-03) and they are
  never out of an adult's sight.
- **A bright outer layer** for every child in unfamiliar places makes them far easier to find
  (→ 11-02).

## Discretion versus being found

Signalling is broadcasting (→ 14-03, → 10-05): a signal fire, a mirror flash or a whistle tells
anyone in range that people are here. **In most situations (a blizzard, a lost child, an injury)
that is exactly what you want.** In a long breakdown where you are avoiding attention, it is a
decision.

**How to hold both:** **quiet signals for routine coordination** (an object in a window, a mark on
a post, a single whistle note) and **loud, unmistakable, universal signals when someone needs
help.** Do not let habitual discretion stop a call for rescue: reaching help is usually what
matters most (→ 12-16).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pealess whistles, one per person and spares** | Carries far, no power, works when exhausted | **Pealess**: pea whistles freeze and fail in cold |
| **Signal mirrors, one per adult** | One of the longest-range signals | Learn to aim it; practise |
| A flashlight or headlamp per person | Night signalling and everything else | → 10-01 |
| **A bright orange panel, cloth or vest** | Very visible on snow and from the air | Also for children |
| Bright outer layers for children | Easier to find | → 11-02 |
| Chemical light sticks | Marking; for children; no heat or flame | → 10-01 |
| Chalk, marker, flagging tape | Marks, trail marking, notes | → 15-03 |
| Air horn (optional) | Very loud, very far | Consumable |
| **The family signal list, written** | Short; everyone knows it | This page; → 25-08 |
| An agreed window object | Discreet neighbourhood signal | Costs nothing |

**If you do not have it:**

- **Whistle:** any whistle. Real ones cost almost nothing; buy them.
- **Mirror:** any mirror, a polished metal lid, a CD, a phone screen, foil on cardboard.
- **Bright panel:** an orange tarp, a bright jacket, a bedsheet, a safety vest.
- **Marking:** tracks stamped in snow, branches laid in an arrow, rocks, a scratched X, torn cloth
  tied to branches.
- **Noise:** metal on metal, a car horn, a pot and spoon.
- **Light:** a headlamp, a vehicle's headlights or hazard lights, a fire.
- **What you cannot improvise is the agreement.** Signals only work if everyone knows what they
  mean **in advance.** That part is free, and it is the part people skip.

## When it runs out

- **Almost nothing here runs out.** A whistle, a mirror, a bright cloth and an agreement last
  indefinitely with no power. **The most durable communications in the binder.**
- **The consumables are batteries for lights** (→ 09-07) and light sticks; both minor.
- **What fades is memory.** Review the signals every year (→ 25-10), and **re-teach children as
  they grow**, because what they can understand and do changes every year.
- **When the last battery is gone, this page still works.** The most valuable thing on it costs
  almost nothing: a whistle on a child's jacket, and ten minutes teaching them to use it.

## By phase

- **A (at home):** whistles for everyone, a window signal agreed with neighbours (→ 18-01), and
  the note spots at the rally points (→ 15-03). Teach and practise.
- **B (on the move):** **where signalling matters most.** Whistles on everyone, bright layers on
  children, a mirror and a light per adult, and **signals agreed before you set off.** In a
  whiteout nobody sees or hears anything (→ 17-01); staying physically together beats any signal.
- **C (rural or a new place):** long distances and few people. **A loud signal at the house (an
  air horn, a bell, a whistle) that everyone knows** is a permanent, low-tech capability that works
  in all weather with no power.
