review_pass.notes: Stranded-vehicle CO advice sourced to NWS winter-storm page; 911 wording tightened.

pages.body:
# Road communications: staying heard on the way

**What this page is for.** Keeping the people at both ends (the "nodes" on → 15-08) informed from
a moving vehicle, including the stretches where the phone shows no bars. The plan is a **PACE
ladder** (Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency): channels written down, agreed with the
nodes, and used **in order** instead of improvised at a rest stop. The route hazards themselves
are on → 17-11 and the maps on → 25-04; this page is only about staying heard.

> **CAUTION.** **If the road stops you, stay with the vehicle, at a named town if you can, note
> the time, and wait**: the overdue trigger on → 15-08 is doing the searching. If you run the
> engine for heat while stopped, keep the tailpipe clear of snow and a window cracked: a blocked
> exhaust fills a car with carbon monoxide. The NWS says: stay in the vehicle, clear snow from the
> exhaust pipe, and open a window a little while the engine runs (NWS, What To Do If You're
> Caught in a Winter Storm; CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics; → 08-02).

## Do this now

1. **Print the visor card** (below), fill it in, and keep it in the vehicle with the node numbers
   from → 15-08.
2. **Drive each route once in good weather with this page out**, and pencil in the truth: where
   the phone really had signal, which check-in towns work, how long each leg took. **Every
   coverage guess is an assumption until you have done this.**
3. **Write down each adult's phone carrier.** A second phone on a different carrier is a real
   backup, because towers fail unevenly. Driver: ____________ Other adult: ____________ Same?
   ☐ (if so, that rung is thinner).
4. **Make sure the charging kit rides along**: a car charger and cables for every phone and radio.
   A dead phone deletes the whole first rung.

## Check-in points for each route

{{#each destinations as x}}### To {{x.name}} ({{x.state_name}}, about {{x.approximate_miles}} miles)

Your route notes: {{x.route_notes}}

| Leg | Check-in town | Signal there (pencil after the test drive) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Departure | Home | ______ | Departure text to the node and the relay (→ 15-08) |
| 1 | ______________ | ______ | |
| Midpoint | ______________ | ______ | The midpoint text, before committing to the next leg |
| 3 | ______________ | ______ | Last good coverage before any known dead zone? |
| Arrival | {{x.name}} | ______ | **The arrival text cancels the overdue trigger** |

{{else}}No destinations are entered in your profile. Use the blank table for any long trip.

| Leg | Check-in town | Signal there | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Departure | Home | ______ | |
| Midpoint | ______________ | ______ | |
| Arrival | ______________ | ______ | |
{{/each}}

**Planning assumptions until a drive proves otherwise:** open country between towns, hills,
valleys and forests have weak or no signal; **assume no coverage at all in a blizzard**, when the
weather that strands you also floods the network (→ 17-01). **A missed midpoint check-in is
information, not an alarm; only the arrival deadline starts the calls** (→ 15-08).

## The PACE ladder on the road

| Rung | Channel | The reality |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | **Phone, and text first** | **A text queues and retries through weak, brief signal that a call cannot hold**; one sent in a dead zone often goes through at the next hilltop. Send check-ins as texts by default. **911 connects from any phone on any carrier's tower**, even when your own carrier shows "No Service", or with no plan, as long as some carrier's tower is in reach: call it rather than texting (47 CFR 9.10). Wi-Fi calling (→ 15-03) works over any gas-station or motel Wi-Fi |
| **A** | **The other adult's phone** | A different carrier means different towers. A stopped trucker's phone or a gas-station phone is also an alternate: the message matters, not whose phone |
| **C** | **GMRS and CB** | GMRS on the family channel near home or the destination where someone is listening (→ 15-03, → 15-08). On the open road, **CB channel 19 is where truckers are**: road news and a message someone will relay; **channel 9 is the traditional emergency channel, but assume nobody official listens.** A radio call to a stranger who will phone your node *is* reach-back |
| **SAT** | **Satellite texting** | Some phones (for example iPhone 14 and later) can send an **emergency SOS by satellite** with your location when there are no bars, and newer software can send ordinary texts by satellite (Apple Support, Emergency SOS via satellite). **Clear sky, step out of the vehicle, hold the phone up, follow the on-screen pointer; it is slow, so send one short line.** A satellite messenger does the same **only with a paid subscription.** Satellite internet in the vehicle needs a plan that allows use while moving (→ 15-02) |
| **E** | **NOAA Weather Radio: listening only** | When you can reach nobody, you can still **hear** warnings ahead (→ 15-01). **The emergency rung is: stop and wait** at a named town (→ 17-11), note the time, and let the arrival deadline do its job. **A vehicle stopped at a named town is what a search finds; one improvising across country is not** |

What our household has on each rung: P ______ A ______ C ______ SAT ______ E ______

## The visor card: print this

One sheet, folded to visor size, one per route (a master copy on → 25-08). Fill the clock lines at
departure, every trip, in pencil.

```
ROUTE TO: ______________    ROUTE: __________
DEPARTED: ____:____      ARRIVAL DUE: ____:____
OVERDUE TRIGGER STARTS AT: ____:____  (15-08)
CHECK-INS: 1)__________ 2)__________ 3)__________
NODE (destination): __________  ph __________
RELAY: {{ contacts.out_of_area.name }}  ph {{ contacts.out_of_area.phone }}
TEXT FIRST. WHO / STATUS (OK - NEED HELP - MOVING)
            / WHERE / NEXT CHECK-IN
C: GMRS ch ____ . CB 19 (truckers) / 9 (emergency)
SAT: SOS by satellite: clear sky, hold phone up
911 works on ANY carrier's tower
E: weather radio - step through all 7 channels
IF STOPPED: stay with vehicle, named town if you
can, note time, wait - the trigger is running
```

**The card is the plan a tired driver actually follows.**

## Charging on the road

The first rung dies with the phone battery.

- **Phones and power banks:** a good USB car charger in the 12 V socket, with a cable for every
  phone. Keep it in the vehicle kit (→ 22-05).
- **GMRS and amateur handhelds:** from the same USB charger, or their own 12 V cords.
- **Satellite internet**, if you carry it: it draws real power, so run it in short windows at
  check-in stops. Phones and radios charge first.
- **Satellite texting uses battery too**: the phone searches the sky at full power. Do it with
  plenty of charge, or on the car charger.
- {{#if has.hybrid}}**Your hybrid** can act as a parked generator while you wait, but keep the
fuel tank well above empty and the **carbon monoxide** rule in mind: tailpipe clear, never in a
closed space (→ 08-02).{{else}}**A running vehicle** charges everything while you wait, but keep
the tailpipe clear and never idle in a closed space (→ 08-02).{{/if}}
- **Phone habit on the road:** airplane mode through known dead zones, off at check-in points. A
  phone hunting for towers all day is dead by evening.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **A printed visor card per route, filled in** | The plan at eye level | → 25-08 |
| A USB car charger and cables | The first rung's lifeline | → 22-05 |
| A GMRS handheld in the vehicle | The contingency rung at both ends | → 15-02 |
| **CB (mobile or handheld) and a real antenna** | Channel 19 is where the road talks | → 15-02 |
| A weather radio in the vehicle | The emergency rung: incoming warnings | → 15-01 |
| A paper road atlas with routes and check-ins marked | Phones die | → 25-04 |
| A charged power bank in the cab | Bridges the phone between stops | → 09-03 |
| A phone with satellite texting, or a messenger with a subscription | The satellite rung | Try the demo at home |

**If you do not have it:**

- **No CB?** A GMRS or amateur handheld, plus asking a trucker at a stop: their CB and phone become
  yours for one message.
- **No car charger?** Any gas station sells one; a poor one beats a dead phone.
- **No working phone at all?** Every open business on the road has one. **The message is three
  lines (WHO, STATUS, WHERE): anyone can pass it to your node.**

## When it runs out

- **On the road, battery runs out first, then coverage.** The charging kit handles the first; the
  ladder handles the second.
- **Over the years the coverage picture changes**: carriers change, towers come and go. **Pencil in
  the dead zones again every time you drive the route.** The card is meant to be corrected.
- **When the whole network is down** (→ 17-08), the ladder shrinks to the contingency and emergency
  rungs, and the plan becomes → 15-08's phones-down routine: the nodes' trigger clocks still run.
  **The deadline you set at departure is the one piece of communication that works with no
  infrastructure at all.**

## By phase

- **A (at home):** preparation: the test drives, the printed card, the carriers written down, the
  charging kit in the vehicle (→ 22-05).
- **B (on the move):** **this page is the trip.** Text at every named point, go down the ladder in
  order, and if the road stops you, **stopping and waiting is a communications strategy**, because
  the overdue trigger (→ 15-08) is doing the searching (→ 01-03).
- **C (at a destination):** the card flips for the trip back: a new departure text, new clock
  lines, the same ladder.

pages.title: Tools and repair: section overview
pages.body:
# Tools and repair

**What this section holds.** 12 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 16-01 **Essential hand tools**: Which hand tools to own, how to keep them, and how to use them without getting hurt.
- → 16-02 **Sharpening knives, axes and saws**: How to put an edge back on every cutting tool you own, with a file, a stone and a strip of leather.
- → 16-03 **Knots and cordage**: Six knots that cover almost every job (tying down, hanging, lashing, tensioning), the rope to stock, how to keep it, how to make cord from plants and cloth, …
- → 16-04 **Sewing and mending gear**: Repairing and making anything of fabric: packs, tarps, tents, boots, canvas, webbing, straps, cushions.
- → 16-05 **Improvised repairs: tape, wire, glue, patch**: Fixing broken things with what is on hand, and knowing which things must never be fixed that way.
- → 16-06 **Axes, saws and wood tools**: Cutting and splitting firewood by hand and with a chainsaw without losing a foot, a leg or a hand.
- → 16-07 **Fasteners, wire and hardware to stock**: The screws, nails, bolts, wire and small hardware that every other repair in this binder depends on.
- → 16-08 **Repairing metal and wood without power**: Fixing tool handles and wooden structures, cutting, bending and joining metal by hand, simple work with fire, and knowing what scrap steel is good for.
- → 16-09 **Bicycles and human-powered transport**: Moving people, water, wood and supplies when fuel is gone: bicycles, bike trailers, carts and sleds, and the three bicycle repairs that cover most failures.
- → 16-10 **Tire failures: roadside diagnosis and repair**: What to do when a tire goes soft, punctures, or fails on the road, with a small kit you carry in the vehicle: a plug kit, a portable inflator, sealant, a jac…
- → 16-11 **Trailer maintenance and repair**: Keeping a small utility or enclosed trailer safe to tow: the walkaround before every trip, the wheel bearings that cause the worst failures, trailer tires, l…
- → 16-12 **Grid-down house repairs: gas, roof, window, burst pipe, sump**: The repairs that keep a house a shelter when no one can come: a gas smell, a torn-open roof, a broken window, a burst pipe, and water rising in a basement.

pages.title: Essential hand tools

photo_slots.caption: Our tool area: where each kind of tool lives, the eye protection and the trauma kit

pages.body:
# Essential hand tools

**What this page is for.** Which hand tools to own, how to keep them, and how to use them
without getting hurt. Hand tools need no fuel and no power, break in ways you can fix, and last
for generations. Power tools are faster while batteries and fuel last. The rule for this whole
section: **own the hand-powered version of every job you depend on.**

> **CAUTION. With no clinic, the tools chapter is a medical chapter.** Cuts, punctures, crushed
> fingers and eye injuries from tool work are among the most likely serious injuries in any
> long emergency (→ 12-02). Sharp tools, the right technique, eye protection, and not working
> when you are exhausted or cold prevent more harm than any first-aid kit can treat.
>
> **Check that every household member's tetanus shot is up to date** (CDC, About Tetanus).
> Tetanus is a serious infection that enters through deep, dirty wounds, and tool punctures are
> exactly that kind of wound (→ 12-04). Adults need a booster every 10 years; ask a clinic now
> while one is open.

## Do this now

1. **Lay out every tool you own** on a table and write it down (→ 22-04). Most households find
   three screwdrivers and no file, no hacksaw and no hand drill.
2. **Buy the hand-powered version of what you depend on:** a hand drill or brace, a hand saw,
   files. These are the tools that still work in year three.
3. **Buy several pairs of eye protection** and keep one at every place where work happens. Eye
   injuries are permanent and there may be no eye doctor.
4. **Buy files and sharpening stones** (→ 16-02). A dull tool is dangerous and useless, and these
   are cheap now and hard to get later.
5. **Organize and label** so anyone can find a tool in the dark, including someone who did not
   put it away.

{{photo tool-area}}

## Buy good ones once, for what you depend on

Cheap tools fail under load, and they fail suddenly, often into your hand. For the tools you
will rely on (axe, saw, knife, pliers, wrenches, files), buy good ones once. For tools you use
now and then, cheap is fine. **Old tools from estate sales, farm auctions and flea markets are
often better than new ones** and cost little: older hand tools were made to be resharpened
for a lifetime.

## The core kit, by job

{{figure fig-core-tool-kit}}

**Cutting and shaping wood** (→ 16-06)
- Axe (for felling and splitting), splitting maul (a heavy, blunt splitting axe) and steel wedges
- Hatchet (a small one-hand axe) for kindling
- Bow saw (a steel frame holding a thin blade) with spare blades; crosscut hand saw; folding saw
- Wood chisels, a draw knife (a two-handled blade pulled toward you to shave wood), a hand plane
- Brace and bit (a crank-shaped hand drill) or an "eggbeater" hand drill, with a set of bits
- Rasp and wood files

**Metal and general** (→ 16-08)
- Hacksaw and a large supply of spare blades (**the blades are what wears out**)
- Metal files: flat, round, half-round, triangular
- Ball-peen hammer (rounded back, for metal), claw hammer, small sledge
- Cold chisels (for cutting metal) and punches
- A bench vise (a clamp bolted to a bench). It is one of the most useful things you can own; a
  portable one also works.
- An anvil, or any heavy flat block of steel

**Gripping and turning**
- Pliers: slip-joint, needle-nose, linesman's (heavy square-jawed pliers that also cut wire),
  locking pliers, and adjustable groove-joint ("channel-lock") pliers
- Wrenches: a full set, plus adjustable wrenches and pipe wrenches
- Sockets and ratchet, in both SAE (inch) and metric sizes
- Screwdrivers: flat, Phillips, Torx (six-point star) and square drive
- Clamps. You will always want more clamps.

**Measuring and marking**
- Tape measure, folding rule, combination square, level, chalk line, pencils and a scribe
  (a sharp steel point for marking metal), calipers

**Digging and earth**
- Round-point and square shovels, a spade, a mattock or pick, a post-hole digger (→ 13-07), a
  garden fork, a pry bar

**Sharpening** (→ 16-02)
- Mill bastard file (a common flat file) for axes; chainsaw files in your chain's size;
  coarse and fine stones; a strop (leather for polishing an edge); a honing guide

**Safety gear. Not optional.**
- Eye protection, several pairs, one at every work area
- Hearing protection. Power tools and chainsaws cause permanent hearing loss (CDC/NIOSH, About
  Noise and Hearing Loss), and there may be no hearing specialist.
- Work gloves, several pairs, plus cut-resistant gloves
- Sturdy boots, steel-toe if you can
- Dust masks or respirators for sawdust, insulation, mold and ash
- A first-aid kit and a bleeding-control kit at the work area, not in the house (→ 12-01,
  → 12-08). A tourniquet and the training to use it are the core of bleeding control (American
  College of Surgeons, Stop the Bleed).

## Power tools and the power you have

Power tools save a great deal of labor while there is power for them. What limits them is fuel,
charged batteries and sun, not the tool.

{{#if has.power_station}}**You own a power station** (about {{ gear.station_wh_total }} watt-hours
in total, → 09-03). Many corded tools can run from a power station's AC outlet if the tool's
running watts are below the station's continuous rating. Read the watts or amps on the tool's
label (→ 29-14) and the station's label; if the tool lists amps, multiply by 120 to get rough
watts (→ 29-02). Motors pull a short burst of extra power when they start, so test each tool on
the station now, unloaded first, before you rely on it. Some stations have a mode for heaters
that lowers the output voltage; read your station's manual and turn any such mode off for
motors.{{else}}If you later own a power station or generator (→ 09-03, → 09-04), many corded tools
can run from it: compare the tool's label watts with the station's continuous rating (→ 29-02,
→ 29-14).{{/if}}

- **Charging cordless tool batteries** is the cheaper habit: a tool-battery charger is a small
  load, and the charged pack then works far from the power source.
- **Power for medical devices and food cold comes first** (→ 09-01). Tool charging uses what is
  left over.
- **Hearing protection** every time a power tool runs.

| Job | Power tool | Hand tool to own as well |
|---|---|---|
| Cutting firewood | Chainsaw (fuel-limited, → 16-06) | Bow saw, crosscut saw, axe, maul |
| Drilling | Cordless or corded drill | Brace and bit, hand drill, gimlet |
| Cutting metal | Angle grinder | Hacksaw and spare blades, cold chisel, files |
| Sharpening | Bench grinder | Files, stones, hand-crank grinder |
| Sawing boards | Circular saw | Hand saw, panel saw |
| Sanding and shaping | Sander | Rasps, files, planes, scrapers |
| Driving screws | Impact driver | Screwdrivers, brace with a screwdriver bit |

**Own the hand version of everything in that table.** The day the power fails is usually the day
the work is urgent.

## Tool inventory (fill in on paper or in → 22-04)

```
CUTTING / WOOD (16-06)
  Chainsaw?  Y / N   Bar length: ____ in
    Chain pitch / gauge (stamped on the bar): ______ / ______
    Chainsaw file size for that chain (16-02): ______ in
  Axe: __________  Hatchet: __________  Maul / wedges: __________
  Saws (bow / crosscut / folding / hand): ______________________
FASTENING / DRIVING
  Drill / driver: __________  Battery platform and packs: __________
  Hand drill or brace?  Y / N    Screwdriver set?  Y / N
  Hammers: ______________________
MECHANICAL (16-05, 16-10)
  Socket set: SAE / metric / both   Largest size: ______
  Wrenches: __________  Pliers / locking pliers: __________
  Hacksaw + spare blades x ____   Files (mill / flat / round): ______
DIGGING
  Shovels: ______  Spade: ____  Mattock / pick: ____  Pry bar: ____
BENCH
  Vise?  Y / N  (size ____)   Work surface?  Y / N
  Clamps x ____   Eye protection x ____   Hearing protection x ____

TOP 10 GAPS TO BUY (copy to 22-01):
  1________ 2________ 3________ 4________ 5________
  6________ 7________ 8________ 9________ 10_______
Inventory done (date / initials): __________
```

## Care, which is what makes tools last

- **Clean and dry after use.** Rust destroys more tools than wear does.
- **Oil the steel.** Wipe every steel tool with light oil each season. A rag kept in a closed can
  of mineral oil or machine oil makes this easy. **Mineral or machine oil only in that can.**
- **Sharpen before the edge is dull** (→ 16-02).
- **Look after handles.** Rub linseed oil into wooden handles and check them for cracks. A loose
  axe head is dangerous (→ 16-06).
- **Linseed-oil rags can catch fire by themselves.** The oil gives off heat as it dries, and a
  bunched rag in a bin, a pocket or on a bench can ignite within hours. Spread used rags flat
  outdoors to dry stiff, or seal them in a metal can filled with water and a lid. Never pile them
  or put them in a pocket, and never near stored fuel.
- **Store tools organized and off the ground.** A tool you cannot find is a tool you do not have.
- **Mark anything you lend** so it comes back.

## Working safely (OSHA basics)

These follow OSHA's hand and power tool guidance (OSHA, Hand and Power Tools).

- **Right tool for the job.** Improvised tool use is where hands get hurt.
- **Tools in good condition.** No cracked handles. No "mushroomed" heads on chisels and punches
  (the struck end spread into a ragged lip): those edges break off and fly. No dull edges.
- **Cut away from yourself.** Before every cut, ask where the tool goes if it slips, and make sure
  no hand, leg or person is there.
- **Eye protection every time**, not just for the jobs that look dangerous.
- **Do not work when exhausted, cold, rushed or in poor light.** In a winter without power that is
  the normal condition, so notice it and stop.
- **Children stay well clear of tool work**, and tools are stored out of small children's reach
  (→ 20-02). Whether and when older children use tools is a household choice: {{choice DC-24}}
  (→ 30-25).
- **Bleeding-control kit at the work area** (→ 12-08), and know how to use it (→ 12-02).

## Getting more tools

- **Estate sales, farm auctions, flea markets and old sheds** have excellent hand tools for very
  little money. Do this now.
- **Abandoned buildings and garages** (→ 22-02): tools, fasteners, wire and hardware. Take only
  what the law and your own ethics allow at the time.
- **Vehicles** often hold a socket set, a jack and a pry bar.
- **Improvised:** a rock as a hammer; a vehicle leaf spring as chisel or blade steel; rebar as a
  pry bar; an old file ground into a knife or scraper (→ 16-08); any heavy steel block as an anvil.
- **What you cannot make: files and saw blades.** They are hardened steel with cut teeth. Stock
  them heavily.

## When it runs out

- **Hand tools barely wear out. Their consumables do:** saw blades, files, sandpaper, drill bits
  and sharpening stones. Over-stock those now (→ 23-02).
- **Count saw blades and files.** A bow saw blade cutting a winter of firewood wears out; a file
  sharpening axes and chains wears out. They are the quiet bottleneck of firewood (→ 06-04).
- **Make them last:** sharpen instead of replacing (→ 16-02); use the right tool so nothing wears
  early; avoid cutting frozen wood where you can, because it is hard on edges.
- **Resupply:** scavenging (→ 22-02) and trade (→ 18-02). Tools are good barter goods, and tool
  skills are better (→ 18-03).
- **The real asset is the skill.** A person who can sharpen, fix and improvise keeps a household
  running on salvage, and is one of the most valuable people in any community (→ 18-03, → 23-05).

## By phase

- **A, sheltering at home:** buy and organize now, while tools are cheap. Build hand-tool backups
  for everything you depend on. Set up a work area with eye protection and a bleeding-control kit.
- **B, on the move:** a very small kit: a good knife, a multi-tool, pliers, a folding saw, a small
  file, cord, tape and wire. Weight is brutal on the move (→ 22-03), and tools compete with water.
- **C, settled somewhere new:** this chapter comes into its own: more building, more repair, no
  store. A vise, an anvil, a full hand-tool kit and a real work area are basic infrastructure.
  Set them up early (→ 01-04).

pages.title: Sharpening knives, axes and saws
pages.body:
# Sharpening knives, axes and saws

**What this page is for.** How to put an edge back on every cutting tool you own, with a file, a
stone and a strip of leather. Sharpening costs little, takes an afternoon to learn, and keeps
every edge tool working for years. When you cannot buy a new axe, restoring the one you have is
what "tools last forever" really means.

> **CAUTION. A dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one.** A dull edge does not bite. It
> skates and glances off, it needs force, and it goes where you did not intend with your weight
> behind it. Many serious knife and axe injuries involve a dull tool and too much force
> (→ 12-02). Learn to sharpen now, on tools you do not depend on, before you have to do it by
> lamplight with cold hands (→ 24-01).

## Do this now

1. **Buy files and stones:** a mill bastard file (a common flat file, 8 to 10 inches) for axes,
   chainsaw files in the exact size for your chain, and sharpening stones in a coarse and a fine
   grit.
2. **Sharpen everything you own this month:** kitchen knives, the axe, the hatchet, the shovel,
   the loppers. You will find half of it is dull, and you will build the skill.
3. **Learn the burr** (next section). It is most of what sharpening is.
4. **Get a strop**, or make one from an old leather belt, and use it. Stropping keeps an edge
   sharp much longer and removes almost no metal.

## The one idea: the burr

{{figure fig-burr-and-bevel}}

An edge is the line where two sloped faces (bevels) meet. **You sharpen by grinding one side
until a tiny wire of metal, the burr, curls over along the whole opposite side.** Then you do the
other side. Then you remove the burr.

- **Feel for the burr** by drawing a fingertip *across* the edge, from the thick back of the
  blade outward. Never along the edge. A burr feels like a slight catch.
- **A burr along the whole length means you have reached the edge everywhere.** No burr means you
  have only polished the slope, not sharpened.
- **Then refine on a finer stone, and strop** to remove the burr and straighten the edge.

Everything else (angles, stones, technique) is refinement of that one idea.

## Angles, roughly

The angle is measured on one face, from the flat of the blade.

| Tool | Rough angle per side | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Kitchen or fillet knife | Shallow, about 15 to 20 degrees | Sharpest; for slicing, not chopping |
| Butchering knife | About 20 degrees | Sharp but durable (→ 05-09) |
| General outdoor knife | About 20 to 25 degrees | Compromise |
| Axe or hatchet | Thicker, with a rounded ("convex") profile | Must survive impact; a thin edge chips (→ 16-06) |
| Machete or brush hook | Thicker | Impact tool |
| Chisel or plane blade | About 25 to 30 degrees, back kept flat | Fine woodwork |
| Scissors and shears | The factory angle, bevelled side only | Never sharpen the flat inner side |

**Thinner cuts better; thicker lasts longer.** An axe sharpened like a kitchen knife chips on the
first knot.

## Sharpening a knife

1. **Coarse stone** if the edge is chipped or very dull. If it is only tired, start on the fine
   stone.
2. **Hold one steady angle.** This is the hard part. A clip-on guide helps while you learn.
3. **Work one side until a burr forms along the whole edge.**
4. **Turn the knife over and repeat** until the burr forms on the first side.
5. **Finer stone**, both sides, lighter pressure.
6. **Strop:** draw the blade along leather with the edge trailing (spine first), to remove the
   burr.
7. **Test** by slicing a sheet of paper. **Never test by running your thumb across the edge.**

**Water or oil on the stone** carries away the metal grit so the stone keeps cutting. Use what
the stone was made for.

## Sharpening an axe

{{figure fig-axe-convex-filing}}

1. **Secure the axe** in a vise, or braced firmly. **Never hold it loose in one hand.**
2. **File first** with a mill bastard file, pushing *into* the edge. A file cuts only on the push
   stroke. Work from the middle of the edge outward, on both sides.
3. **Keep the rounded profile.** An axe edge should be slightly curved in cross-section, not a
   flat bevel. Blend the bevel back a couple of inches into the side of the head.
4. **Then a stone**, in small circles, both sides.
5. **Strop or hone** to finish.
6. **Wear gloves and file away from your hand.** File slips on axes are a common injury.
7. **Grind off any mushrooming** on the striking end of a maul or wedge. Mushroomed steel breaks
   off in flying fragments (OSHA, Hand and Power Tools), a classic eye injury.

A properly sharpened axe cuts far more wood per swing, which matters when you are cutting a
winter's firewood by hand (→ 06-04).

## Saws

- **Bow saw blades are hardened and disposable.** You cannot usefully resharpen them. **Stock many
  spare blades.**
- **Chainsaw chains are not disposable.** They are sharpened with a round file many times over
  their life, a few strokes per tooth every tank or two of fuel. A chain is used up only when the
  teeth are filed back to the wear marks.
- **Traditional hand saws can be sharpened and "set"** with a saw file and a saw set (a plier-like
  tool). This is a learnable skill, and it is why an old hand saw is a better long-term buy than
  a disposable-blade saw.
- **Set** means the teeth are bent slightly left and right in turn, so the cut is wider than the
  blade and the blade does not jam. A saw with no set binds and burns.

## Chainsaw chains

**The file size, the filing angles and the depth-gauge setting come from your saw's and chain's
manufacturer and the Extension guides cited here, not from this page.** Getting them wrong makes
kickback more likely. Kickback is the saw's tip catching and throwing the bar up and back toward
you, one of the main ways chainsaws injure people (University of Missouri Extension, Operating a
Chain Saw Safely; → 16-06).

- **Sharpen often.** A few strokes every tank is far better than a big restoration later.
- **A sharp chain pulls itself into the wood and throws chips. A dull chain makes fine dust and
  you have to push.** That is the test.
- **Depth gauges** (the small humps in front of each cutting tooth, also called rakers) must be
  filed down now and then, or the chain stops cutting even with sharp teeth.
- **Stock the right size files and a depth-gauge tool** (University of Missouri Extension,
  Selecting and Maintaining a Chain Saw). They are small, cheap and specific to your chain. Write
  the size on your tool inventory (→ 16-01).

## Other things worth sharpening

- **Shovels and spades:** a sharpened shovel cuts sod and roots far better.
- **Hoes** (→ 05-01): a sharp hoe makes weeding a fraction of the work.
- **Loppers, pruners and shears** (→ 05-13): a clean cut is better for the plant too.
- **Scissors and kitchen knives:** daily comfort and safety.
- **Drill bits and auger bits** can be filed back to life.
- **A scythe**, if you have one, needs constant honing and "peening" (hammering the edge thin).
  A real skill worth learning for a rural move.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mill bastard file, 8 to 10 in, with a handle | The axe file; general use | Buy several |
| Chainsaw files in your chain's size, and a depth-gauge tool | Chain-specific | Stock many; they wear |
| Sharpening stones, coarse and fine | Knives, chisels, plane blades | Diamond plates last longest |
| Strop (leather and polishing compound) | Keeps an edge without removing metal | An old belt works |
| Metal files: flat, round, half-round, triangular | Tools, hardware, repairs | → 16-08 |
| Saw file and saw set | Sharpen a hand saw indefinitely | The long-term choice |
| **Spare bow saw blades, many** | Cannot be resharpened | Over-stock |
| Bench vise | Holds work safely while filing | → 16-01 |
| Gloves and eye protection | Filing throws metal; edges cut | Every time |
| Honing guide (optional) | Steady angle while learning | Helps most on chisels |

**Substitutes if you have nothing:**
- **Stone:** a flat, fine-grained river stone (people sharpened on them for thousands of years);
  the rough unglazed ring on the bottom of a ceramic mug as a fine hone; a smooth concrete edge as
  a coarse stone.
- **Strop:** a leather belt, a boot tongue, a piece of cardboard. Polishing compound helps but is
  not needed.
- **Wet-and-dry sandpaper on a flat surface** (glass or a tile) is an excellent sharpening system.
  Stock a range of grits.
- **Files** can be salvaged from any shop or farm. A file too worn to cut can be ground into a
  knife or chisel (→ 16-08).
- **What you cannot improvise:** a chainsaw file of the right diameter, and hardened saw blades.
  Buy those now.

## When it runs out

- **Files and stones wear out.** Files dull after a lot of steel; stones wear hollow. Both are
  cheap now. Stock several and add them to → 23-02.
- **Saw blades are the real limit** (→ 06-04, → 16-06). Either stock many, or own a traditional
  hand saw and a saw file. For a plan measured in years, the traditional saw is the sturdier
  choice even though it is slower.
- **Strop often, sharpen rarely.** Stropping removes almost no metal. Heavy sharpening uses up
  the tool. A knife stropped daily may not need a stone for months.
- **The skill is the resource.** Someone who can sharpen keeps every edge in a neighborhood
  working, and that is a service people will trade for (→ 18-03).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** learn now, on your own tools, in daylight. Stock files, stones and blades.
- **B, on the move:** a small file and a pocket stone weigh almost nothing and keep a knife and a
  folding saw working. The knife is the tool you use most.
- **C, settled:** constant edge work: axes, saws, knives, shovels, butchering (→ 05-09). Set up a
  permanent sharpening station with a vise, files and stones. A hand-crank grinder is an
  excellent tool that needs no power.

pages.title: Knots and cordage
pages.body:
# Knots and cordage

**What this page is for.** Six knots that cover almost every job (tying down, hanging, lashing,
tensioning), the rope to stock, how to keep it, how to make cord from plants and cloth, and the
one rope job that kills people: pulling a stuck vehicle. People try to learn thirty knots and
remember none. **Learn six, practice until your hands do them without thinking, and stop.**

> **Nothing on this page is rated for life safety.** These are utility knots for tying
> things down, lashing and hanging. **Do not use them, or any rope in this binder, for climbing,
> lowering a person, rescue, or anything where a failure drops a person.** That needs rated rope,
> rated hardware and training.
>
> **Never pull a stuck vehicle with rope, chain or a ratchet strap, or from a hitch ball.** A
> snapped line or a torn-off ball flies through windshields and people. The safe method is in its
> own block below.

## Do this now

1. **Buy rope in several sizes:** a lot of 550 paracord, 1/4-inch and 3/8-inch utility rope, bank
   line or tarred twine, and jute or sisal twine for anything you will burn or compost. Buy more
   than you think.
2. **Learn the six knots below this week:** bowline, taut-line hitch, clove hitch, two half
   hitches, square knot, trucker's hitch.
3. **Practice them in gloves and in the dark.** That is when you will need them (→ 11-04).
4. **Make a practice cord:** cut a 4-foot length of paracord, tie it to a drawer handle, and do one
   knot each evening against the steps below until all six are hands-only. Tick each one off.
5. {{#if has.child}}**Teach the children one knot**: the overhand first, then the square knot.
   Children enjoy this and it is a real skill (→ 20-07).{{else}}**Teach one knot to someone else.**
   Teaching it is the best test that you know it.{{/if}}

## Two words used in every step

{{figure fig-knot-parts-of-a-rope}}

- The **working end** is the short end you move.
- The **standing part** is the long rest of the rope, going to the load or the anchor.
- A **bight** is a fold of rope, a U-shape, with no crossing.
- A **loop** is a circle where the rope crosses itself.

The pictures for each knot come from the US Army's rigging manual (US Army, FM 5-125, Rigging
Techniques, Procedures, and Applications). The steps are written so each step is one hand motion,
and they work without the picture.

## Warm-up: the overhand knot

{{figure fig-knot-overhand}}

The simplest knot, the one children learn first, and a stopper at the end of a rope.

1. Make a loop near the end of the rope by crossing the working end over the standing part.
2. Push the working end through the loop from behind.
3. Pull both ends.

*Check:* a small lump that will not pass through a hole the rope itself passes through.

## The six knots

### 1. Bowline: a fixed loop that will not slip or jam

{{figure fig-knot-bowline}}

*Use:* a loop in the end of a line, tying to a ring or post, hauling. It unties easily even after
a heavy load.

1. Hold the standing part in your left hand. The last 2 feet of rope is the working end.
2. Make a small loop in the standing part by crossing it over itself, so that **the part of the
   rope leading toward the working end lies on top** of the part going down to the load. This
   small loop is the "rabbit hole".
3. Push the working end up through the small loop from underneath ("the rabbit comes out of the
   hole").
4. Pass the working end behind the standing part ("around the tree").
5. Bring the working end back down through the small loop, the same way it came out ("back down
   the hole").
6. Hold the working end and the side of the big loop together in one hand and the standing part
   in the other. Pull apart to tighten.

*Check:* the working end finishes lying inside the big loop, with a tail about as long as your
fist is wide. **Then pull the big loop hard. If it shrinks or slides, you made the small loop the
wrong way round and tied a slip knot.** Untie it and cross the rope the other way in step 2.

### 2. Taut-line hitch: an adjustable loop that grips under load

{{figure fig-knot-taut-line-hitch}}

*Use:* tent and tarp lines, clotheslines, anything you tighten and re-tighten (→ 11-03). One of
the most useful knots there is, and almost nobody knows it.

1. Pass the working end around the anchor (a stake or a tree). The standing part runs back to the
   tarp. You now have a big open loop between the anchor and the tarp.
2. Bring the working end back alongside the standing part, toward the tarp.
3. Wrap the working end around the standing part, inside the big loop, turning back toward the
   anchor.
4. Make a second wrap the same way, right beside the first, still inside the big loop.
5. Move the working end to the tarp side of those two wraps (outside the big loop) and make one
   more wrap around the standing part.
6. Tuck the working end under that last wrap and pull it snug.

*Check:* hold the knot and slide it along the standing part. It should slide by hand and hold when
the line is pulled.

### 3. Clove hitch: quick fastening to a post or pole

{{figure fig-knot-clove-hitch}}

*Use:* starting a lashing, tying to a rail or post. **It can slip when the pull keeps changing**,
so back it up with a half hitch.

1. Pass the working end over and around the post, then cross it diagonally over the standing part.
2. Take the working end around the post a second time, beside the first wrap.
3. Tuck the working end under its own second wrap, beneath the diagonal crossing.
4. Pull the working end and the standing part in opposite directions to set it.
5. For security, add a half hitch: the working end around the standing part and back through.

*Check:* two wraps sit side by side on the post with the diagonal crossing pinned between them.

### 4. Two half hitches (with a round turn): tying off to anything

{{figure fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches}}

*Use:* tying a rope to a ring, rail, branch or post.

1. Pass the working end around the object. **For a real load, go around twice** (a "round turn");
   the friction does half the work.
2. Bring the working end over the standing part, around behind it, and up through the gap between
   itself and the object. That is one half hitch.
3. Repeat step 2 in the same direction, just beyond the first. That is the second.
4. Pull the working end to slide both hitches down against the object.

*Check:* the two hitches together look like a clove hitch around the standing part.

### 5. Square knot (reef knot): joining two ends of the same size

{{figure fig-knot-square-knot}}

*Use:* tying a bundle, a bandage (→ 12-02), a sack. **Not for joining two ropes under serious
load**; it can roll apart. For that, use the sheet bend below.

1. Hold one end in each hand.
2. Cross the right end over the left and wrap it under, as if starting to tie a shoe.
3. Cross the left end over the right and wrap it under.
4. Pull all four strands to tighten.

*Check:* each rope's two strands leave the knot on the same side, and the knot lies flat. If it
looks twisted and lopsided, it is a "granny knot", which slips. Untie it and start again
("right over left, then left over right").

### 6. Trucker's hitch: a rope pulley for pulling things tight

{{figure fig-knot-truckers-hitch}}

*Use:* strapping a load down, tightening a tarp ridge line, pulling something taut. In theory it
triples your pull; in practice about double, because the rope rubs on itself. Still surprising.

1. Tie the far end of the rope to something fixed (a bowline or two half hitches). Bring the
   working end over the load to your anchor point.
2. In the standing part, about 2 feet above the anchor, make a small loop by crossing the rope
   over itself.
3. Reach through that small loop, grab a bight of the standing part from the anchor side, and pull
   it through to form a hanging loop. This is your "pulley". It will spill free later.
4. Pass the working end down around the anchor (a hook, a rail, a stake).
5. Bring the working end up and through the pulley loop from step 3.
6. Pull down on the working end. Haul until tight.
7. Pinch the tight strands with one hand. With the other, lock the working end off with two half
   hitches around both strands below the pulley loop.

*Check:* undo the half hitches and pull the working end back out; the whole thing should fall
apart at once. That is the point.

### Two worth adding

**Sheet bend: joining two ropes, even of different sizes.** {{figure fig-knot-sheet-bend}}

1. Make a bight (a U) in the end of the thicker rope. Hold it.
2. Push the end of the thinner rope up through the U from underneath.
3. Wrap the thin end around behind both legs of the U.
4. Tuck the thin end under itself, across the front of the U (not through the U).
5. Pull the thin rope's standing part to tighten.

*Check:* both short ends finish on the same side of the knot.

**Prusik: a loop that grips a rope.** {{figure fig-knot-prusik}} A short loop of thinner cord
wrapped around a thicker rope. It slides when loose and grips when pulled. Useful for an
adjustable attachment point on a ridge line. (Again: not for holding a person.)

1. Tie a short length of thin cord into a closed loop (a double overhand or sheet bend joins the
   ends).
2. Lay the loop behind the thick rope. Pass one end of the loop around the rope and through the
   other end of the loop.
3. Repeat twice more, inside the first wrap, so three wraps sit neatly side by side.
4. Pull the loop to tighten. It should grip when pulled and slide when you push the wraps.

### Lashings: turning poles into furniture

A lashing ties two poles together with many turns of rope. With a **square lashing** (poles
crossing at right angles) and a **diagonal lashing** (poles crossing at an angle, or springing
apart), you can build a sawbuck (→ 16-06), a drying rack (→ 11-03), a trellis (→ 05-10), a shelter
frame or an antenna mast support (→ 15-06).

{{figure fig-lashing-square}}

**Square lashing.**
1. Lay the two poles crossed at a right angle. Tie a clove hitch on the upright pole just below
   the crosspiece.
2. Wrap the rope over the crosspiece, behind the upright, under the crosspiece on the other side,
   and behind the upright again. That is one wrap around the joint.
3. Do three or four such wraps, keeping each tight and laid beside the last, not on top.
4. Now make two or three "frapping" turns: wrap between the two poles, around the wraps
   themselves, pulling hard. This tightens everything.
5. Finish with a clove hitch on the crosspiece.

{{figure fig-lashing-diagonal}}

**Diagonal lashing.**
1. Tie a timber hitch (a loop wrapped back around itself) around both poles, across the joint
   diagonally.
2. Make three or four wraps along that same diagonal.
3. Make three or four wraps along the other diagonal.
4. Make two frapping turns between the poles, then finish with a clove hitch.

## Cordage: what to stock and why

| Type | Strength | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 550 paracord | Strong for its size | Everything general | **Its core is seven separate thin strands**: thread, snares, fishing line, repairs (→ 16-04) |
| Bank line or tarred twine | Strong, thin | Lashing, snares, repairs | Resists rot and sunlight; grips well |
| 1/4 to 3/8 in utility rope | Real loads | Hauling, tying down, ridge lines | Nylon stretches; polyester does not |
| Rope 1/2 in and up | Heavy loads | Dragging logs, heavy lifting. **Not vehicle recovery** | See the block below |
| Natural fiber (jute, sisal, hemp) | Moderate | Anything burned or composted: garden ties, kindling bundles | Rots, which is sometimes the point (→ 05-10) |
| Baling wire, mechanic's wire | n/a | The metal version of cord | → 16-07 |
| Ratchet straps | Very strong | Securing loads | Sunlight weakens the webbing |
| Bungee cords | Light | Light securing | Perish; **the hooks cause eye injuries** |

**How much a rope can hold.** Never load a rope past **one-fifth of its labeled breaking
strength**, and remember that **a knot cuts a rope's strength by a third to a half** (US Army,
FM 5-125). Military-specification Type III paracord breaks at 550 lb when new, dry and unknotted,
so about 100 lb is its working load; commercial "550" cord is often weaker. Rubbing, sunlight and
age lower every figure further.

## Pulling a stuck vehicle: rope is the wrong tool

{{figure fig-vehicle-recovery-setup}}

{{#if has.vehicle}}Getting {{#if has.trailer}}a vehicle and a loaded trailer (→ 16-11){{else}}a
vehicle{{/if}} out of a ditch or a snowdrift is the most likely rope job on the road, and one of the
deadliest amateur mistakes.{{else}}If you ever ride in or borrow a vehicle that gets stuck, this is
the most likely rope job on the road, and one of the deadliest amateur mistakes.{{/if}} A snapped
line, a broken hook or a torn-off hitch ball at thousands of pounds of pull goes through windshields
and people.

```
[ ] DIG AND ADD TRACTION FIRST (22-05: shovel, traction mats,
    sand). Most "recoveries" are a shovel job. Pull only when
    that fails.
[ ] ONLY a rated recovery (kinetic) strap or rated tow strap with
    NO metal hooks. Never rope, never a chain, never a ratchet strap.
[ ] ATTACH ONLY to rated recovery points, or to the hitch RECEIVER
    with a rated shackle or soft shackle. NEVER to a hitch ball,
    a bumper, a tie-down loop or a suspension part.
[ ] LINE DAMPER: drape a blanket, coat or floor mat over the middle
    of the strap. It drops a broken strap instead of launching it.
[ ] EVERYONE ELSE stands at least 1.5 x the strap's length away and
    OUT OF LINE with the pull. Children well back or in the far
    vehicle, never beside the line.
[ ] PULL GENTLY, IN LINE, from a slack start. No running starts
    unless the strap is a kinetic rope made for it, and even then
    a few feet of slack, not a run.
[ ] Inspect the strap after every pull. A cut or glazed strap is done.
```

**Your strap's own printed instructions govern over this page.** Keep them with the strap
(→ 22-05).

## Care and failure

- **Sunlight destroys synthetic rope.** Rope left outdoors weakens within a season or two, and you
  cannot see it happen. Store rope out of the sun.
- **Rubbing is the main way rope fails.** A rope running over an edge cuts itself. Pad the edge with
  cloth, a piece of hose or wood.
- **Wet natural fiber rots.** Dry it before storing.
- **Knots weaken rope.** That is normal, and one reason utility rope is not for life safety.
- **Inspect before every load:** fuzz, cuts, shiny glazed patches, stiffness, discolouring.
- **Seal the ends** so they do not fray: melt synthetic rope with a lighter; wrap natural rope ends
  tightly with thin twine ("whipping").
- **Coil it and hang it.** A tangled rope in an emergency is a rope you do not have.

## Making cord from nothing

A real skill, and it works. It is slow; practice in summer with fresh material.

- **Plant fibers:** the inner bark of basswood, elm, willow or dogwood; the stems of stinging
  nettle, milkweed and dogbane; yucca leaves (→ 05-17 for what grows near you, and identify every
  plant with certainty).
- **The reverse-wrap method:** hold two bundles of fiber, twist each one away from you, and wrap
  them around each other toward you. The opposing twists lock. Learn it once and you can make cord
  from a ditch.
- **Rawhide and sinew** from animals you process (→ 05-09): very strong, and rawhide shrinks as it
  dries, which makes it excellent for binding a tool head (→ 16-08).
- **Cloth strips:** cut a sheet, shirt or tarp in one continuous spiral to make a long strip.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **550 paracord, several hundred feet** | The most useful cordage there is | Inner strands are a bonus |
| Bank line or tarred twine | Lashing, snares, repairs | Buy a spool |
| Utility rope, 1/4 and 3/8 in, 100+ ft each | Real loads, ridge lines | Polyester for low stretch |
| Heavier rope, 1/2 in and up | Dragging, lifting. **Not recovery** | Working load is one-fifth of breaking strength |
| **Rated recovery strap (no hooks) and a rated shackle or soft shackle** | The only safe way to pull a vehicle out | → 22-05; keep the strap's instructions |
| Jute or sisal twine | Garden, bundles, anything burned | → 05-10 |
| Ratchet straps, 4 to 6 | Load securing; better than knots on a vehicle | Check webbing for sun damage |
| Baling or mechanic's wire | Metal cordage | → 16-07 |
| Utility carabiners (not climbing-rated) | Quick attachment | Never for people |
| Pulleys | Mechanical advantage for heavy work | Useful |
| Whipping twine and a lighter | Finishing rope ends | Cheap |

**Scavenge:** rope and cord from garages, boats, farms, tarps, tents and curtain pulls; wire from
fencing and coat hangers (→ 16-07); baling twine around any farm; seat belts and webbing from
vehicles (very strong); cloth strips; plant fiber.

## When it runs out

- **Cord barely runs out if you keep it out of the sun.** Synthetic rope stored indoors lasts
  decades.
- **What gets used up:** paracord cut into short pieces (it is so useful it disappears), strap
  webbing, and bungees.
- **Length is the resource.** Do not cut a 100-foot rope into ten short pieces unless you must; you
  can always tie a bowline in the middle.
- **Substitute:** wire (→ 16-07), cloth strips, rawhide, and **lashings instead of hardware**:
  knowing knots means needing fewer brackets, screws and fittings.
- **The skill costs nothing.** Six knots and two lashings is an afternoon of learning that pays for
  years, and it is easy to teach (→ 18-03, → 20-07).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** stock rope, learn the knots, and use them: a clothesline (→ 11-03), a trellis
  (→ 05-10), a tarp over the woodpile, an antenna support (→ 15-06).
- **B, on the move:** paracord is one of the best weight-for-use items you can carry: a hundred
  feet, plus ratchet straps if you are driving.
- **C, settled:** fencing, animals, building, hauling, gates. Lashing skills reduce your need for
  hardware when there is no store.

pages.title: Sewing and mending gear
pages.body:
# Sewing and mending gear

**What this page is for.** Repairing and making anything of fabric: packs, tarps, tents, boots,
canvas, webbing, straps, cushions. Clothing in particular is on → 11-07. The planning point:
fabric is everywhere, in every house and abandoned building, but **thread and needles are tiny,
cheap and almost impossible to make well.** Stock them in amounts that feel absurd. They are what
turn abundant material into usable goods.

> **Sewing needles and thread are not surgical tools.** Nothing here is about closing wounds. That
> is → 12-14, and most wounds in a long emergency should not be closed at all.

## Do this now

1. **Buy a real sewing kit, then far more thread and needles than it holds.** Include heavy-duty
   and upholstery thread, leather or canvas needles, and curved needles.
2. **Learn four stitches this month:** running stitch, backstitch, whipstitch and saddle stitch.
   That is the whole practical set.
3. **Buy a stitching awl and waxed thread** for boots, packs, belts and canvas (→ 11-06). An awl is
   a sharp spike on a handle for punching holes in thick material; a stitching awl also carries
   thread.
4. **Start a parts bin.** Every worn-out garment or bag gets stripped of zippers, buttons, snaps,
   elastic, webbing, buckles and usable fabric before it is thrown away.

## The four stitches

{{figure fig-four-stitches}}

**1. Running stitch.** Needle in and out along a line, evenly spaced. Fast and weak. *Use:*
temporary tacking, gathering fabric.

**2. Backstitch.** Each new stitch goes backward to meet the end of the previous one, so the thread
is continuous on the underside. **Strong.** *Use:* any seam that takes load. Make this your
default. Two passes are stronger still.

**3. Whipstitch.** The thread loops over the edge again and again. *Use:* joining two edges,
binding a raw edge so it does not fray, closing a hole, fixing the edge of a patch.

**4. Saddle stitch.** **Two needles on one thread, passing through the same hole from both
sides.** *Use:* leather, heavy canvas, webbing, boots, packs. It is the strongest hand stitch, and
unlike a machine stitch it **does not unravel when one stitch breaks.** Punch the holes first with
an awl. This is the stitch that makes heavy gear repairable.

1. Punch a line of holes with the awl, evenly spaced.
2. Thread a needle onto each end of one length of waxed thread.
3. Pass one needle through the first hole and pull until the thread is centered.
4. At each next hole, push the left needle through from the left, then the right needle through
   the same hole from the right. Pull both tight.
5. At the end, go back two or three holes the same way to lock it, and trim.

**Plus, for clothing:** darning and patching (→ 11-07).

## Techniques worth knowing

- **Backstitch anything under load.** Running stitch is only for tacking.
- **Round the corners of patches.** Square corners peel up.
- **Patch from the inside** for a flat repair; **from the outside** where it needs to resist
  rubbing.
- **Reinforce before it fails.** Add a second layer at knees, elbows, seat, pack-strap anchors and
  the bottom corners of bags while they are new.
- **Bar-tack the stress points.** A bar-tack is a short, dense block of stitches over the same spot,
  where a strap meets a bag, at a pocket corner, at the end of a zipper. This is where gear fails.
- **Wax your thread** for heavy work. Run it across a block of beeswax: it gets stronger, sheds
  water and stops tangling.
- **Match the thread to the fabric.** If the thread is much stronger than the fabric, the fabric
  tears instead of the thread breaking, which is the worse failure.
- **Seal seams on waterproof gear.** Every needle hole is a leak. Use seam sealer, wax or silicone
  after stitching (→ 11-03).

## Repairing gear

{{figure fig-box-stitch-webbing}}

| Item | How |
|---|---|
| Pack strap torn out | Sew a backing patch inside, then bar-tack heavily. The classic failure |
| Tarp or tent tear | Patch both sides, round the corners, seal the seam. Nylon repair tape for a fast field fix |
| Boot seam or sole | Awl, waxed thread, saddle stitch; glue for soles (→ 11-06, → 16-05) |
| Zipper | Squeeze a loose slider gently with pliers; replace a lost pull with a loop of cord; bar-tack a broken end stop. Spare zippers are gold |
| Webbing or strap | Overlap the ends and sew a box with an X inside it ("box stitch"), the standard strong joint |
| Canvas | Patch and saddle-stitch; wax the seam |
| Leather | Awl, waxed thread, saddle stitch, then rub in leather conditioner |
| Cushions and upholstery | Curved needle; this is what they are for |
| Window screens and netting | Patch with fine mesh. Keeps insects out, which matters for disease |

## Making, not just mending

Once you can sew, the material in every house becomes goods:

{{#if has.child}}- **Cutting adult clothes down for the children** (→ 11-02). This is often the
  most valuable use, because children outgrow clothes and nothing stops that.
{{else}}- **Cutting adult clothes down for children** in your group (→ 11-02). Children outgrow
  clothes and nothing stops that.
{{/if}}- **Wool blankets into mittens, boot liners, vests and ponchos** (→ 11-05).
- **Tarps into shelters, gaiters, over-mittens, aprons and bags.**
- **Bags and packs** from canvas and webbing.
- **Cloth diapers and menstrual pads** from flannel (→ 13-08).
- **Reusable dressings** from clean cotton (→ 12-02).
- **Insulated curtains** for windows (→ 08-03), a large heat saving.

## Machines

- **An electric sewing machine multiplies output** while there is power. It is a modest load.
- **A hand-crank or treadle (foot-pedal) machine needs no power at all.** If you see one at an
  estate sale, buy it. They were built to last a century and can be repaired.
- **Learn hand sewing anyway.** The machine is a bonus, not the plan.

## Teaching it

- **Every adult should be able to sew**, so the skill does not live in one person.
{{#if has.young_child}}- **Young children can start** with a blunt plastic needle, yarn and
  burlap. It builds dexterity and is a calm, indoor, screen-free activity in a long winter
  (→ 20-07, → 21-02).
{{else}}- **Children can start** with a blunt plastic needle, yarn and burlap. It builds dexterity
  and is a calm, indoor activity in a long winter (→ 20-07, → 21-02).
{{/if}}- **Sewing is one of the most tradeable skills there is** (→ 18-03). Everyone's gear fails;
  few can fix it.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Thread: many spools, several weights** | The limiting consumable | Include heavy-duty and upholstery |
| **Needles: a large assortment** | They bend, break and vanish | Include leather or canvas, and curved |
| Stitching awl | Boots, packs, canvas, leather | The heavy-duty tool |
| Waxed thread | Heavy repairs | Or wax your own |
| Beeswax block | Waxing thread; also candles and boots | Multi-use (→ 10-04) |
| Fabric scissors kept only for fabric, and a seam ripper | Sharp scissors make everything easier | Never cut paper with them |
| Thimble, pins, many safety pins | A safety pin is a repair in itself | |
| **Spare zippers, buttons, snaps, hook-and-loop, elastic, buckles, webbing** | The parts that fail and cannot be made | Small and cheap; stock deep |
| Fabric: canvas, denim, ripstop nylon, flannel | Patch and project stock | Plus the rag bag |
| Nylon repair tape | Field fix for tarps and shells | A roll in every kit |
| Seam sealer | Every needle hole is a leak | → 11-03 |
| Sewing machine; hand-crank or treadle if found | Output multiplier | Watch estate sales |
| **Rag bag and parts bin** | Nothing is thrown out whole | Start today |

**Substitutes:**
- **Fabric:** curtains, sheets, upholstery, tarps, tents, clothing, seat covers. Abundant
  (→ 22-02, → 11-05).
- **Thread:** paracord inner strands (excellent, → 16-03), dental floss (very strong), threads
  pulled from fabric edges, fishing line (strong, but it can cut fabric).
- **Needles:** hard to improvise. A sharpened wire with a filed eye works badly. Stock real ones.
- **Awl:** a sharpened nail, an ice pick, a punch.
- **Buttons:** cut from other clothes, or carved from wood, bone or antler.
- **Webbing and buckles:** seat belts from vehicles (very strong), backpack straps, luggage.
- **Wax:** beeswax, candle wax, paraffin.

## When it runs out

- **Thread and needles run out before fabric does.** Stock both in amounts that feel excessive.
  They weigh nothing and never expire.
- **Think in repairs, not spools.** A spool goes a long way on clothing and a short way on heavy
  canvas with doubled thread. Add them to → 23-02.
- **Make it last:** light thread for light work, heavy-duty only where load is carried. **Repair
  early**: a small tear uses a fraction of the thread of a big one.
- **Resupply:** unpicking seams from unwanted clothes yields usable thread, and every discarded
  item yields fasteners. The parts bin is a real supply line.
- **Substitute:** paracord strands, floss, cloth strips, wire (→ 16-07) for some joins, glue
  (→ 16-05) for some repairs. Nothing substitutes for a needle.
- **The long view:** if this lasts years, the chain continues into spinning and weaving, and fiber
  animals (→ 11-05). It starts with a backstitch, which starts with one evening now.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** build the kit, learn the four stitches, start the rag bag and parts bin, and
  reinforce gear before it fails.
- **B, on the move:** a small repair kit: needles, strong thread, safety pins, nylon repair tape, a
  spare zipper pull and a small awl. A blown pack strap or boot seam in winter is a real emergency
  (→ 11-06), and a ten-minute repair prevents it.
- **C, settled:** repair and remaking become routine work. A treadle machine changes everything.
  Sewing is one of the easiest things to trade (→ 18-03).

pages.title: Improvised repairs: tape, wire, glue, patch

photo_slots.caption: Our repair shelf: adhesives with their dates, tapes, wire, clamps, the parts bin

pages.body:
# Improvised repairs: tape, wire, glue, patch

**What this page is for.** Fixing broken things with what is on hand, and knowing which things
must never be fixed that way. With no store, "repair it" replaces "replace it" for good, and the
ability to fix things from a shelf of tape, wire and glue is one of the most valuable skills in a
long emergency.

> **CAUTION. Know what you must NOT improvise.** Some repairs kill people when they fail:
> - **Fuel lines and fuel containers** (fire, → 06-06).
> - **Anything that carries smoke or exhaust:** stovepipe, chimney, vent connectors. A leak lets
>   out carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that kills in minutes (→ 08-02, → 29-03).
>   A taped stovepipe joint is a poisoning waiting to happen.
> - **Pressure vessels and propane or gas fittings.**
> - **Beams, joists and posts holding up a roof or floor.**
> - **Brakes and steering on a vehicle.**
> - **Electrical wiring inside walls** (→ 09-08, → 29-04).
>
> Those get a proper repair or they are taken out of service. Everything else is fair game.

## Do this now

1. **Build a repair shelf** and stock it: tapes, glues, wire, fasteners, patches, sealants. All
   cheap now.
2. **Write the date of purchase on every glue.** Two-part epoxy, super glue and construction
   adhesive all age. Rotate them.
3. **Fix three broken things this month** that you have been putting off. Repair is a skill, and
   skills need practice.
4. **Start a parts bin and a materials pile:** screws, hinges, brackets, wire, scrap wood, sheet
   metal, fabric, anything salvaged from what you throw out (→ 22-02).

{{photo repair-shelf}}

## Three questions before any repair

1. **What happens if this repair fails?** If the answer involves fire, carbon monoxide, a fall or
   a vehicle at speed, do not improvise.
2. **What kind of force is on it?** Pulling (tension), squeezing (compression), sliding
   (shear) or shaking (vibration)? **Vibration breaks glued joints and loosens fasteners.**
   Pulling needs mechanical fastening. Squeezing is forgiving.
3. **Is this temporary or permanent?** Say it out loud. A temporary repair that becomes
   permanent by neglect is how things fail badly later. **Mark temporary repairs with tape and
   write them on a list.**

## Glues, and what each is for

Read every product's label for the cure time and the ventilation it needs (→ 29-14).

| Glue | Best for | Fails at |
|---|---|---|
| **Two-part epoxy** | The strongest general repair: metal, wood, ceramic, filling gaps | Heat; flexing; sunlight over time |
| **Super glue (cyanoacrylate)** | Small, tight, rigid joints; with baking soda as a hard filler | Impact; gaps; damp over time. **Reacts hot with cotton and wool** |
| **Construction adhesive** | Wood, subfloor, large surfaces | Small precise parts |
| **Contact cement** | Boot soles, laminates, large flat bonds. **Coat both sides, wait until dry to the touch (about 10 to 20 minutes), then press together once, hard. No clamping; it grabs on contact** | Gaps; oily surfaces; pressing it while still wet (a weak bond that lets go in the cold) |
| **Flexible urethane shoe adhesive** | Boots, gaskets, gear that bends | Slow cure |
| **PVC cement** | Rigid plastic pipe of that type | Only that plastic |
| **Silicone sealant** | Sealing gaps against water | Any load |
| **Steel-filled epoxy putty** | Metal repair, filling stripped threads and gaps | Heat; high pressure |
| **Wood glue or hide glue** | Wood joints; hide glue can be made and undone with heat | Damp |
| **Pine pitch, powdered charcoal and a little fat** | Traditional glue you can make | Heat; only modest strength |

**Super glue plus baking soda.** Put down a drop of glue, dust it with baking soda, repeat. It
hardens instantly into a hard filler you can file and drill. Good for filling holes and rebuilding
broken plastic tabs. **The fill gets hot for a few seconds: set the part down, do not hold it,
and keep the fumes out of your eyes.**

## Tapes, and their real limits

| Tape | Good for | The truth |
|---|---|---|
| Duct tape | Fast temporary anything | Lets go with heat, cold, sunlight and time. **Never on skin** |
| Heavy cloth tape | Stronger duct tape | Same limits, better glue |
| **Self-fusing (self-amalgamating) silicone or rubber tape** | Sealing and waterproofing; it fuses to itself, not to the object | Excellent for radio cable joints (→ 15-06), hoses, handles |
| Electrical tape | Insulating, wrapping | Unwinds with heat and time |
| Gaffer tape | Temporary; peels off cleanly | Not waterproof |
| **Ripstop nylon repair tape** | Tarps, tents, jackets, sleeping bags | Durable; keep a roll in every kit |
| Aluminum foil tape | Heating ducts | The tape for duct joints, **but never a chimney or stovepipe repair** (→ 08-02) |
| PTFE thread tape | Threaded pipe joints | Seals; adds no strength |

**Duct tape is not a repair, it is a delay.** Use it, then do the real fix.

## Mechanical fixes: the ones that last

Mechanical repairs outlast glued ones, especially with shaking, cold and load.

- **Baling or mechanic's wire.** Twisted tight with pliers, ends tucked in, it holds things
  together indefinitely. The most underrated repair material there is (→ 16-07).
- **A bolt right through, with washers on both sides**, beats a glued joint every time.
- **Screws into a backing block** spread the load into sound material.
- **Sister boards:** a broken wooden piece gets a new board bolted alongside it (→ 16-08).
- **Hose clamps** (screw-tightened metal bands) hold and join round things. Stock many sizes.
- **Cotter pins and safety wire** stop things shaking loose.
- **Pop rivets:** joins sheet metal from one side. A rivet gun is cheap and very useful.
- **Lashing** (→ 16-03): for poles, a good lashing is stronger and more forgiving than most
  hardware.
- **Rawhide:** wrapped wet and left to dry, it shrinks and grips like a clamp. Excellent for tool
  handles (→ 16-08).

## The repairs you will actually face

| Broken | How |
|---|---|
| Tool handle | Replace or re-hang it (→ 16-08); wedge tight. Wire and epoxy a crack only as a stopgap |
| Boot sole coming off | Clean and roughen both faces. **Urethane shoe glue:** apply, press, clamp or weight for 24 hours. **Contact cement:** coat both faces, let dry to the touch, press once hard, no clamp. Follow the label (→ 11-06) |
| Tarp or tent tear | Ripstop tape both sides now; sew and seal later (→ 16-04) |
| Leaking container (water, not fuel) | Epoxy putty, silicone, or a gasket cut from rubber sheet |
| Broken plastic part | Super glue and baking soda; epoxy; a metal splint; or make a metal replacement (→ 16-08) |
| Stripped screw hole in wood | Pack it with wooden matchsticks or toothpicks and glue, let dry, drive the screw again |
| Stripped thread in metal | Fill with epoxy putty and re-cut; a thread insert; or go up one size |
| Broken zipper | → 16-04, → 11-07 |
| Cracked wooden furniture | Glue and clamp; sister a board; bolt through |
| Water hose or pipe leak | Self-fusing tape and a hose clamp. **Never on gas or fuel lines.** Burst pipes: → 16-12 |
| Broken window | Plastic sheet and tape for now; plywood is warmer (→ 08-03, → 16-12) |

## Working safely

- **Ventilate for glues and solvents.** The vapors are toxic and many are flammable. Read the
  label.
- **Never near an open flame or a running stove or heater.** Many glues and solvents catch fire,
  and a wood stove is an ignition source (→ 06-06).
- **Eye protection** for glue, wire ends and springs (→ 16-01).
- **Nitrile gloves, never cotton, around super glue.** Epoxy and super glue stick to skin
  instantly, and **super glue soaking into cotton or wool (a glove, a rag, a sleeve) reacts fast
  and hot enough to smoke and burn.** Never wipe super glue with a cotton rag.
- **Tetanus:** sharp wire and metal edges cause puncture wounds. Keep vaccinations current
  (CDC, About Tetanus; → 12-04).
- **Children away from glues and solvents**, which are a poisoning and eye hazard; store them
  locked (→ 20-02).
- **Never hide a weakness.** A repair you can see is safer than one you cannot.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Two-part epoxy and steel-filled epoxy putty** | The strongest general repairs | Date and rotate |
| **Super glue and baking soda** | Instant filler; many uses | Stock several small tubes |
| Contact cement and urethane shoe glue | Boots, flexible repairs | → 11-06 |
| Construction adhesive, wood glue, silicone | Wood, sealing | |
| **Baling or mechanic's wire, a lot** | Mechanical repairs outlast glue | The most underrated item |
| **Self-fusing tape** | Sealing, waterproofing, cable joints | → 15-06 |
| Duct tape, cloth tape, electrical tape, **ripstop tape**, foil tape | Different jobs | Ripstop in every kit |
| **Hose clamps, assorted** | Clamping and joining | Endlessly useful |
| Pop rivet gun and rivets | Sheet metal and hardware | Cheap |
| Screws, bolts, nuts, washers, nails | → 16-07 | Deep stock |
| Cotter pins, safety wire, cable ties | Stop things shaking loose | Cable ties weaken in sunlight |
| Rubber sheet or old inner tubes | Gaskets, straps, patches | Free from a bike shop |
| Clamps of several types | You always want more | → 16-01 |
| Materials pile and parts bin | Raw material for everything here | Organized enough to find things |

**Substitutes:**
- **Wire:** coat hangers, fencing, electrical cable.
- **Rubber:** inner tubes make gaskets, straps, bindings and rubber bands; also tires, hoses, shoe
  soles.
- **Sheet metal:** cans, roof flashing, ductwork, appliance panels (→ 16-08).
- **Fasteners:** from anything being thrown out (→ 22-02).
- **Glue:** pine pitch with charcoal and a little fat; hide glue from hides and hooves (→ 05-09).
- **Clamping:** a loop of rope twisted tight with a stick (a "Spanish windlass"), wedges, weight,
  drying rawhide.
- **What you cannot make: modern epoxy.** Stock it and rotate it.

## When it runs out

- **Glues run out and expire; wire and fasteners barely do.** So stock wire, fasteners and
  hardware heavily (→ 16-07), and treat glue as precious.
- **Rotate glues every year** at the annual review (→ 25-10). Buy fresh rather than hoarding old.
- **Use mechanical repairs where you can** and save glue for what truly needs it. Repair early and
  small.
- **Resupply:** every abandoned garage, shed and workshop is full of these materials (→ 22-02).
  Hardware and fasteners are good barter goods (→ 18-02).
- **The real resource is the habit.** A household that fixes by default uses a fraction of the
  materials and keeps working far longer. Build the habit now, while replacing is still possible
  (→ 23-05).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** build the repair shelf, fix things, start the parts bin. Practice on things that
  do not matter.
- **B, on the move:** a tiny kit: ripstop tape, a few feet of wire, cable ties, super glue, needle
  and thread (→ 16-04), a multi-tool. Field repairs only need to reach the next stop.
- **C, settled:** repair becomes the default and the workshop becomes real infrastructure: a vise,
  an anvil, a materials pile, a parts bin (→ 16-01, → 16-08). Being the household that can fix
  things is a real position of value (→ 18-03).
