photo_slots.caption: Our wood station: chopping block, sawbuck, the bleeding-control kit and where it hangs

pages.body:
# Axes, saws and wood tools

**What this page is for.** Cutting and splitting firewood by hand and with a chainsaw without
losing a foot, a leg or a hand. Wood processing is the most frequent dangerous work a household
does without the grid: every day, all winter, often cold and tired, with tools that cut through
bone.

> **CAUTION. This is where serious injuries actually happen.**
> - **An axe wound to the foot or shin, and a chainsaw wound to the leg, are among the most likely
>   severe-bleeding injuries in this whole binder** (→ 12-02). A bleeding-control kit with a
>   tourniquet lives at the woodpile, not in the house (→ 12-08).
> - **Chainsaw kickback** is the bar being thrown back toward the operator's face and body when
>   the tip touches something or the wood pinches the chain. The University of Missouri Extension
>   names kickback, pushback and pull-in as the forces that make operators lose control
>   (Operating a Chain Saw Safely). Most chainsaw injuries are deep cuts to the legs and the left
>   hand. **Chaps, a helmet with face shield, hearing protection and real instruction are not
>   optional.**
> - **Felling a standing tree kills experienced people.** Learn it from a person, not a page. A
>   leaning, dead or wind-thrown tree is more dangerous, not less.
> - **Never refuel a hot saw, and never pour fuel near a flame or running engine.** Fuel is never
>   stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance: the vapor ignites (floor,
>   → 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Buy chainsaw chaps, a helmet with face shield and ear muffs, and cut-resistant gloves before
   you next cut anything.** Chaps are made of long fibers that pull out and jam the chain (University
   of Missouri Extension). They cost little next to a leg.
2. **Hang a bleeding-control kit with a tourniquet at the woodpile** (→ 12-08), and learn to use
   it one-handed on yourself (→ 12-02).
3. **Buy the hand set:** a good axe, a splitting maul, steel wedges, a bow saw with many spare
   blades, and a crosscut saw. These are what you will use in year two (→ 06-04).
4. **Get instruction:** a county Extension class, a forestry course, or an experienced person. One
   afternoon changes your risk for good.
5. **Wear wool, not fleece, near fire and hot work** (→ 11-05), and nothing loose near a saw.

{{photo woodpile-station}}

## The tools, by job

| Tool | Job | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Splitting maul** (heavy, blunt wedge-shaped head) | Splitting rounds | The firewood workhorse. Not for chopping |
| **Steel wedges and a sledge** | Knotty or large rounds | Have two wedges |
| **Felling axe** (long handle, thinner head) | Chopping across the grain, removing limbs | Sharp, rounded edge (→ 16-02) |
| **Hatchet** | Kindling | **The most common injury tool**: the short handle puts your leg in its swing |
| **Bow saw** | Cutting logs to length ("bucking") | Fast, cheap; **blades are the consumable** |
| **Crosscut hand saw** | Larger wood, quiet, no fuel | Slower; sharpenable if traditional |
| **Folding saw** | Limbs; carry on the move | Very useful |
| **Chainsaw** | Volume, while fuel lasts | Fastest and most dangerous |
| **Peavey or cant hook** (a lever with a swinging hook) | Rolling logs | Saves backs and fingers |
| **Sawbuck** (an X-shaped stand) | Holds wood at working height while sawing | **Build one**; it prevents many injuries |
| **Chopping block** | **For splitting: low, knee height or less, wide and stable. For kindling with a hatchet: higher**, so hands stay clear | See rule 1 |

{{figure fig-sawbuck}}

## The axe rules that prevent the injury

{{figure fig-chopping-block-height}}

1. **A chopping block at the right height.** This matters most. A round on the bare ground means
   the axe's swing carries on into your shins. **For splitting, a low block (knee height or less)**
   means the head arrives near the bottom of its swing with the handle about level, so a miss
   hits the block or the ground. A waist-high splitting block makes a glancing blow travel forward
   and down into your legs. The higher block is only for hatchet and kindling work.
2. **Feet apart, out of the swing.** Stand so that a glancing blow goes between your feet or into
   the block, not into a leg.
3. **Nothing behind you or overhead.** Check the whole swing path every time.
4. **Sharp** (→ 16-02). A dull axe glances off.
5. **Check the head is tight** every session. A loose head flies off. Re-wedge or re-hang it
   (→ 16-08).
6. **Never chop when exhausted, cold or in poor light.** That is the condition you will most often
   be in, which is why the rule matters. Stop and do it tomorrow.
7. **Children and bystanders well clear**, inside a wide, enforced circle (→ 20-02). Whether older
   children split kindling is a household choice: {{choice DC-24}} (→ 30-25).
8. **Eye protection.** Chips fly; frozen wood shatters.
9. **Never hold wood with your hand while striking it.** Split on a stable surface.
10. **Frozen wood splits more easily but shatters more**, and chips edges. Eye protection
    especially in winter.

## Chainsaws

{{figure fig-chainsaw-kickback-zone}}

**Kickback** happens in a fraction of a second when **the upper tip of the bar** touches wood or
anything else, or when the wood closes and pinches the chain. The bar is thrown up and back toward
you.

**Protective gear** (OSHA, Chain Saw Safety; University of Missouri Extension):
- **Chaps or cut-resistant trousers.** The legs are the most common contact point. Chaps overlap
  the boot tops.
- **Helmet with face shield and ear muffs**: falling limbs, chips, and permanent hearing loss
  (CDC/NIOSH, About Noise and Hearing Loss).
- **Safety glasses** under the shield.
- **Leather gloves.**
- **Steel-toe boots.**
- **No loose clothing.**

**Operating rules:**
- **Both hands on the saw, always, thumb wrapped around the front handle.**
- **Never cut with the upper tip of the bar** (the kickback zone).
- **Never cut above shoulder height.**
- **Firm footing. Never on a ladder. Never in a tree** without specific training.
- **Watch for pinching.** Before cutting, think about which side of the log is being squeezed and
  which stretched, and use wedges. **If the bar is pinched: engine off, then drive a wedge into
  the cut (or lift the log with the peavey) and lift the saw out by hand. Never yank a running saw
  free, and never start it while pinched.**
- **Test the chain brake before every session.** With the engine idling, push the front hand guard
  forward. The chain must stop instantly. If it does not, the saw does not run today.
- **Chain brake on whenever you walk with the saw.**
- **Cut chaps are finished.** Any cut that reaches the fibers means retire them; patched chaps do
  not jam a chain. Replace a cracked helmet too.
- **Let the saw cool before refuelling** (→ 06-06, → 06-07).
- **Do not cut alone if you can avoid it.** With no ambulance coming, cutting alone is a much bigger
  risk than it is today.
- **Sharpen the chain properly** (→ 16-02). A badly sharpened chain kicks back more.

**Chainsaw fuel goes stale.** Gasoline mixed with two-stroke oil does not keep well (→ 29-01).
Whether to use old fuel in a saw is a household choice: {{choice DC-17}} (→ 30-18).

## Felling: the honest version

**Do not learn to fell trees from a book.** Felling means reading lean, tension, rot, wind, trees
hung up in other trees, trunks that split upward ("barber chair"), and escape routes. It kills
professionals every year. Get instruction in person.

**And you mostly do not need to fell.** Most emergency firewood comes from **storm debris, standing
dead trees, downed limbs and wood already on the ground** (→ 06-04), which is safer, already partly
dry, and plentiful after any windstorm. **Cutting to length and splitting downed wood is the job.
Felling is the exception.**

**If you must:** clear two escape paths at 45 degrees behind you, look up for hung-up trees and
loose dead limbs ("widow-makers"), never work under a hung-up tree, and never fell near power
lines.

## Winter

- **Frozen wood is harder on edges and shatters more.** Sharpen more often; wear eye protection.
- **Cold hands are clumsy.** Warm up before precise work (→ 11-04).
- **Short days tempt you to keep working in poor light** (→ 10-01). Do not.
- **Ice underfoot while swinging an axe** is a bad combination. Traction first (→ 11-06).
- **Chainsaws start hard in deep cold**, like any small engine (→ 09-15).
- **This is the work you will do at the worst time, every winter.** Build the safe habits now,
  while it is easy.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Chainsaw chaps** | Legs are the contact point; chaps jam the chain | Overlap the boots |
| **Helmet with face shield and ear muffs** | Falling limbs, chips, hearing | |
| Cut-resistant gloves, steel-toe boots | The rest of the protective gear | |
| **Splitting maul, two steel wedges, sledge** | The firewood workhorse | |
| Felling axe and hatchet | Chopping, limbing, kindling | Keep sharp (→ 16-02) |
| **Bow saw and MANY spare blades** | Bucking; blades are the bottleneck | Over-stock |
| Traditional crosscut saw | The year-three saw | With a saw file (→ 16-02) |
| Folding saw | Limbs; on the move | |
| **Sawbuck** | Holds wood at working height | Build from scrap or lashed poles (→ 16-03) |
| **Chopping block at the right height** | The best injury prevention | A big round on end |
| Peavey or cant hook | Moving logs without hands | |
| Files: mill bastard, chainsaw files, depth-gauge tool | Sharpening (→ 16-02) | Right size for your chain |
| Bar oil, spare chain, spark plug, air filter | Small-engine upkeep | Stock ahead |
| **Bleeding-control kit with a tourniquet, at the woodpile** | Minutes matter | → 12-08 |
| Wool outer layers | Synthetics melt near fire | → 11-05 |

**Substitutes:**
- **Axes and mauls** from estate sales and old sheds. Old axe heads are often excellent steel and
  can be re-handled (→ 16-08).
- **Handles:** buy spare hickory or ash handles, or shape one from a straight-grained hardwood
  limb.
- **Wedges:** hardwood wedges ("gluts") made with an axe work.
- **Sawbuck:** scrap lumber or lashed poles, half an hour (→ 16-03).
- **Peavey:** a stout pole as a lever.
- **What you cannot make: chaps, and hardened saw blades.** Buy both now.

## When it runs out

- **Saw blades are the bottleneck of the whole firewood plan** (→ 06-04). Bow-saw blades are
  disposable; stock many. **Chainsaw chains are the opposite**: they can be filed many times
  (→ 16-02), so stock files deep and chains moderately. **Own a traditional crosscut saw** as the
  tool that still works in year five.
- **Files wear out.** Stock several.
- **Chainsaw fuel and bar oil end.** Plan for the chainsaw as a first-year tool and the axe and
  bow saw as the long-term ones.
- **Handles break.** Stock spares and learn to re-hang a head (→ 16-08).
- **Count it:** blades per cord of wood and files per season. Put both on → 23-02.
- **Hand tools cost calories.** The axe and crosscut saw do everything the chainsaw does, slower
  and with far more effort, which matters when food is short (→ 04-18). Budget labor as well as
  tools.
- **The habits outlast the tools.** A person who splits safely, sharpens well and knows when to
  stop still has all their limbs in year three (→ 12-09).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** storm debris and downed limbs are your wood (→ 06-04). Set up the block and the
  sawbuck, keep the bleeding-control kit there, and enforce a child-free circle (→ 20-02).
  Chainsaw while fuel lasts; hand tools after.
- **B, on the move:** a folding saw and a hatchet, no more. Fires for warmth and cooking, not a
  winter supply.
- **C, settled:** the biggest wood workload and the biggest risk. Do not cut alone if you can avoid
  it, get real instruction before you need it, keep the kit at the work site, and build the
  sawbuck, block and wood shed properly in the first month (→ 01-04).

pages.title: Fasteners, wire and hardware to stock

photo_slots.caption: Our sorted hardware: bins, labels, where the salvage is kept apart

pages.body:
# Fasteners, wire and hardware to stock

**What this page is for.** The screws, nails, bolts, wire and small hardware that every other
repair in this binder depends on. It is the dullest page in the binder and one of the most quietly
important. Fasteners cost almost nothing, never expire, and nobody stocks enough. Running out of
the right screw stops a repair dead. They are also among the best barter goods there are (→ 18-02).

> **Two cautions.** **Do not use salvaged bolts of unknown strength for anything that holds weight
> or holds people.** A bolt that looks fine can be the wrong grade, and you cannot tell by looking.
> **Rusty metal punctures carry a tetanus risk** (CDC, About Tetanus): keep every household
> member's vaccination current (→ 12-04).

## Do this now

1. **Buy assorted fastener kits** (screws, bolts, nuts, washers, nails in many sizes) **plus bulk
   boxes of the sizes you use most.**
2. **Buy wire:** mechanic's or baling wire, galvanized fence wire, stainless safety wire. Wire is
   the most underrated repair material there is (→ 16-05).
3. **Buy hardware:** hinges, brackets, hose clamps, eye bolts, screw eyes, hooks, chain,
   turnbuckles, springs.
4. **Set up sorted, labeled storage** so any size can be found in seconds. Unsorted hardware is
   nearly useless.
5. **Start the salvage habit:** strip fasteners and hardware from anything you throw away (→ 22-02).

{{photo hardware-storage}}

## What to stock

**Screws: the most-used fastener**
- Wood or construction screws in #6, #8 and #10 thickness, from 3/4 inch to 4 inches long. Buy the
  common sizes by the pound.
- Coated deck screws for anything outdoors.
- Drywall screws are cheap and everywhere **but brittle**: fine for light work, not for anything
  structural or under sideways load.
- Sheet-metal (self-tapping) screws for metal, roofing and ductwork.
- Machine screws and nuts in common sizes.
- Lag screws (big, hex-headed wood screws) for heavy timber.

**Nails**
- Common nails from 6d to 16d ("d", or "penny", is the old size system: bigger number, longer nail),
  framing nails, finish nails, roofing nails, masonry nails.
- **Nails are cheaper than screws and hold better against sideways load; screws hold better against
  being pulled straight out.** Stock both.

{{figure fig-nail-vs-screw-shear}}

**Bolts, nuts and washers**
- Carriage bolts and hex bolts, 1/4 inch through 1/2 inch, in a range of lengths.
- Matching nuts, plus nylon-insert lock nuts ("nylock"), which do not shake loose.
- **Washers, flat and lock, in every size.** They are the most commonly missing item, and they
  matter: they spread load and stop a bolt head pulling through.
- Threaded rod in a few lengths. Cut it to make any bolt you need.
- **Both inch (SAE) and metric**, because you will be repairing things of unknown origin.

**Wire**

| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| **Mechanic's or baling wire** (soft, dark annealed steel) | General repair. Twist it and forget it. Buy a big roll |
| Galvanized fence wire | Outdoors; fencing, garden, structures |
| Stainless safety wire | Fine, strong, rust-free; locking bolts so they cannot turn |
| Copper wire | Electrical work (→ 09-08), and soft enough for delicate binding |
| **Hardware cloth** (stiff welded steel mesh) | Rodent-proofing (→ 04-11, → 13-03), tree guards (→ 05-13), screens, sifting |
| Chicken wire | Fencing, plant protection, compost bins |
| Smooth high-tensile wire | Fencing on rural land |

**Hardware**
- Hinges in several sizes, hasps and latches, brackets, angle iron, corner braces, flat mending
  plates.
- **Hose clamps in a full range of sizes.** Endlessly useful (→ 16-05).
- Eye bolts, screw eyes, hooks, S-hooks, shackles, quick links.
- Light and medium chain, and turnbuckles (for tightening a wire or cable).
- Springs, cotter pins, clevis pins, R-clips.
- Casters and wheels. Moving heavy things without a vehicle matters more than you would think.
- Pulleys (→ 16-03).
- Cable ties in several sizes: fast and useful, but **sunlight and cold make them brittle.** Not a
  permanent outdoor fastener.

**Consumables that live with the hardware**
- Sandpaper in a range of grits, steel wool (also stuffs rodent holes), wire brushes, penetrating
  oil, thread-locking liquid, anti-seize paste, grease and machine oil, rust converter, primer and
  paint for exposed steel.

## The details that matter

- **Dissimilar metals corrode each other** when wet. Do not use bare steel fasteners in aluminum,
  or in pressure-treated lumber, which eats plain steel fast. **Use hot-dip galvanized or stainless
  fasteners outdoors.**
- **Drill a pilot hole in hardwood and near board ends**, or the wood splits, especially old, dry
  or frozen lumber.
- **Nails bend; screws snap.** For a joint carrying sideways load, use nails or bolts. For holding
  against pull-out, use screws.
- **Anything that vibrates** gets lock washers, nylock nuts, thread locker or safety wire.
- **On a rusted bolt, penetrating oil and patience beat force**, and heat helps a great deal
  (→ 16-08).
- **Do not over-tighten.** A stripped thread or snapped bolt turns a five-minute job into an hour.
- **Old painted hardware and wood may carry lead paint.** Do not sand or burn it indoors, and keep
  children away from the dust (CDC, About Lead in the Home).

## Storage that makes it usable

- **Labeled, sorted, visible:** jars, parts bins or compartment boxes.
- **Dry.** Rust destroys fasteners in storage. Use sealed containers with a desiccant packet (or a
  little rice).
- **Keep salvage apart from good stock** so an unknown bolt never ends up where it matters.
- **A small grab bin** of mixed common fasteners near the work area for quick jobs.

## As barter goods

Fasteners and hardware are close to ideal trade items (→ 18-02): everyone needs them, they keep
forever, they are compact, and they divide easily into small trades. Each piece is worth little,
which makes them low-risk to trade compared with food, medicine or fuel, because trading them does
not advertise that you have a stockpile (→ 14-03). A coffee can of assorted screws is a valuable
thing to have on a shelf.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Assorted screw kits and bulk common sizes** | The most-used fastener | #6, #8, #10; 3/4 to 4 in |
| Nails, assorted and bulk | Cheaper; better in sideways load | 6d to 16d, roofing, finish |
| Bolts, nuts, **washers**, nylock nuts | Structural and mechanical repair | Inch **and** metric |
| Threaded rod | Make any bolt | Cut to length |
| **Mechanic's or baling wire, big roll** | The most underrated repair material | → 16-05 |
| Galvanized wire, **hardware cloth**, chicken wire | Rodents, garden, structures | |
| Stainless safety wire, copper wire | Fine binding; electrical | |
| Hinges, hasps, brackets, angle iron, mending plates | Structural repairs | |
| **Hose clamps, full range** | Endlessly useful | |
| Eye bolts, hooks, chain, turnbuckles, quick links | Hanging, tightening | |
| Cable ties | Fast; sunlight and cold weaken them | Not permanent outdoors |
| Sandpaper, steel wool, wire brushes | Surface preparation | |
| Penetrating oil, thread locker, anti-seize, grease | Getting things apart and keeping them together | All four |
| Rust converter, primer, paint | Outdoor steel rusts fast | |
| **Labeled, sorted, dry storage** | Unsorted hardware is useless | The part people skip |

**Salvage:** everything on this page is easy to salvage (→ 22-02): appliances, furniture, vehicles,
pallets, decks, fence lines, farm buildings. Coat hangers are the classic improvised wire. You can
also **make** fasteners: a nail cut and re-headed, twisted wire, a wooden peg driven through a
drilled hole (the traditional "treenail" joint, → 16-08), rawhide that shrinks as it dries.
**Do not substitute** graded structural bolts, or anything holding weight over people.

## When it runs out

- **They never expire**, so the only way to run out is not buying enough. Stock deeply now.
- **Track it as "do I still have the common sizes"**, and restock the moment a bin runs low
  (→ 22-04, → 23-02).
- **Salvage before buying, and before improvising.** Straighten and reuse nails; it works.
- **Substitute:** wire (→ 16-05), lashing (→ 16-03), wooden pegs, rawhide, glue. A household that
  knows lashings and pegs needs far less hardware.
- **Over-stocking on purpose is sensible**: surplus screws become things you need, by trade.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** buy and sort now, while hardware stores exist. One of the best returns per dollar
  in the acquisition plan (→ 22-07).
- **B, on the move:** almost none of it travels; it is heavy. Cable ties, some wire and a few screws
  in the repair kit (→ 22-03).
- **C, settled:** very heavy use: building, fencing, animal housing, gates. Bring what you can and
  plan salvage for the rest. Old farm buildings are often full of usable hardware, and an old fence
  line is itself a wire supply.

photo_slots.caption: Our workbench: the vise, the anvil block, where the materials pile is

pages.body:
# Repairing metal and wood without power

**What this page is for.** Fixing tool handles and wooden structures, cutting, bending and joining
metal by hand, simple work with fire, and knowing what scrap steel is good for. The two skills
that matter most here, fitting a new tool handle and turning scrap steel into a working edge, mean
the tools in this section never truly run out: they get remade.

> **CAUTION. Four hazards on this page.**
> 1. **Never heat galvanized steel** (the dull gray, often spangled zinc-coated kind used on
>    fence posts, buckets and some pipe). The zinc gives off fumes that cause "metal fume fever"
>    and worse. **Galvanized: do not heat, do not weld, do not forge.** Check before anything
>    goes in a fire.
> 2. **Any forge or metalworking fire makes carbon monoxide** (→ 29-03; CDC, Carbon Monoxide
>    Poisoning Basics). **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage,
>    or near an open window** (floor, → 30-01): a charcoal forge counts. It goes outdoors.
> 3. **Hot metal and hammering:** burns (→ 12-03), flying scale, eye injuries. Eye protection,
>    leather gloves, and natural-fiber clothing; synthetics melt onto skin (→ 11-05).
> 4. **Lead.** Old paint, old solder and some salvaged metals contain lead (CDC, About Lead in
>    the Home). {{#if has.young_child}}**You have a child under 6, the age most harmed by lead.**
>    {{/if}}Do lead-adjacent work outdoors, away from children, and wash hands and clothes
>    afterward.

## Do this now

1. **Set up a vise and a solid work surface.** A bench vise is the item that most expands what you
   can repair (→ 16-01).
2. **Find a heavy block of steel to use as an anvil:** a railroad tie plate, a short piece of
   rail, a sledge head, a thick plate. Free or nearly free.
3. **Start a materials pile:** scrap steel, sheet metal, angle iron, rebar, pipe, vehicle leaf
   springs, hardwood, lumber. Sort it and keep it dry.
4. **Learn to re-hang an axe head** (below). It is the repair you are most likely to need (→ 16-06).

{{photo workbench}}

## Wood repair

### Re-hanging an axe or hammer head

{{figure fig-rehang-axe-head}}

1. **Remove the old handle.** Saw it off flush under the head, then drill out the wood left in
   the "eye" (the hole in the head) and punch it through. That is the safer first choice. If you
   must burn it out, **bury the whole cutting edge in damp sand or wet earth so only the eye and
   the wood stub sit in the coals.** Heat at the edge softens the steel and ruins the axe.
2. **Fit a new handle** of hickory or ash, straight-grained, with the grain lines running the same
   way as the blade. Shape the top to fit the eye tightly, taking off a little at a time with a
   rasp and trying it often.
3. **Drive it fully home**, then **wedge it**: a wooden wedge driven into the slot cut in the top of
   the handle, then a small steel wedge across it.
4. **Saw off the excess** and rub the handle with boiled linseed oil. **Linseed-oil rags heat up
   by themselves and can catch fire within hours when bunched.** Spread the rag flat outdoors to
   dry stiff, or drop it in a water-filled metal can with a lid (→ 16-01).
5. **Check it every season.** Wood shrinks in a dry, heated house, and **a loose head is
   dangerous.** Soaking the head in water swells it tight for a while; it is not a repair.

### Other wood repairs

- **Split or cracked piece:** glue and clamp, then **sister a board alongside and bolt through**
  (→ 16-05, → 16-07). A sistered repair is often stronger than the original.
- **Rotted post base:** cut out the rot and splice in new wood, or set a new post beside it. Keep
  wood off the ground; ground contact is what rotted it.
- **Loose joint:** wedges, glue, screws, a mending plate, or a lashing (→ 16-03).
- **Stripped screw hole:** matchsticks or toothpicks and glue, then drive the screw again (→ 16-05).
- **Making a handle from scratch:** a straight-grained hardwood limb, a draw knife and a rasp. A
  learnable and very useful skill.
- **Wooden pegs ("treenails")** in drilled holes, instead of metal fasteners: traditional, strong
  in the right joint, and free.
- **Green or dry wood:** freshly cut ("green") wood is easy to work but shrinks as it dries, which
  can tighten a joint or split a board. Dry wood is stable and harder to work. Plan around it.

## Metal repair without a welder

You can do a great deal with cold work and simple heat.

**Cold work:**
- **Cut** with a hacksaw (stock blades), a cold chisel, or tin snips.
- **Drill** with a hand drill and good bits. Go slowly and use oil.
- **Bend** in a vise, with a hammer, or over a form. Thick steel needs heat.
- **File** to shape. Files do a remarkable amount of work with patience (→ 16-02).
- **Join** with bolts, rivets or wire (→ 16-07). Bolted joints are easier to repair than welds.
- **Rivet:** a pop-rivet gun for sheet metal, or solid rivets hammered over ("peened") for real
  strength.

**With heat** (a fire, a charcoal forge or a torch), **outdoors only**:
- **Hot bending and shaping.** Steel becomes workable at red heat. A wood or charcoal fire with
  forced air (a bellows, a hand-crank blower, or a hair dryer if there is spare power) reaches it.
- **Straightening** bent steel.
- **Basic blacksmithing:** stretching steel thinner ("drawing out") and thickening it
  ("upsetting").
- **Brazing and soft soldering:** joining metal with a melted filler instead of a welder. Torch
  brazing is strong and worth learning.
- **Hardening and tempering** (heat-treating) need you to know the steel, and salvaged steel is
  unknown. Expect to experiment and expect failures. Leaf springs and files are reliable
  high-carbon sources.
- **Quenching** (cooling hot steel fast to harden it): use vegetable oil. **Used motor oil flashes
  into a fireball and its smoke is toxic.** Use a deep metal can with a lid to smother a flare-up,
  nothing flammable within arm's reach, and children nowhere near (→ 12-03).

**A basic forge is achievable:** an old brake drum or a fire pit, charcoal you can make (→ 06-05),
forced air, an anvil block, a hammer and tongs. It is a project for a settled phase, but knowing
it is possible changes what "the tools ran out" means.

## What scrap steel is good for

| Source | Steel | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Leaf springs, coil springs** | High-carbon, can be hardened | Knives, chisels, punches. The classic scrap steel |
| **Worn-out files** | Very high carbon | Knives, scrapers, small chisels. **Brittle**: soften by heating and cooling slowly before shaping |
| Rebar | Low carbon, unknown | Stakes, hooks. Will not harden well |
| Angle iron, channel, plate | Mild steel | Brackets, frames |
| Pipe | Mild steel (check it is not galvanized) | Handles, frames, rollers, levers |
| Sheet metal: appliances, ductwork, roofing, cans | Thin mild steel | Patches, flashing, containers |
| Bearings, axles, old tools | Various, often hardenable | Punches, chisels |
| Railroad tie plate or rail | Heavy mild steel | Anvil substitute |
| Copper pipe and wire | Soft | Electrical (→ 09-08), rivets, sheet work |
| Aluminum | Soft and light | Never where steel strength is needed; will not harden |

**The spark test:** touch a piece to a grinding wheel or rough stone. **High-carbon steel throws
bushy, branching sparks; mild steel throws long, straight streaks.** Crude, but it works.

## Rust

- **Prevent:** oil every steel tool each season (→ 16-01); prime and paint anything kept outdoors;
  keep things dry and off the ground.
- **Remove:** wire brush, sandpaper, a vinegar soak (slow but effective), or rust converter.
  Electrolysis with a battery charger works very well if there is spare power.
- **Protect at once.** Bare steel starts to rust within hours in humid air.
- **Rusted bolts:** penetrating oil, patience, and heat (not on galvanized), which breaks the rust
  bond (→ 16-05).

## Workshops at a destination

If you may move to another place (→ 01-05), what is already there changes what you carry.

{{#if has.destinations}}{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{d.name}}** ({{d.status_text}}): what is
  in its shop is ______________________ (surveyed on ____/____/____ by ______).
{{/each}}{{/if}}

**Only rely on a shop at a place whose people have agreed to have you.** At any place not agreed,
or improvised, assume there is no shop at all: your own vise and anvil block are the only ones.
That is why the vise and anvil are bought regardless (→ 16-01).

**The shop check** (run it on a visit, phone camera in hand, about 20 minutes; or on arrival day):

```
[ ] POWER: grid-down options? 240 V outlets? Generator hookup?
    (09-04, 09-13)
[ ] BENCH & VISE: solid bench? Vise size? Anvil or heavy plate?
[ ] WELDING / CUTTING: welder (type, rod or wire on hand)? Torch?
    WHO there knows how to run them?
[ ] MACHINES: drill press, bench grinder, compressor, chop saw?
[ ] HAND TOOLS: full mechanic's set? Wood tools? What duplicates
    ours, what is missing?
[ ] CONSUMABLES: welding rod, hacksaw blades, files, drill bits,
    fasteners, oil and grease, the things that run out (23-02)
[ ] STEEL & WOOD PILE: scrap steel, lumber, handle stock?
[ ] WHAT IS MISSING that we should bring or leave there ahead of time?
```

**What travels and what waits** (feeds the load plan, → 01-03):
- **Travels:** hand tools (→ 16-01), files, hacksaw blades, drill bits, the sharpening kit
  (→ 16-02), fasteners (→ 16-07), the light, valuable, always-scarce layer. Your vise and anvil
  block if there is any doubt about the shop.
- **Waits** at an agreed place: machines, the welder, the materials pile. Spend weight on the
  consumables no shop ever has enough of.
- **Leave duplicates ahead of time** only at a place that has agreed, a box at a time on visits.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Heavy bench vise** | The biggest capability expansion | Bolt it down solid |
| **Anvil or heavy steel block** | Backing for all metalwork | Tie plate, rail, thick plate |
| Ball-peen hammers in several weights, a sledge | Metalwork, riveting | |
| **Hacksaw and many spare blades** | The metal-cutting workhorse | Blades are the consumable |
| Metal files: flat, round, half-round, triangular | Shaping without power | → 16-02 |
| Cold chisels, punches, drifts | Cutting and driving | Grind off mushroomed heads (OSHA) |
| Tin snips | Sheet metal | |
| Hand drill or brace, good bits, cutting oil | Drilling without power | |
| Pop-rivet gun and rivets; solid rivets | Joining without welding | |
| **Draw knife, rasps, spokeshave** | Making and fitting handles | |
| **Spare axe, hammer and tool handles, and wedges** | The repair you will need | Hickory or ash |
| Boiled linseed oil | Handles | Rags dried flat outdoors or in a water-filled lidded can |
| Propane torch, brazing rod, solder and flux | Joining, heating, freeing rusted bolts | Fuel is finite (→ 06-06) |
| Eye protection, leather gloves, natural-fiber clothing | Hot metal, scale | Never synthetics |
| Materials pile | Raw material | Sorted and dry |
| A paper metalwork or blacksmithing book | Heat-treating, technique | |

**Substitutes:**
- **Anvil:** tie plate, rail section, a sledge head set in a stump, thick plate.
- **Forge:** a brake drum or a pit with forced air and charcoal (→ 06-05).
- **Tongs:** locking pliers, or tongs forged from rebar.
- **Steel:** leaf springs, files, angle iron, pipe, appliance panels (→ 22-02).
- **Handle wood:** hickory, ash, oak or elm, split and dried (→ 06-04 for the trees near you).
- **What you cannot make: hacksaw blades and files.** They gate all metalwork. Stock them.

## When it runs out

- **The consumables are hacksaw blades, files and drill bits.** Stock all three and add them to
  → 23-02.
- **Everything else is close to permanent:** vise, anvil, hammers, chisels, draw knife. Scrap steel
  and hardwood are plentiful (→ 22-02).
- **Make them last:** do not force a hacksaw (it strips teeth); clean files with a file card; turn a
  worn file into a knife blank instead of throwing it away.
- **Substitute:** cold work for hot; bolts for welds; wood where it will serve; lashings and pegs for
  hardware (→ 16-03, → 16-07).
- **The person who can make a handle and an edge** is valuable in any community (→ 18-03, → 23-05).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** set up the vise and materials pile; learn to re-hang a handle; collect scrap
  steel and hardwood while people still throw it away. Work with fire outdoors, with children well
  clear (→ 20-02).
- **B, on the move:** none of this travels. A file, a hacksaw blade and wire in the repair kit
  (→ 16-05).
- **C, settled:** this is where it becomes real. Run the shop check on arrival day. Where there is a
  shop, fit in and contribute consumables and hands; where there is none, set up your own vise and
  anvil in the first week (→ 01-04). Old farms are rich in salvageable steel. A household that can
  make and repair tools is the household others come to (→ 18-03).

pages.body:
# Bicycles and human-powered transport

**What this page is for.** Moving people, water, wood and supplies when fuel is gone: bicycles,
bike trailers, carts and sleds, and the three bicycle repairs that cover most failures. A bicycle
carries several times what a person can walk with, at several times walking speed, on nothing but
food. **A bicycle with a trailer is the most capable human-powered transport there is.**

> **CAUTION. Cold and ice.** {{#if is.cold_winters}}Your winters are cold enough that cycling is
> impractical or dangerous for months.{{else}}In ice, deep snow and hard cold, cycling is
> impractical or dangerous.{{/if}} Riding adds your own speed to the wind chill (→ 29-10), and a
> fall on ice is a broken wrist with no emergency room (→ 12-09). In those months, **the sled
> and the cart are the transport, not the bicycle.**{{#if has.young_child}} **A young child
> riding in a trailer makes no heat of their own**; check them constantly in the cold, or do not
> go (→ 11-02, → 12-10).{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Make sure every adult's bicycle actually works:** tires, tubes, brakes, chain. A bike with
   flat tires and a rusted chain is not transport.
2. **Buy the consumables, several of each:** inner tubes, patch kits, tires, chain, quick links,
   brake pads, cables.
3. **Buy a bike trailer** (cargo or child). It turns a bicycle into a hauling vehicle.
4. **Buy a plastic sled and a garden cart.** Between them they cover most winter and summer
   hauling, and both are cheap.
5. **Learn to fix a flat and adjust the brakes** (Procedures 1 and 2). Twenty minutes, once.
6. **Photograph your rear derailleur now** (Procedure 3) and add the photo below.

## Why it matters

Fuel runs out, and vehicles also need tires, batteries and parts. **A bicycle needs food and a
small kit of spares.**
- It moves at three to four times walking speed and carries far more.
- **With a trailer it can haul 100 lb or more:** water (→ 03-02), firewood (→ 06-04), salvage
  (→ 22-02), food.
- It is quiet and does not announce itself the way an engine does (→ 14-03).
- It can be repaired with simple tools and salvaged parts.

**The main use is hauling, not travel:** water from a source, wood from a lot, supplies from a
salvage run. That is what the trailer is for.

## Seasons

| Season | What works |
|---|---|
| Dry and mild | **Bicycle and trailer**: excellent. Cart and wheelbarrow for short hauls |
| Mud | Bike is poor. **Cart with wide wheels**, or walk |
| Ice and snow | **Sled.** A bike on ice is a broken wrist. Studded tires help on packed snow, not in drifts |
| Deep snow or blizzard | **Nothing. Do not move** (→ 17-01) |

{{#if is.snow_region}}**You live in snow country.** Plan on the sled for several months a year.{{/if}}

**The sled is the underrated winter tool.** A cheap plastic toboggan hauls water, firewood,
supplies and children across snow and ice safely. Carrying a heavy load or a child across ice on
foot is one of the most likely ways to break a bone in this whole binder (→ 11-06, → 12-09).

## Choosing and keeping a bicycle

**Choose sturdy over fast:** a hybrid or mountain bike with **wide tires**, a **steel frame** (it
can be brazed if it cracks, → 16-08), **rack mounts**, and simple parts. Complicated modern gears
have more to go wrong and fewer spares.

| Part | Why | Stock |
|---|---|---|
| **Inner tubes** | The number one failure by far | **Two or more per bike** (size is printed on the tire's side) |
| Patch kits with vulcanizing patches and glue | A tube can be patched many times | Several kits; the glue dries out once opened |
| Tires | Wear; sidewalls crack with age and sunlight | A spare pair per bike |
| Chain and quick links | Stretches and snaps | One or two spare chains; two quick links per bike |
| Brake pads and cables | Safety-critical; wear steadily | Several sets |
| Spokes and a spoke wrench | Loaded wheels go out of true | A handful per wheel size |
| Grease, chain lube, oil | Neglect kills bikes | Bulk |
| Tire levers, pump, multi-tool, chain tool | The field kit | On the bike |

**Puncture-resistant tires or tire liners** are worth the money: glass and thorns are constant. A
frame pump on the bike and a floor pump at home. A pump is not optional.

**Upkeep that matters:**
- Keep the chain clean and oiled. A dry chain wears everything fast.
- Keep tires at the pressure printed on the sidewall. Low pressure causes "pinch" flats and rim
  damage.
- Keep the bike dry and under cover. Rust destroys bikes.
- Straighten ("true") a wheel that wobbles.

## Procedure 1: fix a flat

{{figure fig-tube-patch-steps}}

**The practical way: carry two spare tubes per bike and swap**, then patch the punctured tube at
home in good light. A swap takes about 10 minutes; a roadside patch takes longer and fails more.
Patching still matters: it is what lets each tube survive many flats.

1. **Remove the wheel.** Open the brake's quick release (or unhook the curved cable end on rim
   brakes), then open the axle lever or undo the axle nuts. For the rear wheel, shift to the
   smallest rear gear first so the chain drops off easily.
2. Let out all remaining air. Hook a tire lever under the tire's edge (the "bead"), pry it over
   the rim, and hook the lever onto a spoke.
3. Slide a second lever along under the bead until one whole side of the tire is off the rim.
   Leave the other side on.
4. Pull out the tube, valve last. **Then run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire.**
   The nail or glass that caused this is usually still there, waiting for the next tube. Check
   that the rim tape covers every spoke hole.
5. **Find the hole:** pump some air in and listen, or pass it slowly near your lips to feel the
   air; best of all, dunk it a section at a time in water and watch for bubbles. Mark the hole.
6. **Patch:** rub the spot with the kit's sandpaper until dull. Spread a thin film of glue wider
   than the patch. **Wait until the glue looks dry, 2 to 3 minutes. This is the step everyone
   rushes, and why patches fail.** Peel the foil off the patch without touching the black rubber
   underneath, and press that black side onto the glue, centered on the hole. **The clear plastic
   film on top stays on.** Press hard for 30 seconds.
7. **Refit:** put a breath of air in the tube so it holds its shape, push the valve through the
   rim, tuck the tube into the tire all round, then roll the bead back over the rim with your
   palms, finishing opposite the valve. **Use levers only for the last few inches**; levers pinch
   tubes.
8. Before pumping up, squeeze your way round both sides of the tire to check the tube is not caught
   under the bead.
9. Pump to the pressure printed on the tire. Spin the wheel and check the line molded on the tire
   sits evenly above the rim all the way round. Refit the wheel, reconnect the brake, spin it, and
   squeeze the brake once before riding.

**Practice this once at home this month.** Your first flat repair should not be the real one.

## Procedure 2: adjust rim brakes

{{figure fig-rim-brake-adjust}}

1. **The symptom** is weak braking (the lever pulls nearly to the handlebar) or a pad rubbing.
2. **Barrel adjuster first.** This is the small ridged barrel where the cable enters the lever or
   the brake. Unscrewing it tightens the cable. Half a turn at a time; squeeze; repeat. This fixes
   most brake complaints.
3. If the adjuster runs out of thread, screw it most of the way back in, loosen the **cable clamp
   bolt** on the brake arm, pull the cable snug with pliers so the pads almost touch the rim, and
   tighten the bolt firmly.
4. **Test:** spin the wheel; it must turn freely. Squeeze hard; it must stop dead. Release; it
   must spin freely again. If one pad drags, center the brake (most have a small centring screw on
   one arm) or check the wheel is seated straight.
5. **Pads must hit the rim fully**, never the tire (it will cut through) and never below the rim.
   Loosen, line up, tighten. Replace pads worn past their grooves.

Disc brakes work differently; follow the bike maker's manual.

## Procedure 3: replace or rejoin a chain

1. A snapped chain, or a stretched one that skips, is fixed with the **quick link** (a two-piece
   joining link) from the kit, and for a full replacement, a spare chain.
2. **Size a new chain against the old one:** lay them side by side and match them link for link,
   removing extra links with the chain tool (it pushes a pin out). The chain must match your
   gearing's **speed count** (count the rear gears: ____-speed; the chain packet says which it
   fits).
3. **Threading it wrong is the classic failure.** Use your photo:

{{photo derailleur-threading}}

4. Thread the chain to match the photo, bring the two ends together on the bottom run, and join
   them with the quick link: one half on each end, plates together, then press hard on a pedal
   until it clicks shut.
5. **Roadside, with no spare chain:** push out the damaged link's pin with the chain tool, rejoin
   the shorter chain with a quick link, and avoid the biggest gear combinations on the way home.

## How much each method carries

| Method | Rough load | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Walking with a pack | 30 to 50 lb, uncomfortably | The baseline |
| Bicycle with bags | 40 to 60 lb | Steering gets twitchy; keep weight low |
| **Bicycle and trailer** | **100 lb or more** | The workhorse |
| Garden cart or wheelbarrow | 100 to 300 lb, short distances | Water, wood, dirt |
| **Sled on snow** | 100 lb or more, safely | The winter answer |
| Hand cart | 100 to 200 lb | |

**Water is why this matters** (→ 03-02): a gallon weighs about 8.3 lb, so five gallons is over
40 lb and awkward. A cart or sled turns a miserable daily trip into a routine one.

## Children

{{#if has.child}}Children in your household: {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{/if}}

- **A bike trailer** suits a child old enough to sit up well. It is enclosed and visible, and it
  also hauls cargo.
- **An infant** is carried, or rides in a trailer only with a proper infant seat or support.
- **In the cold: a sled, not a bike.** A child in a trailer moving at bike speed in freezing air
  feels a serious wind chill and is making no heat (→ 11-02, → 12-10). Check them constantly, or
  do not go.
- **Bright colors and helmets for everyone.**

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A working bicycle per adult | Fuel-free transport | Steel frame, wide tires, rack mounts |
| **Bike trailer, cargo or child** | Turns a bike into a hauler | The key accessory |
| **Two tubes per bike, correct size** | Swap now, patch later | Wrapped, out of the sun |
| **Patch kits, two or more** | Each tube lasts many flats | Check glue every year |
| Tire levers, three | Procedure 1 | Plastic; on the bike |
| **Quick links, two per bike, matching the chain** | Procedure 3 | Tape one under the saddle |
| Frame pump and floor pump | Every repair ends with air | Not optional |
| Spare tires, chain, cables, brake pads | The other consumables | Several of each |
| Multi-tool and chain tool | Field repair | On the bike |
| Puncture-resistant tires or liners | Flats are the top failure | Worth it |
| Rear rack and bags | Carrying without a trailer | |
| **Plastic sled or toboggan, two** | The winter transport | Cheap; important |
| **Garden cart or wheelbarrow** | Water, wood, dirt, salvage | Wide wheels for soft ground |
| Hand truck | Heavy, awkward loads | |
| Helmets for everyone | Falls happen | |
| Front and rear lights, reflectors | Short winter days | → 10-01 |
| Grease, chain lube, oil | Neglect kills bikes | |
| A paper bike repair manual | Fixing what you did not build | |

**Salvage and substitutes:**
- **Bicycles are everywhere:** garages, sheds, curbs (→ 22-02). Most need only tubes, a chain and
  oil. Any bike is a parts bike.
- **Trailer:** two bike wheels, angle iron or conduit, and a plywood box (→ 16-07, → 16-08).
- **Cart:** wheelbarrow, garden wagon, appliance dolly, or a box on lawnmower or stroller wheels.
- **Sled:** plastic toboggan, a plastic barrel cut in half lengthwise, a truck bed liner, a car
  hood.
- **Tube patches:** pieces of old inner tube glued with contact cement (→ 16-05).
- **Tires:** hard to improvise. Stock them.

## When it runs out

- **Tubes and tires are what stop a bicycle completely.** Stock them heavily. Patch kits stretch
  tubes a long way, so patches are the best-value spare.
- **Count tubes and tires per bike** and add them to → 23-02.
- **Make them last:** patch rather than replace; keep pressure right; fit liners; watch for glass.
- **Last resort:** a flat tire stuffed tight with rope, cloth or hose gets you home slowly.
- **The sled and the cart are the options that cannot fail**: no tires, no chain, no spares, just a
  hull and a rope (→ 16-03). In a very long event, they are what is still working.
- **Walking never runs out:** good boots (→ 11-06), a good pack, reasonable loads.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** bike and trailer for water, wood and salvage in good weather; sled and cart in
  winter. Quiet transport is discreet transport (→ 14-03).
- **B, on the move:** a loaded bicycle you push, not ride, still carries far more than your back
  (→ 01-03). In deep winter it is not workable (→ 01-02, → 11-01); a sled is.
- **C, settled:** a bicycle is valuable for anything within a few miles, and a cart or wagon becomes
  daily infrastructure.

pages.body:
# Tire failures: roadside diagnosis and repair

**What this page is for.** What to do when a tire goes soft, punctures, or fails on the road, with
a small kit you carry in the vehicle: a plug kit, a portable inflator, sealant, a jack, a lug wrench
and, ideally, a spare. Many newer vehicles carry no spare at all, only a sealant kit; for those,
this page is the replacement. In a long emergency there is no tire shop and no tow truck, so these
repairs are how the vehicle keeps moving.

> **CAUTION. Three ways to get hurt at the roadside.**
> - **Traffic.** Get as far off the road as possible. A ruined rim is cheaper than a person.
> - **The jack.** **Everyone out of the vehicle before it is jacked up.** A person shifting in a
>   seat is the movement that rocks a jack over onto the hands of the person working. Never put
>   any part of your body under a vehicle held only by a jack.
> - **Carbon monoxide.** If the engine runs for heat while you wait, **the exhaust pipe must be
>   clear of snow** and a window cracked. A blocked tailpipe fills the cabin with carbon monoxide
>   (→ 08-02, → 29-03).
>
> **Your products' own instructions govern** where they differ from this page. Keep a copy of
> this page, and those instructions, in the kit.

**Your vehicles:**
{{#if has.vehicle}}{{#each vehicles as v}}- {{v.type_text}} ({{v.fuel_text}}; four-wheel drive: {{v.four_wheel_drive}}; can tow: {{v.can_tow}}). Spare tire aboard: yes / no / compact only. Tire size (from the sidewall): __________. Pressure from the door-jamb placard: front ____ rear ____. Lug nut torque from the manual: ____.
{{/each}}{{else}}None entered. Keep this page for any vehicle you ride in or borrow.{{/if}}

{{#if has.trailer}}**Trailer:** every procedure here works the same on your trailer's tires, with
the same kit, **except** the pressure (a trailer uses the maximum pressure molded on its own tire
sidewall, not a door placard) and the trailer's own spare. That, plus wheel bearings and lights, is
→ 16-11.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Find out whether each vehicle has a spare**, and what kind: full-size, compact ("donut"), or
   none. Write it above. If none, put a used full-size wheel and tire for that vehicle on the
   shopping list (→ 26-09).
2. **Build the kit** in the table at the bottom (→ 22-05).
3. **Practice a plug once on a scrap tire.** The insertion tool takes real force the first time,
   and the first time should not be on a freezing roadside.
4. **Do one driveway jack-and-swap.** Find the jacking points in the owner's manual and mark them
   with a paint pen. Add the photo:

{{photo jacking-points}}

5. **Charge the inflator** and put it on your regular charging rotation. Its 12-volt cord is the
   backup.
6. **Keep sealant bottles in the cabin**, not a cold cargo area. Sealant pours badly when cold.
7. **Check tire pressures monthly and before any long trip**, cold, against the door-jamb placard
   (NHTSA, TireWise). Many roadside "flats" began as weeks of slow under-inflation.

{{photo tire-kit}}

## Step 0: every case starts the same way

```
[ ] OFF THE ROAD as far as possible. Flat, firm ground. Hazard
    lights ON. In winter, the stranded-vehicle rules (17-01) apply
    in full.
[ ] For plugging, sealing and inflating: children stay buckled in
    the vehicle. One adult works, one adult watches traffic and
    children. Work on the side away from traffic when you can.
    JACKING is different: everyone OUT first (Case 4).
[ ] Engine may run for heat ONLY with the exhaust pipe clear of
    snow and a window cracked (08-02).
[ ] LOOK BEFORE YOU TOUCH: what failed, and can you see why?
```

## Diagnose it

{{figure fig-tread-vs-sidewall}}

The **tread** is the thick part that touches the road. The **sidewall** is the thin, smooth side
with the writing on it. The **shoulder** is the curved edge between them.

| What you see | It is | Go to |
|---|---|---|
| Tire soft or low, warning light, no visible damage | Slow leak | Case 1 |
| Nail or screw head in the **tread** | Puncture | Case 2 |
| Hissing you cannot find; a hole too ragged for a plug; or no time or too dangerous to plug | Sealant case | Case 3 |
| Cut or bulge in the **sidewall**, tread peeling, tire shredded | Dead tire | Case 4 |
| Loud bang and a pull while driving | Blowout | Case 5 first, then 4 |

## Case 1: slow leak or low tire

1. **Inflate to the placard pressure** with the inflator. Check with a simple pencil gauge too;
   digital gauges are sometimes wrong.
2. **Find the leak:** sponge soapy water (a little soap in any bottle of water) over the tread, the
   valve and the edge where tire meets rim. Bubbles mark it. No soap: listen, and feel with a wet
   finger.
3. **Bubbles at the valve:** use the valve-core tool (a small key, often in plug kits) to tighten the
   valve core a quarter turn. Still bubbling? Swap in a spare core (the tire deflates; reinflate
   after). A 30-second fix few people know.
4. **Bubbles on the tread:** that is a puncture. Go to Case 2.
5. **Bubbles at the rim edge, or nothing found but it keeps dropping:** reinflate and drive on,
   checking about every 30 minutes. Rim leaks are shop work, or Case 3 if it will not hold.

## Case 2: puncture in the tread (the plug kit)

{{figure fig-tire-plug-steps}}

**Plugs are for the tread only. Never the sidewall, never the shoulder.**

```
1. Mark the spot, then PULL THE OBJECT out with pliers.
2. REAM: push the spiral reamer in and out several times for a
   clean, round hole. (A little of the kit's lubricant on the tools
   helps.)
3. THREAD a plug through the eye of the insertion needle, centered.
   A touch of lubricant or cement on the plug.
4. INSERT straight in with steady force until about 1/3 of the plug
   is still outside. This takes muscle; brace yourself and the tire.
5. PULL STRAIGHT OUT quickly. The plug stays; the needle releases.
6. TRIM the plug flush with a knife.
7. REINFLATE to the placard pressure. Check the repair with soapy
   water.
8. Drive. Recheck pressure after 10 minutes, then at each stop.
```

A well-set plug often lasts the life of the tire, but by the tire industry's own standard it is a
temporary repair. In normal times, have a shop fit a patch from the inside soon. **Plugs are the
most renewable tire resource you can carry:** a kit holds many, and each one fixes a puncture.
Prefer a plug to sealant whenever you can.

## Case 3: sealant

**When:** the hole is too ragged for a plug, there are several small punctures, you cannot find the
leak but must move, or plugging is unsafe (traffic, cold, dark).

```
1. Roll the vehicle so the VALVE IS AT THE TOP.
2. REMOVE THE VALVE CORE with the core tool. (The tire deflates
   fully. That is expected.)
3. SQUEEZE IN the amount the bottle's label gives for your tire size.
4. REFIT THE CORE, snug.
5. REINFLATE to the placard pressure.
6. DRIVE AT ONCE, a few miles at moderate speed, to spread the
   sealant. Recheck pressure after 10 minutes; top up.
```

(Some sealant kits pump in through the valve without removing the core. Follow the label.)

**What it costs you:** it is temporary; it gums up the rim and the tire-pressure sensor; and the tire
will need a real repair or replacement. **Each bottle fixes one tire, once.** In a long emergency,
sealant is the scarce resource and plugs are the plentiful one, so sealant is the reserve, not the
default.

## Case 4: dead tire (sidewall cut, bulge, shredded)

**Nothing in a bottle or a plug fixes a sidewall. Ever.** Sidewall damage means the tire is
replaced (NHTSA, TireWise).

**With a spare aboard:**

{{figure fig-lug-star-pattern}}

```
1. EVERYONE OUT before the jack goes under. Children with the second
   adult, well off the road, never between the vehicle and traffic.
   If there is NO safe place to stand (whiteout, deep cold, no
   shoulder), that is the signal to plug or seal instead, or to wait
   for help (17-01). CHOCK the wheel diagonally opposite (a rock or
   block in front of and behind it). Parking brake ON. Shift to park
   (or first gear).
2. LOOSEN each lug nut half a turn WHILE THE WHEEL IS STILL ON THE
   GROUND. Counter-clockwise ("lefty loosey").
3. JACK at the marked jacking point until the tire just clears the
   ground.
4. Lug nuts off, wheel off, SPARE ON. Lug nuts back on, hand-tight,
   in a STAR pattern (across, not round the circle).
5. LOWER the vehicle, then tighten firmly in the star pattern.
6. Tighten to the torque in your owner's manual at the first chance
   (auto parts stores often lend torque wrenches). Recheck the lug
   nuts after about 50 miles regardless.
```

- **A compact spare** has a speed and distance limit printed on it. Respect it.
{{#if has.4wd}}- **Your household has a four-wheel-drive vehicle.** Read its manual about spares and
  tire replacement: many four-wheel and all-wheel-drive vehicles need all four tires closely matched
  in size and wear, and a compact spare may require the vehicle to stay in two-wheel drive or stay
  slow until the tire is replaced. Four-wheel drive does not help you drive on a flat.
{{/if}}- **Without a spare:** this is a stranding, not a repair. In normal times, call roadside help
  or a tow. With no help coming, drive on the flat **at walking speed, on flat ground, only if
  staying where you are is dangerous**. You will ruin the rim; a ruined rim is better than a family
  stranded in danger.
- **This case is why a spare wheel belongs on the shopping list** (→ 26-09).

## Case 5: blowout at speed

```
GRIP the wheel firmly. DO NOT BRAKE HARD. Ease OFF the accelerator,
hold the car straight, let the speed bleed off, signal, and roll
gently onto the shoulder. Then Case 4.
```

Braking hard or swerving with a blown front tire is how a blowout becomes a rollover. Say this
sequence out loud once a year so it becomes reflex.

## Winter

- **The stranded-vehicle rules** (→ 17-01) run alongside the whole time: be visible, stay warm,
  keep the exhaust clear, watch the children.
- **Work in short bursts.** Bare fingers lose their skill within minutes in deep cold; warm your
  hands inside between steps. The plug job gets twice as hard. Sealant kept warm in the cabin may
  beat a plug in a whiteout, even for a pluggable hole. That is a reasonable call.
- **Cold lowers tire pressure** by roughly 1 psi for every 10 °F drop (NHTSA, TireWise). A "low"
  tire on a bitter morning may just be the cold; check against the placard before assuming a leak.

## Gear

| Item | Covers | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **Tire plug kit** (plugs, insertion tool, reamer, pliers, knife, pencil gauge, valve-core tool, spare valve cores) | Cases 1 and 2 | Vehicle, with this page in the lid |
| **Portable inflator** (battery and 12-volt cord) | Every case ends with "reinflate" | Vehicle; on the charging rotation |
| **Tire sealant**, one bottle per tire you want to cover | Case 3 | **Cabin**; date on each bottle |
| **Jack** rated for your vehicle, and its handle | Case 4 | Vehicle |
| **Long-handled lug wrench** in your lug-nut size | Case 4 | With the jack |
| Wheel chocks (or two solid blocks) | Case 4 | With the jack |
| **Spare wheel and tire**, full-size if possible | Turns Case 4 from a stranding into a delay | Vehicle, for every trip beyond town |
| Work gloves, headlamp, reflective triangles | Every case | Vehicle |
| Factory sealant kit, if the vehicle came with one | A backup bottle; check its expiry | Where the maker put it |

**Substitutes:** any air source beats none: a gas-station hose, or a bicycle floor pump (→ 16-09),
slow but real. Plug strings and rubber cement are sold in any auto aisle and worth grabbing.

## When it runs out

- **Plugs:** the renewable workhorse. Restock while stores exist.
- **Sealant:** one use each, and it ages. Write the purchase date on each bottle and check the
  label's shelf life at the rotation check (→ 26-08).
- **Valve cores:** cheap by the card. Keep spares.
- **Tires themselves:** in a long emergency, nobody can make them. Gentle driving, correct pressure
  (NHTSA, TireWise) and moving the least-worn tires to where they matter most are the plan
  (→ 23-04).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** flats are an errand. Plug, then have a shop fix it properly. Keep the kit stocked.
  Practice now.
- **B, on the move:** the kit, a charged inflator, warm sealant and a spare ride along (→ 01-03). A
  flat is a 20-minute delay if, and only if, you practiced.
- **C, settled:** gravel and field work eat tires. A plug kit becomes something the whole community
  uses (→ 18-01). Save sealant for true emergencies.

pages.body:
# Trailer maintenance and repair

**What this page is for.** Keeping a small utility or enclosed trailer safe to tow: the walkaround
before every trip, the wheel bearings that cause the worst failures, trailer tires, lights, and the
hitch. Nothing on a trailer is exotic, and all of it can be checked in ten minutes. This page is
the ten minutes.

{{#if has.trailer}}**You own a trailer.** Fill in the record block below the day you read this.
**Vehicles that can tow:** {{#each vehicles as v}}{{v.type_text}} (can tow: {{v.can_tow}}); {{/each}}{{else}}**You have
no trailer recorded.** Keep this page for a trailer you borrow, buy or find; read it before towing
anything.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY. A wheel bearing that fails at highway speed can lock the wheel, throw it off, or start a
> fire.** Most small trailers have **one axle: no second axle to limp on.** The two checks that
> prevent this are the bearing service (yearly) and the **hot-hub check at every stop** (below).
>
> **Never tow with an unlatched or unpinned coupler, or without both safety chains crossed under
> the tongue** (NHTSA, Trailer Safety). A trailer that comes loose crosses into oncoming traffic.
>
> **Never let anyone ride in a trailer.**
>
> **Your trailer's own axle maker and tire sidewall govern** where they differ from this page.

## Do this now

1. **Fill in the record block** (bottom of the page). A used trailer's history is unknown until you
   write it down. The bearing service date and the tire date codes decide everything else.

{{photo trailer-plate}}

2. **Do the full walkaround once in the driveway**, slowly, with this page in hand. After that it
   takes five minutes.
3. **Have the bearings inspected and repacked now** unless there is paper proof of a recent
   service. On a used trailer, "unknown" means "due". Watch it done, and ask the shop the axle brand
   and whether the hubs have grease fittings.

{{photo trailer-hubs}}

4. **Buy a mounted spare** (a trailer tire on a wheel with the right bolt pattern, plus a carrier or
   strap point) (→ 26-09). It turns a tire failure from abandoning the trailer into a 20-minute
   delay.
5. **Buy a grease gun, a tube of marine wheel-bearing grease, and dielectric grease** (a
   non-conducting grease that keeps water out of electrical plugs). None can be improvised later.

## The walkaround: every hitch-up, no exceptions

{{figure fig-trailer-hitch-checks}}

These checks follow NHTSA's trailer safety guidance (NHTSA, Trailer Safety).

```
[ ] COUPLER fully down on the ball, LATCH CLOSED and PINNED or
    LOCKED. Lift test: crank the tongue jack UP a few inches. The
    back of the vehicle should rise with it. If the coupler pops
    off, you found out in the driveway.
[ ] SAFETY CHAINS crossed in an X under the tongue (so they catch a
    dropped coupler), hooked to the hitch, not to each other. Enough
    slack to turn, not enough to drag.
[ ] TONGUE JACK fully raised (or removed and stowed).
[ ] LIGHTS plugged in. With a helper or a phone video: running
    lights, LEFT signal, RIGHT signal, BRAKE lights. Fix before
    moving.
[ ] TIRES at the MAXIMUM pressure printed on the trailer tire's
    sidewall, checked COLD. Look for cracks, bulges, wear.
[ ] LUG NUTS: check snug with a wrench, in a star pattern. Re-tighten
    after the first ~50 miles on any wheel that has been off; lug
    nuts loosen as they seat.
[ ] LOAD: heavy items forward, over or slightly ahead of the axle,
    so roughly 10 to 12 percent of the loaded trailer's weight
    presses down on the hitch ("tongue weight"). Too little makes
    the trailer sway. Everything strapped (01-03).
[ ] DOOR or gate latched. Anything on the roof or tongue secured.
```

**Carrying fuel** in the trailer rather than the passenger cabin is one of the options on → 30-07.
Your choice: {{choice DC-06}}.

## Wheel bearings: the killer, for a non-mechanic

{{figure fig-wheel-bearing-cutaway}}

Each wheel spins on two cone-shaped steel bearings sitting in grease inside the hub (the metal
center the wheel bolts to). Over time the grease dries out, leaks past a worn seal, or lets water
in. The bearing then runs metal on metal, overheats, and can weld itself to the axle stub. On a
two-axle trailer that is a bad day; on a one-axle trailer it is the whole trip.

**Service rule:** inspect and repack the bearings **every 12 months or 12,000 miles, whichever
comes first** (Dexter Axle, Trailer Axle Operation, Maintenance and Service Manual), and at once on
a used trailer with no records. For a trailer that mostly sits, the yearly rule is the one that
matters.

A **repack** means: hub off, old grease cleaned out, bearings inspected (any pitting, blue heat
marks or roughness means replace; bearings are cheap), packed full of fresh grease, a new seal
fitted, and the axle nut set to the maker's specification, snug and then backed off slightly, not
forced tight. **Learn this once beside someone who has done it before doing it alone.**

**Grease fittings ("easy-lube" hubs).** Some hubs have a grease fitting in the end of the axle so a
grease gun can push fresh grease through. If yours do: jack the wheel up and turn it slowly while
pumping slowly, until fresh grease appears at the cap. **That is a top-up between repacks, not a
replacement for them**: it cannot inspect the bearings, and pumping too fast can burst the rear
seal and push grease onto brakes (etrailer, Trailer Bearings). No fitting means no shortcut:
repack or nothing.

**The hot-hub check: every stop, every time.**

```
Hold the back of your hand NEAR (not on) the center of each hub.
  Warm, like metal left in the sun  -> normal.
  Too hot to hold your hand near    -> STOP. Do not drive on.
A hub you cannot touch is a bearing failing. Driving on means a
seized wheel, a lost wheel, or fire. Let it cool. Add grease if it
has a fitting. Creep at low speed to help, or make the leave-the-
trailer decision (01-03).
```

**What a failing bearing sounds like:** a low growl or rumble that rises and falls with road speed
(not engine speed), sometimes a rhythmic grinding or chirp, often changing in curves. Test with the
windows down at low speed on a quiet road. **Any new speed-linked noise from the trailer: stop and
do the hot-hub check.**

## Trailer tires: different rules from the car's

- **Trailer tires are marked "ST"** (special trailer). They are built stiff for towing, not for
  grip. **A light-truck ("LT") tire of the same or higher load rating is an accepted substitute.**
  A passenger-car ("P") tire is a last resort only, carrying about 10 percent less, because its
  soft sidewalls flex, overheat and encourage sway.
- **Pressure is the MAXIMUM printed on the sidewall, cold.** That is the opposite of a car, which
  uses its door placard (→ 16-10). Under-inflated trailer tires overheat and blow out.
- **Trailer tires age out at roughly 5 to 6 years even with good tread.** Trailers sit, and sun
  kills sidewalls from inside. **Read the date code:** the last four digits of the "DOT" code on the
  sidewall are the week and year it was made ("3921" means week 39 of 2021; → 29-14). A used trailer
  often arrives with tires many years old that look new. **Check the date, not the tread.**
- **Cracks in the sidewall, bulges, or an old date mean replace before the first long tow**, not
  after.

## The trailer spare

- **One mounted spare** with the correct bolt pattern, on a carrier or strapped inside.
- **Your vehicle's roadside kit works on the trailer** (→ 16-10): the plug kit, inflator, jack and
  lug wrench. A small trailer's corner is light; jack under the frame near the axle. Chock the
  vehicle and the trailer's other wheel. Same star-pattern lug-nut rules (→ 16-10, Case 4).
- **Tread punctures plug exactly as on a car** (→ 16-10, Case 2). **Sidewall damage means the
  spare.** That is the whole decision.

## Lights: the troubleshooting ladder

{{figure fig-four-pin-connector}}

Trailer lights fail constantly, and the fix is almost always the same. Work down the ladder and stop
when they work.

1. **The ground wire first. It causes most trailer light faults.** In a common 4-pin plug, the white
   wire and the light housings' mounting screws carry the return path. A bad ground looks crazy: dim
   lights, turn signals that flash everything, lights that work only at an angle. **Fix:** unbolt the
   white wire where it meets the trailer frame, wire-brush the frame and the terminal to bright metal,
   bolt it back tight. Do the same for each light's mounting screws.
2. **The plug itself.** Unplug, look for green corrosion, brush the pins clean, and **pack both
   halves with dielectric grease.** Make that a habit at every hitch-up. A dab in each bulb socket
   ends most repeat failures.
3. **The bulb or lamp.** Swap it (carry spares). Sealed LED lamps swap as a whole unit: two screws,
   two wires. Join wires with crimp connectors or solder, never twist-and-tape (→ 16-07).
4. **The wiring run**, last and rarest: look for a pinched or rubbed-through wire where the harness
   crosses the frame, especially at the tongue.

**Nothing lights at all?** Test the vehicle's socket first, with a cheap plug-in 4-pin tester or a
helper and a test light.

## Coupler, latch and frame

- **Coupler wear check** (every few months and before any long tow): hitched, latched, tongue jack
  lightly loaded, rock the tongue. **A clunk between coupler and ball means a worn coupler or the
  wrong ball size.** The required ball size is stamped on the coupler. A coupler on a ball one size
  too small tows fine until the first hard bump lifts it off.
- The latch moves freely, snaps fully shut, and takes the pin or padlock. Oil it. Replace a bent
  latch; couplers are cheap bolt-on parts.
- **Safety chain hooks and their welds:** look for stretching, cracks or rust-through.
- **Frame, tongue welds, spring hangers and U-bolts:** once a season, look for cracks at welds (a
  crack often leaves a rusty streak down the paint). **Anything cracked goes to a welder before it
  tows again.**
- **Wooden floor:** probe for soft spots; water gets in at door seals.

## Record block (fill in the day you get it)

```
Make / model:          ____________________   Year: ________
VIN / plate:           ____________________
Axle brand and rating: ____________________   Grease fittings? Y / N
Bearing service date:  ____________  by: ____________________
  ("unknown" = due NOW)
Tire size (sidewall):  ____________  Max cold psi: ________
Tire DOT date codes:   L: ________  R: ________  Spare: ________
Bolt pattern:          ____________  Coupler ball size: ________
Empty weight (plate):  ________ lb
Gross weight rating (plate, "GVWR"): ________ lb
Cargo budget = the LOWER of (GVWR - empty weight) and
  (your vehicle's towing limit - empty weight): ________ lb
Vehicle's tongue weight limit (owner's manual): ________ lb
Lug nut torque (axle or wheel maker): ________ ft-lb
```

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Mounted spare wheel and trailer tire, with carrier** | Turns a tire failure into a delay | Match the bolt pattern |
| **Grease gun and marine wheel-bearing grease** | Top-ups and repacks | One tube lasts years |
| Spare bearing and seal kit for your axle | Repack parts; keep on the shelf | Match the axle in the record |
| **Dielectric grease** | Ends most light problems | Plug and bulb sockets |
| Spare bulbs or a spare LED lamp, crimp connectors | Ladder step 3 | → 16-07 |
| 4-pin plug tester | Splits trailer faults from vehicle faults in seconds | Cheap |
| Two wheel chocks | Every jacking job | Wood blocks work |
| Padlocks for the coupler latch and the door | Theft is the everyday risk | |
| The roadside tire kit (→ 16-10) | Covers trailer tires too | Already in the vehicle |
| This page | The walkaround and the ladder | In the trailer |

**Substitutes:** bearings and seals are standard sizes, sold at auto parts and farm stores or taken
from a scrapped trailer with the same axle. A length of wire run from the light housing to bare frame
metal proves a bad ground in the field. A bottle jack or floor jack replaces a scissor jack.

## When it runs out

- **Sealed grease keeps for years.** Stock two tubes.
- **A boxed bearing-and-seal kit** turns a repack into an hour instead of a hunt. They do not age on
  the shelf.
- **Trailer tires age whether you tow or not.** Park out of direct sun, or shade the tires, to slow
  it. In a long event, nobody stocks trailer sizes, so the tire-conservation rules of → 23-04 apply
  twice over.
- **Lights:** sealed LED lamps are the buy-once answer; no filaments to shake apart on gravel.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** service the bearings, fill in the record, practice the walkaround and backing up
  in an empty lot (→ 22-05). Load the trailer as → 01-03 says.
- **B, on the move:** walkaround before leaving; **hot-hub check at every stop**; re-tighten lug
  nuts at the first stop. Winter towing multiplies every rule on → 17-01 and calls for much lower
  speeds. A problem caught at a fuel stop is a delay; one missed is the leave-the-trailer decision
  (→ 01-03).
- **C, settled:** the trailer becomes the hauler. Make the yearly repack a fall routine (→ 26-08).
  At a place with no shop, the grease gun and the boxed bearing kit you carry are the shop. Gravel
  eats lights; the ladder gets used.
