pages.body:
# Grid-down house repairs: gas, roof, window, burst pipe, sump

**What this page is for.** The repairs that keep a house a shelter when no one can come: a gas
smell, a torn-open roof, a broken window, a burst pipe, and water rising in a basement. All are
within reach of a careful person who is not a tradesman, if the materials are already in the house.
None of the materials can be bought after the storm, because everyone else's roof is open too.

> **SAFETY. The danger is not the house. It is you.** With no emergency room, **a fall off a ladder
> is a worse outcome than any leak.** Every repair below starts with a safety gate, and the gates
> are the point of the page.
>
> **Gas comes before every repair.** If you smell gas, nothing else on this page happens until the
> gas block has been run.
>
> **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit
> with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide")
> cord.** It electrocutes line workers and neighbors and starts fires (floor, → 30-01; → 29-04).
> Run cords to single appliances instead.
>
> **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window**
> (floor, → 30-01). Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning (→ 08-02).

## Do this now

1. **Find the gas shutoff and the main water shutoff.** Practice both in the dark. Photograph both
   (blocks below). Write their locations on the family plan (→ 00-04).
2. **Buy the roof kit before storm season:** two heavy tarps sized for your roof (rule below), a
   bundle of 1x2 furring strips (thin wooden strips), and a box of 2-inch exterior screws.
3. **Buy the plumbing kit:** two push-fit couplings in **each** pipe size in the house (measure now),
   a small tube cutter, and two screw-type pipe repair clamps. It fits in a shoebox.
4. **Measure plywood for the windows most likely to break** (the big ones facing your usual storm
   direction) and write the sizes where you store the plywood.
5. **Walk the house and write down what your water pipes are made of** (table under Repair 3):
   ______________________.
{{#if has.basement}}6. **You have a basement.** If it has a sump pit (a hole in the floor with a pump in it), buy a
   battery water alarm for the pit, and read Repair 4.{{/if}}

## Gas: the gate before every repair

{{#if has.gas_any}}**Your home has {{#if has.natural_gas}}natural gas{{else}}propane{{/if}} service.**
This block is for you now.{{else}}**Your home has no gas service recorded.** Read this anyway for
any house you shelter in.{{/if}} Each gas appliance (furnace, water heater, stove) has its own
small valve on the pipe feeding it. **Those are not the house shutoff.** The house shutoff is at the
meter (natural gas) or at the tank (propane).

{{figure fig-gas-valve-on-off}}

{{photo gas-shutoff}}

```
[ ] SMELL GAS (rotten eggs) or HEAR HISSING -> everyone OUT, now.
    Leave doors open behind you. No light switches, no lighters, no
    phone calls until you are outside and away from the house.
[ ] SHUT OFF AT THE METER ONLY IF IT IS SAFE: you can reach it from
    outside, you do not smell gas strongly there, and nothing is
    burning. If in doubt, stay away and keep everyone away.
    NATURAL GAS: the valve is on the pipe coming out of the ground,
    BEFORE the meter. With a 12-inch adjustable wrench or gas wrench,
    turn it ONE QUARTER TURN so the flat bar lies CROSSWISE to the
    pipe = OFF. Bar in line with the pipe = ON (FEMA, Utility
    Shut-off and Safety).
    PROPANE TANK: close the valve under the tank's dome lid, turning
    clockwise ("righty tighty").
[ ] THE WRENCH HANGS AT THE METER. That is the only place it is any
    use. Hung on: ____/____/____
[ ] DO NOT TURN IT BACK ON YOURSELF while the utility exists. Call
    from outside: gas emergency line {{ contacts.utility.gas.phone }}
    ({{ contacts.utility.gas.provider }}), or 911. Only the utility
    restores service and relights pilots (FEMA).
```

**If the utility is gone for good:** FEMA says only a qualified professional turns the gas back
on, and propane safety guidance says only a technician should relight a pilot (Ready.gov, Safety
Skills; Propane Education & Research Council). Waiting may mean no hot water, furnace or stove; relighting yourself risks a fire,
explosion or carbon monoxide. Your household's choice: {{choice DC-28}} → 30-29. Whatever you
chose, the gas stays off until the leak is found and fixed, and nothing is lit while anyone
smells gas (→ 08-02).

A gas smell also changes where you shelter from a tornado: not in a room near the leak (→ 17-06).

## Repair 1: tarping a roof after hail or wind

**The safety gate. All five must pass, or the answer is buckets in the attic until conditions
change.**

{{figure fig-ladder-four-to-one}}

```
[ ] DRY ROOF. Never wet, never icy, never in wind. The leak can
    run another day; you cannot.
[ ] TWO PEOPLE minimum: one on the roof, one holding the ladder and
    watching. NEVER alone.
[ ] ONE STORY ONLY. Higher than one story, or a pitch you would not
    comfortably sit on: the job is off. Tarp from inside the attic
    under the hole, set buckets, wait for help. This is the honest
    limit for someone who is not a roofer (OSHA, Fall Protection).
[ ] SOUND STRUCTURE. Sagging roof deck, a gas smell (gas block
    first), or power lines down on the house = nobody goes up
    (Red Cross / FEMA).
[ ] LADDER (OSHA): base 1 foot out from the wall for every 4 feet
    of height; top at least 3 feet ABOVE the roof edge and TIED OFF;
    three points of contact always. Hands EMPTY: screws and strips go
    up in a bucket on a rope (16-03). Held by the second person,
    always.
```

**The over-the-ridge method.** This is how the US Army Corps of Engineers' temporary "Blue Roof"
crews do it: the tarp is fixed to solid wood, never held by weights (US Army Corps of Engineers,
Blue Roof Information).

{{figure fig-roof-tarp-over-ridge}}

1. **Size the tarp** so it reaches **from over the peak (ridge) and down past the damage by at least
   3 feet on every side**, and far enough down the slope that water runs off onto sound shingles,
   not under the tarp's bottom edge.
2. **Anchor on the far, undamaged side first.** Roll the tarp's top edge twice around a furring
   strip and screw through strip and tarp into the roof deck, at close, even spacing along the whole
   strip. Wind cannot get under an edge that comes over the ridge.
3. **Unroll** over the ridge and down across the damage. Pull it drum-tight. Flapping destroys a
   tarp in days.
4. **Screw furring strips down both side edges**, through the tarp into the deck, working down the
   slope. Strips run **up and down** the slope, so water that gets under an edge still runs out the
   bottom.
5. **Bottom edge:** roll it around a strip and screw it onto sound roof, or let it hang over the eave
   with the roll screwed at the sides.
6. **Never bricks, sandbags or tires alone.** The first gust turns them into missiles and the tarp
   into a sail. Weights are only for an hour while you fetch the screws.
7. **Yes, the screws make holes.** Each is under the tarp or through it into wood, and easy to seal
   later with roofing cement (→ 16-05). A peeled-off tarp is a flooded house now. Count the screws
   so you can seal every hole when the tarp comes off.

### Water coming through the ceiling

Until the roof is tarped, catch the water inside.

{{photo breaker-panel}}

1. **Electricity first.** If water is running near a ceiling light or fan, switch that circuit off
   at the breaker panel before working under it. **Never stand in water to reach a panel.** If the
   panel itself is wet, or there is water on the floor in front of it, leave it alone. The power
   stays off until someone who knows has looked (electric utility while it exists:
   {{ contacts.utility.electric.phone }}).
2. **Find the drip point.** If the ceiling is bulging with water, set a bucket under it and poke a
   small hole at the lowest point, so the water drains in one place instead of bringing the ceiling
   down.
3. **Hang a ceiling leak diverter** (a square of waterproof fabric with a drain fitting in the middle)
   or a plastic sheet under the drip, corners tied or taped up, so the middle sags lowest at the
   drain.
4. **Run a hose from the drain to a bucket, floor drain, sink or out a window**, lower than the
   diverter.
5. **Check every few hours.** Empty the bucket; check the hose. It buys time; the tarp is still the
   repair.

A leak diverter hung upside-down outdoors also works as a rain funnel into a barrel (→ 03-05). That
water is raw: treat it before drinking (→ 03-04).

## Repair 2: broken window

**Glass first:** leather gloves and eye protection before touching anything (→ 12-02). Work loose
pieces out of the frame from the top down. Sweep, then wipe the floor with a damp cloth: the tiny
pieces outlast the cleanup.{{#if has.young_child}} With a small child crawling or barefoot, wipe
twice and keep them out of the room until it is done.{{/if}}

**For now (minutes):** plastic sheeting, or a contractor bag cut open, taped to the **inside** of the
frame all the way round. Inside tape survives wind better. Good for days, not weeks. It stops
weather, not people.

**Board-up (the real fix):**
1. Measure the opening. Cut plywood (1/2 inch or thicker) slightly smaller than the opening, or cut
   it larger and screw it over the outside trim instead.
2. Screw through the plywood into the **frame** (not the moving window sash), evenly spaced all
   round, with screws 2 inches or longer. Screws, not nails, so it comes off later without wrecking
   the trim.
3. **Winter:** trapped air insulates. Plastic inside, plywood outside, and a blanket hung over the
   whole opening (→ 08-03). That room may still drop out of the warm part of the house (→ 08-01).

## Repair 3: burst pipe

**Step 0: turn off the main water shutoff, then open the lowest faucet in the house to drain the
pipes** (→ 03-06). Everything below is done on a drained line with no pressure.

{{photo water-main-shutoff}}

**What pipe do you have?**

| Look | It is | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Dull orange-brown metal, soldered joints | **Copper** | Push-fit works |
| Cream or tan rigid plastic, printed "CPVC" | **CPVC** | Push-fit works; old CPVC is brittle, cut gently |
| Flexible tubing, often red, blue or white, printed "PEX" | **PEX** | Push-fit works; use the stiffener insert that comes with the fitting |
| Gray metal, threaded joints, a magnet sticks | **Galvanized steel** (older houses) | **Push-fit does not fit.** Cap or clamp the branch and live without it; the real repair is threaded fittings and two pipe wrenches |

**The non-plumber's repair: a push-fit coupling on a clean cut.** A push-fit coupling is a short
fitting that seals with rubber rings and grips with steel teeth. No torch, no glue.

{{figure fig-push-fit-coupling}}

1. **Cut out the split** with the tube cutter (or a hacksaw, square across), removing a short
   section centered on the damage. If the split is long, make two cuts and bridge the gap with a
   repair coupling, or a spare piece of pipe and two couplings.
2. **Smooth the cut ends** (remove the sharp lip, "deburr") and wipe clean. A scratch or burr will
   leak. **On copper, use emery cloth only if it is corroded, and lightly**: deep scratches spoil the
   seal (fitting makers' instructions).
3. **Mark the insertion depth** on the pipe (the package states it), so you can see it seated fully.
4. **Push the fitting on**, twisting slightly, until the mark meets the fitting on both sides. It
   takes real force and stops with a solid feel.
5. **Reopen the main slowly** with a dry paper towel wrapped round the joint. Any wet spot within ten
   minutes means it is not seated: release it (with the release tool) and redo it.

**The fast temporary (no cutting):** a screw-type pipe repair clamp, a rubber pad in a hinged steel
sleeve, clamped over the split. No clamp: a strip of inner-tube rubber wrapped tight over the split
and held with two hose clamps or tightly twisted wire (→ 16-05, → 16-07). Temporaries weep and fail;
they buy time for the real repair.

**Frozen pipe, one sequence** (Red Cross, Preventing and Thawing Frozen Pipes):
1. **Main water off** (→ 03-06).
2. **Open the faucet on the frozen line**, so melting ice has somewhere to go.
3. **Warm the pipe starting from the faucet end**, working back toward the frozen section, with a
   hair dryer, a heating pad, or towels soaked in hot water. **Never a torch, a fuel heater or any
   open flame.** That is how a pipe job becomes a house fire.
4. **When water flows, turn the main back on slowly and check the whole run.** A pipe that froze may
   have split without showing it (→ 08-03).

## Repair 4: water rising in a basement sump pit

{{#if has.basement}}**You have a basement.** {{/if}}In a house with a basement sump pump, the most
likely grid-down water problem is not a burst pipe: it is **the sump pump stopping when the power
does**, during snowmelt or a big storm.

1. **Power the pump another way** if you have one: a power station or generator, by cord to the
   pump only, never through house wiring (floor above; → 17-08, → 09-04). Read the pump's label for
   its running watts (→ 29-14) and check your power source can start it. **Test it now, with the pit
   dry**, so you know the cord reaches.
2. **No power, or the pump is dead:** a small 12-volt utility or bilge pump on a power station's
   12-volt port with a garden hose out a door or window; or a bucket line up the stairs. That works.
   A water-powered backup pump works only while town water pressure holds.
3. **Put a battery water alarm at the edge of the pit.** The pump fails silently; the alarm wakes
   you.
4. **Keep nothing that matters on a basement floor.** Power stations, medicine, food, chemicals,
   documents (→ 19-01) on shelves. **Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) that gets wet gives off
   chlorine gas and can start a fire** with organic material (→ 03-04): store it high and dry.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **12-inch adjustable wrench or gas wrench, hung at the gas meter** | The gas gate | Useless anywhere else |
| **Heavy tarps, two, roof-sized** | Repair 1 | Heaviest weave sold |
| **Furring strips (1x2, a bundle) and 2-inch exterior screws** | The tarp anchors | Store flat with the tarps |
| Plywood, 1/2 inch or thicker | Board-up | Sizes written on it |
| Plastic sheeting and tape | Interim window | → 16-05 |
| **Push-fit couplings, two per pipe size, plus a repair coupling** | Repair 3 | Your sizes: ______ |
| **Small tube cutter** | Clean square cuts in tight spots | |
| **Pipe repair clamps, two**, inner-tube rubber, hose clamps | The temporary | |
| Push-fit release tool | Redoing a bad joint | Tape it to the fittings box |
| Ceiling leak diverter or plastic sheet and hose | Inside until the tarp is on | |
| Battery water alarm (if you have a sump) | Repair 4 | Test the battery yearly (→ 25-10) |
| 12-volt utility pump and garden hose (optional) | Repair 4 backup | |
| Leather gloves and eye protection | Glass and overhead work | One set kept with this kit |
| Ladder in good condition | The gate assumes it | |

**Substitutes:** tarps from billboards, pool covers and truck loads; plywood from fences and interior
doors; strips from pallet wood; a garden hose split lengthwise and clamped as a pipe patch. In a long
event, **capping a branch line you can live without** beats repairing it.

## When it runs out

- **Tarps die from sunlight and flapping.** A tight tarp lasts a year or more; a loose one, a month.
  Re-tighten after every wind. The second tarp is the replacement.
- **Push-fit fittings can be reused** with the release tool, and do not age.
- **Prevention is the deeper fix:** winterizing the house (→ 08-03) and draining the water system
  before a hard freeze with no heat (→ 03-06) make Repair 3 unnecessary.
- **Damage beyond tarp scale** (sagging roof, broken roof framing) is a reason to move within the
  house or leave, not to do carpentry (→ 17-02).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** buy the kits, measure pipes and windows, hang the gas wrench, and treat the first
  real tarp job as practice, with the full safety gate.
- **B, on the move:** a tarp, screws and a driver travel{{#if has.trailer}} in the trailer
  (→ 16-11){{/if}}, because the place you arrive may be damaged.
- **C, settled:** barn and outbuilding roofs make this a recurring job. **The one-story,
  two-person gate still applies to every person, every time.**

# Weather and regional hazards

**What this section holds.** 18 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 17-01 **Blizzards, ice storms and winter storms**: Winter storms are the hazard most likely to cut a household off: roads close, the power fails, and help cannot reach you for days.
- → 17-02 **Tornadoes, severe thunderstorms, derechos and lightning**: A tornado warning gives you minutes, not hours.
- → 17-03 **Floods and flash floods**: Flooding kills more people each year than any other thunderstorm-related hazard, and over half of flood drownings happen when a vehicle is driven into floodw…
- → 17-04 **Extreme cold and extreme heat**: Temperature extremes kill quietly, mostly the very young, the old and the sick, and mostly indoors when the power is out.
- → 17-05 **Grassland and wildland fire**: Wildfire is not only a mountain and forest problem.
- → 17-06 **Preparing a storm shelter spot**: In a tornado warning you will have minutes, and someone may be carrying a child.
- → 17-07 **Drought and water scarcity**: Drought is the slow hazard.
- → 17-08 **Power grid failure: hours, days and weeks**: Section 09 is how to make power.
- → 17-09 **Pandemic and widespread illness**: A pandemic (a disease spreading widely across many countries) usually does not break the power grid or the water supply.
- → 17-10 **Reading the sky: forecasting with no forecast**: Every other page in this section assumes a warning reaches you.
- → 17-11 **Hazards on the road to each destination**: A trip to a destination crosses country whose weather you may not know.
- → 17-12 **Earthquakes**: An earthquake gives no warning you can count on and is over in seconds to a minute.
- → 17-13 **Hurricanes and tropical storms**: A hurricane gives days of warning, which is its one gift.
- → 17-14 **Wildfire smoke and fire evacuation**: Wildfire reaches far more people as smoke than as flame: smoke from a fire hundreds of miles away can make the air unhealthy for days or weeks.
- → 17-15 **Tsunamis**: A tsunami is a series of ocean waves, usually caused by an undersea earthquake, that floods the coast far beyond any normal tide.
- → 17-16 **Volcanic ashfall**: An eruption can drop ash over a huge area, hundreds of miles downwind.

pages.body:
# Blizzards, ice storms and winter storms

**What this page is for.** Winter storms are the hazard most likely to cut a household off: roads
close, the power fails, and help cannot reach you for days. This page covers the four winter
hazards, the alert words that come before them, what to do before, during and after, and the one
scenario that kills people every winter: being stranded in a vehicle.
{{#if is.snow_region}}Your home county gets about **{{ region.home.snow_in }} inches of snow a
year**, so plan on this page every winter.{{/if}}
{{#if is.cold_winters}}January nights average about **{{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F** where you
live, and the record low is **{{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F**.{{/if}}

> **SAFETY.** The three killers in a winter storm, in order:
> 1. **Carbon monoxide** (CO, a poison gas you cannot see or smell, → 29-03) from generators,
>    grills and heaters brought indoors during a cold outage. It kills prepared and unprepared
>    people alike. **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near
>    an open window.** (→ 30-01, → 08-02)
> 2. **Travel.** People die in vehicles in blizzards. Do not travel under a blizzard warning. If
>    you are stranded, **stay with the vehicle** (below).
> 3. **The cold itself:** hypothermia (the body's core getting dangerously cold) and frostbite
>    (frozen skin), → 08-05.
>
> **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** In a winter outage, refrigerated
> medicine must be kept from freezing (→ 29-07).

## Do this now

1. **Get a NOAA Weather Radio with SAME programmed** (→ 15-01, → 29-09). Winter storms come with
   hours of warning, and those hours are everything.
2. **CO alarms on every level and where people sleep, tested, before the first heater is lit**
   (→ 08-02). Replace each by the date printed on it.
3. **Do the "three days with no power in deep cold" walk-through on paper:** heat, water, food,
   light, medicine, sanitation (→ 13-05). Find the gaps now.
4. **Winterize the house** (→ 08-03) and **stock the vehicle kit in autumn** (→ 22-05). In a cold
   region the vehicle kit is a survival kit, not a first-aid kit.
5. **Bring firewood and fuel in reach before the storm**, not during (→ 06-04).

## The four winter hazards

| Hazard | What it does | The main danger |
|---|---|---|
| **Blizzard** | Wind plus snow makes a **whiteout**. Travel becomes impossible; drifts bury things | Stranding and getting lost. People have died a few yards from shelter |
| **Ice storm** | Freezing rain coats everything in ice | **Power lines and trees come down**: outages of days to weeks |
| **Extreme cold** | Very low air temperature, often with wind | Frostbite in minutes, hypothermia, frozen pipes, failing equipment (→ 17-04) |
| **Heavy snow** | Deep snow, roof loads, blocked doors and roads | Being cut off; roof damage; heart strain from shoveling |

## The alert words, and what each one means for you

A **watch** means get ready; a **warning** means it is happening or about to; an **advisory**
means take care (→ 29-10). Each NWS office sets its own trigger amounts for snow, ice and cold, so
copy your office's numbers into the blanks. Your office: **{{ region.home.nws_office }}**.

| NWS alert | What it means | What the household does |
|---|---|---|
| **Blizzard Warning** | Blizzard conditions: wind over 35 mph with snow and blowing snow, cutting visibility to a quarter mile or less for at least 3 hours (NSSL, Winter Weather Types) | **Nobody travels.** Lifeline rules in force. Full storm preparation should already be done at the watch |
| **Winter Storm Warning** | Heavy snow or sleet, or a mix with big impact. Your office's amount: snow over ______ in | Run the "before" list below; no travel plans for 48 hours |
| **Ice Storm Warning** | Damaging ice on lines and trees. Your office's amount: ______ in of ice | **Treat it as a power-outage warning** (→ 17-08): charge everything, fill water, stay off roads |
| **Extreme Cold Warning** | Dangerously cold air temperature or wind chill. Your office's line: ______ °F | Outside only for essential minutes, no bare skin, children stay in, no unnecessary travel |
| **Cold Weather Advisory** | Cold enough to be dangerous without care. Your office's line: ______ °F | Short, supervised time outside; full layers (→ 11-01) |
| **Winter Weather Advisory** | Snow, sleet or light ice that makes travel hazardous | Errands early; vehicle kit in the car (→ 22-05) |

> **Old names.** In October 2024 the NWS renamed the Wind Chill Watch, Wind Chill Warning and Wind
> Chill Advisory to the **Extreme Cold Watch**, **Extreme Cold Warning** and **Cold Weather
> Advisory** (NWS, cold product changes, 2024). An old card or radio that says "wind chill
> warning" means the same thing. There is no separate **Blizzard Watch**: since 2017 a possible
> blizzard comes as a **Winter Storm Watch** (NWS, Hazard Simplification, 2017).
>
> **Coming change.** The NWS has announced that it will stop using the word "Advisory" and use
> plain-language headlines that start with the hazard in capitals (for example "SNOW: hazardous
> travel"); watches and warnings stay as they are (NWS, Hazard Simplification FAQ). If your alerts
> read that way, treat them as the advisory rows in this table.

**Wind chill** is how cold it feels on bare skin when wind is added (→ 29-10). The NWS wind chill
chart shows whether bare skin freezes in 30, 10 or 5 minutes at each temperature and wind speed
(NWS, Wind Chill Chart). Use the chart, not a feeling.

{{figure fig-wind-chill-chart}}

## The blizzard: the whiteout is the danger

**A blizzard is defined by wind and visibility, not by how much snow falls.** Wind lifting snow
already on the ground can make a whiteout under a clear sky; this is a **ground blizzard** (NSSL).

- **Visibility can drop to nothing.** People have died walking between a house and a barn. **If
  you must go out in a whiteout, tie a rope from the door to where you are going** and keep a hand
  on it. This is an old, proven practice.
- **Drifts bury doors, vehicles, woodpiles and solar panels** (→ 09-05). Bring in what you will
  need before it starts.
- **Do not travel.** When the NWS or the road authority says do not travel, believe it.
- **Plan on three days or more of complete self-reliance**, with little or no solar power and no
  way to leave.

{{photo whiteout-lifeline}}

## The ice storm: the outage maker

- **Ice brings down power lines and trees.** Outages can last a week or more over a wide area,
  with repair crews working through terrible conditions.
- **Treat every downed line as live**, and keep everyone, children and pets far away.
- **Falling ice and limbs** injure people under trees.
- **Walking is dangerous**: traction devices, sand, wood ash or cat litter on paths (→ 11-06).
- **This is when CO poisoning happens.** People bring generators and grills inside or run heaters
  in closed rooms. Heaters run indoors only under their own pages' rules (→ 08-04, → 08-09,
  → 08-10).

## Stranded in a vehicle

This kills people in cold regions every winter, and the guidance is specific (NWS, What To Do If
You're Caught in a Winter Storm):

- **Stay with the vehicle.** It is shelter, it is visible, and searchers look for vehicles.
  Walking for help in a whiteout is how people die.
- **Run the engine about 10 minutes each hour** for heat, and **first make sure the exhaust pipe
  is clear of snow.** A drifted-in tailpipe pushes CO into the cabin; this is a recurring cause of
  death.
- **Open a window a little** for fresh air while the engine runs.
- **Move arms, legs, fingers and toes** now and then to keep blood flowing and stay warm
  (→ 11-04).
- **Be visible:** a bright cloth, preferably red, on the antenna or door; **raise the hood once
  the snow stops**; dome light on at night while the engine runs (→ 15-07).
- **The vehicle kit is why this works** (→ 22-05): blankets, hats, mittens, hand warmers, food,
  water, a light, a shovel. Stock it before the first storm.

Some households carry a candle in a metal can for heat in a stranded car, with a window cracked.
That is an open flame in a closed space, which is a trade-off: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21

## The household during a winter storm

**Before it hits (at the watch):**
- Firewood and fuel in reach (→ 06-04). Water containers filled (→ 03-02). Everything charged.
- CO alarms tested. Refrigerated medicine plan checked (→ 29-07).
- Warm clothes sorted for every person (→ 11-01, → 11-02).
- Vehicle fuel above half (→ 22-05).

**During:**
- **Heat one room** (→ 08-01). Layers on indoors. Light without flame where you can (→ 10-01).
- **Nothing fuel-burning without ventilation and a working CO alarm** (→ 08-02).
- **Whether an unvented heater runs while people sleep is a household decision with a real risk
  on each side**: cold on one side, carbon monoxide on the other. Read the card before the
  storm: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02
- **Check children and elders by touch**, often: belly and back of the neck (→ 11-02).
- **Water:** let taps on outside walls drip and open cabinet doors under sinks; know where the
  main shutoff is (→ 03-06). Snow is water if you can spend the fuel to melt it (→ 03-05).
- **Medicine:** insulin and other refrigerated medicine must not freeze (→ 29-07). Keep it in the
  heated room with you, off cold floors and outside walls.

**After:**
- **Dig out carefully.** The NWS warns that the strain of cold and hard work such as shoveling
  heavy snow may cause a heart attack; anyone not in good health should avoid it (NWS, What To Do
  If You're Caught in a Winter Storm). Take breaks; share the work.
- **Clear the tailpipe before starting any vehicle**, and clear snow from furnace and dryer vents
  outside the house before running them.
- Sweep snow off solar panels (→ 09-05). Check on neighbours, especially older people living
  alone (→ 18-01). Check the roof, pipes and chimney for damage.

## Sheltering by dwelling type

{{#if has.mobile_home}}**You live in a mobile or manufactured home.** These lose heat fast and
their water lines often run under the floor, where they freeze first. Skirting closed, heat tape
checked, and an agreed sturdier place to go (family, a neighbour, a warming centre) if the power
will be out for long in deep cold.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}**You live in an apartment.** Shared walls help you hold heat. Your
building's heat, water pumps and elevators may stop with the power, so stairs, stored water and
the building's exits matter. Never run a grill or generator on a balcony.{{/if}}
{{#if has.basement}}**You have a basement** ({{ dwelling.basement }}). Below-ground rooms hold
their temperature better than the floors above, but a basement on an outside wall with windows
loses heat. See → 08-01 before choosing the warm room.{{/if}}
Whatever the building: one heated room, the CO rules, stored water, and nobody on the roads.

## The worst realistic case

A blizzard or ice storm **during a longer grid failure** is the case to plan against:
- Little or no solar power for days (→ 09-05).
- No travel, no resupply, no help coming.
- Heating fuel burning faster than on any other day (→ 06-04).
- Everyone in one room for days, which strains tempers and spreads illness (→ 21-02, → 13-11).

If your plan survives that on paper, it is a real plan. Then test it (→ 24-04).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **CO alarms, battery, every level and where people sleep** | The main killer after a winter storm | Installed and tested before any heater runs (→ 08-02) |
| NOAA Weather Radio with SAME | Hours of warning | → 15-01 |
| **Vehicle winter kit** | Stranding is the classic fatal case | Blankets, warmth, food, water, light, shovel (→ 22-05) |
| Snow shovels and a roof rake | Digging out; roof loads; panels | |
| Traction devices; sand or ash for paths | Falls on ice break bones | → 11-06 |
| **Rope for a whiteout lifeline** | Old practice that works | Door to woodpile, door to outbuilding |
| Firewood or fuel inside before the storm | You cannot reach a buried woodpile | → 06-04 |
| Filled water containers | Pipes freeze | → 03-02, → 03-06 |
| Layers, hats, mittens for everyone | Indoors as well as out | → 11-01, → 11-02 |
| Hand warmers | Vehicle kit; pockets | Over clothing, not against skin; not in a small child's mittens (→ 11-04) |
| Headlamps and spare batteries | Long dark evenings | → 10-01 |

**If you do not have it:** snow is water (→ 03-05); snow banked against a wall cuts wind and
heat loss; outdoor cold is a refrigerator (→ 04-09), and a freezing risk for medicine at the same
time; any rope, cord or garden hose makes a lifeline; blankets over windows hold heat (→ 08-03).

## When it runs out

- **Heat, water and battery tighten at once.** That is what makes winter storms hard: the
  firewood burns faster, the pipes freeze, and the solar panels are buried. Work out the storm
  case, not the average day (→ 06-04, → 23-02).
- **Stretch it:** one room, layers indoors, long sleep, cook once a day, and use the free cold for
  food storage instead of burning anything to make it.
- **The habit that matters: prepare when the watch is issued, not when the warning is.**

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the most likely emergency in a cold region and the most survivable if you have
  prepared: fuel in, water filled, CO alarms tested, everything charged, one room warm.
- **B (moving):** **do not move in a winter storm** (→ 01-02, → 01-03). If you are caught out:
  stay with the vehicle, keep the tailpipe clear, stay visible (→ 17-11).
- **C (rural or new site):** longer isolation, longer outages, no plow coming. Provision a rural
  site for a week or more of complete isolation as a normal winter condition. A lifeline between
  buildings is standard practice there.

pages.body:
# Tornadoes, severe thunderstorms, derechos and lightning

**What this page is for.** A tornado warning gives you minutes, not hours. This page is what to
do in those minutes: what the alert words mean, where to go in each kind of building, what to do
in a vehicle, and what comes after. It also covers the same storms' other killers: straight-line
wind (including derechos) and lightning. Hail is on → 17-18; preparing the shelter spot is on
→ 17-06.
{{#if is.tornado_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for tornadoes in the region data:
plan for this every spring and summer.**{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for tornadoes, but
tornadoes have struck every state; keep this page.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY.** **Tornado warning: go now.** Lowest floor, most interior room, away from windows,
> as many walls between you and the outside as you can, and **protect your head and neck**
> (NWS, Tornado Safety). **A mobile home is not a shelter, even tied down. Leave it for a sturdy
> building before the storm arrives** (NWS; SPC). **Never shelter under a highway overpass.**

## Do this now

1. **Put a NOAA Weather Radio with SAME where you sleep** (→ 15-01, → 29-09). Enough tornadoes
   come after dark that a warning you sleep through is the whole problem.
2. **Pick your shelter spot today** and stock it (→ 17-06). Ours: **{{ dwelling.shelter_room }}**.
3. **Put shoes, a light, a whistle, a first-aid kit and water in the spot.** Decide who grabs the
   medicines and who carries whom on the way (below).
4. **Practice twice:** once by day, once at night, timed (→ 24-02). You will find problems both
   times.
5. **Know where you would shelter** at work, school, the store, and the houses you visit.

## Watch, warning, and the words that matter

| Alert | Meaning | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **Tornado Watch** | Conditions favour tornadoes over a wide area, for hours | Radio on, plan reviewed, shoes on everyone, know where everyone is |
| **Tornado Warning** | A tornado is seen or shown on radar near you | **Shelter now** |
| **Severe Thunderstorm Warning** | Damaging wind (58 mph or more) or large hail (1 inch or more). Tornadoes can form from these storms with little added warning | Inside, away from windows; treat "destructive" as a tornado warning |

The NWS adds a **damage threat** tag to severe thunderstorm warnings: **"considerable"** means
hail of 1.75 inches or more or wind of 70 mph or more; **"destructive"** means hail of 2.75 inches
or more or wind of 80 mph or more, and only the destructive tag sets off a Wireless Emergency
Alert on phones (NWS, 2021). Wind like that does tornado-class damage with no funnel at all. More
alert words: → 29-10.

**Outdoor sirens** are an outdoor warning system. They are often not heard indoors, they can fail,
and **silence is not an all-clear**: there is no all-clear signal. Many places test sirens on a
fixed schedule. Your local test time: ______________. A siren at any other time is real. **The
weather radio, not the siren, is your primary warning** (NWS, NOAA Weather Radio).

## Where to go: by building

**The rule:** as low as possible, as far inside as possible, as many walls between you and the
outside as possible, and protect your head (NWS, Tornadoes: During the Event).

{{figure fig-tornado-shelter-choices}}

{{#if has.basement}}- **Your home has a basement** ({{ dwelling.basement }}). Go down. Get under a
  sturdy workbench or the stairs, away from windows, and **not under heavy appliances on the floor
  above** (a refrigerator or piano can come through).{{else}}- **No basement:** the most interior
  room on the lowest floor (a bathroom, closet or hallway), away from windows.{{/if}}
{{#if has.shelter_room}}- **Your named shelter room:** {{ dwelling.shelter_room }}.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **In an apartment:** get to the lowest floor you can reach quickly, into an
  interior hallway, stairwell or bathroom away from windows. Do not use the elevator; the power
  may fail. If you live on an upper floor, agree with a neighbour below where you will go.{{/if}}
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **You live in a mobile or manufactured home. It is not safe in a tornado,
  even if it is tied down. Leave for a sturdy building or a community shelter when the watch is
  issued or the sky turns bad, not when the warning sounds** (NWS; SPC: "Get out!"). Know now
  where you will go and how long it takes to get there: ______________.{{/if}}
- **Cover your head and neck.** Helmets (bicycle helmets work) help: SPC says flying debris is
  the greatest danger in tornadoes.
- **Put a mattress, heavy blankets or couch cushions over you.**
- **Shoes on.** After a tornado the ground is glass, nails and broken wood (→ 12-02).
- **Never:** a room with windows, a big open room (gym, warehouse, big store aisle), a garage, a
  shed, a tent, a mobile home, or a vehicle if a building can be reached.

## Caught in a vehicle or in the open

NWS: **"Being in a vehicle during a tornado is not safe. The best course of action is to drive to
the closest shelter."** A sturdy building always wins. Failing that, in order (SPC, Tornado
Safety FAQ):

1. **If the tornado is far off and roads are open, drive at right angles to its path**, away from
   it, not along its track.
2. **Caught by extreme wind or flying debris:** park quickly, out of traffic lanes. SPC: **"Stay
   in the car with the seat belt on. Put your head down below the windows; cover your head with
   your hands and a blanket, coat, or other cushion if possible."**
3. **The ditch test.** SPC: **"If you can safely get noticeably lower than the level of the
   roadway, leave your car and lie in that area, covering your head with your hands."** It must
   be *noticeably* lower and reachable. A flat shoulder is not a ditch.
   {{#if has.young_child}}With small children buckled into car seats, the realistic choice is
   usually the vehicle, belted, heads below the windows: you cannot unbuckle and carry several
   children through tornado wind.{{/if}}
4. **Never shelter under an overpass.** SPC: overpasses create "deadly traffic hazards while
   offering little protection against flying debris." The wind speeds up in the gap. It feels
   safe; it kills.
5. **In the open with no vehicle:** the lowest spot you can reach, flat on the ground, head
   covered. It is a last resort.

{{figure fig-tornado-vehicle-choices}}

## Children, medicines and pets: solve them before the warning

- **Decide now who carries whom and who grabs what.** Do not negotiate it during a warning.
  {{#each members as m}}
  - {{m.label}} ({{m.age_text}}): goes with __________; grabs __________.{{/each}}
- **Children who have practiced will go; children who have not may freeze or hide** (→ 20-04).
  Practice it as a game. Keep a comfort item and a light a child may hold in the spot (→ 20-08).
- **Shoes on during the watch**, not the warning. It is the single biggest time-saver.
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **Refrigerated medicine** is grabbed on the way, in a small
  insulated container, not stored in the shelter if the spot gets too cold or too warm for its
  label (→ 29-07).{{/if}}
{{#if has.epinephrine}}- **Epinephrine** goes with the person who needs it. Check the storage
  range on the label before storing a spare in a basement (→ 02-03).{{/if}}
- **Phones, medical cards and the family plan** go too (→ 25-09).
{{#if has.pets}}- **Pets:** keep carriers in or beside the shelter spot, doors open. Decide out loud,
  in advance, whether anyone looks for a pet after the warning sounds, and who. During a watch,
  close pets into the shelter side of the house.{{/if}}

## After the tornado

- **Stay in shelter until the warning ends.** Outbreaks bring more than one tornado.
- **Shoes and gloves before you move** (→ 12-02).
- **Downed power lines:** assume every line is live. Keep everyone, children and pets well back.
- **Gas:** if you smell gas, get everyone out and shut the gas off at the meter (→ 16-12). **Do
  not turn it back on yourself while a utility exists.** If no utility will come, relighting
  yourself is a decision card: {{choice DC-28}} → 30-29 (→ 16-12).
- **Do not go into a badly damaged building.**
- **Check on neighbours** (→ 18-01). Right after a tornado, neighbours are the only rescue there
  is.
- **Expect cuts and debris wounds** (→ 12-08). Photograph damage for insurance if that system
  still works (→ 19-04).

{{photo gas-shutoff}}

## Derechos: hurricane-force wind across a whole region

**SPC definition:** a derecho is a **widespread, long-lived windstorm** from a line of storms, with
a damage swath of **at least about 250 miles**, gusts of **at least 58 mph** along most of it, and
several well-separated gusts of **75 mph or more**.

- **What one looks like:** on August 10, 2020, a derecho crossed Iowa and beyond. Its path ran
  **over 750 miles**, winds passed **100 mph** in two areas (gusts near Cedar Rapids were estimated
  at 120 mph or more), and **over 1.9 million customers** lost power, 1.4 million of them at once
  (NWS Des Moines, event summary).
- **Warning signs:** sometimes a shelf cloud across the horizon, an advancing wall of dust or
  rain, then a sudden wind blast. SPC: derechos usually move at 50 mph or more, so these signs
  appear on very short notice, often too short to act on; the radio warning is what gives you
  time (→ 17-10).
- **What you do:** the tornado posture without waiting for rotation. Same shelter, same helmets.
  Trees and power lines come down everywhere at once.
- **Afterward it is a long, wide outage** (→ 17-08). Plan on days, not hours.

## Lightning: the everyday killer in the same storms

- **"When thunder roars, go indoors,"** and stay in until **30 minutes after the last thunder**
  (NWS, Lightning Safety brochure). If you can hear thunder, it is time to get to a safe building
  or vehicle.
- **Safe places:** a substantial building with electricity or plumbing, or a hard-topped metal
  vehicle with the windows up (NWS). Inside, stay off corded phones and other equipment wired to
  the mains, and away from plumbing: sinks, baths and taps (NWS, Lightning Tips).
- **Never safe:** open areas, hilltops, lone trees, water, wire fences and power lines, and
  sheds, picnic shelters, tents or covered porches (NWS); add tractors and mowers in the open.
{{#if has.pool}}- **Pool or hot tub:** thunder means everyone out of the water, and it stays
  closed until 30 minutes after the last thunder.{{/if}}
- **Grid-down life means more hours outside.** The 30-minute clock does not shrink because the
  chores are urgent. Use the time for indoor work.
- **If someone is struck:** NWS says lightning victims do not carry an electrical charge and may
  need first aid at once; cardiac arrest is what kills. Touch them and **start CPR at once**
  (→ 12-18).
  Move everyone else out of the open; lightning does strike the same place twice.

## When the warning systems are gone

In a long grid failure there may be no sirens, no phone alerts, no ambulance and no hospital.
- **A battery or crank NOAA Weather Radio still works** while transmitters run (→ 15-01). Keep
  its batteries as a protected reserve.
- **Read the sky** (→ 17-10).
- **Keep the shelter stocked as if you might lose the house.** Losing the house is a reason to
  move (→ 01-02); when you would leave home is a household decision: {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **NOAA Weather Radio with SAME, where you sleep** | Night tornadoes | → 15-01 |
| Second battery or crank radio in the shelter | You will be down there when the power goes | |
| **Helmets for everyone** (bike helmets are fine) | Head injury from debris | Kept in the shelter |
| **Shoes for everyone in the shelter** | Glass and nails afterward | Children's sizes checked each spring |
| Lights and spare batteries | Power will be out | → 10-01 |
| First-aid and trauma kit | Cuts and debris wounds | → 12-08 |
| Water and some food | You may be there a while | Rotate |
| Whistle per person | Signal from under debris | → 15-07 |
| Mattress or heavy blankets | Debris cover | |
| Work gloves | The aftermath | |
| Printed family plan and medical cards | → 25-09 | In the shelter |

**If you do not have it:** a hard hat, sports helmet or cushion for heads; couch cushions or a
sturdy table for debris; a bathtub with a mattress over it as the no-basement spot; banging on a
pipe to signal.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** shelter spot stocked and practiced; radio by the bed; medicines ready to grab.
  Know your neighbours.
- **B (moving):** a vehicle is a bad place in a tornado. Watch the radio and the sky and do not
  drive into severe weather (→ 01-03, → 17-11).
- **C (rural or new site):** fewer sirens, longer response, neighbours far away. A basement,
  storm cellar or safe room is a main test of any site (→ 01-05, → 17-06).

pages.body:
# Floods and flash floods

**What this page is for.** Flooding kills more people each year than any other
thunderstorm-related hazard, and over half of flood drownings happen when a vehicle is driven into
floodwater (NWS, Turn Around Don't Drown). This page covers the kinds of flooding, the alert words, the rules for water on
roads, getting out fast, and the long tail: contaminated water, food and mold.
{{#if is.flood_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for flooding in the region data.** Do
the "Do this now" list this month.{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for flooding, but
flash floods and basement floods happen almost anywhere it rains.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY. Turn Around, Don't Drown.** Never drive or walk into moving water. The NWS numbers,
> printed so they work offline:
>
> | Moving water depth | What it does (NWS, Turn Around Don't Drown) |
> |---|---|
> | **6 inches** | Knocks an adult off their feet |
> | **12 inches** | Carries away most cars |
> | **2 feet** | Carries away SUVs and trucks |
>
> There is no depth of flowing water across a road that is safe to drive. You cannot judge depth
> or current from the driver's seat, and **the road under the water may be gone**. Floodwater
> also hides open manholes, washed-out culverts and live power lines.
>
> **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.**
> Generators and pumps run indoors during flood cleanup kill people every year (→ 30-01).

{{figure fig-flood-water-depths}}

## Do this now

1. **Find out whether your home is in a mapped flood zone.** FEMA's Flood Map Service Center
   holds the maps; your county keeps them too. Remember that flooding does not stop at a map
   line (Ready.gov, Floods). Mark the result on your map (→ 25-04).
2. **Find two routes to high ground** and mark the low spots on them. The road you would take may
   be the one that floods.
3. **Pack the document grab kit and go-bags and keep them upstairs**, never in a basement
   (→ 19-01, → 22-03).
4. **Flood insurance, while that system exists:** standard homeowner's policies do not cover
   floods, and a new flood policy typically takes up to 30 days to start (Ready.gov, Floods). Buy
   it long before the rain (→ 19-04).
5. **Program the weather radio for flood alerts** (→ 15-01).

{{photo flood-routes}}

## The kinds of flooding

| Type | What it looks like | Warning time |
|---|---|---|
| **River flooding** | A river or its tributaries rising over days, often from snowmelt or long rain | **Days**: the most predictable |
| **Ice jam or rain on snow** | Ice dams a river, then lets go; rain melts deep snow fast | **Hours**: fast and dangerous |
| **Flash flood** | Heavy storm rain overwhelms creeks, gullies and drains | **Minutes to an hour** |
| **Coastal and storm surge** | Sea water pushed ashore by a storm (→ 17-13) | Hours to days |
| **Burn-scar flash flood and debris flow** | Rain on ground bared by wildfire runs off like pavement (→ 17-17) | Minutes |
| **Street and storm-drain flooding** | Streets and basements when drains are overwhelmed | Minutes |
| **Basement flood from a failed sump pump** | **Power out means sump pump out** | Immediate |

**The last one is easy to miss.** In a power outage (→ 17-08), a basement that depends on a sump
pump floods. If your shelter spot, food, medicine or batteries live in the basement, put them on
shelves, and plan a backup pump or a battery-powered water alarm.
{{#if has.basement}}Your home has a basement ({{ dwelling.basement }}): check now what sits on its
floor.{{/if}}

## Alert words

- **Flood Watch:** flooding, including flash flooding, is possible. Get ready. (Older radios and
  some offices still say "flash flood watch.")
- **Flood Warning** or **Flash Flood Warning:** flooding is happening or about to. **Act now:
  move to higher ground.**
- **Flash Flood Emergency:** a rare, severe threat to life in a specific place. Get to high ground
  immediately.
- **Flood Advisory:** minor flooding; be careful on roads.

More on alert words: → 29-10.

## The rules when water is rising

- **Never drive through flooded roads**, and never drive around barricades.
- **Never walk through moving water.** If you must cross still water, probe ahead with a pole.
- **If your car is caught in rushing water, stay inside unless water is rising inside the car;
  then get onto the roof** (Ready.gov, Floods).
- **If you are trapped in a building, go to the highest floor.** Go onto the roof only if you
  must, and signal for help. **Do not climb into a closed attic**: rising water can trap you there
  (Ready.gov, Floods).
- **Stay off bridges over fast water.**
- **Keep children and pets away from floodwater.** It moves fast, it is dirty and it hides
  hazards.
- **Downed power lines in water are live.**
- **Leave early.** Leaving at night, in water, with children is far worse than leaving in daylight
  when it only feels inconvenient. When you would leave is a household decision: {{choice DC-19}}
  → 30-20

## Getting out fast

Flooding is the hazard most likely to force a sudden departure at night (→ 01-03).
- **Go-bags and documents upstairs and reachable** (→ 19-01, → 22-03).
- **Medicines and devices first** (→ 01-07).
- **Vehicle fuelled and parked where water will not trap it**, facing the way out.
- **Children into car seats is a real, minutes-long step: practice it.** Pets into carriers is
  another; start it first, not last.
- **Know two routes out**, because one will flood.

{{#if has.mobile_home}}**Mobile and manufactured homes** can float or shift off their foundations
in moving water. Leave early for a sturdy building on high ground.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}**In an apartment,** an upper floor may keep you dry, but the building may
lose power, water and elevators, and the streets may be cut off for days. Decide early whether
to stay up high with supplies or leave.{{/if}}

## What the water leaves behind

**Even if your house stays dry, a regional flood can foul the water supply.**
- **Town water** may go under a boil notice, or worse. Follow it.
- **Wells** that floodwater reached are not safe because the water looks clear. They must be
  disinfected and tested before use (CDC, How to Disinfect Wells After an Emergency; → 03-07,
  → 03-10).
- **Surface water** carries sewage, fuel, farm chemicals and dead animals.
- **Your stored water becomes the supply** (→ 03-02), and your treatment ability matters
  (→ 03-04). **Boiling and most filters do not remove chemicals**; fuel or chemical contamination
  needs a different source.
- **Toilets and septic systems back up.** Do not use a toilet on a flooded system (→ 13-01).
- **Illness follows floods.** Hand washing and clean water matter more in the weeks after than on
  the day (→ 13-11, → 12-05).

**Food, garden and belongings** (CDC, Preparing for Floods):
- **Throw out food that touched floodwater** if it was in packaging that is not waterproof, in
  cardboard (including juice, milk and formula boxes), in containers with screw caps, snap lids,
  crimped or twist caps or flip tops, home-canned, or in cans that are bulging, open or damaged
  (CDC, Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency, 2025).
- **Undamaged commercial cans and retort pouches can be saved**: remove labels, brush off silt,
  wash in hot soapy water, rinse in safe water, then either soak 15 minutes in 1 cup (8 oz)
  unscented household bleach per 5 gallons of water or boil for 2 minutes; relabel with the
  contents and expiry date, and use them soon (CDC). Food from a freezer that lost power is a
  separate question: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15
- **Do not eat garden produce that floodwater touched.**
- **Porous things that got wet** (mattresses, upholstery, carpet, drywall) grow mold and usually
  have to go.
- **Mold** is a health hazard for weeks. Dry fast; ventilate. Keep people with asthma or other
  lung disease, people with weak immune systems, and children out of moldy buildings and out of
  cleanup work (Ready.gov, Floods).

## Cleanup safety

- **Gloves, boots, eye protection**, and wash hands well afterward (→ 13-02).
- **Keep open wounds out of floodwater**; cover them and watch for infection (→ 12-02, → 12-04).
  Check that everyone's tetanus shot is up to date.
- **Do not touch anything electrical while standing in water.** Turn off power at the panel only
  if you can reach it while dry.
- **Disinfecting with bleach:** follow the label and the CDC dilution. **Bleach or pool shock is
  never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** The mix makes poison gas (→ 29-05, → 30-01).
- **Generators and pumps outdoors only**, far from windows (→ 08-02, → 09-04).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Flood map of your home and routes** | Most people guess their risk wrong | → 25-04 |
| NOAA Weather Radio with SAME | Flood warnings at night | → 15-01 |
| **Document kit and go-bags, upstairs** | The fast-departure hazard | → 19-01, → 22-03 |
| **Water treatment and spare filters; stored water up off the floor** | The supply may fail | → 03-02, → 03-04 |
| Well test kit, if you have a well | A flooded well must be tested | → 03-07 |
| Rubber boots, gloves, eye protection | Cleanup | |
| Battery water alarm; backup sump pump if you can | Power out means sump out | |
| Shelves or pallets in the basement | Keep stores off the floor | |
| Bleach and cleaning supplies | Disinfection after | → 29-05 |

**If you do not have it:** height is the substitute for almost everything: stores up, bags up,
papers up. Sandbags can be feed sacks, pillowcases or heavy trash bags filled with sand or soil,
with plastic sheeting under them. Drying is open windows, fans and time.

## When it runs out

- **Clean water is the consumable that matters.** A flood can take out the town supply, the well
  and every surface source at once. Your runway is what you stored plus what you can treat
  (→ 03-01). Cleanup and hand washing raise the need.
- **Ration** drinking and cooking first, hand washing next (never cut it), cleaning last. Use
  untreated floodwater for nothing.
- **The long tail is illness and mold**, and hygiene is what prevents it.
- **For a new site:** do not choose a site in a flood plain, and put the well uphill and away
  from the latrine (→ 01-05, → 13-07).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** know your flood zone, keep bags and documents high, and know two routes out.
- **B (moving):** flooded roads are the classic fatal error. Turn around. Never cross water you
  cannot see the bottom of, and avoid driving at night when flash floods are possible (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** flood plain status should rule a site out. Learn where the water goes
  in a wet spring by seeing the land then, not only in a dry month.

pages.body:
# Extreme cold and extreme heat

**What this page is for.** Temperature extremes kill quietly, mostly the very young, the old and
the sick, and mostly indoors when the power is out. This page puts cold and heat side by side,
because they fail in opposite directions and one plan has to handle both.
Where you live: January nights average about **{{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F** (record low
**{{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F**); July days average about **{{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F**
(record high **{{ region.home.record_high_f }} °F**).
{{#if is.cold_winters}}**Your winters are cold enough that this page applies every year.**{{/if}}
{{#if is.hot_summers}}**Your summers are hot enough that this page applies every year.**{{/if}}

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Heat stroke is an emergency.** A hot person who is **confused**, slurring, or passing out
>   needs **cooling at once**, before anything else (CDC/NIOSH).
> - **Never leave anyone, especially a child, in a parked vehicle.** Not with windows cracked,
>   not for five minutes.
> - **Cold:** wind chill decides how fast bare skin freezes. Read the NWS chart, not a feeling.
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** In cold, refrigerated medicine must
>   be kept from freezing (→ 29-07, → 30-01).
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Heating in a cold outage is when carbon monoxide kills (→ 08-02).

## Do this now

1. **Look at the wind chill chart and the heat index chart** (below and → 29-10). Use them before
   anyone works outside.
2. **Pick a winter room and a summer room.** In winter it is the room you heat (→ 08-01); in summer
   it is the lowest, shadiest room. They are usually not the same room.
3. **Set the work rule for each season:** winter work in the warmest hours; **summer work at dawn
   and dusk, rest in the middle of the day.**
4. **Check the refrigerated medicine plan at both ends** (→ 29-07, → 09-10): summer is keeping it
   cool; winter is keeping it from freezing.
5. **Write down who checks on whom**, including neighbours who live alone (→ 18-01).

## The two ends, side by side

| | **Extreme cold** | **Extreme heat** |
|---|---|---|
| **What kills** | Hypothermia, frostbite, carbon monoxide from heating | Heat stroke, dehydration |
| **How fast** | Frostbite in minutes at the coldest wind chills | Heat stroke can build over hours, or come fast with work |
| **The multiplier** | **Wind** (wind chill) | **Humidity** (heat index) |
| **The household limit** | **Fuel** (→ 06-04) | **Water** (→ 03-01) |
| **Solar power** | At its worst (→ 09-05) | At its best |
| **Keeping food and medicine cold** | Free: outdoor cold (→ 04-09), with freezing risk | Hard: the biggest electrical load (→ 09-10) |
| **Room** | One heated room (→ 08-01) | The lowest, shadiest room |
| **Work** | Midday, warmest hours | Dawn and dusk |
| **Clothing** | Layers, wool, no cotton (→ 11-01) | Loose, light, covered; cotton is right (→ 11-08) |

The pairing is useful: the hardest electrical job, cooling medicine, is cheapest when solar is
best and free when solar is worst.

## Alert words

| NWS alert | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Cold Weather Advisory** | Cold enough to be dangerous without care |
| **Extreme Cold Watch / Warning** | Dangerously cold air temperature or wind chill possible / expected |
| **Heat Advisory** | Heat that can make people ill, especially with work or no cooling |
| **Extreme Heat Watch / Warning** | Dangerous, possibly deadly heat possible / expected |

**Name changes.** The NWS renamed the wind chill alerts to Extreme Cold and Cold Weather Advisory in
October 2024 (NWS, 2024), and renamed the Excessive Heat Watch and Warning to **Extreme Heat** on
March 4, 2025 (NWS, 2025). Old cards and radios may still use the old words; treat them the same.
The NWS has also announced that it will replace the word "Advisory" with plain-language headlines
that start with the hazard (for example "HEAT: ..."); watches and warnings keep their names (NWS,
Hazard Simplification FAQ). Each office sets its own trigger numbers. Your office,
**{{ region.home.nws_office }}**, issues an Extreme Cold Warning at ______ °F and an Extreme Heat
Warning at a heat index of ______ °F.

## Extreme cold

- **Wind chill is the number that matters.** Find today's temperature and wind on the NWS chart
  and read the frostbite time (NWS, Wind Chill Chart).
- **No bare skin outside at the coldest wind chills.** Children stay in; outdoor work is essential
  minutes only.
- **Cold breaks equipment:** batteries lose capacity and lithium batteries must not be charged
  below freezing (→ 09-07); engines start hard; phones shut off; pipes freeze (→ 03-06).
- **The house is your main defence** (→ 08-01, → 08-03), and fuel is the limit (→ 06-04).
- **Check children and elders by touch**, not by asking: belly and back of the neck (→ 11-02).
- **Warning signs and treatment** of hypothermia and frostbite: → 08-05, → 12-10.

{{figure fig-wind-chill-chart}}

## Extreme heat

**The heat index** (temperature plus humidity) is how hot it feels, because damp air stops sweat
cooling you. The NWS categories (NWS Amarillo, Heat Index; NWS, Heat Index chart):

| Heat index | Category | Effect on the body, with long exposure or physical activity |
|---|---|---|
| 80 to 90 °F | Caution | Fatigue possible |
| 90 to 103 °F | Extreme caution | Heat stroke, heat cramps or heat exhaustion possible |
| 103 to 124 °F | Danger | Heat cramps or heat exhaustion likely; heat stroke possible |
| 125 °F and up | Extreme danger | Heat stroke highly likely |

**The published heat index assumes shade and a light wind. Full sun can add up to 15 °F** (NWS).

{{figure fig-heat-index-chart}}

**Heat illness gets worse in steps** (CDC, Heat-Related Illnesses; CDC/NIOSH):
- **Heat exhaustion:** heavy sweating, cold, pale and clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, nausea or
  vomiting, muscle cramps, tiredness or weakness, dizziness, headache, fainting. **Move to a cool
  place, loosen clothes, cool wet cloths or a cool bath, sips of water.** CDC: get medical help
  right away if they are throwing up, the symptoms get worse, or they last longer than 1 hour.
  With no help coming, keep cooling and watch for the heat stroke signs below.
- **Heat stroke:** a high body temperature (103 °F or higher), hot, red, dry or damp skin, a fast
  strong pulse, headache, dizziness, nausea, **confusion**, passing out (CDC). **Cool hard and at
  once:** a cold water or ice bath if you can, otherwise wet the skin, soak the clothing, move air
  over them, and cold wet cloths or ice on the head, neck, armpits and groin (CDC/NIOSH). **Do not
  give the person anything to drink** (CDC). Call for help if help exists; cooling comes first.
  With no help, see → 12-16.

**Living through heat with no air conditioning** (NWS, Heat Safety; CDC):
- **Close up by day, open up at night**, live on the lowest floor, block sun **outside** the
  glass, move air with a fan (→ 11-08).
- **Fans have a limit.** CDC: use fans only if indoor temperatures are below 90 °F; above 90 °F a
  fan can increase body temperature (CDC, About Heat and Your Health). Cool the body instead: wet
  cloths, a cool shower or bath.
- **Water on a schedule, not on thirst**, and more with work. Over days of heavy sweating, salt
  and electrolytes matter (→ 04-13, → 12-05).
- **Shift the work:** heavy jobs at dawn and evening, rest through the worst of the day. Write your
  household's line: outdoor work stops when ______________.

## Who is hit hardest

- **Infants and young children** lose and gain heat fast and cannot tell you. A carried or seated
  child makes little heat in the cold and cannot move to shade in the heat. Check by touch.
  {{#if has.infant}}An infant in your household is at the highest risk at both ends.{{/if}}
- **Elders and people with heart, lung or kidney disease** may not feel heat or thirst, and some
  medicines change how the body handles heat (CDC, Heat and Your Health). Ask a pharmacist now
  which of the household's medicines do.
  {{#if has.elder}}Plan a check on each elder at least twice a day in a heat wave.{{/if}}
{{#if has.diabetes}}- **Diabetes:** heat and dehydration push blood sugar around and dehydration
  feeds itself; in cold, low blood sugar can look like cold (confusion, clumsiness). **Check the
  glucose before blaming the weather.** See your condition page in Section 02.{{/if}}
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **Refrigerated medicine** that has been too warm is a hard choice
  when no replacement exists. It is a decision card: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09{{/if}}
{{#if has.pregnant}}- **Pregnancy** raises heat risk. Rest in the coolest place and drink
  steadily.{{/if}}

## By dwelling type

{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home:** heats fast in sun and loses heat fast in
  cold. In a long heat wave or a deep-cold outage, agree in advance on a sturdier, cooler or warmer
  place to go.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** upper floors are the hottest. In a heat wave with no power,
  spend the day on a lower floor, in a shared cool space, or with someone below.{{/if}}
{{#if has.basement}}- **Basement:** usually the coolest room in summer and a steady room in winter;
  it is often the right summer room.{{/if}}
- **Any building:** window coverings that block sun in summer and hold heat in winter help twice
  (→ 08-03).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Wind chill and heat index charts** | Turn a feeling into a time limit | Printed on this page and → 29-10 |
| Indoor/outdoor min/max thermometer | Shows what the house is really doing | |
| Cold-weather clothing for everyone | → 11-01, → 11-02 | Layers, wool |
| Hot-weather clothing, hats, shade | → 11-08 | |
| Low-power fans (12 V or USB) | Comfort per watt in summer | → 09-01 |
| Shade cloth or tarps | Block sun outside the glass | |
| Extra stored water | Summer needs far exceed the average | → 03-02 |
| Oral rehydration salts, salt | Days of heavy sweating | → 12-05 |
| Medical thermometers | Both hypothermia and heat stroke | → 12-01 |

**If you do not have it:** layers from any source, newspaper as insulation, snow banked against the
house, body heat and shared sleeping in the cold (an infant sharing an adult bed is a separate
decision: {{choice DC-09}} → 30-10); wet cloths at neck and wrists, a damp sheet in a breezy
window, the lowest room, and night air in the heat. Deep ground is cool in summer and above
freezing in winter, which is why cellars and basements work.

## When it runs out

- **Winter runs out of fuel; summer runs out of water.** Work out each one separately on → 23-02.
  Do not average them: a plan sized for the average fails at both ends.
- **Stretch it** by behaviour first: when you work, where you sleep, what you expect. It costs
  nothing and does more than equipment.
- **Lasting fixes help twice:** insulation, shade trees, window coverings, a cellar.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the house is the tool at both ends: heated room in winter, lowest room in
  summer.
- **B (moving):** both extremes make travel much more dangerous (→ 01-02). Winter risks
  stranding (→ 17-01); summer is a water problem, and water is heavy. Move in mild weather if you
  have any choice.
- **C (rural or new site):** more exposure, less shade, more wind, help further away. Build shade
  and windbreaks early and plan the work calendar around the extremes.

pages.body:
# Grassland and wildland fire

**What this page is for.** Wildfire is not only a mountain and forest problem. Fire in dry grass,
brush and crops happens on the plains, in the desert, in the suburbs and in the woods, and grass
fire is often the fastest of all. This page covers how these fires behave, the weather that
drives them, protecting the house, your own household as the ignition source, and what to do when
a fire is coming. Smoke, evacuation zones and the clean room are on → 17-14.
{{#if is.wildfire_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for wildfire in the region data.**
Do the "Do this now" list before the next dry season.{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for
wildfire, but a grid-down household running fires every day is its own risk; the household part
of this page applies to everyone.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY.**
> - **You cannot outrun a wind-driven grass fire on foot.** It moves at the speed of the wind.
> - **Leave early.** Fire evacuation is a decision of minutes, not hours. Do not wait to see what
>   it does, and **do not go back for things**.
> - **A grid-down household starts fires:** cooking fires, wood heat, ash, lamps, generators,
>   saws. You are the most likely ignition source in your own emergency.
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance** (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Learn what a Red Flag Warning is and make sure your weather radio sounds for it** (→ 15-01).
   **Red flag means: no outdoor fire, no ash dumping, nothing that throws sparks.**
2. **Clear the first five feet around the house** of anything that burns, and **move the woodpile
   away from the house** (below). A woodpile against a wall is a wick.
3. **Set the ash rule and post it** (below).
4. **Make a fire evacuation plan** that works in minutes: bags, documents, medicines, people, pets
   (→ 17-14, → 19-01, → 22-03).
5. **Read the burn conditions off the sky and the radio, not off a notice:** dry grass plus low
   humidity plus wind means no open burning, whether or not anyone is still posting bans.

> **Before the collapse:** while counties and states post burn bans and fire restrictions, check
> them and obey them.

## How these fires behave

- **Speed.** Fire in cured (dead, dry) grass, pushed by wind, often moves faster than a person can
  run, and it speeds up going uphill.
- **A thin flame front.** A grass fire's front is often shallow and passes quickly. That is why
  **"the black", ground that has already burned**, is a refuge: fire does not come back over
  ground with nothing left to burn.
- **Spotting.** Wind carries embers ahead of the fire and starts new fires downwind, sometimes far
  ahead.
- **Wind shifts change everything at once.** A fire moving away can turn toward you.
- **Smoke** cuts visibility to nothing and harms lungs, especially children's (→ 17-14).
- **Houses mostly catch from embers**, not the flame front: in gutters, on decks, under eaves, in
  woodpiles, and in dry grass against the wall.
- **Forest and brush fires** burn hotter and longer than grass fires and can throw embers a long
  way; the same rules apply with more distance and more time.

## The weather that drives fire

**Red Flag Warning:** warm, dry, windy weather in which any fire spreads fast. **Fire Weather
Watch:** those conditions may come in the next day or two (NWS, Wildfire Safety; → 29-10). Watch
for:
- **Spring before green-up:** last year's dead grass, dry air, wind. Easy to underestimate.
- **Late summer and fall after the grass cures**, worst in drought (→ 17-07).
- **Any windy day with low humidity.**

**On a red flag day: no outdoor fire, no ash dumping, no sparks, no machines in dry grass.**

## Protecting the house

Fire agencies describe three zones around a house (USFA, Take Action; Ready.gov, Wildfires):

{{figure fig-defensible-space-zones}}

- **0 to 5 feet: nothing that burns.** Remove wood mulch, dead or dry plants, leaves and pine
  needles, including from the roof and gutters; trim branches that hang over the roof and chimney
  (USFA). No firewood or stored items against the walls; gravel or bare soil is best.
- **5 to 30 feet:** "lean, clean and green": dead branches removed, plants spaced apart and
  watered in dry summers, no low branches that let fire climb into trees (USFA).
- **Woodpiles at least 30 feet from the house**, on bare ground or gravel or in an enclosed shed
  (USFA).
- **30 to 100 feet:** fuel reduced by thinning and spacing plants and limbing up trees (USFA).
- **The house itself:** clean gutters (dry leaves in a gutter catch embers), screened vents, nothing
  stored under decks, nothing burnable on decks or against walls, propane cylinders moved away
  (→ 06-06).

Your state and county may have their own distances for your kind of vegetation; use the larger
number.

## Your own fire risk

| Source | Control |
|---|---|
| **Wood ash** | Metal can with a tight lid, on a non-burnable surface, away from buildings; **treat it as live for days**, and soak it with water before it touches soil, garden or compost. A can that feels cool outside can still hold live coals |
| **Outdoor cooking fire** (→ 07-01) | Cleared ground, contained, water and a shovel at hand, never on a red flag day, never left alone |
| **Chimney and stovepipe sparks** | Spark arrestor; clean flue (→ 06-09) |
| **Fuel** (→ 06-06) | Away from the house and from anything that sparks or burns |
| **Lamps and candles** (→ 10-02) | Contained, watched, never left alone. Flashlights instead in an outage where you can (USFA) |
| **Generator** (→ 09-04) | Hot exhaust lights dry grass. Run it on bare ground or pavement |
| **Saws, mowers, engines** | Sparks and hot exhaust in dry grass; work early in the day, with water at hand |
| **Burn piles and trash** (→ 13-03) | Never on a red flag day; cleared ring; water at hand; never in wind |

**Ash is worth saying twice.** Dumping "cold" ash on grass, in a plastic bin or against the house
has started a huge number of fires.

{{photo ash-can}}

## When a fire is coming

- **Go early.** When you would leave home is a household decision written in advance:
  {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20
- **Medicines first, then documents and bags** (→ 01-07, → 19-01). **Children into car seats and
  pets into carriers are the slow steps; start them first.**
- **Drive away from the fire and across the wind**, not ahead of it along its path.
- **Caught in the open with no way out:** get to the black, or bare ground, a plowed field, a road
  cut, gravel, or water. Get low, cover bare skin, protect your airway. If phones work, call 911
  and give your location, but be aware that emergency response could be delayed or impossible
  (Ready.gov, Wildfires).

**Caught in a vehicle** (Fire Safe Marin, Are Vehicles Safe?). **Stay in the car: driving through
wildfire is dangerous, but much less dangerous than running from it on foot.** The steel body
protects you from flames, heat and embers.
1. **Drive slowly with headlights on**, avoid heavy smoke, and watch for other vehicles and people.
   Never abandon the vehicle in the middle of the road.
2. **If you have to stop, park away from heavy trees and brush.**
3. **Roll up the windows and close the air vents.**
4. **Headlights on, ignition off.**
5. **Get on the floor and cover up with a blanket or coat** (wool if you have it). Children out of
   car seats onto the floor with an adult over them.
6. **Stay in the vehicle until the main fire passes.** It will get hot, smoke and sparks may get
   in, air currents may rock the car, and the engine may stall and be hard to restart. Metal fuel
   tanks rarely explode. Then drive or walk out **into the black**.

**Smoke:** stay low, cover mouth and nose, and get children out of it first. **No mask on a child
under 2**; for them the protection is distance, so leave earlier (→ 17-14).

## When there is no fire department

In a long grid failure a house or grass fire is yours alone. That moves everything toward
**prevention**: defensible space, ash discipline and fire-safe habits become rules, not good
ideas.
- **Losing the house means losing everything in it**: food, water, fuel, medicine. Keep a go-bag
  and a second set of critical medical supplies somewhere other than the house if you can
  (→ 22-03).
- **Water for firefighting:** rain barrels, stock tanks, buckets staged around the property.
  {{#if has.pool}}Your pool is a large firefighting reserve; a pump and a long hose make it usable.{{/if}}
- **A fire extinguisher is for a small fire and a clear way out**; when the fire is bigger than a
  wastebasket, leave (→ 29-12).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Metal ash can with a tight lid** | The most likely ignition source | Non-burnable base, away from the house |
| NOAA Weather Radio | Red flag warnings | → 15-01 |
| **Mower, loppers, rake** | Defensible space is what saves the house | Ongoing work |
| Fire extinguishers (ABC) | Every room with a heat source, plus outdoors | → 29-12 |
| Long garden hoses | Wetting down and small fires | |
| Shovels and rakes | Grass fire is fought with dirt and beating | Keep them where you can reach them |
| Spark arrestor on the chimney | Sparks land in dry grass | → 06-09 |
| Wool blankets | Smothering small fires; vehicle refuge | Not synthetic |
| N95 or better masks | Smoke | Adults and older children; fit matters (→ 17-14) |
| **Go-bags and document kit** | Minutes, not hours | → 22-03, → 19-01 |

**If you do not have it:** a shovel and a rake are the real grass-fire tools; wet burlap or a wool
blanket beats out small fires; **a mowed or disced strip of bare ground around buildings is the
classic plains firebreak** and costs only work; any metal can with a lid is an ash can, never
plastic or cardboard.

## When it runs out

- **Prevention does not run out**; it costs work, not supplies.
- **What runs out:** extinguishers (one use each; check gauges every year), masks, hose.
- **What wears down is discipline.** The tenth month of dumping ash is when someone gets careless.
  Keep the rule posted and the metal can where the ash goes.
- **With no fire department, a house fire is effectively unrecoverable.** That makes every
  prevention step worth more than it looks.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** in town the risk is mostly your own fires and your neighbours': cooking, wood
  heat, ash, lamps. Defensible space, ash discipline, extinguishers.
- **B (moving):** do not camp or cook in dry grass; clear a wide circle; never leave a fire; check
  the wind before lighting anything. Smoke also gives your position away (→ 14-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** grass and wildland fire become a main hazard. Defensible space, a
  firebreak, stored firefighting water and an evacuation plan in the first month (→ 01-04); fire
  risk belongs on the site checklist (→ 01-05).
