pages.body:
# Preparing a storm shelter spot

**What this page is for.** In a tornado warning you will have minutes, and someone may be carrying
a child. This page turns "we would go to the basement" into a chosen, stocked and practiced spot
that works in the dark with nothing in your hands. For most homes it is an afternoon's work, not a
building project, and it is one of the best uses of an afternoon in this binder. What to do in a
warning is on → 17-02.

> **SAFETY.** The spot is: **lowest floor, most interior, as many walls between you and the
> outside as possible, away from windows, heads and necks covered** (NWS, Tornado Safety). **A
> mobile home, a vehicle, a garage or a shed is not a shelter.**

## Do this now

1. **Pick the spot** using the ranking below, and write it here: **{{ dwelling.shelter_room }}**.
   Pick a second spot in case the first is blocked or smells of gas: ______________.
2. **Clear it and keep it clear.** Shelves fixed to the wall, nothing heavy that can fall, stock
   on shelves off the floor.
3. **Stock it with the list below, permanently**, so you can arrive empty-handed.
4. **Shoes and helmets for everyone go in the spot.**
5. **Practice twice, once by day and once at night, timed** (→ 24-02). Fix what goes wrong.

{{photo shelter-spot}}

## Choosing the spot

Ranked, from the NWS and SPC guidance:

1. **An engineered safe room or storm shelter** built to FEMA's safe room criteria (FEMA P-320,
   Taking Shelter from the Storm). This is the best protection. It is a real construction project,
   and it is worth pricing.
2. **A basement**, in a corner away from windows, **under a sturdy workbench or the stairs**, and
   **not under heavy appliances on the floor above**. In a walkout basement, "away from windows"
   means away from the whole at-ground wall: stay on the buried side.
3. **No basement: the most interior room on the lowest floor.** A small bathroom, closet or
   hallway with no outside walls. **A bathtub with a mattress pulled over it** is the classic
   version.
4. **Never:** a room with windows, a large open room, a garage, a mobile home, or a vehicle.

{{figure fig-tornado-shelter-choices}}

**For your home:**
{{#if has.basement}}- You have a basement ({{ dwelling.basement }}). Walk it with this page.{{/if}}
{{#if has.shelter_room}}- Your named windowless room is **{{ dwelling.shelter_room }}**.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** find the lowest interior space you can reach in a minute or
  two: an interior hallway, stairwell or ground-floor interior room. Ask the building manager
  whether there is a designated shelter area. Do not use elevators.{{/if}}
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home: there is no safe spot inside.** Your
  shelter is a sturdy building nearby: a neighbour's basement, a community shelter, a public
  building. Write it here: ______________, and how long it takes to reach: ______ minutes. **You
  go when the watch is issued or the sky turns bad**, because the warning does not leave enough
  time (NWS; SPC).{{/if}}

**Then look up and around.** What is on the floor directly above? (A refrigerator, a piano, a full
bathtub?) What on the shelves could fall on you? Clear it and fix the shelving.

{{photo shelter-overhead}}

**Things that often share a basement corner, and what to do about them:**
- **A gas furnace or water heater:** if you smell gas, you go to the second spot. Make that part of
  the drill.
- **A sump pit:** power out means pump out and possible flooding (→ 17-03). Stock goes on shelves.
{{#if has.pool}}- **Pool chemicals:** pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) gives off chlorine gas when
  wet or heated. Keep it sealed in a lidded container on a shelf, away from the furnace and the
  sump, and never next to acids or other cleaners. **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with
  ammonia, acids or other cleaners** (→ 29-05, → 30-01).{{/if}}

## What lives in the spot, permanently

The goal: **you can go down with nothing in your hands and still be equipped.**

| What | Items |
|---|---|
| **Heads** | **A helmet for everyone** (bike helmets are fine). SPC: flying debris is the greatest danger in tornadoes |
| **Feet** | **Shoes for everyone**, children included: the aftermath is glass and nails (→ 12-02) |
| **Light** | Two or three headlamps or flashlights, spare batteries, a lantern, a chemical light stick (no battery to go flat) |
| **Warning** | **A second battery or crank NOAA Weather Radio** (→ 15-01) |
| **Medical** | First-aid and trauma kit (→ 12-08); a small kit of everyday medicines |
| **Water and food** | Several gallons of water, some shelf-stable food{{#if has.food_allergy}}, safe for every food allergy in the household{{/if}} |
| **Signalling** | **A whistle for everyone** (→ 15-07), to be heard from under debris |
| **Cover** | Mattress, heavy blankets or cushions |
| **Children** | A comfort item, a small toy or book, a blanket (→ 20-08) |
| **Papers** | Copy of the family plan and medical cards (→ 25-09) |
| **Tools** | Work gloves and a pry bar, in case the way out is blocked |
| **Sanitation** | A bucket with a lid and bags (→ 13-01) |

**Rotate water, food and batteries twice a year**, with the household inventory (→ 25-10).

## Medicines: decide the grab in advance

Some medicines should not live in the shelter because the spot gets too cold or too warm for the
label's storage range, or because they are in daily use. Read each label (→ 29-07).
{{#each meds as x}}- **{{x.name}}** ({{x.member}}): lives in the shelter / grabbed on the way
  (circle one). Grabbed by: __________.
{{else}}- No medicines are entered in your profile. If anyone takes a daily or rescue medicine,
  decide here whether it lives in the spot or is grabbed on the way.
{{/each}}
- **Rescue medicines** (epinephrine, inhalers) go with the person who needs them. A spare stored in
  the shelter only if a min/max thermometer shows the spot stays inside the label's range all year
  (→ 02-03).
- **Phones and powered medical devices** go too; a charged power bank lives in the spot.
- **Practice the grab** as part of the drill so it is automatic.

## Children, elders and pets

- **Assign roles now** (→ 00-07): who carries the smallest child, who takes an older child's hand,
  who helps an elder or anyone who uses a wheelchair or walker, who grabs the medicines. Do not
  negotiate it during a warning.
  {{#each members as m}}
  - {{m.label}}: goes with / helps __________.{{/each}}
- **Children who have practiced will go; children who have not may freeze or hide** (→ 20-04).
- **Shoes on during the watch.** This is the single biggest time-saver.
- **Make the spot less frightening:** a lantern a child is allowed to hold, a familiar blanket, a
  routine (→ 20-08).
{{#if has.mobility_aid}}- **Someone uses a wheelchair or walker.** If the spot is down stairs, decide
  how they get there and time it; if that is too slow, choose a ground-floor interior room instead
  and make it as strong a spot as you can.{{/if}}
{{#if has.pets}}- **Pets:** carriers live in or beside the spot with the doors open. Decide out loud,
  before any warning, whether anyone looks for a pet once the warning sounds. During a watch, shut
  pets into the shelter side of the house (→ 20-09).{{/if}}

## The drill

1. Announce a drill at a random time.
2. Everyone goes, carrying what they would carry.
3. Time it.
4. Ask: what went wrong? Shoes upstairs? Medicine not where you thought? A scared child? A dead
   light? Fix it.
5. Repeat once at night.
6. Re-drill every spring, and as children grow (→ 25-10).

## If you come up and the house is gone

That is why the spot holds water, food, medicine, papers, shoes and a pry bar.
- **Signal from under debris** with whistles (→ 15-07).
- **The way out may be blocked**: gloves and a pry bar.
- **The house may be unlivable.** Go-bags (→ 22-03) and the document kit (→ 19-01) should be
  reachable, but the spot's own stock is the fallback. In a long emergency, losing the house is a
  reason to move (→ 01-02).

## A tornado spot is not a fallout room

The spot is chosen for minutes. Sheltering for a day or two from fallout (→ 27-05) needs space,
heat, air and sanitation, and any fuel-burning heater there needs its fresh-air openings kept open
(→ 08-01; a heater running while people sleep is card DC-01, → 30-02). Choose the fallout room
separately on → 27-05; the tornado stock can be its supply.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Helmets for everyone** | Debris head injury | Bike helmets are fine |
| **Shoes for everyone, kept in the spot** | Glass and nails afterward | Check children's sizes each spring |
| Second NOAA Weather Radio | You will be down there with no power | → 15-01 |
| Lights, lantern, spare batteries, light sticks | Power will be out | → 10-01 |
| First-aid and trauma kit | Cuts are the common injury | → 12-08 |
| Water and shelf-stable food | You may be there a while | Rotate |
| Whistles | Signal from under debris | → 15-07 |
| Mattress, blankets, cushions | Debris cover | |
| Gloves and pry bar | Blocked exit | |
| Bucket with lid and bags | Long stays | → 13-01 |
| Rotation date on the wall | Water, food, batteries | → 25-10 |

**If you do not have it:** any helmet, a hard hat, or a cushion held over head and neck; a sturdy
workbench, mattress or bathtub for cover; banging on a pipe to signal. **What you cannot
improvise is the practice, and the decision about who carries whom.**

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here runs out fast, but everything quietly expires:** batteries go flat, water gets
  old, food and medicines pass their dates. Put it on the annual review (→ 25-10).
- **The plan's fit changes** as children grow. Re-drill and re-assign roles every year.
- **If the house is destroyed, the spot's stock is what you have.** Keep more there than feels
  necessary. If you can only do one, do the shelter: it is where you will be.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** spot stocked and practiced, second spot agreed out loud, weather radio where you
  sleep and another in the spot.
- **B (moving):** there is no shelter on the move; the answer is not being out in severe weather
  (→ 17-02, → 17-11). At any house you stay in, **pick the best interior room in the first hour**:
  small, no outside walls, lowest floor, no windows. Do not assume last visit's answer is still
  right.
- **C (rural or new site):** a basement, cellar or safe room is a main test of a site (→ 01-05). A
  storm cellar also works as a root cellar (→ 04-09).

pages.body:
# Drought and water scarcity

**What this page is for.** Drought is the slow hazard. It arrives over a season, and by the time it
is obvious the choices are fewer. Three things fail together: **the water supply** (wells drop,
creeks shrink, rain barrels stay empty), **the garden**, and **fire safety**, because everything
dries out (→ 17-05). This page is about doing the water math honestly, cutting use in a planned
order, and knowing when storage is no longer enough.
{{#if is.drought_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for drought in the region data.**{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).
Your area gets about **{{ region.home.precip_in }} inches** of rain and melted snow in a normal
year.

> **CAUTION.** **Never cut drinking water, cooking water or hand washing.** An illness outbreak
> costs far more water than hand washing ever saves (→ 13-11). In heat, people need more water,
> not less (→ 17-04).

## Do this now

1. **Do the water math for a hot, dry month, not an average one** (→ 03-01). Your household's
   minimum is about **{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons a day** for drinking and basic
   hygiene; the planning figure is **{{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day**. Laundry,
   dishes, bathing and the garden come on top.
2. **Put a barrel on every downspout you can** (→ 03-05).
3. **Set up the greywater cascade** (→ 13-03) so each gallon does two or three jobs. It is the
   biggest saving available.
4. **Mulch the garden deeply.** It is the cheapest water saving there is (→ 05-11).
5. **Write the cutting order below on → 23-02** so it is decided before anyone is thirsty.

> **Before the collapse:** some states limit rainwater collection or set rules for water rights,
> wells and diverting streams. Check your state's rules before building a large system while that
> system still works.

## What drought does to each source

| Source | In a drought |
|---|---|
| **Town water** | Restrictions first, then possibly rationing. Usually the last to fail |
| **Rain barrels** (→ 03-05) | **Empty exactly when you need them** |
| **Wells** | The water table drops; yield falls; shallow wells can go dry first |
| **Creeks, ponds, sloughs** | Shrink, then stop. What is left is warm, concentrated and dirtier (→ 03-04) |
| **Rivers** | Low, warm and poorer in quality; treatable with work |
| **Snowpack** | A dry winter means a dry spring. **Drought often starts the winter before** |
{{#if has.pool}}| **Your pool or hot tub** (about {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons) | The largest single reserve on the property, but not drought-proof: uncovered, it loses water to evaporation every hot, windy day, and with no pump or chlorine it turns green. **Keep it covered** (→ 03-03) |
{{/if}}{{#if has.well}}| **Your well** | Note its depth and normal yield now: ______ ft, ______ gal/min. Watch for sputtering, air or sediment as the level drops (→ 03-10) |
{{/if}}

## Storage math

**In a drought, storage is the buffer.**
- **Stored drinking water:** {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gallons, which lasts about
  **{{ derived.water.stored_days }} days** at the floor rate.
- **Two weeks at the planning rate** is about {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gallons (CDC, Emergency
  Water Supply; → 03-01).
- Add hygiene (→ 13-02), dishes, laundry (→ 13-04), toilet flushing (→ 13-01) and the garden, and the
  real household figure is several times the drinking figure. Most households find their runway
  is days, not weeks. Write it on → 23-02 and recompute weekly in a dry spell.

## The cutting order: decide it in advance

When water is short, cut in this order:
1. **Garden watering.** Painful, and the right first cut. Mulch, shade and save the most valuable
   beds; let the rest go.
2. **Laundry.** Wash less, air more (→ 13-04).
3. **Bathing.** Basin washes instead of full baths.
4. **Dishes.** One-pot meals, scrape well, wash once (→ 13-10).
5. **Flushing.** Greywater only (→ 13-03), or a bucket toilet (→ 13-01).
6. **Never cut: drinking, cooking and hand washing.** Hand washing is the last thing to go.

## Savings that actually move the number

- **Cascade every gallon** (→ 13-03): rinse water becomes wash water becomes flush water or water
  for non-food plants.
- **Deep mulch** cuts evaporation from the soil (→ 05-11).
- **Water the soil, not the leaves**, early in the morning or in the evening.
- **Drip or soaker lines** instead of sprinklers.
- **Shade cloth** over the garden in extreme heat cuts water need.
- **Containers dry fastest:** group them, shade them, mulch them (→ 05-10).
- **Fix every leak.** A dripping tap is a real loss over a month.
- **Cover stored water** against evaporation and dirt (→ 03-02).
- **Grow what survives.** Deep-rooted, drought-tolerant crops and established perennials
  (→ 05-13); give up the thirsty ones.

{{figure fig-water-cascade}}

## Drought and fire are the same event

Dry fuel everywhere, low humidity, and **firefighting water is scarce exactly when fire risk is
highest** (→ 17-05). Cooking fires, ash, generator exhaust and saws all become more dangerous. Read
burn conditions off the sky and the radio. Long droughts also bring smoke from distant fires
(→ 17-14).

## Food

- **A drought year is a poor harvest year.** If the garden is part of the food plan, the stored
  food is the drought plan (→ 04-01).
- **Established plants survive; new plantings do not.** Water what is already invested.
- **Wild food fails too**: fewer berries, nuts and game.

## The multi-year drought

- **Storage buys a season, not a drought.** For years of drought you need a **source**, not a
  buffer.
- **A reliable water source is the first test of any long-term site** (→ 01-05): a deep well, a
  spring or dependable surface water outranks almost everything else.
- **A town lot with barrels and stored water has a fixed, finite reserve.** Long-term water is a
  question of where you live (→ 01-02).
- **People downstream share the water.** Expect disputes and plan to be a good neighbour
  (→ 18-01).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **As much stored water as you can keep** | Storage is the buffer | → 03-02 |
| Rain barrels on every downspout | Free when it rains | → 03-05 |
| Water treatment and spare filters | Shrinking sources are dirtier | → 03-04 |
| **Mulch, lots of it** | The cheapest saving in the garden | Straw, leaves, chips |
| Drip or soaker hose | Targeted watering | |
| Shade cloth | Cuts water need | |
| Greywater basins and buckets | The cascade | → 13-03 |
| Covered containers | Evaporation and dirt | |
| Rain gauge and a water-use log | You cannot manage what you do not measure | → 25-05 |
| Drought-tolerant seed | Grow what survives | |
{{#if has.pool}}| Pool cover; pump and hose | Slows evaporation; makes the pool usable for washing, garden and fire water | A cover is a drowning hazard for small children: → 20-02 |{{/if}}

**If you do not have it:** tarps funnelled into barrels catch a surprising amount from a modest
rain; the bathtub is storage (fill it at the first sign of restrictions); leaves, grass clippings,
cardboard and straw are free mulch; snow in winter is free water (→ 03-06). **What you cannot
substitute is a source.**

**Pool and surface water for drinking:** pool water and untreated surface water need treatment, and
salt-water pools need distilling, which costs fuel (→ 03-03). Drinking them is a trade-off with a
decision card: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14

## When it runs out

- **This whole page is about running out.** Compute the runway at the rationed rate and recompute
  weekly.
- **Substitute in order:** rain (→ 03-05), then stored (→ 03-02), then pool or other non-drinking
  reserves treated or distilled (→ 03-03), then surface water treated (→ 03-04), then hauling from
  a distant source. Each step costs more fuel, work or risk.
- **The trigger to move:** when the runway at rationed use drops below the time it would take to
  relocate, that is a go/no-go decision (→ 01-02). Water has no substitute and cannot be made
  locally.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** town water usually holds longest. **While it works, fill every container you
  own.** Expect restrictions before failure.
- **B (moving):** in summer, water is the limit on travel: heavy, used fast in heat, and sources on
  the route may be dry or fouled. Plan the route around water and carry more than feels necessary
  (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** water is the site. Plan for well yield to drop in drought, build
  storage, and place the garden and animals around the water, not the other way round.

pages.body:
# Power grid failure: hours, days and weeks

**What this page is for.** Section 09 is how to make power. This page is what happens when the
grid goes down, over three very different lengths of time, and the moment when one becomes the
next is where households get caught. Start from the safety box; it is what kills people.

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Carbon monoxide (CO) is the main killer after a power outage. CPSC says one portable
>   generator produces the same amount of CO as hundreds of cars, and opening doors or windows does
>   not make it safe (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Information Center; CPSC, Portable Generator Safety;
>   → 29-03).
> - **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock
>   kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide")
>   cord.** Backfed power can kill line workers and neighbours (→ 29-04, → 30-01).
> - **Battery CO alarms on every level and where people sleep, tested, before any heater or
>   generator runs.** You have {{ gear.co_alarms }} CO alarms.
> - **Flashlights, not candles** (USFA).

{{figure fig-generator-distance}}

{{figure fig-backfeed-path}}

## Do this now

1. **Install and test the CO alarms**, with spare batteries. This is the single most valuable step
   on this page (→ 08-02).
2. **Walk through each duration below on paper:** hours, days, weeks. The answers differ, and the
   gaps show up at once.
3. **Check the medical answer at every duration:** refrigerated medicine, device charging, the
   backup plan for each powered device (→ 09-06, → 09-10).
4. **Learn the manual release on the garage door** and anything else that needs power to open.
5. **Do a blackout weekend** (→ 24-04). Nothing on this page is real until you have.

{{photo garage-release}}

## The three durations

| | **Hours (0 to 12)** | **Days (1 to 7)** | **Weeks or longer** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Typical cause** | Storm, equipment fault | Ice storm, hurricane, derecho, major storm | Cascading failure, long crisis |
| **Food** | Keep the fridge and freezer **closed** (→ 04-17) | Eat down in order; outdoor cold in winter (→ 04-09) | Stored food is the plan (Section 04) |
| **Water** | Town water probably fine | **Pressure may fail: fill containers now; treat anything doubtful** (→ 03-02, → 03-04) | Water is the daily job (→ 03-01) |
| **Heat or cooling** | The house holds its temperature | **One room** (→ 08-01); in summer, the lowest, shadiest room (→ 17-04) | Fuel and wood clocks (→ 23-02) |
| **Light** | Headlamps (→ 10-01) | Batteries, rationed | Solar and LED, then flame (→ 10-02) |
| **Medical** | Little changes | **Refrigerated medicine and device charging matter now** (→ 09-10, → 09-06) | **The medicine supply is the clock** (→ 01-02) |
| **Sanitation** | Fine | Sewer may still work: pour-flush (→ 13-01) | Bucket system; disposal |
| **News** | Phones probably work | Phones degrade; **NOAA and AM radio** (→ 15-01) | Radio only (→ 15-04) |
| **The decision** | Wait | **Prepare for longer** | **Go/no-go** (→ 01-02) |

**The mistake is treating each stage as the last one.** Households that spend day two as if it
were an inconvenience find themselves unprepared on day five. **Prepare for the next-longer stage
from the start.**

## Hours

- **Keep the refrigerator and freezer shut.** A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for about **4
  hours**; a full freezer holds about **48 hours**, a half-full one about **24 hours**
  (FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During a Power Outage). → 04-17
- **Headlamps, not candles.**
- **If the outage was forecast, everything was charged at the warning** (below).
- **Check on neighbours**, especially anyone elderly or on powered medical equipment (→ 18-01).
- **Unplug sensitive electronics** so the return surge does not damage them (Ready.gov, Power
  Outages).

## Days

1. **Heat or cooling first.** One room (→ 08-01, → 09-16). CO alarms up before any heater is lit.
   Run one fuel-burning heater at a time, under its own page's rules (→ 08-04).
   - **Whether an unvented heater runs while people sleep** is a household decision:
     {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02
   - **Whether a propane cylinder larger than 1 lb comes indoors** is another:
     {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03
   {{#if has.gas_any}}- **Gas often keeps flowing** when electricity stops, but most furnaces need
     electricity for the blower and igniter. Powering a furnace from a generator or power station
     needs a safe connection (→ 09-04). Converting the furnace to a plug yourself is a decision
     card: {{choice DC-07}} → 30-08{{/if}}
2. **Food.** Fridge first, then freezer, then pantry. In winter, outdoor cold is free storage
   (→ 04-09). Food from a freezer that thawed is a decision card: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15
3. **Water.** Town pressure often survives on backup power, but not always. **Fill containers when
   the outage starts**, and treat anything doubtful (→ 03-04). In winter, watch for freezing pipes
   (→ 03-06).
   {{#if has.well}}**Your well pump needs electricity.** Without it you have only what is in the
   pressure tank and what you stored (→ 03-10).{{/if}}
4. **Medicine and devices.**
   {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}Refrigerated medicine: keep it in its label range (→ 29-07, → 09-10). In
   winter this is easy; in summer it is the hard problem.{{/if}}
   {{#if has.cpap}}CPAP: battery or power station plan (→ 09-10).{{/if}}
   {{#if has.oxygen}}Oxygen: a concentrator stops without power. Know how many hours of cylinder
   backup you have: ______ (→ 02-08).{{/if}}
   Phones that run medical devices or apps get the power banks first (→ 09-06).
5. **Power.**
   {{#if has.power_station}}Your power stations hold about **{{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh** in total,
   roughly **{{ derived.station_fridge_days }} days** of a typical full-size fridge if nothing else
   ran (an estimate; → 29-02). Give each station a job before the outage, by priority (→ 09-01).{{/if}}
   {{#if has.generator}}Your generator ({{ gear.generator_watts }} running watts, {{ gear.generator_fuel }})
   is a **bridge**: run it outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages
   (Ready.gov, Power Outages), in bursts to charge
   batteries, not all day (→ 09-04). House connection: {{ gear.house_connection }}.{{/if}}
6. **Sump pump.** Power out means sump out (→ 17-03). A pump draws a large surge when it starts;
   read the nameplate and test it on your backup power before you need it. If both the sump and
   heat need the same battery, the sump usually wins: water damage is permanent.
7. **Sanitation.** If the sewer works, pour-flush with non-drinking water (→ 13-01).
8. **News.** Battery or crank NOAA and AM/FM radio (→ 15-01).
9. **Sleep and morale.** Long dark evenings in one room are harder than people expect after two
   days (→ 21-02, → 21-07).

**The charge-at-the-warning rule.** Ice storms, hurricanes and big windstorms come with hours of
notice. **When the warning (not the outage) is issued:** every power station and power bank to
full, every phone charged, the vehicle above half a tank, water containers filled. Grid power in
the warning window is free storage.

## Weeks and longer

The outage stops being an event and becomes **the situation**, and the rest of this binder is the
plan.
- **Solar and batteries become the power system**; generator fuel is finite (→ 09-02, → 09-04).
- **The medicine supply becomes the household clock** and drives the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02).
- **Water, food, heat and sanitation become daily work** instead of utilities.
- **Town water may fail** once treatment and pumping run out of backup fuel. Pressure usually sags
  before it stops.
- **Natural gas may outlast electricity**, but if gas pressure is lost, restoring it takes a long
  time because each house must be checked and relit.
- **Community effects begin** (→ 14-01, → 18-01).

## The cascade: what fails because power failed

- **Water treatment and pumping**: boil notices, then low or no pressure (→ 03-04).
- **Sewage lift stations**: backups (→ 13-01).
- **Cell towers**: batteries for hours, generators for days if fuelled, then quiet.
- **Fuel stations**: pumps need electricity. Fuel becomes hard to get quickly.
- **Refrigeration everywhere**: food supply chains falter within days.
- **Pharmacies**: medicine access narrows. For many households this is the one that matters most.
- **Card payments**: stop. **Cash matters early** (→ 19-02).
- **Heat in an unprepared house**: in a cold winter, a danger to life within a day or two; in a
  heat wave, the same for elders and the sick.

## The blackout weekend

Turn off the main breaker for a weekend, once in winter and once in summer. Live on your plan:
cook, light, heat or cool, wash, run the medical routine. Write down what failed. Everyone finds
three or four things. Fix them, then do it again next year (→ 24-04).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **CO alarms, battery, every level** | The main killer after an outage | → 08-02 |
| Battery or crank NOAA and AM/FM radio | News when everything else is dark | → 15-01 |
| **Power banks, charged** | Phones and medical devices | → 09-06 |
| Headlamps, lanterns, batteries | Light without flame | → 10-01 |
| Power station(s) and a way to recharge them | The quiet, indoor-safe power | → 09-03, → 29-02 |
| Generator and stored fuel, if you choose one | A bridge, in bursts, outdoors only | → 09-04 |
| Fridge and freezer thermometers | Food-safety decisions | → 04-17 |
| Stored water | Pressure may fail | → 03-02 |
| Cash in small bills | Card systems fail at once | → 19-02 |
| Manual can opener, matches, non-electric tools | The things people forget | |

**If you do not have it:** a vehicle can charge phones and devices, **outdoors, never in an
attached garage** (→ 09-11); winter cold is a refrigerator (→ 04-09); neighbours have generators,
wood stoves and wells, and mutual aid works best if you already know each other (→ 18-01). **What
you cannot substitute: the CO alarm, and life-sustaining medicine.**

## When it runs out

- **The outage does not run out; your buffers do**, in a fairly predictable order: phone batteries,
  then refrigerated food, then generator fuel, then water pressure, then heating fuel, then
  medicine. Know the order and watch the shortest one.
- **Ration by priority** (→ 09-01): life-sustaining medical loads first, everything else shed in
  order.
- **Substitute:** solar for grid, wood for furnace, outdoor cold for refrigeration, radio for
  internet, cash for cards, neighbours for services.
- **Decide in advance** the point at which an outage that looks indefinite becomes a reason to
  leave (→ 01-02), and decide it early, while fuel, roads and daylight still exist.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** Section 09's system plus the fallbacks here. Most long outages come with weather
  warnings (→ 15-01).
- **B (moving):** an indefinite outage plus a short medicine supply is the classic trigger to move
  (→ 01-02). Keep the vehicle above half a tank; fuel goes when pumps lose power.
- **C (rural or new site):** no grid to fail, but no restoration either. The household's own power
  is the system from day one (→ 09-09).

# Pandemic and widespread illness

**What this page is for.** A pandemic (a disease spreading widely across many countries) usually
does not break the power grid or the water supply. **It breaks the supply chain and the health
care system.** For a household that depends on a daily medicine, the main danger is often not "we
get sick" but "the pharmacy cannot fill it" and "the clinic is full." This page is household
preparation that works whatever the germ is.

> **CAUTION. Disease-specific guidance must come from CDC and public health authorities at the
> time.** How a disease spreads, how long it incubates, isolation rules, treatment and vaccines
> are specific to each illness. Nothing written in advance replaces current guidance. Where none
> can be had, use the offline default below.

## Do this now

1. **Deepen the medicine supply** (→ 12-07). For a household with a life-sustaining medicine, this
   is the most valuable pandemic preparation by far. Count days on hand for each daily medicine
   and supply, and talk to the prescriber and pharmacy about a longer supply while that system
   works:
   {{#each meds as x}}
   - **{{x.name}}** ({{x.member}}): **{{x.days_on_hand}}** days on hand.{{else}}
   - No medicines are entered in your profile. Add them in settings so this list and → 23-02 can
     track them.{{/each}}
2. **Build food and household supply depth** (→ 04-01, → 04-02) so weeks without going out are
   routine.
3. **Build the hygiene system** (→ 13-02): soap, water, a hand-washing station. It works against
   nearly every germ.
4. **Stock sick-care supplies** (→ 13-11, → 12-05): oral rehydration salts, thermometers, gloves,
   disinfectant, masks, a dedicated sick kit.
5. **Know your household's specific risks** and talk them over with your clinician (→ 12-11).

## The three ways a pandemic hits a household

1. **Direct illness.** Someone gets sick. This is what people plan for, and → 12-05 and → 13-11
   cover it.
2. **Health care saturation.** Often the bigger risk. **An overwhelmed system makes ordinary
   emergencies worse**: an injury, a childbirth, a flare of a chronic condition. Care that is
   normally there becomes unreliable (→ 12-16).
3. **Supply chain disruption.** Medicine shortages, food gaps, shortages of specific goods. For a
   household that depends on a medicine made by few producers, this can matter more than a power
   outage.

## Who in your household is most exposed

| Who | The pandemic-specific risk |
|---|---|
{{#if has.diabetes}}| **Anyone with diabetes** | Medicine and supply disruption; illness raises blood sugar and the risk of emergencies; needs care more than most (see the condition page in Section 02) |
{{/if}}{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}| **Anyone with a severe allergy** | Epinephrine supply; safe food narrows further in a shortage (→ 02-03, → 02-04) |
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}| **Anyone on oxygen or with lung disease** | Respiratory illness hits hardest; oxygen supply (→ 02-08) |
{{/if}}{{#if has.infant}}| **Infants** | Dehydrate fast; cannot report; cannot be separated from carers; too young for a mask |
{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}| **Elders** | More severe illness; isolation and loneliness |
{{/if}}{{#if has.pregnant}}| **Pregnancy** | Prenatal and birth care may be disrupted (→ 02-12) |
{{/if}}| **All adults** | If every adult is ill at once, nobody runs the medical routines or cares for children. Plan for it |

## What reduces risk

Layered, and none is complete alone:
1. **Hand washing** with soap at the key moments (CDC). Works against nearly everything.
2. **Fewer exposures:** fewer trips, fewer contacts, staying home when sick. The most effective
   single step and the hardest to keep up.
3. **Cleaning and disinfecting** often-touched surfaces (CDC; → 13-11).
4. **Fresh air.** Air exchange matters for illnesses spread through the air. In winter it fights
   with keeping warm (→ 08-03); the answer is short, deliberate airing several times a day, not a
   sealed house.
5. **Masks** (below). Germ-specific guidance overrides this.
6. **Vaccination** per current public health guidance, **including routine childhood vaccines**
   (→ 12-04), which matter more when the health system is stretched.
7. **Supply depth** so you do not have to go out.
8. **Separating the sick person inside the house** where you can (→ 13-11).

## The offline default: isolation and masks when there is no current guidance

Germ-specific public health guidance overrides this. When there is none to be had, run this (CDC,
Preventing Spread of Respiratory Viruses When You're Sick):
- **The sick person stays home and apart from others while they have symptoms.** They go back to
  normal activity when, **for at least 24 hours, their symptoms are getting better overall and they
  have had no fever without using fever-reducing medicine**, then take **added precautions over
  the next 5 days**: cleaner air, hygiene, a well-fitted mask, distance.
- **Stomach illness:** the same shape. CDC: a person who has had norovirus does not prepare or
  handle food or care for others until at least 2 days (48 hours) after symptoms stop (CDC, How
  to Prevent Norovirus; → 13-11).
- **Masks, best first:** a NIOSH-approved **N95** respirator, then an international respirator
  such as a **KN95**, then a **surgical** (disposable) mask, then **cloth**. Fit matters: gaps let
  air leak in and out (CDC, Masks and Respiratory Viruses Prevention). **No respirator on a child
  under 2** (EPA, Reduce Your Smoke Exposure): their protection is distance and the sick adult
  wearing one.
- **Hands:** soap and water for **20 seconds**, before eating or feeding a child, after coughing or
  caring for the sick, after the toilet. Hand sanitizer with **at least 60% alcohol** when hands are
  not visibly dirty (CDC, Handwashing; → 13-02).
- **One heated room in winter:** true isolation is nearly impossible. The sick person takes the far
  side, wears a mask, does no food preparation, and the room is aired briefly several times a day.

**Sepsis** (the body's extreme reaction to an infection) can follow any infection. Confusion, fast
breathing, a racing heart, extreme pain or clammy skin in someone who is ill is an emergency (CDC,
About Sepsis; → 12-04).

## The stock-up window

**When a situation is developing, the window to prepare is early and it closes fast.** Shelves
empty, prescriptions get limited, and everyone acts at once.
- **Be prepared beforehand; do not panic-buy during.** That is the whole argument for the depth in
  Section 04 and → 12-07.
- **Panic-buying damages the community you will depend on** (→ 18-01).
- **Medicine is the exception worth acting on at once:** if a supply problem looks likely, call
  the prescriber and pharmacy early. That is not hoarding; it is a medical step for a
  life-sustaining drug.
- **Sharing or borrowing prescription medicine** and **antibiotics without a prescription** are
  decision cards, not things to improvise: {{choice DC-15}} → 30-16; {{choice DC-16}} → 30-17

## Isolation with small children

- **You cannot isolate a baby or toddler from their carers**, and trying makes things worse.
- **You can** reduce spread with hand washing, cleaning, separate personal items, fresh air, and
  separating a sick adult where possible.
- **Assume everyone gets it** and plan for that: water, oral rehydration salts, easy food and fuel
  set out so a fully sick household can still function.
- **Every adult should be able to run every life-sustaining routine**, because the person who
  usually does it may be the one who is sick (→ 00-07).

## The long tail

- **Schools and childcare close** (→ 20-03). **Work changes or stops** (→ 19-08).
- **Supply chains stay disrupted after the worst is over.**
- **Health care backlogs last** (→ 12-11).
- **Mental strain is heavy and long** (→ 21-01, → 21-02, → 12-15). Plan for it on purpose.
- **Communities strain under this kind of stress** (→ 18-06), and community is also what gets
  people through it (→ 18-01).

## When the medicine is the problem and everything else works

A pandemic is the scenario most likely to cut a medicine supply **while the grid, water and roads
still work**:
- **You can still travel**, so the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02) may point toward **seeking supply**,
  not sheltering.
- **You can still communicate**, so clinicians, pharmacies and patient networks matter.
- **Money still works.**
- **The right response can be early, active and outward.** The instinct in a pandemic is to
  shelter; for a household whose central need is a medicine, that may be exactly wrong.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **The longest legitimate medicine supply** | The most valuable step here | → 12-07; talk to the prescriber |
| Deep food and household stock | So you need not go out | → 04-01, → 04-02 |
| **Soap in quantity; a hand-washing station** | Works against nearly everything | → 13-02 |
| Hand sanitizer, at least 60% alcohol | A supplement, not a replacement | |
| **Oral rehydration salts** | Illness and dehydration, especially children | → 12-05 |
| Thermometers and spare batteries | Tracking a sick household | |
| Nitrile gloves; N95 respirators in adult and smaller sizes; surgical masks | Caring for the sick | Fit-check the N95s now |
| Disinfectant and spray bottles | Per the CDC cleaning guidance | → 13-11 |
| **A dedicated sick kit** (bucket, cloths, own cup and towel) | Assembled before you need it | → 13-11 |
| Cash in small bills | Systems degrade | → 19-02 |
| Games, projects, school materials | Months at home | → 20-03, → 21-02 |

**If you do not have it:** soap and water replace almost every product on this page; a surgical
mask under a snug cloth one fits better than either alone; fresh air is free; oral rehydration
solution can be made from salt, sugar and safe water using the published WHO recipe on → 12-05; a
neighbourhood that runs errands for its sick households protects everyone (→ 18-01). **What you
cannot substitute is a life-sustaining medicine.**

## When it runs out

- **The supply that decides the outcome is medicine**, not food or fuel. Track days on hand and
  treat supply-chain news as an early trigger (→ 23-02, → 01-02).
- **Medicine is never rationed below what the condition needs.** That is a clinician's
  conversation, not a household decision (→ 12-11).
- **Resupply is still possible in this scenario**: pharmacies, mail order, other regions,
  clinicians, community. **Act early, before scarcity sets in.**

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** sheltering in place works, provided the medicine supply holds. Use early warning
  to deepen it, reduce exposure, and keep hygiene strict.
- **B (moving):** in a pandemic, movement is usually to get medicine or care, not to relocate.
  Travel raises exposure; weigh it against what you are going for (→ 01-02).
- **C (rural or new site):** distance protects against spread, and worsens the supply and care
  problem. Weigh both honestly (→ 01-05).

# Reading the sky: forecasting with no forecast

**What this page is for.** Every other page in this section assumes a warning reaches you. In a
long grid or internet failure it may not. Then **the sky, an analog barometer and a battery NOAA
Weather Radio** are the whole warning system. This page teaches the signs that matter most.

> **SAFETY.** Reading the sky buys **minutes to hours**, not days, and it gives false alarms.
> **Take the false alarms.** Going to shelter for a shelf cloud that blows through costs ten
> minutes; ignoring a wall cloud can cost everything. When a sign on this page fires, act on the
> matching page (→ 17-02, → 17-06, → 17-01) and argue about it afterward.

## Do this now

1. **Get an analog (aneroid) barometer** and hang it where you pass it every day (→ 22-01). Tap the
   glass gently before reading; the needle sticks. **Write the reading and the time on a card next
   to it twice a day.** A barometer is useless without its trend.
2. **Learn the wall cloud and shelf cloud difference below** until you can say it from memory.
3. **Practice on ordinary storms now**, while forecasts still exist to check yourself against
   (→ 24-02).
4. **Keep the weather radio's batteries as a protected reserve** (→ 15-01). NOAA Weather Radio
   transmitters reach you with no internet at all (NWS, NOAA Weather Radio).

## Quick reference: post this

| You see or feel | It likely means | Do |
|---|---|---|
| **A lowered, often rotating cloud under the rain-free base** (wall cloud) | Tornado possible within minutes | **Shelter now** (→ 17-06) |
| **A long, low, wedge-shaped cloud on the storm's leading edge** (shelf cloud) | Damaging straight-line wind about to arrive | Inside, interior room, away from windows (→ 17-18) |
| **Dark greenish sky** | Not a reliable sign (NSSL): treat it as "a severe storm is near" | Inside; vehicles and portable gear under cover if time |
| **Large hail, or a sudden calm** | A dangerous storm. SPC: these can come before a tornado but are not a reliable sign either way | **Shelter now** |
| **A continuous roar like a freight train** | Tornado, close | **Shelter now** |
| **Shelf cloud plus advancing wall of dust or rain, then a wind blast** | Derecho or severe squall line | Tornado posture (→ 17-02) |
| **Halo around the sun or moon** (thin high cloud, cirrostratus) | Moisture arriving high up; a warm front may bring persistent rain within a day (Met Office) | Check supplies; watch for the sequence below |
| **High thin cloud thickening and lowering until the sun is a dim smear** | The storm system is getting closer: hours, not days | In winter, start storm preparation (→ 17-01) |
| **Wind backing (turning counter-clockwise, for example west to south to east) plus a falling barometer** | A low-pressure storm approaching | Prepare; do not start a trip |
| **Barometer falling more than about 1 millibar an hour** | A storm may be approaching (mariners' rule of thumb) | Storm preparation |
| **Barometer falling faster, or for hours on end** | A stronger storm | Full preparation; no travel |
| **Winter: temperature rising toward freezing as snow starts, east or southeast wind** | Snow that may turn to freezing rain | Ice-storm preparation (→ 17-01, → 17-08) |
| **Winter: sharp wind shift to the northwest and temperature crashing after the snow** | Cold front behind the storm; blowing snow | Nobody travels (→ 17-11) |
| **At the coast: the sea drawing back suddenly, or a roar from the ocean** | Possible tsunami | **High ground now** (→ 17-15) |
| **Night: you can see none of this** | The storm is still there | Radio on, alarm armed, shoes by the bed, light in reach |

## Tornado signs the storm shows you

- **Wall cloud or shelf cloud: the difference that matters** (SPC; NSSL):
  - A **wall cloud** is an **abrupt, isolated lowering** under the storm's **rain-free base**,
    usually at the **back** of the storm (in much of the central US, its southwest side), and
    often **rotating**. It marks the updraft, where tornadoes form. **Rotation you can watch is the
    alarm.**
  - A **shelf cloud** is a **long, low, wedge-shaped** cloud on the **leading edge** of the storm,
    often across the whole horizon. It marks the gust front of cold outflow. It looks terrifying
    and usually means **straight-line wind**, not a tornado. Still get inside.
  - **Memory aid:** shelf cloud = front of the storm, shaped like a shelf, coming at you. Wall
    cloud = back of the storm, hanging down like a wall, often turning.
- **A green sky is folklore-grade.** NSSL says scientists do not agree why the sky turns green,
  though it is often reported near hail; SPC lists no sky colour as a tornado sign.
- **Large hail, or a sudden calm:** SPC says neither is a reliable predictor of a tornado, but
  large hail does mean an unusually dangerous storm. The quiet is not the all-clear.
- **A roar that does not fade like thunder:** tornado.
- **At night:** this is what the radio is for. Lightning flickering in one part of the sky at least
  shows where the storm is.

{{figure fig-wall-vs-shelf-cloud}}

## Derecho signature

A derecho (a long, wide windstorm; → 17-02) may show **a shelf cloud across the horizon** and an
**advancing wall of dust and rain** below it, then an abrupt **wind blast**. SPC is blunt about the
limits: shelf clouds are not always present, and because derechos usually move at 50 mph or more,
the signs appear on very short notice, often too short to act on (SPC, About Derechos). **When
you see them, take the tornado posture at once, without waiting for rotation**; the radio is what
gives real warning.

## Winter storm onset: a day's notice

The classic warm-front cloud sequence. High wispy cirrus is often the first cloud to appear ahead
of a low-pressure system (NOAA JetStream, The Four Core Types of Clouds):
1. **A halo** around the sun or moon (thin ice-crystal cloud, cirrostratus): moisture arriving high
   up. The Met Office says that when a sheet of cirrostratus covers the sky, a warm front is likely
   to bring persistent rain within a day (Met Office, High clouds). The faster the sky thickens,
   the sooner.
2. **High cloud thickens and lowers** until the sun is a dim smear behind grey: the weather is
   hours away, not days.
3. **The wind backs** and **the barometer falls steadily.**
4. **Temperature tells you which storm it is.** Rising toward freezing as precipitation starts
   means snow that can turn to **freezing rain**, the outage maker (→ 17-08). Falling hard behind a
   northwest wind shift means the back side: blowing snow and ground blizzards (→ 17-11).
5. **When step 2 is under way in winter, run the → 17-01 "before" list.** Being half a day early
   costs nothing.

## The barometer

An analog barometer needs no power and no internet. **Set it once** to the sea-level pressure read
out on the NOAA Weather Radio observation (the nearest airport's reading), not to a guessed number.
Your home sits at about **{{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft**, and a barometer set without a real
reading at that height can be far off. **The number matters less than the trend.**
- **Falling more than about 1 millibar an hour:** a storm may be approaching. Read it every hour
  or two while it falls.
- **Falling faster than that, or falling for hours on end:** a stronger storm or a fast-deepening
  low. Full preparation, no travel.
- **Rising fast after a storm:** clearing, but in winter often wind and bitter cold behind it.
- The 1-millibar-an-hour figure is a **mariners' rule of thumb** (Barometer Rules), not an NWS
  product. Treat it as a reason to prepare, never as a reason to relax.

**Pressure and wind together** beat either alone:

| Barometer | Wind from | Read it as |
|---|---|---|
| Falling fast | East to southeast | A major low approaching |
| Falling fast | South to southwest, warm and humid | Severe thunderstorms possible today: watch the sky hourly |
| Steady or rising | West to northwest | Fair, or clearing |
| Rising fast | Northwest, in winter | Clearing, wind and plunging cold: blowing snow on open roads |

These are for the middle latitudes of the US, where weather generally moves west to east. Near
the coasts and in the mountains, local winds can change the pattern; learn yours by logging.

## Folk and animal signs: label them honestly

These only back up the signs above. **Never act on them alone; never let them overrule the table.**
- **"Red sky at night, red sky at morning"**: weakly true where weather moves west to east; wrong
  often.
- **Birds going quiet, animals bunching, insects vanishing:** often true, never reliable, never
  specific.
- **Chimney smoke hanging low, smells carrying far:** a rough low-pressure sign; the barometer says
  it better.
- **Aching joints, "the smell of rain":** real things, useless timing.
- **When a folk sign and the barometer agree, stop and read the sky carefully.**

## What the NOAA radio still gives you

The NWS transmitter network broadcasts on VHF with backup power at many sites, independent of phone
networks and the internet (→ 15-02, → 29-09):
- **Watches and warnings with the SAME alarm**, which wakes you.
- **Routine forecasts and observations**, including the pressure that sets your barometer.
- **If even the transmitters go quiet, this page is what is left.** That is why it is here.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Analog (aneroid) barometer** | The no-power storm detector | Hang at eye level; tap before reading |
| Log card and pencil beside it | The trend is the instrument | Twice a day; more often when falling |
| NOAA Weather Radio, battery or crank | The real warning layer | → 15-01 |
| Outdoor min/max thermometer | Temperature trend is a clue in winter | |
| This page's table, posted | Used under stress | |
| A compass, or known landmarks | Wind direction is half the reading | Know which way is northwest |

**If you do not have it:** a watch or vehicle with a pressure sensor; for wind direction a flag,
smoke, a wet finger or moving trees. **What you cannot improvise is a practiced eye.** Practice on
storms now.

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here wears out** except radio batteries; protect them.
- **What fades is skill.** Keep logging the barometer in quiet weeks and check yourself against
  real storms every season.
- **The failure is alarm fatigue.** After three false alarms the fourth shelf cloud gets ignored.
  The response to a sign is cheap on purpose, so you can afford to take every alarm.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** the radio leads; the sky backs it up. Log the barometer daily so the habit
  exists before it matters.
- **B (moving):** this page and → 17-11 are the trip's weather service. Read the sky at every stop.
  A falling barometer or a darkening western sky is a reason to stop early, not drive faster
  (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** sky reading becomes a daily working skill for field work, travel and
  fire risk (→ 17-05). Teach it to children as they grow.

pages.body:
# Hazards on the road to each destination

**What this page is for.** A trip to a destination crosses country whose weather you may not know.
This page lists, for each of your destinations, what the weather does there and what it is likely
to do on the way, then gives the rules for the hazards that kill people in vehicles: ground
blizzards, tornadoes, flooded roads and high wind. Print it and keep a copy in the vehicle kit
(→ 22-05).

> **SAFETY. The route is checked before departure, not managed after.** A hazard you drive into on
> purpose is not weather; it is a planning failure. Three rules that are never relaxed:
> - **Never drive into flowing water** across a road: 6 inches knocks an adult down, 12 inches
>   carries away most cars, 2 feet carries away SUVs and trucks (NWS, Turn Around Don't Drown).
> - **A closed road means stop.** Never detour onto back roads in a winter storm.
> - **Never shelter under an overpass** in a tornado (SPC).

## Your destinations

{{#each destinations as x}}
### {{x.name}}

- **Where:** {{x.county}}, {{x.state_name}}. Status: **{{x.status_text}}**. About
  **{{x.approximate_miles}} miles**.
- **Climate there:** January nights about {{x.region.jan_low_f}} °F; July days about
  {{x.region.jul_high_f}} °F; about {{x.region.snow_in}} inches of snow a year; elevation about
  {{x.region.elevation_ft}} ft.
- **Weather office there:** {{x.region.nws_office}}. State emergency agency:
  {{x.region.state_em}}.
- **Your route notes:** {{x.route_notes}}
- **Shelter stops on this route** (sturdy buildings, full-service towns, rest areas): ______________
- **Low spots and flood-prone crossings on this route:** ______________
- **The point of no return** (past here, you are committed to open country or a long stretch with
  no services): ______________
{{else}}
No destination is entered. The rules below still apply to any trip, including a move toward town,
family or medical help. Add destinations in settings and regenerate.
{{/each}}

## The honest read for each route

{{ai corridor-hazards-read}}

## Home hazards, for comparison

| Hazard at home | Rating |
|---|---|
{{#each region.home.hazards as h}}| {{h.name}} | {{h.rating_text}} |
{{/each}}

**What the rating means.** The ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index for each county, on a
1-to-3 scale (low, moderate, high). They measure expected harm to people and property, not how
likely the hazard is: a big city can rate high for a rare hazard because so much is exposed (Cook
County, Illinois, rates high for earthquakes), and a thinly settled county can rate low for a
hazard that does strike it. Use them to choose which pages to read first, never to decide that a
hazard on your route cannot happen (→ 29-10). Each destination's full hazard list is on its state
page in Section 32.

## Season and route: decide before you need to

When to leave is a household decision written in advance: {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20. For each
destination, fill in the table before the season starts.

{{#if has.destinations}}| Season or situation | {{#each destinations as x}}{{x.name}} | {{/each}}
|---|{{#each destinations as x}}---|{{/each}}
| Winter, storm anywhere on the route | {{#each destinations as x}}Wait / go: ____ | {{/each}}
| Winter, clear multi-day window | {{#each destinations as x}}Wait / go: ____ | {{/each}}
| Spring and summer storm season | {{#each destinations as x}}Wait / go: ____ | {{/each}}
| Hurricane or wildfire season | {{#each destinations as x}}Wait / go: ____ | {{/each}}
| Short warning, any season | {{#each destinations as x}}Wait / go: ____ | {{/each}}{{else}}| Season or situation | Any trip you might make: wait or go? |
|---|---|
| Winter, storm anywhere on the route | ____ |
| Winter, clear multi-day window | ____ |
| Spring and summer storm season | ____ |
| Hurricane or wildfire season | ____ |
| Short warning, any season | ____ |{{/if}}

**General rules that fit almost any route:**
- **Short trips can wait for a weather window.** A day's delay costs little; driving into a storm
  can cost everything.
- **Long trips suit only an early, seen-it-coming departure in a clear multi-day window** (→ 01-05).
- **In storm season, leave in the morning**; severe thunderstorms peak in the late afternoon and
  evening. Avoid driving at night when flash floods are possible.
- **Main highways are cleared and patrolled first.** In ice or snow, stay on them or do not go.

## Winter: the ground blizzard

A **ground blizzard** needs **no falling snow**: dry snow already on the ground plus strong wind
makes zero visibility at road level, sometimes under a blue sky (NSSL, Winter Weather Types). The
trap: you leave in sunshine and an hour later the road disappears.
- **The setup to recognise** (→ 17-10): fresh dry snow on the ground, a clearing sky, a rising
  barometer and strong northwest wind. **A beautiful cold morning after a snowstorm can be the most
  dangerous travel day of the year** in open country.
- **Closed road means stop.** Never detour onto back roads in winter: they drift shut, nobody plows
  or patrols them, and people die on them.
- **Whiteout while driving:** do not stop in a travel lane. Exit if you can; otherwise pull as far
  off the road as possible, lights on, and **stay with the vehicle** (→ 17-01: tailpipe clear,
  engine about 10 minutes each hour, a bright marker; NWS).
- **Fuel:** keep the tank at least half full in winter and fill at every chance (→ 22-05).

## Tornado while driving

NWS: **"Being in a vehicle during a tornado is not safe. The best course of action is to drive to
the closest shelter."** If a tornado is close and there is no building (SPC, Tornado Safety FAQ):
1. **If you can, drive away at right angles to its path.** Do not try to outrun it along its track.
2. **Caught by extreme wind or debris:** park out of traffic lanes. **"Stay in the car with the
   seat belt on. Put your head down below the windows; cover your head with your hands and a
   blanket, coat, or other cushion."**
3. **"If you can safely get noticeably lower than the level of the roadway, leave your car and lie
   in that area, covering your head with your hands."** Noticeably lower and reachable means
   ditch; otherwise stay belted in the vehicle below the windows.
   {{#if has.young_child}}With small children in car seats, the vehicle is usually the realistic
   choice.{{/if}}
4. **Never under an overpass.**
5. **Mobile home parks are not shelter.** Drive on to something sturdier.

{{figure fig-tornado-vehicle-choices}}

## Floods and low-water crossings

- **Never cross flowing water.** You cannot see whether the road is still there.
- **Back roads in hill country often cross creeks at fords and dips** that flood in minutes.
  When flood watches are up, stay on the main highways and do not drive at night (→ 17-03).
- **If your vehicle is trapped in rushing water, stay inside unless water is rising inside it;
  then get onto the roof** (Ready.gov, Floods; → 17-03).

{{figure fig-flood-water-depths}}

## Hurricanes, wildfire and smoke on the route

- **Hurricane evacuation routes jam.** Leave when told, or earlier, and know the official route
  (→ 17-13).
- **Wildfire closes roads without notice and smoke cuts visibility to nothing.** Never drive toward
  a fire to "get past it" (→ 17-05, → 17-14).

{{#if has.trailer}}## Towing a trailer

A tall trailer catches wind like a sail, and an empty or lightly loaded one is the worst case.
**No agency publishes crosswind limits for a household trailer**, so set your own, conservatively,
and test them on a windy day before it matters (→ 16-11):
- Slow to ______ mph when gusts reach ______ mph.
- Stop towing when gusts reach ______ mph.
- On ice or packed snow: ______ (many experienced towers simply stop).
- **When to drop the trailer:** sheltering from a tornado (seconds matter: leave it), a wind hold
  that is outlasting the daylight, or any time the vehicle must move and the trailer cannot.
  **Cargo can be replaced; people cannot.** Note where you left it and drive on. Practice
  unhitching once so it takes two minutes.
- Load heavy items low and over or just ahead of the axle; check the trailer brakes and lights
  before every trip.
{{/if}}

## Shelter on the road

Ranked, using the rule from → 17-02 (lowest floor, interior, walls between you and outside):
1. **Sturdy public buildings:** truck stops (interior restrooms), stores with interior rooms or walk-in
   coolers, banks, schools, churches, courthouses, hospitals.
2. **Rest areas** with solid masonry restroom buildings: adequate in a tornado warning, good for a
   wind or ice hold.
3. **Motels:** an interior ground-floor bathroom. Also the ice-storm answer: **ice on the route
   means stop early and take the room.** Driving on is how a trip becomes a rescue.
4. **The vehicle:** last resort, per the rules above.

{{photo route-atlas}}

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **This page and a paper atlas with routes and shelter stops marked** | The plan must be on paper | → 25-04 |
| Winter vehicle kit | Stranding | → 22-05 |
| NOAA Weather Radio in the vehicle | Warnings where phones do not reach | → 15-09 |
| Fuel at least half, always | Closures strand you where you are | |
| List of truck stops and rest areas on each route | The shelter plan | On the atlas |

Carrying spare fuel inside the passenger area is a trade-off with its own card:
{{choice DC-06}} → 30-07

**If you do not have it:** any masonry building beats the vehicle; local AM radio reads road
closures; truck drivers at fuel stops know the road ahead. **What you cannot substitute is slack.**
Every rule here is a version of "leave early, stop early, wait a day."

## When it runs out

- **Fuel:** closures and detours burn it. Below a quarter tank in bad weather, stop at the next
  services and fill or stay.
- **Daylight:** winter gives few driving hours. A long trip may not fit in one winter day, which is
  itself a reason to choose the season.
- **Route knowledge:** roads close, bridges wash out. After any real event, the last traveller's
  information beats the map. Update the atlas notes every trip.
- **The decision habit:** at every fuel stop, decide the next leg only (→ 01-03). A trip is a chain
  of short decisions, not one long one.

## Phase notes

- **B (moving):** this whole page is the moving phase. Weather on the route turns "go" into "wait",
  and waiting is almost always right (→ 01-02, → 01-03, → 01-05).

pages.body:
# Earthquakes

**What this page is for.** An earthquake gives no warning you can count on and is over in seconds
to a minute. What protects you is what you did beforehand (heavy things fastened down, a practiced
reflex) and what you do in the first hour after. This page covers both.
{{#if is.earthquake_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for earthquakes in the region
data.** Do the "Do this now" list this month.{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for
earthquakes, but you may travel or move to a place that is not; the reflex below is worth knowing
everywhere.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is. A big city can rate 3 for a rare hazard because so much is exposed (Cook County, Illinois, rates 3 for earthquakes), and a thinly settled county can rate 1 for a hazard that does strike it (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Drop, Cover, and Hold On.** Drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck (under a
>   sturdy table if one is close), and hold on until the shaking stops (Ready.gov, Earthquakes).
> - **If you are inside, stay inside.** Do not run outside, and do not stand in a doorway.
> - **After the shaking:** smell gas, leave and shut it off; expect aftershocks; near the coast,
>   **go to high ground at once** without waiting for an official warning (NWS, During a Tsunami;
>   → 17-15).
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** After an earthquake people lose power and cook and heat improvised; carbon monoxide
>   follows (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On** with everyone, including children, until it is a reflex
   (→ 24-02).
2. **Fasten heavy things:** bookcases, tall dressers, refrigerators and **the water heater** to the
   wall studs. **Move heavy and breakable things to low shelves** (Ready.gov).
3. **Know where the gas, water and electric shutoffs are** and keep the gas wrench at the meter
   (→ 16-12).
4. **Keep shoes and a flashlight by every bed.** After a night quake the floor is broken glass.
5. **Pick an out-of-area contact** everyone calls or texts; local lines jam after a quake (→ 15-03).

{{photo water-heater-strap}}

## Warning and alerts

- **Earthquakes cannot be predicted.** There is no watch.
- **On the West Coast, the USGS ShakeAlert system** can send a phone alert seconds before shaking
  reaches you (USGS, Early Warning). A few seconds is enough to Drop, Cover, and Hold On. If an
  alert sounds, do it at once; do not look outside first.
- **Aftershocks** follow the main shock, sometimes for days or longer. Each one is a reason to Drop,
  Cover, and Hold On again.

## During the shaking

{{figure fig-drop-cover-hold-on}}

| Where you are | What to do (Ready.gov, Earthquakes) |
|---|---|
| **Indoors** | Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Under a sturdy table or desk if one is near; otherwise against an inside wall, away from windows. Stay inside |
| **In bed** | Turn face down and cover your head and neck with a pillow. Stay there |
| **In a wheelchair or with a walker** | Lock the wheels. Bend over, cover your head and neck with your arms, a book or a pillow, and hold on. Get as low as you safely can |
| **Outdoors** | Move to an open area away from buildings, trees, streetlights and power lines. Drop, Cover, and Hold On |
| **Driving** | Pull over, stop and set the parking brake. Stay in the vehicle, away from bridges, overpasses and power lines if you can |
| **Near the coast** | Protect yourself from the shaking first. When it stops, go inland or to high ground at once (→ 17-15) |

**By dwelling:**
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** stay inside and Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Do not use elevators
  or crowd into stairwells during shaking. Upper floors sway more; it is frightening but usually
  not the danger. Falling objects and glass are.{{/if}}
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home:** it can be shaken off its supports. Drop,
  Cover, and Hold On inside; after the shaking, check whether it has shifted before using gas or
  electricity, and leave if it has. Ask a professional about earthquake bracing.{{/if}}
{{#if has.basement}}- **Basement:** no safer than the floor above during shaking; the stairs can
  fail. Drop, Cover, and Hold On where you are.{{/if}}
- **Any building:** the danger is falling objects, breaking glass and heavy furniture. That is why
  fastening things down beforehand matters more than where you stand.

## The first hour after

1. **Check yourself, then others, for injuries** (→ 12-02, → 12-09). Shoes on before you walk.
2. **Gas:** if you smell gas or hear hissing, **get everyone out and shut it off at the meter**
   (→ 16-12). Do not use matches, lighters or switches. Do not turn the gas back on yourself while
   a utility exists; if none will come, relighting yourself is a decision card:
   {{choice DC-28}} → 30-29.
3. **Fire:** small fires are common after earthquakes. Put them out if you safely can (→ 29-12).
4. **Damaged buildings:** leave if there are large cracks, a shifted foundation, or a leaning
   chimney, and do not go back in until it has been checked.
5. **Downed power lines:** keep everyone far away.
6. **Near the coast:** go to high ground now (→ 17-15).
7. **Text, do not call,** your out-of-area contact (→ 15-03).
8. **Check on neighbours** (→ 18-01). After a large earthquake, neighbours are the first rescue.

{{photo gas-meter-quake}}

## The days after

- **Water:** pipes break. Shut the main valve if lines are broken so clean water in the house does
  not drain away. **The water heater tank is a water reserve** (→ 03-02). Treat town water as
  unsafe until told otherwise.
- **Toilets:** do not flush until you know the sewer line is intact; use a bucket toilet (→ 13-01).
- **Chimneys and stoves:** earthquakes crack chimneys and flue liners, which can set the house on
  fire or leak carbon monoxide. Using one before it is checked is a decision card:
  {{choice DC-21}} → 30-22
- **Power:** expect outages (→ 17-08).
- **Landslides:** earthquakes loosen slopes; stay clear of steep ground and cuts (→ 17-17).
- **Aftershocks:** sleep with shoes and a light by the bed; keep heavy things off shelves above
  beds.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Furniture straps, water heater strap kit** | Falling furniture and broken gas lines | Fixed to studs |
| Shoes and a flashlight by every bed | Night quake, broken glass | |
| **Gas shutoff wrench at the meter** | Gas leaks start fires | → 16-12 |
| Stored water | Pipes break | → 03-02 |
| First-aid kit | Cuts and fractures | → 12-08 |
| Fire extinguisher | Fires after the shaking | → 29-12 |
| Work gloves, pry bar | Debris | |
| Go-bag and document kit | You may have to leave a damaged home | → 22-03, → 19-01 |
| Battery radio | News when power and phones fail | → 15-01 |

**If you do not have it:** a sturdy table is your cover; a pillow covers your head in bed; rope or
strapping and screws into studs hold a bookcase; a bucket and bags make a toilet.

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here runs out quickly.** What expires is the practice. Drill once a year and whenever a
  child is old enough to learn it.
- **After a big earthquake,** services can be out for days to weeks across a whole region. Plan
  water, food and sanitation for that (→ 17-08).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** things fastened down, the reflex practiced, shutoffs known.
- **B (moving):** stop the vehicle away from bridges and overpasses; after a large quake expect
  roads cut by slides and broken bridges (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** check the building for heavy unreinforced chimneys and walls, and
  where the slopes above and below it would go (→ 17-17).
