pages.body:
# Hurricanes and tropical storms

**What this page is for.** A hurricane gives days of warning, which is its one gift. Most of the
deaths come from **water**: storm surge at the coast and flooding from rain far inland, and then
from carbon monoxide and accidents in the days after. This page covers the alert words, the
evacuation decision, sheltering, and the long, hot, powerless aftermath.
{{#if is.hurricane_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for hurricanes in the region data.**
Plan before each season.{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for hurricanes, but their rain and
tornadoes can reach hundreds of miles inland.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).
{{#if is.coastal}}**Your home county is on the coast: find your evacuation zone this week.**{{/if}}

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Run from the water; hide from the wind.** Storm surge is historically the leading cause of
>   hurricane deaths in the United States (Ready.gov, Hurricanes; NHC, Storm Surge Overview). **If
>   you live in an evacuation zone and officials tell you to leave, leave.**
> - **A mobile or manufactured home is not a shelter in a hurricane. Leave it for a sturdy
>   building or a public shelter before the storm arrives, whatever the category.**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Carbon monoxide kills many people after hurricanes (CPSC; → 30-01).
> - **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock
>   kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide")
>   cord.**
> - **Turn Around, Don't Drown:** 6 inches of moving water knocks an adult down; 12 inches carries
>   away most cars (NWS).

## Do this now

1. **Find your evacuation zone** on your county's map and write it here: ______. Know the route out
   and a place to go inland: ______________.
2. **Decide your leaving rule now:** {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20. Leaving early, before the roads
   jam, is almost always better.
3. **Plan for the house:** shutters or pre-cut, labelled plywood for windows; a list of what comes
   in from the yard.
4. **Stock for two weeks without power in heat**: water (→ 03-02), food, medicine, cooling
   (→ 17-04).
5. **Insurance while that system works:** wind and flood are often separate policies (→ 19-04).

{{photo evacuation-zone}}

## The words and the scale

**Watches and warnings** (NWS, Hurricane and Tropical Storm Watches and Warnings):

| Alert | Means | Issued about |
|---|---|---|
| **Tropical Storm Watch / Warning** | Sustained winds of 39 to 73 mph possible / expected | 48 / 36 hours ahead |
| **Hurricane Watch / Warning** | Sustained winds of 74 mph or more possible / expected | 48 / 36 hours before tropical-storm-force winds |
| **Storm Surge Watch / Warning** | Life-threatening flooding from sea water pushed inland possible / expected | 48 / 36 hours |
| **Extreme Wind Warning** | The extreme winds of a major hurricane (115 mph or more), usually the eyewall, are about to arrive | Within about an hour |

**A hurricane warning is the last good time to finish preparing.** Once tropical-storm winds
arrive, outside work becomes dangerous. On an Extreme Wind Warning, go at once to the interior
shelter spot as for a tornado (→ 17-06).

**The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale** (NHC) rates **wind only**:

| Category | Sustained wind |
|---|---|
| 1 | 74 to 95 mph |
| 2 | 96 to 110 mph |
| 3 (major) | 111 to 129 mph |
| 4 (major) | 130 to 156 mph |
| 5 (major) | 157 mph or more |

**The category says nothing about surge or rain.** A "weak" storm that moves slowly can flood
worse than a strong fast one.

## The hazards

- **Storm surge:** sea water pushed ashore by the storm, rising over hours and moving inland with
  waves on top. It drowns people in their homes. Your evacuation zone is drawn for it.
  {{figure fig-storm-surge}}
- **Inland flooding from rain:** can reach far from the coast, for days after landfall (→ 17-03).
- **Wind:** breaks windows, peels roofs, throws debris, drops trees and power lines.
- **Tornadoes:** spun off in the storm's bands, often with little warning (→ 17-02).
- **Rip currents and high surf**, even far from the storm.
- **The aftermath:** heat with no power, carbon monoxide, chainsaw and ladder injuries, downed
  lines, contaminated water.

## Leave or stay

- **Leave if you are told to, if you live in a surge zone, if you live in a mobile home, or if
  anyone in the house depends on power for medical equipment** (→ 01-07).
- **Leave early.** Evacuation routes clog. Fill the tank and go while it is light and roads move.
- **The goal is out of the water's reach and into a sturdy building.** That is often tens of miles
  inland, not hundreds; a shorter trip means less time stuck on jammed roads.
{{#if has.pets}}- **Pets go with you.** Find pet-friendly shelters or lodging now (→ 20-09).{{/if}}
- **If you stay**, you are deciding to be without help until the storm passes; emergency services
  stop answering in high winds.

## Sheltering at home (outside the surge zone)

- **An interior room on the lowest floor that will not flood**, away from windows: a closet,
  bathroom or hallway (Ready.gov).
{{#if has.shelter_room}}- **Your named room:** {{ dwelling.shelter_room }}.{{/if}}
{{#if has.basement}}- **Your basement** ({{ dwelling.basement }}) is good for wind but **can flood
  fast** in heavy rain or surge. Do not shelter below ground if flooding is possible; have a way
  up.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** wind is stronger on high floors. Shelter in an interior hallway
  or room on a lower floor that is above any flood or surge level; ask the building manager now
  where that is.{{/if}}
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home: do not stay. Leave for a sturdy building or
  public shelter before the storm.** Write where: ______________.{{/if}}
- **Do not go outside in the calm eye of the storm.** The other side of the eyewall arrives fast,
  with wind from the opposite direction.
- **Do not climb into a closed attic** to escape rising water; you can be trapped. Go to the
  highest floor and signal; go onto the roof only if you must (Ready.gov, Floods).

## Before the storm (at the watch)

- Shutters closed or plywood up; loose outdoor items inside or tied down.
- **Vehicles fuelled**; cash on hand (→ 19-02).
- Water stored; bathtub filled for washing and flushing (→ 03-02).
- Everything charged; refrigerator and freezer set colder; freeze containers of water.
- Medicines refilled; documents in waterproof bags (→ 19-01).
- Generator, if any, tested outdoors and fuel stored safely (→ 09-04).

## After the storm

- **Wait for the all-clear** before going out; flooding can still be rising.
- **Floodwater:** never drive or walk into it (→ 17-03).
- **Downed lines:** assume live.
- **Generators outdoors only, far from windows and doors** (→ 08-02, → 09-04).
- **Heat:** the days after a hurricane are often hot and humid with no power. Cool the body; check
  on elders (→ 17-04).
- **Food:** a closed refrigerator keeps food safe about 4 hours; a full freezer about 48 hours
  (FoodSafety.gov; → 04-17).
- **Water:** follow boil notices; disinfect a flooded well before use (→ 03-07).
- **Chainsaws, ladders and roofs** injure many people after storms. Work in pairs, rested, in
  daylight (→ 16-06).
- **Photograph damage** before cleanup (→ 19-04).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **County evacuation zone map; route out** | Surge is the killer | On this page |
| Shutters or pre-cut labelled plywood, screws, drill | Windows | Fit before the season |
| NOAA Weather Radio | Warnings when phones fail | → 15-01 |
| Two weeks of water, food, medicine | Long outage | → 03-02, → 04-02 |
| Cooling: battery fans, shade, wet cloths | Heat after the storm | → 17-04 |
| CO alarms, battery | Generators after storms | → 08-02 |
| Waterproof document bags | Water gets in | → 19-01 |
| Tarps, rope, nails or screws | Temporary roof and window repairs | → 16-12 |
| Life jackets in a surge or flood zone | If you are caught by water | |

**If you do not have it:** an interior closet with a mattress over you is a wind shelter; trash
bags and duct tape keep papers dry; a full bathtub is washing and flushing water.

## When it runs out

- **Power can be out for weeks after a major hurricane** (→ 17-08). Water, cooling and medicine are
  the clocks.
- **Fuel stations stop pumping** without power; fill before the storm.
- **Help comes from outside the area, slowly.** Plan to be on your own for at least the first days.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** outside the surge zone and in a sturdy building, sheltering can be right; inside
  it, leaving is right.
- **B (moving):** leave early, on the official route, toward the nearest safe inland place rather
  than the farthest (→ 01-03, → 17-11).
- **C (rural or new site):** do not choose a site in a surge zone or a flood plain; look at where
  water went in past storms.

pages.body:
# Wildfire smoke and fire evacuation

**What this page is for.** Wildfire reaches far more people as smoke than as flame: smoke from a
fire hundreds of miles away can make the air unhealthy for days or weeks. And when a fire is close,
leaving early is what saves lives. This page covers reading the air quality number, making one
clean room in the house, masks, and getting out when told. How fires behave and how to protect the
house is on → 17-05.
{{#if is.wildfire_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for wildfire in the region data.**{{else}}Your
home county is rated lower for wildfire, but smoke travels far; the smoke half of this page applies
almost everywhere.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY.**
> - **When officials say evacuate, go at once.** Fire can move faster than the warnings. Do not wait
>   to see the flames.
> - **Smoke harms children, older adults, pregnant women and anyone with heart or lung disease
>   first** (EPA, Reduce Your Smoke Exposure). Act for them at a lower air quality number.
> - **No respirator on a child under 2** (EPA). Their protection is clean indoor air and distance.
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window**, even to power an air cleaner (→ 30-01).

## Do this now

1. **Choose a clean room** (below) and work out how you will filter its air.
2. **Buy N95 respirators** in sizes that fit each adult and older child, and practice the fit.
3. **Pack go-bags and the document kit** and keep them by the door in fire season (→ 22-03,
   → 19-01).
4. **Know how your area announces evacuations** (phone alerts, sirens, door-to-door, radio) and
   your two routes out.
5. **Decide your leaving rule now:** {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20

## Reading the air: the Air Quality Index

The **Air Quality Index (AQI)** is a 0 to 500 scale for how polluted the air is. Smoke shows up as
"particle pollution". The EPA categories (AirNow, AQI Basics):

| AQI | Colour | Category | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 to 50 | Green | Good | Little or no risk |
| 51 to 100 | Yellow | Moderate | Acceptable; some risk for people unusually sensitive to air pollution |
| 101 to 150 | Orange | Unhealthy for sensitive groups | Sensitive groups (children, older adults, pregnant women, heart or lung disease) may have health effects; the general public less likely |
| 151 to 200 | Red | Unhealthy | Some of the general public may have health effects; sensitive groups more serious ones |
| 201 to 300 | Purple | Very unhealthy | Health alert: the risk of health effects is increased for everyone |
| 301 and up | Maroon | Hazardous | Health warning of emergency conditions: everyone is more likely to be affected |

**Alert words:** an **Air Quality Alert** means the air is or will be unhealthy; a **Dense Smoke
Advisory** means smoke is cutting visibility; a **Red Flag Warning** means fire weather (→ 17-05,
→ 29-10).

**With no AQI to read:** if you can see haze indoors, smell smoke, or cannot see landmarks you
normally can, treat the air as unhealthy. If eyes sting and people cough, it is worse.

## What to do when the air is smoky

- **Stay indoors, with windows and doors shut,** and limit hard work outside.
- **Make one clean room** and spend as much time in it as you can, especially at night (EPA, Create
  a Clean Room):
  1. **Pick a room** big enough for everyone, ideally with a bathroom, whose door you can keep
     shut.
  2. **Close its windows and doors**, as long as you can still get out quickly. If the room has an
     exhaust fan or range hood, use it only briefly: it can pull smoke in from elsewhere in the
     house.
  3. **Keep it cool.** If your heating, cooling or window unit has a fresh-air setting, turn it
     off, close the intake, or set it to recirculate.
  4. **Filter the air** with a portable air cleaner sized for the room, on its highest setting, of
     a type that makes no ozone. **If you have none, a box fan with a furnace filter taped to it**
     is a temporary substitute that EPA describes for when better options are not available.
  5. **Make no smoke inside:** no candles, incense, frying, broiling, smoking, aerosol sprays,
     fuel-burning stoves, or vacuuming without a HEPA filter. Dust with a damp cloth.
- **Central air or furnace fan:** set to recirculate, with the best filter the system accepts.
- **In a vehicle:** windows up, air on recirculate.

{{figure fig-box-fan-filter}}

{{photo clean-room}}

**Power for the clean room:** a portable air cleaner or box fan is a modest load a power station
can carry (→ 09-01). The generator stays outside, far from the house.

## Masks

- **A NIOSH-approved N95 or P100 respirator, well fitted,** significantly reduces the smoke you
  breathe. Choose one with two head straps, not ear loops. Do not rely on dust masks or bandanas
  (EPA, Protect Your Lungs From Wildfire Smoke and Ash; EPA, Reduce Your Smoke Exposure).
- **Fit is most of it:** no gaps at the nose and cheeks; a good seal is not possible with facial
  hair (EPA).
- **No respirator on a child under 2** (EPA). Respirators do not come in children's sizes; some
  older children can use an adult small one if it fits and they will keep it on. For them too,
  clean indoor air and distance come first.
- **Ask a doctor first** if you have heart or lung disease or are pregnant: a respirator makes
  breathing harder, and in heat it raises the risk of heat illness (EPA).
- A mask helps when you must be outside; it is not a reason to stay out longer.

## Who needs protecting first

{{#if has.condition.CL-07}}- **Asthma:** keep rescue medicine in reach and follow the asthma action
  plan; smoke is a common trigger (→ 02-07).{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-08}}- **COPD or oxygen:** smoke can turn a stable day into an emergency. Never
  have oxygen near a flame (→ 02-08).{{/if}}
{{#if has.condition.CL-09}}- **Heart disease:** smoke raises the risk of heart trouble; chest pain or
  unusual breathlessness is an emergency (→ 02-09).{{/if}}
{{#if has.young_child}}- **Young children** breathe more air for their size and spend time close to
  the floor and outside; they go into the clean room first.{{/if}}
{{#if has.elder}}- **Elders:** check on them twice a day in smoke.{{/if}}
{{#if has.pregnant}}- **Pregnancy:** limit exposure; clean room and fitted mask outside.{{/if}}
- **Anyone:** trouble breathing, chest pain, or confusion in smoke is an emergency. Get them to the
  cleanest air you can.

**If the clean room cannot keep the air clean**, going to a cleaner place (family, a public cleaner
air shelter, a town upwind) is the next step. Leave before people are struggling.

## Fire evacuation

**Many areas use three steps**: be **ready** (bags packed, plan made), **get set** (prepare to
leave now; leave already if you need extra time, have animals, or have someone who moves slowly),
and **go** (leave now). Names differ by place. Your area's words: ______________.

**When you get the order, go**, and do not return until officials say it is safe (Ready.gov,
Wildfires). Before you leave, if there is time:
- **Medicines and devices first**, then documents, bags, phones, chargers (→ 01-07, → 19-01).
- **People who move slowly leave first.** Children into car seats and pets into carriers take
  time; start them first (→ 20-09).
- **Close all windows and doors** so embers cannot blow in; move burnable furniture away from
  windows.
- **Back the vehicle in**, loaded, facing the way out, windows closed.
- **Leave lights on** so firefighters can see the house through smoke.
- **Do not go back** for anything.

**On the road:** drive with headlights on, windows up, air on recirculate. Never drive toward a
fire to get past it. If you are trapped by fire in a vehicle, the steps are on → 17-05.

## By dwelling type

{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home:** lets smoke in easily and catches fire
  readily. Go to cleaner air sooner, and leave on the first evacuation warning.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** a bedroom with the door shut makes a good clean room. Shared
  ventilation may bring smoke in from the halls; seal the gap under the door with a towel.{{/if}}
- **Any home:** the room with the fewest outside walls and windows is the easiest to keep clean.

## After the fire

- **Return only when officials say it is safe.** Hot spots smoulder for days.
- **Ash:** wear an N95 and gloves to clean; dampen ash before sweeping; keep children away from
  ash and burned areas.
- **Water:** a burned area's water system may be contaminated; follow local notices.
- **Burned slopes flood and slide** in the next rains, for years (→ 17-17).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **N95 respirators, right sizes** | Smoke outdoors | Fit-check now |
| Portable air cleaner (no ozone), or box fan plus furnace filters and tape | Clean room | → 09-01 for power |
| Towels or tape for door gaps | Keep smoke out | |
| Go-bags and document kit by the door in fire season | Minutes to leave | → 22-03 |
| NOAA Weather Radio; phone alerts on | Red flag warnings and evacuation orders | → 15-01 |
| Spare furnace filters | Smoke clogs them fast | |

**If you do not have it:** the smallest interior room with a towel under the door; a damp cloth
over the face is a poor last resort for an adult; leaving early is the best mask there is.

## When it runs out

- **Filters clog.** Smoke seasons can last weeks; keep spares and change them when dark.
- **Patience runs out.** Long smoke episodes wear people down; the clean room rules still apply on
  day ten.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** clean room ready, masks fitted, bags by the door in fire season.
- **B (moving):** smoke cuts visibility and closes roads; check the route and leave early
  (→ 17-11).
- **C (rural or new site):** check how a site would be evacuated: one road in through brush is a
  trap. Defensible space comes first (→ 17-05).

pages.body:
# Tsunamis

**What this page is for.** A tsunami is a series of ocean waves, usually caused by an undersea
earthquake, that floods the coast far beyond any normal tide. Near the earthquake that caused it,
the first wave can arrive in minutes, before any official warning. This page is about recognising
the natural warnings and getting to high ground fast.
{{#if is.tsunami_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for tsunamis in the region data. Learn
your route this week.**{{else}}{{#if is.coastal}}Your home county is on the coast; keep this page
even though the rating is lower.{{else}}Your home is not on the coast, but if you visit or move to
one, this page applies.{{/if}}{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Natural warnings: a strong or long earthquake; the ocean suddenly rising like a fast flood
>   or a wall of water, or draining away; a loud roar from the ocean.** Any one of these means go
>   now (NWS, During a Tsunami).
> - **Do not wait for an official warning.** As soon as you can move safely, **go to high ground or
>   as far inland as you can.**
> - **The first wave may not be the last or the largest.** Stay away until officials say it is
>   safe.

{{figure fig-tsunami-natural-warnings}}

## Do this now

1. **Find out whether home, work and school are in a tsunami hazard zone.** Coastal communities
   post maps and blue-and-white route signs. Write your zone status: ______.
2. **Learn the route to high ground on foot**, and walk it with everyone, timed (→ 24-02). Write it
   here: ______________. Have a second route.
3. **Agree a meeting place on high ground** and an out-of-area contact (→ 15-03).
4. **Keep a go-bag where you can grab it on the way out** (→ 22-03).
5. **Make sure your NOAA Weather Radio and phone alerts are on** (→ 15-01).

{{photo tsunami-route}}

## The alert words

| Alert | Meaning (NWS) | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **Tsunami Warning** | A dangerous tsunami is likely; widespread flooding possible | **Go to high ground or inland now** |
| **Tsunami Advisory** | Strong currents and dangerous waves are expected or happening | Stay out of the water and away from beaches and harbours |
| **Tsunami Watch** | A distant event may cause a tsunami | Stay informed and be ready to act |
| **Tsunami Information Statement** | An earthquake happened; no threat or a very distant one | No action unless that changes |

A **natural warning is as serious as an official one** (NWS). Near the source there may be no time
for an official one.

## During

- **If you feel an earthquake near the coast:** protect yourself first with **Drop, Cover, and Hold
  On** until the shaking stops (→ 17-12). **Then go**, without waiting.
- **Go to high ground or inland** by the route you practised. **On foot is often faster** than
  driving when everyone leaves at once and roads are cracked or jammed.
- **If you cannot reach high ground in time,** some communities name tall, strong buildings for
  vertical evacuation. Know whether yours does: ______________.
- **Stay away from rivers and streams** that lead to the ocean; tsunamis travel up them.
- **Get news** from the NOAA Weather Radio, local radio or phone alerts once you are safe.

**By dwelling:**
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home:** offers no protection from a tsunami. Leave
  for high ground on any natural or official warning.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** if you are in a hazard zone, plan to leave for high ground, not
  to go upstairs, unless your building is an officially named vertical evacuation building.{{/if}}
{{#if has.basement}}- **Basement:** never shelter below ground from a tsunami; it floods first.{{/if}}
- **Any building in the zone:** leave it for high ground.

## After

- **Stay out of the hazard zone until officials say it is safe.** Waves can keep arriving for hours.
- **Avoid damaged buildings, bridges and piers**, and keep away from downed power lines (NWS).
- **Floodwater rules apply:** it is dirty and it hides hazards (→ 17-03).
- **Expect aftershocks** if an earthquake caused it (→ 17-12).
- **Water and sewer:** treat water as unsafe until told otherwise (→ 03-04).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Go-bag by the door** | You leave in minutes | → 22-03 |
| Sturdy shoes by every bed | Night earthquake, debris | |
| NOAA Weather Radio | Official warnings | → 15-01 |
| Written route and meeting place | Phones may fail | On this page |
| Headlamp | Night evacuation | |

**If you do not have it:** nothing replaces knowing the route. Walk it.

## When it runs out

- **The practice fades.** Walk the route each year and when anyone new joins the household.
- **After a major tsunami,** the coast may be without water, power and roads for a long time; plan
  for it as for a hurricane (→ 17-13, → 17-08).

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** route known and walked; go-bag ready.
- **B (moving):** on any coast road, a strong earthquake means turn inland at once.
- **C (rural or new site):** do not choose a site in a mapped tsunami zone; if you must, know the
  high ground within a walk (→ 01-05).

pages.body:
# Volcanic ashfall

**What this page is for.** An eruption can drop ash over a huge area, hundreds of miles downwind.
Volcanic ash is not soft like wood ash: it is tiny, sharp bits of rock and glass. It hurts lungs and
eyes, wrecks engines and electronics, fouls water, and is heavy enough when wet to break roofs.
Closer to a volcano there are other dangers, below. This page is about living through ashfall.
{{#if is.volcano_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for volcanic hazard in the region
data.**{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for volcanic hazard; ash travels far, so keep this
page if you live downwind of the western volcanoes or travel near them.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **CAUTION.**
> - **Stay indoors during ashfall** with windows, doors and vents closed, until officials say it
>   is safe to go out (Ready.gov, Volcanoes).
> - **Outside, wear a well-fitting N95 respirator**; a dust or cloth mask only as a last resort
>   (Ready.gov).
> - **Avoid driving in heavy ash.** It cuts visibility, makes roads slick, and clogs engines.
> - **Do not get on your roof to remove ash** (Ready.gov, Volcanoes). Wet ash is heavy and roofs
>   are slippery.
> - **Near a volcano, valleys and river channels are where mudflows (lahars) run.** Get to high
>   ground out of the valley if one is reported.

## Do this now

1. **Know whether you live near a volcano or downwind of one**, and whether your valley is a lahar
   path. Local emergency plans and the USGS volcano observatories map both.
2. **Keep N95 respirators** for every adult and older child, and **glasses** for anyone who wears
   contact lenses (ash under a lens scratches the eye).
3. **Plan to cover stored water and disconnect rain barrels** from downspouts when ash is forecast
   (→ 03-05).
4. **Keep spare air filters** for the vehicle and the furnace.

## Alerts

- **Ashfall Advisory** and **Ashfall Warning** from the NWS: ash is expected to fall where you are
  (→ 29-10).
- **USGS volcano observatories** issue alert levels for each volcano, from normal through advisory
  and watch to warning. A warning means a hazardous eruption is happening or about to.
- **Evacuation orders** come from local officials, mostly for areas near the volcano and in lahar
  paths. **If told to leave, leave** (Ready.gov).

## During ashfall

- **Stay inside.** Close windows, doors and fireplace dampers; cover vents and seal gaps
  (Ready.gov). Set heating or cooling to recirculate, or turn it off.
- **Make one clean room** as for wildfire smoke (→ 17-14): a closed room, filtered air, no
  indoor dust-raising.
- **Protect electronics and machinery:** cover them; wet ash conducts electricity and can short
  equipment and power lines. Expect outages (→ 17-08).
- **Bring pets and livestock in** or under cover; give them clean water.
- **If you must go out:** N95, goggles or glasses, long sleeves. Change and leave dusty clothes at
  the door.
- **Driving:** avoid driving in heavy ash. If you must, keep the windows up and do not use the air
  conditioning (Ready.gov); go slowly with headlights on. Ash stirred up by traffic stalls
  engines.

{{#if has.mobile_home}}**Mobile or manufactured home:** many have low-pitched roofs with long spans,
the shape most at risk from ash load. Keep gutters clear and plan where you would go if ash builds
up and rain is forecast.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}**Apartment:** shared ventilation can bring ash in; seal your door gaps and
make the clean room inside your unit.{{/if}}

## Roofs: the ash load

- **Roof collapse from ash is rare** and usually needs very thick ash, typically more than about 4
  inches (100 mm) (USGS, Roof Loading).
- **Rain makes it much worse.** Wet ash is up to twice as dense as dry ash, so the load is up to
  twice as heavy (USGS).
- **Long-span, low-pitched roofs that were not engineered** (carports, barns, wide spans) are the
  most at risk, possibly at about 4 inches or less (USGS).
- **Gutters fill with ash,** stop draining and add weight. Clear them.
- **Clearing:** Ready.gov's advice is not to get on the roof. Where you can reach, work from the
  ground with long-handled tools. Damp the ash lightly to keep dust down, but **do not soak it**:
  water adds weight.

## After

- **Clean up with masks on.** Lightly dampen ash before sweeping or shovelling; dry sweeping raises
  thick dust. Bag it; do not wash it into drains, where it sets and blocks them.
- **Water:** ash in an open water source can make it cloudy, acidic or salty-tasting. Use stored
  water (→ 03-02); treat any other source (→ 03-04). Clean rain-barrel systems before reconnecting.
- **Gardens:** wash produce well; light ash can be dug into soil.
- **Vehicles:** change air and oil filters often; wash ash off before it scratches paint and glass.
- **People with asthma or lung disease** stay in clean air and keep rescue medicine close
  (→ 02-07, → 02-08).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **N95 respirators** | Ash in the lungs | Fit-checked |
| Goggles; glasses for contact-lens wearers | Ash in the eyes | |
| Tape and plastic sheeting | Seal vents and cover equipment | |
| Spare vehicle and furnace filters | Ash clogs them | |
| Long-handled push brooms and shovels | Clear ash from the ground | |
| Covers for stored water | Keep ash out | → 03-02 |
| Stored water | Sources may be fouled | |

**If you do not have it:** a damp cloth over nose and mouth is a poor last resort; wet towels along
door gaps; plastic bags over electronics.

## When it runs out

- **Filters and masks run out first** in a long ash event. Stock more than seems needed.
- **Ash keeps coming back** with every wind and every passing car for weeks; clean up in steps.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** stay in, seal up, protect water and equipment.
- **B (moving):** avoid driving through heavy ash; never drive into a valley where a lahar is
  reported (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** check whether a site sits in a lahar path or a common ash plume
  direction from a nearby volcano (→ 01-05).

review_pass.notes: NRI note; Ready.gov and USGS warning signs verified.

pages.body:
# Landslides and debris flows

**What this page is for.** A **landslide** is a mass of earth or rock moving down a slope. A
**debris flow** (often called a mudslide) is a fast, wet landslide: mud, rocks and trees moving like
wet concrete, fast enough to outrun people and to destroy houses. Most are set off by heavy rain,
snowmelt or earthquakes, and **ground burned by wildfire** produces them in ordinary rain. This
page covers the warning signs and what to do before, during and after.
{{#if is.landslide_region}}**Your home county is rated 2 or 3 for landslides in the region
data.**{{else}}Your home county is rated lower for landslides, but any steep slope, road cut or
burned hillside can slide.{{/if}}
Ratings in this binder are FEMA's National Risk Index for your county, on a 1-to-3 scale: they measure expected harm to people and property there, not how likely the hazard is (→ 29-10).

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Stay alert and awake during a storm that could cause a landslide** (Ready.gov). Many debris
>   flow deaths happen to people asleep at night.
> - **Leave if you are told to, or if you feel unsafe staying** (Ready.gov).
> - **If you are caught in the path, move uphill and out of the path as fast as you can.**
> - **Never cross a flowing road or bridge when a flow is coming** (Ready.gov).

## Do this now

1. **Look at the slopes above and below your home** and where water runs (USGS, Landslide
   Preparedness). Do gutters, the driveway or a neighbour's drain send water onto a slope? That
   soaks the ground.
2. **Check your state geological survey or county for landslide maps.** Remember that maps of
   where slides start often do not show how far they run out onto flat ground below (USGS).
3. **Keep plants on slopes** (roots hold soil) and **never dump yard waste or fill on a slope**
   (USGS).
4. **Sign up for local warnings**, and keep a go-bag ready (→ 22-03).
5. **If you see warning signs on your property,** a geologist or engineer with landslide experience
   can assess it while that is possible (USGS).

{{photo slope-check}}

## Warning signs

**Fast-moving flows** (Ready.gov):
- **Rushing water, mud, or unusual sounds**; trees cracking or boulders knocking together upslope.
- A creek suddenly turning muddy, or its flow dropping while rain keeps falling (debris may be
  damming it upstream).

**Slow-moving slides** (Ready.gov; USGS):
- **Doors or windows sticking or jamming for the first time.**
- **New cracks in plaster, tile, brick or foundations.**
- **Bulging ground at the base of a slope.**
- Fences, poles, trees or walls tilting; outside stairs or decks pulling away from the house;
  widening cracks in the ground or pavement; broken water or sewer lines.

{{figure fig-landslide-warning-signs}}

## When they happen

- **During and after intense rain**, especially after a wet period, and during fast snowmelt.
- **On ground burned by wildfire:** the burned soil sheds water like pavement, and even short,
  intense rain can send debris flows down the channels below. This danger lasts for years after a
  fire (→ 17-14). The NWS issues flash flood warnings for burn scars; treat them as debris flow
  warnings.
- **After earthquakes**, which loosen slopes (→ 17-12).
- **Along road cuts, stream banks and coastal bluffs.**

Alert words: **Flash Flood Watch/Warning** and local debris flow warnings cover most of these
(→ 29-10).

## During

- **Stay awake and listening** when heavy rain falls on steep or burned ground.
- **Follow evacuation instructions.** When you would leave on your own is a household decision:
  {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20
- **If you hear or see a flow coming, move uphill and to the side, out of its channel.** Do not run
  downhill or down the channel.
- **Do not cross a flowing road, bridge or creek** in its path.
- **If you cannot get out of the way,** get to the upper floor of a sturdy building on the side away
  from the slope, or curl into a tight ball and protect your head.

**By dwelling:**
{{#if has.basement}}- **Basement:** do not shelter below ground on the uphill side; debris can push
  through walls and fill it.{{/if}}
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Mobile or manufactured home:** offers little resistance to a flow; leave
  early when warnings are out.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** an upper floor on the side away from the slope is safer than the
  ground floor facing it.{{/if}}
- **Any home at the foot of a slope or in a canyon mouth:** these are the debris flow paths. Leave
  before the storm, not during it.

## After

- **Stay away from the slide area.** More slides can follow (Ready.gov).
- **Watch for flooding,** which often comes with or after a slide.
- **Report broken utility lines and damaged roads** where anyone can still act on it (Ready.gov).
- **Have the building checked** before going back in. Look for cracks, tilt and broken lines.
- **Replant bare ground** as soon as you can (Ready.gov).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NOAA Weather Radio; phone alerts on | Flash flood and debris flow warnings | → 15-01 |
| Go-bag by the door in storm season | You leave fast, often at night | → 22-03 |
| Headlamps | Night evacuation | |
| A written uphill route | You will not think clearly in the dark | |

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here is consumed;** what matters is noticing slow changes. Walk the property after big
  storms and once a year, and note new cracks and sticking doors.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** know your slope and your route uphill; stay awake in big storms on steep or
  burned ground.
- **B (moving):** mountain and canyon roads close with slides; never drive into a flowing channel
  (→ 01-03).
- **C (rural or new site):** do not choose a site at a canyon mouth, at the foot of a steep slope,
  or below a recent burn (→ 01-05).

pages.body:
# Hail and damaging wind

**What this page is for.** Thunderstorm wind damages more than tornadoes do: severe thunderstorm
winds make up about half of all severe weather reports in the lower 48 states (NSSL, Damaging
Winds). Hail breaks windows, panels, roofs, gardens and sometimes people. This page covers both,
plus strong wind without a storm (high wind and dust). Tornadoes are on → 17-02.
{{#if is.tornado_region}}Your home county's tornado rating is 2 or 3. That rating is FEMA's
National Risk Index: expected harm to people and property, not how often storms come (→ 29-10).
Hail and damaging wind come from the same severe thunderstorms as tornadoes.{{/if}}

> **CAUTION.**
> - **Treat a severe thunderstorm warning tagged "destructive" like a tornado warning**: wind of
>   80 mph or more or hail of 2.75 inches or more (NWS, 2021). Go to the shelter spot (→ 17-06).
> - **Mobile and manufactured homes are the most dangerous place to be in damaging wind; even
>   anchored ones can be badly damaged when gusts pass 80 mph** (NSSL). **Leave for a sturdy
>   building before the storm arrives.**
> - **Get inside when hail starts and stay away from windows.** Large hail can injure and kill.

## Do this now

1. **Make sure your weather radio sounds for severe thunderstorm warnings** (→ 15-01).
2. **Decide what comes inside or under cover when a warning is issued:** portable solar panels,
   vehicles, outdoor gear, animals. Write the list: ______________.
3. **Trim dead branches** over the house, vehicles and power lines.
4. **Know where to put the vehicles** when hail threatens (garage, carport, a covered public
   place).

## The words and the numbers

- **Severe thunderstorm:** hail of **1 inch (quarter size)** or more, or wind of **58 mph** or more.
- The NWS adds a **damage threat** tag to the warning: **"considerable"** for hail of 1.75 inches
  (golf ball) or more or wind of 70 mph or more; **"destructive"** for hail of 2.75 inches (baseball)
  or more or wind of 80 mph or more. **Only "destructive" sets off a Wireless Emergency Alert on
  phones** (NWS, 2021).
- **High Wind Warning** or **Wind Advisory:** strong wind without a thunderstorm.
- **Dust Storm Warning:** blowing dust cutting visibility to near zero.
More alert words: → 29-10.

## Hail

{{figure fig-hail-sizes}}

- **How fast it falls** (NSSL, rough estimates): hail under 1 inch about 9 to 25 mph; 1 to 1.75
  inches about 25 to 40 mph; 2 to 4 inches about 44 to 72 mph; over 4 inches possibly more than
  100 mph.
- **What it breaks:** windows, skylights, siding, roofs, vehicles, solar panels, greenhouses,
  gardens, and it can kill livestock and people caught outside (NSSL).
- **Wind-driven hail** comes in sideways, through windows and into houses.
- **On the road:** hail deep enough on the pavement drives like ice (NSSL).

**What to do:**
- **Get inside a sturdy building** and away from windows and skylights. Close curtains or blinds to
  catch glass.
- **In a vehicle:** pull off the road if you can do it safely, but **not under an overpass**, where
  stopped cars cause crashes and block the road (SPC). Stay inside, away from the windows, and cover
  your head; lie down with your back to the windows if the glass may break.
- **Outdoors with no shelter:** crouch low and protect your head with your arms or anything you
  have.
- **Solar panels:** portable panels come inside or under hard cover at the warning; it takes
  minutes and a panel may be irreplaceable (→ 09-02). A fixed ground array can sometimes be tilted
  steep or covered.
- **Garden:** row cover and shade cloth give partial protection; a hailstorm can wreck a season's
  crop in minutes (→ 05-01).
- **Animals:** livestock and poultry need shelter (→ 05-04).

## Damaging wind

- **Damaging winds are those above about 50 to 60 mph** and can reach about 100 mph; one storm's
  damage path can run for hundreds of miles (NSSL).
- Most thunderstorm wind damage is **straight-line wind** from the storm's downdraft, not tornadoes.
  A small, intense burst of it is a **downburst**; a long, wide windstorm is a **derecho** (→ 17-02).
- **What it does:** brings down trees and power lines across whole regions at once, rolls mobile
  homes, tears roofs, flips vehicles and trailers, and turns loose objects into missiles.

**What to do when a warning is issued:**
- **Go inside a sturdy building, to an interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows** (the
  tornado spot, → 17-06).
{{#if has.mobile_home}}- **Your mobile or manufactured home: leave for a sturdy building before the
  storm arrives.** Where: ______________.{{/if}}
{{#if has.apartment}}- **Apartment:** a lower-floor interior hallway or bathroom, away from windows
  and glass doors.{{/if}}
{{#if has.basement}}- **Basement:** the best place in the house for damaging wind.{{/if}}
- **Bring in or tie down** anything loose outside.
- **Do not drive** into the storm; high-sided vehicles and trailers blow over (→ 17-11).

**Afterward:**
- **Treat every downed line as live.** Keep everyone, children and pets far away.
- **Tree work after storms injures many people.** Bent trees and trapped limbs spring back. Work in
  daylight, rested, with a partner, and leave anything near power lines alone (→ 16-06).
- **Expect a long, wide outage** after a derecho (→ 17-08).
- **Photograph damage** for insurance while that works (→ 19-04).

## High wind and dust without a storm

- **High wind:** secure loose items; avoid wooded areas; take care with high-sided vehicles and
  trailers.
- **Dust storm while driving** (NWS, Dust Storms and Haboobs): if visibility drops, **pull off the road as
  far as you safely can, turn off all lights, set the parking brake, and keep your foot off the
  brake pedal**, so drivers behind do not follow your lights and hit you. Stay buckled and wait it
  out.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NOAA Weather Radio | Severe thunderstorm warnings | → 15-01 |
| Tarps, rope, plywood, screws | Temporary roof and window repairs | → 16-12 |
| Row cover and shade cloth | Partial hail protection for the garden | |
| Moving blankets | Cover a vehicle or panels in a hurry | |
| Work gloves, eye protection | Cleanup | |

**If you do not have it:** blankets, cardboard or a mattress over things that must stay outside;
the car under any solid roof that is not an overpass.

## Phase notes

- **A (at home):** warning list of what comes inside; dead branches trimmed.
- **B (moving):** do not drive into a severe thunderstorm; a trailer or tall vehicle is at
  particular risk in high wind (→ 17-11).
- **C (rural or new site):** windbreaks of trees, and a sturdy building for the animals.

# Community, barter and governance

**What this section holds.** 8 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 18-01 **Neighbors and mutual aid**: Building the network of people near you who will help, and whom you will help, before anything goes wrong.
- → 18-02 **Barter and trade goods**: What to stock for trading, how to trade without putting your household at risk, what never to trade, and the food and medicine traps in trading.

- → 18-04 **Group organization and decisions**: What to do when cooperation goes beyond neighbors helping neighbors: shared work, shared resources, or households moving in together.

- → 18-07 **Teaching and preserving knowledge**: Keeping what your household knows alive when screens fail, and passing it on.

pages.body:
# Neighbors and mutual aid

**What this page is for.** Building the network of people near you who will help, and whom you will
help, before anything goes wrong. The most under-invested resource in most emergency plans is the
people who live within a hundred yards. No one household can cover medical skill, security,
childcare, repairs and round-the-clock work. **A neighborhood can.**

> **CAUTION. Connection and discretion pull against each other.** The CDC names **social connection
> as a protective factor and social isolation as a risk factor** for both mental and physical health
> (CDC, About Social Connection). In nearly every hard scenario in this binder (a medical emergency
> with no hospital, a tornado, a fire, an illness that takes down every adult, a broken leg), the
> neighbors are the only help that exists. But being known to have supplies has costs (→ 14-03).
> This page is about holding both: **being connected without being careless.**

## Do this now

1. **Learn your neighbors' names**: both sides and across the street. It is free, takes a few
   weeks of ordinary friendliness, and is the highest-return preparedness step there is.
2. **Find out who has which skills:** nurses, paramedics, electricians, plumbers, mechanics,
   vets, radio operators (→ 15-05), gardeners, people with tools or a generator.
3. **Find out who is vulnerable:** elderly, living alone, dependent on medical equipment, with
   small children. Knowing now is what makes checking on them possible later.
{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}4. **Tell close neighbors about the serious allergies in your household**
   (→ 02-03, → 02-04). A kind neighbor handing a child a cookie is a real risk, and the conversation
   is easy now. Allergies to share: {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}); {{/each}}
{{else}}4. **Tell close neighbors about any serious allergy or medical need** in your household, so
   they do not feed or treat someone wrongly (→ 02-03, → 02-04).
{{/if}}5. **Do something small and neighborly this month:** lend a tool, share produce, clear a walk.
   Reciprocity is built in ordinary time, not in a crisis.

## What your household brings and what it needs

Every household both supplies something and lacks something. Write both down honestly; it decides
how you approach the people around you.

**Skills in your household** (from your profile):
{{#each members as m}}- {{m.label}}: {{m.skills}}
{{else}}- (none entered: fill in on paper) ______________________
{{/each}}

**What a neighborhood typically needs, and who might cover it:**

| Need | Who covers it | Ours? / Who nearby? |
|---|---|---|
| Medical and first aid (→ 12-16) | Nurse, paramedic, doctor, anyone trained | ________ |
| Dental first aid (→ 18-08) | Anyone trained; a dental worker if there is one | ________ |
| Mechanical and small engines | Mechanic: generators, vehicles, pumps | ________ |
| Electrical (→ 09-08) | Electrician: generator hookups, solar, wiring | ________ |
| Welding and fabrication | Welder | ________ |
| Animals and farm skills | Farmer, rancher, vet | ________ |
| Every adult sick at once (→ 13-11) | Someone to bring water and check in | ________ |
| An injured adult (→ 12-09) | Hands for wood, water, children | ________ |
| Watch hours (→ 14-01) | More eyes, more hours | ________ |
| Equipment | Generator, chainsaw, tractor, well, truck | ________ |
| Childcare relief | An hour without children is worth a great deal (→ 21-05) | ________ |
| Company and morale (→ 21-02) | Protective, per CDC | ________ |
| Local information (→ 15-04) | First-hand, current | ________ |

**If your household holds a rare skill** (medical, dental, mechanical, electrical), you do not
approach mutual aid as someone asking for help: lead with what you can do, trade skill for skill,
and expect to be wanted. The flip side is that being valuable also means being known (→ 14-03).
**If your household holds no rare skill**, you are in the same position as most households: offer
labor, reliability and the skills you can learn quickly (→ 18-03).

## How mutual aid actually forms

It is not organized in a crisis; **it is revealed in a crisis, from relationships that already
existed.**
- **Ordinary reciprocity now.** Lend, borrow, share, help. Small exchanges build the trust larger
  ones need.
- **Be useful and known for it.** The household that fixes things (→ 16-05), knows first aid
  (→ 12-01) or has a working radio (→ 15-05) is the one people want in their network.
- **Start with the nearest neighbors** and widen out. Depth beats breadth.
- **Use what already exists:** a congregation, a block, a school community, extended family. Far
  easier to activate than something built from scratch.
- **Skills and time are the easiest things to offer** (→ 18-03), and they do not use up supplies.

## Connection and discretion

Both of these are true, and they pull against each other (→ 14-03):
- **Being known and connected makes you safer** in almost every scenario in this binder.
- **Being known to have supplies can make you a target** in a truly broken-down situation.

**How to hold both:**
- **Be known as a person, not as a stockpile.** Neighbors should know you are capable, friendly
  and helpful. They do not need an inventory.
- **Trade skills and labor before goods** (→ 18-03).
- **Be discreet about quantities, not about willingness.** "We can help" is different from "we have
  six months of food".
- **Help visibly with small things and privately with large ones.**
- **Get to know people over time** (→ 18-05) rather than deciding all at once.
- **In an ordinary disaster (a blizzard, an outage, a storm) the balance strongly favors openness
  and helping.** In a long breakdown it shifts, and → 14-03 covers that judgment. Do not bring
  breakdown-level suspicion to a three-day ice storm; that is how households cut themselves off from
  the help they will need.

## What to offer, in order of cost to you

1. **Presence and attention.** Checking on someone costs nothing.
2. **Information** (→ 15-04).
3. **Skills and labor** (→ 18-03). The best trade good there is; it does not run out.
4. **Tools, lent.** Usually returned, and it builds trust.
5. **Small consumables:** a meal, some coffee, a battery.
6. **Real supplies:** considered, and against a real need.

**Give what does not deplete you generously; be careful with what does.** That is sustainable, and
sustainable generosity is what builds a network.

## Organizing a block

If things go long, some coordination will emerge. What helps:
- **A list of who lives where**, who is vulnerable and who has skills (the roster below).
- **A check-in system:** a signal in a window (→ 15-07), an agreed time, someone knocking on the
  elderly neighbor's door.
- **A shared radio channel** (→ 15-02).
- **Shared watch** if it comes to that (→ 14-01): more eyes, fewer sleepless nights.
- **Shared work:** snow clearing, wood cutting, water hauling. Some jobs are far easier with four
  people.
- **Shared equipment:** one working generator, chainsaw or well can serve several households.
- **Skills exchange and teaching** (→ 18-03, → 18-07).
- **A way to make decisions and settle disputes**, agreed before you need it (→ 18-04, → 18-06).

## The neighbor roster

Fill it in over ordinary weeks, in pencil, and update it at the annual review (→ 25-10). **Risks**
means things worth knowing to help (medical needs, alone, an aggressive dog, visible desperation),
noted to help, not to judge. **This roster is private: it stays in the binder** (→ 14-03).

**Already in your contacts:**
{{#each local_contacts as c}}- {{c.name}} ({{c.relationship}}), {{c.phone}}.{{#if c.notes}} {{c.notes}}{{/if}}
{{else}}- none entered
{{/each}}
**Your meeting place near home:** {{ contacts.meet.near_home }}. The household there should be the
first fully filled row: if your plan sends people to their door, you should know their skills, their
household and their needs better than anyone's (→ 00-04, → 15-03).

```
Relationship: S = stranger  N = nodding  F = friendly  T = trusted
(the ladder on 18-05)

House / dir.  Name(s)          Adults+kids  Skills       Resources    Risks        Rel  Last contact
------------  ---------------  -----------  -----------  -----------  -----------  ---  ------------
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
____________  _______________  ___+___      ___________  ___________  ___________  ___  __________
```

## The hard cases

- **People who take and never give.** Common enough to plan for. Set limits early and kindly; the
  alternative is resentment that poisons everything.
- **People in desperate need whom you cannot fully help.** A hard problem with no clean answer
  (→ 12-16, → 18-06). Small, bounded help is usually possible and worth doing.
- **People you do not trust** (→ 18-05). Distance without hostility is usually right.
- **The neighbor who becomes a burden.** Bounded, specific help is sustainable; open-ended help is
  not.
- **Being the household that has, among households that do not.** This is why "known as capable, not
  as stocked" matters, and it is an argument for helping early: a neighborhood that got through the
  first weeks together behaves very differently from one that did not.

## The medical side

- **Find out who nearby has medical training.** A nurse or paramedic is help, relief and a second
  opinion (→ 12-16).
- **Anyone who might feed your children must know their allergies** (→ 02-04). Food from others is
  also a household choice: {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19).
- **Another household managing the same condition** (for example, insulin-dependent diabetes) is a
  partner for sharing knowledge and sourcing.
- **If every adult is down** (→ 13-11), a neighbor bringing water and checking on the children is
  the whole plan.
- **Distress is common.** If a neighbor, or you, are struggling, the Disaster Distress Helpline
  (call or text 1-800-985-5990, SAMHSA) works while phones do (→ 21-02).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **The neighbor roster, filled in** | The core of this page | Pencil; update yearly |
| A list of who is vulnerable nearby | Makes checking possible | |
| Allergy and medical information shared with close neighbors | Concrete safety | |
| Things worth lending: tools, a generator, a chainsaw | Reciprocity is built by lending | |
| Small surplus to give: fasteners, seeds, soap, matches | Cheap, useful, low-risk to share | → 18-02 |
| Radios on an agreed channel | Neighborhood coordination | → 15-02 |
| Skills: first aid, repair, radio | What makes you worth knowing | |
| An agreed "we need help" signal | Agreed with near neighbors | → 15-07 |

**Everything on this page is free:** names, conversations, attention, small acts. **What you cannot
substitute is the relationships themselves, and they take time.** That is why this is a "do it now"
page: one of the few things in this binder that cannot be acquired quickly.

## When it runs out

- **Relationships do not deplete; they compound.** But they decay without upkeep, and they cannot be
  built in a crisis.
- **The common failure:** a household that prepared thoroughly, told nobody, knows nobody, and finds
  that what it cannot do alone is what matters most.
- **Be generous with what does not deplete** (skills, time, information, attention) and careful with
  what does.
- **For any move** (→ 01-05): the people already at a destination matter as much as the land. A place
  with good neighbors is worth more than a better place with none.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** the best chance you will have: neighbors close, low stakes. Do it this year. In a
  blizzard or an outage, this network is what works.
- **B, on the move:** you leave your network behind, a real cost of moving. On the road, other people
  are both the main resource and the main risk (→ 18-05, → 14-01). Most people in a disaster help
  rather than harm.
- **C, settled:** fewer neighbors, farther apart, mattering more. Rural communities often have strong
  traditions of mutual aid and welcome people who contribute. Make relationships an early priority
  (→ 01-04).

pages.body:
# Barter and trade goods

**What this page is for.** What to stock for trading, how to trade without putting your household at
risk, what never to trade, and the food and medicine traps in trading. Barter is a phase, not a
destination: in the long run what lasts is relationships and reputation (→ 18-01).

> **CAUTION. Trading is a security event, not just an exchange** (→ 14-03). Every trade shows that
> you have something, hints at what else you might have, and tells someone where you live. **Trade
> skills before goods, and small things before large ones.**
>
> **Two traps:**
> - **Prescription medicine.** Medicine from a stranger may be the wrong drug, the wrong strength,
>   fake, or spoiled, and casual antibiotic use breeds resistance (CDC, Antibiotic Use; → 12-04,
>   → 12-07). Whether your household ever gives or accepts someone else's prescription is a choice:
>   {{choice DC-15}} (→ 30-16). Antibiotics without a prescription: {{choice DC-16}} (→ 30-17).
> - **Food you did not make.** Traded food has no label and unknown ingredients (FDA, Food
>   Allergies), and home-canned food from someone else's kitchen can carry botulism, which you
>   cannot see, smell or taste. Rules below.

## Do this now

1. **Over-stock the cheap, useful, shelf-stable things.** They are the best trade goods and cost
   little now: fasteners and hardware (→ 16-07), matches and lighters, soap (→ 13-09), salt
   (→ 04-13), batteries, seeds (→ 05-03), needles and thread (→ 16-04), tape and wire (→ 16-05).
2. **Build skills** (→ 18-03). They are the safest thing to trade and they do not run out.
3. **Keep some cash in small bills** (→ 19-02). Early in any disruption, cash still works and barter
   does not.
4. **Write your household's never-trade list** (below) now, calmly. Deciding under pressure is worse.

## How a broken economy goes

| Stage | What works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Cards, cash | Prepare now |
| **Early disruption** | **Cash, and only cash** | Card machines stop when the power does (→ 19-02). Small bills |
| Deeper disruption | Cash still moves; goods start to matter | Prices rise fast |
| Extended | **Barter and reciprocity** | Trust becomes the medium (→ 18-01) |
| Settled | A local exchange system re-emerges | Skills, labor, staple goods |

**Cash matters early, and most people have none.**

## What makes a good trade good

1. **Everyone needs it**, whatever their situation.
2. **It keeps:** no expiry, no upkeep.
3. **It divides:** you can trade a little without trading a lot.
4. **It is compact.**
5. **It is cheap now**, so you can over-stock it.
6. **It is boring to be seen with.** A box of screws does not mark you as a target; a case of
   ammunition does (→ 14-03). This is the point people miss.

## The good ones

| Category | Items | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware (→ 16-07) | Screws, nails, wire, hose clamps, tape | Universal, divisible, boring, cheap |
| Fire | Matches, lighters, ferro rods | Everyone needs fire; tiny |
| Hygiene (→ 13-09) | Soap, toothpaste, toothbrushes, menstrual supplies | Universal; soap can also be made |
| Food staples (→ 04-13) | Salt, sugar, spices, coffee, yeast, baking soda | Salt is the classic; spices rescue bad food |
| Batteries | AA and AAA especially | Compact; everyone needs them |
| Seeds (→ 05-03) | Open-pollinated vegetable seed (seed you can save and replant) | Tiny, cheap, very valuable in spring |
| Sewing (→ 16-04) | Needles, thread, safety pins, buttons, zippers | Cannot be improvised |
| Repair (→ 16-05) | Glue, epoxy, wire, patches, duct tape | Everyone breaks things |
| Light | Candles, lamp oil, headlamps | Long dark winters |
| Water (→ 03-04) | Purification tablets, filters | Life-critical; compact |
| First aid (→ 12-01) | Bandages, gauze, tape, non-prescription pain relievers | Valuable; see the visibility caution |
| Children's things | Diapers, outgrown clothes, shoes | The most natural, least fraught trade there is |
| Tools (→ 16-01) | Files, blades, hand tools | Durable; high value |
| Tobacco and alcohol | | Historically very tradeable; also a source of trouble |

## The ones to be careful with

- **Prescription medicine:** see the caution above and your choices on → 30-16 and → 30-17.
- **Ammunition and firearms** (→ 14-07). High value, but trading them advertises what you have and
  arms people you may not know (→ 18-05). Be very deliberate.
- **Fuel.** Valuable, dangerous to handle, and it marks you as someone with fuel.
- **Food in quantity.** Trading visible amounts of food tells everyone you have food: the single
  most consequential thing to reveal when food is scarce.
- **Anything that reveals depth.** One of something looks like the last one you have; a case of it
  looks like a supply.
- **Water treatment and medical supplies** buy a great deal, and mark you.

## Your never-trade list

Write it now, so nobody ever has to argue it at the door. "That's not something we trade" is the
whole answer. **The list is yours to write.** The rows below are suggestions some households use,
with their reasons, not a default; keep, change or strike any of them.

| Suggestion | Why some households put it here |
|---|---|
| Any medicine or medical supply a member's life depends on (insulin, pump and sensor supplies, epinephrine auto-injectors, inhalers) | Your supply is that person's runway; no trade can make up for running out (→ 12-07) |
| The last month of any medicine | The final weeks of any supply are never surplus |
| Firearms | Arms someone you cannot un-arm, and shows what you hold (→ 14-03) |
| This binder and your written records | A map of your household: people, medical details, places, stores |
| Your water treatment if it is your only means | Water is the first thing that kills |

{{#each meds as m}}- From your settings, worth considering: {{m.name}} ({{m.member}})
{{/each}}

**Our never-trade list:**
1. ______________________ 2. ______________________ 3. ______________________
4. ______________________ 5. ______________________ 6. ______________________

> **Before the collapse:** transferring a firearm is a legal event with federal and state rules
> (→ 14-11). Selling or giving away prescription medicine is unlawful.

## Trade freely: what builds the network without costing you

- **Skills and labor** (→ 18-03, → 18-08): repair, sewing, first aid, teaching. They regenerate.
- **Surplus garden produce.** Visibly seasonal; it does not suggest a stocked pantry.
- **Common batteries** from a deep stock.
- **The boring hardware tier** above: fasteners, matches, soap, salt, seeds, sewing supplies.
- **Information and referrals** (→ 15-04): free and welcome.

## Trading with less risk

- **Skills and labor first.** They reveal nothing about your stores.
- **Trade small.** Repeated small trades build a relationship; one large trade builds a reputation
  you may not want.
- **Meet away from your house**, especially with people you do not know well (→ 18-05).
- **Never let a trade become a tour of your supplies.** Bring only what you are trading.
- **Trade with people you know**, and build up slowly with people you do not.
- **Decline gracefully.** "We don't have any to spare" is a complete answer.
- **Do not haggle hard with neighbors you will depend on.** The relationship is worth more than the
  margin.

## Fairness and reputation

In a small community, your reputation as a trader is a real asset or a real liability.
- **Be fair and be seen to be fair.** Word travels fast.
- **Do not exploit desperation.** Beyond the ethics, it is a terrible strategy: you will need these
  people (→ 18-01).
- **Generosity with small things** buys great goodwill for little.
- **Keep your word.** In a barter economy, reliability is the currency underneath the currency.

## Traded food: the rules

- **Traded food has no label and unknown ingredients**, and anything cooked in someone else's
  kitchen may have touched an allergen (FDA, Food Allergies; → 02-04).
{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}- **Your household has a severe allergy.** {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}). {{/each}}
{{/if}}- **Whether an allergic member ever eats food you did not make** is a household choice: {{choice DC-18}} (→ 30-19).
- **Food that is old, dented or from someone's failed freezer** is a separate choice: {{choice DC-14}}
  (→ 30-15). **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans and jars are never opened. They are discarded**,
  away from children and animals.
- **Home-canned food from someone else's process.** Botulism toxin is invisible, and the jar's look
  and smell tell you nothing reliable. CDC's guidance: **boil all low-acid home-canned food
  (vegetables, beans, meat, fish, soup) for 10 minutes before eating or tasting it, adding 1 minute
  for each additional 1,000 feet of elevation** (CDC, Botulism Prevention; → 04-05). Low-acid foods are
  pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not canned (floor, → 30-01).
  Prefer factory-sealed, labeled goods when you have a choice.
- **Never honey for a child under 1 year** (infant botulism; CDC, Botulism Prevention).
{{#if has.toddler}}- **A toddler trying a genuinely new food:** one new food at a time, at home,
  with an adult watching afterward (→ 20-01).{{/if}}
- **Tell trading partners about allergies.** People are generally glad to know, and it stops a kind
  gift becoming an emergency (→ 18-01).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Cash in small bills** | Works early, when nothing else does | → 19-02 |
| Surplus fasteners, wire, tape | The best trade goods: cheap, boring, universal | Over-stock |
| Matches, lighters, ferro rods | Tiny, cheap, wanted | |
| Soap, toothbrushes, toothpaste | Universal | Bulk |
| Salt, sugar, spices, coffee, yeast | Salt is the classic | → 04-13 |
| AA and AAA batteries | Everyone needs them | |
| Open-pollinated seed | Very valuable in spring | Rotate |
| Needles, thread, safety pins | Cannot be improvised | |
| Candles, lamp oil, headlamps | Dark months | |
| Water purification tablets | Life-critical, compact | |
| Basic non-prescription first-aid supplies | Valuable; think about visibility | |
| **Your never-trade list, written** | Decided calmly, in advance | This page |
{{#if has.trailer}}| One "boring tier" barter box in the trailer | Road trade stock and an arrival gift | Packed apart from the rest of the load (→ 14-03) |
{{/if}}

**Substitutes:** skills for everything (repair, sewing, first aid, radio, sharpening, soap-making,
teaching); a day's labor; made goods such as soap, candles and repaired items; information; salvaged
surplus (→ 22-02).

## When it runs out

- **Stocked trade goods run out; skills do not.** A household that can make soap, fix things,
  sharpen, sew and dress a wound has a permanent trading position.
- **Trade goods are surplus, never core supply.** Never trade into your own runway: food, water
  treatment, fuel or medicine (→ 23-02).
- **Substitute** skills for goods, made goods for stocked goods, labor for both.
- **The long view:** a household known for fair dealing, useful skills and reliable help is in a
  stronger position than one holding a large stockpile and no standing.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** cash first (→ 19-02), then small neighborly exchange (→ 18-01). Do not rush into
  visible trading.
- **B, on the move:** trading on the road is risky (→ 18-05, → 14-01). Use skills, information and
  cash while it works. If you carry trade goods, keep them to one small box of the boring tier, opened
  away from the rest of your load. **Never arrive empty-handed** at a destination (→ 01-05): bring
  goods chosen for the household that takes you in, not only for your own.
- **C, settled:** a local exchange economy is likely to re-emerge around produce, labor, skills and
  equipment. Being able to produce something tradeable (food, soap, repairs, care, teaching) is the
  durable position (→ 18-03, → 18-07).

pages.body:
# Skills as currency

**What this page is for.** Why skills are the best trade good there is, which skills matter most,
and how to get them while courses still exist. A stockpile is finite, visible, and defended only by
you. A skill cannot be used up, cannot be taken, improves with use, and, for a household that values
discretion (→ 14-03), **using it reveals nothing about what you have.** A person with valuable skills
is welcome almost anywhere, which is a different position from a person with valuable things.

## Do this now

1. **Pick three skills from the lists below and actually learn them this year.** Not read about:
   do. **A bleeding-control class (Stop the Bleed) and a first-aid and CPR course** are the highest
   value (→ 12-01). **An amateur ("ham") radio license** is next (→ 15-05).
2. **Practice the ones you have.** A skill last used ten years ago is a memory, not a capability
   (→ 24-01).
3. **Find out what skills your neighbors have** (→ 18-01), and let them know yours.
4. **Teach one skill to someone this year** (→ 18-07). Teaching shows whether you really know it.

## Why skills beat stockpiles

| | Stockpile | Skill |
|---|---|---|
| Runs out | Yes | No; improves with use |
| Can be taken | Yes | No |
| Marks you as a target | Yes (→ 14-03) | No |
| Portable | Poorly | Perfectly |
| Tradeable again and again | No | Yes |
| Makes you welcome | Sometimes | Almost always |
| Cost | Money | Time, which is available now |

This is not an argument against stockpiling; most of this binder is about stockpiling. **It is an
argument for spending some of your preparation on time instead of money.**

## The skills that matter most

**Tier 1: the ones that make you truly valuable in a crisis**

| Skill | Why | How to start |
|---|---|---|
| **Medical, real training** | The most valuable skill when there is no hospital (→ 12-16) | Stop the Bleed, first aid and CPR, then EMT or wilderness first responder courses |
| **Childbirth skills** | The emergency with the worst outcomes and least room to improvise (→ 12-12) | Rare and very valuable |
| **Dental first aid** | Constant, miserable, nothing substitutes (→ 12-06, → 18-08) | Courses are rare; the binder's pages are a start |
| **Veterinary** | Animals, and often the nearest medical training around | |
| **Water treatment** | Life-critical; everyone needs it (→ 03-04) | Learnable in an afternoon |

**Tier 2: constantly needed, learnable now**

| Skill | Pages |
|---|---|
| Repair: mechanical, electrical, general | → 16-05, → 16-08 |
| Sharpening: everyone's tools are dull and almost nobody can fix that | → 16-02 |
| Sewing and gear repair | → 16-04, → 11-07 |
| Food preservation: canning, drying, curing | → 04-04, → 04-06, → 04-07 |
| Gardening and seed saving | → 05-01, → 05-03 |
| Animal keeping and butchering | → 05-04, → 05-09 |
| Radio: operating, antennas, repair | → 15-05, → 15-06 |
| 12-volt power and solar | → 09-08, → 09-09 |
| Soap making: universally needed, almost nobody can do it | → 13-09 |
| Building, carpentry, plumbing | → 16-08, → 16-12 |
| Small-engine repair | → 09-15 |
| Metalwork | → 16-08 |

**Tier 3: valuable and underrated**
- **Teaching** (→ 18-07), including children's schooling (→ 20-03)
- **Cooking well from little** (→ 04-18)
- **Baking.** Bread is morale (→ 21-06).
- **Childcare.** An hour of relief is worth a great deal to any parent (→ 21-05).
- **Organizing and planning.** Truly scarce.
- **Calming disputes** (→ 18-06)
- **Music.** Do not underestimate it over a long winter (→ 21-02).
- **Languages**, depending on the community
- **Being calm and reliable.** Not exactly a skill, and the most valuable trait there is.

## Skills your own household needs first

Some skills matter most for your own people, before any trade:
- **First aid and bleeding control** for every adult (→ 12-01).
{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}- **Every adult fully able to run the type 1 diabetes routine** (→ 02-01, → 02-02). A survival
  requirement, not a trade skill.
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}- **Every adult able to run the pump and sensor, and to fall back to injections** (→ 02-02).
{{/if}}{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}- **Every adult and caregiver able to recognize anaphylaxis and use the auto-injector**
  (→ 02-03).
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-04}}- **Allergen-safe cooking** (→ 02-04), which shapes everything else in the kitchen.
{{/if}}- **Each condition in your household:** every adult knows that module's daily routine and warning
  signs (→ 12-11).
- **Water treatment** (→ 03-04), because illness on top of any condition compounds it.

## Trading a skill safely

- **A repair for a neighbor reveals nothing about your stores** (→ 14-03).
- **You can be generous with skills indefinitely** without running anything down.
- **It builds relationship and reputation** (→ 18-01). It makes you someone people protect rather
  than someone they eye.
- **Do not undervalue it.** A day's skilled work is worth a day's food, and being known as fair
  matters (→ 18-02).
- **Teach as well as do** (→ 18-07). It multiplies your value and costs nothing.
- **Know your limits.** Working beyond your competence, in medicine especially, does real harm
  (→ 12-16). "I can clean and dress that; I can't set it" is a good answer.

## Getting skills now

- **Courses that exist now and will not later:** Stop the Bleed, first aid and CPR, wilderness first
  responder, amateur radio licensing (ARRL, Getting Licensed; → 15-05), canning classes, a welding
  class at a technical college.
- **Practice, do not just read.** Under stress you do what you have practiced (→ 21-01).
- **Do it badly first, at low stakes.** Make bad soap. Sharpen a cheap knife. Sew a crooked patch.
- **Learn from people:** neighbors, clubs, classes. Faster than books, and it builds the network
  (→ 18-01).
- **Teach the children** (→ 20-07, → 20-03).
- **Write down what you learn** (→ 24-01).

## The skills inventory

Keep it on paper (→ 24-01, → 22-04) and review it yearly (→ 25-10).

**From your profile:**
{{#each members as m}}- {{m.label}} ({{m.age_text}}): has {{m.skills}}. Learning next: ______________
{{/each}}

**Missing from the household entirely:** ________________________________
**Who nearby has it** (→ 18-01): ________________________________

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Course fees and time** | The real investment on this page | |
| Cheap practice materials | You learn by doing badly first | Knives to sharpen, fabric to sew |
| **Paper reference books** | Medicine, dentistry, repair, radio, canning | → 25-06 |
| **Written skills inventory** | Have, need, who nearby has it | |
| Tools for the skills you are building | A skill without tools is theory | → 16-01 |
| A notebook | What you would otherwise forget | |
| Club and class memberships | Skills and network at the same time | |

**What you cannot substitute is the time.** Skills take time to build, and the time is available
now.

## When it runs out

- **Skills do not run out. They fade without use and are lost if not passed on.**
- **Practice keeps them** (→ 24-01, → 24-03).
- **Teaching multiplies them** (→ 18-07). A skill you have taught to three people is a skill your
  community has.
- **For a skill you lack, the substitute is a person who has it** (→ 18-01).
- **Supplies get you through months; skills get you through years.** They travel at no weight, cannot
  be taken, and make you welcome.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** acquire. Courses, licenses, clubs and practice, all available now and not later.
- **B, on the move:** skills are the only thing you carry at no weight (→ 22-03).
- **C, settled:** skills become the local economy. Being the household that can fix, treat, teach or
  make is a durable and secure position.
