pages.body:
# Group organization and decisions

**What this page is for.** What to do when cooperation goes beyond neighbors helping neighbors:
shared work, shared resources, or households moving in together. Most cooperation in a disaster is
informal and works fine that way (→ 18-01). **What breaks groups is almost never the outside threat.
It is unclear expectations, unequal contribution and unresolved disputes** (→ 18-06, → 21-05): the
same failures as inside one household, at a larger scale.

> **CAUTION. Decide what your household will not take part in, before you join anything.**
> Detaining, punishing or using force on people are the decisions that most often turn a group into
> something its members never agreed to. Your household's own rule on the use of force is a
> worksheet you write yourselves: {{choice DC-12}} (→ 30-13). A group's agreement should not quietly
> override it.
>
> **Other people's property, labor and children remain theirs.** A group that forgets this breaks
> from the inside.
>
> **Before the collapse:** detaining and punishing people is the job of law enforcement and the
> courts. What a private citizen may lawfully do is narrow and set by state law, and group
> arrangements over property, work or children carry legal obligations (→ 14-11).

## Do this now

1. **You do not need to organize anything yet. You need relationships** (→ 18-01). Structure, if it
   is ever needed, is built on top of them.
2. **Get your own household's roles and decisions right first** (→ 00-07, → 21-04). A household that
   cannot divide its own work will not do better in a group.
3. **Read the agreement checklist below once**, so the conversation is easier if it ever happens.
{{#if has.destinations}}4. **For each place you might go** (→ 01-05), run the arrival agreement below with them now, by
   phone, in ordinary time, and write the answers down.{{else}}4. **If you ever name a place to go**
   (→ 01-05), run the arrival agreement below with its people in ordinary time.{{/if}}

## Levels of organization

**Go no further up this ladder than the situation needs.** Each step adds capability and friction.

| Level | What it is | When |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Informal mutual aid | Neighbors helping neighbors | Almost always; usually enough (→ 18-01) |
| 2. Coordinated tasks | Shared watch, shared wood cutting, a check-in list | Days to weeks; low cost |
| 3. Shared resources | A common generator, well or tool pool | Weeks to months; needs some agreement |
| 4. Combined households | Living together, shared stores and labor | Months or more; **needs real agreement** |
| 5. Formal community structure | Roles, rules, decision procedures | Long term; mostly emerges rather than being designed |

**Most households never need to go past level 2.** Over-organizing creates conflict where none was
needed.

## What to agree before combining anything

From level 3 up, **agree these out loud and write them down.** Vagueness here is what destroys
groups.

1. **Who is in**, and how someone new joins.
2. **What each person contributes:** supplies, labor, skills, space, equipment. Be specific.
3. **What each person receives:** food, shelter, protection, a share of what is produced.
4. **How work is divided and how the unpleasant work rotates.** Rotation matters more than a fair
   first split (→ 21-04).
5. **Who decides what.** Most things should have an owner, not a vote (below).
6. **How disputes are settled** (→ 18-06). Agree it before there are disputes.
7. **How someone leaves, and what they take.** The clause people skip, and the one that causes the
   worst trouble.
8. **What is shared and what stays private.** Not everything has to be pooled.
9. **How the children are looked after, and by whom**, including every member's allergy and medical
   rules, understood by every adult (→ 02-04, → 12-11).
10. **How the agreement is revisited.** Circumstances change.

**Write it down.** Memories differ under stress. A written agreement is not distrust; it is what lets
people trust each other.

## The arrival agreement (moving in with family or friends)

The most likely level-4 case is a household moving in with relatives or friends at a destination.
The hard version is arriving at a working farm or home whose people were not expecting you, with the
terms settled at the kitchen table on day one. **Settle them warmly, once, and in writing.**

{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{d.name}}** ({{d.status_text}}). Who is there: {{d.who_is_there}}. Agreement talked through on: ____/____/____
{{else}}- No destinations entered yet.
{{/each}}

**Only count on a place whose people have agreed.** At a place not asked, arrive self-sufficient,
with nothing assumed and nothing left there ahead of time (→ 01-05).

```
ARRIVAL AGREEMENT                      Date talked through: __________
Place: ______________________   Their household: __________________

1. WHO ARRIVES (names, count): _____________________________________
   Total people at the place: _______

2. WHAT WE CONTRIBUTE
   Labor (daily, each adult; what the children can do): __________
   Skills (18-03), offered plainly: ________________ Accepted? ____
   Supplies we bring or left there ahead of time: _________________
   Equipment (vehicle, trailer, tools, radios): ___________________

3. WHO DECIDES (say it plainly; it is true anyway)
   THEIR PLACE = THEIR FINAL CALL on land, animals, equipment and
   who stays.                                         Agreed: _____
   OUR final call: our own medical care, our children, our own
   medicines and medical devices (never pooled).      Agreed: _____
   Who owns each area (farm work / food / medical / watch): _______

4. POOLED OR SEPARATE
   Pooled: _______________________________ (food? fuel? work?)
   Separate: every medicine and medical device, this binder: ______
   Cold storage for refrigerated medicine there, if needed: _______

5. LEAVING
   Either side can say "this isn't working." What leaves with us:
   what we brought + ______________ Notice / handover: ___________

6. MEDICAL DISCLOSURE: what they need to know about our members'
   conditions and allergies, told to whom, and when:
   ________________________________________________________________
   (Where medicine is stored: need-to-know.)

7. SPACE AND PRIVACY: where we sleep, what is "ours", where a door
   can close: _____________________________________________________

8. CHILDREN: the place's hazards walked with our children (20-02:
   water, machinery, animals, grain, dogs); allergy rules known by
   EVERY adult there: __________ Supervision plan: _______________

9. REVISIT: checked at each visit and yearly (25-10): ____________

Signed and dated (both households): _______________________________
```

**At a place that has agreed:** run the nine questions by phone on the next call (→ 15-08),
especially 3 (whose final call), 4 (what is pooled), 6 (what they should know before you arrive) and
8 (hazards for children).
**At a place that has not:** question 6 happens in the first hour, because there is no "before";
question 2 is whatever you brought (→ 18-02); question 5 matters more, not less, when nobody invited
you.

## Decisions that work

- **Most decisions have an owner, not a vote.** Whoever's area it is decides: water, food, medical,
  watch, children. Voting on everything is slow and exhausting.
- **Group decisions are for what affects everyone:** moving, admitting someone, large commitments.
- **Agree a tie-breaker in advance**, and on safety, prefer the more cautious option.
- **Emergencies have a named decision-maker.** There is no time to deliberate (→ 21-01).
- **Decide when to decide.** "We'll decide Sunday" is often the best answer.
- **Write decisions down.**

## Fairness: what keeps a group together

- **Openness.** People tolerate scarcity far better than secrecy about scarcity.
- **Visible contribution.** Invisible work breeds resentment. Name it and thank people.
- **Rotate the bad jobs.** The single most effective fairness measure.
- **Different capacities, said openly.** Someone with a baby (→ 20-01), an injury (→ 12-09) or a
  chronic condition (→ 12-11) contributes differently. Say so rather than letting it become a
  grievance.
- **Children and the sick are cared for, not weighed.** Say that explicitly.
- **A member's medical needs** (medicine, devices, special food) are stated up front as not pooled
  and not negotiable, rather than discovered as a disagreement later.

## Roles worth naming

Not a hierarchy, just clarity (→ 00-07): water, food and stores, fuel and heat, medical (ideally the
most trained person, → 18-03), watch, repair, communications, children, and coordination (someone
has to hold the whole picture).

## What breaks groups

- **Unclear expectations**, by a wide margin.
- **Unequal contribution**, real or perceived.
- **Resentment left unspoken** (→ 21-05).
- **Disputes left unsettled** (→ 18-06).
- **One person gathering authority** nobody agreed to.
- **Scarcity plus secrecy.**
- **No way to leave**, so people who want out feel trapped and behave badly.
- **Exhaustion** (→ 21-02, → 21-07). Much group conflict in the later months is a sleep problem
  dressed as a governance problem.

## The honest scale

**One household combining with one or two others is realistic** and can work well: more hands,
medical backup (→ 12-16), childcare relief (→ 21-05), better morale (→ 21-02). Anything larger is a
real organizational problem and much harder than people imagine. Start small, go slowly.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Your own household's roles and decision rules, written** | Get this right before scaling it | → 00-07 |
| The agreement checklist, thought through | So the conversation is easy | This page |
| A written skills and resource list | The raw material of cooperation | → 18-03, → 22-04 |
| Paper and pen for agreements and decisions | Memory differs; paper does not | |
| Radios on a shared channel | Coordination | → 15-02 |
| Allergy and medical rules, written and shared | For anyone feeding or minding your children | |
| Relationships built in advance | The real prerequisite | → 18-01 |

**Everything here is a conversation and a piece of paper.** Use structures that already exist: a
congregation, a block association, extended family. What you cannot substitute is trust, and it
takes time (→ 18-05).

## When it runs out

- **What runs out is goodwill**, on the same schedule as everything else in a long event (→ 21-02).
  Upkeep is openness, rotation, thanks, and settling disputes early (→ 18-06).
- **Watch for the drift:** decisions stop being discussed, work stops being shared, someone stops
  showing up, resentment stops being spoken (SAMHSA, Disaster Distress Helpline warning signs).
- **Add structure only when needed, and remove it when not.**
- **When a group is not working, leaving well beats staying badly.** That is why the exit clause
  matters.
- **Most of this page will probably never be needed.** Level 1 and 2 cooperation almost certainly
  will, and needs only relationships built in advance.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** informal mutual aid is the realistic level. Do not try to organize a neighborhood
  that does not want organizing.
- **B, on the move:** traveling with another household is a real decision: more capability, more
  friction, slower. Agree the terms before leaving, including how you would separate (→ 01-03).
- **C, settled:** where combining households makes most sense, and where getting the agreement right
  matters most, because you are in it for a long time (→ 01-04).

pages.body:
# Trust, vetting and strangers

**What this page is for.** How to judge people, answer a knock at the door, decide who learns your
household's sensitive facts, and teach children the family rules, without sliding into either "trust
everyone" or "trust no one". Neither is a plan.

> **CAUTION. Start with what disaster research shows: in real disasters, most people help.**
> Looting and predation are the exception. The common pattern is spontaneous cooperation, sharing
> and rescue by ordinary people. Households that assume the opposite cut themselves off from the
> help they will need (→ 18-01). **And** not everyone is safe, and judgment matters, especially for a
> household with small children or a life-critical medicine.
>
> **This page is about judging people, not about force.** When and whether force is used is a
> separate question your household writes down on its own worksheet: {{choice DC-12}} (→ 30-13,
> → 14-11).

## Do this now

1. **Build relationships now** (→ 18-01). Judging someone is far easier when you have known them for
   years than when you meet them at your gate.
2. **Agree, among the adults, how you will answer a knock at the door**, what you will disclose and
   who decides (→ 00-07, → 21-05).
3. **Agree a duress signal** between the adults (→ 15-07): an ordinary-sounding phrase that means
   "this is not fine".
{{#if has.child}}4. **Teach the children the family rules** about strangers and about not telling (below), simply
   and without frightening them (→ 20-04).{{/if}}

## What disaster research shows

- **Most people behave helpfully in disasters.** They help strangers, share and organize themselves.
- **Panic and mass lawlessness are rare** and are often over-reported.
- **The bigger real risks are usually** disorganization, scarcity, illness, rumors and exhaustion.
- **Neighbors usually respond faster and better than officials** in the first hours and days
  (→ 18-01).

**So a posture of cautious openness is both more accurate and more useful than default suspicion.**
Isolation costs you the help, information, skills and morale that protect you most (CDC, About
Social Connection).

## But judgment still matters

- **Not everyone is safe**, and desperate people do things they otherwise would not.
- **The longer and harder a situation, the more the balance shifts** (→ 14-01).
- **You can be wrong in both directions**, and both errors cost.

## Judging people: practical, not paranoid

**Time is the best test there is.** Almost everything else stands in for it.
- **Known beats unknown.** Someone your neighbors vouch for is a different matter from a stranger.
- **Consistency over time.** Do their story and behavior line up across several meetings?
- **Small tests before large ones.** Trade small (→ 18-02), lend something minor, share information
  before supplies.
- **Reciprocity.** Do they give as well as take? Only taking is information.
- **How they treat people with nothing to offer**: children, the elderly, the sick. One of the most
  reliable signals there is.
- **How they talk about others.** Someone who boasts of cheating people is telling you something.
- **Your instinct.** If something feels wrong, act on it and think later. Instinct is fast but also
  biased, so **use it to create distance, not to justify hostility** (→ 21-01).

## The knock at the door

Decide this in advance (→ 00-07):
- **Answer or not?** Not answering is a complete option and needs no justification.
- **Talk through the door or from a window.** You can help without opening it.
- **Do not let a stranger inside** in an uncertain situation. Once inside, they have seen everything
  (→ 14-03).
- **Meet away from the house** for anything like a trade (→ 18-02).
- **Two adults aware:** one talks; one is present somewhere else.
- **"We don't have anything to spare" is a complete answer.** It needs no argument or apology.
- **You can help without revealing anything:** a cup of water, directions, information.
- **Small, bounded help is usually possible and usually right.** It costs little, and a neighborhood
  where people help each other is safer for you.

## The hard case

**Someone in real need whom you cannot fully help**: hungry, cold, with children. There is no clean
answer, and it is worth having thought about before it happens (→ 12-16, → 21-03).
- **Small, bounded, immediate help** is usually possible: a meal, water, an hour of warmth,
  directions to where help is.
- **Open-ended help you cannot keep up hurts everyone**, them included. A promise you have to
  withdraw is worse than none.
- **Pointing people to real resources** (→ 25-03) is genuine help and costs nothing.
- **Your first duty is to your own household**, and that is not a failing.
- **Decide as a household, in advance where possible** (→ 21-05). Disagreeing about this in the
  moment is corrosive.

## Bringing people in

If a situation goes long, joining with others comes up (→ 18-04):
- **Skills and character matter more than supplies** (→ 18-03).
- **Slowly.** Cooperation before combining.
- **Agree the terms first:** work, resources, decisions, and how someone leaves (→ 18-04, → 18-06).
- **Everyone who might feed or mind your children knows their allergies and medical needs.**
- **Family and close friends are the usual first circle**, and even there the terms are said out
  loud.

## Medical privacy: who learns what, and when

If anyone in your household depends on a medicine or device they cannot live without (insulin,
epinephrine, oxygen, a pump, anti-seizure medicine), that fact is two exposures in one. It says
there is a supply of valuable, hard-to-replace medicine in the house, and it shows exactly what
taking or destroying that supply would do to your family. Most leaks reveal *what you have*; this
one reveals *what you cannot live without*.

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Your household has refrigerated medicine** ({{#each refrigerated_meds as r}}{{r.member}}: {{r.name}}; {{/each}}). This section applies to you.{{/if}}

**A framework many households use.** Decide your own circles and write them below.

| Circle | Usually | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A household you will move in with (→ 18-04) | **Yes, fully**: before arrival where there is a "before", or in the first hour | Living together while hiding a life-support need is planning built on sand: refrigeration, supplies and the "if they are down" plan all depend on them knowing |
| Trusted neighbors (T on the → 18-01 roster) | The fact, if useful; **never quantities or where it is kept** | They may need to help in an emergency |
| Other neighbors | Capabilities, not vulnerabilities | They can know you are a nurse or a mechanic without knowing a member is insulin-dependent |
| Strangers and trading contacts | **Never** | No trade or conversation is worth handing a stranger your household's pressure point |

**Disclosure follows commitment, not acquaintance.** When two households truly commit to live
together, full medical disclosure is owed and essential (→ 18-04). Until then, the same information
is pure exposure. The order is: trust, then commitment, then disclosure. Never disclosure as a way
to build trust.

**Our circles:** told fully: ______________ Told the fact only: ______________ Never told: everyone else.

## Teaching children

{{#if has.child}}Children in your household: {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{/if}}

- **Simple rules for a young child:** stay with a grown-up; do not go anywhere with anyone; do not
  tell people about our house or our things; tell us if someone talks to you (→ 20-04).
- **A rule, not a fear.** "That's our family rule" works better than describing danger (→ 20-08).
- **Let them also see adults being kind to people.** Children learn the whole posture, not just the
  caution. You want them to learn "we're careful and we help", not "people are bad".
- **Babies and toddlers** are kept safe by supervision and barriers, always (→ 20-02).

## The two ways to get it wrong

| Error | What it costs |
|---|---|
| Trusting everyone | Losing supplies, revealing your position, letting the wrong person in |
| **Trusting no one** | **Isolation, a documented risk factor** (CDC); no medical help (→ 12-16); no relief; no information; worse morale (→ 21-02); and a reputation that makes later cooperation impossible |

**The second error is more common in prepared households and less talked about**, and the damage is
hard to undo.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Relationships built in advance** | The only real vetting tool | → 18-01 |
| Your posture and roles, written | Decided calmly, not at the door | → 00-07 |
| **A duress signal agreed between adults** | A phrase that means the opposite of what it says | → 15-07 |
| A way to see who is at the door | Window, peephole | |
| Exterior lighting, used deliberately | Balanced with light discipline | → 10-05, → 14-02 |
| A written list of real local resources | Helping by pointing costs nothing | → 25-03 |
| Something small to give | Bounded help is often right | Water, a meal |

**Time, observation and your neighbors' knowledge** substitute for every other vetting method, and
they are free. **Distance** substitutes for confrontation in almost every case: not answering, not
engaging and not being where a problem is are complete strategies (→ 14-01). **What you cannot
substitute is judgment, and exhaustion, fear and hunger degrade it** (→ 21-01).

## When it runs out

- **What runs out is the benefit of the doubt.** It erodes as things get longer and harder. Notice
  it: a household that has slid into default hostility has cut itself off from its strongest
  protection (CDC).
- **Re-check your posture deliberately** from time to time (→ 14-01). Conditions change both ways: a
  chaotic neighborhood in week two may be organized by month two.
- **For most households, the biggest risks are medical and environmental, not human.** The people
  around you are far more likely to be part of the solution.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** neighbors close, mostly known, mostly helpful. Build relationships, keep ordinary
  discretion, and be someone people are glad lives on their street.
- **B, on the move:** strangers are unavoidable and cannot be judged over time (→ 01-03). Distance and
  avoidance are the main tools (→ 14-01). Help where it is cheap and safe; do not camp near roads or
  where you can be approached unseen.
- **C, settled:** fewer people, more consequential meetings. Rural communities often take time to
  accept newcomers, then are strongly cooperative. Arrive as someone who contributes (→ 18-03) and
  the judging takes care of itself.

pages.body:
# Conflict resolution between households

**What this page is for.** Handling the ordinary disputes with neighbors that a long emergency
brings: water, noise, animals, boundaries, help given and not returned, children, dogs, borrowed
tools. That is normal, and most of it is manageable. **You cannot afford enemies next door.** Every
hard scenario in this binder is better with cooperative neighbors (→ 18-01). A dispute that ends a
relationship costs far more than whatever it was about.

> **CAUTION. This page is about ordinary disputes, not violence.** Threats, violence, theft and
> other crimes are matters for law enforcement wherever it exists. Where it does not, the answer is
> distance, awareness and securing your home (→ 14-02), not confrontation (→ 14-13). Your household's
> written rule on force is a separate worksheet: {{choice DC-12}} (→ 30-13). Nothing on this page
> authorizes anything.

## Do this now

1. **Build relationships now** (→ 18-01). A dispute between people who like each other gets settled;
   a dispute between strangers escalates. That is the whole prevention strategy.
2. **Settle the predictable friction points in advance:** boundaries, shared fences, drainage, where
   the dog goes, where waste water goes (→ 13-03). Most neighborhood conflict is about things that
   could have been agreed beforehand.
3. **Agree among the adults how you will handle a dispute:** who talks, what you will concede, what
   you will not (→ 21-05, → 00-07). A household that argues in front of the neighbor loses twice.
4. **Find out who the natural peacemakers are:** the respected long-timer, the faith leader, the
   person everyone likes. Every neighborhood has them.

## What disputes will actually be about

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Resources | Water access, a shared well, firewood, a generator, tools not returned |
| Boundaries | Where a fence is, where animals go, where waste goes (→ 13-07) |
| Noise and smoke | A generator at night (→ 09-04), a smoky fire, a barking dog |
| Help | Given and not returned; asked for and refused; expected and not offered |
| Children | Kids, dogs, fences, other people's rules |
| Trades | Something that was not as described (→ 18-02) |
| Fairness in a group | Contribution and share (→ 18-04) |
| Built-up irritation | The real cause of most of it (→ 21-02) |

**Most are solvable. Most escalate only because nobody raised them early.**

## Calming a dispute: the practical version

1. **Raise it early and small.** The most effective step on this page. A sentence in week one
   prevents a confrontation in month three.
2. **Go in person, calmly, at a good time.** Not when either of you is exhausted, cold or hungry
   (→ 21-01). Not at night.
3. **One adult, not two.** Two people arriving looks like a confrontation.
4. **Lead with the relationship.** "I want to sort this out because we're going to be neighbors
   for a long time."
5. **Describe the problem, not the person.** "Water is running into our yard," not "you're
   careless."
6. **Ask their side first.** There is often a reason you do not know, and asking changes the whole
   conversation.
7. **Look for the practical fix.** Most people want the problem gone, not a victory.
8. **Concede what you can.** Being right is worth less than being on good terms.
9. **If it heats up, step away.** "Let me think about it. Can we talk tomorrow?" You can always come
   back; you cannot un-say things.
10. **Follow up.** Confirm it is settled, and be pleasant afterward. A settled dispute that leaves
    coldness is only half settled.

## When you cannot settle it yourselves

- **A third person:** a respected neighbor, a mutual friend, a faith leader. Informal mediation
  works remarkably well; it is the traditional way.
- **Choose the mediator together**, and agree in advance whether their view decides it or only
  advises.
- **Each side tells it without interruption**, then everyone looks for the fix.
- **Write down what is agreed** (→ 18-04).
- **In a group, agree the dispute process before there are disputes** (→ 18-04).

## When it cannot be settled at all

- **Distance.** You do not have to be friends with everyone. Civil and separate is a workable
  outcome and often the right one.
- **Reduce contact:** fences, schedules, routes, not sharing what causes friction.
- **Do not feed it.** You can refuse to escalate on your own.
- **Do not recruit the neighborhood.** Turning a two-party dispute into sides is the worst outcome
  and very hard to undo.
- **Accept a loss and move on** when the thing at stake is smaller than the relationship, which it
  usually is.

## When it is a safety matter

A different category, treated differently (→ 14-01):
- **Threats, violence, theft and crimes** go to law enforcement wherever it exists.
- **Where none exists:** distance, awareness and securing your home (→ 14-02), not confrontation. You
  cannot win a feud with a neighbor.
- **Do not go and confront someone** about a safety matter. That is how situations become
  irreversible.
- **Tell other neighbors the facts**, not to build a side, but because shared awareness protects
  everyone (→ 18-01).

## Your own household first

How a dispute goes is decided mostly inside your own house (→ 21-05, → 21-01):
- **Agree the approach among the adults first.** A united, calm household handles disputes well.
- **Check the body before the conversation:** tired, cold, hungry{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}, or low
  blood sugar (→ 02-01){{/if}} makes everything worse.
- **Never in front of the children** (→ 20-08). They absorb it, and repeat it to the neighbor's
  children.
- **Do not let a dispute become a story you keep telling yourselves.** Rehearsed grievances grow.

## Reputation

In a small community, how you handle disputes becomes your reputation (→ 18-02, → 18-03). Being known
as fair means people will deal with you, help you, and give you the benefit of the doubt. Being known
as difficult means the opposite, and it is very hard to reverse. Word travels fast.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Relationships built in advance** | The prevention strategy | → 18-01 |
| Clear boundaries and agreements up front | Most conflict is about undiscussed things | Fences, drainage, waste |
| An agreed household approach | United and calm works | → 21-05 |
| Knowing who the local peacemakers are | Every neighborhood has them | |
| Written agreements for anything shared | Memories differ | → 18-04 |
| Something to give | A conceded point or small gift settles a lot | |

All of this is free: conversation, patience, timing, conceding small things. What cannot be
substituted is the relationship built beforehand.

## When it runs out

- **Patience and goodwill run out** on the same schedule as everything else in a long event
  (→ 21-02). Disputes months in are usually about exhaustion, not the water line.
- **Upkeep:** raise things early and small, keep relationships warm, and look after your own
  household's rest (→ 21-07). A rested household has disputes; an exhausted one has feuds.
- **Substitute:** distance for settlement; mediation for direct talk; concession for victory.
- **Conceding a point to keep your neighbors willing to help you is almost always the right
  trade.** Decide that in advance so you do not have to work it out mid-argument.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** neighbors close, friction unavoidable, stakes highest. Settle the predictable
  things now; raise the rest early and small.
- **B, on the move:** avoidance is the strategy (→ 14-01). Disputes with strangers on the road have
  no upside and no way to settle them. Do not engage; move on.
- **C, settled:** water, boundaries and animals are the classic rural disputes. Settle boundaries and
  water clearly and early (→ 01-04). You will see these people for the rest of your life, which is
  both the pressure and the reason to get it right.

pages.body:
# Teaching and preserving knowledge

**What this page is for.** Keeping what your household knows alive when screens fail, and passing it
on. A dead phone, a burned house, a failed drive or an internet that stops working takes with it
almost everything a modern household knows how to look up. Two jobs: **preserving** knowledge (paper
books, your own written records, copies of this binder) and **passing it on** (teaching your
children and neighbors, and being taught). Teaching costs nothing, multiplies a community's
abilities, and makes the teacher someone a community protects (→ 18-03).

## Do this now

1. **Buy the paper books** in the list below. Printed and on a shelf, not bookmarked. A few hundred
   dollars for a library that cannot be bought later.
2. **Keep this binder on more than one device**, charged (→ 00-10), and **export and print the pages
   you would need first** (the emergency quick reference, the medical pages for your household's
   conditions, the water pages). An app on a dead phone is not a binder.
3. **Start writing things down** (→ 25-05): what you learn, what works, what your household actually
   uses. Your own records will be more useful than any book.
4. **Teach one thing to someone this year** (→ 18-03): a neighbor, one of the children (→ 20-07).
   Teaching shows whether you really know it.

{{photo library-shelf}}

## Why paper

- **No power, device, network or battery needed.** No file format goes out of date.
- **Survives** a dead phone, a lost laptop, a failed drive and, stored sensibly, a wet basement.
- **Anyone can read it**, including someone who is not you; another adult may be the one using it.
- **You do not have to have predicted the question**, as you do when choosing what to download.
- **You can write in it**, which is how a reference becomes yours.
- **Digital storage fails all at once and silently.** You find out when you need it.

## The paper library: the core list

| Subject | What to own |
|---|---|
| **Medical** | A wilderness or "no doctor" style medical book written for laypeople, its dental companion, and a current first-aid manual (→ 12-01) |
| Food preservation | A current, tested canning guide. Tested recipes matter (→ 04-04) |
| Gardening | A guide for your region; a seed-saving reference |
| **Plant identification** | **A field guide for your region, with photographs. Not a national one** (→ 05-06) |
| Animals | Poultry, rabbits, butchering |
| Repair | General home repair, small engines, your vehicle's manual |
| Radio | An amateur radio license manual and antenna book (ARRL, Getting Licensed; → 15-05) |
| Electrical and solar | A 12-volt and off-grid wiring reference |
| Building | Basic carpentry |
| Sewing | Mending and pattern basics |
| Reference | **Local paper maps** (→ 25-04), a dictionary, maths and science basics for the children (→ 20-03) |
| Children | Books to read aloud, and readers a little ahead of their reading age |
| This binder | The printed pages you need first, and the app on more than one device |

**And the one people forget: books for pleasure.** On a long winter night, a stack of novels is a
morale asset (→ 21-02).

## Your own records: more useful than any book

The most valuable reference in a year will be the one you wrote (→ 25-05):
- **What you actually use:** water, wood, food, batteries (→ 23-02). Your real numbers, not planning
  guesses.
- **What worked and what did not:** the vegetable variety that produced, the repair that held, the
  road that was passable.
- **Weather and seasons:** frost dates you saw, when things bloomed, when the ice went out. Over a few
  years this becomes a valuable local record (→ 25-01).
- **A medical log:** illnesses, treatments, results, and the daily records any condition needs
  (→ 12-11).
- **Annotated maps:** where the water is, where the wild fruit is, which routes work (→ 25-04).
- **A household journal:** what happened. Good for morale now (→ 21-06) and for the children later.
- **Pencil or waterproof ink**, in a bound book, kept dry.

## Teaching the children

{{#if has.child}}{{#each children as c}}- {{c.label}}, {{c.age_text}}
{{/each}}{{/if}}{{#each teens as t}}- {{t.label}}, {{t.age_text}}
{{/each}}

- **In ten years they will be capable people, and what they know will be what you taught them.**
- **Teach by doing it alongside them.** That is how young children learn (CDC, Positive Parenting
  Tips).
- **Practical skills as they are ready:** knots (→ 16-03), sewing (→ 16-04), gardening, cooking,
  animals, and later tools, fire and first aid.
- **Reading and arithmetic** are the foundation everything else needs (→ 20-03).
- **Let them see you learning.** It models the most important skill of all.
- **Write down what you want them to know** in case you are not there to teach it. A hard thought,
  and a worthwhile document.

## Teaching neighbors, and being taught

- **Teaching multiplies a community's abilities** and costs you nothing (→ 18-03).
- **A community where three people can do first aid is far safer** than one where one person can
  (→ 12-16), and that protects you too.
- **Being taught is just as valuable.** Asking someone to teach you is one of the best ways to build
  a relationship (→ 18-01). People are glad to be asked.
- **Trade lessons, not just goods** (→ 18-02).
- **Teach other people's children** where it is welcome. It builds the community your children will
  grow up in.

## Keeping it safe

- **Dry, off the floor, out of direct sun.** Basements flood (→ 17-03); attics bake.
- **A waterproof box** for the things you cannot replace: printed binder pages, medical references,
  documents (→ 19-01).
- **A second copy of the critical few stored away from the house** (→ 19-03). A house fire takes
  everything at once.
- **Digital backups as well.** They are cheap and cover different failures (→ 19-03). Just do not
  rely on them alone.
- **Write in the margins.** A used reference is worth more than a clean one.

## The bigger picture

In a long disruption, knowledge decides whether a community recovers or only survives. The skills in
this binder (growing, preserving, treating, building, fixing, communicating) are the same skills
that rebuild. Preserving and teaching them helps beyond your household, and it is the most lasting
security there is: a community that needs what you know wants you in it.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **The paper library above** | Cannot be bought later | This year |
| **Printed key pages of this binder** | For when every screen is dead | Use the app's PDF export |
| Bound notebooks, several | Records, journal, logs | Pencil or waterproof ink |
| **Waterproof box for the irreplaceable** | Fire and flood take everything at once | → 19-01 |
| **A second set stored away from home** | The house-fire case | → 19-03 |
| Local paper maps | Annotate them | → 25-04 |
| Children's books, a little ahead of their age | They grow into them | |
| Books for pleasure | Long winter nights | |
| Pencils, pens and paper in bulk | Records, teaching, schooling | |

**Substitutes:** libraries' sale shelves, thrift stores and estate sales are full of these books.
Swapping books with neighbors is one of the easiest community activities there is. **People are the
other library**: someone who knows how to do something is a reference you cannot print.

## When it runs out

- **Books do not run out.** They get wet, burned or lost: hence the waterproof box and the second
  set.
- **Paper and pencils do run out.** Stock them; they carry everything on this page.
- **What really fades is knowledge nobody teaches.** A skill not passed on is gone in one
  generation. Teaching is the upkeep.
- **Teaching by doing, telling and repeating** is how most human knowledge moved for most of history.
  It still works, and it is how your children will learn most of what they learn.
- **Knowledge is the one asset in this plan that grows in value.**

## By phase

- **A, at home:** buy the library, print the key pages, start the records, teach one thing.
- **B, on the move:** the binder on a charged phone and a few printed pages; a small notebook.
- **C, settled:** records become a local almanac; teaching becomes a contribution the community
  values.

pages.body:
# Dental skills in a community

**What this page is for.** How a community handles teeth when dental offices are closed: who in a
neighborhood can help, what a trained layperson can and cannot do, how dental help is shared fairly,
and what being known for it costs. The clinical first aid is on → 12-06 (prevention and everyday
problems) and → 12-20 (knocked-out teeth, lost fillings, abscess). This page is the community side.

> **CAUTION. A spreading dental infection can kill.** An abscess (a pocket of infection at a tooth)
> can spread into the face, jaw, neck or blood. Infection in the blood can lead to sepsis, the body's
> extreme reaction to infection, which is a medical emergency (CDC, About Sepsis). **Swelling that
> spreads toward the eye, down the neck or under the jaw, trouble swallowing or breathing, or fever
> with a swollen face means the most urgent care you can reach** (→ 12-20; American Dental
> Association, Dental Emergencies). Antibiotics without a prescription are a household choice:
> {{choice DC-16}} (→ 30-17).

## Do this now

1. **Read → 12-06 and → 12-20 together, every adult.** The community side is only as useful as the
   first aid behind it.
2. **Get everyone's dental work done now** while dentists are open: cleanings, fillings, and any tooth
   a dentist says is failing. The best grid-down dentistry is what was finished before.
3. **Find out who near you has dental training** (→ 18-01): a dentist, hygienist, dental assistant,
   oral surgeon, military or wilderness medic. Note it on the neighbor roster.
4. **Stock prevention and first-aid supplies** (table below). Prevention is the part anyone can do.
5. **Decide as a household, before the first request comes**, how you will share dental help or
   supplies (exchange norms below).

## Why teeth matter so much

When regular dental care stops, tooth problems become one of the most common and disabling health
complaints. Tooth decay is an infection that keeps going until the tooth is treated or lost (NIH,
Tooth Decay), and gum disease does the same to the tissue holding teeth in (NIH, Gum Disease).
Dental pain stops people working and sleeping. A community where someone can sort "miserable" from
"dangerous", give sound first aid, and keep teeth from getting worse is measurably safer.

## Who has dental skills, and what each can do

| Who | What they can usually do | What they cannot do without a real practice |
|---|---|---|
| **Licensed dentist or oral surgeon** | Examine, give local anesthetic, extract, drain, place temporary fillings, judge infection, prescribe while the system works | Crowns, root canals, implants, anything needing a lab and a supply chain |
| Dental hygienist or assistant | Assess, clean, teach prevention, assist, recognize infection | Extractions; injections only where their own license allows them |
| Military, wilderness or EMS medic | Assess, first aid, recognize spreading infection | Usually not dental procedures |
| **A trained layperson (anyone who has learned → 12-06 and → 12-20)** | Prevention teaching; knocked-out tooth first aid; temporary filling material from a kit; recognizing danger signs; pain relief per the label | **No extractions, no injections, no cutting.** These do real harm in untrained hands |

**Off-grid, even a dentist's work narrows** to pulling teeth, draining infection, temporary fillings
and pain control: buying time and removing infection, not rebuilding mouths. **"Not today" is a
complete answer** from anyone: poor light, no clean instruments, exhaustion.

**Nobody uses a professional's instruments or anesthetic on someone else.** Injectable anesthetic
and surgical instruments in untrained hands cause nerve damage, broken-off roots and spreading
infection.

## Prevention: dentistry that never runs out

Anyone can teach this, and it saves more teeth than any procedure (CDC, Oral Health):
- **Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste**, and clean between teeth daily.
- **Sugar less often.** How often sugar touches teeth matters more than how much. Sweet drinks sipped
  all day are the worst.
- **Water after eating** when you cannot brush.
- **Check children's teeth** for white or brown spots, the first stage of decay.
- **Teach it to the neighborhood's children** (→ 18-07). Cheap to give; it compounds for years.

## Sharing dental help fairly

If someone in your household or your neighborhood has dental skills, decide the norms before the
first request. The first time you help sets the price of every time after.

- **Never a price list.** Pricing care for pain in a crisis reads as profiting from suffering, and
  the resentment outlasts anything gained (→ 18-02).
- **Help freely, always, with:** children, true emergencies (the spreading abscess, the knocked-out
  tooth), and first contact with a household you want in your network (→ 18-05). Refusing a child
  over payment would destroy a household's standing.
- **For everything else, goods and help given back as neighborliness, not billed.** "We could use
  hands on the woodpile" or "a few eggs", said after care, not demanded before it. A community that
  owes favors to the person who helps with teeth is a strong security arrangement.
- **The arithmetic:** a pulled tooth costs the helper an hour and a little supply, and is worth a
  week of work to the person in pain. Charging at that gap would be extortion; giving generously turns
  it into standing, which still works in year two (→ 18-03).

## The cost of being known for it

Skills cannot be hidden the way supplies can, and should not be: a skill nobody knows about helps
nobody. But a person known for dental work is presumed to hold **anesthetics, sharp instruments and
pain medicine**, three of the most sought-after things there are (→ 14-03, → 12-07).

- **Let the skill become known gradually, person to person, as trust builds** (→ 18-05). Never
  advertised.
- **Supplies are never on show.** Care happens with one small closed case brought to the moment, not
  in front of an open cabinet. Nobody watching should be able to guess what is in the house.
- **Help away from your stores where possible**; at home, one room, one case.
- **The person is the asset; the stock is the secret.** "She can help with teeth" is the reputation
  to have. Quantities, medicines and locations are never told.
- **Being valued is itself protection.** A community defends the person it cannot afford to lose,
  and that protection grows from generosity, not from charging.

> **Before the collapse:** states have "Good Samaritan" laws that protect people who give
> emergency help in good faith, usually without pay. They are written for emergencies, generally not
> for ongoing treatment or paid care. Licensed dental professionals stay bound by their license
> rules, records and standards of care; a three-day outage is not a license to practice from the
> kitchen, and people should be sent to working care while it exists (→ 12-16). Where the line falls
> in a long breakdown cannot be written in advance. Whoever gives the care decides case by case, and
> writes down why (→ 25-05).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Toothbrushes, fluoride toothpaste, floss, in bulk | Prevention for you, and to give | Cheap goodwill (→ 18-02) |
| A dental first-aid kit: temporary filling material, clove-oil product (adults only, per label), gauze, a tooth-saving solution or container | The lay first aid on → 12-20 | |
| Non-prescription pain relievers | Pain control per the label | → 12-13 |
| A small closed carry case | Supplies stay out of sight | |
| A paper dental first-aid book for laypeople | When no one trained is near | → 18-07 |
| Your exchange norms, written | The first case sets the precedent | This page |

**There is no substitute for a trained person.** The lay fallback is → 12-06 and → 12-20; the
regional fallback is whatever care still works. **Prevention substitutes for treatment** at community
scale.

## When it runs out

- **The scarce resource is the trained person:** one pair of hands, who is also a parent and
  sometimes a patient. Emergencies always; everything else on their schedule, not demand's.
- **Supplies run out and anesthetic expires.** When they do, say so honestly; do not let
  expectations outrun stock (→ 23-02).
- **Goodwill compounds and never expires.** Many small acts of help with teeth buy more security and
  standing than almost any trade good.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** dentists are open. Use them, and send others to them. Stock prevention supplies.
- **B, on the move:** dental first-aid supplies in the medical kit (→ 22-06). A dental skill is a safe
  thing to offer on the road (→ 18-02): it reveals no stores and cannot be stolen. Offer it with the
  usual caution (→ 18-05).
- **C, settled:** anyone with real dental skill becomes a regional asset, and word will travel.
  Decide deliberately how far you will help. If you are moving in with another household, name it as
  a contribution (→ 18-04).

# Finances and documents

**What this section holds.** 8 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 19-01 **The document grab kit**: Making sure your household's papers leave with you.
- → 19-02 **Cash, value and a degraded economy**: Having money you can use when card machines, ATMs and phone payments do not work, and understanding what holds value as a disruption gets longer.
- → 19-03 **Records and backups**: Making sure your household's records survive a fire, a flood, a dead phone and a failed drive.
- → 19-04 **Insurance and claims**: Understanding what your insurance covers before the disaster, and making a claim work after it.
- → 19-05 **Identity protection and fraud after a disaster**: Protecting your household from the scams and identity theft that follow every disaster: contractor scams, fake charities, fake officials and adjusters, and t…
- → 19-06 **Bank access in a crisis**: Understanding which parts of banking stop working in an emergency, and arranging your money and papers so that does not hurt.
- → 19-07 **Access continuity: if one adult is gone**: Making sure that if one adult is in hospital, unable to act, or dead, the others can still pay the bills, reach the insurance, keep income coming, and get in…
- → 19-08 **Income continuity for the self-employed and small business**: Keeping a household's income alive when the adult who earns it cannot work, or when a disaster shuts the business.

pages.body:
# The document grab kit

**What this page is for.** Making sure your household's papers leave with you. The scenario: you have
ten minutes to leave and will not come back, because of a fire, a flood, a storm's aftermath or a
fast evacuation (→ 17-03, → 01-03). **Documents are what people forget and most regret.** Replacing
vital records is possible but slow (USA.gov, Replace Your Vital Documents), and much harder when the
offices that issue them were hit too. Without them you may struggle to prove who you are, get money,
file an insurance claim (→ 19-04), get medical care, or enroll a child in school.

> **CAUTION. Never write safe combinations, passwords, PINs or full account numbers into this app.**
> Write them **by hand on paper**, and keep that paper **separately** from the grab folder (→ 19-07).
> A lost phone or a lost folder should never hand someone both your identity and your keys.
>
> This is a one-afternoon project that costs almost nothing. Do it this month.

## Do this now

1. **Decide where the originals live** (birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, titles,
   wills): one fire-resistant, waterproof place, **off the floor**, that every adult can open.
2. **Assemble the grab folder**: a waterproof zip pouch with a handle, kept **with the go-bags**
   (→ 22-03), holding **copies** of the list below. This is the under-a-minute layer.
3. **Scan everything** and keep the digital copies in two places, one at home and one away from home
   (→ 19-03).
4. **Give a copy of the critical few to someone out of the area**: a relative or friend (→ 15-03). A
   house fire takes the originals and the home backup at once.
5. **Put the medical papers in** (→ 25-09). For many households they matter as much as the identity
   papers.
6. **Test the grab:** can one adult, carrying a child or a bag, pick up the folder and leave in under a
   minute?
7. **Write both locations** on the family plan's "documents are at" line (→ 00-04).

{{photo grab-folder}}

## What goes in

Originals or certified copies where noted; good photocopies otherwise.

| Category | Documents |
|---|---|
| **Identity** | Birth certificates (every member), Social Security cards, passports, driver's licenses or state IDs, marriage certificate, adoption or custody papers, immigration documents |
| **Medical** | Family medical summary (→ 25-09), insurance cards, prescription lists, allergy action plans, vaccination records, clinicians' contacts, and for anyone on a life-critical medicine: the medicine names and strengths, any device models and serial numbers, the prescriber, and a recent pharmacy printout (→ 01-07) |
| **Property** | Deed or mortgage, lease, vehicle titles and registration, home inventory with photos (→ 19-04, → 22-04) |
| **Insurance** | Policies (home or renters, auto, life, health, flood); policy numbers and agent contacts (→ 19-04) |
| **Financial** | Names of your banks and card issuers and their phone numbers; recent statements; recent tax returns; safe-deposit box details; some cash (→ 19-02). **Full account numbers: handwritten, on the separate paper** |
| **Legal** | Wills, powers of attorney, advance directives, trusts, divorce decrees |
| **Contacts** | Printed contact list: family, out-of-area contact, clinicians, insurers, employer (→ 15-03, → 25-03) |
| **Pets** | Vaccination and ownership records; shelters ask for them (→ 20-09) |
| **Children** | School and immunization records, medical cards |

## What matters most for your household

**Your members:** {{#each members as m}}{{m.label}} ({{m.age_text}}); {{/each}}

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}- **Allergy action plans** for every member with a severe allergy (→ 02-03), so any caregiver, shelter
  or clinician knows at once.
{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **Prescription and device details for refrigerated or life-critical medicines**: this is what makes
  an emergency refill possible somewhere unfamiliar (→ 01-07, → 12-07).
{{/if}}- **Insurance cards and numbers**, to get those filled.
- **The family medical summary** (→ 25-09), laminated, with a copy in each go-bag (→ 22-03).
{{#if has.pets}}- **Pet records**: vaccination proof, a recent photo of each animal (→ 20-09).
{{/if}}{{#if has.child}}- **Children's records**: birth certificates, immunizations, custody papers if any.
{{/if}}

**If you could grab only one folder, it is this one.**

## Two layers: originals and the grab folder

Originals belong somewhere secure and fire-resistant. That often means a place that takes a key,
a dial or a combination and a few minutes, which is fine for originals and useless for a
one-minute grab. So the kit has two layers.

{{photo originals-location}}

| Layer | Where | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Originals** | A fire-resistant, waterproof box or safe, **off the floor**, that every adult can open | Birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, titles, deed, wills, powers of attorney, an encrypted backup drive (→ 19-03) |
| **2. Grab folder** | **With the go-bags** (→ 22-03), in a waterproof pouch with a handle, known to everyone and findable in the dark | The laminated medical summary, allergy plans, prescription and device sheet, insurance cards and numbers, printed contacts, **photocopies** of every ID, birth certificate and Social Security card, some cash in small bills (→ 19-02) |

- **One handle, one item.** You should be able to pick it up while carrying a child.
- **Never on a basement floor.** Basements flood first (→ 16-12).
- **"Fire-resistant" ratings have limits.** A serious house fire may still destroy a box's contents,
  which is why the copy kept away from home exists (→ 19-03).
- **Every adult can open the originals box.** If one cannot, fix that this week (→ 19-07). Where the
  key or combination is kept is written on paper, not in this app.
- **Write both locations here:** originals: ______________ grab folder: ______________

## Three copies, three ways to fail

1. **Originals** at home, with the grab folder's copies.
2. **Digital scans**, encrypted, stored at home **and** away from home (→ 19-03).
3. **Paper copies with a trusted person out of the area.**

A fire takes the first and maybe the second; a network failure takes the second; **the third
survives both.**

## Rebuilding what you lost

If documents are destroyed, they can be recovered, slowly:
- **Birth, marriage and death records** come from the vital records office of the state or county
  that issued them (USA.gov). For {{ home.state_name }}, write the office and how to request
  here: ______________________ (→ 25-03).
- **Social Security cards** from the Social Security Administration; **driver's licenses** from the
  state; **passports** from the State Department.
- **Tax records:** the IRS has guidance on rebuilding records after a disaster, including getting
  transcripts of past returns (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a Disaster).
- **Bank and card records** from the institutions (CFPB, Disasters and Emergencies).
- **Property records** from the county recorder or register of deeds. Usually recoverable, since the
  county holds them.
- **Medical records** from clinicians and pharmacies: another reason the contact list is in the
  folder.

**All of it is much easier if you know names, dates and which institutions you use**, which is the
argument for the digital and away-from-home copies.

## The photo inventory: one hour

For insurance and for rebuilding (→ 19-04, → 22-04):
- **Walk through the house filming or photographing every room**, opening closets and drawers, saying
  what things are.
- **Photograph serial numbers** on major items.
- **Photograph storage areas**: food, tools, equipment.
- **Store it away from home** (→ 19-03). **Update it every year** (→ 25-10).

This hour is what makes an insurance claim work.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Fire-resistant, waterproof box or safe | Layer 1: the originals | Off the floor |
| **Grab folder: waterproof pouch with a handle** | Layer 2: the one-minute grab | With the go-bags |
| Certified copies of vital records | Faster than replacing later | Order now |
| **Laminated family medical summary and copies** | The medical priority | → 25-09 |
| Photocopies with someone out of the area | Layer 3 | |
| Cash in small bills | Early disruption is cash-only | → 19-02 |
| Scanner or phone, and encrypted storage | The digital layer | → 19-03 |
| Encrypted USB drive plus an online backup | Two digital copies, different failures | → 19-03 |
| Printed contact list | Phones die | → 25-03 |
| Zip bags inside the folder | Findable under stress | |

**Substitutes:** any waterproof container: a dry bag, a sealed metal ammunition can, doubled zip bags
in a hard case. Something today beats something perfect never. **Phone photos of documents** are
better than nothing and worse than paper, since the phone dies. **A relative's house** is a good place
for the third copy.

## When it runs out

- **Documents do not run out; they go out of date.** Review every year (→ 25-10): expired IDs and
  passports, changed policies, changed medicines, new clinicians, children's records as they grow.
- **Renew IDs before they lapse.** Replacement offices may be closed exactly when you need them.
- **Check the digital copies still exist and still open** (→ 19-03). A backup nobody has checked is a
  hope, not a backup.
- **Most documents can be rebuilt; the cost is time**, and time is what you will be short of.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** assemble the grab folder this week, back up three ways, test the grab, do the photo
  inventory.
- **B, on the move:** both layers go: the grab folder on a person, the originals box in the vehicle if
  it is portable. After medicines, papers are the highest-priority cargo that is not used up.
- **C, settled:** same kit, kept the same way. Add the new place's papers, and set up a new
  away-from-home copy with someone you trust. It matters more far from everything, not less.

pages.body:
# Cash, value and a degraded economy

**What this page is for.** Having money you can use when card machines, ATMs and phone payments do
not work, and understanding what holds value as a disruption gets longer. **The single most useful
fact here: in the first hours and days of almost any disruption, cash works and cards do not.** Card
readers, ATMs and payment networks all need power and connections (→ 17-08). Shops that stay open go
cash-only, and ATMs empty fast. Most households have no cash at all.

> **CAUTION. Cash is also a security item** (→ 14-03). Keep it discreet, split up, and do not talk
> about it. **Never type account numbers, PINs or passwords into this app**; anything like that is
> written by hand on paper kept separately (→ 19-07).

## Do this now

1. **Get cash in small bills:** fives, tens and twenties, **not hundreds**, because nobody will make
   change, and trying shows you have more.
2. **Split it:** a main reserve in your most secure place at home, and smaller amounts in the grab
   folder (→ 19-01), each go-bag (→ 22-03) and {{#if has.vehicle}}each vehicle (→ 22-05){{else}}any
   vehicle you use{{/if}}. Never all in one place, and never all behind a lock that takes minutes.
3. **Write on paper** the names and phone numbers of your banks, credit unions and card issuers, and
   keep it in the grab folder (→ 19-01).
4. **Have more than one way to reach money:** two institutions, a credit card with room on it, and
   cash. One point of failure is a real risk (→ 19-06).

> **Before the collapse:** bank deposits are insured by the FDIC, and credit union deposits by the
> NCUA, up to $250,000 per depositor, per institution, per ownership category (FDIC,
> Understanding Deposit Insurance; NCUA, Share Insurance Coverage). Know which insurer covers each
> of your accounts.

## How a broken economy goes

| Stage | What works | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Cards, phone payments, cash | **Prepare now** |
| **Hours to days** (outage, storm) | **Cash only.** ATMs down or empty; card readers dead | This is what the cash is for |
| Weeks (regional disruption) | Cash, but prices rise sharply and some goods are gone | Cash still works; scarcity is the problem |
| Months (severe) | Cash matters less as supply fails; goods and skills start to matter (→ 18-02, → 18-03) | Barter grows beside cash |
| Long-term collapse | Barter, reciprocity, local exchange | Skills and relationships are the currency (→ 18-01) |

**Most real events stop at the second or third stage.** Cash covers the great majority of realistic
scenarios, which makes it the most valuable financial preparation by far.

## How much cash, and how

- **Small bills.**
- **Enough for what?** A useful measure: a full tank of fuel, a few days of food and supplies, and a
  night's lodging, per adult. Adjust to what you can afford.
- **Split it** (step 2 above).
- **Keep some in the vehicle**: evacuation is when you will want it (→ 01-03).
- **Dry and discreet:** a waterproof bag, not an obvious place.
- **A few coins** for vending machines and parking.
- **Do not talk about it** (→ 14-03).

## Banks and access

From the CFPB's disaster guidance (CFPB, Disasters and Emergencies) and the FDIC:
- **Two institutions are better than one**: a bank and a credit union, ideally.
- **Know how to reach each without the internet**: a phone number and a branch address, on paper.
- **Know your available credit.** A card with room on it is a resource while payment systems work.
- **Know what is on automatic payment** and what happens if it fails. Creditors are often
  accommodating after a disaster if you contact them early (CFPB).
- **Disaster financial help exists** (USA.gov, Find Disaster Financial Help). Write down where to
  find it (→ 25-03).

**Account worksheet: fill this in BY HAND, on paper only.** Print or copy this blank and keep the
filled copy with your originals (→ 19-01), not in the app. Use only the **last four digits** and no
passwords, so a lost paper is not a lost account. Full numbers and sign-in details stay on the
separate paper described on → 19-07.

```
ON PAPER ONLY
Institution       Account type     Last 4   How to reach it          Sign-in needs
                                            (branch / phone / app)   (texts a code? to whose phone?)
______________    ____________     ____     ____________________     __________________
______________    ____________     ____     ____________________     __________________
______________    ____________     ____     ____________________     __________________
______________    ____________     ____     ____________________     __________________
Business accounts (19-08):
______________    ____________     ____     ____________________     __________________
Updated (date): __________   Every adult can reach each row: see 19-07
```

## What holds value: the honest version

- **Cash is the most useful store of value for realistic scenarios.** It works in the stages where
  nearly everything actually lands.
- **Precious metals** are a long-term store of value, not a practical way to pay in a crisis. When
  cash has failed, nobody makes change for a gold coin, and most people cannot tell real from fake.
  They also mark you as worth robbing (→ 14-03). **This binder recommends no investment**; buying
  metals is a financial decision, not a preparedness one.
- **The best stores of value in a long disruption are goods and skills** (→ 18-02, → 18-03), and
  unlike metals, they are useful even if nothing bad happens: fasteners, matches, soap, seeds, salt,
  and the ability to fix things.
- **Fuel, food and medicine hold great value in scarcity**, and are exactly what you should be
  slowest to trade.

## Insurance and assistance

- **Insurance is the main financial protection** against realistic disasters: fire, wind, hail,
  flood (→ 19-04). **Standard homeowner's policies usually do not cover flood** (→ 17-03).
- **Disaster assistance programs exist** (USA.gov). Keep the papers that let you use them (→ 19-01,
  → 19-04).
- **The photo inventory** (→ 19-01) is what makes a claim work.

## Medicine: the expense that cannot wait

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Your household has refrigerated or life-critical medicines**
({{#each refrigerated_meds as r}}{{r.name}}; {{/each}}).{{/if}} For any household member whose
medicine cannot be skipped, a money problem quickly becomes a medical emergency (→ 12-11).
- **Know your insurance, your pharmacy, and the manufacturer assistance programs** for each such
  medicine. Look them up now and write them down (→ 12-07).
- **A cash reserve set aside for medicine** is a legitimate part of the plan.
- **For such a household, financial capacity is medical capacity.**

## The ordinary resilience that matters most

Not exciting, and it does more than any stockpile for realistic scenarios:
- **An emergency fund**, the most useful preparedness asset most households can build.
- **Low debt**: less fragility, more room to move.
- **More than one income path** where possible (→ 19-08).
- **Insurance in force and understood** (→ 19-04).
- **Records organized** (→ 19-01, → 19-03).
- **Knowing your fixed bills** and what happens if one is missed.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Cash in small bills, split across places** | Works when nothing else does | 5s, 10s, 20s |
| Cash in the vehicle | Evacuation | → 22-05 |
| **Institution names and phone numbers on paper** | You will need them without a device | → 19-01 |
| Accounts at two institutions | No single point of failure | |
| Insurance policies and agent contacts | → 19-04 | Copies in the grab folder |
| Medicine cost and assistance details | The expense that cannot wait | → 12-07 |
| A waterproof bag for the cash | Fire and flood | |
| An emergency fund | The most useful asset most households can build | |
| Trade goods | When cash stops working | → 18-02 |

**Substitutes:** skills (→ 18-03), goods everyone needs (→ 18-02), labor, and relationships
(→ 18-01). **What you cannot substitute is cash in the first days.**

## When it runs out

- **Cash runs out fast in a long event**, and buys less as goods get scarce. Plan for days to weeks,
  not months.
- **What replaces it, in order:** cash, then goods, then skills, then relationships. Each lasts longer
  and is harder to spend.
- **Spend cash early on what will become unavailable** (fuel, medicine, specific supplies), not on
  what will still be there.
- **In a developing situation, acting early with cash is usually right**; the window closes fast
  (→ 17-09). Panic-buying in front of your neighbors has real costs (→ 18-01). Being ready beforehand
  resolves both.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** cash covers the realistic scenarios. Keep the fund, insurance and records in order,
  and be able to pay for medicine without notice.
- **B, on the move:** cash and the grab folder (→ 19-01) are the financial plan. Split the cash between
  adults and vehicles. Fuel will be the main expense and the first thing to vanish.
- **C, settled:** local exchange matters more (→ 18-02). Cash keeps working a long time in rural
  communities; over years, skills and produce become the practical currency.

pages.body:
# Records and backups

**What this page is for.** Making sure your household's records survive a fire, a flood, a dead phone
and a failed drive. **The rule: three copies, two formats, one away from home.** Three copies, so one
failure does not lose everything. Two formats (paper and digital), because they fail differently. One
away from home, because fire and flood take everything in the house at once (→ 17-03). Most
households have one copy, in one format, in one place.

> **Digital-only records depend on a device, a battery, a file format and a network**, and in this
> binder's scenarios all four are unreliable (→ 09-06, → 17-08). **Paper is the format that
> survives.**
>
> **Passwords, PINs, safe combinations and account numbers are never typed into this app.** The few
> you need in a crisis are written by hand on paper and kept separately (below, and → 19-07).

## Do this now

1. **Print what matters:** the key pages of this binder (use the app's PDF export, → 00-10), the
   medical summary (→ 25-09), the contact list (→ 25-03), the family plan (→ 15-03) and the document
   list (→ 19-01). A file on a dead phone is not a record you can use.
2. **Do the photo inventory of the house**, an hour with a phone (→ 19-01, → 22-04).
3. **Set up the away-from-home copy**: a relative, a friend, a safe-deposit box, or encrypted online
   storage. This month.
4. **Check that a backup actually opens.** An unchecked backup is a hope, not a backup.

## The three copies

| Copy | Format | Where | What kills it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Originals** | Paper | Your originals box, off the floor; grab-folder copies with the go-bags (→ 19-01) | Fire, flood, leaving in a hurry (the grab folder is the fix) |
| **2. Digital scans** | Encrypted files | A drive at home **and** a second drive or online storage away from home | Device failure, ransomware, no power, no network |
| **3. Paper copies** | Photocopies | **Out of the area**, with a relative or friend | Nothing local. This is the one that survives the house burning |

Each layer covers the others' failures. That is the design.

## What to back up

- **Documents** (→ 19-01): identity, medical, property, insurance, financial, legal.
- **Medical records** (→ 25-09): prescriptions, device details, allergy plans, clinicians' contacts,
  vaccination records. For many households, as important as identity papers.
- **The photo inventory** (→ 22-04): every room, closets open, serial numbers, storage areas. It is
  what makes an insurance claim work (→ 19-04).
- **Family photographs.** What people most regret losing, and almost always digital-only. **Print the
  important ones** (→ 21-03).
- **This binder.** On more than one device, with the key pages printed (→ 18-07).
- **Your own household records** (→ 25-05): consumption logs, garden notes, weather, medical logs. Over
  years they become more useful than any published reference.

## Digital, done sensibly

- **Encrypt anything with identity or financial information on it.** A lost unencrypted drive is an
  identity-theft event (FTC, Identity Theft: Report and Recover; → 19-05).
- **Two digital places, not one:** two drives kept in different places, or a drive plus online
  storage. **One drive travels** (with the grab folder or a go-bag) and **one stays home**, never both
  in the same place.
- **Check that it opens.** Restore one file as a test, every year (→ 25-10).
- **Use formats anyone can open:** PDF and plain text outlast formats that need special software.
- **Keep the encryption password where you will still have it**: on the separate paper (below). A
  backup you cannot unlock is not a backup, and this is a very common failure.
- **Online storage works until the internet does not**, which is the scenario this binder plans for.
  It is a layer, not the plan.
- **Protect drives and spare devices from a power surge or worse** (→ 27-03).

## Passwords: the awkward one

- **A password manager is the right answer in normal times.** It depends on a device and possibly a
  network.
- **For a crisis, you need the critical few on paper:** bank access, insurance and medical portals,
  and **the email account that resets everything else** (→ 19-07). Every adult must be able to use
  them without help.
- **Write them by hand. Never type them into this app.** Keep the sheet **in your most secure place
  at home, separate from the grab folder** (→ 19-01). A locked box in the house is reasonable; a pouch
  by the door or a note in a wallet is not. That is a security trade-off; make it knowingly.
- **Do not keep a password on the same paper or drive as the thing it unlocks.** A lost bag should
  never carry both the encrypted drive and its key.
- **Two-step sign-in** (a code sent to your phone) protects you normally and **can lock you out when
  the phone is dead or lost** (→ 09-06). **Print the backup codes** each service offers and keep them
  with the password sheet.

## Paper: the format that survives

- **No power, device, network or format needed; anyone can read it** (→ 18-07).
- **Dry and off the floor.** Basements flood (→ 17-03).
- **Fire is paper's weakness**, which the away-from-home copy solves.
- **Pencil or waterproof ink** for anything handwritten. **Inkjet printing runs when wet.**
- **Laminate the critical cards:** medical summary, family plan, emergency contacts.

## Rebuilding what is lost

Possible, and slow (→ 19-01): vital records from the issuing state or county (USA.gov); tax records
using the IRS's disaster guidance, including transcripts (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a
Disaster); bank records from the institutions (CFPB); property records from the county, usually
intact; medical records from clinicians and pharmacies; insurance from your company (→ 19-04).
**All of it goes faster if you know the names, institutions and dates.**

## The yearly review (→ 25-10)

- Documents current? Expired IDs, changed policies, changed medicines.
- Backups checked? Do they open?
- Away-from-home copy updated?
- Photo inventory refreshed?
- Medical summary current, especially as children grow?
- Contact list current?
- Printed binder pages current?

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Printer, paper, ink, or access to one | The format that survives | Library or workplace printers work |
| Scanner or phone | The digital layer | |
| **Two encrypted USB drives** | Layer 2, in two places | One travels, one stays; check yearly |
| Online storage account | A different failure again | Not the whole plan |
| Waterproof, fire-resistant document box | Layer 1 | → 19-01 |
| **An away-from-home arrangement** | Layer 3: survives the house burning | This month |
| Laminating pouches | Medical cards, family plan | |
| Bound notebooks and pencils | Household records | Pencil survives wet |
| Prints of important photos | What people most regret losing | |

**Substitutes:** a relative's house is a perfect away-from-home copy and costs nothing. Phone photos
of documents are better than nothing and worse than paper. Handwritten copies of contacts and medical
details. **What you cannot substitute is doing it before the event.**

## When it runs out

- **Records do not run out; they go stale and get lost.** The upkeep is the yearly review.
- **Digital storage fails silently:** drives die, accounts lapse, formats age, passwords are lost.
  Check yearly, or assume it is gone.
- **Paper ages slowly and predictably**, which is why it is the main format here.
- **Your own records grow more valuable every year**, and exist only if you write them down.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** do all of it now. Every part of this page needs working infrastructure, which you
  have today.
- **B, on the move:** the grab folder and one drive travel; the away-from-home copy protects you if
  the house is lost while you are gone.
- **C, settled:** set up a new away-from-home copy with someone you trust. Keep the household records
  going; at a new place, your own observations become the reference nobody else has.
