review_pass.notes: NFIP 30-day wait and exceptions verified (FEMA FloodSmart, read live); basement-contents wording corrected; NRI rating caveat added.

pages.body:
# Insurance and claims

**What this page is for.** Understanding what your insurance covers before the disaster, and making a
claim work after it. Insurance is the main financial protection against the disasters that actually
happen to most households: fire, wind, hail, storms, freezing damage and flood. It is also the thing
most households have never read.

**Your home county's main hazards:**
{{#each region.home.hazards as h}}- {{h.name}}: {{h.rating_text}}
{{/each}}
These ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index). They weigh how much
there is to damage as well as how often a hazard strikes, so "low" is not a promise that it will
not happen to you. Your state page in Section 32 explains them.

> **CAUTION. Two things that surprise people, both worth knowing now.**
> 1. **Standard homeowner's and renter's policies usually do not cover flood.** Flood coverage is a
>    separate policy, and **it does not start the day you buy it**: you cannot buy it when the water
>    is rising (→ 17-03).{{#if is.flood_region}} **Your county's flood rating is high: ask about it
>    this week.**{{/if}}
> 2. **Limits, deductibles and exclusions vary enormously**, especially for wind and hail, which
>    sometimes carry a separate, higher deductible{{#if is.hurricane_region}}, and for hurricanes,
>    which often have their own deductible{{/if}}{{#if is.earthquake_region}}; earthquake damage is
>    usually excluded unless you add it{{/if}}.
>
> **This page cannot tell you what your policy covers. Read it, and call your agent.**

> **Before the collapse:** a National Flood Insurance Program policy takes effect 30 days after
> you buy it. The exceptions are narrow, such as buying it while making, increasing, extending or
> renewing a mortgage (FEMA FloodSmart, Buy a Policy). A private flood policy has its own terms;
> ask. NFIP policies do not cover personal property kept in a basement, temporary housing while
> the home is repaired, or sewer backup unless it is caused directly by flooding (FEMA FloodSmart).
> FEMA's flood maps show whether an address is in a mapped flood zone; your agent can look it up.

## Do this now

1. **Read your actual policy:** coverage limits, deductibles, exclusions, and whether wind and hail
   have their own deductible. One afternoon, once.
2. **Ask your agent three questions:** Am I covered for flood? Is my dwelling coverage enough to
   rebuild at today's costs? What is my wind and hail deductible?
3. **Ask two more if you have a basement:** what a flood policy pays for in the basement, and
   whether you can add **sewer and sump-pump backup** coverage (→ 17-08). That is the water event many
   houses actually have.
4. **Do the photo inventory** (→ 19-01, → 22-04), an hour with a phone, stored away from home. This is
   what makes a claim work.
5. **Put policies, policy numbers and agents' phone numbers in the grab folder** (→ 19-01).

## Coverage worth checking

| Hazard | Typical situation. **Check your own policy** |
|---|---|
| Hail | Often a separate, higher deductible; older roofs may be paid at depreciated value, not replacement cost |
| Wind and tornado | Usually covered; check the deductible |
| Hurricane | Often its own deductible; storm surge counts as flood |
| Fire and wildfire | Usually covered |
| Ice and winter storm | Often covered; burst-pipe damage may depend on whether the home was heated and maintained |
| **Flood** | **Usually NOT covered.** Separate policy with a waiting period; NFIP policies do not cover personal property kept in a basement. Seepage and sump failure are not "flood" without wider flooding |
| **Sewer and drain backup** | **Often excluded unless added.** A real risk when power fails and a sump pump stops |
| Earthquake | Usually excluded unless added |
| Food spoiled in an outage | Sometimes covered, with limits (→ 04-17) |
| Additional living expenses | Pays for somewhere to stay if the home cannot be lived in. Check the limit |
| Personal property | **Replacement cost versus "actual cash value" (depreciated) is the big difference** |
| Special limits | Firearms, jewelry, cash and electronics often have low limits. Check, and list valuable items separately if needed |

## Is the house itself insured for enough?

**The most common serious gap is too little coverage on the building.** Building costs rise, and a
policy written years ago may not pay to rebuild today.
- Ask whether your dwelling limit reflects current rebuilding costs.
- Ask about "extended" or "guaranteed" replacement cost if offered.
- It matters most in exactly the case where you need it: a total loss.

## Insuring the people, not just the house

Property policies protect things. These protect the plan:
- **Life insurance on every adult whose income or work the household depends on.** A chronic
  condition often raises the price; it does not always rule coverage out. Get quotes; do not assume
  the answer.
- **Disability insurance** for anyone whose income depends on their ability to do their job,
  especially if self-employed (→ 19-08).
- **Beneficiaries checked on every policy**, and matching your will and other documents (→ 19-07).

**Adults in your household:** {{#each adults as a}}{{a.label}}; {{/each}}

**Coverage worksheet: fill in by hand from the actual documents.** No policy numbers in the app; the
filled copy goes in the grab folder (→ 19-01).

```
ON PAPER
Policy               Company         Policy no.     Amount / benefit   Beneficiary   Reviewed
Life: __________     ____________    ___________    $__________        ___________   ________
Life: __________     ____________    ___________    $__________        ___________   ________
Disability: _______  ____________    ___________    $______/month      n/a           ________
Home or renters      ____________    ___________    $__________        n/a           ________
Auto                 ____________    ___________    $__________        n/a           ________
Umbrella             ____________    ___________    $__________        n/a           ________
Flood                ____________    ___________    $__________        n/a           ________
Business (19-08)     ____________    ___________    $__________        n/a           ________
```

## The inventory decides whether a claim works

The most useful hour you can spend on insurance (→ 22-04, → 19-03):
- **Video every room**, talking as you go. Open closets, cabinets and drawers.
- **Photograph serial numbers** on major items.
- **Photograph storage areas:** food, tools, equipment and your preparedness supplies. They are real
  money, and people routinely forget to claim them.
- **Keep receipts** for significant purchases where you can.
- **Store it away from home** (→ 19-03). An inventory that burns with the house is no inventory.
- **Update it every year** (→ 25-10).

**Without it you rebuild a list from memory under stress, and you will under-claim badly.**

```
PHOTO / VIDEO INVENTORY
Done? ____  Date: __________  By: __________
Stored away from home where (19-03): ____________________
Second copy: ____________________
Supplies and storage areas included? ____  Serial numbers? ____
Refreshed at yearly review (25-10): __________
```

## Making a claim

From the CFPB's disaster guidance (CFPB, Disasters and Emergencies) and common practice:
1. **Safety first** (→ 17-02, → 17-03). The claim can wait.
2. **Contact the insurer as soon as practical.** Many have 24-hour claim lines. Write down the claim
   number and the adjuster's name.
3. **Document the damage before cleaning up:** many photos and video. **Do not throw out damaged
   property until it is documented or the adjuster has seen it**, unless it is a health hazard, such
   as flood-soaked food or moldy materials (CDC, Preparing for Floods).
4. **Make reasonable temporary repairs** to stop more damage: tarp the roof, board the window
   (→ 16-12). Keep receipts; this is usually covered. **No permanent repairs before the adjuster
   sees it.**
5. **Keep a log** of every call: date, name, what was said (→ 25-05).
6. **Keep every receipt** for lodging, meals and supplies if you are displaced. Additional living
   expenses are often covered.
7. **Read what you are asked to sign.**
8. **If you disagree with the settlement**, ask about the appraisal process in your policy. The
   regulator to contact is the {{ home.state_name }} state insurance department. Phone:
   ______________ (also on → 25-03).

## Help beyond insurance

Federal and state disaster assistance exists, separate from insurance (USA.gov, Find Disaster
Financial Help).
- It usually requires a declared disaster and adds to insurance rather than replacing it.
- It requires documents (→ 19-01, → 19-03).
- The IRS has disaster guidance on records and on casualty losses (IRS, Reconstructing Records After
  a Disaster).
- Write down where to find help now (→ 25-03).

## The honest limit

**Insurance works in a working society.** It covers the fire, the tornado, the hailstorm: bounded
disasters, which are also the most likely ones. **In a long collapse, insurance is not a plan**:
claims will not be paid and money may not buy anything (→ 19-02). That is fine; it is not what
insurance is for. Most bad things that actually happen to a household are the bounded kind, and for
those, a policy you have read and an inventory you have made are worth more than almost anything else
in this binder.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Your policy, read** | Almost nobody has | An afternoon, once |
| **Photo and video inventory, stored away from home** | What makes a claim work | → 22-04 |
| Policies, numbers and agent contacts in the grab folder | You will need them when the house is gone | → 19-01 |
| Flood coverage, if it applies | Not in standard policies; waiting period | → 17-03 |
| Sewer and sump backup coverage | Real risk in an outage | → 17-08 |
| Valuable items listed separately on the policy | Above the low sub-limits | |
| Receipts for significant purchases | Support the claim | Photograph them |
| A claim log notebook | Every call, date, name | → 25-05 |
| Tarps, plastic sheeting, boards | Temporary repairs | → 16-12 |

**Substitutes:** the inventory can be done today with a phone. Photos of anything you cannot document
formally. Neighbors as witnesses to damage and to what you had (→ 18-01). **What you cannot
substitute is coverage not bought before the event, or the flood waiting period.**

## When it runs out

- **Coverage lapses if premiums are not paid**, a real risk in a financial disruption (→ 19-02).
  Insurers and lenders are often accommodating if you contact them early (CFPB).
- **Review every year:** coverage against rebuilding costs, the inventory, and changes in your life.
- **Substitutes:** the emergency fund (→ 19-02), disaster assistance, and your neighbors, who are
  the help that actually arrives first (→ 18-01).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** read the policy, close the gaps, do the inventory, store it away from home. All of
  this only works before the event.
- **B, on the move:** the grab folder holds the policy details; the away-from-home inventory supports
  a claim if the house is lost while you are gone.
- **C, settled:** redo it all for the new place. Rural properties raise different questions:
  outbuildings, wells, livestock, distance from a fire station. Ask before you commit (→ 01-05).

review_pass.notes: FTC line 1-877-438-4338, freeze/fraud-alert facts and FTC recovery-step order verified (FTC recovery plan, read live); FEMA no-fee line re-cited.

pages.body:
# Identity protection and fraud after a disaster

**What this page is for.** Protecting your household from the scams and identity theft that follow
every disaster: contractor scams, fake charities, fake officials and adjusters, and theft using
papers and mail lost in the chaos. One of the most consistent harms after a disaster, and largely
preventable. It works two ways: **papers and mail are exposed** (a damaged house, a displaced family,
mail going to an empty address), and **people under stress decide fast**, which is exactly what scams
are built on (→ 21-01).

> **CAUTION. Urgency, plus contact you did not ask for, plus a request for money or personal
> information, is a scam, essentially always.** Hang up, and call back on a number you find yourself:
> the one on your policy, card or statement.
>
> **The FTC is the federal agency for reporting and recovering from identity theft**; its identity
> theft line is 1-877-438-4338 (FTC, Identity Theft: A Recovery Plan). Write it on your contact
> list now (→ 25-03).

## Do this now

1. **Consider a credit freeze at all three national credit bureaus, for every adult.** A freeze stops
   anyone opening new credit in your name. It is free, you can lift it when you need credit, and it is
   the strongest protection against new-account fraud. It does not affect your credit score (FTC,
   What To Know About Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts).
2. **Consider freezes for the children too.** Child identity theft is real and goes unnoticed for
   years, usually until the child first applies for credit as an adult. A parent can request a free
   freeze for a child under 16; each bureau has its own steps (FTC, What To Know About Credit Freezes
   and Fraud Alerts).
3. **Write down** the FTC line above and the three bureaus' phone numbers (→ 25-03).
4. **Secure your papers** (→ 19-01). The same box that protects against loss protects against
   exposure.
5. **Turn on account alerts** with your bank and card issuers while systems work.

**Members to freeze:** {{#each members as m}}{{m.label}} (frozen? __); {{/each}}

## The post-disaster scams

| Scam | How it works | Defense |
|---|---|---|
| Contractor fraud | Door-to-door "we're working in the area", wants a large deposit, disappears | **Never pay much up front.** Check licensing. Get it in writing. Use established local firms |
| Fake adjusters or inspectors | Claim to be from your insurer or the government; ask for information or fees | **Call your insurer yourself** on the number on your policy (→ 19-04). Real officials do not demand payment |
| Charity fraud | Fake relief groups, urgent appeals | Give to organizations you already know |
| Advance-fee "assistance" | "Pay a fee to get your grant" | **Federal agencies never charge you for disaster assistance, and FEMA never charges for an inspection** (FEMA, Disaster Fraud) |
| Identity theft | Using papers, mail or information exposed in the chaos | Freezes, alerts, secured papers |
| Price gouging | Often illegal | Report to the state attorney general (→ 25-03) |
| Phishing | Fake texts and emails about claims, aid or accounts | **Never tap the link.** Contact the organization yourself |

## Why a disaster exposes you

- **Papers scattered or reachable** in a damaged house.
- **Mail going to an empty or damaged address.** If you are displaced, ask the Postal Service to hold
  or forward it.
- **Personal details shared with many parties** during recovery (insurers, contractors, agencies), any
  of whom can be impersonated.
- **Stress and distraction** (→ 21-01), the reason scams work.
- **Debris and discarded paper.** Shred or burn anything with identifying information; do not put it
  on the debris pile (→ 13-03).

## Freezes and alerts

- **A freeze blocks new credit accounts** being opened in your name. Free to place and to lift at all
  three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), and you can lift it temporarily when you apply for
  credit (FTC).
- **A fraud alert** is lighter: it asks lenders to check it is really you. A free alert placed with
  one bureau is passed to the other two and lasts one year (FTC, Identity Theft: A Recovery Plan). A
  freeze is stronger.
- **Do it for every member, children included.**

## If it happens: the recovery path (FTC)

The FTC's first three steps, in its order (FTC, Identity Theft: A Recovery Plan):
1. **Call the companies where you know fraud happened.** Ask them to close or freeze those
   accounts, and change the logins, passwords and PINs.
2. **Place a fraud alert and get your credit reports.** Go through them and note anything you do
   not recognize.
3. **Report it to the FTC** (line above). The online report produces an official identity theft
   report and a recovery plan.

Then:
4. **Consider a freeze** with each bureau, if you have not already.
5. **File a police report** if you know who did it or a company asks for one.
6. **Keep a record of everything:** dates, names, what was said (→ 25-05).
7. **Follow the plan through.** Recovery is a process, not one call.

## Angles that matter for some households

- **Medical identity theft:** someone using your health insurance. Read the "explanation of benefits"
  statements your insurer sends. {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}For a household with expensive ongoing
  prescriptions, this could interfere with getting the medicine you actually need (→ 12-07).{{/if}}
- **Children's identities:** freeze them, and check periodically that no credit file exists.
- **Papers in a go-bag are papers outside a safe** (→ 22-03). Worth knowing; the trade-off still
  favors having copies with you.
- **A displaced household is an exposed household:** mail, address and papers all in flux.

## Information hygiene (→ 14-03)

- **Do not discuss money or accounts in public**, including on radio, which anyone can hear (→ 15-02).
- **Do not post about being away from home.**
- **Check before sharing anything**: call the organization yourself, on a number you looked up.
- **Shred or burn** papers you discard.
- **Distrust urgency.** Legitimate organizations will let you call them back.

## The everyday version, which matters more

Most identity theft has nothing to do with disasters:
- **Freezes on every member.** Free, effective, lasting.
- **Account alerts** on bank accounts and cards.
- **Check credit reports.** A look every few months is plenty.
- **Strong, unique passwords and a password manager** (→ 19-03).
- **Two-step sign-in, with the backup codes printed on paper** (→ 19-03), so a dead phone does not
  lock you out (→ 09-06).
- **Papers secured at home** (→ 19-01).

> **Before the collapse:** federal law lets you get a free credit report from each of the three
> bureaus every 12 months, and the bureaus have permanently extended free weekly reports
> (FTC, Free Credit Reports). Placing and lifting a freeze is free (FTC).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Credit freezes, every member** | Free, reversible, strongest protection | |
| FTC line and bureau numbers, on paper | The official recovery path | → 25-03 |
| Account alerts turned on | Early warning | |
| Waterproof, secure document box | Against exposure and loss | → 19-01 |
| Shredder, or burn safely | Discarded paper is a way in | → 13-03 |
| Password manager and **printed backup codes** | Security that survives a dead phone | → 19-03 |
| Your insurer's real phone number, on paper | To check anyone claiming to be an adjuster | → 19-04 |
| State attorney general or consumer protection number | Gouging and contractor fraud | → 25-03 |
| A log notebook | Dates, names, what was said | → 25-05 |

**Substitutes:** skepticism is free and is most of the defense. **Calling back on a number you found
yourself** defeats nearly every impersonation scam. **Neighbors**: word travels fast about a scammer
working a street (→ 18-01). **What you cannot substitute is the freeze, done in advance.**

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here runs out.** Freezes stay; skepticism does not wear out.
- **Attention lapses.** Review every year (→ 25-10): freezes still on, alerts still set, children's
  files checked, passwords current.
- **Risk rises during and after any disruption and stays high for months.** Stay skeptical longer than
  feels necessary.
- **If something does happen, recovery depends on proving what is yours** (→ 19-03).
- **Fraud after a disaster is far more likely than most scenarios in this binder.** A ten-minute,
  free credit freeze is one of the best returns on any page here.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** freezes and alerts now. After any local disaster, expect contractor and adjuster
  scams within days. Check everything, and warn the neighbors.
- **B, on the move:** keep the grab folder on a person (→ 19-01), hold your mail, and be especially
  wary of anyone offering help that costs money.
- **C, settled:** fewer door-to-door scams, but remote and displaced households are targeted for that
  reason. The freeze protects wherever you are.

pages.title: Bank access in a crisis

review_pass.notes: FDIC 'box contents not insured' verified (FDIC Understanding Deposit Insurance, read live).

pages.body:
# Bank access in a crisis

**What this page is for.** Understanding which parts of banking stop working in an emergency, and
arranging your money and papers so that does not hurt. Card networks, ATMs, online banking, branches
and safe-deposit boxes all depend on power, staff and connections (→ 17-08). In most of this binder's
scenarios, some or all of them stop. **The rule this page exists to print: nothing you need in the
first 72 hours depends on a bank being open.**

> **CAUTION. A safe-deposit box is a vault with banker's hours.** It is excellent at one thing,
> surviving a fire, flood or burglary at your house, and useless at another: being reachable on a bad
> day. Nights, weekends, holidays, outages, evacuations: the box might as well be on the moon. **So
> nothing crisis-needed lives only in the box.**
>
> **This page never asks for account numbers, PINs, passwords or combinations, and you should never
> type them into this app.** Anything like that is written by hand on paper kept separately (→ 19-07).

> **Before the collapse:** the FDIC insures bank **deposits**, not the contents of a safe-deposit box
> (FDIC, Understanding Deposit Insurance). A box rented in one person's name can be sealed for a time when that
> person dies, until the estate is authorized to open it. Rules differ by state and bank; ask yours.

## Do this now

1. **Count how many ways your household can reach money:** institutions, cards, cash. If the answer
   is one, add a second institution (→ 19-02).
2. **Keep cash at home, split** (→ 19-02), because the box, the ATM and the card reader fail on the
   same days.
3. **On paper, list each institution's name, its phone number and the nearest branch address**, and put
   the list in the grab folder (→ 19-01). No account numbers on that list.
4. **If you rent a safe-deposit box:** list what is in it, check each item against the rule below, and
   ask the bank two questions (below).
5. **Make sure more than one adult can reach each account and the box** (→ 19-07).

## What stops working, and when

| Service | Fails when | What covers it |
|---|---|---|
| Card payments | Power or network out at the shop | Cash in small bills (→ 19-02) |
| ATMs | Power out, network down, or emptied | Cash at home |
| Online and app banking | Your phone or the network is down; a sign-in code goes to a dead phone | Paper backup codes (→ 19-03); phone number on paper |
| Branches | Closed for the storm, staff cannot get in, power out | A second institution; cash |
| Safe-deposit box | Nights, weekends, holidays, any closure | Home copies of anything needed soon |
| Transfers and direct deposit | Bank or payment system disruption | Cash; a buffer in more than one account |

## Safe-deposit box rules

| The box is | The box is not |
|---|---|
| The most burglar-, fire- and flood-resistant storage you can rent | **Reachable outside branch hours** |
| A copy that survives your house burning (→ 19-03) | **Reachable in an outage, evacuation or bank disruption** |
| The right home for originals you need only after a crisis | **Insured**: the FDIC covers deposits, not box contents |
| Cheap | **Guaranteed reachable after the renter dies** |

1. **Nothing crisis-needed lives only in the box.** If losing access to the box for a month would
   hurt in that month, a copy lives at home (→ 19-01).
2. **Originals needed for rebuilding, not surviving, belong in the box:** deeds, vehicle titles, extra
   certified birth and marriage certificates, a copy of the will.
3. **The grab folder must work without the box.** Test it against "the bank never reopens".
4. **More than one adult can open it**: joint rental, or the bank's authorized-deputy arrangement,
   confirmed in writing, not assumed (→ 19-07).
5. **The original will does not live only in a box that might be sealed.** The lawyer keeps a copy,
   and its location is written on → 19-07.

**Two questions for your bank** (write the answers here):
- Who besides the renter can open the box today? ______________________
- What happens to the box when a renter dies? ______________________

**Box contents list** (names of items only): ______________________________________

## A home safe has the same problem

A fire-rated safe at home covers part of the box's job without the hours problem. But **to anyone who
does not know how to open it, it has exactly the box's problem.** If only one adult knows the
combination or where the key is, the papers inside are out of reach the day that adult is away, hurt
or dead. Every adult who may need it can open it without help; check it at the yearly review
(→ 19-07, → 25-10). **The combination itself is never written in this app.**

## Cash caches: names only

Write **where**, never **how much**. A written amount turns a lost or stolen page into a shopping list
(→ 14-03). Amounts live in the adults' heads.

```
CASH LOCATIONS (names only, no amounts)
  1. ______________________ (main reserve)       in place? ____
  2. Grab folder (19-01)                          in place? ____
  3. Go-bags (22-03)                              in place? ____
  4. Vehicle kit (22-05)                          in place? ____
  5. ______________________                       in place? ____
Checked (date): __________   Every adult knows all of them: ____
```

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Home copies of everything crisis-needed** | Rule 1 | → 19-01 |
| A second institution | No single point of failure | → 19-02 |
| **Cash at home, split, small bills** | Box and ATM fail together | → 19-02 |
| Institution names, phone numbers and branch addresses on paper | Reach the bank without the internet | In the grab folder |
| Joint or deputy access on any box | The death-sealing fix | Confirm with the bank |
| A box contents list | Know what is there without going | Update yearly |

**No box?** A relative's house out of the area is the traditional away-from-home copy (→ 19-03): less
burglar-proof, more reachable, free.

## When it runs out

- **What runs out first is access**, before cash or supplies. Plan as if the box and the bank do not
  exist until the bounded disaster is over. That is when they matter most: rebuilding, claims
  (→ 19-04), settling an estate.
- **Check the box list and access arrangements every year** (→ 25-10).
- **The box is the deep archive; the grab folder is working memory; cash at home is the reflex.**
  Mixing the layers is the whole failure this page describes.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** the bank works as designed for bounded disasters. Do the access audit and ask the
  two questions this month.
- **B, on the move:** the box's contents are gone for the duration, which is fine if rule 1 held. The
  grab folder and cash are the bank now. Banks in other states may not serve you in person; a national
  bank or credit union network may help (CFPB, Disasters and Emergencies).
- **C, settled:** a box far away is a once-a-season errand at best. Plan one deliberate trip for deeds
  and originals when conditions allow, not before (→ 01-05).

pages.title: Access continuity: if one adult is gone

review_pass.notes: Access map records where/how only; CISA password-manager line verified live; guardian line now covers teens.

pages.body:
# Access continuity: if one adult is gone

**What this page is for.** Making sure that if one adult is in hospital, unable to act, or dead, the
others can still pay the bills, reach the insurance, keep income coming, and get into the accounts,
**this week**, not after months of court. In most households, money and digital life run
disproportionately through one person's logins. If the honest answer to "could the other adult do it
without them?" is "probably not without their thumb on the phone", that is this page's finding.

**Adults in your household:** {{#each adults as a}}{{a.label}}; {{/each}}
If you are the only adult, the "other adult" on this page is the person you trust most to act for
you, and the estate documents below matter even more.

> **CAUTION. Never write passwords, PINs, unlock codes, safe combinations or account numbers in this
> app.** This page records **where and how**, never **what**. The secrets themselves live in a password
> manager and on paper kept separately, written by hand (→ 19-03).
>
> **The failure is quiet.** Everything works until the day it is needed, because the everyday
> arrangement ("she just handles that") hides the missing access. **The fix is the three tests below,
> actually done and dated.** An access plan never tested is a hope.

## Do this now

1. **Each adult runs the three tests below this month, cold**, with no coaching from the other. Date
   the lines.
2. **Fill in the access map in pencil**: locations and methods only.
3. **Share phone unlock codes between the adults today**, if you have not. It costs nothing and is the
   most common gap. (Tell each other in person; do not write it here.)
4. **Check the estate documents exist** (table below). A power of attorney cannot be signed by someone
   who is already unconscious (CFPB, Managing Someone Else's Money).

## The access map

Locations and methods only. Anyone who reads this binder may read this page (→ 14-03).

```
ACCESS MAP (pencil)              ADULT 1: ________    ADULT 2: ________
-------------------------------  -------------------  -------------------
Password manager (which one):    _________________    _________________
  Its emergency or recovery kit,
  printed and kept where:        _________________    _________________
  Can the OTHER adult open it
  TODAY (not "could get")?       YES / NO             YES / NO
Phone unlock code shared?        YES / NO  date: ___  YES / NO  date: ___
THE email account that resets
  everything else:               _________________    _________________
  Its backup codes printed?
  Kept where?                    _________________    _________________
Banks and card issuers (names):  _________________    _________________
Insurance portals (19-04):       _________________    _________________
Business systems (19-08):        _________________    _________________
Employer and benefits systems:   _________________    _________________
Where the paper password sheet
  is kept (19-03):               _________________    _________________
```

A password manager's "emergency kit" or "recovery kit" is a printable sheet that lets you get back
into the account. Many managers also offer a way to grant another person emergency access. Strong,
unique passwords in a manager are the right everyday answer (CISA, Use Strong Passwords).

## The three tests: each adult, dated, no coaching

**A test is passed only when it was done cold**, from memory or from the binder alone.

```
                                        ADULT 1      ADULT 2
TEST 1: Open the OTHER adult's password
  manager (their vault, your hands,
  no help):                             date: _____  date: _____
TEST 2: Reach the critical accounts:
  a bank, the reset email, an insurance
  portal, one employer or business
  system. Sign in, look, sign out:      date: _____  date: _____
TEST 3: Physically find the paper
  password sheet, the originals box,
  and any safe or box key (19-01,
  19-06); open each and close it:       date: _____  date: _____
```

**A failed test is a good result.** It found the gap on a calm afternoon instead of in a hospital
waiting room. Fix it, test again, date it.

## If one adult is gone: the playbook

1. **Medical care and children first** (→ 12-16). This page is for day two onward.
2. **Their phone** is the practical master key, because sign-in codes go to it. **Keep it charged.** A
   dead or wiped phone makes everything below harder.
3. **Open their password manager** (test 1), then **the reset email**, then banks, bills and insurance
   (→ 19-04).
4. **Income:** if they were self-employed or ran a business, start → 19-08. If employed, call their
   employer's HR and benefits line: ______________________. Health insurance through that employer
   may be what covers the family.
5. **Money:** automatic payments keep running, which is good; know what they are (→ 19-02). **A
   financial power of attorney** is what lets you act on accounts in their name alone (CFPB).
6. **Write down what you did and when** (→ 25-05). You will need it for the bank, the insurer and any
   court.

## Estate documents: the paper under all of it

Access gets you through the month; **legal authority gets you through the year** (CFPB, Managing
Someone Else's Money). Fill in honestly:

```
                          EXISTS?  REVIEWED IN LAST 3 YRS?  ORIGINAL KEPT WHERE?
Will (each adult)         ______   ______                   _______________
Financial power of
  attorney (each)         ______   ______                   _______________
Health care power of
  attorney / advance
  directive (each)        ______   ______                   _______________
Guardian named for
  children (in the wills) ______   ______                   _______________
Beneficiaries checked on
  every policy and account ______  ______                   (19-04 worksheet)
```

**Blanks in that table are the real emergency on this page.** A missing power of attorney means courts
and months. {{#if has.child}}**You have children: a missing guardianship nomination means a judge
chooses who raises them.** {{else}}{{#if has.teen}}**You have a child under 18: a missing
guardianship nomination means a judge chooses who raises them.** {{/if}}{{/if}}**The original will should not live only in a box that may be
sealed on death** (→ 19-06).

> **Before the collapse:** wills, powers of attorney and guardianship nominations follow state law,
> and the forms that work differ by state. A lawyer, once, is the usual route; some states offer
> official statutory forms for powers of attorney and advance directives.

## The yearly re-test

**All three tests, every adult, every year** at the review (→ 25-10). Passwords change, phones are
replaced, sign-in methods are re-enrolled, and last year's dated line is this year's hope.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Each password manager's emergency kit, printed and stored** | The cold-start sheet | Kept with the paper password sheet; not in a wallet |
| **Backup codes for the reset email, printed** | The account that resets everything must itself be recoverable | → 19-03 |
| Phone unlock codes shared between adults | The most common gap | In person, not written here |
| **Wills, powers of attorney, guardianship, signed** | Authority, not just access | A lawyer, once |
| This page's map and tests, filled in and dated | The record | Pencil |

**Nothing substitutes for authority arranged in advance.** Afterward there is only the court. The
bank's own procedures after a death (death certificate, court letters) are slow and cover only the
legal side, never this month's bills (→ 19-06).

## When it runs out

- **Access decays silently.** Every password change, new phone or new account un-passes a test.
  That is why the tests are dated and yearly.
- **The gap this page cannot close: every adult gone at once.** The guardianship nomination, the
  estate documents, and a sealed letter to whoever will handle the estate saying where things are
  is the honest best available. Letter kept where: ______________________
- **Access is the cheap half of having a backup adult.** Buy it with an afternoon and three tests.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** do the map, the tests and the lawyer visit now. Every item on this page needs the
  working world.
- **B, on the move:** phones and the grab folder (→ 19-01) carry the access layer. Each adult's
  password-manager emergency kit travels sealed, apart from the devices.
- **C, settled:** connection may be the problem, not knowledge. The printed layer (emergency kits,
  backup codes, this map) is what still works. Re-test whenever you can reach the network.

pages.title: Income continuity for the self-employed and small business

review_pass.notes: No figures; worksheets on paper, no policy or account numbers in the app.

pages.body:
# Income continuity for the self-employed and small business

**What this page is for.** Keeping a household's income alive when the adult who earns it cannot work,
or when a disaster shuts the business. It is written for any adult who is self-employed, runs a small
business or a practice, or depends on their own hands for income: a tradesperson, a clinician, a
shop owner, a farmer, a freelancer. A binder that plans food and medicine to the day and skips the
thing that pays for them has a hole in it.

**For an employed adult**, most of this is covered by the employer's benefits; read the "employed"
box near the end and the playbook on → 19-07.

> **CAUTION. The scenario that matters most is usually not the storm. It is the owner unable to
> work** (an injury, an illness, a complication of a chronic condition; → 12-09, → 12-11) **while
> rent, staff, loans and the household's own bills keep running.** Insurance for exactly that exists,
> and it can only be bought **before** it is needed. **Pull the actual policies and fill in the
> worksheets from the paper.** "I think we have that" is the failure.
>
> **Write worksheets by hand on paper.** No policy numbers, account numbers or passwords in this app
> (→ 19-07).

## Do this now

1. **Pull the actual policies** and fill in every blank below by hand: company, benefit, waiting
   period.
2. **Disability insurance first** (worksheet 1). If it does not exist, or is not the right kind, that
   call goes ahead of any purchase in the rest of this binder.
3. **Name who runs the business, or closes it, if you cannot**, and put their phone numbers on your
   contact list (→ 25-03).
4. **If you hold a license and keep client, patient or customer records, find your licensing board's
   rules** on how long records must be kept and what to do if you close. Write them in worksheet 5.
5. **Write a one-page business continuity plan** (Ready.gov, Business Continuity Planning): what
   stops, what it costs per week, who does what.

## Three kinds of interruption

| Scenario | What stops | What bridges it |
|---|---|---|
| **Short outage or storm** (days) (→ 17-08) | Appointments, sales, perhaps spoiled stock | Cash buffer (→ 19-02); rescheduling; property insurance for losses (→ 19-04) |
| **Regional disaster** (weeks to months) | The business **and** your customers' ability to pay | **Business interruption and overhead insurance** (below); US Small Business Administration disaster loans (SBA, Disaster Assistance) |
| **The owner unable to work** | Income stops completely while every cost keeps running | **Disability insurance, overhead insurance, and a named person to run or close it**: the reason this page exists |

## Worksheets: fill in by hand from the documents

**1. Disability insurance: the critical one.**
**"Own-occupation"** disability pays if you cannot do **your own** occupation, even if you could do
some other work. **"Any-occupation"** pays only if you cannot do any reasonable job. For someone whose
income depends on a specific physical skill (a surgeon's hands, a carpenter's back, a driver's
eyes), the difference is everything.

```
ON PAPER
Company: ____________________
Own-occupation? (true own-occ / modified / any-occ): ____________
Monthly benefit: $________   Waiting ("elimination") period: ___ days
Pays until (age __ / __ years): ______
Extras (inflation increase, partial disability, option to
  increase later): _______________________________________
Any exclusions for existing conditions: _________________________
Premium paid and current, paid from: ____________________________
```

**2. Business overhead expense insurance.** Pays the business's fixed costs (rent, staff, loan
payments) while the owner is disabled, so there is a business to return to or sell.

```
Exists? ____  Company: ______________________
Monthly benefit: $________  Waiting period: ____ days  Pays for: ______
```

**3. Business interruption (on the business property policy).** What events it covers, the waiting
period, the limit, and whether it pays when the government orders an area closed.

```
Company: ____________________  Covers: ________________________
Waiting period: ______  Limit: $________  Agent: ______________
```

**4. Who runs, or closes, the business if you cannot.**

```
Partner, associate or employee who can do the work: ____________
Temporary replacement (agency, colleague) and phone: ____________
Person who carries out this page: ______________________________
Checklist, in order:
 [ ] contact clients and reschedule or refer
 [ ] secure anything dangerous or controlled (chemicals, medicines,
     tools, firearms, client records)
 [ ] payroll decision (line 6)
 [ ] notify insurers (1 to 3 above)
 [ ] a weekly go / no-go decision
Close the business if out of work for more than ____ weeks
Who values or sells it (broker, accountant): ____________________
```

**5. Client, patient or customer records.** An obligation that can outlast the business.

```
Records kept in (system, where hosted): _________________________
Who besides the owner can open and export them TODAY (19-07 test):
  ______________________
Required keeping period (licensing board rule, checked on ___):
  ______________________
Who will hold the records if the business closes: _______________
```

**6. Staff and payroll.** How long can the business pay staff with no income, and from what?

```
Payroll is run by / through: ____________________
Reserve: covers ____ weeks
Line of credit (bank, limit): ____________________
```

**7. What else leans on the business.** Relationships, a building, equipment, a vehicle, health
insurance for the family: ______________________________________

## If you are employed

- **Know your benefits:** short- and long-term disability, life insurance, and how long health
  insurance continues if you cannot work.
- **Write the HR and benefits phone number** on the contact list (→ 25-03, → 19-07).
- **Unemployment insurance** is run by each state; know how to apply.
- **A side skill** that earns in any economy is real insurance (→ 18-03).

## The two honest framings

- **Insurance solves the bounded scenarios**, which are by far the likely ones (→ 19-04). Disability,
  overhead and interruption coverage are a business's version of the grab folder: boring, decisive,
  and buyable today.
- **In a long collapse, most businesses stop with the payment system**, and the owner's skills become
  something to trade and share in the community instead (→ 18-03; for dental skills, → 18-08). Until
  then, the business funds everything else in this binder.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Disability insurance, the right kind** | The most important policy for anyone who lives by their own work | Worksheet 1 |
| Business overhead expense insurance | Keeps the business alive while you are down | Worksheet 2 |
| Business interruption coverage | The regional-disaster bridge | Worksheet 3 |
| **Named people and phone numbers** | A plan is a person with a phone | Worksheet 4 |
| Records access for a second person, tested | The obligation and the asset | Worksheet 5, → 19-07 |
| Copies of all business policies in the grab folder | Claims start from paper | → 19-01 |
| A one-page continuity plan | What stops, what it costs, who does what | Ready.gov |

**Substitutes:** SBA disaster loans and insurer or lender accommodations (→ 19-04) help partly, slowly,
and usually only in declared disasters. Another adult's income is often the real household backstop.
**Nothing substitutes for coverage bought before the disability.**

## When it runs out

- **Benefits have a waiting period at the front and a limit at the back.** The cash buffer (→ 19-02)
  covers the waiting period; the benefit period in worksheet 1 is your household's runway for a long
  disability. Know both numbers.
- **Review every year** (→ 25-10): premiums paid, benefit still matching costs, the named people still
  willing, licensing rules re-checked.
- **If one person is both the household's income and its biggest health risk**, insuring their
  ability to work is as central to this binder as any stockpile.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** everything on this page happens now, while insurers answer phones. The worksheet
  blanks are this month's homework.
- **B, on the move:** the business stays behind; policies, records-access notes and the closure plan
  travel in the grab folder (→ 19-01). Insurance and the business's future get sorted from wherever
  you land, with paper in hand.

pages.title: Kids and family: section overview
pages.body:
# Kids and family

**What this section holds.** 9 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 20-01 **Babies, toddlers and young children: what they need**: The youngest people in a house have the smallest reserves of everything.
- → 20-02 **Keeping children safe in a house without the grid**: Going without power brings back every household hazard that modern life engineered away: a heater in the room where everyone lives, open fire for cooking, fl…
- → 20-03 **Children's routine and schooling**: Routine is not a comfort item.
- → 20-04 **Teaching children the plan**: A child who knows what to do is safer, calmer and easier to keep safe than one who does not.
- → 20-05 **Feeding babies and toddlers without the supply chain**: The household routine for feeding a baby or toddler when stores, power and clean tap water may be gone: the three feeding paths, how to hold each one togethe…
- → 20-06 **Diapering and keeping small children clean**: CDC warns that even a microscopic amount of poop can carry millions of germs.
- → 20-07 **Real jobs for children**: A child with a real job is happier, calmer and safer, and over time a genuinely useful member of the household.
- → 20-08 **Children and fear**: Children know when something is wrong.
- → 20-09 **Pets: food, water, medicine, moving, and hard choices**: Each pet is another mouth, another water need, a waste problem and, if you ever have to move, an animal that must be contained and carried.

pages.title: Babies, toddlers and young children: what they need
pages.body:
# Babies, toddlers and young children: what they need

**What this page is for.** The youngest people in a house have the smallest reserves of
everything. They dry out fast, lose and gain heat fast, and cannot tell you what is wrong. This
page lists what they need, what cannot be improvised, and how to watch a child who cannot
speak for themself. It is written in age bands. Your household's bands are listed first; the
others stay on the page for visiting children, grandchildren and children you may take in.

> **SAFETY.** Small children dehydrate in hours, not days (→ 12-05). **No honey for a child
> under 1 year** (botulism; CDC, Botulism Prevention). **No anti-diarrhoea medicine such as
> loperamide under age 2** (its label says so). **Children do not have access to firearms,
> fuel, medications or chlorine products** (floor, → 30-01): small children explore by mouth and
> by hand, and in a crisis the adults are busier.

**Your children:** {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.child}}none entered. This page stays for children you may care for later.{{/if}}

**Read first for your household:**
{{#if has.infant}}- **Infant (under 12 months)** and **toddler** bands below: a member is under 2.
{{/if}}{{#if has.toddler}}- **Toddler (1 to 3)** band below.
{{/if}}{{#if has.young_child}}- **Preschool (3 to 5)** band below, and the choking list.
{{/if}}{{#if has.nursing}}- **The nursing parent's food and water** (below and → 20-05).
{{/if}}{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}- **Allergies in the house** (below, → 02-03 and → 02-04).
{{/if}}{{#if !has.young_child}}- No member under 6 is entered. Read the "do this now" list if young children may stay with you.
{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Ask your child's doctor now, while you can:** "If we cannot buy formula, milk, diapers or
   this child's medicine for a month, what do we do?" Write the answers on → 20-05 and → 25-09.
2. **Stock the things you cannot improvise:** the right milk for each child's age (→ 20-05),
   diapers (→ 13-08), oral rehydration salts (ORS, → 12-05), any child's medicine, and the
   foods each child reliably eats.
3. **Buy the next two clothing and shoe sizes** for each child (→ 11-02). Growth is the one
   shortage nothing prevents.
4. **Write each child's feeding and medical details on a card** for any caregiver (→ 15-03,
   → 25-09), including every allergy.
5. **Work out on paper how the kitchen runs with no fridge and rationed water** (→ 13-10,
   → 04-17), before you have to.

## What a small child needs, and where each answer lives

| Need | Grid-down answer | Pages |
|---|---|---|
| **Fluid** | Safe water; breast milk or formula for babies; the right milk for toddlers; **ORS if ill** | → 03-04, → 12-05, → 20-05 |
| **Calories and nutrition** | Never rationed. Soft, varied food; fat and protein matter | → 04-01, → 04-18 |
| **Warmth** | Layers, the heated room, body heat | → 11-02, → 08-01 |
| **Sleep** | A warm, safe sleep place and a routine (DC-09 below) | → 11-02, → 21-07, → 20-03 |
| **Clean** | Diapering, washing, contained waste | → 13-08, → 20-06, → 13-02 |
| **Supervision** | Constant for the youngest; barriers do the rest | → 20-02 |
| **Comfort and routine** | Predictability, familiar objects, calm adults | → 20-08, → 21-04 |

**Calories.** The binder's household calorie total uses the USDA/HHS Dietary Guidelines table
by age and sex (→ 04-01). A child's share is **never rationed**; you ration everything else to
protect it. {{#if has.nursing}}**Your nursing member eats and drinks more:** the Dietary
Guidelines add about 330 calories a day in the first 6 months of nursing and about 400 in the
second 6 months, and the water plan adds extra for her (→ 03-01).{{else}}A nursing parent eats
more: the Dietary Guidelines add about 330 calories a day in the first 6 months of nursing and
about 400 in the second 6 months, plus extra water (→ 03-01).{{/if}}

## Age bands

### Infant (under 12 months)

- **Milk is the whole diet for the first months:** breast milk or infant formula, nothing
  else (CDC). Formula is never diluted and never homemade (→ 20-05).
- **Solid foods start around 6 months** alongside milk, soft and mashed (CDC, Foods and Drinks
  for 6 to 24 Month Olds).
- **Safe water** for anything that goes in a bottle or cup (→ 03-04). Babies are the least able
  to survive a water-borne illness.
- **No honey under 1 year** (botulism). Honey appears in this binder as a wound dressing and a
  cough remedy (→ 12-02, → 12-13); the age rule matters more than the memory.
- **Sleep:** the American Academy of Pediatrics says a baby sleeps in the parents' room on a
  separate firm, flat surface. Sharing an adult bed for warmth is a trade-off that the card
  only offers for children over 12 months (→ 30-10). {{choice DC-09}} → 30-10.
- **Watch:** fewer wet diapers plus unusual sleepiness is an emergency (→ 12-05).

### Toddler (1 to 3)

- **Around 12 months a child moves to mostly family foods.** That is a real advantage in a
  crisis: the child increasingly eats what everyone eats.
- **Milk for 12 to 23 months is whole milk** (CDC), about 16 to 24 ounces a day, not the nonfat
  dry milk that most pantries stock. Low-fat milk only from age 2 unless a clinician says
  otherwise. Stock and substitutes: → 20-05, → 04-14.
- **Soft, mashable, small.** Choking is the hazard at this age (list below).
- **Mobile, curious, mouths everything.** This is the band at highest risk on almost every
  hazard in → 20-02: buckets of water, heaters, fuel, button batteries.
- **Sleep:** if the household is considering bed-sharing for warmth, the conditions are on the
  card (over 12 months, firm surface, no heavy covers over the child, sober adults).
  {{choice DC-09}} → 30-10.

### Preschool (3 to 5)

- **Eats family food**, still on the choking list until about 4.
- **Can learn rules and a few jobs** (→ 20-04, → 20-07): "I only eat food a grown-up gives
  me", the fire line, the water rule.
- **Still cannot report illness well.** A change in behaviour is often the first sign.

### School-age (6 to 12) and teen (13 to 17)

Older children need the same never-rationed food and safe water, and can do much more for
themselves. Their pages are → 20-03 (routine and schooling), → 20-04 (teaching the plan),
→ 20-07 (jobs) and → 20-08 (fear). Teens eat as much as adults or more (→ 04-01).

## Choking: the foods to change for children under 4

The American Academy of Pediatrics lists these as choking hazards for young children
(AAP, Choking Prevention), printed so this page works alone:

- Hot dogs, sausages and meat sticks: **cut into very small pieces**, not rounds.
- **Whole grapes:** chop into very small pieces.
- Hard, gooey or sticky candy; chewing gum.
- Nuts and seeds (especially sunflower seeds).
- Raw vegetables such as carrot sticks; raw fruit chunks such as apple pieces: **cook soft or
  grate.**
- Popcorn; marshmallows.
- Thick chunks of peanut butter or other nut butters: **spread thinly.**
- Chunks of meat; chunks of cheese or string cheese.

The AAP advises cutting food for young children into pieces **no bigger than half an inch**,
seating children to eat, and watching every meal. **What to do if a child chokes, and infant and
child CPR, is → 12-18.** Read it before you need it.

## Food rules in a crisis

- **Variety matters.** A stored-food diet is narrow (→ 04-18). Fats, protein and vitamins need
  deliberate attention for growing children.
- **Safe water** for drinking and for mixing any milk powder (→ 03-04, CDC).
- **New foods and allergies.** Introducing a common allergen (peanut, egg and others) to a baby
  or toddler is something to plan with the child's doctor while one is reachable, especially if
  a brother or sister has a food allergy (FDA, Food Allergies).
- **Traded or scavenged food.** Food from another kitchen carries unknown ingredients and
  unknown handling. Home-canned low-acid food from someone else follows the questionable food
  card (→ 30-15) and → 18-02.
{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}- **Your household has a severe allergy:** {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}); {{/each}}
  Feeding an allergic person unlabeled, traded or scavenged food is a trade-off on its own card.
  {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19. The household's food rules are in the food-allergy module (→ 02-04)
  and the emergency response in → 02-03.
{{else}}- **If anyone in the house has a severe food allergy,** the food rules are in the
  food-allergy module (→ 02-04), the emergency response is → 02-03, and unlabeled food is a
  card (→ 30-19).
{{/if}}

### Two food chains in one kitchen (when one person has a food allergy)

1. **Cook one base meal that is safe for the allergic person**, then adapt it for the youngest
   (mash, soften, portion). Making the whole household's food allergen-safe by default is the
   simplest system there is.
2. **Feed a toddler away from any food containing the allergen.** A toddler's hands on a shared
   surface carry it everywhere.
3. **Wash hands and surfaces between**, with soap (→ 13-02), even when water is short.
4. **Label everything.** In a tired household, labels prevent the mistake.

## Sleep and warmth

- **The heated room** (→ 08-01) is where everyone sleeps in a cold house: warmer and safer than a
  cold bedroom.
- **A cold house is answered with warm sleepwear and a sleep sack, not loose blankets** on a
  small child (→ 11-02). Feel the neck and chest for overheating.
- **Hot-water bottles and warmed stones pre-warm the bed and come out before a child gets in.**
  A contact burn develops on small skin in less time than a night (→ 12-03, → 21-07).
- **A heater burning while people sleep** is a separate trade-off on its own card
  (→ 30-02). {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02.
- **Routine matters enormously** for children and for the adults' sanity (→ 21-04, → 21-07).

## Supplies that cannot be improvised

| Item | Why it is hard to improvise |
|---|---|
| **The right milk for each age**: breast milk support, formula if used, whole milk for 12 to 23 months | Formula has no substitute; nonfat powder is the wrong milk for a toddler (→ 20-05, → 04-14) |
| **Diapers** | Cloth works but needs water, soap and drying (→ 13-08) |
| **Foods the child will actually eat** | Small children are particular, and stressed ones more so |
| **Clothing and shoes in the next sizes** | Growth does not stop (→ 11-02) |
| **Children's medicines and a thermometer** | Children's strengths and forms; check every label against everyone's allergies (→ 12-13) |
| **ORS or children's electrolyte drink** | The highest-value item for a small child (→ 12-05) |
| **Comfort objects, with duplicates** | Not sentimental: a lost one is a bad week (→ 20-08) |

## Watching a child who cannot tell you

**Check the body, not the answer** (→ 11-02, → 12-05):

- **Dehydration:** fewer wet diapers, no tears, dry mouth, sunken eyes, floppy or unusually
  sleepy, refusing to drink. **In a baby, unusual sleepiness plus fewer wet diapers is an
  emergency.**
- **Too cold:** cold belly and back of the neck (not hands), unusual sleepiness, weak cry, pale
  or bright red skin (→ 11-02).
- **Too hot:** hot skin, flushing, floppiness, fewer wet diapers (→ 11-08).
- **Illness:** fever, a change in feeding, a change in behaviour. **A change in behaviour is
  often the first sign.**
- **Allergic reaction:** watch any child eating a food for the first time (→ 02-03).

**If a child under 2 has diarrhoea** (WHO, The Treatment of Diarrhoea, as printed on → 12-05):
give **50 to 100 mL (a quarter to half a cup) of ORS after each loose stool**, in sips from a
spoon, on top of normal feeding. Breast milk continues throughout. A child already showing
dehydration signs needs more, as set out on → 12-05. **No anti-diarrhoea medicine under 2.**

## Gear

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Milk for each child's age, and safe water capacity | Mixing and drinking need clean water | → 20-05, → 03-04 |
| Diapers: a disposable buffer plus cloth | The relentless consumable | → 13-08 |
| ORS, plenty | Dehydration is the fast killer at this age | → 12-05 |
| Shelf-stable foods each child eats | Fussy plus stressed is real | Rotate |
| Clothing and shoes, next two sizes | Growth does not stop | → 11-02 |
| Warm sleepwear and a sleep sack | Cold house, no loose blankets on a baby | → 11-02 |
| Separate sleep surface (crib or play yard) | Safe sleep and a safe place by day | → 30-10, → 20-02 |
| Children's thermometer and medicines | Labels checked against all allergies | → 12-13 |
| Baby carrier or sling | Hands free; body heat; child kept close | |
| Car seat for each child, installed | No bulky coat under the harness (AAP) | → 11-02, → 22-05 |
| Labelled feeding gear | Separate chains if anyone has an allergy | → 02-04, → 13-10 |
| Comfort objects, with duplicates | A lost one is a bad night for everyone | → 20-08 |
| Gates, latches, barriers | → 20-02 | |
| Written feeding and medical card per child | For any caregiver | → 15-03, → 25-09 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**

- **Food:** mashed, softened versions of the household's food. This is the direction feeding
  goes anyway after 12 months (CDC): cooked grains, mashed beans, soft cooked vegetables, soft
  fruit.
- **Diapers:** cloth from flannel, towels or sheets (→ 13-08).
- **Carrier:** a long, strong cloth tied as a wrap.
- **Clothing:** cut down from adult clothing (→ 11-02, → 11-07).
- **Comfort:** a familiar cloth, a made toy, a routine. Predictability is itself a comfort.
- **What you cannot substitute:** infant formula (→ 20-05), and a doctor's advice on
  introducing allergens. Ask now.

## When it runs out

- **Milk, diapers and clothing sizes run out on a schedule you can predict.** Put all three on
  the consumables table with dates (→ 23-02). They are the most predictable depletion clocks in
  the binder; use that.
- **Ration everything else, never a child's food or fluid**, and never a nursing parent's.
- **Substitute:** family food mashed; cloth diapers; cut-down clothing; and the community.
  Children's supplies are the easiest barter category there is (→ 18-02): everyone has outgrown
  gear and everyone needs the next size.
- **This problem eases with time.** A 1-year-old becomes a 2-year-old, needs less special
  supply and eats more of what everyone eats. That is unusual in this binder and worth knowing.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** stock deeply, set up the kitchen routine and the safety barriers
  (→ 20-02). Use the time while stores work to buy ahead on sizes and supplies.
- **B (moving):** small children are carried, which shapes everything. An adult carrying a child
  makes heat; the child does not (→ 11-02). Disposables, not cloth. Breast milk or ready-to-feed
  formula, ORS and safe water are the critical load. In the car each child is in a seat, harness
  snug, no puffy coat under it, blanket over the top (AAP; → 11-02, → 22-05).
- **C (establish):** more room and more hazards (→ 20-02). Food improves as a garden and animals
  come in (→ 05-01, → 05-04).
