pages.body:
# Keeping children safe in a house without the grid

**What this page is for.** Going without power brings back every household hazard that modern
life engineered away: a heater in the room where everyone lives, open fire for cooking, flame
for light, fuel on the property, hand tools, and buckets of standing water everywhere. This
page lists those hazards in order of how fast they kill, and the controls that work when the
adults are tired and busy.

> **SAFETY. Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine
> products.** This is a floor, not a choice (→ 30-01): every source agrees, small children
> explore by mouth and by hand, and in a crisis the adults are busier and supervision is thinner,
> which is exactly when storage has to do the work. Lock firearms unloaded, with ammunition
> separate (→ 14-14). Store fuel, medicine and chlorine locked or high, in their own labelled
> containers, never in drink bottles.
>
> **Two hazards dominate, and both kill fast and silently:**
> **(1) Drowning.** A small child can drown in a few inches of water, in minutes, with no splash
> or shout (CPSC; CDC, Preventing Drowning): a bucket, a tub, a rain barrel, a cooler, a pool.
> **(2) Fire and burns:** heaters, cooking fires, lamps and hot liquids (→ 12-03).
>
> **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
> window** (floor, → 30-01). Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning.

**Children in your household:** {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#each teens as t}}{{t.label}} ({{t.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.child}}{{#if !has.teen}}none entered. Keep this page for visiting children.{{/if}}{{/if}}

{{#if has.toddler}}**Your household has a toddler.** A child of 1 to 3 is the highest-risk
person on almost every line of this page: mobile, unable to be reasoned with, and putting
everything in the mouth.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Water first.** Lids on every water container; dump what is not in use. {{#if has.pool}}**Your
   pool:** a four-sided isolation fence at least 4 feet high, fully separating the pool from the
   house and yard, with a self-closing, self-latching gate (CDC; CPSC; AAP). Do it now, not next
   summer.{{else}}If you have or reach a pool, hot tub or pond, the barrier rules below come
   first.{{/if}}
2. **Carbon monoxide alarms** in the room where people sleep, at pillow height, and on each
   level; test them monthly (→ 08-02). No fuel heater is lit until the alarm in its room is up
   and tested.
3. **An anchored barrier around every heater or stove** before it is first lit (block below).
4. **Lock up** fuel, lamp oil, chemicals, lye, pool shock, bleach, medicines and spare button
   batteries (→ 06-06, → 13-09, → 03-04, → 12-07).
5. **Learn CPR, every adult.** CDC recommends it for drowning specifically, and no ambulance may
   come. Infant and child choking and CPR: → 12-18.
6. **Walk every room on your knees** with the checklist below. Button batteries first. Put the
   walk on the drill calendar so it repeats (→ 24-02, → 25-10).

## The hazards, by how fast they kill

| Hazard | Speed | Control |
|---|---|---|
| **Drowning** (pool, bucket, tub, barrel, cooler) | Minutes, silent | Barriers, lids, a named water watcher, CPR |
| **Fire and burns** | Seconds | Anchored barriers; the hot-zone line; hot liquids kept away |
| **Carbon monoxide** | Minutes | Tested alarms; heater and engine rules (→ 08-02) |
| **Poisoning** (fuel, lye, chemicals, medicines, batteries) | Minutes to hours | Locked storage (floor) |
| **Firearms** | Instant | Locked, unloaded, ammunition separate (floor, → 14-14) |
| **Falls** (stairs in the dark, ice, ladders) | Instant | Light, gates, traction (→ 10-01, → 11-06) |
| **Cold and heat** | Minutes to hours | → 11-02, → 11-08, → 17-04 |
| **Tools** | Instant | Locked; a work radius children stay out of (→ 16-01, → 16-06) |
| **Waste and contamination** | Days | Sanitation kept apart (→ 13-01, → 13-11) |
| **Allergen exposure** (if anyone has a food allergy) | Minutes | → 02-03, → 02-04 |

## Drowning: the one to take most seriously

**The layers of protection** (CDC, Preventing Drowning; AAP, Drowning Prevention):

1. **Barriers.** For a pool: a four-sided isolation fence, at least 4 feet, with a self-closing,
   self-latching gate, separating the pool from both the house and the yard. CDC notes that
   four-sided fencing cuts a child's drowning risk substantially compared with a fence around
   the property line only. This is the most effective single measure.
2. **Alarms** on doors and gates to the pool area, and a safety cover.
3. **Close, constant, undistracted supervision** whenever children are near water. **Name one
   adult as the water watcher**, with no phone, no chores, no conversation. "Everyone's
   watching" means nobody is.
4. **Swimming lessons** reduce drowning risk (CDC). Worth doing while they exist.
5. **Life jackets** for any water activity.
6. **CPR for every adult**, and rescue equipment (a reach pole, a float) at the water.
7. **Grid-down rule:** if a pool or pond becomes a water source (→ 03-03), **the gate closes and
   latches every single time**, and **no child goes to fetch water.**

**In-home drowning** (CPSC, In-Home Drowning): buckets, bathtubs, toilets, coolers, rain barrels
and standing water. In a house where water is stored in open containers everywhere, this risk
goes up a great deal. **Lids. Every container.**

**Pool covers and ice in winter.** A covered or frozen pool that is opened repeatedly for water
is a different drowning, not a safer one.
- **Only a safety cover built to the ASTM F1346 standard counts as a barrier** (CPSC, Safety
  Barrier Guidelines for Residential Pools). A tarp or a water-bag winter cover does not.
  Children have drowned in rain and melt water pooled on top of a loose cover.
- **Pump or bail standing water off any non-safety cover** after every thaw or rain.
- **The water-draw opening is re-covered and the gate re-latched after every draw**, by the
  adult who drew the water.
- **Nobody on the ice, and no child in the pool yard**, all year.

{{#if has.pool}}**Your pool holds {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gallons.** Its fence, gate and cover
are the highest-value safety items on the property.{{/if}}{{#if has.hot_tub}} **Your hot tub:**
keep the locking cover on and latched whenever no adult is in it.{{/if}}

## Fire and burns: the daily hazard

You may be running open fire every day (→ 07-01, → 08-01, → 10-02).
- **A physical barrier around every heat source**, anchored so a climbing toddler cannot shift
  it.
- **The hot-zone line:** a line on the floor (tape works) that children do not cross when fire
  is burning. Teach it and hold it (→ 20-04).
- **Hot liquids never travel through where children are.** Scalds are the most common serious
  burn in small children.
- **No flame in children's rooms.** Flameless lights only (USFA, Candle Fire Safety).
- **Lamps and candles out before sleep.** Open flame indoors is a trade-off on its own card
  (→ 30-21). {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21.
- **A young child never carries a flame.** Give them a headlamp instead: a light they are
  allowed to use makes the rule easy to keep (→ 10-01).
- **Smoke alarms on every level; carbon monoxide alarms** as → 08-02.

### Portable heaters and stoves: the barrier block

The heater pages (→ 08-09, → 08-10, → 08-08) point here. The heater and the children's play
area are often in the same room.
- **A fixed, anchored barrier** (metal play-yard panels or a hearth gate, screwed or weighted)
  around the heater **at the clearances printed on its label and manual**: above, in front and
  at the sides. Write yours here: above ______ in, front ______ in, sides ______ in. Mark the
  floor inside the barrier as the hot zone. {{figure fig-heater-barrier-clearances}}
- **Never lit with a child unsupervised in the room.** An adult in the room and awake, or the
  heater is off.
- **Running a fuel heater while people sleep** is a trade-off with its own card; the options
  include running it only with a tested alarm at pillow height, vents, the barrier and wake
  checks. {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02.
- **Never moved or refuelled while lit or hot.** Refuel outdoors, with the heater cold (→ 08-10).
- **The fuel can and funnel live outside the room**, capped and locked (→ 06-06). A mouthful of
  kerosene or lamp oil can be breathed into the lungs and cause a severe pneumonia (CDC MMWR,
  hydrocarbon ingestion in children; → 12-17).
- **Nothing drying on or over the heater; nothing stored inside the barrier.**
- **The play area or crib on the far side of the room** from the heater and from the vent.
- **The heater's own safety switches** (tip-over, low-oxygen) stop a fire, not a burn. They are
  not child-proofing.
- **A wood stove:** the hearth-gate rules on → 08-08 apply; same logic.

{{photo heater-barrier}}

## Poisoning: the grid-down house is full of it

New things in the house that were not there before:
- **Lamp oil, kerosene, gasoline, propane** (→ 06-06, → 10-02; what each is: → 29-01).
- **Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite).** An oxidiser, not "bleach": a mouthful of granules burns
  the mouth and gullet, and it releases chlorine gas if it gets wet or meets acid, ammonia or
  fuel (→ 29-05). Store it sealed, dry, labelled, off the floor, away from fuel and heat, behind
  a latched door (→ 03-04).
- **Lye and soap-making chemicals** (→ 13-09): caustic.
- **Bleach and disinfectants** in larger amounts (→ 13-11). **Never mix bleach or pool shock with
  ammonia, acids or other cleaners** (floor, → 30-01).
- **Medicines**, including any insulin, epinephrine and the stockpile (→ 12-07).
- **Wood ash** (caustic when wet), **antifreeze**, **battery acid** (→ 09-03).
- **Rodent bait** (→ 04-11): a real hazard with children and pets; consider traps instead.

**All of it locked, high and out of reach.** "Out of reach" for a toddler is a moving target:
they climb. Poison Control: **1-800-222-1222** while phones work (→ 12-17).

{{photo locked-storage}}

## Supervision, honestly

Supervision degrades when adults are exhausted and busy, which is the normal state of a
grid-down household. **The answers are structural, not attentional:**
- **Barriers do the work supervision cannot.** Fences, gates, locks and latches do not get tired.
- **Name who has the children** during any hazardous job. "We're both sort of watching" is how
  accidents happen.
- **A safe zone:** a gated area or play yard where the youngest can be while adults work.
- **Older children can help** (→ 20-07), and a helping child is a located child. Which dangerous
  jobs a child may do, at what age, is a worksheet the household fills in (→ 30-25).
  {{choice DC-24}} → 30-25.
- **Do the dangerous work while young children sleep** or are watched elsewhere: chainsaws, fire
  building, chemicals.

**Household-specific hazards:**
{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}- **Severe allergy in the house.** An accidental exposure may be the most
  likely serious emergency you face. Everyone who feeds that person knows the list, and the safe
  food chain holds even when everything else is improvised (→ 02-04, → 02-03).
{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **Refrigerated medicines and injection supplies** (insulin,
  needles, pens) are secured from children while staying instantly reachable for the adult who
  needs them.
{{/if}}{{#if has.pets}}- **Pets** around a toddler: food bowls, litter and the animals
  themselves (→ 20-09).
{{/if}}{{#if has.firearms}}- **Firearms in the house:** locked, unloaded, ammunition separate,
  every time (→ 14-14, → 29-11; AAP, Guns in the Home; NSSF, Project ChildSafe).
{{/if}}- Any of these that apply later: the same rules.

## The room-by-room walk, at a child's eye level

A house changes under crisis load: new gear, new fuel, new cords, staged bags. **Walk every room
on your knees** (that is a toddler's sight line) every few months and whenever the house
changes, and put it on the drill calendar (→ 24-02, → 25-10).

- [ ] **Button and coin batteries, first, every time** (CPSC, Button Batteries). Every headlamp,
      radio, clock, thermometer, remote and key fob: **is the battery door screwed shut?** A
      swallowed coin battery can burn through the gullet in hours. If one is swallowed, the
      steps are on → 12-17 (National Capital Poison Center guideline); read it before you need
      it.
- [ ] **Spare coin batteries stored like medicine:** locked or high, in the original pack,
      never loose in a drawer or kit lid.
- [ ] **Fuel, lamp oil, chemicals, lye, bleach, pool shock:** up high and locked. Anything moved
      down "just for now" goes back up now.
- [ ] **Charging cables and power stations:** cords out of pull-reach (a pulled cord brings down
      the device, the battery or hot liquid with it); stations against a wall and off the floor;
      nothing charging on fabric (→ 09-03).
- [ ] **Staged go-bags hold medicine.** Staged means hung high or behind a latched door, not by
      the front door at toddler height (→ 22-03, → 12-07).
- [ ] **Water containers:** lids on; dump what is not in use (→ 03-02, → 13-01).
- [ ] **Tools and knives** back in locked storage, not where the last job ended (→ 16-01).
- [ ] **Heater season:** barrier anchored at the label clearances; nothing drying on it or stored
      inside it; play area on the far side; carbon monoxide alarm in the room tested this month.
- [ ] **Generator:** runs outside only, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust
      away from the house (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics; → 09-04); its hot muffler is a
      burn; cords routed where a child cannot pull or trip on them.
- [ ] **Car seats:** installed and tight, harness at each child's current size, no bulky coat
      under the harness (AAP; → 11-02, → 22-05).
- [ ] **Matches and lighters:** counted, high and locked. They migrate.
- [ ] **Firearms:** locked, unloaded, ammunition separate (→ 14-14).
- [ ] **What can the youngest reach this time that they could not last time?**

```
WALK DONE: date __________  by __________
FOUND AND FIXED: _____________________________________________
______________________________________________________________
```

## Arriving at a new place: farms, ponds and woods

A destination or a new site has hazards this house does not. **Walk the new place on the first
day, before anything is unpacked and before children roam.** CDC/NIOSH's childhood agricultural
injury work counts farms among the most dangerous places children are ever present, with
machinery and drowning leading the list.

**The first-day walk (ask the hosts to walk it with you):**
- [ ] **Augers and power take-off (PTO) shafts are absolute no-go zones.** Name them, mark them
      with flagging tape at a child's height. There is no safe "quick look" distance.
- [ ] **Stock tanks, ponds, creeks, cisterns and pools:** the same drowning layers as at home; no
      child near water without a named watcher; covers or barriers where possible.
- [ ] **Large animals: no child alone with them, ever.** A cow with a calf is the specific danger.
- [ ] **Equipment cabs locked, keys out of ignitions.**
- [ ] **Chemical storage found and confirmed locked.** A working farm holds drums and jugs this
      house does not (→ 12-17).
- [ ] **Wells and outbuildings:** covers on wells, doors latched.
- [ ] **Kid zones agreed out loud** with the hosts: where children may be without an adult, and
      who is watching when.
- [ ] **Woods and open land:** walk the boundary with the children and pick landmarks ("never
      past the big rock without a grown-up"); **the buddy rule**: nobody in the woods alone;
      "**we don't eat anything from the ground**" (→ 05-19, → 05-06); "**step on logs, never
      blindly over them**" where there are snakes.

{{#if has.agreed_destination}}**Your agreed destinations:** {{#each agreed_destinations as d}}{{d.name}} ({{d.county}}, {{d.state_name}}); {{/each}}
Ask now about pools, ponds, animals and machinery there, and whether a pool fence exists. "We'll
fence it next season" is how children drown.{{/if}}

```
FIRST-DAY WALK DONE: date __________  walked by __________________
NO-GO ZONES AGREED: ___________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________
```

## Gear

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pool isolation fence, self-latching gate, safety cover (if any pool) | The highest-value safety item on a property with a pool | CDC, CPSC, AAP |
| Gate and door alarms | Another layer | Where the house forms a side of the pool area |
| **Lids for every water container** | A bucket is a toddler drowning hazard | → 03-02 |
| **Anchored heater barrier** | Heater and children share a room | → 08-09, → 08-10 |
| Smoke alarms on every level; **carbon monoxide alarms** | The precondition for any fuel heat | → 08-02 |
| Car seat for each child, checked every few months | Moving is a drive | → 11-02, → 22-05 |
| **Lockable cabinets or boxes** for fuel, chemicals, lye, medicines, batteries | The floor | → 06-06, → 12-07 |
| Firearm safe or lock box; ammunition stored separately | The floor | → 14-14 |
| Safety gates, outlet covers, cabinet latches | Ordinary child-proofing | |
| CPR training for every adult | No ambulance may come | → 12-18; take the class |
| Rescue pole and float at any water | Reach, do not go in | |
| Life jackets sized for each child | Water activities | |
| Tape for the hot-zone line | Makes an abstract rule concrete | → 20-04 |
| A headlamp for each young child | Removes the reason to carry a flame | → 10-01 |
| Flameless night lights | USFA's substitute for candles | → 10-02 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Barriers:** plywood, pallets, furniture, improvised gates. **A pool fence should be the real
  thing.**
- **Lids:** any lid, plywood cut to fit, a tarp bungeed down. Something is far better than
  nothing.
- **Hot-zone line:** tape, chalk, a row of stones.
- **Locked storage:** a padlocked box, a high locked closet, a hasp on a cabinet.
- **Safe zone:** a play yard, a gated room, a corner fenced with furniture.
- **What you cannot improvise:** supervision and CPR knowledge.

## When it runs out

- **Safety equipment does not wear out; vigilance does.** The risk on this page rises with time,
  as the household tires and as a 1-year-old becomes a 2-year-old who climbs, opens latches and
  reaches higher. Re-walk the house as children grow.
- **The failure to guard against is convenience erosion:** the pool gate propped open because
  you are hauling water twenty times a day; the heater barrier moved aside because it is in the
  way; the lamp left burning because everyone is tired. Knowing these in advance is most of the
  defence.
- **Structure beats attention, always.** A latch that closes itself is worth more than a promise
  to be careful.
- **Teaching never runs out.** A child who understands the hot zone and the water rule is safer
  than one who is merely watched (→ 20-04).

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** the highest-hazard phase: a normal house plus a heater in the living
  room, open flame, stored fuel, open water containers and any pool. Alarms and the heater
  barrier first, then water barriers, then locked storage.
- **B (moving):** traffic, unfamiliar ground, water crossings, cold (→ 11-02) and separation
  (→ 15-03, → 15-07). Every child in a car seat, harness snug, no puffy coat under it, blanket
  over the top. **Nobody out of arm's reach;** a whistle and an ID card on each child. Carrying
  fuel inside a passenger vehicle is a trade-off on its own card (→ 30-07); wherever the cans
  ride, children cannot reach them. {{choice DC-06}} → 30-07.
- **C (establish):** ponds and creeks, livestock, machinery, wells, outbuildings, and much longer
  help times (→ 12-16). The first-day walk above, then the room-by-room walk restarts at the new
  house, and the heater barrier comes with the heater.

pages.title: Children's routine and schooling
pages.body:
# Children's routine and schooling

**What this page is for.** Routine is not a comfort item. It is one of the most protective
things you can give children in a crisis, and one of the cheapest. A predictable day tells a
child that the adults have things in hand, and that calms fear better than reassurance does
(→ 20-08, → 21-04). It protects the adults too: a household with a shape to its day decides
better, sleeps better and fights less (→ 21-02, → 21-05). This page gives a daily shape and
what "school" looks like at each age when there is no school.

**Your children:** {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#each teens as t}}{{t.label}} ({{t.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.child}}{{#if !has.teen}}none entered.{{/if}}{{/if}}

{{#if is.cold_winters}}**Your winters are long and dark.** With everyone in one heated room
(→ 08-01) and the dark lasting longer than the day, winter is the hardest stretch for children
and adults. It is worth a plan, not just endurance.{{else}}**The hardest stretch** is any long
spell when everyone is confined indoors: winter dark, a heat wave, smoke or storms. It is worth
a plan, not just endurance.{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Buy paper, pencils, crayons and books**, a large box of them. They are cheap, they do not
   expire, and in a long confinement they matter enormously.
2. **Buy physical learning material for the coming years** of each child: alphabet and number
   sets and early readers for the young ones, workbooks and reference books for older ones,
   books each child will want again and again.
3. **Write a rough daily shape** (below) and try it for a week now. You will find what does not
   work while it is still easy to change.
4. **Protect the two routines that matter most: bedtime (→ 21-07) and toothbrushing (→ 12-06).**
   They quietly lapse and cost the most.

## Why routine protects children

CDC's child development guidance describes young children as thriving on predictability
(CDC, Positive Parenting Tips). In a crisis:
- **A known day lowers anxiety:** the child does not have to wonder what is happening.
- **It saves adult capacity:** a day with a shape needs fewer decisions.
- **It marks time.** Days without structure blur together, which wears down everyone (→ 21-02).
- **It gives a sense of progress**, not just endurance.
- **It survives the loss of everything else.** Routine costs nothing.

## A workable daily shape

Adapt it. The point is that there **is** one.

| Block | What | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Wake with the light** | Up when it is light (→ 10-03) | In winter that is late, and that is fine |
| **Morning: chores and work** | Water, wood, fire, animals, cooking. **Children have jobs** (→ 20-07) | Daylight is for work |
| **Learning block** | At a table, at the best window (length by age, below) | Short and every day beats long and now and then |
| **Midday: main meal** | The big cooking event (→ 07-01) | Everyone together |
| **Afternoon: outdoor time** | Even in winter, especially in winter, when safe | → 11-02, → 12-10 |
| **Late afternoon: projects, mending, prep** | Adults work; children play or help | Before the light goes |
| **Evening: together in the warm room** | Light on, everyone together (→ 08-01, → 10-03) | The social block |
| **Bedtime routine** | **Wash, teeth, story, bed. Same order every night** | **Defend this one** (→ 21-07, → 12-06) |

**The two anchors are morning and bedtime.** If everything else falls apart, keep those.

## Learning, by age

### Infant and toddler (under 3)

They learn by play, talk and being read to. **Talk to them constantly**: hearing language is the
main thing at this age. Name things, sing, read the same books again and again.

### Preschool (3 to 5): keep it modest

At this age "school" is mostly play, language and habits. You do not need a curriculum; you need
consistency and materials.
- **20 to 30 minutes a day is plenty**, and consistency beats length.
- **Letters, numbers, drawing, counting things, and being read to.** Reading aloud is the single
  most valuable learning activity at this age.
- **Everything is a lesson:** counting firewood, measuring water, sorting seeds (→ 05-03),
  reading a thermometer, watching plants grow.
- **Practical skills:** knots (→ 16-03), sewing with a blunt needle (→ 16-04), helping cook,
  feeding animals (→ 20-07). Allergy rules apply in the kitchen (→ 02-04).
- **Physical play matters.** A small child kept indoors all winter with no way to move is hard
  to live with.

### School-age (6 to 12)

- **Reading, writing and arithmetic every day**, in a short block (an hour or so, split up, is
  realistic). Use whatever books and workbooks you have; older children can read to younger
  ones.
- **The household is the curriculum:** measuring and doubling recipes (→ 25-02), weather records
  (→ 17-10), the garden calendar (→ 25-01), simple repairs (→ 16-05), map reading (→ 25-04).
- **Keep a journal** of the event: writing practice now, family history later (→ 25-05).
- **Real skills with real tools come with training and the household's own rule** (→ 30-25).

### Teen (13 to 17)

- **Teens can run their own learning** with books and a weekly check-in. Agree goals with them.
- **Give real responsibility and real skill:** first aid (→ 12-01), radio (→ 15-02), cooking for
  the household, gardening, tool work under the household's job rules (→ 30-25).
- **Teaching younger children** is good for both (→ 18-07).
- **Teens lose the most socially** in a long event: friends, school, plans. Name that loss
  (→ 21-03) and protect some time and privacy for them.

## The long-confinement problem

- **Somewhere to move indoors.** Children need to move. Set aside a space and let them.
- **Get outside every day it is safe** (→ 11-02; limits → 12-10). Even 20 minutes changes a day.
  Cold is manageable with the right clothing; darkness and confinement are the real problem.
- **Vary the days:** a special meal, a project, a game, a new job (→ 21-06).
- **Light for the evening block** (→ 10-03). A lit, warm, gathered evening is worth spending
  scarce light on.
- **Stories, games and music:** cards, dice, drawing, singing, reading aloud. Stock them now.
- **Accept that some days are bad**, for children and adults (→ 21-02).

## Routines that protect health

These lapse silently in a hard stretch and cost real damage:
- **Toothbrushing twice a day** with fluoride toothpaste (CDC, Oral Health). A stored-food diet is
  high in starches and sugars and there may be no dentist (→ 12-06).
- **Handwashing at the key moments** (CDC, About Hygiene; → 13-02): it is how outbreaks are
  prevented (→ 13-11).
- **Bedtime and sleep** (→ 21-07).
- **Meals at regular times**, which also matters for anyone with diabetes (→ 02-01, → 02-05).
- **Getting dressed each morning**, even when nobody is going anywhere. It marks the day as a day.

## The adults' side

- **Assign the routine; do not just hope for it** (→ 00-07): who does the morning fire, who does
  the learning block, who does bedtime.
- **Trade off.** Adults with small children in one room for months need breaks from each other.
  Put them on the schedule (→ 21-05).
- **Protect some adult time** in the evening after the children are down.
- **Make one day a week different** (→ 21-06). A week identical to the last is how time
  collapses.

## The children's box

When the household moves, one labelled tote is the children's box, claimed now so it is not
argued over at load time (→ 22-05, → 01-06).
- **Contents:** a rotating dozen books, paper, pencils and crayons, small games (cards, dice,
  dominoes), and **duplicates of the important comfort objects** (→ 20-08).
- **Packed light enough that a child can help carry it**, with the contents list taped inside the
  lid.
- **It is not optional weight.** On the move this tote is the routine: the bedtime story and the
  learning block at a rest stop come out of it.

```
CHILDREN'S BOX packed: __________  contents listed in lid: YES / NO
```

## Gear

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Paper, pencils, crayons in bulk** | Cheap, do not expire, enormously valuable | A big box |
| **Physical books**, including early readers and reference | No power needed, endlessly re-read | Buy ahead of each child's reading age |
| Alphabet and number materials, workbooks | The learning block | |
| Games: cards, dice, dominoes, board games | Evenings, no batteries | |
| Art supplies, modelling clay, blunt scissors | Hands busy for hours | |
| A simple musical instrument | Morale, and a skill | → 21-06 |
| **Toothbrushes and fluoride toothpaste, years' worth** | Protect this routine | → 12-06 |
| Indoor play items | Children must move | Ball, tunnel, cushions |
| Reading light for the evening | Worth the watts | → 10-01, → 10-03 |
| Calendar for crossing off days | Marks time | → 21-06 |
| Written daily routine, posted | Everyone knows the shape of the day | → 21-04 |
| The children's box | Routine on the move | → 22-05 |
| Seeds, magnifier, simple tools | The household is the curriculum | → 05-03, → 16-03 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Paper:** the backs of anything, cardboard, brown paper. Charcoal from the fire draws well
  (→ 06-01).
- **Books:** libraries, free boxes, neighbours. Book swapping is a natural community activity
  (→ 18-01, → 18-07).
- **Games:** cards, dice and pebbles cover a huge number of games. Learn a few good ones now.
- **Toys:** made from wood, cloth and string (→ 16-03, → 16-04). A small child plays with almost
  anything if an adult is engaged.
- **Curriculum:** the household itself: cooking, counting, measuring, weather, plants, animals,
  tools.
- **What you cannot substitute:** adult attention. That is the real input, and the scarcest one
  in a hard stretch, which is why the routine matters.

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here runs out fast.** Paper, pencils and books last, and routine costs nothing.
- **What wears away is the routine itself**, months in, when everyone is tired. The defence is
  having it written down and assigned (→ 00-07, → 21-04) rather than relying on willpower.
- **Ration light** (→ 10-03) **to the evening block and bedtime**; do the learning block by
  daylight at the window.
- **Substitute:** spoken learning (stories, songs, counting, memory games) needs no materials.
  Learn some stories.
- **The return:** a child who spends a crisis year learning, helping and feeling secure comes out
  of it better off, not worse. That depends far more on routine and adult attention than on
  supplies.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** set the routine in the first week. A household that drifts for a
  month rarely recovers the structure.
- **B (moving):** routine collapses on the move and that is expected. Keep two things:
  **bedtime and food times.** A story and a steady bedtime help a young child enormously, even in
  a vehicle (→ 20-08); the children's box makes that possible.
- **C (establish):** more real work and real learning: animals, garden, building, weather. A rural
  household is a rich place for a child to learn (→ 20-07). Re-set the routine in the first week
  at the new site.
