pages.body:
# Teaching children the plan

**What this page is for.** A child who knows what to do is safer, calmer and easier to keep safe
than one who does not. Teaching is a real safety layer, **but it sits on top of barriers and
supervision** (→ 20-02), never in place of them. This page lists what to teach at each age, how
to teach it so it sticks, and the drills to run.

**The tone matters as much as the content.** Taught as competence and routine, this makes a
child feel capable. Taught as danger and fear, it makes anxious children who follow rules less
well (→ 20-08, → 21-01). **Frame everything as "here's what we do", not "here's what could happen
to you."**

**Your children:** {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#each teens as t}}{{t.label}} ({{t.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.child}}{{#if !has.teen}}none entered.{{/if}}{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Teach each child who can talk five things this month:** their full name and their parents'
   full names; any allergies they have; the fire rule; the water rule; and what to do if lost
   (stay put, blow the whistle).
2. **Give them equipment that goes with the rules:** their own **headlamp**, so they never need
   to carry a flame, and their own **whistle** on their jacket (→ 10-01, → 15-07). Children keep
   rules they have tools for.
3. **Practise the shelter drill and the "we got separated" drill as games** (→ 17-06, → 24-02).
   Twice, once at night.
4. **Teach the "grown-up won't wake up" drill** (below). Hang a whistle at the child's height and
   tape an address card beside the phone first, so the steps have tools.
5. **Teach "no puffy coat in the car seat"** as their rule too: coat off, harness snug, blanket
   over the top (AAP; → 11-02).
6. **Put a medical card in each child's pocket** and tell them what it is for (→ 15-03, → 25-09).

## What to teach, by age

### Infant and toddler (under 3)

Almost nothing yet, and that is the planning point. **The environment does the work**: barriers,
latches, lids and constant supervision (→ 20-02). Routine and predictability build their sense of
safety (→ 21-04). They learn by watching older children, which cuts both ways: an older child
keeping the rules helps. Re-teach as they grow; in a year or two they will be learning the
preschool list.

### Preschool (3 to 5)

CDC's development guidance describes preschoolers as able to follow simple rules, remember
routines and learn best by repetition and play rather than explanation (CDC, Positive Parenting
Tips).

| Teach | How | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Full name and parents' full names** | Repetition, a song | Separation (→ 15-03) |
| **Their allergies, if any** | Repetition; a card in the pocket | Life-critical (→ 02-03) |
| **"I only eat food a grown-up gives me"** | Absolute, repeated, no exceptions | Allergies, spoiled food, foraged plants |
| **The fire rule:** fire stays where a grown-up puts it | Show the hot-zone tape; give a headlamp | Daily hazard (→ 12-03) |
| **The water rule:** never near a pool, pond or bucket without a grown-up | Repetition; gates stay latched | Drowning (→ 20-02) |
| **The shelter drill:** where we go, what we do | Practise as a game, twice | → 17-06 |
| **Lost:** stay put, blow the whistle three times, keep blowing | Practise outdoors | → 15-07 |
| **"Grown-up won't wake up"** | The script below, every few months, as a game | Life-critical |
| **"Only people on my list"** | Recite the names | → 00-04 |
| **"Tell a grown-up if..."** hurt, cold, tingly, scared, sees something wrong | Praise every time they do | Turns them into a sensor |
| **Where the kits are**, and that they can fetch an adult | Show them | → 12-08 |
| **The meeting place** | Walk there; make it a landmark they know | → 15-03 |

### School-age (6 to 12)

Everything on the preschool list, plus:
- **Home address and a phone number by heart**, and the out-of-area contact (→ 00-04).
- **How to call 911 and what to say** (AAP, Teaching Your Child How to Use 911): their name,
  the address, what happened, and stay on the line. Any wireless phone can call 911, even without
  service (FCC).
- **The family communications plan** (→ 15-03): meeting places, radio channel, signals.
- **Basic first aid:** pressure on bleeding, cooling a burn, the recovery position (→ 12-01).
- **Carrying and checking their own go-bag** (→ 22-03).
- **Reading the household's own signs:** the carbon monoxide alarm sound and what to do (get
  everyone out), the smoke alarm sound.

### Teen (13 to 17)

Treat teens as junior adults in the plan:
- **The whole family plan** (→ 00-04), the go/no-go triggers (→ 01-02) and their own role
  (→ 00-07).
- **First aid and CPR training**, ideally a real class (→ 12-18).
- **Radio use** (→ 15-02) and the comms plan.
- **How to shut off the utilities** (→ 16-12) and use an extinguisher (→ 29-12).
- **Dangerous jobs** on the household's own worksheet (→ 30-25), and firearm safety rules even in
  a house with no firearms (→ 29-11).
- **How to give help when an adult is down**, including any household member's emergency
  medicine they have been trained to give (→ 02-03, → 02-01).

## How to teach it so it sticks

- **Repetition beats explanation.** "We do this" works far better than "here's why" until about
  school age.
- **Make it a game.** Time the shelter drill. Race to the meeting place. Practise the whistle
  outside. Play is how young children learn.
- **Give a job in the drill** (→ 20-07): carrying a small bag, holding the flashlight. A child with
  a role takes part; a child with no role panics or resists.
- **Praise the behaviour, every time**, above all telling an adult something.
- **Never make a child afraid to report.** "You are never in trouble for being lost, for telling
  us you're cold, for saying you ate something." A child who fears trouble hides things, and a
  hidden food exposure or a hidden fall is dangerous.
- **Keep it short and concrete.** "We stay behind the tape when the fire is on." Not a lecture.
- **Model it.** Children copy what adults do, not what they say.
- **Re-teach as they grow** (→ 25-10). A rule taught at four does not fit at six.

## Allergies: the conversation for a child who has one

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}Your household's allergy list: {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}); {{/each}}{{/if}}

- **The rule is absolute and simple:** "I only eat food a grown-up who knows my allergies gives
  me." Not "be careful". Not "check first".
- **Teach the names** of their allergens as they can manage them. Where an allergy covers a whole
  group (for example tree nuts), teach the whole group as a "no"; a small child cannot tell one nut
  from another in someone else's kitchen. Exceptions are the adults' to manage (→ 02-04).
- **Teach them to say "I'm allergic"** to any adult offering food.
- **Teach what a reaction feels like** and to tell an adult **at once**: tingly mouth, itchy
  throat, tummy hurts, feels funny (CDC, Recognizing and Responding to Anaphylaxis). Frame it as
  "tell us right away and we'll fix it."
- **Do not make a young child responsible for avoidance.** The adults own the safe-food chain
  (→ 02-04). The child's job is to eat only what they are handed and to speak up.
- **Teach every other adult who might feed them:** neighbours, relatives, anyone (→ 18-01). That
  is a bigger risk than the child's own behaviour.

## The "grown-up won't wake up" drill

**Why it exists.** Any adult can collapse: a fall, a seizure, carbon monoxide, a heart problem, a
diabetic low. A young child cannot treat it, but **can be drilled to get help**. The AAP says
young children can learn a simple, rehearsed get-help script, and its first lesson is calling 911
(AAP, Teaching Your Child How to Use 911). While phones work, that is the step that saves the
adult.
{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}**Your household includes insulin-treated diabetes:** a severe low is
the likeliest reason this drill is ever used (→ 02-01). The treatment is an adult's trained job;
the child's job is getting the adult.{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-11}} **Your household includes
a seizure disorder** (→ 02-11): add "move things away and do not hold them down" only for older
children taught by an adult.{{/if}}

**Teach it word for word (put in the names that fit your family):**

```
IF A GROWN-UP WON'T WAKE UP, OR ACTS FUNNY OR WOBBLY:
  1. SHOUT for the other grown-up, as loud as you can.
  2. If no one comes: CALL 9-1-1 on the phone.
     Say: "MY ______ WON'T WAKE UP."
     Then read the ADDRESS CARD by the phone. DON'T hang up.
  3. BLOW THE WHISTLE (the hook by the door). Keep blowing.
  4. STAY with the little ones and KEEP SHOUTING and BLOWING.
     That IS the job.
  5. ONLY if it is DAYTIME and a grown-up said TODAY that the phones
     are broken: go to ________________ and say
     "MY ______ WON'T WAKE UP."
```

Step 5's place: {{ contacts.meet.near_home }} (the near-home meeting place in → 00-04), or a
neighbour named here: ______________________.

- **The phone gesture.** Most mobile phones have an emergency SOS shortcut (often holding the side
  button with a volume button) as well as dialling 911. Write the exact steps for each phone in
  the house: phone 1 ______________ ; phone 2 ______________ . **Practise the gesture with the
  call cancelled, or on a pretend phone. Never dial 911 to practise** (AAP).
- **The address card.** The street address in large print, taped at the child's eye level by the
  phone and the whistle hook, read aloud together until they can say it. A child can read it
  back even if they cannot remember it. Address: __________________________________ {{photo address-card}}
- **Why "stay" comes before "go".** A young child cannot weigh dark, cold or traffic before
  crossing streets alone; they will do whatever they were last praised for. So the default is
  **stay, shout, whistle.** Leaving is the exception, true only when it is daylight **and** an
  adult said that morning, "the phones are broken today; if someone won't wake up, you go to
  ______." When phones are down, one adult says that line every morning; when they work, nobody
  does, and step 5 does not exist.
- **What the child must never do: touch the adult's medicine.** Not pens, pumps, syringes or
  pills. **Their job is noise and feet, never medicine** (→ 20-02). Older children and teens may
  be trained by an adult to give a specific emergency medicine (→ 02-03, → 02-01); that is a
  separate, adult-taught skill.
- **Practise every few months, as a game, never as a fright** (→ 24-02): announced, short, ended
  with a high five, stopped if the child is scared. A grown-up "sleeps" on the floor; the child
  runs the steps. **Never tell them the grown-up could really die.** The frame is "this is how you
  get the grown-ups." After any real event, debrief with → 21-03.

## Pets in an alarm

{{#if has.pets}}Teach it as its own line, because in a real alarm a child **will** think of the
pets:{{else}}If the household ever has pets, teach this as its own line:{{/if}}

> "When the alarm goes, the pets look after themselves. Your job is YOU. Nobody chases a pet,
> not you and not the grown-ups."

Carriers can wait at the shelter spot with doors open; an animal that comes gets crated; one that
does not waits for the all-clear (→ 20-09). Seconds spent chasing an animal are seconds the
family is not in shelter. The comfort to say, because it is often true: animals are good at
finding their own hiding places.

## "Only people on my list": separation and reunification

The child's side of the reunification plan (→ 00-04):
- **The rule: "If my grown-ups don't come, I go only with people on my list."** Practise
  reciting the names the same way as their own name. A stranger, even a kind one, is not on the
  list. A family password the list knows is an easy check.
- **Write the collection plan in pen** for a school or workday event:

```
IF IT HAPPENS ON A SCHOOL OR WORK DAY:
  Collects the children: ______________ (default: whichever adult is
     closer at that hour)
  Goes home / to the meeting place: ______________
  If school or childcare is unreachable: staff follow their release
     list. These names MUST be on it: ________________________
  Any child's emergency medicine plan on file there: YES / NO
```

- **When a child starts a new school or childcare,** re-do the pickup list, the medicine plan with
  the school nurse, and the reunification point, and re-run this page and → 00-04 that month.

## Drills: actually run them

| Drill | How often | What you will learn |
|---|---|---|
| **Shelter** (tornado, storm; → 17-06; NWS Tornado Safety) | Twice now, then each season | It takes longer than you think; a small child freezes; the light is dead |
| **Fire escape** (→ 00-04) | Twice a year | Two ways out; where you meet |
| **Grown-up won't wake up** | Every few months, as a game | Whether they can work the phone, find the whistle, read the card, and stay |
| **"We got separated"** (→ 15-03) | Once, then yearly | They do not remember the meeting place |
| **Lost: stay put and whistle** (→ 15-07) | Outdoors, a few times | They want to walk toward you; that is the habit to break |
| **Blackout evening** (→ 24-04) | Yearly | Everything |

**Debrief each one positively:** "You did great. Next time let's try X." Never scare them with
what would have happened.

## The balance to hold

The household is preparing for serious things and children absorb some of that regardless
(→ 20-08). **The goal is a child who feels capable and safe, not one who is anxious and always on
watch.**
- Tell them the adults have a plan and their job is small and specific.
- Answer questions honestly at their level, and do not volunteer more (→ 20-08).
- Keep normal life normal: play, stories, routine, treats (→ 21-06).
- Watch for signs it is landing badly: new fears, sleep problems, going backwards, clinginess
  (→ 20-08).

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Whistle on each child's jacket** | The lost-child tool; carries far | → 15-07 |
| **Whistle on a hook at child height**, and one in each go-bag | Step 3 of the drill needs a tool | → 22-03 |
| **Address card by each phone**, large print, child's eye level | The 911 operator needs the address | Laminate it |
| **Car seat for each child**, no bulky coat under the harness | Moving is a drive | → 11-02, → 22-05 |
| **A headlamp per child** | A rule with a tool | → 10-01 |
| **Medical card in each child's pocket** | Allergies, names, contacts | → 15-03, → 25-09 |
| Medical ID bracelet or tag | Works when the card is lost | |
| Tape for the hot-zone line | Makes the rule visible | → 12-03 |
| A small go-bag of their own | A role in the plan | → 22-03 |
| Books about weather and helpers | Calm framing | → 20-08 |
| The drill schedule on the calendar | Unscheduled drills do not happen | → 24-02 |

**Scavenge or substitute:** the teaching costs nothing and is the most valuable thing on this
page. A card can be an index card in a zip bag, or written inside a jacket, or written on the
child's arm in marker (a real disaster-response practice). Any whistle works. **What you cannot
substitute:** teaching every adult who might feed an allergic child.

## When it runs out

- **Teaching does not run out; it compounds.** Everything a child learns now they keep and build
  on.
- **What fades is memory and fit.** A drill practised once is forgotten. **Re-teach and re-drill
  every year** (→ 25-10), and as each younger child comes into range.
- **The failure:** teaching once, feeling done, and finding in a real event that the child does
  not remember. Schedule the re-drills.
- **Confidence compounds fastest.** A child who has done the shelter drill six times goes to
  shelter calmly instead of freezing, which frees adult time and attention exactly when both are
  scarce.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** teach and drill now, while it can be play.
- **B (moving):** the training pays off. Before setting out, re-brief: where we are going, what
  to do if separated, the car-seat rule (→ 01-03, → 15-03).
- **C (establish):** new hazards, new rules (→ 20-02). Re-teach everything at the new site on day
  one, walk the boundaries together, and hand out new jobs (→ 20-07).

pages.title: Feeding babies and toddlers without the supply chain
pages.body:
# Feeding babies and toddlers without the supply chain

**What this page is for.** The household routine for feeding a baby or toddler when stores,
power and clean tap water may be gone: the three feeding paths, how to hold each one together,
the right milk at each age, and what to do in a formula shortage. The medical side (the nursing
parent's own medicines, warning signs in a baby, and the formula clock as a condition) is the
infant-feeding module, → 02-13. The water arithmetic is → 03-01.

> **SAFETY. Two rules that are absolute.**
>
> **(1) Never dilute infant formula to make it last longer.** Over-diluted formula causes water
> intoxication, salt imbalance, seizures, brain damage and death in babies. It is one of the most
> dangerous things a loving parent can do in a shortage. Mix exactly as the label says, every
> time.
>
> **(2) Never make homemade infant formula.** Recipes from evaporated milk, goat milk, plant milks
> or "old recipes" have caused serious harm and death. A baby's needs are specific and
> unforgiving. **A formula shortage is a medical and public-health emergency, not a kitchen
> project.**
>
> This page gives **no formula recipes and no dilution ratios**, on purpose. It does print the
> holding times and water temperatures, because off-grid this binder may be the only reference.

**Your youngest:** {{#each infants as i}}{{i.label}} ({{i.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.infant}}no member under 2 is entered.{{/if}}{{#if has.nursing}} **Someone in your household is nursing.**{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Ask your baby's doctor now:** "What happens if we cannot get our milk or formula for a
   month?" Write the answer in the box below.
2. **If formula is in use, stock it deeply and rotate it.** It expires. It is a short-runway,
   no-substitute supply; treat it as seriously as insulin (→ 23-02).
3. **Secure safe water for preparation and cleaning** (→ 03-04). That need does not relax in a
   crisis.
4. **Write each child's actual feeding in pen** and re-date it every few months. Every plan on
   this page branches on it:

```
AS OF: __________  Child: __________  Age: ______
Breastfed?  YES / NO   When: ____________________
Formula?    YES / NO   Brand and type: __________  Amount per day: ______
Family foods?  YES / NO     Milk (12 to 23 months): WHOLE  ______ oz/day
Doctor's answer for "no formula or milk for a month": ______________
____________________________________________________________________
```

## The three feeding paths

| Path | How it holds up in a crisis | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| **Breastfeeding** | **The most robust there is:** no supply chain, no water treatment, no sterilising, right temperature, protection against infection (CDC) | **The nursing parent fed, watered and rested** |
| **Formula** | **The most fragile:** a manufactured product that needs safe water and clean equipment | Supply, safe water, fuel and water for cleaning |
| **Family foods (from about 12 months)** | **More robust every month:** the child eats what the household eats | Household food, allergy care |

Every month a child moves along the third path, the household loses a supply-chain dependency.

## Breastfeeding

- **It is the most crisis-resistant way to feed a baby** (CDC), and the immune protection comes at
  exactly the time infection risk rises (→ 13-11).
- **The nursing parent's food and water are not optional.** The Dietary Guidelines add about 330
  calories a day in the first 6 months of nursing and about 400 in the second 6 months (USDA/HHS,
  Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025), and the water plan adds extra (→ 03-01). This is the
  thing people most often forget. {{#if has.nursing}}Your water floor already includes it:
  {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons a day for the household.{{/if}}
- **Stress and exhaustion affect supply**, and a crisis brings both. Rest, food, water and support
  are the practical help (→ 21-02). Sudden weaning under stress is a real risk: protecting the
  nursing parent **is** the baby's food security.
- **Expressing and storing milk** (CDC, as published):
  - Freshly expressed: **up to 4 hours at room temperature** (77 °F or cooler); **up to 4 days in
    a fridge** (40 °F or colder); frozen, **about 6 months is best, 12 months acceptable**.
  - Thawed milk: 1 to 2 hours at room temperature, 24 hours in the fridge; **never refreeze**.
  - Left over from a feed: use within 2 hours or throw away. Never microwave breast milk.
  - In winter an unheated porch or shed works as a fridge only if a thermometer shows it holding
    between 32 and 40 °F (→ 04-09). In summer it does not (→ 09-10).
- **Clean pump parts and bottles** as in CDC's infant feeding-item guidance: wash, then sanitise
  (CDC, How to Clean, Sanitize, and Store Infant Feeding Items; → 13-10).
- **Medicines while nursing** (the parent's own) are in → 02-13.

## Formula

**Follow CDC's guidance and the label exactly.**
- **Safe water every time** (→ 03-04). **Boil the water** (a rolling boil, then let it cool).
- **For a baby under 2 to 3 months old, born early, or with a weak immune system:** mix the
  powder into water that is still **at least 158 °F (70 °C)**, which kills *Cronobacter* germs
  that can be in the powder (CDC; WHO/FAO, Safe Preparation of Powdered Infant Formula). **Then
  cool the bottle to body temperature** and test a drop on the inside of your wrist before
  feeding.
- **Clean bottles and feeding items:** washed, then sanitised (CDC). This costs real water and
  fuel (→ 13-10); budget it.
- **Holding times** (CDC, as published):
  - Mixed powdered formula: **use within 2 hours of mixing**, or within 24 hours if refrigerated
    straight away.
  - **Once a feed starts, finish or throw away within 1 hour** (saliva seeds the bottle with
    germs).
  - Opened ready-to-feed: capped and refrigerated, **use within 48 hours**; same 1-hour rule once
    a feed starts.
  - **No fridge: mix one feed at a time.**
- **Never add anything to a bottle:** no cereal, no sugar, no honey.
- **Ready-to-feed formula needs no water and no mixing.** That makes it right for go-bags and for
  moving (→ 22-03), despite the weight and cost.
- **Powdered formula stores longest** and is right for the bulk stock.
- **Check every label against the household's allergies.** Formulas based on soy and on cow's
  milk both exist (→ 02-04).

## The right milk after 12 months

- **From 12 to 23 months the milk is plain, pasteurised whole milk** (CDC, Foods and Drinks for
  12 to 24 Month Olds): about **16 to 24 ounces a day**. More than that crowds out iron-rich food.
  Low-fat or fat-free milk only from age 2, unless a clinician says otherwise.
- **Most pantries stock nonfat dry milk.** That is cooking milk and milk for over-2s, **not
  toddler milk**. Stock for a toddler: **whole-milk powder** or **shelf-stable (UHT) whole milk**,
  rotated (→ 04-14).
- **Evaporated milk mixed half and half with safe water is an acceptable whole-milk drink for a
  child over 12 months** (→ 04-14): as milk with meals, **never as infant formula** and never the
  "homemade formula" of the warning above.
- **If none of these is available,** the fat comes from the family plate: butter or ghee, oils,
  full-fat dairy where there is any, eggs if no allergy forbids them. Ask the child's doctor now
  and write the answer in the box above. Milk still needs safe handling (→ 04-17).

## A formula shortage: what to actually do

The right actions all face outward:
1. **Contact the baby's doctor at once.** They have options and information you do not.
2. **Contact the pharmacy, WIC if you use it, and public health.** Shortages are handled as public
   health matters, and relief agencies follow international guidance on feeding babies in
   emergencies (IFE Core Group, Infant and Young Child Feeding in Emergencies).
3. **Ask the clinician which alternatives suit a child of this age.** At 12 months there are more
   options than at 2 months; that is a clinician's call.
4. **Ask other parents and the community** (→ 18-01). Formula sharing happens.
5. **Do not dilute. Do not improvise formula.** Repeated because it is the thing people do.
6. **If there is no access at all, that is a reason to move toward supply** (→ 01-02), the same
   logic as for insulin. It is not a shelter-in-place problem.

## Moving to family foods

From CDC's infant and toddler nutrition guidance (read it in the original if you can):
- **From about 6 months, other foods start alongside breast milk or formula.**
- **By about 12 months, a child eats a good share from the family table.** Lean that way in a
  crisis: every food the child can eat from the household supply removes a dependency.
- **Soft, mashable, small pieces.** The choking list is on → 20-01 (AAP) and the response on
  → 12-18.
- **Variety and nutrient density** need deliberate attention on a stored-food diet (→ 04-18).
- **New allergenic foods:** plan with the child's doctor, especially if a sibling has a food
  allergy (→ 02-04).

## Water for babies

- **Safe water matters more for babies than for adults.** Use CDC's guidance for preparing
  formula and for any water a baby drinks (→ 03-04; what "safe" means: → 29-06).
- **Too much plain water is dangerous for young babies**, which is another reason the no-dilution
  rule exists.
- **In illness, oral rehydration solution (ORS) is the answer, not plain water** (→ 12-05). A
  small child dries out dangerously fast.

## Gear

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Formula (if used), deep stock, rotated** | Short runway, no substitute | Check dates; powdered for bulk |
| **Ready-to-feed formula for the go-bag** | No water, no mixing | → 22-03 |
| **Safe water capacity and spare filters** | Preparation needs it | → 03-04 |
| Bottles, nipples, brushes: spares | They wear out and get lost | And a way to sanitise |
| Pot and fuel for boiling water and equipment | Sanitising costs fuel and water | → 07-01, → 13-10 |
| Breastfeeding supplies | Pump parts, storage bags | And the nursing parent's food and water |
| **Whole-milk powder or UHT whole milk (12 to 23 months)** | Nonfat powder is the wrong milk | → 04-14 |
| Shelf-stable toddler foods the child eats | The direction things go | → 20-01 |
| **ORS** | Illness in a baby is a fast emergency | → 12-05 |
| Thermometer for food and cold storage | Holding times depend on temperature | → 04-09 |
| Written feeding plan on each child's card | Any caregiver needs it | → 15-03, → 25-09 |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Family foods**, mashed and softened, after about 12 months (CDC).
- **Other parents and the community** (→ 18-01).
- **Doctor, pharmacy, WIC, public health:** the right channels in a shortage.
- **Clean cloth and boiled water** for cleaning feeding equipment when soap or hot water is short
  (→ 13-10).
- **What you must not substitute: infant formula itself.** No dilution, no homemade recipes, no
  animal-milk "formula". (Whole cow's milk, or evaporated milk mixed half and half, **as a drink
  for a child over 12 months** is a different thing and is fine.)

## When it runs out

- **Formula is one of the shortest-runway, least replaceable supplies in the binder.** Put it on
  the consumables table (→ 23-02) and check it weekly while it is in use.
- **Runway = cans (or ounces) on hand ÷ daily use.** Work out the number and know it.
- **You cannot ration a baby's food.** Ration everything else to protect it, and answer a
  shortage by **seeking supply**, not stretching what you have.
- **Whole milk's runway:** whole-milk powder, then UHT, then evaporated milk, then fat from the
  family plate (and the doctor's answer above).
- **Escalation trigger:** if a baby's feeding cannot be met, that is a go/no-go event (→ 01-02).
  Decide the threshold in advance.
- **The reassuring part:** this dependency has a natural end. Each month a baby is closer to
  family food.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** stock deeply, keep safe-water capacity, keep in touch with the
  doctor, and move toward family foods as fast as the doctor advises. Stores are the resupply
  window; use it.
- **B (moving):** **ready-to-feed formula** and safe water for everything else. This is the one
  place where the heavy, expensive option is clearly right (→ 22-03). The nursing parent's water
  and food travel first.
- **C (establish):** no resupply. A child eating family food is a much easier problem, and a
  garden, eggs and animals (→ 05-01, → 05-04) make a good toddler diet possible.

pages.title: Diapering and keeping small children clean

photo_slots.caption: Our changing station: supplies in reach, lidded pail, handwashing right there

pages.body:
# Diapering and keeping small children clean

**What this page is for.** CDC warns that even a microscopic amount of poop can carry millions of
germs. In a house with a child in diapers, diapering is the busiest route for germs to travel from
bottom to mouth, and in a grid-down house (no running water, rationed washing, everyone in one
room) that is exactly how a household-wide outbreak starts (→ 13-11, → 12-05). This page is the
routine, the hygiene and the skin. The diaper supply and the laundry system are on → 13-08.

> **The control is simple, and it does not relax when water is short: wash hands with soap and
> water after every single change** (CDC; → 13-02), clean the changing surface, and contain the
> waste (→ 13-01).

**Children in diapers or learning the toilet:** {{#each infants as i}}{{i.label}} ({{i.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.infant}}{{#if !has.toddler}}none entered.{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if has.toddler}} (and any toddler up to about 3){{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Set up one changing station** with everything within arm's reach and **handwashing right
   there** (→ 13-02). If washing means walking to another room, it will not happen every time.
2. **Get a lidded pail** and put it where a toddler cannot reach it (→ 20-02).
3. **Stock barrier ointment** (petroleum jelly or zinc oxide). Preventing rash matters much more
   without a doctor (→ 12-07).
4. **Post the diapering steps** (below) on the wall. Order matters, and it slips at 3 a.m.

{{photo changing-station}}

## The routine

From CDC's hygiene guidance; read the original if you can and post it. What matters most off-grid:

1. **Everything ready before you start:** clean diaper, wipes, ointment, bag. **Never walk away
   from a child on a changing surface.**
2. **Contain the soiled diaper at once:** into the lidded pail or a bag (→ 13-01, → 13-08).
3. **Clean the child front to back**, thoroughly.
4. **Clean the changing surface after every change.** This is the step that gets skipped, and it
   is how the surface becomes a germ route (CDC, When and How to Clean and Disinfect Your Home).
5. **Wash your hands with soap and water, every time.** Hand sanitiser is a supplement, not a
   replacement (CDC, About Handwashing).
6. **Wash the child's hands too.** They have touched everything and they go in the mouth.

## Why this matters more without the grid

- **Water is rationed**, so skipping the wash is tempting. Do not. A tippy-tap at the station
  makes it almost free (→ 13-02).
- **Solids go into the waste system** (→ 13-01), not the laundry. Shake or scrape first.
- **Cloth diapers make the laundry infection control** (→ 13-04): hot water, thorough rinsing,
  complete drying.
- **Everyone in one room** (→ 08-01) is the wrong set-up for stopping an outbreak (→ 13-11).
- **A toddler touches and mouths everything**: the household's most efficient germ carrier, which
  is an age, not a criticism.
- **A sick toddler dries out fast** (→ 12-05), so preventing illness is worth a great deal.

## Diaper rash: ordinary now, a real problem off-grid

Changes may be less frequent, drying incomplete and washing imperfect.
- **Change often.** A wet diaper in a cold house is a rash cause and a heat drain (→ 11-02).
- **Dry the skin completely** before the new diaper.
- **Diaper-free time** on a towel in the warm room: the most effective single thing.
- **Barrier ointment at every change** once a rash starts. Petroleum jelly works.
- **Rinse cloth diapers thoroughly.** Soap left in the cloth is a common cause of rash that will
  not clear (→ 13-04).
- **Dry in the sun when you can**: sunlight helps bleach and sanitise cloth.
- **Watch for rash that is not improving, spreads, has open sores, or comes with fever.** It may
  be a yeast or bacterial infection (→ 12-04).

**Telling yeast rash apart:** **beefy red with a sharp edge, small red "satellite" spots beyond
the main patch, worst in the skin folds** (an ordinary irritant rash spares the folds), and **not
better after 2 to 3 days of barrier cream and diaper-free time.** Yeast needs an antifungal cream
(clotrimazole 1% or miconazole 2%, sold over the counter and stocked on → 12-07), **used as its
label directs**, with barrier ointment over the top; boil-wash the cloth diapers. Spreading
pus-filled blisters, crusting or fever is bacterial, not yeast: → 12-04.

## Washing a small child with little water

- **A basin wash covers most of it:** face, hands, bottom, feet, skin folds. Very little water,
  real results (CDC, Personal Hygiene During an Emergency; → 13-02).
- **Warm the water.** Nobody, least of all a toddler, cooperates with a cold wash in a cold house.
- **Full baths become occasional**, and that is fine. Hands, face and bottom come first.
- **Hands before every meal**: the most valuable wash of the day.
- **Teeth twice a day** (→ 12-06).
- **Nails short**: dirt under nails, and scratching.
- **Lice and scabies** spread in crowded conditions; stock the treatments (→ 12-07).
- **Dry thoroughly and dress warmly afterwards** in a cold house (→ 11-02).

## Toilet learning, by age

- **Toddler (1 to 3):** **a crisis is a bad time to start toilet learning.** Wait for stability
  unless the child is clearly ready and leading.
- **Preschool and school-age:** **going backwards under stress is normal and common** (→ 20-08).
  Treat it as unremarkable and keep some larger cloth options and spare clothes; making it a
  problem makes it worse.
- **A cold, dark trip to a bucket toilet is frightening for a small child** (→ 13-01, → 13-05).
  Keep the toilet indoors, near the warm room, with a light the child can use (→ 10-01), a step
  and a seat reducer if you have one.
- **Older children and teens** need privacy for toileting and washing even in one shared room
  (→ 21-07); a hung blanket is enough. Menstrual supplies for older girls: → 13-08.

## Nights

- **Night changes in a cold, dark house are easy to put off.** Set up so they are fast: everything
  in reach, a headlamp on a hook, the pail right there.
- **Overnight, a well-fitted absorbent diaper matters**: a good use of a disposable when supply
  allows (→ 13-08).
- **A wet child overnight in a cold room loses real heat** (→ 11-02).

## Gear

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Changing station with handwashing at it** | Inconvenient washing does not happen | → 13-02; a tippy-tap works |
| **Lidded pail, out of reach** | Containment and toddler safety | → 13-08, → 20-02 |
| Diapers: a disposable buffer plus cloth | The relentless consumable | → 13-08 |
| **Barrier ointment / petroleum jelly** | Rash prevention without a doctor | Many uses |
| **Antifungal cream** (clotrimazole 1% or miconazole 2%) | Yeast rash, which barrier cream will not fix | → 12-07 |
| Soap in quantity; a way to warm water | The main control | → 13-02, → 13-09 |
| Cloth wipes or disposable wipes | Wipes run out fast; cloth is reusable | Wash with the diapers |
| Washable changing pad and spares | Cleaned after each change | |
| Headlamp on a hook at the station | Night changes | → 10-01 |
| Basin and washcloths, labelled | Low-water washing | |
| Children's toothbrushes and fluoride toothpaste | Protect the routine | → 12-06 |
| Lice and scabies treatments | Crowded conditions | → 12-07 |
| Nail clippers, small comb | Ordinary hygiene | |
| The diapering steps, posted | Order matters at 3 a.m. | On the wall |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Wipes:** cloth squares and warm water: cheaper, kinder to skin, reusable (→ 13-08). Cut from
  flannel or old towels (→ 16-04).
- **Changing pad:** a folded towel over a plastic sheet or a cut trash bag.
- **Pail:** any bucket with a lid.
- **Barrier:** petroleum jelly, lard or tallow (→ 10-04), or a plain oil.
- **Handwashing:** a tippy-tap, a jug with a nail hole, a bottle with a pinhole (→ 13-02).
- **Diapers:** flannel, towels, folded T-shirts (→ 13-08).
- **What you cannot substitute:** handwashing. That is the whole control.

## When it runs out

- **Disposables and wipes run out; cloth does not** (→ 13-08). The change is from a supply
  problem to a water, soap and drying problem: a better problem, but a real one (→ 13-04, → 11-03).
- **Count disposables in days of a toddler.** It is a sobering number. Put it on → 23-02.
- **Use disposables where they count most:** overnight, during illness, in a cold snap when
  drying is impossible, and on the move. Cloth the rest of the time.
- **Never ration handwashing after changes, or change frequency.** Both cost far less than the
  illness or rash they prevent.
- **This problem ends on its own.** A child is out of diapers in a few years.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** cloth as the default **while** water, fuel for a hot wash and indoor
  drying all hold; fall back on the disposable buffer when they do not (→ 13-08, → 13-04,
  → 03-01). Set up the station properly in the first week.
- **B (moving):** **disposables, without hesitation.** You cannot wash and dry cloth on the move,
  and a wet child in the cold is in danger (→ 11-02). Pack out the waste or bury it properly, well
  away from water (→ 13-07); carry hand sanitiser for when washing is impossible.
- **C (establish):** cloth throughout, with more water and drying space and a proper set-up near
  the stove (→ 13-04). Diaper waste is human waste and goes in the same system, away from water
  (→ 13-07).

pages.title: Real jobs for children
pages.body:
# Real jobs for children

**What this page is for.** A child with a real job is happier, calmer and safer, and over time a
genuinely useful member of the household. Contribution protects against fear and helplessness
(→ 20-08, → 21-02), builds skill, and keeps a child near an adult instead of bored and wandering
(→ 20-02). This page lists jobs that fit each age and how to hand them out.

> **SAFETY. Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products**
> (floor, → 30-01). That holds however busy the adults are. **Which dangerous jobs a child may do
> (fire, fuel, blades, power tools, large animals, water, chemicals), at what age, with what
> training and supervision, is the household's own written rule** on the DC-24 worksheet
> (→ 30-25). Nothing on this page overrides it. {{choice DC-24}} → 30-25.
>
> **Infants and toddlers have no jobs. They have supervision.**

**Your children:** {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#each teens as t}}{{t.label}} ({{t.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.child}}{{#if !has.teen}}none entered.{{/if}}{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Give each child old enough two real jobs this week**: things that need doing, that they can
   do, and that visibly matter. Not busywork; children can tell the difference.
2. **Praise the contribution specifically.** "You filled the kindling basket, so we have a fire
   tonight" beats "good job."
3. **Put the jobs on the daily routine** (→ 20-03) so they are expected, not requested.
4. **Give them tools that are theirs:** a small basket, a headlamp (→ 10-01), a whistle (→ 15-07).
   Ownership makes it real.
5. **Fill in the DC-24 worksheet** (→ 30-25) with every adult, before the first dangerous job.

## Why this matters more than it sounds

In a crisis, children are usually on the receiving end of adult worry. That is frightening and
boring, and it produces the behaviour that makes everything harder. **A child with a job is:**
- **Less frightened**: competence protects against fear (→ 20-08, → 21-01).
- **Less bored**: less friction, fewer bad days.
- **Near an adult**: the safety control that matters (→ 20-02).
- **Learning real skills** at the age when skills stick (→ 20-03, → 24-01).
- **Genuinely helpful**, more so every year.
- **Part of the household**, which matters over a long event.

## Jobs by age

The CDC describes preschoolers as able to follow multi-step instructions, wanting to help and
proud of it (CDC, Positive Parenting Tips). NIOSH's farm-safety work matches each job to a child's
age, size, strength and judgement, with training and supervision (CDC/NIOSH, Childhood
Agricultural Injury Prevention Initiative). The tables below are safe-by-default examples; the
household's own worksheet decides anything with a hazard.

### Infant and toddler (under 3)

- **No jobs, only supervision** (→ 20-02).
- **They can be present** while work happens: carried, in a carrier, or in a safe gated area.
  Being near working adults is good for them.
- **Around 2, they want to "help".** Let them, safely and in trivial ways: carrying a diaper or
  a spoon, putting twigs in a basket. That is how the next stage starts.

### Preschool (3 to 5)

| Job | Why it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Fill the kindling basket** | Real, visible, needed daily | Kindling only, never near the fire |
| **Feed and water small animals** with an adult | Useful; children love it | Handwashing after (→ 13-02, CDC); eggs and allergies per → 02-04 |
| **Water plants** with a small can | Real garden work | Never at a pool, pond or barrel |
| **Sort and put away**: cutlery, socks, seeds by size | Real, and a sorting lesson | → 20-03 |
| **Set the table; simple food prep**: washing vegetables, stirring cold food, tearing greens | Real kitchen work | Allergy rules apply (→ 02-04) |
| **Fetch named things** for an adult | Small errands; learns the house | |
| **Hold the flashlight** | Useful, and taken seriously | → 10-01 |
| **Help with a baby**: fetch a diaper, entertain | Real help | **Never unsupervised care** |
| **Sweep; wipe surfaces** with a damp cloth | Real work | Cloths, not chemicals |
| **Read the thermometer and report** | A role in the plan | → 17-04 |
| **Carry their own small pack** | Ownership; matters on the move | → 22-03 |
| **Cross off the day on the calendar** | Marks time | → 21-06 |

### School-age (6 to 12)

Everything above, more reliably, plus jobs that build toward adult skills:
- **Water carrying with small jugs** filled for them (never at an open source); then their own
  run, once the habit is shown.
- **A garden row of their own**, planted to harvest (→ 05-01).
- **Dish duty**, with an adult handling knives (→ 13-10).
- **Animal chores as their own routine** (→ 05-04, → 05-05).
- **Laundry by hand**, wringing and hanging (→ 13-04).
- **Watching the fire with an adult and reporting**; building and lighting only as the worksheet
  allows (→ 30-25, → 06-01).
- **Knife work for food or carving**, taught with an adult every time, under the worksheet
  (→ 16-01).
- **Simple repairs and sewing** (→ 16-04, → 16-05).
- **Keeping a log**: water level, weather, rain gauge (→ 25-05).

### Teen (13 to 17)

Teens can do most adult work once trained, and in a long event their work matters.
- **Wood: splitting and sawing**, after training and under the worksheet (→ 16-06; OSHA, Hand and
  Power Tools). Chainsaws and power tools are a separate line on the worksheet.
- **Cooking whole meals** for the household (→ 07-01).
- **Water treatment** with an adult checking (→ 03-04).
- **Radio watch and the comms log** (→ 15-02, → 15-04).
- **First aid** once trained (→ 12-01).
- **Caring for younger children** for set periods, with a named adult nearby.
- **Teaching younger children** a skill they have (→ 18-07).
- **Fuel, firearms, butchering and large animals** only by the worksheet's rule (→ 30-25), firearms
  also by → 14-14 and → 29-11.

**Unlock by demonstrated habit, not by birthday.** A birthday is when an adult **starts teaching**
the next thing, with the child, every time. Doing it alone comes only after the habit has been
shown over weeks. A careful 7-year-old earns things a careless 10-year-old does not. Review the
worksheet on each child's birthday and at the yearly review (→ 25-10).

**Two lines that never move on a birthday alone:** open water (pools, ponds, wells, barrels) and
firearms. Those follow their own pages (→ 20-02, → 14-14) and the worksheet.

## What young children must not do

These hold however busy the adults are (→ 20-02), unless the household's worksheet says otherwise
for an older child, with training and an adult beside them:
- **Nothing at a pool, pond, rain barrel or open water container.**
- **Nothing involving fire, heaters, the stove, hot liquids or lamps.**
- **No tools with edges:** knives, axes, saws (→ 16-01, → 16-06).
- **No fuel, chemicals, lye, bleach or medicines** (floor; → 06-06, → 13-09, → 12-07).
- **No firearms** (floor; → 14-14).
- **No unsupervised care of a baby or toddler.**
- **No going outside alone** in cold, dark or unfamiliar ground (→ 11-02).
- **No handling human waste or the toilet system** (→ 13-01).
- **No preparing food for an allergic person** (→ 02-04).

## How to give a job so it works

- **Make it real.** Children spot busywork at once and it does none of the good.
- **Make it visible.** A full basket, watered plants, fed animals.
- **Make it theirs.** "The kindling basket is your job" beats "can you help with the wood."
- **Same job, same time, most days** (→ 20-03).
- **Accept imperfect work.** A job done badly by a child is worth more than one done perfectly by
  an adult, because the point is the child. Redoing it in front of them undoes the benefit.
- **Praise the effort specifically**, and connect it to the household.
- **Grow the jobs as they grow.**

## The adult side

- **It is slower.** Everything takes longer with a child helping. Budget for it; the alternative
  is a bored child interrupting anyway.
- **It is supervision**: a helping child is a located child.
- **It is morale for adults too** (→ 21-02). Working beside your children is one of the good
  parts of a hard time.
- **Do not overload.** The jobs are small; play is most of a young child's day. A child made
  responsible for adult-sized worry is being harmed, not helped (→ 20-08). Teens need time off
  and time with friends too.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A child-sized kindling basket or small bucket | Ownership | |
| A headlamp per child | Holding the light; the fire rule | → 10-01 |
| Small watering can | Garden work | |
| Child-sized gloves | Animals, garden, wood | Gloves are not an allergy control |
| A small pack of their own | Matters on the move | → 22-03 |
| Blunt scissors, blunt needle, burlap | Real skills, safely | → 16-04 |
| Step stool | Reach the sink to wash and help | → 13-02 |
| Child-sized eye protection and hearing protection | For older children's tool work | → 30-25 |
| Job chart with pictures for non-readers | Posted | → 20-03 |

**Scavenge or substitute:** every item can be improvised: a small basket, a cut jug as a watering
can, a cloth bag as a pack. **The point is that it is theirs.** The jobs cost nothing. Praise and
attention are the real inputs.

## When it runs out

- **This does not run out; it grows.** Every month a child can do more. A year into a long event,
  they are really contributing.
- **What wears out is adult patience with the slowness.** Months in, letting a child "help" feels
  like an obstacle. That is exactly when it matters most (→ 21-02).
- **When a job stops working, change it.** Interest fades; rotate jobs and add new ones.
- **The long view:** a child who spends a hard year learning to work and be useful comes out of it
  more capable and more confident.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** start now, while it is easy and stakes are low. Build the jobs into the
  routine (→ 20-03) so they survive into harder times.
- **B (moving):** **a young child's job is carrying their own small pack, holding a hand and
  staying close.** That is a real job. Teens carry real loads and watch younger children at stops
  (→ 01-03, → 15-03).
- **C (establish):** the richest place for this: animals, garden, building, real work everywhere.
  **Re-teach the hazards at the new site first** (→ 20-02, → 20-04), then hand out the jobs.

pages.title: Children and fear
pages.body:
# Children and fear

**What this page is for.** Children know when something is wrong. They read adults with great
accuracy, and **being told nothing is more frightening than being told something**, because a
child fills the gap with something worse than the truth. This page covers what to say, what
distress looks like at each age, what helps, and when it is more than ordinary fear.

**The biggest single factor in how children come through a crisis is how the adults around them
are doing** (→ 21-01, → 21-02). That is the uncomfortable part of this page and the most useful.
Looking after your own state is child care.

> **If phones work:** the **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988)** and SAMHSA's
> **Disaster Distress Helpline (1-800-985-5990, call or text)** are there for adults and older
> children alike. Write both on the wall (→ 12-15, → 25-03). For a medical or mental-health
> emergency in anyone, the first-response page is → 12-15.

**Your children:** {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#each teens as t}}{{t.label}} ({{t.age_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if !has.child}}{{#if !has.teen}}none entered.{{/if}}{{/if}}

## Do this now

1. **Agree between the adults what you will tell the children**, and use the same words. Children
   notice when adults disagree, and it worries them.
2. **Practise the honest, brief, reassuring version:** "Something happened with the power (the
   weather). We have a plan. Our job is X. You're safe with us."
3. **Protect the routine** (→ 20-03, → 21-04). It is the single most protective thing you can do
   for a frightened child, and it costs nothing.
4. **Cut children's exposure to disaster news and adult conversation** (→ 15-04). Small children
   absorb far more than people expect and have no way to make sense of it.

## What to tell them

**Honest, at their level, brief, reassuring.** In that order (CDC, Helping Children Cope During
and After a Disaster).

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| **Answer the question actually asked**, at their level | Volunteer more than they asked |
| **Say "I don't know" when you don't**, plus "and here's what we're doing" | Promise what you cannot keep ("everything will be fine") |
| **Name the plan:** "We're staying here, we have food and heat, our job is to keep the fire going" | Describe worst cases |
| **Give them a role** (→ 20-07) | Make them responsible for adult worries |
| **Name feelings:** "It is scary. It's okay to feel scared" | Dismiss them ("don't be silly") |
| **Be calm in front of them** | Have the frightened conversations where they can hear |
| **Repeat.** They will ask the same thing many times | Get impatient; repetition is how they process |

**For a small child, short is best:** "The power is out because of the storm. We have wood and
food and we're all together. It's going to be a bit different for a while. Your job is to help
with the kindling." Add more only if they ask.

**For older children and teens, more truth, and a voice:** tell them what is known, what is not,
and what the plan is; ask what they think; give them real work (→ 20-07) and a say in things that
affect them. Teens resent being managed and handle facts better than secrets.

### Why false reassurance backfires

- If it turns out not to be fine, the child learns you cannot be trusted on exactly the questions
  that matter most.
- Children can tell when adults are pretending, and the gap between your words and your face is
  itself frightening.
- "We have a plan and we're together" is both true and reassuring, and it survives things getting
  worse.

## What distress looks like, by age

### Infant and toddler (under 3)

- Clinginess, changed sleep, changed eating, more crying, harder to soothe.
- **They read the adults' feelings directly** and have no way to process them except through the
  adults.
- The help is the same at every level of the crisis: **calm adults, physical contact, routine.**

### Preschool (3 to 5)

Distress shows in **behaviour**, not words (CDC):
- **Going backwards**: toileting accidents, baby talk, wanting to be carried, thumb sucking.
  Very common, and **not a problem to correct.** Treat it as unremarkable and it usually passes.
- Clinginess and fear of separation.
- Sleep problems: trouble falling asleep, waking, nightmares (→ 21-07).
- New fears: the dark, noises, being alone, weather.
- More and bigger tantrums.
- Changes in eating.
- **Repetitive play about the event.** Normal: it is how children process. Do not stop it.
- Tummy aches and headaches with no medical cause.
- **Unusual quietness**, which is easy to miss because it is convenient.

### School-age (6 to 12)

- Worry about safety of family and pets; asking the same questions over and over.
- Trouble concentrating; falling behind in learning.
- Irritability, fights, withdrawal from play.
- Physical complaints; sleep trouble.
- Guilt ("it happened because I...") and magical thinking. Correct it gently and plainly.

### Teen (13 to 17)

- Withdrawal, irritability, risk-taking, defiance.
- Grief for lost friends, school and plans, often unspoken (→ 21-03).
- Sleeping too much or too little; changes in eating.
- Alcohol or drug use if any is within reach.
- **Hopelessness or talk of self-harm** (CDC, Risk and Protective Factors for Suicide): take it
  seriously at once (→ 12-15).

## What actually helps

1. **Routine, above everything** (→ 20-03, → 21-04). Predictability tells a child the adults have
   things in hand more convincingly than words.
2. **Physical closeness:** holding, carrying, sleeping near. For a baby or toddler this is the
   whole intervention.
3. **Calm adults.** The hardest and the most effective. Manage your own state (→ 21-01), have
   frightened conversations out of earshot, and take turns being the steady one (→ 21-05).
4. **A role** (→ 20-07). Contribution protects against helplessness.
5. **Play.** A young child should mostly still be a young child. Protect play time; it is how
   children recover.
6. **Honest, brief answers**, repeated as often as needed.
7. **Limit exposure** to news (→ 15-04), adult conversations and frightening details. Children do
   not need to know the supply arithmetic.
8. **Name feelings:** "You're scared. That makes sense. I'm here."
9. **Something to look forward to** (→ 21-06): a special meal, a story, a small celebration.
10. **Sleep** (→ 21-07). A tired child is a fragile child.
11. **For older children and teens: friends and other trusted adults** (→ 18-01). Any safe contact
    with peers helps.

## What to avoid

- **Adult conversations within earshot.** They hear everything, and understand less than you
  think while absorbing more than you think.
- **Using a child as an emotional support.** Even a teen is not your counsellor.
- **Punishing regression or fear-driven behaviour.** It makes it worse and damages trust.
- **Threats framed around danger.** "If you go near the pool you'll drown" makes anxiety and
  worse compliance than "we always hold a grown-up's hand near water" (→ 20-04).
- **Letting a child carry the household's medical worry.** A parent's medicine supply or a
  sibling's allergy is not a child's burden, and they cannot fix it.
- **Assuming a child is fine because they are not saying anything.**

## When it is more than ordinary fear

Get professional help if any exists, and use the lines above if phones work:
- Distress that is **severe, lasting, or getting worse over weeks**.
- **Complete withdrawal**, or loss of interest in play or friends.
- **Regression that does not ease** as things settle.
- **Any talk of self-harm, at any age.** Take it seriously (→ 12-15).
- **New and marked aggression.**
- **Sleep trouble that does not improve** with routine.
- **Anything that frightens you as a parent.** That instinct is worth acting on.

**Check the body first** (→ 12-15): **dehydration, infection, fever, pain, hunger, cold, carbon
monoxide, and low blood sugar in a child with diabetes** all change behaviour. Rule out the body
before deciding it is the mind.

## Death and loss

If someone dies, a pet dies, or the house is lost (→ 21-03):
- **Tell the truth simply, in concrete words.** "Died", not "went to sleep" or "we lost him".
  Soft words confuse and frighten small children; a child told someone "went to sleep" may become
  afraid of sleep.
- **Expect the same question again and again.** That is processing.
- **Let them see adults grieve**, in a manageable form. Children who never see adult feeling learn
  to hide their own.
- **Keep the routine** (→ 21-04). It is not disrespectful; it is what holds a child steady.
- **Some ritual helps:** a marker, a drawing, saying goodbye (→ 21-06).
- **If the household may have to give up or lose its pets** (→ 30-11), tell the children honestly
  and simply, and never let them watch a pet's death. → 21-03 covers pet loss.

## Gear

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Comfort objects, and duplicates** | A lost one is a bad week | Buy a spare of the important one |
| **Books, including familiar favourites** | Repetition comforts; reading aloud is the best thing you can do | → 20-03 |
| Games, art supplies, things to play with | Play is processing | |
| **Flameless night lights** | New fear of the dark is very common | → 10-02 |
| Light for the evening together | Worth the watts | → 10-03 |
| **988 and Disaster Distress Helpline, posted** | May work when much else does not | → 12-15, → 25-03 |
| Written daily routine, posted | The most protective thing available | → 21-04 |
| Small treats for occasions | Something to look forward to | → 21-06 |
| Printed photos of family and normal life | Continuity | Print some now |

**Scavenge or substitute:** everything that matters most here is free: routine, closeness, honest
words, calm, play and attention. Stories told aloud need no books. Made toys (→ 16-04, → 16-03),
and the making is itself the activity. **What you cannot substitute: a calm adult.** That is why
→ 21-01 and → 21-02 are part of the child-care plan.

## When it runs out

- **Nothing here runs out, but the adults do.** The limit is adult emotional capacity, and months
  into a long event it is scarce (→ 21-02).
- **Protect it on purpose:** take turns (→ 21-05), protect sleep (→ 21-07), get time apart, and
  treat the adults' state as household infrastructure, because for the children it is.
- **The failure:** exhausted adults, worn-down routine, frightened children, each making the
  others worse. **The way back in is the routine**: the cheapest thing to restore, and it steadies
  the rest.
- **Other adults help:** a neighbour, a relative, another family (→ 18-01). Even brief relief
  changes an adult's capacity, and children benefit from other trusted adults directly.
- **Children are resilient when the adults around them are steady, the routine holds, and they
  are told the truth in a form they can carry.** Those three are within your control.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** the first days are the most frightening. Name the plan, start the
  routine, and switch off the news where children can hear.
- **B (moving):** a short ritual at the end of each day (a story, a song) steadies a child. Keep
  them close and tell them the next stop, not the whole journey (→ 01-03).
- **C (establish):** a new place is both a loss and a relief. Re-start the routine in the first
  week and give children their own corner and jobs (→ 20-07).

pages.body:
# Pets: food, water, medicine, moving, and hard choices

**What this page is for.** Each pet is another mouth, another water need, a waste problem and,
if you ever have to move, an animal that must be contained and carried. Planned now, pets are a
comfort in a hard time. Unplanned, they become an improvised problem at the worst moment. This
page covers dogs, cats and other house pets: food and water arithmetic, medicines, carriers,
moving, and what to do if you cannot keep them (decision card DC-10, → 30-11).

> **SAFETY.**
> - **Antifreeze kills pets** and tastes sweet to them (ASPCA, Ethylene Glycol Poisoning in
>   Pets). Store vehicle fluids sealed and out of reach; wipe up drips (→ 06-06).
> - **Never give a pet a human medicine, or one animal's medicine to another species**, unless a
>   veterinarian said to. Many are toxic, especially to cats.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products** (floor,
>   → 30-01). That includes pet medicines and any firearm used on this page.
> - **Children never watch a pet's death.** → 20-08, → 21-03.

**Your pets:** {{#each pets as p}}{{p.count}} {{p.type}} (food per day: {{p.food_per_day}}; medicines: {{p.medications}}); {{else}}none entered. This page stays for animals you may take in or care for.{{/each}}

## Do this now

1. **Stock pet food the way you stock human food:** deep, rotated, oldest first, in sealed
   rodent-proof containers.
2. **Count pets in the water plan** (→ 03-01). {{#if has.pets}}Your household's daily water floor,
   pets included, is **{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons**.{{/if}}
3. **Refill every pet prescription** and ask the vet for a buffer supply; keep a written list of
   what each animal takes (FEMA/Ready.gov).
4. **One carrier per cat or small animal, and a leash and harness per dog**, stored where you can
   reach them in a hurry, not buried in a closet.
5. **ID:** collar tags and registered microchips, with an out-of-area contact on the
   registration (FEMA/Ready.gov). Take a photo of each pet with a family member. {{photo pet-id-photo}}
6. **Decide now, calmly, as adults, what you would do if you could not keep them** (→ 30-11), and
   ask your vet the questions at the end of this page while you can.

## Food

- **Dry food** stores longest and simplest. **Canned food carries water**, a real advantage when
  water is short. A mix is sensible.
- **Rotate.** The fats in pet food go rancid. Store cool, dark and sealed, in a bucket with a
  gasket lid or the original bag inside a tote (→ 04-11).
- **Sudden diet changes upset stomachs**, and old animals most of all. Stock the food they eat now.
- **Cats are obligate carnivores:** they cannot live on grain and vegetable scraps. If food runs
  short, protein is what matters: plain cooked meat and organ meat, not bread or rice.
- **Dogs** eat a wider diet, but plain cooked meat, fish, eggs and cooked grains are safer stretch
  foods than seasoned table scraps.

**Foods never to give pets** (ASPCA, People Foods to Avoid Feeding Your Pets): alcohol; yeast
dough; chocolate, coffee and caffeine; avocado; citrus; grapes and raisins; **onions, garlic and
chives**; milk and dairy; macadamia and other nuts; raw or undercooked meat, raw eggs and raw
bones; **xylitol** (a sweetener in sugar-free gum and some peanut butters); salt and salty foods.

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**A severe food allergy in the house:** pet bowls live on the floor where
small children live. Pet foods and scraps that contain a household allergen (fish, egg, peanut
and others) are handled under the food-allergy module's separate-cookware rules: their own bowl
and pan, hands washed, pets fed away from the allergic person (→ 02-04).{{/if}}

**Food arithmetic, per animal:** days of food on hand = food stored ÷ food per day. Write it on the
consumables table (→ 23-02).

## Water

- **Pets drink treated water**, the same as people. Raw pool, pond or puddle water can make an
  animal sick, and there may be no vet (→ 03-01, → 03-04).
- **The binder's water plan adds a quarter-gallon a day for each pet** (→ 03-01). CDC advises
  storing extra water for pets beyond the household's own (CDC, How to Create and Store an
  Emergency Water Supply). **A large dog drinks far more:** measure your own animal. Fill the bowl
  from a measured jug for a few ordinary days and see what is gone. Mine: ______ cups a day.
- **More in heat, more on dry food, more when nursing or ill.**
- **Older cats and any animal with kidney disease need more water, not less, when water is
  rationed**, and dry-food-only speeds dehydration. Feed canned food when water is tight, and never
  ration a kidney-compromised animal's water below its normal intake.

## Medicines and health

- **List every pet medicine** (the log below) with the vet's instructions as written. This binder
  gives no animal doses.
- **Ask the vet for a refill buffer** while vets are open, and how long each medicine keeps.
- **Keep pets healthy now:** vaccines, weight, teeth, parasite control. A healthy animal needs less
  later.
- **Basic pet first aid:** gauze, self-adhering wrap, nail clippers, tweezers, a brush.
- **Signs that need help now:** not eating or drinking for a day or more (sooner for a cat or a
  small animal), straining to urinate (above all a male cat), repeated vomiting, collapse.

## Litter and waste

- **Litter runs out fast.** Substitutes: sand, dry dirt, sawdust or wood pellets (pellets work
  well), shredded paper, dried peat, wood ash used sparingly (dusty).
- **Cat and dog waste goes with human waste** (→ 13-01), never into a garden or near food or water.
- **Toxoplasmosis** spreads from cat feces. Keep litter away from food preparation and wash hands
  after handling it (CDC, Preventing Toxoplasmosis). {{#if has.pregnant}}**Someone in your household
  is pregnant:** CDC advises a pregnant person avoid changing cat litter; if she must, gloves and
  handwashing, and change it daily.{{else}}CDC advises a pregnant person avoid changing cat litter.{{/if}}
- **A cat finds a corner** if the box is unusable. Keep it maintained.

## Keeping them safe and quiet

- **Keep pets indoors or contained.** Loose pets in a crisis get lost, injured or killed, and they
  advertise that a house is occupied and supplied (→ 14-03).
- **Cold:** pets seek the heated room, which is fine. Keep them away from open flame, stoves,
  heaters and candles; a curious cat and an unattended flame is a house fire.
- **Noise:** a barking dog or yowling cat carries. Calm and contained matters for security.
- **Stressed animals bite.** Keep dogs and children apart when either is frightened, tired or
  eating (→ 20-02).
- **Other pets:** birds, reptiles, fish and small mammals often depend on power: heat lamps,
  aquarium pumps and filters. Plan how you would keep them warm or aerated without power, and how
  you would move them, or plan to rehome them early.
- **Radiation or fallout emergencies:** bring pets inside with you; if they were outside, wiping or
  washing their fur removes fallout dust (CDC, Pets and Radiation Emergencies; → 27-05).
- **In a storm alarm, nobody chases a pet** (→ 20-04). Carriers can wait at the shelter spot.

## If you have to move

- **FEMA's rule while help exists: if local officials ask you to evacuate, your pets evacuate too.**
  Many public shelters and hotels do not allow pets, so plan a pet-friendly place in advance
  (FEMA/Ready.gov). Write it here: ______________________.
- **Carriers, one per cat or small animal**, and leash and harness for each dog, by the door.
  Catching frightened animals at departure is a delay you can prevent.
- **Pet kit, alongside the human go-bags** (FEMA/Ready.gov): several days of food in a waterproof
  container, several days of water and a bowl, medicine, first aid, collar with ID, a backup leash,
  carrier, sanitation supplies (litter and tray, bags), copies of records in a waterproof bag, a
  photo of you with the pet, and familiar bedding or a toy (→ 22-03). {{photo pet-kit}}
- **Cold weather:** cover and insulate carriers; an animal in a carrier in a cold vehicle chills
  fast.
- **Be honest in the plan.** If leaving on foot, or with no room, is ever the only option, pets are
  a real constraint. That is exactly what DC-10 is for.

## When you cannot keep them (DC-10)

A long emergency may leave too little food or water for people and pets, or force a move the pets
cannot make. FEMA's advice is to plan to take them; when that is impossible the choices are
hard: keep them and share scarce food and water; release them, knowing most house pets do not
survive long alone; or end their lives humanely. The full card, with what each option costs, is
→ 30-11.

**Our choice:** {{choice DC-10}} → 30-11.

**Write the order you would try things,** per animal (you may answer differently for each):

```
1. Someone who would take them: __________________ (agreed? YES / NO, date ______)
2. ____________________________________________________________
3. ____________________________________________________________
```

**If releasing:** leave as much dry food and water as can be spared, a way in and out of shelter,
and a collar with an ID tag; release near people who may take them in (→ 30-11).

## A humane end: the method section for DC-10

Read this once now, calmly, so it is never read for the first time in a crisis.

> **A veterinarian is the right choice whenever one exists.** If any vet, clinic, shelter or
> animal control officer can be reached, even far away and even by trading, that is the answer.

> **Before the collapse:** state and local laws govern how an animal may be killed and where a
> firearm may be fired. While government works, use a veterinarian or animal control.

**What the AVMA says** (American Veterinary Medical Association, Guidelines for the Euthanasia of
Animals, 2020 edition; the full document is bound behind this page in the Large download):

- **The preferred method for dogs, cats and other small pets is an injection of a barbiturate
  drug, given by or under a veterinarian.** Federal drug law restricts these drugs to people
  registered with the Drug Enforcement Administration. A vet can sedate the animal first so it is
  calm, and the family can be present.
- **For dogs and cats, gunshot is "acceptable with conditions".** The AVMA says it should only be
  done **by highly skilled people trained in the use of firearms** (it names animal control and law
  enforcement officers and trained veterinarians), only where firearm use is legal, and that it
  **may be appropriate in remote areas or emergencies where withholding death would leave the animal
  in prolonged, unrelieved pain and suffering, or where human life is in imminent danger.** It is
  not for routine use and not when other methods are available.
- **For cats, the AVMA recommends sedation first whenever possible** (for example, medicine added to
  food), because cats can be difficult to shoot humanely. That medicine comes from a vet: ask
  now.
- **Unacceptable**, by the AVMA's list: **drowning; cold (hypothermia); household chemicals,
  disinfectants, cleaning agents and pesticides;** and injecting drugs by routes or into awake
  animals outside the methods it describes. Do not improvise with human medicines either: a failed
  attempt causes great suffering.
- **Other pets** (rabbits, birds, rodents, reptiles, fish): the AVMA gives each species its own
  methods, which differ from those for dogs and cats. This binder does not print them. Ask your vet
  now, and write the answer below.

**If the household has chosen this option, has no vet, and someone with real firearm skill is
available** (if no one in the household has that skill, ask someone who does before attempting:
a law officer, animal control officer or experienced hunter):

1. **Decide in advance who.** The calmest adult with firearm skill. **Children elsewhere, out of
   sight and hearing** (→ 30-11).
2. **Firearm safety** (AVMA, as published; → 29-11): treat every firearm as loaded; know where the
   muzzle points and never let it point at yourself or anyone; finger off the trigger until ready;
   be sure of the target and what lies beyond it; unload when not in use.
3. **Outdoors, in a place no one else can enter**, with a safe backstop of earth behind and below
   (AVMA: outdoors, in an area where public access is restricted).
4. **Calm the animal.** The AVMA says animals used to people should be handled calmly and
   reassuringly beforehand. A favourite food, a familiar voice, a quiet place.
5. **Placement** (AVMA Figures 8 and 9, after the Canadian Veterinary Journal firearm guidelines):
   {{figure fig-avma-gunshot-sites-dog-cat}}
   - **Dog:** midway between the level of the eyes and the base of the ears, slightly off the
     midline, with the aim directed across the dog toward the spine.
   - **Cat:** a point slightly below a line drawn between the inner bases of the ears, or where
     lines from the outer corner of each eye to the base of the opposite ear cross.
6. **Never hold the muzzle against the animal.** The AVMA warns the barrel can burst. Its general
   guidance is to hold the muzzle 1 to 2 feet from the head, at a right angle to the skull.
7. **Confirm death before anything else** (AVMA): no heartbeat or pulse, no breathing, no blink
   when the surface of the eye is touched, no response to a firm toe pinch, and greying gums. No
   single sign except stiffening of the body (rigor mortis) confirms death on its own. **If any
   sign of life remains, act again at once.** The AVMA says that if one method is proving
   difficult, another should be tried immediately.
8. **Burial.** Bury deeply, away from water and wells (→ 13-07). The AVMA notes that remains can
   carry residues (lead from bullets; drugs from a vet's injection) that poison scavengers and
   pets; if the ground is frozen, cover and store the remains securely until deep burial is
   possible.
9. **Afterwards:** tell the children the truth simply (→ 20-08), mark the loss (→ 21-06), and
   expect grief, including in the adult who did it (→ 21-03).

## Pet log

| | |
|---|---|
| Pets (type, count) | {{#each pets as p}}{{p.count}} {{p.type}}; {{/each}} |
| Food: brand and daily amount | {{#each pets as p}}{{p.type}}: {{p.food_per_day}}; {{/each}} |
| Medicines, as the vet wrote them | {{#each pets as p}}{{p.type}}: {{p.medications}}; {{/each}} |
| Vet name and phone | ______________________ |
| Microchip numbers | ______________________ |
| Days of food on hand | ______________________ |
| Pet-friendly place to go | ______________________ |
| Vet's answers, asked now: sedative for a humane end (cats), methods for our other pets, what to do if you cannot reach us | ______________________ |

## Gear

**Have it now (buy toward this):**

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Deep stock of their usual food | Diet changes upset stomachs | Rotate; rodent-proof bins |
| Sealed storage bins or buckets | Dry and pest-free | Gasket lids |
| Litter and a spare tray (cats) | Sanitation fails fast without it | Wood pellets store well |
| Carriers, leashes, harnesses | Movement without a chase | By the door |
| Collapsible bowls | Go-bag | |
| Prescription medicines and a written list | Continuity of care | Ask the vet for a buffer |
| Nail clippers, brush, pet first aid | Small problems stay small | Gauze, self-adhering wrap |
| Records in a waterproof bag | Shelters and boarding ask for them | FEMA/Ready.gov |

**Scavenge or substitute:**
- **Litter:** sand, dirt, sawdust, wood pellets, shredded paper.
- **Food:** plain cooked meat and organ meat; fish and game scraps from hunting and fishing
  (→ 05-07, → 05-08), prepared without onion, garlic or salt. Not grain-based human food as a cat's
  staple.
- **Carrier:** a sturdy tote with air holes and a secured lid, as a last resort.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** days of pet food on hand, on the consumables table (→ 23-02).
- **Ration:** animals tolerate a modest cut in portion better than a sudden change of food, but cats
  cannot go without protein. Stretch with cooked meat scraps rather than starch.
- **Resupply:** hunting, trapping and fishing scraps (→ 05-07, → 05-08, → 05-15) are real pet food.
- **The honest note:** in a very long event, feeding pets is a real cost. Decide the household's
  position in advance (→ 30-11), not in a moment of scarcity.

## By phase

- **A (shelter in place):** the easiest phase: stock, keep them in, manage litter and noise.
- **B (moving):** carriers, warmth, water and a plan. This is where pets are hardest, and where
  DC-10 matters most.
- **C (establish):** cats earn their keep as rodent control around stored food (→ 04-11). Keep new
  arrivals contained until settled, or they wander off.

pages.title: Morale and mental health: section overview
pages.body:
# Morale and mental health

**What this section holds.** 7 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 21-01 **Stress, panic and judgment**: Stress is not a soft topic.
- → 21-02 **Morale over the long haul**: Almost every preparedness plan is built for month one, and almost every real hardship is decided months later.
- → 21-03 **Grief, loss and trauma**: Nobody wants to read this page, and it is better read in advance.
- → 21-04 **Routine and structure for the household**: Routine is the cheapest, most effective morale and safety tool in this binder.
- → 21-05 **Conflict between adults**: A few adults, possibly children, one heated room, no relief, for months: that is hard on any partnership or household, and **conflict under it is normal, not…
- → 21-06 **Celebration, marking time and meaning**: This page is not decoration.
- → 21-07 **Sleep in a hard time**: Sleep is the biggest single lever on judgment, mood, patience and the body's defence against infection.
