pages.body:
# Master acquisition list

**What this page is for.** Every subject page in this binder ends with a list of things to own.
This page collects all of them in one place, grouped by what they do (water, food, heat and so
on), so you can shop, budget and tick things off. **→ 22-07 puts the same items in buying
order** (what to buy first). **→ 22-02 is the same list read backwards:** what to look for when
there is nothing left to buy. Where your settings already say what you own, the number is
printed; everything else you tick by hand.

## Do this now

1. **Print this page and walk the house with it** (the route is → 26-02). Mark each row
   ✔ have it, ~ partly, ✗ none. Most households find they already own a good share of it and
   have never counted.
2. **Buy the ✗ items in → 22-07's order**, not this page's order. This page is grouped by
   subject; → 22-07 is ordered by what hurts people soonest.
3. **Rows marked ★ are load-bearing:** the plan has a hole without them. If you buy nothing
   else this year, buy those.
4. **Log what you buy in → 22-04** as it arrives, or you will end up guessing at your own
   supplies.
5. **Owning is not the same as working.** The tests (does it turn on, does it fit, is it in
   date) are on → 26-03 to → 26-07.

## How to read the list

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **★** | Load-bearing. The plan has a hole without it |
| **§** | Has a **consumable**: buy the spares at the same time (filter elements, fuel, lids, batteries) |
| **№** | **Quantity matters more than quality.** Several cheap ones beat one good one |
| **⌛** | **Time-sensitive.** Takes months or years to become useful (seasoned wood, soil, skill, seed) |

**The three buying mistakes this list is built to prevent:**

1. **Buying the tool and not the consumable (§).** A water filter with no spare element, a
   canner with no lids, a saw with no file, a radio with no batteries. Many "prepared"
   households fail exactly here.
2. **Buying one of something every person needs (№).** One headlamp in a household of
   {{ household.size }} is an argument.
3. **Buying late what needed years (⌛).** Soil, seed, seasoned firewood and skill cannot be
   bought in a hurry at any price.

## 1. Water (→ 03-01 to → 03-10)

**Your numbers:** stored now {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gal · two-week target
{{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal (→ 03-01).

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★§ Gravity or pump water filter + spare elements** | The element is the consumable. Buy two spares. A filter does not remove salt or dissolved chemicals (→ 29-06) | → 03-04, → 03-09 |
| [ ] | **★ Unscented household bleach**, fresh, plus a dropper | Write the purchase date on it: bleach loses strength over months (→ 29-05) | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | **★№ Food-grade water containers** (5-gal jugs and/or larger drums) | Store cool and dark (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply) | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Water preserver or stabiliser | For long-term stored water; follow its label | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | **§ Distillation setup** (large pot, lid, collection vessel, or a purpose-built still) | The only home method that removes salt. {{#if has.pool}}Your pool or hot tub ({{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gal) is raw material, not drinking water.{{else}}Needed only if your fallback water is salty or chemically contaminated.{{/if}} Drinking pool or untreated surface water is a household choice: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14 | → 03-03 |
| [ ] | Rain barrels + downspout diverter + screen | The screen keeps mosquitoes out. {{#if is.cold_winters}}Drain before the hard freeze or the ice splits it.{{/if}} | → 03-05 |
| [ ] | №Buckets with lids (food grade), and a separate, labelled non-potable set | Never cross-use | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Test strips (limited use: read → 03-07 first) | They say almost nothing about germs | → 03-07 |
| [ ] | Mosquito larvicide (Bti) for standing water | Treats water you are not drinking | → 03-08 |
| [ ] | Hoses, siphon pump, funnel | Moving water is most of the work | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Well bailer (a narrow cylinder bucket) + rope long enough for the well | {{#if has.well}}Your no-power fallback for the well (→ 03-10).{{else}}Only if you have, or may move to, a drilled well.{{/if}} | → 03-10 |

## 2. Food storage (→ 04-01 to → 04-19)

**Your numbers:** pantry about {{ gear.food.pantry_days }} days by your estimate ·
freeze-dried {{ gear.food.freeze_dried_servings }} servings · household need about
{{ derived.calories.day }} kcal a day (→ 04-01).

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★ Staples you actually eat**: rice, beans, oats, flour, sugar, salt, oil | Store what you eat; eat what you store | → 04-01, → 04-02 |
| [ ] | **★ Mylar bags + oxygen absorbers + food-grade buckets** | Turns staples that keep a year into staples that keep many years | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | **§ Pressure canner** + spare gaskets | The only safe method for low-acid food (→ 29-08) | → 04-05 |
| [ ] | **§ Water-bath canner**, jars, **lids** (lids are single-use) | Buy lids by the case | → 04-04 |
| [ ] | § Dehydrator, or screens for sun and oven drying | | → 04-06 |
| [ ] | Canning or pickling salt (not iodised table salt), vinegar, sugar, honey | Preserving, not just cooking | → 04-13, → 04-07 |
| [ ] | **Fats and oils** | The hardest food to store and the easiest to run out of. Rotate | → 04-12 |
| [ ] | Powdered or canned dairy, shelf-stable protein | | → 04-14 |
| [ ] | Coffee, tea, comfort food | Morale is a supply line | → 21-02 |
{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}| [ ] | **★ Allergen-safe staples**, stored and labelled separately | A dedicated bin and dedicated utensils for the allergic person | → 02-04 |
{{else}}| [ ] | Special-diet staples (allergy, celiac, infant), stored separately | Only if someone needs them | → 02-04, → 02-19 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Rodent-proof bins and gamma lids | Rodents find bulk grain | → 04-11 |
| [ ] | Sprouting jars + sprouting seed | Fresh food in the dead of winter | → 04-16 |
| [ ] | Permanent marker, labels, a rotation log | An unlabelled bucket is a mystery in two years | → 04-10 |

## 3. Food production (→ 05-01 to → 05-19)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★⌛ Open-pollinated (heirloom) seed** in quantity | Hybrid seed does not come true when you save it | → 05-03 |
| [ ] | ⌛ Compost bin or pile; a fork to turn it | Soil is a multi-year project | → 05-11 |
| [ ] | Garden hand tools: fork, spade, hoe, rake, trowel | | → 05-01, → 16-01 |
| [ ] | Row cover, cold frame or low-tunnel materials | Lengthens both ends of the season (your season: → 25-01) | → 05-02 |
| [ ] | Containers and potting mix | For a patio, balcony or windowsill | → 05-10, → 05-14 |
| [ ] | Grow light + shelf for seedlings | | → 05-14 |

## 4. Fire, fuel, cooking and heat (→ 06, → 07, → 08)

**Your numbers:** gasoline {{ gear.fuel.gasoline_gal }} gal · diesel {{ gear.fuel.diesel_gal }}
gal · kerosene {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal · propane 1-lb {{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }},
20-lb {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} · firewood {{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords · CO alarms
{{ gear.co_alarms }} · smoke alarms {{ gear.smoke_alarms }} · extinguishers
{{ gear.extinguishers }}. What each fuel is: → 29-01.

| [ ] | CO detector with a number (ppm) display | The number shows a slow leak before the alarm sounds | → 08-02 |
| [ ] | **★ Smoke alarms and fire extinguishers** (ABC type) | → 29-12 | → 26-03 |
| [ ] | **★№ Ignition, three ways**: lighters (many), ferro rod, stormproof matches | Redundancy is cheap here | → 06-01 |
| [ ] | Tinder, bought or homemade | | → 06-01 |
| [ ] | **★⌛ Seasoned firewood**{{#if has.fireplace}} (you have a fireplace){{/if}}{{#if has.wood_stove}} (you have a wood stove){{/if}} | Wood cut today is next year's fuel | → 06-03, → 06-04 |

| [ ] | Approved fuel cans, labelled, and stabiliser | **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Where cans live is a household choice: {{choice DC-05}} → 30-06 | → 06-06 |
| [ ] | Fuel-transport hardware: cans, ratchet straps, an exterior rack | Fuel that cannot ride safely is range you do not have | → 06-08 |
| [ ] | Manual fuel transfer pump, labelled for the one fuel it moves | Can to tank without lifting | → 06-07 |
| [ ] | An indoor-rated heater and its fuel, if heat is your gap | Unvented heaters put all their exhaust in the room. Overnight use: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02 | → 08-04, → 08-09, → 08-10 |
| [ ] | § Heater spares: wicks, filters, hoses, fuses | A heater you cannot fix mid-winter is not a heater | → 08-09, → 08-10, → 08-07 |
| [ ] | Rocket stove or efficient wood stove | A fraction of the wood of an open fire | → 07-02 |
| [ ] | Cast iron: Dutch oven, skillet, griddle | Works on coals; lasts forever | → 07-04 |
| [ ] | Grill grate, tripod, long tongs, heavy gloves | For outdoor cooking | → 07-01 |
| [ ] | Solar oven, bought or built | Free cooking on a sunny day | → 07-03 |
| [ ] | Chimney brush kit sized to your flue + chimney-fire suppressant | {{#if has.fireplace}}You have a fireplace: measure the flue first.{{else}}Only if you burn wood indoors.{{/if}} | → 06-09 |
| [ ] | Moisture meter for firewood | Burn wood under 20 % moisture | → 08-08 |
| [ ] | Vacuum flasks (thermos), large | One boil keeps water hot for hours and saves fuel | → 07-02 |
| [ ] | Window film, weatherstripping, door sweeps, plastic sheeting, tape | One-room heating hardware | → 08-01, → 08-03 |
| [ ] | Heavy quilts, sleeping bags rated for your coldest nights | Your record low: {{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F | → 08-06, → 11-01 |

## 5. Power and light (→ 09, → 10)

**Your numbers:** power stations {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh in total · solar
{{ gear.solar_w_total }} W · generator {{ gear.generator_watts }} W running, fuel

## 6. Medical (→ 12, Section 02) — the full carry kit is → 22-06

{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}| [ ] | **★§ Cold chain for refrigerated medicine**: a 12 V fridge or cooler, a thermometer, an evaporative cooling pouch | → 29-07 | → 12-21, → 09-10 |

| [ ] | Thermometers: one for people, one for the fridge or medicine store | | → 12-05 |
| [ ] | Spare prescription glasses, reading glasses, hearing-aid batteries | Cheap, and you cannot function without them | → 02-23 |

## 7. Sanitation and hygiene (→ 13)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |

| [ ] | **★§ Bleach and/or pool shock (calcium hypochlorite)** | Doubles for water. **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** | → 13-11, → 29-05 |

| [ ] | Toilet paper in bulk, plus washable cloth alternatives | | → 13-01 |
| [ ] | Heavy trash bags | | → 13-03 |
| [ ] | Washboard or plunger washer, tubs, wringer, clothesline | Laundry by hand is real work | → 13-04 |
| [ ] | Menstrual supplies (disposable and reusable){{#if has.infant}}; diapers at this size **and the next**{{/if}} | Reusable is the long game | → 13-08 |
| [ ] | Shovel + lime or ash for latrine work | | → 13-07 |
| [ ] | Heavy rubber gloves, N95 masks, eye protection | Waste handling and clean-up | → 13-11 |
{{#if has.pets}}| [ ] | Pet litter and waste bags, and a plan for when they run out | Sand, ash, shredded paper | → 20-09 |
{{/if}}

## 8. Clothing and warmth (→ 11)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |

| [ ] | **★ Wool or synthetic base layers for every person**, children included | Cotton holds water and steals heat | → 11-01, → 11-05 |
| [ ] | **★ Insulated waterproof boots** + spare liners for everyone | | → 11-06 |

{{#if has.child}}| [ ] | **⌛ The next two sizes of everything for each child** | The clock nobody plans for | → 11-02, → 11-09 |
| [ ] | Car-seat ponchos or blankets that go over the buckled harness | No bulky coat under a harness (AAP) | → 11-02 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Drying rack for indoor drying | Gear that never dries is dangerous gear | → 11-03 |
| [ ] | Chainsaw chaps + eye and ear protection | A saw injury with no emergency room is the scenario | → 11-05 |
| [ ] | Sun protection and light layers for summer | {{#if is.hot_summers}}Your July mean high is {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F.{{/if}} | → 11-08 |

## 9. Tools and repair (→ 16)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★ A good axe, a good knife, a good file** | Best lifetime value of any tools | → 16-01, → 16-02, → 16-06 |
| [ ] | Hand tools: hand drill, hand saws, hammers, pliers, wrenches, vise | Power tools stop; these do not | → 16-01 |
| [ ] | § Sharpening: stones, files, honing compound, strop | A dull tool is a dangerous tool | → 16-02 |
| [ ] | №§ Cordage: paracord, rope, wire, zip ties, duct tape | Never enough | → 16-03 |
| [ ] | Sewing kit: heavy needles, awl, waxed thread, patches | | → 16-04 |

| [ ] | №§ Fasteners: screws, nails, bolts, hose clamps, baling wire | Buy the assortment boxes | → 16-07 |
| [ ] | Tarps, plastic sheeting, lumber, plywood | Roof and window repair | → 08-03, → 16-05 |
| [ ] | Push-fit pipe couplings in your pipe sizes + a small tube cutter | A burst pipe becomes a short repair | → 16-12 |
| [ ] | Bicycle + tubes, patch kit, pump, chain tool; a wagon or sled | Transport when fuel is gone | → 16-09 |
{{#if has.trailer}}| [ ] | Trailer spare wheel, bearing kit, coupler and tongue locks | One bearing or tyre can end a move | → 16-11 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Work gloves (№), safety glasses, ear protection | Injury is what you cannot afford | → 16-01 |

## 10. Security (→ 14)

Firearms pages are in every binder; these rows matter only if you own them, except storage and
home hardening, which matter to everyone.

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★ Locking storage for every firearm**, opened by every adult who needs it | **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.**{{#if has.child}} This household has children.{{/if}} | → 14-14, → 20-02 |
| [ ] | Ammunition for each calibre you own, stored cool and dry{{#if !has.firearms}} (none owned per settings){{/if}} | Match the stamp on the box to the stamp on the gun (→ 29-11) | → 14-07 |
| [ ] | § Cleaning kit, solvent, oil; spare small parts | Small and cheap now, unobtainable later | → 14-05, → 14-06 |
| [ ] | Optic batteries, backup sights | | → 14-09 |
| [ ] | Hearing and eye protection | | → 14-05 |
| [ ] | Home hardening: door reinforcement, locks, window film, exterior lighting | The cheapest security spend there is | → 14-02 |
| [ ] | Outdoor padlocks for gates and sheds, with the keys stored where every adult can find them | A lost key locks you out | → 14-02 |
| [ ] | Pepper spray, one per adult who will carry it | A step between words and a firearm | → 14-13 |
| [ ] | Binoculars, a good light, a whistle | | → 14-01 |

## 11. Communications (→ 15)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★ NOAA Weather Radio** (battery or crank, with SAME county coding){{#if has.noaa_radio}}: owned{{/if}} | The best early warning there is (→ 29-09) | → 15-01 |
| [ ] | FRS/GMRS handhelds (№) + rechargeable batteries{{#if has.gmrs}}: owned{{/if}} | Yard-to-neighbourhood range | → 15-02 |
| [ ] | Shortwave or scanner receiver for listening | | → 15-04 |
| [ ] | Amateur ("ham") radio + **a licence earned now**{{#if has.ham}}: in the household{{/if}} | The exam takes time | → 15-05 |
| [ ] | Antenna wire, connectors, coax | | → 15-06 |
| [ ] | Satellite messenger or satellite internet{{#if has.satellite}}: owned; it is a channel only once activated and tested{{/if}} | | → 15-02 |
| [ ] | Printed family comms plan and contact cards | | → 15-03, → 25-08 |
| [ ] | Analog barometer | The pressure trend is a forecast with no forecast | → 17-10 |

## 12. Children, family, documents, morale (→ 19, → 20, → 21)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **★ Document kit**: copies of everything, waterproof, grab-and-go | | → 19-01 |
| [ ] | **★ Cash in small bills** | Cards stop working with the power | → 19-02 |
| [ ] | Backup drive + paper copies of records | | → 19-03 |
{{#if has.infant}}| [ ] | Diapers and wipes at the current size **and the next**; formula if used | | → 20-06, → 20-05 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.child}}| [ ] | Carriers, child-size work gloves, comfort items | | → 20-01, → 20-07 |
| [ ] | School supplies, printed books, workbooks | The internet goes with the grid | → 20-03 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.pets}}| [ ] | Pet food, carriers, medicines, records | | → 20-09 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Games, cards, instruments, treats, decorations | Morale is a supply line | → 21-02, → 21-06 |
| [ ] | Paper, pencils, notebooks, a wall calendar | Logs, letters, schooling, sanity | → 21-04, → 25-05 |
| [ ] | This binder installed on more than one charged device | → 00-10 | → 00-01 |

## The ★ list, all together

If you do nothing else: water filter + elements, bleach, water containers, staples you eat,
mylar + oxygen absorbers, special-diet food if anyone needs it, open-pollinated seed, ignition
three ways, seasoned firewood, CO alarms, smoke alarms and extinguishers, power for medical
devices, a headlamp per person, the fullest legitimate medicine supply, rescue medicines in
pairs, a trauma kit, a bucket toilet, bleach or pool shock, base layers and boots for everyone,
an axe, knife and file, locked firearm storage if you own firearms, a NOAA radio, the document
kit, and cash. **Audit against the rows, not this paragraph.**

## When the shops close

This is a list of things to acquire, so "runs out" means **the shops close**.

- **Every ⌛ item becomes unobtainable at that moment**, permanently. Seed, seasoned wood and
  soil cannot be improvised. Buy them first even though they feel least urgent.
- **Every § consumable sets the real life of its tool.** Count the spares, not the tools: that
  is → 22-04, and it feeds → 23-02.
- **Everything above has a scavenged equivalent**: → 22-02. The six categories worth picking up
  whenever you see them are **containers, cloth, fasteners, cordage, fuel and blades**.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the whole list applies; the house is the store.
- **B (moving):** only what fits in the vehicle and the bags (→ 22-03, → 22-05). This list is
  what you are leaving behind, which is why the go-bag contents are chosen from it in advance.
- **C (establish):** the ⌛ items and the ones that produce (→ 23-04) matter most: seed, tools
  and skill.

Related: → 22-07 what to buy first · → 22-02 the scavenging version · → 22-04 inventory log ·
→ 22-03 go-bags · → 22-05 vehicle kit · → 22-06 medical kit · → 23-04 which purchases last ·
→ 23-02 counting what you have. A general national kit list: Ready.gov, Build A Kit.

pages.body:
# Scavenging field guide: what to look for

**What this page is for.** Knowing what is valuable before you need it, so that the things you
already own, are given, trade for, or find genuinely abandoned do not get overlooked. "Salvage"
means recovering useful material from things that are broken, discarded or abandoned. It also
carries real hazards (lead, mould, spoiled food, sharp steel, unstable buildings, contaminated
containers), and the second half of this page is about not being hurt by them.

> **CAUTION.** **Taking property that is not yours is theft**, in any scenario, and this page
> does not say otherwise. The most dangerous part of scavenging is not other people: it is a
> preventable injury with no doctor available.

## Do this now

1. **Learn the six categories below.** They are the things that get used up constantly and stop
   being made: **containers, cloth, cordage, fasteners, fuel, blades.**
2. **Start with your own house.** Most households already own hundreds of items on this page:
   the garage, the basement, the shed, the junk drawer, the car. **Inventory before you
   scavenge** (→ 22-04).
3. **Settle the household's ethics now, out loud, before anyone is desperate** (below).
   Deciding under pressure is how people become someone they did not intend to be.
4. **Never let a child handle salvage.** Lead, glass, chemicals and rusted steel.

## The six categories that matter most

Ranked by how fast you use them up, times how impossible they are to make at home.

1. **Containers.** Buckets (food grade especially), fuel cans, drums, jars, bottles, coolers,
   tubs, tanks. You will never have enough. Water (→ 03-02), food (→ 04-03), waste (→ 13-01)
   and transport all compete for them. *Look at:* building sites (drywall-compound buckets),
   restaurants and bakeries (food-grade buckets), farms (drums, large plastic totes), garages.
2. **Cloth and clothing.** Especially **wool**, and especially **children's sizes**, which
   quietly run out as children grow (→ 11-02). Blankets, curtains, canvas, tarps, sheets,
   towels, thread. *Look at:* closets, thrift stores, upholstery, mattress covers, drop cloths.
3. **Cordage and tape.** Rope, paracord, wire, baling wire, chain, ratchet straps, zip ties,
   duct tape (→ 16-03). *Look at:* garages, farms, boats, trailers, job sites.
4. **Fasteners and hardware.** Screws, nails, bolts, nuts, washers, hinges, hose clamps,
   springs. Small, heavy, and impossible to make at home (→ 16-07). *Look at:* junk drawers,
   workshop coffee cans, broken furniture, pallets.
5. **Fuel and things that burn.** Propane cylinders, lamp oil, charcoal, seasoned wood, scrap
   lumber, paper. **Never burn painted, treated or pressure-treated wood indoors, or under
   anything you cook on** (→ 06-05). *Look at:* grills, camping gear, garages, building scrap,
   fallen limbs.
6. **Blades and steel.** Knives, axes, saws, files, drill bits, hand tools. Good steel outlasts
   almost everything else in this binder (→ 16-01). *Look at:* old toolboxes, farm sheds.
   **Rust is not disqualifying:** rusted good steel cleans up; cheap steel never gets good.

## The full list, by need

| Need | Look for | Where it hides | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water storage** | Food-grade buckets, drums, jugs, water heaters (each holds tens of gallons), rain barrels | Restaurants, bakeries, garages, basements | → 03-02 |
| **Water treatment** | Unscented bleach, pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), coffee filters, cloth, sand, pots for boiling | Laundry rooms, pool sheds, kitchens | → 03-04 |
| **Food** | Sealed shelf-stable food, canning jars, **lids**, salt, sugar, oil, spices | Pantries, basements, restaurants | → 04-02 |
| **Growing food** | Seed packets, garden tools, pots, hose, fencing, chicken wire | Sheds, garden centres, farms | → 05-01 |
| **Fire** | Lighters, matches, ferro rods, charcoal, propane, lamp oil, seasoned wood | Grills, camping gear, garages | → 06-01 |
| **Cooking** | Cast iron, stainless pots, grill grates, camp stoves, Dutch ovens | Kitchens, garages, campers | → 07-01 |
| **Heat** | Blankets, sleeping bags, foam, rigid insulation, plastic sheeting, tape, cardboard | Attics, campers, job sites | → 08-01 |
| **Power** | Small solar panels (garden lights, dead RVs), 12 V batteries, battery backups (UPS units), chargers, inverters, wire, fuses | Vehicles, RVs, sheds, offices | → 09-13 |
| **Light** | Headlamps, flashlights, batteries, candles, lamp oil, wicks | Junk drawers, camping gear | → 10-01 |
| **Medical** | **Sealed, in-date** supplies only; OTC medicines; bandages; gloves | See the hard limits below | → 12-01 |
| **Sanitation** | Bleach, soap, bin bags, buckets, lime, ash, gloves, N95 masks | Laundry rooms, workshops | → 13-01 |
| **Clothing** | Wool, boots, socks, **children's next sizes**, needles, thread, buttons, zips | Closets, thrift stores, upholstery | → 11-01 |
| **Tools** | Hand tools, files, sharpening stones, vises, clamps, saw blades | Workshops, farms | → 16-01 |
| **Comms** | Batteries, radios, antenna wire, coax, connectors | Garages, vehicles, offices | → 15-02 |
| **Transport** | Bicycles, tubes, patch kits, wagons, {{#if is.snow_region}}sleds, {{/if}}carts | Garages, sheds | → 16-09 |
| **Children** | Diapers, wipes, formula (**sealed and in date only**), clothing in larger sizes, books, toys | See the allergy limits below | → 20-01 |

## What is worth its weight when moving (Phase B)

Weight is the limit the moment you are moving (→ 01-03). In order of value per pound:
**medication → water treatment → dense high-calorie food → fire → cordage → a blade → a light →
warm dry layers.** Almost everything else on this page is for staying put (Phase A) or
settling (Phase C). **Anything you cannot carry uphill for a mile is not going with you.**

## The hard limits: things not to take or use

| Never take or use | Why |
|---|---|
| **Insulin, epinephrine or any prescription medicine whose storage history you do not know** | Heat and freezing ruin some medicines with no visible sign, and a damaged rescue device may fail exactly when it must not (→ 29-07). **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Your *own* expired stock is a separate household choice: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05. Found antibiotics: {{choice DC-16}} → 30-17 |
| **Food without a full, intact ingredient label, for anyone with a food allergy**{{#if has.anaphylaxis}} (this household has one){{/if}} | Unlabelled or traded food can carry the allergen. Where the household draws that line: {{choice DC-18}} → 30-19, → 02-04 |
| **Refrigerated or frozen food from a dead fridge or freezer** | FoodSafety.gov: refrigerated food is safe about **4 hours** without power; a full freezer about **48 hours** (24 if half full). **When in doubt, throw it out** (USDA/HHS, Food Safety During a Power Outage; → 04-17) |
| **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans** | **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are thrown out, unopened.** Botulism gives no warning taste or smell (→ 29-08). Dented or rusty cans are a household choice: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15 |
| **Containers that held chemicals, fuel or pesticide** | Never for water or food, ever, however well washed |
| **Painted or pressure-treated wood, for indoor burning or cooking** | Lead, arsenic and other preservatives go into the smoke and the ash |
| **Damaged, dropped or unknown-history gas cylinders** | A leaking valve or weakened cylinder is a fire you carry home |
| **Anything inside a building that is unsound** | Burned, flooded or collapsed: nothing in there is worth a broken leg with no emergency room |

## Hazards, and how not to get hurt

- **Lead:** paint from before 1978, some solder, some glazes. Do not sand it, burn it or let
  children near it; wash hands (CDC, About Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention; → 13-02).
- **Mould and floodwater residue:** N95 mask, gloves, ventilation. Treat porous material that
  floodwater touched as lost (→ 17-03).
- **Sharps and rusted steel:** gloves and boots, always. **Know your tetanus status** (→ 12-04).
  Use tools as their makers intend (OSHA, Hand and Power Tools).
- **Buildings:** floors, stairs and roofs fail after fire and flood. Never go in alone.
- **Germs:** treat everything you bring home as contaminated: clean it, then disinfect it, then
  wash your hands (CDC, When and How to Clean and Disinfect Your Home; → 13-11).
- **Injury is the real risk.** A cut hand with no antibiotics is a life-threatening event
  (→ 12-04).

## The ethics question: settle it now

Decide, as a household, **before** anyone is hungry, where these lines fall:

- **Your own property, and goods freely given or traded:** never in question.
- **Material that is genuinely abandoned:** "abandoned" means actually ownerless, not "nobody
  is home right now".
- **A neighbour's property while they are away:** this is theft, and it is also how you lose
  the only network that will keep you alive (→ 18-01). **Ask. Trade. Leave a note and a debt.**
- **While any authority still functions, the law applies**, and so do the consequences.

Our household's line, in our own words: ______________________________________________

**The strategic argument, not only the moral one:** in a long event, **the community is the
resource that lasts** (→ 18-01, → 18-05). People who take get cut off; people who trade, teach
and share get fed. Section 18 is a better survival strategy than this page.

## Keeping quiet about it (OPSEC)

"OPSEC" means not advertising what you have or what you plan (→ 14-03).

- **Do not display what you have.** Carrying visible salvage marks you.
- **Go with someone; tell someone where you are going and when you are due back** (→ 15-03).
- **Daylight, known routes, no fixed pattern.**
- **Carry less than you can carry**, so you can still move quickly.

## Gear for salvage work

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| Heavy work gloves + sturdy boots | Cuts and punctures are the actual risk |
| N95 masks and eye protection | Dust, mould, lead |
| Pry bar, multi-tool, adjustable wrench, hacksaw | Getting things apart |
| Backpack + a tote, wagon{{#if is.snow_region}} or sled (the winter answer){{/if}} | Carrying it |
| Headlamp + spare batteries | Basements and buildings are dark |
| Permanent marker + tape | Label what you take, immediately |
| Small notebook | Where things are, for later trips |
| Soap and water or hand sanitiser | Before you eat, always |

The companion page is → 23-03: what a found item can stand in for.

## When it runs out

Scavenging always runs down. The supply of found goods shrinks every week and the effort per
item rises (→ 23-04).

- **How long:** weeks to months in a town; then it is picked over.
- **Ration:** take what you need and what stores well; leave what you cannot use. Hoarding
  what you cannot maintain costs trust you will need.
- **Replace it with:** **trade** (→ 18-02) and **skill** (→ 18-03), which outlast scavenging
  by years; then producing (→ 05-01), repairing (→ 16-05) and making (→ 13-09, → 10-04).

**Plan for scavenging to end.** The households that do well long-term are the ones producing
food and fuel by the time it does.

## Phase notes

- **A ({{ home.setting }}):** {{#if is.urban}}the most material and the most people. Your own
  house first, then trade with neighbours, then genuinely abandoned material.{{else}}less
  material, fewer people. Outbuildings, farm scrap and your own sheds first, then trade with
  neighbours.{{/if}}
- **B (moving):** almost nothing is worth the weight or the delay. Water, fuel and food only.
  **Do not detour to scavenge while travelling with children.**
- **C (establishing):** farms, outbuildings and abandoned homesteads hold tools, fencing,
  containers and hardware far more often than food.

Related: → 22-01 the buy-it-now version · → 22-04 inventory · → 23-03 substitutes ·
→ 23-04 why scavenging is never the endgame · → 14-03 OPSEC · → 18-01 mutual aid ·
→ 18-02 trade · → 04-17 food after a power cut · → 13-11 cleaning what you bring home ·
→ 12-04 infection.

pages.body:
# Go-bags and kits, one per person

**What this page is for.** A go-bag is a packed bag, one per person, that lets you leave home in
minutes and get through about three days on what you carry (Ready.gov, Build A Kit). This page
builds one bag for each person in this household, from your settings, plus one shared bag for
the vehicle. The medical part of each bag comes from → 22-06 and is packed first.

> **SAFETY — CRITICAL.**
> - **Rescue medicines and daily medicines are packed first and checked most often.**
>   Everything else in a bag is negotiable; those are not. **Quantities come from your
>   prescriptions and your condition pages in Section 02, never from a list.**
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** In cold weather, insulin and
>   other medicines that must not freeze ride inside the coat, against the body, not in the
>   pack (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency; → 29-07).
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** A
>   child's bag holds no medicine; an adult carries it.

## Do this now

1. **Build the medical kit first** (→ 22-06). If the rest of the bag is perfect and the
   medicine is short, the bag has failed.
2. **Pack one bag per person** below ({{ household.size }} people), sized to who carries it,
   plus the shared household bag for the vehicle (→ 22-05).
{{#if has.epinephrine}}3. **Put an epinephrine pair in the allergic person's bag, in each adult's bag and in the
   house kit**, and check every expiry on the same day. The pair that counts travels **on a
   person**, not in a parked vehicle (→ 02-03).
{{else}}3. **Put every rescue medicine where the person who needs it will be**, not only in one bag
   (→ 22-06).
{{/if}}4. **Pick two check dates, six months apart** (for example when the clocks change), and
   write them here: ____________ and ____________. Rotate food and water, check batteries and
   expiry dates{{#if has.child}}, **re-size the children's clothing**{{/if}}, and walk the plan
   (→ 24-02).
5. **Store the bags where you can grab them in 60 seconds in the dark**, by the exit you
   would actually use.

{{photo go-bags-spot}}

## The four levels of kit

| Level | Covers | Where it lives | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Every day ("EDC", everyday carry)** | Right now | On your body | "It happened while I was out" |
| **2. Go-bag** | About 72 hours, on foot | By the door | "We have minutes to leave" |
| **3. Vehicle kit** | Days, with the car | In the vehicle, always | "We are stuck, or driving out" (→ 22-05) |
| **4. Household stores** | Weeks to months | The house | Sheltering in place (→ 01-01) |

**They nest.** Leaving with the go-bag means the vehicle kit is a bonus and the house is gone.
Never plan to fill Level 2 from Level 4 on the way out: under stress you will forget, and
there may be no light.

## Level 1: what is on each body, every day

For most households Level 1 is a small light, a way to make fire, a whistle (→ 15-07) and the
wallet card set from → 25-08. **For anyone with a medical clock, Level 1 is medical:**

| Person | Conditions (from settings) | Allergies | On the body, always |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each members as m}}| {{m.label}} | {{#if m.conditions}}{{m.conditions}}{{else}}none in settings{{/if}} | {{#if m.allergies}}{{m.allergies}}{{else}}none in settings{{/if}} | Rescue medicine if any · medical ID · ____________ |
{{/each}}

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Allergy rule:** whichever adult is with the allergic person carries an **epinephrine pair**
on their body (not in the car, not in a bag on a hook), the person's allergen card, and the
plan from their prescriber (→ 02-03). A second dose may be needed (AAP, Allergy and
Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan).
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}**Diabetes rule:** the person with diabetes carries fast sugar, their meter or sensor reader,
and medical ID (→ 02-01, → 02-02).
{{/if}}**The test:** if it is not on a body when the siren goes or the reaction starts in a parking
lot, it is not Level 1. Pockets and a belt pouch beat everything else.

## The one rule that decides everything else

**A go-bag you cannot carry is not a go-bag.**
{{#if has.child}}This household has {{ household.children }} children. Every small child who cannot walk far is
carried, and that uses most of an adult's carrying capacity before a single item goes in.
{{/if}}{{#if has.mobility_aid}}Someone here uses a wheelchair or walker: decide now who pushes, who carries their bag, and how
the chair travels (→ 02-22).
{{/if}}

- **Weigh each loaded bag and write the weight on its tag.**
- **Walk a mile with the loaded bags** before you believe any of this (→ 24-02). Then take
  things out.
- **Children carry a small bag of their own** (comfort item, a snack, a whistle) because
  carrying something helps a child in a crisis, not because it helps the load.

## One bag per person

Each table is the core bag. The add-ons for each age band follow; pack them into the same bag.

{{#each members as m}}

### Bag: {{m.label}} ({{m.role}}, {{m.age_text}})

| ✔ | Category | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **Medical (first)** | Conditions: {{#if m.conditions}}{{m.conditions}}{{else}}none in settings{{/if}}. Allergies: {{#if m.allergies}}{{m.allergies}}{{else}}none in settings{{/if}}. Medicines: {{#if m.meds}}{{m.meds}}{{else}}none in settings{{/if}}. The matching modules from → 22-06, as one pouch (for anyone under 13, an adult carries it). Printed medicine list and the family medical summary (→ 25-09) |
| [ ] | **Water** | A bottle + a small filter + chemical treatment as a backup (→ 03-04). Planning figure is 1 gallon per person per day (CDC); the bag carries a day's drinking, the vehicle the rest |
| [ ] | **Food** | Three days of high-calorie food this person will actually eat, sealed, in original labelled packaging |
| [ ] | **Warmth** | Base layer, hat, gloves or mittens, spare socks, rain shell, emergency blanket or bivvy |
| [ ] | **Light and tools** | Headlamp + spare batteries, knife or multi-tool (adults), lighter + ferro rod, cordage, duct tape |
| [ ] | **Documents** | Copies of ID, insurance cards, prescription list (→ 19-01) |
| [ ] | **Comms** | Printed contacts and meeting places (→ 15-03), whistle, a charged phone and cable |
| [ ] | **Hygiene** | Toothbrush, small soap, hand sanitiser, toilet paper, any menstrual supplies (→ 13-08) |
| [ ] | **Personal** | Spare glasses, hearing-aid batteries, comfort item, ____________ |

Bag weight: ______ lb · Checked on: ____________
{{/each}}

### Add-on: every adult and elder

For: {{#each adults as a}}{{a.label}} · {{else}}no one listed{{/each}}

Between the adults, divide the **shared** load so the person with the heaviest medical load
carries mainly medical: the main water filter and a collapsible container, the bulk of the
shared food, **the trauma kit** (tourniquet, pressure dressings, wound-packing gauze; → 12-02),
a tarp and emergency blankets, a small stove, fuel and pot, a repair kit, **a second set of any
rescue medicine**, cash (→ 19-02), the document kit or drive (→ 19-03), and this binder on a
charged device or a printed set of the core pages (→ 00-02, → 01-03, → 25-08).

{{#if has.pregnant}}**Pregnancy (in this household):** prenatal vitamins, extra water and food, the prenatal
records, and the hospital-bag items from → 02-12.
{{/if}}{{#if has.nursing}}**Nursing (in this household):** extra water and food for the nursing parent; their supply is
the baby's supply (→ 02-13).
{{/if}}

### Add-on: teenagers (13 to 17)

For: {{#each teens as t}}{{t.label}} ({{t.age_text}}) · {{else}}no one in this age band right now{{/each}}

A teen carries close to an adult load and a real share of the shared kit: their own water
filter or tablets, a headlamp, a knife if the household allows it, and one shared item they are
responsible for. Give them their own copy of the contact card and the meeting places, and walk
them through the plan as an adult would be (→ 20-04).

### Add-on: children under 13

For: {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} ({{c.age_text}}) · {{else}}no one in this age band right now{{/each}}

| ✔ | Category | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **Their own small bag** | The comfort item, a snack, a whistle on a cord. **No medicine in the child's bag**: an adult carries it |
| [ ] | **ID card** | A card with the family's names, a photo of the family, the out-of-area contact's number and the meeting place (→ 15-03) |
| [ ] | **Warmth** | A full change of clothes, hat, mittens (warmer than gloves for small hands), two pairs of socks{{#if is.cold_winters}}, snow gear in season{{/if}} |
| [ ] | **Comfort** | **The specific comfort item.** It is what keeps a small child moving (→ 20-08) |
| [ ] | **Occupation** | A small book, cards, crayons |
| [ ] | **Safe food** | Snacks they reliably eat{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}; for a child with a food allergy, only food in original labelled packaging (→ 02-04){{/if}} |

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**For a child with anaphylaxis:** the epinephrine pair rides with the adult who is with the
child, in an outside pocket, marked, never buried; the written plan from the prescriber,
laminated, so anyone (a stranger included) can act (→ 02-03). Antihistamine only as the plan
says: never instead of epinephrine, never first. Feeding unlabelled or traded food:
{{choice DC-18}} → 30-19.
{{/if}}

### Add-on: babies and toddlers under 2

For: {{#each infants as i}}{{i.label}} ({{i.age_text}}) · {{else}}no one in this age band right now{{/each}}

| ✔ | Category | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **Feeding** | Formula if used, **plus safe water and the means to prepare it cleanly** (CDC, Infant Formula Preparation and Storage); bottles; the foods they take (→ 02-13, → 20-05) |
| [ ] | **Diapers** | Three days at the **current size**, wipes, cream, bags, and cloth as the backup (→ 20-06) |
| [ ] | **Carrier** | **A carrier or child-carrier pack is a survival item.** They cannot walk out of anything |
| [ ] | **Warmth** | Snowsuit or bunting in season, hat, mittens, blanket, two spares of everything (small children get wet) |
| [ ] | **Medical** | Their own medicines and an infant fever reducer as their provider directed, carried by an adult; a thermometer |
| [ ] | **Comfort** | Pacifiers, the specific blanket or toy, a familiar cup |
| [ ] | **Sleep** | Something they will actually sleep on (→ 21-07). Bed-sharing for warmth: {{choice DC-09}} → 30-10 |

### Add-on: elders (over 70)

For: {{#each elders as e}}{{e.label}} ({{e.age_text}}) · {{else}}no one in this age band right now{{/each}}

Lighter bag, more medical. Spare glasses and hearing-aid batteries (→ 02-23), a written list of
every medicine with the prescriber's words, a pill organiser for three days, compression or
mobility aids, an extra warm layer (older bodies cool faster; → 08-05), and a folding seat if
long waits are likely. If memory is a concern, an ID bracelet and one named adult who stays
with them at every stop (→ 02-21).

{{#if has.pets}}
### Pets

{{#each pets as p}}- {{p.type}} ({{p.count}}): food for three days ({{p.food_per_day}} a day), water, bowls, medicines{{#if p.medications}} ({{p.medications}}){{/if}}, leash or carrier, litter or waste bags, vaccination records and a photo (Ready.gov, Pets and Animals; → 20-09).
{{/each}}

Decide the pet plan **now**, not at the door. If it ever becomes impossible to keep them:
{{choice DC-10}} → 30-11.
{{/if}}

## The household bag (rides in the vehicle)

- Larger water containers and the second filter (→ 03-04)
- Extra food for several days, a stove and fuel
- The full first-aid kit (→ 12-01) beyond the trauma kit
- Tent or heavy tarp, sleeping bags rated for the season, ground pads
{{#if has.pets}}- Pet carriers, food, water bowls, litter (→ 20-09)
{{/if}}- Tools, cordage, tape, work gloves
- Paper maps and a compass (→ 25-04)
- **Cash**, documents, backup drive (→ 19-01)
- This binder on a second charged device (→ 00-10)

## The 60-second, 10-minute and 30-minute lists

Post these on the inside of a cupboard door (→ 01-06):

| You have | You take |
|---|---|
| **60 seconds** | People{{#if has.pets}}, pets{{/if}}, **medical kit**, go-bags, phones, keys, wallets |
| **10 minutes** | + document kit, water, food bin, sleeping bags, coats and boots for everyone, the binder device |
| **30 minutes** | + tools, stove and fuel, extra water, extra clothing, whatever else the vehicle holds (→ 22-05) |

**Practise the 60-second list with the family, timed, at least twice a year** (→ 24-02).

## Your climate changes the bag

Home county: {{ home.county }}, {{ home.state_name }} · January mean low {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F
· July mean high {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F.

{{#if is.cold_winters}}- **Winter matters here.** Boots, snow gear and hats live with the bags, not in a closet
  upstairs. Medicines that must not freeze ride inside a coat. Batteries lose capacity in cold:
  carry spares warm (→ 09-05). On foot in a blizzard with small children is extremely dangerous;
  in winter the honest plan is often "get to the vehicle, or stay put" (NWS, During a Winter
  Storm; → 17-01, → 01-02).
{{else}}- **Cold snaps still happen.** Keep a warm layer and a hat in every bag all year.
{{/if}}{{#if is.hot_summers}}- **Heat matters here.** More water than you think, sun hat, light long sleeves, and
  medicines kept out of direct sun and parked cars (→ 29-07, → 17-04).
{{/if}}{{#if is.hurricane_region}}- **Hurricane country:** waterproof everything; dry bags for documents and medicine (→ 17-13).
{{/if}}{{#if is.wildfire_region}}- **Wildfire country:** N95 masks for every person, goggles, and a bag that is ready all
  season, because warnings can be short (→ 17-14).
{{/if}}{{#if is.flood_region}}- **Flood risk:** waterproof bags, and the bag goes up high with you (→ 17-03).
{{/if}}

## Maintenance: the part everyone skips

A go-bag is not a purchase; it is a **rotation**. On the two check dates:

1. **Every expiry date**: medicines, rescue devices, food, water treatment.
2. **Every battery**, including the ones inside devices.
3. **Children's clothing sizes**, the fastest-expiring item in the house.
4. **Weigh the bags.** They gain weight every year.
5. **Reprint the paper pages** (→ 19-01, → 25-09): phone numbers and prescriptions change.
6. Log it in → 22-04 and write the date on each bag's tag.

Medicine that was too hot in a parked car or a summer bag: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09. Using
expired rescue medicine when nothing in date exists: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05.

## Gear for the bags

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| One pack per person, sized to the person carrying it | Fit matters more than brand |
{{#if has.young_child}}| **A child-carrier pack** | A small child is cargo |
{{/if}}| Insulated medicine pouch | Keeps medicine in range in both directions (→ 29-07) |
| Dry bags or heavy zip bags | Everything gets wet eventually |
| Water bottles, a small filter, treatment tablets | Two ways to make water safe (→ 03-04) |
| Emergency bivvies and wool layers | Cold is what kills people outdoors |
| A headlamp per person + batteries | Hands free |
| Laminated plans and contact cards | Anyone must be able to act |
| A luggage scale | Keeps the bags honest |

**If you do not have it:** any backpack works; fit and weight matter more. A wagon{{#if is.snow_region}}
or a sled{{/if}} beats a pack for hauling children and gear. Bedsheets make carriers and
bundles. **There is no substitute for insulin, epinephrine or any other daily or rescue
medicine.** Do not plan around finding them (→ 23-03).

## When it runs out

A go-bag lasts about three days by design. **After that, everything in it is spent**, which is
the whole point of → 01-02: leaving is only a plan if it ends somewhere.

- **How long:** three days of water and food. The medical module's clock is the real number,
  and it comes from your condition pages, not this one.
- **Ration:** water and warmth first. Anyone whose eating is medical (diabetes, a nursing
  parent, a small child) eats to their need, not to a share (→ 23-01).
- **Resupply:** the vehicle kit (→ 22-05), then a destination (→ 01-05).
- **The strategic point:** a go-bag buys **the time to reach somewhere**. If there is no
  somewhere, better bags do not help; a destination does (→ 01-05).

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the bags sit ready and get maintained. Most emergencies are handled
  at home.
- **B (moving):** this page is the plan. Grab, load, go; the 60-second list runs the door. The
  medical load-out follows → 01-07.
- **C (establish):** the bags become the starting kit at the new place and then get **rebuilt
  at once**: a spent bag left empty is the most common failure after any move.

Related: → 22-06 medical kit (build it first) · → 22-05 vehicle kit · → 22-01 where the gear
comes from · → 01-02 when to go · → 01-03 moving · → 01-06 transition checklists ·
→ 19-01 documents · → 25-08 quick-reference cards · → 24-02 practising the grab.

pages.body:
# Household inventory log

**What this page is for.** You cannot ration what you have not counted, and you cannot claim
what you cannot prove. This worksheet does three jobs at once: it feeds the "how many days do
we have" numbers in → 23-02, it shows what is still missing from → 22-01, and it is the record
an insurer or a disaster-assistance programme will ask for (→ 19-04). Numbers your settings
already hold are printed; everything else you write in pencil.

## Do this now

1. **Do the count in one sitting, room by room** (route: → 26-02), with a pencil and a phone
   camera. It takes an afternoon, and nothing else in this binder returns more for one
   afternoon.
2. **Photograph every room and every open storage container**, plus serial numbers on anything
   valuable. Store the photos **off-site**: a copy that burns with the house proves nothing
   (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a Disaster; CFPB, Disasters and Emergencies; → 19-03).
3. **Copy the totals into → 23-02.** That is where quantity becomes days.
4. **Set the recount dates**: the same two dates a year as the go-bag check (→ 22-03).
5. **Count the medical rows against the actual boxes and the actual prescriptions**, not memory.

## Four rules that make an inventory useful

1. **Count in units you will use in a decision.** "3 cases" is useless; "36 cans, about 14,000
   calories" answers a question (→ 04-01).
2. **Record the date, always.** An undated inventory is a guess within a month.
3. **Record where it is.** In an emergency someone else needs to find it.
4. **Record the earliest expiry in a group, not the latest.** Rotation is driven by the front
   of the shelf (→ 04-10).

This page is the **stock** view: what exists, where, how much, expiring when. → 23-02 is the
**runway** view: the same numbers divided by daily use. Fill this one first.

## Header

```
INVENTORY DATE: ____________   COUNTED BY: ____________________
NEXT RECOUNT DUE: ____________ PHOTOS STORED AT (off-site): ____________
```

Household: {{ household.size }} people ({{ household.adults }} adults, {{ household.children }}
children){{#if has.pets}}, pets: {{#each pets as p}}{{p.count}} {{p.type}} · {{/each}}{{/if}}.

## Where things are (fill in once, update when you move them)

| Item | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Electrical panel and main breaker | ____________ | Label the breakers (→ 29-04) |
| Water main shutoff | ____________ | Operate it once (→ 03-02) |
| Gas shutoff and the tool it needs{{#if !has.gas_any}} (none per settings){{/if}} | ____________ | Procedure: → 16-12 |
| Water heater ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal){{#if !has.water_heater_tank}} (tankless or none per settings){{/if}} | ____________ | An emergency water reserve (→ 03-02) |
| Fire extinguishers ({{ gear.extinguishers }}) | ____________ | → 29-12 |
| Smoke alarms ({{ gear.smoke_alarms }}) and CO alarms ({{ gear.co_alarms }}) | ____________ | Battery type? ______ |
| Shelter room{{#if has.shelter_room}}: {{ dwelling.shelter_room }}{{/if}} | ____________ | → 17-06 |
| Medical kit and rescue medicines | ____________ | → 22-06 |
| Go-bags | ____________ | → 22-03 |
| Document kit and cash | ____________ | Location only; never write a safe combination in this binder (→ 19-01) |
| Fuel storage | ____________ | Outside the living space (→ 06-06) |

## A. Medical (count these first, against the boxes)

**The medicines your settings list:**

| Person | Medicine | Strength | Where kept | Expiry | On hand (count) | Days at normal use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as x}}| {{x.member}} | {{x.name}} | {{x.strength}} | {{x.where_kept}} | {{x.expiry}} | ______ | ______ |
{{else}}| none entered | | | | | | |
{{/each}}

**Everything else medical:**

| Item | On hand | Unit | Earliest expiry | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#if has.epinephrine}}| **Epinephrine devices**, every location | | devices | | | Never rationed (→ 02-03) |
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}| Diabetes supplies: syringes or pens, sensors, pump parts, test strips, **ketone strips**, glucagon, fast sugar | | | | | → 02-01, → 02-02 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}| CPAP filters, masks, tubing | | | | | → 02-24 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}| Oxygen cylinders and tubing | | hours | | | → 02-08 |
{{/if}}| Other device supplies: ______________ | | | | | |
{{#if has.infant}}| Infant formula and feeding supplies | | | | | → 02-13 |
{{/if}}| First-aid consumables (gauze, tape, dressings) | | | | | → 12-01 |
| Trauma items: tourniquets ___ · wound-packing gauze ___ · pressure bandages ___ · CPR mask ___ | | | | | → 12-02 |
| Over-the-counter: adult pain and fever ___ · child pain and fever ___ · dosing syringes ___ · anti-diarrhoeal ___ · oral rehydration salts ___ | | | | | Adult-only items kept apart from children's (→ 12-13) |
| Spare glasses, hearing-aid batteries | | | | | → 02-23 |
{{#if has.pets}}| Pet food and pet medicines | | | | | → 20-09 |
{{/if}}

> **Reconcile this block against your condition pages and → 22-06 every time.** It is the block
> that sets the household's real timeline (→ 23-01).

## B. Water

| Item | On hand | Unit | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stored drinking water | {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} | gallons | | Date filled: ______ |
| Water heater and pipes | {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} | gallons | | Know the drain valve (→ 03-02) |
| Pool or hot tub (raw, not drinkable){{#if !has.pool}} (none per settings){{/if}} | {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} | gallons | | Treatment: → 03-03 |
| Filters | | units | | Element life left: ______ |
| **Spare filter elements** | | | | |
| Unscented bleach | | fl oz | | **Purchase date:** ______ |
| Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) | | lb | | Stored sealed, dry, away from fuel (→ 29-05) |
| Purification tablets | | | | Expiry: ______ |
| Empty containers (capacity) | | gallons | | |
| Rain barrels | | gallons | | |

Two-week target for this household: {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gallons (→ 03-01).

## C. Food

| Category | On hand | Unit | Earliest expiry | Location | Est. calories |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rice and grains | | lb | | | |

## H. Summary (copy to → 23-02)

```

Water: ______ days    Food: ______ days    Heat/fuel: ______ days
Power: ______ days    Sanitation: ______ days    Medical: ______ days

1. ______________________  4. ______________________
2. ______________________  5. ______________________
3. ______________________

```

## What to do with the finished sheet

- **One copy in the binder** (or photographed into the app's photo slots), one **stored
  off-site** (→ 19-03), and the photo-inventory status on → 19-04 updated.
- **Copy the numbers to → 23-02** and re-rank → 22-07.
- **Give a copy to every adult.** An inventory only one person knows is a single point of
  failure.
- **Keep last year's sheet.** The difference between two years is your real rate of use,
  better data than any estimate in this binder.

**What you need:** a clipboard, pencils, a tape measure, a kitchen or luggage scale, a
permanent marker and labels, a phone for photos, and a fireproof, waterproof box for the paper
copy (→ 19-01). **Pencil, not pen:** pens freeze and run; pencil works wet and cold and erases
when counts change.

## When it goes stale

- **How long it stays true:** about **six months**, less if you are using your stores.
- **Never skip the medical block** to save time; it is the one that matters.
- **Refresh:** the twice-a-year recount, on the go-bag dates (→ 22-03).
- **A guessed inventory is worse than none**, because it produces confident, wrong decisions on
  → 01-02.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** full inventory twice a year, plus a running log of what is used
  (→ 25-05).
- **B (moving):** the only inventory that matters is what is in the vehicle and the bags.
  **Count it at each stop**, out loud, so every adult knows (→ 01-03).
- **C (establish):** restart the full inventory in the first week. **What you arrived with is
  your whole world** until production starts (→ 23-04).

Related: → 23-02 turns these counts into days · → 22-01 what the gaps mean you should buy ·
→ 22-07 spending order · → 04-10 food rotation · → 19-03 off-site copies · → 19-04 insurance ·
→ 25-05 more blank logs · → 25-10 annual review.

pages.body:
# Vehicle kit

**What this page is for.** The kit that lives in each vehicle all year, the add-ons for your
seasons, and the evacuation load that waits in the house ready to go in. It also covers the
spare tyre, how much a vehicle can really carry, and why medicine and batteries ride in a
vehicle but never live in one.

> **CAUTION.**
> - **If you are stranded in a winter storm, stay with the vehicle.** It is shelter, and it is
>   what searchers look for (NWS, During a Winter Storm).
> - **Before running the engine for heat, clear snow from the exhaust pipe and crack a window.**
>   Carbon monoxide builds up silently (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics; → 29-03).
>   **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.**
> - **Medicine never stays in a parked vehicle.** It leaves with a person at every stop
>   (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency; → 01-07).
> - **Never leave a child or a pet in a parked vehicle**, in any season (NWS, Heat Safety).

## Do this now

1. **Build the all-year kit below for each vehicle**, in one duffel or tote so it stays one
   grabbable unit.
{{#if is.cold_winters}}2. **Add the winter add-on before the first snow** and leave it in until spring. The storm that
   strands you is never the one you planned around.
{{else}}2. **Add the seasonal add-on that fits your weather** (winter or heat, below).
{{/if}}3. **Keep the fuel tank at least half full**{{#if is.cold_winters}} all winter{{/if}}. Our line:
   never below ______ (the American Red Cross advises at least half full; Power Outage Safety).
{{#if has.child}}4. **Put a spare hat, mittens and boots in each vehicle for every child, in the size that fits
   now.** Children get stranded in whatever they wore to school.
{{/if}}5. **Look under the cargo floor today:** is there a spare tyre, a jack and a wrench? Write it
   in the table below. Many newer vehicles, hybrids and EVs carry none.
6. **Check the kit on the go-bag dates** (→ 22-03).

{{photo vehicle-kit-stowed}}

## Our vehicles

| Vehicle | Fuel | Four-wheel drive | Can tow | Spare tyre? | Jack + wrench? | Payload (door sticker) | Kit checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each vehicles as v}}| {{v.type_text}} | {{v.fuel_text}} | {{v.four_wheel_drive}} | {{v.can_tow}} | ____ | ____ | ______ lb | ______ |
{{else}}| No vehicle entered | | | | | | | |
{{/each}}

{{#if !has.vehicle}}No vehicle is entered in settings. Read this page anyway: a borrowed or rental vehicle in an
evacuation needs the same kit, and the rules for medicine and fuel do not change.
{{/if}}

## The three jobs of a vehicle kit

| Job | Example | What it demands |
|---|---|---|
| **Stranded** | Storm, ditch, breakdown, closed highway | **Warmth or cooling, water, light, being seen, patience** |
| **Getting yourself out** | Stuck in snow or mud, dead battery, flat tyre | Traction, tools, a way to jump-start |
| **Evacuation** | The Phase B drive (→ 01-03) | Fuel, water, food, navigation, the family's kit |

Most car-kit lists only cover the second job. In cold or hot country the first one is the one
that kills, and it is mostly a temperature-and-water problem.

## If you are stranded: the rules, in order

1. **Stay in the vehicle.** Walking in a whiteout or extreme heat is how people get lost
   (NWS, During a Winter Storm).
2. **Make yourself visible.** Bright cloth on the antenna or door handle; dome light on at
   night while the engine runs; hazard lights sparingly.
3. **Before running the engine: clear the exhaust pipe**, every time, and **crack a window on
   the side away from the wind.** Run it about **10 minutes an hour**, not continuously
   (NWS, During a Winter Storm; CDC; → 08-02).
4. **Insulate.** Blankets, sleeping bags, everyone in one space. Move arms and legs now and
   then to keep blood moving (OSHA, Cold Stress).
5. **Water first, food second.** Do not eat snow: it costs body heat; melt it (→ 03-06).
6. **Call or text your location** while you still have signal, then save the phone's battery
   (→ 00-10).
7. **Watch the children constantly.** Small bodies cool and overheat faster (→ 11-02, → 08-05).

## The kit: all year, every vehicle

| ✔ | Item | Why |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **Water**, rotated (it may freeze; leave room in the bottle) | The first shortage |
| [ ] | Shelf-stable food{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}, **safe for the person with the food allergy** (→ 02-04){{/if}}; extra snacks for children | |
{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}| [ ] | **Fast sugar**, clearly marked | For anyone with diabetes (→ 02-01) |
{{/if}}| [ ] | First-aid kit + trauma items (→ 12-01, → 12-02) | |
| [ ] | **Headlamp or flashlight + spare batteries** | Roadside work is night work |
| [ ] | Phone cables, 12 V adapter, **jump pack** (also charges devices) | → 09-11 |
| [ ] | Multi-tool, knife, duct tape, zip ties, work gloves | |
| [ ] | Tow strap, jumper cables | |
| [ ] | Spare tyre **checked**, jack, wheel wrench, **tyre plug kit, 12 V compressor**, tyre gauge | A flat you cannot fix is a stranding (→ 16-10) |
| [ ] | Fluids: oil, coolant, washer fluid{{#if is.cold_winters}} rated for winter{{/if}} | |
| [ ] | Fire extinguisher | → 29-12 |
| [ ] | **Paper maps** of home, destinations and the states between, + a compass | Phones and networks fail first (→ 25-04) |
| [ ] | **Printed contact and meeting-place card** (→ 15-03, → 25-08) | Phones die; paper does not |
| [ ] | Cash in small bills (→ 19-02) | |
| [ ] | Whistle, signal mirror, bright cloth | Being seen |
| [ ] | Trash bags, wipes, hand sanitiser{{#if has.infant}}, **diapers and wipes**{{/if}} | → 13-08 |
| [ ] | Rain gear, spare clothing for everyone who rides in it | |
| [ ] | Notebook and **pencil** | Pens fail in the cold |

## Winter add-on{{#if is.cold_winters}} (applies here: January mean low {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F){{/if}}

| ✔ | Item | Why |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **A sleeping bag or heavy wool blanket for every seat** | The single most life-saving item in a winter vehicle |
| [ ] | **Extra hats, mittens, wool socks, insulated boots**{{#if has.child}}, children's in the size that fits now{{/if}} | People get stranded dressed for the car, not the ditch |
| [ ] | Emergency blankets or bivvies, one per person | Cheap, tiny, effective |
| [ ] | Hand and body warmers | **Outside the inner layer** for anyone too young to tell you a warmer is burning them: the packets warn against direct skin contact |
{{#if has.young_child}}| [ ] | **A blanket or poncho that goes over the buckled car-seat harness** | No bulky coat under the harness; the top layer must come off easily so the child does not overheat once the cabin warms (AAP, Winter Car Seat Safety Tips; → 11-02) |
{{/if}}| [ ] | **Full-size shovel** (not a folding toy) | Digging out and clearing the exhaust |
| [ ] | Traction: sand, cat litter or traction boards; tyre chains if you carry them | |
| [ ] | Ice scraper and snow brush | |
| [ ] | Candle in a metal can + lighter | A little heat and light, with a window cracked. Open flame in a closed space is a household choice: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21 |
| [ ] | Bright flagging cloth | Being found |
| [ ] | Snow pants for whoever will dig | |

## Heat add-on{{#if is.hot_summers}} (applies here: July mean high {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F){{/if}}

| ✔ | Item | Why |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Extra water, more than you think | Heat illness starts with dehydration (→ 17-04) |
| [ ] | Sunshade for the windshield, a light-coloured cover for children's seats | A closed car heats far past the outside temperature (NWS, Heat Safety) |
| [ ] | Wide hats, light long sleeves, sunscreen | |
| [ ] | A battery fan and a spray bottle | Moving air and evaporation |
| [ ] | Insulated medicine pouch | Medicine still leaves with a person (→ 29-07) |

{{#if is.wildfire_region}}**Wildfire country:** N95 masks for everyone, goggles, and the tank kept fuller in fire
season; know two ways out (→ 17-14).
{{/if}}{{#if is.hurricane_region}}**Hurricane country:** fill the tank when a storm is first forecast; stations close early
(→ 17-13).
{{/if}}{{#if is.flood_region}}**Flood risk:** never drive into water over the road; a small depth of moving water can float
a car (→ 17-03).
{{/if}}

## The evacuation load (waits in the house, loads in minutes)

Pre-stage it in one place so loading is not a decision (→ 01-06):

1. **First: the medical load-out from → 01-07.**{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}} This household has
   refrigerated medicine: the running cooler goes in first, in the cabin, thermometer in range.{{/if}}
   Medicine and the medical kit (→ 22-06) ride **in the cabin with a person**, never the trunk,
   a trailer or a roof box.
2. The go-bags and the household bag (→ 22-03).
3. Water containers (fill them on the way out if there is time).
4. Food bin, stove and fuel.
{{#if has.pets}}5. Pet carriers, food, litter (→ 20-09).
{{/if}}6. Sleeping bags, tarp or tent, ground pads; tools, cordage, tape.
7. **Documents, cash, drives** (→ 19-01).
8. **Fuel cans, filled and stabilised** (→ 06-06, → 06-08), outside the passenger space: on a
   hitch carrier or in a trailer. Whether cans may ever ride inside the vehicle, in the cargo
   area, for the shortest possible leg, is a household choice: {{choice DC-06}} → 30-07.
   **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.**

## The spare tyre

**Many newer vehicles, most EVs and many hybrids have no spare**; they carry a sealant and
inflator kit, which cannot fix a sidewall cut, a blowout or a hole larger than a nail.
{{#if has.hybrid}}A hybrid is in this household: check its cargo floor today.{{/if}}{{#if has.ev}}
An EV is in this household: check its cargo floor today.{{/if}}

The roadside ladder, cheapest first (→ 16-10 has the full procedure):

1. **A bad valve core** causes many slow leaks: a valve tool and spare cores fix it.
2. **A tyre plug kit with steel T-handles + a 12 V compressor + a pencil gauge.** Plugs fix most
   tread punctures and can be used again and again. They are a get-home repair; never plug a
   sidewall. **Practise one plug on a scrap tyre**: it takes real force the first time.
3. **One can of sealant** as the last layer: tread holes only, temporary, and it gums the tyre
   pressure sensor and the rim, so shops may refuse to patch afterwards.
4. **A real spare for long trips:** a used wheel and tyre matching the size on the door-jamb
   sticker, a jack, a breaker bar and a torque wrench, strapped in the cargo area. **Do one
   practice wheel change in the driveway.**

## How much the vehicle can really carry

{{photo door-jamb-sticker}}

- **Payload is the limit that binds.** The sticker on the driver's door frame gives the most
  the vehicle can carry: every pound of people, pets, cargo **and trailer tongue weight**
  counts against it. Write each vehicle's number in the table above.
- **Add up the people first.** Weigh everyone, add car seats and pet carriers, and subtract from
  payload. What is left is all the cargo you have. Water weighs about 8.3 lb a gallon (→ 25-02),
  which is why a moving family carries a day or two of water plus a way to treat more, never
  its storage tanks (→ 03-01).
- **A hitch carrier** (a tray or box on a rear hitch) carries heavy items outside the cabin:
  fuel cans, the spare, tools. Its weight is on the tongue; the vehicle's tongue limit, not the
  hitch's rating, decides. **One receiver holds one thing:** a tray or a trailer, not both.
- **A roof box** suits the light, bulky half of the load (sleeping bags, clothing, diapers). Read
  the roof load limit in the owner's manual: it is small. **Never medicine** (a roof box is a
  freezer in winter and an oven in summer), **never firearms or documents.** Expect worse fuel
  use and know your new height.
- **A trailer** is the biggest capacity multiplier. Load the heavy items low and slightly
  forward of the trailer's axle, so the tongue presses down on the hitch (too little tongue
  weight makes a trailer sway); the tongue weight the trailer and the vehicle need is in their
  manuals (→ 16-11). Never exceed the vehicle's towing and tongue limits from the owner's manual. Backing a trailer
  is a skill: practise before it matters (→ 16-11). **Nothing alive rides in a trailer**, and
  neither do medicines or documents.
- **Do one test pack:** load the real totes into the real vehicle, seats in family
  configuration. "If it does not fit, it does not go" (→ 01-03) is only knowable by loading.

```
VEHICLE: ________________  PAYLOAD (sticker): ______ lb
People + car seats + pets: ______ lb   Left for cargo: ______ lb
Tow limit (manual): ______ lb   Tongue limit (manual): ______ lb
Roof load limit (manual): ______ lb   Range on a full tank: ______ mi
```

**Loading rules, whatever the setup:** heaviest items low, forward and inside; bulky-light up
top; fuel outside the passenger space; medicine and the medical kit in the cabin with a person.
Firearms travel unloaded, cased and out of reach, so they cannot shift, fire or be grabbed at a
stop. Never load so heavily that the vehicle squats.

> **Before the collapse:** laws on carrying firearms in vehicles differ by state and change at
> state lines. Unloaded and cased is the usual baseline; check each state on the route
> (→ 14-11).

## Fuel discipline

- **Set a refuelling line and keep it.** Ours: ______ of a tank.
- **Each vehicle is a tank of fuel**, plus stabilised cans stored outside the living space,
  away from ignition (→ 06-06).
- **In an evacuation, fuel is the range limit and stations may be down** (→ 01-03). Range in
  the tanks plus what you carry is your true radius: write it on the map (→ 25-04).
- **When fuel is gone, the vehicle becomes shelter and storage.** Bicycles, a wagon{{#if is.snow_region}}
  and a sled{{/if}} are the transport plan after that (→ 16-09).

## Medicine and batteries ride in a vehicle; they never live in one

- **A parked car runs far below freezing in winter and far above most medicine labels in
  summer.** Freezing destroys insulin with no sign; heat degrades insulin and epinephrine
  (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency; → 29-07). **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen
  is discarded.** Heat-exposed medicine: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09.
- Medicine lives in an **insulated pouch that travels with the person**, in and out every time.
- **Fast sugar** can live in the car permanently: it is stable, and it is what you will want
  fastest.
- **A vehicle-stored rescue device is better than none**, but treat it as a backup that is
  replaced on schedule, never the primary.
- **Lithium batteries and power stations** have charge and storage temperature limits on their
  labels that a parked car exceeds for months each year (→ 29-02, → 09-03). Load them at
  departure; bring them in on arrival. Anything battery-shaped that must stay: cabin footwell,
  not trunk; checked monthly.
- **The car is a generator, not a battery.** A running engine charges phones and power stations
  through the 12 V socket or a USB-C car charger (→ 09-11), outdoors only.

## If you do not have it

- **Blankets, sleeping bags and heavy coats** from the house: the warmth layer is the part that
  must not be missing.
- **Floor mats** make traction boards; **cat litter or sand** works as grit.
- **Cardboard and newspaper** insulate people from cold surfaces.
- **A wagon{{#if is.snow_region}}, sled{{/if}} or cart** hauls children and gear when the
  vehicle stops being the answer.

## When it runs out

- **How long:** fuel is the vehicle's clock, and it is short: days of on-and-off heat, or one
  tank's driving range.
- **Ration:** heat in cycles (about 10 minutes an hour), water steadily, food last.
- **Resupply:** stabilised fuel cans. Siphoning has real limits (many tanks block it; the vapour
  is the hazard), and **never siphon by mouth** (→ 06-07).
- **After fuel:** the vehicle is still **shelter, storage and a windbreak**; transport becomes
  bicycle, wagon{{#if is.snow_region}} and sled{{/if}} (→ 16-09).

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the kit is for local emergencies: the ditch, the closed road, the
  school run in a storm. This is the most likely use of anything in this binder.
- **B (moving):** the vehicle is the evacuation. Load the pre-staged pile, keep the medical kit
  in the cabin, and go early rather than perfectly (→ 01-02).
- **C (establish):** the vehicle becomes a **fixed asset**: battery and alternator (→ 09-11),
  storage, shelter, glass, wire, seats and mirrors. Do not scrap it thoughtlessly.

Related: → 22-03 go-bags · → 22-06 medical kit · → 01-07 medical load-out · → 17-01 blizzards ·
→ 08-02 carbon monoxide · → 08-05 hypothermia · → 11-02 keeping children warm · → 06-06 fuel
storage · → 06-08 fuel in transport · → 16-10 tyre failures · → 16-11 trailers · → 25-04 maps.
