pages.body:
# Medical go-kit

**What this page is for.** One bag that holds everything this household's medical conditions
need for the first days away from home, packed so that someone who did not pack it can find
each part by feel, in the dark. It is built from the conditions, allergies and medicines in
your settings: each condition adds its module (its own pouch) from the condition library in
Section 02. Build this kit before any other kit in the binder.

> **SAFETY — CRITICAL.**
> - **This page contains no dosing.** Quantities and doses come from your prescriptions and
>   your prescribers. The binder never works out, adjusts or suggests a dose.
> - **Rescue medicine is never rationed and never delayed.** In anaphylaxis, epinephrine comes
>   first; antihistamines do not treat it (CDC, Recognizing and Responding to Anaphylaxis;
>   AAAAI, Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan).
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.**
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** The kit
>   is closed and rides with an adult.
> - **Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no
>   help will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).**

## Do this now

1. **Build this kit first.** → 22-03 waits; this does not.
2. **Ask every prescriber, at the next appointment, for the most on-hand supply your
   prescriptions and insurance allow**, and about 90-day fills and early-refill ("vacation")
   overrides (→ 12-07). This is the single highest-value medical preparation there is.
3. **Count what you have today** and write the number of days on the front of the kit and in
   the table below (→ 22-04).
{{#if has.epinephrine}}4. **Put an epinephrine pair everywhere the allergic person spends time**: their own bag, each
   adult's bag, the house kit, school or daycare. A vehicle pair is a marked backup only.
{{else}}4. **Put each rescue medicine where the person who needs it will be** (inhaler, glucagon,
   seizure rescue medicine, epinephrine), not only in this bag.
{{/if}}5. **Get each condition's emergency plan from the prescriber, in writing**, laminate it, and put
   one copy in the kit and one on the fridge. A plan a stranger can follow is worth more than
   a plan only you understand.
6. **Check every expiry date on the two kit-check dates** (→ 22-03).

{{photo med-kit-packed}}

## How the kit is organised

| Pouch | For | What it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| **One pouch per condition module** | Each person with a condition (below) | The condition's own emergency (each Section 02 page names it) |
| **Rescue pouch** | Anyone with a rescue medicine | A life-threatening event in minutes: anaphylaxis, a severe low, an asthma attack, a seizure |
| **General pouch** | Everyone | Bleeding, infection, dehydration, fever, wounds |

**Different coloured pouches, labelled on the outside, with that condition's printed plan
inside each.**

## What this household needs

**People and conditions:**

| Person | Age | Conditions | Allergies |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each members as m}}| {{m.label}} | {{m.age_text}} | {{m.conditions}} | {{m.allergies}} |
{{/each}}

**Medicines, exactly as typed from the bottles** (the binder never changes these):

| Person | Medicine | Strength | Schedule | Refrigerated | If doses are missed (prescriber's words) | Where kept | Expiry | Days on hand |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as x}}| {{x.member}} | {{x.name}} | {{x.strength}} | {{x.schedule}} | {{x.refrigerated}} | {{x.if_missed}} | {{x.where_kept}} | {{x.expiry}} | {{x.days_on_hand}} |
{{else}}| none entered | | | | | | | | |
{{/each}}

**Allergies:**

| Person | Allergen | Severity | Carries epinephrine |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each allergies as a}}| {{a.member}} | {{a.allergen}} | {{a.severity}} | {{a.carries_epinephrine}} |
{{else}}| none entered | | | |
{{/each}}

**Shortest medical clock in the household:** ______________ = ______ days. This number sits on
the front of the kit and drives → 01-02.

## The condition modules

Each row is the go-kit part of that condition's page. Rows marked **(in this household)** are
the ones your settings selected; the rest stay here so a condition can be added later.

| Condition | What goes in its pouch | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Type 1 diabetes, injections{{#if has.condition.CL-01}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Every vial or pen, syringes or pen needles, meter + strips + lancets, **ketone strips**, fast sugar, glucagon, the sick-day plan, cooling | → 02-01 |
| Type 1 diabetes, pump and sensor{{#if has.condition.CL-02}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | All of the above **plus** pump supplies, sensors, chargers, the printed pump-failure plan from the prescriber. **The syringe is the survival path** | → 02-02 |
| Anaphylaxis{{#if has.condition.CL-03}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | **Epinephrine pair**, the written plan, medical ID, antihistamine only as the plan says | → 02-03 |
| Food allergy{{#if has.condition.CL-04}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Safe food in original labelled packaging, dedicated utensils, the allergen list | → 02-04 |
| Type 2 diabetes{{#if has.condition.CL-05}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Tablets or injectables, meter + strips, fast sugar if the medicine can cause lows | → 02-05 |
| Type 2 diabetes on insulin{{#if has.condition.CL-06}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Insulin and supplies as for type 1, cooling, meter + strips, fast sugar | → 02-06 |
| Asthma{{#if has.condition.CL-07}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Rescue inhaler (two), spacer, controller inhaler, the written action plan, N95 masks for smoke | → 02-07 |
| COPD and oxygen{{#if has.condition.CL-08}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Inhalers, oxygen hours counted, tubing, concentrator power plan; **no flame near oxygen** | → 02-08 |
| High blood pressure and heart disease{{#if has.condition.CL-09}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Every daily tablet; a home blood-pressure cuff; any chest-pain medicine the prescriber gave | → 02-09 |
| Blood thinners{{#if has.condition.CL-10}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | The tablets, extra pressure dressings and wound-packing gauze, a card saying which thinner | → 02-10 |
| Epilepsy and seizures{{#if has.condition.CL-11}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Every daily medicine, any rescue medicine, the seizure plan, a seizure log | → 02-11 |
| Pregnancy, birth and postpartum{{#if has.condition.CL-12}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Prenatal vitamins, records, the birth supplies list | → 02-12 |
| Infant feeding{{#if has.condition.CL-13}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Formula and safe water, or the nursing parent's extra food and water; bottles and cleaning | → 02-13 |
| Thyroid disease{{#if has.condition.CL-14}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | The tablets, in original bottles | → 02-14 |
| Kidney disease and dialysis{{#if has.condition.CL-15}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Medicines, the fluid and potassium plan, the dialysis centre's emergency plan | → 02-15 |
| Mental-health medicines{{#if has.condition.CL-16}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Every daily medicine (some are dangerous to stop suddenly), the crisis plan | → 02-16 |
| Opioid dependence and chronic pain{{#if has.condition.CL-17}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Medicines as prescribed, **naloxone**, non-drug pain aids | → 02-17 |
| Immunosuppression and transplant{{#if has.condition.CL-18}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Every anti-rejection medicine, masks, hand sanitiser, a thermometer | → 02-18 |
| Celiac and severe gut disease{{#if has.condition.CL-19}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Safe food, oral rehydration salts, any prescribed medicine | → 02-19 |
| Adrenal insufficiency{{#if has.condition.CL-20}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Daily steroid, the prescriber's written stress plan and any emergency injection kit | → 02-20 |
| Dementia and elderly care{{#if has.condition.CL-21}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Medicines in a pill organiser, ID bracelet, a recent photo, a comfort item | → 02-21 |
| Mobility impairment{{#if has.condition.CL-22}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Pressure-injury supplies, toileting supplies, aid repair kit | → 02-22 |
| Hearing and vision aids{{#if has.condition.CL-23}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Spare glasses, the written glasses prescription, hearing-aid batteries | → 02-23 |
| Sleep apnoea (CPAP){{#if has.condition.CL-24}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Mask, tubing, filters, the 12 V cord or battery tested at home | → 02-24 |
| Contraception and menstrual health{{#if has.condition.CL-25}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | The supply, plus reusable menstrual supplies | → 02-25 |
| Severe obesity and bariatric surgery{{#if has.condition.CL-26}} **(in this household)**{{/if}} | Vitamins and supplements as prescribed, larger-size first-aid and mobility items | → 02-26 |
| A condition not in the library | The twelve headings of → 02-27, filled in from the prescriber | → 02-27 |

## Rescue medicines: the rules that do not change

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Anaphylaxis is in this household.**{{else}}No anaphylaxis is entered; read this anyway.{{/if}}

- **Epinephrine in pairs, in date.** A second dose may be needed if symptoms get worse,
  continue or do not get better in 5 minutes (AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan).
  One device is not a kit.
- **The written, signed plan from the prescriber**, laminated, in the pouch. Anyone must be
  able to follow it, including someone who has never met the person (→ 02-03).
- **Medical ID on the person** listing the allergens.
- **Antihistamine only as the plan says: never first, never instead of epinephrine.**
- **Safe food** in original sealed packaging (→ 02-04), and dedicated utensils: cross-contact is
  the usual exposure in an improvised kitchen.
- **After epinephrine, the plan is normally emergency care.** Write down now what you do when
  that is not available (→ 12-16): a second dose may be needed, and a reaction can come back
  hours later. Watch the person.
- **Expired devices when nothing in date exists** is a household choice: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05.

{{#if has.condition.CL-01}}**Insulin-dependent diabetes is in this household.**{{else}}No insulin-dependent diabetes is entered; read this anyway.{{/if}}

- **Every vial or pen you legitimately have**, plus the injection fallback (syringes or pens)
  **even if a pump works**: pumps fail, batteries die (→ 02-02).
- **Meter, strips and lancets.** A sensor is not the fallback; the meter is.
- **Ketone strips**: the most-forgotten life-saving item in the kit. They catch diabetic
  ketoacidosis (DKA) early (CDC, Diabetic Ketoacidosis).
- **Fast sugar** in several places: kit, pocket, car, bedside.
- **Glucagon**, and **a second adult who knows how to use it.**
- **The sick-day plan** from the prescriber (CDC, Managing Sick Days).
- **Rationing insulin is not a household decision.** If supply is short, that is a reason to
  move toward resupply (→ 01-02), not to under-dose (→ 12-11).

## The cold chain

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}This household keeps refrigerated medicine:
{{#each refrigerated_meds as r}}{{r.member}}: {{r.name}} ({{r.where_kept}}) · {{/each}}
{{else}}No refrigerated medicine is entered. Read this anyway: a new prescription can change that.
{{/if}}

- **Insulin's fridge range is 36 to 46 °F.** Many insulins can be kept unrefrigerated between
  59 and 86 °F for up to 28 days, depending on the product; read your product's label (FDA,
  Insulin Storage in an Emergency; ADA, Insulin Storage and Syringe Safety). Other medicines:
  read each label (→ 29-14).
- **Freezing is a cliff; heat is a slope** (→ 29-07). **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen
  is discarded.** In winter, carry it against the body. Heat-exposed medicine:
  {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09.
- **A thermometer decides, not a hand.** Put one in whatever keeps the medicine cold.
- **Layers:** a 12 V fridge or cooler on a power station (tested at home for a day; → 09-10), an
  insulated pouch with cold packs that cannot touch the medicine, and an evaporative cooling
  pouch as the fallback (→ 12-21).

## General pouch (the carry version of → 12-01)

| Category | Items |
|---|---|
| **Bleeding** | Tourniquet (and the training), pressure dressing, wound-packing gauze, gauze rolls, tape (Stop the Bleed, USUHS; → 12-02) |
| **Wounds** | Irrigation syringe, antiseptic, non-stick pads, closure strips; sutures or stapler **only if trained** (→ 12-14) |
| **Infection** | Antibiotic ointment. Prescribed antibiotics only; using them without a prescription is a household choice: {{choice DC-16}} → 30-17 |
| **Burns** | Non-stick dressings, cling film, clean water (→ 12-03) |
| **Fluids** | **Oral rehydration salts**: diarrhoea and dehydration are common when water and sanitation fail (→ 12-05) |
| **Fever and pain** | Adult and **child** forms, each with the dosing tool from its package; a thermometer (→ 12-13) |
| **Splints** | Padded aluminium splint, wrap, triangular bandages (→ 12-09) |
| **Barrier** | Nitrile gloves (several pairs), N95 masks, eye protection, CPR face shield |
| **Dental** | Temporary filling material, clove oil, dental wax (→ 12-06) |
| **Tools** | Trauma shears, tweezers, safety pins, headlamp and spare batteries, permanent marker (write the time on a tourniquet and on dressings) |
| **Personal** | Everyone's prescriptions, spare glasses, sunscreen, insect repellent |
| **Paper** | → 12-01, → 12-02, → 12-16, every condition plan, and the family medical summary (→ 25-09) |

Giving one person's prescription medicine to another: {{choice DC-15}} → 30-16.

## Storage, rotation and where it lives

- **One grab bag, carried in the cabin**, never in the trunk in extreme weather (→ 01-07).
- **Insulated in both directions**: a cold-pack pocket for summer, body-carry for winter.
- **Waterproof**: a dry bag or heavy zip bags inside.
- **Labelled outside** with the household's name, the conditions, and "MEDICAL".
- **A copy of each plan on the fridge**, where responders look.
- **On each kit-check date:** every expiry, every battery, refresh the food, **replace anything
  within six months of expiry**, and read every plan aloud with another adult.

## The honest limits of this kit

It handles **hours to days**, not months. It cannot:

- **Make insulin, epinephrine or any other medicine.** No skill substitutes (→ 23-04).
- **Replace a hospital** for airway management, surgery, imaging or blood (→ 12-16).
- **Solve a supply shortage.** Only resupply does, which is why the count in → 22-04 is the
  number that drives the household's decisions, and why → 01-02 exists.

## If you do not have it

- **The general pouch substitutes broadly:** clean cloth for gauze, boiled water for
  irrigation, improvised splints (→ 12-09). **A tourniquet is the exception:** improvised ones
  often fail (→ 12-02), so firm direct pressure and wound packing come first.
- **Medicines do not substitute.** Found medicine of unknown storage history cannot be trusted
  as the primary: heat and freezing damage are invisible (→ 22-02).
- **The one thing you can always improvise is the written plan.** Copy the essentials onto
  paper and put it where responders look.

## When it runs out

| Item | How long | Ration? | Resupply | Substitute |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Daily medicines** | Count ÷ daily use, from the prescription | **Not a household decision**: ask the prescriber now what to do if it runs short | Pharmacy, clinic, hospital, mutual aid (→ 12-07) | **None** for most |
| **Rescue medicines** | Devices or doses on hand | **Never** | Prescription | **None** |
| **Device supplies** (sensors, pump parts, CPAP filters) | Count | Only as the condition page says | As above | The condition page's fallback |
| **Test and ketone strips** | Count | **Do not skimp on ketone strips** | As above | None reliable |
| General pouch | Weeks | Yes, most items | Trade (→ 18-02), scavenge (→ 22-02) | Widely (→ 23-03) |

**Everything in this binder can be rationed, substituted, improvised or produced except the top
rows of this table.** They are the reason the household has a phase plan at all.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the kit sits packed; the house holds the bulk supply (→ 12-07). Work
  the resupply relationships now, while pharmacies and clinics function.
- **B (moving):** this kit **rides in the cabin with a person**, never left in a parked vehicle
  in heat or cold. First loaded, first checked at every stop (→ 01-07).
- **C (establish):** the supply count becomes the countdown. **Finding a medical supply line
  is a first task at the new place**, not a background chore (→ 01-04, → 18-01).

Related: → 22-03 go-bags · → 22-05 vehicle · → 01-07 the medical load-out · → 12-01 household
first-aid kit · → 12-08 kit tiers · → 12-11 chronic conditions · → 12-16 hard calls ·
→ 25-09 medical summary · → 23-02 the runway table · → 29-07 refrigerated medicines.

pages.body:
# What to buy first: the spending order

**What this page is for.** → 22-01 is what to buy; this page is the order. The rule is not about
comfort: **buy against what hurts people soonest, then against what cannot be bought later.**
Tier 0 and Tier 1 below are cheap and cover most realistic risk. Rows that your settings make
urgent for this household are marked **(this household)**.

## Do this now

1. **Do Tier 0 this week.** It is cheap and small, and several of its items prevent deaths in
   the next month, not the next decade.
2. **Do not skip ahead to solar panels and rifles.** Both are on this list; neither is near the
   top, and buying them first is the most common preparedness mistake.
3. **Fill in the → 22-04 inventory first** if you have not: you may already own half of what you
   are about to buy.
4. **Set a monthly amount you can actually sustain** and work down the tiers. Steady beats a
   spree, because the ⌛ items (seed, wood, soil, skill) need years, not money.

## The ordering rule

Rank every purchase by three questions, in this order:

1. **How fast does its absence hurt someone here?** Minutes, hours, days, weeks, months.
2. **Can it still be bought later?** ⌛ items (seed, seasoned wood, soil, skill, children's next
   sizes) **cannot**. They move up.
3. **How likely is the event it covers?** A power cut lasting days is common enough
   that the American Red Cross tells every household to plan two weeks of food and water for
   one (American Red Cross, Power Outage Safety); a years-long collapse is not. **Buy against the
   likely first**, then the severe.

**For most households that produces:** carbon monoxide → medical dependency →
{{#if is.cold_winters}}cold{{else}}{{#if is.hot_summers}}heat{{else}}cold or heat{{/if}}{{/if}} → water →
injury and infection → food → everything else. **Food is sixth**, and it is where most people
start.

## Tier 0: this week (small money, largest risk reduction)

| # | Item | Why it is first | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Battery CO alarms**, one on every level and outside every sleeping area, plus batteries. You have {{ gear.co_alarms }} | Bringing any burning heat source indoors in an outage is how households die; detecting it is cheap (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics; → 29-03){{#if has.unvented_heater}}. **(this household): you own an unvented heater**{{/if}}{{#if has.generator}}. **(this household): you own a generator**{{/if}} | → 08-02 |
| 2 | **The fullest legitimate supply of every daily and rescue medicine**: start the conversation with each prescriber now{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}} **(this household: refrigerated medicine)**{{/if}} | Nothing else you buy changes this clock | → 12-07, → 22-06 |
{{#if has.epinephrine}}| 3 | **Epinephrine pairs for every location** the allergic person spends time **(this household)** | Minutes matter and there is no substitute | → 02-03 |
{{/if}}| 3a | **Trauma and family first-aid core**: tourniquets, wound-packing gauze, pressure bandages, oral rehydration salts, adult and child fever medicine with dosing tools, a CPR face shield | A bleed, a dehydrated child or a fever with no emergency room is the realistic medical emergency. Count what you have first (→ 22-04) | → 12-01, → 12-02, → 12-05, → 12-13 |
| 4 | **Water: bleach + a filter + containers** toward {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gallons | Days, not weeks (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply) | → 03-02, → 03-04 |
| 5 | **A headlamp per person** ({{ household.size }}) + batteries | Everything else is harder in the dark | → 10-01 |
| 5a | **Smoke alarms and an ABC fire extinguisher** on every level. You have {{ gear.smoke_alarms }} smoke alarms and {{ gear.extinguishers }} extinguishers | Fire with no fire department | → 29-12 |
| 5b | **Labels on every fuel can** | One wrong pour puts gasoline in a heater (→ 29-01) | → 06-06 |
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}| 5c | **A thermometer for the medicine fridge or cooler** **(this household)** | The storage range is unverifiable without one (→ 29-07) | → 22-06 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.child}}| 5d | **A lockable box for medicines** **(this household: children)** | **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** | → 20-02 |
{{/if}}

## Tier 1: this month

| # | Item | Why | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | **Base layers, insulated boots, hats and mittens for everyone**{{#if has.child}}, children included{{/if}} | {{#if is.cold_winters}}Cold is a local killer here (January mean low {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F){{else}}Cold snaps and wet weather still kill{{/if}}; children's sizes ⌛ expire | → 11-01, → 11-02 |
| 7 | **Trauma kit (row 3a) + a Stop the Bleed class** | The class is what makes the tourniquet work | → 12-02 |
| 8 | **Two weeks of shelf-stable food you actually eat**{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}, **including allergen-safe food (this household)**{{/if}} | Cheap, useful at once, rotates naturally | → 04-02 |
| 9 | **NOAA Weather Radio** (battery or crank, SAME){{#if has.noaa_radio}}: owned{{/if}} | The best early warning there is | → 15-01 |
| 10 | **A vehicle kit for each vehicle**{{#if is.cold_winters}}, winter add-on included{{/if}} | Blankets, shovel, traction, children's gear in current sizes | → 22-05 |
| 11 | **Ignition three ways + a way to cook without the grid** | Boiling water is the base skill | → 06-01, → 07-01 |
| 12 | **Document kit + cash in small bills** | Costs almost nothing; cannot be replaced if lost | → 19-01, → 19-02 |
| 13 | **Bucket toilet + cover material** | Sanitation failure causes outbreaks fast (→ 13-11) | → 13-01 |
| 14 | **Power for medical devices**: power banks or a station sized to them{{#if has.cpap}} **(this household: CPAP)**{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}} **(this household: oxygen)**{{/if}} | Devices through a multi-day outage | → 09-10 |
| 14a | **A CO detector with a number (ppm) display** on each level | Catches a slow leak before the alarm threshold | → 08-02 |
| 14b | **Fuel-transport hardware**: approved cans, straps, an exterior rack{{#if has.destinations}} **(this household: you have destinations)**{{/if}} | Fuel that cannot ride safely is range you do not have | → 06-08 |
| 14c | **Spares for any heater you own**: wicks, filters, hoses{{#if has.unvented_heater}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | A heater you cannot fix mid-winter is not a heater | → 08-09, → 08-10 |
{{#if has.trailer}}| 14d | **Trailer spare wheel + bearing kit + coupler lock** **(this household)** | One bearing or one tyre is the whole move | → 16-11 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.vehicle}}| 14e | **Tyre plug kit + 12 V compressor**, and a real spare if the vehicle has none | A flat you cannot fix is a stranding | → 16-10, → 22-05 |
{{/if}}

## Tier 2: this season (and the ⌛ items: do not defer these)

| # | Item | Why | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | **⌛ Open-pollinated seed, in quantity** | Cheap, light, and **unbuyable later** | → 05-03 |
| 16 | **⌛ Firewood, far more than feels sensible, seasoning now**{{#if has.fireplace}} **(this household: fireplace)**{{/if}}{{#if has.wood_stove}} **(this household: wood stove)**{{/if}} | Wood bought today is next winter's fuel | → 06-03, → 06-04 |
| 17 | **⌛ A compost pile started; soil begun**{{#if has.garden}} **(this household: garden space)**{{/if}} | Years to build; free to start | → 05-11 |
| 18 | **⌛ The next two sizes of children's clothing and boots**{{#if has.child}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | The expiry nobody plans for | → 11-02, → 11-09 |
| 19 | **A good axe, saw + file, and a good knife** | Best lifetime value of any tool | → 16-01, → 16-06 |
| 20 | **Bulk staples + mylar + oxygen absorbers + buckets** | Turns cheap food into long-keeping food | → 04-03 |
| 21 | **Ammunition for the calibres you already own**, cleaning kit, spare parts{{#if !has.firearms}} (none owned per settings){{/if}} | Feed and maintain what you have; buy nothing new first | → 14-07, → 14-05 |
| 21a | **Locked storage for every firearm**{{#if has.firearms}}{{#if has.child}} **(this household: firearms and children)**{{/if}}{{/if}} | Child-access prevention, in calm times and crisis | → 14-14 |
| 22 | **Home hardening**: locks, door reinforcement, window film, lighting | The cheapest security spend | → 14-02 |
| 23 | **Go-bags built out** | Most of the contents come from Tiers 0 to 2 | → 22-03 |
| 24 | **Sanitation bulk**: soap, bleach, liners, gloves{{#if has.infant}}, diapers and wipes{{/if}} | Boring; runs out fastest | → 13-01 |
| 25 | **First-aid depth**: oral rehydration salts, dental, splints | | → 12-01, → 12-05, → 12-06 |
| 25a | **Chimney brush sized to your flue + suppressant**{{#if has.fireplace}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | Wood heat means creosote on a schedule | → 06-09 |
| 25b | **Chainsaw chaps + eye and ear protection** | A saw injury with no emergency room | → 11-05 |
| 25c | **Large vacuum flasks** | Saves cooking fuel | → 07-02 |
| 25d | **Push-fit pipe couplings + a tube cutter** | A burst pipe becomes a short repair | → 16-12 |
{{#if has.young_child}}| 25e | **Car-seat ponchos or over-harness blankets** **(this household)** | No bulky coat under the harness (→ 11-02) | → 22-05 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.well}}| 25f | **Well bailer + rope** **(this household: well)** | The no-power fallback; cheap, and unbuyable once needed | → 03-10 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.pets}}| 25g | **Pet food, carriers and medicines for two weeks** **(this household)** | | → 20-09 |
{{/if}}

## Tier 3: this year

| # | Item | Why here and not earlier | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| 26 | **Solar + a battery or power station**: you have {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W and {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh | Size it to medical loads and December sun; insulation, layers and a CO alarm come first | → 09-02, → 09-03 |
| 27 | **Pressure canner + jars + lids** | Pays off only with a harvest and the skill (→ 24-01) | → 04-05 |
| 28 | **Rocket or efficient stove, Dutch oven, cast iron** | Cuts wood use sharply | → 07-02, → 07-04 |
| 29 | **Rain barrels + gutters + screens** | Turns weather into a supply (→ 23-04) | → 03-05 |
| 30 | **Water distillation setup**{{#if has.pool}} **(this household: pool or hot tub)**{{/if}} | The only home method that removes salt | → 03-03 |
| 31 | **Garden built out**: beds, tools, row cover, ⌛ fruit trees | | → 05-01, → 05-02, → 05-13 |
| 32 | **Two-way radios + a ham licence** | The licence takes time | → 15-02, → 15-05 |
| 33 | **Chickens or rabbits** (check local rules) | Ongoing protein and fat | → 05-04, → 05-05 |
| 34 | **Bicycles + trailer + spares** | Transport after fuel | → 16-09 |
| 35 | **Generator**{{#if has.generator}} (owned: {{ gear.generator_watts }} W){{/if}}: outdoor-rated cords, oil and filters, a marked outdoor spot, a first start | Useful, loud, thirsty, and **CO-lethal indoors**. **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** | → 09-04 |
| 35a | **Analog barometer** | Hours of warning with no forecast | → 17-10 |
| 35b | **Moisture meter for firewood** | The difference between heat and creosote | → 08-08 |

## Tier 4: the things money cannot shortcut

These outrank most of Tier 3 and cost little or nothing:

- **Skills** (→ 23-05, → 24-01): the only asset that never runs out.
- **Practice** (→ 24-02, → 24-04): a blackout weekend finds more gaps than a large purchase.
- **A destination** (→ 01-05): {{#if has.agreed_destination}}you have an agreed destination. What
  money cannot buy is the remaining work with the people there: agreed terms (→ 18-04) and a tote
  of supplies left there on each visit.{{else}}no destination is agreed yet. A conversation, a
  visit or an agreement is worth more than another year of gear.{{/if}}
- **Neighbours** (→ 18-01): mutual aid is the highest-return preparation there is.
- **A medical supply relationship** (→ 12-07): the only thing that moves the medical clock.

## Budget shapes

An illustrative split, not prices. Replace with real local numbers as you fill → 22-04.

| If you have | Spend it on |
|---|---|
| **$100** | Tier 0 items 1, 4, 5: CO alarms, bleach + containers, headlamps |
| **$500** | Tier 0 complete + food, base layers, NOAA radio |
| **$1,500** | + vehicle kits, trauma kit, bucket toilet, go-bags, bulk staples, seed |
| **$5,000** | + wood, tools, canning setup, rain barrels, home hardening |
| **$15,000+** | + solar and batteries, distillation, garden build-out, livestock, transport |
| **$0** | **Tier 4.** Inventory, practise, teach the children, meet the neighbours, walk the routes |

## The five most common ways to waste money

1. **Buying the tool without the consumable**: a filter with no element, a canner with no lids,
   an optic with no batteries, a saw with no file.
2. **Buying gear for a skill never practised.** An unused pressure canner is furniture.
3. **Buying one of something everyone needs.**
4. **Buying solar before insulation, layers and a CO alarm.** A warm, safe household uses far
   less power.
5. **Putting off the ⌛ items** because they feel unhurried. Seed, wood, soil, children's sizes
   and skill are the only things here money cannot fix later.

## When the shops close

This page becomes read-only.

- **Every ⌛ item becomes unobtainable at that moment.**
- **Tier 0 and Tier 1 are the items you will most regret skipping**: cheapest and most
  consequential.
- **Almost everything in Tiers 2 and 3 has a scavenged or traded equivalent** (→ 22-02).
  **Nothing in Tier 0 does**: CO alarms and medicines are bought, not found.
- After that, → 22-02 (scavenge), → 18-02 (trade) and → 23-05 (skills) are the only ways left
  to acquire anything, and only the last one grows.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** work down the tiers on a monthly budget; re-rank at every recount
  (→ 22-04). The worksheet version is → 26-09.
- **B (moving):** nothing here can be bought once you are moving.
- **C (establish):** seed, tools and skill make a place viable (→ 23-04), so buy in Phase A with
  Phase C in mind.

Related: → 22-01 the full list by subject · → 22-04 what you already have · → 22-02 what to
look for later · → 23-04 which purchases last · → 23-05 the free ones · → 26-09 the shopping
worksheet · → 25-10 annual review. A national starting list: Ready.gov, Build A Kit.

# Depletion and substitution

**What this section holds.** 5 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 23-01 **The depletion framework**: Everything you stock runs out, and each thing runs out at its own speed.
- → 23-02 **Master consumables table**: Every section of this binder works out how long one kind of supply lasts.
- → 23-03 **Substitution catalog: what replaces what**: A one-page index of "when this runs out, use that", each line pointing to the page that explains it properly.
- → 23-04 **Lifecycles of every major consumable**: Every supply in the house moves through the same four stages, from a pile that only shrinks to something you can make for yourself.
- → 23-05 **Skills that replace supplies**: Everything else in this section is arithmetic on a shrinking pile.

pages.body:
# The depletion framework

**What this page is for.** Everything you stock runs out, and each thing runs out at its own
speed. Planners call the number of days a supply will last its **runway** (think of a
plane running out of runway). This page gives you four questions to ask about every supply,
sorts supplies into three classes, and shows how to find the one that runs out first. **The
supply that runs out first sets your household's timeline.** The worksheet where you write the
numbers is → 23-02.

## Do this now

1. **Fill in the master consumables table** (→ 23-02). It takes an afternoon with a notebook,
   a measuring cup and a scale.
2. **Work out each prescription medicine's runway first** (→ 12-07) and write today's date
   next to it. For most households with a daily medicine, that is the shortest clock.
3. **Put a weekly check on the household routine** (→ 21-04) so the numbers stay true. A
   runway worked out once and never updated is a number you will misremember.
4. **Decide now, calmly, at what runway you act.** When to leave home is a household decision
   (→ 01-02). {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20

## The four questions for every supply

Every "When it runs out" block in this binder answers these four.

**1. Runway: how long does it last?**
- Amount on hand divided by real daily use. **Measure the use, do not guess it.** Most
  households' guesses about their own use are well off until they measure it.
- Use the hard case: winter wood use, summer water use, water use when someone is sick
  (→ 12-05). Not the average.
- Write the date. A runway shrinks every day.

**2. Ration: how do you stretch it?**
- What is the least that keeps the job done, rather than comfortable?
- What gets cut first, second and third. Decide it in advance, in writing.
- What is never rationed (see the rules below).

**3. Resupply: where does more come from?**
- Make or grow it (garden → 05-01, wood → 06-04, rain and snow → 03-05).
- Find it (→ 22-02).
- Trade for it (→ 18-02).
- **Or it cannot be resupplied.** Write that down plainly. It is the important case.

**4. Substitute: what does the job instead?**
- A different material, a different method, or a skill that replaces the supply (→ 23-05).
- **Or nothing does.** Name it (→ 23-03).

## The three classes of supply

Sorting every supply into one of three classes is the key move, because each class needs a
different kind of plan.

{{figure fig-three-classes-of-consumable}}

| Class | What it means | Examples | The plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Renewable** | You can make or gather more for as long as you need | Water (→ 03-05), wood (→ 06-04), garden food (→ 05-01), soap (→ 13-09), cordage (→ 16-03), fat lamps (→ 10-04) | **Build the ability to produce it.** How much you can make matters more than how much you hold |
| **B. Substitutable** | It runs out, but something else does the job | Batteries → daylight; gauze → boiled cloth (→ 12-02); tape → wire (→ 16-05); screws → lashings (→ 16-03) | **Stock it deeply and learn the substitute** |
| **C. Irreplaceable** | No way to make it, nothing replaces it, no local resupply | Prescription medicines the body depends on (insulin → 02-01, epinephrine → 02-03, seizure and heart medicines → 12-11), infant formula for a baby who is not breastfed (→ 20-05), supplies for medical devices | **The runway is the plan.** It drives the go/no-go decision (→ 01-02) |

**Class C is short, and it decides everything.** A household can be well prepared in classes
A and B and still have its whole timeline set by one item in class C.

### Your household's class C items

These come from your settings. Add anything missing by hand.

{{#each meds as m}}- **{{m.name}}** {{m.strength}} for {{m.member}}: about {{m.days_on_hand}} days on hand (from your settings; recount from the boxes).
{{else}}- No medicines are entered in settings. If anyone takes a daily prescription, add it in settings or here: ______________________ days on hand: ______
{{/each}}
{{#if has.infant}}- Infant formula, if the baby is not fully breastfed (→ 20-05). There is no safe homemade formula.
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}- Oxygen: cylinders and concentrator power (→ 02-08, → 09-10).
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}- CPAP power and parts (→ 02-24, → 09-10).
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}- Pump and sensor supplies (→ 02-02).
{{/if}}{{#if has.epinephrine}}- Epinephrine auto-injectors: their clock is the expiry date, not daily use (→ 02-03).
{{/if}}

## The clocks, in a typical order

The order matters more than the numbers. Your own numbers go in → 23-02.

| Clock | Class | Typical runway | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Daily prescription medicines** (→ 12-07) | **C** | **Whatever you hold** | **For most households with one, this is the governing clock** |
| **Epinephrine** (→ 02-03) | **C** | Until it expires | Cannot be made; it expires |
| Phone and medical-device batteries (→ 09-06) | B | Days | Charging plan and manual backups |
| Stored water (→ 03-02) | A | Days | Renewable: rain, snow, treatment (→ 03-04) |
| Refrigerated food (→ 04-17) | B | Hours to days | Winter outdoor cold substitutes for free (→ 04-09) |
| Generator fuel (→ 09-04) | B | Days to weeks | Solar substitutes (→ 09-02) |
| **Wood**, if it is your only heat (→ 06-04) | A | **Weeks** | Renewable but hard work; the winter clock |
| Batteries (→ 09-07) | B | Weeks | Solar plus rechargeables makes them renewable |
| Stored food (→ 04-01) | A/B | Months | Renewable through → 05-01 and → 05-07, slowly |
| First-aid supplies (→ 12-01) | B | Varies | Clean cloth and cleanliness substitute (→ 12-02) |
| Diapers (→ 13-08) | B | Days to weeks | Cloth substitutes; **the child also outgrows them** |
| Screws, wire, thread (→ 16-07, → 16-04) | B | Long | Plentiful to salvage (→ 22-02) |
| Skills (→ 23-05) | none | **Never runs out** | **Gets better with use** |

**Read the first row and the last row together.** The shortest clock is usually something
you have to buy, and the longest is something you know.

## Working it out honestly: the common mistakes

- **Using label or planning figures instead of measured ones.** Measure real use: power
  (→ 09-01), water (→ 03-01), wood (→ 06-04).
- **Averaging the seasons.** A plan built on yearly averages fails at both ends. It is the
  same mistake as sizing solar on yearly sun (→ 09-05) or water on spring conditions (→ 17-07).
- **Forgetting the spikes.** Illness raises water use (→ 12-05); a storm raises wood use
  (→ 17-01); heat raises water use (→ 11-08).
- **Counting the whole stock as usable.** Some of it is hard to reach, spoiled or held back as
  a reserve. Do not count the reserve you will not touch.
- **Ignoring the work.** A renewable supply you are too hurt or tired to produce is not
  renewable that week (→ 12-09, → 21-02).

## Rationing: the general rules

Every "When it runs out" block in this binder uses these.

1. **Ration by function, not comfort.** Keep what keeps you able to work and stay well; cut
   what is only pleasant. Rule 5 is the exception.
2. **Cut the biggest user first** where you can. Usually it is a comfort use.
3. **Never ration** drinking water (→ 03-01), handwashing (→ 13-02), prescribed medicine
   (→ 12-11), children's food (→ 20-01) or sleep (→ 21-07). Each costs far more than it saves.
   **Stretching a prescription by skipping or cutting doses is not a household decision**: talk
   to the prescriber now about what to do if supply is cut off (→ 12-07).
4. **Protect the class C items absolutely.** Everything else can be bargained.
5. **Do not ration morale to zero** (→ 21-06). A household that saves every pleasure for a
   worse day finds that every day is the worse day.
6. **Decide the order of cuts in advance**, in writing, so it is not an argument (→ 21-05).

## What you need

| Item | Why | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **The filled-in master consumables table** | The thing this section exists to produce | → 23-02 |
| A notebook for the weekly check | Runways shrink; numbers must be current | → 21-04, → 25-05 |
| **Measuring tools**: a plug-in watt meter, a marked jug, a kitchen or bathroom scale | Measured beats estimated, every time (→ 29-13) | → 09-01, → 03-01 |
| The household inventory | You cannot work out a runway on an unknown stock | → 22-04 |
| **Written action points** | So the leave-or-stay decision is calm and decided ahead | → 01-02 |
| Calendar reminders for expiry dates | Medicines, batteries, food, epinephrine | → 25-10 |

No money? The framework is free: four questions, a notebook and an afternoon. Estimate where
you cannot measure, but measure the important ones: water, power, wood and medicine.

## When it runs out

- **The framework does not run out; the habit of keeping it does.** Keep the weekly check on
  the routine (→ 21-04).
- **The decision point.** When the shortest clock nears the action point you set in advance,
  go to → 01-02. **Set it early so you act while you still have fuel, roads, daylight and
  choices.** A decision made at the last dose is made with nothing left to carry it out.
- **The direction to push.** Over time, move supplies from class C to B to A: build
  production, learn substitutes, gain skills (→ 23-04, → 23-05). Some prescription medicines
  can never move. Almost everything else can.
- **What this means for the whole plan.** If your timeline is set by a bought medicine, the
  most valuable preparations are: building that supply through legitimate means while
  pharmacies work (→ 12-07); making the decision early (→ 01-02); and building the community
  and skills that make everything else survivable in the meantime (→ 18-01, → 23-05).

# Master consumables table

**What this page is for.** Every section of this binder works out how long one kind of supply
lasts. This page puts all of them on one sheet so you can see **which clock is shortest**
(→ 23-01). Numbers from your settings are printed. Everything else you fill in with a pencil
and update at the weekly check (→ 21-04). **If you fill in only one thing, fill in the summary
line at the bottom.**

> **SAFETY.** The medicine rows are counts, not plans for stretching doses. **Never skip,
> split or space out a prescribed dose to make it last** without your prescriber's
> instructions; ask now what to do if supply is cut off and write the answer on → 12-07.
> **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded** (floor, → 30-01): freezing breaks
> it with no visible sign. Infant formula is never diluted to make it last (→ 20-05).

## Do this now

1. **Fill in the class C block first**: medicines and anything else nothing can replace. That
   is a today task.
2. **Measure the big four over a few real days**: water (→ 03-01), power (→ 09-01), wood or
   heating fuel (→ 06-04), food (→ 04-01). Measured, not guessed (→ 29-13).
3. **Write your own action point on each block.** The binder does not set them for you.
4. **Put the update on the weekly check** (→ 21-04) and the full review on the yearly calendar
   (→ 25-10). Blank copies: → 25-05.

**Household:** {{ household.size }} people ({{ household.adults }} adults, {{ household.children }}
children){{#if has.pets}}; pets: {{#each pets as p}}{{p.count}} {{p.type}}; {{/each}}{{/if}}.
Date of this update: ____________

## Class C: irreplaceable (the governing clocks)

No production, no substitute, no local resupply. **This block drives the leave-or-stay
decision** (→ 01-02).

| Item | Who | Days on hand (settings) | Recounted today | Date checked | Our action point | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as m}}| **{{m.name}}** {{m.strength}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}} (refrigerated: {{m.refrigerated}}){{/if}} | {{m.member}} | {{m.days_on_hand}} | ______ | ______ | ______ | → 12-07 |

| Epinephrine auto-injectors (the clock is the **expiry date**, not use) | ______ | expires: ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | → 02-03 |
| Other emergency medicines kept for a reaction (glucagon and similar): expiry, not use | ______ | expires: ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | → 02-01 |
| Infant formula{{#if has.infant}} (a baby is in the household){{/if}} | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ | → 20-05 |

How to fill a medicine row: count what is in the house (unopened plus open), divide by the
amount used per day **as prescribed**, and write the date. Insulin storage limits without a
fridge are on → 02-01 and → 29-07 (FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching
Between Products in an Emergency).

> **The shortest number in this block is the household's timeline.** When it reaches your
> action point, go to → 01-02. When to leave: {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20

## Water

| Item | On hand | Daily use | Days | Notes | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stored drinking water | {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gal | floor {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gal/day; plan {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal/day | about {{ derived.water.stored_days }} days at the floor | The floor is at least 1 gallon per person per day, more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply); how your figure is built is on → 03-01. Two weeks at the planning figure: {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal | → 03-01, → 03-02 |
| Filter life left, tablets, bleach | ______ | — | — | Spare filter cartridges? Bleach loses strength in storage (→ 29-05) | → 03-04, → 03-09 |
| Rain and snow catchment | ______ | — | — | Seasonal (→ 03-05, → 03-06) | → 03-05 |
{{#if has.pool}}| Pool or hot tub (not drinking water as it stands) | {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gal | — | — | Drinking it is a household choice: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14 | → 03-03 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}| Water-heater tank | {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal | — | — | Drain from the bottom valve with the power or gas off (→ 03-02) | → 03-02 |
{{/if}}

**Our action point:** stored water below ______ days → harvest-and-treat mode (catchment out,
treatment running, → 03-05, → 03-04).

Use goes up with illness (→ 12-05), summer heat (→ 11-08), laundry (→ 13-04) and the garden
(→ 05-10).

## Food

| Item | On hand | Daily use | Days | Notes | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total stored calories | ______ kcal | {{ derived.calories.day }} kcal/day | ______ | Days = stored calories ÷ daily need. The daily figure is from the USDA Dietary Guidelines table for your members at a moderately active level; hard physical work in cold weather needs more. Two weeks: {{ derived.calories.two_weeks }} kcal. Your estimate in settings: {{ gear.food.pantry_days }} days | → 04-01 |
| Freeze-dried food | {{ gear.food.freeze_dried_servings }} servings | ______ | ______ | Add its calories to the line above. Needs hot water, little fuel (→ 04-19) | → 04-19 |
{{#if has.food_allergy}}| **Allergy-safe food, counted separately** | ______ | ______ | ______ | A narrower supply than the pantry; it runs out first (→ 02-04) | → 02-04 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.infant}}| Baby and toddler food | ______ | ______ | ______ | → 20-01 | → 20-05 |
{{/if}}| Fats and oils | ______ | ______ | ______ | Also soap and lamp fuel (→ 13-09, → 10-04) | → 04-12 |
| Salt | ______ | ______ | ______ | Preserving and trade | → 04-13 |
| Cooking fuel (propane, white gas, butane) | ______ | ______ | ______ | Count only the share set aside for cooking if the same fuel also heats or runs the generator | → 07-05, → 06-05 |
{{#each pets as p}}| Pet food: {{p.count}} {{p.type}} | ______ | {{p.food_per_day}} | ______ | | → 20-09 |
{{/each}}

**Our action point:** stored food below ______ days → → 04-18 (meal planning in scarcity).

## Heat and fuel

| Item | On hand | Daily use | Days | Notes | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Firewood | {{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords | ______ | ______ | Work it out for a cold week, not an average one (MU Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating) | → 06-04 |
| Propane, 20-lb cylinders | {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} | ______ | ______ | Propane does not go stale. If the same cylinders heat, cook and run the generator, split them on paper (→ 06-05) and track each share | → 06-05, → 06-06 |
| Propane, 1-lb cylinders | {{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }} | ______ | ______ | | → 07-05 |
| Kerosene (K-1) | {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal | heater's gal per hour × hours run | ______ | The burn rate is on the heater's label or manual. Jar-test before filling (→ 30-18) | → 08-10, → 06-06 |
| Diesel | {{ gear.fuel.diesel_gal }} gal | ______ | ______ | | → 06-06 |
| Gasoline | {{ gear.fuel.gasoline_gal }} gal | ______ | ______ | Shared between generator and vehicles: every gallon burned at home is range lost on the road (→ 01-03). Untreated gasoline keeps for months, not years (→ 23-04) | → 09-04, → 06-06 |
| Generator fuel{{#if has.generator}} ({{ gear.generator_fuel }}){{/if}} | see above | measure gal per hour on first run | ______ | | → 09-04 |
| Lamp oil and candles | ______ | ______ | ______ | Count in hours of light | → 10-02 |

Old fuel: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18

**Our action points:** heater fuel below ______ → heat only in waking hours, layers carry the
rest; below ______ → step down the heat chain (→ 23-03) and do the heat check on → 01-02.
Heater fuel below ______ before winter → buy now.

## Power

| Item | Capacity | Daily use | Days | Notes | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Power stations | {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh | ______ Wh | ______ | A full-size fridge alone: about {{ derived.station_fridge_days }} days with no sun (an estimate; the battery's own percentage screen is the truth) | → 09-03 |
| Medicine fridge or cooler on battery | ______ Wh/day (measure) | — | ______ | Days = station Wh ÷ measured Wh per day, less if anything else is plugged in | → 09-10 |
| Power banks | ______ Wh each × ______ | — | ______ | | → 09-06 |
| AA and AAA cells (rechargeable / alkaline) | ______ / ______ | ______ per night | ______ | | → 09-07, → 10-06 |
| Solar | {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W | — | — | Rough clear-day harvest: about {{ derived.solar_wh_dec }} Wh in December, {{ derived.solar_wh_jun }} Wh in June (estimates). Overcast days give far less; snow-covered panels give none. **Size on December** | → 09-05 |

**Our action point:** cells below ______ → count, charge and restage the rotation (→ 10-06).

## Medical and sanitation

| Item | On hand | Use rate | Days | Notes | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Oral rehydration salts** | ______ | ______ | ______ | Count in litres and sick-days | → 12-05 |
| Gauze and dressings | ______ | ______ | ______ | Count in dressing changes | → 12-02 |
| Over-the-counter medicines | ______ | ______ | ______ | Check expiry dates | → 12-07, → 12-13 |
| **Soap** | ______ | ______ | ______ | The most valuable medical supply | → 13-02, → 13-09 |
| Bleach | ______ | ______ | ______ | Loses strength in storage (→ 29-05) | → 13-11 |
| Toilet paper and cover material | ______ | ______ | ______ | Measure a real week | → 13-01 |
| Waste bags | ______ | ______ | ______ | | → 13-01, → 13-03 |
| Diapers{{#if has.infant}} (a baby is in the household){{/if}} | ______ | count a real day | ______ | The child also outgrows the size | → 13-08 |
{{#if has.cats}}| Cat litter | ______ | ______ | ______ | Never compost it; bag it like human waste. Dirt, sand or ash substitute | → 13-03 |
{{/if}}| Menstrual supplies | ______ | ______ | ______ | Reusables end this line | → 13-08 |

**Our action point:** diapers below ______ days → start the cloth transition (→ 13-08); do
not wait for the last pack.

## Tools and materials

| Item | On hand | Notes | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Saw blades, chainsaw chains** | ______ | The firewood bottleneck | → 16-06, → 16-02 |
| Files and sharpening stones | ______ | Hard to improvise | → 16-02 |
| Hacksaw blades, drill bits | ______ | Hard to improvise | → 16-08 |
| **Thread and needles** | ______ | Cannot be made at home; stock far more than seems sensible | → 16-04 |
| Screws, nails, wire, tape | ______ | Plentiful to salvage | → 16-07, → 16-05 |
| Glues | ______ | Expire; rotate | → 16-05 |
| Radio cable and connectors | ______ | Fail without visible signs | → 15-06 |
| Bicycle tubes and tires | ______ | | → 16-09 |
| Heater wicks and fuel filters | ______ | A worn wick burns smoky and makes more carbon monoxide; replace, never turn down | → 08-10, → 08-09 |
| Igniter batteries for heaters and stoves | ______ | | → 28-04 |
| **CO and smoke alarm batteries** | ______ | For {{ gear.co_alarms }} CO and {{ gear.smoke_alarms }} smoke alarms. Replace at the chirp and by the date on the unit; test before any fuel-burning heater is lit (→ 08-02) | → 08-02 |
| Fire extinguishers | {{ gear.extinguishers }} | Check the gauge (→ 29-12) | → 29-12 |
| Seeds | ______ | Germination falls each year | → 05-03 |
| Potting mix, fertiliser | ______ | Slow to scavenge | → 05-10, → 05-11 |

## The summary line: fill this in every week

| | Value | Date |
|---|---|---|
| **Shortest class C clock (days)** | ______ | ______ |
| **What it is** | ______ | ______ |
| **Our action point** (→ 01-02) | ______ | ______ |
| **Shortest non-medical clock (days)** | ______ | ______ |
| **Did anything cross an action point this week?** | ______ | ______ |

## How to use it

- **Pencil.** It changes all the time.
- **Update at the weekly check** (→ 21-04): about fifteen minutes with every adult.
- **Measure the big ones over real days** (→ 23-01) and work them out for the hard case: a
  cold week, a hot week, a sick week.
- **Every block has an action point line.** Write your own and change it whenever you have a
  better number.

What the table is for:
1. Seeing which clock is shortest. In most households with a daily prescription, it is a
   medicine.
2. Making the leave-or-stay decision on numbers rather than feelings (→ 01-02).
3. Knowing what to buy next (→ 22-07): whatever has the shortest runway for how much it
   matters.
4. Knowing what to ration, and when (→ 23-01).
5. Catching a problem while it can still be fixed.

**What most households find when they fill it in honestly:** the medical clock is far shorter
than everything else and cannot be stretched by effort, only by supply (→ 12-07) and by acting
early (→ 01-02). And the renewable lines (water, wood, food) look worse on paper than they
are, because a runway leaves out what you can produce (→ 23-04).

## When it runs out

- **This table is the tool for that question.** When the summary line crosses an action
  point, go to → 01-02 and carry out the decision you already wrote down.
- **Failure one:** filling it in once, feeling prepared, and never updating it. The weekly
  check is the fix.
- **Failure two:** filling it in with hopeful numbers. Measure.
- **The reassurance:** most lines are class A or B (→ 23-01), renewable or substitutable. The
  table looks alarming, and most of it is not. The class C block is the real content, and it
  is short enough to check in two minutes.

# Substitution catalog: what replaces what

**What this page is for.** A one-page index of "when this runs out, use that", each line
pointing to the page that explains it properly. **Read the linked page before acting on any
line.** Most substitutes carry safety limits that do not fit in a table cell. The catalog opens
with the most important rows: the ones where the answer is **nothing**.

> **Caution.** Several substitutes involve fuel, flame or chlorine. The floors apply to every
> line (→ 30-01): **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or
> near an open window.** **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a
> running appliance.** **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other
> cleaners.**

## The rows where there is no substitute

Knowing these matters more than any clever improvisation.

| Need | Substitute | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| **Insulin** | **None** | Supply and runway (→ 02-01, → 12-07). Syringes can replace a pump or pen as a way of *giving* insulin (→ 02-02), but nothing replaces the drug. The leave-or-stay decision is the plan (→ 01-02) |
| **Epinephrine for anaphylaxis** | **None.** Antihistamines are not a substitute | Supply and expiry (→ 02-03); avoiding the trigger is the strategy (→ 02-04) |
| **Other daily prescription medicines** (seizure, heart, thyroid, transplant, steroid replacement and others) | **None you can make or improvise** | Build the supply while pharmacies work (→ 12-07); the condition pages (→ 12-11) |
| **Infant formula** | **None. Never dilute it, never make it at home** | Clinician, community, public health (→ 20-05, → 02-13) |
| **A skilled attendant at a difficult birth** | None | Be near care (→ 02-12, → 01-05) |
| **Surgery, imaging, blood transfusion** | None | Know the limit (→ 12-16) |
| **A working smoke or carbon monoxide alarm** | None | Keep spares and batteries; test before any fuel-burning heater is lit (→ 08-02, → 29-12) |
| **Safe water for an infant** | None | Treat it properly (→ 03-04, → 20-05) |

## Water

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| Tap water | Stored → rain or snow → pool or hot tub (distilled) → surface water, treated | → 03-02, → 03-05, → 03-03, → 03-04 |
| The well pump (no power) | A bailer down the casing; a hand pump fitted alongside the electric pump | → 03-10 |
| A filter | **Boiling** (kills germs; does not remove chemicals) or chlorine disinfection by the EPA method | → 03-04 |
| Household bleach (used up or too old) | **Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), only by the two-step method:** granules into a stock solution first, then 1 part stock to 100 parts water (EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water). **Never granules straight into drinking water** | → 03-04, → 29-05 |
| Hot running water for washing | A tippy-tap; a jug with a nail hole; basin washing (CDC, handwashing) | → 13-02 |
| Water for flushing | Greywater, non-drinking water, snowmelt | → 13-03, → 13-01 |
| A dishwasher | Three-tub washing | → 13-10 |

## Heat and cooking

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| The furnace | **The heat chain below, in order** | → 08-04 |
| Kerosene for a wick heater (used up) | **Nothing else. Gasoline is never put in a kerosene heater**: it causes a fire or explosion. Step down the chain instead | → 08-10, → 06-06 |
| Propane for a propane heater or camp stove (used up) | **Nothing else.** Kerosene and lamp oil are never propane-appliance fuels. Step down the chain; cook outdoors on wood | → 08-09, → 07-01 |
| Firewood | Storm debris, standing dead wood, untreated scrap lumber, compressed logs. **Never painted or pressure-treated wood** | → 06-04, → 06-05 |
| An open cooking fire | **A rocket stove: a fraction of the wood** | → 07-02 |
| The kitchen stove | Outdoor fire, Dutch oven, solar cooker, camp stove (outdoors) | → 07-01, → 07-04, → 07-03, → 07-05 |
| The refrigerator | **Winter: outdoor cold, free.** Summer: cellar, evaporative cooling, 12-volt cooler | → 04-09, → 09-10 |
| A bed warmer | A hot water bottle; a wrapped warm stone | → 21-07 |

**The winter heat chain: step down only when the step above is gone.**

| Step | Use | Its limits | Ref |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The furnace, run in short bursts** on a generator or power station{{#if has.gas_any}}, if your gas or propane still flows{{/if}} | Only through a transfer switch or interlock, or a furnace already given its own plug. **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide") cord.** Who does a plug conversion: {{choice DC-07}} → 30-08 | → 08-04, → 09-04 |
| 2 | **One warm room**: blankets, layers, shared body heat, low-watt heated blankets on a power station | Uses no fuel. Infants follow safe-sleep rules: no electric blanket on or around an infant (→ 20-01) | → 08-01, → 08-06, → 11-02 |
| 3 | **Wood stove or fireplace**{{#if has.wood_stove}} (you have one){{/if}} | Only if inspected and the chimney is clear (→ 06-09, → 08-08) | → 08-08 |
| 4 | **An unvented fuel heater** (kerosene wick or indoor-rated propane){{#if has.unvented_heater}} (you have one){{/if}} | Carbon monoxide alarm working first; fresh air openings as the manual says; fill outdoors with the heater off and cool; correct fuel only; never two heaters in one room. Running one while people sleep is a household choice: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb indoors: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03 | → 08-10, → 08-09, → 08-02 |
| 5 | **A vehicle as a warming refuge** | **Outdoors, never in a garage.** Clear snow from the exhaust pipe; run the engine about 10 minutes each hour, with a window open a little while it runs (National Weather Service, Winter Weather Safety); never leave a child alone in it; hours, not nights | → 08-06 |
| 6 | **Leave** | When the warm room keeps cooling and no heat is coming back. Your trigger: {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20 | → 01-02, → 08-01 |

Open flame or candles indoors: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21

## Light

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| House lighting | LED lights, rechargeable cells, solar | → 10-01, → 09-02 |
| Batteries | **Daylight and an earlier day**: the biggest saving | → 10-03 |
| A lantern | A headlamp strapped to a translucent jug of water | → 10-03 |
| Shop candles | Fat lamps; remelted wax | → 10-04 |
| Reflectors | Foil, white walls, a white ceiling | → 10-03 |

## Power

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| The grid | Solar and battery; a generator in short runs, outdoors | → 09-02, → 09-04 |
| An inverter (the box that turns battery power into household power) | **Run 12-volt devices straight from the battery**: no conversion loss (→ 29-02) | → 09-08 |
| A generator | A vehicle's alternator, engine running **outdoors only** | → 09-11 |
| Lithium batteries | Salvaged lead-acid batteries, in quantity | → 09-03, → 09-14 |
| Electric space heat | **Not a 1,500-watt space heater**: that is about 36 kWh a day if left on, more than most home battery banks hold. Low-watt, targeted loads only (heated blankets, a furnace blower in bursts) | → 08-04, → 09-01 |

## Food

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| The grocery store | Stores → garden → foraging → hunting, fishing and trapping | → 04-01, → 05-01 |
| Cooking fuel for stored food | Ready-to-eat food and freeze-dried food (needs only hot water) | → 04-19 |
| A freezer for preserving | Canning, drying, curing, fermenting, cold storage | → 04-04 to → 04-09 |
| Shop yeast | Sourdough starter | → 04-18 |
| Cooking oil | Rendered animal fat | → 04-12, → 05-16 |
| Fresh vegetables in winter | Sprouts and microgreens indoors | → 05-14, → 04-16 |
| Shop fertiliser | Compost, manure, diluted urine, wood ash, crushed shell | → 05-11 |

Low-acid food: **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not
canned** (floor, → 30-01). Wild plants: **No wild plant or mushroom is eaten on a "test";
identification or nothing.**

## Medical

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| Sterile gauze | Boiled clean cotton cloth; sanitary pads | → 12-02 |
| Antibiotic ointment | **Cleaning and flushing the wound**; honey (**never for a child under 1 year**; CDC, Botulism Prevention) | → 12-02, → 12-04 |
| Sterile saline | Clean drinking water, squirted with pressure | → 12-02 |
| A splint | Cardboard, rolled magazines, sticks, a foam pad, always padded | → 12-09 |
| Crutches | A padded forked branch; a rake handle | → 12-09 |
| Cold packs | Snow, ice, cold water | → 12-09 |
| Shop oral rehydration salts | **The WHO recipe, measured exactly** | → 12-05 |
| A tourniquet | **Buy real ones.** Improvised ones often fail | → 12-02 |
| Antiseptic | Soap and plenty of water | → 12-02, → 13-02 |

## Sanitation

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| A flushing toilet | Pour-flush if the sewer still drains; otherwise a bucket with cover material | → 13-01 |
| Cover material | Sawdust, leaves, ash, soil, shredded paper | → 13-01 |
| Shop soap | Lye from wood ash and rendered fat | → 13-09 |
| Toilet paper | A bidet bottle; washed cloth; newspaper | → 13-01 |
| Disposable diapers | Cloth from flannel, towels, sheets | → 13-08 |
| Menstrual products | A menstrual cup (lasts years); cloth pads | → 13-08 |
| A washing machine | A plunger, two tubs and a wringer | → 13-04 |
| A dryer | Line-drying outdoors (it works even below freezing); a high line in the warm room | → 11-03 |

## Clothing and shelter

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| New clothing | Repair, patch, darn, cut down adult clothing | → 11-07, → 16-04 |
| Insulation | Wool (stays warm damp), newspaper between layers, comforters | → 11-05 |
| A rain shell | A tarp, a trash bag (cut breathing and face holes; never on a small child's head), waxed canvas | → 11-05 |
| Outgrown children's gear | Cut-down adult clothing; trade with other families | → 11-02, → 18-02 |
| Boot liners | Felted wool, layered socks, sheepskin | → 11-06 |
| Ice traction devices | Short screws in the soles; wire wrapped round the boot | → 11-06 |

## Tools and repair

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| Power tools | **Hand tools: own one for everything you depend on** | → 16-01 |
| A chainsaw | Bow saw, crosscut saw, axe, maul | → 16-06 |
| Sharpening stones | A flat river stone; the unglazed ring under a ceramic mug; wet sandpaper on glass | → 16-02 |
| Glue | Wire and screws (often stronger anyway); pine pitch; hide glue | → 16-05 |
| Hardware | Lashings and wooden pegs | → 16-03, → 16-07 |
| Thread | Inner strands of paracord; dental floss; unravelled fabric | → 16-04, → 16-03 |
| An anvil | A rail tie plate; a heavy steel plate; a sledgehammer head | → 16-08 |
| A tool handle | Shaped hardwood; a straight-grained branch | → 16-08 |

## Communications

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| Cell phone | Short-range family radios → amateur (ham) radio → notes at agreed meeting points → walking over | → 15-02, → 15-05, → 15-03 |
| Shop-bought antennas | A wire antenna in a tree works well (→ 29-09) | → 15-06 |
| Internet news | NOAA Weather Radio → AM radio at night → shortwave → ham → your own eyes | → 15-01, → 15-04 |
| Any radio | Whistles, mirrors, lights, signals agreed in advance | → 15-07 |

## Transport and money

| Instead of | Use | Ref |
|---|---|---|
| A vehicle | Bicycle and trailer; a sled in snow; walking | → 16-09 |
| Fuel | Human power; shorter trips. Fuel travels sealed, upright and outside the passenger space where possible. Carrying it inside the vehicle is a household choice: {{choice DC-06}} → 30-07 | → 16-09, → 06-08 |
| Cards | Cash in small bills | → 19-02 |
| Cash | Goods → skills → neighbours helping neighbours | → 18-02, → 18-03, → 18-01 |
| Services that no longer exist | Skills: yours and your neighbours' | → 23-05, → 18-01 |

## How to read the catalog

- **Every line points to a page.** Go there before acting; the limits are on the page.
- **Most substitutes are worse than the original**: slower, harder, less output. That is
  expected. The point is that the job still gets done.
- **Some substitutes are better.** Outdoor winter cold beats a refrigerator and costs nothing;
  a wire antenna can beat a shop one; a mechanical repair outlasts a glued one.
- **The top block matters most.** Knowing what has no substitute keeps the rest of the plan
  honest.

### The pattern across the catalog

- **Water, heat, food, light and sanitation have deep chains.** These are class A problems
  (→ 23-01): solvable with work, materials and knowledge.
- **Tools, repair and clothing substitute easily**, because a town is full of materials
  (→ 22-02).
- **Communications and transport step down gracefully** to low-tech options that work.
- **Medical substitutes exist for supplies but not for skill or equipment**: cloth for gauze,
  yes; surgery, no (→ 12-16).
- **The top block substitutes for nothing.**

## When it runs out

- **When a substitute runs out, go one step further down its chain.** Most have three or four
  steps.
- **When a chain ends, the answer is either a skill (→ 23-05) or a decision (→ 01-02).**
- **Push upward over time**: from "substituted" to "produced" (→ 23-04). Soap made, wood grown,
  food raised.
- **The honest close.** For the items at the top of this page there is no chain. Everything
  else in the catalog buys time and ability, so the household can act on that one problem early,
  deliberately, and with resources still in hand.
