pages.body:
# Running a blackout weekend

**What this page is for.** The most valuable exercise in this binder. Forty-eight hours with the
main breaker off finds more real gaps than a lot of money spent on gear or a year of reading,
and it finds them while the fix is a trip to the hardware store. This page gives four levels,
from one evening to a winter weekend, the safety limits, a schedule, and the measurements that
make the rest of the binder's numbers real.

> **Caution: the exercise has hard limits.** Three things are **never** part of the test:
> **medical devices stay powered**, **medicines that need cold stay cold**, and **the ability
> to call 911 or end the exercise at once stays available.** Everything else can go dark.
> **A working, tested battery carbon monoxide alarm is required.** **Never run a generator,
> charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.**

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}> **Medicine first, breakers second.** Your household has refrigerated medicine
> ({{#each refrigerated_meds as r}}{{r.name}} for {{r.member}}; {{/each}}). Before any breaker goes
> off, do **one** of these: **(a)** leave the fridge's circuit on (find and label that breaker
> now), or **(b)** set up the real outage method first: the medicine cooler running on battery,
> a thermometer inside showing the label's temperature range, and only then move the medicine
> (→ 09-10, → 12-21, → 29-07). Medicine left in a dark fridge for 48 hours may be pushed onto its
> label's room-temperature time limit (FDA, Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching
> Between Products in an Emergency). **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.**
{{/if}}

{{photo breaker-labels}}

## Do this now

1. **Pick a date and put it on the calendar**: spring and autumn (→ 24-03). A date on a calendar
   is the only version of this that ever happens.
2. **Tell the household a week ahead**{{#if has.child}}, children included, and **call it an
   adventure** (→ 20-08){{/if}}. Announced, not sprung.
3. **Do the first one in mild weather.** Winter versions come later and teach the most.
4. **Print the debrief worksheet below** (or keep it open) for the whole weekend.

## What you are actually testing

Not "can we survive". You can; it is 48 hours. You are testing **whether this binder's plan
fits the house you actually live in**:
1. **Do the systems work?** Not in theory: the actual filter, stove, panel, bucket toilet.
2. **What do we reach for that is not there?** This list is always longer than you expect, and
   it is the main result of the weekend.
3. **How much do we really use?** Water per person per day, fuel per meal, battery per evening.
   **These numbers make → 23-02 real**; everything before them is a guess.
4. {{#if has.child}}**How do the children cope?** A young child's tolerance for dark and boredom is a real planning
   number (→ 20-08, → 21-04).{{else}}**How do the adults cope** with dark, cold and boredom (→ 21-02)?{{/if}}
5. **What breaks first, the equipment or the mood?** Usually the mood, which is why Section 21
   is in this binder.

## The safety limits: read these twice

| Never part of the test | Why |
|---|---|
| **Medical device power**{{#if has.cpap}} (CPAP){{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}} (oxygen){{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-02}} (pump, sensor, phone){{/if}} | You may **measure** the battery drain, but the devices stay powered. Do not test them by doing without (→ 09-10) |
| **Medicines that need cold** | Correctly stored the whole time (FDA): fridge circuit left on, or the battery cooler running and checked before the main goes off |
| **Epinephrine**{{#if !has.epinephrine}} (if anyone carries it){{/if}} | In place, in date, findable, always |
| **The phone and 911** | One charged phone stays available all the time |
| **Ending the exercise** | Anyone can call it off, for any reason, without argument. Especially a child |

| Absolute rules |
|---|
| **Battery carbon monoxide alarms, tested**: one where people sleep and one on every level ({{ gear.co_alarms }} in settings), installed and tested **before** any fuel-burning heater is lit (→ 08-02) |
| **Indoor heat only from an appliance rated for indoor use**, run exactly by its manual and its page (→ 08-10, → 08-09, → 08-08), with the alarm up first and the fresh-air openings the manual gives. Never two fuel heaters in one room. **Never indoors, under any circumstances:** camp stove, grill, generator, charcoal |
| **Overnight heat** is a household decision: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb indoors: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03. **Anyone waking with a headache or feeling sick = everyone out**, then call (→ 29-03) |
| **Candles and open flame indoors:** {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21. Battery lights are safer (→ 10-01) |
| **Generators outdoors only**, at least 20 feet from windows and doors, never in a garage (CDC; → 09-04) |
| **Cooking happens outdoors** (fire, rocket stove, camp stove) or on an appliance made for indoor use (→ 07-01) |
| **Do not let the pipes freeze.** In cold weather keep the house above freezing, or shut off and drain the water (→ 17-01, → 08-03) |
| **Food safety is real, not simulated:** a closed fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours; a full closed freezer about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24 (FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During a Power Outage; → 04-17) |
| **Do not drive anywhere for supplies.** If you must, the exercise is over: write down why |

## Level 1: an evening blackout (start here)

**Four to six hours, one evening.** Switch off every breaker except any circuit that must stay
on (above). Cook, light the house, do dishes, do bedtime. **Turn the power back on before bed the
first time.**
*What it usually finds:* flashlights with dead batteries, matches nobody can find, an electric
can opener, bedtime in the dark harder than expected{{#if has.young_child}}, and a small child who
thinks it is the best night of the year{{/if}}.

## Level 2: a 24-hour blackout

**Friday evening to Saturday evening.** One full night and three meals.
*What it usually finds:* charging is the bottleneck, water is heavier than you think, cooking
takes far longer, and nobody planned lunch.

## Level 3: a full weekend, water off too

**48 hours, breakers off, main water valve off.** This is the real exercise.
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}Level 3 is the right weekend to do the medicine-cooler option (b) for real.{{/if}}
*What it usually finds:* your real water use (almost always higher than the planning figure of
{{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal a day), that washing dishes and laundry by hand is a job
(→ 13-04), that the bucket toilet works but the cover material runs out, and that the shortest
runway in the house is not the one you assumed.

## Level 4: a winter weekend

**Only after levels 1 to 3 have gone well, and with a plan for stopping.** One room heated,
everything else cold. {{#if has.gas_any}}With the breakers off, most gas furnaces do not run: their fan and controls need
power.{{/if}} "One room heated" means the warm-room plan on → 08-01, with your heat source
run exactly by its page. **Watch the pipes, watch the CO alarm, watch the
{{#if has.child}}children{{else}}people{{/if}}.** Drill 8's practice lights (→ 24-02) get their first
overnight here.
*What it usually finds:* how much fuel a night really costs (→ 23-02){{#if has.child}}, that keeping
children warm is a full-time job (→ 11-02){{/if}}, that batteries die fast in cold (→ 09-05), and
that the one-room plan needs adjusting to your actual house.{{#if !is.cold_winters}} Where winters are
mild, run Level 4 in your hottest week instead: no air conditioning, and watch for heat illness
(→ 11-08, → 17-04).{{/if}}

## The schedule for a level 3 weekend

| When | Do |
|---|---|
| **The week before** | Tell everyone. Fill water containers. **Install and test the CO alarms** (→ 08-02). Lay out the gear. Plan meals. Charge the medical power banks and every power station to full. **Find and label every breaker**, especially any that stays on |
| **Friday, 5 p.m.** | {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Medicine step first:** fridge breaker confirmed on and labelled, or the cooler running, thermometer reading in range, medicine moved. **Do not touch the panel until this is done.**{{else}}Medical devices on battery and charged; phones charged.{{/if}} |
| **Friday, 6 p.m.** | **Breakers off** (except any circuit you decided stays on). **Water main off.** Write down the time and the meter readings if you can |
| **Friday evening** | Cook dinner off-grid. Light the house. Bedtime by lamplight. **Log everything used** |
| **Saturday morning** | Breakfast. A water-treatment run (EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water). Bucket toilet in service. {{#if has.child}}Children's jobs given out (→ 20-07){{else}}Jobs shared out{{/if}} |
| **Saturday midday** | A normal day: {{#if has.child}}schoolwork (→ 20-03), {{/if}}chores, laundry by hand, a walk. **Measure the solar output**{{#if !has.solar}} if you have panels{{/if}} |
| **Saturday afternoon** | Practise one skill from → 24-01: fire in bad conditions, sharpening, sewing |
| **Saturday evening** | Cook, eat, and **make the evening good**: a game, a story, something that turns it into a good memory (→ 21-06) |
| **Sunday morning** | Breakfast. **Read the numbers**: water, fuel, battery used |
| **Sunday midday** | **Debrief while it is fresh.** Fill in the worksheet. Restore power and water |
| **Sunday afternoon** | **Fix the top three findings the same day**, while they are vivid |

## The measurements: the real result

Write these down; they replace guesses on → 23-02 with facts.

```
WATER used, total: ______ gal  ÷ {{ household.size }} people ÷ 2 days = ______ gal/person/day
   (compare with the planning figure on 03-01: ______)
FUEL or WOOD burned: ______   meals cooked: ______   per meal: ______
BATTERY / SOLAR: started ____ %  ended ____ %   solar produced: ______ Wh
MEDICAL device battery drain: ______ % over ____ hours → projected runtime: ______ h
LIGHT: hours of lamp use ______   fuel or battery used ______
FOOD: meals cooked ____   eaten versus planned: ______
TIME: hours spent on water, cooking, heating, sanitation: ______  <- the real finding
```

**The last line is the one nobody expects.** Living without the grid is a full-time job before
anything productive happens, and knowing your number changes how you plan phase C.

## The debrief worksheet

```
DATE: __________  LEVEL: ____  WEATHER: ______________  LENGTH: ______

THINGS THAT DID NOT WORK
1. ______________________________  fix: ______________________
2. ______________________________  fix: ______________________
3. ______________________________  fix: ______________________

THINGS WE REACHED FOR AND DID NOT HAVE
1. ______________  2. ______________  3. ______________  4. ______________

WHAT SURPRISED US
______________________________________________________________________

HARDEST PART (be honest: it is usually not the gear)
______________________________________________________________________

CHILDREN'S EXPERIENCE (what worked / what to change)
______________________________________________________________________

BINDER PAGES TO UPDATE
______  ______  ______  ______

BUY THIS WEEK (add to 22-07)
1. ______________  2. ______________  3. ______________

NEXT BLACKOUT WEEKEND: __________  LEVEL: ____
```

## Making it good for {{#if has.child}}the children{{else}}everyone{{/if}}

{{#if has.child}}The exercise **fails** if the children come out of it frightened, and it **succeeds beyond its
purpose** if they come out thinking blackouts are fun.
- **Call it camping.** It is.
- **Give each child a real job**: carrying the lamp, counting the water jugs{{#if has.pets}}, feeding the pets{{/if}} (→ 20-07).
- **Keep bedtimes and mealtimes normal.** Routine keeps children steady (→ 21-04, → 20-03).
- **Plan one deliberately great thing**: a fire, a Dutch-oven dessert, shadow puppets, everyone
  sleeping in one room (→ 21-06).
{{#if has.infant}}- **Babies just need warmth, feeding, sleep and clean diapers on the usual schedule.** If any of
  that is at risk, end the exercise. That is not a failure; it is the finding (→ 20-01).
{{/if}}- **In a winter weekend, watch the children for cold all the time** (→ 11-02, → 08-05).
{{else}}- **Plan one deliberately good thing** each evening: a fire, a good meal, a game (→ 21-06).
- **Keep normal mealtimes and bedtimes** (→ 21-04).
{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}- **Older adults** feel cold and heat sooner and may hide it. Check on them on a schedule, and
  end the exercise if they are struggling (→ 02-21, → 08-05).
{{/if}}

## The most common findings (you will probably hit these)

1. **Charging is the bottleneck**, not lighting.
2. **Water is heavy**, and moving it is most of the work.
3. **Cooking takes about three times longer** and uses more fuel than expected.
4. **Nobody planned lunch.** Or the dishes. Or where the wash water goes.
5. **The bucket toilet works; the cover material runs out.**
6. **Sleep gets worse**, and everything is harder because of it (→ 21-07).
7. **The evenings are long.** Boredom, not danger, is the mood problem (→ 21-02).
8. **The house is colder or hotter than you assumed** without heating or cooling.

## What you need

Nothing new: **that is the point.** Use exactly what you own. The list of things to buy is a
**result** of the weekend, and it goes on → 22-07. Two things worth having first: **battery CO
alarms, installed**, and **a way to measure** (a bucket marked in gallons, a kitchen scale, a
battery monitor or a cheap plug-in watt meter, a fridge thermometer).

No money? Improvise during the weekend and **write down what you improvised**. That is the most
valuable page of notes you will make all year, and it feeds → 23-03.

## When it runs out

The exercise ends after 48 hours by design. What runs out is **how long the findings stay
true**:
- **Runway:** about a year. {{#if has.child}}Children grow, {{/if}}gear changes, the house changes.
- **Ration:** if a full weekend is impossible, **do a level 1 evening.** About a quarter of the
  value for a small part of the effort, and far better than nothing.
- **Resupply:** twice a year (→ 24-03).
- **Substitute:** none. Every other page in this binder is theory until this weekend tests it.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** this rehearses the most likely emergency: a multi-day outage at home
  {{#if is.cold_winters}}in winter {{/if}}is not a hypothetical in {{ home.state_name }}.
- **B, moving:** add a travel version: do the grab (→ 22-03), load the vehicle, drive an hour of
  the route, and camp out of the vehicle overnight (→ 22-05, → 01-03).
- **C, establishing:** a blackout weekend is a **preview of ordinary life** somewhere rural. If 48
  hours is miserable, list what would make it bearable: that list is your phase C build order
  (→ 01-04, → 23-04).

# Reference and appendices

**What this section holds.** 9 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 25-01 **Planting and harvest calendar for your frost dates**: Almost every garden date hangs off two dates: the **last spring frost** and the **first fall frost**.
- → 25-02 **Conversions, water and calorie math**: The tables you will want at 2 a.m.
- → 25-03 **Regional contacts and resources**: The phone numbers and offices you will want when the phone's contact list is dead or the internet is gone, in one place you can print or copy.
- → 25-04 **Maps: local, regional and routes**: Which maps to own, what to mark on them, and how to find your way when the phone is dead.
- → 25-05 **Blank logs and worksheets**: Forms to print (or copy into a notebook) for keeping track of a long event and of ordinary preparation.
- → 25-07 **Glossary: every term in plain words**: If a word in this binder is unfamiliar, it should be here, in plain words, with the page that explains it properly.
- → 25-08 **Quick-reference cards**: Short cards for the minute when you cannot read a whole page.
- → 25-09 **Family medical summary sheet**: This sheet lets **someone who has never met your family keep them alive**: a paramedic, an emergency-room nurse, a neighbour, a relative, a shelter volunteer.
- → 25-10 **Annual review checklist**: A binder that is never reviewed becomes fiction.

pages.body:
# Planting and harvest calendar for your frost dates

**What this page is for.** Almost every garden date hangs off two dates: the **last spring
frost** and the **first fall frost**. A frost is a night cold enough (32 °F or below) to kill
tender plants. This page prints your county's median dates from the region data and then gives
a method that works in any climate: count weeks backwards and forwards from those dates. It
never needs a month-by-month calendar for one place.

## Your numbers

| | Home: {{ home.county }}, {{ home.state_name }} |
|---|---|
| **Last spring frost (median)** | {{ region.home.last_frost }} |
| **First fall frost (median)** | {{ region.home.first_frost }} |
| **Frost-free days (median)** | {{ region.home.growing_days }} |
| **USDA hardiness zone** | {{ region.home.zone }} |
| **July mean high** | {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F |
| **Elevation** | {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft |

{{#if has.destinations}}| Destination | Last frost | First frost | Frost-free days | Zone |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each destinations as d}}| {{d.name}} ({{d.county}}, {{d.state_name}}) | {{d.region.last_frost}} | {{d.region.first_frost}} | {{d.region.growing_days}} | {{d.region.zone}} |
{{/each}}

The destination garden plan is → 05-18.
{{/if}}

**Median means half of years are worse.** A median last frost is the date after which a frost
happens in about half of years, so a late frost after it is normal, and low spots in a yard
frost earlier than the street. Plan to cover tender plants for two or three weeks either side,
and keep your own record (→ 25-05): two years of your own dates beat any published table.

**The hardiness zone is about winter, not summer.** It is the coldest winter night on average,
and it tells you which **perennials** (fruit trees, bushes, asparagus, rhubarb) survive the
winter (USDA, Plant Hardiness Zone Map). It does not tell you when to plant vegetables; the
frost dates do.

## Do this now

1. **Copy the two frost dates onto a wall calendar** and mark the weeks before and after each
   (the timeline below).
2. **Order seed in mid-winter.** Popular open-pollinated varieties sell out, and seed is the
   cheapest, lightest, most time-sensitive purchase in the binder (→ 05-03, → 22-07).
3. **Count backwards from the last frost** to get every indoor sowing date (table below), and
   write them on the calendar.
4. **Start a garden log** (→ 25-05).

## Read your season length first

{{figure fig-planting-timeline}}

| Your season | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Short**: frost-free days not much more than the "days to maturity" of tomatoes or winter squash on their packets | Warm-season crops barely finish. Cool-season crops do well | Start tomatoes, peppers and squash indoors; choose short-season ("days to maturity" well under your frost-free days) varieties; season extension matters most (→ 05-02) |
| **Middle**: room for slow crops with weeks to spare | A full spring-summer-fall garden | Use the tables as written; cool crops in spring and again for fall |
| **Long**: frost comes late or rarely, and summers are hot | Summer heat, not frost, is the limit. Lettuce and peas bolt (go to seed) in heat | Plant cool-season crops in late summer to grow through fall and winter; warm crops in spring; shade cloth and mulch in midsummer |
| **No regular frost** | Frost dates are blank or rare | Plant by season and soil temperature: cool crops in the cool months, warm crops in the warm months; watch for the hottest, driest weeks instead |

{{#if is.hot_summers}}**Your summers are hot** (July mean high {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F): expect the long-season pattern.
Spring cool crops must be in early; plan a second, larger cool-season planting in late summer.
{{/if}}{{#if is.cold_winters}}**Your winters are cold** (January mean low {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F): perennials must be
hardy to your zone, and root crops can stay in the ground under heavy mulch into early winter.
{{/if}}{{#if is.high_altitude}}**You are above 5,000 ft:** nights are colder than the frost dates suggest, sun is strong, and the
season is often shorter than the county median. Use frost cover generously.
{{/if}}

**Check every seed packet's "days to maturity"** against your frost-free days. A crop needing
more days than your season gives must be started indoors or swapped for a faster variety.

## Indoor sowing: count backwards from the last frost

Seedlings started indoors need a sunny window or a grow light, and warmth to sprout
(University of Minnesota Extension, Starting Seeds Indoors).

| Crop | Start indoors | Plant out | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Onions, leeks** | **10 to 12 weeks before** last frost | About 4 weeks **before** last frost | Very cold-tolerant |
| **Celery** | 10 to 12 weeks before | After last frost | Slow |
| **Peppers, eggplant** | **8 to 10 weeks before** | About **2 weeks after** last frost, in warm soil | Dislike cold soil |
| **Tomatoes** | **6 to 8 weeks before** | After last frost | Do not start too early: leggy plants transplant badly |
| **Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower** | 6 to 8 weeks before | 2 to 4 weeks **before** last frost | Hardy |
| **Lettuce, greens** | 4 to 6 weeks before | 3 to 4 weeks before | Or sow directly |
| **Cucumbers, melons, squash** | **3 to 4 weeks only** | After last frost | Dislike transplanting: sow in pots that go into the ground whole |
| **Basil and tender herbs** | 6 to 8 weeks before | After last frost, warm | Frost-tender |

**Harden off everything over one to two weeks** before it goes out: set seedlings outside for a few
hours, then longer each day, so sun and wind do not kill them in an afternoon (University of
Minnesota Extension, Planting the Vegetable Garden; → 05-14).

My dates this year: onions ______ · peppers ______ · tomatoes ______ · brassicas ______ ·
squash ______ · plant out ______.

## Direct sowing, relative to the frost dates

| When | Crops |
|---|---|
| **4 to 6 weeks before last frost** (as soon as the soil can be worked) | Peas, spinach, radish, turnip, mustard |
| **2 to 4 weeks before** | Carrots, beets, chard, lettuce, kale, potatoes, onion sets |
| **At or after last frost** | Beans, corn, squash, cucumber, melon, sunflower |
| **2 weeks after** | Anything that wants truly warm soil |
| **For a fall crop** | Beets, carrots, kale, lettuce, spinach, radish, turnip: count back from the **first fall frost** by the packet's days to maturity, plus a couple of weeks for slower autumn growth |
| **Fall** | **Garlic** (a few weeks before the ground freezes, or in the cool season where it does not) and cover crops |

A soil thermometer is the honest test: it tells you when the ground is ready better than any
date (→ 29-13).

## The year as weeks around your frost dates

| When | Garden work |
|---|---|
| **12 weeks before last frost** | Order seed. Test saved seed for germination. Plan beds and rotation |
| **10 to 12 weeks before** | Start onions and leeks. Prune fruit trees while dormant (→ 05-13). Set up lights |
| **6 to 10 weeks before** | Start peppers, eggplant, brassicas, then tomatoes. Build and repair beds. Turn compost (→ 05-11) |
| **2 to 6 weeks before** | Sow peas, spinach, radish as the soil works. Potatoes and onion sets. Row cover on |
| **Last frost to 2 weeks after** | Harden off, then transplant. Sow beans, corn, squash. **Be ready to cover for a late frost** |
| **Early summer** | Succession-sow lettuce, beans, carrots every 2 to 3 weeks. Mulch heavily. Watch pests (→ 05-12) |
| **Midsummer** | Water deeply. **Sow the fall crops.** Harvest and preserve as things come in (→ 04-04, → 04-06) |
| **Late summer** | Peak harvest and preservation. Save seed from the best plants (→ 05-03) |
| **Around the first frost** | Harvest tender crops ahead of it. **Cover for early frosts**: warm weeks often follow. Plant garlic and cover crops |
| **After the first frost** | Root crops into cold storage (→ 04-09). Clean up, mulch, compost. **Write down what worked** |
| **Winter** | Clean, oil and sharpen tools (→ 16-02). Plan. Check stored crops for spoilage |

## What actually feeds a family

Ranked by calories per square foot, with storage in mind:

| Rank | Crop | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Potatoes** (or **sweet potatoes** in long, hot seasons) | Most calories per square foot; store well (→ 04-09) |
| **2** | **Winter squash** | Dense calories; keeps for months at room temperature |
| **3** | **Dry beans** | Protein, stores dry, no processing |
| **4** | **Corn (flour or flint types)** | Calories and long storage; needs space |
| **5** | **Beets, carrots, turnips, rutabaga** | Store in damp sand, or in the ground under mulch where winters allow |
| **6** | **Onions, garlic** | Keep long; flavour matters for morale |
| **7** | **Cabbage** | Stores, and ferments into sauerkraut (→ 04-08) |
| **8** | **Kale, chard, spinach** | Vitamins and cold tolerance, few calories |
| **9** | Tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers | Vitamins, preserving and morale, **not calories** |

**The honest note:** a good home garden is a **meaningful supplement and a large morale and
vitamin asset.** It will not feed a family for a year. Grain and fat are the gaps (→ 23-04).

## Frost protection: what buys how much

| Method | Buys | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Floating row cover | 2 to 4 °F | Cheap; also keeps insects off |
| Doubled row cover or a low tunnel | 4 to 8 °F | The workhorse |
| Cold frame | Several weeks at each end of the season | → 05-02 |
| Water jugs among the plants | A few degrees overnight | Free |
| Mulch | Protects roots and moisture | Also stops weeds |
| Sheets and blankets, for one night | A few degrees | The emergency answer to a late frost |

## How long the harvest keeps (approximate, in a cold room)

| Crop | Keeps | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| Potatoes | 4 to 6 months | Dark, about 40 °F, humid; **never with apples or onions** |
| Winter squash | 3 to 6 months | Cool and **dry**, about 50 °F |
| Onions, garlic | 4 to 8 months | Cool, dry, airy |
| Carrots, beets, turnips | 4 to 6 months | Cold and damp: sand or damp sawdust |
| Cabbage | 2 to 4 months | Cold and damp |
| Apples | 2 to 5 months | Cold; **away from potatoes** |

Full detail: → 04-09. In warm climates without a cold room, the storage crops are squash, sweet
potatoes, dry beans and grain, and the rest is preserved (→ 04-04 to → 04-08).

## Blanks to fill in (once, then every year)

```
MY LAST SPRING FROST: ____________   EARLIEST I HAVE SEEN: ____________
MY FIRST FALL FROST:  ____________   LATEST I HAVE SEEN:   ____________
FROST-FREE DAYS: ______

LAST YEAR: last frost ________  first frost ________  first hard freeze ________
BEST PERFORMERS: __________________________________________
FAILURES (and why): _______________________________________
CHANGE NEXT YEAR: _________________________________________
```

## Gear

**Buy toward:** **open-pollinated seed** (bought in mid-winter), a soil thermometer, row cover
and hoops, a grow light and heat mat, seed trays and mix, plant labels and a pencil, a garden
notebook.

**If you do not have it:** milk jugs make cloches; old windows make cold frames; bedsheets cover
a frost night; yogurt pots and newspaper pots start seed; a sunny window substitutes, poorly,
for a grow light. **Seed saved from open-pollinated plants is free forever** (→ 05-03).

## When it runs out

Seasons, not supplies.

- **Each planting window is one to three weeks wide. Miss it and you wait a year.**
- **If you can only do part of a garden**, plant **potatoes, squash and beans** (the calorie
  crops) plus greens for vitamins.
- **Save your own seed** (→ 05-03): the only way this calendar keeps working when seed cannot
  be bought.
- Indoor growing and sprouting stretch the season at the edges (→ 05-14, → 04-16), and cold
  storage stretches the harvest into spring (→ 04-09).

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** garden the yard, containers and any balcony (→ 05-01, → 05-10).
  Learn the calendar in your own soil while mistakes are cheap.
- **B (moving):** carry seed. **It weighs nothing and is the most valuable thing you can bring
  to a new place.**
- **C (establish):** this calendar is the year's work, recalculated for the new place's frost
  dates (→ 05-18). Scale up and add grain and storage crops.

Related: → 05-01 the garden · → 05-02 season extension · → 05-03 seed saving · → 05-11 soil ·
→ 04-09 cold storage · → 04-04 and → 04-06 preserving · → 24-03 the practice calendar ·
→ 25-05 the garden log · → 05-13 fruit (plant now, harvest in years).

# Conversions, water and calorie math

**What this page is for.** The tables you will want at 2 a.m. with no phone. Everything here is
arithmetic or a planning estimate. **Where a number carries a safety consequence (how much
bleach to put in water, cooking temperatures, wind chill), this page points to the page that
owns it instead of repeating it.** That is deliberate: a mis-copied bleach amount is a real
hazard. Measuring without tools: → 29-13.

## Do this now

1. **Check this household's own numbers** in the worksheet at the bottom; the binder filled in
   what your settings allow. Write the rest in once, in pencil.
2. **Learn three numbers by heart:** water for this household,
   **{{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day** to plan with (→ 03-01); about
   **{{ derived.calories.day }} calories a day** for the household (→ 04-01); and **8.34 lb per
   gallon of water**.
3. **Do not use this page to dose bleach.** Go to → 03-04.

## Volume

| From | To | Multiply by |
|---|---|---|
| Gallons | Litres | 3.785 |
| Litres | Gallons | 0.264 |
| Gallons | Quarts | 4 |
| Quarts | Cups | 4 |
| Cups | Fluid ounces | 8 |
| Fluid ounces | Millilitres | 29.57 |
| Tablespoons | Teaspoons | 3 |
| Cups | Tablespoons | 16 |
| Cubic feet | Gallons | 7.48 |
| Gallons | Cubic feet | 0.134 |

## Weight

| From | To | Multiply by |
|---|---|---|
| Pounds | Kilograms | 0.454 |
| Kilograms | Pounds | 2.205 |
| Ounces | Grams | 28.35 |
| **Gallons of water** | **Pounds** | **8.34** |
| Cubic foot of water | Pounds | 62.4 |
| A 5-gallon bucket of water | Pounds | about 42, plus the bucket |
| A 55-gallon drum of water | Pounds | about 460: **it will not move once full** |

## Length, area, temperature

| Conversion | Formula |
|---|---|
| Inches to centimetres | × 2.54 |
| Feet to metres | × 0.305 |
| Miles to kilometres | × 1.609 |
| Acres to square feet | × 43,560 |
| **°F to °C** | **(°F − 32) × 5 ÷ 9** |
| **°C to °F** | **(°C × 9 ÷ 5) + 32** |

**Reference points:** 32 °F = 0 °C (freezing) · 40 °F = 4.4 °C (fridge) · 98.6 °F = 37 °C (body)
· 212 °F = 100 °C (boiling at sea level).

## Water math

| Question | Figure |
|---|---|
| **Minimum planning figure** | **1 gallon per person per day** for drinking and basic hygiene (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply) |
| **This household, floor** | **{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gal a day**: 1 gal per person, plus extra for nursing or pregnant members, infants and pets (→ 03-01) |
| **This household, plan** | **{{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal a day**; two weeks = **{{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal** |
| **Stored now** | {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gal = **{{ derived.water.stored_days }} days** at the floor rate |
| Realistic with cooking and washing | 2 to 3 gal per person per day |
| Absolute drinking minimum, short term | About 0.5 gal per person per day: **not sustainable, and worse when hot or working** |
| Toilet flush (conventional) | 1.6 to 3.5 gal, which is why the bucket toilet exists (→ 13-01) |
| Shower | 2 to 2.5 gal a minute |
| Sponge bath | About 1 gal |
| Hand-washing a load of laundry | 10 to 20 gal (→ 13-04) |
| Washing dishes carefully, two basins | 2 to 4 gal |

**Containers:** bathtub about 40 to 50 gal · this household's water heater
{{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal (a reserve: know the drain valve, → 03-02) · toilet
tanks (never the bowls), the last reserve: FEMA says not to drink tank water, so keep it for
flushing and washing, or disinfect it first if nothing else is left, and never if a cleaning
tablet or dye is in it (FEMA, Food and Water in an Emergency; → 03-04) · {{#if has.pool}}pool or hot tub {{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gal, **none of
it drinkable without treatment** (→ 03-03){{else}}a 55-gal drum · a 5-gal bucket{{/if}}.

**Days of water = gallons on hand ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }}** (the plan rate). Use the
floor rate, {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }}, only when rationing. Do it on → 23-02.

## Calorie math

| Person or situation | Calories a day (planning) |
|---|---|
| Adult | About 1,600 to 3,000, by age, sex and activity (USDA/HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans, Appendix 2) |
| Adult, **hard physical work or cold** | The table's "active" column: for most adults **200 to 400 more** a day than the moderate one (→ 04-01) |
| Children and teenagers | By age and sex from the same table |
| **This household, normal** | **{{ derived.calories.day }}** (two weeks: {{ derived.calories.two_weeks }}) |
| **This household, working hard in the cold** | {{ derived.calories.day }} + 200 to 400 for each working adult = ______ |

**Two things people miss:** cold and hard work together can push the household's need far above
normal, and the eating of anyone with diabetes, a nursing parent or a small child is a
**medical** matter, not a rationing decision (→ 23-01).

**Rough calories per pound (dry):**

| Food | Calories per lb |
|---|---|
| **Oil and fat** | **About 4,000**: the densest thing you can store (→ 04-12) |
| Nuts and seeds | About 2,600 (an allergy constraint for some: → 02-04) |
| Powdered milk | About 1,650 (nonfat) to 2,250 (whole) |
| Sugar | About 1,750 |
| Honey | About 1,400 |
| Rolled oats | About 1,700 |
| **Rice, flour, pasta (dry)** | **About 1,600** |
| Dry beans | About 1,500 |
| Potatoes (fresh) | About 350 |
| **Canned goods**, mixed | About 400 to 600: you are carrying their water (→ 04-01) |

**Quick check:** 1 lb of mixed dry staples is about 1,500 to 1,800 calories, so an adult needs
roughly 1.5 lb a day. This household: {{ derived.calories.day }} ÷ about 1,600 = ______ lb a day,
× 30 = ______ lb a month, plus fat. A sanity check on → 04-01, not a substitute for counting.

## Fuel and heat

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| **A cord of wood** | 4 ft × 4 ft × 8 ft = **128 cubic feet stacked** |
| **A face cord (rick)** | 4 ft × 8 ft × the log length (often 16 in): about **1/3 of a cord** |
| Weight of a cord at 20 % moisture | About 2,700 lb (pine) to 3,700 lb (oak) (University of Missouri Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating) |
| Heat per cord | Dense hardwoods (oak, ash, hickory) give much more heat per cord than softwoods or cottonwood: **species matters** (University of Missouri Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating; → 06-03) |
| **Seasoning time** | **6 to 12 months, split and stacked; dense hardwoods a year or more** (→ 06-03) |
| Moisture target | **Under 20 %**: wet wood wastes heat boiling its own water and fouls the chimney |
| **Propane** | **91,420 BTU a gallon** (DOE AFDC). A refill receipt gives gallons; an exchange cylinder's label gives only the weight of propane, and the heater's manual often gives hours per cylinder |
| **Kerosene (1-K)** | **About 135,000 BTU a gallon** (typical figure; read your heater's label for its own rating) |
| Gasoline (pump gas with about 10 % ethanol) | **About 114,000 BTU a gallon** (DOE AFDC) ≈ 33 kWh of heat |
| **1 kWh of electricity** | **= 3,412 BTU.** A 1,500 W space heater gives about 5,100 BTU an hour and uses 1.5 kWh every hour |

A **BTU** (British thermal unit) is a unit of heat. Heaters are labelled in **BTU/h**: heat per
hour (→ 29-14).

**Heater runtime = fuel BTU ÷ the heater's BTU/h.** Example: 4 gallons of propane (from the
refill receipt) is 4 × 91,420 ≈ 366,000 BTU; in a heater burning 9,000 BTU/h it lasts about
366,000 ÷ 9,000 ≈ 40 hours, if nothing else uses that cylinder. Your heaters: {{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}} ({{h.model}}): ______ BTU/h → ______ hours per tank · {{else}}none entered{{/each}}.

**Cooking on an open fire uses far more wood** than an efficient stove for the same meal
(→ 07-02). **Measure yours during a blackout weekend** (→ 24-04).

## Electricity

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Watts (W)** | Rate of use: volts × amps |
| **Watt-hours (Wh)** | Energy: watts × hours. **The unit that matters for batteries** |
| **Amp-hours (Ah)** | Battery capacity at a voltage. **Wh = Ah × volts** |
| 100 Ah at 12 V | 1,200 Wh on paper; **usable is less**, depending on chemistry (→ 09-07) |

**Typical loads (check your own labels; → 29-14):** LED bulb 5 to 10 W · headlamp 1 to 3 W ·
phone charge 10 to 20 Wh · laptop 30 to 60 W · CPAP 30 to 60 W · **fridge 100 to 200 W running,
about 1,000 to 2,000 Wh a day** · microwave 1,000 to 1,500 W · well pump 500 to 1,500 W, with a
higher start-up surge.

**This household:** power stations {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh · solar {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W ·
estimated solar harvest **{{ derived.solar_wh_jun }} Wh a day in June** and
**{{ derived.solar_wh_dec }} Wh a day in December** (your panels × your county's sun hours ×
0.75 for losses; an estimate). **Size for December, not June**, if the load is medical
(→ 09-05, → 09-10). A full-size fridge on the stations: about {{ derived.station_fridge_days }}
days (estimate).

## Temperature, weather and the body

- **Wind chill:** use the NWS chart (NWS, Wind Chill Chart; → 29-10). At extreme wind chill,
  exposed skin can freeze in minutes (→ 08-05).
- **Hypothermia** can happen well above freezing when wet and windy (→ 08-05).
- **Fridge 40 °F or colder; freezer 0 °F or colder.** After the power goes out: about **4
  hours** for refrigerated food, **48 hours** for a full freezer (24 if half full)
  (USDA/HHS, Food Safety During a Power Outage; → 04-17).
- **Safe cooking temperatures** for meat, poultry and leftovers, with rest times: **use the
  FoodSafety.gov chart** (Cook to a Safe Minimum Internal Temperature) and → 07-04. Do not
  estimate.
- **Boiling to make water safe:** a **rolling boil for 1 minute**; above about 5,000 ft,
  **3 minutes** (EPA says above 5,000 ft; CDC says above 6,500 ft; use the lower, safer figure)
  (EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water; → 03-04). Your elevation: about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft{{#if is.high_altitude}},
  **so boil for 3 minutes**{{/if}}.

## Time and distance (planning a move)

| How | Rate |
|---|---|
| Adult walking, unloaded, good ground | About 3 mph |
| **Adults walking loaded, with a small child** | **1 to 1.5 mph, with frequent stops** |
| Walking in snow or at night | **Half that or worse** |
| Bicycle, loaded | 8 to 12 mph |
| **A realistic day on foot with small children** | **5 to 8 miles** |

Take the last row seriously on → 01-03: it decides whether leaving on foot is a plan or a hope.

## This household's numbers

```
PEOPLE: {{ household.size }} ({{ household.adults }} adults, {{ household.children }} children)
WATER   floor/day: {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gal   plan/day: {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal   realistic/day: ______ gal
CALORIES/day, normal: {{ derived.calories.day }}   cold + hard work: ______
DRY STAPLES/day: ______ lb        per month: ______ lb
WOOD per day (measured in a blackout weekend): ______
MEDICAL power use/day: ______ Wh
SOLAR, June: {{ derived.solar_wh_jun }} Wh/day (est.)   December: {{ derived.solar_wh_dec }} Wh/day (est.)
VEHICLE range on a full tank: ______ mi   + fuel cans: ______ mi
```

## Gear

**Buy toward:** a kitchen scale, a measuring jug, a fridge thermometer and a body thermometer, a
moisture meter for firewood, a watt-meter or battery monitor, a tape measure, and a calculator
with a solar cell. **And pencil and paper**: the actual instrument for all of this.

**If you do not have it:** a marked bucket measures water; a known weight checks a guess; **a cord
of wood is a fixed size**, so a tape measure is a scale; counting steps measures distance
(→ 29-13). **The most useful substitute of all is a written record of what you actually used
last time** (→ 24-04).

## When it goes stale

- These tables do not change; **the household's numbers change as children grow.** Redo the
  worksheet each year (→ 25-10).
- **Measure during every blackout weekend** and replace estimates with your real figures.
- **A measured number beats a table every time**, including the tables on this page.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** measure everything now, while meters, scales and the internet work.
- **B (moving):** the travel table and the water figure matter most; carry them on a card
  (→ 25-08).
- **C (establish):** wood, calories and solar output are all different at a new place.
  **Re-measure in the first month.**

Related: → 03-01 water needs · → 04-01 calorie and stockpile math · → 23-02 runway table ·
→ 06-03 firewood · → 09-03 batteries · → 09-05 winter solar · → 04-17 food after an outage ·
→ 03-04 water treatment (**dosing lives there**) · → 25-08 the card version.

# Regional contacts and resources

**What this page is for.** The phone numbers and offices you will want when the phone's contact
list is dead or the internet is gone, in one place you can print or copy. Three kinds of entry:
**national numbers** that are the same everywhere (printed); **your region's offices** from the
binder's region data (printed by name); and **local numbers** you type in settings or write by
hand. **This binder never looks up or guesses a local phone number**: one wrong digit in an
emergency is worse than a blank.

## Do this now

1. **Fill in every blank row in pencil, today.** The printed rows are the easy half; the blank
   ones (your clinic, your pharmacy, your neighbours) are the half that actually gets used.
2. **Make copies**: one in each go-bag (→ 22-03), each vehicle (→ 22-05), and one with the
   out-of-area contact.
3. **Program your NOAA Weather Radio** with your county's SAME code below, and check that the
   radio receives the transmitter (→ 15-01).
4. **Call each local number once** and tick its box. A number you have never dialled is a guess.
5. **Introduce yourself to two neighbours** and get their numbers. That one act is worth more in
   a real emergency than most of the gear in → 22-01 (→ 18-01).

## Emergency: the same everywhere

| Who | Number |
|---|---|
| **Police, fire, ambulance** | **911**. Any working cell phone can call 911, on any carrier's tower, even without service of its own (FCC, 9-1-1 and E9-1-1 Services) |
| **Poison Help (24 hours)** | **1-800-222-1222**: connects to your local poison center (Poison Control) |
| **988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline** (call or text) | **988** |
| **Disaster Distress Helpline** (call or text, 24 hours) | **1-800-985-5990** (SAMHSA) |
| **National Domestic Violence Hotline** (24 hours) | **1-800-799-7233** · text **START** to **88788** |
| Road conditions | In many states, dial **511** |

Animal poisoning: your vet, or a pet poison line written here: ______________________

## Utilities (as typed in settings)

| Service | Provider | Number | Dialled once ☐ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Electric outage** | {{ contacts.utility.electric.provider }} | {{ contacts.utility.electric.phone }} | ☐ |

| **Water** | {{ contacts.utility.water.provider }} | {{ contacts.utility.water.phone }} | ☐ |

**If you smell gas: leave the building first, then call 911 and the gas company from outside**
(FEMA, Utility Shut-off and Safety; → 16-12). Shutoffs: → 00-04.

{{/if}}

## Weather and hazards: home

| Resource | Detail |

six-digit county code that makes it sound only for your county; → 29-09):

Coverage changes; the NWS publishes which transmitters cover each county (NOAA/NWS, NOAA Weather
Radio Coverage by County). Re-check at the annual review (→ 25-10). Neighbouring counties' SAME
codes, if you want warnings for them too: ______ ______ ______

## Medical

## Food, farming and skills

| Resource | Name and phone |

| **County Extension office** (the land-grant university's local office) | ______________________ |

**Extension is the most underused resource in this binder.** It is free, local, and staffed by
people whose job is teaching gardening, food preservation and livestock, and it is the best
answer to much of → 24-01. The National Center for Home Food Preservation is the national
authority for tested canning methods (→ 04-04, → 04-05).

## Community and mutual aid (these matter most)

| Contact | Name | Phone |
|---|---|---|
| **Out-of-area contact** (everyone reports here if separated; → 15-03) | {{ contacts.out_of_area.name }} | {{ contacts.out_of_area.phone }} |

{{/each}}| Neighbour | ______________________ | ______________ |
| Neighbour | ______________________ | ______________ |
| Family, local | ______________________ | ______________ |
| Family, out of state | ______________________ | ______________ |
{{#if has.child}}| School or daycare | ______________________ | ______________ |
{{/if}}| Faith community | ______________________ | ______________ |
| Local ham radio club | ______________________ | ______________ |
| Skilled people we know (mechanic, nurse, welder, gardener, hunter) | ______________________ | ______________ |

## Practical services

| Service | Name and phone |
|---|---|
| Bank or credit union | ______________________ |
| Home and auto insurance (policy numbers) | ______________________ |
| State insurance department (consumer line, pre-collapse) | ______________________ |
| Fuel or propane supplier | ______________________ |
| Firewood supplier | ______________________ |
| {{#if has.well}}Well service{{else}}Plumber{{/if}} | ______________________ |
| {{#if has.septic}}Septic service{{else}}Electrician{{/if}} | ______________________ |
| Hardware store | ______________________ |
| Auto repair and towing | ______________________ |

## National resources worth knowing by name

You cannot reach these without the internet or a phone line, but their documents are behind the
pages that cite them in this binder{{#if size.large}} (this is the Large copy){{else}} (the Large copy holds the full documents; this Small copy names them){{/if}}.

| Resource | Use |
|---|---|
| USA.gov, Replace Your Vital Documents | Replacing lost documents (→ 19-01) |
| IRS, Reconstructing Records After a Disaster | Tax and property records after a loss (→ 19-03) |
| FoodSafety.gov | Food after a power cut; cooking temperatures (→ 04-17) |
| EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water | Water treatment (→ 03-04) |
| CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply | Storage and quantities (→ 03-02) |

## The offline problem

**Every website is useless the moment the internet is.** That is why the binder carries its
sources inside, why this page holds numbers and not links, and why **the most valuable contacts
here are the human ones**: neighbours, family, the ham club, the person who keeps chickens two
streets over. They work when nothing else does (→ 18-01).

**What you need:** a printed copy in every bag and vehicle, laminated wallet cards with the
essentials (→ 25-08), a pencil, and a small paper address book kept with the document kit
(→ 19-01). **The best substitute of all is memorised numbers**: make sure everyone old enough to
speak knows the out-of-area contact's number.

## When it goes stale

- **Numbers stay right for about a year.** Offices move; people move more.
- **Do not skip the blank rows**: they are the ones that fail silently.
- **Re-check at the annual review** (→ 25-10), then reprint.
- **When phones and agencies are gone**, the contacts that still work are the ones you can walk
  to (→ 18-01, → 18-03).

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** all of these work. Use them now, especially Extension, your
  prescribers and the neighbours.
- **B (moving):** the out-of-area contact and the meeting places are what matter; most
  institutional rows stop working (→ 15-03).
- **C (establish):** rebuild this page for the new place on arrival: county Extension office,
  nearest clinic and pharmacy, the local emergency manager, and the neighbours. Do it in the
  first week.

Related: → 15-01 weather alerts and SAME codes · → 15-03 the family comms plan · → 25-08 the
card version · → 19-01 document kit · → 25-09 medical summary · → 12-07 medicine supply ·
→ 18-01 mutual aid · → 25-10 annual re-check · Section 32 for every state's offices.

pages.body:
# Maps: local, regional and routes

**What this page is for.** Which maps to own, what to mark on them, and how to find your way
when the phone is dead. A phone's GPS position comes from satellites and keeps working without
cell service, but **maps, routing and search need either the internet or maps already
downloaded**, and every screen needs a charged battery. **A paper map and a compass work in a
dead-battery storm.**

## What maps this binder carries

{{#if size.large}}**This is the Large copy.** It carries **US Geological Survey (USGS) topographic maps**
(below) for your home county, {{ home.county }}, {{ home.state_name }}{{#if has.destinations}}, for each destination's county{{/if}}{{#if has.destinations}}, and for the counties a straight line
between home and each destination crosses (the "route counties"){{/if}}, fetched when you
downloaded the binder. A topographic ("topo") map shows the shape of the ground with contour
lines, plus water, roads, buildings and woods (USGS, The National Map, US Topo). They are free
public maps; **print the ones you will carry**, because a phone may not be there.
{{else}}**This is the Small copy.** It carries a state outline map and **the paper-map list
below**: what to buy and how to read it. The **Large** copy also carries **USGS topographic maps**
for your home county, each destination's county and the counties between them, fetched at
download. You can upgrade to Large later from your saved profile without rebuilding the pages
(→ 29-15), or print the same free USGS maps yourself while the internet works.
{{/if}}

Either way, **buy paper maps**: a phone or a printout of one county does not replace a road atlas.

## Do this now

1. **Buy the paper maps in the list below this month.** They cost little and are the only
   navigation that never fails.
2. **Mark them up at the kitchen table**, not on the road. The marks are the value; a blank map
   is just paper.
3. **Drive the routes out of town yourself**, and walk the first miles of one. A route you have
   not travelled is a guess (→ 01-03).
4. **Draw your vehicle's range as a circle** on the regional map: full tank plus fuel cans
   (→ 22-05, → 25-02). That circle is your real radius when moving, and it is usually smaller
   than people assume.
5. **Put a map set in each vehicle and the household bag**, in a zip bag.

## The maps to own

| # | Map | Why | Where to get it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Street map of {{ home.town }}** | Your own area at walking scale: every street, cut-through and bridge | Bookstores, visitor centres, gas stations, or print one while you can |
| **2** | **{{ home.state_name }} highway map** | Regional movement and the road network | Free from the state's travel or transport department; rest areas; gas stations |
| **3** | **A current road atlas, plus a county-detail atlas (gazetteer) for home{{#if has.destinations}} and each destination state{{/if}}** | The regional picture and the back roads a state map leaves out | Any road-atlas publisher; a gazetteer shows every county and gravel road |
| **4** | **USGS topographic maps** for home{{#if has.destinations}} and each destination{{/if}} | **Terrain, water, elevation, structures, woods**: what the ground is really like | {{#if size.large}}In this binder (above); print them{{else}}Free from USGS while the internet works; print them{{/if}} |

Also worth having: **county plat maps** (who owns which land: matters when settling somewhere,
Phase C), **public land maps**, and a **floodplain map** for home.

{{#if has.destinations}}
### Our destinations

| Destination | County, state | Status | About how far | Route notes (as typed) | State map ☐ | Atlas pages marked ☐ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each destinations as d}}| {{d.name}} | {{d.county}}, {{d.state_name}} | {{d.status_text}} | {{d.approximate_miles}} mi | {{d.route_notes}} | ☐ | ☐ |
{{/each}}

You need a highway map for **every state you would cross**, not only the ones at each end:
______________________________.
{{/if}}

## How to mark them up

{{photo annotated-map}}

{{figure fig-map-symbols}}

**On the home street map, mark:**

- **Home and the meeting places**: near home ({{ contacts.meet.near_home }}), in town
  ({{ contacts.meet.in_town }}), out of town ({{ contacts.meet.out_of_town }}) (→ 00-04, → 15-03)
{{#if has.child}}- **Each school or daycare** and the route to it
{{/if}}- **Hospitals, urgent care and pharmacies** (→ 25-03)
- **Water**: rivers, creeks, ponds, springs (→ 03-07)
- **Hazards**: floodplain, industrial sites, fuel storage, bridges (bridges are choke points and
  fail first)
- **Three walking routes out**, in different directions
- Neighbours and friendly houses (→ 18-01)

**On the regional map, mark:**

- **Primary route out** (interstate or highway), **secondary** (state roads), **tertiary**
  (county and back roads)
- **Your vehicle range circle**
- **Family and contacts** across the region
- **River crossings**: every one is a choke point (→ 17-03)
{{#if has.destinations}}- **Each destination, with a symbol, not a name** (→ 14-03), and the route to it
{{/if}}- **Fuel, water and towns** along each route, with sturdy buildings for shelter (→ 17-11)
- **Distances in days on foot**, not just miles: at 5 to 8 miles a day with small children
  (→ 25-02), the map looks very different

**On the topo map, mark:**

- Water sources and whether they are above or below you
- High ground (flood safety, → 17-03) and low ground (cold air settles there, but it is out of
  the wind)
- Woods: fuel that town does not have (→ 06-04)
- Ridges and valleys that shape where you can travel

## The three-route rule

Always have **three ways out**, known well enough to drive at night:

| Route | What it is | When it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | Interstate or highway: fastest, best surface | Closed, jammed or blocked: **the most likely failure in an evacuation** |
| **Secondary** | State and county highways | {{#if is.snow_region}}Drifted or unploughed, {{/if}}flooded, or closed at a bridge |
| **Tertiary** | Gravel and back roads | Mud{{#if is.snow_region}} or deep snow{{/if}}; slowest |

**Drive each one, in each season if you can.** Write the real drive time and fuel used on the
map. **Then walk the first few miles of one**: it is the version you will use if the vehicle
stops.

## What belongs on your maps in this region

Home hazards (rated 1 to 3; → 29-10):
{{#each region.home.hazards as z}}{{z.name}} {{z.rating_text}} · {{/each}}

- **Rivers and flooding:** **never drive through water over a road**; a foot of moving water can
  move a car (NWS, Flood Safety; CDC, Preparing for Floods). Mark a way around every crossing.
{{#if is.snow_region}}- **Winter closures:** highways close in storms, often as a whole route. **Mark shelter points
  along each route**: towns, fuel stations, sturdy buildings (NWS, Winter Weather Safety; → 17-01).
{{/if}}{{#if is.wildfire_region}}- **Wildfire:** mark two ways out of your neighbourhood that do not pass through brush or
  timber, and open areas to wait in (→ 17-14).
{{/if}}{{#if is.hurricane_region}}- **Hurricanes:** mark your evacuation zone and the official evacuation route (→ 17-13).
{{/if}}{{#if is.coastal}}- **Coast:** mark ground high enough to be out of storm-surge{{#if is.tsunami_region}} and tsunami{{/if}} reach (→ 17-15).
{{/if}}- **Distances and services:** between towns there can be long stretches with nothing. **Mark fuel,
  water and towns**, and plan legs around them.

## Offline maps on phones: set them up now

**GPS satellites do not depend on the power grid.** A phone's GPS chip finds your position
without cell service or an account. **What disappears is the map download**, so the whole game
is having maps already on the device.

- **Install an offline map app that routes without internet** on every phone, and download the
  map data for home{{#if has.destinations}}, each destination and every state between{{/if}} while the internet works.
- **Offline map areas in some apps expire** and silently vanish unless refreshed: put the
  refresh on the calendar with the go-bag checks (→ 22-03).
- **An offline map knows roads, not conditions.** No closures, floods or missing bridges. The
  radio (→ 15-01) and your own eyes supply conditions. **Never let an app argue you into water
  (→ 17-03).** The marked paper route is the plan; the app is the position fix.
- **Navigation with the screen on drains a phone fast.** Charge from the vehicle (→ 09-11); never
  use the phone a medical device depends on for navigation (→ 09-06).
- **Paper stays the master.** Screens break, batteries die, and a passenger cannot spread a phone
  across their lap. **Print strip maps** of each route: one page per leg, with fuel, bridges and
  turns marked.

## Navigation without GPS: the minimum skills

- **Read a map and turn it to match the ground.** Practise on a walk (→ 24-01).
- **Use a compass:** take and follow a bearing. Learn **declination** for your area: the
  difference between true north (the map) and magnetic north (the compass), printed in the
  margin of USGS topo maps.
- **Estimate distance:** count paces, use time and speed, match landmarks (→ 29-13).
- **The sun and stars:** the sun rises roughly east and sets roughly west; **Polaris (the North
  Star) marks north** and is found from the Big Dipper.
- **Match what you see to the map:** river, road, water tower, ridge, grain elevator.

**Practise all of it on an ordinary weekend walk**, before it matters.

## OPSEC: what not to write on a map

A marked map tells a stranger where you live, where your children are and where you would go
(→ 14-03).

- **Do not label a destination "our place".** Use a symbol you know.
- **Do not mark caches, stores or firearms.**
- **Do not write names next to houses.**
- **Keep the heavily marked master at home**; carry a lighter copy.
- **Do not hand your marked map to a stranger.** Give directions instead.

## Storage

- **Zip bag or dry bag**: a wet map is a lost map.
- **A set in each vehicle and in the household bag**; the master at home.
- **A compass with each set.**
- **Pencil, not pen**: pen bleeds when wet and cannot be corrected.

## Map worksheet

```
PRIMARY ROUTE OUT: _________________________________________________
   distance ______ mi   drive time ______   fuel used ______   driven on ______
SECONDARY: _________________________________________________________
   distance ______ mi   drive time ______   fuel used ______   driven on ______
TERTIARY: __________________________________________________________
   distance ______ mi   drive time ______   fuel used ______   driven on ______

VEHICLE RANGE (full tank): ______ mi    + fuel cans: ______ mi
WALKING RANGE, whole family, per day: ______ mi   (25-02)

RIVER CROSSINGS ON EACH ROUTE: _____________________________________
SHELTER POINTS ALONG EACH ROUTE: ___________________________________
STATES CROSSED: ____________________  state maps bought? ____
DESTINATION ROUTES: atlas pages marked? ____  strip maps printed? ____
```

## Gear

| Item | Why |
|---|---|
| Home street, state and regional paper maps; a county-detail atlas | Never need a battery |
| USGS topo maps for home{{#if has.destinations}} and destinations{{/if}}, printed | Terrain, water, woods |
| **Baseplate compass with declination adjustment** | Bearings |
| A second, simple compass | Backup |
| Map case or dry bags | Wet maps tear |
| Pencils and a fine marker; highlighters | Marking up |
| A ruler and a piece of string | String follows curved roads to measure distance |

**If you do not have it:** gas-station and visitor-centre maps (often free); route printouts made
now, while the internet works; and a hand-drawn sketch map of your own neighbourhood, which is
surprisingly useful and teaches you the ground.

## When it goes stale

- Roads change slowly; **bridges, closures and conditions change fast**, and no printed map shows
  them.
- **Make copies** rather than carrying the only original.
- **Update each year** (→ 25-10): re-drive the routes and note what changed.
- **Local knowledge beats any map**: someone who drives those roads every day knows what the map
  cannot show. Ask, then check against the ground.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the home street map is the working document: water, hazards,
  neighbours and walking routes.
- **B (moving):** this page is the plan. Routes marked, range known, meeting places fixed, and
  **the maps in the vehicle, not the house** (→ 22-05).
- **C (establish):** get **topo and plat maps of the new area at once**: water, woods, high
  ground, neighbours, and who owns what (→ 01-04).

Related: → 01-03 moving · → 01-05 destinations · → 22-05 where the maps ride · → 17-03 floods ·
→ 17-01 winter closures · → 14-03 OPSEC · → 25-02 range and walking-rate math · → 15-03 meeting
places.

pages.body:
# Blank logs and worksheets

**What this page is for.** Forms to print (or copy into a notebook) for keeping track of a long
event and of ordinary preparation. Written records turn guesses into numbers (→ 23-02), let a
second person pick up where you left off, and are the proof an insurer or the tax authority asks
for later (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a Disaster; → 19-04). **Use pencil.** Pens freeze and
run.

## Do this now

1. **Print at least five copies of each log**, or set aside a notebook, with two pencils.
2. **Start the daily log the day anything unusual begins**: an outage, an illness, a storm. The
   first entry is always "we didn't think this would last."
3. **Start the water and fuel logs during your next blackout weekend** (→ 24-04): that is where
   the real use numbers come from.

## Why logs matter more than they seem

1. **They replace estimates with facts.** Everything on → 23-02 is arithmetic on numbers you
   either measured or guessed.
2. **They hand over cleanly.** If one adult is ill or away, another can read the log and know
   exactly where things stand.
3. **They catch slow problems.** A slow drop in stored water, a slowly worsening symptom, a
   shrinking woodpile: invisible day to day, obvious in a log.
4. **They are the record afterwards**, for insurance, tax and disaster assistance (→ 19-04).
5. **They anchor morale.** Writing the day down gives shape to time when the calendar has
   stopped meaning anything (→ 21-04).

**Rule for every log: date, time, who wrote it. Always.**

## Daily situation log

```
DATE: __________  DAY # ______  WEATHER: ______________  TEMP high/low: ______

WATER    on hand ______ gal   used today ______ gal   treated today ______ gal
FOOD     meals ______   notable use ____________________  days left ______
POWER    battery start ____%  end ____%   solar made ______ Wh
HEAT     fuel used ______     indoor temp ______        wood left ______
MEDICAL  shortest supply: ____________ ______ days left
         anything unusual: _____________________________________________
```

| Person | Sleep | Mood | Health | Anything to watch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each members as m}}| {{m.label}} | | | | |

## Home-preserving log (→ 04-04, → 04-05, → 04-06)

## Health log (one per person)

for (CDC, Managing Sick Days).

```

## Garden log (→ 25-01)

CROP          VARIETY        SOWN     TRANSPLANTED   FIRST HARVEST   YIELD

SEED SAVED FROM: ______________________________________________
WHAT WORKED: __________________________________________________
WHAT FAILED (and why): ________________________________________
CHANGE NEXT YEAR: _____________________________________________
```

## Barometer and sky log (→ 17-10; the trend is the instrument, two rows a day)

```
SET TO THE LOCAL REPORTED PRESSURE ON: __________   (17-10)

DATE   TIME   READING    CHANGE since last    SKY (clouds, wind direction)   WHAT I EXPECT
              (mb/inHg)  (rise/steady/fall,   and anything odd
                          how fast)
_____  _____  ________   __________________   ____________________________   __________
_____  _____  ________   __________________   ____________________________   __________
_____  _____  ________   __________________   ____________________________   __________

CHECK THE CALL AGAINST WHAT HAPPENED: that is how the skill builds (17-10).
```

## Maintenance and repair log

```

_____  ________________  ______________________  _____________  __________
_____  ________________  ______________________  _____________  __________
```

## Drill and practice log (→ 24-01, → 24-02)

```
DATE   DRILL / SKILL            RESULT / TIME   WHAT WE CHANGED
_____  _______________________  ____________    ______________________________
_____  _______________________  ____________    ______________________________
```

## Visitor and trade log (→ 18-02)

```
DATE   WHO                  WHAT WAS TRADED OR GIVEN      OWED?    NOTES
_____  __________________   ____________________________  _______  __________
```

> Trade records prevent the misunderstandings that break the relationships you depend on
> (→ 18-05).

## Binder change log

```
DATE   PAGE        WHAT CHANGED (note it; change it in settings at the next rebuild)
_____  __________  ______________________________________________________________
_____  __________  ______________________________________________________________
```

> **This one keeps the binder true.** Every drill, blackout weekend and real event should
> produce at least one line here, and the next rebuild picks it up (→ 29-15).

## Gear

**Buy toward:** a stack of printed forms or a notebook, several pencils and a sharpener, a
clipboard, a waterproof notebook for outdoor use, a wall calendar, and a waterproof folder for
finished logs. A phone or camera for photo records of the inventory and any damage (→ 19-04).

**If you do not have it:** any notebook, the backs of old pages, or a wall you write on. **The
form matters far less than the habit**: a dated line in a spiral notebook beats a beautiful
blank form nobody fills in.

## When it runs out

- Paper and pencil last essentially forever; **the habit is what runs out**, usually in the
  second week of an event.
- **If you can keep only one log, keep the daily situation log**: it holds a little of
  everything.
- Blank paper and pencils are worth stocking (→ 22-01).
- **Written beats remembered**, especially when tired, cold and handing over to another adult.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** logs are for practice and inventory. Start them during the blackout
  weekend (→ 24-04).
- **B (moving):** the daily log becomes a travel log: where you stopped, what you used, what you
  saw, what the route was really like.
- **C (establish):** logs become the operating record of a small homestead: garden, wood,
  animals, weather, repairs. **Years of your own data make a place work.**
