pages.body:
# Glossary: every term in plain words

**What this page is for.** If a word in this binder is unfamiliar, it should be here, in plain
words, with the page that explains it properly. **Nothing on this page is a procedure.** The
definitions orient you; the page in the last column does the work. The explainers in Section 29
(→ 29-01 to → 29-15) teach most of these words in context, one subject per page.

## Do this now

1. **Read "How this binder works" first.** Those terms explain how the whole book is organised.
2. **Make sure every adult knows the medical words in bold.** Under stress, a shared vocabulary
   is the difference between "they're acting funny" and "this is anaphylaxis, get the
   epinephrine."

## How this binder works

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Phase A, B, C** | The three-part plan: **A** = stay home (shelter in place); **B** = move (evacuate); **C** = settle somewhere new (establish) | → 01-01 to → 01-04 |
| **Go/no-go** | The decision to leave or stay, made against triggers the household wrote in advance | → 01-02 |
| **Floor** | One of nine rules that are not choices, because the failure kills without warning and nothing makes it safe | → 30-01 |
| **Decision card** | A one-page trade-off (DC-01 to DC-29) where the household chooses its own risk; your answer prints wherever the subject comes up | → 30-02 to → 30-30 |
| **Explainer** | A one-page lesson on a subject newcomers are not expected to know (EX-01 to EX-15) | → 29-01 to → 29-15 |
| **Condition module** | The pages for one medical condition (CL-01 to CL-26); the ones you ticked are moved forward | Section 02 |
| **Core, region, household layers** | Core: the same for every household. Region: your state's climate, hazards, offices and plants. Household: your people, gear and plans, filled from settings | → 29-15 |
| **Small and Large copy** | Small: every page, citations by title only. Large: the same plus the cited documents and topographic maps inside | → 00-09, → 29-15 |
| **AI-reviewed, not human-verified** | The stamp on every page: an AI checked it; no professional did. Where a professional disagrees, the professional is right | → 29-15 |
| **Fill-in blank** | A line marked "(fill in)": an answer you skipped in settings | → 00-01 |
| **Before the collapse** | A boxed note about laws, licences or codes: true while government works, never deciding a survival procedure | → 29-15 |
| **Runway, clock** | How many days a supply lasts at the rate you use it. The household's **shortest clock** governs the plan | → 23-02 |
| **Consumable** | Something used up: fuel, filters, lids, batteries, medicine. It sets the real life of the tool that uses it | → 22-01 |
| **Class A, B, C consumable** | **A** can be produced, **B** can be substituted, **C** has no substitute (some medicines, infant formula) | → 23-01 |
| **Stage 1 to 4** | A resource's life: stock only, stretch it, substitute, produce it | → 23-04 |
| **Have-it-now / scavenge-substitute** | The two lists on many pages: buy toward the first (→ 22-01), look for the second (→ 22-02) | → 22-01 |
| **Shelter in place** | Staying inside your home (or a named room) until a danger passes | → 01-01 |
| **EDC (everyday carry)** | What is on your body every day; the kit most likely to be the only one with you | → 22-03 |
| **Go-bag** | A packed bag per person for about three days on foot | → 22-03 |
| **PACE plan** | Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency: four ways to reach each other, tried in order | → 15-03 |
| **OPSEC** | "Operational security": not advertising what you have or what you plan | → 14-03 |
| **Mutual aid** | Neighbours helping each other on purpose, with agreed expectations | → 18-01 |

## Medical

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Anaphylaxis** | A severe, fast, life-threatening allergic reaction affecting breathing or circulation. **Epinephrine is the treatment; antihistamines are not** | → 02-03 |
| **Epinephrine** | The medicine that treats anaphylaxis (adrenaline). Comes in **auto-injectors** (a pen pressed into the outer thigh) and a nasal spray. **A second dose may be needed** | → 02-03 |
| **Antihistamine** | An allergy medicine for itching and hives. **Never instead of epinephrine, never first** in anaphylaxis | → 02-03 |
| **Cross-contact** | An allergen carried onto safe food by a shared surface, utensil or hands | → 02-04 |
| **Type 1 diabetes** | The pancreas makes almost no insulin. **Insulin is not optional and has no substitute** | → 02-01 |
| **Type 2 diabetes** | The body does not use insulin well; treated with diet, tablets, injectables or insulin | → 02-05 |
| **Insulin** | The hormone that lets the body use sugar; a refrigerated protein medicine. **Frozen insulin is discarded** | → 02-01, → 29-07 |
| **Basal / bolus** | Background insulin / mealtime or correction insulin | → 02-01 |
| **Hypoglycaemia ("a low")** | Blood sugar too low: shaky, sweaty, confused. Can kill in minutes | → 02-01 |
| **Hyperglycaemia ("a high")** | Blood sugar too high | → 02-01 |
| **DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis)** | A life-threatening emergency when the body lacks insulin and burns fat, making **ketones** that acidify the blood. **Ketone strips catch it early** (CDC, Diabetic Ketoacidosis) | → 02-01 |
| **Ketones** | Acids made when the body burns fat for fuel; measured with urine or blood strips | → 02-01 |
| **CGM (continuous glucose monitor)** | A sensor worn on the skin that reads sugar levels all day | → 02-02 |
| **Insulin pump** | A worn device that delivers insulin; needs supplies, batteries and a backup plan | → 02-02 |
| **Glucagon** | A rescue medicine for a severe low when the person cannot swallow | → 02-01 |
| **Asthma / rescue inhaler** | Narrowing of the airways / the fast-acting inhaler that opens them | → 02-07 |
| **COPD** | Long-term lung disease; some people need **oxygen** from a concentrator (needs power) or cylinders | → 02-08 |
| **CPAP** | A powered machine that keeps the airway open during sleep | → 02-24 |
| **Anticoagulant (blood thinner)** | Medicine that slows clotting; bleeding is harder to stop | → 02-10 |
| **Seizure** | A burst of abnormal brain activity, often with jerking or blank staring | → 02-11 |
| **Naloxone** | A medicine that reverses an opioid overdose | → 02-17 |
| **Prescriber** | The doctor, nurse practitioner or other clinician who prescribes a medicine | → 12-07 |
| **OTC (over the counter)** | Medicine sold without a prescription; its box carries a **Drug Facts** label | → 29-14 |
| **Drug Facts label** | The standard box label: active ingredient, uses, warnings, directions | → 29-14 |
| **Expiry date (EXP) / lot number (LOT)** | The last date the maker guarantees full strength / the batch it came from | → 29-14 |
| **Cold chain** | Keeping a medicine within its temperature range from start to finish | → 29-07 |
| **Excursion** | A time a medicine spent outside its labelled range. **Freezing is a cliff; heat is a slope** | → 29-07 |
| **Evaporative cooling pouch** | A wetted pouch that cools medicine as water evaporates; no power needed | → 12-21 |
| **Hypothermia** | Dangerous drop in core body temperature; **happens above freezing when wet and windy** | → 08-05 |
| **Frostbite** | Frozen skin and tissue, usually fingers, toes, ears, nose. **Minutes at extreme wind chill** | → 08-05 |
| **Heat exhaustion / heat stroke** | Overheating with heavy sweating and weakness / a life-threatening emergency with confusion and very high body temperature | → 17-04 |
| **ORS (oral rehydration solution)** | Water with the right salt and sugar to replace what diarrhoea and vomiting lose | → 12-05 |
| **Tourniquet** | A tight band above a bleeding arm or leg wound that stops the blood. The floor (→ 30-01): **Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no help will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).** | → 12-02 |
| **Wound packing** | Stuffing gauze firmly into a deep wound and pressing to stop bleeding | → 12-02 |
| **Triage** | Sorting injured people by who benefits most from limited help | → 12-16 |
| **Sepsis** | A life-threatening body-wide response to infection | → 12-04 |
| **CPR** | Chest compressions (and breaths) to keep blood moving when the heart stops | → 12-18 |
| **Medical ID** | A bracelet, tag or card naming a condition or allergy for responders | → 25-09 |

## Water

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Potable** | Safe to drink | → 29-06 |
| **Clear is not clean** | Water can look perfect and still carry germs or chemicals | → 29-06 |
| **Germs: bacteria, viruses, parasites** | Bacteria are tiny living cells; viruses are far smaller and need a host; parasites (such as Giardia) include tough cysts that resist chlorine | → 29-06 |
| **Rolling boil** | Big bubbles that keep coming when stirred; **1 minute**, or **3 minutes** at high altitude, makes water safe from germs (EPA) | → 03-04 |
| **Filtration** | Straining out particles and many germs. **A filter does not remove salt**, and plain filters do not remove dissolved chemicals | → 03-04 |
| **Micron; absolute vs nominal** | A millionth of a metre. "Absolute" is the largest gap a filter lets through; "nominal" is an average and promises less | → 29-06 |
| **Disinfection** | Killing germs, by boiling, chemicals or ultraviolet light (UV) | → 03-04 |
| **Distillation** | Boiling water and collecting the steam. **Removes salt** and most chemicals | → 03-03 |
| **Turbidity** | Cloudiness. **Settle and pre-filter cloudy water before disinfecting** | → 29-06 |
| **Residual** | Chlorine left over after it has done its work: a faint smell means it is still protecting the water | → 29-06 |
| **ppm (parts per million)** | How strong a chemical is in water: 1 ppm is one part in a million | → 29-05 |
| **Sodium hypochlorite** | The active chemical in household bleach | → 29-05 |
| **Calcium hypochlorite ("pool shock", "cal-hypo")** | A dry chlorine powder or granule; made into a stock solution for water | → 29-05 |
| **Trichlor / dichlor** | Pool tablets with stabilisers: **not** for drinking water | → 29-05 |
| **Never-mix rule** | **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** Chlorine gas | → 30-01 |
| **Greywater / blackwater** | Used wash water / sewage | → 13-03, → 13-01 |
| **Bti** | A natural larvicide that kills mosquito larvae in standing water | → 03-08 |
| **SAME, NWR** | See Communications | |

## Food, canning and growing

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **pH** | How acid something is. **Lower is more acid** | → 29-08 |
| **High-acid / low-acid food** | pH 4.6 or lower (most fruit, pickles) / above 4.6 (vegetables, beans, meat, soups) | → 29-08 |
| **Botulism** | A deadly illness from a toxin made by spores in sealed low-acid food. **No warning taste or smell** | → 29-08 |
| **Spores** | Dormant, heat-resistant forms of bacteria that survive boiling | → 29-08 |
| **Boiling-water canner** | A deep pot that holds jars under boiling water; for **high-acid** foods only | → 04-04 |
| **Pressure canner** | A heavy pot that holds jars under pressure to reach about 240 to 250 °F; **required for low-acid foods**. **A pressure cooker is not a pressure canner** | → 04-05 |
| **Dial gauge / weighted gauge; psi** | Two ways a canner shows pressure / pounds per square inch | → 29-08 |
| **Venting** | Letting steam escape from a canner for a set time before pressurising | → 29-08 |
| **Altitude adjustment** | Higher places need longer times or more pressure; the recipe's table governs | → 29-08 |
| **Headspace** | The gap between the food and the lid, set by the recipe | → 29-08 |
| **Hot pack / raw pack** | Filling jars with hot, cooked food / raw food | → 29-08 |
| **Tested recipe** | A process proven safe by a recognised authority (USDA, NCHFP, Extension). **Use only tested recipes** | → 04-05 |
| **The seal** | The lid pulled down by vacuum as a jar cools; an unsealed jar is refrigerated or reprocessed | → 29-08 |
| **Curing / fermentation** | Preserving with salt (and sometimes nitrite) / with helpful microbes that make acid | → 04-07, → 04-08 |
| **Oxygen absorber / mylar** | A sachet that removes oxygen / a metallised bag that keeps it out; together they make dry food keep for years | → 04-03 |
| **"Best if used by", "Sell by", "Use by"** | Quality and display dates, not safety dates. Infant formula is the exception: its date is required by federal law, and it is followed | → 29-14 |
| **Open-pollinated (heirloom) / hybrid (F1)** | Seed that comes true when saved / seed from a cross that does not | → 05-03 |
| **Frost date** | The median date of the last spring or first fall frost; half of years are worse | → 25-01 |
| **Hardiness zone** | The USDA zone for a place's average coldest winter night; tells which perennials survive | → 25-01 |
| **Days to maturity** | On a seed packet: days from planting to harvest | → 25-01 |
| **Hardening off / succession sowing** | Getting seedlings used to outdoors over one to two weeks / small sowings every few weeks | → 25-01 |

## Fire, fuel and heat

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Gasoline** | Thin, very volatile engine fuel. **Never in a heater or lamp, never indoors** | → 29-01 |
| **Diesel** | Heavier oily fuel for diesel engines and ducted heaters vented outdoors | → 29-01 |
| **Kerosene (1-K, K-1)** | A lighter oily fuel; **1-K** is the clear grade for indoor wick heaters | → 29-01 |
| **Propane / butane** | Gases stored as liquid under pressure in cylinders; butane fails in freezing cold | → 29-01 |
| **White gas (camp fuel)** | A very volatile liquid for camp stoves; as dangerous to store as gasoline | → 29-01 |
| **Lamp oil** | Refined liquid paraffin for oil lamps; a swallowed mouthful can enter the lungs (call Poison Help) | → 29-01 |
| **Ethanol blend** | Pump gasoline with alcohol in it (often about 10 %); it pulls in water and ages | → 29-01 |
| **Stabiliser** | An additive that slows fuel ageing; it cannot fix stale fuel | → 06-06 |
| **Jar test** | Pouring a sample of fuel into a clear jar to check for water or cloudiness | → 29-01 |
| **Carbon monoxide (CO)** | A gas from anything that burns: **no colour, no smell, no taste, and lethal** (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics) | → 29-03 |
| **CO alarm (and ppm display)** | A battery device that sounds when CO builds up; a model with a number shows low levels the alarm waits on | → 29-03 |
| **Vented / unvented** | Exhaust goes outdoors through a pipe / exhaust stays in the room | → 08-04 |
| **Pilot light** | A small flame that is always lit on some gas appliances; it can ignite leaking gas or vapour | → 29-01 |
| **Seasoned wood** | Split and dried **6 to 12 months** to under about 20 % moisture | → 06-03 |
| **Cord / face cord** | 4 × 4 × 8 ft of stacked wood (128 cubic ft) / about a third of that | → 25-02 |
| **BTU, BTU/h** | A unit of heat / heat per hour, how heaters are rated | → 25-02 |
| **Creosote** | Tar that builds up in chimneys from smoky fires; it causes chimney fires | → 06-09 |
| **Rocket stove** | A small, efficient wood stove that burns sticks hot and clean | → 07-02 |
| **Banking a fire** | Covering coals so the fire survives overnight | → 06-02 |
| **Tare weight (TW)** | The empty weight stamped on a propane cylinder's collar | → 29-14 |
| **DOT specification** | The federal standard stamped on a pressure cylinder | → 29-14 |
| **Flame mitigation device** | A mesh in a newer fuel can's spout that helps stop flame entering the can | → 29-14 |
| **ABC extinguisher; PASS** | A fire extinguisher for ordinary, liquid and electrical fires / Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep | → 29-12 |
| **Fire blanket** | A flame-resistant sheet to smother a small fire, such as a pan fire | → 29-12 |
| **Smoke alarm: ionisation / photoelectric** | Two sensor types: quicker to flaming fires / quicker to smouldering fires. **Smoke alarms do not detect CO** | → 29-12 |

## Power and electricity

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Volts, amps, watts** | Electrical "pressure", "flow", and the rate of use (**watts = volts × amps**) | → 29-02 |
| **Watt-hours (Wh), kilowatt-hours (kWh)** | Energy: watts × hours. **What batteries are sized in.** 1 kWh = 1,000 Wh | → 29-02 |
| **Amp-hours (Ah)** | Battery capacity at a voltage: **Wh = Ah × volts** | → 29-02 |
| **Power station** | A portable battery with outlets and an inverter inside | → 29-02 |
| **Inverter** | Turns battery (DC) power into household (AC) power; loses some energy doing it | → 29-02 |
| **AC / DC** | Alternating current from wall outlets / direct current from batteries and solar | → 09-12 |
| **LiFePO4 (LFP)** | Lithium iron phosphate, a long-lived, safer lithium battery; **must not be charged below freezing** unless its battery system blocks cold charging | → 29-02 |
| **Lead-acid** | Car, marine and AGM batteries: heavy, and damaged by deep draining | → 29-02 |
| **Depth of discharge** | How far a battery is drained; deeper shortens its life | → 09-07 |
| **Solar panel; charge controller** | Turns sunlight into DC power / regulates it into the battery | → 09-02 |
| **Voc, Isc** | A panel label's open-circuit volts and short-circuit amps; they limit what a station can accept | → 28-07 |
| **Peak sun hours** | Hours of full-strength sun a day; far fewer in December | → 09-05 |
| **Data plate** | The label on an appliance with its volts, watts or amps, and model | → 29-14 |
| **Phantom load** | Power drawn by things you forgot were on | → 09-01 |
| **Panel, breaker, main breaker** | The box where house wiring starts / a switch that trips on overload / the one switch that cuts the whole house | → 29-04 |
| **GFCI** | An outlet or breaker that cuts power fast if current leaks, as in a wet location | → 29-04 |
| **Transfer switch / interlock / inlet** | Ways to feed house circuits from a generator safely, with the grid locked out / the outdoor socket the generator cord plugs into | → 29-04 |
| **Backfeeding; "suicide cord"** | Pushing generator power into house wiring without a transfer switch or interlock, often with a double-plug cord. **Never.** It electrocutes line workers | → 30-01 |
| **Cord-and-plug conversion** | Giving a hard-wired appliance (furnace, well pump) a plug so it can run from a generator cord | → 30-08 |
| **Wire gauge (AWG)** | Wire thickness: **a lower number is a thicker wire** | → 29-04 |

## Sanitation

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Bucket toilet** | A sealed bucket with a seat and a liner, plus dry cover material | → 13-01 |
| **Cover material** | Sawdust, peat or ash added after each use for smell and flies | → 13-01 |
| **Latrine** | A dug pit toilet, sited well away from water and homes | → 13-07 |
| **Humanure** | Composted human waste: long timelines, real germ risks, never on food crops without the full process | → 13-06 |
| **Fecal-oral route** | How most outbreak diseases spread: from waste to hands to mouth. **Handwashing breaks it** | → 13-11 |

## Communications

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **NOAA Weather Radio (NWR)** | National Weather Service broadcasts of forecasts and warnings, 24 hours | → 15-01 |
| **SAME code** | A six-digit county code that makes a weather radio sound only for chosen counties | → 29-09 |
| **FRS / GMRS** | Short-range family radios / higher-power family radios; GMRS needs a licence (no exam) | → 29-09 |
| **MURS / CB** | Licence-free VHF handheld radios / citizens band, common on highways | → 29-09 |
| **Amateur ("ham") radio** | Licensed radio (exam required) with long-range ability | → 15-05 |
| **Repeater / simplex** | A hilltop station that relays your signal for range / radio to radio directly | → 29-09 |
| **Line of sight** | Most handheld radios reach only what the antenna could "see"; height helps more than power | → 29-09 |
| **Privacy codes** | Tones that filter what *you* hear. **Everyone can still hear you** | → 29-09 |
| **Scanner** | A receiver that listens across many channels | → 15-04 |

## Weather and hazards

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Watch** | Conditions are favourable for the hazard. **Get ready** | → 29-10 |
| **Warning** | It is happening or about to. **Act now** | → 29-10 |
| **Advisory** | Hazardous but less severe; adjust plans | → 29-10 |
| **Wind chill** | How cold the air feels on skin with wind; it sets how fast frostbite happens (NWS, Wind Chill Chart) | → 29-10 |
| **Heat index** | How hot it feels with humidity; full sun can add more | → 29-10 |
| **Hazard rating 1 to 3** | The region appendix's rating of each natural hazard for a county: 1 lower, 3 higher. It says how much the hazard deserves planning, not how likely it is on any day | → 29-10 |
| **Blizzard / ground blizzard** | Wind and blowing snow that cut visibility, **not a snowfall total** / the same with no new snow, closing roads in clear weather | → 17-01 |
| **Derecho** | A long, wide, fast-moving line of damaging straight-line wind | → 17-18 |
| **Flash flood** | Fast flooding with little warning. **Never drive into water over a road** | → 17-03 |
| **Storm surge** | Seawater pushed ashore by a hurricane: its deadliest part | → 17-13 |
| **Red flag warning** | Weather that lets wildfire spread fast | → 17-05 |
| **Barometric pressure (mb, inHg)** | Air pressure, in millibars or inches of mercury; **a fast fall means a storm is coming** | → 17-10 |

## Firearms and security

Firearms pages are in every binder so that a non-shooter can make one safe (→ 29-11).

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **The four rules** | Treat every gun as loaded; never point it at anything you are not willing to destroy; finger off the trigger until ready; know your target and what is beyond it | → 29-11 |
| **Muzzle, barrel, chamber, action** | The open front end / the tube / where the cartridge sits to fire / the moving parts that load and unload | → 29-11 |
| **Magazine / cylinder** | The removable or fixed holder of cartridges / a revolver's rotating holder | → 29-11 |
| **Safety** | A switch that blocks firing on some guns; **not** a substitute for the rules | → 29-11 |
| **Cartridge, caliber, headstamp** | One round / its size / the markings on its base. **The headstamp must match the marking on the gun** | → 29-11 |
| **Zero** | The distance at which the sights and the bullet's path meet | → 14-09 |
| **MOA / mil** | Angle units for adjusting sights | → 14-09 |
| **De-escalation** | Deliberately calming a confrontation: the cheapest security tool there is | → 14-13 |
| **Safe storage** | Unloaded, locked, with ammunition locked separately. **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products** | → 14-14 |

## Measuring and labels

| Term | Meaning | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Calibrating** | Checking a guess against something whose size is known | → 29-13 |
| **Pace count** | Your steps per 100 yards or per mile, measured once and used to estimate distance | → 29-13 |
| **Hz (hertz)** | Cycles per second; US household power is 60 Hz | → 29-14 |
| **Declination** | The angle between true north (the map) and magnetic north (the compass) where you are | → 25-04 |

Related: → 29-01 to → 29-15 the explainers · → 25-02 the numbers behind the units ·
→ 00-01 how to use the binder · → 25-06 the sources behind the definitions.

review_pass.notes: Floors checked word for word against 30-01/docs 05; anaphylaxis card re-sourced to AAP plan; tourniquet, hypo, boil, winter-vehicle and lightning rows corrected and sourced. Wave 2 (R18): tourniquet floor now verbatim from 30-01 (both sentences); toilet tank last reserve, disinfect first (FEMA 477); boil line EPA 5,000 / CDC 6,500 as 03-04; NWS winter key merged to nws-winter-storm-during.

pages.body:
# Quick-reference cards

**What this page is for.** Short cards for the minute when you cannot read a whole page. Each
is a memory aid for something you have already read and practised (→ 24-01), not a substitute
for training. **The full page always governs**; each card names it. Print them, cut them out,
laminate them (or slip them into zip bags), and put a set wherever an emergency could start.

> **SAFETY — CRITICAL.**
> - **These cards are compressed.** When a card and its page differ, the page is right; reprint
>   the card.
> - **No card contains a calculated dose.** A medical card is replaced by the person's own
>   written plan from their prescriber before it goes in a bag.
> - The floors that appear on these cards are printed word for word from → 30-01.

## Do this now

1. **Print, cut and laminate.** One set on the fridge, one in each go-bag, one in each vehicle,
   one in the medical kit (→ 22-06), one at the shelter spot.
2. **Replace cards 2 and 3 with the prescriber's written plans** for anyone in the household who
   has one (→ 02-03, → 02-01).
3. **Fill in every blank.** A card with blanks is a card that fails. Numbers you typed in
   settings are already printed; everything else comes from → 25-03.
4. **Reprint any card whose page changes** and swap every copy.

## Card 1: Emergency numbers

| | |
|---|---|
| **Emergency (police, fire, ambulance)** | **911** |
| **Poison Help** | **1-800-222-1222** |
| **988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline** | **988** |
| **Disaster Distress Helpline** | **1-800-985-5990** |
| **Out-of-area contact** (text first, then call) | {{ contacts.out_of_area.name }} · {{ contacts.out_of_area.phone }} |
| **Meeting place near home** | {{ contacts.meet.near_home }} |
| **Meeting place in town** | {{ contacts.meet.in_town }} |
| **Meeting place out of town** | {{ contacts.meet.out_of_town }} |
| **Gas leak** (leave the building first) | {{ contacts.utility.gas.provider }} · {{ contacts.utility.gas.phone }} |
| **Electric outage** | {{ contacts.utility.electric.provider }} · {{ contacts.utility.electric.phone }} |
| **Water** | {{ contacts.utility.water.provider }} · {{ contacts.utility.water.phone }} |
| **Doctor / pharmacy / vet** | ______________ / ______________ / ______________ |
| **Nearest emergency room** | ______________________ |
| **NWS office** | {{ region.home.nws_office }} |
| **Weather radio** | {{#each region.home.nwr as t}}{{t.call}} {{t.freq}} MHz, SAME {{t.same}} · {{else}}______ MHz, SAME ______{{/each}} |
| **If no phone works** | Medical: the cards and pages govern (poisoning → 12-17, CPR → 12-18). Nearest neighbour with medical skills: ______________ |

## Card 2: Anaphylaxis (replace with the person's signed plan, → 02-03)

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**In this household:** {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}) · {{/each}}
Epinephrine is kept: ______________________
{{else}}No anaphylaxis is entered. Keep the card: a reaction can happen to a guest, or a first time.
{{/if}}

| | |
|---|---|
| **Signs** | Any one severe sign: trouble breathing, wheeze or cough, tight or hoarse throat, trouble swallowing, swollen lips or tongue, pale or blue skin, weak pulse, faint or dizzy, many hives over the body, severe vomiting, confusion. Or more than one mild sign at once (AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan) |
| **1. Epinephrine first** | Outer thigh, through clothing if needed. **Do not wait.** Note the time (AAP; CDC, Recognizing and Responding to Anaphylaxis) |
| **2. Call 911** | Or get to care |
| **3. Position** | Lie flat, legs raised. Vomiting: on the side. Struggling to breathe: sitting up. **Never stand or walk them** |
| **4. Second dose** | If symptoms get worse, continue, or do not get better in **5 minutes** (AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan) |
| **5. Stay** | Reactions can return hours later. No 911: that watch is yours, epinephrine in reach |
| **Antihistamine** | **Not a treatment for anaphylaxis.** Never delay epinephrine for anything |
| **Expired or out-of-range device, nothing else available** | Household choice: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05 |

## Card 3: Diabetes emergency (no dosing; replace with the prescriber's plan, → 02-01)

| | |
|---|---|
| **LOW (hypoglycaemia)** | Shaky, sweaty, confused, irritable, pale, slurred, unsteady (CDC, Low Blood Sugar) |
| **Awake and can swallow** | Fast sugar now; **recheck in about 15 minutes**; repeat until back in range, then a snack or meal (CDC, Treatment of Low Blood Sugar) |
| **Unconscious, seizing, or cannot swallow** | **Nothing by mouth. Give glucagon. Call 911.** On their side. Sugar by mouth only once awake and able to swallow |
| **HIGH with ketones (DKA risk)** | Thirst, peeing a lot, nausea or vomiting, belly pain, fruity breath, fast deep breathing, confusion (CDC, Diabetic Ketoacidosis) |
| **What to do** | **Check ketones.** Fluids. Follow the prescriber's sick-day plan. **DKA is an emergency: get help** |
| **Pump or sensor failure** | The prescriber's written fallback plan (→ 02-02) |
| **Insulin** | **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.** Heat-exposed: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09. Fridge range 36 to 46 °F (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency). Never ration on your own judgement |
| **Days of insulin left** | ______ (update weekly) |

## Card 4: Water

| | |
|---|---|
| **This household, floor** | **{{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gal a day** (the rationing line) |
| **This household, plan** | **{{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal a day**; two weeks = {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal |
| **Days of water** | Stored gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} |
| **1. Settle** | Let cloudy water settle, then pour it through cloth or a coffee filter |
| **2. Disinfect** | **Boil: a rolling boil for 1 minute** (3 minutes above about 5,000 ft: EPA's line; CDC's is 6,500 ft, use the lower) (EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water), **or** chemicals: **amounts are on → 03-04, not here**, because bleach strength varies by product and age |
| **3. Store** | Covered, cool, dark, labelled with the date |
| **Pool or salt water** | Filtering and boiling **do not remove salt or pool chemicals**. Distillation only (→ 03-03) |
| **Reserves in the house** | Water heater {{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal · pipes · ice (FEMA). **Toilet tanks** (never the bowls) are the last reserve: FEMA says not to drink tank water, so keep it for flushing and washing, or disinfect it first if nothing else is left (→ 03-04), and never if a cleaning tablet or dye is in it (FEMA, Food and Water in an Emergency) |

## Card 5: Carbon monoxide

| | |
|---|---|
| **The floor** | **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** |
| **What it is** | A gas with **no colour, no smell, no taste** that kills silently (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics; → 29-03) |
| **Never indoors** | Generator, grill, charcoal, camp stove, any heater not rated for indoor use, a running vehicle (including in an attached garage, door open or not) |
| **Symptoms** | Headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, confusion, sleepiness. **Several people sick at once, or better outside = suspect CO** |
| **Alarm sounds or you suspect it** | **1. Everyone outside into fresh air, now. 2. Call 911. 3. Nobody goes back in** until it is cleared. Count heads |
| **No 911** | Fresh air is the treatment: rest outside for hours; turn off the source; air the house fully; symptoms can return, so anyone affected takes it easy |
| **Alarms** | Battery CO alarm on every level and outside every sleeping area. Test monthly. We have {{ gear.co_alarms }} |

## Card 6: Severe bleeding

| | |
|---|---|
| **1. Pressure** | Hard, direct, both hands, and **hold** |
| **2. Limb bleeding that will not stop** | **Tourniquet** 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding **stops**. It will hurt. If it still bleeds, a second one above the first (Stop the Bleed, USUHS) |
| **3. The floor** | **Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no help will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).** Write the time on the strap or the skin, and say it aloud. {{choice DC-25}} |
| **4. Body or groin wound** | **Pack** the wound with gauze and press hard |
| **5. Keep them warm** | Cold makes bleeding worse |
| **6. Get help** | → 12-02 |
| **Tourniquets are kept** | ______________________ |

## Card 7: Tornado

| | |
|---|---|
| **Watch** | Conditions favourable: be ready, stay alert |
| **Warning** | Happening or imminent: **go now** |
| **Go to** | {{#if has.shelter_room}}**{{ dwelling.shelter_room }}**{{else}}the lowest floor, the innermost room with no windows: ______________{{/if}} |
| **Do** | Cover head and neck; helmets on children if you have them; shoes on |
| **Take** | Shoes, light, weather radio, phone, water, **rescue medicines and the medical kit** (the house may not be there afterwards) |
| **Not** | Not in a vehicle, not under an overpass (NOAA Storm Prediction Center, Tornado Safety FAQ). {{#if has.mobile_home}}**You live in a mobile home: it is not shelter. Go to a sturdy building before the warning** (→ 17-06).{{else}}A mobile home is not shelter.{{/if}} |
| **Gas smell after** | Get out; shut the gas off only if you know how; call from outside |

Full page: → 17-02, → 17-06 (NWS, Tornado Safety).

## Card 8: Stranded in a vehicle in winter

| | |
|---|---|
| **Stay with the vehicle** | It is shelter, and it is what searchers find (NWS, During a Winter Storm) |
| **Be seen** | Bright cloth on the antenna; dome light on at night when running; hazards sparingly |
| **Before running the engine** | **Clear the exhaust pipe** and **crack a window away from the wind**. About 10 minutes an hour (NWS, During a Winter Storm) |
| **Insulate** | Blankets, everyone together, move arms and legs now and then |
| **Water** | Do not eat snow: melt it |
| **Phone** | Text your location while you have signal, then save the battery |
| **Children** | Watch them constantly: they cool much faster |
| **Frostbite** | At extreme wind chill, minutes. Cover all skin (→ 08-05) |

## Card 9: Power cut and food safety

| | |
|---|---|
| **Keep the fridge and freezer closed** | Refrigerated food about **4 hours**; full freezer about **48 hours**, half full about **24** (USDA/HHS, Food Safety During a Power Outage) |
| **When in doubt, throw it out** | Never taste to test |
| **Power goes to, in order** | 1. Medical devices · 2. Light · 3. Communications · 4. Refrigeration · 5. Everything else (→ 09-01) |
| **Check** | CO alarms · water · the heat plan · the neighbours |
| **Eat down** | Fridge first, then freezer, then pantry |
| **Generator** | **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide") cord.** |

## Card 10: Grab and go

| You have | You take |
|---|---|
| **60 seconds** | People{{#if has.pets}}, pets{{/if}}, **medical kit**, go-bags, phones, keys, wallets |
| **10 minutes** | + document kit, water, food bin, sleeping bags, coats and boots for everyone |
| **30 minutes** | + tools, stove and fuel, extra water, extra clothing (→ 22-05) |

Who carries or leads whom: {{#each children as c}}{{c.label}} → ______ · {{else}}______{{/each}}

Go-bags are at: ______________ · Medical kit is at: ______________{{#if has.pets}} · Pet carriers are at: ______________{{/if}}

## Card 11: Daily priorities when it has gone on a long time

| Every day, in this order |
|---|
| 1. **Medical**: medicines, supplies, rescue medicines in date and in reach |
| 2. **Water**: treated, stored, tomorrow's secured |
| 3. **Warmth or cooling**: the one room, fuel for tomorrow |
| 4. **Food**: cook it, ration it; children eat properly |
| 5. **Sanitation**: waste out, hands washed |
| 6. **Security**: doors, light discipline, awareness |
| 7. **People**: sleep, routine, children, each other |

**Never ration:** drinking water, handwashing, medicine, children's food, sleep. Log the day
(→ 25-05). Shortest clock: ______ days.

## Card 12: Choking and CPR (memory aid: the class governs, → 12-18)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Coughing hard** | Let them cough. Watch |
| **Silent, no air, turning blue** | **Act now** |
| **Under 1 year** | 5 back blows (face down along your forearm) + 5 chest thrusts (two fingers). Repeat. **Never abdominal thrusts on a baby** (MedlinePlus, Choking: infant under 1 year) |
| **Age 1 and up** | 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts (in and up, hard). Alternate until clear |
| **Goes limp** | Start CPR. Remove from the mouth only what you can see |
| **CPR** | Not breathing, or only gasping: **push hard, push fast, centre of the chest, 100 to 120 a minute; 30 pushes : 2 breaths** (MedlinePlus, CPR) |
| **Depth** | Baby about 1½ in (two fingers; cover mouth **and** nose for gentle puffs) · child about 2 in (one or two hands) · adult 2 to 2.4 in (two hands) |
| **Untrained or unwilling to give breaths** | Pushes only |
| **More than one rescuer** | Swap every 2 minutes |

## Card 13: Six knots (utility only: never for climbing or lifting people, → 16-03)

| Knot | Use | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Words** | | **Working end** = the short end you move. **Standing part** = the long rope to the load |
| **Bowline** | A fixed loop | Small loop in the standing part; working end up through it, behind the standing part, back down the loop; snug. The end finishes inside the loop |
| **Taut-line hitch** | An adjustable guy line | Round the anchor; two wraps round the standing part inside the loop; one wrap outside; tuck under itself. Slides by hand, holds under pull |
| **Clove hitch** | Onto a post | Over and around; cross over the standing part; around again; tuck under the second wrap. Add a half hitch: it slips under changing loads |
| **Two half hitches** | Tying off | Round the object, over, behind, up through; repeat in front |
| **Square knot** | Bundles, same-size rope | Right over left and under; left over right and under. It lies flat, or it is a granny: retie. **Not for joining ropes under load** |
| **Trucker's hitch** | Tightening a load | Fix the far end; a small loop in the standing part; pull a fold through it; working end round the anchor, up through the fold; haul; lock with two half hitches |

Text cannot draw a knot: the US Army rigging manual (FM 5-125) plates behind → 16-03 are the
pictures.

## Card 14: Communications (PACE; fill the blanks or this card fails, → 15-03)

PACE = **P**rimary, **A**lternate, **C**ontingency, **E**mergency: four ways to reach each other,
tried in that order.

| | Primary | Alternate | Contingency | Emergency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Local** | Text, then call | Out-of-area contact relays | Radio channel ______ | Go to the meeting place; leave a note |
| **Regional** | Text (it queues) | Out-of-area contact at a set time: ______ | ______________ | ______________ |
| **At a destination** | Call or text home and the out-of-area contact | Destination phones | Radio window: ______ | ______________ |

**Out-of-area contact:** {{ contacts.out_of_area.name }} · {{ contacts.out_of_area.phone }} ·
backup ______________. **No bars:** 911 works on any carrier's tower; some phones can text by
satellite (clear sky). **Weather radio:** {{#each region.home.nwr as t}}{{t.freq}} MHz ({{t.call}}) · {{else}}______ MHz{{/each}}.
**Overdue rule:** no word by ______ hours after departure, the contact calls ______________.

## Card 15: Watch, warning, advisory (→ 29-10)

| Level | Meaning | Do |
|---|---|---|
| **Advisory** | Hazardous but lesser | Adjust plans; errands early; kit in the vehicle |
| **Watch** | Conditions **favourable** | **Get ready now:** water filled, everything charging, tank topped up, plan out. Prepare at the watch, not the warning |
| **Warning** | Happening or imminent | **Act** on the row below |

| Warning | Our action |
|---|---|
| **Tornado** | Shelter spot now, heads covered (Card 7) |
| **Severe thunderstorm** | Inside; away from windows; lightning means indoors (NWS, Lightning Safety) |
| **Blizzard, winter storm, ice storm** | No travel. One-room plan ready; everything charged; expect days without power |
| **Extreme cold** | Outside only for essential minutes; children stay in |
| **Flood or flash flood** | Higher ground. **Never drive into water over a road** (NWS, Flood Safety) |
| **Red flag, fire** | Leave early; do not wait to see (NWS, Wildfire Safety) |
| **Extreme heat** | Shade, fluids, the coolest room; watch children, elders and medicines (NWS, Heat Safety) |
| **Hurricane** | Leave when told to; if staying, the interior room above flood level (Ready.gov, Hurricanes) |

Home hazards rated 2 or 3 move to the top of this card:
{{#each region.home.hazards as z}}{{z.name}} {{z.rating_text}} · {{/each}}

## Card 16: Indoor heaters

| | |
|---|---|
| **Before any heater is lit** | **A battery CO alarm installed and tested** in that room and where people sleep |
| **Only heaters rated for indoor use** | Read the label (→ 29-14). Everything else stays outside |
| **One heater at a time** | Never unattended. Clearances and ventilation **as the manual states** |
| **Overnight while people sleep** | Household choice: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02 |
| **Propane cylinder bigger than 1 lb indoors** | Household choice: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03. Refilling 1-lb cylinders: {{choice DC-03}} → 30-04 |
| **Kerosene** | **1-K only**, clear, no water layer in a jar check. **Gasoline in a kerosene heater = fire or explosion** (University of Missouri Extension, Unvented Portable Kerosene Heaters). Old fuel: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18 |
| **Filling** | **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Outdoors, heater off and cold |
| **Fuel cans** | Read the label aloud, smell, then pour. An unlabelled can is not poured (→ 29-01) |
| **Leak check (propane)** | Soapy water on every joint, every time. Gas smell: valve off, everyone out |
| **Children** | A barrier around the heater; nothing drying on top |
| **Alarm, headache, dizziness, nausea** | Heater off if in reach, **everyone out**, then air the room (Card 5) |

Open-flame cooking and candles indoors: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21. Our heaters:
{{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}} ({{h.model}}) · {{else}}none entered{{/each}}.

## Card 17: Other hazards in one line each

| Hazard | First move | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Earthquake** | **Drop, cover and hold on**; stay inside until the shaking stops; then check for gas and fire (Ready.gov, Earthquakes) | → 17-12 |
| **Hurricane** | Leave when officials say; if not, an interior room above flood level; **never in a flooded car** (Ready.gov, Hurricanes) | → 17-13 |
| **Wildfire or smoke** | Leave early; N95 masks; windows shut; a clean-air room (NWS, Wildfire Safety) | → 17-14 |
| **Extreme heat** | Shade, water, the coolest room; **never leave a child or pet in a car** (NWS, Heat Safety) | → 17-04 |
| **Lightning** | When thunder roars, go indoors; a hard-topped car is next best (NWS, Lightning Safety) | → 17-02 |
| **Flood** | Higher ground; **turn around, do not drown** (NWS, Flood Safety) | → 17-03 |
| **Poisoning** | **Poison Help 1-800-222-1222**; do not make the person vomit unless told to | → 12-17 |
{{#if is.coastal}}| **Tsunami (coast)** | Strong shaking or the sea pulling back: go to high ground or inland at once (Ready.gov, Tsunamis) | → 17-15 |
{{/if}}

## Printing and keeping them current

- **Print at full size, cut, laminate** (or a zip bag and tape). **Punch a corner and keep them
  on a ring** so a set stays together.
- **Where:** fridge · each go-bag · each vehicle · medical kit · shelter spot. **Card 16 goes
  with each heater** too.
- **Every card is a compressed page.** When the page changes, reprint and swap every copy: **a
  stale card in a bag is worse than none.**
- **Cards 2 and 3 are the ones a stranger may have to use.** Make them legible, complete, and
  in the outside pocket.

Related: → 00-02 emergency quick reference · → 00-06 the first 60 minutes · → 25-09 medical
summary · → 25-03 contacts · → 22-03 where the cards live · → 30-01 the floors.

review_pass.notes: Second-dose line re-cited to AAP; renders for all three profiles; no dosing.

pages.body:
# Family medical summary sheet

**What this page is for.** This sheet lets **someone who has never met your family keep them
alive**: a paramedic, an emergency-room nurse, a neighbour, a relative, a shelter volunteer. It
holds conditions, allergies, medicines, devices and contacts, filled from your settings, with
blanks for the rest. **It contains no treatment instructions on purpose.** Those are the
prescribers' written plans, which are attached to it.

> **SAFETY — CRITICAL.**
> - **Fill it in with your prescribers, not from memory**, and have them check it.
> - **Medicines are printed exactly as typed from the bottles.** The binder never works out or
>   changes a dose.
> - **Attach each condition's signed or written plan** (anaphylaxis action plan, pump-failure
>   plan, seizure plan, sick-day plan). A summary without the plans is half a document.

## Do this now

1. **Check every printed line against the bottles and devices**, and fill the blanks at your
   next appointments.
2. **Make copies**: the medical kit (→ 22-06), every go-bag (→ 22-03), every vehicle, one with
   the out-of-area contact{{#if has.child}}, and one at each school or daycare{{/if}}.
3. **Attach the plans** to every copy.
4. **Photograph it and store the photo off-site** (→ 19-03); keep a copy in the document kit
   (→ 19-01).
5. **Re-check it every year and after any change** in medicine, device, weight of a growing
   child, or prescriber (→ 25-10).

## What this sheet is, and is not

| It IS | It is NOT |
|---|---|
| A **record**: conditions, allergies, medicines, devices, contacts | A prescription or a dosing sheet |
| What you hand to a responder | A substitute for the prescribers' written plans |
| A supply snapshot for planning (→ 22-04, → 23-02) | Medical advice of any kind |

**Two rules:** write **exactly** what the label and the prescriber say (medicine, strength,
device model), and **date every version**. An undated medical summary is dangerous because
nobody can tell how old it is.

## First, in a box at the top

{{ai responder-first-three}}

Copy these lines by hand onto an index card for every wallet today, before the full sheet is
finished.

## Household medical summary

```
DATE COMPLETED: ____________   VERSION: ______   COMPLETED BY: ____________
NEXT REVIEW DUE: ____________
ADDRESS (write by hand): __________________________________________
```

Emergency contact (out of area): {{ contacts.out_of_area.name }} · {{ contacts.out_of_area.phone }}

{{#each members as m}}

### {{m.label}} ({{m.role}}, {{m.age_text}})

| | |
|---|---|
| **Full name** | ______________________________ |
| **Date of birth** | ____________ |
| **Weight** | {{m.weight_text}} · re-weighed on ______: ______ |
| **Blood type** | ______ |
| **Conditions** | {{m.conditions}} |
| **Allergies** | {{m.allergies}} |
| **Medicines** | {{m.meds}} (details in the table below) |
| **Pregnant or nursing** | {{m.pregnant_or_nursing}} |
| **Devices** (model and serial; device support phone from the box) | ______________________________ |
| **Plans attached** (name and date of each) | ______________________________ |
| **Other conditions, surgeries, implants** | ______________________________ |
| **Immunisations; last tetanus booster** | ______________________________ |
| **Glasses or hearing aids** (prescription, where spares are) | ______________________________ |
| **Prescribers and phones** | ______________________________ |
| **Pharmacy and phone** | ______________________________ |
| **Insurance and member number** | ______________________________ |
| **Medical ID worn? Wording** | ______________________________ |
| **Communication needs** (language, hearing, memory) | ______________________________ |
{{/each}}

## Medicines, exactly as typed from the bottles

| Person | Medicine | Strength | Schedule | Refrigerated | If doses are missed (prescriber's words) | Where kept | Expiry | Days on hand |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as x}}| {{x.member}} | {{x.name}} | {{x.strength}} | {{x.schedule}} | {{x.refrigerated}} | {{x.if_missed}} | {{x.where_kept}} | {{x.expiry}} | {{x.days_on_hand}} |
{{else}}| none entered | | | | | | | | |
{{/each}}

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}**Refrigerated medicine is in this household.** It must not freeze; **a frozen-then-thawed
insulin vial or pen is discarded** (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency; → 29-07).
{{/if}}

## Allergies

| Person | Allergen | Severity | Carries epinephrine |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each allergies as a}}| {{a.member}} | {{a.allergen}} | {{a.severity}} | {{a.carries_epinephrine}} |
{{else}}| none entered | | | |
{{/each}}

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}**Anaphylaxis risk in this household. Epinephrine is the first treatment; antihistamines are
not. A second dose may be needed** (AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan; AAAAI,
Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan). Epinephrine locations, all of them: ______________________
Total devices: ______ · earliest expiry: ______
{{/if}}

## Supply snapshot (update weekly in a long event; → 23-02)

| Item | Count | Days at normal use | Earliest expiry |
|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as x}}| {{x.member}}: {{x.name}} | ______ | {{x.days_on_hand}} | {{x.expiry}} |
{{/each}}| Device supplies: ______________ | ______ | ______ | ______ |
| Rescue medicines: ______________ | ______ | n/a: never rationed | ______ |

{{#if has.pets}}
## Pets

| Pet | Count | Medicines | Food per day | Vet and phone | Microchip numbers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each pets as p}}| {{p.type}} | {{p.count}} | {{p.medications}} | {{p.food_per_day}} | ______________ | ______________ |
{{/each}}
{{/if}}

## Household notes

```
BLOOD TYPES (all): ______________________________________________
DRUG ALLERGIES (all, together): _________________________________
ADVANCE DIRECTIVES / MEDICAL POWER OF ATTORNEY, where kept: ______
WHERE THE MEDICAL KIT LIVES: ____________________________________
WHERE THE PLANS ARE POSTED: _____________________________________
COPIES OF THIS SHEET ARE AT: ____________________________________
```

## Gear

**Buy toward:** a waterproof sleeve or laminator for each copy, **medical ID jewellery or tags**
for anyone with a life-threatening condition or allergy, a small stapler to attach the plans, a
phone for the off-site photo, and **each prescriber's written plan, printed, signed and dated**.

**If you do not have it:** a hand-written index card carrying the box at the top of this page
is a real, useful substitute: **write it today.** Perfect is the enemy of having anything at all
in a wallet.

## When it goes stale

The sheet does not run out; **its accuracy does, quickly.**

- **About a year at most**, and **at once** after any change of medicine, device, prescriber,
  or a growing child's weight.
- **Never make fewer copies to save paper.** A copy that is not where the emergency is does
  nothing.
- **Re-check at the annual review and after every appointment** (→ 25-10).
- The cards (→ 25-08) carry the emergency part, but not the prescriber contacts, device serials
  or supply counts that make **this** sheet the one a clinic needs.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** keep it current and spread around. Most of its value is in ordinary
  life: a hospital visit, a babysitter, a school form.
- **B (moving):** it travels in the medical kit and the document kit, and a copy is with the
  out-of-area contact. **It lets someone else speak for your family** if you cannot (→ 01-07).
- **C (establish):** it is what you hand a clinician, a pharmacist or a mutual-aid group in a
  new place. Keep the supply snapshot current: it decides what you have to ask for (→ 12-07).

Related: → 22-06 the medical kit this lives in · → 25-08 the card version · → 19-01 document kit
· → 19-03 off-site copies · → 25-03 prescriber contacts · → 25-10 review · → 01-07 medical needs
on the road.

pages.body:
# Annual review checklist

**What this page is for.** A binder that is never reviewed becomes fiction. Numbers drift,
children grow, medicines change, and gear expires. **One afternoon a year** keeps every other
page true, and ends with a **rebuild of this binder** from your updated settings. Pick a fixed
date (a birthday, New Year, the first cold snap) and never move it.

## Do this now

1. **Put a recurring yearly date on the calendar** and block three hours. Ours: ____________.
2. **Do this year's review now if it has been more than a year.** The most common failure of
   any binder is that it was correct once.
3. **Do it with every adult present.** Half the value is the conversation; a plan only one
   adult knows has a single point of failure.

## The rhythm this binder runs on

| How often | What | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Monthly** | Press every smoke and CO alarm's test button | → 29-12 |
| **Twice a year** | Kit checks, expiry dates, children's sizes, inventory, a blackout weekend | → 22-03, → 22-04, → 24-04 |
| **Each season** | That season's skills, garden and wood work | → 24-03 |
| **Before each device's own deadline** | Anything a medical device or app needs renewed (a sensor, an app, a battery), written on that condition's page | Section 02 |
| **Yearly (this page)** | Everything else: plans, contacts, budget, the honest assessment, and a rebuild | |

The annual review **does not repeat** the twice-a-year checks; it assumes they happened and
looks at what nobody else looks at.

## What goes stale, worst first

1. **Medical**: prescriptions, devices, weights of growing children, expiry dates, prescribers.
2. **The children**: sizes, abilities, needs, what they can be taught, what frightens them.
3. **Contacts**: people move, numbers change, offices reorganise (→ 25-03).
4. **Numbers**: water, calories, days of supply, all of which change as children grow.
5. **Gear**: expiry, wear, batteries, things that broke and were never replaced.
6. **The plan itself**: destinations, routes, the triggers for leaving.

## The review

```
REVIEW DATE: ____________   PEOPLE PRESENT: ______________________________
LAST REVIEW: ____________
```

### 1. Medical (always first)

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Family medical summary re-checked against the bottles and devices, and reprinted | → 25-09 |
| [ ] | Each prescriber's written plan current, re-signed or re-dated | Section 02 |
{{#if has.epinephrine}}| [ ] | **Every epinephrine device counted and dated in every location**; count and earliest expiry written on → 22-04 | → 02-03 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Every rescue medicine counted and in date | → 22-06 |
| [ ] | Every daily medicine and device supply counted; days on hand updated in settings | → 22-04 |
| [ ] | Asked each prescriber about emergency and 90-day supply this year | → 12-07 |
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}| [ ] | Cold-chain gear tested: the cooler runs a day on its battery and holds range on a thermometer | → 29-07 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Potassium iodide, if kept: in date, with the published age table attached | → 27-06 |
| [ ] | First-aid and trauma supplies checked and restocked | → 12-01 |
| [ ] | Tetanus status current for every adult | → 12-04 |
{{#if has.child}}| [ ] | **Every child weighed and measured**; new weights in settings and on the summary sheet | → 25-09 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Spare glasses and written glasses prescriptions current; hearing-aid batteries | → 02-23 |

Shortest medical clock this year: ______________ = ______ days.

### 2. Life safety

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Every smoke alarm tested; batteries replaced | → 29-12 |
| [ ] | Every CO alarm tested; batteries replaced; one on every level and outside every sleeping area | → 08-02 |
| [ ] | Fire extinguishers in date, pressure gauge in the green, reachable | → 29-12 |
| [ ] | Chimney, fireplace or stove inspected and cleaned{{#if !has.fireplace}} (if any){{/if}} | → 06-09 |
| [ ] | Every heater and fuel appliance checked | → 08-04 |
| [ ] | Gas and water shutoffs found and operable; every adult knows them | → 00-04 |
| [ ] | Shelter spot cleared and stocked | → 17-06 |
| [ ] | Window escape routes clear; ladders for upstairs bedrooms | → 24-02 |
| [ ] | Every decision card still says what the household wants; change any in settings | → 30-02 to → 30-30 |

### 3. Inventory and numbers

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Full inventory done | → 22-04 |
| [ ] | Days of supply recalculated for every consumable | → 23-02 |
| [ ] | Household changes (new people, new ages, pets) entered in settings so water and calorie figures update | → 25-02 |
| [ ] | Stored water rotated; bleach replaced (note the purchase date) | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Food rotated; anything near expiry moved to the kitchen | → 04-10 |
| [ ] | Home-canned jars checked; methods re-checked against current tested recipes (NCHFP) | → 04-05 |
| [ ] | Wood counted and seasoning noted; stored fuel checked and dated | → 06-03, → 06-06 |
| [ ] | Batteries checked; power banks and stations cycled | → 09-03 |

Shortest supply this year: ______________ = ______ days · last year: ______ days · better /
worse?

{{#if has.child}}
### 4. The children (the fastest-changing part of the plan)

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Clothing and boots fit **now**; the next two sizes on hand | → 11-02, → 11-09 |
| [ ] | Go-bag contents re-sized | → 22-03 |
| [ ] | Diaper size and feeding needs current | → 20-05, → 20-06 |
| [ ] | Vehicle kits restocked with current-size children's gear | → 22-05 |
| [ ] | What each child can be taught this year has moved on | → 20-04 |
| [ ] | Jobs updated to what they can actually do now | → 20-07 |
| [ ] | School or daycare has current plans, rescue medicines and contacts | → 25-09 |
{{else}}
### 4. The people

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Clothing and boots still fit and are sound | → 11-01 |
| [ ] | Anyone whose needs changed this year (a new condition, a pregnancy, an elder moving in) entered in settings | → 29-15 |
{{/if}}

### 5. Kits and gear

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Go-bags emptied, checked, repacked and **weighed** | → 22-03 |
| [ ] | Vehicle kits refreshed; seasonal add-on in before the season | → 22-05 |
| [ ] | Medical go-kit checked against its page | → 22-06 |
| [ ] | Water filters: element life noted; spares on hand | → 03-09 |
| [ ] | Tools sharpened, oiled, repaired | → 16-02 |
{{#if has.firearms}}| [ ] | Firearms cleaned, stored locked, ammunition counted | → 14-05, → 14-14 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Radios tested; batteries checked; SAME code confirmed | → 15-01 |
| [ ] | Any frequencies, repeaters or radio licences on → 25-03 re-checked | → 25-03 |
| [ ] | Shielded spares (if kept) opened, tested and re-sealed | → 27-03 |
{{#if has.power_station}}| [ ] | Power stations and solar tested under load; output recorded | → 09-09 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.generator}}| [ ] | Generator run under load outdoors; oil changed as the manual says | → 09-15 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Anything that broke this year: repaired or replaced? | |

### 6. Documents, money, records

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Document kit current (IDs, insurance, deeds, titles) | → 19-01 |
| [ ] | Off-site copies refreshed; photos of the house and contents updated (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a Disaster) | → 19-03 |
| [ ] | Insurance reviewed: coverage, deductible, flood, contents | → 19-04 |
| [ ] | Cash on hand refreshed in small bills | → 19-02 |
| [ ] | Password and record backups opened and readable | → 19-03 |
| [ ] | Advance directives and medical powers of attorney current and findable | → 25-09 |

### 7. Contacts and community

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Every number on → 25-03 checked by calling | → 25-03 |
| [ ] | Out-of-area contact confirmed and still willing | → 15-03 |
| [ ] | Neighbours: added anyone this year? | → 18-01 |
| [ ] | Meeting places still valid (anything built or demolished?) | → 00-04 |
| [ ] | Contact cards reprinted and handed out | → 25-08 |

### 8. Skills and practice

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Skills checklist re-scored for every adult | → 24-01 |
| [ ] | Drills run this year: ______ | → 24-02 |
| [ ] | Blackout weekends run this year: ______ | → 24-04 |
| [ ] | Measurements from the blackout weekend copied into → 23-02 | → 24-04 |
| [ ] | Three skills chosen for next year: ________ ________ ________ | → 24-01 |

### 9. The plan itself (the conversation, not the checklist)

| ✔ | Question | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Staying home: still workable? What changed? | → 01-01 |
| [ ] | The triggers for leaving: still the right ones? | → 01-02 |
| [ ] | Routes re-driven; closures and changes noted | → 25-04 |
| [ ] | **Destination: any progress this year?** Status: ______ · one concrete step for next year: ______ | → 01-05 |
| [ ] | Household roles still make sense | → 00-07 |
| [ ] | Anything in this binder we now know is **wrong**? ______________ | → 25-05 |

> **The destination line is the one to be honest about.** It is the gap that cannot be closed
> by buying something. **A conversation, a visit, an agreement, a piece of ground is worth more
> than another year of gear.**

### 10. The binder itself

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Settings updated with everything this review changed: people, ages, weights, medicines, gear, contacts, destinations, decision cards | → 29-15 |
| [ ] | **Binder rebuilt from the saved profile file**, and the new copy installed on every device; old copies deleted | → 00-10 |
| [ ] | The review-notes page of the new copy read; anything it flags fixed | → 29-15 |
| [ ] | Notes from the binder change log (→ 25-05) carried into settings or written onto the pages they concern | → 25-05 |
| [ ] | Small or Large: still the right size? {{#if size.large}}(this is Large){{else}}(this is Small){{/if}} | → 00-09 |
| [ ] | The saved profile file backed up off-site | → 19-03 |

### 11. Spending

| ✔ | Check | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Spending order re-ranked from this year's gaps | → 22-07 |
| [ ] | Budget for next year: ______ | → 26-09 |
| [ ] | Top three purchases: 1. ______ 2. ______ 3. ______ | → 26-09 |
| [ ] | Time-sensitive items (seed, wood, children's sizes) ordered or scheduled | → 23-04 |

### 12. The one-page summary (write it, keep it)

```
WHAT CHANGED THIS YEAR: ___________________________________________
WHAT WE LEARNED (drills, blackout weekend, real events): __________
___________________________________________________________________
BIGGEST REMAINING GAP: ____________________________________________
THE ONE THING TO FIX NEXT YEAR: ___________________________________
NEXT REVIEW: ____________
```

## How to run it well

- **Three hours, every adult, no screens** except the settings page at the end. Work in order.
- **Do sections 1 and 2 first**: if the afternoon collapses, those are the ones that mattered.
- **Argue about section 9.** It is the only section that is a judgement, not a check.
- **Write everything down.** Next year's review starts by reading this year's summary.
{{#if has.child}}- **Make the children part of it** where you can: a child repacking their own go-bag is doing
  the review and learning the plan at once (→ 20-04).
{{/if}}

**What you need:** this checklist printed, a pencil, a clipboard, a luggage scale for the
go-bags, fresh batteries for every alarm, a phone for record photos, and the year's replacement
consumables (bleach, batteries, expired medicines replaced through the pharmacy), so the review
ends with things fixed rather than a list of things to fix. **If you have nothing else**, the
review needs only time and honesty; but a checklist beats a habit, because what goes stale is
exactly what you stop noticing.

## When it goes stale

- **About twelve months** before medical, contacts and children's sizes are meaningfully wrong.
- **If you only have an hour:** sections 1, 2 and 4.
- **Between reviews,** the twice-a-year checks (→ 22-03, → 22-04) carry the load.
- **An unreviewed binder is a confident document full of stale numbers**, which is more
  dangerous than none.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the annual review is a luxury of normal times; do it while it is easy.
- **B (moving):** no review while moving; **what you reviewed last is what you have.**
- **C (establish):** review **every three months** for the first year at a new place, and
  change the home base in settings and rebuild: water, fuel, routes, neighbours, seasons and
  numbers are all different there.

Related: → 22-04 inventory · → 23-02 runway · → 24-01 skills · → 24-03 seasonal cadence ·
→ 25-09 medical summary · → 25-03 contacts · → 22-07 spending · → 29-15 how the binder is
rebuilt · → 01-05 the gap this review keeps asking about.

pages.body:
# Pre-disaster acquisition checklist

**What this section holds.** 9 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 26-01 **How to run the check**: This section is the clipboard version of the binder.
- → 26-02 **Walk the house, room by room**: The checklists are organised by subject (water, heat, tools).
- → 26-03 **Checklist 1: life safety and medical**: The first sheet of the walk (→ 26-01), and the one to do properly even if you do no other.
- → 26-04 **Checklist 2: water and food**: The second sheet of the walk (→ 26-01).
- → 26-05 **Checklist 3: heat, power and light**: The third sheet of the walk (→ 26-01): how you will stay warm (or cool), make power, see after dark, and cook when the grid is down.
- → 26-06 **Checklist 4: sanitation, clothing, tools, security and comms**: The fourth sheet of the walk (→ 26-01): the weeks-to-months items.
- → 26-07 **Checklist 5: children, elders, pets, records and morale**: The last sheet of the walk (→ 26-01): the months items, and the cheapest.
- → 26-08 **Expiry and rotation tracker**: Expiry is the failure nobody notices until the morning it matters.
- → 26-09 **The result: ranked shopping list and budget**: The walk is not finished until this page is filled in.

pages.body:
# How to run the check

**What this page is for.** This section is the clipboard version of the binder. → 22-01 says
**what** to own and **why**; this section finds **what you already have** and **what to buy
next**. You walk the house once with a pencil and these sheets, mark what you find, and finish
with a ranked shopping list. **About two hours, two people, one afternoon.** No experience
needed: every item says what it is for and points to the page that explains it.

## Do this now

1. **Print (or open on a second device) checklists → 26-03 to → 26-07**, plus → 26-08 (expiry
   dates) and → 26-09 (the shopping list). Put the printouts on a clipboard.
2. **Block two hours and do it with another adult** if there is one. One reads items, the other
   looks. It goes twice as fast, and you both learn where things are.
3. **Start with → 26-03 (life safety and medical).** If the afternoon collapses, that is the
   one that mattered.
4. **Finish by filling in → 26-09.** A walk that produces no shopping list was just tidying.

## What this section is, and what it is not

| | This section (26) | The other two |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Do we have it? What do we buy? | → 22-01: what should we own, and why |
| **Form** | Tick-box sheets you carry | → 22-04: how many, to work out days of supply |
| **Result** | A ranked shopping list (→ 26-09) | → 23-02: the shortest supply in the house |
| **How often** | Once, then yearly | → 22-04 twice a year |

**Do not do all three at once.** Run this section first: you cannot count what you have not
found. → 22-04 comes later, when you want quantities rather than presence.

## The four marks

Use these four and nothing else.

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **✔** | **Have it, it works, and I know where it is.** All three, or it is not a ✔ |
| **~** | **Partly**: some but not enough, or it needs a spare, a battery or a repair |
| **✗** | **Do not have it** |
| **n/a** | Genuinely does not apply to us |

**The "~" is where the truth lives.** Most households are mostly "~": a filter with no spare
element, a canner with no lids, one headlamp for {{ household.size }} people. **A "~" is
usually cheaper to fix than a "✗" and matters just as much.**

## Four rules for an honest walk

1. **Touch it.** If you did not lay hands on it, it is not a ✔. Memory is optimistic, and things
   get borrowed, moved and used up.
2. **Test anything with a battery or a moving part.** Turn on every flashlight. Press every
   alarm's test button. A dead device is a ✗.
3. **Write the location in the same pass.** Half the value of this walk is that every adult ends
   up knowing where things are.
4. **Read every expiry date as you go** (how: → 29-14) and copy it to → 26-08.

## The order, and why

The checklists run in the order that things hurt people, not the order that is fun to shop for:

| # | Checklist | Why it is here |
|---|---|---|
| **→ 26-03** | **Life safety and medical** | Minutes to hours: CO alarms, rescue medicines, the trauma kit, every daily medicine{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}. **This household has refrigerated medicine**{{/if}}{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}. **This household has anaphylaxis risk**{{/if}} |
| **→ 26-04** | **Water and food** | Days. Water is the first shortage in almost every emergency (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply) |
| **→ 26-05** | **Heat, power and light** | Days. {{#if is.cold_winters}}In your winters, heat is a life-safety item too.{{else}}{{#if is.hot_summers}}In your summers, cooling is a life-safety item too.{{else}}A long power cut changes everything (American Red Cross, Power Outage Safety).{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}} Power for medical devices is here.{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}} Power for oxygen is here.{{/if}} |
| **→ 26-06** | **Sanitation, shelter, tools, security, comms** | Weeks |
| **→ 26-07** | **Children, pets, records, morale** | Months, and the records cost almost nothing and cannot be replaced if lost (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a Disaster) |

**Food is not first.** Most people start there because it is the easy, satisfying purchase. It is
rarely what runs out first.

## Two hours, roughly

```
0:00   Print, clipboard, pencil, phone for photos.
0:05   26-03 LIFE SAFETY & MEDICAL: do this one properly
0:35   26-04 WATER & FOOD: kitchen, pantry, basement, garage
1:05   26-05 HEAT, POWER & LIGHT: garage, shed, junk drawers, vehicles
1:25   26-06 SANITATION, SHELTER, TOOLS, SECURITY, COMMS: garage and workshop
1:45   26-07 CHILDREN, PETS, RECORDS, MORALE: closets, files, bedrooms
1:55   26-08 copy every expiry date you found
2:00   26-09 fill in the shopping list. STOP. Do not shop tonight.
```

**Do not shop the same day.** Sleep on it, then buy in → 26-09's order, which is → 22-07's
order: what hurts people soonest, then what cannot be bought later.

## What to bring

- **A pencil** (marks change), a clipboard and the sheets.
- **A phone or camera**: photograph each room and open container as you go. That record is also
  your insurance and disaster-assistance evidence (IRS; → 19-04).
- **A tape measure and a kitchen or luggage scale**, if you want quantities as well.
- **A box** for everything expired, broken or the wrong size. Deal with it at the end rather
  than interrupting the walk.
- **A cheap battery tester**: it turns "probably fine" into ✔ or ✗ in two seconds.

## What people always find

Expect these, and do not be discouraged:

1. **Dead batteries** in half the flashlights.
2. **Expired medicine**, usually including something that matters.
3. **Clothing and boots that no longer fit**{{#if has.child}}, often a child's whole current size{{/if}}.
4. **One of something everyone needs.**
5. **A tool with no consumable**: a filter with no element, a saw with no file, a canner with no
   lids.
6. **Far more food than expected, and far less water.**

## After the walk

1. **Fill in → 26-09** and buy in that order.
2. **Then do → 22-04** when you want quantities; it feeds the days-of-supply math on → 23-02.
3. **Re-run this section yearly** (→ 25-10), and re-run → 26-08 twice a year: expiry dates move
   faster than anything else.
4. **Update settings** with anything you found (gear, medicines, fuel on hand) and rebuild the
   binder so the numbers on every page are yours (→ 29-15).

**If you have nothing to print with:** any notebook and pencil. The method matters, not the
stationery. **The one thing not to do is the walk from memory.**

## When it goes stale

- A completed walk is good for about a year, less with growing children.
- **Short on time?** Do → 26-03 alone: a fraction of the sheets and most of the risk.
- **A guessed inventory produces confident, wrong decisions**, which is worse than knowing you
  do not know.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** this is a Phase A job by definition: it only works while shops are
  open.
- **B (moving):** irrelevant while moving. What you own is what you have.
- **C (establish):** re-run the whole section in the first week at a new place, against what
  actually arrived.

Related: → 26-02 the room-by-room route · → 26-03 to → 26-07 the checklists · → 26-09 the result
· → 22-01 what to own and why · → 22-07 the spending order · → 22-04 quantities · → 23-02 days of
supply · → 25-10 the yearly re-run. A national starting list: Ready.gov, Build A Kit.
