pages.body:
# Walk the house, room by room

**What this page is for.** The checklists are organised by subject (water, heat, tools). Your
home is organised by room. This page is the route that joins the two: walk it once, in order,
and you cover everything without doubling back. **Photograph each room and each open container
as you go**: that record is also your insurance evidence (IRS, Reconstructing Records After a
Disaster; → 19-04).

Our home: {{ dwelling.type }}, {{ home.setting }}. Basement: {{ dwelling.basement }}. Water:
{{ dwelling.water_supply }}. Sewer: {{ dwelling.sewer }}. Main heat: {{ dwelling.primary_heat }}.

## Do this now

1. **Follow the route below in order.** It ends at the door with the go-bags, which is where the
   walk should finish.
2. **Check the fixed safety items where they are** (alarms, extinguishers, shutoffs). They
   cannot be judged from a shelf.
3. **Open every closed container.** The unlabelled bucket in the basement is exactly what this
   walk is for.

## The route

Work from the inside rooms outward and top down, so you never carry things past a room you have
finished. Skip any room you do not have; do not skip a room because it is messy.

### 1. Kitchen

| Look for | Checklist |
|---|---|
| Pantry staples, canned goods, oils, salt, sugar{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}; **the allergen-safe bin**{{/if}} | → 26-04 |
| Fridge and freezer contents (and what a two-day power cut would cost) | → 26-04 |
| Water containers, bottled water, filter, bleach (**note the purchase date**) | → 26-04 |
| Pots big enough to boil water, cast iron, a manual can opener, a kettle | → 26-04, → 26-05 |
| Canning gear: canner, jars, **lids** (single-use: count them) | → 26-04 |
| Refrigerated medicine, if it lives here: is it out of children's reach? | → 26-03 |
| First-aid kit if it lives here; fire extinguisher; **smoke alarm nearby** | → 26-03 |
| Matches, lighters, candles in drawers | → 26-05 |

**The kitchen question:** *if the power went off right now, what could I cook, and how?*

### 2. Bathrooms

Medicine cabinet (**every expiry date: copy to → 26-08**), over-the-counter medicines,
first-aid supplies, soap, toilet paper, menstrual supplies{{#if has.infant}}, diapers and wipes{{/if}},
**spare glasses**, a thermometer. **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or
chlorine products.**

**The bathroom question:** *how many days of every medicine are actually here?*

### 3. Bedrooms and closets

Base layers, coats, boots, hats, mittens, wool socks: **for each person, in the size that fits
now**. Blankets, sleeping bags (note the temperature rating), spare bedding.{{#if has.child}}
**Each child's next two sizes.**{{/if}} A smoke alarm in or outside every sleeping area, and a CO
alarm outside every sleeping area (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

**The bedroom question:** *could everyone dress for {{#if is.cold_winters}}the coldest night here ({{ region.home.record_low_f }} °F on record){{else}}a cold, wet night{{/if}}, right now?*

{{#if has.child}}
### 4. Children's rooms

Comfort items, children's medicines (out of reach), books and games that need no screen,
whistles, clothing in the next sizes{{#if has.infant}}; diapers and wipes at the **current** size,
formula and feeding gear, carriers{{/if}}.

**The children's question:** *what will each child need in the next three months that we do not
have?*
{{/if}}

### 5. Living areas

Lighting: lamps, candles, headlamps, flashlights: **turn each one on**. Board games, cards,
books, paper and pencils.{{#if has.fireplace}} Fireplace tools; the damper works.{{/if}} Blackout
curtains.

### 6. {{#if has.basement}}Basement and utility room{{else}}Utility closet or laundry{{/if}}

| Look for | Checklist |
|---|---|
| **Water heater**{{#if has.water_heater_tank}} ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal){{/if}}: **find the drain valve** | → 26-04 |
| **Water main shutoff. Operate it.**{{#if has.gas_any}} **Gas shutoff and the tool it needs**{{/if}} (FEMA, Utility Shut-off and Safety) | → 26-06 |
| Electrical panel: which breaker is which; the main breaker (→ 29-04) | → 26-05 |
| Bulk food storage, buckets, mylar, cool storage space | → 26-04 |
| Bucket-toilet supplies, cover material, liners, bleach | → 26-06 |
| Sump pump and any backup | → 26-06 |
{{#if has.well}}| **Well pump, pressure tank, and how the pump is wired** | → 03-10 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.septic}}| Septic access and what a long outage means for it | → 13-12 |
{{/if}}

**The utility question:** *can every adult find and operate every shutoff in the dark?*

### 7. {{#if has.garage}}Garage, shed{{else}}Storage space, shed or storage unit{{/if}}

| Look for | Checklist |
|---|---|
| Hand tools, axes, saws, files, sharpening stones, vise | → 26-06 |
| **Fuel: propane cylinders, gasoline, kerosene, stabiliser**: labelled, caps tight, away from ignition. Where fuel is stored is a household choice: {{choice DC-05}} → 30-06 | → 26-05 |
| Generator, solar gear, batteries, power banks, chargers, extension cords | → 26-05 |
| Cordage, tape, fasteners, tarps, plastic sheeting, lumber | → 26-06 |
| Camping gear: stove, lanterns, sleeping pads, tent | → 26-05, → 26-06 |
| Garden tools, seed, containers, hose, compost | → 26-04 |
| Bicycles, tubes, patch kit, pump, wagon{{#if is.snow_region}}, sled{{/if}} | → 26-06 |
| Firearms, ammunition by calibre, cleaning kit, spare parts: **locked** | → 26-06 |

**Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.**
**The garage question:** *which tool do I own whose consumable I do not?*

### 8. Vehicles

{{#each vehicles as v}}- {{v.type_text}}: kit, blankets, shovel, traction, jump pack, first aid, water,{{#if has.child}} children's gear in the current size,{{/if}} paper maps, cash, **fuel level**, spare tyre and jack.
{{else}}- No vehicle entered. If you borrow or rent one in an emergency, the vehicle kit (→ 22-05) goes with you.
{{/each}}

Note anything a parked car's summer heat or winter cold has ruined (→ 22-05).
**The vehicle question:** *if we were stranded tonight, in tonight's weather, for twelve hours?*

### 9. Office and files

Documents (IDs, passports, deeds, titles, insurance, prescriptions), cash, backup drive,
**off-site copies**, printed contact list, this binder on a charged device. **Photograph the
document kit** (→ 19-03).
**The office question:** *if the house burned tonight, what could we not replace?*

### 10. Yard and outside{{#if has.apartment}} (balcony, building, shared spaces){{/if}}

{{#if has.apartment}}Stairwells and exits (two ways out), the building's water and gas shutoffs and who has the
keys, any storage unit, a balcony for a grill or solar panel if the building allows it.{{else}}Firewood: **how much, and is it really seasoned?** Rain barrels and gutters, garden beds,
{{#if has.pool}}the pool or hot tub and its equipment, {{/if}}{{#if has.outdoor_fire}}the fire pit or outdoor fireplace, {{/if}}fencing, outdoor
lighting, downspouts{{#if is.snow_region}}, snow shovels{{/if}}.{{/if}}
**The outside question:** *how many days of cooking and heating are really out there?*

### 11. Finish at the door

Go-bags: **open each one and check it against → 22-03**, weigh it, check every expiry, and
re-size the clothing inside.{{#if has.pets}} Pet carriers.{{/if}} The medical kit.
**The door question:** *could we be out of here in sixty seconds with everything that matters?*

### 12. Anything kept somewhere else

The rooms cannot answer this one: **what already lives somewhere else, and what should?**

{{#each destinations as d}}- **{{d.name}}** ({{d.status_text}}): what is already there? ______ · what should ride there on the next visit? ______ · has anyone there agreed to hold it, and where? ______
{{else}}- No destination entered. If you agree one later, a tote per visit beats hauling everything on the worst day (→ 01-05).
{{/each}}
- Storage unit, workplace, a relative's house: ______________________
- Where is the list of things kept elsewhere, so it counts in → 22-04? ______________________

## Fixed safety items: check these where they are

| ✔ | Item |
|---|---|
| [ ] | **Smoke alarm** in or near every sleeping area and on every level: test pressed, battery fresh (we have {{ gear.smoke_alarms }}) |
| [ ] | **CO alarms** on every level and outside every sleeping area: test pressed (we have {{ gear.co_alarms }}) (→ 08-02) |
| [ ] | **Fire extinguishers**: in date, reachable, every adult knows how (PASS: → 29-12) (we have {{ gear.extinguishers }}) |
| [ ] | **Water main shutoff**: found, **operated**, the tool present if one is needed |
| [ ] | **Gas shutoff**{{#if !has.gas_any}} (none per settings){{/if}}: found; the wrench hung beside it; every adult has seen it |
| [ ] | **Electrical panel**: labelled; every adult knows the main breaker |
| [ ] | **Water heater drain valve**: found, and a hose that fits it (→ 03-02) |
| [ ] | **Shelter spot**{{#if has.shelter_room}} ({{ dwelling.shelter_room }}){{/if}}: clear, stocked, shoes and a light there (→ 17-06) |
| [ ] | **Window escape routes** clear; ladders for upstairs bedrooms |
| [ ] | **Fuel** stored away from the living space and ignition, in labelled containers (→ 06-06) |

## The room-by-room tally

```
ROOM              ✔    ~    ✗    BIGGEST GAP FOUND
Kitchen         ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Bathrooms       ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Bedrooms        ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Children's      ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Living areas    ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Utility         ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Garage / shed   ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Vehicles        ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Office / files  ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Outside         ____ ____ ____  ________________________________
Go-bags         ____ ____ ____  ________________________________

PHOTOS TAKEN? ____    STORED OFF-SITE? ____        (19-03)
```

**What you need:** a clipboard, pencils, a battery tester, a headlamp (basements and crawl
spaces), a tape measure, and a phone for photos. Nothing else but time; **do not skip the photo
record**: it takes minutes and it is what an insurer asks for.

## When it goes stale

- The walk is good for a year; **the expiry dates you collect are good for months**.
- **If you only walk three places,** walk the **bathroom cabinet, the garage and the go-bags**:
  that is where the worst gaps hide.
- Re-walk the go-bags on the two kit-check dates (→ 22-03), and everything yearly (→ 25-10).

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** the whole route.
- **B (moving):** only the vehicle and go-bag stops matter.
- **C (establish):** re-walk everything in the first week; a new building has different
  shutoffs, storage and hazards.

Related: → 26-01 the method · → 26-03 to → 26-07 the checklists · → 26-08 expiry · → 08-02 CO
alarms · → 06-06 fuel storage · → 03-02 the water heater as a reserve · → 19-03 and → 19-04 the
photo record · → 22-03 the go-bag check · → 00-04 shutoff photos.

pages.body:
# Checklist 1: life safety and medical

**What this page is for.** The first sheet of the walk (→ 26-01), and the one to do properly
even if you do no other. It covers the alarms that warn you of fire and carbon monoxide, every
medicine and device someone in the household depends on, and the first-aid kit. **No quantity on
this page is a recommendation**: amounts come from your prescriptions and your prescribers.

> **SAFETY — CRITICAL.**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** A battery CO alarm is the cheapest life-saving item in the house (CDC, Carbon
>   Monoxide Poisoning: Basics; → 29-03).
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.**
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.**

**Marks:** ✔ have it, it works, I know where it is · ~ partly, or needs a spare · ✗ do not have ·
n/a

## A. Alarms and fixed safety (check these where they are)

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Where / notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **CO alarm, battery or battery-backup type, on every level and outside every sleeping area** (we have {{ gear.co_alarms }}) | | → 08-02 |
| [ ] | A CO alarm in any room where anything burns{{#if has.unvented_heater}} (**you own an unvented heater**){{/if}}, installed and tested **before** it is lit | | → 08-02 |
| [ ] | Spare batteries for every alarm | | |
| [ ] | **Smoke alarm in every sleeping area, outside each one, and on every level**, tested (we have {{ gear.smoke_alarms }}) (USFA, Smoke Alarms) | | → 29-12 |
| [ ] | Fire extinguishers, in date, reachable (we have {{ gear.extinguishers }}) | | → 29-12 |
| [ ] | Every adult has operated the **gas shutoff**{{#if !has.gas_any}} (none per settings){{/if}} and knows where the tool is | | → 00-04 |
| [ ] | Every adult has operated the **water main** | | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Escape ladder for any upstairs bedroom | | → 24-02 |

> **The CO alarm is the best value per dollar in this binder.** Bringing anything that burns
> indoors in an outage is the most likely way a household dies, and it is cheap to detect.

## B. Every medicine someone depends on

Printed from settings, exactly as typed. Count against the bottles.

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Person | Medicine | Strength | Refrigerated | On hand | Earliest expiry | Days on hand |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as x}}| [ ] | {{x.member}} | {{x.name}} | {{x.strength}} | {{x.refrigerated}} | ______ | {{x.expiry}} | {{x.days_on_hand}} |
{{else}}| [ ] | none entered | | | | | | |
{{/each}}| [ ] | Any medicine not yet in settings: ______________ | | | | ______ | ______ | ______ |

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Page |
|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **A written list of every prescription**, and the family medical summary filled in | → 25-09 |
| [ ] | Asked each prescriber this year about emergency supply, 90-day fills and early-refill overrides: Y / N | → 12-07 |
| [ ] | Each condition's written plan from the prescriber, laminated | Section 02 |
{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}| [ ] | **Cold chain (this household):** a thermometer in the fridge or cooler that holds the medicine; an insulated pouch and cold packs; an evaporative cooling pouch; a way to run a 12 V cooler in an outage | → 29-07, → 12-21 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Medicine stored out of children's reach, locked if there are children | → 20-02 |
| [ ] | Spare glasses or the written glasses prescription; hearing-aid batteries | → 02-23 |

> **Medicine that must not freeze or overheat** (insulin and many others): if you have no way to
> keep it in range in a winter power cut or a summer car, that is a "~", not a "✔" (FDA, Insulin
> Storage in an Emergency). Heat-exposed medicine: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09.

## C. Rescue medicines

{{#if has.epinephrine}}**Epinephrine (this household):**

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Location | Count | Expiry |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | The allergic person's own bag | ______ | ______ |
| [ ] | Each adult's bag | ______ | ______ |
| [ ] | House medical kit | ______ | ______ |
| [ ] | School, daycare or work, on file | ______ | ______ |
| [ ] | Each vehicle: a **backup only**, in a pouch that comes inside in extreme heat or cold | ______ | ______ |
| [ ] | The written action plan, laminated, with every caregiver | | |
| [ ] | Medical ID worn | | |
| [ ] | Antihistamine as the plan says (**never instead of epinephrine**) | ______ | ______ |
| [ ] | A trainer device for practice | | |

> **A pair, not one.** A second dose may be needed (AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency
> Plan). Any location holding a single device is a "~". Expired devices when nothing in
> date exists: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05.
{{/if}}

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Rescue item | Count | Expiry | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Glucagon and fast sugar{{#if has.condition.CL-01}} **(this household)**{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-06}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | ______ | → 02-01 |
| [ ] | Rescue inhaler and spacer{{#if has.condition.CL-07}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | ______ | → 02-07 |
| [ ] | Seizure rescue medicine{{#if has.condition.CL-11}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | ______ | → 02-11 |
| [ ] | Naloxone{{#if has.condition.CL-17}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | ______ | → 02-17 |
| [ ] | Emergency steroid kit{{#if has.condition.CL-20}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | ______ | → 02-20 |
| [ ] | Other: ______________ | ______ | ______ | |

## D. Devices and their supplies

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Count / runtime | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Diabetes: meter + strips, **ketone strips**, syringes or pens as the fallback, sensors, pump supplies{{#if has.condition.CL-02}} **(this household: pump and sensor)**{{/if}} | ______ | → 02-01, → 02-02 |
| [ ] | Oxygen: cylinders (hours), concentrator power plan, tubing{{#if has.oxygen}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ h | → 02-08 |
| [ ] | CPAP: mask, tubing, filters, 12 V cord or battery tested for a night{{#if has.cpap}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | → 02-24 |
| [ ] | Wheelchair or walker: repair kit, spare tyre or tips{{#if has.mobility_aid}} **(this household)**{{/if}} | ______ | → 02-22 |
| [ ] | Power for every medical device, measured in watt-hours a day | ______ Wh | → 09-10 |
| [ ] | Sharps container (or a hard-sided substitute) | | → 13-03 |

> **Ketone strips are the most-forgotten item on this page** for anyone with diabetes, and they
> catch DKA early (CDC, Diabetic Ketoacidosis).

## E. Trauma and first aid

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Count | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Tourniquets, and the training (Stop the Bleed). **Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no help will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).** | ______ | → 12-02 |
| [ ] | Pressure dressings; wound-packing gauze | ______ | → 12-02 |
| [ ] | Trauma shears | ______ | → 12-02 |
| [ ] | Gauze, tape, non-stick pads | ______ | → 12-01 |
| [ ] | Wound irrigation syringe | ______ | → 12-14 |
| [ ] | Closure strips (stapler or sutures only if trained) | ______ | → 12-14 |
| [ ] | Nitrile gloves, several pairs | ______ | → 12-01 |
| [ ] | Burn dressings | ______ | → 12-03 |
| [ ] | Padded splint, wrap, triangular bandages | ______ | → 12-09 |
| [ ] | **Oral rehydration salts** | ______ | → 12-05 |
| [ ] | Pain and fever medicine, **adult and child** forms, each with its dosing tool{{#if has.child}} **(this household has children)**{{/if}} | ______ | → 12-13 |
| [ ] | A working thermometer | ______ | → 12-05 |
| [ ] | Dental first aid (temporary filling, clove oil) | ______ | → 12-06 |
| [ ] | CPR face shield, N95 masks, eye protection | ______ | → 12-01 |
| [ ] | A second full kit for the house | | → 12-01 |
| [ ] | Stop the Bleed course taken by every adult | | → 12-02 |
| [ ] | First aid and CPR course{{#if has.infant}}, **including infant CPR**{{/if}}, every adult | | → 12-18 |

> **Diarrhoea, dehydration and infection are far more common in a long event than a wound that
> needs a tourniquet.** Oral rehydration salts and infection care are not glamorous, and you
> are more likely to need them (→ 12-04, → 12-05).

## The lines that decide the rest

```
SHORTEST MEDICAL CLOCK:     ________ = ______ days  <- the household's governing number (23-01)
RESCUE MEDICINE IN DATE, IN EVERY LOCATION:  Y / N
CO ALARMS WORKING:          ________   <- should equal levels + sleeping areas + burning points
SMOKE ALARMS WORKING:       ________

BIGGEST GAP ON THIS PAGE: ______________________________________________
FIRST THING TO BUY:       ______________________________________________
```

**Copy these to → 26-09.** Anything on this page marked ✗ goes to the top of the shopping list,
ahead of everything on the other checklists, whatever it costs.

Related: → 22-06 the medical go-kit this stocks · → 12-07 medicine supply · → 08-02 carbon
monoxide · → 12-01 the household kit · → 26-08 where the expiry dates go · → 26-09 the shopping
list · → 25-09 medical summary.

# Checklist 2: water and food

**What this page is for.** The second sheet of the walk (→ 26-01). Water first, because it is
the shortage that arrives first in almost every emergency and the one most households are
least ready for (CDC, How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply). Then food, food
storage and growing.

> **CAUTION.** **This household's water floor is {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} gallons a
> day; plan on {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gallons a day, so two weeks is
> {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gallons** (→ 03-01). Cooking and washing come on top, from
> water you treat. **No bleach amounts or canning times on this page**: read → 03-04 and → 04-05.
> **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.**

**Marks:** ✔ have it, it works, I know where it is · ~ partly, or needs a spare · ✗ do not have

## A. Water storage

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Gallons / count | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Stored drinking water (settings: {{ gear.water.stored_gal }} gal) | ______ | Filled on: ______ | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Food-grade containers (jugs, drums) | ______ | | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Food-grade 5-gal buckets + lids | ______ | | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Separate **non-drinking** buckets, labelled | ______ | | → 13-03 |
| [ ] | Water heater{{#if has.water_heater_tank}} ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal){{/if}}: drain valve found + a hose that fits | | Power or gas off first; let it cool; close the cold inlet | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Bathtub liner (a water bladder for the tub) | ______ | | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | Rain barrels + diverter + **screen** | ______ | {{#if is.cold_winters}}Drained before the hard freeze{{else}}Mosquito screen on{{/if}} | → 03-05 |
| [ ] | Rainwater treatment supplies located (rain is not drinking water until treated) | | | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | Siphon pump, hose, funnel, **marked for water only** | | | → 03-02 |
| [ ] | {{#if has.pool}}**Pool or hot tub ({{ dwelling.pool_gallons }} gal): raw water**, plan for treating it{{else}}Nearby raw water (pond, creek, a neighbour's pool) and a plan for treating it{{/if}} | | Drinking it is a household choice: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14 | → 03-03 |
{{#if has.well}}| [ ] | **Well: a way to get water with no power** (bailer + rope, hand pump, or generator wiring) **(this household)** | | | → 03-10 |
{{/if}}

## B. Water treatment

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Count | Expiry or life | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Gravity or pump filter | ______ | | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | **Spare filter elements** (at least two) | ______ | Element life: ______ | → 03-09 |
| [ ] | Unscented household bleach | ______ | **Bought on:** ______ | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), stored sealed, dry, away from fuel and other chemicals | ______ | | → 29-05 |
| [ ] | Purification tablets | ______ | ______ | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | Dropper or measuring syringe, marked for bleach only | ______ | | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | Large pot with a lid for boiling | ______ | | → 07-01 |
| [ ] | Distillation setup (removes salt) | ______ | | → 03-03 |
| [ ] | Cloth or coffee filters for pre-filtering cloudy water | ______ | | → 03-04 |
| [ ] | Mosquito larvicide (Bti) for standing water | ______ | ______ | → 03-08 |

> **A filter with no spare element is a "~", not a "✔".** The element is the consumable, and it
> sets how long the filter works.

## C. Food staples

**This household needs about {{ derived.calories.day }} calories a day** (→ 04-01). Pantry by
your estimate: {{ gear.food.pantry_days }} days. Freeze-dried: {{ gear.food.freeze_dried_servings }}
servings.

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Amount (lb or cans) | Earliest expiry | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Rice and grains | ______ | ______ | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | Beans and lentils | ______ | ______ | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | Flour, oats, pasta | ______ | ______ | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | Canned meat and fish | ______ | ______ | → 04-02 |
| [ ] | Canned vegetables and fruit | ______ | ______ | → 04-02 |
| [ ] | **Fats and oils** | ______ | ______ | → 04-12 |
| [ ] | Sugar and honey | ______ | ______ | → 04-13 |
| [ ] | **Salt** (canning or pickling, not only iodised table salt) | ______ | | → 04-13 |
| [ ] | Powdered or canned milk | ______ | ______ | → 04-14 |
{{#if has.child}}| [ ] | Shelf-stable milk and foods the children reliably eat | ______ | ______ | → 20-05 |
{{/if}}{{#if has.infant}}| [ ] | **Infant formula** (if used), unopened, in date, and safe water to mix it | ______ | ______ | → 02-13 |
{{/if}}| [ ] | Spices, vinegar, baking supplies | ______ | ______ | → 04-13 |
| [ ] | Coffee, tea, comfort food | ______ | ______ | → 21-02 |
| [ ] | Manual can opener (two) | ______ | | → 04-02 |

```
TOTAL ESTIMATED CALORIES: __________ ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }} a day = ________ DAYS
```

> **Fats are the hardest food to store and the easiest to run short of** (→ 04-12). Households
> almost always have more grain and less fat than they think.

## D. Special-diet food{{#if has.anaphylaxis}} (this household: food allergy){{/if}}

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Amount | Expiry | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | A **dedicated bin**, kept apart from shared food | ______ | | → 02-04 |

| [ ] | Dedicated utensils, cutting board, pans | ______ | | → 02-04 |
| [ ] | A written list of safe brands (makers change recipes; re-read labels) | ______ | | → 29-14 |
| [ ] | Freeze-dried or bulk food **checked against the allergen list before buying** | ______ | ______ | → 04-19 |

{{#if has.anaphylaxis}}Allergens in this household: {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}: {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}) · {{/each}}
{{/if}}A shared scoop in a shared bin is a "~" at best. Celiac disease and other medical diets follow
the same rules (→ 02-19).

## E. Food storage and preserving gear

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Count | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | Mylar bags + **oxygen absorbers** | ______ | | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | Food-grade buckets + gamma (screw-top) lids | ______ | | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | Rodent-proof bins | ______ | | → 04-11 |
| [ ] | Pressure canner{{#if has.pressure_canner}} (owned){{/if}} + **spare gasket** | ______ | Dial gauge tested this year? | → 04-05 |
| [ ] | Boiling-water canner | ______ | | → 04-04 |
| [ ] | Jars | ______ | | → 04-04 |
| [ ] | **Lids** (single use: count them) | ______ | | → 04-04 |
| [ ] | Dehydrator and/or drying screens | ______ | | → 04-06 |
| [ ] | Fermenting crocks or jars with airlocks | ______ | | → 04-08 |
| [ ] | Vacuum sealer + bags | ______ | | → 04-03 |
| [ ] | Labels + permanent marker | ______ | | → 04-10 |
| [ ] | **A current tested-recipe book** (USDA, NCHFP or Extension) | ______ | | → 04-05 |

> **Canning lids are single use.** A canner with no lids is a "✗" dressed as a "✔" (NCHFP,
> General Canning Information). **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and
> pressure, or not canned.**

## F. Growing food

| ✔ ~ ✗ | Item | Count | Notes | Page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [ ] | **Open-pollinated seed** (not hybrid) | ______ | Packet year: ______ | → 05-03 |
| [ ] | Seed-starting trays, mix, grow light | ______ | | → 05-14 |
| [ ] | Garden hand tools | ______ | | → 05-01 |
| [ ] | Row cover, hoops, cold frame | ______ | | → 05-02 |
| [ ] | Containers + potting mix{{#if has.apartment}} (balcony or windowsill){{/if}} | ______ | | → 05-10 |
| [ ] | Compost bin or pile started | ______ | | → 05-11 |
| [ ] | Watering cans, soaker hose | ______ | | → 05-01 |
| [ ] | Fruit trees or bushes **planted** | ______ | Planted on: ______ | → 05-13 |
| [ ] | Sprouting jars + sprouting seed | ______ | ______ | → 04-16 |
| [ ] | Fishing tackle | ______ | | → 05-08 |
| [ ] | Traps and snare wire | ______ | | → 05-15 |
| [ ] | Game-processing knives, saw, gambrel | ______ | | → 05-09 |
| [ ] | Two regional field guides **with photographs** | ______ | | → 05-06 |

> **Seed and soil are the two things money cannot buy in a hurry.** Seed needs a season; soil
> takes years. Both are cheap now and unobtainable later (→ 23-04). Your frost dates: → 25-01.

## The lines that matter

```
DAYS OF WATER STORED:     ________  (gallons ÷ {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} a day, the plan rate;
                                      ÷ {{ derived.water.floor_gal_day }} is the rationing floor)
   TARGET: two weeks = {{ derived.water.two_weeks_gal }} gal.
   Under a week of water is a TODAY problem, not a someday problem.
DAYS OF FOOD:             ________  (calories ÷ {{ derived.calories.day }})
SPARE FILTER ELEMENTS:    ________  (zero = the filter has a deadline)
BLEACH PURCHASE DATE:     ________  (it weakens on the shelf)
CANNING LIDS ON HAND:     ________

BIGGEST GAP: ______________________________________________
```

Food from a fridge or freezer after a power cut: about 4 hours for the fridge, 48 for a full
freezer (USDA/HHS, Food Safety During a Power Outage; → 04-17).

Related: → 03-02 storage · → 03-04 treatment (**amounts live there**) · → 03-03 pool and salt
water · → 04-01 pantry math · → 04-03 bulk staples · → 04-05 pressure canning · → 02-04 food
allergy · → 05-03 seed saving · → 26-08 expiry tracker · → 26-09 the shopping list.

pages.body:
# Checklist 3: heat, power and light

**What this page is for.** The third sheet of the walk (→ 26-01): how you will stay warm (or
cool), make power, see after dark, and cook when the grid is down. {{#if is.cold_winters}}In your
winters (January mean low {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F) heat is a life-safety item, not a comfort
one.{{else}}{{#if is.hot_summers}}In your summers (July mean high {{ region.home.jul_high_f }} °F) cooling is a life-safety item,
not a comfort one.{{else}}A long outage in the worst week of your year is the case to plan for.{{/if}}{{/if}}

> **CAUTION: the safety rules on this page are not optional.**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** CPSC: one generator makes as much carbon monoxide as hundreds of idling cars
>   (CPSC, news release, 2006). Run it outdoors, at least 20 feet from the house (CPSC, Portable
>   Generator Safety).
> - **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock
>   kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male
>   ("suicide") cord.**
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.**
> - **Anything that burns indoors needs a working battery CO alarm first** (CDC, Carbon Monoxide
>   Poisoning: Basics; → 08-02), and only heaters rated for indoor use belong inside.

# Checklist 4: sanitation, clothing, tools, security and comms

**What this page is for.** The fourth sheet of the walk (→ 26-01): the weeks-to-months items.
Nothing here kills you tonight; all of it decides whether month three is manageable or
miserable. **Sanitation is first on purpose**: a sanitation failure turns into a medical
emergency fast, especially with small children or elders in the house (→ 13-11).

**Marks:** ✔ have it, it works, I know where it is · ~ partly, or needs a spare · ✗ do not have

> **Long events are lost to isolation, despair and boredom as often as to running out of
> something.** Staying connected to other people protects health (CDC, About Social Connection;
> → 21-02). Budget for morale the way you budget for food.

pages.body:
# Expiry and rotation tracker

**What this page is for.** Expiry is the failure nobody notices until the morning it matters.
This sheet puts every date found on the walk (→ 26-02) in one place you can scan in thirty
seconds. **It prints no shelf-life figures on purpose**: the label is the authority, and for
medicine so are your pharmacist and prescriber. How to read the dates: → 29-14.

> **CAUTION.**
> - **Never quietly rely on an expired medicine.** If something critical is close to expiry,
>   that is a conversation with the prescriber now, not a decision in an emergency (→ 12-07).
>   What the household does when nothing in date exists: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05.
> - **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded**, whatever its date.
> - **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are thrown out, unopened.**

## Do this now

1. **Copy every date you found on the walk** onto this sheet, soonest first.
2. **Circle anything expiring within six months.** That is this year's replacement list; it
   goes to → 26-09.
3. **Re-run this sheet on the two kit-check dates** with the go-bags (→ 22-03).

## Three kinds of expiry

| Kind | What it means | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Hard** | Stops working or becomes unsafe. **Replace on schedule** | Rescue medicines, insulin and other refrigerated medicines, glucagon, test and ketone strips, infant formula, canning lids |
| **Fading** | Loses strength or performance slowly: still there, works less well | **Bleach** (weakens on the shelf; → 29-05), batteries, sunscreen, fuel, seed |
| **Quality** | A best-quality date, not a safety cliff (USDA FSIS, Food Product Dating) | Most dry staples; canned goods stored cool and dry. Dented or rusty cans: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15 |

**Treat every medical row as hard, always.** Everything else can be judged; those cannot.

## The rule for rotation

**Store what you eat, eat what you store, oldest first** (→ 04-10). Anything used only in an
emergency is the thing most likely to be expired when the emergency comes, which is why go-bag
and vehicle food need a set rotation date, not good intentions.

## Dates that are not printed on the product

Some things have no stamp but still have a clock. Write the date you got them, in marker, on
the item:

- **Bleach**: the **purchase** date; it loses strength over months (EPA, Emergency Disinfection
  of Drinking Water; → 03-04).
- **Stored water**: the **fill** date (→ 03-02).
- **Firewood**: when it was **split and stacked**; seasoning takes 6 to 12 months (→ 06-03).
- **Seed**: the **packet year**; germination falls each year (→ 05-03).
- **Fuel**: when it was bought and when stabiliser was added (→ 06-06).
- **Filter elements**: **gallons used**, not a date (→ 03-09).
- **Home-canned food**: the **date canned** and the recipe (NCHFP; → 04-05).
{{#if has.child}}- **Children's clothing**: the **size**, which expires faster than any date on this page.
{{/if}}

## The tracker, soonest first

```
DATE COMPLETED: ____________        NEXT REVIEW: ____________

KIND   ITEM                              LOCATION            EXPIRES     ACTION
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________
_____  ________________________________  __________________  __________  ________

KIND:   H = hard (replace on schedule) · F = fading · Q = quality only
ACTION: R = replace now · 6 = replace within 6 months · U = use it up first · OK
```

## The medical block: check this one separately, every time

**Medicines from settings:**

| Person | Medicine | Where kept | Expires | Days on hand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as x}}| {{x.member}} | {{x.name}} | {{x.where_kept}} | {{x.expiry}} | {{x.days_on_hand}} |
{{else}}| none entered | | | | |
{{/each}}

**Everything else medical:**

| Item | Location | Expires |
|---|---|---|
{{#if has.epinephrine}}| Epinephrine: the allergic person's bag | ______ | ______ |
| Epinephrine: each adult's bag | ______ | ______ |
| Epinephrine: house kit | ______ | ______ |
| Epinephrine: school, daycare or work | ______ | ______ |
| Epinephrine: each vehicle (backup) | ______ | ______ |
{{/if}}| Other rescue medicines (glucagon, inhaler, seizure, naloxone) | ______ | ______ |
| Device supplies (sensors, pump parts, test and ketone strips, CPAP filters) | ______ | ______ |
{{#if has.infant}}| Infant formula | ______ | ______ |
| Infant fever reducer | ______ | ______ |
{{/if}}{{#if has.child}}| Children's pain and fever medicine | ______ | ______ |
{{/if}}| Adult pain and fever medicine | ______ | ______ |
| Antibiotics, if prescribed | ______ | ______ |
| Oral rehydration salts | ______ | ______ |
{{#if has.pets}}| Pet medicines | ______ | ______ |
{{/if}}

```
SOONEST MEDICAL EXPIRY: ______________________ on ____________
SHORTEST MEDICAL CLOCK: ______________________ = ______ days   (23-01)
```

{{#if has.epinephrine}}> **Every location holding epinephrine gets its own line**, because the one that expires is
> always the one nobody checks: the spare in the car. A second dose may be needed, so each
> location needs a pair (AAP, Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan).
{{/if}}

## The date-stamped items

| Item | Date got or done | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Bleach | ______ | Replace on schedule (→ 03-04) |
| Stored water | ______ | Rotate (→ 03-02) |
| Firewood stacked | ______ | Seasoned when? (→ 06-03) |
| Seed packets | ______ | Year (→ 05-03) |
| Fuel + stabiliser | ______ | (→ 06-06) |
| Filter element | ______ gal used of ______ | (→ 03-09) |
| Smoke and CO alarm batteries | ______ | The alarms themselves wear out: read the date on the back (USFA, Smoke Alarms; → 29-12) |
| Fire extinguisher | ______ | Gauge in the green? |
| Go-bag food rotated | ______ | (→ 22-03) |
| Vehicle kit food rotated | ______ | (→ 22-05) |
{{#each members as m}}| {{m.label}}: clothing size now | ______ | Next size on hand? |
{{/each}}

## Gear

**Buy toward:** a permanent marker (write the purchase date on each item the day it comes home:
the single habit that makes most of this page unnecessary), labels, and a wall calendar with the
two kit-check dates marked.

**If you do not have it:** any notebook. **The substitute for tracking is discovering it in an
emergency**, which is not a substitute.

## When it goes stale

- **About six months**, less for anything medical.
- **If you track only one block, track the medical block.**
- **Refresh** on the two kit-check dates (→ 22-03), fully at the yearly review (→ 25-10).

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** keep it current; most of its value is in ordinary life.
- **B (moving):** only the medical block matters, and it travels with → 25-09.
- **C (establish):** restart it in the first month; the clocks keep running wherever you are.

Related: → 26-03 where the medical dates come from · → 04-10 food rotation · → 22-03 and → 22-05
kit checks · → 12-07 medicine supply · → 03-04 bleach strength · → 29-14 reading a label ·
→ 25-10 review.

# The result: ranked shopping list and budget

**What this page is for.** The walk is not finished until this page is filled in. Everything
before it was diagnosis; this is the prescription. **Do not shop the same day you walk**: sleep
on it, then buy in the order below, which is → 22-07's order: *what hurts people soonest, then
what cannot be bought later.* Typical rows for this household are already printed in each tier,
from your settings; add your own ✗ and ~ items in the blank rows.

## Do this now

1. **Move every ✗ and every ~ from the five checklists** into the right tier below.
2. **Anything from → 26-03 (life safety and medical) goes in Tier 0**, whatever it costs and
   whatever else is on the list.
3. **Set a monthly amount you can actually sustain** and work down. Steady beats a spree,
   because the ⌛ items need years, not money.
4. **Put the ⌛ items on the calendar now**, even if you cannot buy them yet.

## The ordering rule

Three questions, in order:

1. **How fast does its absence hurt someone here?** Minutes, hours, days, weeks.
2. **Can it still be bought later?** ⌛ items (seed, seasoned wood, soil, children's next sizes,
   skill) **cannot**. They move up regardless.
3. **How likely is the event it covers?** A power cut lasting days is common enough
   that the American Red Cross tells every household to plan two weeks of food and water for
   one (American Red Cross, Power Outage Safety){{#if is.cold_winters}}, and here it will come in
   winter sooner or later (American Red Cross, Winter Storm Safety){{/if}}. Buy against the likely
   first, then the severe.

**Two marks worth carrying over:**

- **§ = has a consumable.** Buy the spare in the same order: the element, the lids, the file, the
  batteries. Forgetting it is the most common preparedness mistake.
- **⌛ = time-sensitive.** Money cannot fix it later.

| [ ] | **Destination: one concrete step this year**{{#if has.agreed_destination}} (you have an agreed destination: settle terms, leave a tote on each visit){{else}} (none agreed yet: a conversation, a visit, an agreement){{/if}}: ______________ | ______ | → 01-05 |

## The summary

```

COUNTS      ✔ ______   ~ ______   ✗ ______

TOTAL ESTIMATED SPEND:  Tier 0 ______  Tier 1 ______
                        Tier 2 ______  Tier 3 ______   ALL: ________

_______________________________________________________________

NEXT WALK DUE: ____________                                    (25-10)
```

**What you need:** nothing: this page is the result, not an input. The one useful extra is a
short list on your phone or in your wallet, so Tier 0 and Tier 1 get bought when you pass the
shop rather than waiting for a special trip.

**Second-hand and scavenged:** much of Tiers 2 and 3 has a second-hand or scavenged equivalent
(→ 22-02). **Nothing in Tier 0 does**: CO alarms and medicines are bought, not found.

## When the shops close

This page becomes read-only.

- **The list is good until the next walk**, about a year.
- **If the budget is small,** buy **Tier 0 complete, then the ⌛ items in Tier 2**, and let Tier 1
  wait. Cheap-and-unbuyable-later beats expensive-and-still-available.
- **Re-walk yearly** (→ 25-10) and re-rank from what you find.
- **Tier 4** (skills, practice, neighbours, a destination) is free and outranks most of what is
  above it.

## Phase notes

- **A (shelter in place):** work down the tiers monthly.
- **B (moving):** nothing on this page can be bought once you are moving.
- **C (establish):** the ⌛ and producing items make a place viable; buy in Phase A with Phase C
  in mind (→ 23-04).

Related: → 26-01 to → 26-08 the walk that produced this · → 22-07 the same order, explained ·
→ 22-01 what to own and why · → 23-04 which purchases last · → 01-05 the destination money cannot
settle for you · → 25-10 the yearly re-run.

pages.body:
# CBRN and EMP

**What this section holds.** 7 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 27-01 **How to think about CBRN and EMP**: CBRN means chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear.
- → 27-02 **EMP and geomagnetic storms: what actually happens**: Two very different things get called "EMP".
- → 27-03 **Protecting electronics, and the medical devices**: Which of your household's electronics actually matter, what really threatens them, and the cheap, honest hedge for spares.
- → 27-04 **Nuclear detonation: the first hour**: The actions for the first hour after a nuclear explosion, in order, for a household that is not at the blast itself.
- → 27-05 **Fallout: sheltering, time and decontamination**: How to shelter for the 24 to 48 hours after a nuclear explosion: where in your home, how to add protection with what you own, how to get contamination off pe…
- → 27-06 **Potassium iodide: what it does and does not do**: Potassium iodide (KI) is the most misunderstood item in preparedness, and the misunderstanding is dangerous both ways.
- → 27-07 **Chemical and biological release**: Chemical and biological releases get named together, but they need almost opposite responses.

review_pass.notes: No changes; NOAA G-scale frequencies and FDA/Ready.gov/CDC claims traced to archived sources.

pages.body:
# How to think about CBRN and EMP

**What this page is for.** CBRN means chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear. EMP means
electromagnetic pulse: a burst of energy that can damage electronics. This is the part of
preparedness where published advice goes furthest wrong: much of what is written about EMP and
nuclear survival is unsourced, mistaken, or selling something. This section is small, sourced to
federal agencies, and built on one honest observation: **for almost every one of these events,
what actually happens to you is a long loss of power, water and services, which the rest of this
binder already covers.**

> **Caution.** Read this page before the rest of the section, so the other six are read in
> proportion. Nothing here replaces official instructions during a real event: listen for them
> (→ 15-01).

## Do this now

1. **Read this page first.** Then the others in order.
2. **Do not buy anything because of this section** until the basics on → 26-09 are done. A
   carbon monoxide alarm and a month of prescription medicine outrank every item any CBRN page
   could suggest.
3. **The two things in this section that really add something** are → 27-03 (protecting the
   electronics your household cannot lose) and → 27-04 with → 27-05 (the first 48 hours after a
   nuclear detonation, which are short, specific and time-critical).

## The one idea that organises this section

Every event here has **two phases**, and they need different pages:

| | **The event** | **The aftermath** |
|---|---|---|
| **How long** | Minutes to about 48 hours | Weeks to years |
| **What decides survival** | A few specific, time-critical actions | Water, heat, food, medicine, sanitation, people |
| **Where it lives** | **This section** | **The rest of the binder** |

**That is why this section is seven pages and not seventy.** The aftermath of an EMP is a grid
failure (→ 17-08). The aftermath of a pandemic is → 17-09. The aftermath of a nuclear detonation
you survived at a distance is sheltering at home (→ 01-01) with a radiation-shaped first two days
on the front.

## What is realistic, ranked

Ranked by how likely you are to live through it, not by how frightening it is:

| Event | How likely | What is really different |
|---|---|---|
| **Geomagnetic storm** (a storm from the sun hitting Earth's magnetic field; "space weather") | **Recurring and real.** NOAA's scale expects about 4 G5 "extreme" storms and about 100 G4 "severe" storms per 11-year solar cycle (NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, NOAA Space Weather Scales) | Strain on the power grid and possible damage to large transformers. **NOAA issues warnings**: you can watch for it (→ 27-02) |
| **Pandemic or natural outbreak** | Happens | Already covered: → 17-09, → 13-11 |
| **Chemical release** from industry, rail or highway | Plausible anywhere near rail lines, highways or plants | Seal a room and shelter, or leave (→ 27-07) |
| **Deliberate biological release** | Low | Mostly the pandemic playbook (→ 27-07, → 17-09) |
| **High-altitude EMP** from a nuclear weapon | Low, and needs a nuclear attack | In practice the same aftermath as a long grid failure (→ 27-02) |
| **Nuclear detonation nearby** | Low | The first 48 hours, and only those (→ 27-04, → 27-05) |

**Notice what the table says.** The most likely item is a space-weather event that NOAA forecasts
publicly, and the least likely gets the most attention.

## Five common claims that are not true

1. **"EMP destroys all electronics everywhere."** It does not. Effects vary hugely with the
   event, the device, whether it is plugged into a long wire, and whether it is switched on.
   Plan for **losing the grid**, the reliable consequence, rather than for a pattern of device
   failure nobody can predict (→ 27-02).
2. **"Potassium iodide protects you from radiation."** **It does not.** FDA says potassium
   iodide only stops the thyroid gland taking up radioactive iodine; it is not a general
   protection against radiation, and taking more than directed can cause severe illness or death
   (FDA, Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium Iodide; → 27-06).
3. **"You need a gas mask."** A respirator works only with the right cartridge for the specific
   chemical, a proper fit and training. Without all three it is theatre{{#if has.child}}, and adult
   masks do not fit children{{/if}} (→ 27-07).
4. **"If it happens, run."** For fallout, the federal advice is the opposite: **get inside, stay
   inside, stay tuned** (Ready.gov, Nuclear Explosion; CDC, Radiation Emergencies). Driving
   through fallout is worse than sheltering from it (→ 27-04).
5. **"You can't survive a nuclear event, so why plan?"** At a distance from a detonation, what
   you do in the first 24 hours makes a very large difference, and fallout radiation drops fast
   (HHS REMM, Nuclear Explosion; → 27-05). The fatalism is as wrong as the fantasy.

## What this section will not contain

In line with the safety page (→ 00-05):
- **No dosing, with one exception:** → 27-06 prints FDA's own potassium iodide table by age and
  FDA's home-preparation method for children, as published, because an offline household cannot
  look them up. Even there, the **when** does not change: only on official public-health
  direction, and your clinician's advice comes first. Adults over 40 are a decision card:
  {{choice DC-22}} → 30-23
- **No radiation-measuring instructions** beyond what a household instrument can honestly do.
- **No blast-effect tables, weapon sizes or target lists.** They change nothing you would do.
- **No product recommendations** for gear that has not been tested against a real threat.

## What matters most for your household

{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}- **An insulin pump and glucose sensor are electronics, and they keep someone alive.** Any event
  that damages electronics is, for your household, first a **medical continuity** problem.
  That is → 27-03, the page in this section most worth acting on. The real answer to every
  electronics scenario is the **injection backup** (→ 02-02): no power, no radio, no batteries.
  Practise it (→ 24-01).
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}- **Oxygen equipment depends on power.** Cylinders, a regulator that needs no power and a backup
  plan are the answer to any grid or electronics event (→ 02-08, → 27-03).
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}- **A CPAP needs power every night.** Battery and a plan for nights without it (→ 02-24, → 27-03).
{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **Refrigerated medicine** depends on the fridge, which depends on the grid. Every scenario
  here ends in a cold-chain problem (→ 29-07, → 12-21).
{{/if}}{{#if has.child}}- **Sheltering with children** for 24 to 48 hours in one interior space is a logistics problem
  (water, food{{#if has.infant}}, diapers{{/if}}, toilet, boredom) long before it is a radiation
  problem (→ 27-05, → 20-08).
{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}- **Older members** may need medicines, warmth and help with stairs in a shelter space; plan the
  space around them (→ 27-05).
{{/if}}- For every household: the electronics that matter most are the ones that keep someone
  well, and the ones that tell you what is happening (a battery radio, → 15-01).

## What you need

Almost nothing that is not already on → 22-01. The honest list this section adds is short:
a battery or hand-crank radio you need anyway (→ 15-01), a shielded container for **backup**
medical and communication electronics (→ 27-03), and pre-cut plastic sheeting and tape for
sealing one room (→ 27-07). **Everything else is already in the binder for other reasons.**

No money? **Mass is mass.** Books, water containers and earth shield against fallout radiation
whatever they were bought for (→ 27-05). The best fallout shelter in most houses is the lowest,
most central space you already have.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the event actions in this section last hours to about two days. After that, every
  clock on → 23-02 takes over.
- **Ration:** nothing here is a consumable except attention. **Do not let this section take money
  that belongs to the basics** (→ 26-09).
- **Resupply:** read it again after any change to your medical devices (→ 27-03).
- **Substitute:** the rest of the binder. That is the point of this page.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** sheltering in place is the answer for nearly every scenario here, and the home
  you have is the shelter you have.
- **B, moving:** **moving during fallout or a chemical plume is the wrong call** unless officials
  tell you to (→ 27-04). It is the one situation where staying put is most clearly right
  (→ 01-02).
- **C, establishing:** distance from likely targets and from heavy industry is a real but minor
  factor in choosing a destination (→ 01-05), well below water, timber, ground and people.

pages.body:
# EMP and geomagnetic storms: what actually happens

**What this page is for.** Two very different things get called "EMP". This page explains both,
prints NOAA's storm scale, and says what to do with the one real early warning you can get. The
short version: **the reliable result of every scenario here is that the grid goes away and stays
away**, which the rest of this binder already plans for.

> **Caution.** What is **not** predictable is which individual devices survive. **Plan for the
> outage, not for a particular pattern of gadget failure**, and be sceptical of anyone who tells
> you exactly what will and will not work.

## Do this now

1. **Know that the likely version is watched and forecast.** NOAA's Space Weather Prediction
   Center issues public watches and warnings for geomagnetic storms. That is a real early-warning
   channel; there is none for a weapon (→ 15-01).
2. **Do the electronics protection on → 27-03** for the devices someone in your household
   depends on{{#if has.condition.CL-02}} (the pump, the sensor, a backup meter){{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}} (the CPAP){{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}} (oxygen equipment){{/if}}.
3. {{#if has.condition.CL-02}}**Practise the injection backup** (→ 02-02). It answers every electronics-failure scenario
   and needs no power at all.{{else}}**Give every device you depend on a non-electronic backup** (→ 27-03), and practise using
   it.{{/if}}
4. **Treat the rest as a grid failure**, because that is what it is: → 17-08, → 09-01, → 23-02.

## Two different things get called "EMP"

| | **Geomagnetic storm (space weather)** | **High-altitude EMP** |
|---|---|---|
| **Cause** | The sun: a burst of charged particles (a coronal mass ejection) hitting Earth's magnetic field | A nuclear weapon set off high in the atmosphere |
| **How likely** | **Recurring.** NOAA expects about 4 G5 storms per 11-year solar cycle | Low, and needs a nuclear attack |
| **Warning** | **Yes: hours to days.** NOAA: the fastest Earth-directed solar storms arrive in as little as 15 to 18 hours, slower ones take several days (NOAA SWPC, Coronal Mass Ejections) | None |
| **Main way it does damage** | Currents pushed into **very long conductors**: power lines, pipelines, and the large transformers at their ends (NOAA scale) | CISA: it may damage or disable large sections of the national electric grid, and can harm electronics that are not protected, directly or through the systems they depend on (CISA, Electromagnetic Pulse) |
| **Household electronics** | NOAA's scale lists effects on power grids, satellites, radio and navigation, not on household devices; you lose power because the grid does | Unpredictable; published claims vary wildly |

**The practical point:** both end in the same place for you: **no grid, possibly for a long time,
possibly over a wide area.** This binder already treats that as its starting point.

## The NOAA scale, in NOAA's words

NOAA rates geomagnetic storms from **G1 (minor) to G5 (extreme)** (NOAA Space Weather Prediction
Center, NOAA Space Weather Scales):

| Scale | Effect on the power system | About how often, per 11-year cycle |
|---|---|---|
| **G1** minor | Weak power-grid fluctuations | about 1,700 |
| **G2** moderate | Voltage alarms in high-latitude power systems; long storms can damage transformers | about 600 |
| **G3** strong | Voltage corrections may be needed; false alarms on some protection devices | about 200 |
| **G4** severe | *"Possible widespread voltage control problems and some protective systems will mistakenly trip out key assets from the grid."* | about 100 |
| **G5** extreme | *"Widespread voltage control problems and protective system problems can occur, some grid systems may experience complete collapse or blackouts. Transformers may experience damage."* | **about 4** |

**Read the last row honestly, both ways.** A G5 is not science fiction: it happens several times
a solar cycle. And its stated effect is *blackouts and transformer damage*, not the end of
technology.

## Why "which devices survive" is the wrong question

You will find confident, contradictory lists. They disagree because the answer depends on the
event, the device, whether it is plugged into the mains or a long antenna, whether it is switched
on, and where it sits. **Nobody can give you a reliable list.**

So do not plan around one. Plan around the two things that are reliable:
1. **The grid is gone**, over a possibly large area, possibly for a long time. Repair is slow
   because everyone needs the same parts (→ 23-04).
2. **Anything you depend on needs a non-electronic backup**: {{#if has.condition.CL-02}}injections
   instead of the pump (→ 02-02), a simple glucose meter, {{/if}}paper copies of documents
   (→ 19-01), and this binder installed on more than one device (→ 00-10).

## What a long, wide-area outage changes

The honest difference between "the power is out" and these scenarios:
- **It is regional, not local.** No repair crews coming from the next state, because the next
  state has the same problem. Neighbours matter more, not less (→ 18-01).
- **Repair can be slow.** NOAA's scale says a G5 storm can damage transformers, and large
  transformers are not kept on a shelf.
- **Fuel stops moving** once pumps and card payments are down (→ 06-06, → 22-05).
- **Water and sewage run on electricity.** Town water may fail or lose pressure (→ 03-02)
  {{#if has.well}}, and your well pump stops (→ 03-10){{/if}}.
- **Nothing else about your day changes.** You still need water, heat, food, medicine and
  sanitation, in that order: the whole binder.

## The one early warning worth knowing

For **space weather only**, there is real forecasting:
- **NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center** issues public watches, warnings and alerts. News and
  weather services usually pass on the big ones (→ 15-01).
- A **G4 or G5 watch** is the one realistic case in which you get hours to days of notice that a
  serious grid event may be coming.
- **What to do with that notice:** top up stored water (→ 03-02), fill the vehicles' tanks
  (→ 22-05), charge every power bank, power station and medical device (→ 09-10), and count the
  medicines (→ 23-02). It is the same two-hour routine as any storm warning (→ 00-06).
- **Unplugging is a household judgement, not an agency instruction.** NOAA's scale describes
  effects on the **grid**; no agency tells households to unplug anything for a geomagnetic storm.
  Some households choose to unplug fully charged power stations and non-essential electronics
  during a G4 or G5 watch, as a cheap hedge: a full battery gains nothing by staying plugged in.
  {{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}If you do, the medicine cooler then runs on the station's battery:
  know how many hours that gives you (→ 09-10) and plug back in when NOAA ends the watch.{{/if}}
  Near the peak of a solar cycle G4 watches come several times a year; if the hedge costs you,
  keep the top-up and drop the unplugging.

**There is no such warning for a weapon.** Which is another reason routine preparation matters
more than scenario gear.

## What you need

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Battery or hand-crank NOAA Weather Radio** | Already needed (→ 15-01); also your news source here (NOAA, NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards) | Buy it for storms; it works for this too |
| **Simple backups for medical devices**{{#if has.diabetes}} (a basic glucose meter and strips){{/if}} | Not networked, battery-powered, cheap | → 22-06, → 27-03 |
| **A shielded container for backup electronics** | A cheap hedge for spares | → 27-03; read its honest limits |
| **Power banks and solar** | The medical loads are the ones that matter | → 09-10 |
| Paper copies of key documents and numbers | Paper does not care about any of this | → 19-01 |
| Hand tools, a manual can opener, matches | The general non-electronic backup | → 16-01 |

No money? Vehicles hold batteries and alternators (→ 09-11; engine running outdoors only). Older,
simpler equipment tends to be easier to repair.{{#if has.condition.CL-02}} **The injection backup
replaces the whole electronic diabetes setup** (→ 02-02): that is the substitution that matters
here.{{/if}}

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** in a long, wide-area outage every clock on → 23-02 starts at once, and the shortest
  one governs (→ 23-01).
- **Ration:** power goes first to medical devices, then light, then communications (→ 09-01).
- **Resupply:** none from the grid. Solar and vehicle charging are the only inputs (→ 09-02,
  → 09-11), and winter solar is thin (→ 09-05).
- **Substitute:** the non-electronic way of doing everything: paper, hand tools, manual methods,
  and the binder in front of you.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** shelter in place. This is a services problem, not a danger to the house.
- **B, moving:** a wide-area outage makes travel **harder**: no fuel pumps, no card payments, no
  traffic lights. It weakens the case for leaving (→ 01-02).
- **C, establishing:** a rural place with wood, water and its own power copes with this scenario
  much better than a town lot (→ 23-04).

pages.body:
# Protecting electronics, and the medical devices

**What this page is for.** Which of your household's electronics actually matter, what really
threatens them, and the cheap, honest hedge for spares. The answer that protects people is
**redundancy and a backup that needs no electricity**, not a box.

> **SAFETY: read this limit first.** **Nothing on this page will protect a device from an event
> nobody can describe in advance.** Home shielding is untested against any real threat, and anyone
> who tells you a container is "EMP-proof" is selling something. **What protects people is a
> backup that needs no power, practised in advance** (→ 24-01). **No dosing appears here**: every
> backup plan for a medicine or device comes from the person's own prescriber, written down now.
> **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded** (floor, → 30-01).

## Your household's devices

From your settings. Add anything missing by hand.

{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}- **Insulin pump, glucose sensor (CGM) and the phone or controller that runs them** (→ 02-02).
  Backup: **syringes or pens, a simple meter, strips, lancets, ketone strips**, and the
  prescriber's written plan for switching to injections.
{{/if}}{{#if has.diabetes}}- **Blood glucose meter** (→ 02-01, → 02-05, → 02-06). Backup: a second meter and strips, in date.
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}- **Oxygen concentrator** (→ 02-08). Backup: **oxygen cylinders with a regulator that needs no
  power**, a written plan from the supplier, and the supplier's emergency number on paper.
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}- **CPAP machine** (→ 02-24). Backup: a battery made for it or a power station with a DC cable,
  and the clinician's advice now on what to do on nights without it.
{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- **The medicine fridge or cooler and its thermometer** (→ 29-07, → 12-21). Backup:
  evaporative cooling pouches and a non-electronic thermometer. Your refrigerated medicines:
  {{#each refrigerated_meds as r}}{{r.name}} ({{r.member}}); {{/each}}
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-23}}- **Hearing aids and their batteries or charger** (→ 02-23). Backup: spare disposable-battery
  aids or an older pair, spare batteries, and the glasses prescription on paper.
{{/if}}{{#if has.mobility_aid}}- **Power wheelchair or scooter, if used** (→ 02-22). Backup: a manual chair.
{{/if}}- Every household: **phones**, **a battery or hand-crank radio** (→ 15-01), **flashlights**.
- Other devices someone depends on: ______________________ backup: ______________________

## Do this now

1. **Practise the no-power backup for each device above**, with the prescriber's or supplier's
   written instructions (→ 24-01, → 24-02). It works for a dead battery, a failed part, a lost
   phone, a flood, and every scenario in this section.
2. {{#if has.diabetes}}**Keep a backup glucose meter, strips and lancets that need no network**, in date (→ 26-08).
   A meter is the backup for a sensor; a sensor is not the backup for anything.{{else}}**Keep the simple, non-electronic version of every medical tool** (a manual thermometer, a
   manual blood-pressure cuff if one is used), in date (→ 26-08).{{/if}}
3. {{#if has.condition.CL-02}}**Keep enough syringes or pens for the insulin you hold**, as prescribed (→ 02-01).{{else}}**Keep the supplies each backup needs**, as prescribed or as the supplier advises.{{/if}}
4. **Store backups apart from the daily devices.** Same house, different place. Most real losses
   are ordinary: a bag left in a hot car, a flooded basement, a dropped phone.
5. **If you want the shielded-container hedge, do it cheaply** (below), and never let it replace
   any of the above.

## The honest threat model

The question is never "will my devices survive an EMP?" It is:

> **What happens to the person who depends on this device if it, its controller and its power
> all stop working at once, and stay stopped?**

That question has a good answer, and it does not involve shielding: **the no-power backup.**
{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}For type 1 diabetes, insulin cannot simply stop: without it,
diabetic ketoacidosis (a dangerous build-up of acids in the blood) can develop (CDC, Diabetic
Ketoacidosis). So the plan has to be **continuity**, not protection.{{/if}}

**Every failure has the same answer**, which is why it is worth practising:

| What fails | Answer |
|---|---|
| Phone or controller dies, is lost or breaks | The device's own backup controls if it has any, then the no-power backup |
| Device supplies run out (pump sets, sensors, filters, tubing) | The no-power backup |
| Batteries and charging are gone | → 09-10, then the no-power backup |
| Devices damaged by any event | The no-power backup |
| **All of these at once** | **The no-power backup** |

## Where the real risk is (it is not exotic)

The likely ways a household loses its medical electronics, most likely first:
1. **Ordinary breakage or loss**: dropped, wet, left behind, stolen.
2. **Supplies run out** because resupply stopped (→ 12-07). This binder plans for it.
3. **A power cut long enough to drain everything** (→ 09-10).
4. **Heat or cold in a vehicle**: common, and it damages **medicines** too (FDA, Information
   Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency; → 29-07). Using
   medicine after a heat excursion is a decision card: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09
5. **A wide-area electromagnetic event.** Last, and least (NOAA, Space Weather Scales; → 27-02).

**Preparing fully for 1 to 4 also covers 5.** Preparing for 5 alone covers nothing.

## The shielded container: what it can and cannot be

**What is reasonable to say:** a sealed, fully enclosing metal container, with the contents
insulated from the metal, will weaken some radiated fields. That is basic physics, and it costs
nothing with things you own. (A container like this is often called a **Faraday cage**.)

**What is not reasonable to say:** that it is "EMP-proof", that it is tested, or that it makes any
particular device survive any particular event. **None of that can be known at home**, and this
binder will not print it.

**So treat it as** a cheap hedge for **spare** equipment you are not using: never as protection
for devices in daily use, and never as a reason to hold fewer spares.

{{figure fig-shielded-container}}

```
[ ] A metal container that FULLY encloses: a metal trash can with a tight metal
    lid, an ammo can, a metal toolbox. Unbroken metal contact all round the lid
    matters more than thickness.
[ ] Contents INSULATED from the metal: a cardboard box, bubble wrap or foam inside.
[ ] Contents are SPARES ONLY, checked and rotated like anything else (26-08).
[ ] Nothing in it that expires unnoticed, and nothing you need daily.
[ ] Stored dry. Rust and damp are far likelier to ruin the contents than any pulse.
```

{{photo shielded-spares}}

### What is worth putting in it

Small spares whose loss would really hurt, and that you can afford to leave idle:
{{#if has.condition.CL-02}}- **Pump and sensor spares** you are not using: a spare controller or phone set up for the
  device, if your clinic and supplier provide one, with the settings printed on paper beside it
  (→ 02-02). Never all spares in one container or one room.
{{/if}}{{#if has.diabetes}}- **A backup glucose meter, strips and lancets** (in date, → 26-08).
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}- **A spare CPAP power supply and DC cable**, if you have one.
{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-23}}- **Spare hearing aids** and a charger.
{{/if}}- **A small power station or power bank, a folding solar panel and the cables**: a reserve
  power tier you never use day to day (→ 09-03). It comes out for its quarterly charge check
  (→ 24-03) and goes straight back.
- **A small 12-volt inverter** (the box that turns 12-volt battery power into household
  power, → 29-02) that can run from a vehicle's 12-volt socket.
- **A spare battery or hand-crank radio** (→ 15-01) and **a spare handheld radio** (→ 15-02).
- **A spare phone with this binder installed** (→ 00-10) and **a drive with copies of your
  documents** (→ 19-03).
- **A spare headlamp and spare batteries** (→ 10-01).

**Testing a shielding bag:** seal a phone inside and call it. If it rings, the bag leaks. That only
checks phone frequencies: **a bag that fails is certainly leaking; a bag that passes proves
little.** Each quarter, check the stored spares still hold a charge and still work with the
devices they back up (→ 24-03).

**What never goes in it: medicine.** Medicines need a temperature range, not shielding (FDA). A
sealed metal box in a garage or car is a way to destroy them (→ 29-07).

## Working units and the reserve: the honest trade-off

A power station kept plugged into the wall as a backup for a medicine fridge, a CPAP or an oxygen
concentrator is connected to the longest conductor in the house: the power line. That is the path
an electromagnetic event uses. **It is still usually the right choice**: it gives instant backup
power in every ordinary outage, and ordinary outages are far more likely than an electromagnetic
event (ranked 1 to 4 above, against 5). A daily medical benefit outweighs a rare,
unpredictable hedge.

The way to have both:
```
NORMAL TIMES
[ ] Working power stations: connected and doing their job (09-03, 09-16).
    Their protection is the reserve tier below, not a box.
RESERVE TIER (never in daily use)
[ ] A small station or power bank + a folding panel + cables, kept IN the
    shielded container or at least stored unplugged and uncoupled.
SOLAR PANELS AND WIRING
[ ] Panels and their cable runs stored UNCONNECTED when not in use. A connected
    string of panels is a long conductor; a stack of disconnected panels is
    close to inert. Connect a string only to use it.
```

{{#if has.power_station}}Your stations: {{#each stations as s}}{{s.model}} ({{s.wh}} Wh); {{/each}}decide which one is the reserve: ______________{{/if}}

## The things that need no protection at all

This is the more important list:
{{#if has.diabetes}}- **Syringes and insulin pens.** Mechanical.
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}- **Oxygen cylinders and a regulator that needs no power.**
{{/if}}- **Paper**: printed copies of the medical summary (→ 25-09), each person's emergency plans,
  contact cards (→ 25-03), maps (→ 25-04).
- **Manual tools, matches, hand pumps, the woodpile.**
- **Skills** (→ 23-05).

**A household whose critical paths are all mechanical or on paper need not worry much about this
section.** Getting there is the real goal.

## What you need

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **The no-power backup for each device** (syringes or pens, oxygen cylinders, a manual chair, as applies) | The backup that always works | As prescribed; → 12-07 |
| {{#if has.diabetes}}**Backup meter, strips, lancets**{{else}}**Simple non-electronic medical tools**{{/if}} | Not networked, cheap, in date | → 26-08 |
| **A second power bank** | Runtime for the devices and phones | → 09-10 |
| A metal container with a tight lid, and an insulating liner | The honest hedge, cheaply | See the limits above |
| A small 12-volt inverter | Gives the reserve tier household power from a vehicle | → 09-11 |
| A spare battery or hand-crank radio | News when nothing else works | → 15-01 |
| Printed plans and medical summary | Paper is immune to all of this | → 25-09 |

No money? An ammo can, a metal filing-cabinet drawer or a metal trash can all enclose. **The
substitute that matters is not a container at all: it is a practised no-power routine and the
supplies it needs.**

## When it runs out

| Item | Runway | Ration? | Resupply | Substitute |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Prescription medicine** | Your count (→ 23-02) | **No: never a household decision** (→ 12-11) | → 12-07 | **None** |
| Device supplies (pump sets, sensors, tubing, filters) | Count | Only as the prescriber or supplier says | → 12-07 | The no-power backup |
| Test strips | Count | Test as the clinician advises (CDC, Managing Sick Days) | → 12-07 | Poor |
| Device batteries | Days | → 09-01 | Solar, vehicle (→ 09-11) | The no-power backup |

**The point:** every row except the first has a substitute, and the first has none. **The
electronics can be replaced and the medicine cannot** (→ 23-04).

## By phase

- **A, at home:** hold spares, practise the backup, keep the printed plans current.
- **B, moving:** the medical kit rides in the passenger space, not the trunk (→ 22-05); the backup
  plan travels on paper.
- **C, establishing:** electronics get harder to replace and to charge (→ 09-05). The mechanical
  path becomes the normal one, not the backup.
