pages.body:
# Nuclear detonation: the first hour

**What this page is for.** The actions for the first hour after a nuclear explosion, in order,
for a household that is not at the blast itself. Fallout is radioactive dust that the explosion
throws up and that falls back over a wide area in the hours afterwards. It is the main danger at
a distance, and **sheltering inside is what protects you from it.**

> **SAFETY. If this is happening, the message is three words:**
> **GET INSIDE. STAY INSIDE. STAY TUNED.** (Ready.gov, Nuclear Explosion; CDC, Radiation
> Emergencies.)
> Do not go outside to look. Do not drive to collect anyone. Do not leave unless officials tell
> you to. **Sheltering beats travelling**: fallout is worst early and fades fast (→ 27-05), and a
> vehicle gives almost no protection. **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors,
> in a garage, or near an open window**, even now.

## The first hour: do it in this order

```
IF YOU SEE A BRIGHT FLASH
[ ] DO NOT LOOK AT IT. Take cover behind anything that might protect you;
    outside, lie face down to protect bare skin from heat and flying
    debris (Ready.gov). Inside, get down away from windows.
[ ] STAY DOWN until the blast wave has passed. It can arrive some time
    after the flash, and it breaks windows and throws debris.

THEN, AT ONCE
[ ] GET INSIDE the best building you can reach in a FEW MINUTES. Ready.gov:
    you will have 10 minutes or more to find an adequate shelter before
    fallout arrives; if a multi-story building or basement is a few minutes
    away, go there immediately. Do not travel further for a "better" one:
    time outside is what hurts you.
[ ] GO DOWN AND IN: below ground if you can, otherwise the centre of the
    building, away from outside walls, windows and the roof. YOUR SPOT is
    in the box below this list.
[ ] COUNT EVERYONE: every person, and the pets.
[ ] TAKE THE MEDICAL KIT with you (22-06): medicines, epinephrine, go-bags.
[ ] CLOSE windows, doors and vents. Turn off fans, air conditioners and
    forced-air heating units that BRING AIR IN FROM OUTSIDE (Ready.gov;
    CDC): bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans, fresh-air intakes, window
    units. Close the fireplace damper.
    A furnace that only recirculates indoor air may keep running if it has
    power: in winter it is the shelter's heat.

WITHIN THE FIRST 10 TO 15 MINUTES
[ ] IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING IN THROUGH FALLOUT: cover mouth and nose with a
    mask, cloth or towel (CDC). Imperfect beats nothing. Do NOT spend extra
    minutes outside perfecting it.
[ ] IF YOU WERE OUTSIDE: take off outer clothing before going into the
    shelter space, bag it, leave it outside the living space, and wash
    exposed skin and hair gently with soap and water. Removing the outer
    layer of clothing can remove up to 90% of radioactive material (CDC).
    No hair conditioner (FEMA). Do not scrub skin raw. Full routine: 27-05.
[ ] Bring pets in (CDC). If they were outside, brush and wipe the coat
    before they join you (Ready.gov).
[ ] TURN ON A BATTERY RADIO (NOAA Weather Radio or AM/FM). It is your only
    reliable source of instructions. (15-01)

WITHIN THE FIRST HOUR
[ ] SETTLE IN FOR AT LEAST 24 HOURS (Ready.gov): water, food, light, toilet,
    bedding into the shelter space. (27-05)
[ ] MEDICAL: count medicine days, confirm epinephrine is with you, put the
    phone on a power bank. (23-02, 09-10)
[ ] Do NOT take potassium iodide unless public health officials say to. (27-06)
[ ] Write down the time of the event and what you see. (25-05)
[ ] Text, do not call, if phones work at all. Then save the battery. (15-03)
```

### Your shelter spot

{{figure fig-shelter-by-dwelling}}

{{#if has.mobile_home}}**You live in a mobile or manufactured home. It gives very little protection from fallout**: it is
a light frame building, the weakest kind in HHS REMM's ranking. If a sturdy brick or concrete
building (a school, church, store, a neighbour's basement) is a few minutes away, **go there
now**, before fallout arrives: Ready.gov says the safest buildings have brick or concrete walls. If not, go to the centre of the home,
the lowest point, and pile the heaviest things you own around you. Nearby sturdy building:
______________ minutes away: ______
{{/if}}{{#if has.basement}}**Basement.** Go to the corner that is most below ground, away from windows and window wells, and
stack heavy things between you and any glass or exposed wall.{{#if has.walkout}} **Your basement is a walkout**: one
side is at ground level with doors or windows, so it is much weaker. Use the buried side or
corner, and stack mass across the walkout glass and door (→ 27-05).{{/if}}
{{/if}}{{#if has.shelter_room}}**Your named interior room**: {{ dwelling.shelter_room }}. Good if it is on the lowest floor and has no
outside walls; stack mass on any side that faces outside.
{{/if}}{{#if has.apartment}}**Apartment.** In a large building, the best places are underground (a basement or underground
garage) or the **centre of the middle floors**, away from the roof, the ground floor's outside
walls and all windows. Not the top floor; not the ground floor near glass. Use the stairs.
{{/if}}Our spot: ______________. Second choice: ______________.

{{photo fallout-shelter-spot}}

**Shelter with heat in winter.** If the spot you pick is not where you normally keep warm, plan
now how you will heat it. An unvented heater in a closed shelter room is a carbon monoxide risk
that is immediate, while fallout through a cracked window is small and fading: keep the heater's
air openings open (→ 08-01). Running one while people sleep: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02

## Why sheltering beats running

This is the part that goes most against instinct, and where people get hurt.
- **Fallout is most intense early and fades quickly** (→ 27-05). The hours when it is worst
  outside are the hours you would spend driving.
- **A car gives almost no protection.** It is thin metal and glass; Ready.gov marks a car as not
  safe, and CDC says to get inside a building right away.
- **You do not know where the fallout is heading.** Officials, with monitoring, do. That is what
  the radio is for.
- **Roads will be blocked** by everyone else who decided to run.

**Federal guidance is consistent.** CDC: the best way to protect yourself in a radiation
emergency is to **get inside, stay inside, and stay tuned** (CDC, Radiation Emergencies). FEMA's
message for the public after a detonation is the same, and adds: prepare to stay inside for at
least 24 hours unless officials say otherwise or the building is threatened by fire or collapse
(FEMA, Nuclear Detonation Response Guidance, 2023). The exception is when officials order an
evacuation: then follow the route they give.

## What protects you: mass and distance

HHS REMM puts it plainly: a brick building protects better than a brick-veneer one, which
protects better than a wood-frame one, and there is less exposure in interior rooms and below
ground (HHS REMM, Nuclear Explosion).

Planners measure a shelter by its **protection factor** (also called a dose reduction factor).
FEMA's example: a factor of 200 means a person in that spot would receive 1/200th of the dose of
a person out in the open (FEMA, Nuclear Detonation Response Guidance: Planning for the First 72
Hours, 2023; HHS REMM). So a protection factor of 10 means one-tenth. Higher is better.

| Best to worst | Where |
|---|---|
| **Best** | Below ground, in the middle, surrounded by earth; the centre of a large concrete or brick building |
| Good | Middle floors of a large masonry building, interior rooms, away from windows; a basement corner |
| Poor | Ground floor near windows and outside walls; the top floor under the roof; a small wood-frame house above ground |
| **Worst** | Outdoors, in a vehicle, or in a mobile home |

**Two directions matter:** away from the **outside walls**, and away from the **roof**, because
fallout settles on the roof and the ground around you.

A tornado spot and a fallout spot can be different rooms. A tornado spot is for twenty minutes; a
fallout spot is for a day or two, and needs room for water, a toilet, bedding, and heat or
cooling (→ 17-06, → 27-05).

## How far away matters

- **The realistic concern for most households is fallout arriving from far away, hours after an
  explosion somewhere else**, not blast or heat. Distant fallout is exactly the case that
  sheltering handles well: hours of warning, the best space in the house, and 24 to 48 hours of
  supplies is a truly effective response. It is also when the radio matters most, because there
  will be time to be told what is coming.
- Which way the wind usually blows where you live, and what lies upwind, is worth knowing as
  geography. It changes nothing in the list above.

## What this page does not contain

No weapon sizes, blast-radius tables, target lists or dose calculations. **None of them change
a single action above.** If you are close enough for those numbers to matter, no page helps; if
you are far enough away to act, the actions are the ones listed (→ 00-05).

## If someone is outside and cannot reach you

Hard, and best decided now rather than in the moment:
- **They shelter where they are**, in the best building they can reach, for the same 24 hours.
  That is better for them than travelling to you.
- **The family plan says so in advance** (→ 00-04): everyone knows the rule is **shelter where
  you are, reunite when officials say it is safe**, not "everyone come home now".
{{#if has.child}}- **Schools and daycares have shelter plans.** Find out now what your children's are, and write it
  on → 25-03.
{{/if}}

## After the first hour

Go to **→ 27-05**: sheltering through 24 to 48 hours, cleaning off contamination, and judging
when it is reasonable to come out. Then the rest of the binder takes over: this becomes a long
shelter-in-place with no power (→ 01-01).

## What you need

Nothing on this page is unique to nuclear events. The shelter spot needs the 24-to-48-hour
supplies on → 27-05: **water, the medical kit, a battery radio, light, a bucket toilet, bedding,
food{{#if has.child}}, and something to keep children busy{{/if}}.**

No money? **Mass is mass.** Filled water containers, books, boxes of earth, furniture and
appliances stacked between you and the outside walls all add protection, and you already own them
(→ 27-05).

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** the acute phase is roughly **24 to 48 hours**; the supplies are for that window
  plus whatever follows.
- **Ration:** do not ration water or children's food, even in the shelter (→ 23-01).
- **Resupply:** none until officials say it is safe to move.
- **Substitute:** after the acute phase, this is an ordinary long grid-down event and every
  other section applies.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** shelter in place, firmly, against the urge to move.
- **B, moving:** **do not travel during or soon after fallout** unless officials direct it. This
  overrides the usual stay-or-go reasoning (→ 01-02). If officials do direct movement, **follow
  their route, not your own plan**: they know where the fallout is going. **Do not spend minutes
  standing outside hitching a trailer or loading a roof box**: in the one scenario where minutes
  outside matter, speed beats capacity.
- **C, establishing:** distance from likely targets is a minor factor in choosing a destination
  (→ 01-05), well below water and ground.

Potassium iodide is for later and only on official direction (→ 27-06). Adults over 40:
{{choice DC-22}} → 30-23

pages.body:
# Fallout: sheltering, time and decontamination

**What this page is for.** How to shelter for the 24 to 48 hours after a nuclear explosion: where
in your home, how to add protection with what you own, how to get contamination off people and
pets, what to eat and drink, and when to come out. The first hour is → 27-04.

> **SAFETY.** The fact that makes sheltering work: **fallout fades fast.** HHS REMM: the level
> *"decays quickly, roughly by a factor of 10 for every 7-fold increase in time."* **Time inside
> is the most protective thing you can do, and the first day buys the most.** Stay inside at
> least 24 hours unless officials say otherwise (Ready.gov, Nuclear Explosion). **Never run a
> generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** **Bleach or
> pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.**

## Do this now (before anything happens)

1. **Choose the shelter spot** using the guide below, write it down, and photograph it. It may not
   be your tornado spot: a tornado spot is for twenty minutes; a fallout spot is for a day or two
   and needs room for water, a toilet, bedding and heat or cooling (→ 17-06).
2. **Keep stored, covered water near it** (→ 03-02). CDC: **boiling tap water will not get rid
   of radioactive material**, and chlorine only kills germs (→ 03-04). Water in sealed containers
   from before the event{{#if has.water_heater_tank}}, then the water heater
   ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal){{/if}} and the toilet tank (not the bowl), is the answer,
   not treatment (CDC, Food, Drinking Water, and Medicine Safety in a Radiation Emergency).
3. **Put a bucket toilet and cover material there** (→ 13-01). Two days with
   {{ household.size }} people and no plan for waste is its own emergency.
4. {{#if has.child}}**Put something there for the children** (→ 20-08).{{else}}**Put something there to pass the time**: cards, books (→ 21-02).{{/if}}

## The decay rule, and why it decides everything

{{figure fig-fallout-decay-7-10}}

Because fallout fades **about tenfold for every sevenfold increase in time** (HHS REMM):

| Time after the explosion | Roughly |
|---|---|
| **1 hour** | The starting level |
| **7 hours** | About **1/10** of it |
| **2 days (49 hours)** | About **1/100** |
| **2 weeks** | About **1/1,000** |

**What it means:** going outside at hour 1 versus hour 24 is an enormous difference. Day 3 versus
day 4 is small. **That is why the advice is "at least 24 hours" and why the first day is not up
for debate.**

**It is also why the plan is achievable.** Nobody is asking you to live underground for months.
You are being asked to stay put for a day or two with supplies you should have anyway.

## The three protections, in order

1. **Time**: every hour inside counts, and the early ones count most.
2. **Distance**: from the fallout itself, which settles on the roof, the ground and the outside
   walls. Go to the middle of the building and below ground level.
3. **Shielding (mass)**: put heavy material between you and the outside. Earth is best;
   concrete, brick, water and books all work.

**Shelters are measured by protection factor** (a "dose reduction factor"): a factor of 200 means
a person in that spot gets 1/200th of the dose of a person out in the open, so a factor of 10
means one-tenth; higher is better (FEMA, Nuclear Detonation Response Guidance, 2023; HHS REMM).
Interior spots and below ground score higher, and a brick building beats brick veneer, which
beats a wood frame (HHS REMM, Nuclear Explosion).

## The best shelter for your home

{{figure fig-shelter-by-dwelling}}

Your home: {{ dwelling.type }}{{#if has.basement}}, basement: {{ dwelling.basement }}{{/if}}.

{{#if has.basement}}**You have a basement: use it.** Pick the corner most below ground, farthest from windows, window
wells and outside doors. Stack mass against any window well and, if there is living space above,
consider a sturdy table with heavy things on it to sit under.
{{#if has.walkout}}**Your basement is a walkout.** One side is at ground level with glass or a door, so that side
gives little protection. Shelter on the buried side or in the buried corner, and **stack mass
across the walkout glass and door**: it is the room's weak side. If the walkout area is where you
keep warm in winter, the trade is real: the buried corner shields better, the warm side is
heatable. Stack the mass and decide which matters more for your household this night.
{{/if}}{{/if}}{{#if has.shelter_room}}**Your named room**: {{ dwelling.shelter_room }}. An interior room with no outside walls, on the lowest
floor, is a reasonable shelter in a house without a basement. Stack mass on any wall that faces
outside and keep away from the ceiling under the roof if it is a one-storey house.
{{/if}}{{#if has.apartment}}**Apartment.** In a large building, the best places are **below ground** (a basement, an underground
garage) or **the centre of the middle floors**, away from the roof and the outside walls. The top
floor and the ground floor near glass are poor. If your own unit is on the top floor or has
mostly outside walls, a central stairwell or an interior corridor on a middle floor is often
better: agree it with neighbours now. Never use the lifts.
{{/if}}{{#if has.mobile_home}}**Mobile or manufactured home.** It gives very little protection. **The plan is to reach a sturdy
building within minutes**, before fallout arrives (→ 27-04): a school, church, store or a
neighbour's basement that you have agreed in advance. If you cannot reach one in time, go to the
centre of the home, the lowest point, and pile everything heavy you own around you, then move to a
sturdy building only when officials say it is safe.
{{/if}}{{#if !has.basement}}{{#if !has.apartment}}{{#if !has.mobile_home}}**No basement.** Use the most central room on the ground floor, with the fewest outside walls and
windows: often a bathroom, closet or hallway. Stack mass on every side that faces outside.
{{/if}}{{/if}}{{/if}}
Our spot: ______________. Second choice: ______________.

{{photo fallout-shelter-spot}}

### Building shielding from what you have

Stack mass between you and the outside, especially across windows, glass doors and window wells,
and overhead if there is living space or roof above:
- **Water containers**: filled, they are heavy and you need them anyway.
- **Books, full boxes, bags of soil or sand, bins of canned food.**
- **Furniture, mattresses, appliances** against window wells and glass.
- **Earth**, if you can bank it against a window well from inside.

**A smaller, denser space beats a large comfortable one.** You are trading room for mass, and for
a day or two it is the right trade.

## Heat and air in the shelter

- **A furnace that only recirculates indoor air may run if it has power.** Ready.gov's instruction
  is to turn off fans and units that **bring air in from outside** (Ready.gov, Nuclear Explosion).
- **With no furnace, heat the shelter the way you heat one room in any outage** (→ 08-01), with a
  carbon monoxide alarm working where people sleep. **Keep the heater's fresh-air openings open**,
  even here: a closed, heated room without them is a carbon monoxide risk that is immediate, while
  fallout through a cracked window is small and fading. Overnight: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02. A
  propane cylinder over 1 lb indoors: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03
{{#if is.hot_summers}}- **In summer heat**, a closed room gets dangerously hot. Water, wet cloths and rest; watch the
  young and old for heat illness (→ 11-08). Short, early-morning ventilation is a trade-off to make
  only after the first 24 hours, or when officials say so.
{{/if}}

## Decontamination: simple and effective

Most outside contamination is dust on the outside of you. Removing it is straightforward (HHS
REMM; CDC, Radiation Emergencies).

```
[ ] TAKE OFF OUTER CLOTHING before entering the shelter space. Peel it away
    from the face. CDC: removing your outer layer of clothing can remove up to
    90% of radioactive material. This one step is most of it.
[ ] BAG IT and put it outside the living space, well away from people.
[ ] WASH exposed skin and hair with soap and lukewarm water, gently.
    Do NOT scrub skin raw: broken skin lets contamination in.
    Do NOT use hair conditioner (FEMA): it can hold contamination in hair.
[ ] Blow your nose; wipe eyelids and ears with a clean damp cloth.
[ ] Put on clean clothing that was stored inside.
[ ] Wipe down pets that were outside before they come into the shelter space.
```

**Do it at the edge of the shelter space**, so contamination stays on one side of a line everyone
understands. Bagged clothing and gear go **outside the living space**: an outbuilding, a closed
garage, a trailer or a bin outside, away from doors and people.

{{photo decon-boundary}}

{{#if has.child}}**Decontaminating children: the order and the details matter.**
```
[ ] ADULT HANDS FIRST. Clean your own hands (and face if exposed) before you
    touch a child. Dirty hands put contamination back on everything.
[ ] CUT, DON'T PULL. Cut contaminated clothing off rather than pulling it
    over the head: pulling drags the dirty layer across mouth, nose and eyes.
    Keep blunt-tipped trauma shears in the medical kit (22-06).
[ ] EYES AND NOSE: wipe OUTWARD, from the inner corner of the eye out, from
    the nose out and down, with a clean damp part of the cloth for each wipe.
    Never wipe toward the eyes or mouth.
[ ] KEEP THEM WARM. Small children chill fast. Use warm water, wash gently
    and quickly, dry at once, dress in clothes stored inside (11-02).
[ ] TALK THE WHOLE WAY. Say what is happening in plain words, keep your voice
    level, and give an older child a job ("you hold the towel"). A drill
    voice, not an emergency voice (20-08).
```
{{#if has.infant}}**For a baby, warmth outranks speed.** A baby washed in a cold room can get dangerously cold faster
than outside contamination can plausibly hurt them. Warm the water first.
{{/if}}{{/if}}

{{#if has.pets}}**Pets** (Ready.gov: pets come inside too; gently brush the coat, then wash with soap
and water if you have it):
```
[ ] BRING PETS IN and CONFINE them (crate or small room) as soon as you can.
    An animal that grooms a contaminated coat swallows the contamination.
[ ] GLOVES ON. Gently wash or brush the coat out; with cats, wiping
    head-to-tail with damp cloths in or beside the crate is what two people
    can actually do. Change cloths often; bag used cloths with the clothing.
[ ] PAWS: do them thoroughly. Paws carry contamination into bedding and
    litter. Treat the first litter change as contaminated waste: bag it
    with the clothing.
[ ] Pets then stay inside the shelter space with you. Nobody goes outside
    to chase a pet that bolts: it is crated and wiped when it comes back.
```
{{/if}}

## Food and water in the shelter

- **Water: use stored, covered water** (→ 03-02). CDC: drinks in sealed containers are safe, and
  water in the toilet tank (not the bowl) or the water heater is free of radioactive material.
  **Boiling tap water will not get rid of radioactive material** (CDC, Food, Drinking Water, and
  Medicine Safety in a Radiation Emergency); chlorine only kills germs (→ 03-04). Other water is
  a last resort once stored water is gone, not a plan.
- **Food: sealed, packaged food is fine**, and so is food that was in the refrigerator or freezer
  (CDC). Wipe the outside of a container with a damp cloth before opening it (CDC).{{#if has.pets}}
  Pet food in sealed containers is safe for the animals (CDC).{{/if}}
- **Do not pick or eat food from the garden** until officials say it is safe (CDC), and do not
  collect rainwater or use open water until then (→ 03-05).
- **Fallout can contaminate soil, food and water** (HHS REMM); official advisories will say what
  local food is safe.

## 48 hours in one space: the list

This is the part nobody plans and everybody struggles with. It is a logistics and morale problem,
not a physics one.

```
[ ] WATER for {{ household.size }} people for 48 hours: at least 2 days at your
    planning figure of {{ derived.water.plan_gal_day }} gal a day (03-01)
[ ] MEDICAL KIT: every medicine, epinephrine, device and charger      (22-06)
[ ] Bucket toilet, liners, cover material, hand sanitiser             (13-01)
[ ] Food that needs no cooking, for everyone                          (04-01)
[ ] Bedding, and something each person will actually sleep on       (21-07)
[ ] LIGHT: headlamps and spare batteries; a lantern for the space     (10-01)
[ ] Battery radio and spare batteries: your only instruction channel (15-01)
[ ] Warm layers; the heat plan and its CO alarm                       (08-01)
[ ] Cards, books, paper, pencils                                       (21-06)
[ ] This binder, charged                                               (00-10)
```
{{#if has.infant}}- [ ] Diapers, wipes, a changing surface (→ 20-06), and the baby's feeding plan: nursing parent's
  extra water and food, or formula with **sealed bottled water** (→ 20-05, → 02-13).
{{/if}}{{#if has.young_child}}- [ ] Each young child's comfort item, and a few new small activities saved for this (→ 20-08).
{{/if}}{{#if has.food_allergy}}- [ ] Allergy-safe food, sealed and labelled (→ 02-04).
{{/if}}{{#if has.pets}}- [ ] Pet carriers, litter or waste bags, pet food and water (→ 20-09).
{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}- [ ] For older members: medicines, glasses, hearing aids and batteries, a chair they can get up from,
  and a plan for the toilet (→ 02-21).
{{/if}}{{#if has.oxygen}}- [ ] Oxygen cylinders and the regulator (→ 02-08).
{{/if}}{{#if has.cpap}}- [ ] CPAP and its battery (→ 02-24).
{{/if}}{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}- [ ] The medicine cooler and its thermometer (→ 29-07).
{{/if}}

> **Keep the routine.** Meals at meal times, sleep at bedtime{{#if has.child}}, a job for each
> child{{/if}}. It is the most effective thing you can do for people in a small space (→ 21-04,
> → 20-08).

## When can you come out?

**When officials say so.** That is the honest answer, and why the radio is on the list.

With no instruction at all:
- **Do not go out in the first 24 hours** if you can possibly avoid it (Ready.gov).
- **Brief, essential trips only** after that, and brief means minutes.
- **Every trip outside ends with the decontamination routine above.**
- **The longer you wait, the better**: the improvement is steep early and shallow later.

**A home radiation meter** is optional and mostly not useful: a meaningful one is expensive,
needs calibration, and needs interpretation you will not have. **The radio and the clock are the
instruments this plan runs on.**

Potassium iodide is a separate question, only on official direction (→ 27-06). Adults over 40:
{{choice DC-22}} → 30-23

## What you need

Everything on the 48-hour list, and **almost all of it is already in this binder for other
reasons**: stocking one warm room for a winter outage (→ 08-01) stocks it for this. The only
additions worth making are **pre-cut plastic sheeting and tape** for sealing a room (→ 27-07) and
a **second radio**.

No money? Mass from anything heavy; a bucket and bags for the toilet; blankets for warmth; the
water you already store. **There is no substitute for having stored water before the event**:
it is the thing this scenario forgives least.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** stock the shelter for **48 hours**, and the aftermath for as long as → 23-02 says.
- **Ration:** never ration drinking water or children's food (→ 23-01). Ration light and
  battery.
- **Resupply:** only when officials say moving is safe.
- **Substitute:** after the acute phase this becomes an ordinary long outage (→ 01-01), with the
  whole binder behind it.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** this **is** sheltering at home, squeezed into one space for two days.
- **B, moving:** do not move during the acute phase (→ 27-04). Afterwards, → 01-02 applies
  as normal.
- **C, establishing:** a basement with earth around it shelters better than most above-ground
  construction: a small point in a site's favour, well below water and timber (→ 01-05).

pages.body:
# Potassium iodide: what it does and does not do

**What this page is for.** Potassium iodide (KI) is the most misunderstood item in preparedness,
and the misunderstanding is dangerous both ways. This page explains what it does, who should not
take it, and prints FDA's dose table and FDA's home recipe for children **exactly as FDA publishes
them**, because an offline household cannot look them up. Nothing here tells you **when** to take
it: only public health officials do that.

> **SAFETY.** **It is not an anti-radiation pill.** FDA: KI works only to stop the thyroid gland
> taking up radioactive iodine; it is not a general protection against radiation. **"KI should not
> be taken as a preventative before radiation exposure"**: take it **only when public health or
> emergency officials say to.** Taking more than directed does not protect more and can cause
> severe illness or death (FDA, Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium Iodide). **Sheltering
> protects far more than KI does** (→ 27-05). This binder does not work out anyone's dose: find
> each person's row in FDA's table yourself.

## Do this now

1. **Understand what it is for** before deciding whether to keep any: it protects **one gland**
   from **one kind** of contamination. Nothing else.
2. **If you decide to keep some, talk to your clinicians first.** There are real reasons some
   people should not take it (below){{#if has.condition.CL-14}}, and someone in your household has thyroid disease
   (→ 02-14){{/if}}.
3. **Never take it "just in case."** Only on official direction.
4. **Write on the family medical summary (→ 25-09)** anyone who should not take it, and anyone
   in the special groups below.

## The one-sentence version

**KI fills the thyroid with ordinary iodine so it cannot absorb radioactive iodine.** That is the
whole mechanism, and everything true about KI follows from it. The **thyroid** is a gland in the
neck; **radioactive iodine** is one of the materials a nuclear accident or explosion can release,
and the thyroid absorbs it.

## What it does not do

| Belief | What FDA says |
|---|---|
| "It protects you from radiation" | **No.** It is not a general protection against radiation |
| "It protects your whole body" | **No.** The thyroid only |
| "It protects against fallout in general" | **No.** Only against **radioactive iodine**, not other radioactive materials or radiation from outside the body |
| "Take it as soon as you hear about an event" | **No.** Not before exposure; take it when officials say |
| "More is safer" | **No.** More does not protect more and can cause severe illness or death |
| "It's harmless, so why not" | **No.** Some people should not take it (below) |
| "It replaces sheltering" | **No.** **Sheltering is the protection** (→ 27-05). KI covers one narrow route |

## Who should not take it, or should take care

From FDA's KI FAQ:
- **People with a known iodine sensitivity** should avoid it.
- **People with dermatitis herpetiformis or hypocomplementemic vasculitis** (rare conditions
  linked to iodine sensitivity) should avoid it.
- **People with nodular thyroid disease together with heart disease** should not take it.
- **People with multinodular goitre, Graves' disease or autoimmune thyroiditis** should use
  caution, especially if dosing goes on for more than a few days.
- A seafood or shellfish allergy does not necessarily mean iodine sensitivity.

**This is a conversation with your clinician, not a checklist decision**, and another reason not
to buy a bottle and assume it is good for everyone (HHS REMM, Potassium Iodide).

## Where sheltering fits, and why it matters more

| | **Sheltering (→ 27-05)** | **KI** |
|---|---|---|
| **Protects against** | Radiation from outside, breathing in fallout, contamination: broadly | The thyroid taking up radioactive iodine, only |
| **Who it helps** | Everyone | Everyone, but only their thyroid |
| **When** | At once; the first 24 hours matter most | Only when officials direct |
| **Cost** | Free: you already have the building | A purchase, with people who should not take it |
| **If you could only do one** | **This one, by a wide margin** | |

**If a page in this section changes what you do, it should be → 27-05, not this one.**

## Children, and why this page names them

Children are the group most sensitive to radioactive iodine (HHS REMM, Potassium Iodide), and
children exposed to it have a greater risk of thyroid cancer than adults do, which is why public
health guidance puts them first (FDA, KI Preparation and Dosing Instructions, 2012). **That changes none of the rules above**: it is given on official direction, with a
clinician's advice where you can get it. Children's doses are fractions of an adult tablet, and
guessing fractions from memory in the dark is the error this page exists to prevent: so FDA's
table **and** FDA's measuring method are both printed below.

If you keep KI, keep the children's guidance from your paediatrician with it, and note it on
→ 25-09.

## FDA's dose table, as published

> **The when-rule comes first and does not change: KI ONLY when public health officials direct
> it.** Nothing in this table starts a dose. Officials start it; the table only answers how much,
> in FDA's own numbers.

**FDA, Frequently Asked Questions on Potassium Iodide (KI)**, question 5, "Threshold Thyroid
Radioactive Exposures and Recommended Doses of KI for Different Risk Groups", printed as FDA
publishes it. "Predicted thyroid gland exposure" is the radiation dose to the thyroid at which FDA
recommends KI for that group; officials work this out, not households.

| | Predicted Thyroid gland exposure (cGy) | KI dose (mg) | Number or fraction of 130 mg tablets | Number or fraction of 65 mg tablets | Milliliters (mL) of oral solution, 65 mg/mL\*\*\* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adults over 40 years | > 500 | 130 | 1 | 2 | 2 mL |
| Adults over 18 through 40 years | > 10 | 130 | 1 | 2 | 2 mL |
| Pregnant or Lactating Women | > 5 | 130 | 1 | 2 | 2 mL |
| Adolescents, 12 through 18 years\* | > 5 | 65 | ½ | 1 | 1 mL |
| Children over 3 years through 12 years | > 5 | 65 | ½ | 1 | 1 mL |
| Children over 1 month through 3 years | > 5 | 32 | Use KI oral solution\*\* | ½ | 0.5 mL |
| Infants birth through 1 month | > 5 | 16 | Use KI oral solution\*\* | Use KI oral solution\*\* | 0.25 mL |

\* Adolescents approaching adult size (> 150 lbs or > 70 kg) should receive the full adult dose
(130 mg)

\*\* Potassium iodide oral solution is supplied in 1 oz (30 mL) bottles with a dropper marked for
1, 0.5, and 0.25 mL dosing. Each mL contains 65 mg potassium iodide.

\*\*\* See the Home Preparation and Dosing Instructions for Making KI Solution using KI Tablets
for the Emergency Administration of Potassium Iodide to Infants and Small Children (printed
below on this page).

**About the ">" sign.** FDA's 2001 guidance, which this table comes from, prints each threshold as
"at or above" (≥ 500, ≥ 10, ≥ 5 cGy) and the adolescent footnote as ≥ 70 kg; FDA's FAQ web page,
copied above, prints ">" (FDA, Potassium Iodide as a Thyroid Blocking Agent in Radiation
Emergencies, 2001). The difference never matters to a household: officials, not you, decide
whether a threshold has been reached.

**The rules FDA attaches to the table:**
- **One dose a day**, only while officials say the exposure risk continues. More often is not
  more protection.
- **Pregnant women and newborns: FDA does not recommend repeat dosing** unless other protective
  measures are not available. FDA also says pregnant women and newborns should get priority for
  evacuation and sheltering.{{#if has.pregnant}} **Someone in your household is pregnant.**{{/if}}{{#if has.infant}} **There is a baby in your household**: check whether they are in the birth-to-1-month row.{{/if}}{{#if has.nursing}} **Someone in your household is breastfeeding**: they are in the "pregnant or lactating" row; ask a clinician now about repeat doses and write the answer on → 25-09.{{/if}}
- **Adults over 40:** FDA says anyone over 40 should take KI only if the predicted exposure is high
  enough to destroy the thyroid and cause lifelong hypothyroidism (the 500 cGy row) (FDA). HHS
  REMM gives the reason: adults over 40 have the lowest risk of thyroid cancer from radioactive
  iodine and a greater risk of an allergic reaction to KI than younger people (HHS REMM,
  Potassium Iodide). Whether your household follows that is a
  decision card: {{choice DC-22}} → 30-23{{#if has.adult_over_40}} **Your household has at least one adult aged 40 or over.**{{/if}}
- **A dose given wrongly is not corrected with another dose.** Write down who got what and when
  (→ 25-05). Do not re-dose early.

### Your household's rows

Find each person's row in the table yourself and write the row (not a calculated amount) here.
Check it against the label of the product you hold.

{{#each members as m}}- **{{m.label}}** ({{m.age_text}}{{#if has.pregnant}}; pregnant or nursing: {{m.pregnant_or_nursing}}{{/if}}): FDA row ______________________ · should not take / take care (clinician): ______
{{/each}}

## FDA's home recipe for children, using one 130 mg tablet

FDA, *Potassium Iodide (KI) Preparation and Dosing Instructions for Use During a Nuclear
Emergency: To Make KI Solution (Liquid Form), using one 130 mg KI Tablet* (August 22, 2012). For
anyone who cannot swallow tablets. Printed as published.

**You will need:** one 130 mg KI tablet; a teaspoon; a small bowl; four teaspoons of water; four
teaspoons of a drink. FDA recommends any one of: white milk, chocolate milk, orange juice, soda
(for example, cola), infant formula, raspberry syrup, water.

```
Step 1. Soften the KI tablet:
        Put one 130 mg KI tablet into a small bowl. Add four teaspoons of
        water. Soak the tablet for one minute.
Step 2. Crush the softened KI tablet:
        Use the back of the teaspoon to crush the tablet in the water. At the
        end of this step, there should not be any large pieces of KI. This
        makes the KI and water mixture.
Step 3. Add a drink to the KI and water mixture:
        Choose a drink from the list above. Mix four teaspoons of the desired
        drink with the KI and water mixture made in Step 2. Adding the desired
        drink makes the final KI solution.
Step 4. Give the right amount of the final KI solution, using the chart
        below.
```

**How much of the final KI solution to give each day (FDA).** Give this amount once a day until
your healthcare provider or public health official says you may stop.

| Age | Once-daily dose of KI solution |
|---|---|
| 19 years and older | 8 teaspoons |
| 13 to 18 years (150 pounds or more) | 8 teaspoons |
| 13 to 18 years (149 pounds or less) | 4 teaspoons |
| 4 to 12 years | 4 teaspoons |
| Older than 1 month to 3 years | 2 teaspoons |
| Birth to 1 month | 1 teaspoon |

**Storing extra solution (FDA):** store any extra final KI solution in a refrigerator. It can be
used another day. After 7 days, throw out any unused solution.

Use **measuring** teaspoons, not table spoons from the drawer; keep a set in the bag with the KI
(→ 22-06). Do not cut tablets into small pieces by eye for a young child: the solution is the
method FDA gives.

## If officials do direct it

1. **Listen to the actual instruction**: it will say who should take it and when (→ 15-01).
2. **Follow the product label and your clinician's advice.** The tables above are FDA's own,
   printed for when the label is not in hand, not a replacement for either.
3. **Do not take extra**, and not more often than directed (FDA).
4. **Keep sheltering.** KI adds to sheltering; it never replaces it (→ 27-05).
5. **Write down what was given, to whom, and when** (→ 25-05).

## Storage, if you keep it

- Put the **expiry date on → 26-08** like any other medicine.
- Store it **with the medical kit** (→ 22-06), with this page printed or the binder to hand, and
  the measuring spoons.
- **It is not something you grab in the first hour.** Sheltering is (→ 27-04).

## What you need

Honestly, **this is optional and ranks below almost everything on → 26-09.** If you want it: an
in-date supply suited to your household, chosen with your clinicians, stored with the medical
kit, with the children's guidance attached and the expiry tracked (→ 26-08).

**No substitute, and do not improvise one.** CDC: do not use table salt or foods that contain
iodine as a substitute for KI; they do not help, and eating large amounts could be harmful.
Dietary supplements that contain iodine may not work to protect the thyroid and can hurt you
(CDC, Potassium Iodide (KI), 2025). Iodine antiseptics (tincture of iodine, povidone-iodine) are
for skin, not for swallowing, and are not substitutes either. **If you have no KI and
officials recommend it, shelter and follow their instructions**, which is the bigger protection
anyway.

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** it has an expiry date; track it (→ 26-08).
- **Ration:** **never take more than directed**: more is not better and can be fatal (FDA).
- **Resupply:** a pharmacy now; in a real emergency, public health distribution.
- **Substitute:** none. But note what that means: unlike a daily prescription, **not having KI is
  not life-threatening on its own.** Sheltering carries the protection.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** the only phase where it applies, and only on official direction.
- **B, moving:** it does not change the rule that you shelter rather than travel (→ 27-04).
- **C, establishing:** the same rules apply anywhere; what changes is how you hear the
  instruction (→ 15-01).

pages.body:
# Chemical and biological release

**What this page is for.** Chemical and biological releases get named together, but they need
almost opposite responses. **Chemical:** fast, local, and a **seal-the-room-and-listen** problem
lasting hours. **Biological:** slow, wide, and handled by **the pandemic plan** already on → 17-09
and → 13-11. This page is mostly about the chemical half.

> **Caution.** **For fallout you go down; for chemical vapour you go up.** Getting this backwards
> is one of the few truly dangerous mistakes in this section. **The radio tells you which one you
> are in** (→ 15-01). **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other
> cleaners**: that mixing is itself a common household chemical release.

## Do this now

1. **Know that the likely version is an accident, not an attack.** A rail, highway or plant
   release{{#if is.rural}}, or an anhydrous ammonia release from farm storage or a field tank{{/if}}, is far more likely, and
   the response is the same.
2. **Pick the room you would seal**: interior, upper floor if you have one, few windows, water
   nearby if possible. Pre-cut plastic sheeting and tape for it and store them there (→ 08-03).
3. **Set the rule now: go inside and listen. Do not drive into or through a cloud.**
4. **For anything biological, go to → 17-09 and → 13-11.** That is the plan.

## The two are not alike

| | **Chemical release** | **Biological release** |
|---|---|---|
| **Starts** | Minutes | Days to weeks |
| **Spread** | A local cloud (a "plume"), driven by wind | Possibly everywhere |
| **You find out because** | You are told, or you see or smell it | Public health announces it, later |
| **Core response** | **Get inside, seal, listen** | Distance, hygiene, isolate the sick |
| **Lasts** | Hours | Weeks to months |
| **Where in this binder** | **This page** | → 17-09, → 13-11 |

## Chemical: shelter in place, properly

The cloud passes. Your job is to be inside and sealed while it does (FEMA/Ready.gov, Shelter;
Ready.gov, Hazardous Materials Incidents).

{{figure fig-up-for-vapour-down-for-fallout}}

```
[ ] GET INSIDE. Bring everyone and the pets in. Close all doors and windows.
[ ] SHUT OFF anything that moves outside air in: furnace and air-conditioning
    fans, bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans, fireplace dampers, the dryer.
[ ] GO UP, NOT DOWN. Ready.gov: an above-ground room with as few openings as
    possible. Some chemical gases, chlorine among them, are heavier than air
    and collect low (ATSDR), so a basement is the WRONG place here: the
    opposite of the fallout answer (27-05).
[ ] SEAL that room: plastic sheeting and tape over windows, vents and the gaps
    round the door. A wet towel along the bottom of the door helps.
[ ] TAKE IN: water, the medical kit (22-06), phones, a battery radio, and
    something to pass the time.
[ ] LISTEN. Weather radio and local broadcast. Officials will say when it is
    over and whether to leave. (15-01)
[ ] DO NOT LEAVE unless told to. Driving into a cloud is worse than sitting
    it out.
[ ] AFTERWARDS: air the house out thoroughly and follow any official cleaning
    advice (CDC, When and How to Clean and Disinfect Your Home). (13-11)
```

Your sealing room: ______________ {{#if has.apartment}}(in an apartment: an interior room of your own unit, away from the corridor
door and windows; the building's ventilation may need the building manager to turn it off){{/if}}{{#if has.mobile_home}}(a mobile home leaks air badly: seal the smallest interior room, and leave early if officials
advise it){{/if}}

{{photo seal-room}}

### The sealed room, by the numbers

- **Room size: about 10 square feet of floor space per person.** FEMA: that gives enough air to
  prevent carbon dioxide build-up for up to 5 hours, assuming a normal breathing rate while
  resting, and many chemical releases would be diluted within a few hours (FEMA, How long to
  remain in a shelter-in-place room?). For
  {{ household.size }} people{{#if has.pets}} and the pets{{/if}}, most normal bedrooms clear that
  bar; pick the room for its position (interior, upstairs, few windows), not its size.
- **It is temporary.** A taped room with people breathing in it goes stale in **hours**. You seal,
  listen, and unseal on the all-clear. It is not a bunker.
- **The judgement line:** if hours have passed with no all-clear and the room is getting stuffy
  (headache, heavy air{{#if has.child}}, a drowsy child{{/if}}), **open the seal, refresh the air
  briefly, and reseal.** Stale air is a certainty on a clock; the cloud outside has probably
  passed. Do not let a taped window outrank the people inside.

**Pre-cut the plastic now, to the room's actual openings.** Cutting sheeting during a release
wastes the minutes that matter. Ready.gov: cut the plastic several inches wider than the openings,
label each sheet, and tape the corners first, then all the edges (Ready.gov, Shelter). Write the
sizes here:

| Opening | Width | Height | Cut size (several inches extra per side) | Piece labelled? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Window 1 | ____ | ____ | ____ | [ ] |
| Window 2 | ____ | ____ | ____ | [ ] |
| Door | ____ | ____ | ____ | [ ] |
| Vent or return | ____ | ____ | ____ | [ ] |
| Outlets and gaps | ____ | ____ | ____ | [ ] |

### If you were outside and exposed

The same idea as → 27-05: most of it is on the outside of you.

```
[ ] TAKE OFF outer clothing before going inside. Cut it off rather than
    pulling it over the face if it is contaminated.
[ ] BAG it and leave it outside the living space.
[ ] WASH with soap and lukewarm water. Flush eyes with clean water.
[ ] Put on clean clothing stored inside.
[ ] GET MEDICAL ADVICE. Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, is staffed and
    handles exposures. (25-03)
    NO PHONE: the offline poisoning page (12-17). Cleaning off as above is
    the treatment; do not make anyone vomit, do not try to "neutralise"
    a chemical on skin, watch breathing.
```

## Why this page does not recommend gas masks

A respirator helps only if **all three** are true: the **right cartridge for that exact
chemical**, a **proper seal on the face**, and **training to use it**. In a real release you will
not know the chemical in time to choose a cartridge.{{#if has.child}} And **adult respirators do not
fit young children**: there is no protective mask you can put on a small child.{{/if}}

**So the household's protection is the building, not the face.** Sealing a room protects
everyone, costs almost nothing, and does not depend on knowing what was released. **N95 masks are
still worth having** for dust, clean-up and outbreaks (→ 13-11), just not as chemical protection.

## The two you are most likely to meet

Rail lines, highways and industry carry hazardous chemicals almost everywhere, and farm country
adds its own. Two are worth knowing by sight and smell (CDC/ATSDR, Medical Management Guidelines
for Ammonia; for Chlorine):

| Chemical | Where it comes from | What you would notice | Where the cloud goes (ATSDR) | The trap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Anhydrous ammonia** | Rail, and farm supply stores and field tanks in farming areas{{#if is.rural}} (likely near you){{/if}} | Sharp, choking, suffocating smell; you may see a cloud | ATSDR: the gas is **lighter than air and will rise**, **but** vapour from the liquefied gas is **at first heavier than air and may spread along the ground** | Do not read "lighter than air" as "safe low down". The early cloud, the dangerous one, behaves heavy. Treat it as ground-hugging until it visibly lifts |
| **Chlorine** | Rail (water treatment and industry) | **Yellow-green gas**; sharp, irritating smell, like strong bleach | ATSDR: **heavier than air** and **may collect in low-lying areas** | **A basement is the worst room in a chlorine release.** This is the down-for-fallout, up-for-vapour reversal at its sharpest |

**You will not identify the chemical in time, and you do not need to.** Caught outside near a
visible cloud or a choking smell: **move away at once, in a direction upwind of the source**
(Ready.gov, Hazardous Materials Incidents), never through the cloud and never downwind along it,
**then get inside, seal, listen** (→ 15-01). Both chemicals above, and everything else on a rail car, are answered by the
same sealed upstairs room.

## Biological: read → 17-09, not this page

For a household, a deliberate biological release and a natural pandemic look the same and are
handled the same way. You will learn about it from public health, not your own senses. The
response:
- **Distance and less contact** (→ 17-09).
- **Handwashing**: the measure that actually works (CDC, About Handwashing; → 13-02).
- **Isolate anyone who is sick** inside the household (→ 13-11).
- **Protect the most vulnerable**{{#if has.infant}}: babies{{/if}}{{#if has.elder}}, older members{{/if}}{{#if has.condition.CL-18}}, anyone on immune-suppressing medicine (→ 02-18){{/if}}, anyone with a chronic condition (→ 12-11).
- **Follow public health instructions** on treatment and preventive medicine, if any exist.

**Do not stockpile antibiotics against an unknown germ.** They do nothing for viruses, the right
drug depends on the organism, and misuse causes harm (→ 12-04). Antibiotics without a
prescription are a decision card: {{choice DC-16}} → 30-17

## What you need

| Item | Why | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-cut plastic sheeting and strong tape** | The whole chemical response | Cut and label it now (table above) |
| **A battery weather radio** | How you learn what it is and when it ends (NOAA, NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards) | → 15-01 |
| Water and the medical kit in the room | You may be there for hours | → 22-06 |
| N95 masks, nitrile gloves, eye protection | Clean-up and outbreaks, **not** chemical protection | → 13-11 |
| Soap, plenty | Cleaning off, and the biological half | → 13-02 |
| Poison Control number posted | Staffed and fast while phones work | → 25-03; offline → 12-17 |

No money? Any plastic and tape seals a room: bin bags, shower curtains, painter's plastic. Wet
towels at the bottoms of doors. **The room matters more than the materials.**

## When it runs out

- **Runway:** a chemical shelter-in-place lasts **hours**. Stock the room for a day and you have
  over-prepared, which is the right way round.
- **Ration:** nothing, at these lengths of time.
- **Resupply:** afterwards, as normal.
- **Substitute:** for the biological half, the whole of → 17-09 and → 13-11.

## By phase

- **A, at home:** shelter and seal. This is an event of hours, not a change of phase.
- **B, moving:** **do not drive through a cloud.** If officials order an evacuation, take the route
  they give, not the fastest one (→ 01-02).
- **C, establishing:** distance from rail lines, highways and large chemical storage is a modest
  factor in choosing a place (→ 01-05).

- → 28-04 **Portable fuel heaters: the specs that keep you safe, and common models**: A portable fuel heater burns propane or kerosene in the room and lets the exhaust out into the room.

# Power stations: the specs that keep you safe, and common models

**What this page is for.** A power station is a big battery in a box with its own charger, its
own solar charge controller and its own inverter (the part that makes household-style 120 V AC
power). New to the words volts, amps, watts and watt-hours? Read → 29-02 first. This page lists
the handful of numbers on a power station that decide whether it powers what you need, survives
the cold, and survives the solar panels you plug into it. Then it gives those numbers, from the
makers' own manuals and spec pages, for common models. **The label on your own unit wins over
this table every time** (→ 28-07).

## What matters and why

1. **Capacity, in watt-hours (Wh).** How much energy it holds. A 1,000 Wh station runs a 100 W
   load for very roughly 10 hours, less after inverter losses (→ 29-02). Some makers print the
   cell rating (for example "51.2 V, 20 Ah"); volts × amp-hours = watt-hours.
2. **Chemistry.** "LiFePO4" or "LFP" (lithium iron phosphate) is the longer-lived, less
   fire-prone kind; "NMC" or plain "lithium-ion" packs more energy into less weight. Both are
   lithium and both need the care in → 09-07. The warning signs of a failing lithium battery are
   heat, an odd smell, swelling, leaking, smoke or unusual noise: get people out and do not try to
   carry it (NFPA, Lithium-Ion Batteries; → 09-07).
3. **AC continuous (rated) watts.** The most the inverter delivers all day. Add up what will be
   plugged in at once and stay under it.
4. **AC surge or peak watts.** A short burst for motors starting (fridge, pump, furnace blower).
   Motors can need several times their running watts for a moment (→ 09-04). Some makers also
   advertise a "boost" or "lifting" mode that runs **heating-type** loads (kettle, hair dryer)
   above the rated watts by lowering the voltage; the manuals say it is not for motors.
5. **Solar input: maximum voltage (V), current (A), watts (W) and the connector.** This is the
   number that destroys stations. The station's built-in controller has a voltage ceiling. The
   panels' **Voc** (open-circuit voltage, printed on every panel) added up for panels wired in a
   chain, **times 1.20 for cold mornings**, must stay under that ceiling (→ 09-02, → 28-02). Too
   much current or too many watts only wastes power; too many volts breaks the controller for
   good and the warranty does not cover it. There is also a minimum voltage below which charging
   will not start.
6. **Car-charging input.** Whether it charges from a vehicle's 12 V socket, and at what rate.
   Some share the solar port. Goal Zero, for one, says to use its own 12 V lithium charging cable
   because an ordinary cable can damage the unit (Goal Zero, Yeti 1500X).
7. **Pass-through and UPS.** Many stations pass wall power straight to their outlets while
   charging and switch to battery when the power fails. The makers state a switch-over time
   (10 to 30 milliseconds in the table) and **all of them say it is not a true 0 ms UPS**: test
   any medical or computer device on it before you rely on it (→ 09-06).
8. **Charging and operating temperature.** Lithium must not be **charged** below freezing; most
   stations refuse to charge below 32 °F (0 °C) and some stop discharging below 14 °F or −4 °F.
   A station in a cold garage or car may show full and still refuse to charge from the sun.
   Bring it into the warm room (→ 08-01, → 09-07).
9. **Expansion and the AC output.** Extra battery packs fit only the models the maker lists. The
   AC outlets are for plugging appliances in. **They are never connected to the house wiring**
   except through equipment made for it and installed for it, for the same reason a generator is
   not (→ 30-01, → 29-04, → 09-04).

## Common models, from the makers' own documents

Every number is copied from the document named in the last column. "See label" means the maker's
document read for this kit did not publish it. The EcoFlow DELTA 2 manual read is the European
edition (230 V outlets) and the Anker F3800 guide the British one. The F3800 row takes its US
outlet figures from Anker's US page; the DELTA 2 row is marked, and a US unit's AC outlet figures
may differ. Check those two rows against your own label, the solar input line first. Solar input is per port unless it says total.

| Model | Capacity, chemistry | AC continuous / surge | Solar (DC) input: volts, amps, watts, connector | Car charging | UPS switch-over | Charge / discharge temperature | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EcoFlow RIVER 2 Pro | 768 Wh, LFP | 800 W / 1,600 W surge, 120 V | 11–50 V, 13 A, 220 W max; XT60 | See label (shares the DC input) | See label | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | EcoFlow, RIVER 2 Pro user manual |
| EcoFlow DELTA 2 | 1,024 Wh, LFP | 1,800 W / 2,700 W surge in the EU edition (230 V); US outlets: see label | 11–60 V, 15 A, 500 W max; XT60 | 12 V or 24 V battery, default 8 A | Within 30 ms (EPS) | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | EcoFlow, DELTA 2 user manual |
| EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max | 2,048 Wh, LFP | 2,400 W / 4,800 W surge, 120 V | 2 ports, each 11–60 V, 15 A, 500 W; 1,000 W both; XT60 | 12 V or 24 V battery, default 8 A | Within 30 ms (EPS) | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | EcoFlow, DELTA 2 Max user manual |
| EcoFlow DELTA 3 Max Plus | 2,048 Wh, LFP | 3,000 W / 6,000 W surge, 120 V (US) | 2 ports, each 11–60 V, 18 A; watts: see label; XT60i | 12 V or 24 V at 8 A; 48 V at 10.4 A (same ports) | See label | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | EcoFlow, DELTA 3 Max Plus user manual |
| Jackery Explorer 300 Plus | 288 Wh, lithium-ion | 300 W / 600 W surge, 120 V | USB-C input, 12–27 V, 5 A, 100 W max | 12 V car charger; rate: see label | Within 20 ms | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | Jackery, Explorer 300 Plus user manual (JE-300B) |
| Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | 1,070 Wh, LiFePO4 | 1,500 W / 3,000 W surge, 120 V | 2 × 8 mm (DC8020): 16–60 V at up to 10.5 A each, 400 W max both | Low-voltage range of the same ports: 12–16 V, up to 8 A | Within 20 ms (manual) | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | Jackery, Explorer 1000 v2 US product page; user manual (JE-1000D) for the switch-over time |
| Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus | 2,042.8 Wh, lithium-ion | 3,000 W / 6,000 W surge, 120 V | 2 × 8 mm (DC8020): 17.5–60 V at up to 12 A each, 1,400 W max both | Low-voltage range of the same ports: 11–17.5 V, up to 8 A | Within 20 ms | 32–113 °F / 14–113 °F | Jackery, Explorer 2000 Plus user manual (JE-2000C) |
| Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 | 1,024 Wh, LFP | 2,000 W; heating loads up to 2,400 W ("SurgePad"); not for motors per Anker | See label | See label | Within 10 ms | 32–104 °F / −4–104 °F | Anker, C1000 Gen 2 user guide |
| Anker SOLIX F3800 | 3,840 Wh, LiFePO4 | 6,000 W max; 120 V and 120/240 V (US, from Anker's comparison table) | 2 ports, each 11–60 V, 1,200 W each; XT-60. Current limit depends on firmware: 10 A below 32 V and 25 A from 32 to 60 V (older), or 10 A below 15 V and 27 A from 15 to 60 V (newer). **Over 60 V damages it** | Shares the solar ports; see label | 20 ms | 32–104 °F / −4–104 °F (given in °C) | Anker, F3800 user guide (A1790, UK edition), and the F3800 vs F3800 Plus table on Anker's US F3800 Plus page |
| Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus | 3,840 Wh, LFP | 6,000 W max; 120 V and 120/240 V (L14-30R) | 2 ports, each 11–165 V, 17 A, 1,600 W | See label | 20 ms, on the UPS outlets, when plugged into a 120 V wall outlet | See label | Anker, F3800 Plus product page |
| BLUETTI AC70 | 768 Wh, LiFePO4 | 1,000 W; resistive loads to 2,000 W ("Power Lifting") | 12–58 V, 10 A, 500 W max; XT60. **Panels over 58 V Voc must not be used** | 12 V or 24 V socket, through the DC input | 20 ms or less | 32–104 °F / −4–104 °F | BLUETTI, AC70 user manual |
| BLUETTI AC180 | 1,152 Wh, LiFePO4 | 1,800 W; resistive loads to 2,700 W ("Power Lifting") | 12–60 V, 10 A, 500 W max; DC7909 (MC4 cable supplied). **Over 60 V Voc damages it** | 12 V socket, through the DC input | 20 ms or less | 32–104 °F / −4–104 °F (1,500 W max above 86 °F) | BLUETTI, AC180 user manual |
| Goal Zero Yeti 1500X | 1,516 Wh, lithium-ion NMC | 2,000 W / 3,500 W surge, 120 V | High-power port 14–50 V, up to 50 A, 600 W max; 8 mm ports 14–50 V, up to 10 A, 150 W max | Goal Zero 12 V lithium car cable only | See label | Operating 32–104 °F | Goal Zero, Yeti 1500X product page |

**Two lessons hide in this table.** First, the Anker F3800 and F3800 Plus look alike and their
solar ceilings differ by more than 100 volts: a string that suits one destroys the other. Second,
stations from the same maker take panels in different voltage windows (50 V, 58 V, 60 V). **Never
move a panel string from one station to another without redoing the cold check** (→ 28-02).

Models from these makers that the kit looked for but could not confirm from a maker's own
document are left out rather than guessed. Many brands share these designs; whatever you own,
the rating label next to the solar input is the authority (→ 28-07).

## Habits that protect a station

- **Connect panels in the order your manual gives.** Some makers say to connect the panels
  before switching the station on. Write your manual's order on the label photo.
- **Measure Voc with a multimeter** before the first connection of any new panel or string, on a
  cold sunny morning if you can (→ 09-12, → 28-02).
- **One connector fits many things.** An adapter that lets a panel plug in does not make it safe:
  check volts first.
- **Store at part charge in a cool, dry place**, check it monthly, and top it up as the manual
  says (→ 09-03, → 09-07).

# Solar panels and charge controllers: the label numbers and common models

**What this page is for.** Every solar panel carries a label with four electrical numbers, and
every charge controller (the box, separate or built into a power station, that turns panel power
into battery charge) carries its limits. Matching the two is the whole job. This page explains
the numbers in plain words, shows the cold-weather check with real published figures, and lists
common panels and controllers from the makers' own documents. How solar works and how much it
makes in your season: → 09-02 and → 09-05. Connectors and adapters: → 09-12.

## What matters on a panel, and why

| Label word | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Pmax** (rated watts) | Power at the test lab's bright light, 77 °F (25 °C) | Real panels make less: haze, angle, heat. Plan on less |
| **Voc** (open-circuit voltage) | Volts with nothing connected. **The highest voltage the panel makes** | Decides whether you destroy a controller. Always check against Voc, never Vmp |
| **Isc** (short-circuit current) | The most current it can push | Some controllers print a maximum input Isc too. Exceed that and it may be damaged |
| **Vmp, Imp** | Volts and amps while working at its best point | Vmp × Imp ≈ rated watts. Useful for sizing cable, not for safety limits |
| **Temperature coefficient of Voc** | How much Voc rises per degree colder, in % per °C | Lets you work the cold check exactly (below) |
| **Maximum system voltage, maximum series fuse** | Limits for the panel itself in a big array | Matter for fused, multi-panel arrays (→ 09-08) |
| **Connector** | MC4, Anderson, 8 mm (DC8020), DC7909, XT60, USB | A panel that plugs in is not necessarily safe to plug in |

**Series and parallel.** Panels chained plus-to-minus (series) **add their volts**; current stays
that of one panel. Panels joined plus-to-plus and minus-to-minus (parallel) **add their amps**;
volts stay those of one panel. Mixing models in one series string drags every panel down to the
weakest one's current. More on wiring: → 09-02, → 09-08.

## The cold check, every time

Panels are rated at 77 °F. **Colder panels make higher voltage**, and the highest voltage of the
year comes at sunrise on a clear, frozen morning (→ 09-02). The rule this kit uses:

1. Add up the label **Voc** of every panel wired in series.
2. **Multiply by 1.20.**
3. That number must be **below** the controller's or station's maximum solar input voltage.

**A worked example with published numbers.** The Renogy RSP200D datasheet (third-generation
sheet) gives Voc 23.0 V and a Voc coefficient of −0.28 % per °C. At −40 °F (−40 °C, 65 °C below the
lab's 77 °F) that panel's Voc rises by 0.28 × 65 ≈ 18 %, so the 1.20 factor covers it. A panel
with a larger coefficient, or a place colder than that, needs its own factor (method: → 09-02).

- Two in series: 46.0 V × 1.20 = **55.2 V cold**. Under a 60 V station limit. **Over** a 50 V
  limit: on such a station, that string will damage it.
- Three in series: 69.0 V × 1.20 = **82.8 V cold**. Over any 60 V station; under a 100 V
  controller.
- Four Rich Solar MEGA 100 panels in series: 4 × 22.8 V = 91.2 V; × 1.20 = **109.4 V cold**. Over
  a 100 V controller even though the warm number looks fine.

**Same name, different numbers.** Makers revise panels and mark it only with a small revision
code (the sheet above is "G3"). **Use the label on your own panel, and a multimeter reading in
full sun, not the catalogue** (→ 28-07).

**The three controller limits are not equally dangerous.** Too many volts breaks the controller
input at once and for good. Too many watts or amps is usually clipped: the controller takes what
it can and wastes the rest. The exception is a **maximum PV short-circuit current**, where the
maker prints one: Victron says an array with a higher short-circuit current may damage the
controller, and EcoFlow tells you to keep total Isc within 18 A on the DELTA 3 Max Plus ports
(Victron, SmartSolar MPPT 100/30 and 100/50 datasheet; EcoFlow, DELTA 3 Max Plus user manual).
**When in doubt, choose the wiring that keeps volts lower.** Wasted watts are free; a dead
controller is not.

## Common panels, from the makers' own documents

STC means the lab's standard test: bright sun (1,000 W per square metre) and a 77 °F panel.
"See label" means the maker's document read for this kit did not give it.

| Panel | Rated W | Voc | Isc | Vmp | Imp | Connector, other limits | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Renogy RSP200D (rigid, glass) | 200 | 23.0 V | 11.05 A | 19.2 V | 10.42 A | MC4; Voc coefficient −0.28 %/°C; max series fuse 20 A; operating −40 to 185 °F | Renogy, RSP200D datasheet (G3) |
| Rich Solar MEGA 100 (rigid) | 100 | 22.8 V | 5.78 A | 18.6 V | 5.38 A | MC4; max series fuse 10 A; operating −40 to 185 °F | Rich Solar, MEGA 100 product page |
| EcoFlow NextGen 220 W bifacial portable | 220 front (175 rear) | 21.5 V | 12.4 A front | 18.4 V | 11.9 A front | "Photovoltaic connectors"; IP68 | EcoFlow, 220 W bifacial panel product page |
| EcoFlow 400 W lightweight portable | 400 | 39.3 V | 12.2 A | See label | See label | Cable to XT60/XT60i station input | EcoFlow, 400 W lightweight panel user manual |
| BLUETTI PV200 (folding) | 200 | 26.1 V | 10.3 A | 20.5 V | 9.7 A | MC4; operating 14 to 149 °F (given as −10 to +65 °C); IP65, not waterproof | BLUETTI, PV200 user guide |
| Jackery SolarSaga 100 (JS-100C) | 100 | 24.8 V | 5.6 A | 20 V | 5 A | DC7909 plug, DC7909–DC8020 adapter; USB-A and USB-C outputs; operating −4 to 149 °F | Jackery, SolarSaga 100 user guide |

Notice the folding panels: **two of the 26.1 V panels in series reach about 62.6 V cold**, already
over a 60 V station. Folding panels made for one brand's station are often meant to be used one
at a time or in parallel; their manual says which.

## Charge controllers

A separate controller sits between panels and a battery (a 12 V or 24 V battery bank, not a power
station, which has its own). The model name of many controllers is the limits: "100/30" means a
100 V solar input ceiling and 30 A of charging current.

| Controller | Battery | Charge current | Max solar Voc | Max solar Isc | Panel watts it uses at 12 V / 24 V | Notes | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Victron SmartSolar MPPT 100/30 | 12/24 V auto | 30 A | 100 V | 35 A | 440 W / 880 W | Solar volts must be at least battery volts + 5 V to start; full output to 104 °F, operating −22 to 140 °F | Victron, SmartSolar 100/30 and 100/50 datasheet |
| Victron SmartSolar MPPT 100/50 | 12/24 V auto | 50 A | 100 V | 60 A | 700 W / 1,400 W | As above | Victron, same datasheet |

More panel than the "watts it uses" figure is allowed by Victron: the controller limits what it
takes. More **volts** than 100 is never allowed. Other controllers (Renogy, Rich Solar, EPEver and
others) print the same three limits on their side label; the kit could not confirm a Renogy
controller sheet from Renogy's own site and left it out rather than guess.

## Our panels

From the back of each panel (→ 28-07). The cold column is your series string's total Voc × 1.20.

| Panel | Watts | How many | Voc | Isc | Vmp / Imp | Connector | Wired as | String Voc cold (× 1.20) |

{{else}}| ______ | ______ | ______ | ______ V | ______ A | ______ / ______ | ______ | series / parallel | ______ V |
{{/each}}

{{#if has.solar}}Our panels total **{{ gear.solar_w_total }} W**. A rough December day gives about
**{{ derived.solar_wh_dec }} Wh** and a June day about **{{ derived.solar_wh_jun }} Wh**
(estimates, → 09-05).{{/if}}

**Our controllers and what each panel string feeds:**

| Controller or station input | Max solar volts | Max Isc | Which string | Cold string Voc | Under the limit? |

# Portable generators: the specs that keep you safe, and common models

**What this page is for.** A portable generator is a small engine that turns a generator head and
gives you household power wherever you park it. This page lists the numbers on a generator that
decide what it can run, how long, on what fuel, and how it may be connected, then gives those
numbers for common models from the makers' own manuals and spec pages. How to run, refuel and
connect one safely is on → 09-04; upkeep on → 09-15.

> **SAFETY.** Two floors apply to every generator (→ 30-01).
> **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.**
> Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no mitigation that works
> every time. Run it outdoors, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed
> away (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics; CPSC, Portable Generator Safety).
> **Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide") cord.**
> Backfeeding electrocutes line workers and neighbours and starts fires (→ 29-04).

## What matters and why

1. **Running (rated) watts and starting (surge, peak, maximum) watts.** Running watts is what it
   gives all day. Starting watts is a brief burst for motors. A fridge, well pump or furnace
   blower needs several times its running watts for a moment when it starts (→ 09-04). Add the
   running watts of everything on at once and keep a margin; check the biggest motor against the
   starting figure. Some makers print kVA (kilovolt-amps) instead: for planning, 1.8 kVA reads as
   1,800 W.
2. **Fuel.** Gasoline, propane, or both ("dual fuel"); some also natural gas ("tri-fuel").
   **Output is lower on propane**: about 10 % less in the table. Gasoline goes stale in months;
   propane keeps (→ 29-01, → 06-05). Whether stale fuel may be used is a decision card
   (→ 30-18).
3. **Tank and run time, with the load it was measured at.** Makers quote run time at 25 % or 50 %
   of rated load. At full load it is much shorter. Compare like with like.
4. **Inverter or not.** An **inverter generator** makes steady, clean power, throttles down at
   light load and is quieter. A **conventional** ("open frame") generator is cheaper per watt and
   often bigger. Sensitive electronics and some battery chargers are fussy about rougher power:
   test your own charger on your own generator before you need it.
5. **120 V only, or 120/240 V.** Many well pumps run on **240 V**, and a standard residential
   inlet and interlock are 240 V, usually fed from a four-prong twist-lock outlet (L14-30R) or a
   50 A outlet (14-50R). A 120 V-only generator cannot properly drive them. If the manual says it
   is not transfer-switch ready, it is not for one (→ 09-04, → 29-04).
6. **CO shutoff.** Newer models carry a carbon-monoxide sensor that stops the engine when CO
   builds up around it. Makers name it differently: CO-MINDER (Honda), CO Shield (Champion),
   CO SECURE (Predator), CO sensor (Westinghouse). **It protects people near the generator; it
   is not a CO alarm for the house** (Champion says so on its page). Keep battery CO alarms on
   every level and by the beds (→ 08-02).
7. **Altitude and temperature.** Engines lose power in thin air: Honda and Generac both give
   **about 3.5 % less per 1,000 feet** of elevation, and some carburettors need a high-altitude
   kit (Predator: above 3,280 ft). Generac also gives an operating range of 8 to 104 °F and less
   power when hot. {{#if is.high_altitude}}At about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft, plan on
   your generator giving noticeably less than its plate says.{{/if}}
8. **Outlets.** 5-20R is the ordinary household duplex (20 A); TT-30R is the RV outlet (120 V,
   30 A); L5-30R is a 120 V twist-lock; L14-30R and 14-50R are 120/240 V. The outlet decides
   which cord and which connection are possible (→ 09-12).
9. **Distance from the house for fire, too.** Honda's manuals also say to keep the generator at
   least 3 feet from buildings for cooling and fire. That is **in addition to** the 20 feet from
   windows, doors and vents for carbon monoxide, not instead of it.

## Common models, from the makers' own documents

"See label" means the maker's document read for this kit did not give it. Run times say the load
they were measured at.

| Model | Fuel | Running / starting W | Volts | Inverter | Tank | Run time | CO shutoff | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Honda EU2200i | Gasoline | 1,800 / 2,200 (1.8 / 2.2 kVA) | 120 V | Yes | 0.95 gal | See label | Not in the manual edition read; CO-MINDER units: see label | Honda, EU2200i owner's manual |
| Honda EU7000iS | Gasoline | 5,500 / 7,000 (5.5 / 7.0 kVA) | 120/240 V | Yes | 5.07 gal | See label | Yes (CO-MINDER) | Honda, EU7000is owner's manual |
| Westinghouse iGen2200 | Gasoline | 1,800 / 2,200 | 120 V | Yes | 1.14 gal | 12 h at 25 % | No | Westinghouse, iGen2200 product page |
| Predator 3500 inverter (item 59137) | Gasoline | 3,000 / 3,500 | 120 V | Yes | 2.64 gal | 11 h at 25 % | Yes | Harbor Freight (Predator), owner's manual |
| Generac GP3500iO | Gasoline | 3,000 / 3,500 | 120 V | Yes | 2.37 gal | 8.0 h at 50 % | Not in the manual edition read; see label | Generac, GP3500iO owner's manual |
| Champion 3500 W dual fuel (201297) | Gasoline / propane | 3,500 / 4,375 gas; 3,150 / 3,951 propane | 120 V | No | 4.7 gal; propane from a 20-lb cylinder | 14 h gas, 10.5 h propane, at 50 % | Yes (CO Shield) | Champion, model 201297 product page |
| Westinghouse WGen9500DFc | Gasoline / propane | 9,500 / 12,500 gas; 8,500 / 11,200 propane | 120/240 V (L14-30R and 14-50R) | No (conventional) | 6.6 gal | 8 h gas and 7 h propane at 50 %; 12 h gas at 25 % | Yes | Westinghouse, WGen9500DFc product page |

**Read the letters after the model number.** Westinghouse sells the WGen9500DF **without** a CO
sensor and the WGen9500DF**c** with one; the "c" is the only difference in the name. Honda's
manuals for the same model differ by edition. Your data plate and your own manual are the
authority (→ 28-07).

Models from DuroMax and others are left out because the kit could not read their specifications
on the maker's own pages; that is not a judgement of the product.

## Connecting a generator to the house

The floors above decide the first part: a **transfer switch** or an **interlock kit** (with the
main breaker off whenever the generator feeds the panel), or extension cords to single appliances.
Never backfeed. What each one is: → 29-04. How to do it: → 09-04.

A **cord-and-plug conversion** gives one appliance, such as a furnace or well pump, its own plug so
it can be unplugged from the house outlet and plugged into the generator cord. That is not a
connection to house wiring, but whether to do that conversion yourself or have an electrician do
it is a trade-off between cost and the risk of a wiring mistake: {{choice DC-07}} → 30-08.

{{#if has.house_connection}}Our connection: **{{ gear.house_connection }}**.{{/if}}

## Our generator

{{#if has.generator}}From settings: **{{ gear.generator_watts }} running watts**,
**{{ gear.generator_fuel }}**, output volts: **{{ gear.generator_volts }}**.
{{#if has.inverter_generator}}It is an inverter generator.{{else}}It is a conventional (not
inverter) generator: test your battery chargers and electronics on it before you rely on it.{{/if}}
{{else}}We have not entered a generator. If you get one, fill this in from its data plate.{{/if}}

| Item | From our data plate and manual |

| Model and serial number | ______________________ |
| Running / starting watts, gasoline | ______ / ______ W |
| Running / starting watts, propane (if dual fuel) | ______ / ______ W |
| Volts; 240 V outlet type | ______ ; ______ |
| Tank; run time and the load it was measured at | ______ gal; ______ h at ______ % |
| CO shutoff? | yes / no |
| Oil type and amount | ______ |
| Lowest temperature in the manual; altitude kit needed? | ______ °F; ______ |
| Where it runs (20 ft or more from every window, door and vent) | ______________________ |
