pages.body:
# Portable fuel heaters: the specs that keep you safe, and common models

**What this page is for.** A portable fuel heater burns propane or kerosene in the room and lets
the exhaust out into the room. That is what "unvented" means. Every one of them makes carbon
monoxide (CO), uses up the room's oxygen and can start a fire. This page lists the numbers and
words on a heater's label and manual that decide where it may run, how much air it needs, and how
fast it uses fuel, then gives them for common models from the makers' own manuals. How to set up
and run one: propane → 08-09, kerosene wick → 08-10, the warm room → 08-01.

> **SAFETY.** Battery CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas, tested, whenever any
> fuel burns indoors (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Questions and Answers; → 08-02). An ODS or tip-over
> switch is **not** a CO alarm.
> **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
> ignites. Refuel and change cylinders outdoors, with the heater off and cool (→ 30-01).
> A heater labelled **"For Outdoor Use Only"**, and any construction-type forced-air heater, is
> never run in living or sleeping space.

## What matters and why

1. **Heat, in BTU per hour (BTU/h).** A BTU is a unit of heat. More BTU/h warms more space and
   burns fuel faster. Many heaters have LO and HI settings; the manual may limit which setting is
   allowed in a small room.
2. **Fuel use per hour, or run time per cylinder or tank.** Lets you work out how long your fuel
   lasts (method: → 06-05). Run times are shorter in hard cold.
3. **Indoor or outdoor, in the maker's own words.** Read the exact wording on the label and in the
   manual: "for indoor use", "emergency indoor use", "small recreational enclosures", "for outdoor
   use only", "never use in living or sleeping areas". **The same family name can carry different
   wording**: the Big Buddy manual read for this kit says "For Outdoor Use Only" on its cover,
   while the Portable Buddy and Little Buddy manuals describe indoor use with fresh-air openings.
   Go by the label on yours.
4. **Oxygen depletion sensor (ODS) and tip-over switch.** An ODS shuts off the gas when the room's
   oxygen drops. A tip-over switch shuts it off if knocked over. Wick kerosene heaters usually
   have a tip-and-jar shut-off and **no ODS**: the Dyna-Glo WK11C8 manual lists only its automatic
   shut-off for when the heater is jarred or tipped. **Neither device measures
   CO** (→ 08-09).
5. **The fresh-air opening the manual specifies.** Each manual gives its own: a size of opening in
   square inches, or a rule based on room volume. It is part of the heater's safe operation, not
   a suggestion (examples in the table).
6. **Altitude limit.** Propane radiant heaters burn weakly and may shut off above 7,000 feet (Mr.
   Heater manuals). {{#if is.high_altitude}}Your home is about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft
   up: read your heater's altitude line before you need it.{{/if}}
7. **Clearances** to anything that burns, and **the sleeping rule**: the Buddy manuals say never
   operate the heater while sleeping; the Dyna-Glo kerosene manual says turn it off before bed.
8. **Fuel type and connection.** Kerosene heaters take water-clear 1-K kerosene only (→ 29-01).
   Propane heaters take 1-lb cylinders, or a larger cylinder **kept outdoors** on the maker's
   hose, with the regulator in place.

**The two decisions this page does not make for you.** Running an unvented heater while people
sleep: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house:
{{choice DC-02}} → 30-03. Refilling 1-lb cylinders: {{choice DC-03}} → 30-04. Old kerosene in a
heater: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18. Each card explains the hazard, the maker's rule and the options.

## How much gas is in a propane cylinder

- A "20-lb" cylinder is named for the most propane it can safely hold. **Most are filled and
  labelled to 15 lb net**, even though the cylinder can safely hold 20 lb (NIST, Liquefied
  Petroleum Gas 20 Pound Cylinders). Weigh it: empty weight (stamped "TW" on the collar, → 28-07)
  plus the propane.
- One pound of propane makes about **8.6 cubic feet of gas** (8.62 cu ft per lb at 70 °F;
  Matheson, propane physical properties). So a full 20-lb cylinder holds about **170 cubic feet
  of gas**, and a 15-lb fill about 130. **Watch the decimal point: 170, not 1,700.**
- Propane burns when it makes up between 2.1 % and 9.5 % of the air (Matheson). At 2.1 %, the
  170 cubic feet in a full cylinder is enough to make about 8,000 cubic feet of air able to
  burn: more than a whole room. The Buddy heater manuals allow a 20-lb cylinder only outdoors
  (→ 08-09); whether one ever comes inside is a decision card (→ 30-03).
- Gallons, total BTU and the hours-per-cylinder method: → 06-05.

## Common models, from the makers' own manuals

"See label" means the document read for this kit did not give it. Rows marked with a manual
summary come from the kit pages that were written from that manual (→ 08-09, → 08-10).

| Model | Fuel | Heat, BTU/h | Fuel use or run time | Indoor wording in its manual | ODS | Tip-over | Fresh-air opening the manual specifies | Altitude | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mr. Heater Little Buddy MH4B | Propane, 1-lb cylinder | 3,800 | About 5 h per 1-lb cylinder | "Emergency indoor use"; recreational or commercial enclosure with a window or roof vent; outdoors | Yes | Yes | **4 sq in** (2 × 2 in) | May shut off above 7,000 ft | Mr. Heater, MH4B owner's manual |

# Two-way and weather radios: what the specs mean, and common models

**What this page is for.** When phones and the internet are down, radios are how a household
talks across the block and hears warnings. This page explains the numbers and words on a radio's
box and label, then lists common models with the makers' own figures. What each radio service is
for and how far it really reaches: → 29-09 and → 15-02. Family channel plan: → 15-03.

## What matters and why

1. **Service.** Which set of frequencies and rules the radio is built for. **FRS** (Family Radio
   Service) bubble-pack radios, **GMRS** (General Mobile Radio Service) handhelds and mobiles,
   **CB** (Citizens Band) for vehicles, **amateur ("ham")** radios, and receive-only **NOAA
   Weather Radio**. Radios on the same service talk to each other; across services, mostly not.
   FRS and GMRS share channel numbers 1 to 22, so FRS and GMRS radios can talk.
2. **Transmit power, in watts.** The federal limits are fixed by service: FRS up to 2 W on
   channels 1–7 and 15–22 and 0.5 W on 8–14; GMRS up to 5 W on 1–7, 0.5 W (handhelds only) on
   8–14, and up to 50 W from a mobile, base or repeater on the main channels 15–22; CB 4 W AM or FM, 12 W single-sideband;
   MURS 2 W (47 CFR Part 95). More watts helps a little. **Antenna height helps far more**
   (→ 15-06).
3. **Range claims.** "Up to 30 miles" or "35 miles" on a box is mountain-top to valley in ideal
   conditions; makers say so in the small print. Plan on the everyday ranges on → 29-09, and
   test your own (→ 15-06).
4. **Licence (before the collapse).** See the box below.
5. **NOAA weather and SAME alert.** Many two-way radios can listen to the seven NOAA weather
   channels. A **SAME** radio sounds an alarm only for the counties you program (→ 15-01,
   → 29-10). Transmitters near our home, from the region appendix:
   {{#each region.home.nwr as t}}{{t.call}} on {{t.freq}} MHz (SAME code {{t.same}}).
   {{else}}none listed for our county; see → 15-01.{{/each}}
6. **Power source.** Radios that also take ordinary AA or AAA cells keep working when the
   rechargeable pack is flat and you have no way to charge it. Mobiles run from 12 V.
7. **Repeater capable and removable antenna.** GMRS radios that work through a repeater (a relay
   on a tower or hill) reach much farther. A removable antenna lets you fit a better one; FRS
   antennas are fixed by rule.
8. **Privacy codes are not privacy.** They only stop you hearing other users; anyone on the
   channel without a code hears you.

> **Before the collapse:** transmitting on **GMRS** needs an FCC individual licence; the rule says
> one licence lets the holder's immediate family operate the holder's stations, and it normally
> runs ten years (47 CFR 95.1705). Midland gives the fee as $35. **Amateur** radio needs an exam
> and a licence. **FRS** radios are sold as licence-free. Listening needs no licence. The maker of
> one popular inexpensive dual-band handheld describes it as legal for use on amateur frequencies,
> which means transmitting needs an amateur licence. → 15-05, → 29-09.

## Common models, from the makers' own pages

"See label" means the maker's page read for this kit did not give it.

| Midland GXT1000VP4 | GMRS handheld (drops to FRS power on 8–14) | See label | GMRS licence required (Midland) | Weather alert and scan | Rechargeable packs; desktop, AC and DC chargers | 50 channels | Midland, GXT1000VP4 page |
| Midland MXT275 | GMRS mobile ("MicroMobile") | 15 W | GMRS licence | Weather scan and alert | 12 V vehicle power cord | 15 high-power channels; 8 repeater channels; external magnetic antenna | Midland, MXT275 page |
| BTECH GMRS-V2 | GMRS handheld, repeater compatible | 0.5 W / 5 W; low power only on 8–14 | GMRS licence (47 CFR 95.1705) | NOAA receiver and scan | 7.4 V Li-ion pack, USB-C charging | 200 programmable channels; IP54 splash resistant; −4 to 140 °F | BTECH, GMRS-V2 page |

pages.body:
# Water filters and purifiers: what they remove, and common models

**What this page is for.** Portable water filters differ in the one thing that matters most:
which germs they stop. This page explains the words on the box, then lists common filters with
what each maker says it removes and how much water it is rated for. How to make water safe, step
by step: → 03-04. Looking after a filter, including freezing: → 03-09. The words micron, bacteria,
protozoa and virus: → 29-06.

## What matters and why

1. **What it removes, by germ type, in the maker's own words.**
   - **Bacteria** (for example *E. coli*, cholera).
   - **Protozoa**, also called parasites or cysts (*Giardia*, *Cryptosporidium*).
   - **Viruses**, which are far smaller than bacteria.
   **If the box does not say viruses, assume it does not remove them**, and disinfect the water
   after filtering (chlorine or boiling, → 03-04, → 29-05). Makers call a device that is rated
   for viruses a **purifier**.
2. **How sure: the percentage or "log" figure.** 99.9999 % is "6 log": one germ in a million gets
   through. More nines is better. A maker may also name a test protocol (NSF P231, NSF P248).
3. **Pore size, in microns.** A micron is a thousandth of a millimetre. In the table, 0.1 to
   0.2 micron filters are rated for bacteria and protozoa; the two 0.02 micron purifiers are also
   rated for viruses.
4. **Rated capacity.** How much water before the filter element is worn out, "depending on water
   quality". Dirty water wears it out far sooner. Count what goes through it.
5. **Flow rate.** Litres per minute or per hour. A family needs a gravity or pump filter, not a
   drinking straw.
6. **What it does not do.** None of these remove dissolved chemicals, fuel, salt or most metals
   unless the maker says so; some say plainly they do not (→ 03-03, → 03-07).
7. **Freezing.** A hollow-fiber filter that has frozen wet may be cracked inside with nothing to
   see. **If a used filter has been below freezing, or you cannot be sure, retire it** (→ 03-09).
8. **"For clear water only."** Some makers say this. Let muddy water settle or pre-filter it
   through cloth first (→ 03-04).

Drinking from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface water is a decision card that says which
treatment steps go with each choice: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14.

## Common filters and purifiers, from the makers' own pages

"Not stated" means the maker's page read for this kit did not claim it; treat it as **no**.

| Sawyer MINI | Hollow fiber, squeeze, straw or inline | 99.99999 % | 99.9999 % | Not stated | 0.1 micron absolute | Up to 100,000 gal | See label | Sawyer, MINI product page |
| LifeStraw Personal | Hollow fiber, drinking straw | 99.999999 % | 99.999 % | Not stated | 0.2 micron | Up to 1,000 gal (4,000 L) | Drink through it | LifeStraw, Personal product page |
| LifeStraw Family | Gravity purifier | 99.999999 % | 99.999 % | **99.999 %** | 0.02 micron | Up to 4,755 gal (18,000 L) | Up to 12 L per hour | LifeStraw, Family product page |
| Katadyn BeFree 0.6 L | Hollow fiber, soft bottle | Removes (no % given) | "Cysts" removed | Not stated | 0.1 micron | Up to 1,000 L | Up to 2 L per minute | Katadyn, BeFree 0.6 L product page |
| Katadyn Hiker Pro | Pump; glass fiber with activated carbon | Removes | Removes (*Giardia*, *Cryptosporidium*) | Not stated | Not stated | Up to 1,150 L (300 gal) | About 1 L per minute | Katadyn, Hiker Pro product page |

# Reading your own gear: data plates, panel labels, BTU plates, safety marks and dates

**What this page is for.** The tables in this section cover popular models. Yours may be another
brand, an older version, or a revision with different numbers under the same name. Every piece of
gear carries its own limits on a label or plate, and **that label is the authority**. This page
shows where to find the label on each kind of gear, what each number means, and which numbers to
copy into the "Our gear" tables (→ 28-01 to → 28-06). The general guide to labels, fuel cans,
cylinders and medicines is → 29-14.

**Do this now, while the power is on and you can still look things up:**

1. Find the label on every power station, panel, generator, heater, radio, filter and alarm.
2. Photograph each one into the app, close and sharp, and a second photo of where it is.
3. Copy the key numbers into the "Our gear" table on that kind of gear's page.
4. Write the date on anything that wears out: filters, CO alarms, batteries, fuel.

## Where the label is

| Gear | Usually found |
|---|---|
| Power station | Underside or back; input limits also printed beside each input port |
| Solar panel | Back of the panel, near the junction box; on folding panels inside a flap |
| Generator | Sticker or plate on the frame or engine cover; engine and emissions labels separate |
| Heater | Rating plate on the back, base or inside a door |
| Radio | Inside the battery compartment |
| Filter | Box, leaflet or the element itself; often not on the device. Keep the box |
| CO and smoke alarm | Back of the alarm: take it off its base |

## Electrical nameplates: volts, amps, watts

- **V (volts)**, **A (amps)**, **W (watts)**, and sometimes **VA** or **kVA** instead of watts
  (for planning, read 1.8 kVA as 1,800 W). Watts = volts × amps (→ 29-02).
- **"~" means AC** (household-type power); **"⎓" means DC** (battery-type power). "120V~ 15A"
  is an AC rating; "11–60V⎓15A" is a DC input range and current.
- **Rated, continuous or running** is what it does all day. **Max, peak, surge or starting** is a
  short burst.
- **Hz** (60 in the US) and **phase** (1 for household gear).
- **Input** lines tell you what may feed it. **Output** lines tell you what it can power. On a
  power station, copy every input line, especially the solar (PV or DC) input **voltage range**:
  that top number is the one never to exceed (→ 28-01).
- **Generators** also print the outlet types and often whether they are "transfer switch ready".
  The manual adds what the plate leaves out: Generac's, for example, says maximum power drops
  about 3.5 % per 1,000 ft of altitude (→ 28-03).

## Solar panel labels: Voc and Isc first

The panel label lists **Pmax** (watts), **Voc**, **Isc**, **Vmp** and **Imp** at **STC** (the
lab's standard bright sun at 77 °F), plus **maximum system voltage** and **maximum series fuse**.
A datasheet may add the **temperature coefficient of Voc** (Renogy's RSP200D sheet gives −0.28 %
per °C). Copy Voc and Isc for every panel; they set the cold check (→ 28-02, → 09-02).

**Check Voc with a multimeter** before the first connection of any panel or string:

1. Panel in full sun, **not connected to anything**.
2. Multimeter on **DC volts**, range above the expected reading.
3. Red probe to the panel's positive lead, black to negative (→ 09-12 for connector tips).
4. The reading should be close to the label Voc, higher on a cold morning. A string reads the sum.
5. Write the reading, the date and the air temperature on the label photo.

A controller label gives its limits the same way. Victron's model number carries two of them:
"100/30" is 100 V maximum solar voltage and 30 A charging current (→ 28-02).

## Heater rating plates: BTU and fuel

- **Input in BTU/h**, for each setting (LO, MED, HI).
- **Fuel type**: "Propane (LP)", "1-K kerosene", "natural gas". Never another fuel (→ 29-01).
- **Gas pressure** on propane heaters with hoses or quick-connects, for example "regulated to
  11 in W.C." (inches of water column) on the Big Buddy manual. That tells you which regulator
  and hose it needs.
- **The use wording**: "for indoor use", "emergency indoor use", "for outdoor use only", "not for
  use in living or sleeping areas". Copy it exactly (→ 28-04).
- **Clearances**, the **minimum fresh-air opening**, and any **altitude** line. Many are in the
  manual, not on the plate: keep the manual with the heater.

## Fuel cylinders

Propane cylinder collars are stamped with the DOT specification, **TW** (tare weight, the empty
weight) and the date of manufacture: → 29-14. A "20-lb" cylinder is often sold filled to 15 lb
(NIST); weigh it against TW to know what is in it (→ 28-04).

## Safety marks: UL, ETL, CSA and others

A small mark such as **UL**, **ETL** (Intertek) or **CSA**, often in a circle, means a **Nationally
Recognized Testing Laboratory** tested and certified the product to a product safety standard;
OSHA recognises these laboratories, and each uses its own registered mark, which the maker may
apply only after certification (OSHA, Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory Program). The
words "listed" or "certified" go with the mark. **A mark does not make an outdoor-only heater
safe indoors**: it certifies the product for the use on its label.

## Dates: date codes, alarms and anything that wears out

- **Serial number and date code.** Most gear carries a serial number and often a date of
  manufacture, sometimes as a code. Write the purchase date beside it. Recall notices and
  manuals are matched by model and serial number (→ 29-14).
- **CO alarms.** Alarms have a recommended replacement age, given in the product literature or by
  the maker (CPSC, Carbon Monoxide Questions and Answers). Look on the back for the manufacture
  date and any "replace by" date, and write the replacement date on the front with a marker.
  **The test button tests the circuit, not whether the sensor still detects CO** (CPSC). An alarm
  past its date is replaced, not trusted. If the leaflet describes an end-of-life signal (a
  pattern of chirps), tape that page inside a cupboard door so nobody mistakes it for a low
  battery.
- **Smoke alarms:** follow the replacement age in their leaflet the same way (→ 29-12).
- **Batteries, filters, fuel:** write the first-use or fill date on each (→ 03-09, → 06-06).

{{figure fig-data-plate-example}}

## What we copied, and where

| Power stations | ______ | yes / no | → 28-01 | — |
| Solar panels | ______ | yes / no | → 28-02 | — |
| Generator | ______ | yes / no | → 28-03 | — |
| Heaters | ______ | yes / no | → 28-04 | — |
| Radios | ______ | yes / no | → 28-05 | — |
| Water filters | ______ | yes / no | → 28-06 | ______ |
| CO alarms ({{ gear.co_alarms }}) | ______ | yes / no | this page | ______ |
| Smoke alarms ({{ gear.smoke_alarms }}) | ______ | yes / no | this page | ______ |

pages.body:
# Explainers

**What this section holds.** 15 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 29-01 **Fuels: gasoline, diesel, kerosene, propane, butane, white gas, lamp oil, wood, charcoal**: Most fuel accidents happen because someone did not know which liquid was in the can, or did not know that a fuel is only safe in the appliance built for it.
- → 29-02 **Batteries and power stations: volts, amps, watts and watt-hours**: When the power is out, stored electricity is counted in four words: volts, amps, watts and watt-hours.
- → 29-03 **Carbon monoxide: the gas you cannot see or smell**: Every winter power outage kills families who brought a generator, grill or stove inside to stay warm.
- → 29-04 **Electricity in the house: the panel, breakers, transfer switches and backfeeding**: In an outage you may want to shut the power off, run a generator, or power the furnace.
- → 29-05 **Chlorine products: bleach, pool shock, tablets and ppm**: Chlorine kills germs in water and on surfaces, and a household may have it in three or four forms.
- → 29-06 **Water words: boil, filter, micron, germs, turbidity, potable**: Water treatment advice uses a handful of words that sound alike but mean different jobs.
- → 29-07 **Refrigerated medicines: the cold chain without power**: Some medicines, insulin above all, lose strength if they get too warm and are ruined if they freeze.
- → 29-08 **Canning words: acid, pH, pressure canner, headspace, the seal, botulism**: Home canning keeps food for years without power, and done wrong it makes a poison you cannot see, smell or taste.
- → 29-09 **Radios: FRS, GMRS, CB, MURS, ham and NOAA Weather Radio**: When phones are down, radios are how a family stays in touch and how you hear warnings.
- → 29-10 **Weather alert words: watch, warning, advisory, wind chill, heat index**: A weather alert is only useful if everyone in the house knows what the words mean and what to do at once.
- → 29-11 **Firearms basics for a non-shooter in the house**: This page is for the person in the house who does not use guns but may one day have to move one, store one, or keep children away from one.
- → 29-12 **Fire extinguishers, fire blankets and smoke alarms**: In an outage, a household burns more things indoors (heaters, lamps, candles, stoves) and the fire department may not come.
- → 29-13 **Measuring things without instruments: volume, weight, temperature, distance, time**: Many survival jobs depend on a measurement: how much water is left, how much bleach goes in, whether the freezer is still cold, how far the next town is.
- → 29-14 **Reading a label: data plates, fuel cans, cylinders, medicines, dates and lot numbers**: Almost every limit that keeps you safe is printed on the thing itself: how much power an appliance draws, what fuel a can held, when a cylinder must be retir…
- → 29-15 **How this binder was made, and what to trust**: Before you rely on a reference in an emergency, you should know who wrote it, how it was checked, and where its limits are.

pages.body:
# Fuels, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Most fuel accidents happen because someone did not know which liquid
was in the can, or did not know that a fuel is only safe in the appliance built for it. This
page says what each common fuel is, what burns it, how long it keeps, whether it can ever be
used indoors and why, and how to tell them apart.

> **SAFETY — the floors that apply (→ 30-01).**
> - **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open
>   window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no warning; alarms fail; there is no
>   mitigation that works every time.
> - **Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.** Vapour
>   ignition.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in
>   every source.

## Two ideas that explain every fuel rule

1. **Everything that burns makes carbon monoxide (CO)**, a gas you cannot see or smell (CDC,
   Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics). Only an appliance built and rated for indoor use, run the
   way its manual says, belongs inside. → 29-03
2. **The vapour burns, not the liquid.** Gasoline gives off vapour even when cold. The vapour is
   heavier than air, flows along the floor and can be lit by a pilot light or a spark across the
   room. Kerosene and diesel give off far less vapour, which is why they are easier to store, but
   they still burn.

## What each fuel is, and how to tell them apart

| Fuel | What it is | What burns it | How to recognise it | Usual can colour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gasoline** | Liquid fuel refined from crude oil. Most US pump gasoline is about 10% ethanol (EIA) | Cars, lawn and garden engines, most portable generators | Sharp smell that stings the eyes; very thin; evaporates fast | Red |
| **Diesel** | A heavier "distillate" fuel oil for diesel engines; road diesel is ultra-low sulfur, 15 ppm or less (EIA) | Diesel cars and trucks, tractors, diesel generators, ducted diesel heaters that vent outdoors | Oily, heavy smell; feels greasy; off-road diesel and **heating oil** are dyed red by IRS rule (EIA) | Yellow |
| **Kerosene** | A lighter distillate than diesel. **1-K (K-1)** is the clear, low-sulfur grade (University of Missouri Extension, G1999) | Wick kerosene heaters, kerosene lamps, some ducted heaters | Oily smell like lamp fuel; K-1 is water-clear. Red-dyed or yellowed kerosene is not K-1 | Blue |
| **Propane** | A gas at normal pressure that turns liquid under pressure, so it is sold in steel cylinders (EIA) | Grills, camp stoves, portable propane heaters, some generators, house furnaces on tank service | Comes only in pressure cylinders or tanks. A smell is added so leaks are noticed: if you smell gas, get everyone out (FEMA, Utility Shut-off and Safety) | White, grey or steel cylinder |
| **Butane** | A close relative of propane, also stored as a liquid under pressure (EIA) | Small canister stoves, lighters | Small thin metal canisters | Printed canister |
| **White gas** ("camp fuel") | A very volatile refined petroleum liquid, as dangerous to store as gasoline | Liquid-fuel camp stoves and pressurised lanterns | Clear, solvent smell; sold in metal cans labelled camp fuel | Printed metal can |
| **Lamp oil** | Refined liquid paraffin for oil lamps. "Tiki" or citronella oil is a different product, outdoor only | Oil lamps made for it; K-1 kerosene also burns in flat-wick kerosene lamps | Clear or coloured; often sold in bottles that look like drinks | Plastic bottle |
| **Wood** | Logs, split and dried ("seasoned") | Fireplaces, wood stoves, outdoor fires | Seasoned wood is lighter, cracked at the ends, and sounds hollow when two pieces are knocked together | — |
| **Charcoal** | Wood already partly burned, sold as lumps or briquettes | Outdoor grills only | Black, light, dusty | Paper bag |

**Colours are a habit, not a guarantee.** Red for gasoline, yellow for diesel and blue for
kerosene are the usual US convention; your heater's manual may name a colour too. But cans get
reused and households use their own colours. **The label is
what you trust:** read it aloud, smell it, then pour. A can with no readable label is not poured
into anything until you know what is in it. → 29-14

{{figure fig-fuel-can-colours}}

## How long each keeps, and whether it can ever be used indoors

| Fuel | How long it keeps | Indoors? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Gasoline** | Months, not years. Air and heat age it; ethanol pulls water from the air; stabiliser slows ageing but cannot fix stale fuel and has its own shelf life (Honda Power Equipment, Fuel Recommendations) | **Never.** Not in a heater, a lamp or a stove | Too volatile. In a kerosene heater it is an explosion. Engines that burn it make lethal CO (floor above) |
| **Diesel** | Ages too: water collects at the bottom of a tank and it thickens in hard cold. Follow your additive's label | **Only** in a heater whose exhaust is ducted outdoors, installed as its manual says | Burning it in the room puts the exhaust in the room |
| **Kerosene** | Keeps longer than gasoline when full, sealed and dark, but water creeps in. Before use, a sample in a clear jar must be clear, with no water layer and no cloudiness. How old is too old is a choice → 30-18 | **Only** K-1, only in a heater or lamp made for indoor use, with the ventilation its manual requires and a CO alarm | Unvented heaters put all their exhaust into the room. Overnight use is a choice → 30-02 |
| **Propane** | Does not go stale in a sealed cylinder; the cylinder itself has a date (→ 29-14) | **Only** appliances rated for indoor use. The propane code (NFPA 58) allows only 1-lb cylinders to be kept inside a home, two at most (Flame King filling training, citing NFPA 58) | A leaking valve lays heavy gas along the floor where a pilot light can light it. Larger cylinders inside → 30-03 |
| **Butane** | Keeps sealed; check the canister | **No.** CDC: never use a portable camp stove indoors | Fails in freezing weather because it stops turning to gas |
| **White gas** | Keeps sealed | **No** | Same reasons as gasoline. Never in a wick lamp or kerosene heater |
| **Lamp oil** | Keeps sealed | In a lamp made for it, in a ventilated room | A swallowed mouthful can enter the lungs. **Do not make the person vomit; call Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222** (CDC MMWR; Poison Control) → 12-17 |
| **Wood** | Years if dry; split, covered and aged at least 6 months before it burns well (EPA, Burn Wise tips) | **Only** in an installed, vented fireplace or wood stove | The chimney carries the smoke and CO out. Never burn trash or treated wood (EPA) |
| **Charcoal** | Years if dry | **Never.** Not in a fireplace, not "for a while" | Very high CO output (CDC). This is a floor |

## If the wrong fuel goes in

- **Gasoline or white gas in a kerosene heater or lamp:** flare-up, uncontrolled flame,
  explosion. Do not light it. Outdoors, cold, drain it, new wick (→ 08-10).
- **Gasoline in a diesel engine, or diesel in a gasoline engine:** do not start it. Drain the
  tank. The vehicle or generator manual says which fuel it takes.
- **Any fuel in a drink bottle:** this is how children are poisoned. Never decant fuel into a
  food or drink container (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety).
- **Gasoline to start or restart a fire:** never (CPSC).

## Decisions on this page

These are trade-offs with no single right answer. Each card explains the hazard and the options.

- Storing fuel in an attached garage: {{choice DC-05}} → 30-06
- Carrying fuel inside a passenger vehicle: {{choice DC-06}} → 30-07
- Using old kerosene, diesel or gasoline: {{choice DC-17}} → 30-18
- An unvented heater running while people sleep: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02
- A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03
- Refilling 1-lb cylinders: {{choice DC-03}} → 30-04
- Open-flame cooking or candles indoors: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21
- A fireplace or stove not inspected this year: {{choice DC-21}} → 30-22

## What this household keeps

| Fuel | On hand |
|---|---|
| Gasoline | {{ gear.fuel.gasoline_gal }} gal |
| Diesel | {{ gear.fuel.diesel_gal }} gal |
| Kerosene | {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal |
| Propane, 1-lb cylinders | {{ gear.fuel.propane_1lb }} |
| Propane, 20-lb cylinders | {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }} |
| Firewood | {{ gear.fuel.firewood_cords }} cords |

{{photo fuel-cans}}

Storage rules: → 06-06. Moving and pouring fuel: → 06-07. Carbon monoxide: → 29-03.

pages.body:
# Batteries and power stations, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** When the power is out, stored electricity is counted in four words:
volts, amps, watts and watt-hours. With those, you can read any battery or appliance label and
work out how long something will run. This page also says what a power station is, which
battery types last, and why a car battery makes a poor house battery.

> **SAFETY.** A lithium battery that is **hot, swelling, leaking, smoking, smells odd or makes
> an unusual noise** is a fire about to happen: get people away from it and call for help; do not
> carry it (NFPA, Lithium-Ion Batteries; USFA, Lithium-Ion Batteries: Everyday Convenience,
> Hidden Fire Risks). Lead-acid batteries give off explosive hydrogen while
> charging and hold sulfuric acid: charge them only where the air moves, with eye protection
> (OSHA, 29 CFR 1926.441).

## The four words

Think of water in a hose.

| Word | Symbol | Water picture | In plain words |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Volts** | V | Pressure | How hard the electricity pushes. A car battery is 12 V; a wall outlet is 120 V |
| **Amps** | A | How much water flows | How much electricity is moving right now |
| **Watts** | W | Pressure × flow | **Watts = volts × amps.** How fast something uses power while it runs |
| **Watt-hours** | Wh | Water in the bucket | **Watt-hours = watts × hours.** How much energy a battery holds, or a device uses over time |

A battery label may give **amp-hours (Ah)** instead. Turn them into watt-hours by multiplying by
the volts: 100 Ah at 12 V is 1,200 Wh. That is the nominal figure; you can safely use only part
of it (below).

**Household examples** (typical planning ranges; read your own appliance's label, → 29-14):

| Thing | Watts while running | Energy |
|---|---|---|
| Phone, full charge | — | 10 to 20 Wh |
| Electric kettle | 1,200 to 1,800 W | A few minutes per boil |
| Full-size fridge | 100 to 200 W while the motor runs | 1,000 to 2,000 Wh a day |

**The one sum to remember:** a 1,000 Wh battery runs a 100 W load for roughly 10 hours, less the
losses below. Heat-making things (kettles, heaters, hair dryers) use the most; lights, radios and
phone charging use the least.

{{figure fig-watts-and-watt-hours}}

## What a power station is

A **power station** is a battery in a box with everything needed to use it: a **charge
controller** (lets solar panels, a wall outlet or a car charge the battery safely), an
**inverter** (turns the battery's direct current into household alternating current, → 29-04),
and outlets (wall-style AC, 12 V car-style, USB). The label shows three numbers that matter:
**Wh** (how much it holds), **output watts** (the biggest load it can run at once), and the
**input** limits (how fast it can be refilled). → 28-01

**Why "watts in" is limited.** Every station has a maximum charging rate, and for solar a
voltage and current window printed on it. Panels connected beyond that window can damage the
station; inside it, the station takes only what it can. Panels also make much less than their
rated watts on short, low-sun winter days (US DOE, Solar Photovoltaic System Design Basics). → 09-02, 09-05

**Inverter losses.** Turning DC into AC wastes some energy as heat, and an inverter left switched
on draws power even when nothing is plugged in. Run 12 V and USB devices from the 12 V and USB
ports where you can, and switch the AC side off when you are not using it. → 09-12

## Battery types

| Type | What it is like | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4, "LFP")** | The usual chemistry in newer power stations. Light, lasts thousands of charge cycles, needs no maintenance, most of its capacity is usable | **Must not be charged below freezing** unless its battery management system blocks cold charging. Read the datasheet |
| **Other lithium-ion** (phones, laptops, tools, many older stations) | Light and powerful | Shorter life; more prone to fire when damaged. Never take packs apart |
| **Lead-acid (car, marine, AGM)** | Heavy, cheap, found everywhere | Using more than about half its charge shortens its life sharply; flooded types vent hydrogen and need distilled-water top-ups (→ 09-03, → 09-07) |
| **NiMH rechargeable AA/AAA** | Small, safe, common | Lose charge sitting on a shelf unless "pre-charged" type |

**Cold and heat.** Cold reduces what any battery delivers; lithium cannot be charged when
frozen. Heat shortens every battery's life. Keep batteries indoors, above freezing, out of the
sun. → 09-07

**Why a car battery is a poor house battery.** A car's starting battery is built to give a big
burst for a few seconds and then be recharged at once by the engine. Drained deeply, again and
again, it wears out quickly. A deep-cycle battery (marine, golf cart) is better, and a car can
still charge phones and small devices from its 12 V socket. Never run the engine in an attached
garage (→ 29-03). → 09-14

## This household

{{#if has.power_station}}Your power stations hold about {{ gear.station_wh_total }} Wh in total.
As a rough estimate, that would run a typical full-size fridge for about
{{ derived.station_fridge_days }} days with no recharging. Your own fridge and your own
percentage screen are the truth.{{else}}No power station is listed in your profile. A phone power
bank is the smallest useful battery; → 09-03 explains the sizes.{{/if}}
{{#if has.solar}} Your solar panels total {{ gear.solar_w_total }} W on their labels.{{/if}}

What to power first: → 09-01. Wiring and fuses: → 09-08.

pages.body:
# Carbon monoxide, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Every winter power outage kills families who brought a generator,
grill or stove inside to stay warm. They die from carbon monoxide. This page says what it is,
where it comes from, why your senses will not warn you, what an alarm does and does not do, and
what to do if you suspect it.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Never run a generator, charcoal, or any
> engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.** Carbon monoxide kills in minutes with no
> warning; alarms fail; there is no mitigation that works every time.

## What it is

**Carbon monoxide (CO)** is a gas made whenever a fuel burns: gasoline, diesel, kerosene,
propane, natural gas, wood, charcoal (→ 29-01). It has **no colour, no smell and no taste**
(CDC). When you breathe it, it takes the place of oxygen in your blood, so the body slowly
starves of oxygen. More than 400 Americans die each year from CO poisoning that is not caused
by fire, and more than 100,000 go to an emergency room (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

## Where it comes from in a house

Furnaces, water heaters, gas ranges, fireplaces and wood stoves, portable generators, charcoal
grills, camp stoves, kerosene and propane heaters, and cars. A properly vented appliance sends
its CO up a flue or chimney. **Trouble starts when the exhaust stays in the room**: a generator
or grill brought inside, a camp stove used indoors, a blocked chimney, or a vent buried by snow.

## Why you will not notice it

The first symptoms feel like flu: **headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting,
chest pain, confusion** (CDC). People feel tired, lie down, and do not wake up. **People who are
asleep or drunk can die from CO before they have any symptoms** (CDC). Infants, older adults, and
people with heart or lung disease or anaemia are hurt first and worst (CDC). A clue: several
people, or the pets, feel ill at the same time and feel better outdoors.

## What a CO alarm does and does not do

An alarm measures CO in **parts per million (ppm)**: how many CO molecules there are in every
million molecules of air. Alarms are designed to stay **silent at low levels** so they do not
go off constantly. The home CO alarm standard, UL 2034, sets these alarm points (as printed in
a First Alert CO alarm manual; CPSC says alarms are designed to sound before levels become
life-threatening):

| CO level | What the alarm standard requires |
|---|---|
| 30 ppm, steady | No alarm, even after 30 days |
| 70 ppm | Alarm within 1 to 4 hours |
| 150 ppm | Alarm within 10 to 50 minutes |
| 400 ppm | Alarm within 4 to 15 minutes |

For comparison, homes without gas stoves average 0.5 to 5 ppm, and the air near a properly
adjusted gas stove 5 to 15 ppm (EPA, Carbon Monoxide's Impact on Indoor Air Quality). So **a
quiet alarm is not proof the air is clean**, and a reading that stays above those levels means something
is making CO. An alarm with a number display tells you more than one that only beeps.

- **Where:** on every level of the home and outside each sleeping area (CPSC). In a room where
  people sleep near a heater, at the height of sleeping heads, on the wall away from the heater,
  not in a dead-air corner, not next to an open window. The alarm's own manual gives the height.
- **Power:** battery or battery backup (CDC). A plug-in alarm with no battery does nothing in an
  outage.
- **Replace** the alarm at the end-of-life date printed on it, and at once if it chirps that it
  has reached end of life.
- **An alarm is a backup, not permission.** It can fail, have a dead battery, or be in the wrong
  room. It does not make a generator in the garage safe.

## If you suspect CO

1. **Get everyone outside into fresh air now**, pets included. Do not stop to open windows or
   look for the cause.
2. **Call 911** if it works. CO poisoning needs medical care; some effects show up later.
3. **Count heads.** Confusion is a symptom; someone may not follow you out.
4. **Nobody goes back in** until the source is found and shut off and the house is aired out.
5. **No 911:** fresh air is the treatment. Keep everyone outside, warm and resting, for hours,
   with someone watching anyone who was confused, vomiting or passed out. The full offline
   procedure is on → 08-02.

## Rules that follow from this

- Generators run **outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house**, exhaust pointed away
  (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety). Never in a garage, even with the door open.
- **Never** burn charcoal indoors. **Never** heat the house with a gas oven or range. **Never**
  use a portable camp stove indoors (CDC).
- **After heavy snow**, clear the snow from furnace, water-heater and dryer vents.

## Decisions on this page

- An unvented heater running while people sleep: {{choice DC-01}} → 30-02
- A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside: {{choice DC-02}} → 30-03
- Open-flame cooking or candles indoors: {{choice DC-20}} → 30-21

## This household

CO alarms on hand: {{ gear.co_alarms }}.
{{#if has.unvented_heater}}You have a portable heater that vents into the room. Install and test
the alarms before it is lit the first time. → 08-01{{/if}}
{{#if has.generator}}You have a generator. Mark its outdoor spot now, at least 20 feet out. → 09-04{{/if}}

{{photo co-alarm-spot}}

pages.body:
# Electricity in the house, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** In an outage you may want to shut the power off, run a generator, or
power the furnace. Each of those touches the house wiring, where mistakes kill. This page names
the parts, explains backfeeding (the mistake that kills line workers), and says what a safe
generator connection looks like.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Never connect a generator to house wiring
> except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never
> backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide") cord.** Electrocutes line workers
> and neighbours; fire. A cord-and-plug conversion is not a connection to house wiring: the
> appliance is unplugged from the house outlet and plugged into the generator cord, so nothing
> reaches the panel.

## The parts

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Service** | The wires from the utility pole or underground line to your meter. They carry power **both ways**: whatever is on your side can flow out to the street |
| **Meter** | Measures what you use. Belongs to the utility |
| **Panel** (breaker box) | The metal box where the incoming power is split into **circuits**, each feeding a group of outlets, lights or one big appliance |
| **Main breaker** | The large switch at the top of the panel. Off = the whole house is cut off from the utility line. Learn where it is now (FEMA, Utility Shut-off and Safety) |
| **Breaker** | One switch per circuit. It trips (shuts off) by itself if the circuit draws too much current, which protects the wiring from overheating |
| **GFCI** | An outlet or breaker that shuts off in a fraction of a second if current leaks to ground, for example through a person. Required near water: kitchen, bathroom, outdoors |
| **Transfer switch** | A switch installed by an electrician next to the panel. It connects the chosen circuits **either** to the utility **or** to a generator inlet, never both at once |
| **Interlock** | A metal plate fitted to the panel so the main breaker and a generator breaker cannot both be on at the same time. Same job as a transfer switch, done inside the panel |
| **Inlet** | A recessed, outdoor-rated plug on the house wall that a generator cord plugs into. Used with a transfer switch or interlock |

Most US household outlets are 120 volts; large appliances such as dryers, ranges, central air
and many well pumps run on 240 volts. Your generator or power station label says which it can
supply. → 29-02, → 28-03

{{figure fig-panel-transfer-switch-interlock}}

## Backfeeding: why it kills

**Backfeeding** means pushing power from a generator into the house wiring in a way that lets it
flow out through the service to the street. The usual way people do it is a homemade cord with a
plug on both ends, pushed into a wall outlet. The power goes backward through your meter, up to
the transformer, which raises it to the high voltage of the street line, and **can electrocute a utility worker
repairing a line they believe is dead**, or a neighbour served by the same transformer. It also
bypasses some of the house's own circuit protection (CPSC, Safety Alert: Portable Generator
Hazards).

OSHA's rule: **never attach a generator directly to a building's electrical system unless it
has a properly installed transfer switch**, because of the electrocution risk to utility
workers. A cord with two plug ends is never used for anything.

## The safe ways to use a generator

1. **Extension cords to individual appliances.** Plug the appliance into a cord, the cord into
   the generator. Nothing touches the house wiring. This is always allowed.
2. **A transfer switch or interlock with an inlet**, installed by an electrician. You then power
   chosen circuits through the panel with no path to the street.
3. **A cord-and-plug conversion** of one hard-wired appliance (such as a furnace) so it can be
   unplugged from the house outlet and plugged into a generator cord. Nothing then reaches the
   panel. Whether you do this yourself or have an electrician do it is a choice:
   {{choice DC-07}} → 30-08

Generators run outdoors, at least 20 feet from the house (CPSC). → 29-03

## Extension cords

- **Gauge** is the thickness of the wire inside. **A lower gauge number means a thicker wire**
  that carries more current without overheating: 12-gauge is thicker than 16-gauge.
- Use **heavy-duty, outdoor-rated, grounded (3-prong) cords** with no damage (OSHA, Portable
  Generator Safety). The cord's tag gives its rating; it must be at least the total of what is
  plugged into it.
- **Unroll the whole cord.** A coiled cord under load heats up.
- **Never chain cords together or plug power strips into each other.**
- Do not run a cord through a door or window that then has to stay open: exhaust gets in.

## Shutting the power off

To switch off the whole house, turn the **main breaker** off (FEMA, Utility Shut-off and
Safety). Stand on a dry surface. If there is water near the panel, or you smell burning, or see
scorching, stay away and get help. Any work inside the panel, any permanent wiring, any
connection to house circuits: a qualified electrician (OSHA, Electrical).

## This household

{{#if has.generator}}Your generator connects to the house by: {{ gear.house_connection }}.
{{#if has.house_connection}}Before you ever use it, check that the transfer switch is set to
generator, or with an interlock that the main breaker is off, every single time. → 09-04{{else}}Use extension cords to
individual appliances only. → 09-04{{/if}}{{else}}No generator is listed. Extension cords from a
power station follow the same cord rules. → 09-03{{/if}}

{{photo main-breaker}}

pages.body:
# Chlorine products, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Chlorine kills germs in water and on surfaces, and a household may
have it in three or four forms. They differ in strength by hundreds of times, and two of them
together can make a poison gas. This page says what each one is, what "ppm" means, and how to use
the published tables without guessing.

> **SAFETY — the floors that apply (→ 30-01).**
> - **Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.** Chlorine gas.
> - **Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in
>   every source.
>
> Water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals **cannot be made safe** by chlorine or boiling
> (CDC). Swallowed chlorine product: **Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222**, → 12-17.

## The forms you will meet

| Product | What it is | Strength | Keeps | Drinking water? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Household bleach** | Liquid **sodium hypochlorite** in water | Regular unscented bleach is 5 to 9% (CDC); the % is on the label | EPA says use bleach stored at room temperature for less than a year; write the purchase date on it. Mixed with water, it works less well after 24 hours (CDC) | **Yes**, unscented only, using the table below |
| **Pool shock (cal-hypo)** | Granular **calcium hypochlorite** | Concentrated: one heaping teaspoon makes 2 gallons of stock at about 500 ppm (EPA); the % is on the label | Water or heat breaks it down: sealed, dry, below 120°F (CDC/ATSDR) | **Yes**, only if the label shows calcium hypochlorite with **no** algaecides, clarifiers or stabilisers, using EPA's two-step method (→ 03-04) |
| **Pool tablets (trichlor, dichlor)** | Slow-dissolving chlorine compounds for pools | Per label | Per label | **No** — pool use only. Never stored with cal-hypo: CDC/ATSDR says to keep cal-hypo apart from other chlorinating agents |
| **Chlorine dioxide tablets** | A different chemical sold for drinking water | Per label | Per label | **Yes**, following the label's times exactly; the one chemical that handles *Cryptosporidium* (CDC) |

Scented, "splashless", gel or "multi-action" products are **not** used for water or disinfection:
they are weaker or carry additives.

## What ppm means

**ppm** is **parts per million**. In water, 1 ppm is 1 milligram of chlorine in each litre
(mg/L). It is how strengths are compared:

- **Drinking water** gets the lowest strength: just enough to leave a faint chlorine smell after
  30 minutes.
- **Surface disinfection** uses 1,000 to 5,000 ppm for the hardest jobs (CDC, Preventing
  Norovirus).
- A **cal-hypo stock solution** made by EPA's method is about 500 ppm (500 mg/L), and is then
  diluted 1 part to 100 parts water for drinking. The stock itself is a poison: labelled, lidded
  and kept from children.

Surface strength in drinking water is poisoning. Drinking strength on a vomit spill does
nothing. **Never mix up the two tables. An unlabelled jug of mixed bleach is surface solution:
pour it out.**

## Drinking water with bleach (CDC)

Clear cloudy water first (let it settle, pour off, filter through cloth). Then, from CDC's
table (How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency):

| Water | 5 to 9% bleach | 1% bleach |
|---|---|---|
| 1 quart or litre | 2 drops | 10 drops |
| 1 gallon | 8 drops (0.5 mL) | 40 drops (2.5 mL) |
| 5 gallons | 40 drops (2.5 mL, 1/2 tsp) | 200 drops (12.5 mL) |

Stir, wait **at least 30 minutes**. **Double the dose** if the water is cloudy, coloured or very
cold. If the label gives drinking-water directions, follow the label. EPA's own table is for
bleach labelled 6 or 8.25 percent: 8 drops of 6% or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon (EPA,
Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water). Both tables, and the full method: → 03-04.

## Surfaces and dishes (CDC)

| Job | Recipe, per gallon of room-temperature water, 5 to 9% bleach | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| Sanitising washed dishes and food surfaces | 1 tablespoon | Then air dry |
| General surface disinfection | 5 tablespoons (1/3 cup) | At least 1 minute, visibly wet |
| Vomit or diarrhoea (norovirus) | 5 to 25 tablespoons (1,000 to 5,000 ppm); the strong end for the spill itself (→ 13-11) | At least 5 minutes |

Clean first, then disinfect: bleach does not work on visible dirt. Make it fresh every day.
Rinse food surfaces with safe water afterward. Ventilate. → 13-10, → 13-11

## Storing chlorine safely (CDC/ATSDR)

Cal-hypo is an **oxidiser**: it feeds a fire, releases chlorine gas when wet or heated, and its
dust burns skin and lungs. Keep it sealed and dry in its original container, off the floor,
below 120°F, away from fuel, acids, ammonia, trichlor or dichlor, and anything that gets wet. Add granules to
water, never water to granules. Bleach goes up high, away from ammonia cleaners and acids.

## Decisions on this page

- Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14
- Chlorinating beyond label strength when water is very dirty: {{choice DC-23}} → 30-24

{{#if has.pool}}You have a pool: its chemicals belong on this page's storage rules. → 03-03, → 03-08{{/if}}

pages.body:
# Water words, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Water treatment advice uses a handful of words that sound alike but
mean different jobs. Mixing them up is how people drink water they thought was safe. This page
defines them.

> **SAFETY.** **Clear is not clean.** Water can look perfect and carry enough germs to cause
> days of diarrhoea, which in a small child, an elder or someone with diabetes is a medical
> emergency. And **no boiling, filtering or chlorine makes water safe if it may contain fuel,
> toxic chemicals or radioactive material** (CDC). Find another source.

## Three different jobs

| Job | What it does | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Clarifying** | Removes dirt and particles so the water is clear | Settle and pour off; strain through cloth or a coffee filter |
| **Disinfecting** | Kills or removes germs | Boiling, chlorine (→ 29-05), a fine enough filter plus chlorine, UV |
| **Distilling** | Removes salts and many chemicals by boiling water and collecting the steam | A still (→ 03-03). Needed for salt water and pool water with salts |

Boiling and chlorine disinfect. **They do not remove salt or chemicals.** A filter removes some
germs but, on its own, not all of them.

## The words

- **Potable** — safe to drink. Tap water from a working public system is potable; after a main
  break or a boil-water notice it is not, until the utility says so.
- **Boil** — a **rolling boil**: big bubbles that keep rolling when stirred, not the first small
  bubbles. Hold it **1 minute**; above 5,000 ft (EPA) or 6,500 ft (CDC) hold it **3 minutes**.
  Boiling is the most reliable way to kill germs (CDC).
  {{#if is.high_altitude}}Your home is above 5,000 ft: boil 3 minutes.{{/if}}
- **Germs** come in three kinds that behave differently:
  - **Bacteria** — single cells, such as *E. coli*. Killed by boiling and chlorine; removed by a
    filter of 0.3 micron or finer.
  - **Parasites** (protozoa), such as *Giardia* and *Cryptosporidium*. Larger. Killed by
    boiling; removed by a filter of 1 micron or finer. **Chlorine works poorly on them, and
    iodine does not kill *Cryptosporidium*** (CDC).
  - **Viruses** — far smaller than either. Killed by boiling and chlorine. **Most portable filters
    do not remove viruses** (CDC); only a few, sold as purifiers, are rated for them (→ 28-06).
    Unless the box says viruses, filtered water still needs chlorine or boiling.
- **Micron** — one millionth of a metre. A filter's **absolute** pore size is the largest gap it
  lets through; a "nominal" size is an average and promises less. Read which one the package
  states (→ 28-06).
- **Turbidity** — cloudiness. Cloudy water shields germs from chlorine and UV and uses up the
  chlorine, so it is cleared first and dosed double (CDC; → 29-05).
- **Residual** — the chlorine left over after it has done its work. A faint smell after 30
  minutes means some remains; no smell means the dose was used up, so treat again.
- **UV** — ultraviolet light from a pen-style device or the sun. Works on small amounts of clear
  water only. Sunlight method: clear plastic bottles of 2 litres or less, 6 hours in full sun or
  2 days if cloudy (CDC) (→ 03-04).
- **Contaminated vs. dirty** — dirty water has mud and germs and can be treated. Contaminated
  water has fuel, chemicals, sewage overflow or floodwater from industrial areas; treat it as
  unusable unless distilled, and even then not if fuel or solvents are the problem.

{{figure fig-micron-scale-germs}}

## Stored water

Store water in clean, food-grade containers, sealed, cool and dark, and replace stored tap water
every 6 months (CDC, Creating and Storing an Emergency Water Supply). → 03-02

## Wells and testing

A private well is not tested by anyone but you. Test it for bacteria at least once a year and
after a flood (CDC, Guidelines for Testing Well Water).
{{#if has.well}}Your home has a well: → 03-07 and → 03-10.{{/if}}

## Decisions on this page

- Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source: {{choice DC-13}} → 30-14

pages.body:
# Refrigerated medicines, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Some medicines, insulin above all, lose strength if they get too warm
and are ruined if they freeze. When the power goes, the kitchen fridge stops protecting them.
This page explains the "cold chain", how to read a storage label, and the order of things to try
when there is no working fridge. It gives no doses.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is
> discarded.** Loss of potency with no way to tell; the published guidance is unanimous.
>
> **No derived dosing.** Never change a dose because a medicine got warm. Your prescriber's plan
> and the condition page govern (→ 02-01, → 02-03).

## What "cold chain" means

The **cold chain** is the unbroken run of correct temperatures from the factory to the moment of
use. Every link counts: pharmacy, car, home fridge, cooler, pocket. A break is called an
**excursion**. **Heat is a slope**: the warmer and longer, the more strength is lost, usually
without any visible change. **Freezing is a cliff**: one freeze can ruin the medicine.

## Reading a storage label

The box and the package insert say how to store the product. The words mean:

| Label says | Means |
|---|---|
| "Store refrigerated, 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C)" | Fridge temperature, never the freezer, never against the cooling plate |
| "Do not freeze" / "Discard if frozen" | One freeze ends it, even if it thaws and looks normal |
| "Store at room temperature, 68°F to 77°F (20°C to 25°C); excursions permitted 59°F to 86°F (15°C to 30°C)" | The usual range, and the short swings the maker tested and allows |
| "Once opened (in use), may be kept at room temperature up to N days" | A countdown starts when the vial or pen is first used or taken out of the fridge. Write the date on it |
| "Protect from light" | Keep it in its box |
| "Inspect before use; do not use if cloudy, discoloured or contains particles" | The look-test the maker allows. A normal look does not prove full strength |

Two examples, as published:
- **Insulin:** unopened, in the fridge at 36°F to 46°F. In an emergency, insulin can be kept
  unrefrigerated at 59°F to 86°F for up to 28 days (FDA, Insulin Storage in an Emergency;
  American Diabetes Association). Never frozen. Each product's own label gives its in-use days.
- **Epinephrine auto-injector:** room temperature, 68°F to 77°F, with excursions to 59°F to 86°F
  allowed; **do not refrigerate**; keep it in its carrier tube to protect it from light; replace
  it if the liquid is discoloured, cloudy or has particles (FDA, EpiPen prescribing information).

Expiry dates and lot numbers: → 29-14.

## The fridge-without-power ladder

Try these in order. **At every step, a thermometer decides, not a guess.** A min/max thermometer
(it records the highest and lowest temperature since you last reset it) in each place medicine is
kept, read and written down morning and evening.

1. **A powered fridge kept running.** A small 12-volt medical or travel fridge on a power station
   or generator-charged battery is the most reliable cold chain (→ 09-10, → 29-02). Some go cold
   enough to freeze: set it and check it with the thermometer, not the display.
2. **A cooler with ice or cold packs**, with a towel or box between the ice and the medicine so
   it **cannot freeze**. Keep it shut; add ice before it is gone.
3. **The coolest stable place in the house**: a basement, an interior closet, a cooler set on a
   concrete floor. More stable than living space, but measure it.
4. **An evaporative cooling pouch or clay-pot cooler** for warm weather: water evaporating from
   its surface cools what is inside below the air temperature, but not to fridge cold. The
   pouch maker's instructions set how to soak it and how long it lasts (→ 12-21).
5. **Winter cold, carefully.** An unheated room or porch may sit at fridge temperature, but it
   swings below freezing. Only inside an insulated cooler as a buffer, with the min/max
   thermometer, never below 36°F.

## Decisions on this page

- Using insulin or other refrigerated medicine after a heat excursion: {{choice DC-08}} → 30-09
- Using expired or heat-exposed epinephrine or other expired medicine: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05

## This household

{{#if has.refrigerated_meds}}Medicines in your profile, with whether each is marked refrigerated:

| Person | Medicine | Refrigerated |
|---|---|---|
{{#each meds as m}}| {{m.member}} | {{m.name}} | {{m.refrigerated}} |
{{/each}}

Put a thermometer with each refrigerated one today.{{else}}No refrigerated medicine is listed in
your profile. If that changes, add it in settings and regenerate.{{/if}}

pages.body:
# Canning words, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Home canning keeps food for years without power, and done wrong it
makes a poison you cannot see, smell or taste. Every canning rule comes from a few words. This
page explains them so the tested recipes in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning make sense.
It does not give process times: those come only from a tested recipe (→ 04-04, → 04-05).

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the
> published time and pressure, or not canned.** Botulism has no field treatment and the food
> looks and smells normal.

## Botulism in one paragraph

*Clostridium botulinum* is a germ that lives in soil and on vegetables as tough **spores** that
survive boiling. In a sealed jar with no air, little acid and room temperature, the spores wake
up and make **botulinum toxin**, one of the most poisonous substances known. It causes paralysis
that starts with the eyes, face and swallowing and can stop breathing. **The jar can look, smell
and taste normal** (USDA; CDC). Acid stops the spores growing; very high heat kills them; heat
also destroys the toxin. That is the whole logic of canning.

## The words

- **pH** — a scale of how acidic something is, from 0 to 14. **Lower is more acidic**; 7 is
  neutral (plain water). Lemon juice and vinegar are low; meat and most vegetables are near
  neutral.
- **High-acid food** — pH **4.6 or lower**: most fruit, pickles, jams, and tomatoes **with added
  lemon juice or citric acid**. Botulism spores cannot grow, so a **boiling-water canner** is
  enough (USDA, Principles of Home Canning).
- **Low-acid food** — pH **above 4.6**: vegetables, beans, meat, poultry, fish, soups, and plain
  tomatoes with nothing added. These **must** be processed in a **pressure canner** (USDA).
- **Boiling-water canner** (water bath) — a big pot with a rack; jars covered by boiling water.
  Water cannot get hotter than boiling: **212°F at sea level**, and lower the higher you live.
- **Pressure canner** — a heavy pot with a locking lid, a vent, and a **gauge**. Holding steam
  under pressure raises the temperature to **about 240°F to 250°F**, which kills botulism spores
  in the tested time (NCHFP, Using Pressure Canners). USDA processes for low-acid vegetables have
  used pressure only since 1943.
- **Pressure cooker vs. pressure canner** — a pressure cooker cooks dinner. **Many pressure
  cookers and electric multi-cookers are not tested for canning** and may not hold the
  temperature for long enough. Use equipment the maker states is for canning.
- **Dial gauge vs. weighted gauge** — a **dial gauge** shows pressure on a needle and must be
  tested yearly; one that reads more than 2 psi off is replaced. A **weighted gauge** rocks or
  jiggles at its set pressure and needs no testing (NCHFP).
- **psi** — pounds per square inch, the unit of pressure on the gauge.
- **Altitude adjustment** — because water boils cooler up high, recipes add time (water bath) or
  pressure (pressure canner) above 1,000 ft. **The recipe's altitude table governs.**
  {{#if is.high_altitude}}Your home is above 5,000 ft: every recipe needs its altitude row.{{else}}Your home elevation is about {{ region.home.elevation_ft }} ft; find that row in every recipe.{{/if}}
- **Venting** — letting steam pour out of a pressure canner for the time the recipe says before
  closing the vent, to push out the air. Trapped air means a lower temperature.
- **Headspace** — the empty space between the food and the top of the jar, set by the recipe.
  Too little and food bubbles out and the lid fails; too much and air stays in.
- **Hot pack / raw pack** — filling jars with hot, cooked food or with raw food. The recipe's
  time is tested for one or the other, not both.
- **The seal** — as the jar cools, a vacuum pulls the lid down. A sealed lid is concave and does
  not flex or pop when pressed in the centre. **Unsealed after 24 hours:** refrigerate and eat, or
  reprocess with a new lid.
- **Tested recipe** — a recipe whose time, pressure, jar size and pack were measured in a
  laboratory. USDA and the National Center for Home Food Preservation publish them. **A family
  recipe card is not a tested recipe.**

{{figure fig-jar-headspace-and-seal}}

## Before eating home-canned low-acid food

CDC's backstop: boil it hard in an open pan **10 minutes, plus 1 minute for every 1,000 ft of
elevation**, liquid included, before eating (CDC, Botulism Prevention). This destroys the toxin.
It does not rescue a jar that is **bulging, leaking, spurting, mouldy or foul-smelling**: those
are thrown out unopened, where children and animals cannot reach them.

## Decisions on this page

- Eating food past its date, from dented cans or a failed freezer: {{choice DC-14}} → 30-15
  (Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are not a choice: discard.)

{{#if has.pressure_canner}}You have a pressure canner: check what kind of gauge it has.{{/if}}

pages.body:
# Radios, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** When phones are down, radios are how a family stays in touch and how
you hear warnings. The radios on sale use different "services" with different rules, power and
reach. This page says what each one is, what range to honestly expect, what a repeater is, and
how NOAA Weather Radio works.

## Words first

- **Handheld** — a walkie-talkie. **Mobile** — mounted in a vehicle. **Base** — at home with an
  outside antenna.
- **Watts** — transmit power. More power helps a little; **antenna height helps far more**.
- **Line of sight** — the radios these services use travel roughly in straight lines. Hills,
  buildings and the curve of the earth block them. Two people on rooftops talk much farther than
  two people in basements.
- **Repeater** — a radio on a tall tower or building that receives you on one frequency and
  re-transmits on another at once, so two handhelds that cannot reach each other can both reach
  it. GMRS repeaters listen 5 MHz above the frequency they transmit on (47 CFR Part 95).
- **"Privacy codes"** (CTCSS/DCS tones) only stop **your** radio from playing other people's
  traffic. **Everyone can still hear you.** Nothing on these radios is private.
- **Simplex** — radio to radio directly, no repeater.

{{figure fig-line-of-sight-and-repeater}}

## The services

| Service | Licence | Power (47 CFR Parts 95 and 97) | Honest everyday range | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FRS** (Family Radio Service) | None | 2 W on channels 1–7 and 15–22; 0.5 W on 8–14; fixed antenna | A few hundred yards to about a mile in town | The yard, the block, a campsite |
| **GMRS** (General Mobile Radio Service) | Yes; **no exam**; one licence covers the family | Up to 5 W on 1–7, 50 W on 15–22; removable antennas; repeaters allowed | 1 to 5 miles handheld; more with a repeater or a roof antenna | Family coordination around a town |
| **MURS** | None | 2 W, 5 channels near 151–154 MHz; external antennas allowed | 1 to 3 miles | A quiet alternative to FRS |
| **CB** (Citizens Band) | None | 4 W AM, 12 W single-sideband; 40 channels near 27 MHz | 1 to 5 miles; occasionally very far | Road and traffic information from truckers |
| **Amateur ("ham")** | Yes; **exam** | Depends on licence class and band | Across town to across the world, depending on band and antenna | Real distance; organised emergency nets |
| **Scanner / receiver** | None to listen | — | — | Hearing what is going on without being heard |

FRS and GMRS share the same 22 channels, so FRS and GMRS radios can talk to each other on them.
The "35-mile" figure on a blister pack is a mountaintop-to-mountaintop number; expect the
everyday column. **Test your own:** one person walks or drives away calling every block until
contact is lost, and you write that distance down (→ 15-06).

> **Before the collapse:** transmitting on GMRS or amateur bands requires an FCC licence while
> the FCC operates; GMRS needs no exam, amateur radio does (47 CFR Parts 95 and 97). A licence
> you hold and a radio you have practised on now are worth far more than one you are guessing at
> later. Listening needs no licence. → 15-05

## NOAA Weather Radio

The National Weather Service runs a network of transmitters that broadcast forecasts and warnings
around the clock. It does not depend on the internet, cell towers or your house power, only on
the transmitter and your radio's batteries. **Every transmitter in the country uses one of seven
frequencies: 162.400, 162.425, 162.450, 162.475, 162.500, 162.525 and 162.550 MHz** (NWS). Any
radio that tunes those finds the local one by stepping through seven channels.

**SAME** (Specific Area Message Encoding) is a code for each county. A weather radio with SAME,
programmed with your county's code, stays silent until an alert for that county arrives, then
sounds an alarm. Program the counties around yours too: storms arrive from neighbouring counties
first. What the alerts mean: → 29-10.

Your home transmitters (from the region appendix):

| Call sign | Frequency (MHz) | SAME code |
|---|---|---|
{{#each region.home.nwr as t}}| {{t.call}} | {{t.freq}} | {{t.same}} |
{{/each}}

{{#if has.noaa_radio}}You have a weather radio: program the SAME code above and test it.{{else}}A weather radio with SAME and battery backup is one of the cheapest life-saving purchases there is. → 15-01{{/if}}
{{#if has.gmrs}} You have FRS or GMRS radios: agree a family channel and practise. → 15-03{{/if}}
{{#if has.ham}} Someone in the household is licensed or has a ham radio. → 15-05{{/if}}

pages.body:
# Weather alert words, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** A weather alert is only useful if everyone in the house knows what
the words mean and what to do at once. This page explains the three alert levels, the two
"feels like" numbers, and the hazard ratings printed for your region.

## Watch, warning, advisory

| Word | What it means | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **Watch** | Conditions are right for the hazard to develop. It has not happened yet. Watches cover large areas and last hours | Get ready. Charge things, check the plan, know where everyone is, shoes on |
| **Warning** | The hazard is happening, or is about to, where you are | **Act now.** For a tornado warning: to the shelter spot, immediately |
| **Advisory** | Less serious, but still a hazard that can hurt people who ignore it | Take care; change plans for travel or outdoor work |

**Tornado warning** means a tornado has been seen or shown by radar: the warning time is minutes
(NWS, Tornado Safety). A **severe thunderstorm warning** means damaging wind or large hail, and
tornadoes can form from these storms with little extra warning. → 17-02, → 17-06

Other alerts you will hear:
- **Flood or flash flood warning** — water is rising or about to. Never drive or walk into
  moving water: 6 inches can knock an adult down and 12 inches can carry away most cars (NWS,
  Turn Around Don't Drown). → 17-03
- **Red flag warning** — warm, dry, windy weather in which any fire spreads fast. No outdoor
  burning (NWS Glossary). → 17-05
- **Winter storm, ice storm, blizzard warning** — travel becomes dangerous and power loss is
  likely. → 17-01
- **Extreme cold warning** and **extreme heat warning** — dangerous cold or heat. The NWS
  renamed these in 2024 (cold: Wind Chill Warning became Extreme Cold Warning, and the cold
  advisory is now a **Cold Weather Advisory**) and 2025 (Excessive Heat Warning became Extreme
  Heat Warning). Older radios and pages may use the old names; treat them the same.

Each NWS office sets its own trigger numbers for its area, so the same word can start at a
different temperature in different states. Your office: {{ region.home.nws_office }}.

## The two "feels like" numbers

**Wind chill** is how cold it feels on bare skin when wind is added to cold air, because wind
strips heat away faster. It is the number that predicts **frostbite**. The NWS wind chill chart
shows, for each air temperature and wind speed, whether bare skin freezes in 30, 10 or 5 minutes
(NWS, Wind Chill Chart). Use the chart, not a feeling. → 08-05

**Heat index** is how hot it feels when humidity is added to heat, because damp air stops sweat
from cooling you. The NWS categories (NWS Amarillo, Heat Index):

| Heat index | Category | What can happen with long exposure or work |
|---|---|---|
| 80°F to 90°F | Caution | Tiredness |
| 90°F to 103°F | Extreme caution | Heat stroke, heat cramps or heat exhaustion possible |
| 103°F to 124°F | Danger | Heat cramps or heat exhaustion likely; heat stroke possible |
| 125°F and up | Extreme danger | Heat stroke highly likely |

The published heat index assumes shade and a light wind. **Full sun can add up to 15°F** (NWS).
→ 17-04

{{figure fig-wind-chill-chart}}

{{figure fig-heat-index-chart}}

## The hazard ratings in your region pages

The region appendix rates each natural hazard for every county on a scale of **1 to 3**, from
FEMA's National Risk Index: **3** means FEMA rates the county's risk from that hazard very high or
relatively high, **2** relatively moderate, and **1** relatively low, very low or not rated. The
index weighs how much a hazard could cost the county (what there is to damage, and how well the
community recovers), **not how likely it is on any day**: a big city can rate high for a rare
hazard, and a thinly settled county can rate low for a real one. Use it to decide what to plan
for, then read the hazard page. Your home county:

| Hazard | Rating | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
{{#each region.home.hazards as h}}| {{h.name}} | {{h.rating}} | {{h.rating_text}} |
{{/each}}

Pages for the hazards rated 2 or 3 are moved to the front of their sections in your binder.

## Hearing the alert

The alert only helps if it reaches you at 3 a.m. with the power and phones out: a NOAA Weather
Radio with SAME and fresh batteries (→ 29-09). When to leave home altogether is a decision your
household writes down in advance: {{choice DC-19}} → 30-20
