pages.body:
# Firearms basics, for someone who does not shoot

**What this page is for.** This page is for the person in the house who does not use guns but
may one day have to move one, store one, or keep children away from one. It covers the four
safety rules, how to tell in general terms whether a gun is loaded, how to match ammunition to a
gun, and safe storage. It does not teach shooting or tactics. The page is in every binder,
whether or not the household owns a firearm, because guns turn up in other people's homes.

> **SAFETY — the floor that applies (→ 30-01).** **Children do not have access to firearms,
> fuel, medications or chlorine products.** Fixed in every source.

## The four rules

These four are taught in every safety course. NSSF's longer list of ten starts from the same
ideas: keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction, never touch the trigger until you mean to
shoot, be sure of your target and what is beyond it, and a gun is only certain not to fire when
its action is open and it is completely empty (NSSF, Firearm Safety). Every accident breaks at
least one of them.

1. **Treat every gun as if it is loaded.** Always, including one someone just told you is empty.
2. **Never point a gun at anything you are not willing to destroy.** Keep the muzzle (the open
   end of the barrel) pointed in a safe direction: usually at the floor, away from people, or at
   something that would stop a bullet.
3. **Keep your finger off the trigger** and outside the trigger guard, resting along the side of
   the gun, unless you are about to shoot.
4. **Know your target and what is beyond it.** Bullets go through walls, doors and people.

## Words you will hear

- **Muzzle** — the open end the bullet comes out of. **Barrel** — the tube.
- **Chamber** — where the cartridge sits, ready to fire, at the back of the barrel.
- **Action** — the moving parts that load, fire and unload. Opening the action shows the chamber.
- **Magazine** — a removable box (or a fixed tube) that holds cartridges and feeds them in.
  Removing the magazine does **not** empty the chamber.
- **Cylinder** — the turning drum on a revolver, with several chambers.
- **Safety** — a switch that blocks firing on some guns. It is a mechanical part and can fail.
  It never replaces the four rules.
- **Cartridge** (round) — one unit of ammunition. **Caliber** (or gauge, for shotguns) — the size
  and type of cartridge a gun is made for.

## Is it loaded? (general terms)

If you do not know how a particular gun opens, **do not experiment**. Leave it where it is,
pointed in a safe direction, keep others away, and get the person who knows it. If you must
check one you know how to open:

1. Muzzle in a safe direction, finger outside the trigger guard, the whole time.
2. **Remove the magazine first**, if it has a removable one. Then open the action.
3. **Look into the chamber, and feel it with a finger**: dim light fools eyes. On a revolver,
   open the cylinder and look at every chamber. On a gun with a tube magazine under the barrel,
   the tube may still hold cartridges.
4. If you closed it or put it down, it is **loaded again in your mind**: rule 1.

## Matching ammunition to the gun

Use only the ammunition the gun's maker designates. **The caliber is stamped on the barrel**, or
sometimes on the frame or receiver. The **headstamp** is the lettering on the flat base of each
cartridge. **The headstamp must match the marking on the gun** (SAAMI, Generally Accepted
Firearms and Ammunition Interchangeability). Some cartridges, such as rimfire and some military
rounds, have no caliber on the headstamp: then the original box must say, and if it does not,
the ammunition is not used until a knowledgeable person identifies it. **A cartridge that fits
is not proof it is safe**: the wrong one can burst the gun. SAAMI lists a few accepted
alternatives (for example, a gun marked 357 Magnum may fire 38 Special, not the reverse); the
gun's manual is the authority.

{{figure fig-barrel-marking-and-headstamp}}

## Safe storage

- The safest storage is **unloaded, locked, with ammunition locked separately** (American Academy
  of Pediatrics, Guns in the Home). Locks include cable locks through the action, lock boxes and
  gun safes (CPSC; NSSF Project ChildSafe). Keys and combinations are kept from children.
- **Teach children:** if you see a gun, do not touch it, leave the area, and tell an adult
  (AAP). Ask about guns at homes where children visit.
- **Ammunition:** in its original box, cool and dry, away from fuel and pool chemicals; avoid
  temperatures over 150°F (SAAMI).
- **Lead:** handling ammunition and cleaning guns leaves lead on the hands. Wash hands before
  eating or touching children; no cleaning on the kitchen table (CDC, Childhood Lead Poisoning
  Prevention). → 14-05

## Decisions on this page

- Firing on your own property for practice: {{choice DC-11}} → 30-12

## This household

{{#if has.firearms}}Your profile says there are firearms in the home. {{#if has.safe}}They have
a safe: write who holds the key or combination on → 14-14.{{else}}No safe is listed: a lock for
each firearm is the first purchase. → 14-14{{/if}}{{else}}No firearms are listed in your profile.
This page still applies at other people's homes.{{/if}}
{{#if has.child}} There are children in the house: storage rules above are not optional. → 20-02{{/if}}

{{photo barrel-marking}}

pages.body:
# Fire extinguishers, fire blankets and alarms, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** In an outage, a household burns more things indoors (heaters, lamps,
candles, stoves) and the fire department may not come. This page explains the alarm that wakes
you, the extinguisher that stops a small fire, the blanket that smothers one, and the moment to
stop fighting and leave.

> **SAFETY.** **People first, then the fire.** A home fire can fill a house with smoke very
> fast. If the fire is bigger than a wastebasket, spreading, or between you and the exit, **get
> everyone out, stay out, and call 911 from outside** (USFA, Choosing and Using Fire
> Extinguishers). Young children and older adults should not use extinguishers (USFA).

## Smoke alarms

- **Where:** inside each bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level including the
  basement (USFA, Smoke Alarms).
- **Test monthly** with the test button. Replace 9-volt batteries yearly; hard-wired alarms need
  their backup battery replaced yearly. **Replace the whole alarm 10 years from the manufacture
  date** printed on it (USFA).
- **Two kinds of sensor:** ionization and photoelectric. They detect different kinds of fire,
  and you cannot predict which fire you will have, so have both kinds or dual-sensor alarms
  (USFA).
- **Smoke alarms do not detect carbon monoxide.** A combination alarm does both; otherwise you
  need separate CO alarms. → 29-03

## Fire classes

An extinguisher's label shows the letters of the fires it is for (USFA):

| Class | Fire in | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Ordinary materials | Wood, paper, cloth, bedding |
| **B** | Flammable liquids | Gasoline, oil, grease, oil-based paint |
| **C** | Electrical equipment that is plugged in | Appliances, tools, power strips |
| **D** | Burning metals | Workshop and industrial metals |
| **K** | Cooking oils and fats in cooking appliances | Deep fryers |

A household **"ABC"** extinguisher covers the first three. The numbers before the letters rate
its size: on "1A:10B:C", the 1A matches 1.25 gallons of water on a class A fire and the 10B
covers a liquid fire of about 10 square feet (USFA). A bigger number is a bigger fire.

## Using an extinguisher: PASS

Use it **only if** everyone else is out or leaving, 911 has been called, the fire is small and
not spreading, you are not breathing smoke, and **your back is to a clear exit** (USFA). Then:

1. **Pull** the pin, nozzle pointing away from you.
2. **Aim** low, at the base of the fire, not the flames.
3. **Squeeze** the lever slowly and evenly.
4. **Sweep** side to side across the base until it is out.

Small extinguishers empty in seconds. If it is not out when the extinguisher is empty, leave.
Watch the spot afterwards: fires can re-light. Check that the gauge needle is in the green; some types need shaking monthly and pressure testing every few years (USFA).

{{figure fig-extinguisher-pass}}

## Fire blankets

A fire blanket is a sheet of fire-resistant fabric in a quick-pull pouch. It smothers a small
fire by cutting off air: laid over a burning pan (heat off, leave it covered until cold), or
wrapped around a person whose clothes are burning after they **stop, drop and roll**. Read its
pouch now, before you need it. **Never throw water on burning fat or oil.** Put a lid or the
blanket on it and turn off the heat. A wool blanket can stand in; synthetic blankets melt. → 12-03

## When to leave instead

- The fire is spreading, or bigger than you can cover with one extinguisher.
- Smoke is filling the room, or you cannot see the exit.
- It is a **lithium battery** fire (power station, e-bike, tool pack): it can throw very hot
  jets of flame, spreads fast, is hard to put out, and the smoke is toxic. Get out and call for
  help (USFA, Lithium-Ion Batteries: Everyday Convenience, Hidden Fire Risks). → 29-02
- Fuel is involved and the fire is near more fuel. → 29-01

**Plan two ways out of every room** and a meeting place outside, and practise it. Close doors
behind you: a closed door slows fire and smoke.

## In an outage

Flashlights, not candles (USFA, Candle Fire Safety). Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from
every heater, fireplace, stove and candle (USFA, Heating Fire Safety). Open flame indoors is a decision your household makes:
{{choice DC-20}} → 30-21

## This household

Smoke alarms: {{ gear.smoke_alarms }}. Extinguishers: {{ gear.extinguishers }}.
Hang an extinguisher near each room with a heat source, by the exit, not beside the stove or
heater, so you never reach through the fire to get it.

{{photo extinguisher-spots}}

pages.body:
# Measuring without instruments, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Many survival jobs depend on a measurement: how much water is left,
how much bleach goes in, whether the freezer is still cold, how far the next town is. When the
scale's battery is dead and the phone is off, you can still measure, by **calibrating** ordinary
things against something whose size you know. Do the calibrating now, while you still have
instruments, and write the results on this page. Unit conversions are on → 25-02.

> **Where a number keeps someone safe** (a bleach dose, a cooking temperature, a canning time),
> measure it properly or use the published method that needs no instrument: a rolling boil
> (→ 03-04), drops from a dropper (→ 29-05), a tested recipe (→ 29-08). Do not estimate those.

## The idea: one known thing

Every method below works the same way. You find **one thing whose size is known**, compare the
unknown thing to it, and count. Then you write the answer down so nobody has to do it twice.

## Volume

- **Mark a bucket.** Pour in a known measure (a 1-gallon jug, a 1-litre bottle) one at a time
  and draw a line at each level with a marker. That bucket now measures water, feed and fuel.
- **Labels carry volumes:** water jugs, milk jugs, soda bottles, paint cans, the water heater's
  data plate ({{ dwelling.water_heater_gallons }} gal for yours).
- **A box of known size:** volume = length × width × height. One cubic foot holds about 7.5
  gallons (→ 25-02).
- **Firewood:** a cord is a stack 4 ft high, 4 ft deep and 8 ft long, 128 cubic feet
  (University of Missouri Extension, Wood Fuel for Heating). A tape measure is the scale.
- **Small amounts:** a medicine dropper or syringe from a first-aid kit is your most accurate
  small measure. Kitchen spoons vary; check one against the dropper's marks.

## Weight

- **Water is the reference weight:** a gallon of water weighs about 8.34 lb (→ 25-02). Two
  full gallon jugs are close to 17 lb.
- **A balance:** a board over a round log or pipe, the unknown on one end, jugs of water on the
  other, slid until it balances. Count the jugs.
- **A bathroom scale for heavy things:** weigh yourself holding it, then without it, and
  subtract.
- **Count what is packed:** cans and bags carry their weight on the label; a pantry can be
  weighed by counting labels.

## Temperature

- **Check a thermometer** in a glass packed with ice and a little water, stirred: it should read
  32°F. In boiling water it reads 212°F at sea level, less the higher you live.
- **The fridge and freezer:** a refrigerator should be at 40°F or below and a freezer at 0°F or
  below. With the door shut, a fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours without power and a full
  freezer about 48 hours (FoodSafety.gov, Food Safety During a Power Outage). Ice crystals still
  in frozen food are a useful sign; a cheap appliance thermometer is the real answer.
- **Hand feel is not a thermometer.** Cooked meat is safe at the temperature on the published
  chart, not by colour (FoodSafety.gov, Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures). Keep one probe
  thermometer with spare batteries, and a min/max thermometer for medicine (→ 29-07).

## Distance

- **Your pace.** Walk a measured 100 feet (along a tape, or a known length such as a lot line
  from your deed) and count your steps. Do it on rough ground and with a pack too. Write it down:
  _____ steps per 100 ft.
- **Time it.** Walk for 15 minutes on a road whose length you know and work out your own walking
  speed, then your speed carrying a load and with children. Write both down. → 24-04
- **Maps** have a scale bar: mark its length on a strip of paper and step it along the route.
- **Vehicles:** the odometer, while the car still runs.

## Time

- **A wind-up or battery wall clock** outlasts phones. Keep one, with batteries.
- **Count seconds** ("one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand") against a clock now, until your count
  matches; then you can time a minute without one.
- **Measure what burns:** light a candle or an oil lamp with a full tank and note how many hours
  it lasts. That tells you hours of light per candle or per fill.
- **The sun** is highest at local noon, when shadows are shortest. A stick in the ground makes a
  rough clock.

## Your calibrations (fill in once, in pen)

| Thing | My number |
|---|---|
| Steps per 100 ft, flat / rough / loaded | _____ / _____ / _____ |
| Walking speed, alone / with children | _____ / _____ |
| Marked bucket: lines at | _____ |
| Hours per candle / per lamp fill | _____ / _____ |
| Drops per mL from our dropper | _____ |
| Wood burned per day in a blackout weekend | _____ |

pages.body:
# Reading a label, explained from the beginning

**What this page is for.** Almost every limit that keeps you safe is printed on the thing
itself: how much power an appliance draws, what fuel a can held, when a cylinder must be
retired, how a medicine is stored, when food stops being good. This page shows where to look
and what the abbreviations mean. Photograph your own labels into the app now: labels fade, peel
and get lost. → 28-07

## Appliance and gear data plates

A **data plate** (or rating label) is the sticker or metal plate on the back or bottom of an
appliance, generator, power station or heater.

| Mark | Means |
|---|---|
| **V** (volts) | The electrical "pressure" it needs or supplies: 120 V household, 12 V car-style |
| **A** (amps) | The current it draws or can supply |
| **W** (watts) | Power while running. Watts = volts × amps. "Rated" or "running" watts is what it does all day; "surge", "peak" or "starting" watts is a short burst for motors starting |
| **Wh / kWh** | Stored or used energy (power stations, batteries) |
| **Ah** | Battery capacity; × volts = Wh |
| **Hz** | Mains frequency; US is 60 Hz |
| **Input / PV input** | What can charge it: a voltage range and a maximum current or watts. Stay inside it |
| **BTU/h** | Heat output (or gas burned) per hour on heaters and stoves. 1 kWh of electricity = 3,412 BTU (EIA, British Thermal Units) |
| **"For indoor use" / "outdoor use only"** | Where the maker allows it to run. An outdoor-only heater, stove or generator is never brought inside → 29-03 |
| **Model / serial number** | What to quote for a manual or part |

Meaning of the electrical words: → 29-02.

{{figure fig-data-plate-example}}

## Fuel cans

- **What was in it:** the printed or written label, not the colour (→ 29-01). Write the fuel and
  the fill date on every can.
- **Safety features by date:** updated child-resistance rules for the closures of gas, diesel and
  kerosene cans took effect on December 22, 2022, and since July 2023 portable fuel containers
  must carry a **flame mitigation device**, such as a flame arrestor, which protects against
  burning vapour jetting out of the can (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety, 2023). Older cans may lack
  them; they are worth replacing.

## Propane cylinders

The collar or foot ring of a cylinder is stamped. On a refillable 1-lb cylinder you will find the
**DOT specification**, **TW (tare weight)**, the weight of the empty cylinder, and the **date of
manufacture**; a refillable cylinder must be requalified within 12 years of its manufacture date
(YSN/Flame King, Training Program 1A). The training's fill method stops when white fog shows at
the bleed vent, the 80 % liquid mark; a filled cylinder should weigh no more than its TW plus the
1 lb it is rated to hold (→ 08-09). A cylinder that hisses, is dented or rusted, or has a bent or stiff
valve is retired. Refilling 1-lb cylinders at home is a decision card: {{choice DC-03}} → 30-04

## Chlorine products

Look for the **% sodium hypochlorite** (bleach) or **% calcium hypochlorite** (pool shock), the
words unscented or regular, and any **drinking-water directions**; if the label gives them,
follow the label (CDC). Additives (scents, algaecides, clarifiers, stabilisers) rule a product
out for water. → 29-05

## Medicines

**Over-the-counter medicines** carry a **Drug Facts** box in the same order on every package
(FDA, OTC Drug Facts Label):

1. **Active ingredient** and the amount in each tablet or dose. Brands with similar names can
   have different active ingredients (FDA), so read this line every time, and do not give two
   products that list the same active ingredient.
2. **Purpose** (for example, pain reliever, antihistamine).
3. **Uses**.
4. **Warnings**: who should not take it, when to stop, when to ask a doctor.
5. **Directions**: the dose by age, as published. **Follow it as printed; never work out a
   dose of your own.**
6. **Other information**: how to store it.
7. **Inactive ingredients**: what matters for allergies.

**Prescription labels** show the patient's name, the drug and strength, directions, the pharmacy,
the prescription number and refills. The package insert gives storage (→ 29-07).

**Expiry date ("EXP")** is the date the maker guarantees full strength under the stated storage.
FDA says an OTC medicine with no expiry date on the label should be treated as expired three years
after purchase.
**Lot number ("LOT")** identifies the batch: recalls are announced by lot, so keep the box or
write the lot down. Using a medicine past its date is a decision card: {{choice DC-04}} → 30-05

## Food dates

USDA explains the phrases (USDA FSIS, Food Product Dating). **"Best if used by"** is about flavour and
quality, not safety. **"Sell by"** tells the store how long to display it. **"Use by"** is the last
date recommended for peak quality. **"Freeze by"** says when to freeze it. Except for infant
formula, these dates are not required by federal law and are not safety dates. Cans may also
carry a packing code ("closed dating", letters and numbers) instead of a readable date (FSIS). Spoilage signs and dented cans: {{choice DC-14}}
→ 30-15. **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans are thrown out, unopened.**

{{photo data-plates}}

pages.body:
# How this binder was made, and what to trust

**What this page is for.** Before you rely on a reference in an emergency, you should know who
wrote it, how it was checked, and where its limits are. This page explains how
this binder was put together, what the stamp on every page means, and how to
change or rebuild it later.

## Built in layers

| Layer | What it is | Who wrote it |
|---|---|---|
| **Core** | Method and fact that are true everywhere: water, food, fire and fuel, heat, power, first aid, sanitation, tools, communications. Plus these explainers (Section 29) and the decision cards (Section 30) | Written once from a fact-checked family binder, with that family's details removed, then frozen. Every household gets the same text |
| **Region** | Climate, hazards, plants, trees, weather offices and radio codes for every state and DC (Section 32). Your home base is moved to the front; the rest stays one tap away, because you may have to cross the country | Built from public datasets, not from memory |
| **Household** | Your people, contacts, meeting places, destinations, house, gear and supply lists | Filled in from your answers in settings; a few paragraphs, such as the story of the route to a destination, are written by the AI from those answers. Every number on these pages traces to something you typed or to a dataset |
| **Condition library** | Modules for common medical conditions (Section 02). The whole library is in every binder; the ones you ticked are moved to the front | Written once and frozen. No doses are worked out for anyone; published tables are printed as published |
| **Gear library** | How to read and run common classes of gear (Section 28) | Written once; your models are filled in from your answers |

Your copy was made at the **{{#if experience.new}}"new to all of this"{{/if}}{{#if experience.some}}"some experience"{{/if}}{{#if experience.experienced}}"experienced"{{/if}}**
level you chose: that sets whether these explainers sit at the front of each section or in the
back.

## "AI-reviewed, not human-verified": what the stamp means

Every page carries this stamp. It means exactly what it says. **No doctor, engineer,
electrician or other professional has checked your copy.** Two kinds of automatic check were run
instead:

- **When the kit was built**, an AI reviewed every page of the shared text once. Every number on
  a page marked critical or caution was traced to a named source that was read, or the number
  was corrected or removed. Pages were compared so that one rule, one number and one name are
  used throughout, and the floors are worded the same everywhere. Anything left over from the
  family whose binder the core came from was removed, and the text was checked for plain
  language.
- **When your binder was generated**, checks ran on your copy: no web address anywhere, nothing
  left from that family, and every fill-in slot checked against your answers. The pages whose
  text depends on your answers were then reviewed again by the AI for consistency, numbers,
  stray names and plain language.

Anything the review could not fix is listed on the **review notes** page. **The known limit:**
if every public source is wrong in the same way, an AI review will not catch it. Where this
binder and a professional disagree, **the professional is right**. While normal services work,
use them.

## Sources, and why there are no links

There is no internet in the situation this binder is for, so it never prints a web address.
Each fact names its source by title, publisher and date in the sentence, preferring US federal
agencies (CDC, EPA, FDA, USDA, NWS, FEMA, CPSC, OSHA, FCC), then national societies and
manufacturers, then university Extension services. **Laws, licences and codes** appear only in
boxes marked **Before the collapse**: they are true while government works, and they never
decide a survival procedure.

## Decision cards and floors

Some choices have no single right answer: running a heater overnight, keeping fuel in the
garage, using an expired medicine. For each, a **decision card** (Section 30) explains the
hazard, why the maker or agency set its rule, how people actually get hurt, what makes it safer,
and the options. **Your household chooses**; your answer is printed wherever the subject comes
up, or "not decided yet". The choice, and the responsibility for it, are yours.

A few things are **floors**, not choices: where there is no mitigation and the failure is death
or permanent injury without warning, such as an engine running indoors or mixing bleach with
ammonia. They are stated as rules with the reason, the same words every time, and no options
box. → 30-01

## Small, Large and Everything

{{#if size.everything}}**This is the Everything copy.**{{else}}{{#if size.large}}**This is the Large copy.**{{else}}**This is the Small copy.**{{/if}}{{/if}}

- **Small** has every page, explainer, card, condition and gear module, the national region
  appendix and all plant plates. Each citation shows title, publisher and date; no source
  document is bound inside. It carries only this kit's own text and public-domain material, and
  fits on any phone.
- **Large** is Small plus the full documents cited by the life-safety sections (medical
  conditions, water, fire and fuel, heating, power, first aid, hazards, kids, CBRN, and the
  decision cards and floors), each bound behind the page that cites it. It also carries
  topographic maps for your home county and destinations, and for the counties along your routes
  if you chose them. Documents cited only by other sections are listed as "in the Everything
  download". It needs a phone with room to spare.
- **Everything** is Large plus every other cited document. It is the largest file and is meant
  for a laptop.
- In Large and Everything, the documents are fetched for your household when you download. Some
  publishers refuse automatic fetching: those are listed on the **Sources not captured** page.
  The page that cites each one still stands on its own text; save the document yourself while
  the internet works.
- A Small copy can be upgraded to Large or Everything later from your saved answers file and
  this binder file, without the pages being written again.

## Changing it later

- **Your answers are never stored by us.** If you chose to save them, they are in a file called
  `profile.json` on your own device. Keep a copy somewhere safe.
- **To add a medical condition, a person, a pet or new gear:** open the settings page, load your
  `profile.json`, change the answer, and generate again. The whole condition library stays in the
  app, so a condition added later gets its full module. A condition that is not in the library
  has its own page: → 02-27.
- **To rebuild from scratch** (a new phone, a lost file): load `profile.json` and generate.
  Without the file, you answer the questions again.
- **Photos you add** to pages stay in your copy on your device and are never sent anywhere.

## This file is your private copy

{{#if size.large}}Your copy contains the full text of documents written by other people and
organisations, fetched for your personal use when you downloaded it. Those documents are
copyrighted by their publishers. **Giving this file to someone else copies their work without
permission and breaks copyright. Keep it within your household.**{{else}}Your Small copy carries
only this kit's own text and public-domain material, but it is still built from your household's
private answers. **Keep it within your household.**{{/if}} If a friend wants a binder, send them
to the settings page so they can make their own. → 00-09

pages.title: Decisions and floors: section overview
pages.body:
# Decisions and floors

**What this section holds.** 30 pages in this build. Pages marked FOR YOU matter most for your household and come first.

- → 30-01 **The floors: nine rules that are not choices**: Most hard calls in this binder are trade-offs, and the household makes them on the decision cards (→ 30-02 to → 30-30).
- → 30-02 **DC-01. An unvented heater running while people sleep**: In a winter outage the coldest hours are the sleeping hours.
- → 30-03 **DC-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house**: When the power is out and it is very cold, it is tempting to bring the grill tank inside to run a heater.
- → 30-04 **DC-03. Refilling 1-lb propane cylinders from a 20-lb tank**: The small 1-lb propane cylinders run out fast and cost a lot.
- → 30-05 **DC-04. Expired or heat-exposed epinephrine, and other expired medication**: When supplies stop, the medicine you have may be past its date, or may have frozen in a car or cooked in a hot room.
- → 30-06 **DC-05. Storing gasoline, kerosene or propane in an attached garage**: Stored fuel is one of the most dangerous things in a prepared house.
- → 30-07 **DC-06. Carrying fuel inside a passenger vehicle**: If the household ever has to drive somewhere far away with no working fuel stations, it may want to carry extra fuel.
- → 30-08 **DC-07. Converting a furnace or well pump to cord-and-plug yourself**: Many households buy a generator and then learn it cannot run the furnace or the well pump, because those are wired straight into the house.
- → 30-09 **DC-08. Using insulin or other refrigerated medication after a heat excursion**: Insulin and some other medicines need to stay cool.
- → 30-10 **DC-09. An infant or toddler sharing a bed with adults for warmth**: In a house with no heat, parents naturally want the baby in bed with them.
- → 30-11 **DC-10. Pets when food, water or movement makes keeping them impossible**: Nobody wants to think about this.
- → 30-12 **DC-11. Firing weapons on your own property for practice, pests or zeroing**: When ranges are closed and gunsmiths are gone, a household may want to fire on its own land: to practise, to "zero" (sight in) a rifle, or to kill pests.
- → 30-13 **DC-12. Defensive use of force: our household rule**: This card is a worksheet, not a multiple choice.
- → 30-14 **DC-13. Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source**: When stored water runs low, a pool, hot tub or nearby stream can look like the answer.
- → 30-15 **DC-14. Food past its date, dented or rusted cans, or food from a failed freezer**: Throwing out food that might be fine is a real loss when no more is coming.
- → 30-16 **DC-15. Giving someone else's prescription medication**: When a person runs out of a medicine and nobody can write a new prescription, the bottle on the next shelf is tempting.
- → 30-17 **DC-16. Antibiotics without a prescription (stockpiled or veterinary)**: An infected wound or a serious infection with no doctor is one of the most likely ways a survivable injury becomes fatal.
- → 30-18 **DC-17. Old kerosene, diesel or gasoline in a heater or engine**: Stored fuel gets old.
- → 30-19 **DC-18. Feeding a food-allergic person unlabeled, traded or scavenged food**: In a long emergency, food stops coming with labels.
- → 30-20 **DC-19. When to leave home: our triggers**: This card is a worksheet.
- → 30-21 **DC-20. Open-flame cooking, candles or oil lamps indoors**: When the power goes out, the house gets dark and the electric stove stops.
- → 30-22 **DC-21. Using a fireplace or wood stove that has not been inspected this year**: A fireplace or wood stove is one of the best heat sources without power.
- → 30-23 **DC-22. Potassium iodide for adults over 40**: Potassium iodide is often sold as an "anti-radiation pill".
- → 30-24 **DC-23. Chlorinating very dirty water beyond the published dose**: Some emergency water is clear; some is brown.
- → 30-25 **DC-24. Children doing dangerous jobs because hands are short**: This card is a worksheet.
- → 30-26 **DC-25. Converting a tourniquet to a pressure dressing when no help will ever come**: The binder's rule is that a tourniquet stays on.
- → 30-27 **DC-26. Holding the allergy-safe food in reserve for the allergic person**: In a household where one person has a food allergy, the food that is safe for them is usually a small part of the whole stockpile.
- → 30-28 **DC-27. Water-glassing fresh eggs (storing them in lime water)**: Hens lay most in summer and least in winter, which is when a household with no fridge most wants eggs.
- → 30-29 **DC-28. Relighting gas appliance pilots yourself when the gas company will not come**: After the gas has been shut off at the meter or tank, or after a propane tank runs dry, every pilot flame in the house goes out.
- → 30-30 **DC-29. One traction attempt on a fractured limb with no pulse below it, when no care is coming**: The usual first-aid rule for a broken bone is "splint it as you find it".

pages.title: The floors: nine rules that are not choices
pages.body:
# The floors: nine rules that are not choices

**What this page is for.** Most hard calls in this binder are trade-offs, and the household
makes them on the decision cards (→ 30-02 to → 30-30). The nine rules on this page are
different. Each one guards against something that kills or maims **without warning and with no
fix afterwards**. No mitigation makes the risky version safe every time, so there is no card,
no options box and no "our choice" line. Other pages copy the rule sentences below word for
word.

> **SAFETY.** If you are reading this in an emergency, the nine bold sentences are the whole
> page. Everything else explains why.

## 1. Engines and charcoal stay outside

**Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window.**

**Why there is no choice.** Burning fuel makes carbon monoxide (CO), a gas you cannot see,
smell or taste (→ 29-03). It takes the place of oxygen in your blood. The first signs feel
like flu: headache, dizziness, sick stomach. People lie down and do not get up. CDC says
people who are asleep or drunk can die before they ever feel ill, and more than 400
Americans die from it each year (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics). A generator is the
worst source: CPSC says one makes as much CO as hundreds of cars, and an open garage door or
window does not make it safe (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety). CO alarms help, but batteries
die, alarms sit in the wrong place, and they are built to wait before sounding (CPSC, Carbon
Monoxide Questions and Answers). Nothing you can add makes an engine indoors safe every time.
The same applies to camp stoves and grills built for outdoor use (CDC).

**Do this instead.** Run the generator outdoors, at least 20 feet from any window, door or
vent, with the exhaust pointed away from every house (CDC). Cook on charcoal and camp stoves
outdoors. Keep battery CO alarms on every level and where people sleep. → 08-02, → 09-04.

{{figure fig-generator-distance}}

## 2. A generator never feeds the house wiring by itself

**Never connect a generator to house wiring except through a transfer switch, or an interlock kit with the main breaker off. Never backfeed through an outlet with a double-male ("suicide") cord.**

A cord-and-plug conversion is not a connection to house wiring: the appliance is unplugged from
the house outlet and plugged into the generator cord, so nothing reaches the panel (whether to do
that conversion yourself is DC-07, → 30-08).

**Why there is no choice.** "Backfeeding" means pushing generator power into the house
wiring, usually with a cord that has a plug on both ends (→ 29-04). That power does not stay
in your house. It flows out through the meter to the transformer on the pole, which raises it
to the voltage of the power line. A line worker who believes the line is dead, or a
neighbour near a downed wire, is electrocuted. CPSC names backfeeding as a cause of
electrocution of utility workers and neighbours (CPSC, Portable Generator Safety). When grid
power comes back, it can also wreck the generator and start a fire. A double-plug cord also
has bare live pins in someone's hand. There is no way to backfeed "carefully".

**Do this instead.** Run extension cords from the generator to single appliances. If you need
a furnace or well pump on generator power, either have a transfer switch or interlock kit
installed for your panel (with an interlock, the main breaker is off whenever the generator
feeds the panel), or give the appliance its own plug by a cord-and-plug conversion so it can be
unplugged from the wall and plugged into the generator cord (→ 09-04). Who does the conversion
work is a decision card (→ 30-08). Backfeeding is never on that card.

{{figure fig-backfeed-path}}

## 3. A tourniquet stays on

**Never loosen a tourniquet once placed while help can still come; mark the time. If no help will ever come, the conversion decision is DC-25 (→ 30-26).**

**Why there is no choice.** A tourniquet is a tight band that stops blood flow to a bleeding
arm or leg. Loosening it "to check" or "to give the limb some blood" lets the bleeding start
again. The person has already lost blood, so the second bleed can be the one that kills, and
the clots that had begun to form are washed away. Writing the time lets anyone who takes over
know how long it has been on (Stop the Bleed, American College of Surgeons).

The rule assumes someone will take over: an ambulance, a clinic, a trained medic. When no help
will ever come, military guidance for long, remote care (TCCC Guidelines, 2026) describes converting a tourniquet to
wound packing and a pressure bandage under strict conditions, and a limb left without blood for
many hours is lost. That is a trade-off, not a floor, so it is a decision card (→ 30-26). While
any help can still come, the tourniquet stays on.

**Do this instead.** Place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint, and tighten
until the bleeding stops. If it still bleeds, add a second one above the first. Write the
time on the strap or the skin. Take a Stop the Bleed course while courses exist. → 12-02,
→ 30-26.

## 4. Low-acid food is pressure-canned or not canned

**Low-acid foods are pressure-canned to the published time and pressure, or not canned.**

**Why there is no choice.** Low-acid foods are vegetables, beans, meat, fish and soups
(→ 29-08). In a sealed jar with no air, botulism spores grow and make a toxin that paralyses
the muscles, including the ones you breathe with. The spores survive boiling water, which
cannot get hotter than 212 °F; only a pressure canner reaches the higher temperature that
kills them (National Center for Home Food Preservation, Principles of Home Canning). The
times and pressures in the USDA tables were tested in a laboratory; guessing them is not the
same thing (USDA, Complete Guide to Home Canning, 2015). The bad jar looks, smells and tastes
normal, so you cannot catch it at the table. Treatment needs a hospital: antitoxin and often
weeks on a breathing machine (CDC, Botulism Prevention). With no hospital, there is no
treatment.

**Do this instead.** Use a real pressure canner (not a pressure cooker) and the USDA time and
pressure for that food, jar size and your altitude. If you have no canner, dry, salt, ferment
by a tested recipe, or eat the food fresh. Throw out any can or jar that is bulging, leaking,
spurting or foul (CDC). → 04-05, → 04-04.

## 5. Wild plants and mushrooms: identification or nothing

**No wild plant or mushroom is eaten on a "test"; identification or nothing.**

**Why there is no choice.** Some survival books, including the military handbook reprinted in
Section 31, describe an "edibility test": touch it, taste a little, wait. That test does not
protect you from the plants that kill. A small amount of water hemlock can kill, with
seizures that start within minutes to hours (USDA Agricultural Research Service,
Poisonous Plant Research Laboratory; CDC MMWR, Water Hemlock Poisoning, 1992). The deadliest
mushrooms cause no symptoms for many hours, by which time the liver damage is done. Taste
tells you nothing about either. Where Section 31 describes an edibility test, this floor
governs.

**Do this instead.** Eat only what you can name with certainty: several matching features,
the right habitat and season, checked against two sources. Leave all mushrooms alone. Use the
plant plates for your region. → 05-06.

## 6. Fuel and flame never meet

**Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.**

**Why there is no choice.** Gasoline gives off vapour even in cold weather (→ 29-01). The
vapour is heavier than air. It flows along the floor, collects in low spots and lights from a
pilot flame, a furnace igniter, a spark or a hot engine across the room (CDC/ATSDR, ToxFAQs for
Automotive Gasoline). The flash reaches back to the can in an instant. CPSC has recorded
deaths and severe burns from fuel cans flashing near a flame (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety,
2023). Propane does the same thing: it is heavier than air and pools.

**Do this instead.** Pour and refill outdoors, away from any flame, with engines and heaters
turned off and cool. Store fuel away from water heaters, furnaces, heaters and anything that
sparks. Where your household stores it is a decision card (→ 30-06). → 06-06, → 06-07.

## 7. Frozen insulin is thrown away

**A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded.**

**Why there is no choice.** Insulin is a protein. Freezing breaks it, and the damage cannot be
undone (→ 29-07). It can look completely normal afterwards, so you cannot tell how much
strength is left. A dose that does nothing, given to someone with type 1 diabetes, can lead to
a dangerous buildup of acids in the blood (diabetic ketoacidosis) without anyone noticing in
time. FDA and the American Diabetes Association both say do not use insulin that has been
frozen (FDA, Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency; ADA, Insulin
Storage and Syringe Safety). Heat is different: heat-exposed insulin is a decision card
(→ 30-09).

**Do this instead.** Keep insulin from freezing: a barrier between insulin and any ice, a
thermometer in the box, the box in the warm room in winter. → 02-01, → 29-07.

## 8. Bleach and pool shock are never mixed

**Bleach or pool shock is never mixed with ammonia, acids or other cleaners.**

**Why there is no choice.** Bleach and pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) are chlorine
products (→ 29-05). Mixed with an acid (some toilet and rust cleaners, vinegar), they release
chlorine gas. Mixed with ammonia (glass cleaners, urine), they release chloramine gas. Both
burn the eyes, throat and lungs, and in a closed room they can kill (CDC, Cleaning and
Disinfecting with Bleach; CDC/ATSDR, Medical Management Guidelines for Chlorine). Pool shock
is also an oxidizer: next to fuel, oil or other organic matter it can start a fire, and it
gives off chlorine when it gets wet (CDC/ATSDR, Calcium Hypochlorite).

**Do this instead.** Use one cleaning product at a time, with water only. Store pool shock
dry, sealed, off the floor and away from fuel, acids and ammonia. → 03-04, → 29-05.

## 9. Children cannot get to the dangerous things

**Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products.**

**Why there is no choice.** Every source agrees on this one. Young children explore by
putting things in their mouths and pulling triggers they find. A mouthful of kerosene or lamp
oil can be breathed into the lungs and cause a severe pneumonia (CDC MMWR, hydrocarbon
ingestion in children). Medicines and chlorine are among the most common child poisonings
(AAP, Poison Prevention). A found, loaded gun is a death in a second (AAP, Guns in the Home;
NSSF, Project ChildSafe). In a crisis the adults are busier and the supervision is thinner,
which is exactly when storage has to do the work.

**Do this instead.** Lock firearms unloaded, with ammunition separate. Store fuel, medicine
and chlorine locked or high, in their own labelled containers, never in drink bottles. Teach
the rule as an absolute. Which jobs children may help with under supervision is a worksheet
(→ 30-25). → 20-02, → 14-14.

## Lines inside the cards that are also fixed

A few cards contain one fixed line that is a floor, not an option:

- **Backfeeding** is never an option on the generator card (→ 30-08); see floor 2.
- **Frozen insulin** is never an option on the heat-exposed medication card (→ 30-09); see
  floor 7.
- **Bulging, leaking or spurting cans and jars** are thrown out; the questionable food card
  (→ 30-15) covers everything else.

pages.title: DC-01. An unvented heater running while people sleep

options.label: Never while anyone sleeps
options.summary: The heater is off and confirmed out before anyone sleeps. Warmth overnight comes from one small room, shared body heat, layers, sleeping bags and pre-warmed beds.

options.label: Lowest setting, alarm, vents, barrier, 3-hour wake
options.summary: Lowest safe setting; tested CO alarm at pillow height installed first; the manual's vents open; heater behind a barrier; one adult wakes every 3 hours to check flame and alarm; headache or nausea means everyone out.

options.label: Run it with alarms and vents
options.summary: The heater runs overnight with a tested CO alarm in the room and the manual's vents open, but no one is set to wake and check it.

pages.settings_summary: Portable propane and kerosene heaters sold for indoor use are 'unvented': their exhaust, including carbon monoxide (CO), stays in the room. Both common types' manuals say never run them while you sleep. CO has no smell; CDC says sleeping people can die before they feel any symptom, and children are affected first. Fire from bedding or a tipped heater is the second risk. What helps most: heater off while people sleep (removes the risk); a tested CO alarm at pillow height, the manual's vent openings, the lowest correct flame, a barrier, and an adult who wakes every 3 hours to check (reduces it a lot). The cost of 'never' is a cold night, which matters most for babies and frail elders in deep cold.
pages.body:
# DC-01. An unvented heater running while people sleep

**What this page is for.** In a winter outage the coldest hours are the sleeping hours. This
card explains what can go wrong when a portable fuel heater keeps burning while everyone is
asleep, why the makers say never do it, and what the household decides. The choice box at the
bottom is the household's answer; every heater page points here.

> **SAFETY.** Never run a generator, charcoal, or any engine indoors, in a garage, or near an
> open window. That is a floor (→ 30-01), not this card. This card is only about heaters sold
> for indoor use. If a CO alarm sounds, or anyone wakes with a headache, dizziness or nausea:
> heater off, everyone out into fresh air, → 08-02.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

A **portable fuel heater** burns propane (the gas in grill tanks) or kerosene (a clear liquid
fuel, → 29-01) to make heat. **Unvented** means it has no chimney or pipe to the outside. Its
exhaust stays in the room you are in. That exhaust includes **carbon monoxide (CO)**, a gas you
cannot see or smell that stops your blood from carrying oxygen (→ 29-03). The heater also uses
up the oxygen in the room and adds water vapour.

Some propane heaters have an **oxygen depletion sensor (ODS)**: it shuts the heater off when
the room's oxygen drops. It does **not** measure CO. Most wick kerosene heaters have no ODS at
all.

{{#if has.unvented_heater}}Your household listed these heaters: {{#each heaters as h}}{{h.kind_text}}; {{/each}}CO alarms on hand: {{ gear.co_alarms }}.{{else}}Your household has not listed a portable fuel heater. Read this card anyway: a borrowed or scavenged heater raises the same question.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why the makers set it

- The owner's manual of one widely sold indoor-rated propane heater says, in capitals,
  **never operate the heater while sleeping**, and requires fresh-air openings high and low in
  the room while it burns (Enerco/Mr. Heater, portable propane heater owner's manual).
- A common wick kerosene heater's manual says never leave it unattended and turn it off and
  check that it is out **before going to bed** (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo, Portable Kerosene Heater
  owner's manual).
- University of Missouri Extension warns that unvented kerosene heaters raise indoor CO and
  other pollutants, more so in small closed rooms (MU Extension, Unvented Portable Kerosene
  Heaters, G1999).

**Why:** a sleeping person cannot notice a flame going wrong, a blanket falling on the heater,
or the first signs of CO. The makers cannot see your room, your fuel or your ventilation, so
they draw the line where a sleeping person is never the only safety system.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

The usual sequence: the house is cold, so the family closes the warm room tightly. The heater
is turned down to save fuel. On a wick heater a turned-down or tarred wick burns badly and
makes more CO (manufacturer's manual). Over several hours the CO level climbs. Children and
anyone with heart or lung disease feel it first (CDC). Everyone gets drowsy, which feels like
ordinary sleep. **CDC says people who are asleep can die from CO before having any
symptoms** (CDC, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Basics).

The second path is fire: bedding, clothes drying nearby, or a curtain within the heater's
clearance, or a heater knocked over in the dark.

The other side is real too. A very cold room can hurt a baby or a frail elder, and CDC lists
infants sleeping in cold bedrooms and older adults among the people most at risk of
hypothermia (CDC, Preventing Hypothermia). {{#if is.cold_winters}}Your home's January average
low is about {{ region.home.jan_low_f }} °F, so this is a real question for your household.{{/if}}

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes the risk**
- Heater off and confirmed out before anyone sleeps. Keep warm by other means: everyone in
  one small room, shared body heat, dry layers and hats, sleeping bags, a warm drink and food
  before bed (→ 08-01, → 21-07). Hot-water bottles pre-warm a bed and come out before a child
  gets in; skin that is asleep burns without waking (→ 11-02).

**Reduces it a lot**
- A **tested, battery CO alarm in the room at the height of sleeping heads**, opposite the
  heater, installed before the heater is ever lit (→ 08-02). No alarm, no overnight heater.
- The **manual's ventilation**, open the whole time: for the propane heater above, an opening
  of 9 square inches high and another low; for the kerosene heater above, a window open at
  least 1 inch in a small room (each manufacturer's manual). Your heater's manual sets its own.
- A heater **with an ODS** rather than one without.
- The **lowest correct setting**: low on a propane heater; on a wick heater, the flame height
  the manual specifies, never turned down below it.
- **One adult wakes about every 3 hours** to look at the flame, the alarm and the openings.
- The heater **behind a barrier** on the far side of the room, with the manual's clearances.

**Reduces it a little**
- Fill the kerosene tank before bed so it does not run dry and smoke at 3 a.m.
- A second CO alarm elsewhere in the house.
- A standing rule: **anyone who wakes with a headache or nausea means everyone out.**

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never while anyone sleeps.**
You give up: overnight heat. On the coldest nights the room may fall well below comfortable,
and you must manage the cold with bodies, layers and bedding. You accept: a cold night.

**`alarm-and-wake`: Lowest setting, alarm, vents, barrier, 3-hour wake.**
You give up: the manuals' rule, and an adult's unbroken sleep every night it runs. You accept:
that the alarm and the wake checks are what stand between the family and CO, and that on a
heater without an ODS they are the only things watching.

**`run-it`: Run it with alarms and vents.**
You give up: the manuals' rule and the human check. You accept: that if the alarm fails, is
placed wrong or sleeps through a slow rise, nobody is awake to notice. This is the riskiest
option.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-01}}

pages.title: DC-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house

options.label: Never indoors
options.summary: Cylinders over 1 lb stay outdoors. If the hose-through-a-window route fails, use another heat source or the cold-night methods; the tank does not come in.

options.label: Last resort: cylinder outside, hose through a window
options.summary: The cylinder always stays outdoors. Only a heater rated for a remote cylinder is fed through the maker's hose, passed through a cracked window or door. The tank never comes inside.

options.label: Indoors with rules
options.summary: Only when the outdoor-hose route is impossible: an above-ground room, never a basement; valve closed whenever the heater is off; no pilot-light appliances nearby; leak test; CO alarm; adult awake; tank out as soon as possible.

pages.settings_summary: A 20-lb propane cylinder (the grill size) holds about twenty times the gas of a 1-lb camping cylinder. Heater makers and the national propane code keep anything over the 1-lb size out of the house. The reason: propane is heavier than air. A leak at the valve, hose or regulator flows along the floor, collects in low places such as basements, and explodes when it reaches a flame such as a pilot light or the heater itself. A cylinder warmed indoors can also vent gas through its safety valve on purpose. What helps most: tank outdoors (removes the risk); maker's hose through a window (reduces it a lot); if it must come in, above-ground room, valve closed when off, leak test, no pilot flames nearby, adult awake (reduces it a little).
pages.body:
# DC-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house

**What this page is for.** When the power is out and it is very cold, it is tempting to bring
the grill tank inside to run a heater. This card explains why makers and the propane code say
no, what actually goes wrong, and what the household decides.

> **SAFETY.** Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance
> (floor, → 30-01). If you smell gas (a rotten-egg smell) near a cylinder indoors: do not
> switch anything on or off, close the tank valve if you can reach it, put out flames, get
> everyone out and open doors on the way.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

**Propane** is a fuel gas stored as a liquid under pressure in steel cylinders (→ 29-01). The
small green **1-lb cylinder** is the camping size. The **20-lb cylinder** is the grill tank.
Bigger tanks hold more. Propane in the air is **heavier than air**: it sinks and spreads along
the floor like invisible water. A rotten-egg smell is added so you can smell a leak, but only
if your nose is near where it pools.

Some indoor-rated propane heaters can run from a large cylinder through a hose. The heater
maker designs that for **the cylinder outdoors**, the hose through a window.

{{#if has.basement}}Your home has a basement. Propane that leaks anywhere in the house can
drain down to it.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- One widely sold indoor-rated propane heater's manual says, in a DANGER box, **never bring a
  refillable propane cylinder indoors**, and allows a cylinder up to 20 lb **only when the
  cylinder is located outdoors** (Enerco/Mr. Heater, propane heater owner's manual).
- NFPA 58, the national propane code, limits cylinders kept inside a home, attached garage
  included, to the 1-lb class (NFPA 58, storage of cylinders within residential buildings).
- The Propane Education & Research Council says store cylinders outdoors, upright, valve
  closed (PERC, Safety Guide for Portable Propane Cylinders).

**Why:** quantity, sinking gas and heat. A 20-lb cylinder holds about twenty times the propane
of a 1-lb cylinder, so a leak indoors is not a whiff; it can be enough to fill a room to the
point where it burns. Because propane sinks, the leak collects at floor level, below your nose,
and flows toward low rooms, stairwells and basements, where furnaces and water heaters often
have a pilot flame or igniter. And a cold cylinder brought into a warm house builds pressure;
its relief valve is designed to vent gas when that happens (PERC).

## 3. How it actually hurts people

A connection is not quite tight, a hose is cracked, or a valve seal is worn. Gas leaks slowly
overnight and spreads along the floor. Nobody smells it at standing height. Someone lights the
heater in the morning, or a water-heater pilot across the room catches the edge of the cloud.
The gas burns all at once: a flash fire or an explosion that injures everyone in the room and
can bring down walls. A second risk is the heater itself: running a heater in the same room as
its own fuel supply puts the flame and the leak side by side. The CO risks of the heater
(→ 30-02) come on top.

{{figure fig-propane-pools-low}}

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes the risk**
- **The cylinder stays outdoors**, upright, valve closed until needed (PERC). Inside, use only
  heaters and 1-lb cylinders the heater maker allows indoors, or heat by other means
  (→ 08-04).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Cylinder outdoors, the heater maker's own hose through a cracked window or door**, with
  the gap packed with a towel. The hose route is the maker's design; inspect the hose every
  use. The cracked window does not replace the heater's required ventilation (→ 08-09).

**Reduces it a little** (only if the cylinder must come in)
- An **above-ground room only**, never a basement or any room below ground level, so a leak
  can drain out a door at floor level.
- **Valve closed every time the heater is off.** Not turned low: closed.
- **Soapy-water leak test** at the valve and both hose ends before opening and again after
  lighting. Bubbles mean stop.
- **No pilot-light appliances** in or open to the room: doors to the furnace and water-heater
  area closed.
- The cylinder as far from the heater as the hose allows, never in front of it, never near
  any other heat.
- **An adult awake in the room** the whole time; no overnight burn with the tank inside.
- **Tank back outside the moment the hose route works again.**

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never indoors.**
You give up: heat from the big cylinder on a night when the window route fails. You accept:
falling back on other heat sources or cold-night methods (→ 08-04, → 08-01).

**`last-resort`: Last resort, cylinder outside, hose through a window.**
You give up: nothing the maker forbids; you need a heater rated for a remote cylinder and the
maker's hose, and a window or door you can crack. You accept: a small leak risk at the hose
inside the room, and a draft.

**`indoors-with-rules`: Indoors with rules.**
You give up: the maker's and the code's rule. You accept: a house-filling quantity of a
heavier-than-air fuel gas in the living space, controlled only by the rules above and an adult
who stays awake.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-02}}

pages.title: DC-03. Refilling 1-lb propane cylinders from a 20-lb tank

options.label: Never refill (the makers' position)
options.summary: Use only new, factory-filled 1-lb cylinders indoors and on camp gear. When they run out, use a 20-lb tank outdoors with the maker's hose, or another fuel.

options.label: Refill by weight, refillable-rated cylinders only
options.summary: Only cylinders built and stamped as refillable; never a disposable. Fill outdoors, away from flame, weighed on a scale to the stamped empty weight plus the rated content and no more; leak-test; retire any cylinder that hisses or has a stiff valve.

pages.settings_summary: The small green 1-lb propane cylinders sold for camp stoves and indoor heaters are made to be filled once at the factory. Adapters sold online let you refill them from a grill tank. Heater makers allow only factory-filled disposable cylinders indoors, and refillable cylinder makers say never refill a disposable. The real dangers are overfilling (a 1-lb cylinder has no overfill stop, so an overfilled one vents gas when it warms indoors) and a worn valve that leaks in the room. What helps most: buy new cylinders, or use a 20-lb tank outdoors with a hose (removes it); cylinders built to be refilled, filled outdoors by weight on a scale and leak-tested (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-03. Refilling 1-lb propane cylinders from a 20-lb tank

**What this page is for.** The small 1-lb propane cylinders run out fast and cost a lot.
Adapters let you refill them from a grill tank. This card explains what the makers say, what
actually goes wrong, and what the household decides.

> **SAFETY.** Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance
> (floor, → 30-01). Refilling, if you do it at all, happens outdoors, with nothing burning
> nearby. Liquid propane on bare skin causes frostbite burns: gloves and long sleeves.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

The **1-lb cylinder** is the small green camping bottle of propane (→ 29-01). Most are
**disposable**: built and certified to be filled once, at the factory. A few makers sell
**refillable** 1-lb cylinders, stamped as refillable with a tare (empty) weight on the foot
ring. A **refill adapter** connects a 20-lb grill tank, turned upside down so liquid flows, to
the small cylinder.

Propane is stored as a liquid with a gas space on top. That gas space is deliberate: when the
cylinder warms, the liquid expands into it. Fill the space with liquid and there is nowhere
for the expansion to go.

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- One widely sold indoor-rated propane heater's manual allows **only disposable cylinders**
  on the heater indoors and says never bring a refillable cylinder indoors (Enerco/Mr. Heater,
  propane heater owner's manual).
- A maker of refillable 1-lb cylinders trains users that a disposable **single-trip cylinder
  must not be refilled**: its valve and seals are built for one fill (YSN/Flame King, Training
  Program 1A, Filling 1 lb Refillable Propane Cylinders).
- The same training sets the fill limit: the cylinder's rated content of propane and no more,
  checked by weight, and says never chill a cylinder in a fridge or freezer to speed filling.

**Why:** the heater maker cannot know who filled a cylinder, how full, or with what valve
condition. The cylinder maker knows the disposable's valve was not designed for repeat use.
The fill limit protects the expansion space.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

**Overfilling.** Small cylinders have no automatic overfill stop. Filling by "chill it and
fill until it stops" or by guesswork leaves too much liquid. The cylinder comes indoors, warms
to room temperature, the liquid expands, and the relief valve opens and releases propane into
the room, next to a lit heater or stove.

**A worn or damaged valve.** A disposable valve reused, or a refillable one that is bent or
stiff, weeps gas slowly. Propane is heavier than air, so the leak flows along the floor toward
a flame (→ 30-03).

**The fill itself.** Liquid propane sprays from a loose connection and freezes skin. A leak
during filling near a flame or a running engine ignites.

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes the risk**
- **Do not refill.** Buy new factory-filled 1-lb cylinders, or run the heater or stove from a
  20-lb tank **outdoors** through the maker's hose (→ 08-09, → 30-03).

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Refillable-rated cylinders only**, stamped as such. **Never a disposable.**
- **Fill by weight on a scale**: full weight is the stamped tare weight plus the cylinder's
  rated content, and never more (refillable cylinder maker's training). If heavy, bleed it
  down outdoors until the weight is right.
- **Outdoors, away from any flame or running engine**, with gloves; the large tank's valve
  closed before connecting; the large tank upside down only as long as the maker says.
- **Soapy-water leak test** on every filled cylinder's valve before it goes anywhere.
- **Retire any cylinder that hisses or has a bent or stiff valve.** It never comes indoors
  again.

**Reduces it a little**
- One trained adult does all refilling; nobody else improvises it.
- Write the fill date on each cylinder and keep a log of how many times it has been filled.
- Store filled cylinders outdoors or in a ventilated shed, out of the sun.

## 5. The options

**`never`: Never refill (the makers' position).**
You give up: cheap small cylinders; you rely on new ones, which run out, or on a 20-lb tank
outdoors with a hose. You accept: fewer hours of small-cylinder heat or cooking once the stock
is gone.

**`by-weight`: Refill by weight, refillable-rated cylinders only.**
You give up: the heater maker's disposable-only rule. You accept: that the scale, the leak
test and the retire-a-bad-valve rule are the only things preventing an overfilled or leaking
cylinder from venting gas indoors. Refilling disposables is not part of this option.

> **Before the collapse:** refilling and transporting single-trip (disposable) cylinders is
> restricted under US transport rules. That is a legal point; the safety reason not to refill
> them is in part 2.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-03}}

options.label: Discard at the printed date
options.summary: Expired, frozen-and-thawed or heat-damaged medication is replaced and not used. The household keeps enough in-date supply that it never faces the question.

options.label: Use if clear and colourless; keep seeking in-date stock
options.summary: When no in-date supply exists: in anaphylaxis, an expired or thawed epinephrine device whose liquid is clear and colourless is used at once. Intact tablets past date may be used. Liquids that changed are not. Keep looking for in-date stock.

pages.settings_summary: Every medicine has an expiry date: the date until which the maker guarantees full strength. Labels also give a storage range; epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPen type) should not freeze or get hot. After the date, or after freezing or heat, strength can drop slowly, and some liquids can change. In anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction), a weak dose is worse than a full one, but no dose can be fatal. Published studies found most expired auto-injectors still held most of their dose, and frozen-then-thawed ones delivered a normal dose. What helps most: keep enough in-date supply, rotated, at the right temperature (removes it); check the window for clear, colourless liquid (reduces it a lot). This card does not cover insulin: frozen insulin is always thrown away.
pages.body:
# DC-04. Expired or heat-exposed epinephrine, and other expired medication

**What this page is for.** When supplies stop, the medicine you have may be past its date, or
may have frozen in a car or cooked in a hot room. This card is about whether to use it when
nothing in-date exists. It is not a dosing guide.

> **SAFETY.** A frozen-then-thawed insulin vial or pen is discarded (floor, → 30-01). That
> floor is not part of this card. In anaphylaxis, give epinephrine first and think second;
> → 02-03.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

**Epinephrine** (adrenaline) is the drug that treats **anaphylaxis**, a severe allergic
reaction that can close the airway and drop blood pressure within minutes. It usually comes in
an **auto-injector** (EpiPen type), a pen you press against the thigh. It has a small window to
see the liquid.

An **expiry date** is the date until which the maker guarantees full strength and safety when
stored as the label says (→ 29-14). After it, most medicines lose strength slowly; a few change
in ways that matter. **Storage range** is the temperature band on the label.

Your household's allergy rows: {{#each allergies as a}}{{a.member}}, {{a.allergen}} ({{a.severity}}); {{else}}none entered.{{/each}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- The FDA prescribing information for the EpiPen says store it at room temperature (68 to
  77 °F, brief trips 59 to 86 °F), do not refrigerate or freeze it, and replace it if the
  liquid is discoloured or has particles (FDA, EpiPen prescribing information).
- FDA advises the public not to use expired medicines, because strength and safety after the
  date are not guaranteed (FDA, Don't Be Tempted to Use Expired Medicines).

**Why:** a maker can only promise what it has tested. Strength and stability are tested up to
the printed date under the printed storage conditions. Beyond that, the maker does not know,
so the label says replace.

**What testing outside the label has found:**
- 40 EpiPen and EpiPen Jr devices tested up to 50 months past their date all still held at
  least 80 percent of the labelled dose, most over 90 percent (Cantrell and others, Annals of
  Internal Medicine, 2017).
- EpiPens frozen for 24 hours and thawed delivered the same dose volume as unfrozen ones
  (Cooper and others, American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, 2018).
- The US military's Shelf Life Extension Program found most intact tablets and capsules,
  stored well, stayed potent years past their dates; liquids and some drugs were exceptions
  (Lyon and others, Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences, 2006).

## 3. How it actually hurts people

**Using it:** an older or heat-damaged device may give somewhat less drug. In anaphylaxis a
weaker first dose can mean the reaction is not stopped and a second dose is needed sooner.
A liquid that has turned brown, pink or cloudy has broken down and may do little.

**Not using it:** anaphylaxis treated with no epinephrine can kill within minutes to hours
(CDC, Recognizing and Responding to Anaphylaxis). Waiting to find an in-date pen is the
failure that kills.

**Other medicines:** an expired liquid (children's syrups, mixed antibiotic suspensions, eye
drops) may have lost strength or grown germs. Some drugs where small strength losses matter
(heart, seizure, thyroid, transplant medicines) can fail quietly. Insulin and frozen
medicines follow their own rules (→ 30-09, → 30-01).

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes the risk**
- **Never be in the position**: keep enough in-date supply, replaced before expiry, logged on
  the rotation tracker (→ 26-08), stored inside the label's temperature range.

**Reduces it a lot**
- **Look through the window first.** Use only epinephrine that is **clear and colourless**,
  with no flakes or crystals (FDA label's own check).
- **Keep devices on a person in the cold** (inside the coat, never in a car or pack) and out of
  hot cars in summer (→ 02-03).
- **Use the newest expired device first**; keep expired stock sorted by date.
- **Give the second dose sooner** if the first device was old and the person is not improving,
  following the written anaphylaxis plan (AAAAI, Anaphylaxis Emergency Action Plan).

**Reduces it a little**
- For tablets and capsules: use only intact ones stored cool and dry; discard anything
  crumbling, discoloured, sticky or smelling different.
- Do not use expired liquids, eye drops or anything that has changed in look or smell.
- Ask a pharmacist or clinician about each long-term medicine while you still can, and write
  their answer on → 12-07.

## 5. The options

**`discard`: Discard at the printed date.**
You give up: whatever strength the old medicine still had. You accept: that if in-date
supply runs out, there may be nothing to give.

**`use-if-clear`: Use if clear and colourless; keep seeking in-date stock.**
You give up: the label's guarantee. You accept: that an older device or tablet may be weaker,
and that you must watch more closely and be ready to give another dose. Discoloured or cloudy
epinephrine is a last resort only when nothing else exists.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-04}}

pages.settings_summary: Many households keep gas cans in the attached garage, next to the car, the lawn mower and often a water heater or furnace. The danger is not the liquid but its vapour. Gasoline vapour forms even in the cold, is heavier than air, flows along the floor and catches fire from a pilot light, igniter, spark or hot engine. A garage fire spreads into the house. Propane cylinders in a garage can vent gas when they warm. What helps most: fuel in a detached shed or outdoor locker (removes most of it); approved sealed cans, far from ignition sources, never opened inside, small quantity (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-05. Storing gasoline, kerosene or propane in an attached garage

**What this page is for.** Stored fuel is one of the most dangerous things in a prepared house.
The garage is the convenient spot. This card explains what the risk is, why codes limit it,
and what the household decides.

> **SAFETY.** Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance.
> Children do not have access to firearms, fuel, medications or chlorine products. (Both are
> floors, → 30-01.) If you smell strong fuel vapour in the garage: no switches, no engines,
> open the big door from outside if you can, keep everyone away until it clears.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

- **Gasoline** is car fuel: thin, sharp-smelling, and it evaporates fast (→ 29-01).
- **Kerosene** is a heavier, oily fuel for wick heaters and lamps. It gives off much less
  vapour than gasoline.
- **Propane** is a gas stored as a liquid in steel cylinders.
- An **attached garage** shares a wall, a door and often air with the house. Many hold a
  water heater, furnace or garage heater with a **pilot light** (a small flame that is always
  lit) or an **electronic igniter** (a spark when it starts).

{{#if has.garage}}Your home has an attached garage. Fuel on hand from your settings: gasoline
{{ gear.fuel.gasoline_gal }} gal, kerosene {{ gear.fuel.kerosene_gal }} gal, 20-lb propane
cylinders {{ gear.fuel.propane_20lb }}.{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- Model fire codes cap how much flammable liquid may be kept in an attached garage and push
  larger amounts into listed cabinets or separate buildings.
- NFPA 58, the propane code, does not allow cylinders larger than the 1-lb class inside a
  home, attached garages included (NFPA 58, storage within residential buildings).
- A common kerosene heater maker says store kerosene only in a container clearly marked
  "kerosene", away from heat and living space (GHP Group/Dyna-Glo, kerosene heater manual).

**Why:** gasoline vapour is heavier than air, so it does not rise and disperse; it flows along
the floor and pools (CDC/ATSDR, ToxFAQs for Automotive Gasoline). It ignites from tiny
sources. A garage gathers exactly those sources: pilot lights, igniters, light switches, a car
or generator engine, tools that spark. A fire there reaches the house through the shared wall
and door.

> **Before the collapse:** your local fire code sets a number for how much gasoline may sit in
> an attached garage. Check it while your fire department can answer. It is a legal limit; the
> physics below is the same with or without it.

## 3. How it actually hurts people

A can's cap is loose, a can cracks in a freeze, or someone tops up the mower inside on a cold
day. Vapour spreads across the floor. The water heater's burner lights on its own, or a car
starts. The vapour cloud flashes back to the can. CPSC has recorded deaths and severe burns
from exactly this flashback (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety, 2023). The fire spreads into the
house through the door. If the fire reaches a propane cylinder, its relief valve vents and
feeds the fire.

A second path: a child finds a can, or fuel ends up in a drink bottle (→ 30-01, floor 9).

## 4. What makes it safer

**Removes most of the risk**
- **Fuel out of the house and garage**: a detached shed or a ventilated, lockable outdoor
  steel locker, shaded. Propane cylinders outdoors, upright, valves closed, at least a few feet
  from doors, windows and anything that sparks (PERC).

**Reduces it a lot** (if fuel stays in the garage)
- **Approved fuel cans only**, caps tight, labelled by fuel, kerosene and gasoline on separate
  shelves. Newer cans have a flame arrester at the spout (CPSC).
- **As far from any pilot light, igniter, heater or engine as the garage allows**, on the
  floor rather than above anything hot.
- **Never pour or transfer fuel inside the garage**, grid up or down. Carry the can out, pour
  outside, cap it, bring it back (→ 06-07).
- **A small, written quantity cap**: only what you rotate through vehicles and the generator.
- **Propane cylinders never in the garage**, whatever the liquids rule.

**Reduces it a little**
- A listed flammables cabinet.
- An ABC fire extinguisher mounted **outside** the storage spot, so you never reach through a
  fire for it (→ 29-12).
- Spill absorbent (cat litter or sand) and a locked door against children.

{{photo fuel-storage-spot}}

## 5. The options

**`outbuilding-only`: Outbuilding or outdoor locker only.**
You give up: convenience, and the cost of a shed or locker. Fuel kept outdoors can be harder
to reach in a storm and easier to steal. You accept: a short walk.

**`garage-with-rules`: Attached garage with rules.**
You give up: the code's limit and the safest location. You accept: a store of vapour-producing
fuel sharing a wall with the house, controlled by caps, distance, the never-pour-inside rule
and a quantity cap. Write the cap here: ______ gal gasoline · ______ gal kerosene.

## 6. Our choice

{{card DC-05}}

pages.title: DC-06. Carrying fuel inside a passenger vehicle

options.label: Never inside: roof, hitch carrier or trailer only
options.summary: Fuel rides outside the passenger space: a roof rack, a hitch-mounted carrier, a pickup bed or an open trailer. If none is available, fuel stays behind and the route is planned on the tank.

options.label: Cargo area, sealed cans, shortest time
options.summary: Only when no outside carry exists: approved sealed cans, caps tight, upright and strapped in the rear cargo area, windows cracked, emptied into the tank at the first chance. Propane cylinders upright, valves closed.

pages.settings_summary: When a family has to drive a long way with no fuel stations working, extra gasoline in cans can be the difference between arriving and being stranded. Fuel safety guidance says it rides outside the passenger space. Inside a closed car, vapour from a can collects in the cabin, can make people sick, and can ignite from a spark. In a rear-end crash, a can behind the back seat can split and burn next to the passengers. Propane in a closed car can leak and pool on the floor. What helps most: carry fuel outside the cabin on a rack, hitch carrier or trailer (removes most of it); approved sealed full cans, strapped upright, windows cracked, shortest possible time (reduces it a lot).
pages.body:
# DC-06. Carrying fuel inside a passenger vehicle

**What this page is for.** If the household ever has to drive somewhere far away with no
working fuel stations, it may want to carry extra fuel. This card explains why guidance says
keep fuel out of the passenger space, what actually goes wrong, and what the household
decides.

> **SAFETY.** Fuel is never stored or transferred near an open flame or a running appliance
> (floor, → 30-01). Refuel the vehicle from a can with the engine off, outdoors, nobody
> smoking, children kept away.

## 1. The thing, in plain words

A **jerrican** or **fuel can** is a container made and approved for gasoline or diesel
(→ 29-01). **Passenger space** means anywhere people sit and the cargo area of an SUV, van or
hatchback that shares their air. **Outside carry** means a roof rack, a hitch-mounted cargo
carrier, a pickup bed or a trailer.

{{#if has.vehicle}}Your vehicles: {{#each vehicles as v}}{{v.type_text}} ({{v.fuel_text}}); {{/each}}{{#if has.trailer}}You have a trailer.{{/if}}{{/if}}

## 2. The rule, and why it was set

- The Propane Education & Research Council says carry propane cylinders **upright, valve
  closed, secured, in a ventilated space**, and do not leave them in a closed vehicle (PERC,
  Safety Guide for Portable Propane Cylinders).
- CPSC promotes approved fuel containers with flame arresters because vapour ignition at the
  can causes deaths and burns (CPSC, Fuel Container Safety, 2023).
