pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Alaska: climate by area and by borough or census area, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each borough or census area, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home borough or census area is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 30 boroughs and census areas.
- Hardiness zones: 1b to 8b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: -23 to 31 F. July mean high: 51 to 72 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -76 F and 98 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the boroughs and census areas: NWS Anchorage, AK; NWS Fairbanks, AK; NWS Juneau, AK.
- Ecoregions at borough or census area centres: Alaska Peninsula Mountains; Aleutian Islands; Pacific Coastal Mountains; Ahklun and Kilbuck Mountains; Bristol Bay-Nushagak Lowlands; Coastal Western Hemlock-Sitka Spruce Forests; Wrangell Mountains; Alaska Range; Interior Highlands; Cook Inlet; Subarctic Coastal Plains; Seward Peninsula; Arctic Foothills; Interior Forested Lowlands and Uplands.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each borough or census area (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest borough or census area value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Arizona: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Arizona Department of Emergency and Military Affairs, Division of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 15 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 9b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 18 to 43 F. July mean high: 85 to 109 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -30 F and 126 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Flagstaff, AZ; NWS Tucson, AZ; NWS PSRFGZ; NWS Phoenix, AZ; NWS Las Vegas, NV; NWS PSRTWC.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Arizona/New Mexico Plateau; Madrean Archipelago; Arizona/New Mexico Mountains; Chihuahuan Deserts; Sonoran Basin and Range.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Arkansas: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Arkansas Division of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 75 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 7a to 8b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 24 to 35 F. July mean high: 82 to 95 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -28 F and 124 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Little Rock, AR; NWS Jackson, MS; NWS Tulsa, OK; NWS Memphis, TN; NWS Shreveport, LA.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Mississippi Alluvial Plain; South Central Plains; Ozark Highlands; Boston Mountains; Arkansas Valley; Mississippi Valley Loess Plains; Ouachita Mountains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for California: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** California Governor's Office of Emergency Services (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 58 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 10b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 15 to 47 F. July mean high: 62 to 110 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -36 F and 124 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS San Francisco, CA; NWS STOREV; NWS Sacramento, CA; NWS Eureka, CA; NWS Hanford, CA; NWS Phoenix, AZ; NWS Las Vegas, NV; NWS REVSTO; NWS Los Angeles/Oxnard, CA; NWS MFRREV; NWS Reno, NV; NWS San Diego, CA; NWS SGXPSR; NWS VEFSGXPSR; NWS Medford, OR; NWS HNXSTO.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Central California Foothills and Coastal Mountains; Sierra Nevada; Central California Valley; Klamath Mountains/California High North Coast Range; Coast Range; Sonoran Basin and Range; Mojave Basin and Range; Eastern Cascades Slopes and Foothills; Southern California/Northern Baja Coast; Central Basin and Range; Southern California Mountains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Colorado: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Colorado Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 64 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4b to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: -6 to 21 F. July mean high: 67 to 94 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -61 F and 114 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Denver, CO; NWS Pueblo, CO; NWS Grand Junction, CO; NWS Goodland, KS.
- Ecoregions at county centres: High Plains; Arizona/New Mexico Plateau; Southern Rockies; Southwestern Tablelands; Colorado Plateaus; Wyoming Basin.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Connecticut: climate by area and by planning region, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each planning region, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home planning region is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Connecticut Division of Emergency Management and Homeland Security (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 9 planning regions.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 14 to 24 F. July mean high: 78 to 85 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -25 F and 106 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the planning regions: NWS Norton, MA; NWS Upton, NY; NWS Albany, NY.
- Ecoregions at planning region centres: Northeastern Coastal Zone; Northeastern Highlands.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each planning region (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest planning region value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

| Area (NWS office) | Planning regions | Zone | Jan low F | Jul high F | Record low / high F | Precip in | Snow in | Last frost | First frost | Frost-free days | Sun hrs Dec / Jun |

| NWS Norton, MA | 2 | 6b | 15 to 20 | 82 to 85 | -24 / 103 | 42.8 to 50.1 | 38 to 52 | Apr 17 to May 1 | Oct 9 to Oct 26 | 161 to 191 | 2.6 / 5.2 to 5.3 |
| NWS Albany, NY | 1 | 6a | 14 | 78 | -25 / 98 | 52.9 | 75 | May 3 | Oct 11 | 161 | 2.4 / 5.1 |

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by planning region

One line per planning region, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain planning regions can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each planning region with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled planning region can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Georgia: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Georgia: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 159 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 7b to 9a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 25 to 44 F. July mean high: 80 to 94 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -16 F and 113 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Jacksonville, FL; NWS Tallahassee, FL; NWS Peachtree City, GA; NWS Charleston, SC; NWS Columbia, SC; NWS Greenville-Spartanburg, SC.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Southern Coastal Plain; Southeastern Plains; Piedmont; Ridge and Valley; Blue Ridge.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. pages.title: Hawaii: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Hawaii: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Hawaii Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 5 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 10a to 12b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 35 to 65 F. July mean high: 58 to 87 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: 34 F and 100 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Honolulu, HI.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Hawaiian Islands (not mapped at EPA Level III).

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

| Area (NWS office) | Counties | Zone | Jan low F | Jul high F | Record low / high F | Precip in | Snow in | Last frost | First frost | Frost-free days | Sun hrs Dec / Jun |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NWS Honolulu, HI | 5 | 10a to 12b | 35 to 65 | 58 to 87 | 34 / 100 | 17.8 to 31 | 0 | Apr 12; none in most years in 4 | Dec 1; none in most years in 4 | 235 to 365 | 4.8 to 5.3 / 5.4 to 6.6 |

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by county

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

| County | Zone | Elev ft | Jan low | Jul high | Rec low / high | Precip in | Snow in | Last frost | First frost | Days |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hawaii | 10a | 8,250 | 35 | 58 | 34 / 87 | 23.9 | 0 | Apr 12 | Dec 1 | 235 |
| Honolulu | 12b | 20 | 65 | 85 | 50 / 100 | 21.8 | 0 | None in most years | None in most years | 365 |
| Kalawao | 12b | 0 | 64 | 86 | 46 / 94 | 21.7 | 0 | None in most years | None in most years | 365 |
| Kauai | 12a | 830 | 62 | 87 | 43 / 97 | 17.8 | 0 | None in most years | None in most years | 365 |
| Maui | 11a | 2,760 | 51 | 74 | 38 / 91 | 31 | 0 | None in most years | None in most years | 365 |

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

| Hazard | High (counties) | Moderate (counties) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tornado | 0 | 0 |
| Blizzard and winter storm | 0 | 0 |
| Ice storm | 0 | 1 |
| Flood (river and coastal) | 3 | 1 |
| Wildfire | 2 | 2 |
| Earthquake | 2 | 1 |
| Hurricane | 0 | 0 |
| Extreme heat | 0 | 0 |
| Extreme cold | 0 | 0 |
| Drought | 0 | 0 |
| Volcano | 2 | 0 |
| Tsunami | 2 | 2 |
| Landslide | 1 | 1 |

Rated Low in every county of Hawaii: tornado, blizzard and winter storm, hurricane, extreme heat, extreme cold, drought.

### Hazard ratings by county

Key: Ice = ice storm; Flood = flood (river and coastal); Fire = wildfire; Quake = earthquake; Volc = volcano; Tsun = tsunami; Land = landslide. 3 = High, 2 = Moderate, 1 = Low.

| Hawaii | 1 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 1 |

| Maui | 1 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 1 |

## National Weather Service offices

Each office issues the watches and warnings for its counties (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). A county split between two offices is listed under both.

A weather radio receives these transmitters with no power grid or internet. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Illinois: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 102 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 5a to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 10 to 26 F. July mean high: 81 to 90 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -38 F and 116 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS St Louis, MO; NWS Paducah, KY; NWS Chicago, IL; NWS Quad Cities, IL; NWS Lincoln, IL.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Interior River Valleys and Hills; Central Corn Belt Plains; Interior Plateau; Driftless Area.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Indiana: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Indiana Department of Homeland Security (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 92 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 5b to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 15 to 26 F. July mean high: 81 to 92 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -35 F and 116 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Northern Indiana, IN; NWS Indianapolis, IN; NWS Chicago, IL; NWS Louisville, KY; NWS Wilmington, OH; NWS Paducah, KY.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Eastern Corn Belt Plains; Central Corn Belt Plains; Interior Plateau; Interior River Valleys and Hills; Southern Michigan/Northern Indiana Drift Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Iowa: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Iowa: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 99 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4b to 6a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 4 to 16 F. July mean high: 79 to 87 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -47 F and 117 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Des Moines, IA; NWS La Crosse, WI; NWS Quad Cities, IL; NWS Sioux Falls, SD; NWS Omaha/Valley, NE.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Western Corn Belt Plains; Driftless Area; Central Irregular Plains; Interior River Valleys and Hills.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Kansas: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Kansas: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Kansas Division of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 105 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 14 to 24 F. July mean high: 87 to 95 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -35 F and 121 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Wichita, KS; NWS Topeka, KS; NWS Kansas City/Pleasant Hill, MO; NWS Dodge City, KS; NWS Springfield, MO; NWS Goodland, KS; NWS Hastings, NE.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Central Irregular Plains; Western Corn Belt Plains; Southwestern Tablelands; Central Great Plains; Flint Hills; Cross Timbers; High Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Kentucky: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Kentucky: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Kentucky Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 120 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6b to 7b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 19 to 30 F. July mean high: 82 to 91 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -37 F and 114 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Louisville, KY; NWS Paducah, KY; NWS Jackson, KY; NWS Wilmington, OH; NWS Charleston, WV.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Interior Plateau; Mississippi Valley Loess Plains; Central Appalachians; Western Allegheny Plateau; Interior River Valleys and Hills; Southwestern Appalachians.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Louisiana: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Louisiana: climate by area and by parish, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each parish, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home parish is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Governor's Office of Homeland Security and Emergency Preparedness (Louisiana) (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 64 parishes.
- Hardiness zones: 8b to 10a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 32 to 47 F. July mean high: 88 to 95 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -16 F and 112 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the parishes: NWS Lake Charles, LA; NWS New Orleans, LA; NWS Shreveport, LA; NWS Jackson, MS.
- Ecoregions at parish centres: Western Gulf Coastal Plain; South Central Plains; Mississippi Valley Loess Plains; Mississippi Alluvial Plain; Southeastern Plains; Southern Coastal Plain.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each parish (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest parish value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

| NWS Shreveport, LA | 17 | 8b to 9a | 32 to 39 | 89 to 95 | -16 / 112 | 48.9 to 60.8 | 0 to 1 | Feb 28 to Mar 30 | Nov 6 to Dec 1 | 221 to 275 | 3.5 to 3.6 / 5.3 to 5.5 |

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by parish

One line per parish, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain parishes can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

pages.title: Maine: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Maine: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Maine Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 16 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4a to 6a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 1 to 17 F. July mean high: 74 to 81 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -45 F and 104 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Gray, ME; NWS Caribou, ME; NWS GYXCAR.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Acadian Plains and Hills; Northeastern Coastal Zone; Northeastern Highlands.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by county

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Michigan: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Michigan State Police, Emergency Management and Homeland Security Division (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 83 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4a to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 0 to 22 F. July mean high: 73 to 84 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -48 F and 112 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Gaylord, MI; NWS Marquette, MI; NWS Grand Rapids, MI; NWS Detroit/Pontiac, MI; NWS Northern Indiana, IN.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Northern Lakes and Forests; Southern Michigan/Northern Indiana Drift Plains; Huron/Erie Lake Plains; North Central Hardwood Forests; Eastern Corn Belt Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Minnesota: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Minnesota Homeland Security and Emergency Management Division (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 87 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 3b to 5a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: -8 to 11 F. July mean high: 70 to 85 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -59 F and 114 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Duluth, MN; NWS Twin Cities/Chanhassen, MN; NWS Grand Forks, ND; NWS Aberdeen, SD; NWS Sioux Falls, SD; NWS La Crosse, WI.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Northern Lakes and Forests; North Central Hardwood Forests; Northern Glaciated Plains; Western Corn Belt Plains; Lake Agassiz Plain; Driftless Area; Northern Minnesota Wetlands.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Mississippi: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Mississippi: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Mississippi Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 82 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 7b to 9a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 28 to 42 F. July mean high: 88 to 96 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -19 F and 114 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Jackson, MS; NWS Memphis, TN; NWS New Orleans, LA; NWS Mobile, AL.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Mississippi Valley Loess Plains; Southeastern Plains; Mississippi Alluvial Plain; Southern Coastal Plain.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

| NWS Memphis, TN | 22 | 7b to 8b | 28 to 36 | 88 to 92 | -19 / 114 | 54.3 to 62.3 | 0 to 3 | Mar 7 to Apr 9 | Oct 28 to Nov 17 | 202 to 254 | 3.4 to 3.5 / 5.6 to 5.8 |

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by county

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Missouri: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Missouri: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Missouri State Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 115 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 5b to 7b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 13 to 30 F. July mean high: 85 to 92 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -34 F and 118 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Kansas City/Pleasant Hill, MO; NWS St Louis, MO; NWS Springfield, MO; NWS Paducah, KY; NWS Quad Cities, IL; NWS Memphis, TN.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Central Irregular Plains; Western Corn Belt Plains; Ozark Highlands; Mississippi Alluvial Plain; Interior River Valleys and Hills; Mississippi Valley Loess Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Montana: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Montana: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Montana Disaster and Emergency Services (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 56 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 3b to 6a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: -2 to 22 F. July mean high: 70 to 91 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -58 F and 117 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Great Falls, MT; NWS Billings, MT; NWS Glasgow, MT; NWS Missoula, MT.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Middle Rockies; Northwestern Great Plains; Northwestern Glaciated Plains; Canadian Rockies; Northern Rockies.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Nebraska: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Nebraska Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 93 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4b to 6a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 9 to 18 F. July mean high: 83 to 92 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -47 F and 118 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Hastings, NE; NWS Omaha/Valley, NE; NWS North Platte, NE; NWS Cheyenne, WY; NWS Sioux Falls, SD; NWS Goodland, KS.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Central Great Plains; Western Corn Belt Plains; Nebraska Sand Hills; High Plains; Northwestern Glaciated Plains; Northwestern Great Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Nevada: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Nevada: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Nevada Division of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 17 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 5a to 9a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 9 to 38 F. July mean high: 84 to 106 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -42 F and 120 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Reno, NV; NWS Las Vegas, NV; NWS Elko, NV; NWS VEFLKN.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Central Basin and Range; Mojave Basin and Range; Northern Basin and Range.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

| NWS Elko, NV | 5 | 5a to 6b | 9 to 19 | 84 to 94 | -42 / 115 | 8.9 to 12.6 | 16 to 84 | May 28 to Jun 2; none in most years in 2 | Sep 11 to Sep 21; none in most years in 2 | 71 to 114 | 2.9 to 3.8 / 6.7 to 7.1 |

| NWS VEFLKN | 1 | 6b | 15 | 94 | -15 / 103 | 4.9 | 10 | May 10 | Sep 30 | 141 | 4.4 / 7.5 |

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by county

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

## NOAA Weather Radio

A weather radio receives these transmitters with no power grid or internet. Program the SAME code of every county you care about so the radio sounds only for warnings there; reception is reliable to about 40 miles over flat ground and less in hills (NOAA National Weather Service, NOAA Weather Radio Coverage by County, 2026). → 15-01

## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for North Carolina: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** North Carolina Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 100 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6b to 9a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 21 to 38 F. July mean high: 74 to 93 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -31 F and 110 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Raleigh, NC; NWS Greenville-Spartanburg, SC; NWS Blacksburg, VA; NWS Newport/Morehead City, NC; NWS Wakefield, VA; NWS Wilmington, NC; NWS Morristown, TN.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Piedmont; Blue Ridge; Middle Atlantic Coastal Plain; Southeastern Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for North Dakota: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** North Dakota Department of Emergency Services (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 53 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 3b to 4b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: -8 to 9 F. July mean high: 77 to 86 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -58 F and 121 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Bismarck, ND; NWS Grand Forks, ND.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Northwestern Great Plains; Northern Glaciated Plains; Northwestern Glaciated Plains; Lake Agassiz Plain.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Ohio: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Ohio Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 88 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 7a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 15 to 24 F. July mean high: 81 to 87 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -37 F and 113 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Wilmington, OH; NWS Northern Indiana, IN; NWS Cleveland, OH; NWS Charleston, WV; NWS Pittsburgh, PA.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Interior Plateau; Eastern Corn Belt Plains; Erie Drift Plain; Eastern Great Lakes Lowlands; Western Allegheny Plateau; Huron/Erie Lake Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet.
