## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

An ecoregion is an area where the land, climate, soils and plants are alike (US EPA, Level III Ecoregions of the Continental United States, 2013; Level III Ecoregions of Alaska). The plant and tree plates for each ecoregion are what to learn before you forage or cut firewood there. → 05-06 → 05-17

pages.title: Oklahoma: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Oklahoma: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Oklahoma Department of Emergency Management and Homeland Security (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 77 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6b to 8a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 19 to 33 F. July mean high: 90 to 97 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -29 F and 120 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Tulsa, OK; NWS Norman, OK; NWS Amarillo, TX; NWS Shreveport, LA.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Ozark Highlands; Central Great Plains; Ouachita Mountains; Southwestern Tablelands; East Central Texas Plains; Cross Timbers; South Central Plains; High Plains; Arkansas Valley; Central Irregular Plains; Flint Hills.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Oregon: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Oregon: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Oregon Department of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 36 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 9b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 19 to 42 F. July mean high: 65 to 94 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -34 F and 117 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Boise, ID; NWS Portland, OR; NWS Medford, OR; NWS Pendleton, OR.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Blue Mountains; Willamette Valley; Cascades; Coast Range; Klamath Mountains/California High North Coast Range; Eastern Cascades Slopes and Foothills; Columbia Plateau; Northern Basin and Range.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Pennsylvania: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 67 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 5b to 7b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 12 to 28 F. July mean high: 77 to 89 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -35 F and 108 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS State College, PA; NWS Pittsburgh, PA; NWS Mount Holly, NJ; NWS Binghamton, NY; NWS Cleveland, OH.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Northern Piedmont; Western Allegheny Plateau; Ridge and Valley; Northern Allegheny Plateau; Central Appalachians; North Central Appalachians; Erie Drift Plain; Eastern Great Lakes Lowlands.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Rhode Island: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Rhode Island Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).

## At a glance

- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -23 F and 104 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Norton, MA.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Northeastern Coastal Zone.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). ## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for South Dakota: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** South Dakota Office of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 66 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4a to 5b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 0 to 18 F. July mean high: 80 to 90 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -58 F and 120 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Sioux Falls, SD; NWS Rapid City, SD; NWS Aberdeen, SD.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Northwestern Glaciated Plains; Northern Glaciated Plains; Northwestern Great Plains; Middle Rockies; Western Corn Belt Plains.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.title: Tennessee: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Tennessee: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Tennessee Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 95 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 7a to 8a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 22 to 32 F. July mean high: 80 to 91 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -29 F and 112 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Morristown, TN; NWS Nashville, TN; NWS Memphis, TN; NWS Huntsville, AL.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Ridge and Valley; Interior Plateau; Southeastern Plains; Southwestern Appalachians; Central Appalachians; Blue Ridge; Mississippi Valley Loess Plains; Mississippi Alluvial Plain.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Texas: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Texas Division of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 254 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6b to 10a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 18 to 52 F. July mean high: 85 to 99 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -23 F and 120 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Fort Worth, TX; NWS Midland/Odessa, TX; NWS Shreveport, LA; NWS Corpus Christi, TX; NWS Norman, OK; NWS Amarillo, TX; NWS Austin/San Antonio, TX; NWS Houston/Galveston, TX; NWS Lubbock, TX; NWS Brownsville, TX; NWS San Angelo, TX; NWS El Paso Tx/Santa Teresa, NM; NWS Lake Charles, LA.
- Ecoregions at county centres: South Central Plains; High Plains; Western Gulf Coastal Plain; Central Great Plains; Southern Texas Plains; East Central Texas Plains; Edwards Plateau; Cross Timbers; Texas Blackland Prairies; Southwestern Tablelands; Chihuahuan Deserts.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. A weather radio receives these transmitters with no power grid or internet. pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Utah: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Utah Division of Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 29 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4b to 7b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 4 to 28 F. July mean high: 72 to 96 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -43 F and 110 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Salt Lake City, UT; NWS Grand Junction, CO; NWS GJTSLC.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Central Basin and Range; Wasatch and Uinta Mountains; Colorado Plateaus; Wyoming Basin.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Vermont: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Vermont Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 14 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4b to 5b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: -1 to 11 F. July mean high: 75 to 82 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -44 F and 104 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Burlington, VT; NWS Albany, NY.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Eastern Great Lakes Lowlands; Northeastern Highlands.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

| NWS Albany, NY | 2 | 5a to 5b | 8 to 11 | 75 | -22 / 89 | 51 to 56.2 | 130 | May 14 to May 16 | Oct 2 to Oct 4 | 140 to 143 | 2.1 to 2.5 / 5 |

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Climate by county

One line per county, for a point near its centre. Elevation is in feet. Mountain counties can be much colder or wetter away from that point (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021) (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. ## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Washington: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Washington Emergency Management Division (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 39 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 6a to 9a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 16 to 37 F. July mean high: 68 to 90 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -48 F and 116 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Spokane, WA; NWS Pendleton, OR; NWS Seattle, WA; NWS Portland, OR.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Columbia Plateau; North Cascades; Coast Range; Willamette Valley; Cascades; Northern Rockies; Puget Lowland; Eastern Cascades Slopes and Foothills.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

Sun hours are peak sun hours: the average daily solar energy on a south-facing panel tilted at the local latitude, in kilowatt-hours per square metre (NASA POWER project, Climatology 2001-2025, 2026). A 100-watt panel makes roughly 100 watt-hours per peak sun hour before losses. → 09-05

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Wisconsin: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Wisconsin Emergency Management (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 72 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4a to 6a (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 0 to 16 F. July mean high: 73 to 85 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -54 F and 112 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS La Crosse, WI; NWS Duluth, MN; NWS Twin Cities/Chanhassen, MN; NWS Green Bay, WI; NWS Milwaukee/Sullivan, WI.
- Ecoregions at county centres: North Central Hardwood Forests; Northern Lakes and Forests; Southeastern Wisconsin Till Plains; Driftless Area; Central Corn Belt Plains; Western Corn Belt Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. pages.title: Wyoming: climate, hazards, weather radio
pages.body:
## What this page is for

This page holds the public reference data for Wyoming: climate by area and by county, the natural hazards FEMA rates for each county, the National Weather Service offices, the NOAA Weather Radio transmitters with the SAME codes to program into a weather radio, the state emergency management agency, and the ecoregions (natural regions) that decide which plants and trees you meet. Your own home county is filled into the subject pages automatically; use this page for any place you might have to go. How the numbers were made, and their limits, is on → 32-00.

## Who to call

- **Emergency:** 911.
- **State emergency management agency:** Wyoming Office of Homeland Security (FEMA, Emergency Management Agencies list, archived 2016, with later renames).
- **Poison control (anywhere in the US):** 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours, connects you to the local poison center (HRSA, Poison Help, 2026). → 12-17
- **Weather warnings without power or internet:** a NOAA Weather Radio set to the transmitter and SAME code below. → 15-01

## At a glance

- 23 counties.
- Hardiness zones: 4b to 5b (USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023).
- January mean low: 1 to 17 F. July mean high: 77 to 91 F (NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, 2021).
- Coldest and hottest on record at the stations used: -56 F and 112 F (NOAA Regional Climate Centers, Applied Climate Information System, station records through 2025).
- NWS forecast offices serving the counties: NWS Cheyenne, WY; NWS Riverton, WY; NWS Rapid City, SD; NWS Billings, MT; NWS Salt Lake City, UT.
- Ecoregions at county centres: Wyoming Basin; Northwestern Great Plains; Middle Rockies; High Plains.

## Climate by area

Areas follow the National Weather Service office that forecasts for each county (NOAA National Weather Service, AWIPS Counties and County Warning Areas, April 2026). Ranges run from the lowest to the highest county value in the area. Temperatures are 30-year averages; a hard winter or a heat wave goes well past them. Frost dates are the median: in half of years the last spring frost comes later than the date shown.

## Natural hazards

Ratings come from FEMA's National Risk Index (FEMA, National Risk Index, December 2025 release): 3 = High (FEMA "Very High" or "Relatively High"), 2 = Moderate ("Relatively Moderate"), 1 = Low (everything lower, including hazards FEMA does not expect here). They compare each county with every other county in the country, and they weigh how much there is to damage as well as how often the hazard strikes, so a thinly settled county can rate Low for a hazard that still happens there. Prepare for anything rated 2 or 3. → 17-01 → 17-02 → 17-03 → 17-04 → 17-05 → 17-07

cards.title: DC-01. An unvented heater running while people sleep

options.label: Never while anyone sleeps
options.summary: The heater is off and confirmed out before anyone sleeps. Warmth overnight comes from one small room, shared body heat, layers, sleeping bags and pre-warmed beds.

options.label: Lowest setting, alarm, vents, barrier, 3-hour wake
options.summary: Lowest safe setting; tested CO alarm at pillow height installed first; the manual's vents open; heater behind a barrier; one adult wakes every 3 hours to check flame and alarm; headache or nausea means everyone out.

options.label: Run it with alarms and vents
options.summary: The heater runs overnight with a tested CO alarm in the room and the manual's vents open, but no one is set to wake and check it.

cards.settings_summary: Portable propane and kerosene heaters sold for indoor use are 'unvented': their exhaust, including carbon monoxide (CO), stays in the room. Both common types' manuals say never run them while you sleep. CO has no smell; CDC says sleeping people can die before they feel any symptom, and children are affected first. Fire from bedding or a tipped heater is the second risk. What helps most: heater off while people sleep (removes the risk); a tested CO alarm at pillow height, the manual's vent openings, the lowest correct flame, a barrier, and an adult who wakes every 3 hours to check (reduces it a lot). The cost of 'never' is a cold night, which matters most for babies and frail elders in deep cold.

cards.title: DC-02. A propane cylinder larger than 1 lb inside the house

options.label: Never indoors
options.summary: Cylinders over 1 lb stay outdoors. If the hose-through-a-window route fails, use another heat source or the cold-night methods; the tank does not come in.

options.label: Last resort: cylinder outside, hose through a window
options.summary: The cylinder always stays outdoors. Only a heater rated for a remote cylinder is fed through the maker's hose, passed through a cracked window or door. The tank never comes inside.

options.label: Indoors with rules
options.summary: Only when the outdoor-hose route is impossible: an above-ground room, never a basement; valve closed whenever the heater is off; no pilot-light appliances nearby; leak test; CO alarm; adult awake; tank out as soon as possible.

cards.settings_summary: A 20-lb propane cylinder (the grill size) holds about twenty times the gas of a 1-lb camping cylinder. Heater makers and the national propane code keep anything over the 1-lb size out of the house. The reason: propane is heavier than air. A leak at the valve, hose or regulator flows along the floor, collects in low places such as basements, and explodes when it reaches a flame such as a pilot light or the heater itself. A cylinder warmed indoors can also vent gas through its safety valve on purpose. What helps most: tank outdoors (removes the risk); maker's hose through a window (reduces it a lot); if it must come in, above-ground room, valve closed when off, leak test, no pilot flames nearby, adult awake (reduces it a little).

cards.title: DC-03. Refilling 1-lb propane cylinders from a 20-lb tank

options.label: Never refill (the makers' position)
options.summary: Use only new, factory-filled 1-lb cylinders indoors and on camp gear. When they run out, use a 20-lb tank outdoors with the maker's hose, or another fuel.

options.label: Refill by weight, refillable-rated cylinders only
options.summary: Only cylinders built and stamped as refillable; never a disposable. Fill outdoors, away from flame, weighed on a scale to the stamped empty weight plus the rated content and no more; leak-test; retire any cylinder that hisses or has a stiff valve.

cards.settings_summary: The small green 1-lb propane cylinders sold for camp stoves and indoor heaters are made to be filled once at the factory. Adapters sold online let you refill them from a grill tank. Heater makers allow only factory-filled disposable cylinders indoors, and refillable cylinder makers say never refill a disposable. The real dangers are overfilling (a 1-lb cylinder has no overfill stop, so an overfilled one vents gas when it warms indoors) and a worn valve that leaks in the room. What helps most: buy new cylinders, or use a 20-lb tank outdoors with a hose (removes it); cylinders built to be refilled, filled outdoors by weight on a scale and leak-tested (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-04. Expired or heat-exposed epinephrine, and other expired medication

options.label: Discard at the printed date
options.summary: Expired, frozen-and-thawed or heat-damaged medication is replaced and not used. The household keeps enough in-date supply that it never faces the question.

options.label: Use if clear and colourless; keep seeking in-date stock
options.summary: When no in-date supply exists: in anaphylaxis, an expired or thawed epinephrine device whose liquid is clear and colourless is used at once. Intact tablets past date may be used. Liquids that changed are not. Keep looking for in-date stock.

cards.settings_summary: Every medicine has an expiry date: the date until which the maker guarantees full strength. Labels also give a storage range; epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPen type) should not freeze or get hot. After the date, or after freezing or heat, strength can drop slowly, and some liquids can change. In anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction), a weak dose is worse than a full one, but no dose can be fatal. Published studies found most expired auto-injectors still held most of their dose, and frozen-then-thawed ones delivered a normal dose. What helps most: keep enough in-date supply, rotated, at the right temperature (removes it); check the window for clear, colourless liquid (reduces it a lot). This card does not cover insulin: frozen insulin is always thrown away.

cards.title: DC-05. Storing gasoline, kerosene or propane in an attached garage

options.label: Outbuilding or outdoor locker only
options.summary: Gasoline and kerosene live in a detached shed or ventilated outdoor locker; propane cylinders outdoors, upright. Nothing in the attached garage or the house.

options.label: Attached garage with rules
options.summary: Approved, labelled cans, caps tight, as far from any heater, water heater or spark as the garage allows; never poured or transferred inside; propane cylinders never in the garage; a written quantity cap.

cards.settings_summary: Many households keep gas cans in the attached garage, next to the car, the lawn mower and often a water heater or furnace. The danger is not the liquid but its vapour. Gasoline vapour forms even in the cold, is heavier than air, flows along the floor and catches fire from a pilot light, igniter, spark or hot engine. A garage fire spreads into the house. Propane cylinders in a garage can vent gas when they warm. What helps most: fuel in a detached shed or outdoor locker (removes most of it); approved sealed cans, far from ignition sources, never opened inside, small quantity (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-06. Carrying fuel inside a passenger vehicle

options.label: Never inside: roof, hitch carrier or trailer only
options.summary: Fuel rides outside the passenger space: a roof rack, a hitch-mounted carrier, a pickup bed or an open trailer. If none is available, fuel stays behind and the route is planned on the tank.

options.label: Cargo area, sealed cans, shortest time
options.summary: Only when no outside carry exists: approved sealed cans, caps tight, upright and strapped in the rear cargo area, windows cracked, emptied into the tank at the first chance. Propane cylinders upright, valves closed.

cards.settings_summary: When a family has to drive a long way with no fuel stations working, extra gasoline in cans can be the difference between arriving and being stranded. Fuel safety guidance says it rides outside the passenger space. Inside a closed car, vapour from a can collects in the cabin, can make people sick, and can ignite from a spark. In a rear-end crash, a can behind the back seat can split and burn next to the passengers. Propane in a closed car can leak and pool on the floor. What helps most: carry fuel outside the cabin on a rack, hitch carrier or trailer (removes most of it); approved sealed full cans, strapped upright, windows cracked, shortest possible time (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-07. Converting a furnace or well pump to cord-and-plug yourself

options.label: Electrician only
options.summary: The cord-and-plug conversion of the furnace or well pump is done by a licensed electrician, now, while one is available. If none did it in time, the appliance stays hard-wired.

options.label: Do it ourselves with the write-up
options.summary: A competent adult converts it following the kit's write-up: that circuit's breaker off and tested dead; cord and plug rated for the circuit; strain relief; ground kept; labelled; tested on the generator before it is needed.

cards.settings_summary: A gas furnace needs electricity for its blower and controls, and a well needs it for the pump, so neither runs in an outage even with a generator. They are wired directly into the house, with no plug. A cord-and-plug conversion gives the appliance its own plug and turns its old supply into an outlet: normally it plugs into that outlet; in an outage you unplug it and plug it into the generator's cord. Nothing reaches the house panel, so it is not backfeeding. The risk is the wiring work itself: working on a live circuit, a missing ground, a loose connection, a plug or cord too small for the load, no strain relief. Those cause shock and fire, sometimes long after the work. What helps most: a licensed electrician now (removes most of it); the circuit's breaker off and tested dead, the written steps, correct parts, a test run before winter (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-08. Using insulin or other refrigerated medication after a heat excursion

options.label: Follow the published window exactly
options.summary: Insulin out of the fridge is used only inside the published room-temperature window (FDA emergency guidance: 59 to 86 °F for up to 28 days) or the product label; after that, or after heat above it, it is replaced.

options.label: Use beyond the window if nothing else; watch closely
options.summary: If no properly stored supply exists, heat-exposed or out-of-window insulin is used rather than none, with more frequent glucose checks and ketone checks, expecting it may work less well. Replaced as soon as possible.

cards.settings_summary: Insulin and some other medicines are stored in the fridge. Without power, FDA's emergency guidance says insulin can be kept at 59 to 86 °F for up to 28 days. Above that, or for longer, it slowly loses strength, and you cannot see the loss. Weaker insulin means higher blood sugar and, for type 1 diabetes, a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which can kill. But no insulin at all causes DKA for certain. FDA says that in an emergency you may still need to use insulin stored above 86 °F until proper supply returns. What helps most: keep it in the band with a powered fridge or cooler and a thermometer (removes it); evaporative pouches, cool spots, rotation (reduces it a lot). Frozen insulin is never used (floor).

cards.title: DC-09. An infant or toddler sharing a bed with adults for warmth

options.label: Own firm sleep surface beside the adults
options.summary: The child sleeps on a separate firm, flat surface (crib, play yard, firm mat on the floor) next to the adults in the warm room, dressed in layers and a sleep sack, checked by touch. Never in the adult bed.

options.label: Bed-share on cold nights, over 12 months only, with rules
options.summary: Only for a child over 12 months: firm mattress (on the floor if the bed is high), no pillows or heavy covers near the child, sleep sack instead, sober and unsedated adults, no older child beside them, nothing hot in the bed.

cards.settings_summary: In a cold house, sharing a bed keeps a small child warm with body heat. The American Academy of Pediatrics says babies under 1 year should sleep in the parents' room but on their own firm, flat surface, never in an adult bed, because about 3,500 US babies die each year from sleep-related causes, including suffocation in soft bedding and being lain on. The risk is highest under 4 months, with soft bedding, sofas, smoking, or an adult who has had alcohol or sedating medicine. Cold is a real risk too: CDC lists infants in cold bedrooms among those most at risk of hypothermia. What helps most: own firm surface next to the adults, warm room, layers and a sleep sack (removes most of it). Bed-sharing on this card is only offered for children over 12 months.

cards.title: DC-10. Pets when food, water or movement makes keeping them impossible

options.label: Keep them at all costs
options.summary: The pets stay with the household and share its food and water, and travel with it. Their needs are counted in every supply plan, and the household accepts going without to keep them.

options.label: Release with food and water left out
options.summary: If they cannot stay or come along, the pets are left or released with as much food and water as can be spared, a way in and out of shelter, and an ID tag, accepting that many will not survive.

options.label: A humane end, by the method page
options.summary: If the pets cannot be kept, carried or rehomed, a calm adult ends their lives humanely using only the method described on the pets page, not an improvised one, away from the children.

cards.settings_summary: Pets need food, water and room in the vehicle. In a long emergency a household may not be able to feed them, or may have to leave on foot or with no space. FEMA's advice while help exists is to plan to take your pets with you. When that is not possible, the choices are hard: keep them and share scarce food and water; release them, knowing most house pets do not survive long alone outdoors; or end their lives humanely, which the American Veterinary Medical Association says must be done by a method that causes no fear or pain. What helps most: plan pet food, water and carriers now, and find someone who could take them (removes most of it); decide in advance, calmly, so the decision is not made in panic.

cards.title: DC-11. Firing weapons on your own property for practice, pests or zeroing

options.label: Never on our property
options.summary: No shots fired on or from the property for practice, pests or sighting in. Practice is dry (unloaded) at home; pests are trapped; live fire happens only at a proper range or open land with a real backstop elsewhere.

options.label: Only into a known backstop, nobody downrange
options.summary: Shots only into an earth bank or backstop that will stop that ammunition, never toward a house, road or path, never at a target above the horizon, never at night, nobody downrange, neighbours told beforehand.

cards.settings_summary: In a long emergency, ranges close, and households may want to practise, sight in a rifle or deal with pests at home. Every firearms safety rule says be sure of your target and what is beyond it: a bullet that misses or passes through keeps going (NSSF: a .22 short bullet over 1 1/4 miles, a .30-06 more than 3 miles) and can ricochet off water, rock or frozen ground. In town, what is beyond is a neighbour's house. Shots also tell everyone nearby that the house is armed and occupied, and damage hearing. What helps most: no live fire at home, dry practice and traps instead (removes it); only into a solid earth backstop, never toward houses or roads, never at a target above the horizon, nobody downrange, neighbours told (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-12. Defensive use of force: our household rule

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults read this page together and write the household's use-of-force rule in their own words on the worksheet, sign and date it, and rehearse it.

cards.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. Every household that keeps any means of defence, firearm or not, needs a rule written in calm advance about when force may be used against another person. Without courts or police, nobody else will draw that line. The traditional tests are: the threat is happening now; nothing less will stop it; the force matches the threat; and a calm person would see it the same way. Mistakes cannot be undone: a bullet passes through walls into neighbours' homes, people are shot by family members who misidentified them in the dark, and with no surgeon any wound may be fatal. The neighbourhood remembers. Read the page, then write the rule in your own words on the worksheet.

cards.title: DC-13. Drinking water from a pool, hot tub or untreated surface source

options.label: Distil before drinking
options.summary: Water from a pool, hot tub or untreated stream, pond or lake is drunk only after distilling (boil it and collect the steam). Undistilled, it is used for flushing, washing and cleaning only.

options.label: Fresh pools: filter and chlorinate
options.summary: A freshwater (not salt) pool known to hold no algaecide or other additive may be drunk after settling, filtering and disinfecting by the published method. Salt pools and hot tubs still need distilling; surface water still needs distilling.

options.label: Surface water through the treatment ladder
options.summary: Streams, ponds and lakes away from obvious fuel, chemical or farm runoff are drunk after the full ladder: settle, filter, then boil or disinfect by the published method. Fresh pools as in the option above; salt pools and hot tubs are still distilled.

cards.settings_summary: A swimming pool or a nearby stream can look like a large water supply. Germs in water (bacteria, viruses, parasites) are killed by boiling, and most by chlorine used as CDC and EPA describe. Chemicals are not. Pool water holds chlorine, stabilizer, often algaecide, and in a salt pool, salt that no boiling or filter removes. Hot tubs hold bromine and body oils. Streams and ponds can carry fuel, farm or industrial runoff. CDC says water containing fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfecting. FEMA and the Red Cross say not to drink from pools or spas. Distillation (boil and catch the steam) removes salt and most chemicals, but it is slow and uses fuel. What helps most: pool and hot-tub water for flushing and washing, stored water for drinking (removes most of it); distil what you drink from them (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-14. Food past its date, dented or rusted cans, or food from a failed freezer

options.label: Follow the label and the published rules strictly
options.summary: Food past its printed date is discarded, even though USDA treats most dates as quality dates; any dented, rusted or swollen can is discarded; perishable food above 40 °F for 2 hours or more is discarded, as USDA advises.

options.label: Inspect and eat, with the rules for each case
options.summary: Shelf-stable food past its quality date is eaten if the package is intact and it looks and smells normal; cans with a small dent and sound seams are eaten; thawed food still holding ice crystals or at 40 °F or below is cooked or refrozen; bulging, leaking or spurting cans are still discarded.

cards.settings_summary: In a long emergency a household will have food past its printed date, dented or rusty cans, and fridges and freezers that have warmed. USDA says dates mark quality, not safety, except on infant formula, and its chart gives canned food 12 months to 5 years on the shelf. The dangers are a can whose seal has failed, which can carry botulism, a toxin that paralyses and does not show by look or smell, and perishable food held warm, which grows bacteria that cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea. USDA says discard perishables above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. What helps most: rotate stock and check fridge and freezer with a thermometer (removes much of it); inspect every can and package, discard any bulging, leaking or spurting can (floor), and cook thoroughly (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-15. Giving someone else's prescription medication

options.label: Never
options.summary: Each prescription medicine is taken only by the person it was prescribed for. If someone runs out, the household looks for a clinician, pharmacy or the same prescription elsewhere.

options.label: Same drug and strength, already prescribed to them
options.summary: Only when the person was already prescribed the same drug at the same strength and has run out: they take it as their own label said, after checking allergies and their other medicines. Never a new drug for a new problem; never to a child from an adult's supply.

cards.settings_summary: When pharmacies close, one person may run out of a medicine that someone else in the house or the neighbourhood still has. Prescriptions are written for one person because the right drug and dose depend on the illness, allergies, other medicines, kidney and liver function, weight and age. Shared medicine can cause an allergic reaction, a dangerous interaction, a dose far too strong (for example a painkiller or sleeping medicine that stops the breathing of someone not used to it), or the wrong insulin causing severe low blood sugar. What helps most: get each person's own supply and a written plan from their clinician now (removes most of it); share only the same drug at the same strength the person already takes, after an allergy and interaction check (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-16. Antibiotics without a prescription (stockpiled or veterinary)

options.label: Never without a clinician
options.summary: Antibiotics are taken only when a clinician prescribed them for that person and that illness, or wrote a plan in advance. No stockpiled, shared, veterinary or aquarium antibiotics are used on a guess.

options.label: Last resort for adults, with the infection page
options.summary: Only for an adult showing the signs of a spreading or serious bacterial infection on the infection page, with no clinician reachable: a human antibiotic, with the drug and dose taken from a clinician's written plan or a published adult table printed as published. Never for children.

cards.settings_summary: Before antibiotics, ordinary wounds and infections killed healthy adults, so many preppers stockpile them, sometimes as fish or farm-animal products. Antibiotics are prescription drugs because the right one depends on the infection, the person's allergies and other medicines, and the dose depends on weight and kidney function. Most coughs, colds and stomach bugs are viral, and antibiotics do nothing for them. The wrong antibiotic can cause a severe allergic reaction or severe diarrhoea, hide a worsening infection, and breed resistant bacteria. Products sold for animals are not made or checked for human use. What helps most: ask a clinician now for a written plan and supply (removes most of it); use only for adults with clear signs of a serious bacterial infection, by a written or published adult table, never for children (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-17. Old kerosene, diesel or gasoline in a heater or engine

options.label: Fresh fuel only, on a rotation schedule
options.summary: Every can is dated. Gasoline is stabilised when bought and rotated into vehicles on a schedule; kerosene and diesel are used and replaced on a schedule. Fuel past the household's age limit is not burned in heaters or the generator.

options.label: Jar-test old fuel and use it if it passes
options.summary: Old fuel may be used if a sample in a clear jar, left to stand, is clear and bright with no water layer, cloudiness, sludge or colour change, and it smells like the right fuel. Any doubt, or an unlabelled can, and it is not used.

cards.settings_summary: Fuel ages. Gasoline loses the parts that help it start, can absorb water and leaves gum that blocks small-engine carburettors. Kerosene and diesel take up water from the air in part-full cans and can grow sludge. One common wick-heater maker says never use kerosene stored from one season to the next. The real danger is in heaters: old or wet kerosene fouls the wick, so the flame burns badly and makes more smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) indoors. Old gasoline in a generator mostly means it will not start when needed. What helps most: date, stabilise and rotate (removes most of it); store full, sealed, cool and dark, and jar-test before every fill (reduces it a lot). An unlabelled or unknown can is never poured.

cards.title: DC-18. Feeding a food-allergic person unlabeled, traded or scavenged food

options.label: Never: only food with a full, readable label
options.summary: The allergic person eats only food whose full ingredient label has been read, or food the household made itself from labelled ingredients in a clean kitchen. No traded, donated, scavenged or foraged food, ever.

options.label: Single-ingredient foods only
options.summary: Unlabelled or traded food is allowed only if it is one plain, recognisable ingredient (whole rice, dry beans, a whole vegetable or fruit, a whole cut of meat) that is not on the person's allergen list, washed and cooked in the household's own clean pots.

options.label: With epinephrine in hand, by our own line
options.summary: Unlabelled food may be tried by the household's own written line, only with in-date epinephrine in hand, an adult who knows the plan watching, the first taste small, and never alone or at night.

cards.settings_summary: When stores close, food arrives without labels: bartered, donated, scavenged, repackaged or foraged. For a person with a food allergy, a label is how you find the hidden egg, peanut, milk, sesame or soy. US law requires the nine major allergens to be declared on packaged food, but only while labels exist. Without one, a trace of the allergen, or a pot or spoon that touched it, can cause anaphylaxis: throat swelling, trouble breathing, collapse, death within minutes to hours without epinephrine. With no ambulance, epinephrine is the only treatment, and a reaction can need more than one dose. What helps most: a deep stock of verified safe food and kept labels (removes most of it); single-ingredient foods cooked in the household's own pots (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-19. When to leave home: our triggers

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults fill in the trigger table on this page with their own thresholds and destinations, agree it, sign and date it, and review it each year.

cards.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. Leaving home is the highest-stakes decision a household makes in a long emergency, and the one most often made badly: too late, in a panic, in bad weather, with children. Staying in a stocked, known home is usually safer than moving. Leaving into a storm or extreme cold kills people every winter, and the Red Cross and National Weather Service both say avoid travel in winter storms unless you must. But staying past the point where medicine, heat, water or safety runs out forces a move in the worst condition. The answer is thresholds written now, while calm, that turn a 3 a.m. judgement into a checklist. Fill in the trigger table on the page.

cards.title: DC-20. Open-flame cooking, candles or oil lamps indoors

options.label: No open flame indoors
options.summary: Light comes from flashlights, headlamps and battery lanterns; cooking happens outdoors or on electric appliances run from stored power. No candles, oil lamps or flame cooking inside.

options.label: Indoors with extinguisher, alarms and rules
options.summary: Candles, oil lamps or stove-top flame cooking are allowed only with working smoke and CO alarms, an extinguisher within reach, 12 inches clear all round, an adult in the room, never where anyone sleeps, out when the room is left.

cards.settings_summary: In an outage, candles, oil lamps and cooking on a match-lit gas stove are the oldest answers to dark and cold food. US Fire Administration advice is to use flashlights, not candles, in a power outage, because candles cause many home fires, often when they are left burning, placed too close to something that burns, or reached by children or pets. Any flame indoors also adds carbon monoxide and uses oxygen, and CDC says never use a gas stove or oven to heat a home. Lamp oil and kerosene are poisonous if a child swallows them. What helps most: battery lights and outdoor cooking (removes it); working smoke and CO alarms, an extinguisher in reach, an adult present, nothing within 12 inches, never in sleeping areas (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-21. Using a fireplace or wood stove that has not been inspected this year

options.label: Inspect first, using the chimney page
options.summary: No fire until the household has done the inspection on the chimney page (cold flue, light and mirror, scrape test, cap and blockages) or a professional has. A flue with glaze, cracks or a blockage is not used until fixed.

options.label: Use it with small hot fires and a watch
options.summary: If it cannot be inspected now: small, hot fires of dry wood only, never smouldering overnight, CO and smoke alarms in the room, an extinguisher in reach, someone checking the chimney and attic, and an inspection at the first chance.

cards.settings_summary: A fireplace or wood stove can heat a house with no power, but the chimney is part of the appliance. Wood smoke leaves a tar called creosote on the inside of the chimney; it builds up faster with damp wood and slow, smoky fires, and it burns. A chimney fire can crack the chimney and set the house alight. A chimney blocked by a nest, leaves or fallen brick sends smoke and carbon monoxide back into the room. The national fire code for chimneys (NFPA 211) and chimney safety groups say inspect at least once a year. What helps most: inspect first, by a professional or with the household's own light-and-mirror check (removes most of it); dry wood, small hot fires, alarms, an extinguisher and a watch on the chimney (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-22. Potassium iodide for adults over 40

options.label: Follow FDA: over 40 only at very large exposure
options.summary: Adults over 40 take potassium iodide only if officials say a very large dose of radioactive iodine is expected, as FDA advises. Everyone younger follows the FDA table on the potassium iodide page, on official direction.

options.label: Adults over 40 take it whenever others do
options.summary: When officials direct potassium iodide for the area, adults over 40 in the household take the FDA adult dose too, after checking the FDA list of people who should not take it, accepting a higher chance of side effects.

cards.settings_summary: Potassium iodide (KI) is a tablet that fills the thyroid gland with ordinary iodine so it does not absorb radioactive iodine released by a nuclear accident or bomb. It protects only the thyroid, only from radioactive iodine, and only when taken on official direction. FDA's guidance says adults over 40 have the lowest risk of thyroid cancer from radioactive iodine and a higher chance of side effects from KI (thyroid problems and allergic reactions), so they should take it only if a very large exposure is expected. Sheltering indoors protects far more than KI does. What helps most: shelter first; know who should not take it; decide now with a clinician; take it only when officials say so.

cards.title: DC-23. Chlorinating very dirty water beyond the published dose

options.label: Clear it first, then the published dose
options.summary: Very dirty water is settled and filtered until it is as clear as possible, then disinfected at the published dose (doubled only if it is still cloudy, coloured or very cold, as CDC and EPA say), with the full wait.

options.label: Heavy dose and a longer wait when it cannot be cleared
options.summary: When the water cannot be settled or filtered, it gets the doubled published dose, a longer wait, and a smell check; if no chlorine smell, dose again and wait again. The household accepts strong taste and that some germs may survive.

cards.settings_summary: Household bleach and dissolved pool shock kill most germs in water at the dose CDC and EPA publish, and they say to double that dose for cloudy, coloured or very cold water. Very dirty water is the problem: mud and plant matter use up the chlorine and hide germs inside particles, so even a big dose may not disinfect it, and a parasite called Cryptosporidium survives ordinary chlorine anyway. Pouring in much more chlorine than published mostly makes water taste and smell harsh and can upset stomachs; mistakes with concentrated pool shock are dangerous. What helps most: settle and filter first, then the published dose (reduces it a lot); boiling clear water instead (removes most germ risk). Never mix chlorine with other cleaners (floor).

cards.title: DC-24. Children doing dangerous jobs because hands are short

options.label: Write our own rule
options.summary: The adults fill in the job table on this page with the age, training and supervision each child needs for each dangerous job, agree it, sign and date it, and review it on each child's birthday.

cards.settings_summary: This card has no multiple choice. In a long emergency there is more work than adults to do it, and children want and need real jobs. But fire, fuel, cutting tools, chainsaws, large animals and open water injure and kill children every year on farms, where the same jobs are done. The US farm-safety programme at NIOSH matches each job to a child's age, size, strength and judgement, and stresses training and adult supervision. The answer is a rule written in advance: for each job, the age to start learning, the training, the supervision, and the habit a child must show before doing it alone. Fill in the table on the page. Locked storage of firearms, fuel, medicines and chlorine stays a floor.

cards.title: DC-25. Converting a tourniquet to a pressure dressing when no help will ever come

options.label: Never loosen: keep it on and accept the limb may be lost
options.summary: Once a tourniquet is on, it stays on, even when no help will ever come. The household accepts that the arm or leg below it may die and be lost, in exchange for never risking the bleeding starting again.

options.label: Convert by the published prolonged-care criteria
options.summary: If no help will ever come, a trained household member converts the tourniquet to packing and a pressure bandage only if every published criterion is met: not in shock, wound watched closely, not an amputation, ideally within 2 hours, never after 6, tourniquet left loose in place.

cards.settings_summary: A tourniquet is a tight band that stops blood flow to a bleeding arm or leg. The rule is never loosen it, because the bleeding can start again and kill. That rule assumes a hospital takes over within hours. If no help will ever come, an arm or leg left without blood for many hours dies. Military prolonged-care guidance (TCCC, 2026) lets medics convert a tourniquet to wound packing and a pressure bandage only if the person is not in shock, the wound can be watched closely and it is not an amputation, ideally within 2 hours, and not after 6 hours without laboratory monitoring. People without that training are told to leave it on. What helps most: reaching care (removes the question); hands-on training, hemostatic gauze and pressure bandages (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-26. Holding the allergy-safe food in reserve for the allergic person

options.label: Share everything: all safe food is eaten by everyone
options.summary: Food that is safe for the allergic person is part of the household's general stock and is eaten by everyone, in the normal order. The household plans one menu that suits all, for as long as it lasts.

options.label: Reserve it: everyone else eats other stock first
options.summary: Food verified safe for the allergic person is set aside as that person's reserve. Everyone else eats the food the allergic person cannot eat first, and the safe stock is used by others only when nothing else is left.

cards.settings_summary: When someone has a food allergy, only part of the stockpile is safe for them: food whose label has been read and checked against their allergens. Everyone else can eat almost anything. If the whole household eats the safe food in the normal order, it runs out first for the one person who has no other choice, and the pressure to give them doubtful food grows every day. A reaction with no ambulance may need more than one dose of epinephrine. Keeping the safe food as their reserve stretches it, but the others eat less-liked food first, which can feel unfair and can be hard to keep to. What helps most: stocking enough safe food for everyone (removes most of the question); tracking the safe food's own runway (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-27. Water-glassing fresh eggs (storing them in lime water)

options.label: Do not water-glass: follow the Extension position
options.summary: Eggs are refrigerated, frozen out of the shell, or cooked and dried. No eggs are stored in lime water. When cold storage fails, eggs are eaten fresh or not kept.

options.label: Water-glass with rules
options.summary: Only clean, unwashed, uncracked fresh eggs, in food-grade pickling lime solution, in a sealed container kept as cool as possible. Every egg is checked before use; any cracked, floating or off egg is discarded; every egg is cooked until yolk and white are firm; none go to anyone allergic to egg.

cards.settings_summary: Water-glassing is an old way of keeping fresh eggs without a fridge: unwashed eggs sit in a bucket of pickling lime and water for months. University Extension services say do not do it. The germ Salmonella can be inside an egg before it is laid, the shell lets water and germs through, and a basement or pantry is not cold enough to stop them growing. Salmonella causes diarrhoea, fever, cramps and vomiting; for children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weak immune systems it can be severe, and with no hospital that matters more. The alternative may be no eggs through a winter. What helps most: freezing eggs out of the shell or drying cooked egg (removes it); cooking every stored egg until firm and checking each one (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-28. Relighting gas appliance pilots yourself when the gas company will not come

options.label: Utility only: wait for the gas company or a technician
options.summary: Once the gas is shut off or a pilot goes out, the household does not turn the gas back on or relight anything itself. It waits for the gas utility, the propane supplier or a qualified technician, however long that takes, and heats and cooks by other means meanwhile.

options.label: Relight ourselves, with rules
options.summary: Only when no one qualified will come: every appliance valve closed before gas is restored, no gas smell anywhere (floor level too), nothing that has been under water, each appliance relit one at a time by its own lighting label, a working CO alarm, gas off at once if a smell returns.

cards.settings_summary: Gas appliances such as water heaters, furnaces and some stoves have a pilot: a small flame that lights the main burner. When the gas is shut off or runs out, every pilot goes out. FEMA says that once gas is turned off, only a qualified professional should turn it back on, and propane safety guidance strongly recommends that only a technician relight a pilot. The danger is gas that has leaked or pooled: propane is heavier than air and settles at the floor, and a flame or spark sets it off. A damaged appliance can also make carbon monoxide. With no gas company coming, waiting may mean no hot water, no furnace, no stove. What helps most: a technician or the utility does it (removes it); every appliance valve closed first, the appliance's own lighting label followed exactly, and a CO alarm (reduces it a lot).

cards.title: DC-29. One traction attempt on a fractured limb with no pulse below it, when no care is coming

options.label: Splint as found: never pull on a broken limb
options.summary: A broken arm or leg is always splinted in the position found, even when the hand or foot beyond it has no pulse and no care is coming. The household accepts that the limb may be lost rather than risk making the injury worse.

options.label: One gentle traction attempt, then splint
options.summary: Only for a deformed broken arm or leg whose hand or foot is pale or blue, cold and pulseless, with no trained help reachable: one gentle, steady pull along the limb toward its normal line, then re-check the pulse and splint. Never on the spine, hip or pelvis, or a break with bone showing.

cards.settings_summary: A badly broken arm or leg can cut off the blood flowing past the break to the hand or foot. It turns pale or blue, cold and numb, with no pulse. First-aid teaching says splint a break as you find it and do not straighten it, because moving it hurts and can do more damage. The same published first-aid guidance makes one exception: if circulation is poor and no trained person is quickly available, try to bring the limb back toward its normal position, which reduces damage from lack of blood. Wilderness first-aid standards teach gentle traction for this. Not doing it may cost the limb; doing it may cause pain and further injury. What helps most: reaching care (removes the question); hands-on wilderness training (reduces it a lot).
