Read by R15 on 2026-11-16: keeps insulin within 18-26 C (64.4-78.8 F) for 45 hours minimum even at a constant 37.8 C (100 F); re-immerse every 45 hours or sooner if crystals can be felt; soak times by size (Mini 2-3 min to Extra Large 15-19 min), strictly timed because over-soaking renders the wallet unusable until it dries; drain 15-30 minutes and towel dry; not in an airtight or waterproof container; not in a refrigerator or freezer; insulin must be at the maker's recommended temperature before it goes in; drying out takes 2-4 weeks; no washing machine or tumble dryer; with age soak time increases; replace when crystals fail to expand.

who-maternal-mortality-fact-sheet-r15.title: Maternal mortality (fact sheet)
who-maternal-mortality-fact-sheet-r15.licence_note: Copyright WHO. Read by R15 on 2026-11-16: the major complications that account for around 75% of maternal deaths are severe bleeding (mostly after childbirth), infections (usually after childbirth), high blood pressure in pregnancy (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia), complications from delivery and unsafe abortion; severe bleeding after birth can kill a healthy woman within hours if she is unattended.

usda-fsis-shelf-stable-food-safety-2014-.title: Shelf-Stable Food Safety (Food Safety Information fact sheet, updated August 2014)
usda-fsis-shelf-stable-food-safety-2014-.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), via GovInfo
usda-fsis-shelf-stable-food-safety-2014-.licence_note: US federal government work; FSIS encourages reprint (the PhotoDisc cover image is excluded). Read 2026-11-16 by R17 (GovInfo copy; fsis.usda.gov refuses automated fetch): dating is for quality, not safety, except infant formula; discard deeply dented cans (a dent you can lay a finger into) and any deep dent on a seam; small dent otherwise sound is safe; discard heavily rusted cans; discard swollen frozen cans and frozen cans thawed at 40 F or higher; below 85 F best, over 100 F harmful; chart: low-acid canned goods 2 to 5 years, high-acid 12 to 18 months; botulism warnings: leaking, bulging or badly dented cans, cracked jars, loose or bulging lids, foul odour, spurting.

cdc-botulism-home-canned-foods-r17.title: Home-Canned Foods (Botulism: Prevention)
cdc-botulism-home-canned-foods-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17 via the fetch tool (curl gets 403): when in doubt, throw it out: container leaking, bulging or swollen; looks damaged, cracked or abnormal; spurts liquid or foam when opened; food discoloured, mouldy or smells bad. At altitudes below 1,000 feet, boil foods for 10 minutes; add 1 minute for each additional 1,000 feet.

cdc-botulism-signs-symptoms-r17.title: Botulism: Signs and Symptoms
cdc-botulism-signs-symptoms-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17 via the fetch tool: difficulty swallowing, muscle weakness, double vision, drooping eyelids, blurry vision, slurred speech, difficulty breathing, difficulty moving the eyes.

cdc-antibiotic-dos-and-donts-r17.title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts
cdc-antibiotic-dos-and-donts-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17 via the fetch tool: take antibiotics only when you need them; antibiotics do not work on viruses (colds, flu); do not share your antibiotics; do not take antibiotics prescribed for someone else; side effects include C. diff diarrhoea and severe allergic reactions; use contributes to resistance.

niosh-nagcat-effectiveness-2011-r17.title: Guidelines for Children's Agricultural Tasks Demonstrate Effectiveness (NIOSH Publication 2011-129, March 2011)
niosh-nagcat-effectiveness-2011-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17 on archive.cdc.gov via the fetch tool (live cdc.gov copy 404/403): NAGCAT, built on child-development principles, matched a child's physical, mental and psychosocial abilities with the requirements of specific farm work, to help parents assign farm work appropriately.

osha-3269-chainsaw-safety-quickcard-r17.title: Chainsaw Safety QuickCard (OSHA 3269)
osha-3269-chainsaw-safety-quickcard-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17: proper personal protective equipment must be worn when operating the saw: hand, foot, leg, eye, face, hearing and head protection. osha-3080-hand-and-power-tools-r17.title: Hand and Power Tools (OSHA 3080, 2002 revised)
osha-3080-hand-and-power-tools-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17: employees should be trained in the proper use of all tools; appropriate personal protective equipment such as safety goggles and gloves.

fda-ki-guidance-2001-r17.title: Guidance: Potassium Iodide as a Thyroid Blocking Agent in Radiation Emergencies (December 2001), PDF
fda-ki-guidance-2001-r17.licence_note: US federal government work. Read 2026-11-16 by R17 (the archived copy of us-fda-potassium-iodide-as-a-thyroid-blocking-agent-fcadee holds no text): adults over 40 need take KI only in the case of a projected large internal radiation dose to the thyroid (>500 cGy) to prevent hypothyroidism; iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis is more common in older people and in iodine-deficient areas but usually requires repeated doses.

water-hemlock.note: Every part, most of all the root, contains cicutoxin. A 2 to 3 cm piece of root can kill an adult (CDC MMWR, 1994). Nausea and stomach pain start within 15 to 90 minutes; in severe poisoning, seizures follow (CDC MMWR, 1994). Sap can be absorbed through skin. Where: Wet ground in every lower-48 state.

fig-backfeed-path.caption: Backfeeding: generator power pushed into an outlet flows out through the panel and meter to the pole transformer, which raises it to the street line's voltage and kills a line worker who believes the line is dead. The safe path: an inlet and a transfer switch or interlock, with the main breaker off.
fig-backfeed-path.alt: Two house cutaways with the service wires, the meter, the panel, a pole transformer and a line worker on the next pole. Top, crossed out: a generator outside with a cord that has two male ends pushed into a wall outlet; red arrows run from the outlet to the panel, out through the meter and the service wires to the transformer and along the street line to the worker. Bottom, ticked: the generator cord goes to an outdoor inlet and a transfer switch or interlock; the main breaker is off and nothing reaches the street.

fig-cal-hypo-two-step.caption: Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), the EPA two-step method: 1, one heaping teaspoon (about 1/4 oz) of granules into 2 gallons of water makes the stock, labelled DO NOT DRINK; 2, one part stock to 100 parts water (1 pint per 12.5 gallons), stir, wait 30 minutes, expect a slight chlorine smell.
fig-cal-hypo-two-step.alt: Step 1: a heaping teaspoon of granules going into a 2-gallon bucket of water, the bucket labelled CHLORINE STOCK: DO NOT DRINK. Step 2: a pint of stock poured into 12.5 gallons of water, with the equivalents per gallon and per 5 gallons, a 30-minute clock, and a check for a slight chlorine smell. A label panel shows 65 to 73 percent calcium hypochlorite with no algaecides, clarifiers or stabilizers.

fig-choking-child-adult.caption: Choking, age 1 to adult: bend them forward and give five back blows between the shoulder blades, then five abdominal thrusts from behind, fist just above the navel, in and up. Kneel behind a small child. Pregnant or too big to reach round: chest thrusts.
fig-choking-child-adult.alt: Three panels. Left: a standing person bent forward at the waist, a rescuer beside them supporting the chest with one arm and striking between the shoulder blades with the heel of the other hand, marked 5 back blows. Middle: the rescuer standing behind with arms around, a fist just above the navel, arrow in and up, marked 5 abdominal thrusts. Right: the rescuer kneeling behind a small child doing the same.

fig-choking-infant.caption: Choking infant under 1: five firm back blows with the baby face-down along your forearm, head lower than chest, jaw supported; then turn face-up for five chest thrusts with two fingers just below the nipple line. Never abdominal thrusts under 1.
fig-choking-infant.alt: Two panels. Left: a seated adult rests a forearm on the thigh with the infant lying face-down along it, head lower than the chest and the jaw held in the hand; the other hand strikes between the shoulder blades, marked 5 back blows. Right: the infant face-up along the forearm, head lower, with two fingers on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, marked 5 chest thrusts.

fig-co-alarm-placement.caption: Carbon monoxide alarms: one on every level and one outside each sleeping area; in the warm room, on the wall opposite the heater at pillow height. Never above the heater, in a ceiling corner, beside a window, door, vent or fan, or in a bathroom.

Red crossed-out alarms: directly above the heater, in the corner where wall meets ceiling, beside the cracked window, and in the bathroom.

fig-cord-and-plug-conversion.caption: Cord-and-plug conversion (DC-07): the furnace gets its own plug. Normal: it plugs into the receptacle where its old house circuit now ends. Outage: main breaker off and locked, furnace unplugged from the wall and plugged into the generator cord, which has one male and one female end.
fig-cord-and-plug-conversion.alt: Two rows. Normal: the panel with breakers on feeds a wall receptacle; the furnace cord and plug are plugged into it; plug and receptacle are labelled. Outage: the main breaker is off with a lock; the wall receptacle is empty; the furnace plug goes into the female end of an extension cord whose male end is in the generator outdoors. A red note says never a cord with two male ends and never into house wiring.

fig-fallout-decay-7-10.caption: The 7-10 rule (HHS REMM): fallout radiation falls about tenfold for every sevenfold increase in time. 1 hour: the starting level; 7 hours: about 1/10; 2 days: about 1/100; 2 weeks: about 1/1,000.
fig-fallout-decay-7-10.alt: Four bars on a logarithmic scale. 1 hour after the explosion, a full bar labelled the starting level; 7 hours, a bar one step lower labelled about 1/10; 2 days (49 hours), another step lower, about 1/100; 2 weeks, the lowest, about 1/1,000.

fig-generator-connection-options.caption: Five ways a generator can reach something in the house. Four are allowed with the right person doing the work; backfeeding through an outlet is never allowed.
fig-generator-connection-options.alt: Five rows, each with a generator outdoors on the left and the house wall: (a) an extension cord to one appliance, always allowed; (b) a cord to an inlet on the wall and a transfer switch beside the panel, licensed electrician; (c) a cord to an inlet and an interlock plate on the panel so the main breaker and the generator breaker are never on together, licensed electrician; (d) a furnace unplugged from its wall receptacle and plugged into the generator cord, a cord-and-plug conversion, decision card DC-07; (e) a cord with two male ends pushed into a wall outlet, crossed out in red: backfeed, never.

fig-generator-distance.caption: Where the generator runs: outdoors, 20 feet or more from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away from every house, never in a garage or under a deck or overhang.
fig-generator-distance.alt: Plan view from above. A house with windows, a door and a vent, an attached garage and a deck. Inside the garage and under the deck a generator is crossed out in red. Out in the yard a generator sits 20 feet or more from the nearest window, its exhaust arrow pointing away from the house and away from the neighbour's house. A checklist below repeats the rules and says to keep battery carbon monoxide alarms on inside.

fig-jar-headspace-and-seal.caption: Canning jar: headspace is the empty space between the food and the lid, set by the recipe. Sealed: the lid is pulled down (concave) and does not flex. Unsealed: fridge and eat now, or reprocess with a new lid. Bulging lid: throw away without tasting.
fig-jar-headspace-and-seal.alt: Left: cross-section of a canning jar with band and flat lid, the food level, and the headspace between food and lid marked as the recipe says. Right, three lids side by side: sealed, dipped in the centre, ticked; unsealed, flexing up and down when pressed, marked fridge and eat now or reprocess; bulging, domed up, crossed out and marked throw away, do not taste.

fig-knot-bowline.caption: Bowline in four steps: the small loop, the working end up through it, around behind the standing part, back down the loop, tightened. The tail finishes inside the big loop.
fig-knot-bowline.alt: Four photographs of a rope on a table: 1, a small loop made in the standing part with the working end lying beside it; 2, the working end passed up through the small loop; 3, the end taken around behind the standing part; 4, the finished bowline with a fixed loop.
fig-knot-bowline.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-31 (printed page 257). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-clove-hitch.caption: Clove hitch. Top row: tied in the hand as two loops laid one over the other and dropped over a post or clip. Bottom row: tied around a pole, two wraps side by side with the crossing pinned between them.
fig-knot-clove-hitch.alt: Six photographs. Top: two loops in a rope, the loops overlapped, then dropped over a carabiner and pulled snug. Bottom: a rope wrapped around a green pole, crossed over itself, and tucked under the second wrap to form a clove hitch.
fig-knot-clove-hitch.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-36 (printed page 261). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-overhand.caption: Overhand knot: a loop, the working end pushed through from behind, both ends pulled.
fig-knot-overhand.alt: Photograph of a red and black rope tied in a single overhand knot on a wooden table.
fig-knot-overhand.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-25 (printed page 253). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-parts-of-a-rope.caption: The words used in every knot step: working end, standing part, bight, loop.
fig-knot-parts-of-a-rope.alt: One rope drawn across the frame. The short free end on the right is labelled working end; the long rest on the left is labelled standing part. Below, a U-shaped fold with no crossing is labelled bight, and a circle where the rope crosses itself is labelled loop.

fig-knot-prusik.caption: Prusik: a closed loop of thinner cord wrapped three times around a thicker rope. It slides when you push the wraps and grips when the loop is pulled. Not for holding a person.
fig-knot-prusik.alt: A thick horizontal ridge line. A closed loop of thin cord is passed around it three times, each wrap inside the last, so three neat turns sit side by side; the loop hangs down below with an arrow showing the pull that makes it grip.

fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches.caption: Round turn and two half hitches: two turns around the pole, then two half hitches around the standing part, slid down against the pole.
fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches.alt: Three photographs of a rope tied to a green pole: the round turn, the first half hitch around the standing part, and the finished knot with two half hitches.
fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-37 (printed page 261). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-sheet-bend.caption: Sheet bend: a bight in the thicker rope, the thin end up through it, around behind both legs, tucked under itself. Both short ends finish on the same side.
fig-knot-sheet-bend.alt: Three photographs: a white thick rope folded into a U with a thinner red rope coming up through it, the red rope wrapped behind the U, and the finished sheet bend.
fig-knot-sheet-bend.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-29 (printed page 256). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-square-knot.caption: Square knot: right over left, then left over right; each rope's two strands leave the knot on the same side and it lies flat. Below, crossed out: the granny knot, which slips.
fig-knot-square-knot.alt: Top: three photographs of a red rope and a blue rope tied into a square knot step by step. Bottom: two photographs of a granny knot, crossed out in red with the words granny knot slips, untie and start again.
fig-knot-square-knot.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-27 and 15-28 (granny knot panels) (printed page 255). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work). Titles and red cross added by GoettschePreppy.

The working end makes wraps 1 and 2 around the standing part inside the big loop, then wrap 3 on the tarp side outside the loop, and is tucked under that last wrap. fig-knot-truckers-hitch.caption: Trucker's hitch: far end tied off, a pulley loop in the standing part, the working end around the anchor and back up through the loop, pulled tight, locked with two half hitches.
fig-knot-truckers-hitch.alt: Side view of a load on a trailer bed. The rope is tied to a fixed point on the far side, runs over the load and down toward the anchor hook. About two feet above the anchor a hanging loop is formed in the standing part. The working end goes down around the anchor, back up through the loop, and is pulled down; two half hitches lock it around both strands below the loop.

fig-lashing-diagonal.caption: Diagonal lashing: timber hitch around both poles, wraps along one diagonal, then the other, frapping turns, clove hitch to finish.
fig-lashing-diagonal.alt: Three photographs of a cord lashing two crossed poles: the timber hitch and first diagonal wraps, the wraps on the other diagonal, and the finished lashing with frapping turns.
fig-lashing-diagonal.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-41 (printed page 264). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-lashing-square.caption: Square lashing: clove hitch on the upright, three or four wraps around the joint, frapping turns between the poles, clove hitch to finish.
fig-lashing-square.alt: Four photographs of a cord lashing a horizontal yellow pole across an upright wooden pole: the starting hitch, the wraps, the frapping turns, and the finished lashing.
fig-lashing-square.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-40 (printed page 263). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-latrine-setbacks.caption: Latrine siting: downhill of the well and at least 100 ft from it and from any surface water, 50 ft or more from the house, never in a drainage path or floodplain; at least 5 ft of dry soil under the bottom of the pit.

fig-panel-transfer-switch-interlock.caption: Backfeeding: generator power pushed into an outlet flows out through the panel and meter to the pole transformer, which raises it to the street line's voltage and kills a line worker who believes the line is dead. The safe path: an inlet and a transfer switch or interlock, with the main breaker off.
fig-panel-transfer-switch-interlock.alt: Two house cutaways with the service wires, the meter, the panel, a pole transformer and a line worker on the next pole. Top, crossed out: a generator outside with a cord that has two male ends pushed into a wall outlet; red arrows run from the outlet to the panel, out through the meter and the service wires to the transformer and along the street line to the worker. Bottom, ticked: the generator cord goes to an outdoor inlet and a transfer switch or interlock; the main breaker is off and nothing reaches the street.

fig-propane-heater-hose-route.caption: Portable propane heater on a 20-lb tank: the tank outdoors on a board, the maker's hose through a cracked ground-level window or door with a towel at the gap, the fuel filter at the heater's regulator, both air openings open, and the CO alarm on the opposite wall at pillow height.
fig-propane-heater-hose-route.alt: Cutaway of a room at ground level and the yard outside. Outside, a 20-lb propane tank stands upright on a board. The maker's hose runs from the tank valve through a window cracked at ground level, with a towel round the gap, to the heater on the floor inside. The fuel filter sits between the hose and the heater regulator. The heater has its clearances marked, 30 inches above, 24 inches in front, 6 inches each side. A 3 by 3 inch opening at ceiling level and another at floor level are open. The CO alarm is on the far wall at pillow height.

fig-series-vs-parallel.caption: Series adds voltage, parallel adds current. Do the cold-voltage check before any series string, and never put a series string into a station with a low input-voltage ceiling.
fig-series-vs-parallel.alt: Top: three panels of about 20 V wired plus to minus in a chain make about 60 V. A box says add the label Voc of every panel, multiply by 1.20, and the result must be below the station maximum PV input voltage. A station with a high voltage ceiling is ticked; a station with a low ceiling is crossed out. Bottom: two panels joined plus to plus and minus to minus with Y-branch connectors make about 20 V with the currents added.

fig-tourniquet-placement.caption: Tourniquet: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, on the limb, never over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops and there is no pulse below, lock the windlass, write the time on it, never loosen it. Still bleeding: a second tourniquet above the first.
fig-tourniquet-placement.alt: Two legs drawn lying flat. Top: a wound on the thigh; a windlass tourniquet sits 2 to 3 inches above it, between the wound and the body, with the windlass rod locked in its clip and TIME written on the strap; a dashed second tourniquet is shown above the first for when bleeding continues. Bottom: a wound just below the knee; a tourniquet over the knee is crossed out in red, and the correct one is above the knee on the thigh.

fig-vehicle-recovery-setup.caption: Pulling a stuck vehicle: a rated strap with no metal hooks, attached to rated recovery points or the hitch receiver with a rated shackle, never the hitch ball; a blanket or mat over the middle of the strap; everyone else at least 1.5 times the strap length away and out of line with the pull.
fig-vehicle-recovery-setup.alt: Two vehicles nose to tail, seen from the side and from above. A blanket hangs over the middle of the strap. From above, a shaded no-standing zone covers the line of pull and extends past both vehicles; people stand to the side, at least 1.5 times the strap length away.

fig-warm-room-layout.caption: The warm room: heater behind a barrier at its label clearances, the heater's air openings, the door closed and hung with a blanket, everyone sleeping in the room, the CO alarm on the wall opposite the heater at pillow height.
fig-warm-room-layout.alt: Plan view of one room. The heater stands near the outside wall with the window, inside a barrier drawn at the clearances on its label. The door is closed with a blanket hung over it. Mattresses and a small tent are at the far side, pillows toward the wall opposite the heater, where the CO alarm is mounted at pillow height. An inset shows the window wall from inside: a 3 by 3 inch opening at ceiling level and another at floor level for a propane heater, or the window cracked at least 1 inch for a wick kerosene heater when the room is smaller than its manual requires.

fig-water-heater-valves.caption: Getting water out of a tank water heater: heat off (gas control to OFF, or the breaker off), close the cold-water inlet valve on top, open a hot tap higher in the house, then open the drain valve at the base slowly into a hose or bucket. The water can be scalding.
fig-water-heater-valves.alt: A tank water heater seen from the front. On top, the cold-water inlet pipe with its valve, marked close, and the hot outlet pipe. Low on the front, the gas control knob marked OFF, not pilot, or for an electric heater the breaker off. At the base, the drain valve with a hose running to a bucket, marked open slowly, scalding. A note shows a hot tap upstairs left open to let air in. Numbers 1 to 4 follow the draining steps.

fig-wind-chill-chart.credit: NOAA National Weather Service, Wind Chill Chart (effective 1 November 2001). Public domain (US Government work).

fig-wound-packing.caption: Wound packing for the groin, armpit or neck, where a tourniquet cannot go: push gauze in until the wound is full, then press hard on top and keep pressing. Never pack the chest or belly: cover and press.
fig-wound-packing.alt: Left: a simple body outline. The groin, armpit and neck are marked in green as places to pack; the chest and belly are shaded red with "do not pack: cover and press". Right, two cross-sections of a wound below the skin: first, fingers push a long strip of gauze into the wound until it is filled; second, two hands stacked on top press straight down hard.

# ai block: corridor-hazards-read - **Used on:** `17-11-corridor-hazards` (household layer), under "The honest read for each route", after the per-destination facts and before the home hazard table.
- **Written by:** C12a, 2026-11-16. ## Purpose The template can print each destination's climate numbers, but it cannot loop over a
destination's hazard list (nested lists are not available in templates) and it cannot compare
that list with home's or say which hazards the trip itself has to cross. This block writes one
short paragraph per destination naming the weather hazards that matter most for that place and
for the drive there, in the order a traveller meets them, so the household knows which rules on
the page apply to which trip. The owner household's binder had one such paragraph per route
("the open-prairie ground blizzard west; tornadoes end to end, ice in the hills and low-water
crossings south"); this block writes the equivalent for any household from region data only. ## Inputs (exact context paths; nothing else) - `destinations[]`: `name`, `state_name`, `county`, `status_text`, `approximate_miles`, `route_notes`, and from its `region`: `state_name`, `jan_low_f`, `jul_high_f`, `snow_in`, `elevation_ft`, `hazards`
- `region.home.hazards`, `home.state_name`, `home.county`
- `has.trailer`, `has.young_child`, `has.mobility_aid`, `has.refrigerated_meds`, `has.vehicle` ## Output - Markdown. One paragraph per destination, in profile order, starting with the destination name in bold followed by a colon: `**Name**: ...`.
- Each paragraph covers, in this order and only where the inputs support it: 1. The destination's hazards rated 3, then those rated 2, by name, using the `rating_text` words. Say which of them home does not share or rates lower ("more tornado risk than home", "a hurricane hazard home does not have"). 2. Its winter and summer in the region values as given, with units, and what that means for the trip: snow and January lows mean the → 17-01 winter rules and the ground blizzard section; high July values mean the heat and water points on → 17-04. 3. If the destination and home are in different states, say that the drive crosses country between `home.state_name` and the destination's `state_name` whose weather is not in the inputs, and that the household should read the state pages in Section 32 for each state the route crosses. Never name intermediate states, roads or towns unless they appear verbatim in `route_notes`. 4. The season the inputs suggest is safest, in words only (for example "late spring or early autumn, outside both the snow season and the worst storm months"), and the one rule on the page that matters most for this trip, as a cross-reference: → 17-01, → 17-02, → 17-03, → 17-04, → 17-13 or → 17-14. 5. If `has.trailer` is true, one sentence that wind hazards on this route make the household's own towing limits on this page apply. If `has.young_child`, `has.mobility_aid` or `has.refrigerated_meds` is true, one sentence pointing to → 01-07 or → 17-02's vehicle rules as relevant.
- If `destinations[]` is empty: output exactly: "No destination is entered, so there is no route to read. The rules on this page apply to any trip."
- If a destination's `hazards` list is empty or missing: say "Hazard ratings for this destination are not available; read its state page in Section 32." and continue with the climate values. ## Constraints - **Never introduce** a number, distance, drive time, road, town, landmark, facility, season date, law or procedure that is not in the inputs. Print region values exactly as given; do not convert or round them. Do not estimate driving hours or fuel.
- Use only hazards present in the inputs. Do not add hazards from general knowledge of a state (for example, do not mention hurricanes for a destination whose list does not rate them 2 or 3).
- Do not change or soften `status_text`. Do not recommend one destination over another and do not make the go/no-go decision; the household does that on → 01-02 and the table on this page.
- Quote `route_notes` only briefly and only as what the household wrote.
- Plain words, short sentences, calm. No headings, no tables, no bullet lists. ## Length Each paragraph 50 to 110 words. At most three paragraphs. ## Example shape (illustrative only; never copy) **The farm**: rated high for tornado and flood and moderate for ice storm; home is rated lower for
tornado. January nights there average 18 °F with 30 inches of snow a year, so a winter trip falls
under the winter rules and the ground blizzard section. The drive leaves your home state, so read
the Section 32 page for each state the route crosses. The quietest time to travel is likely early
autumn, outside the snow season and the spring storm months; the rule that matters most on this
route is → 17-02's tornado-while-driving section. Your own towing limits on this page apply.

destination-honest-read.text:
# ai block: destination-honest-read - **Used on:** `01-05-choosing-a-destination` (household layer), under "The honest read", after the destinations table and the status definitions.
- **Written by:** C01, 2026-11-16. ## Purpose One short, honest paragraph per destination that pulls together what the template can only print
in separate cells: how its status, distance, climate and hazards, the people there, and this
household's needs fit together, and what remains to be done to make it real. The owner household's
binder had such a paragraph per destination ("the distance is the whole problem: a one-shot early
trip, never a reactive winter one"); this block writes the equivalent for any household from its
own answers and the region data. ## Inputs (exact context paths; nothing else) - For each `destinations[]` entry, in profile order: `name`, `state_name`, `county`, `status_text` (agreed / unannounced / property only / undecided), `who_is_there`, `route_notes`, `approximate_miles`, and from its `region`: `jan_low_f`, `jul_high_f`, `snow_in`, `zone`, `hazards` (name, rating, rating_text).
- Excluded on purpose (do **not** use `how_to_reach_them`): it holds phone numbers, which the page prints in its own table.
- Household: `household.size`, `home.county`, `home.state_name`, `region.home.hazards`.
- Flags: `has.refrigerated_meds`, `has.oxygen`, `has.cpap`, `has.mobility_aid`, `has.anaphylaxis`, `has.infant`, `has.young_child`, `has.elder`, `has.pregnant`, `has.pets`, `has.vehicle`, `has.trailer`, `has.condition.CL-NN`. ## Output - Markdown. For each destination, one paragraph starting with the destination name in bold and its status in bold, e.g. `**Name** (**agreed**): ...`. Paragraphs in profile order.
- Each paragraph covers, in this order and only where the inputs support it: 1. What the status means for this place in practice (expected or not; can supplies be cached). 2. Distance in the household's own miles, and what that implies for timing: a long trip suits only an early, seen-it-coming departure in good weather; a short one can be a later move. Say "the fuel worksheet on → 01-03" rather than computing fuel. 3. Winter and climate from the region values (state the values as given, with units), and the destination hazards rated 2 or 3 by name, compared with home's in words ("more", "fewer", "different"). 4. The household's needs that make this place harder or easier, in words (for example refrigerated medicine and an unknown power source; a wheelchair and an unknown house; a small child and a working farm), pointing to → 01-07 for medical needs. 5. The one or two most important open items, chosen from: ask them; visit; place a cache; settle water, heat, storm shelter or medical distance; drive the route.
- If `destinations[]` is empty: output exactly: "No destination is entered. Until one is agreed, staying is strongly preferred, and the realistic move is toward town, family or medical help. Add destinations in settings and regenerate." ## Constraints - **Never introduce** a number, distance, drive time, road, town, facility, phone number, law or procedure that is not in the inputs. **Never print a phone number or address at all**, even one that appears in `who_is_there` or `route_notes`: contact details live in the page's table, not in this paragraph. Do not describe a medical, heating, water or travel procedure; point to the page that has it (→ 01-03, → 01-04, → 01-07). Use `approximate_miles` exactly as given; do not convert it to hours or fuel. Do not name highways, hospitals or pharmacies unless they appear verbatim in `route_notes` or `who_is_there`.
- Do not change or soften the status. An unannounced or undecided destination is never described as safe, expected or reliable. Property only is never described as having anyone there.
- Do not recommend one destination over another, and do not make the go/no-go decision; the household does that on → 01-02.
- Quote the household's free text (`who_is_there`, `route_notes`) only briefly and only as fact about what they wrote; never invent relationships or agreements.
- Plain words, short sentences, calm. No headings, no tables, no bullet lists. ## Length Each paragraph 50 to 110 words. At most three paragraphs (the profile allows three destinations). ## Example shape (illustrative only; never copy) **The cabin** (**property only**): nobody lives there, so nothing has been kept warm or stocked
unless you did it, and someone may be there before you. At about 140 miles it is within reach of a
later departure, but check → 01-03's fuel worksheet. January lows of 4 °F and 60 inches of snow a
year make it a hard winter arrival. With refrigerated medicine in the household and no known power
source there, the cold chain has to ride with you (→ 01-07). Next: visit, and decide what can be
cached there safely.

responder-first-three.text:
# ai block: responder-first-three - **Used on:** `25-09-family-medical-summary` (household layer), under "First, in a box at the top", above the per-person tables.
- **Written by:** C02, 2026-11-16. ## Purpose The household binder's medical summary opened with a hand-written box: "the three things a
responder must know first" (who is dependent on which medicine or device, who has anaphylaxis
and to what, and what has no substitute). A template can print every row, but it cannot pick out
the few life-critical facts across members, conditions, allergies, medicines and devices and
order them by urgency. This block does that, from the household's own answers only. ## Inputs (exact context paths; nothing else) - `members[]`: `label`, `role`, `age_text`, `conditions` (condition-library titles, plus any free-text "other" condition), `pregnant_or_nursing`
- `allergies[]`: `member`, `allergen`, `severity`, `carries_epinephrine`
- `meds[]`: `member`, `name`, `refrigerated` (do **not** use `strength`, `schedule`, `if_missed`, `days_on_hand`)
- flags: `has.anaphylaxis`, `has.epinephrine`, `has.refrigerated_meds`, `has.oxygen`, `has.cpap`, `has.mobility_aid`, `has.pregnant`, `has.nursing`, `has.infant`, `has.condition.CL-NN` ## Output - A Markdown blockquote of **one to five numbered lines**, most urgent first, each in capitals for the person's label and the key fact, in this shape: `> 1. LABEL (age): CONDITION OR ALLERGY. What it depends on. → 02-NN`
- Order of urgency: anaphylaxis (any `allergies` row with severity anaphylaxis); dependence on a medicine whose absence is an emergency within days (insulin, adrenal insufficiency, anti-seizure, anti-rejection, as named by the person's conditions); oxygen or other powered device; pregnancy or a newborn; mobility or memory needs that change how a responder moves the person; then anything else a condition page marks as an emergency.
- For anaphylaxis lines: name the allergen(s) exactly as typed and add "EPINEPHRINE FIRST" if `has.anaphylaxis` is true. Do not add device strengths.
- For medicine lines: name the medicine exactly as typed and add "REFRIGERATED" if `refrigerated` is true. Never a dose, strength or schedule.
- End with one final line, always: `> Medicines and devices listed below have no substitute in this household's plan. Plans from the prescribers are attached.`
- If no member has any condition, allergy, medicine or device marked in settings, output exactly: `> No condition, allergy, medicine or device is entered for this household. If that changes, update settings and regenerate.` ## Constraints - **Never introduce** a dose, strength, timing, number, phone number, product name, diagnosis, law or procedure not in the inputs. Do not infer a condition from a medicine name or a medicine from a condition.
- Do not describe treatment beyond "EPINEPHRINE FIRST" for anaphylaxis. Treatment lives in the attached plans and the condition pages.
- Medicine and allergen names exactly as typed. Labels exactly as typed.
- Use only the page references `→ 02-NN` where NN is the CL number of a selected condition, and `→ 02-03` for anaphylaxis.
- Plain words, calm. No headings, no tables. ## Length At most six lines in total, each at most 25 words. ## Example shape (illustrative only; never copy) > 1. SAM (6): ANAPHYLAXIS TO PEANUT. EPINEPHRINE FIRST. → 02-03
> 2. ALEX (41): TYPE 1 DIABETES, INSULIN DEPENDENT. Insulin (REFRIGERATED). → 02-01
> 3. RIVER (9 months): INFANT; FEEDING PLAN ATTACHED. → 02-13
> Medicines and devices listed below have no substitute in this household's plan. Plans from the prescribers are attached.

roles-must-know.text:
# ai block: roles-must-know - **Used on:** `00-07-household-roles` (household layer), directly under "The one that is not optional".
- **Written by:** C01, 2026-11-16. ## Purpose Name, for this household, the life-sustaining routines that every adult must be able to run, and
whose routine each one is, so the generic paragraph above it becomes concrete. The template cannot
do this because it needs to pick out, from members, conditions, allergies, medicines and devices,
only the items that are life-sustaining, and group them by person. ## Inputs (exact context paths; nothing else) - `members[]`: `label`, `role`, `age_text`, `conditions` (condition-library ids and titles, plus the free-text "other" condition if present)
- `allergies[]`: `member`, `allergen`, `severity`, `carries_epinephrine`
- `meds[]`: `member`, `name`, `refrigerated` (do **not** use `strength`, `schedule` or `if_missed`)
- flags: `has.anaphylaxis`, `has.epinephrine`, `has.refrigerated_meds`, `has.oxygen`, `has.cpap`, `has.mobility_aid`, `has.infant`, `has.pregnant`, `has.nursing`, `has.condition.CL-NN`
- the titles and kit page ids of the selected condition-library modules (Section 02 page ids, `02-NN`, where `NN` is the CL number) ## Output - A Markdown bullet list, one bullet per person who has at least one life-sustaining routine, in the order of `members[]`. Each bullet: the person's label in bold, then the routine(s) in plain words, each followed by the page reference in the form `→ 02-NN` (the condition module) or `→ 02-03` (anaphylaxis), `→ 29-07` (refrigerated medicines), `→ 09-06` (powered devices).
- What counts as a routine: giving or backing up a refrigerated or daily medicine; recognising and treating that condition's emergency as the module describes it (name it only, e.g. "a severe low", "anaphylaxis", "a seizure"; do not describe treatment steps); keeping a powered device running (oxygen, CPAP); moving someone who uses a wheelchair or walker; infant feeding.
- After the list, one sentence: "Each of these has its own page; every adult reads it and practises the emergency part with a trainer or the prescriber (→ 24-01)."
- If no member has any such routine: output exactly one sentence: "No one in this household has a condition, allergy, medicine or device marked life-sustaining in settings. If that changes, regenerate the binder, and the routine will be listed here." ## Constraints - **Never introduce** a number, dose, timing, phone number, product name, law or procedure that is not in the inputs, and never print a number from the inputs other than an age as typed in `age_text`. Do not restate strengths or schedules. Do not explain how to treat anything: the condition pages do that.
- Do not infer a condition from a medicine name, or a medicine from a condition. Use only what is typed.
- Do not rank people or judge the household. No reassurance, no alarm.
- Plain words, short sentences, the binder's voice (calm, direct). No headings, no tables.
- Medicine names exactly as typed. ## Length At most 8 bullets, each at most 30 words; total at most 220 words. ## Example shape (illustrative only; never copy) - **Alex**: daily refrigerated medicine and its cold chain (→ 29-07); recognising a severe low (→ 02-01).
- **Sam**: anaphylaxis to a food; epinephrine first (→ 02-03). Each of these has its own page; every adult reads it and practises the emergency part with a
trainer or the prescriber (→ 24-01).

owner_tokens.description: Words that identify the owner household. Any match in a kit page (body or frontmatter) fails validation. Case-sensitive whole-word unless noted. Section 31 (verbatim handbook), Section 32 (generated national region appendix, which must print public place names) and this file are exempt.
owner_tokens.note_removed: Drug names (NovoLog, glargine, Gvoke) removed 2026-11-16: common prescriptions, not personal; FDA text must be quotable.

notice_md:
# Notice shown inside every generated binder

This text appears (1) on the settings page while the household fills it in, (2) on the download
screen, and (3) as the second page of the generated binder, after the safety disclaimer. It is
written for someone who has never thought about any of this before.

---

## Your answers are never stored

Nothing you type on this page is saved by us. There is no account, no database and no log of your
answers. Your answers live only in this browser tab. If you close the tab before you download your
binder, they are gone and you start over. You may choose to save a copy of your answers as a file
on your own device so you can come back and regenerate later; that file stays with you.

When you press **Generate**, your answers are sent once to the AI service that writes your binder
(Anthropic's Claude API), through a small relay program whose only jobs are to check your access
key and pass the request along. The relay keeps a count of requests and nothing else. Its source
code is shown on the settings page's privacy section so you can check this. Cloudflare, which
hosts the page and the relay, keeps its own standard request metrics (times, sizes, rough location)
like any web host; it does not see your answers' meaning unless it inspected the request, and we
have not asked it to keep anything. The AI provider's own data-handling terms apply to the
request; we do not control those and we say so here rather than promise more than we can.

## This file is your private copy. Do not share it.

A **Large** or **Everything** binder contains the full text of documents written by other people
and organisations: appliance manuals, first-aid guides, fire-safety standards, medical-society fact
sheets, university publications. They were fetched for **your personal use** when you downloaded
this file, because in an emergency you need the whole document in your hand, not a web address that
no longer works. A **Small** binder carries only this project's own text and public-domain
material, and names the other documents without including them.

Those documents are copyrighted by their publishers. Giving a Large or Everything binder to someone
else copies their work without permission and breaks copyright. **Keep this file to your own household.** If a
friend wants a binder, send them to the settings page and they can make their own.

## What this binder is, and is not

This binder was assembled and checked by an AI from a verified core text, public datasets and the
answers you gave. **No doctor, engineer, electrician or other professional has reviewed your copy.**
It is a reference for a time when the normal references, services and professionals are not
available. While they are available, use them. Where this binder and a professional disagree, the
professional is right.

Several pages ask you to choose between options that carry real risk. Those pages explain the
hazard, what the manufacturer or agency says and why, what reduces the risk, and the choices. The
choice is yours and so is the responsibility for it.

sizes.note: Measured: 257 of 645 cited documents (page pictures rendered at 1100 px). The other 388 are counted at the measured average (PDF 2.4 MB, web page 19 KB). Each topographic map adds 27 to 80 MB.
